units.la: QUOTIENS cumq; sæculi huius, in quo vivimus, indolem intueor, Nobilissime Payere, subire protinus solet Caligula Imperatoris, cateroquin parum laudati Principis, institutum nō omninō ineptum, quo ætatis suæ luxuriantem scribendi pruriginem compescere sopiréve voluit, luit, & Aquinorum, Cassiorum, Volusiorum, & id genus βιβλιοσεσβλων scripta spongiâ linguáve deleri jußit. Scilicet jam tum insanum illud χαχόηθες, de quo & Salomonis Sapientis novimus sententiam, increbuerat: ut promi-scuè quid vis chartis illinere cuivis maximum esset prolubium. Plus scire velle (addo ego, & scribere) inquit Philosophus, intemperan-tiæ genus quoddam est. Antisthenes olim, quod multa volumina conscripsisset, à Timo-ne dictus παντοφυὴς φλεδων, h. e. ingeniosus nugator. Aristarchus Grammaticus Alexandrinus supra mille Commentarios exara-vit. Didymum item Grammaticum quatuor millia librorum scripsisse legimus. Quadra-ginta millia Alexandria arsisse, memorant historia. Parum, meo judicio, prout hodie im-manem struem hujus supellectilis conspicimus.
units.tr: Whenever I consider the character of this age in which we live, most noble Payer, there immediately comes to mind a policy of the Emperor Caligula, a prince otherwise little praised, which was not altogether foolish. He wished to check and quiet the rank itch for writing that flourished in his own age, and ordered the writings of Aquinus, Cassius, Volusius and that sort of bookworm to be wiped out with a sponge or with the tongue. Clearly, even then that mad malignant disposition [κακόηθες], of which we also know the saying of Solomon the wise, had taken hold: so that smearing paper with whatever one pleased was the greatest delight of anyone. Plus scire velle (I add, and to write) says the philosopher, is a kind of intemperance. Antisthenes once, because he had written many volumes, was called by Timon an all-producing babbler [παντοφυὴς φλέδων], that is, a clever trifler. Aristarchus the Alexandrian grammarian wrote more than a thousand commentaries. We read that the grammarian Didymus also wrote four thousand books. Histories report that forty thousand books burned at Alexandria. Few, in my judgment, compared with the huge heap of this stuff that we see today.

units.la: Quis est enim, cui non nigra —infusa vanescat sepia lymphâ?
units.tr: For who is there, whose writing the black cuttlefish ink, poured into water, does not dissolve away?

units.la: Immò quò infelicius quidam ab ingenij dotibus instructi sunt, eò locupletiores de se edere solent solent fœtus : velut abiecta mendicabula plarumq; abundare liberis videmus.
units.tr: Indeed, the less favoured some men are in gifts of mind, the more abundant the offspring they are wont to produce; just as we see that abject beggar-folk are usually rich in children.

units.la: Hæc dum serio sic cogito, ipse mihi aurem vello: & tamen quid in utramq; partem hEIC sapere oporteat, è vestigio suggerunt veterum sapientissimi. Non est effœta prorsus mater Natura. semper aliquid novi gignit, quod priori suboli suppar sit: aut eandem quod ornet ; certè haud planè devenustet. Quisquis bonam juvandi voluntatem præ se fert, jam juvisse existimatur. Emersit ex opicâ barbarie res litteraria. At incolumem planitus ex suis virtutibus nec dum esse, palam tot Heroum ἀληξικάκων ausus evincunt, qui omnem vim in illa penitus profligandâ indefesso conatu experiuntur. Horum ego agmen tamquam suppedaneus quidam sequi desidero. Nomen meum sacramento iam pridem obstrinxi. Ad communem ἀγῶνα animum intrepidum fero : ut ut viribus aliis impar. Soccum antiquum mihi selegeram è Sarsinatium colonia effabre expoliendum. Ornamentum tum ultimum restabat; quod iam nunc promo. ELECTA inquam hac, quæ vides: quaq; Tibi, Virprastantissime, ex antiquá formu- lá L.M.Q. DICO. DONO. DEDICO. Atque hoc ardentis affectûs illicium apud me tum reliquisti, cùm anno hoc in Nemétibus filium tuum, spem tuam, adeoq; generis vestri furculum germanissimum incoràm mihi tra- deres. Neque sanè aliter repensare aut pos- sum, aut debeo benigna tua ergà me voluntatis τεχμήρια, quæ tàm largè hucusq; mihi exprom- sisti. planissumè ex Genio gentis vestrae, quæ ab ipsis Charifin non facta, sed nata est. Huma- nitatis illius hospitalitatisq; prorsus edecuma- ta memoriam mecum servo,
units.tr: While I think on these things seriously in this way, I pull my own ear; and yet the wisest of the ancients at once suggest what one ought to think on both sides. Mother Nature is not utterly worn out; she always brings forth something new, which matches the earlier offspring, or which adorns the same, or at least does not quite spoil it. Whoever shows a good will to help is thought already to have helped. Literature has emerged from rustic barbarism. But that we are not yet safe from the vices, the bold efforts of so many heroes who ward off evils [ἀληξικάκων], who strive with tireless effort to root out all that evil, plainly show. I desire to follow their band, like a sort of footstool. I have long ago bound my name by oath. I bring a fearless spirit to the common contest [ἀγῶνα], although unequal in other strengths. I had chosen an old comic slipper from the colony of Sarsina to be finely polished. The final ornament remained, which I now bring forth. Here, I say, are these Selected Pieces, which I give, dedicate and offer to you, most distinguished sir, in the old formula L.M.Q. DICO. DONO. DEDICO. And you left this enticement of ardent affection with me when, this year at Nemetes, you handed over to me your son, your hope, and the most genuine shoot of your family, in my presence. Nor indeed can I otherwise repay, or am I able or obliged to repay, your kindly tokens of good will [τεχμήρια] towards me, which you have so far shown me so generously; most clearly they come from the Genius of your people, which was not made by the Graces [Χάριτες] but born of them. I keep that humanity and hospitality fully in my memory,

units.la: dum res & ætas, & sororum Filiatrium patienter atra.
units.tr: while circumstance and age allow, and the black sisters, the spinning Fates, bear it patiently.

units.la: Me Basiléa aluit, fovit, decoravit: Me Tigurum suscepit: Me Berna iterùm iterumq; amplexata est: Cántones reliqui æternam sui admirationem apud me reliquerunt. Helvetios itaq; dum me amare profiteor, cur te éprimaria inter illos civitate & prosapiá oriundum, non deperire simul queam? Merentur idipsum prater hac insignes illa tua & animi, & fortuna dotes, qua & domi & foris te nobilem iam diu reddiderunt. Ego autem verecundè illis prolixius recensendis supersedeo: quòd norim, praconio meo ultrà ijs addi nihil posse. Interim huncce animum meum tui cupientissimum Excellentia Tua totum totum devoveo: perenne hoc statuens
units.tr: Basel nourished, cherished and adorned me; Zurich received me; Bern embraced me again and again; the rest of the cantons left me with an everlasting admiration for themselves. So, while I profess to love the Swiss, why should I not at the same time be fond of you, born of a foremost citizenship and lineage among them? Those outstanding gifts of yours, of both mind and fortune, deserve this too, which have long made you noble both at home and abroad. I, however, modestly refrain from listing them at greater length, because I know that nothing can be added to them by my praise. Meanwhile I devote this my mind, most eager for you, wholly to Your Excellency, establishing this as a lasting

units.la: nostri monumentum & pignus amoris.
units.tr: monument and pledge of our love.

units.la: Vir Clarißime:
units.tr: Most distinguished sir:

units.la: {*}Ocos tuos Communes Philosophicos Plautinos accepi; quos & non semel, sed sæpius ac sæpius percurri. Diligentiam tuam mirificè laudo. Accuratißimus enim & exactißimus fuisti: nec adeò tàm multa abillo Comicorum Principe exspectassem, quàm multa nobis exhibuisti. Placent etiam Emblemata, quæ subinde sententijs Plautinis à te sunt adjecta. Utinam plures in idem animi tui propositum concurrerent: & exemplo tuo Platonem, Aristotelem, Tullium, Plutarchum, cæteroque hujusmodi notæ prioris Authotes Locos in Communes distribuerent! sanè Commentarijs quotquot sunt Veterum multis intervallis ac spatijs eos anteponerem. Sed his de rebus inter nos aliquando, Deo dante, plenius ac familiarius agemus. *** Vale.
units.tr: I have received your Commonplaces on Plautus, the philosophical ones, and I have gone through them not once but again and again. I warmly praise your diligence. You have been most accurate and most exact, and I would not have expected from that prince of comic writers as much as you have shown us. The emblems you have from time to time added beside the Plautine sayings also please me. I wish more men would share the aim of your mind and, following your example, would arrange Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, Plutarch and the other well-known authors of earlier times into commonplaces. Indeed, I would put such works far ahead of all the commentaries of the ancients, by a long interval. But we will discuss these matters together at some later time, God willing, more fully and more familiarly. Farewell.

units.la: IDEM AD EVMDEM.
units.tr: THE SAME, TO THE SAME.

units.la: {Q}Uæ à te magno studio ad Comicorum Latinorum Principem sunt notata, modis omnibus mihi probantur, adeò ut Livoris Invidia què morsus metuere nullâ cogitatione debeas. Resipsa te non superstitibus modò, sed & posteris prodesse voluisse: immò jam multis profuisse, ac quotidiè prodesse, satis superque declarat. Carpant invidi, dummodò meliore successu, meliora, si postsint, audeant vel præstent. Labor tuus, crede, nec tempore veterascet, nec ab alio superabitur. Adeò namque fundum illum Plautinum necessarijs omnibus luculenter instruere cœpisti, ut qui te sequi qui posthac vel imitari voluerint, à te passim mutuum sint sumturi, tuáque reposituri. Faustis ac felicibus auspicijs tantum perge: & Platonica (quorum specimen mihi misisti) Aristotelica, & id genus Electa, bono publico, per succedaneas vices nobis edE. Hoc si feceris, (quod te velle ac destinare video) futura sæcula uni tibi, quantum multis interpretibus alijs, debitura præsagio. Vale Vir Clarissime. a. d. 31. Julij. Haidelbergæ. Anno 1617.
units.tr: What you have marked with great zeal in the prince of Latin comedy pleases me in every way, so that you need have no fear at all of the bite of envy and spite. The work itself, and the fact that you have wished to benefit not only the living but also posterity, and indeed have already benefited many and benefit them daily, declares this sufficiently and more. Let the envious carp; provided that, with better success, they dare or achieve better things, if any there are. Your labour, believe me, will not grow old with time, nor will it be surpassed by another. For you have begun to furnish that Plautine field so splendidly with all the necessary tools that those who henceforth wish to follow or imitate you will borrow from you on every side, and will return what they have borrowed. Only go on with favourable and happy auspices, and in turn give us, in successive instalments, your Platonica (of which you sent me a specimen), your Aristotelica, and that kind of Electa, for the public good. If you do this, which I see you wish and intend, I foresee that coming ages will owe you alone as much as they owe many other interpreters. Farewell, most distinguished sir. 31 July, Heidelberg, in the year 1617.

units.la: JACOBVS GOTHOFREDVS In Parlamento Parisiensi Advocatus CL. V. JOH. PHILIPPO PAREO Salutem plur.
units.tr: JACOBUS GOTHOFREDUS, advocate in the Parisian Parliament, to the most distinguished man JOHANN PHILIPP PAREUS: greetings.

units.la: LABORES in Plautum tuos dudum est, cum ego, vel ob hoc amare coepi, quòd publici saporis non sunt. Nam quos hodie videmus plærosque, vel vani immensarum allegationum hamaxarij, vel reduviarum medici sunt. Et post hæc omnia tamen, si DIs placet, Induperatores Optimi-Maximi. At quàm diversâ tu longè viâ insistendum putares, ostendisti denuò nunc nuper Eclogis illis tuis, electis verè. Nihil ad gratiam dici puta: Opus istud tuum, ut Thesaurus est, itainscribi quoq; velim. Nisi quòd & hoc supra Thesaurum habet, quod omnibus in communestudijs nimium quantum prodest. Thesaurus defossus, nulli: effossus paucis prodest. Jam ego denuncio, Ordinem nostrum eâ re debiturum tibi juxtà cæteros plurimùm: Cui sparsæ per Authorem verè tuum, veteris Jurisprudentiæ ramenta, in obryzæ nunc demùm massam redintegrata offers. ††† Vale.
units.tr: Your labours on Plautus have long been admired by me, and I began to love them for this very reason: they do not have a popular flavour. For most of those we see today are either empty carters of huge citations or physicians of the bedbug. And yet, after all of that, if it pleases the gods, they are emperors, "Best and Greatest." But by how very different a path you thought one ought to proceed, you have shown again just lately in those Eclogues of yours, truly "Selections." Do not take this as flattery: I would wish your work to be titled a Thesaurus, just as it is one. There is only this about it that is more than a treasury: it is of enormous use to everyone in common studies. A buried treasure benefits no one; one that has been dug up benefits few. Now I declare that our Order will owe you very much for this, more than the rest. For you offer it the scattered scraps of ancient jurisprudence, scattered through the author who is truly yours, now at last restored into a mass of pure gold. Farewell.

units.la: JOH. FORBESII SCOTO-BRITANNI ODA Ad Clarissimum Virum: Dn. M. JOH. PHILIPPVM PAREUM: Dav. Fil. Poëtam Laureatum: & Sacri Palatij ac Consistorij Imperialis Vice-Comitem Palatinum: Illustris Scholæ Neostadiensis Rectorem.
units.tr: JOHN FORBES OF SCOTLAND-BRITAIN, AN ODE to the most distinguished man, Mr. John Philip Pareus, son of David, poet laureate, count palatine of the sacred palace and of the imperial consistory, rector of the illustrious school at Neustadt.

units.la: QVI tibi par esse volet, PAREE, Ille terreni haud capiatur oris Punctuli angustis: superet necesse est Vertice nubes.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to be your equal, Pareus, cannot be confined within the narrow bounds of this small earthly region; he must of necessity rise above the clouds with his peak.

units.la: Sæpe te Pindi juga transvolantem, Sæpe Parnassi volucri vehentem Pallados curru, gelidúmq; sæpe Suspicit Hæmum.
units.tr: Often the ridges of Pindus watch you flying across, often Parnassus, and often Haemus looks up at you as you are carried in Pallas's winged chariot.

units.la: O novem turbâ quoties sororum Vidit in notis comitante ripis, Rhenus, agnatúmq; NICER, Deúmq; Haidelus aula!
units.tr: O how often has the Rhine seen you on its banks, accompanied by the crowd of the nine sisters, and Neckar, your kinsman, and Heidelberg, the court of the gods!

units.la: Tu nites intra patrios, & extra Limites, magno celeber Parente, Quà Deus mundum beat, & triumphat Lampade mundus.
units.tr: You shine within and beyond your fatherland's borders, famous through your great parent, where God blesses the world and the world triumphs in the light of his lamp.

units.la: Gloria hæc magni Patris in recentem Transfit ramum: neq; dignus hæres Deficis tanti decoris, PAREE, Nate PAREO.
units.tr: This glory of your great father passes over to the new branch, and you, Pareus, son, do not fall short of such a great honour; you are a worthy heir.

units.la: Et tui splendor procul in remotas Nominis terras penetravit: oris Lacteo quondam est hilarata rivo Gallia felix.
units.tr: Your splendour has also penetrated far into remote lands, to the regions where your name is known; happy Gaul was once gladdened by the milky stream of your mouth.

units.la: SARSINAS per te redivivus aurâVescitur Vates, tibi Scena plausumLæta dat, Risus redit & locus, Comœdia gaudet.Per tuæ mellita fluenta linguæGratus es Phœbo, Aonidumq; turbæ,Quæ tuam cingunt meritâ decoramDaphnide frontem.At tibi mellita fluenta linguæPortio tantum decoris, per ArtesAltiùm rimaris iter, Lycéi inIntima dux es.Doctła testantur monumenta acutiIngenî, rectæ Rationis VsumQuæ docent, contraq; dolos ΣοφισῶνArma ministrant.Plurima ut paucis loquar: haud PAREE esDegener. notum mihi jam Parentis;Et tuum novi studium. Atq; AmorisSum memor wq;.Nec PAREANÆ Δυάδος prioresArguent horâ immemorem, per artusDum mihi sanguis calidos meabit,Vsq; ero vester.
units.tr: Sarsinas, the poet brought back to life by you, feeds on gold. The stage gladly gives you applause; laughter returns to its place, and Comedy rejoices. You are pleasing to Phoebus and to the throng of the Muses through the honeyed streams of your tongue, which deservedly crown your brow with the laurel of Daphne. Your honeyed tongue has only a share of the grace; through the arts you explore a higher path, and you are a guide to the innermost parts of the Lyceum. Learned monuments of keen wit bear witness to you, which teach the use of right reason and supply weapons against the tricks of the sophists. To say much in few words: Paree, you are not unworthy of your father, whom I already know; and I know your zeal. I am also mindful of love. Nor will the earlier pair of the Pareanae prove that I forget the hour, while blood warms my limbs; I shall always be yours.

units.tr: "For I do not gather the thorns from books, but the most fragrant things, those worth hearing." [Οὐ γὰρ ἐγὼ τὰς ἐν τῶν βιβλίων ἀχάνθας, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἡδυσιμώτατα, ὡς ἀκοῆς ἄξια.] Not, as you do, do I select the thorns of books to be read; but only those things which are most useful, culled, and worth recalling everywhere.

units.tr: It is no wonder that each person gathers from the same material what suits his own studies. In the same meadow the ox seeks grass, the dog a hare, the stork a lizard.

units.la: OPERIS mei est, & studij, multos legere, ut ex plurimis diversos flores carpam: non tàm probaturus omnia, quàm quæ bona sunt. ELECTURUS, assumo multos in manus meas, ut à multis multa cognoscam.
units.tr: It is my task and my study to read many authors, so that I may pluck diverse flowers from many; not so much to approve everything, as to take what is good. Choosing, I take many into my hands, so that from many I may learn many things.

units.la: IN Theologo accuratum illud Antiquitatis studium, si abest, fortasse non requiram: si adfert, vehementer amplectar: nec solùm quasi ornamentum, sed etiam, fas sit dicere, adjumentum. Nam in sacrâ historiâ multa esse, quorum penitior intelligentia pendeat à MORIBUS, & litteris ANTIQUIS, nomo negabit.
units.tr: In a theologian I shall not perhaps look for that exact study of antiquity if it is absent; if it brings something, I shall embrace it warmly: and not only as an ornament but, it is right to say, as an aid. For no one will deny that in sacred history there are many things whose deeper understanding depends on ancient customs and literature.

units.tr: Press on in these studies, and do not neglect those selected passages (as I am accustomed to call them), the harvest of true learning. He who gathers nothing from varied reading, sorts, arranges and does nothing but trifle; and brings back little to what he has received.

units.la: PLAUTUS Mare quasi quoddam est, in quo omnes omnium scientiarum fluvij, omnes omnis sapientiæ rivuli confluxerunt. Nam quæ sedes in ejus fabulis de Deo leguntur sententiæ? quàm piæ? quàm doctæ? quàm denique jucundæ? quæ de RERUM NATURA notulæ, passim instar gemmularum distinctæ? ut suavitate suâ legentes afficiunt! quæ deniquè MORUM & Virtutum icunculæ è regione positis vitijs! scil. ut horum turpitudine tamquam tenebris lux illa eluceat magis, & conspicua fiat, passim resplendent. De Veterum RITIBUS, & LEGIBUS plenæ omnes paginæ: quodque alij HISTORICI magno egere studio, hic per jocum & ludum tangit: nec tangit modò: sed & explicat, atque evolvit.
units.tr: Plautus is a kind of sea, into which all the rivers of all sciences and all the streamlets of all wisdom have flowed together. For what sentences about God are read in his plays? How pious, how learned, and finally how pleasant! What little notes on the nature of things, scattered everywhere like little gems, so that they delight readers with their sweetness! And finally, what little images of morals and virtues set over against the vices! So that, by the baseness of these, that light shines forth the more and becomes conspicuous; they gleam everywhere. All his pages are full of the customs and laws of the ancients; and what other historians have treated with great zeal, he touches here by way of jest and play: and not merely touches, but also explains and unrolls.

units.la: Age igitur, doctissime PICCARTE, rem experiamur: & ex ipsâ Phœbi cortinâ te profatum patefecit.
units.tr: Come then, most learned Piccart, let us try the matter: and from the very tripod of Phoebus, he has revealed you as speaker.

units.tr: Johannes Philippus Pareus, Electa Plautina.

units.la: A. ABOMINATIONIS. DIRARUM. EXECRATIONUM. IMPRECATIONUM.
units.tr: A. Of Abomination, Dire Curses, Execrations and Imprecations.

units.la: ESPVEBANT veteres, quæ abominabantur, ne evenirent. Asin. I.I. v.26. Te obsecro hercle, ut quæ locutus, despuas.
units.tr: The ancients spat to avert whatever they dreaded, lest it should come to pass. Asin. I.1 v.26. I beg you, by Hercules, spit out what you have just said.

units.la: IMPRECATIONES parentum ominis aliquid habent. Asin. 33. v. 155. De argento si mater ma sciat, ut sit factum. Heja benedicite! Terentius Adelphis I.I. v. 60. Nolo in illum graviùs dicere: Orpheus: Δεινὰ ᾧ κατὰ ᾔσειαν ἐξίννυς ἐσ᾽ τοκήων. Valde gravant natos diræ, & malefacta parentum. Videndus Plato lib. XI. de Legg. πᾶς δὴ νοῦν ἔχων φοβεῖται τὴν παρὰ γονέων εὐχὰς, εἰδὼς πολλοῖς καὶ πολλάκις ἐπιτελεῖς γενομένας. Hæ scilicet sunt Furiæ, quæ consequuntur immoimmorigeros, & contumaces liberos, quæ exiguntab eis pænas: quando parentibus sunt causa mærorum, & sollicitudinum, tunc sunt ultrices istius inobedientiæ. Vide etiam Richteri A-xiomata Oecon. cap. 9. In sacris hæc exempla nunc succur-runt: Genef. cap. 9. verf. 25. Ubi Noah maledicit filio Cham. Maledictus Chanaan: servus servorum erit fratribus suis. Item, Judic. c.17.v.2. de Michâ: Dixit matri suæ: Mille & centum argenteis, qui oblati fuerint tibi, propter quos maledixisti, me audien-te: ecce argentum illud apud me est: ego accepi illud: Et dixit mater ejus: Benedictus filius à Jehovâ.
units.tr: Parents' curses carry some omen. Asin. 33 v.155: If my mother learns about the silver, how it was done. Heja, bless us! Terence, Adelphi I.1 v.60: I do not want to say anything harsher against him. Orpheus: Δεινὰ ᾧ κατὰ ᾔσειαν ἐξίννυς ἐσ᾽ τοκήων [Terrible things, which you stir up against your parents]. The curses of parents, and the wrongdoings of parents, weigh heavily on their children. See also Plato, Laws XI: every sensible man fears the prayers of parents, knowing that they are often and in many cases fulfilled: πᾶς δὴ νοῦν ἔχων φοβεῖται τὴν παρὰ γονέων εὐχὰς, εἰδὼς πολλοῖς καὶ πολλάκις ἐπιτελεῖς γενομένας. These, of course, are the Furies, which pursue disobedient and stubborn children and exact punishment from them. Since children are the cause of grief and anxiety to their parents, they become avengers of that disobedience. See also Richter's Axiomata Oeconomica, cap. 9. In Scripture the following examples come to mind. Genesis 9:25, where Noah curses the son of Ham: Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers. Likewise Judges 17:2, of Micah: He said to his mother: The eleven hundred pieces of silver that were taken from you, over which you cursed, and which I heard you utter, behold, the silver is with me; I took it. And his mother said: Blessed be my son by Jehovah.

units.la: Mos veteribus solemnis fuit, sæva, & infelicia hostibus suis impre-cari. Asin. ꝯ.I.v.13. Utinam male qui mihi volunt, sic rideant! Merc. 1.2.v.25. Ac. Perÿmus. C H. Principium inimicis dato. Terentius Heaut. Illud inimicis nostris fiet! Ovidius: Hostibus eveniant conviviatalia nostra! Horatius lib.3.Od. 27.v.21. Hostium uxores, pueriq; cæcos sentiant motus orientis Hadi, & æquoris nigri fremitum, & trementis verbere ripas. Sophocles Electra: Εἰ μὴ πέφυκεν ἐχθρὰ, ... Xenophon ἀναβάδ. Homerus Iliad. φ. τίς ... Dionys. Alexand. Virgil. lib. 3. Georg. Di meliora pii, errorem hostibus illum! Cicero Catone: Mirari solitum Cajum Fabricium, quòd cum apud Regem Pyrrhum legatus esset, audisset à Thessalo Cineâ Athenis quendam esse, qui se sapientem profiteretur, eumq; dicere, omnia, quæ faceremus, ad voluptatem esse referenda, quod ex eo audientes, M. Curium, & T. Coruncanum optare solutos, ut id Samnitibus, ipsiq; Pyrrho persuaderetur, quo facilius vinci possent, cum se voluptatib. dedissent. Propert. lib. 3. Hostibus eveniat lenta puella meis! Idem lib.2. Eleg.5. Hostis si quis erit nobis, amet ipse puellas: Gaudeat in puero, si quis amicus erit! Vide Lamb. ad locum Horatij: Et opus Adag. Pag. 416. Si quid mali in Pyrrham.
units.tr: It was customary for the ancients to invoke harsh and unhappy fates on their enemies. Asin. 5.1 v.13: Would that those who wish me ill might laugh like this! Merc. 1.2 v.25: Give the beginning to my enemies. Terence, Heaut.: That will happen to our enemies! Ovid: May our feasts turn into funerals for our enemies! Horace, Odes III.27 v.21: May the wives of our enemies and their boys feel the stirrings of the rising Hades, and the roar of the dark sea, and the shores trembling under the lash. Sophocles, Electra: Εἰ μὴ πέφυκεν ἐχθρὰ, ... [If enmity is not innate, ...]. Xenophon, Anabasis. Homer, Iliad φ. τίς ... Dionysius of Alexandria. Virgil, Georgics III: May the gods grant better things to the pious, and that error to our enemies! Cicero, Cato: Gaius Fabricius was accustomed to marvel that when he was an envoy to King Pyrrhus, he heard from the Thessalian Cineas that there was a man at Athens who professed to be wise, and who said that all our actions are to be referred to pleasure. Hearing this, Marcus Curius and Tiberius Coruncanius prayed that the Samnites and Pyrrhus himself might be persuaded of it, so that they might be more easily conquered once they had given themselves over to pleasures. Propertius III: May a slow girl fall to my enemies! The same, II Elegies 5: If anyone is our enemy, let him love girls himself; if anyone is our friend, let him rejoice in a boy! See Lambinus on the passage of Horace, and the Adagia, p. 416: If anything evil [happens] to Pyrrha.

units.la: INIMICIS suis quandoq; imprecabantur, jubêtes eos calidam picem cem bibere. Merc. 1.2. v. 29. Calidam picim bibito: & resinam Ægyptiam! Quò pertinet vetus Inscriptio apud Gruter. Pag. MCXCI. 9. HÆC. STIGMATA. ÆTERNA. ACTE. LIBERTÆ INUSTA. SUNT. VENENARIÆ. ET. PERFIDÆ DOLOSÆ. PURI. PECTORIS. CLAVOM. ET. RESTIM. SPARTEAM. UTI. SIBI. COLLUM. ALLIGET. ET. PICEM. CALENTEM. PECTUS. MALUM. COMBURAT. SUUM.
units.tr: Sometimes they called down curses on their enemies, bidding them drink hot pitch. Merc. 1.2 v.29: Drink hot pitch and Egyptian resin! To this belongs the old inscription in Gruter, p. MCXCI.9: THESE BRANDS OF ETERNAL SHAME HAVE BEEN BURNED ON THE POISONERS, THE TREACHEROUS AND THE DECEITFUL. MAY A NAIL AND A SPARTAN ROPE BIND THEIR NECKS, AND MAY BURNING PITCH SCORCH THEIR EVIL BREAST.

units.la: VENENI haustum quoq; imprecabantur inimicis. Perf. ş. 2. v. 42. DI faciant, ut id bibatis, quod vos nunquam transeat!
units.tr: They also invoked the drinking of poison on their enemies. Persa 2.2 v.42: May the gods grant that you drink that which never passes through you!

units.la: SOLEBANT & restim imprecari, & clavum, unde se suspenderent. Poen. 1.2. v. 184. Capias restim, ac suspendas cum hero, ac vostra familiâ! Et 3. 5. v. 1. Suspendant omnes posthac se haruspices! Vide etiam præcedentem Inscriptionem.
units.tr: They were also in the habit of invoking the rope and the nail on which they might hang themselves. Poen. 1.2 v.184: May you take a rope and hang yourself with your master and your whole household! And 3.5 v.1: From now on may all the soothsayers hang themselves! See also the preceding inscription.

units.la: ABSTINENTIÆ. CONTINENTIÆ.
units.tr: Of Abstinence and Continence.

units.la: HOMINEM servum suos domitos oportet habere oculos, & manus, orationemq;. Mil. 2. 6. v. 80. Sic Pericles apud Cicer. lib. 1. de Offic. p. 57. Prætorem decet non solum manus, sed etiam oculos abstinentes habere.
units.tr: A slave ought to have his eyes, his hands and his speech under control, as a man who has been broken in. Mil. 2.6, v. 80. So Pericles, in Cicero, De Officiis book 1, p. 57: "A praetor ought to keep not only his hands but also his eyes from what is not his."

units.la: ACCUSATORUM. QUADRUPLATORUM.
units.tr: Of Accusers and Quadruplators.

units.la: Vide de his Titulo Bonorum: Furti: Rapina.
units.tr: See on this subject under the titles Of Goods, Theft, and Robbery.

units.la: ACCUSATIONUM. INIURIARUM. VIOLENTIÆ.
units.tr: ACCUSATIONS. INJURIES. VIOLENCE.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Iurù.
units.tr: See also the title Of Right.

units.la: NON temere accusandi sunt alij: quia sæpe non sine periculo id fit. Curc. 5. 2. v. 25.
units.tr: Men are not to be accused rashly, since this is often done not without danger. Curc. 5. 2. v. 25.

units.la: QUIBUS visficbat olim in urbe, si cives essent, solebant quiritare: & civium opem implorare: O cives! cives! Curc. 5. 2. v. 27. Ter. Adelph. Obsecro populares, ferte misero, atq; innocenti auxilium. Si verò ruri agerent, solebant jubilare. Vide Ræyardum ad LL. xii. Tab.
units.tr: Those who were wronged in the city of old, if they were citizens, used to cry out "Quiritare" and implore the help of their fellow citizens: O citizens! citizens! Curc. 5. 2. v. 27. Ter. Adelph. I beseech you, fellow citizens, bring aid to a wretched and innocent man. But if they were working in the country, they used to shout jubilare. See Raevardus on the Laws of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: ACTIONUM. NEGOTIORUM. FACINORUM. PRUDENTIÆ.
units.tr: ACTIONS. BUSINESS. DEEDS. PRUDENCE.

units.la: Vide etiam Factis.
units.tr: See also Deeds.

units.la: VOLUPE est, quod agas, si id procedit lepidè ex sententiâ, Mil. 4. 1. v. 1.
units.tr: It is a pleasure to do what you are doing, if it goes well and according to your wishes. Mil. 4. 1. v. 1.

units.la: UT volupe est homini! si quod agit, eluct victoriâ. Pœn. 5. 4. v. 20.
units.tr: How pleasant it is for a man when what he is doing ends in victory! Pœn. 5. 4. v. 20.

units.la: PRÆSTAT in propriâ causâ suam rem agere, quàm per alium. Mil. 4. 3. v. 21. 24.
units.tr: It is better to manage one's own affair oneself than to have another do it. Mil. 4. 3. v. 21, 24.

units.la: CÙM ad rem præsentem pervenimus, ibi tum demum rectè consulimus rebus nostris. Amph. 1. 1. v. 92. Caf. 2. 8. v. 65.
units.tr: Only when we come to the matter at hand do we properly consider our affairs. Amph. 1. 1. v. 92. Cas. 2. 8. v. 65.

units.la: QUOD factum est, infectum fieri nequit. Aul. 4. 10. v. 11. Factum est illud, infectum fieri non potest: inquit adolescens amator. Capt. 5. 3. v. 19. Facta infecta fieri non possunt. Truc. 4. 2. v. 17. Stultus est, qui facta infecta fieri postulat. Vide ibi exemplum Thetidis.
units.tr: What has been done cannot be undone. Aul. 4. 10. v. 11. "What has been done cannot be undone," says the young lover. Capt. 5. 3. v. 19. Things done cannot be made undone. Truc. 4. 2. v. 17. He is a fool who asks that things already done be undone. See there the example of Thetis.

units.la: JOVEM invocabant, ut actiones suas prosperaret. Pœn. 5. 4. v. 15. Jupiter, quem penes spes vitæ fiunt hominum omnium: da diem hunc sospitem quæso!
units.tr: They invoked Jupiter that he would make their actions prosper. Pœn. 5. 4. v. 15. "Jupiter, in whose power lie the hopes of life for all men: grant that this day may be safe for us, I pray!"

units.la: Stultitia est, facinus magnum timido cordi credere. Pseud. 2. 1. v. 3. Proh Juppiter! ut mihi quicquid ago, lepidè omnia prosperè que eveniunt! Neq; quod dubitem, neq; quod timeam meo in pe- ctore conditum est consilium. Res perinde sunt, ut agas, ut easma- gnifacias.
units.tr: It is folly to entrust a great undertaking to a timid heart. Pseud. 2. 1. v. 3. "O Jupiter! Whatever I do, may everything turn out pleasantly and prosperously! Nor is there in my breast any plan to doubt or fear. Things turn out just as you act, and as you make them great."

units.la: In seriis actionibus, ubi intentè quid agendum, utebantur hac formulâ: Hoc age: quæ, teste Plautarcho, è sacrificiis antiquorum petita est. Asin. Prol. Captiv. 2. 3. v. 84. Perf. 4. 4. v. 35. Vide Tit. Sacrificiorum.
units.tr: In serious undertakings, when something must be done with attention, they used this formula: "Do this!" This, according to Plutarch, was taken from the sacrifices of the ancients. Asin. Prol.; Capt. 2. 3. v. 84.; Pers. 4. 4. v. 35. See the title Sacrifices.

units.la: Invitæ actiones non prosperè succedunt. Stich. 1. 2. v. 82. Stultitia est, venatum ducere invitas canes. Quod proverbialiter dictum.
units.tr: Unwilling actions do not succeed well. Stich. 1. 2. v. 82. It is folly to lead unwilling dogs to the hunt. This is said proverbially.

units.la: Audenter agendum, cum bonâ fortunâ. Pœn. 5. 2. v. 13.
units.tr: Action should be taken boldly, when fortune is good. Pœn. 5. 2. v. 13.

units.la: Incipere multò est, quàm impetrare facilius. Ubi alij patrare legunt. Pœn. 5. 2. v. 14. Græci alias dicunt: ἥμισυ ἀλέον παντός.
units.tr: The beginning is much more than obtaining it, and is easier. Some editions read "accomplishing" here. Pœn. 5. 2. v. 14. The Greeks say it otherwise: "half is better than the whole" [ἥμισυ ἀλέον παντός].

units.la: Actiones tùm serió agendæ, quando res calet. Pœn. 4. 2. v. 92. At enim nihil est, nisi, dum calet, hoc agitur. Germani dicunt: Wann das Eysen heiß ist/ so soll man schmieden.
units.tr: Actions should be carried out in earnest when the matter is hot. Pœn. 4. 2. v. 92. "But there is nothing, unless the thing is done while it is hot." The Germans say: "When the iron is hot, one should strike."

units.la: Ad actiones commodas; commodus quoq; actor requiritur, qui eas conficiat. Pœn. 4. 2. v. 93. Probæ materies data est, si probum adhibet fabrum.
units.tr: For suitable actions a suitable doer is also needed, who carries them out. Pœn. 4. 2. v. 93. "Good material is given if a good smith is applied."

units.la: In alienis negotijs dormitamus oës: in nostris maximè vigilamus. Merc. 5. 4. v. 51. Suam quisque rem homo meminit. Pœn. 3. 1. v. 54. Itane tentas? an sciamus nos meminisse nostra. Sic Ennius: Ne quid exspectes amicos, facere quod per te queas.
units.tr: In other people's affairs we all doze; in our own we are most watchful. Merc. 5. 4. v. 51. Each man remembers his own affair. Pœn. 3. 1. v. 54. "Are you trying that? As if we did not know that we remember our own affairs!" So Ennius: "Do not expect friends to do what you can do yourself."

units.la: In negotijs procurandis, solemnis erat ista formula: SI QUID OPUS ESSET. Asin. 1. 1. v. 104. Cicero ad Attic. Erat enim, si meministi, in consulatus petitione per te mihi pollicitus, SI QUID OPUS ESSET. Martial. lib. 7. 21. Si quid opus fuerit, scis me non esse rogandum.
units.tr: In arranging affairs this formula was customary: "IF THERE SHOULD BE ANY NEED." Asin. 1. 1. v. 104. Cicero to Atticus: "For there was, if you remember, your promise to me, made in the canvass for the consulship, IF THERE SHOULD BE ANY NEED." Martial, book 7, 21: "If there is any need, you know I am not to be asked."

units.la: Prout quisque negotia & actiones suas curat: ita etiam eventum sortiuntur. Perf. 4. 1. v. 1 Si quam rem accures sobrie, aut fruga-liter, solet illa retle sub manu succedere: atq; adipol fermè, ut quis-que quæ rem accurat suam, sic etiam procedunt post- principia deniq.
units.tr: According as each man looks after his affairs and actions, so also they turn out in the outcome. Pers. 4. 1. v. 1. "If you attend to any matter soberly or thriftily, it usually goes well in hand; and for the most part things turn out for each man as he takes care of his own affair, so in the end they proceed well from the beginning."

units.la: NEGOTIA, quæ mane suscipiuntur, optimè procedunt. Perf. 1.3.v.35. Hesiod. ὡς γὰρ τοι ... ἔργα.
units.tr: Business undertaken in the morning goes best. Pers. 1. 3. v. 35. Hesiod: "for ... works" [ὡς γὰρ τοι ... ἔργα].

units.la: QUANTI est adhibere hominem amicum, ubi quid geras! Perf. 4.4.v.46.
units.tr: How valuable it is to have a friend present when you are doing something! Pers. 4. 4. v. 46.

units.la: NEGOTIUM qui parare volet, Navem & Mulierem comparet. Pœn. 1.2.v.1.
units.tr: He who wishes to set up a business should get a ship and a woman. Pœn. 1. 2. v. 1.

units.la: INITIO rei gerendæ solebant profari hanc formulam: Quod BONUM FAUSTUM FELIXQUE SIT! Aul. 2.1.v.26. Asin. Prol. v. 2. Quæ RES BENE VORTAT! Addam huc, quæ olim mihi adolescenti observata boni ominis ergo in Noctib° Palatinis Vigilia 1. cap.1. Petronius: Hiu sta ordinatis, quod BENE FELICITERQUE eveniret, precati Deos, viam ingredimur. Apulejus: Et osculato tuo capite, quàm invita discedeꝛet, vultu prodidit, denique sæpe retrorsum respiciens subsistit, Quod BONUM FELIX ET FAUSTUM: itaq; licet salutare non sit, Fotis illa tenetur. Omen itaque plenum in rebus agendis erat: Quod BONUM FELIX FAUSTUM ET SALUTARE SIT. Juvenal. Signata tabula, dictum FELICITER. Hæc Religio an Superstitio eṗdé fuit Græcorum. Theocritus: ὡς τοῦτον ... τέλκω. Ac sicut illi BONUM FACTUM, hi ΑΓΑΘΗ: ΤΥΧΗ: quod apud Theophrastum in characteribus observavi: & Zachariam Callierigum in præcedentem locum Theocriti. Inscriptio vetus pag. MLXXIII. 2. quæ est Ancyræ: ΑΓΑΔΗ; ΤΥΧΗ. ΕΙC. ΑΙΩΝΑ ΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ.
units.tr: At the beginning of an undertaking they used to say this formula: "May it be good, lucky and fortunate!" Aul. 2. 1. v. 26. Asin. Prol. v. 2. "May the thing turn out well!" I will add here what I once observed as a young man, for the sake of a good omen, in the Noctes Palatinae, Vigil 1, chapter 1. Petronius: "Things being arranged, so that it might turn out well and happily, we set out on our way, praying to the gods." Apuleius: "And having kissed your head, she showed by her face how unwillingly she was leaving; at last, often looking back, she stops. 'May it be good, lucky and fortunate!' So although it is not proper to say farewell, Fotis is held back." Thus there was a full omen in doing things: "May it be good, lucky, fortunate and safe!" Juvenal: "The tablet being sealed, he said 'happily.'" Whether this was a religion or a superstition of the Greeks, I do not know exactly. Theocritus: "Thus ... I ..." [ὡς τοῦτον ... τέλκω]. And as the Romans said bonum factum, these said "good fortune" [ΑΓΑΘΗ ΤΥΧΗ], which I observed in Theophrastus in the Characters, and Zacharias Callierigus on the passage of Theocritus just mentioned. An old inscription, p. MLXXIII. 2, which is at Ancyra: "Good fortune. To the Lord for ever" [ΑΓΑΔΗ ΤΥΧΗ. ΕΙΣ ΑΙΩΝΑ ΤΟΝ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ].

units.la: Socrates de morte sua certior factus per Critonem, inquit apud Platonem Criton. pag. 43: Ἀλλ' ὦ κριτων, Τυχη ἀγαθη. εἰ ταύτα τοῖς θεοῖς φίλον, ταύτη ἔσω. Ab hoc ritu explico Catullum in fine Epithalamij ad Mallium: BONA TE VENUS JUVERIT! Vide infra Tit. Nuptiarum. Musæus in Leandro: δ δὲ αὐτικα λύζατο μίτρην, ᾧ θεσμῶν ἐπέβησαν ἀγεισονόυ Ἀφροδίτης.
units.tr: Socrates, informed of his death by Crito, says in Plato, Crito, p. 43: "But, Crito, good fortune! If these things are pleasing to the gods, so let it be" [Ἀλλ' ὦ Κρίτων, Τύχη ἀγαθή. εἰ ταῦτα τοῖς θεοῖς φίλον, ταύτῃ ἔστω]. From this custom I explain Catullus at the end of his Epithalamium for Manlius: "May good Venus help you!" See below, under Marriages. Musaeus in Leander: "And straightway she loosed her headband, by which they stepped into the laws of Aphrodite" [δ δὲ αὐτικα λύζατο μίτρην, ᾧ θεσμῶν ἐπέβησαν ἀγεισονόυ Ἀφροδίτης].

units.la: QUOTIDIE pridie cavendum est, ne quis faciat, quod pigeat posti-ridie. Stich. 1. 2. v. 65. Augustinus: Cave pridie quotidie, ne quid agas hodie, cujus te pœniteat postridie.
units.tr: Every day one must take care for the day before, lest someone do something that he regrets the next day. Stich. 1. 2. v. 65. Augustine: "Beware each day in advance, lest you do anything today which you may regret tomorrow."

units.la: Re bene gestâ, DIs supplicabant. Curc. 4. 2. v. 41.
units.tr: When a matter has gone well, they gave thanks to the gods. Curc. 4. 2. v. 41.

units.la: ADMONITIONUM. MONITIONUM. CASTIGATIONUM. CORRECTIONUM. OBJURGATIONUM. REPREHENSIONUM.
units.tr: Admonitions, Warnings, Chastisements, Corrections, Rebukes, Reprimands.

units.la: Vide etiam, Erroris: Peccati.
units.tr: See also Error: Sin.

units.la: QUI alium monere vult: ne sit ipse monendus. Pseud. 4. 1. v. 11 Monendus ne me moneat. Prov. Ne sis Minervam. Horat. lib. 1. Ep. 17. Disce docendus adhuc, quae censet amiculus. Ausonius ad Symm. Ego te docebo docendus adhuc, si essem id ætatis, ut discerem: atque ego te vegetum, atque alacrem commonebo.
units.tr: He who wants to warn another should not need to be warned himself. Pseud. 4. 1. v. 11 Let the one to be warned not warn me. Proverb: Do not be a Minerva. Horace, Epistles 1.17: Still to be taught, learn what your little friend thinks. Ausonius to Symmachus: I will teach you, though I myself still need to be taught, if I were of an age to learn; and I will advise you, being vigorous and lively.

units.la: AMICUM castigare ob meritam noxiam, immune est facinus. Trin. 1. 1. v. 1. Vide Tit. Amicitia.
units.tr: To chastise a friend for a deserved offence is a blameless act. Trin. 1. 1. v. 1. See the title Friendship.

units.la: Qui monet, quasi adjuvat. Curc. 3. 1. v. 89.
units.tr: He who warns, as it were, helps. Curc. 3. 1. v. 89.

units.la: ERRANTES in viam reducere convenit, ne percant. Aul. 4. 1. v. 6.
units.tr: It is fitting to lead wanderers back onto the road, lest they perish. Aul. 4. 1. v. 6.

units.la: OB castigationes gratia debetur. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 99.
units.tr: Thanks are owed for rebukes. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 99.

units.la: VITUPERIA benivolentiæ signa sæpe sunt. Most. 1. 3. v. 14.
units.tr: Reproaches are often signs of goodwill. Most. 1. 3. v. 14.

units.la: STULTUM est, memorem monere. Sic ait ille Captiv. 2. 3. v. 36. Quæ memini, mora mera est monerier.
units.tr: It is foolish to warn one who remembers. So says that man: Captiv. 2. 3. v. 36. What I remember, it is pure delay to be warned.

units.la: MINOR frater, vel soror, etiam majorem potest admonere officij. Stich. 1. 1. v. 35.
units.tr: A younger brother or sister can even owe a duty of admonition to an elder. Stich. 1. 1. v. 35.

units.la: FILII quandoque possunt parentes admonere: exemplo illius a-doledolescentis : qui parentem in viam reduxit, male sentiente in de beneficientiâ erga amicos. Trin. 2. 2, v. 65.
units.tr: Sons can sometimes admonish their parents, as in the example of that young man who led his father back onto the right path when he was thinking badly about kindness towards friends. Trin. 2. 2, v. 65.

units.la: Adolescentiae. Pueritiae. Juventutis. Ætatis.
units.tr: Adolescence. Boyhood. Youth. Age.

units.la: Vide etiam Temporis: Educationis: Disciplinæ: Animi.
units.tr: See also Time, Education, Discipline, Mind.

units.la: PUeris septuennibus dentes excidunt. Merc 3. 1. v. 44. in jo-co. Nam illi quidem haud sane diu est, cum dentes exciderunt. Vide etiam Men. 5. 9. v. 57.
units.tr: Boys lose their front teeth at seven years old. Merc. 3.1 v.44, in jest: For it is not very long at all since his teeth fell out. See also Men. 5.9 v.57.

units.la: ÆTATEM senilem bene se habere, nimiò est æquius. Merc. 3. 2. v. 6.
units.tr: It is far too fair that old age should be comfortable.

units.la: Adolescens cùm sis, tum cùm est sanguis integer, rei tuæ quærendæ convenit operam dare. Demum igitur cùm senex sis, tunc in otium te, dum potestur, colloces. Ibid.
units.tr: While you are young, and while your blood is sound, it is right to work at getting your property. Then, when you are old at last, you may settle into leisure while you still can.

units.la: In puerilem ætatem multa dicteria jaciuntur: quæ ad regulam juris non examinanda. Perf. 2. 4. vers. 5. Scio ego, quid ætatis sim: eò istum maledictum impunè auferes.
units.tr: Many insults are hurled at childhood, and these are not to be judged by the rules of law. Perf. 2.4 v.5: I know how old I am, so you will get away with that insult unpunished.

units.la: Sæpe ætate pueri, ingenio senes sunt. Merc. 5. 4. v. 15. Novus amator, vetus puer. Vide etiam 1 it. Amatorum. Et Adagia Zecneri Cent. 4. 53. Sic Trin. 2. 2. v. 86. Non ætate, verum ingenio adipiscitur sapientia. Sapienti ætas condimentum est: sapiens ætati cibus est. In hanc sententiam plura apud alios Authores occurrunt, quæ huc congeram. Persius Sat. 4. v. 4. de Nerone: Scilicet ingenium, & rerum prudentia velox Ante pilos venit.
units.tr: Often boys are old by intellect, and old men are boys by age. Merc. 5.4 v.15: A new lover, an old boy. See also 1 it. Amatorum, and the Adages of Zecner, Cent. 4.53. So Trin. 2.2 v.86: Wisdom is gained not by age but by intellect. Age is seasoning for the wise; for the wise, age is food. Many more sayings to this effect occur in other authors, which I will gather here. Persius, Sat. 4 v.4, of Nero: Surely quick intellect and prudence in affairs come before the beard.

units.la: Æschylus in Septem - Thebanâ de Lasthene:
units.tr: Aeschylus, in Seven against Thebes, on Lasthenes:

units.la: Gregorius Nazianzenus in Apologetico : ... Idem Gregor. Basilium adhuc juvenem, vocat ... Idem in carmine de virginitate:
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen, in the Apologetic: ... The same Gregory, calling Basil while he was still a young man ... The same, in his poem on virginity:

units.la: κἀ πολὴν ἀνέτειλε νέος, ἢ γῆρας ἐλαφρότερον ἐλαυνον, ἀρηχθοῖτο πολὺ ἑνεαρωτέρου ἀνδρός.
units.tr: And, having risen young over much, or driving old age away more lightly, he is praised far more than a much younger man. [kai pole aneteilen neos, e gēras elaphroteron elaunon, arēchthoit' polu eneaōterou andros.]

units.la: Sic Gunth. Ligur. de Friderico Barbarossa lib. I. v. III. — meritisq; supervenit annos. Et lib. I. v. 288. Mente senex, ætate puer. Marcellinus de Juliano lib. 25. Virtute senior, quam ætate. Silius lib. 8. de Pisone. v. 386. Orè puer, pueriq; habitu: sed corde sagaci Æquabat senium, atq; ætu superaverat annos. Cornelius Nepos de bello Trojano; sive alius quicumq;: Canescant alii mente: nos pectore, tempora quippe Virtutem non prima negant, non ultima donant. Ambrosius: Non annorum canities est laudanda, sed morum.
units.tr: So Gunther of Liguria on Frederick Barbarossa, book 1 v.111: and by his merits he came to years. And book 1 v.288: old in mind, a boy in age. Marcellinus on Julian, book 25: senior in virtue rather than in age. Silius, book 8, on Piso, v.386: a boy in face and boyish bearing, yet with a shrewd heart he matched old age, and by his spirit had outstripped the years. Cornelius Nepos, on the Trojan War, or whoever else it was: Let others grow grey in mind; we in heart, for time denies virtue to no first, and grants it to no last. Ambrose: The grey hair of years is not to be praised, but that of character.

units.la: Philo Anthol. lib. I. tit. 16. αἱ πολιαὶ σωὸ νῷ γεραρώτεραι, αἱ δ᾽ ἄτερ νῦ μᾶλλον τῶν πολλῶν εἰσὶν ὀνειδος ἐτῶν.
units.tr: Philo, Anthologia, book 1, title 16: Grey hairs are more venerable when joined with mind; without mind they are rather a reproach to many years. [hai poliai sun noi gerarōterai, hai d' ater nou mallon tōn pollōn eisin oneidos etōn.]

units.la: Ibid. αἱ τείχες ὑν σιγῆς, γεραρώτεραι. ἡνδε λαλήσης, ὡς αἱ τῆς ἡβης, ὑ φρένες, ἀλλὰ τείχες.
units.tr: Ibid.: Silent walls are more venerable; when you speak, the mind is not of youth, but of walls. [hai teichēs hyn sigēs, gerarōterai. ēnde lalēsēs, hōs hai tēs hēbēs, hyph' phrenes, alla teichēs.]

units.la: Virgilius lib. 9. Æneid. Audite ô mentibus æquis Æneada: neve hac nostris spectentur ab annis Quaeferimus.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid 9: Hear me, O Aeneadae, with fair minds, and do not let these things be looked upon by our years, which we seek.

units.la: Huc quoq; pertinet vetus Inscriptio Pag. DCCV. 10. P. SCANTIO. JULIANO. P. SCANTIUS. AUGUSTALIS PATER. ET. SERVILIA. C. F. ISIAS MATER. FILIO. PIISS. FECERUNT QUI. VIXIT. ANNOS VIII. M.V. DIEBUS. XII. HOR.*VI. CUIUS. ANNOS. INGENIUM EXCEDEBAT. Item alia Pag. DCCII. 12. L. PROCULO. L. F. XVI. ANN. NATO. QUI. NIHIL. CUM. ADOLESCEN. COMMUNE. HABET. SENES. SAPIEN. ANTEIVIT.
units.tr: This inscription also belongs here: To Publius Scantius Julianus. Publius Scantius Augustalis, his father, and Servilia Isias, his mother, made this for their dutiful son. He lived 8 years, 5 months, 12 days, 6 hours. His intellect exceeded his years. Another, To Lucius Proculus, son of Lucius, aged 16, who had nothing in common with the young, anticipated the wise old.

units.la: Sex. Tertulia. Mater. Ad. Lacrimas. Relic. Hoc. Monumen. Erexit.
units.tr: Sextus. Tertulia. Mother. Left to tears. Erected this monument.

units.la: Ætas alia media, alia mala dicitur. Mediam Cicero conflantem appellat. Et eleganter describit Seneca Oedipo. — Quaspacia morientes Laius vitæ tulit? Primone in ævo viridis, an fraudo occidit? Iocasta: Inter senem juvenemq;, sed proptor seni. Mala ætas, est senilis. Aul. 2 1. v. 37. Vide Lexicon.
units.tr: Age is called one thing middle, another bad. Cicero calls the middle one flaming. Seneca describes it elegantly in Oedipus: What span of life did Laius bear before dying? Did he fall in the green age of the first, or in the dotage? Jocasta: Between old man and youth, but nearer to the old. Bad age is senile age. Aul. 2.1 v.37. See the Lexicon.

units.la: Iam ab anno decimo pueri sub Veneris imperio credebantur esse. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 13. Vide quæ notavimus ad Tit. Amoris.
units.tr: Already from the tenth year boys were believed to be under Venus' rule. Pseud. 1.1 v.13. See what we noted at the title Amoris.

units.la: Minus mirandum est, illæ ætas, si quid illorum facit: Quàm si non facit: Feci ego item (inquit senex) in adolescentiâ. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 6.
units.tr: It is less surprising that that age does something, than if it did not: I did the same too (says the old man) in my youth. Bacch. 3.3 v.6.

units.la: Adolescentes indulgentiâ & assentatione corrumpuntur. Secus enim recti haberentur, ad iugenium bonum: nisi propter aliorum fiduciam pravi fierent. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 8. & seqq. quos vide, ut quei blandiantur multi adolescentibus in æternam corrum perniciem, intelligas.
units.tr: Adolescents are corrupted by indulgence and flattery. Otherwise they would be regarded as upright, with a good nature, unless they became depraved through the trust others placed in them. Bacch. 3.3 v.8 ff. See these lines, so that you may understand how many flatter young men to their eternal ruin.

units.la: Præceptoris fidi munus est, operam sedulò dare, ne discipuli etiam corrumpantur. Ibid. v. 15.
units.tr: It is the duty of a faithful tutor to take care diligently that his pupils are not corrupted too. Ibid. v.15.

units.la: Quæ fuerit olim disciplina, & ratio instituendæ juventutis ad vitum explicat pædagogus, & præceptor adolescentis. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 18. & seqq. Nego tibi hoc annis viginti fecisse primis copiâ, Digitum longe à pædagogo pedem ut efferret ædibus, Idq; ubi obtigerat, hoc etiam ad malum accersebatur malum, Et discipulus & magister perhibebantur improbi. Ante solem exorientem nisi in palæstram veneras, Gymnasij præfecto haud mediocres pœnas penderes. Ibi cursu, hastâ, disco, pugillatu, pila, Saliendo sese exercebant magis, quàm scorto, aut saviis. Ibi suam ætatem extendebant non in latebrosis locis. Inde de hippodromo, & palæstrâ ubi revenisses domum, Cincticulo præcinctus in sella apud magistrum assideres: Tum librum legeres: si unam peccavisses syllabam Fieret corium tàm maculosum, quàm esl nutricis pallium. Locus plane elegans: cui geminus est alter. Most. 1.2.v.72. Unde apparet, quæ vetus fuerit disciplina.
units.tr: What discipline was in former times, and what method was used in bringing up youth, the pedagogue and the tutor of the young man explain. Bacch. 3.3 v.18 ff.: I tell you that for twenty years, in your early years, you did not dare to set one toe outside the house without the pedagogue. And if that happened, evil was added to evil, and both pupil and master were called wicked. Before the sun rose, unless you had come to the wrestling school, you paid no small penalty to the superintendent of the gymnasium. There they trained in running, the spear, the discus, boxing, the ball, and leaping, rather than with whores or kisses. There they spent their youth not in hidden places. Then, when you returned home from the hippodrome and the wrestling ground, you sat girded with a little belt before the teacher. Then you read a book; if you had made a single mistake in a syllable, your hide would be as spotted as a nurse's cloak. A passage quite elegant, to which there is another similar one. Most. 1.2 v.72. From which it is clear what the old discipline was.

units.la: Discipulus magistro olim parebat usque ad eam ætatem, quâ petere magistratus per leges liceret. At nunc priusquam septen-nis est si attigas eum manu,
units.tr: A pupil used to obey his teacher until the age at which the laws permitted him to seek magistracies. But now, if you so much as touch him with your hand before he is seven years old,

units.la: Extemplo puer pædagogo tabulâ dirumpit caput.
units.tr: at once the boy smashes the pedagogue's head with a tablet.

units.la: Cùm patrem adeas postulatum, puero sic dicit pater:
units.tr: When you approach the father to make a complaint, the father speaks thus to the boy:

units.la: Nolter esto: dum te poteris defensare injuriâ.
units.tr: Do not be a coward: defend yourself from injury while you can.

units.la: Provocatur pædagogus. Ebo! senex minimi pretii,
units.tr: The pedagogue is challenged. "Hey! Old man of little worth,

units.la: Ne attigas puerum istâ causâ, quando fecit strenuè.
units.tr: do not touch the boy in this matter, since he has acted bravely."

units.la: It magister quasi lucerna, unctlo exspretus linteo.
units.tr: The teacher goes off like a lamp put out with an oily rag.

units.la: Ibid. Bacch. 3.3.v.42.
units.tr: Ibid. Bacch. 3.3 v.42.

units.la: Adolescentes corrupti, sunt corrigendi. Quo nomine senex graviter objurgatur ab amico: quod neglexerit ad frugem corrigere, & restituere adolescentem deperditum. Trin. 1.2.v.81.
units.tr: Corrupted adolescents must be corrected. For this reason an old man is sharply rebuked by a friend, because he neglected to correct the young man to virtue and to restore the one who had been lost. Trin. 1.2 v.81.

units.la: Qui adolescentibus dant argentum: gladium dant, quo se occidant. Trin. 1.2.v.93. Quid si quit us est, aut quid interest? dare te in manus argentum amanti adolescenti, animi impoti, qui exaedificaret suam ignaviam?
units.tr: Those who give silver to young men give them a sword with which to kill themselves. Trin. 1.2 v.93: What does it matter, or what difference does it make? To put silver into the hands of a young man in love, a youth without self-control, who would build up his own laziness?

units.la: Ætatis habenda est ratio: ne cum juvene illo tandem ea deplo-randa fit. Most. 1.2.v.70. Neq; tempus resarciri potest. Ib.
units.tr: Regard must be had for age, lest at last the time is to be lamented together with that young man. Most. 1.2 v.70. Nor can time be made good again. Ibid.

units.la: Adolescentes debent animum suum vincere, non vinci ab animo: h. e. debent ex præcepto Apostoli fugere juvenilis cupiditates. Trin. 2.2.v.28. Vide etiam Tit. Victoria.
units.tr: Adolescents ought to conquer their own minds, not be conquered by their minds; that is, by the precept of the Apostle they ought to flee youthful lusts. Trin. 2.2 v.28. See also the title Victoria.

units.la: Qui homo cum animo inde ab ineunte ætate depugnat suo, utrum is ita ne esse malit, ut cum animo æquum censeat, an ita potius, ut parentes cum esse, & cognati (& præceptores) velint. Si animus hominem perpulit, actum est: animo servivit, non sibi. Si ipse animum perpulit, dum vivit, victor victorum cluet. Tu si animum vicisti potius, quàm animus te, est quod gaudeas. Nimiò satius est, ut opus est, te ita esse, quàm ut animo lubet. Qui animum vincunt, quàm quos animus, semper probiores cluent. Philosophica hæc est disputatio de juvenilibus cupiditatibus. Trin. 2.2.v.24. & seqq. ubi adolescens frugi aliis in exemplum virtutes suas enumerat.
units.tr: A man who from his earliest age fights with his own mind, whether he prefers to be such as he judges right in his own mind, or rather such as his parents, relatives and teachers wish him to be. If the mind has driven the man, it is all over: he has served the mind, not himself. If he himself has driven out the mind, then while he lives he will be called the victor of victors. If you have conquered your mind rather than your mind conquering you, you have cause to rejoice. It is far better that you be as you ought to be than as your mind pleases. Those who conquer their minds will always be counted better than those whom their minds conquer. This is a philosophical discussion of youthful lusts. Trin. 2.2 v.24 ff., where a thrifty young man lists his own virtues as an example to others.

units.la: Romana juventus variis ludis exercebatur. Most. I. 2. v. 72. Vide Tit. Gymnastica.
units.tr: Roman youth was trained in various games. Most. 1.2 v.72. See the title Gymnastica.

units.la: Adolescentes nisi ad frugem redeant, accidet eis, quod monet Lysiteles. Trin. 3. 2. v. 37. Nisi me auscultas, atque hoc ut dico, facis, tute pone te latebis facile, ne inveniat te Honor in occulto jacebis, cum te maxime clarum voles.
units.tr: Adolescents, unless they return to virtue, will suffer what Lysiteles warns of. Trin. 3.2 v.37: Unless you listen to me and do as I say, you will easily hide yourself away; lest Honour find you lying hidden in a corner when you most want to be famous.

units.la: Qui adolescentem à vitiis reprehendit: servat eum. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 95. Vide paulò ante Tit. Admonitionum.
units.tr: One who rebukes a young man for his vices saves him. Bacch. 3.3 v. 95. See a little above under the title Admonitions.

units.la: Decet verecundum esse adolescentem. Asin. 5. 1. v. 6.
units.tr: A young man ought to be modest. Asin. 5.1 v. 6.

units.la: Adolescentis maximum est ornamentum, pudor & verecundia. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 81.
units.tr: Modesty and shamefastness are the greatest ornament of a young man. Bacch. 3.3 v. 81.

units.la: Adolescentes in suis rebus fluctuant incliti, utrum amori potius operam dent, an rei familiari. Trin. 2. 1. v. 5.
units.tr: Young men of distinction waver over their affairs, whether they should devote their effort to love or to household property. Trin. 2.1 v. 5.

units.la: Adolescentes etiam optimi, prava conversatione corrumpi solent, Most. 1. 1. v. 20.
units.tr: Even the best young men are commonly corrupted by bad company. Most. 1.1 v. 20.

units.la: Adolescentes plærumq; securi rerum suarum, ætatem prodigunt luxu. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 32.
units.tr: Young men, for the most part careless of their affairs, squander their age in luxury. Pseud. 4.7 v. 32.

units.la: Ætas juvenum acerba, & indomita emansuefcit, & domatur cum ætate. Quò allusum Merc. 5. 2. v. 102.
units.tr: The harsh and untamed age of youths grows tame and is subdued with age. This is alluded to in Merc. 5.2 v. 102.

units.la: Adolescentes ætatem suam luxu consumentes, ad egestatem rediguntur. Trinum. Prolog. v. 1. & seqq. lege. Vide etiam Tit. Luxus.
units.tr: Young men who spend their age in luxury are reduced to poverty. Read the Trinummus prologue, v. 1 and following. See also the title Luxury.

units.la: Adolescentibus loca latebrosa, ut ganea, & lustra, sunt vitanda. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 22. & 33. v. 26.
units.tr: Young men must avoid hiding places, such as gaming houses and brothels. Bacch. 1.1 v. 22 and 3.3 v. 26.

units.la: Adolescentem amare, non est novum. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 20.
units.tr: To love a young man is nothing new. Pseud. 1.5 v. 20. ## Of Adoration, of Invocation.

units.la: Adorationis, Invocationis.
Vide etiam Titul. Sacrorum: Religionis: Deorum: Supplicationum: Ara.
units.tr: See also the titles Sacrifices, Religion, Gods, Supplications, Altar.

units.la: ADORATURI ad aram sedebant, & precabantur. Moft. 5. 1. v. 54. Itemque qui de re aliquâ consultabant. Vide Tit. Iudicij. Propert. lib. 2.
units.tr: Those who were about to worship sat down at the altar and prayed. Most. 5.1 v. 54. Likewise those who consulted about some matter. See the title Judgment. Propertius, book 2.

units.la: Ante tuos q; pedes illa ipsa adoperta sedebit.
units.tr: "Before your feet that same veiled woman will sit."

units.la: IDEM faciebant quoque supplices, & ij, qui tutelæ sui causâ confugiebant ad aras. Vide infra Asyli. Templorum. Item Injuriarum. Nec non Colv. ad x 1. Apul.
units.tr: Suppliants did the same, and those who fled to the altars for their own protection. See below, under Asylum, Temples. Likewise under Injuries. Nor Colv. on x 1 of Apuleius.

units.la: QUI magno affectu & studio Deos colebant, aut in magno periculo erant, ut Deorum fide tuti essent, aut à Dijs magni periculi liberationem petebant, aut Aras, aut Divûm simulacra amplectebantur. Rud. 2. 7. v. 2. Quid istuc est obsecro negotij ? quòd duæ mulierculæ hic in fano Veneris signum flentes amplexæ tenent, nisi quem metuentes miseræ, nocte hac verò proximâ sejactatas, atque ejectas hodiè esse ajunt è mari. Virgil. lib. 2. Æneid. &c. Divûm amplexæ simulacra tenebant. Turneb. l. 26. c. 2. & lib. 14. c. 15. Vide infra Tit. Templorum: Asyli: & Injuriarum.
units.tr: Those who worshipped the gods with great devotion, or who were in great danger, either sought to be safe under the protection of the gods' faith, or asked the gods for deliverance from great peril, or embraced altars or statues of the gods. Rud. 2.7 v. 2: "What business is this, I ask you? That two little women here in the temple of Venus are weeping and clinging to the statue, unless they fear someone, the wretched things, who they say were tossed about last night and cast out from the sea today." Virgil, Aeneid book 2, etc.: "They clung to the images of the gods." Turnebus, book 26, ch. 2, and book 14, ch. 15. See below under the titles Temples, Asylum, and Injuries.

units.la: CREATURAS, ut sidera, & stellas, non licet adorare: quia iuvare homines non possunt. Merc. Prol. v. 3. Non ego idem facio, ut alios in Comœdijs Vidi facere amantes, qui aut Nocti, aut Dy, Aut Soli, aut Lunæ miserias narrant suas. Quos pol ego credo humanas querimonias Non tanti facere, quid velint, quid non velint.
units.tr: Creatures, such as the sky and the stars, may not be adored, because they cannot help men. Merc. Prol. v. 3: "I do not do what I have seen other lovers do in comedies, who tell of their miseries to Night, or to Dawn, or to the Sun, or to the Moon. By Pollux, I think such people do not set much store by human complaints, nor do they care what we want or do not want." ## Of Flatterers.

units.la: ADULATORUM.
Vide Parasitorum. Sycophantarum.
units.tr: See Parasites, Sycophants.

units.la: ALTERA manu, fert lapidem, panem ostentat alterâ. Nemini credo, qui largè blandus est, dives pauperi. Ubi manum injicit benignè, ibi onerat aliquam Zamiam. Aul. 2. 2. v. 18.
units.tr: With one hand he carries a stone, with the other he shows bread. I trust no one who is lavishly fawning; the rich man is not kind to the poor. When he kindly lays a hand on you, there he loads someone with a burden. Aul. 2.2 v. 18.

units.la: ADULTERII. SCORTATIONIS. INCESTUS. REI VENEREAE. COITUS. LENONUM. LENARUM. MERETRICUM. CINAEDORUM. LIBIDINIS. MOLLITIEI PELLECEBRARUM. VIRGINUM. PUELLARUM. FEMINARUM, MULIERUM.
units.tr: ADULTERY. FORNICATION. INCEST. SEXUAL INTERCOURSE. COITION. PIMPS. BAWDS. PROSTITUTES. CATAMITES. LUST. EFFEMINACY. ALLUREMENTS. VIRGINS. GIRLS. WOMEN AND MARRIED WOMEN.

units.la: Vide etiam Titul. Amoris: Amationum: Amatorum: Lupanaris: Lustrorum: Ganei. Item Gynaecei: Luxus. Vide etiam infra Tit. Conjugij.
units.tr: See also the headings Love: Lovemaking: Lovers: Brothels: Stews: Revelry. Likewise Women's Quarters: Luxury. See also below the heading Marriage.

units.la: MOECHIS ἐπ' ἀλοφάγῳ deprehensis, virilia amputata, per φαντισμὸν. Poen. 4. 2. v. 41. Refero mea vasa. De hac poena intelligendus locus Terentij Eun. 5. 4. v. 35. Nunc minatur porro sese id, quod mæchis solet: quod ego numquam vidi fieri, nec velim. Facit & mentionem Aristophanes in Nubibus p. 209. Edit. Frischlin. Τίδ', ἵν φαφανίδωθῇ γε πεισομένος σοι, τέφρα δὲ τιλθῇ. De παραπλῷ vide paulò post. Meminit quoque Lucianus in Morte Peregrini.
units.tr: Adulterers caught at the mallow [ἐπ' ἀλοφάγῳ] had their genitals cut off by depilation [φαντισμὸν]. Poen. 4. 2. v. 41. I carry back my wares. The passage of Terence should be understood in light of this punishment, Eun. 5. 4. v. 35. "Now he threatens to do to me what is usually done to adulterers, which I have never seen done and would not wish to see." Aristophanes also mentions it in the Clouds, p. 209, ed. Frischlin: "Why? So that he may suffer the radish, and the ashes be plucked" [Τίδ', ἵν φαφανίδωθῇ γε πεισομένος σοι, τέφρα δὲ τιλθῇ]. Lucian mentions it too, in The Death of Peregrinus. On paraplē see a little later.

units.la: ADULTERÆ feminæ, non domo solum exactæ, & dote privatæ fuerunt, sed etiam necatæ. Alludit Amphit. 2. 2. v. 222. Vide etiam Lipsium ad Annales Taciti lib. I V.
units.tr: Adulterous women were not only driven from the house and deprived of their dowry but were also put to death. Amphitryo 2. 2. v. 222 alludes to this. See also Lipsius on Tacitus's Annals, book 4.

units.la: IN manifesto adulterio deprehensi, poterant interfici. Bacch. 4. 8. v. 17. 26. 77.
units.tr: Those caught in manifest adultery could be killed. Bacchides 4. 8. vv. 17, 26, 77.

units.la: IN adulterijs manifestò deprehensis nates pervellebātur. Ad quem morem alluditur Perf. 5. 2. v. 66. De eo more sic Suidas: Παραπίλλεται, διασείται, ἢ τρίχας ἕ πωγωνὶ διασείειλαι. Aristoph. Pluto: ὁ δὲ ἀλῆς γε μοιχὸς διὰ σε πυ παραπιλλεται. Scholiastes: ἐθῶ ἵν τὸν ἀλόνλα μοιχεῖας παραπίλλεδαι, ἵνα δῆς ἀργύρειον ποιῆς λυθῇ. παραπίλλεσαι ἵν, διασείεται, τὰς τρίχας ἕ πωγωνὶ τιλλεσθαι. De hoc παραπαραπλμῷ lege fis Perf. Sat. 4. Martial. lib. 2. Epig. 62. lib. 6. Epist. 55. Et lib. 9. ep. 98. Ausón. Epig. 123. Juvenal. Sat. 11.
units.tr: Those caught in manifest adultery had their buttocks plucked. Persa 5. 2. v. 66 alludes to this custom. On it Suidas says: "He is plucked, shaken, or plucks out the hairs of his beard." Aristophanes, Plutus: "...the adulterer is plucked on account of you..." The scholiast: "...to be plucked for adultery, so that he may be made to pay silver...; he is plucked, that is, shaken, and his beard-hairs are plucked out." On this paraplēx see Persa, Satire 4; Martial, book 2, epigram 62, book 6, epistle 55, and book 9, epistle 98; Ausonius, epigram 123; Juvenal, Satire 11.

units.la: Qui Lacædemonium pitteumate lubricat Orbem.
units.tr: "Who makes the Spartan orb slippery with pitch."

units.la: Per Orbem & Anulum notabant posticam partem, ut patet ex Demonact. Luciani. De pitteumatis lege Victor. lib. 8. cap. 14. Var. Lect. & Junium de Comâ cap. 2. Glossæ Δρωπαχιςῆς Dropacisla, culipilarius. Coleis namque tale quid factum, constat ex Lampr. Heliogabali, & Martiale.
units.tr: By "orb" and "ring" they meant the back parts, as is clear from Lucian's Demonax. On pitch-smearing see Victorius, Variae Lectiones, book 8, ch. 14, and Junius, De Coma, ch. 2. The gloss Dropacistes is rendered "culipilarius" (a depilator of the backside). Something of this kind was done to the Coleis, as is clear from Lampridius's Heliogabalus and from Martial.

units.la: Libido & metus in hominibus voluptarijs ita pugnant, ut metus succumbat. Baccb. 5. 2. v. 78. Talis adulter apud Horatium lib. 2. Sat. 7. Talis Verres apud Ciceronem: Ita q, æstuabat dubita-tione: versabat se in utramq, partem, non solum mente, verum et-jam corpore: ut omnes qui aderant, intelligere possent, in animo e-ju metum cum cupiditate pugnare Videetiam Aristotelem lib. 7. Ethicorum, ubi luctam ejusmodi Rationis & libidinis, eleganter depingit.
units.tr: In pleasure-loving men desire and fear struggle in such a way that fear gives way. Bacchides 5. 2. v. 78. Horace, Satires 2. 7, presents such an adulterer. Cicero presents such a Verres: "So he was seething with doubt; he turned himself to each side, not only in mind but also in body, so that all who were present could understand that in his mind fear was fighting with desire." See also Aristotle, Ethics book 7, where he elegantly depicts this kind of wrestling between reason and lust.

units.la: Opera meretricum nimium pretiosa est. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 41.
units.tr: The earnings of a prostitute are excessively costly. Bacchides 1. 1. v. 41.

units.la: Meretrices in suis conciliabulis prandium, cænamve amatoribus paratam semper habuerunt. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 47. & 1. 2. v. 23. & 5. 2. v. 62.
units.tr: Prostitutes always kept a lunch or supper ready for their lovers in their meeting-places. Bacchides 1. 1. v. 47; 1. 2. v. 23; 5. 2. v. 62.

units.la: Meretricum fallacie ab adolescentibus non facile possunt pertransiri: Quia rapidus sunt fluvius, quà temere transiri vix potest. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 52.
units.tr: The deceits of prostitutes cannot easily be got past by young men, because they are a swift river, which can hardly be crossed rashly. Bacchides 1. 1. v. 52.

units.la: Isto c illecebrosius fieri nihil potest: nox, mulieri, vinum, homini adolescentulo. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 55.
units.tr: Nothing can be more enticing than this: night, wine, and a woman for a young man. Bacchides 1. 1. v. 55.

units.la: Meretrices venaturam faciunt oculis, & aucupium auribus. Mil. 4. 1. v. 43. Phædrus: —tres reliquit filias; Unam formosam, & oculis venantem viros.
units.tr: Prostitutes make their eyes the hunting-net and their ears the fowler's snare. Miles 4. 1. v. 43. Phaedrus: "She left three daughters: one beautiful, hunting men with her eyes."

units.la: Formosa namque femina, tamquam visco volucres, sic ipsa adolescentes capit & attrahit.
units.tr: A beautiful woman, like birdlime for birds, so catches and draws young men to herself.

units.la: In Casto aut Pervigilio Isidis votivas decem noctes matronis & meretricibus secubandum erat: neque aliter rem divinam facere sine piaculo poterant. Quorsum alludit noster Asin. 4. 1. v. 61.
units.tr: At the Castum or Pervigilium of Isis, matrons and prostitutes had to keep ten votive nights apart, and they could not otherwise perform the sacred rite without sin. Our author alludes to this at Asinaria 4. 1. v. 61.

units.la: Si forte purè velle habere dixerit,
units.tr: "If perhaps she says she wishes to have it pure,"

units.la: Tot reddat spurcas noctes, quot purè habuerit.
units.tr: "let her give back as many foul nights as she has had pure."

units.la: Hoc enim dicebant purè habere : ἀγυνέιν, ἀγνὰς ἔχειν. Tibul. lib.1. Eleg. 3.
units.tr: For they said "to have pure" [ἁγνεύειν, ἁγνὰς ἔχειν]. Tibullus, book 1, elegy 3.

units.la: Quidve piè dum sacra colis, purèq; lavari Tum memini, & puro secubuisse toro.
units.tr: "Or when you devoutly attend the sacred rites and bathe purely, then I remember you also kept apart on a pure bed."

units.la: Propert. lib. 2. Eleg. 33.
units.tr: Propertius, book 2, elegy 33.

units.la: Cynthia jam noctes est operata decem.
units.tr: "Cynthia has now already kept ten nights."

units.la: Idem lib. 2. Eleg. 28.
units.tr: The same, book 2, elegy 28.

units.la: Votivas noctes & mihi redde decem.
units.tr: "Give back to me also my ten votive nights."

units.la: Tangit & Livius lib. 39. Decem dierum castimoniâ opus est in Bacchanalibus.
units.tr: Livy also touches on this, book 39: "Ten days of chastity are required in the Bacchanalia."

units.la: Apul. lib. 2. Mil. Præcipit decem continuis illis diebus cibariam voluptatem coercerem, nec quicquam animal essem, & invius essem.
units.tr: Apuleius, Metamorphoses book 2: "He instructs that for those ten continuous days I restrain my pleasure in food, that I eat nothing of living creatures, and that I be kept apart."

units.la: Meretrices utplurimùm luteâ veste introductæ; quia color auro, cujus illæ cupientes maximè sunt, similis. Asin. 1.3.v.3. Aurummerum est, quod in nos dicis. Et Asin. 1.2.v.7. Mare haud est mare : vos mare acerrimum. Nam in mari repperi: hic clavi bonis. Vide paulò post ex Trucul. & aliis Plauti comœdijs pænè infinitaloca. Vide etiam Titulo Amoris.
units.tr: Prostitutes were usually introduced wearing yellow, because yellow is like gold, which they especially desire. Asinaria 1. 3. v. 3: "It is gold-money you are saying against us." And Asinaria 1. 2. v. 7: "The sea is not a sea; you are the fiercest sea. For I found in the sea: here are nails for good things." See a little later, from Truculentus and other comedies of Plautus, almost endless examples. See also under the heading Love.

units.la: Meretrices sine modo accipiunt. Asin. 1. 3. v. 15.
units.tr: Prostitutes take without limit. Asinaria 1. 3. v. 15.

units.la: Meretrices sine auro & argento nequicquam præstant. Asin. 1. 3. v. 46.
units.tr: Prostitutes accomplish nothing without gold and silver. Asinaria 1. 3. v. 46.

units.la: Diem, aquam, Solem, Lunam, noctem, hæc argento non emo: Cætera quaq; volumus uti : Græca mercamur fide, Quum a pistore panem petimus, vinum ex œnopolio, Si as habent, dant mercem ; eàdem nos disciplinâ utimur.
units.tr: "Day, water, sun, moon, night: these I do not buy with silver. Other things we want to use for free; we buy Greek things on credit. When we ask the baker for bread, or the wine-seller for wine, if they have coin they give the goods; we use the same discipline."

units.la: Vide sequentia.
units.tr: See what follows.

units.la: Ibidem Asin. 1. 3. v. 63.
units.tr: In the same place, Asinaria 1. 3. v. 63.

units.la: Non tu scis? hic noster quastus aucupij similimus est. Eòq; rectè comparantur lenæ: & lenones aucupibus. Ibid. v. 68. Esca est meretrix, leclus illi x est, amatores aves.
units.tr: "Don't you know? This trade of ours is very like fowling." And so bawds are rightly compared with fowlers and pimps with birdcatchers. Ibid. v. 68: "The bait is the prostitute, the bed is her snare, the lovers are the birds."

units.la: Lenonia januæ similimæ sunt portitorum, si affers, tum patent; si non est, quod des; ædes non patent. Ibidem Asin. 1. 3. v. 88.
units.tr: Pimps' doors are very like customs gates: if you bring something, they open; if you have nothing to give, the house does not open. Asinaria 1. 3. v. 88.

units.la: Turpilius Pedio.
units.tr: Turpilius, to Pedio.

units.la: Quaeso omitte ac desere: quae te semel nacta semper studuit
units.tr: "I beg you, leave off and desist. She who once got hold of you has always striven

units.la: Perdere, detegere, despoliare, opplere, adeo fama ac flagitio.
units.tr: to ruin you, to strip you bare, to despoil you, to fill you with shame and disgrace."

units.la: Phaedrus l. 2. Fab. 33.
units.tr: Phaedrus, book 2, fable 33.

units.la: Afeminis utrinq; spoliari viros
units.tr: "Men are despoiled by women on both sides."

units.la: Ament, amentur: nempe exemplis discimus.
units.tr: "Let them love and be loved: indeed we learn by examples."

units.la: Juvenalis Sat. VI. Illa docet spolijs nudi gaudere mariti.
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire 6: "She teaches a woman to rejoice in the spoils of a stripped husband."

units.la: Martial. lib. 4. Dispensatorem fallax spoliabit amica.
units.tr: Martial, book 4: "A deceitful mistress will strip her steward of his money."

units.la: Ovidius:
units.tr: Ovid:

units.la: Sola viro mulier spolijs exsultat ademtis,
units.tr: "Only a woman exults in men's goods taken from them;

units.la: Sola locat noctes: sola locanda venit.
units.tr: only she lets out her nights; only she comes to be let out."

units.la: Sic Meleager meretricem πολύμισθον appellat lib. 4.
units.tr: So Meleager calls the prostitute polymisthos, much-paid, in book 4.

units.la: Anthol.
units.tr: The Anthology.

units.la: τὴν καταφλεξίπολιν Στεφανίδα τὴν πολύμισθον,
units.tr: "Stephanis, the city-burner, the much-paid one, [τὴν καταφλεξίπολιν Στεφανίδα τὴν πολύμισθον,]

units.la: τὴν τοῖς βουλομένοις χρυσὸν ἐφευρομένην.
units.tr: she who discovers gold for those who are willing." [τὴν τοῖς βουλομένοις χρυσὸν ἐφευρομένην.]

units.la: γυμνὴν μοι διὰ νυκτὸς ὅλης παρέκλινεν ὀνειρῷ
units.tr: "All night long she came to me in a dream, naked, [γυμνὴν μοι διὰ νυκτὸς ὅλης παρέκλινεν ὀνειρῷ]

units.la: ἔχει φίλης ἡνὶς πρὸς κα χαρίζομένῳ.
units.tr: holding the reins of a friend who gratifies her." [ἔχει φίλης ἡνία πρὸς κα χαρίζομένῳ.]

units.la: Aristenaetus lib. 2. Epist. 18. ἐφιλωζάντων χρυμάτων ἡ κατέσπεζαν
units.tr: Aristaenetus, book 2, letter 18: "The gold-lovers either stripped [ἐφιλοχρημάτων ἢ κατέσπαζον]

units.la: πατρίδλα γυμνότερον.
units.tr: their fatherland more nakedly." [πατρίδα γυμνότερον.]

units.la: Euripides Hippol. v. 642.
units.tr: Euripides, Hippolytus v. 642.

units.la: τὸ δ᾽ πανύεργον μᾶλλον ἐκτίλλει κύπρεις ἐντοῖς σοφεῖσι.
units.tr: "Cypris uproots most thoroughly the bold ones with her cunning arts." [τὸ δ᾽ ἀνύεργον μᾶλλον ἐκτίλλει κύπρις ἐν τοῖς σοφεῖσι.]

units.la: Σόφας vocat Meretrices callidas & subdolas emungendi ac detegendi viros.
units.tr: He calls prostitutes Sophas [Σόφας], clever and crafty at fleecing men and exposing them.

units.la: Propertius lib. 3. Eleg. 12.
units.tr: Propertius, book 3, elegy 12.

units.la: Nulla est poscendi: nulla est reverentia dandi.
units.tr: "There is no demanding; there is no reverence in giving."

units.la: Martial. lib. 11.
units.tr: Martial, book 11.

units.la: Nulla est hora tibi, quàm non me Phylli furentem
units.tr: "There is no hour for you, Phyllis, when I, raging, am not despoiled by you;

units.la: Despolies, tantâ calliditate rapis.
units.tr: you snatch with such cunning."

units.la: Idem lib. 4. Sic spoliatricem commendat factus amicam.
units.tr: The same, book 4: "Thus the made friend commends the despoiling mistress."

units.la: Vide de vulturiâ hac rapacitate Meretricum infr. eodem hoc Titulo plura loca παρεάλλησα ex Plauto nostro: itemque Jani Gebhardi Crepund. lib. 3. cap. 22.
units.tr: On this vulture-like rapacity of prostitutes, see more passages below under this same heading, from our Plautus, and also Jan Gebhard, Crepundia, book 3, ch. 22.

units.la: Nefas est senes amare. Merc. 5.4.v.55. Dicamus, inquit adolescens, sensibus leges, quibus sese teneant, contentiq; sint. Annos natus sexaginta qui erit, si quem subimus, seu maritum, sive hercle a deo calibem scortarier, cum eo nos hic lege agemus, insicitum (h.e. ineptum)
units.tr: "It is wrong to love old men." Merc. 5. 4. v. 55. "Let us say," says the young man, "let laws be laid down for the senses by which they may hold themselves and be content. A man who is sixty years old, if we take him as a husband, or, by god, a bachelor who consorts with a prostitute, with him we shall proceed here by law, considering him unfit (that is, inept) for love.

units.la: C ineptum ad Venerem) arbitrabimur. Neu quisquam posthac prohibeto adolescentem filium, quin amet, & scortum ducat, quod bono fiat modo. At lex haec non placet, cum impia sit: & voluntati divinae contraria. Ad eamdem legem allusit Terentius Hecyr. 5i. Nam si facit facturave es, bonas quod par est facere, Insicitum offerre injuriam tibi immerenti, iniquum est.
