Sensus ejus loci est: Iniquum est, si homo senex, qui ex rebus amoenis, & voluptarijs exaruit, injuriam inferat meretrici: cum hoc sit potius calidae juventutis.
units.tr: We shall judge him so. And from now on let no one forbid a young son from loving and taking a prostitute, provided it is done in a proper way." But this law does not please, since it is impious and contrary to the divine will. Terence alludes to the same law in Hecyra 5. 1: "For if you do, or are about to do, what it is right to do, it is unfair to offer an insult to you, who deserve none." The sense of that passage is: it is unfair for an old man, who has dried up from pleasant and pleasurable things, to inflict an injury on a prostitute, since this is more properly the business of hot-blooded youth.

units.la: ADULTERIA, scortationes, adolescentes adigunt ad egestatem. Cavendae igitur. Mero. 5. 4. v. 62.
units.tr: Adulteries and whoredoms reduce young men to poverty. They must therefore be avoided. Plautus, Mercator 5.4, v. 62.

units.la: MERETRICES dicte prosedae, a profedendo in meritorijs, vel fornicibus. Poen. 1. 2. v. 55. Ubi varie describuntur ista pecora. Prostibula dicebatur, teste Marcello, quod ante stabulum stant, quaestus diurni ac nocturni gratia. Stabulum enim est meritorium, seu lupanar: quod inibi consistant. Horat. Nullam nisi olenti in fornice stantem. Seneca: Meretrix vocata es: in communi loco stetisti: stetisti puella in lupanari. Tertullianus lib. 2. ad uxorem: Lupanar vocat Consistorium libidinum publicarum. Quamquam meretrices non semper steterunt: interdum sellis insederunt, ut patet ex dicto loco Plauti. v. 56. Quae tibi olant stabulum, statumque & sellam, & sessibulum merum. Juvenal. Sat. VI.
units.tr: Harlots were called prosedae from profedendo, standing forth, in brothels or vaults. Poen. 1.2, v. 55, where these creatures are described in various ways. They were called prostibula, according to Marcellus, because they stood before the stabulum to earn by day and by night. For the stabulum is a brothel, or whorehouse, and they stood there. Horace: nullam nisi olenti in fornice stantem ("none except one standing in a stinking vault"). Seneca: "You were called a harlot; you stood in a common place; you stood, girl, in a brothel." Tertullian, Ad uxorem book 2, calls the brothel consistorium libidinum publicarum, "the meeting-place of public lusts." Yet harlots did not always stand; sometimes they sat in chairs, as is clear from the passage of Plautus at v. 56: quae tibi olant stabulum, statumque & sellam, & sessibulum merum ("who smell to you of the stable, the stand, the chair, and the bare seat"). Juvenal, Satire 6.

units.la: Et dubitas alta Chionem deducere sella?
units.tr: And do you hesitate to draw Chione down from the high chair?

units.la: Ubi commentator: Inde sellaria dicta. Tertullianus de cultu Feminarum: Thamar illa, quia se expinxerat, iccirco justa suspicioni visa est quaestui sedere. Ita Jehova gentem Israeliticam scortationis spiritualis accusat Jeremiae cap. 2. Ubi non fuisti vitiata? juxta vias sedisti illis. Sic Thamar Genef. 38. operuit se peplo, & obtexit se confeditq, in porta oculorum: h. e. in bivio. Vide Wower. ad Petron. & Coleri Parerga cap. 8. Dicebantur etiam Alicariae meretrices eodem loco Plauti v. 55. quod in Campania solitae essent ante pistrina alicariorum quaestus gratia versari: teste Festo Pompejo.
units.tr: The commentator there: "Hence they were called sellariae." Tertullian, De cultu feminarum: "That Tamar, because she had painted her face, was therefore thought rightly suspected of sitting for gain." So Jehovah accuses the Israelite nation of spiritual whoredom, Jeremiah ch. 2: "Where have you not been defiled? You have sat by the roads for them." Likewise Tamar, Genesis 38: she "covered herself with a veil, and wrapped herself, and sat in the gate of the eyes," that is, at the crossroads. See Wower on Petronius, and Coler's Parerga ch. 8. Harlots were also called alicariae in the same passage of Plautus, v. 55, because in Campania they were accustomed to loiter in front of the mills of the alicarii* for gain, according to Festus Pompeius.

units.la: Vocantur & Caeno delibuta ibid. Poen. 1. 2. v. 56. quia Trucul. 4. 4. 2. 1. Blitea & lutea est meretrix: nisi quae sapit in vino ad rem rem suam. Dicuntur & servilicolæ sordidæ: quia servulorum sordidulorum scorta sunt diobolaria: h. e. Græcè Δυλαρίων διωτροί-βων ταλακάδες Διώβολοι. Nempe meretriculæ diobolares vilissimi generis erant, quæ binos merebant obulos, h. e. dupondium.
units.tr: They are also called caeno delibuta ("smeared with mud"), ibid., Poen. 1.2, v. 56, because Truc. 4.4, v. 1: "She is a blitea and lutea, a harlot, unless she tastes wine for her own purpose." They are also called servilicolae sordidae, because they are the harlots of dirty little slaves: diobolaria, that is, in Greek, diobolai [Διώβολοι]. The diobolares were of the cheapest sort, who earned two obols each, that is, a dupondius.

units.la: Seneca Controv. V I. Itane decem invenes perierunt propter duos dupondios? Pacuvius apud Fulgentium: non ego ita fui, uti nunc sunt meretrices diobolares, suam quæ nummi causa parvipendunt gratiam. Cæstius Pius apud Senecam: Pretia stupri accepisti, & manus, quæ Diis datura erat sacra, capturas tulit. Captura, est pretium, quod datur scorto. Plautus Clitellariâ: Non quasi ut hæc sunt hic limaces lividæ. Diobolares, schænicolæ, miraculæ, Cum extritis talu, cum crotilis crusculis, Capillo scisso, atq; excissatis auribus
units.tr: Seneca, Controversiae V.1: "So have ten young men perished because of two dupondii?" Pacuvius, in Fulgentius: "I was not as the now-cheap harlots are, who make light of their favour for the sake of a coin." Caestius Pius, in Seneca: "You took the price of defilement, and a hand which was to be given sacred to the gods took the captura." A captura is the price given to a whore. Plautus, Clitellaria: "Not like these livid slugs here: two-obol girls, dancers, marvels, with worn-down ankles and little rattling feet, hair torn, and ears cut open."

units.la: Διώβολοι καὶ μορμόναι, χοινοφελίδες Græc. Miraculæ sunt φοβητρα, & μορμόνες. Sic Festus: Miracula, quæ nunc digna admiratione dicimus, antiqui in rebus turpibus utebantur. Catullus vocat eadem de causa monstra. Vide Scaligeri conjectanea ad Varronem.
units.tr: Greek: "two-obol girls and bogeys, basket-sprites." Miraculae are frightful things and bogeys. So Festus: "The ancients used miracula, which we now call things worthy of admiration, of shameful things." For the same reason Catullus calls them monstra. See Scaliger's Conjectanea on Varro.

units.la: Meretrices etiam Gallinæ dictæ: quia ut gallinæ absumunt, & spargunt omnia. Quò forte allusum. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 28. Fulgent. in Mythol. lib. 2. de Siren. Inde Gallinaceæ pedes, quia libidinis affectus omnia quæ habet, spargit. Sic dicebantur etiam Charybdis domesticæ. Sidon. lib. 9. Epist. 6. Ut primum intelligere capit, & retractare, quantum de bonusculis avitis paternisq; sumtuositas domesticæ charybdis absorbuisset. Ad quem locum vide Notas Joh. Savar. Ita Lupæ dictæ rapacitate. Item Capræ & Ignis. Donatus Eunuch. 1. 2. Accede adignem hunc: quia avidæ & avaræ sunt, ut ignis alimentorum.
units.tr: Harlots were also called gallinae, hens, because, like hens, they consume and scatter everything. Perhaps this is alluded to at Pseud. 1.1, v. 28. Fulgentius, Mythologia book 2, on the Sirens: "Hence the feet of a hen, because the passion of lust scatters all that it has." So they were also called domesticae Charybdes. Sidonius, book 9, letter 6: "As soon as she began to understand and to reckon how much of the good ancestral and paternal property the extravagance of her domestic Charybdis had swallowed." On this passage see the notes of Joh. Savaro. Thus they were called lupae (she-wolves) for their rapacity; likewise caprae and ignes. Donatus on Eunuchus 1.2: "Come to this fire: because they are greedy and avaricious, like fire for fuel."

units.la: Matronæ magis conducibile est, unum amare, & cum eo ætatem exigere, cui nupta est semel. Verùm enim Meretrix fortunati est oppidi similima. Non potest suam rem obtinere sola, sine multis viris. Cist. 1. 1. v. 80. & seqq. Sic Turpilius: Numquam unius me comparavi servire elegantiæ. Puellæ bene pudicæque docentur atque educantur, quæ in quæstu non sedent, neque in eam spem producuntur. Sed tales habentur etiam, si quæ uni soli se dant: ut Antiphila Ter. Heaut. & Glycerium : & Silenium in Ciftell. dicto loc. quæ se meretrices dici nolunt, quamvis muliebris patientiæ legem acceperint: dum ne corpus vulgarint. Quo exemplo Tibullus suam pudicam esse optat.
units.tr: For a matron it is more suitable to love one man and spend her life with the one to whom she has been married once. Truly a harlot is most like a town under siege: she cannot keep her business going alone, without many men. Cist. 1.1, v. 80 ff. So Turpilius: "I never bound myself to serve the refinement of one man." Girls who are well-brought-up and chaste are taught and educated so that they do not sit for gain, nor are reared with that hope. But such girls are regarded as harlots even if they give themselves to one man only, like Antiphila in Terence's Heautontimorumenos, and Glycerium, and Silenium in the Cistellaria* passage cited, who do not wish to be called harlots, although they have accepted the law of female submission, provided they have not made their bodies common. By this example Tibullus wishes his mistress to be chaste.

units.la: BLITEA & lutea est meretrix, nisi quæ sapit in vino ad rem suam. Si alia membra vino madeant, cor sit saltem sobrium. Truc. 4. 4. v. 1.
units.tr: Blitea and lutea is a harlot, unless she tastes wine for her own purpose. If other limbs are soaked in wine, let the heart at least be sober. Truc. 4.4, v. 1.

units.la: MULIERES, quæ stupri licentiam apud Ædiles professæ meretricium instituerent quæstum, nomen mutare consueverunt. Pœn. 5. 3. v. 20. Illæ etiam, quæ capturis quæstuiq; meretricio renunciabant, liberum sibi ingenuumque nomen, priori illo cum persona deposito, assumere solitæ fuerunt. Vide P. Pith. Adverf. Jacobi Durantij Var. lib. 1. c. 2.
units.tr: Women who, having declared before the aediles their licence for defilement, set up a harlot's trade, were accustomed to change their name. Poen. 5.3, v. 20. Those also who renounced the captura and the harlot's gain were accustomed to assume a free and honourable name, having laid aside that former persona. See P. Pithou's Adversaria; and Jacobus Durantius, Variae, book 1, ch. 2.

units.la: MERETRICES quoties pensum suum nequam absolvissent, & quot ( ut Propert. loquitur lib. 2. Eleg. 33. ) itinera nocte unâ confecissent: tot corollas ludicro cuipiam & minoi um gentium Deo donarunt, ut Trephallo, Marsyæ, Hermæ, &c. Alludit noster Asin. 4. 1. v. 58.
units.tr: Harlots, whenever they had badly completed their task, and as many journeys as they had made in one night (as Propertius says, Eleg. 2.33), donated as many garlands to some playful god of the lesser nations, such as Trephallus, Marsyas, Hermes, and so on. Our author alludes to Asinaria 4.1, v. 58.

units.la: Tum si coronas ferta, unguenta jusserit
units.tr: "Then if he orders garlands and perfumes to be brought,"

units.la: Ancillam ferre suam Veneri aut Cupidini.
units.tr: "to carry his maidservant to Venus or to Cupid."

units.la: Unde colligimus, ut milites exautorati arma sua ad Martis, Gladiatores rude donati, ad Herculis ponebant: ita & Comessatores, & puellas, quæ Veneri militarent, languidas corollas demptas suo capiti, DEO cupiam in munus dedisse. Vide etiam Tit. Deorum.
units.tr: From this we gather that just as discharged soldiers laid their arms at the altar of Mars, and gladiators given the wooden sword dedicated them to Hercules, so revellers and girls who served Venus, having taken the wilted garlands from their heads, offered them as a gift to some god. See also the title Deorum.

units.la: ITA me DIament! ut Lycurgus mihi quidem videtur posse hic ad nequitiam adducier: Nempe apud pompam meretriciam, quam adversâ avi adolescentes frequentant: commercium habentes cum DIs damnosissimis: quales sunt, Amor, Voluptas, Venus, Venustas, Gaudium, Locus, Ludus, Sermo, Suavis suaviatio. Baccb. 1. 2. v. 3 & seqq.
units.tr: "So help me, Diana! Lycurgus seems to me able to be led to wantonness here." Indeed, in the harlots' procession, which young men frequent from across the street, they have dealings with the most ruinous gods: such as Love, Pleasure, Venus, Loveliness, Joy, Place, Play, Talk, and Sweet Kissing. Bacch. 1.2, v. 3 ff.

units.la: MERETRICES retia habent sub vestimentis: quibus adolescentes irretire solent. Epid. 2. 2. v. 32. Vide etiam Amatorum.
units.tr: Harlots have nets under their clothes, with which they are accustomed to ensnare young men. Epid. 2.2, v. 32. See also Amatorum.

units.la: MERETRICVM blanditiæ memoratu quidem lepidæ sunt: Ani- mum autem sodicant, bona destimulant, facta & famam fau- ciant. Apage à me, apage! Bacch. 1. 1. v. 29. 36. inquit adole- scens.
units.tr: The flatteries of harlots are indeed pleasant to recount, but they tickle the mind, they goad the goods, and they cut down deeds and reputation. "Away from me, away!" says the young man. Bacch. 1.1, vv. 29–36.

units.la: Ibidem: Ego homo adolescentulus metuo penetrare in hujusmodi palæstram, ubi damnis desudascitur, ubi pro disco damnum ca- piam, pro cursura dedecus. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 33. 34. 35. 36. 37. 38. Vide totum locum.
units.tr: Likewise there: "I, a young man, fear to enter such a wrestling-school, where one sweats away his losses, where instead of a discus I would catch a loss, and instead of a race, disgrace." Bacch. 1.1, vv. 33–38. See the whole passage.

units.la: INTER obscenas res ponebant pilos sub alis. Sic enim florem illum seu lanuginem sub axillis notarunt. Pœn. 4. 2. v. 50. Nolito ade- pol te velle: jam his duobus mensibus volucres tibi erunt hirci- na. Vellebantur autem & pilabantur homines cinædi. Inde et- jam impudicis hircus sub alis dicebatur habitare, apud Catullum: quod & quidam exprimunt Pœn. 2. 4. v. 48. Hircum ab alis, E- go aliam lectionem expressi, utpote illi loco convenientissimam ex mente Lipsii, Gruteri, & Acidalij.
units.tr: Among obscene things they counted hair under the armpits, for they marked that flower or down under the arms as obscene. Poen. 4.2, v. 50: "Don't wish to be... in these two months you'll have goat-like wings." Men called cinaedi used to pluck and depilate themselves. Hence in Catullus the "goat under the arms" was said to dwell in shameless men. Some also express it so at Poen. 2.4, v. 48: "a goat from the armpits." I have followed another reading, which suits that place best, in the view of Lipsius, Gruter, and Acidalius.

units.la: Ad hanc obscenitatem hircosum alludunt multi Authores: Ovid. lib. 1. de Arte: Nec ledat nares, virgaæ patergæ gregis. Seneca Epist. 115. Alter se justo plus colit, alter se justo plus negligit: illè & crura, hic nec alas quidem vellit. Neglectum forte ijs, qui- bus longè omnis mollities. Unde de adspirante ad Centuriona- tum Juvenal. Sat. 14.
units.tr: Many authors allude to this goatish obscenity. Ovid, Ars amatoria book 1: "Nor let the smell of the goat-flock offend your nostrils." Seneca, Epistle 115: "One cultivates himself more than is right, another neglects himself more than is right: the first plucks his legs too, the other not even his armpits." Perhaps this neglect belongs to those for whom all softness is far off. Whence Juvenal, Satire 14, of one aspiring to the centurionate: "—and hairy nostrils…"

units.la: —— naresq; pilosus
units.tr: —— and a hairy man

units.la: Annotet, & grandes miretur Lælius alas.
units.tr: Takes note of his nostrils, and Laelius marvels at his great armpits.

units.la: Eâ de causâ Athenienses illâ parte fœtidi, ut patet ex sermone mulieris apud Aristophanem concionantis, quæ inter viros vir videri volucrat: πρῶτον μὲν γ' ἐγὼ τὰς μασχάλας λόχμης ἀφαυτέ- ξαι. Et erat peculiaris ars apud Romanos vellendi alas. Seneca Epist. 56. Alipilum cogita: h. e. alarum pilos vellentem. Gloss. Alipilarius: ἀλοπέκτος: qui dropace, h. e. unguento è pice, aut volsellis pilos alarum evellit. Vulsi lævigabantur pumicibus. Vide Theophrast. Character. cap. 19. Animad. Wower. ad Petro- nium p. 427. Edit. Goldast.
units.tr: For this reason the Athenians were hairless in that part, as appears from the speech of the woman in Aristophanes who harangues the people and wished to be thought a man among men: first of all, I will pluck out the thickets of my armpits [πρῶτον μὲν γ' ἐγὼ τὰς μασχάλας λόχμης ἀφαυτέξαι]. The Romans also had a special trade of plucking the armpits. Seneca, Epist. 56: Consider the alipilus, that is, one who plucks the hair of the armpits. Gloss: alipilarius, [ἀλοπέκτος], one who removes the armpit hair with a depilatory of pitch, that is, with a salve, or with tweezers. The plucked places were smoothed with pumice. See Theophrastus, Characters, ch. 19; Wower's notes on Petronius, p. 427, Goldast edition.

units.la: CINÆDI cauponij cum longis manicatis tunicis incedebant. Pseud. 2. 4. v. 48. Vide Tit. Cultus: Vestium.
units.tr: The cinaedi of the cookshops walked about in long-sleeved tunics. Pseudolus 2.4, v. 48. See the title Cultus: Vestium.

units.la: Cinaedi μαλακοὶ saltationibus gaudent. Mil. 3. 1. v. 73.
units.tr: The cinaedi, [μαλακοί], delight in dancing. Miles gloriosus 3.1, v. 73.

units.la: Cinaedi calamistrati erant. Asin. 3. 3. v. 37.
units.tr: The cinaedi were curled with the curling-iron. Asinaria 3.3, v. 37.

units.la: Cinaedi sunt semiviri, ut sacerdotes Cybeles. Poen. 5. 5. v. 39.
units.tr: The cinaedi are half-men, like the priests of Cybele. Poenulus 5.5, v. 39.

units.la: Meretrix tantisper blanditur, dum illud, quod rapiat, videt. Men. 1. 3. v. 11.
units.tr: A harlot flatters only so long as she sees what she may snatch. Menaechmi 1.3, v. 11.

units.la: Turpissima & Sodomitica Venus puerorum, erat facere equum, ut catamiti solebant suis Jovibus. Tangitur illa turpitudo Asin. 3. 3. v. 144. quamquam ibi admitti possit casliorsensus: ut nimirum dicatur parvus quadrupes incedere, ut olim cum puer esset. Allusit quoque Aristoph. Equit. act. 5. scen. 2. ἐχε νυν απι τούτοις τυτου ἀ ὀκλασιαν, ἡ κατα ἐνοχην. &c. Idem Plautus noster Ciftell. 4. 1. v. 5. appellat puerile officium. Seneca Pater lib. 4. Controv. Procemio: Impudicitia in ingenuo crimen est, in servo necessitas, in liberto officium. Eodem trahitur illud Terent. Adelph. 2. 2. Adolescenti morem gestum oportuit. S A. qui potui melius: quin hodie usq; os praebui. Vide, quae Taubmannus notat ad locum Ciftell. Abominandam autem illam Ταυδοτογιαν, ibi vocat Plautus puerile officium, quo pueri scilicet sefubsternebant incurvatos ad paedicationem catamitorum: quamquam honestiori sensu capi potest locus ille, de crepundijs puerorum, quomodo & locus Mil. 5. v. 6. Vide nostrum Lexicon. Alterum autem faedum officium, praeter Senecam, & Terentium, tangit quoq; Martial. lib. 9. Epigr. 69.
units.tr: The most disgraceful and Sodomitical lust of boys was to make a horse, as the catamites used to do with their Joves. That filthiness is touched on in Asinaria 3.3, v. 144, although there a more innocent sense can be admitted there: namely, that a little four-footed creature is said to move about, as once when he was a boy. Aristophanes also alludes to it in Equites, act 5, scene 2: [ἔχε νυν ἀπὸ τούτων τοῦ ... ὀκλασίαν, ἢ κατὰ ἔνοχην] etc. Our Plautus in Cistellaria 4.1, v. 5 calls it a boyish service. Seneca the Elder, Controversiae book 4, preface: Lust is a crime in a freeborn man, a necessity in a slave, a duty in a freedman. To the same point belongs the line of Terence, Adelphi 2.2: The young man ought to have been humoured. Sostrata: How could I do better? Indeed, today I have even offered my mouth. See what Taubmann notes on the passage of the Cistellaria. Plautus there calls that abominable [ταὐδοτογίαν]... a boyish service, by which boys, of course, bent themselves over for the buggery of catamites; although that passage may be taken in a more decent sense, of the children's toys, as also the passage in Miles gloriosus 5, v. 6. See our Lexicon. Apart from Seneca and Terence, Martial also touches on the other foul service, Epigrams book 9, no. 69:

units.la: Lascivam totam possedi noctle puellam,
units.tr: I had possessed the wanton girl through the whole night,

units.la: Cujus nequitias vincere nemo potest.
units.tr: whose wantonness no one can surpass.

units.la: Fessus mille modis, illud puerile poposci:
units.tr: Weary in a thousand ways, I asked for that boyish thing,

units.la: Ante preces totas primaq; verba dedit.
units.tr: and before all my prayers she gave her first words.

units.la: Ad istam impuritiem trahitur quoque verbum illud Conclinisco: de quo vide Lexicon Plautinum. De officio lenonio vide paulo post ex Pseud. 1. 3. v. 142. Vide etiam totam sc. Caf. 5. 2. imo non vide. Sunt enim nefanda prorsus, & petulantiae plena omnia: ut & scena sequenti ultima. Idem scelus vocabant Irrumationem, & linguae compressionem Amphit. 1. 1. v. 191. Rud. 4. 4. v. 20. 31.
units.tr: To this same impurity belongs also the word conclinisco, on which see the Plautine Lexicon. For the service of the procurer, see a little later from Pseudolus 1.3, v. 142. See also the whole of Casina 5.2; indeed, do not look there. For these things are utterly unspeakable and full of wantonness, as is also the last scene of the following act. They called the same crime irrumatio, and the compression of the tongue: Amphitruo 1.1, v. 191; Rudens 4.4, vv. 20, 31.

units.la: Meretricem ego item esse reor, mare ut est; quod des, devorat: vorat: nec umquam abundat. At hoc saltim interest; nam illi æstuanti, ejectum apparet: huic das quantumvis, nusquam apparet, neque datori, neque acceptricæ: Velut meretrix meum herum miserum suâ blanditiâ impulit in pauperiem, privavit bonis, luce, honore, atque amicis, Truc. 2. 7. v. 16. & seqq. Vide sup. ex Asin.
units.tr: I think a harlot is likewise like the sea: whatever you give, she devours and swallows, and never has enough. Yet there is this difference: to the one who burns, it is evident what has been thrown away; to the other, however much you give, nothing appears, neither to the giver nor to the receiver. Thus a harlot pushed my poor master into poverty by her flattery, and deprived him of goods, light, honour, and friends. Truculentus 2.7, vv. 16 ff. See above from Asinaria.

units.la: Meretrices solent alienum fœtum supponere. Truc. 4. 3. v. 30. & seqq. Ter. Eun. Prolog. v. 59.
units.tr: Harlots are accustomed to substitute another's offspring. Truculentus 4.3, vv. 30 ff.; Terence, Eunuchus, prologue, v. 59.

units.la: Pudicus insidias locare, turpe erat. Curc. 1. 1. v. 25. Solebant enim ijs, qui Venerem legibus vetitam sectarentur, partes necessariæ, sive testes, exsecari. Quò pertinet jocus servi Curc. 1. 1. v. 30. Vide locum integrum. Nec non ea, quæ huic rei illustrandæ adfert doctissimus Jurisconsultorum Joh. Langlæus lib. 8. c. 7. Otij semestris pag. 505. ubi docet, stupratorem meretricis Romanorum legibus nullâ pœnâ affici: cum in publicis lupanaribus palàm se prostituant. Quæ verò Venus sit vetita, explicat Plautus eleganter dicto loco: quem vide.
units.tr: It was shameful for a chaste man to lay snares. Curculio 1.1, v. 25. For they used to cut off the necessary parts, or witnesses, of those who pursued Venus forbidden by law. To this belongs the slave's joke in Curculio 1.1, v. 30; see the whole passage. Also what the most learned jurist Johann Langlaeus adds to illustrate this matter, in book 8, ch. 7 of his Otium semestre, p. 505, where he teaches that under Roman law a seducer of a harlot was punished by no penalty, since they openly prostituted themselves in public brothels. What Venus was forbidden, Plautus explains elegantly in the passage cited; see it.

units.la: Meretrices studiolè cavebant, ne complerentur, gravidæque jacerent, ut loquitur Lucretius: eòque impregnationem impensè præpedire cupiebant: at sæpe falsæ erant: eòque dicebantur sibi malum quærere. Cist. 1. 2. v. 22. Unde partumeia dicuntur per convitium, quòd non tam pariant, quam mingant suum partum: quemadmodum hujusmodi meretricem traducit Horat. Epod. 17. Tumque venter Partumejus, & tuo Cruore rubros obstetrix pannos lavit, Utcumq; fortis exilii puerpera, Et Lucil. Sat. l. 3. 26. Non peperit, verum posticâ parte profudit. Sulpitia de Domitiano: Non trabe, sed tergo prolapsus.
units.tr: Harlots took care, with some diligence, that they should not be filled and lie heavy with child, as Lucretius puts it; and so they eagerly wished to hinder conception, but often they were deceived, and so were said to seek trouble for themselves. Cistellaria 1.2, v. 22. Hence they are called partumeia by way of abuse, because they do not so much give birth as pour out their birth-pangs; as Horace in Epode 17 describes such a harlot: and the midwife, the puerperal woman of the exile, however strong, washes her red rags with your blood. And Lucilius, Satires book 3, line 26: she did not give birth, but poured it out from the back part. Sulpicia on Domitian: not fallen from a beam, but from the back.

units.la: Meretrices sunt pilæ amatorum, dum se publicant.
units.tr: Harlots are the balls of their lovers, while they make themselves public.

units.la: Truc. 4. 1. v. 8. Nævius Tarentillâ: quasi in foro pila Ludens datatim dat se, & communem facit.
units.tr: Truculentus 4.1, v. 8. Naevius, of Tarentilla: as if in the forum, a ball, playing, she gives herself to each and makes herself common.

units.la: Meretrices captant bolos amatorios, non minus atque pi-scatores suos pisculentos. Truc. 4. 2. v. 12.
units.tr: Harlots catch lovers with baits, no less than fishermen catch their fish. Truculentus 4.2, v. 12.

units.la: Amatores meretricum fundus sunt: è quo direscant. Ib. v. 15.
units.tr: Lovers are the harlots' bottom, from which they are drained dry. Ibid., v. 15.

units.la: Meretrices sumtuosas sibi faciunt vestes, quibus ipsæ sua indunt nomina. Epid. 2. 2. v. 39. Quid istuc mirabile est? Quasi non fundis e xornata multa incedant per vias: atq; tributum cum imperatus est, potesse pendi negant. Illis quibus tributum maior pen-ditur, perdi potest. Vide Luxus: Cultus: Habitus.
units.tr: Harlots make for themselves costly garments, in which they dress up their own names. Epidicus 2.2, v. 39: What is that remarkable? As if many do not walk about the streets adorned with purses. And when a tax is imposed, they say they cannot pay it. Those on whom a greater tax is levied can be ruined. See Luxus: Cultus: Habitus.

units.la: Meretricum Ædes & conventicula sunt veluti Orcus: quip-pe quò nemo advenit, nisi quem spes reliquére omnes, esse ut frugi possiet. Sunt enim Meretrices limaces, hominum sorben-tes sanguinem, ut author est Plautus in Nervolariâ. Bacch. 3. 1. v. 1. & seqq. quos vide.
units.tr: The houses and gatherings of harlots are like Orcus: for no one comes there unless he is one whom all hopes have abandoned, so that he can be thrifty. For harlots are slugs, sucking the blood of men, as Plautus says in the Nervolaria, Bacchides 3.1, vv. 1 ff.; see those lines.

units.la: Sectantes lustra & ganea dedecus inurunt parentibus & præ-ceptoribus. Bacch. 3. 1. v. 14. & 3. 3. v. 95.
units.tr: Those who pursue brothels and feasts brand their parents and teachers with disgrace. Bacchides 3.1, v. 14, and 3.3, v. 95.

units.la: Mercatus meretricius celebrabatur Aphrodisijs, seu sacris Ve-neris. Pœn. 1. 2. v. 120. Ad Æde m Veneris hodie est mercatus meretricius: eò conveniunt mercatores: ibi ego me ostendi volo: inquit meretricula.
units.tr: The harlot's market was held at the Aphrodisia, or rites of Venus. Poenulus 1.2, v. 120: There is today a harlot's market at the temple of Venus; the merchants gather there; there I want to show myself, says the little harlot.

units.la: Alienam uxorem subagitare, grave scelus fuit: & poena rapha-nisini punitum. Mil. 5. v. 5. 9. Vide paulò post.
units.tr: To seduce another's wife was a grave crime, and was punished by the raphanisinus. Miles gloriosus 5, vv. 5, 9. See a little below.

units.la: Nec admittitur causa, tametsi ultrò venerit scortum. Ibid. v. 10.
units.tr: Nor is a plea admitted, even if the whore came of her own accord. Ibid., v. 10.

units.la: Magnum probrum erat, ante justas nuptias partum edere. Aul. 2. 3. v. 9.
units.tr: It was a great disgrace to bear a child before lawful marriage. Aulularia 2.3, v. 9.

units.la: Prostibula per ludos publicos in scenam introduci solebant, & exponi omnium non libidini solum, sed & licentiæ: scilicet, ut quæ perditi homines in Mimis, & cæterâ obscenitate Fabu-larum paulò ante natantibus oculis viderant, ea post ludos in re-liquo corpore peccarent. Alludit ad hunc morem Prologus Cas-sinæ v. 14. 15. & Prol. Pœnoli v. 17. Amplius verò explicat Lipsius lib. 1. Elect. c. 11.
units.tr: Prostitutes were accustomed to be brought on stage at the public games and exposed not only to the lust but to the licence of all: so that what wretched men had seen with swimming eyes in the mimes and the other obscenity of the plays a little before, they might then, after the games, commit upon the rest of the body. The prologue of Casina, vv. 14–15, and the prologue of Poenulus, v. 17, allude to this custom. Lipsius explains it more fully, Electa book 1, ch. 11.

units.la: Morem hunc meretrices habent, Ad portum mittunt servulos, ancillulas:
units.tr: Harlots have this custom: they send their little servants and maids to the harbour.

units.la: Si quæ peregrina navis in portum advenit, Rogant cujatis sit, quid ei nomen sit, Post ille extemplò se applicant, aggl tinant, Si pellexerunt, perditum amittunt domum. Men. 2. 2. v. 63.
units.tr: If some foreign ship has come into harbour, they ask whose it is and what its name is; then straightway they attach themselves to the men, bind them fast; if they have enticed them, they lose their ruined house. Menaechmi 2.2, v. 63.

units.la: Improbitas amantium per gradus sese exerit. Manus fert ad papillas: in gremio osculantem tenet mulierem: Manum sub vestimenta ad corpus fert. Exinde majora mala attentat: & ut loquitur Petronius, in unum omnia vota conijcit. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 74.
units.tr: The wickedness of lovers advances by degrees. He brings his hands to her breasts; he holds the woman kissing him in his lap; he puts his hand under her clothes to her body. Thereafter he attempts greater evils, and, as Petronius puts it, he throws all his wishes into one. Bacchides 3.3, v. 74.

units.la: Meretrices quò blandiores, eò damnosiores. Men. 2. 1. v. 37.
units.tr: Harlots are the more damaging the more charming they are. Men. 2. 1. v. 37.

units.la: Scorta non altbant longos crines, sed breviores. Vide Tit. Matrimonij.
units.tr: Harlots did not wear their hair long but cut short. See the title Matrimony.

units.la: Meretrices quoque non minus atque honestæ matronæ amicitiam inter se colere solent. Cist. 1. 1. v. 24. & seqq.
units.tr: Harlots too are wont to cultivate friendship among themselves no less than respectable matrons do. Cist. 1. 1. v. 24 and following.

units.la: Mores meretricios memorant ipsæ meretrices satis copiosè Cist. 1. 1. v. 24. & seqq.
units.tr: The harlots themselves recount their harlots' ways quite fully. Cist. 1. 1. v. 24 and following.

units.la: Scortatores in adulterio deprehensi, vestes deseruerunt, & fugâ sibi consuluerunt. Caf. 5. 4. v. 6.
units.tr: Whoremongers caught in adultery left their clothes behind and saved themselves by flight. Caf. 5. 4. v. 6.

units.la: Mæchi malaci cincinnati, umbraticolæ, differuntur passim, & tympanotribæ. Truc. 2. 7. v. 48.Ibid. Fons vitij & perjurij.
units.tr: Adulterers, soft-haired, curled, shade-loving, are everywhere denounced, and as drum-beaters. Truc. 2. 7. v. 48. Likewise: the source of vice and perjury.

units.la: Scortari & potare de die turpe erat. Pseud. 5. 2. v. 8. Vide Tit. Ebrietatis:
units.tr: To whore and to drink in the daytime was shameful. Pseud. 5. 2. v. 8. See the title Drunkenness.

units.la: Lenoniæ matres ad pellendam inopiam elocabant filias suas ad meretricium quæstum. Asin. 3. 1. v. 33.
units.tr: Procuresses' mothers used to hire out their daughters to the trade of harlotry to drive off poverty. Asin. 3. 1. v. 33.

units.la: Meretriculæ suis amatoribus carere nequeunt, non minus ac cibo. Asin. 3. 1. v. 32. Unum sibi eligunt, quæ præcipue amant, uti opilio aliquam habet ovem peculiarem, quâ se soletur. Ibid.
units.tr: Little harlots cannot do without their lovers, no more than without food. Asin. 3. 1. v. 32. They choose for themselves one whom they love especially, as a shepherd has one ewe of his own with which he consoles himself. Ibid.

units.la: Uxorem usurariam perinde est præbere, ac si agrum sterilem fodiendum loces. Amph. 4. 2. v. 41.
units.tr: To offer a usurious wife is just like setting a barren field out for digging. Amph. 4. 2. v. 41.

units.la: Meretrices comparantur τῇ φάτνῃ præsepi: ubi scilicet pabulum adolescentum. Curc. 2. 1. v. 13.
units.tr: Harlots are compared to the manger [τῇ φάτνῃ], where, of course, the young men's fodder is kept. Curc. 2. 1. v. 13.

units.la: Meretrices lenas suas matres nominabant : quia ab illis educabantur. Cist. I. I. v. 48. 85.
units.tr: Harlots called their procuresses "mothers," because they were brought up by them. Cist. 1. 1. v. 48, 85.

units.la: Meretrices vocabantur pellices matronarum. Cist. I. I. v. 39.
units.tr: Harlots were called the concubines of respectable matrons. Cist. 1. 1. v. 39.

units.la: In libertinis non vindicabantur furta Veneris. Cist. I. I. v. 40. Vide Libertinorum.
units.tr: Among freedmen the thefts of Venus were not punished. Cist. 1. 1. v. 40. See Freedmen.

units.la: Meretrices natae ex patribus conventitiis. Cist. I. I. v. 42. Vide Lexicon Plaut.
units.tr: Harlots were born of fathers who were mere customers. Cist. 1. 1. v. 42. See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: Meretrices dicuntur quotidie nubere. Cist. I. I. v. 45.
units.tr: Harlots are said to marry every day. Cist. 1. 1. v. 45.

units.la: Meretrices famis pellendae causa suas artes exercent. Cist. I. I. v. 43. 47.
units.tr: Harlots practise their arts to drive off hunger. Cist. 1. 1. v. 43, 47.

units.la: Meretricibus etiam lex posita, ne nimis acciperent. Truc. 42. 47. Quae adversum legem accepisti a plurimis pecuniam. Jam hercle apud omnes magistratus faxo erit nomen tuum. Postidea ego te manum iniiciam quadrupli, venefica, suppostrix puerum: Perdidi omne, quod fuit, impudens fui.
units.tr: A law was also laid down for harlots, that they should not take too much. Truc. 42, 47. "You have taken money from very many men against the law. Indeed, by Hercules, I will see to it that your name is before all the magistrates. Afterwards I will lay hands on you, you poisoner, you procuress of boys: I have lost everything I had; I was shameless."

units.la: Salaces verri comparantur. Mil. 4. 2. v. 67.
units.tr: Lustful men are compared to boars. Mil. 4. 2. v. 67.

units.la: Meretrices, ut amatores extruderent foras, simulabant se peperisse. Truc. I. I. v. 67.
units.tr: Harlots, to drive their lovers out of doors, pretended they had given birth. Truc. 1. 1. v. 67.

units.la: Amatores in amoribus sape furta exercent. Truc. 1. 2. v. 9.
units.tr: Lovers in their love affairs often practise thefts. Truc. 1. 2. v. 9.

units.la: Scortatores noctu cubabant in cellis meretricum. Amph. I. I. v. 132.
units.tr: Whoremongers used to sleep at night in the rooms of harlots. Amph. 1. 1. v. 132.

units.la: Turtur in nequitia usurpatur: ut alia nomina avium. Bacch. I. I. v. 35.
units.tr: The turtle-dove is used for wantonness, as are other names of birds. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 35.

units.la: Meretrices gloriosae. Truc. 4. 4. v. 35. Ita sunt gloriae meretricum.
units.tr: Harlots are boastful. Truc. 4. 4. v. 35. Such are the boasts of harlots.

units.la: Qui scortantur cum puella libera, ei injuriam faciunt. Cist. I. 3. v. 32. Ergo stuprum injuria est.
units.tr: Those who consort with a free girl do her an injury. Cist. 1. 3. v. 32. Therefore seduction is an injury.

units.la: Pudicas se autumabant, quni tantum morem gerebant. Most. I. 3. v. 43.
units.tr: They claimed to be chaste women, since they only humoured their men. Most. 1. 3. v. 43.

units.la: Lenae malesuadae, stimulatrices, corruptrices puellarum, vitilenae, venefícae dictae. Most. I. 3. v. 56.
units.tr: Procuresses were called bad advisers, instigators, corrupters of girls, vile procuresses, poisoners. Most. 1. 3. v. 56.

units.la: In hominem lascivum & μαλακὸν congruit illud Mil. 4. 1. v. 18. Nam ta quidem Ad equas fuisti scitus admissarius, Qui confectlare quà mares, quà feminas.
units.tr: That line fits a lewd and soft [μαλακὸν] man: Mil. 4. 1. v. 18. "For you were indeed a clever stallion sent to the mares, one who has his way with both males and females."

units.la: Divortunt mores virgini longè, ac lupæ. h. e. Multum inter-est inter virginem & lupam. Epid. 3. 3. v. 22.
units.tr: Manners of a virgin differ far from those of a she-wolf, i.e. "There is a great difference between a virgin and a she-wolf." Epid. 3. 3. v. 22.

units.la: Non nimis potest pudicitiam quisquam suæ servare filiæ. Epid. 3. 3. v. 24.
units.tr: No one can keep his daughter's chastity too closely. Epid. 3. 3. v. 24.

units.la: Ornamentis vestiarijs mirum quantum inescantur lenæ, & meretrices. Mil. 2. 1. v. 29.
units.tr: Procuresses and harlots are wondrously enticed by clothes and ornaments. Mil. 2. 1. v. 29.

units.la: Meretrices ex quæstu sui corporis sibi dotem quærebant: præsertim Tuscorum filiæ. Cist. 2. 3. v. 20. Curc. 4. 1. v. 21.
units.tr: Harlots sought a dowry for themselves from the profit of their bodies, especially the daughters of the Tuscans. Cist. 2. 3. v. 20. Curc. 4. 1. v. 21.

units.la: Meretrices ἀλληγορικῶς & sc, & suum quæstum comparant rei nauticæ. Asin. 3. 1. v. 16. Elegantèr, sed tamen improbè, inquit Philenium: Quin pol si repositvi remunt, sola ego in cisterna, ubi quiesco omnu familia cassa confissit tibi.
units.tr: Harlots, allegorically [ἀλληγορικῶς], also liken their profit to seafaring. Asin. 3. 1. v. 16. Philaenium says this elegantly but still shamelessly: "Indeed, by Pollux, if the oars are put back, I alone, in the cistern where I rest, will sink, with my whole household wrecked, for you."

units.la: Idem mihi, magnæ quod partiest vitium mulieɼum, Quæ hunc quæstum facimus: quæ ubi saburrata sumus, Largiloquæ extemplò sumus, plus loquimur, quàm sat est. Cist. 1. 2. v. 1. 2. 3. & seqq.
units.tr: The same is true for me, the great fault of women who practise this trade: when we are loaded with ballast we at once become talkative; we say more than is enough. Cist. 1. 2. v. 1, 2, 3 and following.

units.la: Mala nulla est meretrix: pejora ibus conveniunt, hoc est, plus est, quàm mala, nempe pejor, immò pessima. Mil. 3. 3. v. 21.
units.tr: No harlot is bad; the worse words suit them, that is, she is more than bad, indeed she is worse, indeed the worst. Mil. 3. 3. v. 21.

units.la: Sine Cerere & Baccho friget Venus. Bacch. 4. 10. v. 6.
units.tr: Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold. Bacch. 4. 10. v. 6.

units.la: Mulier mala holitori numquam supplicat, si domi habeat hortum. ἀλληγορικῶς. Mil. 2. 2. v. 38.
units.tr: A bad woman never begs the gardener, if she has a garden at home. Allegorically [ἀλληγορικῶς]. Mil. 2. 2. v. 38.

units.la: Meretrices infantem ex stupro natum, expositerunt ad necem, si authorem certum nescirent. Cist. 1. 3. v. 18.
units.tr: Harlots exposed to death an infant born of seduction, if they did not know the certain father. Cist. 1. 3. v. 18.

units.la: Meretrices sunt elecebræ argentariæ. Men. 2. 3. v. 26. 33. Truc. 1. 2. v. 8t. Vide paulò ante multa loca in hanc rem.
units.tr: Harlots are the lures of the money-changers. Men. 2. 3. v. 26, 33. Truc. 1. 2. v. 81. See a little earlier for many passages on this matter.

units.la: Post rem sequitur conceptio. Perf. 4. 4. v. 18. Cum optimis arris rem habebis, gratiam concipient tuam. ἀλληγορικῶς.
units.tr: After the deed follows conception. Perf. 4. 4. v. 18. "You will have intercourse with the best of pledges; they will conceive your favour." Allegorically [ἀλληγορικῶς].

units.la: In re venereâ liberos sibi quærentes, alius alium scandere dicitur. IMPURI nefandà Venere usi alijs pro culcitellâ. Mos. 4. 2. v. 14. Perf. 1. 3. v. 52. MERETRICES apud lenones etiam vino dedita fuerunt. Pseud. 12. v. 50.
units.tr: In sexual intercourse, those seeking children for themselves are said to mount one another. The impure, using unspeakable lust, use others as a pillow. Mos. 4. 2. v. 14. Perf. 1. 3. v. 52. Harlots among the procurers were also given to wine. Pseud. 12. v. 50.

units.la: MERETRICES libertatem affectabant. Perf. 4. 4. v. 107. Idque faciebant sæpe subeundo legem patientiæ multebris, unde summulam pecuniæ corradebant, quâ se in libertatem vindicabant.
units.tr: Harlots aspired to freedom. Perf. 4. 4. v. 107. They did this often by submitting to the law of endurance in many things, from which they scraped together a little sum of money with which they bought their freedom.

units.la: IN sacris nefas fuit attrectare puellas. Pæn. 1. 2. v. 137. Vide Tit. Religionis.
units.tr: In sacred rites it was wrong to touch girls. Poen. 1. 2. v. 137. See the title Religion.

units.la: SOROREM violare nefas. Unde ille Curc. 1. 1. v. 51. Tamâme putaret, quasi soror mea sit.
units.tr: To violate a sister is wrong. Hence that line in Curc. 1. 1. v. 51: "So that he would think her as if she were my sister."

units.la: NON matronarum officium, sed meretricium, viris alienis sub-blandirier. Caf. 3. 3. v. 22. MERETRICES sunt malæ bestiæ, κακὰ θηρία. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 21.
units.tr: It is not the duty of matrons but of harlots to flatter other men. Caf. 3. 3. v. 22. Harlots are evil beasts [κακὰ θηρία]. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 21.

units.la: MERETRICES sectabantur milites magno numero. Epid. 2. 2. v. 29. MERETRICES damnosæ sunt adolescentibus. Cist. 1. 1. v. 52.
units.tr: Harlots pursued soldiers in great numbers. Epid. 2. 2. v. 29. Harlots are ruinous to young men. Cist. 1. 1. v. 52.

units.la: MERETRICES damnum sunt, quà juvenum, quà senum. Men. 1. 2. v. 42.
units.tr: Harlots are a loss, both of young men and of old. Men. 1. 2. v. 42.

units.la: MERETRICES canes alebant, quibus nova nomini indebant. Epid. 2. 2. v. 50.
units.tr: Harlots used to keep dogs, to which they gave new names. Epid. 2. 2. v. 50.

units.la: MERETRICES vulgò suum corpus publicant. Bacch. 4 8. v. 22.
units.tr: Harlots commonly expose their bodies to the public. Bacch. 4. 8. v. 22.

units.la: MERETRICES acerbè ac æstuosè absorbent vivos, instar maris. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 67.
units.tr: Harlots bitterly and greedily swallow men alive, like the sea. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 67.

units.la: ARGENTARII alebant pueros catamitos usurarios. Curc. 3. 1. v. 12. SCORTATIO exebrietate sæpe evenit. Aul. 4. 10. v. 8. MÆCHI UNGUENTATI erant, Mil. 3. 3. v. 50.
units.tr: Money-changers used to keep boys as catamites and as usurers. Curc. 3. 1. v. 12. Whoring often comes from drunkenness. Aul. 4. 10. v. 8. Adulterers were anointed with perfume. Mil. 3. 3. v. 50.

units.la: MERETRICUM mos est fallere, mentiri, Men. 5. 5. v. 8.
units.tr: It is the custom of harlots to deceive and to lie. Men. 5. 5. v. 8.

units.la: Meretrices usi aquarijs, amorum internuntijs. Pœn. 1. 2. v. 14. Vide Tit. Aquariorum.
units.tr: Harlots made use of go-betweens, the messengers of love. Poen. 1. 2. v. 14. See the title Go-betweens.

units.la: Meretriculæ sunt elecebræ adolescentum: quæ etiam lapidem silicem subigere possunt, ut se amet. Pœnol. 1. 2. v. 77. & Truc. 4. 2. v. 46. Vide paulò ante.
units.tr: Little harlots are the lures of young men; they can even soften a flint stone so that it loves them. Poenul. 1. 2. v. 77 and Truc. 4. 2. v. 46. See a little earlier.

units.la: Meretrix nihil eorum, quæ accepit, reddit: velut Acheruns. Truc. 4. 2. v. 36.
units.tr: A harlot gives back none of what she has received, like Acheron. Truc. 4. 2. v. 36.

units.la: Meretrices amatores suos labijs ductare solent. Mil. 2. 1. v. 16.
units.tr: Harlots are wont to lead their lovers on with their lips. Mil. 2. 1. v. 16.

units.la: Qui scortatuntur, malam rem merent: & tenentur lege constitutâ in corruptores virginum. Cist. 1. 3. v. 12.
units.tr: Those who consort with harlots deserve a bad fate, and are bound by the law established against corrupters of virgins. Cist. 1. 3. v. 12.

units.la: Apud lenones rivales filijs fiebant patres. Bacch. Grec. v. 4. In hanc rem memorabilis est illa inscriptio Romana apud Gruter. Pag. DCCLXXXIX. 6. Semicapri. Quicumque. Subis. Sacraria. Fauni. Hæc lege. Romana. Verba. Notata. Manu. Hersilus. Hic. Jaceo. Mecum. Marcella. Quiescit. Quæ. Soror. Et. Genitrix. Quæ. Mihi. Sponsa. Fuit. Vera. Negas. Frontemque. Trahis? Ænigmata. Sphingis. Credis? Sunt. Pythio. Vera. Magis. Tripode. Me. Pater. Et. Nata. Genuit. Mihi. Jungitur. Illa. Sic. Soror. Et. Coniunx. Sic. Fuit. Illa. Parens.
units.tr: Among procurers, rivals became fathers to their sons. Bacch. Greek v. 4. Worth remembering in this connection is that Roman inscription in Gruter, p. DCCLXXXIX, no. 6: "Half-goat, whoever you are, satyr, fauns, sacred places: read these Roman words, written by the hand of Hersilus. Here I lie with Marcella, who rests with me; she was my sister and mother, who was my bride. Do you deny it and frown? Do you think these are riddles of the Sphinx? They are truer than the Pythian tripod: a father and his daughter begot me, and she is joined to me; thus she was sister and wife, thus she was mother."

units.la: Ita quidem edidit Smetius: paulò aliter Gruterus. Cicero pro Cluent. Uxor generi, noverea filij, filiæ pellex. Sic Jocasta ejusdem uxor & mater Senec. Oedip. act. 5. telam utero infigens, exclamat: — hunc dextra, hunc pete
units.tr: Smetius has printed it thus, but Gruter a little differently. Cicero, Pro Cluentio: a wife to her son-in-law, a stepmother to her son, a concubine to her daughter. So Jocasta, the same man's wife and mother, in Seneca's Oedipus, act 5, driving the spindle into her womb, cries out:

units.la: Uterum capacem, qui virum, & gnatum tulit.
units.tr: The womb that bore both husband and son, a capacious one.

units.la: Et Thebaide act. 1.
units.tr: And in the Thebaid, act 1:

units.la: Avi generperatrü, patrisq; rivalis sui: Frater suorum liberum, & fratrum parens: Uno avia partu liberos peperit viro, Ac sibi nepotes: Monstra quis tanta explicet?
units.tr: Grandson-in-law, father, and rival of her own: sister of her children and parent of her brothers. With one birth the grandmother bore children to her husband and grandchildren to herself. Who could explain such monsters?

units.la: Meretrices nihil bene consulunt. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 6.
units.tr: Prostitutes give no good advice. Bacchides 1.1, v. 6.

units.la: Lenonibus nihil est, nisi una lingua, qui abjurant, si quid creditum est. Curc. 4. 2. v. 10. & seqq.
units.tr: Pimps have nothing but a tongue, and they deny whatever has been entrusted to them. Curculio 4.2, v. 10 and following.

units.la: Ibidem sic describit Lenonias virtutes:
units.tr: In the same play he describes the virtues of pimps thus:

units.la: — alienos mancupatis, Alienos manumititis, alienisq; imperatis. Nec vobis author ullus est, nec vosmet testesulli. Item genus est lenonium, inter homines, meo quidem animo, Uti muscas, calices, pedesq; pulices q. Odio & malo, & molestiae bono usui est iis nulli. Nec vobiscum quisquam in foro frugi consistere audet. Qui consistit, conspuitur, vituperatur, Eum rem fidemq; perdere, tametsi nihil facit, ajunt.
units.tr: You buy up other people's goods, you manumit other people's slaves, and you give orders with other people's property. No one vouches for you, and you yourselves call no witnesses. There is a race of pimps among men, in my opinion, like flies, gnats, and fleas: they are of no use to anyone except as a nuisance and a plague. No one dares to stand honestly with you in the forum. Whoever stands there is spat upon and reviled, and they say he loses his property and reputation, even though he has done nothing.

units.la: Lenonum adjuncta varia fuerunt ob mores & disciplinam planè sceleratam. Perf. 3. 3. v. 2. Lutum lenonium, commissum canum, sterquilinium publicum: Impure, inhonestè, injure, illex, labes populi, pecuniarum accipiter, avide, atq; invide, procax, rapax, trahax: trecentis versibus tuas impuritas tuas loqui nemo potest.
units.tr: Pimps had various attachments because of their manners and a thoroughly wicked way of life. Persa 3.3, v. 2: A pimp's mud, a dog's refuse, the public dunghill. Impure, dishonourable, unjust, a lure, the ruin of the people, a hawk for money, greedy, envious, bold, rapacious, grasping: no one could tell of your impurities in three hundred verses.

units.la: Lenones circum forum ad argentarias tabernas versabantur, ubi homines nauci. Truc. 1. 1. v. 48.
units.tr: Pimps hung about the forum by the money-changers' shops, where men are worth nothing. Truculentus 1.1, v. 48.

units.la: Lenones inhiabant aliorum pecunijs. Poen. 3. 3. v. 57. Rex sum, si ego illum cum trecentis numis Philippeis ad me illexero.
units.tr: Poenulus 3.3, v. 57: I am a king if I can lure that man to me with three hundred Philippic coins. Pimps were greedy for other people's money.

units.la: Lenones solebanr in Comœdijs à pueris convitijs excipi. Pseud. 4. 6. v. 19. Nugae theatri: verba quae in Comœdijs solent lenoni dici, quae pueri sciunt.
units.tr: Pseudolus 4.6, v. 19: Theatrical trifles, the words that are usually said to a pimp in comedies, which boys know. Pimps were customarily greeted with insults from boys in the comedies.

units.la: LENONES perjuri. Rud. 5. 2. v. 68. Meum arbitratus est, lingua quod juret mea. Et Rud. 5. 3. v. 5. Si quidem hercle Jovis fuit hic vidulus, Jovis est tamen. Et ibid. v. 17. Juratus sum; & nunc ju-rabo, si quid voluptati est mihi.
units.tr: PIMPS are perjurers. Rudens 5.2, v. 68: He thought my tongue was his own, so it swears. And Rudens 5.3, v. 5: Even if this little chest was Jupiter's, it is still Jupiter's. And ibid., v. 17: I have sworn, and now I will swear again, if it gives me any pleasure.

units.la: LENONES ex gaudio procreati. Ita omnes mortales, si quid est mali lenoni, gaudent. Rud. 5. 1. v. 4.
units.tr: PIMPS are born of joy. Thus all mortals rejoice at whatever misfortune befalls a pimp. Rudens 5.1, v. 4.

units.la: NULLUM genus hominum Reip. nocentius, quàm lenones. Poen. 4. 2. v. 7. Quid illuc est genus? Quæ illic hominum corruptela siunt? Quodvis genus ibi hominum videas, quasi Acheruntem ve-neris. Vide totum locum graphicè depingentem disciplinam le-nonìam.
units.tr: NO class of men is more harmful to the state than pimps. Poenulus 4.2, v. 7: What sort of class is that? What corruption of men is there? You would see every kind of man there, as if you had come to Acheron. See the whole passage, which vividly depicts the pimp's way of life.

units.la: LENONUM genus salacissimum. Pers. 4. 8. v. 7. Jam inclinabo me cum libertatuâ. Vide Senec. Controv. 2. lib. 1. Et ibi Gruteri Notas: ut & ejusdem Suspiciones.
units.tr: The pimp class is most lecherous. Persa 4.8, v. 7: Now I shall turn myself over to freedom. See Seneca, Controversiae 2, book 1, and there Gruter's notes, as well as his own Suspiciones.

units.la: IN lenonìa familiâ lautius curari solebant pueri: qui amatores inve-nirent, in domini quastum. Id est, quod queritur puer lenonum. Pseud. 3. 1. v. 8.
units.tr: In a pimp's household boys were kept more luxuriously, so that they might find lovers for the master's profit. That is, what the pimp's boy complains of. Pseudolus 3.1, v. 8.

units.la: NATUM quantum est hominum sacrilegissimi lenones. Rud. 3. 4. v. 1. & 4. Legirupio.
units.tr: How terribly sacrilegious pimps are as a class! Rudens 3.4, vv. 1 and 4: a law-breaker.

units.la: PALLIA varij coloris tribuebantur lenonibus: ut notat Dona-tus in Terent. Inde Pseud. 4. 2. v. 23. Ut vestitus est, perfossor pa-rietum. Inducebantur etiam quandoq; raso capite: & calvi. E-rant enim ἀναφαλαντρίαι ἢ ψαλακροί, ut ait Pollux: ꝭ notat Turn. l. 29. c. 36. Advers.
units.tr: Pimps were given cloaks of various colours, as Donatus notes on Terence. Hence Pseudolus 4.2, v. 23: As he is dressed, a wall-breaker. They were also sometimes brought in with shaved heads, and bald. For they were [ἀναφαλαντρίαι ἢ ψαλακροί], bald men, as Pollux says; Turnebus notes this, book 29, chapter 36, Adversaria.

units.la: LENÆ comparantur portitoribus. Asin. 1. 3. v. 7. Quemadmo-dum portitores travehunt vectores à littore in littus p medium mare: ita lenæ trajiciunt amantes à limine domus meretriciæ ad Egestatem per domum & consuetudinem meretriciam.
units.tr: Pimps are compared to ferrymen. Asinaria 1.3, v. 7: Just as ferrymen carry passengers from shore to shore across the middle of the sea, so pimps ferry lovers from the threshold of the brothel to Poverty, through the house and the habits of the brothel.

units.la: NUMQUAM fictum, neque pictum, neque scriptum est in poë-matis, ubi Lena bene agat cum quiquam amante, quæ frugi esse volt. Asin. 1. 3. 23.
units.tr: Never has it been invented, painted, or written in poems that a pimp behaves well toward any lover, if she wishes to be honest. Asinaria 1.3, v. 23.

units.la: LENONUM ac servorum lenoniorum ex re ipsâ hæc nomina assi-cta: Vaniloquidorum, virginis-vendonides, nugidololoquides, ar-genti genti exterebronides, tedigniloquides, nummorum expalponi- des. Quod semel arripides, numquam postea cripides. Perf. 4. 6. v. 20.
units.tr: Names of pimps and of slaves belonging to pimps, taken from the actual business: Windbag-ides, virgin-sellers, prattle-ides, silver-scrapers, tedious-talkers, money-pilferers. Those who snatch things once never afterwards give them back. Persa 4.6, v. 20.

units.la: OMNES sunt Lenæ levisidæ: neque tipulæ levius pondus est, quàm fidei lenoniæ. Perf. 2. 2. v. 61.
units.tr: All pimps are light as feathers: a gnat weighs no less than the good faith of a pimp. Persa 2.2, v. 61.

units.la: LENONES vix homines censendi. Pœn. Prol. v. 89. Leno, si est homo, quantum hominum terra sustinet facerrimus.
units.tr: Pimps are scarcely to be counted as men. Poenulus, Prologue, v. 89: A pimp, if he is a man, is the most worthless creature the earth supports.

units.la: MERETRICES omnem suam rem æstimant quæstu. Qui plus dat, potior est. Turc. 1. 1. v. 62. Elegantes isti sunt versiculi, qui de hac lenonia natione circumferuntur: Mulier melle mollior: Et quò nitentior: eò nocentior, Quæ dum te fovet, sibi favet. Et dum videt, rodit, ac radit. Quæ corpus carpit, & aurum haurit: Idq; latenter ac latentor: Non virgo, nec virago, sed vorago, Quæ viros vorat, & amando mandit.
units.tr: Prostitutes value all their business by profit: whoever gives more has the better claim. Truculentus 1.1, v. 62. These are the elegant little verses that circulate about this race of pimps: a woman softer than honey; and the more brilliant she is, the more harmful; while she cherishes you, she cherishes herself; and while she looks at you, she gnaws and scrapes you. She devours your body and drains your gold, and does so secretly, and more secretly still: not a virgin, nor a warrior-woman, but a whirlpool, who swallows men and chews them up by loving them.

units.la: LENONES homines erant molles: qui μαλακὸς quoque curabant corpus suum: utentes hisce instrumentis: Volsellis, calamistro, pectine, speculo, exicià, linteis: de quibus vide Lexicon Plautinum. Curc. 4. 4. v. 21.
units.tr: Pimps were effeminate men who took care of their bodies with soft ways, using these instruments: tweezers, curling-iron, comb, mirror, sandals, linen cloths. On these see the Plautine Lexicon. Curculio 4.4, v. 21.

units.la: LENONUM indoles graphicè describitur in convitiis servi. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 125. & seqq.
units.tr: The character of pimps is vividly described in a slave's insults. Pseudolus 1.3, v. 125 and following.

units.la: OMNES lenones iniqui. Curc. 1. 1. v. 66.
units.tr: All pimps are unjust. Curculio 1.1, v. 66.

units.la: LENONES instructi erant ςωμάτι olei ob amatores. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 77.
units.tr: Pimps were supplied with oil for the body [σώματι], on account of their lovers. Pseudolus 1.2, v. 77.

units.la: LENONES importuni, perfidi, injusti in amatores. Merc. Prol. v. 44. 47.
units.tr: Pimps are troublesome, faithless, and unjust toward their lovers. Mercator, Prologue, vv. 44, 47.

units.la: LENONES ab amatoribus pro Jove habiti. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 93.
units.tr: Pimps were regarded by their lovers as Jove. Pseudolus 1.3, v. 93.

units.la: LENONES non nisi pecuniâ placari poterant. Ibid. v. 94.
units.tr: Pimps could be appeased only with money. Ibid., v. 94.

units.la: LENO Deos parvipendit: fraudis, sceleris, parricidij plenissimus, legilegirupa impudens, impurus, invercundissimus: uno verbo absolvam, Leno. Rud. 3. 2. v. 37.
units.tr: The pimp despises the gods: he is full of fraud, wickedness, and murder, shameless in law-breaking, impure, most shameless. In one word, I shall sum him up: Pimp. Rudens 3.2, v. 37.

units.la: Lenones pestis populi. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 70.
units.tr: Pimps are a plague upon the people. Pseudolus 1.2, v. 70.

units.la: Lenones nihilominus adolescentibus in delitijs, & amore. Pseu. 1. 2. v. 72.
units.tr: Pimps nonetheless take delight in young men and in love. Pseudolus 1.2, v. 72.

units.la: Lenones ob rapacitatem, dictifeles virginarie. Pers. 4. 9. v. 14. & Rud. 3. 4. v. 42.
units.tr: Pimps, out of greed, are virgin-sellers. Persa 4.9, v. 14, and Rudens 3.4, v. 42.

units.la: Lenones alebant meretriculas suas ex muneribus amatorum: ac vestes etiam comparabant ex eodem quaestu: imo totum victum annuum. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 48. 49. Lege etiam seqq. versus.
units.tr: Pimps fed their little prostitutes from the gifts of lovers, and bought clothes from the same profit, indeed their whole yearly livelihood. Pseudolus 1.2, vv. 48, 49. Read also the following verses.

units.la: Probrosum erat ad lenones abire in lupanaria: ideoque eos operto capite adibant. Capt. 3. 1. v. 15.
units.tr: It was disgraceful to go to pimps in the brothels, and so they approached them with their heads covered. Captivi 3.1, v. 15.

units.la: Etiam per internuncios & sequestros appellabantur lenones. Ibi. Quod & patet ex Asinariae Diabolo: & Phadromo Curculionis.
units.tr: Pimps were also called upon through go-betweens and agents. Ibid. This is also clear from the Devil of the Asinaria and from Phaedromus in the Curculio.

units.la: Generi lenonio numquam ullus Deus tam benignus fuit, qui fuerit propitius. Pers. 4. 4. v. 34.
units.tr: No god was ever so kind to the pimp class as to be gracious to it. Persa 4.4, v. 34.

units.la: Lenonum fidem flocci non faciunt: sed perjuri sunt. Rud. Prol. v. 47.
units.tr: Pimps do not care a straw for their word, but are perjurers. Rudens, Prologue, v. 47.

units.la: Lenones Veneri vota solvebant in fano Veneris. Rud. Prol. v. 61. 61.
units.tr: Pimps paid their vows to Venus in Venus's temple. Rudens, Prologue, vv. 61, 61.

units.la: Familia lenonis nauci homines educat. Pers. 2. 2. v. 31.
units.tr: A pimp's household rears men who are worth nothing. Persa 2.2, v. 31.

units.la: Lenones & Deos & homines decipiunt. Rud. 2. 3. v. 16.
units.tr: Pimps deceive both gods and men. Rudens 2.3, v. 16.

units.la: Non lutum est lutulentius lenone. Poen. 1. 1. v. 30. & 4 2. v. 4. Homo lutetus: & cano collitus.
units.tr: Nothing is more muddy than a pimp. Poenulus 1.1, v. 30, and 4.2, v. 4: A muddy man, smeared with grey filth.

units.la: Lenones lupi: & fures auri sunt. Poen. 5. 5. v. 55.
units.tr: Pimps are wolves, and thieves of gold. Poenulus 5.5, v. 55.

units.la: Lenones impuri & avari sunt, lucrifici. Pers. 4. 6. v. 5.
units.tr: Pimps are impure and greedy, profit-hunters. Persa 4.6, v. 5.

units.la: ÆDILIUM.
units.tr: ÆDILIUM.

units.la: Vide Magistratus.
units.tr: See Magistratus.

units.la: ÆDIUM. ÆDIFICIORUM. DOMUS. FORIUM; OSTII.
units.tr: OF HOUSES, OF BUILDINGS, OF THE HOUSE; OF DOORS AND THE DOORWAY.

units.la: IN ædibus tintinnabula erant. Trin. 4. 2. v. 62.
units.tr: Inside the house there were bells. Trin. 4. 2. v. 62.

units.la: MULIERCULÆ fallendis maritis ad januæ cardines aquam affundebant, ne streperent. Curc. 1. 3. v. 3.
units.tr: Wives, to deceive their husbands, poured water on the hinges of the door so that they would not creak. Curc. 1. 3. v. 3.

units.la: IN Græciâ omnes omnium ædium fores non introrsum trahendo, sed in viam publicam pellendo trahebantur: quoniam autem periculum erat, ne quispiam, qui aut præteriret, aut pro foribus staret, ab impulsâ januâ pellieretur, ideo qui exituri erant domo, folebant prius ipsimet intrinsecus aut fores ædium suarum percutere; aut crepitu digitorum indicium facere: ut illo strepitu admonerentur, qui foris erant, caverent sibi, atque ea nus absistere, ut ne lœderentur. Hinc factum, ut in Plautiac Terentij fabulis numquam fere quisquam egrederetur, ut non antea FORES CREPUISSE dicerentur. Ita Græci habent suum Ἰσχύς & κόπτειν, quorum illud est exeuntium, hoc ingredientium. Hunc morem διαψόφησιν exponit his verbis Helladius Besantinus in Bibliothecâ Photij Pag. 547. Edit. Lat. Schotti: Græc. p.857. Ideo, inquit, apud Comicos pulsant fores, quia non, ut apud nos nunc, ostia olim aperiebantur interius, sed adversò modo. Foras enim trudentes exibant, manu pulsantes prius, ut audirent, si qui ad fores essent, & caverent, ne incsci lederentur, foribus repente in viam protrusis. Loxiam enim (Apollinem) adorabant, quem pro foribus singuli ponebant. Præterea aram ibi rotundam collocabant, & myrteis coronabant, cui prætereuntes adstabant, aram autem illam ἀγυιὰν λοξίαν viam obliquam vocarunt, hoc Deinomen aræ tribuentes. At ἀγυιὰς apud Hesiodum significat Deis
units.tr: In Greece the doors of all houses were not drawn inward but pushed outward into the public street. Because there was a danger that someone passing by, or standing before the door, might be struck by a door swung open, those who were about to go out of the house would first knock on their own doors from the inside, or make a sign by snapping their fingers, so that those outside would be warned by the noise, take care, and stand back so as not to be hurt. Hence in the comedies of Plautus and Terence almost no one ever came out without the doors first being said to have creaked. So the Greeks have their ischys [Ἰσχύς] and koptein [κόπτειν], of which the former belongs to those going out and the latter to those coming in. Helladius of Byzantium, in the Bibliotheca of Photius, p. 547 of the Latin edition of Schott (Greek p. 857), explains this custom (diapsophesin [διαψόφησιν]) in these words: For this reason, he says, the comic poets knock on doors, because formerly doors were not opened inward as they are now with us, but in the opposite way. For people went out pushing them outward, knocking first with their hands so that they might hear if anyone was at the doors, and take care not to be hurt when the doors were suddenly thrust out into the street. For they worshipped Loxias (Apollo), whom each man placed before his door. Moreover, they set up there a round altar and crowned it with myrtle, beside which passers-by stood; and they called that altar agyian loxian [ἀγυιὰν λοξίαν], the oblique way, giving this name to the altar. But agyias [ἀγυιὰς] in Hesiod means to sacrifice to the gods.

units.la: Deis sacrificare. Eundem notat Plutarchus in Popliçola. Scholiast. in Nubibus Aristophanis, & Euripid. in Oresiem pag. 129. Muretus libr. 1. Var. lect. cap. 17. Turneb. Adversf. libr. 11. cap. 15. Quamquam Fridericus Lindebruch existimat, publicas tantum Ædes, vel Nobilium ita ædificatas fuisse, ut in publicum aperirentur: & conjecturam facit ex Aristot lib.2.c.2.Oecon. At verò omnia loca Comicorum repugnant. Quæ huc ex Plauto & Terentio coacervanda. Plauti quidem hæc sunt: Amph. 1. 2. v.34. Aul. 4.5. v.5. Cas 2.1. v. 15. & 4.3. v.15. Curc 4.1.v.2.5. Bacch. 2.2. v.6. Most. 2.2. v.47. & 5.1. v.14. Men. 2.2. v.73 & 3.2. v.57. Mil. 2.1. v.76. & 2.2. v.115. & 2.4. v.56. & 48. v.67. Pseud. 1.1. v.128. Poen. 3.2. v.34. Perf 3.2. v.5.
units.tr: Plutarch in the Life of Publicola, the scholiast on Aristophanes' Clouds, and Euripides in Orestes, p. 129, mention the same custom. Muretus, Var. lect. book 1, ch. 17, and Turnebus, Adversaria book 11, ch. 15, also do. Although Friedrich Lindebruch thinks that only public buildings, or those of nobles, were built so that they opened outward to the public, and bases this guess on Aristotle, Oeconomica book 2, ch. 2, all the passages of the comic poets are against him. From Plautus the following should be gathered here: Amph. 1. 2. v. 34; Aul. 4. 5. v. 5; Cas. 2. 1. v. 15 and 4. 3. v. 15; Curc. 4. 1. v. 25; Bacch. 2. 2. v. 6; Most. 2. 2. v. 47 and 5. 1. v. 14; Men. 2. 2. v. 73 and 3. 2. v. 57; Mil. 2. 1. v. 76, 2. 2. v. 115, 2. 4. v. 56 and 48. v. 67; Pseud. 1. 1. v. 128; Poen. 3. 2. v. 34; Pers. 3. 2. v. 5.

units.la: Loca ex Terentio vide in Electis Terentianis: quæ scorsim dabimus.
units.tr: For passages from Terence see the Electa Terentiana, which we shall give separately.

units.la: Ædificium emturi, illud prius inspicicbant. Most. 3. 2. v. 67.
units.tr: Those about to buy a building first inspected it. Most. 3. 2. v. 67.

units.la: In ædibus ædificabant vestibulum, ambulacrũ, porticum, balneas, & Gynæceum, seu locum mulieribus destinatum, in quo textrinæ lanificioque darent operam. Most.3.2.v.69.70.135.
units.tr: In houses they built a vestibule, a walkway, a portico, baths, and a gynaeceum, that is, a room set aside for women, in which they should devote themselves to weaving and wool-working. Most. 3. 2. v. 69, 70, 135.

units.la: Architectones exemplum capere solent ab ædibus pulcrè ædificatis. Most. 1.2. v.21. & 3.2. v.76.
units.tr: Architects are accustomed to take their model from well-built houses. Most. 1. 2. v. 21 and 3. 2. v. 76.

units.la: Ædes commodæ erant, quæ umbram habebant: quæ foli non minimum essent expositæ. Most. 3.2. v. 83.
units.tr: Houses were convenient if they had shade and were not too exposed to the sun. Most. 3. 2. v. 83.

units.la: Clavi Laconica, adulterinâ intus aperiebant ædes, & forinsecus claudebant. Most. 2.1. v.57 77. Germani appellant, ein Dietc/trich). Theon: ... Aristophani dicuntur ... quòd impactæ claustris vix apparerent. Vide Scalig.in Moretum Virgilij: & Isaac. Casaub. Animadv. ad Athenæum. lib.7. cap. 14.
units.tr: With Laconian keys, which were called "adulterine" keys, they opened houses from inside and locked them from outside. Most. 2. 1. v. 57, 77. The Germans call it ein Dietrich. Theon: ... are said by Aristophanes ... because, when pushed into the lock, they could hardly be seen. See Scaliger on the Moretum of Virgil, and Isaac Casaubon, Animadversions on Athenaeus, book 7, ch. 14.

units.la: Ædes vendituti proscribebant bonas, probas, pulchréque ædificatas esse. Merc. 5.2. v. 59. Sic Cicero lib. 3. offic. Quod si qui proscribunt Villam bonam beneque ædifica-tam, non existimantur fefellisse, etiamsi illa nec bona esset, nec ædificata ficata ratione. Cato: Patremfamilia villam rusticam BENE ÆDIFICATAM habere expedit.
units.tr: Those selling houses advertised them as good, sound, and handsomely built. Merc. 5. 2. v. 59. So Cicero, De Officiis book 3: But if those who advertise a farm as good and well built are not thought to have deceived, even if it was neither good nor well built. Cato: It is advantageous for the head of the household to have a rustic farm WELL BUILT.

units.la: In introitu domus mordax canis erat: eoque limini superscriptum CAVE CAVE CANEM: qui catenarius canis dicitur Senecæ lib.3.c.37. de Irâ. Mostl. 3. 2. v.165. Petronius in domo Trimalchionis: Ad sinistram intrantibus non longe ab ostiarij cella, canis ingens catenâ vinctus, in pariete erat pictus, superq; scriptum CAVE CAVE CANEM. Vide Popmam ad Varronem. Et Casaub. ad Theophrasti characteres. Turneb lib.16 c.4.
units.tr: At the entrance of the house there was a snapping dog, and therefore written over the threshold CAVE CAVE CANEM (beware, beware of the dog). This is called a chained dog by Seneca, On Anger, book 3, ch. 37. Most. 3. 2. v. 165. Petronius, in the house of Trimalchio: To those entering on the left, not far from the porter's room, was painted on the wall a huge dog bound with a chain, and above it was written CAVE CAVE CANEM. See Pomp on Varro, Casaubon on the Characters of Theophrastus, and Turnebus book 16, ch. 4.

units.la: Ad ostium ædium sedebant ostiarij seu janitores in catenâ cum cane ferreo: & alio oblatratore, quasi vicario. Quò alluditur Trin. 4.2. v.28. Truc. 2.4.v.1. Num tibi janua est mordax, quò introire metuas? Poëta vet": Janitoris tintinire impedimenta audio. Et vetus est inscriptio ostiorum apud Petronium (ut modò dictû) CAVE CAVE CANEM. Quo loco videndi interpretes ex Editione Goldastiana. Item P. Faber lib.2. Semestr. cap.2. Casaub. ad Suet. Vitell. c.16. Grut. & Lipsius ad Senec. lib.3. de Irâ. c.37.
units.tr: At the door of the house sat the doorkeepers or janitors, chained, with an iron dog and another barking dog as a deputy. This alludes to Trin. 4. 2. v. 28; Truc. 2. 4. v. 1: Is there a snapping door for you, that you fear to go in? An old poet: I hear the rattling of the janitor's chains. And there is an old inscription on doors in Petronius (as just said): CAVE CAVE CANEM. On this passage see the commentators in the Goldast edition; likewise P. Faber, Semestria book 2, ch. 2; Casaubon on Suetonius, Vitellius ch. 16; Gruter and Lipsius on Seneca, On Anger book 3, ch. 37.

units.la: Veteres Romani studiosè fores suas ornarunt sigillis Deorum, vel fictilibus, vel æneis, vel inauratis: imò etiam bullis. Asin. 2.4.v.20. quas servi mundare cogebantur. Vide Scalig. Festum in Antefixa Inde Perf. bullatas nugas vocat. Et Petronius bullatos clavos.
units.tr: The old Romans carefully adorned their doors with images of the gods, whether of clay, bronze, or gilded; indeed even with bullae. Asin. 2. 4. v. 20, which slaves were forced to clean. See Scaliger on Festus under Antefixa. Hence Persius calls them bullatas nugas (bulla-adorned trifles), and Petronius bullatos clavos (bulla-adorned nails).

units.la: Humum ædium conspergebant floribus: ut sic omnia, & munda, & fragrantia essent. Stich. 2.3.v.29.
units.tr: They sprinkled the floor of the house with flowers, so that everything would be clean and fragrant. Stich. 2. 3. v. 29.

units.la: Lectos item discubitorios diligenter sternebant pro hospitibus. Ibid. v.32. Vide Triclinij.
units.tr: Likewise they carefully made up dining couches for guests. Ibid. v. 32. See Triclinium.

units.la: Qui domum in perpetuum deferere animati erant, limina solebant salutare. Romani enim liminibus & postibus aliquid religionis tribuebant. Merc. 5.1.v.1. Vide Turneb.lib.26.23. & lib.12.c.5.
units.tr: Those who were resolved to leave the house forever used to kiss the threshold, for the Romans attributed a certain sacredness to thresholds and doorposts. Merc. 5. 1. v. 1. See Turnebus book 26, ch. 23, and book 12, ch. 5.

units.la: Deos etiam Penates invocabant: & rem suam mandabant. Ib.
units.tr: They also invoked the household gods (Penates) and entrusted their property to them. Ib.

units.la: Interdiu januas ædium non occludebant. Mostl. 2.2.v.14.
units.tr: By day they did not lock the doors of their houses. Most. 2. 2. v. 14.

units.la: Ædes capitales monstris infestari credebant. Mostl. 2.2.v.73.
units.tr: They believed that houses were haunted by monsters. Most. 2. 2. v. 73.

units.la: In medio ædium locus erat, qui impluvium dicebatur, unde & lucetra & plurium excipiebant. Mil. 2. 2. v. 4.
units.tr: In the middle of the house there was a place called the impluvium, through which they also received light and rain. Mil. 2. 2. v. 4.

units.la: In ædificijs alebant omnis generis animalia, gallinas, columbas, simias. Mil. 2. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: In their buildings they kept all kinds of animals: hens, pigeons, monkeys. Mil. 2. 2. v. 7.

units.la: Ubi aliquandiu ædes non inhabitassent, religionis causâ terram tangebant. Most. 2. 2. v. 37. Vide Religionis.
units.tr: When a house had not been inhabited for some time, they touched the ground for the sake of religion. Most. 2. 2. v. 37. See Religion.

units.la: Ædes capitales habebantur: in quibus capital admissum. Most. 2. 2. v. 44. 7l.
units.tr: Houses were regarded as sacred, in which a capital crime had been committed. Most. 2. 2. v. 44, 71.

units.la: Novæ ædes examussim expolitæ
units.tr: New houses, finished with the greatest precision:

units.la: 1. Laudant fabrum.
units.tr: 1. They praise the builder.

units.la: 2. Alijs sunt exemplo.
units.tr: 2. They serve as an example to others.

units.la: 3. Non admittunt hominem nequam.
units.tr: 3. They do not admit a worthless man.

units.la: 4. Volunt diligenter curari.
units.tr: 4. They want to be carefully looked after.

units.la: 5. Periculum imbrium metuunt.
units.tr: 5. They fear the danger of rain.

units.la: 6. A fidei domino restitui debent.
units.tr: 6. They ought to be restored by a faithful master.

units.la: 7. Ab indiligenti domino segniter curantur.
units.tr: 7. When the master is careless, they are neglected in a lazy way.

units.la: Vide Most. 1. 2. v. 8. & seqq.
units.tr: See Most. 1. 2. v. 8 and following.

units.la: Munditiem in ædibus diligenter curabant. Stich. 2. 3. v. 22. Munditias volo fieri: afferte huc scopas, simulq; arundinem, ut operam omnem aranearum perdam, & texturam improbem, dejiciamq; omnes earum telas.
units.tr: They kept the cleanliness of the house with great care. Stich. 2. 3. v. 22: I want cleaning done: bring brooms here, and a reed too, so that I may destroy all the work of the spiders, and undo their web, and sweep down all their cobwebs.

units.la: Idque faciebant ob metum Ædilium. Truc. 2. 7. v. 6. de Amatoribus.
units.tr: And they did this out of fear of the aediles. Truc. 2. 7. v. 6, concerning lovers.

units.la: Inprimis autem mundas curabant peregrinis adventantibus. Stich. 5. 3. v. 5. Lectu sternendis studuimus ancilla nos, mundi ijsq; apparandis.
units.tr: Above all, they kept things clean for foreign visitors arriving. Stich. 5. 3. v. 5: We have taken pains to make the beds ready and to clean and prepare them, as servants.

units.la: Claræ ædes in pretio habitæ. Most. 3. 1. v. 107.
units.tr: Bright houses were held in esteem. Most. 3. 1. v. 107.

units.la: Ædibus domesticum Deum adjunxerunt Larem: quem coronâ exornabant, in Latio è spicis & aristis: in Græciâ è platano. Eum exorabant, ut habitatio esset bona, fausta, felix, fortunataque. Trin. 1. 2. v. 1. Tibullus lib. 2. Eleg. 1. Ornatos Deos vocat.
units.tr: They joined a Lar, a household god, to their houses, which they adorned with a garland: in Latium of ears of grain and of spikes, in Greece of plane-tree leaves. They prayed to him that the dwelling might be good, prosperous, happy, and fortunate. Trin. 1. 2. v. 1. Tibullus, book 2, Elegy 1, calls them adorned gods.

units.la: Fenestris clatratis utebantur olim. Mil. 2. 4. v. 26.
units.tr: In former times they used windows with grates. Mil. 2. 4. v. 26.

units.la: ÆDES venales proscribebantur. Trin. 1. 2. v. 131. Vide Tit. Venditionis.
units.tr: Houses for sale were advertised. Trin. 1. 2. v. 131. See the title Sale.

units.la: DUO pessuli, ut duo limina, addebantur foribus. Aul. 1. 2. v. 25. βάλανοι, sive μοχλοί.
units.tr: Two bolts, like two thresholds, were added to the doors. Aul. 1. 2. v. 25: balanoi [βάλανοι], or mochloi [μοχλοί].

units.la: ÆDES cogebantur mundè-servare: ob metum Ædilium. Truc. 2. 7. v. 6. de Amatoribus.
units.tr: Houses were compelled to be kept clean, for fear of the aediles. Truc. 2.7. v. 6, of the lovers.

units.la: IN ædibus posticum erat: h. e. posterius ostium quoddam. Most. 3. 3. v. 27. Trin. 1. 2. v. 157.
units.tr: In the house there was a back door: that is, a certain second door. Most. 3.3. v. 27. Trin. 1.2. v. 157.

units.la: IN emtione ædium etiam locus observandus. Most. 3. 1. v. 139.
units.tr: In the purchase of a house the site also must be examined. Most. 3.1. v. 139.

units.la: IN ædibus habebant solarium, ubi apricabantur: itemque pone eas Hortum. Mil. 2. 3. v. 69. Most. 5. 1. v. 4. Caf. 3. 4. v. 23.
units.tr: In the houses they had a solarium, where they sunned themselves; and likewise a garden behind them. Mil. 2.3. v. 69. Most. 5.1. v. 4. Caf. 3.4. v. 23.

units.la: IN ædibus effodiebant puteos. Rud. 2. 4. v. 19.
units.tr: In the houses they dug wells. Rud. 2.4. v. 19.

units.la: DOMOS tegebant arundinibus in palude crescentibus. Rud. 1. 2. v. 34.
units.tr: They roofed houses with reeds growing in the marsh. Rud. 1.2. v. 34.

units.la: ÆDIFICANTES columnas solent suffulcire. Mil. 2. 2. v. 54. ἀληθευκῶς de homine cogitabundo.
units.tr: Builders are accustomed to prop up columns. Mil. 2.2. v. 54. ἀληθευκῶς, of a man lost in thought.

units.la: NOVIS ædibus quomodo comparetur Homo Vide Most. 1. 2. v. 8. & seqq. quos lege.
units.tr: On how a man is to be provided with new houses, see Most. 1.2. v. 8 and following, which you should read.

units.la: IN ædibus erat impluvium: quia tecta non erant decussata, sed lata. Amph. 5. 1. v. 56.
units.tr: In the house there was an impluvium, because the roofs were not latticed but flat. Amph. 5.1. v. 56.

units.la: CLAVE referebantur cubilia. Caf. 5. 2. v. 7. 47. & pessulis obdebantur. Ibid. v. 15. Et Cist. 1. 1. v. 113.
units.tr: The bedrooms were locked with a key. Caf. 5.2. v. 7, 47; and they were barred with bolts. Ibid. v. 15. And Cist. 1.1. v. 113.

units.la: AD reficiendas ædes utebantur luto. Rud. 1. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: To repair houses they used mud. Rud. 1.2. v. 7.

units.la: AERIS.
units.tr: AERIS.

units.la: AERIS. NEBULÆ.
units.tr: AIR. CLOUDS.

units.la: NEBULA mollis est. Cas. 4. 4. v. 21.
units.tr: A MIST is soft. Cas. 4. 4. v. 21.

units.la: ÆGRITUDINIS. ÆRUMNARUM. LABORIS. CURÆ. MISERIÆ. INFORTUNII. CALAMITATIS. TRISTITIÆ. AFFLICTIONUM. INFELICITATIS, MALI. DAMNI. MAERORIS. ÆGRIMONIAE. PASSIONIS. VIOLENTIAE.
units.tr: SICKNESS. TOILS. LABOUR. CARE. WRETCHEDNESS. MISFORTUNE. CALAMITY. SADNESS. AFFLICTIONS. UNHAPPINESS. EVIL. LOSS. GRIEF. BITTERNESS. SUFFERING. VIOLENCE.

units.la: AMANTES Noctiaut Diei, aut Soli, aut Lunæ miserias suas narrant. Merc. Prol v. 4.
units.tr: LOVERS tell of their troubles to the night, or to the day, or to the sun, or to the moon. Merc. Prol. v. 4.

units.la: VETERES cùm violentius, & arduus tenebantur, pellebantur, trudebantur, exclamare solebant: HÆC VIS EST. Captiv. 3. 5. v. 92. Sic J. Cæsar petisse videns pugnonibus: Ista quidem vis est.
units.tr: When the ancients were held more violently and forcibly, pushed and shoved, they used to cry out: "This is force!" Captiv. 3. 5. v. 92. So too Julius Caesar, seeing himself set upon with fists, said: "Indeed, that is force."

units.la: IN miseriis constituti, invocabant DEOS. Rud. 1. 4. v. 37. ubi naufragæ mulieres sic precantur: Nunc quisquis es, veneror, Deus, ut nos ex hac arumna eximat miseras, inopes, arumnosas, aliquo auxilio adjuvet.
units.tr: Placed in wretchedness, they called upon the gods. Rud. 1. 4. v. 37. where the shipwrecked women pray thus: "Now, whoever you are, I pray to you, God, that you free us wretched, poor, afflicted women from this calamity and help us with some aid."

units.la: TRISTITIÆ signum est terram obtueri. Bacch. 4. 4. v. 16.
units.tr: To stare at the ground is a sign of sadness. Bacch. 4. 4. v. 16.

units.la: MISERIA unauni quidem homini est affatim. Trin. 5. 2. v. 61.
units.tr: Wretchedness indeed comes to every man in abundance. Trin. 5. 2. v. 61.
