units.la: TRISTES non magis afficiendi tristitiâ. Most. 3. 2. v. 126.
units.tr: The sad are not to be afflicted with sadness any more. Most. 3. 2. v. 126.

units.la: ÆRUMNÆ & molestiæ gravissimæ, comparantur cum ærumnis Herculis: quas recensetPlaut. Persa 1. 1. v. 3. Vide etiam de ijs Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: Toils and most grievous troubles are compared with the labours of Hercules, which Plautus recounts. Persa 1. 1. v. 3. See also on these the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: CURÆ tabem inducunt in cor. Merc. 1. 2. v. 62. Ædepol cor miserum meum, quod guttatim contabescit: quasi in aquam indideris salem.
units.tr: Cares bring a wasting into the heart. Merc. 1. 2. v. 62. "Truly my wretched heart wastes away drop by drop; it is as if you had put salt into water."

units.la: SÆPE multorum annorum miserias unà voluptate sedamus. Poen. 5. 4. v. 91.
units.tr: Often we allay the troubles of many years with a single pleasure. Poen. 5. 4. v. 91.

units.la: ANIMUS æquus optimum est ærumnæ condimentum. Rud. 2. 3. v. 71.
units.tr: An equable mind is the best seasoning of hardship. Rud. 2. 3. v. 71.

units.la: IN ægritudine cōstituti, dicebantur bibere malum mærorem. Aul. 2. 3. v. 12. Vide Lex. Plaut. Bibere.
units.tr: Those placed in sickness were said to drink bitter grief. Aul. 2. 3. v. 12. See the Plautine Lexicon, under Bibere.

units.la: HOMINI misero, si ad malum accidit malum, Major libido est fugere, & facere nequiter. Men. i. i. v. 5.
units.tr: For a wretched man, if evil comes upon evil, the greater desire is to flee and to act wickedly. Men. 1. 1. v. 5.

units.la: IN afflictionibus constituti pij, Deum sæpe accusant, quod pietatis suæ nullum reportent præmium. Rud. 1. 3. v. 10.
units.tr: The godly, placed in afflictions, often accuse God because they receive no reward for their piety. Rud. 1. 3. v. 10.

units.la: ÆGRE in memoriam descendimus miseriarum nostrarum. Perf. 4. 4. v. 92.
units.tr: We are slow to call to mind our miseries. Perf. 4. 4. v. 92.

units.la: MISERI & improbi alios ex suo ingenio æstimant: & soccos mali habere gestarint. Meu. 3. 2. v. 48.
units.tr: The wretched and the wicked judge others by their own disposition, and they have been known to wear the slippers of the wicked. Men. 3. 2. v. 48.

units.la: SUSPENDIUM meditabatur in infortunio aliquo positi. Rud. 4. 4. v. 140.
units.tr: One placed in some misfortune was contemplating suicide. Rud. 4. 4. v. 140.

units.la: QUI cura & corde læri sunt, aliena damna non facile æstimare possunt. Epid. 1. 2. v. 43.
units.tr: Those who are dull in care and heart cannot easily estimate the losses of others. Epid. 1. 2. v. 43.

units.la: UNUM hoc scio: nimiò celerius venire, quam molestum est, quàm id, quod cupide petas. Most. 1. 1. v. 70. αἱ γὰρ βλοίαι, secundum Sophocl. sunt πολλάκις. Democritus: Bona vix quaerentibus evenient: mala vero etiam ultro contingunt.
units.tr: This one thing I know: things come more quickly than is troublesome, than what you eagerly seek. Most. 1. 1. v. 70. The Greek αἱ γὰρ βλάβαι [the harms], according to Sophocles, are πολλάκις [often]. Democritus: "Good things scarcely come to those who seek them, but evils come even unasked."

units.la: QUIBUS exanimi sententiâ res minimè succederent. DIs inimicis se natos dicebant. Most. 3. 1. v. 32, Mil. 2. 3. v.
units.tr: Those whose resolve was lifeless did not succeed at all. They said they were born enemies of the gods. Most. 3. 1. v. 32. Mil. 2. 3. v.

units.la: ÆRIS-ALIENI. CONTRACTUUM. MUTUI. DEBITORUM. CREDITORUM. PECUNIAE. SOLUTIONIS.
units.tr: Debt (aes alienum). Contracts. Loans. Debtors. Creditors. Money. Payment.

units.la: ALIENO uti, & in ære alieno esse, molestum admodum, & periculosum. Capt. Prol. v.19. Alieno uti non moror. Et Cist. 1. 1. 3. v. 40.
units.tr: To use another's money and be in debt is very troublesome and dangerous. Capt. Prol. v.19. I do not mind using another's money. And Cist. 1. 1. 3. v. 40.

units.la: Nunc quod reliquum restat, volo persolvere: Ut expungatur nomen, ne quid debeam.
units.tr: Now I want to pay what remains, so that the name is struck out and I owe nothing.

units.la: DEBITORES quod acceperunt mutuò, raro reddunt fideliter. Trin. 4. 3. v. 44. Ideoq; si quis mutuum quid dederit, fit pro proprio perditum cum repetas, inimicum amicum beneficio invenias tuo. Si mage exigere cupias, duarum rerum exoritur optio: vel illud, quod credideris, perdas, vel illum amicum amiseris. Ibid. 4. 3. v. 45. Germani dicunt: Wann einer etwas hinweg leyhet/ so macht er ihm nur ein eigenen Feind. Sic enim pergit Servus inibi. Talentum mutuum quod dederam, talento inimicum mihi emi, amicum vendidi.
units.tr: DEBTORS seldom repay loans faithfully. Trin. 4. 3. v. 44. Therefore, if someone has lent something, when you demand it back you lose it as if it were your own, and you find your friend turned into an enemy by your kindness. If you press harder, a choice of two things arises: either you lose what you lent, or you lose the friend. Ibid. 4. 3. v. 45. The Germans say: "When someone lends something away, he only makes an enemy of it." For the slave goes on there: "The talent I lent out, I bought an enemy with a talent; I sold a friend."

units.la: IN contractibus syngraphum dabant. Asin. 4, 1. v. 1. Idq; certis & pactis legibus. Ibid. 3. 3. v. 146.
units.tr: IN contracts they gave a written bond. Asin. 4, 1. v. 1. And this under fixed and agreed terms. Ibid. 3. 3. v. 146.

units.la: CREDITORIBUS cavebatur syngraphâ, quæ constabat ex tabulis ceratis. Curc. 3. 1. v. 40.
units.tr: CREDITORS were secured by a written bond, which consisted of waxed tablets. Curc. 3. 1. v. 40.

units.la: AD solutionem debiti solebant repromittere: hoc est, obligatione datâ spondere sibi satisfactum. Asin. 2. 4 v. 48. Vide Lexic.
units.tr: FOR payment of a debt they used to give a counter-promise, that is, by giving a bond to declare themselves satisfied. Asin. 2. 4 v. 48. See the Lexicon.

units.la: Æs alienum curas parit, somnum impedit. Men. 5. 5. v. 30. Germani dicunt: Borgen macht sorgen.
units.tr: Debt brings cares and prevents sleep. Men. 5. 5. v. 30. The Germans say: "Borrowing brings sorrow."

units.la: IN contractibus jurejurando sese obstringebant: ut nisi pecunia præsens detur die dictâ: jusjurandum amittatur. Perf. 3. 2. v. 4.
units.tr: IN contracts they bound themselves by oath, so that unless the money was paid in hand on the appointed day, the oath was forfeited. Perf. 3. 2. v. 4.

units.la: QUI plus peterent, causâ ceciderunt. Most. 3. 1. v. 118. De hoc vide I C. Ræverd. Var. lib. 3. cap. 13. De plus petentibus. Cujac. Hotman. ad §. 28. Si quis agens. Briss. de V.sign. Torrent. Comment. in Suet. Claud. c. 14. Stephani Proodop. lib. 2. c. 11. Gruter. ad Sen. Ep. 48.
units.tr: Those who demanded more lost their case. Most. 3. 1. v. 118. On this see Rævardus, Var. lib. 3, cap. 13, De plus petentibus; Cujacius and Hotman on §28, Si quis agens; Brisson, De V. sign.; Torrentius, commentary on Suetonius, Claudius c. 14; Stephanus, Proodop. lib. 2, c. 11; Gruter on Seneca, Ep. 48.

units.la: ADDICTI dicebantur olim, qui cùm non essent solvendo, creditoribus addicebantur: nec servitute eorum liberabantur, nisi debitis quocumque modo persolutis. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 86. Vide Rævardum cap. 8. lib. singul. ad leges XII. Tab.
units.tr: THOSE were once called addicti, who, being unable to pay, were handed over to their creditors; nor were they freed from that servitude unless the debts were paid off in some way. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 86. See Rævardus, cap. 8, lib. singul., on the Twelve Tables.

units.la: IN solutione caute agendum: cui denumeretur pecunia. Most. 3 3. v. 19. Potest enim ea solutio captioni esse.
units.tr: IN payment one must be careful to whom the money is counted out. Most. 3 3. v. 19. For such a payment can be a trap.

units.la: QUOD redditum est, reddi non potest, aut debet jure. Curc. 4. 3. v. 8.
units.tr: What has been paid back cannot, and by law ought not, be paid again. Curc. 4. 3. v. 8.

units.la: QUOD datum est utendum, id repetendi copia est. Trin. 5. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: What has been given to be used, there is a right to demand back. Trin. 5. 2. v. 7.

units.la: IN contractibus non integram protinus summam solvebant, sed reliquum alio tempore persolvebant. Cist. 1. 3. v. 40. Actum nomen eorum dicebatur expungi, ne quid deberent.
units.tr: IN contracts they did not pay the whole sum at once, but paid the remainder at another time. Cist. 1. 3. v. 40. Their account was said to be "struck out" (expungi), so that they owed nothing.

units.la: AFFABILITATIS. HUMANITATIS.
units.tr: Affability. Humanity.

units.la: ERGA propinquos maxime decet humanitatem exercere: Nunquam erit alienis gravis: qui suis se concinnat levem. Trin. 3. 2. v. 58.
units.tr: TOWARD relatives especially one ought to show kindness: he will never be burdensome to strangers who makes himself agreeable to his own. Trin. 3. 2. v. 58.

units.la: HUMANITATE saepe mores duriores corrigi possunt. Truc. 2. 2. v. 63.
units.tr: BY kindness harsher manners can often be corrected. Truc. 2. 2. v. 63.

units.la: AFFINITATIS. PROPINQUITATIS. COGNATIONIS. CONSANGUINITATIS.
units.tr: AFFINITY. NEARNESS OF KIN. KINSHIP BY BLOOD. CONSANGUINITY.

units.la: Vide paulò post Titul. Amicitia:
units.tr: See shortly after, under the heading Friendship:

units.la: AGRICULTURAE. AGRICOLARUM. RUSTICORUM. VILLICORUM. REI RUSTICAE. AGRORUM. ARATIONIS.
units.tr: AGRICULTURE. FARMING. COUNTRYMEN. BAILIFFS. RURAL AFFAIRS. FIELDS. PLOUGHING.

units.la: AGRI tanquam nutrices alebantur, ob felices eorum proventus. Trin. 2.4. v. III.
units.tr: Fields were, as it were, nursed, because of their happy yields. Trin. 2.4. v. III.

units.la: AGRI sæpe infelices. Quod sic fingit servus. Trin. 2.4. v.122. Terra cum proscinditur, in quinto quoq; sulco moriuntur boves.
units.tr: Fields are often unlucky. A slave feigns this thus: Trin. 2.4. v.122. When the earth is ploughed, oxen die even in the fifth furrow.

units.la: BOBUS arabant, non equis. Ibid.
units.tr: Oxen, not horses, did the ploughing. Ibid.

units.la: OCCATIO præcedere solet sationem & messem: uti jocatur captivus. Capt 3. 5. v. 4.
units.tr: Harrowing usually precedes sowing and reaping, as the captive jokes: Capt 3.5. v. 4.

units.la: Nam semper occant prius, quàm sarriunt rustici.
units.tr: For they always harrow before the farmers hoe.

units.la: AGRORUM vitia quæ soleant esse, vide Trin. 2.4. v.122. Et de ijs plura Tit. Venditionis.
units.tr: For the faults that fields are wont to have, see Trin. 2.4. v.122. And more about them under the heading Venditionis (Sale).

units.la: PER fundum septum non licet facere semitam. Curc. 1.1. v. 36.
units.tr: Through a fenced field it is not lawful to make a path. Curc. 1.1. v. 36.

units.la: OLIM filios ad agriculturam mittebant rus. Merc. Prol. v. 68.
units.tr: Formerly they used to send sons into the country to learn farming. Merc. Prol. v. 68.

units.la: CALAMITAS agrorum, quæ esse soleat, vide Trin. 2. 4. v.122. & sequentib.
units.tr: For the calamity of fields, which is wont to occur, see Trin. 2.4. v.122. and following.

units.la: RUSTICI sculponeis calceis utebantur. Cas. 2.8. v. 61.
units.tr: Countrymen wore wooden-soled shoes. Cas. 2.8. v. 61.

units.la: AGRI, horti, &c. calamitate premuntur: & pereunt. Cas. 5.2.v.30.
units.tr: Fields and gardens, etc., are oppressed by calamity and perish. Cas. 5.2. v.30.

units.la: BOVES plaustra & aratra trahebant. Truc. 2. 2. v. 22.
units.tr: Oxen drew wagons and ploughs. Truc. 2. 2. v. 22.

units.la: Ut ego me ruri hamaxari mavelim patulum bovem!
units.tr: Oh, how I would rather be a broad ox in the country, yoked to a cart!

units.la: ALLEGORIAE.
units.tr: ALLEGORIES.

units.la: ALLEGORIA exemplum prorsus admirandum recitatur Bacch. 4. 9. per totam scenam de Excidio Trojano : & fallacijs servorum in heros. Vide etiam Bacch. 5.2. sub initium scenæ.
units.tr: An entirely admirable example of allegory is recited at Bacch. 4.9, throughout the whole scene on the destruction of Troy, and on the slaves' tricks against their masters. See also Bacch. 5.2 at the beginning of the scene.

units.la: AMBITIONIS OSTENTATIONIS. SUPERBIAE. ΦΤΑΑΤΤΙΑΣ. AMORIS-SUI. ARROGANTIAE. GLORIAE. JACTANTIAE. GLORIATIONIS, VANITATIS.
units.tr: AMBITION, OSTENTATION. PRIDE. SELF-LOVE [ΦΙΛΑΥΤΙΑΣ]. ARROGANCE. GLORY. BOASTING. VAINGLORY, VANITY.

units.la: GLORIOSULI in re minimâ sæpe magnos agunt triumphos. Aul. 5. v. 11. Quod pueri clamitant in fabâ se reperisse.
units.tr: Little braggarts often make great triumphs over trifling matters. Aul. 5. v. 11. As boys shout that they have found a bean.

units.la: ARROGANTES in conviviis solent publicas res clamare, & leges crepare. Mil. 3. 1. v. 56.
units.tr: Arrogant men at dinner parties tend to proclaim public affairs and rattle off laws. Mil. 3. 1. v. 56.

units.la: LAUS propria sordet. Quod accinit servus seni, laudes suas nimis depraedicanti. Mil. 3. 1. v. 63. Cedo tres mihi homines contra aus-richalco emtos cum istis moribus.
units.tr: Self-praise stinks. The slave sings this to the old man who boasts too loudly of his own merits. Mil. 3. 1. v. 63. Give me three men bought in Aurichalcum with such manners.

units.la: HOMINES jactabundi magnas res agitant in mente suâ instruere: quemadmodum piscator ille Gripus. Rud. 4.2. v. 30.
units.tr: Boastful men plan great things in their minds, like that fisherman Gripus. Rud. 4. 2. v. 30.

units.la: ARROGANTIAE summae est, res falsas de se praedicare: quod faciunt milites. Truc. 2.6. v. 5. Vide Tit. Militum.
units.tr: To state false things about oneself is the height of arrogance, as soldiers do. Truc. 2. 6. v. 5. See the title Militum.

units.la: HOMINES superbi & reliquos omnes praefe fastidientes: solebant hanc formulam semper in ore habere : Casin. 3. 6. v. 9. Vide etiam Casaub. ad Theophrasti characteres.
units.tr: Proud men, who despise everyone else, were always accustomed to keep this formula on their lips: Casin. 3. 6. v. 9. See also Casaubon on the Characters of Theophrastus.

units.la: ARROGANTES etiam externo habitu & gestu corporis produnt animum suum jactabundum. Pers. 2. 5. v. 7. Quis ansatus ambulat? S A. magnificè consprcabor. Vide Sreatus: Sputi.
units.tr: Arrogant men also betray their boastful spirit by their outward dress and bodily gesture. Pers. 2. 5. v. 7. Who walks with his nose in the air? I shall strut magnificently. See Sreatus: Sputi.

units.la: SUPERBI se collaudari volunt. Mil. 4.2. v. 54. 71. Et mirificè se jactant. Exemplum insigne Miles per totam hanc scenam, ut & anteriore 4. 1. v. 2.
units.tr: Proud men want to be praised. Mil. 4. 2. v. 54, 71. And they boast wonderfully. A notable example is the soldier throughout this whole scene, as also in the preceding 4. 1. v. 2.

units.la: ARROGANTES genus & prosapiam, itemque formam suam jactare solent. Mil. 4. 2. v. 90.
units.tr: Arrogant men are accustomed to boast of their birth and lineage, and likewise of their good looks. Mil. 4. 2. v. 90.

units.la: PRÆ re nitorem, & gloriam præ copiâ qui habent, meminerint se, unde oriundi sient. Aul. 3. 6. v. 5. inquit avarus Euclio.
units.tr: Let those who have a show of splendour and glory beyond their means remember where they came from. Aul. 3. 6. v. 5, says the miser Euclio.

units.la: ARROGANTES sibi adblandiuntur in amore sui. Mil. 4. 6. v. 8. Ut amari videor! &c v. 50. Nepos sum Veneris.
units.tr: Arrogant men flatter themselves in self-love. Mil. 4. 6. v. 8. That I seem to be loved! etc. v. 50. I am the grandson of Venus.

units.la: MEUS mihi, suus cuique est carus. Capt. 2. 3. v. 40. Sic Cicero ad Att. lib. 15. Quin sua cuiq; sponsa placet, mihi mea: suus cuique amor, mihi meus.
units.tr: Each man's own is dear to him: mine to me, each man's own to each. Capt. 2. 3. v. 40. So Cicero, to Atticus, book 15: Indeed each man's own sweetheart pleases him, mine pleases me; each man's love is his own, mine is mine.

units.la: EXEMPLUM arrogantissimi hominis est Pyrgopolinices Miles gloriosus, impudens, stercoreus, plenus perjurij, atque adulterij. Mil. >1. v. 11. Sic Varro ait: Omnes videmur nobis esse bellulí, Et festivi saperda, cum simus σαπρoί.
units.tr: The example of the most arrogant man is Pyrgopolinices, the braggart soldier, shameless, filthy, full of perjury and adultery. Mil. 1. v. 11. Thus Varro says: We all seem to ourselves handsome and charming, like salted fish, though we are rotten [σαπροί].

units.la: MILITES magnifici & inermes, urbes verbis capiunt. Unde dicti Urbicapi. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 42. 51. Mil. 4. 2. v. 64.
units.tr: Magnificent but unarmed soldiers capture cities with words; hence they are called Urbicapi, city-takers. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 42, 51. Mil. 4. 2. v. 64.

units.la: SUPERBI animi indicium est, quasi ando undare vestes. Epid. 3. 3. v. 50. Vide Habitus.
units.tr: A sign of a proud spirit is, as it were, trailing one's clothes. Epid. 3. 3. v. 50. See Habitus.

units.la: QUI seipsus contemnit, in eo est indoles industriæ. Trin. 2. 2. v. 42. Vide Tit. Virtutis. Sic Socrates: Unum hoc scio, quod nihil scio.
units.tr: He who despises himself has the makings of industry. Trin. 2. 2. v. 42. See the title Virtutis. Thus Socrates: This one thing I know, that I know nothing.

units.la: QUI nihil aliud, nisi quod sibi soli placet, consulit, nugas agit. Trin. 2. 3. v. 4.
units.tr: He who consults nothing but what pleases himself alone is busy with trifles. Trin. 2. 3. v. 4.

units.la: Ambulationum.
units.tr: Walking.

units.la: Ambulationibus famem nobis conciliamus. Cicero V. Tusc. Socratem ferunt, cum usque ad vesperam contentius ambularet, quaesitumq; esset eo, quare id faceret, respondisse, se quo melius canaret, obsonare ambulando famem.
units.tr: By walking we gain an appetite for ourselves. Cicero, Tusc. V: They say that Socrates, when he walked more intently until evening, and was asked why he did so, answered that by walking he bought an appetite, so that he might dine the better.

units.la: Amicitiae. Amicorum. Consuetudinis. Conversationis. Benevolentiae. Familiaritatis. Favoris. Gratiae. Benevolentiae. Inimicitiae. Adversarii. Hostis. Defensionis. Reconciliationis. Amnestiae. Sodalitatis. Benignitatis. Cognationis. Affinitatis. Coniunctionis. Consanguinitatis.
units.tr: Friendship. Of friends. Custom. Conversation. Goodwill. Familiarity. Favour. Grace. Benevolence. Enmity. Adversary. Enemy. Defence. Reconciliation. Amnesty. Fellowship. Kindness. Kinship. Affinity. Connection. Consanguinity.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Beneficiorum. Item Morum.
units.tr: See also the title Beneficiorum. Likewise Morum.

units.la: Amici pauci sunt ferentarij: qui praesentariam operam praestant amico. Sic pauci sublevant inopiam amici, cum opus est: sed fere respondere solent: Non est. Perf. i. 1. v. 6. Trin. 3. 3. v. 30. Potin' est ab amico aliunde exorarier? Gerra! ne tu illud verbum adlutum inveneris: Mihi quidem hercle non est, quod dem mutuum. Itaque miser quaerendo argento mutuo: nequicquam, nisi Non est, sciunt mihi respondere, quos rogo.
units.tr: Friends are few who are ferentarii: those who give present help to a friend. Thus few relieve a friend's want when there is need, but they usually answer: "It isn't there." Perf. 1. 1. v. 6. Trin. 3. 3. v. 30. Can I be begged from a friend elsewhere? Gerra! Don't you find that stale phrase: "Indeed I have nothing to lend"? So wretched, seeking money on loan in vain, unless the people I ask know only how to answer "It isn't there."

units.la: Amicos decet promptos esse in ferendo ope. Trin. 2. 4. v. 5. 5.
units.tr: Friends ought to be ready to lend a hand. Trin. 2. 4. v. 5, 5.

units.la: Sunt quos scio esse amicos: sunt, quos suspicor: sunt quorum ingenia, atque amicos non possum noscere, ad amici partem, an ad inimici perveniant. Trin. 1. 2. v. 54. Vide etiam Merc. 5. 1. v. 9. ubi tres amicorum differentiæ constituuntur. Nam ubi mores deteriores increbescunt indies: ubi qui amici, qui infideles sint, nequeas pernoscere, ubique eripiatur, animo tuo, quod placeat maximè: ibi quidem si regnum detur, non est cupita civitas. Vide etiam Chrysf. ad Ephesios Homil. 16.
units.tr: There are some I know to be friends, some I suspect, and some whose natures I cannot tell whether they belong to the side of a friend or of an enemy. Trin. 1. 2. v. 54. See also Merc. 5. 1. v. 9, where three kinds of friends are distinguished. For when morals grow worse daily, and you cannot make out who are friends and who are faithless, then, wherever what pleases you most is snatched from your mind, even if a kingdom were offered, the city is not desired. See also Chrysostom on Ephesians, Homily 16.

units.la: Amici est, alterum monere, objurgare. Trin. 1. 2. v. 59. Si quid scis, me fecisse inscite, aut improbè, si id me non accusas, tu ipse objurgandus es.
units.tr: It is a friend's part to warn another and to rebuke him. Trin. 1. 2. v. 59. If you know that I have acted foolishly or wrongly, and you do not accuse me of it, you yourself deserve to be rebuked.

units.la: Ut cuiq; homini res parata est, firmi amici sunt: si res labat, itidem amici collabascunt. Res amicos invenit. Stich. 4. 1. v. 16. Immò adulatores adversa fortuna fugat, non amicos: quibus nullum pretium in amicitia placet, præter ipsam. Paupertas sola amicos retinet, & ostendit in vero suo vultu. Seneca Epist. 20. Quod tu beneficio tuo non potes scire, paupertatis scies: illa veros certosq; amicos retinebit: discedet, quisquis non te, sed aliud sequebatur. Non est autem vilob hunc unum amanda paupertas, quod a quibus ameris, ostendit. Vide Joh. Bernartium ad Boeth. Consolat.
units.tr: As each man's affairs are prosperous, so his friends are firm; if his fortune totters, his friends likewise collapse. Adversity finds out friends. Stich. 4. 1. v. 16. Indeed, adverse fortune drives away flatterers, not friends, who want no reward in friendship except friendship itself. Poverty alone keeps friends and shows them in their true face. Seneca, Epist. 20: What you cannot learn from your benefaction, you will learn from poverty: it will keep true and certain friends; whoever followed not you but something else will depart. Yet poverty is not to be loved for this reason alone, that it shows by whom you are loved. See Joh. Bernartius on Boethius' Consolation.

units.la: Maxima pars morem hunc homines habent, quod sibi volunt, Dum id impetrant, boni sunt: sed ubi jam penes se habent, Ex bonis pessimi, & fraudulentissimi sunt. Capt. 2. 1. v. 36. Cicero pro Murena astutos, & ingratos tales nominat.
units.tr: Most men have this habit: they want what they want, and while they obtain it they are good; but once they have it in their power, from good they become the worst and most fraudulent. Capt. 2. 1. v. 36. Cicero in the pro Murena calls such men astute and ungrateful.

units.la: Catullus in Epithal. Pelei. Qui dum aliquid cupient, animum prægestit apisci, Nil metuunt jurare, nihil promittere parcunt. Sed simul ac cupida mentis satiata libido est, Dicta nihil metuere, nihil perjuria curant.
units.tr: Catullus, in the Epithalamium of Peleus: While they desire something, they eagerly strive to get it; they fear nothing in swearing, and spare nothing in promising. But as soon as the greedy desire of the mind is satisfied, they fear no word they have spoken and care nothing for perjuries.

units.la: Callimachus: περὶ τι λαβεῖν, φιλύσι: ἀλλὰ συγύσι λαβόντες.
units.tr: Callimachus: They are fond of you while they are about to get something, but once they have got it... [περὶ τι λαβεῖν, φιλοῦσι· ἀλλὰ συγόντες λαβόντες].

units.la: Phalaris Epist. 83. ait, ejusmodi homines imitari mores Chamaeleontis, qui pro ingenio temporum colores mutat.
units.tr: Phalaris, Epist. 83, says such men imitate the ways of the chameleon, which changes its colours according to the nature of the times.

units.la: Quid rettulit
units.tr: What has it profited

units.la: Beneficum esse oratione, si ad rem auxilium emortuum est?
units.tr: To be beneficent in words, if the help has died out in the deed?

units.la: Malim ifliusmodi mihi amicos furno mersos, quàm foro. Epid. 1. 2. v. 14. 16.
units.tr: I would rather have such friends drowned in an oven than in the forum. Epid. 1. 2. v. 14, 16.

units.la: Nequam illud verbum est: Benevult: nisi qui (h.e. aliquâ re) benefacit. Trin. 2. 4. v. 38.
units.tr: Nequam is the word for "benevolent" unless he does good by some deed. Trin. 2. 4. v. 38.

units.la: Qui bene volunt, bene vsitent. Poen. 1.2.v.160. Sic Scal. Epidor. lib. 4.
units.tr: Let those who wish well act well. Poen. 1. 2. v. 160. So Scaliger, Epidorum book 4.

units.la: Tu si ex animo forte velis cui bene facium; Addas operam: sola cadaver est voluntas.
units.tr: If you truly wish well to anyone from your heart, add effort: the will alone is a corpse.

units.la: Ita esse arbitror hominis amico, qui est amicus, ita uti nomen (scilicet Amici) possidet, nisi Deos, cinihil praestare. Bacch. 3. 2. v. 2.
units.tr: I think it is so with a man: a friend who is a friend, as he holds the name (namely of friend), can do nothing for you, except the gods. Bacch. 3. 2. v. 2.

units.la: Nimium difficile est reperiri amicum, ita ut nomen cluet: cuituam cum rem credideris, sine omni curâ dormias. Trin. 3. 2. v. 19.
units.tr: It is very hard to find a friend who lives up to the name, to whom, when you have entrusted your affairs, you may sleep without any care. Trin. 3. 2. v. 19.

units.la: Amicis semper vacandum. Merc. 2. 2. v. 27. Quamquam negotium est, si quid vis Demipho, Non sum occupatus unquam amico operam dare.
units.tr: Always make time for friends. Merc. 2. 2. v. 27. Although I have business, Demipho, if you wish, I am never too busy to lend a hand to a friend.

units.la: RECONCILIATIONIS
units.tr: RECONCILIATION

units.la: ea est vis, ut gratiam farciat, & simultatem sempiternâ delcat oblivione: ita quidem, ut ex reconciliatione firmior quandoque nascatur amicitia. Amph. 3.2. v.60. Exempla apud veteres extant quamplurima eorum, qui cum prius simultates invicem exercuissent, in gratiam reducti, dehinc amicitiam pfanctè coluerunt: ut de P. Affricano, ac Tiber. Gracch. M. Æmilio Lepido, & Fulvio Flacco, Cælio Russo, & Q. Pompejo apud Ciceronem Orat. de Provinc. Consul. & Val. Max. lib.4. Illud nobilissimum apud Senec. l.1. de clem. c.9. de L. Cinnâ, quem cum vitæ suæ insidias molitum Octavius Augustus comperisset, verbis tantum correptum dimisit: nec ita multo post ultrò ei (cùm petere non auderet) consulatum detulit, amicissimumque & fidelissimum posthac habuit. Vide plura apud doctissimum Langlæum lib.3. c.5. p.161. Otij Semestris.
units.tr: Reconciliation has the power to restore favour and to wipe out enmity with everlasting oblivion, so that the friendship which springs from it is sometimes firmer than before. Amph. 3.2. v.60. There are very many examples of this among the ancients: of men who, having first been at odds with one another, were restored to favour and afterwards cultivated friendship sincerely. Such are P. Africanus and Tiberius Gracchus, M. Aemilius Lepidus and Fulvius Flaccus, Caelius Rufus and Q. Pompeius, in Cicero's De provinciis consularibus and in Valerius Maximus, book 4. The most noble case is in Seneca, De clementia 1.9, concerning L. Cinna. When Octavius Augustus discovered that Cinna had plotted against his life, he rebuked him only with words and let him go. Not long after, of his own accord, since Cinna did not dare to ask, Augustus offered him the consulship, and thereafter held him as his most loyal and dearest friend. See more in the learned Langlaeus, book 3, ch. 5, p. 161, Otium Semestre.

units.la: Iniquum est amico facere iniuriam. Trin. 3.2. v.5.
units.tr: It is wrong to do an injury to a friend. Trin. 3.2. v.5.

units.la: Vera amicitia non est nisi inter similes. Boves non sunt conjungendi cum asinis. Aul. 2.2. v. 52. Quam ad probos propinquitate proximè te adjunxerit : tam optimum est. Vide Titul. Matrimonij.
units.tr: True friendship exists only between like people. Oxen are not to be yoked with asses. Aul. 2.2. v. 52. The closer you join yourself to upright people, the better it is. See the title Marriage.

units.la: Decipitur nemo quidem, mea sententia, qui suis amicis narrat recte res suas. Poen. 5.6. v. 1. Sed tamen in re turpi & detrimentosa, non est sequendum consilium amicorum: ut hoc loco.
units.tr: In my opinion, no one who tells his friends the truth about his affairs is deceived. Poen. 5.6. v. 1. But in a shameful and harmful matter, one should not follow the advice of friends, as in this case.

units.la: Modeste fidelitatem suam amico laudet senex. Trin. 5.2. v. 4. Si quid amicum erga benefeci, aut consului fideliter, non videor meruisse laudem, culpa caruisse arbitror.
units.tr: An old man should modestly commend his own loyalty to a friend. Trin. 5.2. v. 4. If I have done a friend a good turn or given him faithful advice, I do not think I deserve praise; I think I have been free of blame.

units.la: Pessimi amici colubrino ingenio, qui duplices habent linguas. Truc. 4.3. v. 6.
units.tr: The worst friends have a snake-like nature, with forked tongues. Truc. 4.3. v. 6.

units.la: Multi more isto, atque exemplo vivunt, quos cum censeas Esse amicos, reperiuntur falsi falsimonijs, Lingua factiosi, inertes operâ, sublesti fide. Nullus est, cui non invideant, rem secundam obtingere. Nesibi invideatur ipsis, ignavi recte cavent. Bacch. 3.6. v. 11. & seqq. Item Trucul. 4.2. v. 30. Mavelim mihi inimicos invidere, quam me inimicis meis. Nam invidere aliy bene esse, tibi male esse, miseria est. Qui invident, egent: illi quibus invidetur, rem habent. Vide etiam Tit. Invidia.
units.tr: Many live by that custom and example. Whom you would take to be friends, they are found to be false in their deceits, busy with their tongues, idle in their work, and weak in their loyalty. There is no one to whom they do not begrudge good fortune. Lest envy be turned on themselves, the idle take careful care. Bacch. 3.6. v. 11. and following. Likewise Truc. 4.2. v. 30. I would rather have my enemies envy me than have me envy my enemies. For to envy others their prosperity while you are unfortunate is wretchedness. Those who envy are needy; those who are envied have something. See also the title Envy.

units.la: Nihil agit qui diffidentem verbis solatur suis. Is est amicus, qui in re dubiâ operâ juvat, ubi res est opus. Epid. 1.2. v. 9.10.
units.tr: He does nothing who comforts a discouraged man with words. A friend is one who helps with deeds when the matter is doubtful and needs help. Epid. 1.2. v. 9.10.

units.la: Amici mortui nobis videntur, quos diu non visitamus. Perf. 1.1. v. 19.
units.tr: Friends whom we do not visit for a long time seem dead to us. Perf. 1.1. v. 19.

units.la: Veri amici opem serunt amicis. Perf 1.1.v. 36. Amicum me tibi potis es facere sempiternum : si mihi des numos sexcentos, quos pro capite illius pendam.
units.tr: True friends bring help to friends. Perf. 1.1. v. 36. You can make me your friend for ever, if you give me six hundred coins, which I will pay for his life.

units.la: Amici solent vinum propinare amicis suis in signum suavissimae amicitiae. Pseud. 5.1. v. 19.
units.tr: Friends are accustomed to offer wine to their friends as a sign of the sweetest friendship. Pseud. 5.1. v. 19.

units.la: Ægre ferimus vel nomen hostis nostri nominari. Bacch. 2. 3. v. 19.
units.tr: We bear it with difficulty even when the name of our enemy is mentioned. Bacch. 2.3. v. 19.

units.la: Amici dum dant: amici sunt: sin minus: dicuntur esse mortui: sicut de amatoribus dicitur. Pseud. 1.3.v.76. Truc. 1.2.v.61. Nam me fuisse huius fateor summum, atq; intimum, quoad amantis inul- ta peßum ÿt pecunia, Eadem postquam alium reperit, qui plus da- ret, damnosiorem me exunde amovit loco.
units.tr: Friends are friends while they give; otherwise they are said to be dead, as is said of lovers. Pseud. 1.3. v. 76. Truc. 1.2. v. 61. For I confess I was her highest and most intimate friend, as long as a lover's money was being wasted unavenged. Once she found another who would give more, she removed me from her place as a more costly loss.

units.la: ETIAM inimici salutandi. (apt. 3. s. v.86.
units.tr: EVEN enemies are to be greeted. (apt. 3. s. v.86.

units.la: AMICUM non tam decet esse consiliarium, quam auxiliarium. Truc. 2.1. v.6.
units.tr: A friend ought to be less a counsellor than a helper. Truc. 2.1. v.6.

units.la: TUNICA propior est pallio. Trin 5.2. v.3. Deijs, quæ nobis affinia magis sunt, & chara. Simile est illud: Sura geun propius. Sunt enim gradus amicorum: & officiorum.
units.tr: A tunic is nearer than a cloak. Trin 5.2. v.3. That is, of those things which are more akin to us and dearer. A similar saying is: Sura geun propius. For there are degrees of friends and of duties.

units.la: AMICI peregre abituri amicis omnem familiam credunt. Trin. 1. 2. v. 78.
units.tr: Friends who are about to go abroad entrust their whole household to their friends. Trin. 1.2. v. 78.

units.la: NIHIL homini amico est opportuno amicius. Sine tuo labore, quod velis, actum est tamen. Epid. 3 3. v. 43.
units.tr: Nothing is more friendly to a friend who is in need. Without your labour, what you wish has nonetheless been done. Epid. 3.3. v. 43.

units.la: AMICITIA inter meretricium ordinem quoque esse solet. Cist. 1.1. v.24. non minus, atque inter honestas matronas. Ibid.
units.tr: Friendship is wont to exist even within the class of prostitutes, no less than among respectable matrons. Cist. 1.1. v.24. Ibid.

units.la: AMICI opes plæriq; quæritant: & tum simulant amicitias. Aul. 1.2. v.37.
units.tr: Most people seek out a friend's wealth, and then they pretend friendship. Aul. 1.2. v.37.

units.la: AMICUM castigare ob meritam noxiam, immune est facinus: verum in ætate utile, & conducibile. Trin. 1.1, v.1. Scite Hieronymus: Meliora sunt amici vulnera, quam inimici oscula.
units.tr: To rebuke a friend for a fault he has deserved is a blameless act, and useful and profitable in one's lifetime. Trin. 1.1. v.1. Hieronymus rightly says: The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy.

units.la: UBI sunt amici, ibidem est negotium, & molestia. Amicorum enim causa nos interdum laborare necesse est, aut jus amicitiæ perdere. Truc. 4.4, v.32. Verum est verbum: Ubi Amici, esse ibidem opes. Apud Scythas, authore Luciano, is habebatur ditissimus, qui certissimos amicos possideret. Vide Adag. Erasmi. Et Adag. Ben-Sirae, quae collegit Janus Drusus: Melior est amicus in platea, quam aurum in cista.
units.tr: Where there are friends, there are also business and trouble. For we must sometimes labour for our friends' sake, or else lose the rights of friendship. Truc. 4.4. v.32. It is a true saying: where there are friends, there also is wealth. According to Lucian, among the Scythians he was considered richest who possessed the most reliable friends. See the Adages of Erasmus, and the Adages of Ben-Sira, which Janus Drusus collected: A friend in the street is better than gold in the chest.

units.la: VERAE amicitiae nota est, sublevare pauperes amicos, cum non sunt solvendi. Cure. 5.3. v.7. Vide Tit. Pauperta-tis.
units.tr: It is a mark of true friendship to help poor friends when they cannot repay. Curc. 5.3. v.7. See the title Poverty.

units.la: AMICI in rebus dubijs & egenis, factis & fide debent amicorum egestatem sublevare. Capt. 2.3. v.46.79. exemplo duorum captivorum Philocratis, & Tyndari. Vide etiam Trin. 2.2. v. 63. 66. &
units.tr: Friends in doubtful and needy circumstances ought to relieve their friends' want by deeds and by loyalty. Capt. 2.3. v.46.79. Example of the two captives, Philocrates and Tyndarus. See also Trin. 2.2. v. 63.

units.la: 66. Et Curc. 2. 3. v. 53. Hominem amicum amico decet opitulari.
units.tr: 66. And Curc. 2.3. v. 53. It is fitting for a friend to help a friend.

units.la: Amicos in rebus dubijs consulere solemus. Men. 4. 3. v. 26. Et Merc. 3. 4. v. 35. Sodalem æquum esse sodali bene consulere.
units.tr: We are accustomed to consult friends in doubtful matters. Men. 4.3. v. 26. And Merc. 3.4. v. 35. A comrade ought to give fair counsel to a comrade.

units.la: Non placet, qui amicos inter dentes conclusos habet. Trin. 4. 2. v. 64.
units.tr: I do not like a man who keeps his friends shut up between his teeth. Trin. 4.2. v. 64.

units.la: Tardo amico nihil est quicquam iniquius. Pœn. 3. 1. v. 1.
units.tr: Nothing is more unfair than a slow friend. Poen. 3.1. v. 1.

units.la: Quanti est adhibere hominem amicum, ubi quid geras? Perf. 4. 4. v. 46.
units.tr: How valuable it is to have a friend at hand when you are doing something! Perf. 4.4. v. 46.

units.la: Amici interdum in discrimen nos vocant: quod minime sperabamus. Pœn. 5. 4. v. 62. Etiam mea in me latrant canes.
units.tr: Friends sometimes bring us into danger, which we least expected. Poen. 5.4. v. 62. Even my own dogs bark at me.

units.la: Amicos absentes ac bene meritos recte flemus, ac deflemus, praesertim in infortunio constitutos. Capt. 1. 2. v. 30.
units.tr: We rightly weep and mourn for absent friends who have deserved well, especially when they are in misfortune. Capt. 1.2. v. 30.

units.la: Dextris amicitiæ firmantur. Merc. 5. 4. v. 4. Vide Tiraq. ad Alex. lib. 1. c. 19.
units.tr: Friendships are confirmed by handshakes. Merc. 5.4. v. 4. See Tiraquellus on Alexander, book 1, ch. 19.

units.la: Amicum non decet esse ὀλίγαυξένον. Trin. 1. 2. v. 16. Omnibus amicis, quod mihi est, cupio esse idem.
units.tr: A friend should not be a niggard [ὀλίγαυξένον]. Trin. 1.2. v. 16. I wish to be to all my friends what I am to myself.

units.la: Si opulentus it petitum pauperioris gratiam, pauper metuit congredi, per metum male rem gerit. Aul. 2. 2. v. 69.
units.tr: If a wealthy man seeks the favour of a poorer one, the poor man fears to meet him, and through fear he manages the matter badly. Aul. 2.2. v. 69.

units.la: Amicorum est, alterum alterius commodum quaerere. Aul. 2. 1. v. 10 praesertim si sint consanguinei: ut Eunomia, & Megadorus, frater, & soror.
units.tr: It is the duty of friends to seek each other's advantage. Aul. 2.1. v. 10, especially if they are blood relations, such as Eunomia and Megadorus, brother and sister.

units.la: Saepe benignus noster animus, quem praestamus amico, in crimen & infamiam ponitur. Trin. 3. 3. v. 11.
units.tr: Often our kindly disposition, which we show to a friend, is put down to crime and disgrace. Trin. 3.3. v. 11.

units.la: Ubi qui amici, qui infideles sint, nequeas pernoscere, ibi mala est habitatio. Merc. 5. 1. v. 9.
units.tr: Where you cannot discern which people are friends and which are faithless, the dwelling is bad. Merc. 5.1. v. 9.

units.la: Amici soli liberè & tutò loquuntur. Unde Proverb. Soli summus. Pœn. 4. 2. v. 69. Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: Only friends speak freely and safely. Hence the proverb: Soli summus. Poen. 4.2. v. 69. See the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: Pauci ex multis sunt amici boni, qui certi sient. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 155.
units.tr: Among many, few are good friends who are reliable. Pseud. 1.3. v. 155.

units.la: Amicitias quibuscumque de causis dissolutas, conciliat rursum pecunia. Stich. 3. 1. v. 9.
units.tr: Money restores friendships which have been dissolved for whatever reasons. Stich. 3.1. v. 9.

units.la: Amico absenti maledicere nefas. Trin. 4.2. v.81 Vide Tit. Calumnia.
units.tr: It is wrong to speak ill of an absent friend. Trin. 4.2. v. 81. See the title Slander.

units.la: Amicos etiam absentibus amicis benedicere convenit. Mil. 4. 8. v. 30.
units.tr: It is fitting to speak well even of friends who are absent. Mil. 4.8. v. 30.

units.la: Contagione nocet, quod ab uno ad alium transit. Sic Mercurius se metuere dicit, co quod & pater ejus Jupiter metuat. Sic conversatione pravorum ceu pestis vitanda. Amph. Prol. v. 31. Contagione met patris metuo malum.
units.tr: By contagion it does harm, what passes from one to another. So Mercury says that he fears, because his father Jupiter also fears. So one must avoid the company of the wicked as one avoids a plague. Amph. Prol. v. 31. I fear the evil through contagion of my father's fear.

units.la: Prava conversatio optimis quoque adolescentibus damnosa. Most. 1.1.v.20. Vide totum locum. Sic Trinummo Lysiteles adolescens recte sapit. 2.2. v.33.
units.tr: Bad company is harmful even to the best young men. Most. 1.1. v. 20. See the whole passage. So in the Trinummus, the young man Lysiteles rightly reasons. 2.2. v. 33.

units.la: Isthaec ego mihi semper habui aetati tegumentum meae, Ne penetrarem me unquam, ubi esset damni conciliabulum.
units.tr: "These things I have always kept as a covering for my age, so that I should never go into a place where there is a gathering for loss."

units.la: Qui cum malis versantur, tales quoque habere solent. Curc. 4.2. v. 17. Nec vobiscum quisquam in foro frugi consistere audet: qui constitit, culpam eum, conspicitur, vituperatur, eum rem fidemq; perdere, tametsi nihil fecit, ajunt.
units.tr: Those who associate with bad men are wont to have such companions as well. Curc. 4.2. v. 17. "Nor does anyone dare to stand with you in the forum as an honest man. Whoever takes his stand there, they say, is seen to be at fault, is reviled, and has lost his reputation and credit, even though he has done nothing."

units.la: Consuetudine & conversatione Amor conciliatur. Cist. 1.1.v.96. Lucret. 1.4. Consuetudo concinnat Amorem.
units.tr: Love is won by custom and association. Cist. 1.1. v. 96. Lucretius 1.4: "Custom knits love together."

units.la: Quibuscum aetatem exegimus, absurdum est non amplius nosse: ex sententia sycophantae. Trin. 4.2. v.110.
units.tr: With whom we have spent our life, it is absurd not to know any longer: so says the flatterer. Trin. 4.2. v. 110.

units.la: Amici potiores sunt, quam pecunia. Perf. 4.4. v. 104. Etsi res sunt fragilia, amici sunt tamen.
units.tr: Friends are more valuable than money. Perf. 4.4. v. 104. "Though things are fragile, friends nonetheless endure."

units.la: In bono hospite atque amico, quaestus est, quod sumitur. Mil. 3. 1.v.79.
units.tr: With a good host and friend, what is taken is a profit. Mil. 3.1. v. 79.

units.la: Amici malum nostrum ducimus malum. Capt. 1.2. v.42.
units.tr: We regard our friend's trouble as our own trouble. Capt. 1.2. v. 42.

units.la: Quam veterrimus homini optimus est amicus. Truc. 1.2. v. 70.
units.tr: The best friend is the oldest one for a man. Truc. 1.2. v. 70.

units.la: In mala uxore atque inimico si quid sumas, sumtus es. Mil. 3.1. v.78.
units.tr: If you take anything from a bad wife or an enemy, you have been taken for a fool. Mil. 3.1. v. 78.

units.la: Numquam erit alienis gravis: qui suis se concinnat levem. Trin. 3.2.v.58. AMICUM decet esse taciturnum. Trin. 1.2. v. 105. OPES facile inveniunt amicos. Mil. 3.1. v. 120.
units.tr: He will never be a burden to strangers who makes himself light to his own. Trin. 3.2. v. 58. A friend ought to be a man of few words. Trin. 1.2. v. 105. Wealth easily finds friends. Mil. 3.1. v. 120.

units.la: AMORUM. AMATORUM. AMORIS. CUPIDINIS. REI-VENEREÆ. AMANTIUM. AMATIONIS. VOLUPTATIS-AMATORIÆ.
units.tr: LOVES. LOVERS. LOVE. DESIRE. THE THING OF VENUS. LOVERS. LOVING. AMATORY PLEASURE.

units.la: Vide etiam Titul. Adulterij, &c. de Meretricibus & Lenonibus. Item Titul. Matrimonij. Conjugij.
units.tr: See also the titles Adultery, etc., on harlots and pimps. Likewise the titles Marriage and Wedlock.

units.la: IN melle sitæ sunt linguæ vestræ, atque orationes, lacteque corda in felle sunt ita, atque acerbo aceto. Linguis dicta dulcia datis, corde amata facitis amantes, si qui dent non habent. Truc. I. 2. v. 75.
units.tr: Your tongues and speeches are set in honey, but your hearts are in gall, as if in bitter vinegar. You give sweet words with your tongues, and you make lovers of those whose hearts you have, if they give you what they do not have. Truc. I. 2. v. 75.

units.la: MERETRICES sunt electebræ argenti. Ibid. v. 81.
units.tr: Harlots are baits of silver. Ibid. v. 81.

units.la: HOC nobis vitium maximum est, inquit adolescens: cum amamus, tum perimus, si illud quod volumus dicitur: palam cum mentiuntur, verum esse insciti credimus, ne ut in estu motitamur irâ! Trucul. I. 2. v. 87. Sic Terent. Amantium iræ, amoris redingratio.
units.tr: "This is our greatest fault," says the young man, "when we love, then we are ruined, if what we want is told: when they lie openly, we believe, being unskilled, that it is true, so that we are tossed about in the heat of anger!" Trucul. I. 2. v. 87. So Terence: The angers of lovers are the renewal of love.

units.la: PROCUL quidem abesse amantem, haud consentaneum est. Curc. I. 3. v. 9.
units.tr: For a lover to be far away is hardly fitting. Curc. I. 3. v. 9.

units.la: IPSUS se excruciat, qui homo, quod amas, videt, nec potitur, dum licet. Curc. I. 3. v. 14.
units.tr: He torments himself who sees what he loves and does not possess it, while he may. Curc. I. 3. v. 14.

units.la: AMATORES delitias amorum pro adulterâ habent vitâ. Curc. I. 3. v. 16. Ibidem quoque parasiti delitias epularum. Pseud. 5. I. v. 11.
units.tr: Lovers hold the delights of love to be like an adulterous life. Curc. I. 3. v. 16. Likewise parasites hold the delights of feasts. Pseud. 5. I. v. 11.

units.la: BONUM est pauxillum amare sane, insane non bonum est. Curc. I. 3. v. 20.
units.tr: It is good to love a little, and sanely; to love insanely is not good. Curc. I. 3. v. 20.

units.la: AMATORES rivales invidos ferre nequeunt: cæteraque omnia parviparvipendunt profuo amore. Curc. 3. v. 22.
units.tr: Lovers cannot bear envious rivals, and in their headlong love they care little for all other things. Curc. 3. v. 22.

units.la: AMATORES dormiuntinfuis amasijs. Curc. 1. 3. v. 28.
units.tr: LOVERS sleep in their love affairs. Curc. 1. 3. v. 28.

units.la: AMOR est condimentum omnium rerum. Eum sic commendat senex Stalino Cafin. 2. 3. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: LOVE is the seasoning of all things. So the old man Stalinus commends it: Cafin. 2. 3. v. 1. & seqq.

units.la: Omnibus rebus ego Amorem credo, & nitoribus nitore antevenire.
units.tr: I believe Love surpasses all things in brilliance and polish.

units.la: Nec potis quicquam commemorari, quod plus salis, plusque leporis hodie (tis,
units.tr: Nothing can be mentioned that has more salt and more charm today

units.la: Habeat: Coquos equidem nimis demiror, qui utuntur condimen-
units.tr: I greatly wonder at the cooks who use seasonings

units.la: Eos eo condimento uno non utier, omnibus quod praestat.
units.tr: and do not use that one seasoning which surpasses all others.

units.la: Namq; ubi Amor condimentum inerit, quidvis placiturum credo,
units.tr: For when Love is the seasoning, I believe anything will please.

units.la: Neq; salsum, neq; suave esse potest quicquam, ubi Amor non admi- scetur. (lenem.
units.tr: Nothing can be salty or sweet where Love is not mixed in.

units.la: Fel quod amarum est, id mel facit, hominem ex tristi, lepidum &
units.tr: Love makes the bitter gall into honey, turning a man from sour to pleasant and gentle.

units.la: Hanc ego de me conjecturam facio domi, magis, quàm ex auditis.
units.tr: I make this conjecture about myself at home, rather than from what I have heard.

units.la: IN amore non protinus licet potiri, sed sæpe lenta est materies: uti queritur Miles. Mil. 4. 5. v. 4.
units.tr: In love one cannot at once gain possession, but the matter is often slow, as the soldier complains. Mil. 4. 5. v. 4.

units.la: QVI amat hercle si esurit, myllum estet. Caf. 4. 2. v. 16. Cujus quidem versus sententiam expressi eo loco satis commodam, ex hariolatione Gruteri: cum quâ cõgruit planè altera Merc. 4. 4. v. 25.
units.tr: He who loves, by Hercules, if he is hungry, eats a mullet. Caf. 4. 2. v. 16. I have expressed the sense of this verse in a fairly suitable way at that place, following Gruter's conjecture; with which another passage, Merc. 4. 4. v. 25., plainly agrees.

units.la: Nam qui amat, quod amat, si id habet, id habet pro cibo, Videre, amplecti, osculari, alloqui.
units.tr: For he who loves, if he has what he loves, has it as food: to see, to embrace, to kiss, to address.

units.la: Taubmannus in suâ Editione novissimâ sic expressit versum Cassinæ:
units.tr: Taubmann, in his latest edition, rendered the verse of the Casina thus:

units.la: Qui amat, tamen hercle si esurit, nullum esurit.
units.tr: He who loves, though by Hercules he is hungry, is hungry for nothing.

units.la: Nullo sane sensu, ne Grammatico quidem. Proinde si quid mutandum, uti sane locus hic depravatus omninò est, approbanda præter cæteras est lectio JANI DOUZÆ, qui legit, nullus esurit: quam puto esse verissimam. Nam de myllo Gruteriano, quod scripsi, non tam hebes sum, mi Taubmane, quin videam ab ipso Plauto minimè usurpatum. Arripui autem, quia ad sensum nuptæ hujus Comœdiæ: & sententia sic commodissimè staret. Si ægrè quis ferat, arreptam à me, si non veram, ingeniosam tamen conjecturam: legatur post deinde, ac quidem in margine, ut mea, qui & altero verbo esitandi sublevavi totam sententiam versùs. Palam verò edico, illam me ut lectionem Plautinam nullo modo a-gnognoscere; sed lectori hæsitanti dumtaxat sic consultum ire sategisse: eóq; in alterâ Editione lubens ad marginem appositi; in textu autem sic expressi ex antiquâ Editione Argentinensi Adelphi Mulingi: & commodè & verè:
units.tr: That has no sense at all, not even grammatical. Therefore, if anything must be changed (since this place is certainly corrupt throughout), the reading of Janus Dousa is to be preferred above the rest, who reads nullus esurit ("nobody is hungry"), which I think is most true. For I am not so dull, my Taubmann, as not to see that the Gruterian myllum which I wrote was hardly ever used by Plautus himself. I seized on it, however, because it suits the sense of this comedy and the sentence would stand most conveniently with it. If anyone takes it badly, let the conjecture which I seized, if not true, at least be read as ingenious and as mine, afterwards, and indeed in the margin; for I also relieved the whole sentence of the verse by changing one word to esitandi. I openly declare that I do not at all acknowledge that reading as Plautine; I was only eager to provide for the hesitant reader in this way. Therefore in the second edition I gladly placed it in the margin, but in the text I have expressed it thus, from the old Strasbourg edition of Mulingus's Adelphi, both suitably and truly:

units.la: Qui amat tantum hercle: si esurit, nullus esurit.
units.tr: He who loves so much, by Hercules: if he is hungry, nobody is hungry.

units.la: AMOR stultus nos nostri immemores facit. Cist. I. I. v. 63.
units.tr: Foolish love makes us forget ourselves. Cist. I. I. v. 63.

units.la: AMARE occipere amarum est. Nam Amor & mel le, & fel le est fecundissimus: Gustu vix dat dulce, amarum ad satietatem usq; ogerit. Cist. I. I. v. 71. Sententia è tripode prolata: cum quâ consentiunt plures nostri authoris. Amph. 2. 2. v. 1. Satin' parva res voluptatum. Pseud I. I. v. 61. Truc. 2. 3. v. 25. Eurip. Hippolyto: τί τοῦτο λέγεις ἀνθρώπους ἐχεῖν; ἡδίσον, ὦ παῖ, ταύτὸν ἀλγίσον ϑ' ἁμα. In hanc rem egregia est admonitio viri docti, q; hic in gratiam juventutis appingam: Vix primoribus, inquit ille, labris delibandū datur, quod in Amore si quid est, suave est; partem alteram potissimam, & maximam plenis manibus, fauci bus haurias, & haurire coget ris vel invitus, non ad satietatem modo, sed nauseam, & fastidium quoq;. Fugiamus, mea juventus, fugiamus hunc pocillatorem, & ne illud sitiamus: unde laboro.
units.tr: To begin to love is bitter. For Love is most fertile both of honey and of gall: at first taste it scarcely gives sweetness, but bitterness it drives on to satiety. This is a saying brought forth from the tripod, and several passages of our author agree with it: Amph. 2. 2. v. 1. Is a thing of pleasures a small matter enough? Pseud. I. I. v. 61. Truc. 2. 3. v. 25. In Euripides' Hippolytus: [τί τοῦτο λέγεις ἀνθρώπους ἐχεῖν; ἡδίσον, ὦ παῖ, ταύτὸν ἀλγίσον ϑ' ἁμα.] "What do you mean by saying men have this? It is sweetest, boy, and at the same time most painful." On this matter there is an excellent warning from a learned man, which I will add here for the benefit of young people: "Scarcely on the first lips is it given to taste; that in love, if there is anything, it is sweet; the other part, the greater and chief, you will swallow with full hands and full throat, and you will be forced to swallow it, even unwilling, not only to satiety but also to nausea and disgust. Let us flee, my youth, let us flee this cupbearer, and let us not thirst for that," whence my labour.

units.la: Plus haurire mali est, quam ex re decerpere fructum.
units.tr: It is a greater evil to swallow than to pluck the fruit from the thing.

units.la: Quemadmodum in tepido, inquit alius: remissi caloris ac frigoris, quidam quasi cinnus est: ita multa sunt voluptatis, & doloris permistiones, ut cum alibi, tum in amatoria levitate.
units.tr: As in lukewarm water, says another, which is a kind of mixture of diminished heat and cold, so there are many mixtures of pleasure and pain, both elsewhere and especially in amorous levity.

units.la: Musæ ius inde stimulum Amoris vocat γλυκύπικρον.
units.tr: The Muses, therefore, call the goad of Love [γλυκύπικρον] "sweet-bitter."

units.la: Catullus: A Venere dulcis miscetur amaritics.
units.tr: Catullus: Sweetness is mixed with bitterness from Venus.

units.la: AMATORES apud Ienones excepti vino veteri: unguentis, balneis. Poen. 3. 3. v. 86. Omnia autem pro præsenti pecunia; instar militum.
units.tr: Lovers are received by pimps with old wine, unguents and baths. Poen. 3. 3. v. 86. All, however, for ready money, like soldiers.

units.la: AMANTES cùm non reciperentur à puellis intra ædes, deficientes faculas sub auroram ad ostium abjicere solebant. Alij etiam servidiores, accensâ et lumina ostio illidebant, & minitabantur exusti onem domus. De illis Merc. 2. 3. v. 74. Impleantur meæ fores clo giorum carbonibus.
units.tr: When lovers were not admitted into the house by the girls, they used to throw down torches at dawn at the door. Others, more ardent, struck their lit lamps against the door and threatened to burn down the house. Of these, Merc. 2. 3. v. 74.: Let my doors be filled with the coals of revelry.

units.la: De his Persius 4. 4. v. 20. Erant & medij inter hos, quibus sufficiebat, januas amicarum calcibus, impetere, aut ferro incidere, aut re, aut conscribillare, extincto titione. Petronius: Totam faciem ejus fuligine longa perfricuit, & non sentientis labra, humerque, sopitis titionibus pinxit. Sic Virgil. 8. Æn. Impositum cinerem, & sopitos suscitat ignes.
units.tr: Of these, Persius 4. 4. v. 20. There were also middling ones, for whom it was enough to strike their friends' doors with their feet, or to cut them with iron, or to scribble on them with charcoal, the brand having been extinguished. Petronius: He rubbed her whole face with long soot, and painted the lips and shoulder of the unfeeling one while she slept, with the embers smothered. So Virgil, Aeneid 8: He stirs up the ashes laid on, and the smouldering fires.

units.la: Nempe mala, carbone: bona, creta solebant notari. Persius Sat. 5.
units.tr: Bad things were usually marked with charcoal, good things with chalk. Persius, Sat. 5.

units.la: Quaq; sequenda forent, & quae vitanda vicissim, Illa prius creta, mox haec carbone notasti.
units.tr: And what was to be followed, and what was to be avoided in turn, you marked the former with chalk, the latter soon with charcoal.

units.la: Qui amans egens ingressus est praeceps in amoris vias, superavit arumnis is suis aerumnas Herculis. Nam cum Lenone, & cum Excetrâ, cum Cervo, cum Apro Ætolico, cum Avib° Stymphalicis, cum Antaeo deluctari mavelim, quàm cum Amore. Perf. 1. 1. v. 1. & seqq. Amatores itaque pauperes feruntur praecipites, & velut in barathrum quoddam, & profundam Amatoris foveam demerguntur: multi magis quàm divites: cum vix sit spes amore suo potiundi.
units.tr: A needy lover who has rushed headlong into the paths of love has surpassed the troubles of Hercules with his own distresses. For I would rather wrestle with the pimp, with the Hydra, with the stag, with the Aetolian boar, with the Stymphalian birds, with Antaeus, than with Love. Pers. 1. 1. v. 1. & seqq. Poor lovers are therefore carried headlong and sunk, as it were, into a certain pit and deep trench of Love, many more than the rich, since there is scarcely any hope of obtaining their love.

units.la: Amantes in convivijs has sibi delitias faciunt, ut una poscant, bibant. Asin. 4. 1. v. 26.
units.tr: Lovers at feasts make these delights for themselves, so that they call for and drink the same cups together. Asin. 4. 1. v. 26.

units.la: Tecum una poscat: aquè pocula potitet.
units.tr: Let him call for a cup with you together, and drink equally.

units.la: Amantes, ut sunt utrinque suspiciosi valde: ita admodum oderunt suspiciones paßivas. Asin. 4. 1. v. 29.
units.tr: Since lovers are very suspicious on both sides, they greatly hate suspicions directed at themselves. Asin. 4. 1. v. 29.

units.la: In convivijs sibi propinabant pocula: pedem premebant surgentes è lecto tricliniari. Ibid. Nictabant, nutabant, annuebant. Ibid. v. 39.
units.tr: At feasts they drank toasts to each other; rising from the dining couch they pressed each other's foot. Ibid. They winked, nodded and signalled assent. Ibid. v. 39.

units.la: Amatores muneri-gerùli sunt. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 48. Et Muneri-damni-geruli, Foras-gerones: Bonorum hamaxagoga. Truc. 2. 7. v. 1. 2. & seqq. Satinne, qui amat, nequit, quin nihil sit, neq; impro-bis se artibus expoliet? Improbafacta facit amator, bona sua prostercore habet: foras jubet ferri: mutuit publicos adiles.
units.tr: Lovers are bearers of gifts. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 48. And they are bearers of gifts and losses, carriers out, drawers-in of goods (bonorum hamaxagoga). Truc. 2. 7. v. 1. 2. & seqq. Is it not so that the lover, who is in want, cannot help but refine himself by wicked arts? The lover, making wicked deeds, regards his goods as dung; he has them carried out of doors and borrows from the public aediles.

units.la: Non omnis aetas ad perdiscendum sat est amanti, dum id perdiscat; quot pereat modis. Neque eam rationem eumpse umquam edocet Venus, quam penes amantem summa summarum redit. Trucul. 1. 1. v. 1. & seqq. quos omnes huc refer de incommodis, & periculis amantium.
units.tr: Not every age is long enough for a lover to learn, while he is learning it, all the ways he may come to ruin; nor does Venus ever teach him that reckoning, to which the sum of all sums for a lover comes back. Trucul. 1. 1. v. 1. & seqq. Refer all of these here, on the troubles and dangers of lovers.

units.la: Amantes sibi tabellas de suis amoribus scribebant. Pseud. I. I. v. 8.
units.tr: Lovers used to write letters to one another about their loves. Pseud. I. I. v. 8.

units.la: Amantes miseri: & sub Veneris regno se miserõr credebant. Quibus si quid mali accidisset, ejus iræ idipsum imputabant. Mathematici quoque eos à decimo anno ad 18. sub Venere esse dicunt. Itaque sacra ei faciebant, ut amore suo potirentur. Virginies icuncuclas ei conscerabant. Pseud. I. I. v. 13. Vide Meurs. Exerc. Crit. I 2. c. 8. p. 83.
units.tr: Wretched lovers, who believed they were miserable under the rule of Venus. If anything bad happened to them, they blamed it on her anger. The mathematicians also say that from the tenth to the eighteenth year people are under Venus. So they made sacrifices to her, so that they might gain possession of their love, and hung virginal little garlands for her. Pseud. I. I. v. 13. See Meursius, Exercitationes Criticae 1.2, c. 8, p. 83.

units.la: Non est justus amator, nisi qui perpetuat data; sive munera, detq; usq; quo nihil sit: simul amare desinat. Pseud. I. 3. v. 71. & Truc. 2. I. v. 23.
units.tr: A lover is not a just one unless he keeps up the gifts he has promised, and keeps giving until nothing is left; as soon as he stops giving, he stops loving. Pseud. I. 3. v. 71. & Truc. 2. I. v. 23.

units.la: Amori accedunt etiam hæc: Insomnia, ærumna, error, terror, & fuga, Ineptia, stultitiaque adeò & temeritas, Incogitantia, excors immodestia. Petulantia, cupiditas, & malevolentia: Inhæret etiam aviditas, desidia, incuria, Inopia, contumelia, & dispendium, Multiloquium, pauciloquium, hoc ideo fit, quia Quæ nihil attingunt ad rem, nec sunt usui, hæc Amator profert sæpe adverso tempore. Hoc pauciloquium rursum iccirco prædico. Quia nullus Amator unquam adeò est callidè Facundus, quæ in rem sint suam, ut possit loqui. Mercat. Prol. v. 24. & seqq.
units.tr: These also go with love: sleeplessness, distress, wandering, terror, flight; silliness, foolishness and rashness; thoughtlessness, witless immodesty, wantonness, desire and ill will; greed, idleness, carelessness, want, insult and loss; much talking and little talking. He often utters, at the wrong time, things that have nothing to do with the matter and are of no use. That is why I call his speaking little. For no lover is ever so skilled at speech that he can say what is to his own advantage. Mercat. Prol. v. 24. & seqq.

units.la: Morbos Amatorum accuratè exprimit Iena illa apud nostrum Asin. 1. 3. v. 6. Quam magis te in altum capessis, tam altius te in portum refert. Propriè. Sic enim vadati vinctique amore attinemur, ut Veneres nostras in oculis semper habere capiamur. Similitudo eadem Ovidio Epist. Cydippes Acontium: Ipsa velut navis factor, quam certus in altum Propellit Boreas: astu & unda refert.
units.tr: That famous procuress in our author, Asin. 1. 3. v. 6, describes the sicknesses of lovers accurately: The more you make for the open sea, the deeper it carries you back into harbour. That is exactly right, for lovers are so bound and fettered by love that they are caught always keeping their desires before their eyes. Ovid uses the same comparison in the letter of Cydippe to Acontius: just as a ship, which the north wind drives out to sea, is carried back by the wave and the wind.

units.la: Item Seneca Hyppolito act. 1. v. 176.
units.tr: Likewise Seneca, Hippolytus, act 1, v. 176.

units.la: --- quamemorasscio
units.tr: --- what you recall, nurse, I know

units.la: Vera esse nutrix. sed furor cogit sequi
units.tr: is true. But madness compels me to follow

units.la: Pejora. vadit animus in praeceps sciens,
units.tr: worse things. The mind rushes headlong, knowing

units.la: Rei meatq; frustra sana consilia expetens.
units.tr: its ruin, seeking in vain sane counsels.

units.la: Sic cum gravatam navita adversa ratem
units.tr: So when the sailor's ship, weighed down

units.la: Propellit unda: cedit in vanum labor,
units.tr: by an adverse wave is pushed back, the labour comes to nothing,

units.la: Et vitio pro puppis aufertur vado.
units.tr: and through the fault of the shoal is carried off its course.

units.la: Et Thyeste act. 3. v. 434.
units.tr: And in Thyestes, act 3, v. 434:

units.la: Placet ire pigris membris, sed genibus labant,
units.tr: It pleases me to go with sluggish limbs, but my knees give way;

units.la: Alioqui quam quo nitor, abductus feror.
units.tr: otherwise I am dragged off, carried where I strive not to go.

units.la: Sic insitator remige & vento ratem
units.tr: So the steersman, with oar and wind, drives the ship

units.la: Aestus resistens remigi & vento refert.
units.tr: against the surge, and with oar and wind brings it back.

units.la: Idem Seneca Medea v. 936. & Agamemnone v. 134. Et Ovid. Metam. VII.
units.tr: The same Seneca, Medea v. 936 and Agamemnon v. 134. And Ovid, Metamorphoses book 7.

units.la: utque carina
units.tr: As a keel which a contrary wind and a contrary tide

units.la: Quam ventus ventoq; rapit contrarius aestus,
units.tr: seize, and which the wind and the tide carry in opposite directions,

units.la: Vim geminam sentit, paretq; incerta duobus:
units.tr: feels a double force and obeys two uncertain powers,

units.la: Thesias haud aliter dubiis affectibus errat.
units.tr: so Thesias wanders with divided feelings.

units.la: Horat. lib. 2. Od. 7. Sed me per hostes, &c. Similia legas apud Statium lib. 1. 2. & 3. Thebaidos. Vide etiam Suspiciones Jani Gruteri.
units.tr: Horace, Odes 2.7: "But through enemies..." You will find similar passages in Statius, Thebaid books 1, 2 and 3. See also the Suspiciones of Janus Gruterus.

units.la: ITA est AMOR: balista ut jacitur: nihil sic celere est, neque volat: atque is hominum morös, & morosos efficit, minus placet magis, quod suadetur: quod dissuadetur placet: cum inopia est, cupias: quando ejus copia est, tum non velis. Ille qui aspellit, is compellit: ille qui consuadet, vetat. In sanum est malum in hospitium devorti ad Cupidinem. Trin. 3. 2. v. 42. & seqq.
units.tr: This is what love is like: as a ballista shoots a stone, nothing is so swift nor flies so fast; and it makes men fretful and peevish. What is urged pleases less, and what is forbidden pleases more; when it is lacking you desire it, and when it is plentiful you no longer want it. He who drives away, compels; he who advises, forbids. It is a bad thing to lodge with Cupid as a guest. Trin. 3. 2. v. 42. & seqq.

units.la: CORDE amantes sunt cati. Ibid. v. 51.
units.tr: Lovers are clever at heart. Ibid. v. 51.

units.la: MAGNA est amantium rabies, adeo ut amoribus satiari nequeant. Curc. 1. 3. v. 32. Viden' ut moliuntur? nequeunt completi satis.
units.tr: The rage of lovers is great, so that they cannot be sated with love. Curc. 1. 3. v. 32. See how they strive? Once sated, they cannot be satisfied.

units.la: Eandem rabiem exprimit Lucret. lib. 4.
units.tr: Lucretius, book 4, expresses the same rage.

units.la: Etenim potiundi tempore in ipso
units.tr: For at the very moment of possessing

units.la: Fluctuet Fluctuat incertis erroribus ardor amantum,Nec constat, quid primum oculis manibusq; fruantur.
units.tr: the ardour of lovers wavers in uncertain wanderings, nor is it settled which they should first enjoy with their eyes and hands.

units.la: Amantes in litteris puellarum animum defixum habent, non in pectore. Pseud. I.I. v.32.
units.tr: Lovers keep their mind fixed on the letters of girls, not on their heart. Pseud. I. I. v. 32.

units.la: Alium alio pacto propter amorem nisciam fecisse multa nequiter, verear magis me amoris causa isthoc ornatu (nauclerico) incedere. Verum cum multos multa admisse acceperim, inhonesta propter amorem, atque aliena a bonis. Mil. 4.7.v.1. & sequentibus.
units.tr: I do not know how another has done many wicked things for love; I am more afraid that I walk about in this dress (the sailor's) for love's sake. But since I have heard that many have done many things for love that were dishonourable and foreign to what is good, Mil. 4. 7. v. 1. & following.

units.la: Exemplo est Achilles, qui propter amorem Briseidis, cum ea sibi esset erepta, iratus Graecis, a proelio diu se abstinuit: & propter amorem Patrocli vitam brevem longae antepositi. Sic Jupiter libidinis & amoris causa omnia factus est, ac in omnes animalium ac rerum formas versus est.
units.tr: Achilles is an example, who, when Briseis had been taken from him, was angry at the Greeks and held back from battle for a long time; and because of his love for Patroclus he preferred a short life to a long one. So Jupiter was turned into everything for the sake of lust and love, and changed into all the shapes of animals and things.

units.la: Amatores hilaritatem & prandia amant. Esmuß getechtsfym.
units.tr: Lovers love merriment and feasts. Esmuß getechtsfym.

units.la: Unde Amatorie id dicuntur agere. Merc. 3.3. v. 20.
units.tr: Hence they are said to act amatorie. Merc. 3. 3. v. 20.

units.la: Amore nihil inquietius esse ostendit adolescens Mercat. 3. 4. v.1.
units.tr: A young man shows that nothing is more restless than love. Mercat. 3. 4. v. 1.

units.la: Summe ego homo miser, qui nunquam bene queo quiescere? Si dom' sum, foris est animus: sin foris sum, animus domi est. Ita mihi in pectore, atq; in corde facit Amor incendium.
units.tr: Oh, how wretched I am, who can never rest well! If I am at home, my mind is out; if I am out, my mind is at home. So Love makes a fire in my breast and in my heart.

units.la: Assimulate amare oportet: extemplo Melius illi multo quem amies, consulas, quam rei tuae. Cist. I.I.v 98.
units.tr: One must pretend to love: at once you will look after the one you love far better than your own affairs. Cist. I. I. v. 98.

units.la: Nihil amori injurium est: h.e. ludus est amantibus, fallere & inescare alios: quod de se Lena dicit. Cist. 1.1.v. 105.
units.tr: Nothing is wrong for love; that is, it is a game for lovers to deceive and entice others, as the procuress says of herself. Cist. 1. 1. v. 105.

units.la: Conciliaturus tibi puellam, primum matris tibi favorem acquires, secundum praeceptum Nasonis. Cist. I. v.94. Etjam muneribus ac donis opus est. Ibid. v.95. longa item consuetudine. Ibid. v.96.
units.tr: Wishing to win a girl for yourself, first gain the favour of her mother, following the precept of Naso. Cist. I. v. 94. And gifts and presents are needed too. Ibid. v. 95. A long acquaintance as well. Ibid. v. 96.

units.la: Animus amantum mundicia puellarum velut illecebra quadam capitur. Men. 2.3. v. 4.
units.tr: The mind of lovers is caught by the neatness of girls, as by a kind of lure. Men. 2. 3. v. 4.

units.la: Amaenitas loci allicit amantes. Ibid. v.5.
units.tr: The pleasantness of the place attracts lovers. Ibid. v. 5.

units.la: AMASIÆ forces nolunt claudi: ut intromittantur amatores. Men. 2.3.v.1.
units.tr: MISTRESSES do not want their doors shut, so that lovers may be let in. Men. 2. 3. v. 1.

units.la: IN amore solebant alij alijs esse potiores. Men. 3.3.v.8. De quo Amatorum regno vide, quæ adnotavi in Calligraphiâ Romanâ Tit. Amoris. Et Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: IN love some have always been more powerful than others. Men. 3. 3. v. 8. On this kingdom of lovers see what I have noted in my Calligraphia Romana, under the title Amoris, and in the Lexicon Plautinum.

units.la: OCULI sunt in amore duces. Sic Cistellariâ 1.1. v.93. ubi adolescens conspicillo consecutus est puellam usque ad fores. Et Bacch. 4.9.v.92.
units.tr: EYES are the leaders in love. So in Cistellaria 1. 1. v. 93, where the young man followed the girl with a spyglass right up to her door; and in Bacchides 4. 9. v. 92.

units.la: Ego animo cupido, atque oculis indomitis sui.
units.tr: I, eager in mind, and with eyes that cannot be restrained from her.
And Mercator 2. 1. v. 16.

units.la: Atque ego eam conspicio formâ eximiâ mulierem,Quam ego post quam aspexi, non ita amo, ut sani solent homines:sed eodem pacto, ut insani solent.
units.tr: And I see that woman of outstanding beauty; after I caught sight of her I do not love her as sane men usually do, but in the way that madmen do.

units.la: Ita de Tiberio Suetonius cap. 7. Et semel omnino ex occursu visum Agrippinam: adeo contentus & tumentibus oculis prosecutus est, ut custoditum fit, ne umquam in conspectum ejus postea veniret. Sic enim inquit Ausonius Epist. 10. amatoribus accidit, quando, ut ait Virgil. oculos in virgine figunt: Virgil. Eclog. 8. Ut vidi, ut perii! ut me malus abstulit error! Ovid. Epist. 12. Et vidi perii, nec notis ignibus arsi. Sic dicitur: κἀγὼ ὀφθαλμῶν γλυκὺς αἰδοίων.
units.tr: Suetonius says this of Tiberius, chapter 7: He saw Agrippina by chance only once, and followed her with such eager and swollen eyes that it was arranged that he should never come into her sight again. For Ausonius says, Epist. 10: this happens to lovers, when, as Virgil says, they fix their eyes on a maiden; Virgil, Eclogue 8: As soon as I saw her, I perished! How that wicked error carried me off! Ovid, Epist. 12: I saw, and perished, and did not burn with familiar fires. Thus it is said: And I too, sweet to the eyes of the modest [κἀγὼ ὀφθαλμῶν γλυκὺς αἰδοίων].

units.la: Contine oculos, ventrem: & quæ sub ventre sunt.
units.tr: Restrain your eyes, your belly, and what lies beneath the belly.

units.la: INDE Hesychio ὀμμάτια dicitur, hoc est, totus oculeus: quia sci-licet ex adspectu nascitur Amor.
units.tr: Hence in Hesychius ommatia [ὀμμάτια] is used, that is, all eye, because love is born from the sight.

units.la: Propert. lib. 2. & 15.
units.tr: Propertius, book 2 and 15.

units.la: Si nescis, oculi sunt in amore duces.
units.tr: If you do not know, eyes are the leaders in love.

units.la: Idem lib. 1. Eleg. 19.
units.tr: The same, book 1, elegy 19.

units.la: Non adeo leviter nostris puer hæsit ocellis.
units.tr: The boy did not cling so lightly to my eyes.

units.la: Idem lib. 1. Eleg. 32.
units.tr: The same, book 1, elegy 32.

units.la: Qui videt, is peccat; qui te non viderit ergo,Non cupiet: fallit crimina lumen habet.
units.tr: Whoever sees, sins; so whoever has not seen you will not desire you; the eye holds the guilt.

units.la: Idem lib. 3. Eleg. 2 1.
units.tr: The same, book 3, elegy 21.

units.la: Crescit enim assidue spectando cura puella.
units.tr: For care grows constantly as the girl is gazed upon.

units.la: Vide Prælectiones Passeratij ad Propert. lib. I. Eleg. I.
units.tr: See Passerat's Prelections on Propertius, book 1, elegy 1.

units.la: U L T R Ò in amore se offerre, temeritatis est, & contemtum parit. Mil. 4. 6. v. 28.
units.tr: To offer oneself too readily in love is rashness, and it brings contempt. Mil. 4. 6. v. 28.

units.la: P E R D I T E se amarunt Phaon Lesbius & Sappho. Mil. 4. 6. v. 32. Vide Ep. Ovid. & Scal. Ausón. Lect. lib. 2. c. 18.
units.tr: Phaon the Lesbian and Sappho loved each other to their ruin. Mil. 4. 6. v. 32. See Ovid's Epistles, and Scaliger on Ausonius, Lectiones, book 2, ch. 18.

units.la: A M O R omnia excusat. Mil. 4. 6. 37.
units.tr: Love excuses everything. Mil. 4. 6. 37.

units.la: Per amorem si quid fecero, ignoscet,
units.tr: If I have done anything through love, he will forgive it.

units.la: A M A N T E S præ suo amore flocci pendunt omnia sacra. Sic adolescens ille vel violari matrem suam nihili duxit, dum modo potiretur puella suâ. Pseud. I. I. v. 120. quamquam jocus est ambiguo té Tangere.
units.tr: Lovers care nothing for any sacred thing for the sake of their love. So that young man thought it of no account even that his mother should be violated, provided only he could have his girl. Pseud. I. I. v. 120. Though the joke turns on the ambiguous phrase to touch you.

units.la: C R E D O ego Amorem primum apud homines carnificinam commentum.
units.tr: I believe that Love was first invented among men as a torturer.

units.la: Hanc ego de me conjecturam domi facio, ne foras quæram, Qui omnes homines supero, atque antideo cruciabilitatibus animi, Jactor, crucior, agitor, stimulor, versor in Amoris rotâ misesr, Exanimor, feror, differor, distrahor, diripior. Ita nubilam mentem Animi habeo; ubi sum, ibi non sum, ubi non sum, ibi est animus. Ita mihi omnia ingenia sunt: quod lubet, non lubet jam id continuò. Ita me amor lassum animi ludificat, fugit, agit, appetit, Raptat, retinet, lactat, largitur, quod dat, non dat, deludit, Modò quod suasit, dissuadet, quod dissuasit, id ostentat. Maritumis moribus mecum experitur, ita meum frangit amantem Animum, neque nisi quia miser non eo pessum, mihi ulla abest Perdito pernicies. Cist. 2. I. v. I. & seqq.
units.tr: I make this conjecture about myself at home, so that I need not seek it abroad. I surpass all men and outdo them in the torments of the mind. I am tossed, tormented, driven, goaded, turned on the wheel of Love, wretched; I am breathless, carried off, torn apart, snatched in pieces. So my mind is clouded: where I am, I am not; where I am not, there is my mind. So all my moods are such that what pleases me does not please me for long. Thus Love mocks me, wearied with my mind: it puts me to flight, drives me, seeks me, snatches me, holds me, flatters me, bestows, and what it gives it does not give, it deceives; what it has just urged it dissuades, and what it has dissuaded it displays again. It deals with me like a husband, and so it breaks my lover's mind; nor is there any destruction lacking to me, except that, being wretched, I am not yet utterly undone. Cist. 2. I. v. I. & seqq.

units.la: A N I M A est amica amanti: si abest, nullus est: hoc est, mortuus est. Bacch. 2. 2. v. 16.
units.tr: The mistress is life to her lover: if she is absent, he is nothing, that is, he is dead. Bacch. 2. 2. v. 16.

units.la: H 3 Qna-
units.tr: H 3 Qna-

units.la: Quasi piscis, itidem est amator lenæ: nequam est nisi recens. Is habet succum, is suavitatem: cum quovis pacto condias, vel patinarium, vel assum verses quo pacto lubet. Asin. 1. 3. v. 28, &c.
units.tr: Like a fish, a lover of a procuress is the same: worthless unless he is fresh. He has juice, he has sweetness; season him in whatever way you like, as a dish of fish or as a roast, turn him as you please. Asin. 1. 3. v. 28, &c.

units.la: In amore nulius pudor. Mil. 3. 1. v. 29. 30.
units.tr: In love there is no shame. Mil. 3. 1. v. 29. 30.

units.la: Novo modo, tu homo, amas, si quidem te quicquam quod faxis, pudet.
units.tr: What a new fashion: you are a man, you love, if indeed you are ashamed of anything you do.

units.la: Nihil amas, umbra et amantum, magis quam amator.
units.tr: You love nothing more than a lover does; you are the shadow of lovers.

units.la: Amator sibi meretricis mores emit auro & purpurâ. Purpurâ extas occultanda est, auro turpe mulieris Mostell. 1. 3. v. 127. Vide Conjugij.
units.tr: A lover buys for himself a harlot's manners with gold and purple. The purple ought to be hidden; gold is a disgrace for a woman. Mostell. 1. 3. v. 127. See Conjugij.

units.la: Miser est homo, qui amat. Asin. 3. 3. v. 26. Theocritus in Hylâ sub finem: hoc est, miseri amantes: ut loquitur Propertius Eleg. 5. & 6. lib. 1. & Eleg. 20. lib. 2. Durius in terris nihil est, quod vivat amante. Unde infelix Dido identidem appellatur Virgil. & Catull. Dis invitis desinit esse miser: hoc est, desinit amare.
units.tr: He is a wretched man who loves. Asin. 3. 3. v. 26. Theocritus in the Hylas near the end: that is, wretched lovers, as Propertius speaks in Elegies 5 and 6 of book 1, and Elegy 20 of book 2: There is nothing on earth more hard than a lover who is alive. Hence Dido is repeatedly called unhappy by Virgil and Catullus. He ceases to be wretched against the will of the gods: that is, he ceases to love.

units.la: Vide etiam ex Persâ: Qui amat, ærumnas Herculis superat.
units.tr: See also from the Persa: He who loves surpasses the labours of Hercules.

units.la: Et Cistell. 2. 1. Amor commentum est carnificinam.
units.tr: And in the Cistellaria 2.1: Love is an invention of torture.

units.la: Amantes simul mori optant. Asin. 3. 3. v. 26. Propert. lib. 2. Eleg. 15.
units.tr: Lovers wish to die together. Asin. 3. 3. v. 26. Propertius, book 2, Elegy 15.

units.la: Atq; utinam hærentes sic nos vincire catenâVelles, ut numquam solveret una dies.
units.tr: Ah, would that you were willing to bind us, clinging together, with such a chain that no day would ever loosen it.

units.la: Ovid. Epist. Phedræ:
units.tr: Ovid, Epistle of Phaedra:

units.la: Iuppiter esse pium statuit quodcumque juvaret;Et fas omne facit fratre marita soror.Illa coit firmâ generis junctura catenâ:Impositit nodos cui Venus ipsa suos.
units.tr: Jupiter has decreed that whatever pleases is right, and a wife who is a sister makes every law lawful for her brother. She joins in the firm bond of kinship, the knot which Venus herself has tied.

units.la: Tibullus lib. 4. Eleg. 5.
units.tr: Tibullus, book 4, Elegy 5.

units.la: Nec sis nunc injusta Venus, vel serviat æqueVinctus uterq; tibi, vel mea vincla leva,Sed potius validâ teneamur uterq; catenâ,Nulla queat posthac quam solvisse dies.
