units.tr: Do not be unjust now, Venus; either let us both be equally bound to you, or lighten my chains; but rather let us both be held by a strong chain, which no day hereafter can loosen.

units.la: Numquam Amor quemquam, nisi cupidum hominem postulat se in plagas conjicere: eos cupit: eos insectatur, subdole blanditur, ab re consulit blandiloquentulus, harpago, mendax, cupipes, avarus, elegans, despoliator, latebricolarum hominum corruptor, blandus, inops, celati indagator. Nam qui ab eo, quod amat; quàm extemplo savijs sagittatis percussus est, illico res foras labitur, liquitur. Trin. 2. 1. v. 10. & seqq.
units.tr: Love never asks anyone but an eager man to cast himself into snares; it desires them, it hunts them down, it flatters them slyly, it gives crafty counsel with honeyed words: a hook, a liar, greedy-footed, avaricious, elegant, a despoiler, a corrupter of men who hide in corners, smooth-tongued, needy, a hunter of the hidden. For whoever is struck at once by the savage arrows of the one he loves, his property at once slips away and melts. Trin. 2. 1. v. 10. & seqq.

units.la: Qui in amore praecipitavit, pejus perit, quàm si saxo saliat: apage sis Amor. Tuas res tibi habe. Amor mihi amicus ne fias umquam: sunt tamen, quos miseros maleque habeas, quos tibi obnoxios fecisti. Trin. 2. 1. v. 30.
units.tr: He who has rushed headlong into love perishes worse than if he leapt from a rock. Away with you, Love! Keep your own affairs to yourself. Never become my friend; yet there are some whom you may hold as wretched and ill-used, whom you have made subject to you. Trin. 2. 1. v. 30.

units.la: Illecebrae feminarum, quibus juventus permulceri solet, olim Lege cohibitae fuerunt, quod ijs juventus corrumperetur. Quod equidem institutum sanctissimum esse, nemo non dixerit: ut ad famam, pudicitiam, remq; adolescentum conservandam plurimùm conferat. Ejus consuetudinis vestigia aliquot habemus in Plauto nostro. Asin. 1. 2. v. 5. 7. 26. ubi Argirippus adolescens, cùm bonam substantiae suae partem luxui, genioque indulgens, apud Lenam & Philenium meretricem, perlecebris utriusq; delinitus, insumsisset, atque domo, quod pecuniam tum nullam referret, excluderetur, minatur se illas delaturum ad Trium-viros capitales, & ibi earum nomina rei capitalis accusaturum. Sic antem ille: Bene merenti mala es, male merenti bona es: At cum malo tuo, nam nunc jam ex hoc loco Ibo ad tres-viros ego: vostrae ibi nomina Faxo capitis erunt: te perdam ego, et filiam. Perlecebrae, pernicies, adolescentum exitium. Nam Mare haud est mare: mare est vos acerrumum. Nam bona in mari repperi: hic clavi me bonis.
units.tr: The allurements of women, by which youth is usually softened, were once restrained by law, because youth was corrupted by them. Indeed no one would deny that this institution is most holy, since it greatly contributes to preserving the reputation, chastity and property of young men. We have some traces of this custom in our Plautus, Asin. 1. 2. v. 5. 7. 26., where the young man Argyrippus, indulging in luxury and his own pleasure, and charmed by the enticements of both, had spent a good part of his substance on the procuress Lena and the courtesan Philenium. Being shut out of the house because he then had no money to repay, he threatens to denounce them to the capital triumvirs and to accuse them there by name of a capital crime. He speaks thus: You are bad to one who deserves well, good to one who deserves ill. But to your cost, for from this place I will now go to the triumvirs; your names will be capital charges there. I will destroy you and your daughter. Allurements, ruin, the destruction of young men! For the sea is not the sea; the sea is you, most bitter. For I found my goods at sea; here I am nailed down by my goods.

units.la: Sic Trucul. 4. 2. verf. 47. 50. Dinarchus adolescens Phronesium meretricem, cujus blanditijs & illectibus, ipse cum alijs quam plurimis ad egestatis fere terminos redactus erat, cum intromittere cum ipsa nollet, comminatur se ream criminis apud magistratus postulaturum : neque etiam à manuum injectione in eam temperaturum : quòd dicat eam adversus praescripta legum pecuniam à plurimis corrasisse. Sic enim infit :
units.tr: Thus in the Truculentus 4. 2. vv. 47. 50. the young man Dinarchus, whose blandishments and enticements had reduced him, together with very many others, almost to beggary, when she refused to let him in with her, threatens to bring her before the magistrates as a defendant on a charge, and not to refrain from laying hands on her, because she has extorted money from very many men contrary to the prescriptions of the laws. For he begins thus:

units.la: Abiit intro, induit, ego ut hac mihi patiar fieri? jam hercle Ego tibi illecebra ludos faciam clamore in via, quae Adversum legem accepisti à plurimis pecuniam.
units.tr: She has gone inside. Am I to suffer this? By Hercules, I will make a show of you, enticer, with a shout in the street, because you have received money from many men contrary to the law.

units.la: Jam hercle apud omnes magistratus saxo erit nomen tuum. Posti id ego in te manum injiciam quadrupes venefica, Suppositrix puerum, ego Ædepol tua probra aperibo omnia.
units.tr: By Hercules, your name will be on a stone before all the magistrates. Then I will lay hands on you, four-footed poisoner, layer of substituted children; by Pollux, I will expose all your shames.

units.la: Ita Bacch. v.47. Nicobulus senex, cujus filium Mnesilochum, & sodalem ejus Pistoclerum, Bacchides meretrices corrupisse dicebantur, atque domi conclusos habere, introductus cum Philoxeno Pistoclerì patre, minitatur Bacchidibus, in jus eas se pertracturum, & vi majore in ipsas experturum, ni filios, & servum Chrysalum reddere maluit. Ait enim :
units.tr: So in the Bacchides v. 47. old Nicobulus, whose son Mnesilochus and his companion Pistoclerus the courtesans Bacchides were said to have corrupted and to keep shut up at home, comes in with Philoxenus, Pistoclerus' father, and threatens the Bacchides that he will drag them into court and proceed against them with greater force, unless they prefer to return the sons and the slave Chrysalus. For he says:

units.la: NI. Eccas tandem probri Perlecebra : & persuasrices : quid nunc? etiam redditis Nobis & filios, & servum. an ego experior tecum Vi majore?
units.tr: NI. Look at last, you allurements of disgrace and you persuaders! What now? Will you give back to us both the sons and the slave? Or shall I try you with greater force?

units.la: Quibus verbis Nicobulus comminatur, se in eas meretrices de vi publica accusationem instituturum, quòd se invito filium suum domi inclusum detineant : aut sanè talem vim illaturum, cui ab illis resisti non possit : nisi filios reddant.
units.tr: In these words Nicobulus threatens that he will bring a public accusation of violence against those courtesans, because they detain his son shut up at home against his will; or else he will inflict such force as they cannot resist, unless they return the sons.

units.la: Disputant autem Jurisconsulti : An & jure civili criminale judicium intendi in eam mulierem possit, per quam adolescens amator, luxuriosus; factus sit, & sumtibus immodicis exinanitus. Affirmantem partem tuetur Magnus ille Britanniæ Celticæ Jurisconsultus Janus Langlæus lib.8. Semestr. Otij c.6. Ego, inquit ille, Jure quoque civili adversus corruptorem, corruptricemve agi posse non dubitaverim. Nam & Alphenus, cùm Dominus servo dispensatori manumisso, rationes ab eo recepisset, & cùm de eis non constaret, comperisset apud quandam mulierculam pecuniam eum consumsisse : respondit, posse cùm servi corrupti cum eâ muliere agere : quamvis is servus jam liber esset : & etjam furti de pecuniis, quas ad eam servus detulisset. l. penult. ff. de serv. serv. corrupt. Quamobrem si filius obsonatorve meus aleâ luse-rit, scribit Baldus rub. C. de cond. ob tur. causas per tex. in l. sin. §. 1. de alea lusu, & aleat. posse me victorem cogere, ut meas pecu-nias mihi restituat. Sibi enim imputare debet aleator, qui collu-soris conditionem non exploravit. l. qui cum eo. ff. de reg. jur. Quod si sciverit eum de meo ludere, dubium non est, quin furti etiam adversus eum agere possim. l. servus. cujusdam. ff. de cond. ind. Unde perspicuum fit, Romano jure in eum, eamve, qui, quæve liberi hominis animum corruperit, extra ordine animad-verti posse. Nam ut & Gregorius ait Can. ex merit. 16. q. 1. Qui vitam morèsque bonorum corrumpunt, deteriores sunt his, qui substantias aliorum prædiaque diripiunt. Unde & apud Terentium Andr. ş. 4. Simo senex Critonem vehementer objurgat, quòd cum Athenas venisse dicat, ad fallendos adolescêtes rerum imperitos, eosdemque meretricijs amoribus & corruptelarum illecebris irretiendos, ejusque scelerâs cum pœnam daturum comminatur: solere enim Athenis malefi cia vindicari. Sic enim ait:
units.tr: The jurists debate whether a criminal action under civil law can be brought against the woman through whom a young man became a lover and a wastrel, and was drained by immoderate expenses. The great British-Celtic jurist Janus Langlaeus upholds the affirmative in Semestr. Otij book 8, ch. 6. "I would not hesitate," he says, "to hold that an action can be brought under civil law against a corrupter, male or female. For Alphenus, when a master had received accounts from a steward who had been freed, and found that these were not in order, and discovered that the man had spent money on a certain little woman, replied that the master could bring an action against that woman for corrupting the slave, even though he was now free, and also for theft of the money which the slave had conveyed to her. l. penult. ff. de serv. corrupt. Wherefore, if my son or my caterer gambles away money at dice, Baldus writes, rub. C. de cond. ob tur. causas, through the text in l. sin. §. 1. de alea lusu, & aleat., that I can compel the winner to restore my money to me. For a gambler must blame himself, if he has not inquired into the status of his partner. l. qui cum eo. ff. de reg. jur. But if he knew that the man was gambling with my money, there is no doubt that I can also bring an action for theft against him. l. servus. cujusdam. ff. de cond. ind." Hence it is clear that under Roman law a man or woman who has corrupted the mind of a free man can be punished extra ordinem. For, as Gregory also says, Can. ex merit. 16. q. 1. those who corrupt the lives and morals of good men are worse than those who tear apart the substance and estates of others. Hence also in Terence, Andr. 4., old Simo vehemently rebukes Critus, because, although he says he came to Athens to deceive young men inexperienced in affairs, and to ensnare them in courtesans' loves and the enticements of corruption, he threatens him with punishment for his crime, since at Athens crimes are usually avenged. He speaks thus:

units.la: S. Tune impunè facies? tunè hic homines adolescentulos Imperitos rerum, eductos liberè, in fraudem illicis? Sollicitando, & pollicitando eorum animos laetas? C R. Sanus nees?
units.tr: Sim. Will you get away with it? Will you here lure young men inexperienced in the world, reared as free men, into deceit, by enticing and promising to win their hearts? Cr. Are you in your right mind?

units.la: S. Ac meretricios amores nuptijs conglutinas?
units.tr: Sim. And you glue meretricious love affairs onto marriage?

units.la: Præterea & hoc sciendum, in mulierem, quòd adolescentem in fraudem pellexisse dicitur, non prius animadverti oportere, quàm apertis probationibus, vel perspicuis indicijs, ejus rei facta fides fuerit. Alb. d. l. pen. de serv. corr. Credendum enim in dubio potius est, eam adolescentis calliditate seductam, circumventamque fuisse. l. unic. in sin. C de rapt. virg. Nisi versuta subdolaque mulier fit, adolescens vero simplex & fraudis insciusss, cui facile imponi possit. Tales autem persuasrices seu allectatrices, sive, ut nostèr appellat Moss. 1. 3. v. 6. malesuadas feminas reperiri, mirum videri non debet, cum & traditum sit, fuisse, quæ vel ex professo huic rei operam darent. Nam & Demosthenem Theodorita vatidicam feminam, quòd servos ad fallendum instituerit accusasse, morteque multasse. Plutarchus memoriæ prodidit in Demosth.
units.tr: Moreover, this should also be noted: when a woman is said to have enticed a young man into deceit, she should not be punished until it has been established by clear proofs or plain indications that the fact is true. Alb. d. l. pen. de serv. corr. For in doubt it is rather to be believed that she was led astray and cheated by the young man's cunning. l. unic. in sin. C de rapt. virg. Unless the woman is crafty and deceitful, and the young man simple and ignorant of fraud, and so easily imposed upon. That such women who persuade or entice, or, as our author calls them, Moss. 1. 3. v. 6. "evil-counselling women," are to be found should not seem strange, since it is also recorded that some practised this trade as a profession. For Theodorus the seeress is said to have accused Demosthenes of training slaves to deceive, and to have had him put to death; Plutarch records this in his Life of Demosthenes.

units.la: Adolescentes amatores absentibus parentibus vocabant meretrices mulieres, quibus eam rem patris concedebant. Most. 2.1. v.32.
units.tr: Young lovers, when their parents were absent, used to summon courtesans, to whom they granted that privilege of their fathers. Most. 2.1 v.32.

units.la: Amatores filij, parentum mortem exoptant, ut liberius possint vivere. Bacch. 4.4. v.80. & 5.2. v.85. Most. 1.3. v.76.
units.tr: Lovers' sons long for their parents' death so that they may live more freely. Bacch. 4.4 v.80 and 5.2 v.85. Most. 1.3 v.76.

units.la: Amore pereunt quà juvenes quàm senes. Bacch. 5.2. v.85. Propertius: Tu verò quoniam semel es periturus amore, utere.
units.tr: By love men perish, young as well as old. Bacch. 5.2 v.85. Propertius: "Since you are destined once to perish for love, then make use of it."

units.la: Amoris summa est impatientia, quàm amator Calliodorus exprimit. Pseud. 1.1. v.92. Profecto nullo pacto possum vivere, si illa à me alienatur, atq; abducitur. Eandem exprimit adolescens Charinus Merc. 2.4. v.1.2.3.4.5. Vide locum.
units.tr: The sum of love is impatience, which the lover Calliodorus expresses: "Truly, I cannot live in any way if she is estranged and taken away from me." The young man Charinus expresses the same feeling. Merc. 2.4 v.1–5. See the passage.

units.la: Multi adolescentes Amorem virtuti anteponunt: adeóque decorant famam majorum suorum. Trin. 3.2. v.22.
units.tr: Many young men put love before virtue, and so disgrace the fame of their ancestors. Trin. 3.2 v.22.

units.la: Novus amator, vetus puer. In proverbio est Mercat. 5.4. v.15. Philostr. ἐν ταυτὶ ... Dicitur quoq; proverbio: Puer centum annorum. Esai. c.65.
units.tr: A new lover, an old boy. This is a proverb. Mercat. 5.4 v.15. Philostratus: [ἐν ταυτὶ ...]. It is also used as a proverb: a boy of a hundred years. Isaiah 65.

units.la: Amantium mos fuit, amicarum fores spargere mero, & ornare floribus. Curc. 1.1. v.89. & 1.3. v.4. Vide Muretum ad Fibull. & Lipf. Epist. Quæst. lib.4.22.
units.tr: It was the custom of lovers to sprinkle the doors of their mistresses with wine and to adorn them with flowers. Curc. 1.1 v.89 and 1.3 v.4. See Muretus on Tibullus, and Lipsius, Epist. Quaest. lib. 4, 22.

units.la: Nihil amat, qui ingratam, seu invitam amat. Perf. 2.2. v.46.
units.tr: No one loves who loves an ungrateful or unwilling woman. Perf. 2.2 v.46.

units.la: Amantes confidentes esse solent, Perf. 2.2. v.5. Confidentia illa militia militatur, non pondere.
units.tr: Lovers are wont to be confident. Perf. 2.2 v.5. "That warfare is waged with confidence, not with weight."

units.la: Amor non aliter alios complectitur, quàm se, & Genium suum. Lucr. 5.2. v.29.
units.tr: Love embraces others no differently than it embraces itself and its own Genius. Lucr. 5.2 v.29.

units.la: Mos est mulierum: omnes id faciunt, cum se amari intelligunt. Numquam ab amatore suo postulant, id, quod datum est: sed reliquum. True. Prol. v.14.
units.tr: It is the custom of women: all of them do this when they perceive they are loved. They never demand from their lover what has been given, but always the remainder. True. Prol. v.14.

units.la: Senes salaces, ebriosi, vomiturientes miseri amatores. Caf. 3.6. v.7.10. Vide Tit. Senum.
units.tr: Old men are lecherous, drunken, wretched lovers who vomit. Caf. 3.6 v.7–10. See the title Senum.

units.la: Amatores post cænam solebant comessari. Mostel. 1. 4. v. 5. 14. 22. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: Lovers used to revel after dinner. Mostel. 1.4 v.5, 14, 22. See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: Amatores parum agunt cum ratione: neque τὸ πρέπον observant, nullius habentes respectum. Merc. Prol. v. 16.
units.tr: Lovers act with little reason; they do not observe what is fitting, having regard for no one. Merc. Prol. v.16.

units.la: Amorem hæc cuncta vitia sectari solent, cura, ægritudo, nimiaqs elegantia. Merc. Prol. v. 18. Vide etiam Cultus.
units.tr: All these vices are wont to follow love: care, sickness, and excessive finery. Merc. Prol. v.18. See also Cultus.

units.la: Ab amore excusant vitia adolescentes. Aul. 4. 10. v. 15. Quæ tamen excusatio nulla. Ib.
units.tr: Young men excuse their vices by love. Yet that excuse is worth nothing. Aul. 4.10 v.15. Ib.

units.la: Amantes nisi votis suis potiantur, perpetuo fluctuant. Merc. 3. 4. v. 15. Tristis incedit, pectus ardet, quassat caput. Nesciunt ubi sint, an vivi an mortui. Ib.
units.tr: Lovers, unless they obtain their wishes, fluctuate endlessly. Merc. 3.4 v.15. "He walks sadly, his breast burns, he shakes his head." They do not know where they are, whether alive or dead. Ib.

units.la: Amicæ ut placerent suis amatoribus, ad speculum se exornabant. Mostel. 1. 3. v. 90. Vide Speculorum.
units.tr: Mistresses, so that they might please their lovers, adorned themselves before the mirror. Mostel. 1.3 v.90. See Speculorum.

units.la: Quem impensa amabant, ei dicere solebant, paratos se partem annorum suorum dare. Asin. 3. 3. v. 20. Seneca de Brev. vitæ c. 8. vide Muret. Var. Lect. lib. 9. c. 1.
units.tr: To the one whom they loved most intensely, they used to say they were ready to give part of their own years. Asin. 3.3 v.20. Seneca, De brevitate vitae c. 8; see Muretus, Var. Lect. lib. 9, c. 1.

units.la: Servire amanti miseria est, præsertim qui quod amat, caret. Pœn. 4. 1. v. 4.
units.tr: To serve a lover is misery, especially for one who lacks what he loves. Poen. 4.1 v.4.

units.la: Amantes sibi somnia fingunt. Sic adolescens audiens legi litteras ab puella scriptas, videbat sibi cum ea fabulari. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 60.
units.tr: Lovers invent dreams for themselves. Thus a young man, hearing letters written by a girl being read aloud, seemed to himself to be conversing with her. Pseud. 1.1 v.60.

units.la: Amatores sunt instar signi picti in pariete, absque omni sensu. Merc. 2. 2. v. 44.
units.tr: Lovers are like a painted image on a wall, without any sense at all. Merc. 2.2 v.44.

units.la: Humanum amare est: humanum autem ignoscere est. Ib. v. 48.
units.tr: To love is human; but to forgive is human too. Ib. v.48.

units.la: Amor facit, ut sæpe disparis formæ, ætatis, &c. copulentur. Asin. 1. 3. v. 4.
units.tr: Love causes people often of unequal beauty, age, and so on, to be joined together. Asin. 1.3 v.4.

units.la: Horatius lib. 1. Od. 33. Sic visum Veneri, &c.
units.tr: Horace, Odes 1.33: "So it seemed good to Venus," etc.

units.la: Amatores ferre moram nequeunt. Pœnol. 3. 1. v. 1. Tardo amico nihil est quicquam iniquius: præsertim homini amanti, qui quicquid agit, properat omnia: sicut ego his duco advocatis homines spissigradissimos tardiores, quam corbita sunt in tranquillo mari.
units.tr: Lovers cannot bear delay. Poenul. 3.1 v.1. "Nothing is more unfair than a slow friend, especially to a man in love, who hurries in everything he does; so I consider those slow-moving men, whom I summon as witnesses, slower than merchant ships on a calm sea."

units.la: AMATORES pallio reprehendebantur ab amasijs. Mil. I. I. v. 60. Eosdem Achilles laudant ob formam. Ib.
units.tr: LOVERS were rebuked by their mistresses for their cloak. Mil. I.1 v.60. The same men are praised by Achilles for their beauty. Ib.

units.la: AMATORES dum florent divitijs: & dum possunt dare, dicuntur vivere; Sin minus, mortui sunt. Pseud. I. 3. v. 76. Trucul. I. 2. v. 61.
units.tr: LOVERS, while they flourish in riches, and while they can give, are said to live; if not, they are dead. Pseud. I.3 v.76. Truc. I.2 v.61.

units.la: AMOR caecitatem inducit. Sic Pleusides: Honoris causa hercle ego oculo utor minus. Nam si amore abstinuissem, tamquam hoc utere. Mil. 4. 7. v. 25.
units.tr: LOVE induces blindness. So Pleusicles: "By Hercules, for the sake of honour I use my eye less. For if I had abstained from love, I would use it as you do." Mil. 4.7 v.25.

units.la: AMOR mutuus est optimus cultu, & suavissimus. Cist. I. 3. v. 45. Mil. 2. I. v. 23.
units.tr: Mutual LOVE is the best and most pleasant companionship. Cist. I.3 v.45. Mil. 2.1 v.23.

units.la: NON jucundum est, nisi amans facit stultè. Asend. I. 3. v. 8.
units.tr: Nothing is pleasant unless the lover acts foolishly. Asin. I.3 v.8.

units.la: AMANTES nihili sunt. Ibid. v. 10.
units.tr: Lovers are worth nothing. Ibid. v.10.

units.la: O CUPID O, quantus es? Nam tu quemvis confidentem facile tuis factis facis. Eundem ex confidente, a stutum diffidentem denuò. Merc. 5. 2. v. 16. Lege totam scenam, quae desperati amoris affectibus abundat.
units.tr: O CUPID, O, how great you are! For you easily make anyone confident by your deeds, and again you make the same man from confident become diffident and despairing. Merc. 5.2 v.16. Read the whole scene, which abounds in the feelings of hopeless love.

units.la: AMANTES dum differuntur hominum sermonibus, non audire solent: eoq; surdi dicuntur esse. Contra tamen uxor senis. Cas. 3. 3. v. 12.
units.tr: Lovers, while they are discussed in people's talk, are wont not to hear, and so are said to be deaf. On the contrary, however, the old man's wife. Cas. 3.3 v.12.

units.la: AMATORES saepe solent verba dare suis amasijs. Asin. 3. I. v. 22. An tu tibi verba blanda esse aurum rere?
units.tr: Lovers are often wont to deceive their mistresses with words. Asin. 3.1 v.22. "Do you think your flattering words are gold?"

units.la: AMATORES saepe decipiunt amasias inani spe mortis propinquorum suorum. Asin. 3. I. v. 26.
units.tr: Lovers often deceive their mistresses with the empty hope of their relatives' death. Asin. 3.1 v.26.

units.la: Quid mirum fecit, quid novum? adolescens homo, si amat, si amicam liberat? Pseud. I. 5. v. 20.
units.tr: What is strange, what is new about it? A young man, if he loves, if he sets his mistress free? Pseud. I.5 v.20.

units.la: AMATORES initiabant Deo munditianti, h.e. Veneri. Casin. 2. 3. v. 9.
units.tr: Lovers used to initiate themselves into the god of adornment, that is, Venus. Casin. 2.3 v.9.

units.la: UNGEBANT quoq; se lepido unguento. Ib. v. 10.
units.tr: They also anointed themselves with a pleasant ointment. Ib. v.10.

units.la: AMATORES olium diligenter observare solebant. Curc. I. I. v. 15. 20. etiam vino perfundebant. Ib. v. 80.
units.tr: Lovers used carefully to observe leisure; they also drenched themselves with wine. Curc. I.1 v.15, 20. Ib. v.80.

units.la: LIMIS oculis sese amantes intuentur. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 12. Terent. Eun. 3. 5. Quintil. lib. 2. c. 3. quadam voluptate suffusi: aut limi, aut sic. ut sic dicam, Venerei. Apil. Mil. 11. Ad me conversa limis, & morsicantibus oculis. Varro apud Nonium: Multi qui limina intrarent integris oculis strabones sunt facti.
units.tr: Lovers gaze at each other with bleary eyes. Bacch. 5.2 v.12. Terence, Eun. 3.5. Quintilian, lib. 2, c. 3: "suffused with a certain pleasure: bleary, or so to speak, Venereal." Apuleius, Met. 11: "turned towards me with bleary and biting eyes." Varro, quoted by Nonius: "Many who entered the threshold with sound eyes became squinting."

units.la: Qui sefeamant, feriatos dies agitant. Caf. I. 1. v. 49. Meum festus dies: meus pullus. Capt. 3.1.v.8. Epid. 3.4.v.37. Mil. 1.1.v.7. Terent. Eun. 4.4. Vide etiam Martial. lib. 3.47. Symm. l.1. Ep. 1. & lib.3. Ep.81.
units.tr: Those who take holiday keep feast days. Casin. I.1 v.49. "My festal day, my little chick." Capt. 3.1 v.8. Epid. 3.4 v.37. Mil. 1.1 v.7. Terence, Eun. 4.4. See also Martial lib. 3, 47; Symmachus lib. 1, Ep. 1, and lib. 3, Ep. 81.

units.la: Amatores comparantur salsis muriaticis. Toen. 1.2.v.31. Cogita amabo, item nos perhiberi, quasi falsa muriatica esse autumantur sine omni lepore, & sine suavitate, nisi multa aqua usq; & diu macerantur, olent, falsa sunt, tangere, ut non velis: item nos sumus: ejus feminis mulieres sunt insulsa admodum, atque invenusta sine munditie & summa.
units.tr: Lovers are compared to salted, brined fish. Toen. 1.2 v.31. "Consider, I beg you, that we too are said to be like brined fish, without any charm or sweetness, which, unless they are soaked long and thoroughly in much water, smell and are unpleasant to touch, so that you do not want them; so we are, and women of that kind are very insipid and unlovely, without neatness and grace."

units.la: Amantes vitam omnem ponunt in delitijs, & amoribus suis. Curc. 1.3.v.16. Pseud. 5.1.v.10.
units.tr: Lovers put their whole life into their pleasures and loves. Curc. 1.3.v.16. Pseud. 5.1.v.10.

units.la: Amantium gestus disciplinam & indolem exponit servus. Pseud. 5.1.v.13. Ubi amans complexus est amantem, ubi labra ad labella adjungit: ubi alter alterum bilinguij manuscripto inter se prehendunt, ubi mamma manicula opprimitur alia, aut si lubet corpora conduplicant.
units.tr: The gestures of lovers are set out, with their manners and character, by a slave. Pseud. 5.1.v.13. Where the lover embraces the beloved, where he joins lip to lip, where they clasp each other with bilingual hands, where one hand grips a breast, or, if they please, they press their bodies together.

units.la: Nefandae Veneris posticae exemplum vide Caf. 2.8. v. 25. & sequentibus.
units.tr: For an example of unspeakable back-door intercourse, see Cas. 2.8.v.25 and following.

units.la: Amoris summa est impotentia, an impudentia, ut voluptates illas vanas vaniffimis nugis comparare satagat. Sic Caf. 2.8.v.21.
units.tr: Love is supreme folly, or shamelessness, when a man labours to win those empty pleasures with the emptiest trifles. So Cas. 2.8.v.21.

units.la: Quia te tango, mel videor lingere.
units.tr: Because I touch you, I seem to be licking honey.

units.la: Haec facetia est amare inter se rivales duos. Stich. 5.4.v.47. Hoc memorabile est, ego tu sum, tu es ego, uni amici sumus. Vide simREFERENCE lem locum in Querolo Gildae, Scen. 6.
units.tr: It is a witty point that two rivals love the same woman. Stich. 5.4.v.47. This is memorable: "I am you, you are I, we are one friend." See a similar passage in Gildas's Querolus, Scene 6.

units.la: Amantes spem, & vitam omnem in amoribus collocatam habent. Mil. 4.2.v.60.
units.tr: Lovers place their hope and their whole life in their loves. Mil. 4.2.v.60.

units.la: De superbo & glorioso amatore, qualis fuit Miles, dici potest. Mil. 4.2.v.67. Dixi hoc tibi dudum, & nunc dico, nisi huic Verri affertur merces,
units.tr: What is said of the proud and boastful lover may be said of the Soldier. Mil. 4.2.v.67. I told you this before and I say it now: unless merchandise is brought to this Verres,

units.la: Non hic suo seminio quamq; porecclam impertiturus est.
units.tr: He will not bestow on her his seed, however much he cares for her.

units.la: TALUS ludus amatorum. Bacch. i.i. v.38. Vide Tit. Talorum. Itemque malacum pallium gestabant amatores Graeci in scenis. Bacch. i.i. v.38. Pallium hoc appellabant σίνθεσιν.
units.tr: DICE are the game of lovers. Bacch. 1.1.v.38. See the title Talorum. Likewise lovers among the Greeks wore a soft cloak on the stage. Bacch. 1.1.v.38. They called this cloak sinthesis [σίνθεσιν].

units.la: AMANTES puellae per Venerem jurabant. Stich. 5. f. v.i. Ita me Venus amena amet!
units.tr: GIRLS in love swore by Venus. Stich. 5.f.v.1. So may lovely Venus love me!

units.la: IN amore apud meretrices vapulat peculium. Stich. 5. f. v.10.
units.tr: IN love the purse is beaten among courtesans. Stich. 5.f.v.10.

units.la: ANIMA est amica amanti. Vita enim amicae, vita est amantis. Bacch. 2.2. v.16.
units.tr: The soul is the beloved to the lover, for the life of the beloved is the life of the lover. Bacch. 2.2.v.16.

units.la: AMOR pallorem inducit. Terf. i. i. v.24. Palleo, quia paucium salus sum in Veneris praelio: Sagitta Cupido cor meum transfixit.
units.tr: LOVE brings on paleness. Ter. 1.1.v.24. I am pale, because I am scarcely safe in the battle of Venus: Cupid's arrow has pierced my heart.

units.la: AMANS quid cupiat, scit: quid sapiat, non videt: inquit Syrus. Merc. 2. 3. v.
units.tr: A LOVER knows what he desires, but does not see what is wise, says Syrus. Merc. 2.3.v.

units.la: Animi in pectore incerti certant decem: nec quid corde nunc consilij capere possim scio: tantus cum cura meus est error animo.
units.tr: My mind, uncertain, is pulled in ten directions in my breast: I know not what counsel I can now take in my heart; so great is the error of my mind in its trouble.

units.la: AMOR fastidit omnia adversa, unde adolescens ille: Ararre malerlim, quam sic amare. Ibid.
units.tr: LOVE scorns all adverse things, whence that young man: I would rather perish than love like this. Ibid.

units.la: Qui amat, quod amat, si id habet, id habet pro cibo. Merc. 4. 4. v.4. Vide paulo ante.
units.tr: Whoever loves what he loves, if he has it, has it as food. Merc. 4.4.v.4. See a little above.

units.la: AMASIAE solent amatoribus ebibere sanguinem. Curc. i. 2. v. 65. Ita apud Thean. Idyll. 2. Puella inquit: αἰ αἰ ἔρως ἀμφεί. τί μεν μέλαν ἐν χροῒ ἅμα ἀμφὶς, ὡς λιμνᾶτις ἅπαν ἐν βδέλλα πέπωλας.
units.tr: MISTRESSES are wont to drink the blood of their lovers. Curc. 1.2.v.65. So in Theocritus, Idyll 2, the girl says: "Ah, ah, Eros hovers round me. Why, like a leech in a pool, have you sucked up all the dark blood from my skin?" [αἰ αἰ ἔρως ἀμφεί. τί μεν μέλαν ἐν χροῒ ἅμα ἀμφὶς, ὡς λιμνᾶτις ἅπαν ἐν βδέλλα πέπωλας.]

units.la: Heu mihi tristis Amor; quam mihi atrum e corpore sanguinem veluti palustris hirundo inhaerens omnem exsuxisti!
units.tr: Alas, sad Love; how like a swallow clinging to a marsh you have sucked all the dark blood out of my body!

units.la: AMANTES nomina sua cieri, & nominari amant. Asin. 4. i. v.34.
units.tr: LOVERS like their names to be called and spoken. Asin. 4.1.v.34.

units.la: ZELOTUS piam amantium egregie exprimit Plautus. Asin. 4. i. initio scenae.
units.tr: Plautus admirably expresses the zeal of lovers' piety. Asin. 4.1, at the beginning of the scene.

units.la: Ludus amatorum & disciplina notatur Asin. 1.3,v.73.
units.tr: The game and discipline of lovers is noted in Asin. 1.3.v.73.

units.la: Amatores ægre ferunt alios quoque rivales admitti. Asin. 1.3, v.83.
units.tr: Lovers take it ill that other rivals too are admitted. Asin. 1.3.v.83.

units.la: Malus clandestinus est: Amor, damnum est merum. Curc. 1.1, v.49.
units.tr: A clandestine lover is a bad thing: love is pure loss. Curc. 1.1.v.49.

units.la: Amor cæcitatem inducit. Mil. 4.6. v.4.4.45.
units.tr: Love brings on blindness. Mil. 4.6.v.44-45.

units.la: Amantes mortem sibi præoptabant, videntes se spoliari suis a-moribus. Cist. 3.1. v.9. Merc. 2.4.v.3. Vide Tit. Mortis.
units.tr: Lovers prayed for death for themselves, seeing that they were stripped of their loves. Cist. 3.1.v.9. Merc. 2.4.v.3. See the title Mortis.

units.la: Amor facit morosogos, & stultos homines Perf. 1,1.v.50. Amoris vitio, non meo nunc tibi morologus fio.
units.tr: Love makes men morose and foolish. Pers. 1.1.v.50. "Through love's fault, not my own, I now become a grumbler to you."

units.la: Adolescentes amoribus indulgentes, pereunt. Bacch. 3.3. v. 64. & seqq.
units.tr: Young men who indulge in love perish. Bacch. 3.3.v.64 and following.

units.la: Celerem oportet esse amatoris manum in scribendis libris ad amicam. Bacch. 4.4. v. 85.
units.tr: A lover's hand should be quick in writing books to his mistress. Bacch. 4.4.v.85.

units.la: Amatores solent omne aurum, quod a parentibus accipiunt, in lustris comedere: & congræcare. Bacch. 4.4. v.91.
units.tr: Lovers are wont to eat up in brothels all the gold they receive from their parents, and to squander it on Greek living. Bacch. 4.4.v.91.

units.la: Qui ipse haud amavit, ægre amantis ingenium inspicit. Mil. 3. 1. v. 43.
units.tr: One who has never loved himself scarcely understands the nature of a lover. Mil. 3.1.v.43.

units.la: Summa in Amore felicitas, invicem æque amori. Cistell. 1.3. v.45. Mil. 2.1.v.23. Et illo illum contra, qui est amor cultu optimus, li-cet in Cist. amor suavissimus. Catullus: Mutuis animis amant, amantur. Bion: ἀγλον ... (Greek)
units.tr: The highest happiness in love is mutual love equal on both sides. Cist. 1.3.v.45. Mil. 2.1.v.23. And the best love is that which answers love in kind, though in Cistellaria it is the sweetest love. Catullus: "They love with mutual hearts, and are loved." Bion: [ἀγλον ...]

units.la: Amatores dicuntur litteras discere in ludo Venereo. Sic gehen auch in die Schul. Truc. 4.2. v.22.
units.tr: Lovers are said to learn their letters in the school of Venus. So they also go to school. Truc. 4.2.v.22.

units.la: Amor morbus est: & mutatur perfidiose illos magistratus, qui pecuniam sibi commissam depeculantur. Cist. 1.1. v.74.
units.tr: Love is a sickness, and those magistrates change treacherously who plunder the money entrusted to them. Cist. 1.1.v.74.

units.la: Amor est impatiens moræ. Spissum istud amanti verbum est Venit, nisi venit. Cist. 1.1.v.77.
units.tr: Love is impatient of delay. That word "Come, unless he comes" is a hard one for a lover. Cist. 1.1.v.77.

units.la: Amare mare est: & cavendum amare tamquam a mari. Trucul. 5, v. 1.
units.tr: To love is to be at sea, and one must beware of loving as one would beware of the sea. Truc. 5.v.1.

units.la: Amantes quei soleant affectus suos exprimere, quibus gestibus ac factis, graphicè depingit amasia adolescentis. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 62. & seqq.
units.tr: How lovers are wont to express their feelings, by what gestures and acts, the mistress of a young man depicts vividly. Pseud. 1.1.v.62 and following.

units.la: Quod amamus, osculari licet. Merc. 3. 3. v. 12.
units.tr: What we love it is permitted to kiss. Merc. 3.3.v.12.

units.la: Senem osculari mulierem turpe est. Ib. v. 13. Quia nimirum vomitum excutit mulieri. Ibid. Ideò Vervece dicti. Ibid.
units.tr: It is shameful for an old man to kiss a woman, since indeed it stirs up her vomit. For this reason they were called Vervece. Ibid.

units.la: Adolescentes quasi religioni sibi ducunt, amicæ maledicere, & minari. Bacch. 3. 4. v. 5.
units.tr: Young men think it a kind of religious duty not to speak ill of, or threaten, their mistresses. Bacch. 3.4.v.5.

units.la: Amorum conciliatrix est Venus. Mil. 4. 6. v. 12. Illam adorabant ut propitiam sibi. Ib. v. 15.
units.tr: Venus is the go-between of loves. Mil. 4.6.v.12. They worshipped her as one favourable to them. Ibid. v.15.

units.la: Amatores in foro stabant. Capt. 3. 1. v. 18.
units.tr: Lovers used to stand in the forum. Capt. 3.1.v.18.

units.la: Amor vetus non tamen obsolescit. Cistell. 1. 1. v. III.
units.tr: An old love does not however grow stale. Cist. 1.1.v.111.

units.la: Amoris comes egestas. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 38. Quid agitur? C A. amatur, atq; egetur acriter.
units.tr: Poverty is the companion of love. Pseud. 1.3.v.38. "What is going on? C. He is loved, and sorely in want."

units.la: In amore dona sint oportet. Most. 1. 3. v. 28.
units.tr: In love there should be gifts. Most. 1.3.v.28.

units.la: Matronæ, non meretricium est, unum inservire amantem. Most. 1. 3. v. 33.
units.tr: It is not the business of a matron, but of a courtesan, to serve one lover. Most. 1.3.v.33.

units.la: Amatores solent esse cavillatores faceti, commodi convivæ. Mil. 3. 1. v. 46.
units.tr: Lovers are wont to be jesters, witty and agreeable table companions. Mil. 3.1.v.46.

units.la: Amatores vovebant mane Veneri jentaculum. Curc. 1. 1. v. 72.
units.tr: Lovers used to vow a breakfast to Venus in the morning. Curc. 1.1.v.72.

units.la: Non decet senes amare, sed adolescentes. Merc. 5. 4. v. 23. 25. 27. Vide etiam Tit. Adulteri.
units.tr: It is not fitting for old men to love, but for young men. Merc. 5.4.v.23, 25, 27. See also the title Adulteri.

units.la: Non vestem amatores mulieris amant, sed vestis fartum: h.e. corpus ipsum, quod in veste. Most. 1. 3. v. 13.
units.tr: Lovers love not a woman's dress but the stuffing of the dress, that is, the body itself which is within the dress. Most. 1.3.v.13.

units.la: Amoris arrhabonem annulum dabant. Mil. 4. 1. v. 11.
units.tr: They gave a ring as a pledge of love. Mil. 4.1.v.11.

units.la: Amantes Oculum appellabant amicas suas. Most. 1. 3. v. 152. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: Lovers called their mistresses their eye. Most. 1.3.v.152. See the Lexicon to Plautus.

units.la: Amor multos illexit in dispendium. Merc.Prol. v. 53.
units.tr: Love has enticed many to their loss. Merc. Prol. v.53.

units.la: Amantes non possunt pati suas ab alijs basiari. Mortem potius volunt. Truc. 5. v. 34.
units.tr: Lovers cannot bear that their mistresses be kissed by others; they would rather die. Truc. 5.v.34.

units.la: Amor omnia celat vitia. Trucul. 5. v. 42. Quamquam hic horridus est, quamquam hic squalidus est: at est bellus mihi.
units.tr: Love conceals all faults. Truc. 5.v.42. Although she is rough, although she is squalid, yet she is lovely to me.

units.la: Amatores inungebant se oleo. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 77. coq; lenones olei δωάμει probè instructi erant.
units.tr: Lovers anointed themselves with oil. Pseud. 1.2.v.77. And pimps were well supplied with oil for its scent [δωάμει].

units.la: Ex Amore tantum est homini incendium. Asin. 5. 2. v. 69.
units.tr: From love alone comes a fire to man. Asin. 5.2.v.69.

units.la: Amor velut imber adobruit, & prosternit adolescentiam. Mostell. 1. 2. v. 61.
units.tr: Love, like a storm of rain, overwhelms and lays low youth. Mostell. 1.2.v.61.

units.la: Amantes solent insistere plantam pedum. Asin. 4. 1. v. Casin. 4. 4. v. 20. & 23.
units.tr: Lovers are wont to stand on tiptoe. Asin. 4.1.v.; Cas. 4.4.v.20 and 23.

units.la: Ovidius;
units.tr: Ovid

units.la: Velle latus digitis: & pede tange pedem.
units.tr: Let him wish to touch your side with his fingers, and touch your foot with his foot.

units.la: Amatores luxuriæ & Genio suo indulgentes tandem ad inopiam rediguntur. Prol. Trin. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: Lovers who indulge in luxury and their own Genius are at last reduced to poverty. Prol. Trin. v. 1 and following.

units.la: Amatores decet esse dicaces & facetos. Caf. 3. 1. v. 15.
units.tr: Lovers ought to be witty and charming. Caf. 3. 1. v. 15.

units.la: Amoribus & luxu adolescentes, vel optimi corrumpi solent. Most. 1. 1. v. 20. & seqq.
units.tr: Young men, even the best of them, are usually corrupted by love and luxury. Most. 1. 1. v. 20 and following.

units.la: In amoribus mater puellæ primum compellanda. Mil. 2. 1. v. 28.
units.tr: In love affairs, the girl's mother is to be addressed first. Mil. 2. 1. v. 28.

units.la: Amatores jurabant per Dionam & Venerem. Mil. 3. v. 21.
units.tr: Lovers used to swear by Dione and Venus. Mil. 3. v. 21.

units.la: Amor locuples piscatus est bonus. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 69.
units.tr: A wealthy lover makes a good catch, like a fish. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 69.

units.la: Amantes sæpe Nocti, aut Diei, aut Soli, aut Lunæ miserias suas narrant. Merc. Prol. v. 4.
units.tr: Lovers often tell their troubles to the Night, or the Day, or the Sun, or the Moon. Merc. Prol. v. 4.

units.la: Amantes moram nullam ferre possunt, Merc. 5. 2. v. 55. Longinquum istuc amanti est.
units.tr: Lovers cannot bear any delay: "That is a long way off for a lover." Merc. 5. 2. v. 55.

units.la: Amatores decet esse morigeros probè. Men. 1. 3. v. 20.
units.tr: Lovers ought to be truly obliging. Men. 1. 3. v. 20.

units.la: Amatores meretricias artes sectantes fidem, remque, teq;, suosque properant perdere. Epid. 2. 2. v. 36.
units.tr: Lovers who pursue the arts of harlots hasten to lose their credit, their property, and themselves and their own. Epid. 2. 2. v. 36.

units.la: Amatoribus in amationibus solet pallium abripi. Caf. 5. 2. v. 45. & 5. 3. v. 6.
units.tr: In love affairs, lovers are often stripped of their cloak. Caf. 5. 2. v. 45 and 5. 3. v. 6.

units.la: Quasi piscis, itidem amator nequam est, nisi recens. Asin. 1. 3. v. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 25.
units.tr: Like a fish, a lover is worthless unless he is fresh. Asin. 1. 3. v. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 25.

units.la: Amor læ1vos facit homines. Amph. 1. 3. v. 43.
units.tr: Love makes men foolish. Amph. 1. 3. v. 43.

units.la: AMANTES sese perpetuo nominant. Bacch. 2.2.v.32.
units.tr: Lovers are forever calling themselves by name. Bacch. 2. 2. v. 32.

units.la: AMOR ebrietatem conciliat. Rud. 2.7.v.8.
units.tr: Love brings on drunkenness. Rud. 2. 7. v. 8.

units.la: AMATORES culpam in Cupidinem transferunt. Aul. 4.10.v.7. Deus mihi impulsor fuit.
units.tr: Lovers shift the blame onto Cupid: "God was the instigator of me." Aul. 4. 10. v. 7.

units.la: AMATORES solent nutare & nictare puellis per vias incedentib». Merc. 2.3.v.74. Mil. 2.1.v.45.
units.tr: Lovers are wont to nod and wink at girls as they walk through the streets. Merc. 2. 3. v. 74. Mil. 2. 1. v. 45.

units.la: PROSTIBILE est, stantem stanti savium dare amicum amicæ: Eugesic furi datur. Stich. 5.5.v.25.
units.tr: It is disgraceful for a man to give a standing kiss to his lady friend while his friend stands by; such a kiss is given to a thief. Stich. 5. 5. v. 25.

units.la: AMANTES studentsaltando placere amicæ. Pseud. 5.1.v.29.
units.tr: Lovers strive to please their sweetheart by dancing. Pseud. 5. 1. v. 29.

units.la: AMANTES circumferebant imagines suorum in cera. Vide Tit. Pictura: Imaginum.
units.tr: Lovers used to carry around images of their beloveds made of wax. See the title "Pictura: Imaginum."

units.la: BONA amatorum quasi sepeliuntur in ganeis & lustris. Trucul.2.1.
units.tr: The goods of lovers are, as it were, buried in brothels and dens of vice. Truc. 2. 1.

units.la: BLANDIENDI formulas legein Calligraph. Rom. Tit. Amandi. Blandiendi.
units.tr: Formulas of flattery: see Calligraph. Rom., the title "Amandi. Blandiendi."

units.la: AMANTES laboriosi: & egeni plærumque. Pseud. 2.4.v.2. Sciu amorem, scius laborem, scu egestatem meam; inquit adolescens.
units.tr: Lovers are often hard-working, and generally needy. Pseud. 2. 4. v. 2. "I know love, I know labour, I know my poverty," says the young man.

units.la: In convivijs amatores postquam bibissent, sauium dabant. Bacch. 1.1.v.15.
units.tr: At banquets, lovers, after they had drunk, gave kisses. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 15.

units.la: VISCUS merus est blanditia. Bacch 1.1.v.16.17.
units.tr: Flattery is pure bird-lime. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 16 and 17.

units.la: AMOR absorbet omne patrimonium, Merc. Prol. v.43.
units.tr: Love swallows up the whole patrimony. Merc. Prol. v. 43.

units.la: OSCULIS concubitus proximus esse solet. Flamma enim fumo proxima est. Curc. 1.1.v.35.16. Qui vulcu cubare, pandit saltum savys.
units.tr: Kisses are usually followed by intercourse, for a flame is next to smoke. Curc. 1. 1. v. 35 and 16. "He who lies down by the fire opens the way for kisses."

units.la: Ovidius:
units.tr: Ovid:

units.la: Osculaquisumsit, si non & cetera sumsit,
units.tr: Whoever has taken kisses, if he has not also taken the rest,

units.la: Hoc quicquid sumsit, perdere dignus erat.
units.tr: Whatever he has taken, he deserved to lose.

units.la: Osculaautem libidinis Antecania vocantur ab Angelo J C. & proœmium Adulterÿ. Vulgò frequentantur versiculi ab Accursio & Hostiensi usurpati:
units.tr: Kisses of lust are called "Antecania" by Angelus the jurist, and the prelude to adultery. Little verses taken up by Accursius and Hostiensis are commonly repeated:

units.la: Visus & Alloquium, Tactus, post osculu Factum
units.tr: Sight and speech, touch, after the kiss has been given,

units.la: Ni fugias tactus, vix evitabitur actus.
units.tr: Unless you flee from touch, the act will hardly be avoided.

units.la: Petronius: Itaq; primum implevi lactentibus papillis manum: mox basio inhæsi: deinde in unum omnia vota conjeci. Vide etiam Hot-man. Observat. de ritibus Nuptiarum: & Alberic. Gentil. J C. lib. 7. c. 9. p. 781.
units.tr: Petronius: "Therefore first I filled my hand with the milk-swollen breasts; soon I clung to the kiss; then I threw all my desires into one." See also Hotman, on the rites of weddings, and Alberic Gentilis, jurist, book 7, ch. 9, p. 781.

units.la: AMANTES fortunas omnes censent suos amores. Asin. 3.1.v.12.
units.tr: Lovers think all fortunes are their loves. Asin. 3. 1. v. 12.

units.la: AMATOR similis est oppidi hostilis: quam primum expugnari potest, optimum est amicæ. Truc. 1. 2. v.67.
units.tr: A lover is like a hostile town: the sooner it can be taken, the better for his sweetheart. Truc. 1. 2. v. 67.

units.la: AMANTIUM voluntas eadem esse debet. Mil. 4.2.v.79.
units.tr: The wills of lovers ought to be the same. Mil. 4. 2. v. 79.

units.la: AMATORES nihili sunt absque argento. Pseud. 4.7. v.23.
units.tr: Lovers are worth nothing without money. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 23.

units.la: AMATORES ad forum procedebant, prædam suæ libidini inda-gantes. Cas. 3.3.v. 2.
units.tr: Lovers used to go to the forum, seeking prey for their lust. Cas. 3. 3. v. 2.

units.la: QUI amant, visco tanguntur, & cor stimulo fodiuntur. Bacch. 5. 2. v.39. de sene petulanti.
units.tr: Those who love are caught by bird-lime, and their hearts are pierced by a goad. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 39, said of a wanton old man.

units.la: TURPE est senilis amor. Bacch. 5.2. v. 44.
units.tr: An old man's love is shameful. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 44.

units.la: AMATORIBUS omnia pro spisso procedunt, nec moram ferre possunt. Merc. 5.2.v.III.
units.tr: For lovers everything goes wrong, and they cannot bear delay. Merc. 5. 2. v. 111.

units.la: AMATORES amant nocturnas grassationes: ij olim incedebant cum æreo funali in manu. Curc. 1.1. v.2.
units.tr: Lovers love nocturnal raids; in former times they walked with a bronze lantern in hand. Curc. 1. 1. v. 2.

units.la: IN amore cor vehementer salire solet. Mil. 4 2. v. 96.
units.tr: In love the heart is wont to throb violently. Mil. 4. 2. v. 96.

units.la: AMANTIBUS caput prurire dicitur, cum sentiunt se amore peri-re. Bacch. 5.2. v.74.
units.tr: Lovers are said to have an itching head when they feel they are perishing from love. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 74.

units.la: LUCRUM amare nullum amatorem decet. Pæn. 1.2.v.II5.
units.tr: A lover should never love gain. Poen. 1. 2. v. 115.

units.la: QUI amat, si eget, miserâ afficitur Ærumnâ. Curc. 1.2. v.53.
units.tr: He who loves, if he is needy, is afflicted with wretched distress. Curc. 1. 2. v. 53.

units.la: AMATORES luxu diffluunt, comedunt omnem rem. Estur, bibitur, neque quicquam parsimoniam adhibet: sagina plane est. Moft. 1.3. v. 78.
units.tr: Lovers squander everything in luxury and eat up all their property. They eat and drink, and show no thrift at all: they are simply being fattened. Most. 1. 3. v. 78.

units.la: AMATORES ungebant se: & amasiæ purpurisso se allinebant. Trin. 2.1. v. 22. Vide Tit. Gynæcei.
units.tr: Lovers anointed themselves, and their mistresses smeared themselves with purple rouge. Trin. 2. 1. v. 22. See the title "Gynaeceum."

units.la: MISER est, qui amat. Certo is quidem nihili est, qui amat: quid ei homini opus vitâ est? Perf. 2. 1. v. 10.11.
units.tr: He is wretched who loves. "Surely he who loves is worth nothing; what need has such a man for life?" Pers. 2. 1. v. 10 and 11.

units.la: AMANTES omnia ineptè agunt. Merc. 2.3.v.47.
units.tr: Lovers do everything foolishly. Merc. 2. 3. v. 47.

units.la: AMANTIUM animi varij sunt. Quò alluditur Epid. 1. 1. v.43.
units.tr: The minds of lovers are fickle, an allusion to Epid. 1. 1. v. 43.

units.la: ANIMALIUM. BRUTORUM. ASINORUM. ANSERUM. BOUM. CANUM. CERVORUM. COCHLEARUM. ELEPHANTIS. EQUORUM. FORMICARUM. GALLINARUM. HIRCORUM. HIRUDINIS. LUMBRICORUM. LUPORUM. MURIS. MUSTELÆ. MULORUM. OVIUM. PORCORUM. SUUM. SIMIÆ. SERPENTIS. TIPULAE. TESTUDINIS. VERVECIS. VULPIS.
units.tr: ANIMALS. BEASTS. ASSES. GEESE. OXEN. DOGS. STAGS. SNAILS. ELEPHANTS. HORSES. ANTS. HENS. GOATS. LEECHES. EARTHWORMS. WOLVES. MICE. WEASELS. MULES. SHEEP. PIGS. SWINE. APES. SERPENTS. GNATS. TORTOISES. RAMS. FOXES.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Avium & Vermium.
units.tr: See also the titles Birds and Worms.

units.la: ANSERES frumentum edunt: & inter edendum clamore sæpe absterrentur. Truc. 2.1. v. 41.
units.tr: GEESE eat grain, and while eating they are often scared off by shouting. Truc. 2.1. v. 41.

units.la: ASINI Mordicibus scindunt. Aul. 2.2. v. 57.
units.tr: ASSES bite with their teeth. Aul. 2.2. v. 57.

units.la: ASINIS costæ callent plagis. Pseud. 1.2. v. 4.
units.tr: ASSES' ribs grow hard from blows. Pseud. 1.2. v. 4.

units.la: ASINUS ferociens retrorsum cædit calcibus. Inde proverbium natum: Illuc, quorsum asinus cædit calcibus. Poen. 3.3. v. 70.
units.tr: An ass, when it grows wild, kicks backwards with its heels. From this the proverb arose: Going there is like an ass kicking backwards with its heels. Poen. 3.3. v. 70.

units.la: ASINIS abundat Arcadia. Asin. 2.2 v. 67.
units.tr: Arcadia abounds in asses. Asin. 2.2. v. 67.

units.la: BOVES incursant cornibus. Aul. 2.2. v. 57.
units.tr: OXEN attack with their horns. Aul. 2.2. v. 57.

units.la: BUBUS glandes dabant quoque in pabulum. Trucul. 3.1. v. 2. Idem docet Cato c. 54. & 60. Bubus cibaria annua in juga singula lupini modio 120. aut glandis modios 260. Columell. l. 6. c. 3. & lib. 11. c. 2.
units.tr: OXEN were given acorns as fodder too. Trucul. 3.1. v. 2. Cato teaches the same at chapters 54 and 60: For oxen, the yearly feed for each yoke is 120 modii of lupine or 260 modii of acorns. Columella, book 6, chapter 3, and book 11, chapter 2.

units.la: BOVES lupino pascebantur. Poen. 3. 2. v. 21. Lupino macerato pingues fiunt in barbarià boves.
units.tr: OXEN were fed on lupine. Poen. 3.2. v. 21. When soaked in lupine, the oxen in Barbary grow fat.

units.la: BUBUS dabatur ervum, hordei genus. Most. 11. v. 59.
units.tr: OXEN were given vetch, a kind of barley. Most. 11. v. 59.

units.la: CATELLOS majusculos solebant commodare amicis, ad diem unum alterumque, ut suo femine impertirent caniculas, quibus cuperent provenire bellos catellos. Alluditur co Cafin. 3. 2. v. 22.
units.tr: They used to lend fairly large puppies to friends for a day or two, so that they might mate their bitches with them and hope for handsome puppies. This is alluded to in Casina 3.2 v. 22.

units.la: CANINA scæva comparatur latratibus mulieris. Caf. 5.4. v. 4.
units.tr: A dog's bark is compared with the screeching of a woman. Caf. 5.4. v. 4.

units.la: CANES nasum habent sagacem. Curc. 1. 2. v. 17. Virgil. Odora canum vis. Livius Andronicus: Odorisequi canes.
units.tr: DOGS have a keen nose. Curc. 1.2. v. 17. Virgil: the keen power of dogs' scent. Livius Andronicus: hounds that follow by scent.

units.la: SUES catulos suos solent pedibus proterere. Unde proverbij loco usurpatur. Truc. 2.2. v. 13.
units.tr: SOWS are accustomed to trample their own puppies underfoot. This is used as a proverb. Truc. 2.2. v. 13.

units.la: DITIORES in delitijs habere solent catulos Melitæos, quos secum faciunt cubare: ad quos allusum Curc. 5. 2. v. 13.
units.tr: Wealthier people are accustomed to keep Maltese puppies as pets, and they let them sleep with them. This is alluded to in Curc. 5.2. v. 13.

units.la: CANIS venaticus omnia odoratur, usque donec vulpem vestigijs persecutus sit. Mil. 2. 2. v. 114.
units.tr: A hunting dog sniffs out everything until it has tracked the fox by its footprints. Mil. 2.2. v. 114.

units.la: ALITER catuli olent, aliter sues. Proverbialiter. Epid. 4.2. v. 9.
units.tr: Puppies smell one way, pigs another. Proverbial. Epid. 4.2. v. 9.

units.la: CANIBUS nomina indebant etiam delicatæ mulieres, meretricu-læ. Epid. 2. 2. v. 50.
units.tr: Even delicate women, courtesans, gave dogs' names. Epid. 2.2. v. 50.

units.la: CANES fustibus & lapidibus petuntur. Rud. 3. 6. v. 4.
units.tr: DOGS are attacked with clubs and stones. Rud. 3.6. v. 4.

units.la: Quid ego quasi canem hominem insectarer lapidibus?
units.tr: Why should I hunt a man with stones as if he were a dog?

units.la: IUVENCUM equidem vidi ex indomito domitum fieri. Truc. 2. 2. v. 64.
units.tr: I have indeed seen a bullock made tame from being untamed. Truc. 2.2. v. 64.

units.la: CERVI animal velocissimum. Inde vincere cervum cursu. Pœn. 3. 1. v. 27.
units.tr: The STAG is the swiftest of animals. Hence the phrase to outrun a stag in a race. Poen. 3.1. v. 27.

units.la: COCHLEIS æstus solet esse infestus. Captiv. 1. 1. v. 12. Quasi cum caletur, cochleæ in occulto latent, suo sibi succo vivunt, ros sinen cadit. Vide etiam Symmach. Epist. lib. 1. Epist. 33. Ajunt cochleas, cum sitiunt aeris, atq; illis de calo nihil quitur, succo proprio vîcitare. Idem testatur Varro lib. 3. de re Rustica. c. 14. & Ammianus lib. 23. in fine.
units.tr: SNAILS are usually harmed by heat. Captiv. 1.1. v. 12. When it is hot, snails hide in shade and live on their own moisture, since no dew falls on them. See also Symmachus, Letters, book 1, letter 33: They say that snails, when they are thirsty for air and nothing falls on them from heaven, feed on their own juice. Varro also testifies to the same in On Farming, book 3, chapter 14, and Ammianus, book 23, near the end.

units.la: COCHLEÆ tardissimum animal. Pœn. 3. 1. v. 29.
units.tr: The SNAIL is the slowest of animals. Poen. 3.1. v. 29.

units.la: ELEPHANTUM creditur gravidam esse perpetuos decem annos. Stich. 2.1. v.13. Vide Plin. lib. 8.cap.10. Aristotel.lib.6.de Nat. Animal.
units.tr: An ELEPHANT is believed to be pregnant for ten full years. Stich. 2.1. v. 13. See Pliny, book 8, chapter 10, and Aristotle, On the Natural History of Animals, book 6.

units.la: ELEPHANTUS in India capitur: Ejus proboscis manus & brachium dicebatur. Mil. 1. 1. v. 25. ἀλλη̃γοεικω̂ς.
units.tr: An ELEPHANT is caught in India. Its trunk was called a hand and arm. Mil. 1.1. v. 25. [allegorically, ἀλληγορικῶς]

units.la: CUTIS elephanti durissima & crassissima. Mil. 2.2. v.80. Elephanti corio circumtentus est. Vide etiam Cafaub. Animadverf. ad Athen. lib. 3. c. 30.
units.tr: An elephant's hide is very hard and very thick. Mil. 2.2. v. 80. He is wrapped in an elephant's hide. See also Casaubon's Animadversions on Athenaeus, book 3, chapter 30.

units.la: EQUI libidine prurientes solent adhinnire equulis. Cistell. 4.2. v. 88.
units.tr: HORSES in heat neigh after mares. Cistell. 4.2. v. 88.

units.la: EQUI cantherij castrati stantes somniant. Men. 2.3. v.44.
units.tr: Gelded stallions dream while standing. Men. 2.3. v. 44.

units.la: EQUUS Gallicus cantherius viliori pretio vendebatur, quàm mulus. Aul. 3. 5. v.20. Quid sit equus cantherius vide Lexic. Plautinum: & Marcellum Donatum in Vopiscum pag. 1030. Mulis utebantur honestiores matronæ. Vide Tit. Vehiculorum & Nupttiarum.
units.tr: A Gallic stallion was sold for a lower price than a mule. Aul. 5.5. v. 20. For what a stallion (cantherius) is, see the Plautine Lexicon, and Marcellus Donatus on Vopiscus, p. 1030. Respectable matrons used mules. See the titles Carriages and Weddings.

units.la: EQUIS clitellæ impositæ. Mostl. 3.2. v. 92. ἀλλη̃γοεικω̂ς. Itemque mulionibus. Ibid. Nam mulliones malos clitellarios habent.
units.tr: Pack-saddles were put on horses. Mostell. 3.2. v. 92. [allegorically, ἀλληγορικῶς] Likewise on muleteers. Ibid.: For muleteers have bad pack-animals.

units.la: IN hippodromo equis de pernicitate currùs certabant. Cist. 2.3.v.7.
units.tr: In the hippodrome horses competed in the speed of their chariots. Cist. 2.3. v. 7.

units.la: EQUI ungulis suis sonitum concitant. Men. 5.2. v. 113.
units.tr: HORSES make a noise with their hooves. Men. 5.2. v. 113.

units.la: FELES rapacissimum animal, Persius 4.9. v. 14. & Rud. 3.4. v. 42.
units.tr: The CAT is a most rapacious animal. Persius 4.9. v. 14, and Rud. 3.4. v. 42.

units.la: FORMICÆ tardo gradu moventur & incedunt: adeò ut in proverbio sit formicinus gradus. Men. 5.3. v.12. Catull. Carm. 39. Incedere myrmicè. Et Martial. crusculum formicæ dixit.
units.tr: ANTS move and walk with a slow step, so much so that there is a proverb, an ant's step. Men. 5.3. v. 12. Catullus, poem 39: to walk like an ant. And Martial spoke of the little leg of an ant.

units.la: FORMICÆ papaverem comedunt. Trin. 2.4. v.8.
units.tr: ANTS eat poppy. Trin. 2.4. v. 8.

units.la: GALLINACEI PULLI in cavea solebant concludi. Curc. 3.1. v. 80.
units.tr: Young CHICKENS were usually shut up in a coop. Curc. 3.1. v. 80.

units.la: HIRCUS unctus nauteâ fœtet amplius. Casinaria. Grex. versu 7.
units.tr: A GOAT smeared with ship's pitch stinks more. Casinaria. Grex. verse 7.

units.la: Hircus, canis, capra commissa, animalia fœtida.
units.tr: A goat, a dog, and a goat-hair mixed together: foul-smelling animals.

units.la: Hirci castrabantur quoq;. Merc. 2.2.v.1. ἀλλ᾽ηγοσιαῶς.
units.tr: Goats were also castrated. Merc. 2.2. v. 1. [allegorically, ἀλληγορικῶς]

units.la: HIRUDO
units.tr: THE LEECH

units.la: Hirudo exugit sanguinem. Epid. 2.2.v.4.
units.tr: The leech sucks blood. Epid. 2.2.v.4.

units.la: Leones generosi in Getuliâ erant. Men. 5.2. v.iii. Et Leonis halitus olens, Ibid. & Plin. lib. 11. c.53.
units.tr: Lions were noble in Getulia. Men. 5.2. v.iii. And the breath of a lion is foul, Ibid. and Pliny, bk 11, ch.53.

units.la: Lupus animal esuriens. Stich. 4.2.v.25. Hic homo hereditatem tuam inhiat, quasi esuriens lupus.
units.tr: The wolf is a hungry animal. Stich. 4.2.v.25. This man is gaping for your inheritance, like a hungry wolf.

units.la: Lupas Marti sacras putabant: quòd genitores Urbis à Marte geniti essent. Truc. 3.1.v.11. Pœn. 3.3.v.31.
units.tr: They thought she-wolves were sacred to Mars, because the founders of the City were born of Mars. Truc. 3.1.v.11. Pœn. 3.3.v.31.

units.la: Lupi animal rapacissimum: quo cum comparantur servi ob rapacitatem. Pseud. 1.2.v.8.
units.tr: The wolf is a most rapacious animal, and slaves are compared with it for their rapacity. Pseud. 1.2.v.8.

units.la: Lupo agnum eripere est difficile & periculosum. Pœn. 3.5.v.31. Lupo agnum eripere postulant: nugas agunt.
units.tr: To snatch a lamb from a wolf is difficult and dangerous. Pœn. 3.5.v.31. They ask to snatch a lamb from a wolf: they are talking nonsense.

units.la: Mulorum inscitia in proverbium abijt. Cist. 4.2.v.12.
units.tr: The stupidity of mules has passed into a proverb. Cist. 4.2.v.12.

units.la: Mures Africanos putant aliqui esse pantheras. Pœn. 5.2.v.51. Vide Lipsi. l.2. Electa. c.4. Alciatus verò eosdem putat esse, quos Plinius lib.10. c.65. vocat Niloticos, & Ægyptios. Ubi videatur etiam Plinij Commentator Dalecampius.
units.tr: Some think the African mice are panthers. Pœn. 5.2.v.51. See Lipsius, bk 2 of the Electa, ch.4. Alciatus, however, thinks they are the same as those Pliny, bk 10, ch.65, calls Nilotic and Egyptian. See also Dalechamps, Pliny's commentator.

units.la: Mus pusillus sapiens bestia, ætatem qui uni cubili numquam committit suam: quia si unum ostium obsideatur, aliud perfugium gerit. Truc. 4.4.v.15. Sic Lactant. de Irâ Dei. cap.7. Sunt animalia, quæ latebulis suis diversos & plures exitus prendant; ut si quod periculum inciderit, fuga pateat obsessis: quod non faceret, nisi inesset illis intelligentia, & cogitatio.
units.tr: The mouse is a small and wise creature, which never entrusts its life to a single hole, because if one door is blocked it has another way out. Truc. 4.4.v.15. So Lactantius, On the Anger of God, ch.7: There are animals which make several and multiple exits from their hiding places, so that if any danger arises, a way of flight lies open to those beset; which they would not do unless they had understanding and thought.

units.la: Sic de Echino scribit Aristotel. Histor. Animal. lib. 5. cap. 6. Et Basil. Oratione 9. in Hexaem. eum in cavernâ suâ duo foramina facere, spectantia ad oppositas mundi plagas. Vide Erasm. Adag. & Rittershusium J C. ad Oppianum.
units.tr: So Aristotle writes of the hedgehog, History of Animals, bk 5, ch.6. And Basil, Homily 9 on the Hexaemeron, says it makes two holes in its cave, facing opposite quarters of the world. See Erasmus, Adages, and Rittershusius the jurist on Oppian.

units.la: SOREX in muscipula confessus solet næniam soricinam ædere. Bacch. 4. 8. v. 48.
units.tr: A shrew caught in a trap is accustomed to sing the mouse's dirge. Bacch. 4.8.v.48.

units.la: QUASI mus in medio pariete versabere. Caf. 1.1. v. 52.
units.tr: You will turn about like a mouse in the middle of a wall. Caf. 1.1.v.52.

units.la: MUSCARUM tum abundè est, cùm caletur maximè. Trucul. 1. 1. v. 46.
units.tr: There are flies in abundance when it is hottest. Truc. 1.1.v.46.

units.la: MUSCA animal impudens: & ob id parasiti muscis comparantur. Pæn. 3. 3. v. 76.
units.tr: The fly is a shameless creature, and for that reason parasites are compared to flies. Pœn. 3.3.v.76.

units.la: MUSCÆ frequenter in omnibus ædibus: adeò ut in proverbio est, sent ædes vacuæ sine musca. Truc. 2. 2. v. 30.
units.tr: Flies are frequent in all houses, so much so that the proverb runs: there is never a house without a fly. Truc. 2.2.v.30.

units.la: MUSTELA decies in die mutat locum. Stich. 3. 2. v. 45.
units.tr: The weasel changes its place ten times a day. Stich. 3.2.v.45.

units.la: OVES & lanam Tarentinam laudavit antiquitas. Truc. 3. 1. v. 5. Facit & Horatius mentionem lib. 2. Od. 6. Dulce pellitus ovibus Galesi Flumen. Galeus enim Calabriæ & Tarenti fluvius.
units.tr: Antiquity praised sheep and Tarentine wool. Truc. 3.1.v.5. Horace also mentions it, Odes, bk 2, ode 6: Sweet the river Galaesus, with its fleecy sheep. For the Galaesus is a river of Calabria and Tarentum.

units.la: OVES Tarentinæ tectæ & pellitæ pascebantur, ob lanæ vellerisque præstantiam. Quò allusum Merc. 3. 1. v. 27. Vide Turneb. lib. 7. Adversar. c. 17.
units.tr: Tarentine sheep were pastured covered and fleeced, because of the excellence of their wool. This is alluded to in Merc. 3.1.v.27. See Turnebus, bk 7 of the Adversaria, ch.17.

units.la: OVES Græciæ ter in anno tonsitabantur. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 9. Vide Lex. Mina.
units.tr: Greek sheep were shorn three times a year. Bacch. 5.2.v.9. See the lexicon, Mina.

units.la: OVES cum à cætero penè absunt, balare solent. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 20.
units.tr: When sheep are almost entirely separated from the rest of the flock, they are accustomed to bleat. Bacch. 5.2.v.20.

units.la: PRODIGIUM est oves loqui. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 22. per jocum, de senibus.
units.tr: It is a portent for sheep to speak. Bacch. 5.2.v.22. Said in jest, of old men.

units.la: PANTHERINUM & CAPRINUM genus varium est: ob maculas corporis, ut pantheræ: & ob febrim: ut capræ: quæ numquam febri carent, teste Plinio, quia sunt omnicarpæ, ut loquitur vetus scriptor apud Varronem. Epid. 1. 1. v. 16.
units.tr: The panther and goat kinds are a varied genus: in respect of the spots on the body, like panthers; and in respect of fever, like goats, which are never free of fever, according to Pliny, because they are omnivorous, as an old writer says in Varro. Epid. 1.1.v.16.

units.la: SUES immundum animal alienum ab omni mundicie. Stich. 1. 1. v. 6.
units.tr: The pig is an unclean animal, alien to all cleanliness. Stich. 1.1.v.6.

units.la: PORCI sacres immolabantur ab insanis. Men. 2.2. v. 16. Rud. 4.6. v.4. Vide Tit. Deorum, Sacrificiorum. & Lexicon Plautinum.
units.tr: Sacred pigs were sacrificed by madmen. Men. 2.2.v.16. Rud. 4.6.v.4. See the title Gods, Sacrifices, and the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: SUES anginâ infestari solent. Mostell. 1. 3. verf. 61. Trin. 2. 4. verf. 139. Plin. l. 8. Obnoxium genus morbis: anginæ maximè, & strumis. Vide J. Nicol. Loënf. Miscell. lib. 9. c. 22.
units.tr: Pigs are commonly troubled by quinsy. Mostell. 1.3, verse 61. Trin. 2.4, verse 139. Pliny, bk 8: a kind liable to diseases, above all quinsy and scrofula. See J. Nicolaus Loënfeld, Miscellanea, bk 9, ch.22.

units.la: PORCINA caro in delitijs. Men. 1.3, v.26. Vide Ciborum.
units.tr: Pork is among the delicacies. Men. 1.3.v.26. See Food.

units.la: SUES occisæ porricebantur. Rud 3. 2, v. 46. Vide Tit. Funerie.
units.tr: Slaughtered pigs were offered up. Rud. 3.2.v.46. See the title Funerals.

units.la: Sus fœtidum animal à pisloribus alisolet. Capt. 4.2.v.27.
units.tr: The pig is a stinking animal, commonly reared by butchers. Capt. 4.2.v.27.

units.la: CARO suilla omnium sapidissima. Mil. 2. 6. v. 104. Certò scio, occisam sæpe sapere plus multò suem, cùm manducatur.
units.tr: Of all meats, pork is the most savoury. Mil. 2.6.v.104. I know for certain that a pig, once killed, often tastes much better when it is eaten.

units.la: SERPENS animal aslutum, callidum. Pœn. 5.2. v. 75.
units.tr: THE SERPENT: an animal crafty and cunning. Pœn. 5.2.v.75.

units.la: SERPENTES bilingues sunt. Perf 2.4. v.28.
units.tr: Serpents have two tongues. Pers. 2.4.v.28.

units.la: SIMIA animal sagax, versipelle. Pseud 2.4. v.54.
units.tr: The ape is a sagacious, versatile animal. Pseud. 2.4.v.54.

units.la: INTER alias bestias, & aviculas, etiam SIMIAS alebant in ædibus. Mil. 2.2. v.7.
units.tr: Among other beasts and small birds, they even kept apes in the house. Mil. 2.2.v.7.

units.la: SIMIA animal deforme. Most. 4.2. v.4. Simia: in convitio.
units.tr: The ape is an ugly animal. Most. 4.2.v.4. Simia is used as an insult.

units.la: SIMIA, seu pithecium, & spinturnix avis deformis. Mil. 4.1.v.42. Enn. Simia quàm similis turpissima bestia, nobis!
units.tr: The ape, or pithecium, and the spinturnix are ugly birds. Mil. 4.1.v.42. Ennius: How like us, the most wretched of beasts, is the ape!

units.la: SIMIA nihili bestia. Mil. 2.2. v.24.
units.tr: The ape is a worthless beast. Mil. 2.2.v.24.

units.la: SIMIA bestia nequissima. Rud. 3.1. v.18.
units.tr: The ape is a most wicked beast. Rud. 3.1.v.18.

units.la: INVOLVOLI in pampino folio implicant, ac perdunt. Cistell. 4.2. v. 63.
units.tr: The involvoli entangle themselves in a vine leaf and perish. Cistell. 4.2.v.63.

units.la: TIPULA erat bestiola, sex pedes habens, summæ levitatis. Perf. 2. 2. v. 62. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: The tipula was a little creature with six feet, of extreme lightness. Pers. 2.2.v.62. See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: VERVEX animal stupidum. Inde in convitium abijt: Verveccum caput. Perf. 2. 2. v. 2. Vide Calligraphiam Romanam nostram pag. 815. Titul. Nominum ignominiosorum.
units.tr: The vervex is a stupid animal. From this it passed into an insult: "wether's head." Pers. 2.2.v.2. See our Roman Calligraphy, p.815, title Infamous Names.

units.la: L VUL-
units.tr: L VUL-

units.la: VULPES etiam pirum comest. Mostell. 3.1. v.28. Tam facile vinces, quam pirum vulpes comest. Proverb. cui respondet illud Senecae de Claudio Caesare: Tam facile homines occidebat, quam canis extra colit.
units.tr: Foxes even eat pears. Mostell. 3.1.v.28. You will conquer as easily as a fox eats a pear. This is a proverb, to which Seneca's remark about the Emperor Claudius answers: He killed men as easily as a dog keeps watch outside.

units.la: ANIMI-TRANQUILLITATIS. ANIMI-DELIQUII. EXAMINATIONIS. INFIRMITATIS.
units.tr: Tranquillity of Mind. Faintness of Mind. Examination. Weakness.

units.la: POL si animus est aequus tibi, satis habes, qui bene vitam colas. Aul. 2.2. v.10. Cicero de Senectute: Quid quod sapientissimus quisque animo aequissimo moritur, stultissimus inquissimo. Lucret. lib.5. Divitiae grandes homini sunt, vivere parce, aequo animo.
units.tr: By Pollux, if your mind is calm, you have enough to live a good life well. Aulularia 2.2, v. 10. Cicero, On Old Age: "What of this, that the wisest man dies with the most even mind, and the most foolish with the most restless?" Lucretius, book 5: "Great riches for a man are to live sparingly and with an even mind."

units.la: Ex deliquio animi sibi restituti solent lucem, qua aliquandiu visi carere, salutare. Mil. 4.8. v.34. Sed quid hoc? quaeres est? quid video? lux salve candida.
units.tr: Those who have come back to themselves after a faint are wont to greet the light, of which they have been deprived for a while, as a welcome thing. Miles Gloriosus 4.8, v. 34: "But what is this? Do I ask where I am? What do I see? Hail, bright light!"

units.la: AQUA sevitiebat animi deliquio. Bacch. 2.3. v.14. Curc. 2.3. v.33. Truc. 2.4. v.15. Cist. 2.3. v.38. Mil. 4.8. v.22. Ter. And. 2.1. Reddidisti animum.
units.tr: WATER was pouring over him in his fainting fit. Bacchides 2.3, v. 14; Curculio 2.3, v. 33; Truculentus 2.4, v. 15; Cistellaria 2.3, v. 38; Miles Gloriosus 4.8, v. 22. Terence, Andria 2.1: "You have restored my senses."

units.la: ANNONÆ.
units.tr: Corn Prices.

units.la: Annona vilior esset, si Dij improbis brevem, probis autem longam vitam darent. Mil. 3. 1. v. 139. τὰ δὲ σπάνιον, τίμιον, inquit Plato.
units.tr: Grain would be cheaper if the gods gave short life to the wicked and long life to the good. Miles Gloriosus 3.1, v. 139. "What is rare is precious," says Plato. [τὰ δὲ σπάνιον, τίμιον]

units.la: ANNULORUM.
units.tr: Rings.

units.la: Annulorum usus, & sculptura, unde primùm, & qualis fuerit, jucundum scitu. Ex nostro Authore haec constant. Interdum illis historia aliqua, aut fabula insculpta fuit: ut Amph. 1. 1. v. 264. Cum quadrigis Sol exoriens. Interdum munus illud, qp gerebant, expressum. Sic Therapontigonus insculptum habebat militem clipeatum, qui elephantem machaerâ dissecaret. Curc. 3. v. 54. Nonnumquam imaginem propriam effingebant. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 54. & Cicer. 3. Catilin. Sueton. August. cap. 50. Postremò, non semper eodem utebantur, sed mutabant pro libitu, aut si casu amissent. Trin. 3. 3. v. 63. Alia in hanc rem vide apud Meursium part. 2. Exerc. Critic. c. 9. itemque Abrahami Gorlaei librum de Annulis.
units.tr: The use of rings, and their engraving: where it first arose and what it was like, is pleasant to know. From our author these points are established. Sometimes some story or fable was engraved on them, as in Amphitryon 1.1, v. 264: "The sun rising with its four-horse chariot." Sometimes the office which they held was represented: thus Therapontigonus had engraved a shield-bearing soldier who cut an elephant in two with a sword. Curculio 3, v. 54. Sometimes they had their own likeness carved. Pseudolus 1.1, v. 54; and Cicero, Third Catilinarian; Suetonius, Augustus, chap. 50. Finally, they did not always use the same ring, but changed them at pleasure, or if they had lost them by chance. Trinummus 3.3, v. 63. Other things on this matter see in Meursius, part 2, Exercitationes Criticae, chap. 9, and likewise Abraham Gorlaeus's book on Rings.

units.la: Annulus non erat nisi ingenuorum, ingenuarumve, Casin. 3. 5. v. 63. Vide Meurs. ad Catonem de Re rustica. c. 59.
units.tr: A ring was reserved only for freeborn men and women. Casina 3.5, v. 63. See Meursius on Cato's De Re Rustica, chap. 59.

units.la: Servi annuli genus condalium gesserunt digitis. Trin. 4. 3. v. 7.
units.tr: Slaves wore a kind of ring, the condalium, on their fingers. Trinummus 4.3, v. 7.

units.la: Annulis signatorijs obsignabant tabulas. Curc. 2. 3. v. 67.
units.tr: With signet rings they sealed documents. Curculio 2.3, v. 67.

units.la: Annulos aureolos donabant die natali. Epid 5. 1. v. 33.
units.tr: They gave little golden rings on birthdays. Epidicus 5.1, v. 33.

units.la: Annulos dabant in signum & certitudinem rei. Bacch. 2. 3. v. 93. Vide etiam Tit. Hospitalitatis: Convivij: Emtionis.
units.tr: They gave rings as a sign and guarantee of a matter. Bacchides 2.3, v. 93. See also the titles Hospitality, Banquet, Purchase.

units.la: Antiquitatis. Vetustatis. Novitatis.
units.tr: Of Antiquity, Of Age, Of Novelty.

units.la: ANTIQUA opera & verba, ut & veteres fabulæ placere solent. Nam nunc novæ quæ prodeunt Comœdiæ, Multò sunt nequiores, quàm numinovi Cas. Prol. v. 7. Vide Tit. Fabularum, Comœdiæ.
units.tr: ANCIENT works and words, as well as old plays, are usually pleasing. For the new comedies that now come forth are much worse than those of recent times (the old ones) Cas. Prol. v. 7. See the title Of Plays, Comedies.

units.la: Anûs. Vetulæ.
units.tr: Old Women. Little Old Women.

units.la: ANICULÆ solent screare: Curc. 1. 2. v. 22. Ac quia bibaces, venter illarum comparatur barathro, & cloacæ: quæ est prolucenda. Ibid. v. 29. Itemque Iridi, quæ aquam bibit, ut pluat, Ibid. v. 41.
units.tr: OLD women are wont to hawk and spit: Curc. 1. 2. v. 22. And because they are great drinkers, their belly is compared to a pit and a sewer, which must be rinsed out. Ibid. v. 29. Likewise to Iris, who drinks water so that she may rain: Ibid. v. 41.

units.la: ANICULÆ plerumque sunt bibaces: qualis introducitur lena apud Plautum Curcul. 1. 2. v. 77. 78. & 1. 2. v. 16. Vinacemia hæc huic anus non est satis soli.
units.tr: OLD women are mostly great drinkers, such as the procuress introduced by Plautus in the Curculio 1. 2. vv. 77, 78, and 1. 2. v. 16: This old woman's wine-jug is not enough for her alone.

units.la: Apprecationum.
units.tr: Blessings.

units.la: Vide Votorum.
units.tr: See Vows.

units.la: BONA multa aliis apprecantes, ut sunt hac formulâ: Di dent, quæ velis. Multa tibi Di dent bona! Asin. 1. 1. v. Epid. 1 v. 4. Pæn. 5. 2. v. 95. & cb. 3. 2. v. 15.
units.tr: Wishing many good things to others, in such formulas as: May the gods give what you wish. May the gods give you many blessings! Asin. 1. 1. v. Epid. 1 v. 4. Poen. 5. 2. v. 95, and Cist. 3. 2. v. 15.

units.la: APUM.
units.tr: BEES.

units.la: NON tantum mel antiquis in delitijs. Sed & apum jucunda ac dulcis, ob mellificium, erat memoria. Curc. 1.1, v.10. Poenol. 1.2, v.112. Mulsa loquitur: Turn. 8. 8.
units.tr: Not only was honey a delight to the ancients, but the memory of bees was also pleasant and sweet on account of their honey-making. Curc. 1.1, v.10. Poenol. 1.2, v.112. The honey-wine speaks: Turn. 8.8.

units.la: AQUAE. AQUARIORUM.
units.tr: WATER. WATER-CARRIERS.

units.la: Vide etiam Balnei: Fontium: Putei.
units.tr: See also Baths: Fountains: Wells.

units.la: NON tu scis, cùm ex alto puteo sursum ad summum escen-deris, Maximum periculum inde esse ab summo, ne rursum cadas? Mil. 4.4. v.14. ἀλληγορικῶς.
units.tr: Do you not know that when you climb from a deep well up to the top, the greatest danger is at the top, that you may fall back again? Mil. 4.4. v.14. allegorically [ἀλληγορικῶς].

units.la: PUTEOS fodiebant in aedibus. Rud. 2.4. v.19.
units.tr: They dug wells in the houses. Rud. 2.4. v.19.

units.la: AQUAM etiam hostis hosti commodat: coque nemini negari potest, Rud 2.4. v.21.
units.tr: Even an enemy lends water to an enemy, and no one can deny this. Rud 2.4. v.21.

units.la: AQUA fontibus est anima. Amph. 2 2.v.41. joculariter inquit: Ni ego illi puteo omnem animam intertraxero.
units.tr: Water is the life of springs. Amph. 2.2. v.41. He says jokingly: Unless I drain every last drop out of that well.

units.la: AQUA vim habet hominem in deliquio positum reficiendi. Amph. 5.1.v.6. Mil.4.8.v.22. Bacch. 2.3 v.14. Trin. 4.3.v 84. Cist. 2.3, v.38. Curc. 2.3, v 33. Epid.4.1,v.27. Vide Adagium: Adspersi aquam.
units.tr: Water has the power to revive a person who has fainted. Amph. 5.1. v.6. Mil. 4.8. v.22. Bacch. 2.3 v.14. Trin. 4.3. v.84. Cist. 2.3, v.38. Curc. 2.3, v.33. Epid. 4.1, v.27. See the proverb: Sprinkled with water.

units.la: Vide paulò ante: Animi - deliquii.
units.tr: See a little above: of the mind… of a faint.

units.la: AQUARII aquam in aedes portabant: quâ utebantur mulieres ad balneum: sèsqueeluendas. Inde Aquarij māle caeperunt audire. Poenol. 1.2.v 14. Sic Festus: Aquarij sunt impudicarum mulierum sordidi affecle. Is enim tamquam amorum internuntijs solebant uti mulieres. Juven. Sat. 6. --- veniet conductus Aquarius. Aquarioli illi dicti προσυοδιάκονοι. Glossae: Aquaculat: lenocinatur. Vide Turn. 1.14. c.12.
units.tr: Water-carriers carried water into the houses, which the women used for the bath and for washing their feet. From this the water-carriers began to be spoken of badly. Poenulus 1.2. v.14. So Festus: Water-carriers are the dirty servants of unchaste women. For they, as go-betweens of love affairs, were commonly used by the women. Juvenal, Sat. 6: the hired water-carrier will come. Those little water-carriers were called prosyodiakonoi [προσυοδιάκονοι]. Glosses: Aquaculat: he acts as a pimp. See Turnebus 1.14, c.12.

units.la: NIHIL viliori pretio emitur, quàm aqua: quia communis. Unde notatur avaritia Euclionis, qui etiam ploravit aquam profunde-re, cùm lavaret. Aul. 2.4. v. 29.
units.tr: Nothing is bought at a cheaper price than water, because it is common. Hence the avarice of Euclio is noted, who even lamented having to pour out water in abundance while he washed. Aul. 2.4. v.29.

units.la: AQUA calida serviebat ijs, qui timuerunt, vel laborarunt vehe-mentius: sicut frigida ijs, qui deliquium animi patiuntur. Bacch. 1.1. v.73. Vide Delrio ad Agamemn. Senec. v.784.
units.tr: Warm water was useful for those who were frightened or suffered more severely, just as cold water is for those who suffer a faint of the spirit. Bacch. 1.1. v.73. See Delrio on Seneca's Agamemnon, v.784.

units.la: AQUA in convivijs lavabant & manus, & pedes. Perf 5.1.v.17. Vide Tit. Convivÿ. & Stuckij Antiq. l.3. c.6.
units.tr: At banquets they washed both hands and feet with water. Persa 5.1. v.17. See the title Convivium, and Stuckius, Antiq. l.3, c.6.

units.la: AQUÆ inest magna voluptas. Rud. 2.5. v.1.
units.tr: Great pleasure is found in water. Rud. 2.5. v.1.

units.la: URNA hauriebant aquam. Rud. 2.5. v.10.
units.tr: They drew water with urns. Rud. 2.5. v.10.

units.la: FONTIBUS præerat DEUS Fontinalis; ut Vino Bacchus. Stich. 5.2. v.17.
units.tr: The god Fontinalis presided over the springs, as Bacchus over wine. Stich. 5.2. v.17.

units.la: AQUA macerantur muriatica: & pisces alij. Pœn. 1.2. v.32.
units.tr: Fish and other things are steeped in brine with water. Poen. 1.2. v.32.

units.la: UMBRA in puteis. Moft. 3.2. v.83.
units.tr: Shade in wells. Most. 3.2. v.83.

units.la: NIHIL similius aquæ, quàm aqua. Men. 5.9. v.
units.tr: Nothing is more like water than water. Men. 5.9. v.

units.la: PUTEOS è terrâ fodiebant. Moft. 2.1. v.32.
units.tr: They dug wells out of the earth. Most. 2.1. v.32.

units.la: AQUA salem consumit. Merc. 1.2. v.93.
units.tr: Water consumes salt. Merc. 1.2. v.93.

units.la: ARBORUM. FRUCTUUM. FRUTICUM. ULVÆ. SCIRPI. FUNGORUM. NUCIS.
units.tr: TREES. FRUITS. SHRUBS. SEAWEED. RUSHES. MUSHROOMS. NUTS.

units.la: MYRTUS Veneri sacra. Offerebantur etiam fasciculi myrto-rum Veneri. Rud. 3 4.v.27. Quasi murteta juncis: item ego vos virgis circumvinciam.
units.tr: The myrtle is sacred to Venus; bundles of myrtle were also offered to Venus. Rud. 3.4. v.27. Like myrtle-beds with rushes; likewise I will bind you with rods.

units.la: Qui è nuce nucleum esse vult: nucem frangat oportet. Cur. 1.1.v.55.
units.tr: Whoever wants the kernel out of a nut must crack the nut. Curc. 1.1. v.55.

units.la: SCIRPUS palustris semper aridus est. Rud. 2.6.v.39.
units.tr: A marsh rush is always dry. Rud. 2.6. v.39.

units.la: MORA nigra sunt. Pœn. 5.5.v.10. Martial. lib. 1. Epig. 22. Nigrior est cadente moro.
