units.tr: Mulberries are black. Poen. 5.5. v.10. Martial, lib. 1, Epig. 22: Blacker than a fallen mulberry.

units.la: FUNGI nihil habent præter caput. Trin. 4.2.v.9. Hic fungino genere est, capite se totum tegit.
units.tr: Mushrooms have nothing but a head. Trin. 4.2. v.9. He is of the mushroom kind; he covers himself entirely with his head.

units.la: ARCHITECTONICAE.
units.tr: ARCHITECTONICAE.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Ædium.
units.tr: See also the title Of Buildings.

units.la: Hoc cogitato, ubi probus est architectus, Bene lineatam si semel carinam collocavit, Facile esse navem facere, ubi fundata, & constituta est.
units.tr: With this in mind: when a skilled architect has laid a well-drawn keel, it is easy to build the ship once its foundation is fixed and it stands.

units.la: In architectonicis materiarius non debet remorari.
units.tr: In architectural matters the builder should not delay.

units.la: Architecti palos figere solent in parietem.
units.tr: Architects are accustomed to drive stakes into the wall.

units.la: ARGENTARIORUM. DANISTAE. FOENORIS. VSURAE. TRAPEZITARUM. PECUNIAE. REI-MONETARIAE. NUMMULARIORUM.
units.tr: BANKERS. DANISTS. INTEREST. USURY. MONEY-CHANGERS. MONEY. COINAGE. MONEYCHANGERS.

units.la: ARGENTI.
units.tr: SILVER.

units.la: Argentariis bene: & male creditur pecuniâ. Male: quia non reddunt totam summam: Bene, quia non omnis summa perit. Curc. 5.3.v.1.2. & seqq. vide.
units.tr: Money is lent to bankers both well and badly. Badly, because they do not repay the whole sum; well, because the whole sum is not lost. See Curc. 5.3.v.1.2 and following.

units.la: Etiam per jurgia vix reddunt: imo in jus vocant postulantes. Ib.
units.tr: They scarcely repay even through quarrels; indeed they summon their creditors to court. Ib.

units.la: Nullum hodie genus est, hominum deterius, nec minus bono cum jure, quàm danisticum. Most. 3.1. v. 124.
units.tr: There is today no kind of men worse than the danists, nor one less entitled to good law. Most. 3.1. v. 124.

units.la: Danistae alium prae alio annum faustiorem suo fœnori experti sunt. Most. 3.1. v. 2.
units.tr: The danists have found one year more fortunate than another for their interest. Most. 3.1. v. 2.

units.la: Foenus & usura ex cautela juris prius reddi debet, quàm sors: ne sortem accipiendo, usuras remisisse videamur. Mostell. 3.1. v.
units.tr: By the caution of the law, interest and usury must be paid before the principal, lest by accepting the principal we seem to have remitted the interest. Mostell. 3.1. v.

units.la: tantum de fœnore suo loquuntur. Mostell. 3.1.v. 70. Ter. Fœnus illic, fœnus hic.
units.tr: They speak only of their interest. Mostell. 3.1. v. 70. Ter. Interest here, interest there.

units.la: Nescit quidem, nisi fœnus fabulariér veterator.
units.tr: Indeed the old hand knows nothing but to talk of interest.

units.la: Sic Hipponax de Pythermo apud Athen. lib. 14.
units.tr: So Hipponax, concerning Pythermus, in Athenaeus, book 14.

units.la: χρυσὸν λέγει πύθερμον, ὡς ὑδὲν τ᾽ ἄλλα.
units.tr: He calls gold "pytherm," as if it were nothing else [χρυσὸν λέγει πύθερμον, ὡς οὐδὲν τἄλλα].

units.la: DANISTÆ genus improbissimum. Most. 3.1. v.93.
units.tr: The danists are a most wicked kind. Most. 3.1. v. 93.

units.la: ARGENTARII sæpe neque fœnus, neque sortem acceperunt. Most. 3.1. v.30.
units.tr: Bankers have often received neither interest nor principal. Most. 3.1. v. 30.

units.la: ARGENTUM purum & excoctum habet sonum magis tinnulum quàm uvidum in venis suis adhuc delitescens, Rud. 3.4. v.21. ἀλ-ληγοεικῶς.
units.tr: Pure and refined silver has a more ringing sound than the moist silver still hidden in its veins, Rud. 3.4. v. 21, echoing [ἀλληχοϊκῶς].

units.la: ARGENTARII Romæ in foro conductas habebant mensas seu tabernas. Asin. 2.4. v.22. Curc. 4.1. v. Pers. 3.3. v. 37.
units.tr: At Rome the bankers had rented tables or booths in the forum. Asin. 2.4. v. 22. Curc. 4.1. v. Pers. 3.3. v. 37.

units.la: Juvenal.
units.tr: Juvenal.

units.la: ---- erat à multum in arcâ
units.tr: There was much money in his chest,

units.la: Nummus, & ad vigilem ponendi Castora nummi.
units.tr: and coin to be deposited at the Castor by the night watch.

units.la: Vide Sigonium de antiquo jure civium. c.11.
units.tr: See Sigonius, on the ancient law of citizens, ch. 11.

units.la: ARGENTARIIS etiam ostendebatur pecunia, proba esset, annon. Pers. 3.3. v.35. Donatus ad Eunuch. Terent, 3.5. ait, dictos propterea Spectatores pecuniæ. Græcis δοκιμασταί.
units.tr: Money was also displayed to the bankers, to see whether it was sound. Pers. 3.3. v. 35. Donatus, on Terence's Eunuch 3.5, says that they were therefore called spectators of money. In Greek they are called δοκιμασταί [dokimastai].

units.la: DUOBUS modis apud nummularios deponi pecuniæ solebant: nimirùm aut custodiæ, aut fœnoris causâ. De priori agit noster Capt. 1.2.v.84. de posteriori Most. 3 1.v 4. Curc. 2.3. v. 66. & 4. 3. v. 4.
units.tr: Money was customarily deposited with the moneychangers in two ways, namely either for safekeeping or for interest. Our author treats the former in Capt. 1.2. v. 84, and the latter in Most. 3.1. v. 4, Curc. 2.3. v. 66, and 4.3. v. 4.

units.la: Vide etiam Ræv ard, Var. lib.1. c.15.
units.tr: See also Ravard, Var. book 1, ch. 15.

units.la: PECUNIAM solebant occupare, ne otiosa languesceret. Epid. 2.2. v.113.
units.tr: They used to seize money so that it would not lie idle and waste away. Epid. 2.2. v. 113.

units.la: AB Danistis fœnore sumebant argentum, in certam singularum dierum usuram. Epid 1.1.v.51, & 1.2.v.12.
units.tr: They borrowed silver from the danists at a fixed interest for each day. Epid. 1.1. v. 51, and 1.2. v. 12.

units.la: HABENT hunc morem pleriq; argentarij: Ut alius alium poscant, reddant nemini. Curc.3, 1.v.7.
units.tr: Most bankers have this custom: each demands from the other, and repays no one. Curc. 3.1. v. 7.

units.la: ARGENTARII alebant pueros catamitos. Curc.3.1,v 12.
units.tr: Bankers kept catamites as boys. Curc. 3.1. v. 12.

units.la: AERA usuraria perscribebantur in tabulis. Truc. I. I. v. 52.
units.tr: Usurious sums were entered in the account books. Truc. 1.1. v. 52.

units.la: ARITHMETICES. NUMERATIONUM, SUPPUTATIONUM. COMPUTATIONUM.
units.tr: ARITHMETIC. NUMERATIONS, RECKONINGS, COMPUTATIONS.

units.la: NON numeris solùm computabant veteres Arithmetici, sed digitis etiam: quod colligere est ex multis scriptoribus, quà Græcis, quà Latinis. Rationem illam primus, ut puto, aperuit venerabilis Beda peculiari libello, quam postremis temporibus hæsisse adhuc in Ecclesiasticis Authoribus apertè ex his ejus verbis constat: Nunc prolixius, inquit, de Temporum ratione, Domino juvante, dicturi, necessarium duximus utilissimam primo, promtissimamque flexus digitorum paucis præmonstrare solertiam, ut cùm maxima computandi facilitatem dederimus, tum parationre legentium ingenio ad investigandam, dilucidandamq; computando seriem temporum veniamus, neque enim contemnenda parvivependenda est regula, cujus omnes fere sacræ expositores scripturæ non minus quàm litterarum figuras monstrantur complexi. Expositi caydè luculenter Petrus Colvius Brugensis: Apuleij commentator clarissimus: cui succenturiatus quasi Apollo lucem addidit Janus Gruterus, in libris Suspicionum. His ego tamquam veles quispiam aliquid apportabo supellectilis, citra ullius damnum aut periculum, vel meum etiam. Nimirum mihi jam olim adolescenti in Noctibus meis Palatinis Vigil. I. c. 63. hæc sic collecta sunt: quæ quia nunc occasio est, huc congeram pleno quasi horreo.
units.tr: NOT only with numbers did the ancient arithmeticians reckon, but also with the fingers. This may be gathered from many writers, both Greek and Latin. The venerable Bede was, I think, the first to explain this method, in a special little book. From his words it is clear that the practice still persisted among ecclesiastical authors in later times: Now, the Lord helping, we are going to speak at greater length about the reckoning of times. We have judged it necessary first to set out briefly the most useful and ready skill of bending the fingers, so that, while we give the greatest ease in computing, we may also prepare the minds of readers to investigate and make clear the sequence of times by computation. For the rule is not to be despised or held in small esteem, since almost all the sacred expositors of Scripture are shown to have embraced it no less than the shapes of letters. Petrus Colvius of Bruges has explained it most clearly, the most distinguished commentator on Apuleius. To him, as a kind of Apollo in reserve, Janus Gruterus added light in his Suspicions. Like one willing to help, I shall bring some furniture of my own to these, without loss or risk to anyone. Indeed, when I was a young man long ago in my Palatine Nights, these things were collected in this way (Vigil. I. c. 63). Since there is an occasion now, I will heap them here as from a full granary.

units.la: PRIMUM itaque tenendum nomen cujusq; digiti. Primus: Pollex: Alter Index nonnullis, alijs etiam ἀσπασμὸς, & ἐπιδεικτικὸς, salutatorius, & demonstratorius. Tertius, Impudicus, Acroni Famosus, Græcis ἰατρὸς, sicut Medicus Martiali, itemque Bridferto Ramesiensi Presbytero. Impudicus, ineptâ prorsus ratione, meo judicio dicitur, quia Medici eo digito vulnerum putredines tangere solent. Fortasse rectius Medium dixeris. Quartus AnnuAnnularis, δακτυλιώτης, Acroni & Isidoro medicus & medicina-le; præposterè. Quintus minimus, & ὠτίτης vocabatur. Hos digitos Supputationibus adhibebant: idq; aut apertis & porrectis, aut constrictis, & complicatis digitis, facto initio à manu lævâ ab uno usque ad centum, quem numerum centenarium in dextram posteà transferebant. Res igitur sic habet: Minimus digitus auricularis lævę manus & medio artui palma inflexus Unitatem notabat. Annularis eodem modo inflexus, & positus: Duo. Et sic quoque inflexus impudicus sive medicus significabat Tria: minimus sublatus Quatuor: annularis erectus Quinq,: sublatus Index, ita ut pausa fiat manus solo medio ad palmam affixo Sex indigitabat. Omnes reliqui elevati, manente solùm minimo in radice palmæ Septenarium numerabant. Octo annularius similiter erectus. Novem fiunt, si annulari erecto componas ad latùs digitum medium. Decem numerabis, si unguem Indicis in medio pollicis membro, ubi flectitur introrsum constitutum habeas, Apulejus Apolog. O falsum, audax & nimium! o mendacium, viginti annorum exilio puniendum! dimidio tanta, Æmiliane, mentiri, falsa audes sequialterâ? Si triginta annos pro decem dixisses, posses videri pro computationis gestu errasse, quos circulare debueris digitos, operuisse. Undecim, si præter apertam illam Indicis cum pollice circulationem, quâ decem exprimebas, digitum minimum suppresseris, duobus intermedijs erectis, & sic in reliquis, donec ad denarium iterùm perveneris. Sic novendecim fiunt, si decem primùm, eo quo diximus modo, exprimas, dein tres reliquos digitos erigas & extendas, quæ nota est novenarij. Jam verò cùm ad Viginti perveneris, non potes uni decem alterum, similiter eorumdem digitorum κἀμψεω expressum addere: quare, Viginti si computare velis, summitatem pollicis intermedios Indicis, & Impudici artus immittes, ita ut utrumq; contingat. Si Triginta, utrumq; unguem Indicis & pollicis columbatim summo, ut itâ dicam, rostello junges. Apulejus Apolog. Si triginta annos pro decem dixisses, posses videri pro computationis gestu errasse, quos circulare debueris digitos aperuisse.
units.tr: FIRST, then, the name of each finger must be kept in mind. The first is Pollex (thumb). The second is Index (forefinger) to some, but to others ἀσπασμὸς [aspasmos] and ἐπιδεικτικὸς [epideiktikos], the greeting finger and the pointing finger. The third is Impudicus (the shameless one), Famosus (the infamous) to Acron, ἰατρὸς [iatros] to the Greeks, and Medicus (the physician) in Martial, and likewise to Bridferth of Ramsey, a presbyter. In my judgement, Impudicus is called so on quite a senseless principle, because doctors usually touch the putrefaction of wounds with that finger. You might more fittingly call it the Middle finger. The fourth is Annularis (ring finger), δακτυλιώτης [daktyliotes], and medicus and medicinalis to Acron and Isidore, which is wrong. The fifth, minimus (little finger), was called ὠτίτης [otites]. They used these fingers in reckoning, either with the fingers open and extended, or closed and folded, beginning with the left hand from one up to a hundred. Afterwards they transferred that hundred to the right hand. The matter stands thus. The little finger of the left hand, bent at the middle joint and pressed to the palm, marked Unitatem (one). The ring finger, bent and placed in the same way, marked Duo (two). Likewise the bent Impudicus, or medius, signified Tria (three). The little finger raised signified Quatuor (four), the ring finger erect Quinq(ue) (five), and the index raised, so that a pause is made with the middle finger alone fixed to the palm, indicated Sex (six). All the others raised, with only the little finger remaining at the root of the palm, they counted as Septenarium (seven). Octo (eight) is the ring finger likewise erect. Novem (nine) results if, with the ring finger erect, you set the middle finger beside it. You will count Decem (ten) if you hold the nail of the index at the middle joint of the thumb, where it bends inward. Apuleius, Apology: "O false, bold, and excessive man! O lie to be punished with twenty years' exile! Are you so bold, Aemilianus, as to lie by half, to make falsehoods of one and a half? If you had said thirty years for ten, you might seem to have erred in the gesture of counting, having had to open the fingers that ought to have been circled." Undecim (eleven): if, besides that open circle of index and thumb with which you expressed ten, you hold down the little finger, with the two middle fingers erect, and so on through the rest, until you again reach ten. So novendecim (nineteen) results if you first express ten in the way we have said, then raise and extend the other three fingers. This is the sign of nineteen. Now when you come to Viginti (twenty), you cannot add to one ten another ten expressed by the bending [κάμψεως] of the same fingers. So if you wish to count twenty, you put the tip of the thumb to the middle joints of the index and of the Impudicus, so that both touch. For Triginta (thirty), you join the nails of the index and thumb together, as it were in a dove's beak. Apuleius, Apology: "If you had said thirty years for ten, you might seem to have erred in the gesture of counting, having had to open the fingers that ought to have been circled."

units.la: Ausonius Ep. ad Theonem, cùm illi triginta ostrea misisset: Ostrea Bajanis certantia, quæ Meduloram
units.tr: Ausonius, in his letter to Theon, when he had sent him thirty oysters: Ostrea Bajanis certantia, quae Meduloram

units.la: Dulcibus in stagnis refluì maris æstus opimat,
units.tr: The oysters, which vie with those of Baiae, which the tide of the sea, flowing back, fattens in the sweet pools,

units.la: Accepi dilecte Theon, numerabile manus.
units.tr: I received, dear Theon, countable on the hand.

units.la: Verum quot fuerint, subjecta monosticha signant,
units.tr: But how many they were, the lines set below show:

units.la: Quot ter lustratus cum pollice computat Index,
units.tr: As many as the index, circling three times with the thumb, counts,

units.la: Geryones quot erant, decies si multiplicentur.
units.tr: As many as Geryon had, if ten is multiplied by ten.

units.la: Hieronymus lib. 1. ad Jovinianum: Triginta referuntur ad Nuptias. Nam & ipsa digitorum conjunctio, quasi molli osculo se complexans, & fœderans, maritum pingit, & conjugem. Sexaginta vero ad viduas, ꝏ quod in angustia & tribulatione sunt positæ: unde & superiori digito deprimuntur. Quantoq; major est difficultas experta quondam voluptatis illecebris abstinere, tanto majus est præmium. Porrò Centesimus numerus de sinistâ transfertur ad dextram, & ijsdem quidem digitis, sed non eâdem manu, quibus in læva nuptæ, & viduæ circulum faciens, virginitatis exprimit coronam. Idem hucalludens in cap. xiii. D. Matthæi.
units.tr: Jerome, book 1 against Jovinian: Thirty is referred to marriage. For the very joining of the fingers, embracing and clasping each other as with a soft kiss, depicts a husband and a wife. Sixty refers to widows, because they are placed in straits and tribulation; hence they are also pressed down by the upper finger. And the greater the difficulty of abstaining from pleasures once experienced, the greater the reward. Further, the hundredth number is transferred from the left hand to the right, and indeed with the same fingers but not the same hand. Making a circle with the left hand for wives and widows, it expresses the crown of virginity. He alludes to this again in chapter 13 of Matthew:

units.la: Primum ergo, inquit, debemus audire, deinde intelligere. & post intelligentiam fructus reddere doctrinarum, & facere vel centesimum fructum, & sexagesimum, atq; tricesimum, de quibus plenius in libro contra Jovinianum diximus, & nunc breviter perstringemus, centesimum fructum virginibus, sexagesimum viduis & continentibus, tricesimum sanctło matrimonio deputantes.
units.tr: First, he says, we ought to hear, then to understand, and after understanding to yield the fruit of teachings, and to bear a hundredfold fruit, and sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. Of these we have spoken more fully in the book against Jovinian, and now we will touch on them briefly, assigning the hundredfold fruit to virgins, the sixtyfold to widows and the continent, and the thirtyfold to holy matrimony.

units.la: Quadraginta compones, si concavum pollicis convexo sive dorso, ut loquitur Beda, vel etiam lateri Indicis superinduxeris, reliquis tribus digitis porrectis. Sic enim palma fiet. Apulejus: Cùm verò quadraginta, quæ facilius cæterù porrectâ palmâ significantur, ea quadraginta tu dimidio auges; non potes digitorum gestu errasse. Plautus noster Epid. i. i. v.50. Quid istanc quam emit, quanti emit? T H. Tot. E P. Quadraginta minis! T H. Id adeò argentum ab Danista, apud Thebas sumsit fenore, in dies minasq; argenti singulas, nummus. Sic enim ex Mss. & edd. restituì illum locum.
units.tr: You will compound Quadraginta (forty) if you place the hollow of the thumb over the convex back of it, or, as Bede says, over the side of the index, with the other three fingers extended. For so the palm is formed. Apuleius: "But when forty, which is more easily signified by the outstretched palm, you increase by half, you cannot have erred in the gesture of the fingers." Our Plautus, Epidicus 1.1.50: "What did he buy her for, and at what price? TH. Just so much. EP. For forty minae! TH. Yes, and that silver he took at interest from the moneylender at Thebes, one coin a day for each mina of silver." For so I have restored that passage from the manuscripts and editions.

units.la: Quinquagenarij autem forma simplicissima, Gammæ elementi vice functa, palmam intrinsecus spectans. Sexaginta si vis numerare, pollicem in formam Gammæ curvatum diligenter à fronte circumducto Indice præcingas. Notat Hieronymus nymus dicto loco. Si Septuaginta, Indicem itidem flexum immisso pollice superimple, ungulâ pollicis duntaxat erectâ trans medium indicis articulum: Si Octoginta, pollicem protensum in Indicem curvatum immittas, ungulâ pollicis in medio Indicis articulo haerente. Si Nonaginta, Indicis inflexi unguiculam iiso pollici infige. Hucusq; sinistrae manus numeri. Hinc à Centenario ad decem millia in dextrâ supputabant, ut colligimus tum ex Hieronymo: tum ex Macrobij loco lib.i. Saturn. c. vii. Inde & simulacrum Jani fingitur plerumq; manu dextera trecentum: at sinistra sexaginta quinq; numerum tenens ad demonstrandam anni dimensionem. Pro lxv reponuntalij lv. quàm bene, nescio. Scribit enim Plinii lib. xxxiv. c. vi. Praeterea Janus Geminus à Numâ Rege dicatus, qui pacis belliq; argumento colitur, digitis ita figuratis, ut trecentorum quinquaginta quinq; dierum per significationem anni, temporis & aevi se Deum indicaret. Decem Macrobio minus. Nec Macrobius solum lxv exprimit, sed & Suidas voce Ιανουάριος, & Georgius Codinus in libello Statuarum, quae Constantinopoli ejus tempore exstabant. Vide etiam David Haeschel ad Horapollinem pag.171. Esto autem, scripserit ita Plinius. Sed loquitur ille de primo Jani simulachro à Numâ dicato, qui Numa annum cccl v dierum quoque numero instituit. Macrobius ac reliqui de ijs Jani simulachris, qualia suo tempore erant, nec unum ea, sed plurima, in quibus correcto praesertim jam anno à Julio Caesare, acad cccl v dies redacto, quis tam ineptus erit, ut depositi illius, ac antiquiani annii numeros remansisse, vel etiam revixisse credat? In manu igitur sinistra ultimus erat numerus nonaginta novem: à quo transit erat ad dextram, quod ignorasse videtur Erasmus Roterodamus Notis ad Hieronymum. Irenaeus lib.i. adverf. Haereses cap. xiii. ...
units.tr: The form for Quinquagenarij (fifty) is very simple: it takes the place of the letter Gamma, with the palm facing inward. If you want to count Sexaginta (sixty), carefully bend the thumb into the shape of a Gamma and encircle it from the front with the index. Jerome notes this in the passage cited. For Septuaginta (seventy), put the thumb into the similarly bent index and fill it up, with only the nail of the thumb raised across the middle joint of the index. For Octoginta (eighty), put the extended thumb into the curved index, the nail of the thumb sticking at the middle joint of the index. For Nonaginta (ninety), press the little nail of the bent index onto the thumb. So far the numbers of the left hand. From Centenario (a hundred) up to ten thousand they reckoned on the right hand, as we gather both from Jerome and from the passage of Macrobius, Saturnalia book 1, ch. 7: "Hence the statue of Janus is commonly fashioned with the right hand holding three hundred, but the left holding sixty-five, to show the measure of the year." Others read lv in place of lxv; how rightly, I do not know. For Pliny, book 34, ch. 6, writes: "Moreover, Janus Geminus, dedicated by King Numa, who is worshipped as a sign of peace and war, had his fingers so shaped that by their signification he showed himself to be God of the three hundred and fifty-five days of the year, of time and of the age." Macrobius has ten less. Not only Macrobius expresses sixty-five, but also Suidas under the word Ἰανουάριος [Ianouarios], and George Codinus in his little book on statues, which still stood at Constantinople in his time. See also David Hoeschel on Horapollo, p. 171. Be that as it may, let Pliny have written so. But he speaks of the first statue of Janus, dedicated by Numa, who also set up a year of 355 days. Macrobius and the rest speak of those statues of Janus as they were in their own time, and not of one but of many, in which, the year having been corrected by Julius Caesar and reduced to 365 days, who would be so foolish as to believe that the numbers of that abandoned and older year remained, or even came back to life? In the left hand, therefore, the last number was nonaginta novem, ninety-nine, from which one passed to the right hand. Erasmus of Rotterdam seems to have been ignorant of this, in his Notes on Jerome. Irenaeus, book 1 Against Heresies, ch. 13 ...

units.la: Quae latinè sic vertas: Quapropter etiam ipsum pro prudentâ suâ fugisse locum illum, qui est nonaginta novem, id est, defectum, numerum in sinistrâ manu exprimi solitum. Unitatem vero amplius insectari, quae nonaginta istis addita, in dextram ejus manum num transtulit. Igitur in dextrâ nihil nisi centena numerabis veluti; Centum, Ducenta, Sexcenta, & porrò Mille, sive, Decies centum, duo millia, sive vicies centum, octo millia, sive octuagies centum. Quod si verbi causâ, centum ac duodecim computare velis, itemq; centum viginti sex: in manu dextrâ computabis cen-tum, in sinistrâ duodecim; viginti sex. Eo modo Janus Geminus manu dextrâ significabat c c c. sinistrâ lxv. Sic quod è Mar-tiano Capellâ lib. vii. de Arithmeticâ à Colvio & Grutero ad-ducitur: Digiti verò virginis recursantes, & quadam incompre-henfa mobilitatis scaturigine vermiculati, quæ mox ingressa septi-ngentos decem, & septem numeros complicatis in eos digitis, jovem falutabunda subvexit; ita intelligendum est, quod virgo illa Arithmetica, septingentos numeros manu dextrâ ostênderit eâ for-mâ, quâ in levâ formantur septuaginta, septemdecim verò fini-ftrâ. Lepidum admodum Epigramma Nicarchi è xi. Anthol. adducunt Erafmus & Colvius de anu Cotittari.
units.tr: Which you would render into Latin thus: Wherefore he also, out of his prudence, avoided that place which is ninety-nine, that is, the deficient number customarily expressed in the left hand. But he pursued the unit more fully, and when he had added it to those ninety, he transferred it into his right hand. Therefore in the right hand you will count only hundreds, as it were: Hundred, Two hundred, Six hundred, and further Thousand, or Ten hundred, two thousand, or twenty hundred, eight thousand, or eighty hundred. But if, for example, you wish to count one hundred and twelve, and likewise one hundred and twenty-six: in the right hand you will count the hundred, in the left the twelve; the twenty-six in the same way. In this manner Janus Geminus signified with the right hand three hundred and with the left sixty-five. So too what is cited from Martianus Capella, book 7, On Arithmetic, by Colvius and Gruter: But the fingers of the virgin, flexing back and quivering with a certain uncomprehended spring of mobility, soon entered upon seven hundred and seventeen numbers, and with fingers folded upon them, she lifted up Jupiter with a greeting. This should be understood thus: that the virgin Arithmetic showed seven hundred with the right hand in the form in which seventy is formed on the left, and seventeen on the left. Erasmus and Colvius cite a very charming epigram of Nicarchus, from book 11 of the Anthology, about the old woman of Cotyttus.

units.la: Ἡ πολιὴ ἡρτάφοισι κοτυτασίς, ἡ πολύμυθος γραῖα, δὴ ἦν Νέσωρ ἐν ἑπ πρεσβύταρος, ἡ φάος ἀξιήσασ' ἑλαφρὸ πλέον, ἡ χρεὶ λαὴν γῆρας ἀειθμέ ἄλλοτε ... ζώει ἢ λευκὰ ... ὡς τε μὴ δισάζειν μή τι πέπορθ' ἀδίης.
units.tr: The grey-haired, garrulous old woman, who was an elder like Nestor, judged that the light (of life) was worth a little more; she who ... still lives, white ... so that she does not grieve over any misfortune of old age. [Ἡ πολιὴ ἡρτάφοισι κοτυτασίς, ἡ πολύμυθος γραῖα, δὴ ἦν Νέσωρ ἐν ἑπ πρεσβύταρος, ἡ φάος ἀξιήσασ' ἑλαφρὸ πλέον, ἡ χρεὶ λαὴν γῆρας ἀειθμέ ἄλλοτε ... ζώει ἢ λευκὰ ... ὡς τε μὴ δισάζειν μή τι πέπορθ' ἀδίης.]

units.la: Quos versus sic Latine reddidi: Temporibus niveis, dicaxq; venefica facla Euboici vincit Neftoris, & senium. Longius at cervo gaudet vixisse, sinistrâ Connumerans ævi fœcla fecunda fui. Mens viget, atq; oculi retinent sua lumina, pesq; Integer: an Stygium credimus esse Deum?
units.tr: I have rendered these verses into Latin thus: With snowy temples, and a witty old crone, she surpasses the Euboean Nestor in age. But she rejoices to have lived longer than a stag, counting on her left hand the fruitful years of her life. Her mind is vigorous, her eyes keep their light, and her feet are whole: can we believe that she is a Stygian goddess?

units.la: Est jocus in anum, quæ ultrà centum annos prove ēta in sinistrâ manu cæpit annos suos numerare, dein redijt ad dextram, ac du-centesimum attigit. Sic intelligendus Juvenalis de Neftore Sa-tyr. X. Felix nimirum, qui per tot fæcula mortem Distulit, atq; suos in dextrâ computat annos.
units.tr: There is a joke about an old woman who, having lived beyond a hundred years, began to count her years on her left hand, then returned to the right, and reached two hundred. Juvenal's line about Nestor (Satire 10) should be understood in this way: Fortunate indeed is he who has put off death through so many ages, and counts his years on his right hand.

units.la: M
units.tr: M

units.la: Igitur Centum numerantur in dextrâ manu, sicut in lævâ decem, posito ungue Indicis in medio pollice: ita ut circulatio quidem fiat, aperta tamen, id est, ut residuum relinquatur primum pollicis membrum. Ducenta in dextrâ, quæ in lævâ viginti. Trecenta, quæ in illâ triginta. Quadringenta, quæ in alterâ quadraginta. Quintilianus Institut. Orat. lib. XI. cap. III. Nam gestum poculum poscentis, aut verbera minantis, aut numerum quingentorum flexo pollice efficientis, &c.
units.tr: Thus one hundred is counted on the right hand, just as ten on the left, with the nail of the index finger placed on the middle of the thumb; the circle is indeed formed, but left open, so that the first joint of the thumb remains free. Two hundred on the right hand, which is twenty on the left. Three hundred, which on that hand is thirty. Four hundred, which on the other is forty. Quintilian, Institutes of Oratory, book 11, chapter 3: For the gesture of one asking for a cup, or of one threatening blows, or of one showing five hundred by a bent thumb, and so on.

units.la: Efficiuntur autem quinquaginta in sinistrâ flexo pollice, ac in Gammæ elementi figuram decussato.
units.tr: Fifty is made on the left hand with the thumb bent, and crossed in the shape of the letter gamma.

units.la: Sexcenta in dextrâ, quod in sinistrâ sexaginta. Et sic porrò, usque ad mille, quod in dextrâ vocatur uti unum in lævâ: duo millia, ut in lævâ duo: tria millia, ut in eadem tria: novem millia, ut ibi novem: ad decem millia usque. Quod si centum duo millia computes, utrumque & centum, & duo millia singilla-tim exprimis suis digitis eădem manu dextrâ. Sic si tria millia octingenta, cujus summæ mentio est apud Artemidorum lib. II. cap. LXV. unumquemque numerum suo modo in manu dextrâ significas: unde in pugnum ferè manus claudi-tur, nisi quod pollex Indici immittitur, non super inducitur, quam formam in lævâ esse diximus octogenarij. Atq; istis duo-bus numeris MMM & DCC manuque ita in pugnum coactâ, nihil plané significari solitum, etiam idem Artemidorus author est. Cùm ad decem millia, quam Græci μυριάδα vocant, Barbari Milionem, ventum est, non amplius solæ sufficiunt manus, sed jam præter illas corpus solidum assumitur, ut pectus, femora, aliaque corporis membra. In quibus membris indigetatio fit cum manu sinistrâ usque ad decem μυριάδας centum millia. De-cem millia fiunt, si lævam in medio pectore supines, ut musculus tuæ manus pectus tangat, digitis collum spectantibus, precan-tium prorsus in morem. Viginti millia, si eandem decussatim pectori imponas, ita ut summitates digitorum dextram tui cor-poris partem respiciant.
units.tr: Six hundred on the right hand, which on the left is sixty. And so on, up to a thousand, which is shown on the right as one is on the left; two thousand, as two on the left; three thousand, as three on the same hand; nine thousand as nine there, up to ten thousand. If you wish to count two thousand one hundred, you express each of the two numbers, the hundred and the two thousand, separately with your fingers on the same right hand. So too if you signify three thousand eight hundred, the sum mentioned by Artemidorus in book 2, chapter 65, you signify each number in its own way on the right hand; thus the hand is nearly closed into a fist, except that the thumb is placed against the index finger, not laid over it, which we said is the form of eighty on the left. Artemidorus also tells us that with these two numbers, three thousand and eight hundred, and the hand thus clenched into a fist, nothing at all was customarily signified. When one comes to ten thousand, which the Greeks call myriad and the barbarians a million, the hands alone no longer suffice, but the solid body is also employed, such as the breast, the thighs and other limbs of the body. With these limbs the counting proceeds, with the left hand, up to a hundred thousand myriads. Ten thousand is made if you lay the left hand supine on the middle of the chest, so that the back of the hand touches the breast, the fingers pointing toward the neck, exactly in the manner of those who pray. Twenty thousand, if you place the same hand crosswise on the breast, so that the tips of the fingers face the right side of your body.

units.la: Triginta millia, si ibidem pronam ponas, & erectam pollice carti-lagini medij pectoris immisso. Quadraginta millia, si in umbilico erectam supines. Quinqua-ginta millia, si ejusdem pronæ & erectæ pollicem umbilico imponas. Sexaginta millia, si eadem prona fœmur lævum desuper comprehendas: si supinam femori superimponas.
units.tr: Thirty thousand, if you place the hand there prone, and upright, with the thumb pressed into the cartilage of the middle of the chest. Forty thousand, if you lay the upright hand supine on the navel. Fifty thousand, if you place the thumb of the same hand, prone and upright, on the navel. Sixty thousand, if with the same hand prone you grasp the left thigh from above; if you lay the hand supine on the thigh, placed on top.

units.la: Septuaginta millia; si pronam, octuaginta. Sinonaginta millia eadem lævâ lumbos apprehendes, pollice ad inguina converso, eorum more, qui, ut loquitur Plautus noster, ansati incedunt, Hæc sinistræ cum corpore munia. Nunc capè etiam dextræ.
units.tr: Seventy thousand, if prone; eighty thousand. Ninety thousand: with the same left hand you take hold of the loins, with the thumb turned toward the groin, as those do who, as our Plautus says, walk with their arms akimbo. These are the duties of the left hand with the body. Now take the right hand as well.

units.la: Centum fiunt millia, sive μυριάδες decem, ut μυριάς in sinistrâ, dexterâ videlicet manu in medio pectoris supinatâ digitis collum spectantibus. Ducenta millia, ut illic viginti millia. Trecenta, ut illic triginta, & sic in cæteris, ut Octingenta millia, quemadmodum octuaginta in lævâ, dextrâ videlicet prona in fœmur ingestâ, cique superpositâ. Ad quem modum ludere mihi videtur Periplectomenes apud Plautum nostrum. Mil. 2. 2. v. 48.
units.tr: One hundred thousand, or ten myriads, is made as a myriad on the left, that is, with the right hand supine on the middle of the chest, the fingers pointing toward the neck. Two hundred thousand, as twenty thousand there. Three hundred, as thirty there, and so on for the rest; so eight hundred thousand, just as eighty on the left, namely with the right hand prone, laid on the thigh and placed upon it. Plautus's Periplectomenus seems to me to play in this manner, in our Plautus, Miles Gloriosus 2.2, verse 48.

units.la: Pellus digitis pulsat, cor credo evocaturus est foras.
units.tr: He strikes the pulse with his fingers; I think he is going to call the heart out.

units.la: Ecce autem avortit, nisus lævâ, in femine habet lavam manum..
units.tr: But look, he turns away, straining with his left hand; he has his hand on his thigh.

units.la: Dexterâ digitis rationem computat, feriens femur
units.tr: With the right hand he counts the reckoning on his fingers, striking the thigh

units.la: Dexteram ita vehementer, quod tactu agre suppetit.
units.tr: with the right hand so vigorously that it can scarcely be reached by touch.

units.la: Nongenta millia notabis in dextrâ; ut in sinistrâ nonaginta. Ad centies centum, sive centena millia si computes, dextram manum sinistræ inseras, digitosque si dicere liceat, congenues, mutuo inter se nexu complicatos.
units.tr: You will mark nine hundred thousand on the right hand, as ninety on the left. If you wish to count a hundred times a hundred, or a hundred thousand, you put the right hand into the left, and, if one may say so, the fingers interlock, folded together in mutual connection.

units.la: Atque ita Prodromo Bedâ, satis ut opinor, dilucidè exposuit hanc rationem veterum per digitos, quam ille Indigitationem appellat.
units.tr: And thus, I think, Beda in his Prodromus has sufficiently explained this method of the ancients by means of the fingers, which he calls indigitation.

units.la: Solent & Latini sic loqui: In digitos mittere, ut Macrob. lib. 11. cap. x 1. in Somn. Scipionis. Et lib. 1. Saturn. cap. 1. Sic etiam Græci. Pollux: ἐπὶ δακτύλων θέσεω, λογίζεσθαι. Vocant quoq; Ducere: & Subducere.
units.tr: Latin writers also speak in this way: to put into the fingers, as Macrobius, book 1, chapter 11 (?), on the Dream of Scipio; and book 1 of the Saturnalia, chapter 1. So too the Greeks; Pollux: to reckon on the placing of the fingers [ἐπὶ δακτύλων θέσεω, λογίζεσθαι]. They also say to lead and to subduct.

units.la: Terent. Adelph. Numquam ita quisquam tam bene subduxit ratione ad vitam fuit. Quo loco Donatus: Bene subductâ: est, bene dine disposita, bene computata. Ducere enim, est digitis computare Sed Ducere est apud alium palam: Subducere apud seipsum, & secreto.
units.tr: Terence, Adelphi: Never did anyone reckon so well in his life. On this passage Donatus says: Bene subductâ means well arranged, well computed. For ducere means to compute with the fingers, but ducere is used when speaking openly to another; subducere when one reckons with oneself, and in secret.

units.la: Nobis hodie difficilis hæc ratio numerandi videtur: immò impossibilis, ob miras digitorum flexiones, quas sine duratione alicujus membri vix fieri credas. Unde Græcus Poëta eam calculationem δακτυλοκαμψίοδωὴν vocat, epigrammate illo, quod est apud Stobæum pag. 128. Edit. Gesner.
units.tr: To us today this method of counting seems difficult, indeed impossible, on account of the remarkable bending of the fingers, which you would hardly believe could be done without the strain of some limb. Hence the Greek poet calls this kind of calculation finger-bending counting [δακτυλοκαμψίοδωὴν], in that epigram which is in Stobaeus, page 128, Gesner's edition.

units.la: περὶ δανειζομένων τὴν σὴν φρένα, τοῖς δὲ δανείσαις, καὶ λίπτε τὴν ψῆφον δακτυλοκαμψίοδωὴν οὐ?
units.tr: [περὶ δανειζομένων τὴν σὴν φρένα, τοῖς δὲ δανείσαις, καὶ λίπτε τὴν ψῆφον δακτυλοκαμψίοδωὴν οὐ?]

units.la: Quod sic verto:
units.tr: Which I render thus:

units.la: Fœnora tu captans, mentem oblectare memento:Atq; aliis numeros linquito flexibiles.
units.tr: While you chase after interest, remember to amuse your mind, and leave the flexible numbers to others.

units.la: Interim familiariter hanc norunt Græci, & Latini: etiam pueri; ac ideò, si actor fortè digitorum saltè incerto aut indecoro gestu à computatione dissentiret, judicabatur olim indoctus, authore Quintiliano lib. i. Instit. c. 10. Et fortasse huc facit Alcimi Aviti illud lib. ad Fuscinam sororem.
units.tr: Meanwhile the Greeks and Latins knew this practice well, even boys; and therefore, if an advocate, by chance, departed from the computation with some uncertain or unseemly gesture of his fingers, he was once judged unlearned, on the authority of Quintilian, Institutes, book 1, chapter 10. And perhaps Alcimus Avitus's line in his book to his sister Fuscina bears on this.

units.la: Succiduoq; simul, quod quieq; in tempore judex Gesserit, ut digitos, soror, isthæc omnia dudum Doctatenes----
units.tr: And at the same time, whatever the judge at each moment had done, sister, you had long since learned all these things by your fingers ...

units.la: Inprimis fœneratoribus eam fuisse notissimā, constat ex vetustissimis Epigrammatis: tum eo, quod modò adduxeram, tum hoc Palladæ ex 11. Anthol.
units.tr: That usury was very well known is clear from the most ancient epigrams: both from the passage I have just cited, and from this one of Palladas, in Anthology book 11.

units.la: ὃ τῆς ταχίσης ἀρπαγῆς τῆς Ἐ βίω!αἰνὴς δανειστῆς τῶν χρόνων γλύφων τόκης,τέθνηκεν εὐθὺς ἐν ροπῆς καιρῷ ἔραχεῖ,ἐν δακτύλοισι τοὺς τόκες σφίγγων ἔτι
units.tr: O the swift rapacity of life! The cruel moneylender of time, the carver of interest, has died suddenly, in the instant of a turning scale, while still clutching the interest in his fingers. [ὦ τῆς ταχείης ἁρπαγῆς τοῦ βίου, αἰνὴς δανειστὴς τῶν χρόνων, γλύφων τόκους, τέθνηκεν εὐθὺς ἐν ῥοπῆς καιρῷ σμικρῷ, ἐν δακτύλοισι τοὺς τόκους σφίγγων ἔτι]

units.la: Hoc est, me interprete:
units.tr: This, with me as interpreter, is:

units.la: O pol fugacem pranimis vitæ modum!Notat examussim tempora Usurarius:Quem Mors repente sternit usq; calculosLaboriose jactitantem dexterâ.
units.tr: Oh, by Pollux, how fleeting is the measure of life, too swift! The usurer marks the times exactly, whom Death suddenly lays low, still laboriously tossing the counters with his right hand.

units.la: Non absimile est ejusdem Palladæ. Anthol. 11. pag. 184. Alciphron. etiam Epistolâ xxvi meminit. μέγα τι κακὸν εἰσὶν οἱ πε-ρὶ τὰς ψήφους ἢ τῶν ψακτύλων τὰς κάμψεις κιλινδήμενοι. Scævola J C. ff. de Fidei com. lib. ἄχεις ἂν τὰς ψήφους ἀποκατασήσασιν: Donec rationes reddiderint. Meminerunt hujus supputatio-nis & alij scriptores multi, quorum Testimonia, quia semel huc descendi, addam quoq;.
units.tr: Not unlike this is another passage of the same Palladas, Anthology book 11, p. 184. Alciphron also mentions it in Epistle 26: "They are a great evil, those who fuss over the counters or the bending of their fingers" [μέγα τι κακόν εἰσιν οἱ περὶ τὰς ψήφους ἢ τῶν δακτύλων τὰς κάμψεις κυλινδούμενοι]. Scaevola the jurist, in the Digest, on fideicommissa, book [...], has: "until they have restored the counters" [ἄχρις ἂν τὰς ψήφους ἀποκαταστήσωσιν], that is, "until they have rendered their accounts." Many other writers also mention this method of reckoning, and since I have once gone down this path, I will add their testimonies too.

units.la: Ovid. lib. 1. de Ponto Eleg. 111.
units.tr: Ovid, Epistulae ex Ponto, book 1, elegy 111.

units.la: At reditu jam quùq; suos amat, & sibi quid sit Utile, sollicitis computat articulis.
units.tr: But now, too, he loves his return, and with anxious knuckles he counts up what is useful to himself.

units.la: Seneca lib. 111. cap. xxxiii. de Irâ: Quid si propter usuram aut millesimam valetudinariu fenerator distortu pedibus, & manibus ad computandum, non relictis clamat, ac per vadimonia assis suos in ipsum morbi accessionibus vindicat.
units.tr: Seneca, On Anger, book 3, chapter 33: What if a moneylender, crippled in feet and hands from counting for the sake of interest or a thousandth part, does not stop, but shouts out, and through sureties claims his dues even in the attacks of his illness?

units.la: Plinius Secundus lib. 11. Epist. x x. Quo die, quâ horâ, nata esset, interrogavit: ubi audivit, componit vultum, intendit oculos, movet labra, agitat digitos, computat diu.
units.tr: Pliny the Younger, Letters, book 2, letter 20: He asked on what day and at what hour she was born; when he heard, he composes his face, fixes his eyes, moves his lips, works his fingers, and counts for a long time.

units.la: Suetonius Claud. c. xxx i. Nec ullo spectaculi genere comior, aut remissior erat: adeò ut oblatos victoribus aureos, prolatâq; sinistrâ pariter cum vulgo, voce digitiq; numeraret.
units.tr: Suetonius, Claudius, chapter 31: Nor was he more affable or relaxed at any kind of spectacle, so much so that when gold coins were offered to the victors, he counted them out aloud with the crowd, raising his left hand and working his fingers.

units.la: Spartianus in D. Juliano dicit: Populum sibi adversum placasse pollicitatione aureorum, quos digitis ostendebat, ut fidem faceret.
units.tr: Spartianus, in the life of Didius Julianus, says: He placated the people, who were hostile to him, by promising gold pieces, which he showed on his fingers, so as to make them believe him.

units.la: Latinus Pacatus initio Panegyrici dicti Theodosio: Cum igitur impediat turba delectum, atque tandem prastet gesta in summam referre, quam enumerando tenuari, dixisse sufficiat, unum illum divinitus exstitisse, in quo virtutes simul omnes vigerent, quæ singulæ in omnibus prædicantur.
units.tr: Latinus Pacatus, at the beginning of the panegyric delivered to Theodosius: Since therefore the crowd hinders the selection, and since, finally, it is enough to sum up the deeds, which are weakened by being enumerated one by one, let it suffice to say that one man existed by divine providence in whom all the virtues flourished together, which are praised singly in all others.

units.la: Augustinus lib. xvi ii. de Civitate Dei. cap. l iii. Omnium vero de hac calculantium digitos resolvit, & quiescere jubet ille, qui dicit: Non est vestrum scire tempora, quæ Pater in suâ posuit potestate.
units.tr: Augustine, City of God, book 18, chapter 53: But he unbends the fingers of all who calculate about this, and bids them be still, he who says: "It is not for you to know the times, which the Father has put in his own power."

units.la: Seneca Epist. l xxxvii. Numerare docet me Arithmetica, & Avaritiæ commodare digitos.
units.tr: Seneca, Letters, letter 87: Arithmetic teaches me to count, and to lend my fingers to avarice.

units.la: Tertull. Apolog. Sed interim longum multis instrumentis cum digitorum supputatorijs gesticulis adsidendum.
units.tr: Tertullian, Apology: But meanwhile one must sit a long time over many instruments, with the finger gestures of reckoning.

units.la: Sidonius Apollinaris lib. ix. Epist. ix. Chrysippus digitis propter numerorum indicia constrictis.
units.tr: Sidonius Apollinaris, book 9, letter 9: Chrysippus, with his fingers bent together for the indication of numbers.

units.la: Plutarchus Apophthegmatis: Ο ἐφόρος ὁ βασιλεὺς τοῦ Ἀγησιλάου, γαμβρὸς, ἀπὸ μιᾶς πεντάδος ... Ατque haec abunde sufficiant de veterum ratione supputandi: de qua quidem meam sententiam duobus locis Plauti admonitus, in gratiam Antiquitatis studiosorum tam prolixè addere non piguit.
units.tr: Plutarch, Apophthegms: The ephor, the king of Agesilaus, his son-in-law, from one pentad... [ὁ ἔφορος ὁ βασιλεὺς τοῦ Ἀγησιλάου, γαμβρὸς, ἀπὸ μιᾶς πεντάδος ...] And these things will suffice abundantly concerning the ancient manner of reckoning. About this, prompted by two passages of Plautus, I have not been reluctant to set out my own opinion at such length, for the sake of those who study antiquity.

units.la: AVARITIÆ.
units.tr: Avarice.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Divitiarum: Pecuniæ: Liberalitatis.
units.tr: See also the titles Riches: Money: Liberality.

units.la: AVARI in thesauro suo cor defixum habent: quorum scilicet Deus Mammon est. Aul. 3.3. v. 1.
units.tr: Misers keep their heart fixed on their treasure, that is, their god is Mammon. Aul. 3.3. v. 1.

units.la: CHARACTER hominis avari est Euclio: de cujus sordibus vide totam scen. 4. Act. 2. Aul.
units.tr: The character of the miser is Euclio; for his meanness see the whole of scene 4, act 2, Aul.

units.la: AVARI sæpe decipiuntur in suâ aviditate. Rud. 4.7. v.13.
units.tr: Misers are often deceived in their greed. Rud. 4.7. v.13.

units.la: AVARI thesauros suos recondebant in sepulchris. Pseud. 1.4. v.20. Vide Tit. Sepulchri.
units.tr: Misers used to hide their treasures in tombs. Pseud. 1.4. v.20. See the title Sepulchre.

units.la: AVARI etiam araneas in ædibus sibi servari volunt, ut Euclio. Aul. 1. 2. v. 9.
units.tr: Misers even want spiders kept in their houses, as Euclio does. Aul. 1. 2. v. 9.

units.la: PAUPERES sceappellant. Aul. 1.2. v. 10.
units.tr: They call themselves paupers. Aul. 1.2. v. 10.

units.la: NEGANT ignem & aquam. Aul. 1. 2. v. 12.16.
units.tr: They deny fire and water. Aul. 1. 2. v. 12.16.

units.la: AVARI servis edacitatem objicere solent. Trin. 4.3.v. 9.
units.tr: Misers are wont to charge their slaves with gluttony. Trin. 4.3.v. 9.

units.la: AVARI suspicaces: ut Euclio suspicabatur omnibus constare de suâ ollâ. Aul. 1.2. v.37.
units.tr: Misers are suspicious: as Euclio suspected that everyone knew the contents of his pot. Aul. 1.2. v.37.

units.la: OB avaritiæ nomen male solemus audire. Trin. 1.2. v.62.
units.tr: We are used to hearing the name of avarice spoken with ill will. Trin. 1.2. v.62.

units.la: AVARI ne quidem ipsi Fidei credunt.
units.tr: Misers do not even trust Faith herself.

units.la: AVARI male semper audiunt. Trin. 2. 2. v. 69.
units.tr: Misers always hear bad things said of them. Trin. 2. 2. v. 69.

units.la: AVARI perpetuo queruntur sibi nihil esse. Trin. 2. 2. v. 73.
units.tr: Misers constantly complain that they have nothing. Trin. 2. 2. v. 73.

units.la: AVARI aurum vitam suam æstimant. Aul. 4. 9. v. 13.
units.tr: Misers value their life in gold. Aul. 4. 9. v. 13.

units.la: AVARI defraudant Genium suum: ut thesauros congerant. Ibid.
units.tr: Misers cheat their own Genius so that they may pile up treasure. Ibid.

units.la: AVARI miseri admodum omnes sensus suos amittunt. Euclio enim in pervestigando suo thesauro etiam tertiam manum servi excutere cupit; quæ scilicet nusquam erat gentium. Aulular. 4. 4. v. 14.
units.tr: Misers, poor wretches, lose all their senses. Euclio, in searching for his treasure, even wants to shake out the slave's third hand, which of course was nowhere in the world. Aulular. 4. 4. v. 14.

units.la: AVARI nec festorum nec profestorum dierum habent rationem: ut Euclio Plautinus. Aul. 2. 8. v. 10.
units.tr: Misers take no account of holidays or workdays, like Plautus' Euclio. Aul. 2. 8. v. 10.

units.la: AVARI omnia sua extenuant: & κᾶλ' ὑπεροχείσμὸν loquuntur de suis opibus. Aul. 2. 8. v. 15. Nunc tusculum erui.
units.tr: Misers belittle all their possessions and speak of their wealth in an exaggerated manner [καθ' ὑπερβολήν]. Aul. 2. 8. v. 15. Now my hoard has been dug out.

units.la: AVARI etiam probri causâ audiunt mendici. Aul. 3. 2. v. 9.
units.tr: Misers even hear themselves called beggars, as a reproach. Aul. 3. 2. v. 9.

units.la: AVARI eò usque insaniunt, ut clament suam rem perisse, seque eradicarier, de tigillo si quà fumus exeat. Etiam saccos seu folles occludunt, ne spiritus evolet. Aquam plorant profundere, cùm lavant. Ipsam etiam Famem, si roges, numquam utendam dabunt. Præsegmina unguium in tonstrinâ colligunt. Ist das nit genaw gesucht? Vide Aul. 2. 4. v. 20. & seqq. inprimis v. 42. 43.
units.tr: Misers go so mad that they cry out that their property is lost and that they are being rooted out if any smoke comes out from the roof beam. They even seal up their sacks or bellows so the breath does not escape. When they wash, they weep to pour out the water. Even Hunger herself, if you ask, they will never let you use. They gather up the clippings of their nails in the barber's shop. Is this not carefully sought out? See Aul. 2. 4. v. 20. & seqq., especially v. 42. 43.

units.la: AVARI pumice aridiores. Aul. 2. 4. v. 18.
units.tr: Misers are drier than pumice. Aul. 2. 4. v. 18.

units.la: AVARITIA hominum sæpè bonos artifices corrumpit: ut dese profitetur coquus. Pseud. 3. 2. v. 12.
units.tr: Avarice of men often corrupts good craftsmen, as the cook professes of himself. Pseud. 3. 2. v. 12.

units.la: AVARITIA palliatur sub nomine parsimoniæ. Aul. 2. 4. v. 4. & 2. 5. v. 9. De Euclione.
units.tr: Avarice is cloaked under the name of thrift. Aul. 2. 4. v. 4. & 2. 5. v. 9. Said of Euclio.

units.la: AVARI semper egent, & sua bona extenuant. Aul. 3. 6. v. 7.
units.tr: Misers are always in want, and belittle their goods. Aul. 3. 6. v. 7.

units.la: AVARI suspicaces. Putant enim suum thesaurum omnibus notum. Aul. 3. 6. v. 11.
units.tr: Misers are suspicious, for they think their treasure is known to everyone. Aul. 3. 6. v. 11.

units.la: AVARIS numquam sat est. Euclio perpetuò solicitus est de filiâ elocandâ. Aul. 2. 2. v. 14.
units.tr: The miser is never satisfied: Euclio is constantly anxious about marrying off his daughter. Aul. 2. 2. v. 14.

units.la: AVARI quod sibi comparcunt: alij eo lætificantur. Aulular. 4. 8. v. 15.
units.tr: Misers grudge what they spare for themselves, while others rejoice in it. Aulular. 4. 8. v. 15.

units.la: ARTIFICUM. FABRORUM. OPIFICUM OLEARIORUM. OPERARIORUM. PELLIONUM. TONSORUM. CARBONARIORUM. FIGULORUM.
units.tr: CRAFTSMEN. SMITHS. MANUAL WORKERS. OIL-MAKERS. LABOURERS. TANNERS. BARBERS. CHARCOAL-BURNERS. POTTERS.

units.la: OPIFICES manuarij in urbe fuerunt innumerabiles variarum artium. Quamplurimos recenset Plauto, qui sectabantur Gynæceas & luxum muliebrem. Aul. 3 4. v.34. Fullo Phrygio Aurifex, Linarius, Caupones, Patagiarij, Indusiarij, Flamearij, Violarij, Carinarij, Mantiliarij, Murrhobatarij, Propolæ, Lintrones, Caleconarij, Sutores, Diabathrarij, Solearij, Molochinarij, Sarcinatores, Strophiarij, Semizonarij, Phylacistæ, Textores, Limborarij, Arcularij, Crocotarij, Argentarij. Quod opificium cujusq; fuerit, vide in Lexico Plautino: ubi singula nomina explicata invenies. Confer etiam Epid. 22. v.14. & seqq.
units.tr: There were countless manual craftsmen of various trades in the city. Plautus lists very many of them, who attended on the women's quarters and female luxury. Aul. 3 4. v.34. Fuller, Phrygian embroiderer, goldsmith, linen-weaver, innkeepers, makers of trimmings, makers of undergarments, makers of flame-coloured cloth, violet-dyers, makers of ... , makers of mantles, dealers in murrhine ware, hucksters, boatmen, makers of ... , cobblers, makers of sandals, makers of soles, mallow-dyers, menders, makers of breast-bands, makers of half-belts, keepers of ..., weavers, hem-makers, makers of chests, saffron-dyers, silversmiths. What each of these crafts was may be seen in the Plautine lexicon, where you will find each name explained. Compare also Epid. 2.2. v.14 and following.

units.la: SUTORES fuerunt sedentarij & plærumque claudi. Aul. 3.5. v.39. & Aul. 1.1.v.35. Pervigilat totas noctes, tum autem interdiu quasi claudus sutor domi sedet totas dies.
units.tr: The cobblers were sedentary and mostly lame. Aul. 3.5. v.39. and Aul. 1.1. v.35. He keeps watch all night, and by day, like a lame cobbler, he sits at home the whole day long.

units.la: AMPULLARII ampullas corio integebant. Rud. 3.4. v.50. vide Lex. Plaut. Ampulla.
units.tr: The bottle-makers covered flasks with leather. Rud. 3.4. v.50. See the Plautine lexicon, under Ampulla.

units.la: OPIFICES manuarij avaritiâ hominum sæpe redduntur improbiores: ut desc profitetur coquus ille. Pseud. 3.2. v.12.
units.tr: Manual craftsmen are often made more dishonest by the greed of men, as that cook professes. Pseud. 3.2. v.12.

units.la: ROMÆ carbones venundati per carbonarios cum furcâ. Caf. 2. 8. v.2. Glossæ: ἀνθρακοπώλης, carbonarius. Illiq; habebant cellas certas, in quibus carbones imponebant. Glossæ: ἀνθρακοβύκη, cella carbonaria. Qualis cella memorabilis est illa Angliæ in Westmonasterio, basilicâ regis, quâ conjurati proditores abusi sunt ad impietatem suam nefandam, è medio tollere satagētes Regem cum omni familiâ, & regni proceribus. Legatur historia. Auctor de viris illustribus: M. Æmilius Scaurus nobilis, pauper, nam pater ejus quamvis patritius, ob paupertatem carbonarium negotium exercuit.
units.tr: At Rome charcoal was sold by charcoal-dealers with a yoke-pole. Caf. 2.8. v.2. Glosses: ἀνθρακοπώλης [anthrakopōlēs], a charcoal-dealer. They had certain set storerooms in which they stacked the charcoal. Glosses: ἀνθρακοβύκη [anthrakobykē], a charcoal store. Such a store is notable in England, that one at Westminster in the king's basilica, which the conspirators and traitors abused for their unspeakable impiety, striving to remove the King with his whole household and the nobles of the realm. Let the account be read. The writer on illustrious men: Marcus Aemilius Scaurus was of noble birth but poor; for his father, although a patrician, followed the charcoal trade because of his poverty.

units.la: Fabri ferrarij apud carbones assident, semper calent. Rud. 2. 6. v. 47.
units.tr: Iron-smiths sit beside the charcoal; they are always warm. Rud. 2.6. v.47.

units.la: Tonsores homines garruli. Amph. 4:1.v.5. Epid. 2.2.ver.29. Vide libellum Plutarchi de Garrulitate.
units.tr: Barbers are talkative men. Amph. 4.1. v.5. Epid. 2.2. v.29. See Plutarch's little book on Talkativeness.

units.la: In officinâ pellionum crebri & multi sunt pali ligneì ad distendendas pelles. Men. 2.3.v.53.
units.tr: In the workshop of the tanners there are many wooden stakes for stretching hides. Men. 2.3. v.53.

units.la: Phrygiones acu pingebant vestes. Men. 2.3. v.72. & 3.2.v 4. Plin. lib. 8. c. 48.
units.tr: Embroiderers decorated garments with the needle. Men. 2.3. v.72. and 3.2. v.4. Plin. lib. 8. c. 48.

units.la: Figuli versant rotam figularem. Epid. 3.2.v.35.
units.tr: Potters turn the potter's wheel. Epid. 3.2. v.35.

units.la: Olearium tabernæ in Velabro erant Romæ. Capt. 3. 1. v. 29.
units.tr: At Rome there were oil-shops in the Velabrum. Capt. 3.1. v.29.

units.la: ARTIUM, STUDIORUM, LITTERARUM, DOCTORUM, PROFESSORUM, MAGISTRORUM, STUDIOSORUM, SCIENTIÆ, DOCTRINÆ, ERUDITIONIS, PHILOSOPHIÆ, PHILOSOPHORUM, LOGICAE, DIALECTICAE, &c.
units.tr: ARTS, STUDIES, LETTERS, TEACHERS, PROFESSORS, MASTERS, STUDENTS, SCIENCE, LEARNING, ERUDITION, PHILOSOPHY, PHILOSOPHERS, LOGIC, DIALECTIC, etc.

units.la: Vide etiam Titul. Bibliotheca: Litterarum: Scribendi.
units.tr: See also the title Library: Literature: Writing.

units.la: PLautus bonus fuit Dialecticus: qui egregiè novit discernere Diversa: & fallacias Sophisticas. Exemplum evidentissimum in colloquio Servi & Piscatoris. Rud. 4.3. v.36. Vide totum locum, ubi invenies geminum elenchum servi refutari à diversis : & quatuor terminorum in syllogismo. Ibidem nota Philosophum sumi pro Dialectico v. 47. & 64. Thales pro sapienti. Vide etiam Aul. 2.6.v.9. & 4.8. v.1,
units.tr: Plautus was a good dialectician, who knew well how to distinguish differences and sophistical fallacies. The clearest example is the conversation between the slave and the fisherman. Rud. 4.3 v.36. See the whole passage, where you will find the slave's double elenchus refuted in different ways, and the four terms in a syllogism. In the same place note that "philosopher" is taken for dialectician at vv. 47 and 64, and Thales for a wise man. See also Aul. 2.6 v.9 and 4.8 v.1.

units.la: THALES Milesius sapientissimus Philosophorum ob divinam sa-pientiam in proverbium abijt. Captiv. 2. 2. ver. 26. Bacch. 1. 2. v. 14.
units.tr: Thales of Miletus, the wisest of the philosophers, passed into a proverb on account of his divine wisdom. Captiv. 2.2 v.26; Bacch. 1.2 v.14.

units.la: PHILOSOPHI é Gynicâ gente impudentissimi. Perf. 1. 3. v. 43.
units.tr: Philosophers are of the Cynic tribe, the most shameless of men. Perf. 1.3 v.43.

units.la: PÆDAGOGI dabantur pueris, qui velut assectæ, puerorum progressus, actiones, mores observabant: & distinguebantur à præceptoribus, qui docebât, & artes scientiasq: infundebant. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 32. Senecalib. 2. de Ira. c. 22. Præceptores pædagogiq; pueris placidi dentur. Proximis applicatur omne, quod tenerum est: in eorum similitudinem crescit: nutricum & pædagogorum retulere mox in adolescentiâ mores. Apud Platonem educatus puer, cum ad parentes relatus, vociferantem videret patrem: Numquam, inquit, hoc apud Platonem vidi. Non dubito, quin citius patrem imitatus sit, quàm Platonem.
units.tr: Pedagogues were assigned to boys. As attendants, they watched the boys' progress, actions and manners. They were distinguished from teachers, who taught and instilled the arts and sciences. Pseud. 1.5 v.32. Seneca, De Ira 2, c.22: "Let teachers and tutors be given to boys who are gentle. Everything tender takes after what is nearest to it, and grows in their likeness; the manners of nurses and tutors soon show again in adolescence. A boy educated under Plato, when taken back to his parents and seeing his father in a rage, said: 'I never saw this at Plato's.' I have no doubt he imitated his father sooner than Plato."

units.la: IN hominem indocilem, & stupidum convenit illud Perf. 2. 1. v. 6. Cucus si in ludum iret, potuisset jam fieri, ut probè litteras sciret.
units.tr: The line of Persius (Pers. 2.1 v.6) fits an unteachable and stupid man: "If the cuckoo had gone to school, he might by now have learned his letters well."

units.la: QUI litteras sciunt, sinant & alios discere. Truc. 4. 2. v. 22. immò quisciunt: commentari debent, ne oblivisci antur. Ibid.
units.tr: Those who know letters should let others learn too. Truc. 4.2 v.22. Or rather, those who know should write commentaries, so that they do not forget. Ibid.

units.la: TURPE est doctori, cùm culpa redarguit ipsum. Certè virtutem multi docent, parùm interim virtuosi ipsi: quod de Comicis dicit Plautus Rud. 4. 7. v. 23. ubi senex: Spectavi ego pridem Comicos ad istum modum Sapienter dicta dicere, atq; ijs plaudier, Cùm illos sapientes mores monstrabant poplo: Sed cùm inde suam quisq; ibant divorsi domum, Nullus erat illo pacto, ut illi jusserant.
units.tr: It is shameful for a teacher when his own fault refutes him. Surely many teach virtue while being themselves little virtuous. Plautus says this of the comic actors, Rud. 4.7 v.23, where an old man says: "Long ago I watched comic actors speak wise sayings in this manner and be applauded for them, when they showed the people wise conduct. But when each went off divided to his home, there was no one who lived in the way they had prescribed."

units.la: Sententia planè ex tripode. Idem de Pharisæis passim queritur Christus. Et annon hodie de præconibus quibusdam verbi Dei idem dici queat?
units.tr: A saying straight from the tripod. Christ complains of the same thing about the Pharisees everywhere. And can the same not be said today of certain heralds of God's word?

units.la: HAUD æquum facit, qui quod didicit, dedisçit. Amphitr. 2. 2. v. 58. Elegans est γνῶμη de ijs, quæ rectè & verè discuntur. Nam si quid didiceris pravum, & injustum, id dedisçere laudabile est.
units.tr: He does not act fairly who unlearns what he has learned. Amphitr. 2.2 v.58. It is an elegant maxim about things that are learned rightly and truly. For if you have learned something wicked and unjust, unlearning it is praiseworthy.

units.la: LITTERA V geminum habet sonum: pleniorem, & exilem, prout Galli pronunciant. Men. 4. 2. v. 89.
units.tr: The letter V has a double sound: a fuller and a thinner one, as the French pronounce it. Men. 4.2 v.89.

units.la: PE. Tu, Tu, istic, inquam. Vin' afferri noctuam? Quæ Tu, Tu, unq; dicat tibi?
units.tr: PE. You, you, there, I say. Shall I bring an owl? The one that will say "you, you" to you forever?

units.la: Quò loci Parasitus crassum sonum litteræ V exprimit, comparans illum cum gemitu Noctuæ, quem Tou omnes esse scimus.
units.tr: Here the parasite expresses the thick sound of the letter V, comparing it with the cry of the owl, which we all know to be "tu."

units.la: Eundem expressit Ausonius, cùm de hac litterâ sic scribit:
units.tr: Ausonius expressed the same thing when he wrote about this letter thus:

units.la: Cecropiysignota sonù, ferale sonans V.
units.tr: Known by its Attic sound, the V sounds ominously.

units.la: Ferale ideò, quia refert feralem illam avem.
units.tr: It is "ominous" because it recalls that deadly bird.

units.la: Idem Ausonius:
units.tr: The same Ausonius:

units.la: Una fuit tantum, quâ respondere Laconei, Littera, & irato Regi placuere negantes.
units.tr: There was only one letter by which the Laconians answered, and they pleased the angry king by refusing.

units.la: Illa littera erat O'v. Et hinc doctissimus Palmerius corrigit locum Pomponij in Haruspice apud Nonium:
units.tr: That letter was the diphthong OU. Hence the very learned Palmerius corrects the passage of Pomponius in Haruspex, as quoted in Nonius:

units.la: – – fac puriter,
units.tr: – – do it cleanly,

units.la: Bucco, vel pecorei eustico comtem tractu. N. lavi dudum manu.
units.tr: Bucco, or with a rustic, neatly combed stroke. N., I washed my hands of it long ago.

units.la: Quem locum tamen paulò aliter lego & interpretor infra in Tit. Balnei.
units.tr: I read and interpret this passage somewhat differently below, under the title Bath.

units.la: Vide plura in hanc rem apud Just. Lipsium de Pronunciatione Linguæ Latinæ cap. 10. nec non Jacobum Matthiam de Litteris lib. 1. pag. 27.
units.tr: See more on this subject in Justus Lipsius, On the Pronunciation of the Latin Language, ch. 10, and also Jacobus Matthias, On Letters, book 1, p. 27.

units.la: (ornament)
units.tr: (ornament)

units.la: AUCTIONIS. VENDITIONIS. EMTIONIS. CONTRACTUUM. MANCIPATIONIS. MERCATURÆ. LOCATIONUM. BONORUM. MERCATUS. MERCIS. ARGENTARIORUM. STIPULATIONIS.
units.tr: AUCTION. SALE. PURCHASE. CONTRACTS. MANCIPATION. TRADE. LETTINGS. GOODS. MARKET. MERCHANDISE. BANKERS. STIPULATION.

units.la: Vide etiam Pecuniæ: Mutui.
units.tr: See also Money: Loan.

units.la: IN contractibus & emtionibus, quod si summa integra non data, symbolum sive arrham relinquebant. Pseud. I.I. v.53. Quemadmodum locum illum proprie accipiendum autumo: secus quàm Casaubonus alijque, de symbolis hospitalitatis, & conviviorum. Inspiciatur totus contextus: & rei veritas patescet.
units.tr: In contracts and purchases, if the full sum was not paid, they left a token or earnest money. Pseud. I.I. v.53. I hold that this passage should be understood in its proper sense, not as Casaubon and others take it, of tokens of hospitality and banquets. Let the whole context be examined, and the truth of the matter will be plain.

units.la: IN emtionibus adhibiti sences. Bacch. 4.9. v.52. Vide etiam Turn. l.1. c.28. & Cic. lib.7. Ep.29. ibiq; Manutium & Gotofredum. & Hotom. de ritu Nupt. c.25. Cicer. pro Muræna: & Liv. lib.3. sub finem.
units.tr: Sesterces were used in purchases. Bacch. 4.9. v.52. See also Turnebus, book 1, chapter 28; Cicero, letters book 7, letter 29, with the notes of Manutius and Gothofredus there; Hotomanus, on the rite of marriage, chapter 25; Cicero, Pro Murena; and Livy, book 3, near the end.

units.la: EMTIO & venditio, ut alij omnes contractus, constabant interrogationibus & responsionibus, uti patet ex formulis, quas condiderunt JCti, & Varro in de Re Rustica: itemque apud Cicero- nem pro Murena. Et apud nostrum Capt. 1.2. v.70. Stich. 2.1. v.68.
units.tr: Buying and selling, like all other contracts, consisted of questions and answers, as appears from the formulas which the jurists drew up, and from Varro in De Re Rustica; likewise in Cicero's Pro Murena. And in our author: Captivi 1.2. v.70; Stichus 2.1. v.68.

units.la: EMERE quoque solebant in conditionem meliorem. Captiv. 1, 2. v.70.
units.tr: They were also accustomed to buy on better terms. Captivi 1.2. v.70.

units.la: QUI alteri quicquam mancupio tradit, ita dat, quasi suum: ut accipientis illico faciat, dominiumque transferat pure, atque in perpetuum, h.e. sine dici atque conditionis adjectione: cum sit Mancipatio actus legitimus: atque adeò cum author sit, de evictione teneatur authoritatis nomine, qui rem accipientis non fecerit. Sic intelligenda loca apud nostrum Curc. 4.2. v.5. Perf. 4.3. v.55.62. Vide Petr.Fabr. Semestr.lib.2. cap.23. & ad Regg. Juris. Itemque Rævard. ad LL. xii. Tabb. cap. 16.
units.tr: Whoever hands anything over to another by mancipium gives it as if it were his own, so that it immediately becomes the acquirer's and passes ownership purely and forever, that is, without the addition of a day or a condition, since mancipation is a legal act. Therefore, if he is the transferor, he is bound to warranty on account of the title, if he has not made the thing the acquirer's. The passages of our author are to be understood thus: Curculio 4.2. v.5; Persa 4.3. v.55, 62. See Petrus Faber, Semestria, book 2, chapter 23, and on the Regulae Iuris; likewise Ravardus on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, chapter 16.

units.la: Nihil non nisi pecuniâ emitur. Si as habent, dant mercem. Asin. 1. 3. v. 49. Expromtâ pecuniâ opus est: quod est Græcâ mercari fide. Ibid. Græcorum quippe tale fuit ingenium, ut ægrè suas merces cuiquam absque præsenti pecuniâ crederent. Sic Truc. 5. v. 9. Manus vetat priusquam penes se habeat, quicquam credere.
units.tr: Nothing is bought except for money. If they have cash, they give the goods. Asinaria 1.3. v.49. Ready money is needed, which is what the Greeks called trading on credit. Ibid. For the Greeks were of such a disposition that they were reluctant to trust their goods to anyone without money in hand. So in Truculentus 5.9. The hand forbids trusting anything before it has it in its own keeping.

units.la: Nihil Cocio est, si est cæcus. Asin. 1. 3. v. 51. h. e. attentum esse oportet negotiatorem in rem suam. Vide Lex. Plaut. Cocio.
units.tr: Nothing is Cocio, if he is blind. Asinaria 1.3. v.51. That is, the merchant must be attentive to his own interest. See the Lexicon of Plautus, under Cocio.

units.la: Mercatores Mercurium invocant, ut fœtum lucris efficiat. Amph. Prol. v. 21. Ubi tamen latum retineri potest.
units.tr: Merchants call on Mercury, that he may make their profit fruitful. Amphitruo, Prologue, v.21. Here, however, latum may be retained.

units.la: Mercaturam exercebant navigationibus: & quasi à teneris eò assuefiebant. Merc. Prol. v. 76.
units.tr: They carried on trade by sea voyages, and were accustomed to it almost from childhood. Mercator, Prologue, v.76.

units.la: Merci stat pretium, ut pro virtute væneat. Quæ improba est merces pro vitio dominum pauperat. Mil. 3. 1. v. 132.
units.tr: A price is set for goods, so that they sell according to their worth. Wicked is the merchandise that impoverishes its owner through its vice. Miles Gloriosus 3.1. v.132.

units.la: In legitimis contractibus non æquum est redhibere: sed quod emtum est, emtum est. Merc. 2. 3. v. 84. Vide Rævard. ad LL. xii. Tabb. c. 16. & Lex. Plaut. Lege vendere.
units.tr: In lawful contracts it is not fair to take back; what has been bought is bought. Mercator 2.3. v.84. See Ravardus on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, chapter 16, and the Lexicon of Plautus under Lege vendere.

units.la: Qui emebant aliquid, mancupio accipiebant: & periculum evictionis in se recipiebant: hoc est, utebantur, ut suo. Merc. 2. 3. v. 112.
units.tr: Those who bought something took it by mancipium, and took upon themselves the risk of eviction; that is, they used it as their own. Mercator 2.3. v.112.

units.la: In venditionibus periculum evictionis excipiebant. Trinum. 2. 4. v. 19.
units.tr: In sales they took upon themselves the risk of eviction. Trinummus 2.4. v.19.

units.la: Res venales in auctione per Præconem prædicabantur. Bacch. 4. 7. v. 17.
units.tr: Goods for sale at auction were proclaimed by the crier. Bacchides 4.7. v.17.

units.la: In eo ipso astas lapide, ubi præco prædicat.
units.tr: At that very spot the auction stone, where the crier makes his proclamation.

units.la: Igitur præco in lapide stabat. Vide Turn. lib. 10. c. 3.
units.tr: So the crier stood upon the stone. See Turnebus, book 10, chapter 3.

units.la: Venalia prædia veteri more proscribebantur, h. e. propositò divulgatoque libello venum ire, venumque exponi significabantur. Quin & hoc idem in locandis ædibus servatum, ut pendente de ædibus tabulâ proscriberetur facienda locatio. Trin. 1. 2. 9. 131. Ædes venales inscribit litteris. Cic. lib. 3. offic. Claudius ædes, quas in Calio monte habebat, proscripsit, insulamvendidit.
units.tr: Estates for sale were posted in the old manner; that is, by publishing a notice and making it known that they were being put up for sale. Indeed the same practice was observed in letting houses: a notice hung on the house announced that letting was to take place. Trinummus 1.2. v.131. He writes on the house, in letters, that it is for sale. Cicero, On Duties, book 3: Claudius posted notices on the houses he had on the Caelian hill and sold the block.

units.la: O Terent. Heaut. Inscripsi illico ædes mercede. Cicer. lib.16. ad Att. Iste locare incipit, non proscriptâ neque edictâ die.
units.tr: O Terence, Heautontimorumenos: I at once put up the house for rent. Cicero, letters to Atticus, book 16: He begins to let, without a day having been posted or announced.

units.la: In emtionibus & venditionibus arrhabo datus, ut constaret fides de pretio. Mostl. 3.1. v.110. Agell. lib.17. c.2.
units.tr: In purchases and sales an earnest was given, so that there would be assurance about the price. Mostellaria 3.1. v.110. Gellius, book 17, chapter 2.

units.la: Emtio fiebat per auctionem. Men. 5.9. v. 91. per præconem enim conclamata auctio. Ibid. Et Epid. 2.2.v.51.
units.tr: Purchase was made by auction, for the auction was proclaimed by the crier. Menaechmi 5.9. v.91. Also Epidicus 2.2. v.51.

units.la: Quod palàm est venale, si argentum est, emas. Curc. 1.1.v.34.
units.tr: What is openly for sale, if it is silver, buy it. Curculio 1.1. v.34.

units.la: In venditionibus is, qui vendebat: indicabat pretium mercis. Aul. 2.8.v. Perf. 4.4.v.26.37.110. Vide Briss. Formul. lib. 6. Florileg. Merx cujus est; &c ejus indicatio est.
units.tr: In sales, the seller stated the price of the goods. Aulularia 2.8. v.?; Persa 4.4. v.26, 37, 110. See Brissonius, Formulae, book 6; Florilegium: Whose the goods are, and its indication is his.

units.la: In venditionibus venditor tenebatur præstare periculum evictionis. Curc. 4.2.v.8. Perf. 4.4. v.40.114. & 4.7.v.57. Vide Lexic. Plaut. Mancupio dare.
units.tr: In sales the seller was bound to furnish warranty against eviction. Curculio 4.2. v.8; Persa 4.4. v.40, 114; and 4.7. v.57. See the Lexicon of Plautus under Mancupio dare.

units.la: In venditione servorum vestimenta separatim vendi solebant. Stich. 2.1.v.16. Perf. 4.4 v.119. Vide Turn. lib.18.c.21. & Desfid. Herald. Animadverf.
units.tr: In the sale of slaves, their clothing was customarily sold separately. Stichus 2.1. v.16; Persa 4.4. v.119. See Turnebus, book 18, chapter 21, and Des Fides, Herald, Animadversiones.

units.la: Agros vel vineas vendere volentes, aut qui ægrè serebant vendi: solebant ijs maculam quandam, aut infaustam notam affingere. Quod fecit servus ille Trin. 2.4.v.122.125. Lege totum locum: & videbis affutiam servi. Rationes ejus hæ sunt: 1. Ager est fune-flus bobus arantibus. 2. Vinum ibi crescit putidum ac pendulum in uvis. 3. Est sterilis: minus profert: quàm acceperit. 4. Est infelix à possessoribus. 5. Arbores ejus fulmine petuntur. 6. Sues moriuntur angina. 7. Oves scabrae fiunt. 8. Servi morbo solutiali peccant.
units.tr: Those who wished to sell fields or vineyards, or who sold with difficulty, used to attach some stain or unlucky mark to them, as that slave in Trinummus 2.4. v.122, 125 did. Read the whole passage and you will see the slave's cunning. His reasons are these: (1) the field is deadly to oxen at the plough; (2) the wine grown there is rank and hangs sour on the grapes; (3) it is barren and yields less than it received; (4) it is unlucky for its possessors; (5) its trees are struck by lightning; (6) its pigs die of quinsy; (7) its sheep become mangy; (8) its slaves are afflicted with a wasting disease.

units.la: In venditione ædium auctio quoq; fiebat. Pœn. 1.3.v.2.
units.tr: In the sale of houses an auction also took place. Poenulus 1.3. v.2.

units.la: Mercatores nihil prius habent, quàm si expromtâ pecuniâ merces emantur: h.e. fide Græcâ Asin. 2.4.v.33.
units.tr: Merchants have nothing before them unless goods are bought with ready money; that is, on Greek credit. Asinaria 2.4. v.33.

units.la: Solebant quandoque scribere numos in certum diem exsolvendos. Asin. 2.4.v.34.
units.tr: They used sometimes to write that coins were to be paid on a fixed day. Asinaria 2.4. v.34.

units.la: Decima pars bonorum in auctione Herculi consecrabatur. Stich. 2.1.v.80. & 2.3. v.61.69. Vide Tit. Decorum: Herculis.
units.tr: A tenth part of the goods sold at auction was consecrated to Hercules. Stichus 2.1. v.80; 2.3. v.61, 69. See the title Decorum: Herculis.

units.la: IN emtione quanti possumus minimo emere solemus. Epid. 2. 2. v. 110.
units.tr: In buying, we are usually accustomed to buy as cheaply as we can. Epidicus 2.2. v.110.

units.la: IN auctionibus praeconis voce utebantur. Stich. 2. 1. v. 41. Caussas evictionis bonorum aliquot ibi ponit parasitus. Ibid. v. 49.
units.tr: At auctions they used the crier's voice. A parasite there sets out some causes of the eviction of goods. Stichus 2.1. v.41; ibid. v.49.

units.la: IN vendendis aedibus solebant excipere aliquam aedium partem. Trin. 1. 2. v. 157.
units.tr: In selling houses they were accustomed to reserve some part of the house. Trinummus 1.2. v.157.

units.la: AERE alieno nimium obstricti: ut essent solvendo, auctionem faciebant. Poen. 5. 6. v. 27.
units.tr: Those too heavily bound by debt, so that they might be able to pay, held an auction. Poenulus 5.6. v.27.

units.la: TRAPEZITAE illi, qui bonis suis cedere coguntur ob non solutum aes alienum, plerunque hoc agunt, ut debita sua exigant prius: q. a mensa cedant: nec quicquam mutuantur. Wann sie Bankerott spielen: Germanicè. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 61.
units.tr: Those bankers who are compelled to surrender their goods because of unpaid debt usually act so that they first collect what is owed to them, and only then leave the table, lending nothing. In German: When they go bankrupt. Pseudolus 1.3. v.61.

units.la: LEX vetabat, ne quis minori annis quinque & viginti mutuo quid daret. Nam qui dedisset, nullum jus repetendi habebat. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 68. Rud. 5. 3. v. 25. Lex illa erat lex Laetoria. De quibus Lipsius Com. in Tac. lib. 11. & Hotom. in Ind. Legg. Rom. Alciat. Parerg. lib. 6. c. 16. Turn. lib. 11. c. 23. Briss. Antiq. lib 3. c. 2. Propert. Qui dare multa potest, multum & amare potest.
units.tr: A law forbade anyone to lend money to one under twenty-five years of age; for whoever had lent had no right to reclaim it. Pseudolus 1.3. v.68; Rudens 5.3. v.25. That law was the Laetorian law. On it see Lipsius, commentary on Tacitus, book 11, and Hotomanus, in the Index of Roman Laws; Alciatus, Parerga, book 6, chapter 16; Turnebus, book 11, chapter 23; Brissonius, Antiquitates, book 3, chapter 2. Propertius: He who can give much can also love much.

units.la: MERCATUS meretricius celebrabat Aphrodisijs. Poen. 1. 2. v. 126.
units.tr: A meretricious trade was carried on at the festival of Aphrodite. Poenulus 1.2. v.126.

units.la: INVENDIBILI merce oportet ultrò emtorem adducere. Proba verò merx facile emtorem reperit: tametsi in abstrusò sita est. Poen. 1. 2. v. 128.
units.tr: Unsaleable goods must bring their buyer forward of their own accord. Good goods, however, readily find a buyer, even if they lie in some hidden place. Poenulus 1.2. v.128.

units.la: IN portu Atheniensi Piraeo rerum venalium magnus proventus. Most. 1. 1. v. 63.
units.tr: In the Athenian port of Piraeus there was a great supply of goods for sale. Mostellaria 1.1. v.63.

units.la: MERCATORUM Deus est Mercurius. Poen. 1. 2. v. 114.
units.tr: The god of merchants is Mercury. Poenulus 1.2. v.114.

units.la: MERCATORES domum reversi Mercurio grates agebant. Stich. 3. 1. v. 3.
units.tr: Merchants returning home gave thanks to Mercury. Stichus 3.1. v.3.

units.la: AVDITVS.
units.tr: HEARING.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See also under Man (Tit. Hominis).

units.la: VENTVS & spiritus aureæque, atque ore percipiuntur: sensu valde arguto. Mil. 4.8. v. 26. Aurem admotam oportuit. Sic ibi legitur à nonnullis.
units.tr: Wind and breath and gold are perceived by the mouth; the sense is very keen. Mil. 4.8. v. 26. The ear ought to have been brought close. So it is read there by some.

units.la: ATTENTIONEM imperantes utebantur hac formulâ: H o c AGE, Asin.Prol. v.1. Vide Tit. Sacrificiorum.
units.tr: Those who commanded attention used this formula: Hoc age, Asin. Prol. v. 1. See the title Sacrificiorum.

units.la: AUGURII. AUSPICII. OMINIS. AUGURUM. DIVINATIONIS. HARUSPICINÆ. SOMNIORUM. ARIOLORUM. STERNUTATIONUM, AVIUM. AUCUPII, AUSPICUM. RELIGIONIS. SUPERSTITIONIS. VATUM.
units.tr: AUGURIES. AUSPICES. OMENS. AUGURS. DIVINATION. HARUSPICY. DREAMS. SOOTHSAYERS. SNEEZES. BIRDS. BIRD-CATCHING, AUSPICES. RELIGION. SUPERSTITION. PROPHETS.
