units.la: IN omnibus ferè actionibus Augures folebant consulere. Asin.2, 1. ver. 11. ac per certas aves id fiebat, ut picum, cornicem, & parrham. Ib. Inde quoque ex avium volatu certa omina captabant. Ibid. v. 15. Attende ibidem verba Auguralia; Impetrire: Inaugurare: observare. Explicationem invenies in Lexico Plaut.
units.tr: Augurs were accustomed to consult the omens in almost every undertaking (Asin. 2.1, v. 11), and this was done through certain birds, such as the woodpecker, the crow and the jay. Ibid. From the flight of birds they also drew particular omens (ibid. v. 15). Notice in the same place the augural words: impetrire, inaugurare, observare. You will find explanations in the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: Ex nomine sæpe omina captabant. Perf.4.4.v.74. Mos namq; fuit religionis prisce: quibus magnę curę in his talib° initijs, homines præessent aut interessent bono nomine: h e. e quorum nominibus captari velut augurium aliquod posset prosperitatis & diuturnitatis. Talia sunt: Salvius: Longinus: Statorius. Mala contra, à quibus triste aliquod, infirmum, breve: ut, Curtius, Minutius, Furius, Hostilius. Tale vaticinium Lenonis dicto loco: Lucridi nomen fuit in patria. To. Nomen atq; omen quantivis est pretiy.
units.tr: They often drew omens from a name (Persa 4.4, v. 74). For it was an custom of old religion that men in such beginnings took great care that those who presided over or took part in them had a good name, that is, that from their names some omen of prosperity and long life could be taken. Such names are Salvius, Longinus, Statorius. Contrary to these are bad names, from which something sad, weak or short-lived is taken: Curtius, Minutius, Furius, Hostilius. The pimp's prophecy in the passage cited is of this kind: There was a man named Lucridus in his country. Tod. Name and omen, both are of whatever worth you like.

units.la: Vide Lipf. ad lib. 4. Hist. Tac. ad illud: Ingressi milites, quibus fausta nomina.
units.tr: See Lipsius on the fourth book of Tacitus' Histories, on the words: The soldiers entered, to whom were lucky names.

units.la: Vide etiam Festum in Lacus Lucrinas.
units.tr: See also Festus under Lacus Lucrinus.

units.la: VANITAS augurum auspicia corvorum fausta, à dextrâ; à lævâ infausta jactabat. Aulul. 4. 3. v. 1. Non temere est, quod corvus cantat mihi ab lævâ manu. & 4. 6. v. 3. Itaque cùm partes mundi ab ortu auguribus Romanis lævæ essent, Horatius scripsit Od. 27. lib. 3.
units.tr: VANITY The augurs boasted that the auspices of ravens were favourable on the right and unfavourable on the left (Aulularia 4.3, v. 1): It is not for nothing that the raven sings to me from the left hand. And (4.6, v. 3): Accordingly, when the quarters of the sky were on the left for the Roman augurs from the east, Horace wrote in Odes 3.27:

units.la: Oscinem corvorum prece suscitaboSolis ab ortu.
units.tr: I shall summon the raven's song from the rising of the sun,

units.la: ut scilicet cantu suo iter institutum dirimat. A dextrâ autem suadebat corvus, ut patet Asin. 2. 1. v.
units.tr: that is, so that by its song it may break off a journey that has been begun. But the raven advised on the right, as is clear from Asinaria 2.1, v.

units.la: Picus & cornix est ab lævâ, corvus porrò ab dextrâ cōsuadent.
units.tr: The woodpecker and the jay advise from the left, but the raven advises from the right.

units.la: Hinc apparet contrariam in cornice fuisse observationem, quod & à Cicerone scriptum est lib. 1. de Divinat.
units.tr: From this it appears that there was an opposite observation for the jay, which is also written by Cicero in book 1 of On Divination.

units.la: Cur à dextra corvus, à sinistrâ cornix faciat ratum?
units.tr: Why does the raven make it valid from the right and the jay from the left?

units.la: Sinistrâ tamen cornix Maroni inauspicata est. Sape sinistrâ cavâ prædixit ab ilice cornix. Ubi augurium malum etiam adjuvat arboris vitium. Vide Turn. lib. 6. c. 26.
units.tr: Yet Virgil regarded the jay on the left as ill-omened: Often the jay on the left has foretold from the hollow holm-oak. Here the defect of the tree also helps the bad omen. See Turnebus, book 6, chapter 26.

units.la: AUSPICIUM observabant in omnibus actionibus. Ne ego edepol huc veni auspicio malo. Aul. 3. 2. v. 33.
units.tr: They observed auspices in all undertakings: Truly, I came here by no means under an evil auspice (Aulularia 3.2, v. 33).

units.la: OMNE principium rei, omen erat bonum. Stich 5. 2. v. 23. Domum redeunti principium placet. Bonâ sceva sinena obviam occessit mihi.
units.tr: Every beginning of a matter was a good omen: It pleases the beginning for one returning home. A good, left-handed sneeze met me. (Stichus 5.2, v. 23).

units.la: OMEN nostrum est, non adversariorum. Sic Caf. 2. 8. v. 76. Nostro omine et dies.
units.tr: The omen is ours, not our adversaries': so Casina 2.8, v. 76: Both the day too is under our omen.

units.la: AUGURES collegium habebant. Iidem dicebantur capere locum ad effandos templorum fines. Men. 1. 2. v. 54. Vide Lcx.
units.tr: The augurs had a college. The same men were said to take a place for marking out the boundaries of temples (Menaechmi 1.2, v. 54). See the Lexicon.

units.la: MALA nomina omen malum notabant. Asin. 3. 3. v. 155. Vide Tit. Nominum. & Briff. Formul. lib. 1. p. 83.
units.tr: Bad names marked an evil omen (Asinaria 3.3, v. 155). See the title Names, and Brisson's Formulae, book 1, p. 83.

units.la: VETERES nihil nisi auspicato fuscipiebant. Rud. 3.4. v.12. Non hodie isti rei auspicavi, ut cum furcifero fabulor.
units.tr: The ancients undertook nothing except after taking the auspices: I have not taken the auspices for this business today, that I should talk with a gallows-bird (Rudens 3.4, v. 12).

units.la: Ex observatione ominis religionem cōcipiebant. Merc. s.2. v.40. v. 40.
units.tr: From the observation of an omen they conceived a religious scruple (Mercator 5.2, v. 40, v. 40).

units.la: AUSPICIA domi à Ducibus repeti solita,si quid malè cessistet publicè. Capt 3.s.v.108.
units.tr: It was customary for auspices to be taken again at home by the commanders if something had gone badly in public (Captivi 3.5, v. 108).

units.la: Ex superstitione veterum, si digitus, vel unguis salijsset, aliquid indefibi eventurum ominabantur boni, vel mali. Alludit ad hunc morem Plautus noster Epid. 4.1.v.33. Cedo manum: MV. Accipe: arumnosam, & inferiarum compotem mulierem tenes. PE. Quid est, quod digitus titubat tuus? Sic enim ex veteri codice correxit Meursius: qui & morem hunc explicat, ex nescio cujus Melampodis Hierogrammatei libro Περὶ ταλμῶν μαντικῆς, ὡς ἐπολεμεῖον βασιλέα: quæ huc adscribam,quia alias nullibi memini me legere illum Authorem.
units.tr: From the superstition of the ancients, if a finger or a nail jumped, they foretold that some good or evil would happen to someone. Our Plautus alludes to this custom in Epidicus 4.1, v. 33: Give me your hand. MV. Take it: you hold a wretched woman, claimed for the dead. PE. Why does your finger twitch? For so Meursius corrected it from an old manuscript, and he also explains this custom from a book of an unknown Melampus, a hierogrammateus, On the divination of the twitching of limbs, which I shall set down here, since I do not remember reading that author anywhere else:

units.la: Δάκτυλος μικρὸς τῆς δεξιᾶς χειρὸς ἀλλόμενος, πίστεως μέζονος ἀξιωθήσεται ἀπλοῖ. ἐπειδὴ ἐρμῆ ἐστιν ὁ Δάκτυλος, ἐν ἄλλοις σείεσιν ἁπλοῖ, ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτίαν, παρθένῳ φόγον χήρᾳ ὕβριν. ὁ μετάτον μικρὸν λεύτερος Δάκτυλος τῆς δεξιᾶς χειρὸς, ὁ καλούμενος παράμεσος, ἀλλόμενος, πολλῶν χρημάτων κυρίευσιν σημαίνει. ἐσὶ ὁ ἥλιου ὁ Δάκτυλος, ἄλλοις πολλῶν ἀγαθῶν ἐπίκτησιν ἁπλοῖ, ἀλλὰ κακόν.
units.tr: [Greek text, garbled in the scan; sense:] The little finger of the right hand, when it twitches, signifies that one will receive greater trust; for a finger signifies a simple man, and in other respects a sin; for a virgin a disgrace; for a widow an insult. The next finger, the ring finger of the right hand, called the paramesos, when it twitches, signifies the acquisition of many goods; it is the forefinger; for a simple man it signifies the gaining of many good things, but for a bad man an evil.

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] Δάκτυλος ὁ τρίτος τῆς δεξιᾶς χειρὸς, ἤτοι ὁ μέσος, ἐασκανίας ἁπλοῖ, ἢ λοιδορίας, χρόνῳ ὁ Δάκτυλος, ἐν ἄλλοις ἀδέλφῳ ἐνσέδω ἁπλοῖ.
units.tr: [illegible, about 40 letters] [Greek; sense:] The third finger of the right hand, that is, the middle finger, signifies for a simple man deceit or reproach; in time, the finger; in other respects, it signifies a brother's injury.

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: [illegible, about 30 letters]

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters] Δάκτυλος τέταρτος ἀλλόμενος, ζημίαν μεθ᾽ ὕβρεως ἁπλοῖ. ἀρεως ᾧδεῖ ἐσὶ ὁ Δάκτυλος. ἐν ἄλλοις διβλιά-βην ἁπλοῖ ἐλευθέρῳ ἐκκοπὴν.
units.tr: [illegible, about 30 letters] [Greek; sense:] The fourth finger, when it twitches, signifies loss together with insult. It is the finger of ... For a free man it signifies the cutting off of a bird-shaped (?) freedom.

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: [illegible, about 40 letters]

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] Δάκτυλος ὁ μέγας, ὁ ἀντίχειρ καλούμενος, ἀλλόμενος ἐπίκτησιν πολλῶν ἀγαθῶν ἁπλοῖ, ἢ ἐπὶ τέκνοις, ἢ ἐπὶ γυναικί χαρήσεται.
units.tr: [illegible, about 40 letters] [Greek; sense:] The great finger, called the thumb, when it twitches, signifies the acquisition of many goods for a simple man, or he will rejoice in children or in a wife.

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] τῆς ὁ Δάκτυλος. ἄλλοις ἀπαλλάξει ἁπλοῖ. ἁπλῳ ἀγαθὸν. παρθένῳ ἀ-γαθὸν. χήρᾳ ὠφέλειαν, ὄνυχες τῆς δεξιᾶς χειρὸς ἐαν ἀλλωνται, κέρδος ἁπλοῦσιν ἀπερσόκοπον.
units.tr: [illegible, about 40 letters] [Greek; sense:] The finger ... will be released in other respects. For a simple man, good; for a virgin, good; for a widow, profit. If the nails of the right hand twitch, they signify gain for the simple, a profit...

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] μικρὸς Δακτύλου τῆς δεξιᾶς χειρὸς ἐαν ἄλλησι ἢ μυρμηκιᾶν, κακοπα-θείαν ἁπλοῖ. ἁπλῳ τέκνον. παρθένῳ ἀνδρα. χήρᾳ κόπον. ὁ δ᾽ λευτέρος ἐαν ἀλλήται, ἐξυσίαν ἁπλοῖ.
units.tr: [illegible, about 40 letters] [Greek; sense:] The little finger of the right hand, if it twitches or itches, signifies suffering. For a simple man, a child; for a virgin, a husband; for a widow, toil. If the free finger twitches, it signifies power.

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] ὁ δὲ τρίτος, ἢ τέταρτος λύπας ἁπλοῦσιν. ἁπλῳ δὲ ἀ-γαθὸν. γαῦον. ὁ δὲ μεγάλου, αὐξησιν δηλοῖ βίς. Δάκτυλο͞ μικρὸς ἐναντίμ͞ χειρὸς ἀλλόμεν͞, πολλὰ ἀγαθὰ δηλοῖ πᾶσιν. ὁ λεύτερ͞ ἀπὸ ἐγκλι-ματικὸς δηλοῖ λύπην. ἢ ἀπολογον δὴ μεγάλων πεσσῶν. λέλφ ἐν πίσει ὑπὸ κατηγορίαν. ὁ μέσος λύπην δηλοῖ διὰ πᾶγμάτιδιον. ἢ αὐ-ξησιν βίν, ἢ τέλνων, ἢ χρημάτων σημαίνει κομίσεσθαι. ὑνυχες ἐναντίμου χειρὸς ἀπωλειαν σημαίνη κομίσεσθαι. ὑνυχες ἐναντίμ χειρὸς ἀλλόμενοι, ἀφέλειαν δηλῶσι μετὰ δυσκολίας πνὸς. Sanè per quam ridicula haec est superstitio.
units.tr: [illegible, about 40 letters] [Greek; sense:] The third or fourth finger signifies sorrows for the simple, but for the simple man good things. The great finger signifies an increase of life. The little finger of the left hand, when it twitches, signifies many good things for all. The free finger, the one next to the thumb, signifies grief. Or it signifies the loss of great things; a sorrow on account of a charge. The middle finger signifies grief on account of a small matter, or an increase of life, or of children, or the acquisition of money. The nails of the left hand, when they twitch, signify loss. The nails of the left hand, when they twitch, signify profit with some difficulty. Truly, how very ridiculous this superstition is.

units.la: ERANT praecantatrices, conjectrices, aruspicæ & ariolæ, quæ incantamentis & carminibus mala ab hominibus amolirentur: quæ significationem somniorum interpretabantur: quæ halitu folebant mortalem animam velut excludere & exhalare, ut divinam reciperent. Mil. 3.1. v.98.
units.tr: There were charmers, enchantresses, haruspices and soothsayers, who by incantations and songs drove away evils from men; who interpreted the meaning of dreams; who used to breathe out, as it were, and exhale the mortal soul so that they might receive a divine one (Miles 3.1, v. 98).

units.la: Vide Turn. lib.2. Adv. cap. 29. & Donatum ad Terent.Phorm. 4.4. Interdixit hariolis.
units.tr: See Turnebus, book 2 of Adversaria, chapter 29, and Donatus on Terence's Phormio 4.4: He forbade the soothsayers.

units.la: Illis festis Quinquatribus dona offerebant, ex dicto loco Plauti.
units.tr: At those Quinquatria festivals gifts were offered, from the passage of Plautus cited.

units.la: ARUSPICES exta inspiciebant, antequam DIs offerrentur. Pœn. 2.1. v.19.
units.tr: The haruspices inspected the entrails before they were offered to the gods (Poenulus 2.1, v. 19).

units.la: AVES visco capiebantur, & fundis: quibus aucupes folia farfari substernebant: ne ad fundas viscus adhærescceret. Pœn. 2.1. v.33. ἀλληγοεικῶς.
units.tr: Birds were caught with birdlime and with snares, for which the bird-catchers spread leaves of coltsfoot beneath, so that the birdlime would not stick to the snares (Poenulus 2.1, v. 33). Allegorically.

units.la: AUGURES crediderunt, quòd homine in meridiem spectante, ad sinistram ejus partes mundi exorientes sint: ad dextram occidentes. Similiter ex volatu avium judicabant. Epid. 2.2. v.2. Vide de auspiciis Cæl. Rhod. lib. 1. cap. 10. & Alexand. ab Alex. lib. 5. cap. 19. Gotofred. ad II. 12. Tabb. Meurs. Aucts. Philolog. cap. 6. & Fit. Militiæ.
units.tr: The augurs believed that when a man faces south, the quarters of the sky rising are on his left side, and those setting on his right. In the same way they judged from the flight of birds. See Epidicus 2.2, v. 2. On auspices see Caelius Rhodiginus, book 1, chapter 10, and Alexander ab Alexandro, book 5, chapter 19; Gothofredus on Tabb. Meursius, Auctarium Philologicum, chapter 6, and the title Militia.

units.la: VETERES ominibus & auspicijs plurimùm superstitiosè tribue-runt. Amph. 2.2. v. 58. Ante auspicium commoratum est? h. e. an tibi religio aliqua obiecta est, vel omen aliquod. Vide de omini-bus apud Isaacum Pontanum in Notis Macrob. p. 694.
units.tr: The ancients attributed very superstitious weight to omens and auspices (Amphitruo 2.2, v. 58): Has the delay been caused by the auspices? That is, has some religious scruple or some omen been put in your way? See on omens in Isaac Pontanus' notes to Macrobius, p. 694.

units.la: SOLEBANT omina captare ex indirecto aliquo corporis motu. Asin. 2.2. v. 49. Scapula gestibant mihi. Pseud. 1.1. v. 105. Supercilium salit.
units.tr: They used to take omens from some indirect movement of the body: My shoulder-blades twitched for me (Asinaria 2.2, v. 49). My eyebrow is jumping (Pseudolus 1.1, v. 105).

units.la: QUAE malo omine fiebant: adversâ avi facta esse dicebant. Bacch. 1. 2. v. 5.
units.tr: Those things that happened with a bad omen they said had come about with an unfavourable bird (Bacchides 1.2, v. 5).

units.la: FORAS exeuntes observabant auspicia. Stich. 3.2. verf. 6. 43. Auspicio hercle optimo exivi foras: mustela murem mihi abstu-lit praeter pedes: eam strenuè obsonavit, &c. Vide Cafaub. ad Theoph. & Frid. Lindenbr. ad Ter. Phorm. 4. 4. Introijt in ae-des ater alienus canis: Gallina cecinit.
units.tr: Those going out of doors observed the auspices (Stichus 3.2, v. 6 and 43): Truly, I have gone out with the best of auspices: a weasel carried off a mouse right before my feet; I have feasted on it vigorously, etc. See Casaubon on Theophrastus, and Fridericus Lindenbrog on Terence's Phormio 4.4: A black strange dog entered the house; a hen crowed.

units.la: AVES, ut turdi, & aliae aviculae transfennâ seu funiculo extento ca-piebantur, quem vocabant tensa: ei perticae lumbricum impo-nebant in escam. Bacch. 4 6. v. 22. Vide Lex. Transfenna.
units.tr: BIRDS: thrushes and other small birds were caught with a cross-bar, or a stretched cord, which they called a tensa; on this pole they placed a worm as bait. Bacch. 4.6, v. 22. See Lexicon, under Transfenna.

units.la: AVI sinistrâ inominatò res agebantur. Pseud. 2.4. v. 72.
units.tr: By the left bird, matters were transacted without a name. Pseud. 2.4, v. 72.

units.la: AUSPICUM curae quoq; erant, Nubentes profiteri, se liberorum procreandorum causâ convenire. Capt. 4.2. v. 109.
units.tr: Omens were also a concern for those about to marry, who professed that they came together for the sake of begetting children. Capt. 4.2, v. 109.

units.la: EX saltu supercilij omen captabant: nempe vel prosperi vel adver-si quid ominantes. Pseud. 1.1. v. 105. Unde dicam nescio. Nisi quia futurum est: ita supercilium salit. Hinc & Salisatores vo-cati sunt: quia dum eis membrorum quaecumque partes salie-rint, aliquid exinde sibi prosperum seu triste significari praedi-cant. Ad haec omina pertinent & ligaturae exsecrabilium reme-diorum, quae ars Medicorum condemnat: id est: Falcina. Isid. lib.8. Sic Asin. 2.2. v. 49. Scapula gestibant mihi. Vide plura de hac Ominandi superstitione, quam Graeci vocabant apud Muret. l. 9. c. 6. & inprimis Isaaci Cafaub. Lection. Theo-crit. 5.
units.tr: From a twitch of the eyebrow they took an omen, namely either favourable or unfavourable. Pseud. 1.1, v. 105. "Whence I cannot say. Unless because something is about to happen: so the eyebrow twitches." Hence they were also called Salisatores, because whenever any part of the body had twitched, they declared that something fortunate or sad was thereby signified to them. To these omens belong also the wearing of amulets of detestable remedies, which the art of physicians condemns: that is, the Falcina. Isidore, book 8. So in Asin. 2.2, v. 49: "They wore a shoulder-blade for me." See more on this superstition of omens, which the Greeks called [ὠμομαντεία], in Muretus, book 9, chapter 6, and especially Isaac Casaubon, Lectiones Theocriteae 5.

units.la: SI digitus vel unguis salijsset, ita ut palpitationem aliquam senti-rent: aliquid inde vel boni, vel mali eventurum ominabantur. Epid. 4.1. v.33. & Capt. 4.2. v.79. Vide Meurs. Exerc. Crit. parte 1. cap. 5.
units.tr: If a finger or a nail had twitched, so that they felt some throbbing, they foretold that something either good or evil would follow from it. Epid. 4.1, v. 33, and Capt. 4.2, v. 79. See Meursius, Exercitationes Criticae, part 1, chapter 5.

units.la: BENE ominantes OPTIMUM. BONUM. FACTUM dicebant. Pseud. 1. 2. verf. 52. Vide Calligr. Romanam. Titul. Omnia, pagin. 835.
units.tr: Those who augured well used to say "Best! Good! Done!" [optimum, bonum, factum]. Pseud. 1. 2. verf. 52. See Calligr. Romanam, title "Omnia", p. 835.

units.la: BONI ominis ergo utebantur hac formula, initio rei agendae. Quae res feliciter eveniat! Aul. 4.10.v.58.
units.tr: Using a good omen, they used this formula at the beginning of an undertaking: "May the matter turn out happily!" Aul. 4.10, v. 58.

units.la: Vide Formulas Briff. & Calligraphiam nostram.
units.tr: See our collections of formulas and our Calligraphy.

units.la: IN rebus prosperis constituti solebant bene precari hac formula: DI Deaeque te adjuvant. Epid. 3.3. v.15.16.
units.tr: Those established in prosperous circumstances were accustomed to pray well with this formula: "May the gods, male and female, help you." Epid. 3.3, vv. 15–16.

units.la: BONUM omen alicui volentes, utebantur hac formula: Quod BONUM atque FORTUNATUM sit. Cas. 2.6. v. 50. Aul. 2.1.v.26.
units.tr: Wishing someone a good omen, they used this formula: "May it be GOOD and FORTUNATE." Cas. 2.6, v. 50. Aul. 2.1, v. 26.

units.la: IN causis Reipublicae, si quando ominabantur, utebantur hac formula BENE REM GERERE. Capt. 3.2. v.1.
units.tr: In affairs of the commonwealth, when they were augurying, they used this formula: "MAY THE AFFAIR BE WELL CONDUCTED." Capt. 3.2, v. 1.

units.la: IN infantia, adeoque ipsa nativitate omina studiose observata. Amphit. 5.1. v.56. de nativitate Herculis.
units.tr: Omens were also studiously observed in infancy, and indeed at the very moment of birth. Amphit. 5.1, v. 56, concerning the birth of Hercules.

units.la: AVIUM. GALLI-GALLINACEI. HIRUNDI-NUM. VULTURUM. GALLINARUM. CORVO-RUM. INVOLVULORUM. CU-CULI.
units.tr: BIRDS. COCKS. SWALLOWS. VULTURES. HENS. CROWS. BINDWEEDS. CUCKOOS.

units.la: Vide etiam supra Animalium Brutorum.
units.tr: See also above, under Brute Animals.

units.la: AVES visco capi solent: quando arundo illita visco alas verbe-rat. Bacch. I. i. v. 17. Cum eo comparantur blanditiæ, & ille-ctûs mulierum.
units.tr: Birds are usually caught with birdlime, when a reed smeared with birdlime beats their wings. Bacchides 1.1 v.17. To this are compared the flatteries and enticements of women.

units.la: AVES DELICATÆ pueris patricijs in delitijs erant. Andi-cula, columba, catellus, Hirundo, monedula, turtures, merulæ, quas docebant canere versus. Asin. 3. 3. v. 103. Capt. 5. 4. v. 5. Caf. 1. 1. v. 50, & 31. v. 9. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 15. Arnobius lib 7. Ut parvuli pusiones abstineant ploratibus, passercules accipiunt. Plin. lib. 4. Epist. 2. Habebat puer canes majores minoresq.; habebat lusci-nias, psittacos, merulas. Vide Plin. lib. 4. Epist. 2. Vide infra Tit. Lusus.
units.tr: Delicate birds were the delights of patrician boys: a little dove, a pigeon, a little dog, a swallow, a jackdaw, turtledoves, blackbirds, which they taught to sing verses. Asinaria 3.3 v.103; Captivi 5.4 v.5; Casina 1.1 v.50 and 3.1 v.9; Bacchides 1.1 v.15. Arnobius, book 7: "As little boys stop crying when they are given sparrows." Pliny, book 4, letter 2: "The boy had larger and smaller dogs; he had nightingales, parrots, blackbirds." See Pliny, book 4, letter 2. See below under the title Play.

units.la: ALCEDO pullos suos excludit ad mare. Pœn. 1. 2. v. 143.
units.tr: The kingfisher hatches its young by the sea. Poenulus 1.2 v.143.

units.la: AQUILÆ generosiores vulturibus. Rud. 2. 4. v. 9.
units.tr: Eagles are nobler than vultures. Rudens 2.4 v.9.

units.la: COLUMBARUM improbitas in osculando notatur Asin. 1. 3. v. 57. Catull. Carm. 65. Osculા mordenti semper decerpere rostro, &c.
units.tr: The wantonness of doves is noted in their kissing. Asinaria 1.3 v.57. Catullus, poem 65: "always to pluck kisses with a biting beak," etc.

units.la: COLUMBÆ nidamenta congerunt, pinnas, muscum, tomentum, pilos, acus: & id genus alia, unde nidos conficiant. Rud. 3. 6. v. 51.
units.tr: Doves gather materials for their nests: feathers, moss, down, hair, straw, and other such things from which they build their nests. Rudens 3.6 v.51.

units.la: Propert. lib. 2. Eleg. 12.
units.tr: Propertius, book 2, elegy 12.

units.la: Exemplo juncta si sint in amore columbæ, Masculus et totum femina conjugium.
units.tr: "If doves are joined in love by example, the male and the female make up a whole marriage."

units.la: CORVORUM vox est crocitus. Aul. 4 3. v.2.
units.tr: The cry of crows is a croak. Aulularia 4.3 v.2.

units.la: CORVI cornices ac monedulæ, ubi pedibus aliquem locum insistunt modò ἀναιδείσι, modò ὀπνεύτε: quod erat corvitare. Casin. 4.1. v.20. de mulieribus cibo sese injurgitantibus ad mensam.
units.tr: Crows, jackdaws and daws, when they plant themselves on some spot with their feet, are now shameless [ἀναιδείσι], now [ὀπνεύτε]; this was called corvitare. Casina 4.1 v.20, said of women who thrust themselves at the table to get food.

units.la: CUCUS, sive CUCÚLUS avis indocilis. Pers. 2.1. v.6.
units.tr: The cuckoo, or cuckoo-bird, is an untrainable bird. Persius 2.1 v.6.

units.la: GALLI-GALLINACEI ungulis scalpuriunt circumcirca. Aul. 3.4. v. 10.
units.tr: Cocks scratch about on all sides with their claws. Aulularia 3.4 v.10.

units.la: GALLINARUM pulli solebant pipare, aut pipire. A quo pipatu orta formula; Pipulo aliquem differre. Aul. 3.2. v.32. Vide Lex.
units.tr: Chicks of hens used to peep, or pipe. From this peeping arose the phrase pipulo aliquem differre (to put someone off with a peep). Aulularia 3.2 v.32. See the lexicon.

units.la: HIRUNDINES nidos effingunt. Rud. 3.1. v.6. HIRUNDINES natæ ex Philomela, atque ex Progne. Rud. 3.1. v. 12.
units.tr: Swallows build nests. Rudens 3.1 v.6. Swallows were born from Philomela and Procne. Rudens 3.1 v.12.

units.la: INVOLVVLI in pampini folio se implicant: ac perdunt illud. Cist. 4.2. v.63.
units.tr: Bindweeds wind themselves around a vine leaf, and so ruin it. Cistellaria 4.2 v.63.

units.la: LOCUSTÆ carent palpebris: eóque oculos habent duriores. Men. 5.5. v.25. Plin.lib.11.cap.37.
units.tr: Locusts lack eyelids, and therefore have harder eyes. Menaechmi 5.5 v.25. Pliny, book 11, chapter 37.

units.la: MERULA avis tota est nigra. Pænol. 5.5.v. 10. Sic enim quidam legunt ex Mss. Vide Turn.lib.10.cap.29. & Aldrovandum de Avibus lib. 16.
units.tr: The blackbird is entirely black. Poenulus 5.5 v.10. For so some read it, from the manuscripts. See Turnebus, book 10, chapter 29, and Aldrovandi, On Birds, book 16.

units.la: MILVUS avium rapacissima: ut & AQUILA, Aul, 2.4.v.42. Euclioni milvum deripuit pulmentum. Milvi clangor appellabatur Jugitus. Jugere est γιγγεῖν, γιγγαivεν. Pœn. 5.5. v.13. Pseud. 3.2.v.62. de coquis, qui sunt milvinis & aquilinis ungulis.
units.tr: The kite is the most rapacious of birds, as is the eagle. Aulularia 2.4 v.42: "The kite snatched Euclio's pulmentum." The cry of the kite was called jugitus; to jugere is [γιγγεῖν, γιγγαίνειν]. Poenulus 5.5 v.13. Pseudolus 3.2 v.62, of cooks, who have kite-like and eagle-like claws.

units.la: MILVUS avis appetentissima. Unde milvina. Men. 1.3 v.29.
units.tr: The kite is a very greedy bird, whence milvina (kite-like). Menaechmi 1.3 v.29.

units.la: NOCTUÆ sonus est Tou, Tou. Men. 4.2. v.89.
units.tr: The sound of the owl is "tou, tou." Menaechmi 4.2 v.89.

units.la: SPINTURNIX avis deformis. Mil. 4.1. v.42.
units.tr: The spinturnix is a misshapen bird. Miles Gloriosus 4.1 v.42.

units.la: VULTURES triduo ante volant, ubi cadavera futura sint. Al-ludit nostèr. Trucul. 2. 3. v. 16. Illud vide, ut jam quasi Vulturij triduo prius praedivinant, quo die esuri sient. Confirmat Plinius lib. 10. c. 6. Umbricius haruspicum nostro aevo peritissimus tradit, triduo ante, aut biduo vultures Volare, ubi cadavera futura sint.
units.tr: Vultures fly three days before, where carcasses are going to be. Our author alludes to this: Truculentus 2.3 v.16: "Note that, as if they were vultures, they foresee three days ahead the day on which they will be hungry." Pliny confirms it, book 10, chapter 6: "Umbricius, the most skilled of the haruspices of our age, reports that three or two days before, vultures fly to where carcasses are going to be."

units.la: Vultures rapaces. Most. 3. 2. v. 15. Viden' pilluram, ubi cornix unâ vulturios duos vellicat. ἀλλὰ γε οὐκ ὥς de senibus.
units.tr: Vultures are rapacious. Mostellaria 3.2 v.15. "Do you see the plucking, where a crow pulls at two vultures at once?" [ἀλλὰ γε οὐκ ὥς], said of old men.

units.la: VULTURIO in depascendis carnibus humanis occupatus est. Mil. 4. 2. v. 53.
units.tr: The vulture is busy devouring human flesh. Miles Gloriosus 4.2 v.53.

units.la: VULTURES & aquilae aves magnae sunt. Rud. 3. 4. v. 64.
units.tr: Vultures and eagles are large birds. Rudens 3.4 v.64.

units.la: Te ambustulatum obiciam magnis avibus pabulum.
units.tr: "I will throw you, singed, to the large birds as their food."

units.la: AULÆ. AULICORUM.
units.tr: COURTS. COURTIERS.

units.la: QUI primas tenent in Aulâ, dicebantur Oculi Regis. Poen. 3. 3. v. 80. Suidas: ὀφθαλμὸς βασιλέως, ἀντὶ δὲ μέγα δυνάμενος παρὰ βασιλεῖ: οὗτοι δὲ ἐπίλυγ τὸς σαφέστερας, δι᾽ ὧν πάντα ὁ βασιλεὺς ὁπισκοπεῖ.
units.tr: Those who held the first places at court were called "the king's eyes." Poenulus 3.3 v.80. Suidas: "the king's eye [ὀφθαλμὸς βασιλέως]" means one who is of great power with the king; these are the clearer ones, through whom the king oversees everything.

units.la: Hesych. βασιλέως ὀφθαλμὸς. ἐπίμετρος τὸς βασιλέως ἐπίσκοπος, ὁ ἐφωράτο τὰ φράγματα, ὧν τοῦ βασιλέως ὀφθαλμὸν ἐπάλλει. Pollux lib. 2. c. 37. ἐπιλέγοντο ἀτὰρ ὀφθαλμοὶ βασιλέως.
units.tr: Hesychius: "the king's eye [βασιλέως ὀφθαλμός]": an overseer of the king, who was informed of the fences, and whose eye the king was said to be. Pollux, book 2, chapter 37: the king's eyes [ὀφθαλμοὶ βασιλέως] were so called.

units.la: Apulejus de Mundo. Inter Persarum Regg. ministrir Aurea regia, & Imperatoris Oculi quidam homines vocabantur. Vide Brisson de Regno Persarum.
units.tr: Apuleius, On the World: "Among the kings of Persia, the men of the royal household and certain attendants of the emperor were called the Emperor's Eyes." See Brisson, on the kingdom of Persia.

units.la: [ornament]
units.tr: [ornament]

units.la: B.
units.tr: B.

units.la: BALNEARUM. THERMARUM. LAVATIO-NUM. ABLUTIONUM.
units.tr: BATHS. HOT BATHS. WASHINGS. ABLUTIONS.

units.la: MAGNA veterum & religiosa fuit superstitio in lavatio-nibus adhibendis ante rem sacram: quam Plautus no-ster sæpe tangit. Aul. 3.6.v.42. Ego nisi quid me vis, eo lavatum, ut sacrificem: & 4.2.v. 5. Nunc lavabo, ut rem divinam faciam. Vide alia loca infra Titulo Sacri-ficicrum.
units.tr: MANY of the ancients had a great and religious superstition about bathing before a sacred rite, which our Plautus often touches on. Aul. 3.6.v.42. Unless you want something of me, I am going to wash so that I may sacrifice; and 4.2.v.5. Now I will wash so that I may perform the divine rite. See other passages below under the title Sacrificium.

units.la: De hac consuetudine olim adolescens quædam annotaveram in taveram in Noctibus meis Palatinis Vigil.1. c. 14. quæ opportu-nè huc collocabuntur. Authores enim multi in hac re.
units.tr: I once made some notes on this custom in my Palatine Nights, Vigil. 1, c. 14, and they may conveniently be placed here, since many authors write on this matter.

units.la: Tibullus: Lota tibi est hodie: tibi se latissima compsit, Staret ut ante tuos conspicienda focos.
units.tr: Tibullus: You have bathed today, and the whole of you is adorned so that you may stand to be looked at before your hearth.

units.la: Vovet amator Cerinthus Junoni Genitali pro Sulpitiâ,
units.tr: The lover Cerinthus vows to Juno Genitalis on behalf of Sulpicia.

units.la: Livius lib. 1.
units.tr: Livy, book 1.

units.la: Ibi Antistes Romanus cum eum magnitudo vitiime celebratâ famâ movisset, memor responsi Sabinum ita alloquitur: Quidnam tu hospes paras, incestè sacrificium Dianæ facere? quin tu ante vivo perfunderis flumine? Infimâ valle præfluit Tiberis.
units.tr: When the Roman priest, moved by the great fame of the man, who had been celebrated for his virtue, recalled the response and addressed the Sabine: "What are you preparing, stranger, to make a sacrifice to Diana while unclean? Why do you not first bathe yourself in the living stream? The Tiber flows past in the lowest part of the valley."

units.la: Vivo autem flumine dicit: quòd sacra facturus D I s superis corporis ablutione purificabatur.
units.tr: He says "living stream" because a person about to perform sacred rites was purified by washing the body in running water.

units.la: Virgilius: Tu genitor cape sacra manu, patriosq; pendates, Me bello e tanto digressum, & cæde recentem Attrectare nefas, donec me flumine vivo Abluere. ----
units.tr: Virgil: "You, father, take the sacred things in your hand and the household gods of your country, since it is unlawful for me, just come from so great a war and recently stained with slaughter, to touch them until I have washed myself in the living stream."

units.la: Inferis solà adspersione, quæ laureolâ fiebat. Æneas apud inferos ramum Proserpinæ sacraturus:
units.tr: For the dead, purification was by sprinkling alone, which was done with a little laurel branch. Aeneas, about to consecrate the bough to Proserpina in the underworld:

units.la: Occupat Æneas aditum, corpusq; recenti Spargit aquâ.----
units.tr: Aeneas seizes the entrance and sprinkles his body with fresh water.

units.la: Martialis ad Domitianum: Meminerit non nisi religiosa purifica-tione lustratus accedere ad templa debere. Præ reliquis autem locus elegantèr dolatus apud Varronem Serano, περὶ ἀρχαιρεσιῶν. Occipitium: a vivo Deo ostendo, ex oraculo elimino me. Occipitium dixit, ut Virgilius: Transq; caput jace, ne respexeris.----
units.tr: Martial, to Domitian: Let him remember that he ought not to approach the temples unless he has been cleansed by a religious purification. Among the rest, a passage elegantly worded in Varro's Seranus, On the Elections: "Occipitium: I show the back of my head to the living god; I am purged by the oracle." He said occipitium (the back of the head) as Virgil does: and throw it over your head, do not look back.

units.la: Deo ostendit autem occipitium. Unde videtur, delubra non ea tantum fuisse, quæ fontem, aquam, vel lacum, ut vocant authores, haberent; sed & quæ Dei simulachrum. Ergò delubrum, ubi aqua pura cum Deo. Ut autem hic moneam, non prætereundum, quod Servius ait, Lacum in quo manus abluuntur. Ab illo enim Poëta:
units.tr: He shows the back of his head to the god. From this it seems that shrines were not only those that had a spring, water, or a lake, as the authors call them, but also those that housed the image of the god. So there was a shrine where pure water stood beside the god. But I should note here, and not pass over, what Servius says: a basin in which the hands are washed. For the poet says from that:

units.la: Et manibus puras sumite fontis aquas.
units.tr: And take up pure water from the spring in your hands.

units.la: Apud Græcos Hesiodus lib. II.
units.tr: Among the Greeks, Hesiod, book 2.

units.la: μηδέ ποτ' ἐξ ἀνοὺς δι' λείβειν αἴθοπι οἶνον χεροῖν ἀνιπτοισιν.----
units.tr: [μηδέ ποτ' ἐξ ἀνόσου δι' λείβειν αἴθοπα οἶνον χερσὶν ἀνίπτοισιν.] Never pour out dark wine to the gods with unwashed hands.

units.la: Apud Pomponium Atellanarum Auspice:
units.tr: In Pomponius's Atellan Farces, under the title Auspex:

units.la: ----A. Fac puriter,
units.tr: A. Do it cleanly,

units.la: Vel pectore rustico uti tractes. B. Lavi jam dudum manus.
units.tr: or handle it with a rustic heart. B. I have already washed my hands a while ago.

units.la: In quibus versibus corrigendis acutior Palmerius, quàm verior, secundum quod in reliquis omnibus. Ego ut propositui, ita ex Nonio, nudà ferè distinctione, & dispositione lego: eosque ita expono. Dicit Augur purè, vel simplici animo peragat religionem: cui alter respondet, se manus jam lavisse. Putabant scilicet se piari hac lavatione Veteres. Unde legimus apud S. Matthæum cap XXVII. Ἰδὼν δὲ ὁ Πιλᾶτος, ὅτι οὐδὲν ὠφελεῖ, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον θόρυβος γίνεται: λαβὼν ὕδωρ ἀπενιψατο τὰς χεῖρας ἀπέναντι τοῦ ὄχλου, λέγων, Ἀθῷός εἰμι ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος τούτου. Lucianus: τὰδὲ προσχρᾶμα φησὶ μὴ πᾶσιν ἔσω πεῖρα ἐν τηλίων ὅτι μὴ καθαρὸς ἐστι τὰς χεῖρας. Idem de homine impurissimo: ὅσων πεῖρα ἐν τηλίων ὅσων ποταμῶν δεῖ? Meminit & Porphyphyrius Λόγῳ α περὶ Ἐ Γνῶθι σεαυτὸν. Sed & Adspergillum adhi-bebant. Theodoretus in Historia: ἐκατέρωθεν δὲ τῶν ὑγρῶν εἰσὶ-κεισαν νεωκόροι πειρῶνται τοὺς εἰσιόντας προχαλέοντες, ὡς ἐσό-μιζον. Et Socrates Ecclesiastica Historia. ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐμελλεν ὑπερα μεί-ξειν Ἐ ναοῦ τὸν οὐδὸν, ἀλλοὺς τινας διαβρόχως κατέχων ὁ Ἰησοῦς νόμῳ ἑλληνικῷ πειρᾶσθαι τὰς εἰσιόντας.
units.tr: In correcting these verses Palmerius is more clever than correct, unlike in all the rest. I read them as I proposed, following Nonius, with little more than a change of punctuation and arrangement, and I explain them thus: the augur tells the other to perform the rite purely, or with a simple mind; the other replies that he has already washed his hands. The men of old evidently believed that they were cleansed by this washing. Hence we read in St Matthew, chapter 27: "When Pilate saw that he was getting nowhere, but rather that a tumult was arising, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying: I am innocent of the blood of this man." [Ἰδὼν δὲ ὁ Πιλᾶτος, ὅτι οὐδὲν ὠφελεῖ, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον θόρυβος γίνεται: λαβὼν ὕδωρ ἀπενίψατο τὰς χεῖρας ἀπέναντι τοῦ ὄχλου, λέγων, Ἀθῷός εἰμι ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος τούτου.] Lucian says that one who is not clean in his hands must be tested in ... Lucian says the same of a most impure man, asking how many rivers he would need. Porphyry also mentions it, in the first book of his work on "Know thyself." But they also used a sprinkler. Theodoret in his History says that on either side of the entrances there were temple-keepers who sprinkled those entering, as they used to do. And Socrates in his Ecclesiastical History: when Jesus was about to cross the threshold of the temple, he sprinkled those entering with water, according to the Greek custom.

units.la: Ab hoc ritu explico Apulejum Florid. iv. Ita ut contra in male-ficiis etiam cogitata scelera vindicantur, cruenta mente, pura ma-nu. Quamquam & hoc non ignorandum est: In omnibus fere rebus sanctioribus lavabant manus. Dion vetustissimus author, & ipse sacerdos & τ᾽ ὅης. Καὶ βέβν λαβὼν κατὰ χειρῶν κατα χέου, καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ἱεροσωπίην τρέπῳ Bedae in sacris aqua: Orpheus & Clemens Alexandrinus, De ista aquâ in Templis sacrâ, locus est Achillis Tatij lib. viii. de amoribus Leucippis & Clitiphontis: ubi inducit Clitiphontem graviter non solum laesum à Thersandro injusto, & falso domino, sed etiam verberatum: χαὶ γυὶ σεσ-σελδεῖν μὲ δὲν ἀπανιλαῦσα τὸ σεσοπον ἐξω. μὴ δ᾽ ἐνδον τοτο ποιῆ-ζωμιέγωγε, μὴ χ τὸ ἱερὸν ὕδωρ τὸ τῆς ὕβρεως ἀιμαπ μανθῆ. Philostratus lib. iii. de Brachmanibus: Post unguentum: ἐιταἐρρίψαν ἐ-αὐτὴς εἰς τὸ ὕδωρ, χ λουόμενοι ᾧδε πεῖς τὸ ἱερὸν βάδιζον ἐσεφανωμένοι.
units.tr: From this custom I explain Apuleius, Florida 4: Thus, conversely, in the case of evil deeds, even wicked thoughts are punished: a bloody mind, a pure hand. Yet this must also not be overlooked: in almost all more sacred matters they washed their hands. Dion, a very ancient author, himself a priest, and ... taking water and pouring it over the hands, he turned to the sacred face. Bede on sacred water. Orpheus and Clement of Alexandria. There is a passage about this water sacred in temples in Achilles Tatius, book 8, on the loves of Leucippe and Clitophon, where he presents Clitophon as not only grievously wronged by the unjust and false master Thersander, but also beaten. [And he says: "I am no longer able to bear the stench of this place," and "Do not do this inside, lest the sacred water of the outrage be found out."] Philostratus, book 3, on the Brahmans: after the ointment they threw themselves into the water and bathed, and then walked to the temple garlanded.

units.la: Caeterum disceptatur inter viros doctos, utrùm Romani quoti-die usi balneis, & lavationibus. Controversiam hanc dirimit faci-le Romanorum sapientissimus Seneca Epist. 86. Quanta, inquit, nunc aliqui rusticitatis damnant Scipionem, quòd non in Caldari-um suum latiùs specularibus diem admiserat, quod non in multâ luce decoquebatur & spectabat, ut in balneo concoqueret? O hominem calamitosum! nescit vivere. Non pacatâ aquâ lavabatur: sed sepè turbidâ & cùm plueret vehementius pene luculenta. Nec multum ejus intererat, an sic lavaretur: veniebat enim, ut sudorem illic ab-lueret, non ut unguentum. Quas nunc quorundam futuras voces credis? non invideo Scipioni: vere in exilio vixit, qui sic lava-batur. Nam ut ajunt, qui prisćos mores urbis tradiderunt, brachia & crura quotidie ablue bant, quas scil. sordes opere collegerant. Cae-terum totis Nundinis lavabatur. Hoc loco, dicet aliquis: liquet, immundissimos fuisse, quid putas illos oluisse militiam, laborem, vi-rum? postquam munda balnea inventa sunt, spurciores sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, learned men dispute whether the Romans used baths and washings every day. The wisest of the Romans, Seneca, settles this controversy easily, Letter 86: "How much, he says, some now condemn Scipio for rusticity, because he did not admit more daylight into his hot room through windows, because he did not bathe and sweat in a bright light so as to digest his food in the bath! O wretched man! He does not know how to live. He bathed in water that was not clear, often muddy, and when it was raining rather hard, not much better than dirty. Nor did it matter much to him whether he bathed like this; for he came there to wash off his sweat, not to have ointment. What words do you think some people will utter in future? I do not envy Scipio: he truly lived in exile, who bathed like that. For, as those say who handed down the old customs of the city, they washed their arms and legs every day, because of the filth they had gathered from work. Otherwise they bathed only on market days. Here someone will say: it is clear they were most unclean. What do you think they smelled of, soldiering, labour, manhood? Since clean baths were invented, men have become filthier."

units.la: MORIBUS Romanis virgines à balneis publicis arcebantur. Unde per Lautam Lipsius intelligit Feminam, quæ muliebris patientiæ legem jam accepit, per Illautam virginem. Mil. 3.1. v.191.
units.tr: By Roman custom, virgins were kept from public baths. Hence Lipsius understands by "bathed" (lauta) a woman who has already accepted the law of womanly endurance, and by "unbathed" (illauta) a virgin. Mil. 3.1.v.191.

units.la: Juvenalis de pueris:
units.tr: Juvenal, about boys:

units.la: Nec pueri credunt, nisi qui nondum ære lavantur.
units.tr: Nor do boys believe it, except those who have not yet been bathed for money.

units.la: Ego vero simpliciorem sensum tolerari posse autumo.
units.tr: I, however, think that a simpler sense can be tolerated.

units.la: TRES ædes seu cellæ in balneis fuerunt. Prima est caldaria, τὸ λα- κωνικὸν. Dioni συεατήειον, Seneca Sudatorium. Nam sicco calore in eo sudorem eliciebant. Secunda est Media, quæ & Tepidaria. Tertia est frigidaria. Plin. Epist. Post Solem frigidâ lavabatur. Seneca Epist. 84. Ab hac fatigatione in frigidam descendi. Plautus Mostel. 1.3.v.9. Jam pridem ecastor frigidâ non lavi: nec unde me melius, rem esse defæcatum.
units.tr: There were three rooms or cells in baths. The first is the caldarium, which is the Laconian room; Dion calls it the sweating room, Seneca the sudatorium, because in it they drew out sweat by dry heat. The second is the middle room, also called the tepidarium. The third is the frigidarium. Pliny, Letters: After the sun he bathed in cold water. Seneca, Letter 84: From this exhaustion I went down into the cold bath. Plautus, Mostellaria 1.3.v.9: Indeed, for a long time I have not bathed in cold water, nor is there anything from which I would be better cleansed.

units.la: PRÆ lassitudine lavare solebant Amph. 2.2.v.24. Ep. 5.1.v.48. Mer. 1.2.v.17. Bacch. 1.1. v.72. Truc 2.3.v.7. Sic Artemidorus lib.1.c. 66. Oneirocrit. [Greek text].
units.tr: They used to bathe for weariness: Amph. 2.2.v.24; Ep. 5.1.v.48; Mer. 1.2.v.17; Bacch. 1.1.v.72; Truc. 2.3.v.7. So Artemidorus, book 1, chapter 66, of the Oneirocritica.

units.la: MULIERES immodicæ in balneis, in se lavando, & fricando. Pœn. 1.2.v.21. Modus muliebris nullus est: neque umquam lavando, & fricando simus saturæ. Nam quæ elauta est, nisi perculta est, meo quidem animo, quasi illauta est. Et Truc. 2.3.v.3. Si proinde amentur mulieres, dum quam lavant, omnes amantes balneatores fient.
units.tr: Women were immoderate in baths, in washing and rubbing themselves. Poen. 1.2.v.21: A woman's measure is none, nor should we ever be satisfied with washing and rubbing. For she who has been bathed, unless she has been made up, in my opinion is as though unbathed. And Truc. 2.3.v.3: If women are loved in such a way, while they are bathing, all lovers will become bath-attendants.

units.la: ETIAM viri crebri in balneis. Pœn. 5.2.v.16. Num it à balneis circumductus pallio? Vide paulò antè ex Senecâ.
units.tr: Men too were frequent in baths. Poen. 5.2.v.16: Does he go away from the baths, led around in his cloak? See a little above, from Seneca.

units.la: LAVATIONEM sequebatur cæna. Perf. 1.3.v.10.
units.tr: A dinner followed the bath. Persius 1.3.v.10.

units.la: IN balneis luxu lavandi rem profligabant. Trin. 2.4.v.5. Rud. 2.7. v.21. Asin. 1.2. v.9.
units.tr: In baths they wasted the luxury of washing: Trin. 2.4.v.5; Rud. 2.7.v.21; Asin. 1.2.v.9.

units.la: Vide Turneb. in Orat. Cicer. contra Rull. & lib. 21. cap. 12. Adversar.
units.tr: See Turnebus on Cicero's oration against Rullus, and book 21, chapter 12 of his Adversaria.

units.la: In balneis lotiones sequebatur unctio. Rud. 2. 7. v. 22.
units.tr: After the bath came anointing: Rud. 2.7.v.22.

units.la: Latrina, balneum erat privatum, quod ancilla lavabant, seren- tes aquam. Curc. 4. 4. v. 24. Quamquam sensus potius est de latrina, ubi excrementa corporis. Sic etiam Culina vocabulum ambiguum.
units.tr: A latrina was a private bath, which maidservants washed out by sprinkling water. Curc. 4. 4. v. 24. Yet the sense is rather of a latrine, where the excrement of the body is. So also culina is an ambiguous word.

units.la: Vide Meurs. Cassandr. pag. 487.
units.tr: See Meursius, Cassandra, p. 487.

units.la: Strigilem & scaphium, in balneis habebant. Persi. 3. ver. 44. Vide de singulis Lexicon Plaut. Item Mercurialem in Gymnast. & Lauren. Pignorium de Servis: nec non Wowerum ad Petronium.
units.tr: They had a strigilis and a scaphium in the baths. Persi. 3. ver. 44. On the individual items see the Lexicon of Plautus. Likewise Mercuriale on Gymnastics, and Lorenzo Pignorio on Slaves; and also Wower on Petronius.

units.la: In balneis ampullis usi. Stich. 2. 1. v. 74. Cavillationes malacas ampullarias. Ampullam rubidam, rubigonosam strigilem: quâ sc. divites in balneis defricabantur à parasitis.
units.tr: They used flasks in the baths. Stich. 2. 1. v. 74. Cavillationes malacas ampullarias. A reddish flask, a rust-covered strigil, with which, namely, the rich were rubbed down in the baths by the parasites.

units.la: Post lotionem puram sacrificabant. Rud. 3. 3. v. 37.
units.tr: After the pure washing they made sacrifice. Rud. 3. 3. v. 37.

units.la: Belli. Militiae. Obsidionis. Imperatorum. Fetialium. Deditionis. Pugnae. Excidii. Aciei.
units.tr: War. Military service. Siege. Generals. Fetials. Surrender. Battle. Destruction. Battle line.

units.la: Bellum indicturi, solebant delegatos viros, primorum principes mittere. Amph. 1. 1. v. 49. Eos nominabant Fetiales: de quibus Agellius lib. 16. cap. 4. Et Brissonius, qui omnem rationem Fetialium, & clarigandi accuratissimè explicavit lib. iv. Formularum pag. 349. Edit. Francofurt. Wechelianæ. Inde repetet Lector harum rerum studiosus. Liber enim doctorum manibus merito teritur. Excute etiam verba Sofiæ apud nostrum loco dicto: unde lux magna illi antiquitati.
units.tr: When about to declare war, they used to send as envoys the chief men of the first rank. Amph. 1.1 v. 49. These they called Fetials, concerning whom see Aulus Gellius, book 16, chapter 4. And Brisson, who explained most accurately the whole system of the Fetials and of the clarigatio, in book 4 of his Formulae, p. 349, edition of Frankfurt, Wechel's press. The reader keen on these matters may go there for more; for a book is rightly worn by the hands of the learned. Look also at the words of Sophia in our author in the passage cited, whence great light is shed on that antiquity.

units.la: AD deditionem militarem allusum Amph. i.i.v.71.101. Quibus verbis illa facta, dilucidè explicat Brissonius verbis Livij. lib. i v. Formul. pag. 354-355.
units.tr: The military surrender is alluded to at Amph. 1.1 v. 71, 101. Brisson explains that act clearly in the words of Livy, book 1, Formulae, pp. 354-355.

units.la: Bellum incepturi, vota Jovi faciebant, antequam ad pugnam devenirent. Amph. i.i.v.75.
units.tr: When about to begin war, they made vows to Jupiter before coming to battle. Amph. 1.1 v. 75.

units.la: Militis boni officium est, de suo loco & statione non recedere: quod faciunt perduelles, qui se in fugam penetrant. Amph. i. i. v.83. 93. Sic Sallust. Conjurat.Catil.cap.ult. Namferè quem quisque vivus pugnando locum ceperat,eum,amissâ animâ, corpore tegebat.
units.tr: It is the duty of a good soldier not to withdraw from his place and station, which deserters do when they run off in flight. Amph. 1.1 v. 83, 93. So Sallust, Catiline's Conspiracy, last chapter: "For nearly every man, while alive, covered with his body the place he had taken by fighting, even when his soul was lost."

units.la: Justinus lib. 8.
units.tr: Justin, book 8.

units.la: Non tamen immemores pristinæ gloriæ cecidere, quippe adversis vulneribus omnes loca, quæ tuenda à ducibus acceperant, morientes corporibus texerunt.
units.tr: "Yet they did not forget their former glory, but fell; indeed, with wounds on every side, all of them, dying, covered with their bodies the places which they had received from their leaders to defend."

units.la: Seneca lib. de Tranq. cap. 9.
units.tr: Seneca, book on Tranquillity, chapter 9.

units.la: Sanè tantæ curæ fuit in gradu consistere, ut contenderint cæsi eundem obtinere.
units.tr: "Indeed there was such concern to hold their ground that, though cut down, they contended that they held the same spot."

units.la: Latinus Pacatus in Paneg. ad Theodof. Aug.
units.tr: Latinus Pacatus, in the Panegyric to the Emperor Theodosius.

units.la: Gladiatorià desperatione pugnare: nec gradu cedere: sed vestigio stare, vel cadere.
units.tr: "To fight with gladiatorial despair: not to yield ground, but to stand fast on the spot, or fall."

units.la: FORTIUM virorum videtur in prælijs aut vincere, aut mori. Qui enim capiuntur, vix interdum effugiunt ignaviæ, aut certè διλο-λυχίας notam. Quod significavit Philocrates Capt.2.2.v.12. Sed tamen Lacedæmonius quidam ex ijs, qui ab Atheniensibus ca pti sunt in Pylo, urbanè à se ignaviæ notâ amolitus dicitur. Cùm enim Atheniensis quidam ei per ludibrium dixisset: Ex vestris videlicet optimi ac fortissimi quique ceciderunt: Magni, inquit, faciendum esset fusus, si virosfortes dignoscere ac discernere ab ignavis posset. Fuisum autem Lacedæmoniorum more vocabat sagittam: & significabat, non fortissimos quosque mortuos esse: sed eos, qui casu sagittis icti fuissent! ut qui hostium potiti erant, non propterea minus fortes habendi essent, quàm qui ceciderant. Eminus enim cum illis prælisti erant Athenienses.
units.tr: It seems to belong to brave men in battles either to conquer or to die. For those who are captured hardly escape the mark of cowardice, or at least of διλολυχία [being captured alive]. Philocrates pointed this out, Capt. 2.2 v. 12. Yet a certain Lacedaemonian, one of those captured by the Athenians at Pylos, is said to have wiped the mark of cowardice from himself wittily. For when a certain Athenian, mocking him, had said, "Obviously the best and bravest of your men have fallen," he replied: "It would be of great importance to be able to pick out and tell brave men from cowards, if one could." He called the arrow, in the Spartan manner, a "fusus," and meant that not all the bravest had died, but those who had been struck by arrows by chance; so that those who had got the better of the enemy were not on that account to be counted less brave than those who had fallen. For the Athenians had fought with them at long range.

units.la: MILITES aut ornantes, fugam, aut castrametantes, vasa sua colligebant. Pseud. 4.3 v.16.
units.tr: Soldiers either decorated their flight, or, while encamping, gathered up their baggage. Pseud. 4.3 v. 16.

units.la: GRADU militari horis quinque æstivis 20000. passuum conficiebant Calones seu Caculæ. Pseud. 4. 4. v. 11. Ubi vide Lambin. ex Vegetio.
units.tr: The camp-followers, or sutlers, covered 20,000 paces in five summer hours at the military march. Pseud. 4.4 v. 11. See there Lambinus, from Vegetius.

units.la: BELLI dux Rempublicam proferre debet amori uxoris. Amphit. 1.3.v.30.
units.tr: A general of war ought to put the state before love of his wife. Amphit. 1.3 v. 30.

units.la: SOLEBANT Proconsules & Imperatores provincialibus imperare milites: & ijsdem, si ita meriti viderentur, cùm alia, tùm hoc onus militum mittendorum remittere. Quorsum allusit noster in ἀλληγορία de Parasito. Capt. 1.2. v.46.
units.tr: Proconsuls and generals used to command soldiers over the provincials, and to remit to the same, if they seemed to have deserved it, this burden of sending soldiers among other things. Our author alludes to this in an allegory about the Parasite. Capt. 1.2 v. 46.

units.la: IN militiâ machinis utebantur vineis, & pluteis. Mil. 2.2.v. III.
units.tr: In warfare they used siege engines, sheds and mantlets. Mil. 2.2 v. 111.

units.la: Vide Lipsij Poliorcetica lib.1.Dial.7. Noster usurpat ἀλληγορικῶς de fallacijs.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Poliorcetica, book 1, Dialogue 7. Our author uses it allegorically of deceits.

units.la: IN militia caute dispiciendum, & cavendum, ne inimici spolia capiant de nostro commeatu. Mil. 3.1. v.4. ἀλληγορικῶς.
units.tr: In war one must carefully watch and guard against enemies seizing the spoils of our provisions. Mil. 3.1 v. 4. Used allegorically.

units.la: AD militiam ituri calones sarcinam constringebant, clypeum ad dorsum accommodabant, fulmentas appingebant soccis: arcum, pharetram, & sagittas sumebant, cassidem in caput: quandoque dormiebant in tabernaculo. Trin. 3.1.v. 93. & seqq.
units.tr: Setting out for war, the camp-followers bound up their packs, fitted a shield to their back, attached straps to their shoes, and took a bow, quiver and arrows, a helmet on the head; sometimes they slept in the tent. Trin. 3.1 v. 93 and following.

units.la: MILITES ob Rempublicam militare docet. Curc. 3.1. v.19. Petronius initio: Pro libertate publica.
units.tr: He teaches that soldiers serve for the sake of the state. Curc. 3.1 v. 19. Petronius at the beginning: "For public liberty."

units.la: IN militiam abituri viatico se instruebant. Trin. 3.2. v. 102.
units.tr: Those setting out to the army equipped themselves with provisions for the journey. Trin. 3.2 v. 102.

units.la: DUPLEX instrumentum bellicum erat veteribus, quo in hostes emitterent, & jacularentur: altero tela, vel grandiores sagittas, altero lapides & saxa. Id prius Catapultam dixêre: posterius Balistam. Utrunque ἀλληγορικῶς exprimitur Curc. 3. 1. ver.24. 28. Capt. 4.2.v.16. Pœn. 1.1. v.73.
units.tr: The ancients had a double engine of war, by which they hurled and cast at the enemy: with one, spears or larger arrows; with the other, stones and rocks. The former they called the catapult, the latter the ballista. Both are expressed allegorically at Curc. 3.1 v. 24, 28; Capt. 4.2 v. 16; Poen. 1.1 v. 73.

units.la: Vide Lexicon Plautinum, & Justi Lipsij Poliorcet. lib. 3. Dialog. 2.
units.tr: See the Plautine Lexicon, and Justus Lipsius, Poliorcetica, book 3, Dialogue 2.

units.la: Intendam balistam in senem. Eâ balistâ, si pervortam turrim, & propugnácula, rectâ portâ invadam extemplò in oppidum antiquum. Sic capso, gritote amicis vostris aurâ corbibus. Bacch. 4.4. v.60. ἀλληγοεινῶς.
units.tr: "I will aim the ballista at the old man. With that ballista, if I overturn the tower and the bulwarks, I will at once invade the old town straight through the gate. Thus, having been caught, take care to cry to your friends with your gold-bearing crows." Bacch. 4.4 v. 60. Used allegorically.

units.la: Milites machaerâ & clypeo usi. Truc. 2.6. v.25.
units.tr: Soldiers armed with sword and shield. Truc. 2.6 v. 25.

units.la: Milites ignavi dicti Mulieres. Vide Tit. Mulierum.
units.tr: Soldiers are called cowards, women. See the title "Women."

units.la: Militum, tàm apud Græcos, quàm apud Romanos duo erant genera. Illi sumtu suo militabant, & Assidui dicebantur: hi publico, & Ærarij, atque Metelli sunt nominati. Mil. 1.1. v.74.
units.tr: Among soldiers, both with the Greeks and with the Romans, there were two kinds. The former served at their own expense and were called "assidui"; the latter at public expense, and were named "aerarii" and "Metelli." Mil. 1.1 v. 74.

units.la: Vide Cassand.Meurs.pag.335.
units.tr: See Cassander, Meursius, p. 335.

units.la: Milites se antemunire solent,& circumducere exercitum, currere in obsidium perduelles, præsidium suis parare, intercludere inimicis commeatum, munire sibi viam, quâ cibatus, commeatusque ad se & legiones suas tutò possit pervenire. Mil. 2.2. v.66. inde locum.
units.tr: Soldiers are accustomed to fortify themselves in advance, to lead the army round, to run to besiege the enemy, to prepare a garrison for their own people, to cut off provisions from the enemy, to fortify a road for themselves by which food and supplies may reach them and their legions safely. Mil. 2.2 v. 66, and the passage there.

units.la: Troiani excidij (ἀπεῖτο) & summa, eleganter describitur à Plauto. Bacch. 4.9. per totam scenam.
units.tr: The destruction and sum of Troy (ἀπεῖτο) is elegantly described by Plautus. Bacch. 4.9, through the whole scene.

units.la: Equus Troianus qualis fuerit, describit Q. Calaber. lib.12. & Homer. Odyss. δ & 9. aliiqueauthores.
units.tr: What kind of Trojan horse it was is described by Quintus Calaber, book 12, and Homer, Odyssey δ and θ, and other authors.

units.la: Vide ad præditum locum, quæ compilavit Taubman. ex variis scriptoribus. pag.502.
units.tr: See on the passage what Taubmann has gathered from various writers, p. 502.

units.la: Successus belli animos facit. Bacch. 4.9. v.18.
units.tr: Success in war makes men's spirits high. Bacch. 4.9 v. 18.

units.la: Pilum telum erat, quod injiciebant hosti. Mostell. 3.1.v.39.
units.tr: The pilum was a missile which they threw at the enemy. Mostell. 3.1 v. 39.

units.la: Vide Stewech. ad Vegetium: & Lips. Poliorcetica lib. 4.
units.tr: See Stewechius on Vegetius, and Lipsius, Poliorcetica, book 4.

units.la: Balistis expugnabantur urbes. Pseud. 2.1.v.10. ἀλληγοεινῶς. Ballionem exbalistabo lepidè, date operam modo, hoc ego oppidum Admunire,ut hoc die capiatur, volo: atq; ad hoc meas legiones ad-ducam; si hoc expugno, facile ego hinc rem civibus meis faciam. Post ad oppidum hoc vetus continuò meum exercitum protinus obducam. Inde me, & simul participes omnes meos prædâ onerabo, atq; opplebo. Metum & fugam perduellibus meis injiciam.
units.tr: Cities were taken by ballistae. Pseud. 2.1 v. 10. Used allegorically. "I will charmingly ballista Ballio out of the way; just give your attention. I want to fortify this town, so that it may be captured this day; and to this end I will bring up my legions. If I take this, I will easily make things go well for my citizens from here. Afterwards I will at once lead my army round this old town. Then I will load myself and all my partners with booty and fill them up. I will strike fear and flight into my enemies."

units.la: E bello re bene gestâ læti domum redibant, inprimis ad conjuges. ges. Amph. 2.2. v. 16. 22.
units.tr: Returning home happy from a war well waged, especially to their wives. Amph. 2.2 v. 16, 22.

units.la: SUPREMI omnium ducum Imperatoris ductu atque auspicio omnia gesta dicebantur. Amph. 2.2, ver. 25. Videndus Dialogus Lipsij de Militia Romana libr. 2. Dial. 12. nec non Torrentius in Sueton. August. cap. 21.
units.tr: Everything was said to be done under the leadership and auspices of the supreme general, the commander of all. Amph. 2.2 v. 25. See Lipsius's Dialogue on the Roman Army, book 2, Dialogue 12, and also Torrentius on Suetonius, Augustus, chapter 21.

units.la: COPIÆ per acies duplices triplices instructæ fuerunt. Quò alludit servus Pseud. 2.1. v. 5.
units.tr: Troops were drawn up in double and triple battle lines. To this the slave alludes, Pseud. 2.1 v. 5.

units.la: Vide Cæsarem lib. 1. de bello Gallico. Et lib. 1. de bello Civili.
units.tr: See Caesar, On the Gallic War, book 1, and On the Civil War, book 1.

units.la: ÆS militare sunt pugni. Poen. 5. 5. v. 7. Aere militari tetigero tenunculum.
units.tr: Military bronze are fists. Poen. 5.5 v. 7. "I have touched a little cudgel with military bronze."

units.la: AD militiam solent plærumque confugere nepotes, qui rem suam confregerunt omnem: actum gestare clipeum, galeam, sarcinam. Trin. 2.4. v. 195.
units.tr: Grandsons who have squandered all their property usually flee to military service, bearing a shield, helmet and pack as their business. Trin. 2.4 v. 195.

units.la: MILITES prædam & manubium sectabantur. Aul. 3.4. v. 12. ἀλλὰ ληγοειηῶς. Exemi e manu manubium.
units.tr: Soldiers pursued plunder and booty. Aul. 3.4 v. 12. Used allegorically. "I have taken the booty out of his hand."

units.la: OPPIDUM quodvis videtur posse expugnari dolis. Mil. 4. 4. v. 21.
units.tr: Any town seems able to be taken by tricks. Mil. 4.4 v. 21.

units.la: MILITES ob rapacitatem Milvis comparantur. Poenol. 5.5. v. 13. Male ego metuo Milvos.
units.tr: Soldiers, for their rapacity, are compared to kites. Poenulus 5.5 v. 13. "I fear the kites badly."

units.la: MILITES prædones, fures, ὡς ὅπι τὸ πολύ. Poenol. 3. 6. v. 7. Non sum nequicquam miles factus, paulum prædæ intus feci.
units.tr: Soldiers are plunderers and thieves, as is mostly the case. Poenulus 3.6 v. 7. "I have not been made a soldier for nothing; I have made a little plunder inside."

units.la: IN militiâ Caculæ sive Calones subserviebant militibus. Trin. 3. 2. v. 95. Illorum officium fuit, militibus ligna suppeditare: sicut Lixæ, aquam.
units.tr: In war, camp-followers or sutlers served the soldiers. Trin. 3.2 v. 95. Their duty was to supply the soldiers with wood, as the sutlers did with water.

units.la: IN militiâ erant adjutores sive optiones, qui ægrorum, vel aliàs impeditorum munera subibant. Asin. 1.1. v. 88. eò alludit senex.
units.tr: In war there were helpers or orderlies, who undertook the duties of the sick or otherwise hindered. Asin. 1.1 v. 88. The old man alludes to this.

units.la: Vide de his Adjutoribus Langlæi Otij Semestr. lib. 7. c. 4. p. 312. & Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: On these helpers see Lange, Otia Semestria, book 7, chapter 4, p. 312, and the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: JUVENES primâ ætate ad militiam mittebantur cum custode e cognatis. Mostell. 1. 4. ver. 49. Turneb. lib. 7. cap 3. & lib. 26. capit. 22.
units.tr: Young men of early age were sent to military service with a guardian from among their kinsmen. Mostell. 1.4 v. 49. Turnebus, book 7, chapter 3, and book 26, chapter 22.

units.la: UBI unum emeritum est stipendium, igitur tum specimen cernitur, quò eveniant: hoc est, cujus spei sint futuri. Mostell. 2. 1. v. §1.
units.tr: When one term of service has been completed, then the proof is seen of what they will turn out to be, that is, of what hope they will hold. Mostell. 2. 1. v. §1.

units.la: MILITES clypeo, machera utebantur: & expolibant nitidè. Mil. 1.1. v. 1. Qui quidem splendor armorum hostibus terriculamento esse solet. Veget. lib. 2. c. 14. Plurimum terroris hostibus armorum splendor importat. Quis credat militem bellicosum, cujus dissimulatione, situ, ac rubigine arma sedantur.
units.tr: Soldiers used the shield and the sword, and they polished them brightly. Mil. 1.1. v. 1. This brilliance of arms is usually a terror to the enemy. Veget. lib. 2. c. 14. The brilliance of arms brings the greatest terror to the enemy. Who would believe a warlike soldier whose arms are kept quiet by neglect, dirt and rust?

units.la: Laberius apud Agellium lib. 10. cap. 17.
units.tr: Laberius, quoted by Agellius, book 10, chapter 17.

units.la: Democritus Abderites, Physicus Philosophus Clypeum constituit contra exortum Hyperionis Oculos, ut possit effodere splendore æreo, &c.
units.tr: Democritus of Abdera, the natural philosopher, set up a shield against the rising of Hyperion's eyes, so that he could dazzle them with its bronze gleam, etc.

units.la: PUGNÆ præliares opponuntur velitationibus. Curc. 4. 4. v. 17.
units.tr: Actual battle is set against skirmishing. Curc. 4. 4. v. 17.

units.la: MILITES in suis armis confidere solent. Curc. 4. 4. v. 18. At ita me machæra, & clipeus bene juvent!
units.tr: Soldiers usually put their trust in their arms. Curc. 4. 4. v. 18. But so may my sword and shield help me well!

units.la: MILITES habebant servos calones, seu calatores, qui ligna portabant: ἀπὸ τῶν ξύλων. Alij tamen ἀπὸ ξυλεῖν. Vide Lexic. Plaut. Pseud. 4. 2. v. 52.
units.tr: Soldiers had slaves called camp-servants or carriers, who carried wood: from ξύλα [ἀπὸ τῶν ξύλων]. Others, however, derive it from ξυλεῖν [ἀπὸ ξυλεῖν]. See the Plautine lexicon. Pseud. 4. 2. v. 52.

units.la: DEVICTI bello totos se in arbitratum hostium dedebant. Amph. 1. 1. v. 102. Sic apud Polybium in Excerptis Legationum CXLII. Qui Pop. Romani Arbitrio se suaq; victi permittunt, ÿ agrû primò illis dant omnem, quem habent: & urbes, quacumq; sunt in illo: adhæc viros pariter & faeminas, quotquot in agro fuerint; annes, portus, sacra, monumenta denique: ita ut omnium domini fiant Romani.
units.tr: Those defeated in war gave themselves wholly into the power of their enemies. Amph. 1. 1. v. 102. So too in Polybius, in the Excerpts from Embassies, 142: Those who, being conquered, put themselves and their possessions at the discretion of the Roman people, first give them all the land they have, and the cities that are in it; besides, the men and women alike, however many are in the land; the rivers, harbours, sacred things and monuments, in short everything, so that the Romans become masters of all.

units.la: MILITES certos dicuntur coitus, & pedatus, seu periodos congrediendi facere. Cist. 2 1. v. 49. Vide Lex. Plaut. Scipio Affric. Vt atq; ingratis coatlus cum illo sponsionem feci: fallâ sponsione, ad judicem adduxi: adductum primo coetu damnavi. Cato apud Nonium: Igitur tertio pedatu nobis bellum fecere.
units.tr: Soldiers are said to make fixed meetings and marching-appointments, or periods for engaging. Cist. 2. 1. v. 49. See the Plautine lexicon. Scipio Africanus: So I made a bargain with him against his will, and, the bargain having failed, I brought him before the judge; having been brought, I condemned him at the first meeting. Cato, quoted by Nonius: So they made war on us at the third march.

units.la: QUEMADMODUM lecti milites in tabulas & codices referebantur, & scribebantur: ita delebantur non milites, & rejecti. Curc. 4. 4. v. 29. Miles pulcre excenturiatus est expunctio in manipulo. Vide Lipf. Analecta ad Militiam.
units.tr: Just as soldiers who were enlisted were recorded and written in the tablets and registers, so those who were not soldiers, or were rejected, were erased. Curc. 4. 4. v. 29. A soldier has been well promoted, the removal being made in the maniple. See Lipsius, Analecta on military service.

units.la: MILITES ad Militiam abituri, non satis habebant aves observaf- se: sed insuper folicitè explorabant antè pugnæ initium: indeet- jam aliquid ominis captantes. Epid. 2.2. v.2. sic ἀλλ᾽ηγοεικῶς, in- quit Servus: liquido ex eo foràs auspicio, avi sinistrà: cultrum ha- beo: qui excuterem senis marsupium. Atq; hoc dicebant Ex acu- minibus auspicare. Arnobius lib. ii. Aut Martium discrimen ob- euntes spem praeli sumitis: & ex acuminibus auspicatis? Cic. lib. ii. de Nat. Deorum: Itaque maximae Reipub. partes, in his bella, quibus Respub: salus continetur, nullis auspiciis administrantur, nulla perennia servantur: nulla ex acuminibus, nulli viri vocan- tur.
units.tr: Soldiers about to set off for service did not think it enough to observe the birds; they also carefully searched out omens before the start of the battle, thus seeking some sign already. Epid. 2. 2. v. 2. So, says the slave, [ἀλλ᾽ ἠγοραικῶς]: From this clear omen outside, a bird on the left: I have a knife, with which I may cut open the old man's purse. And they called this to take auspices from the points. Arnobius, book 2: Or do you, facing the peril of war, take hope of battle and auspices from the points? Cicero, book 2 On the Nature of the Gods: Therefore the greatest parts of the commonwealth, in those wars on which the safety of the commonwealth depends, are managed with no auspices, no omens are observed; no auspices from the points are taken, no men are called.

units.la: Atq; hoc auspicij genus primus M. Marcellus neglexit, teste Ci- cerone lib. ii. de Divinatione: Bellicam rem administrari majo- res nostri, nisi auspicato noluerunt: quàm multi anni sunt, cum bel- la à propratoribus & Proconsulibus administrantur, qui auspicia non habent! Itaq; nec amnes transeunt auspicato: nec tripudio au- spicantur. nam Ex Acuminibus quidem, quod totum auspi- cium militare est, jam M. Marcellus ille quinquies consul totum omisit, idem Imperator, idem Augur optimus.
units.tr: This kind of augury was first neglected by M. Marcellus, as Cicero testifies in book 2 On Divination: Our ancestors did not want warfare to be conducted without auspices. How many years have passed since wars have been conducted by propraetors and proconsuls, who have no auspices! So they do not cross rivers with auspices, nor take auspices from the sacred chickens. For the auspices from the points, which is the whole of military augury, that famous M. Marcellus, five times consul, altogether omitted; he was an excellent general and an excellent augur.

units.la: STIPENDIUM militare nimis tenue erant tres asses. Most. 2. i. v. 10. Ubi sunt isti, qui trium numorum causa subeunt sub falas? Ubi aliì quiq; hastis corpus transfigi solet. Ita enim ibi legendum ex Mss. Camerario - Pall. & omnibus omninò editionib° levi istâ immu- tatione verborum censeo. Camerarius fecerat quindenis hastis. Vide Lipsl.lib.i. Elect.cap.2. Et Poliorc. lib.5. cap.5.
units.tr: Military pay was very small, only three asses. Most. 2. 1. v. 10. Where are those who undergo the yoke for the sake of three coins? Where, as is usual, the body is pierced by spears. For so it is to be read there from the manuscripts of Camerarius, the Palatine, and all the editions in general, with this slight change of words; I think so. Camerarius had written quindenis hastis. See Lipsius, Elections, book 1, chapter 2, and Poliorcetica, book 5, chapter 5.

units.la: ERANT etiam excursores ἀκέφομα levis armaturæ milites. Most. 2.1.v.12. Cic. lib.2. de Divin. Sed hæc erit nobis tanquam levio- ris armaturæ prima excursio.
units.tr: There were also skirmishers, [ἀκροβολισταί] light-armed soldiers. Most. 2. 1. v. 12. Cicero, book 2 On Divination: But this will be for us, as it were, the first sally of light-armed troops.

units.la: MUROS etiam scalis ascendebant. Quò referri potest illud Most. 2.1. vers.12. Ego dabo et talentum, primus qui in crucem excur- rerit.
units.tr: They also climbed the walls by ladders. To this may be referred that line, Most. 2. 1. v. 12. I will give a talent too to the first man who runs out onto the cross.

units.la: MILITIBUS abituris in militiam: & ex eâdem redeuntibus da- batur syngraphus: quem nostri milites appellant Paspoorten. Capt. 2.3.v.90. & 3.2. v.6.
units.tr: To soldiers departing for service, and returning from it, a written pass was given, which our soldiers call Paspoorten. Capt. 2. 3. v. 90, and 3. 2. v. 6.

units.la: MILITES sæpe falsis pugnis gloriari solent. Trucul. 2. 6. v. 4. Mille memorari potest, qui & convitii & condemnati satis de pugnis sient.
units.tr: Soldiers often like to boast of false battles. Trucul. 2. 6. v. 4. One can recall a thousand who, both for boasting and for being condemned, have had enough of battles.

units.la: Ridiculi igitur habiti etiam Principes, qui falsis victorijs gloriam quærebant apud vulgum: nam plebs sola fallitur his præstigijs: Ideoque cùm plebs plurimùm posset suffragijs, judicijs, in libera Republica legibus cautum, ne quis ejusmodi mendacijs clare-sceret. Nam & statuta pœna: si quis militum falsò strenuum quid factum à se retulisset ad tribunum aut ducem. Polybius: ἐὰν τι- νὲς ψευδῆ πρὸς ἀντῶν ἀνδραγαθίαν ἐπαγγελλωνταις τοῖς χιλιάρχοις ἐνσκα ἐ πύας λαβεῖν. Crimen hoc proprie vocabant De falsis pugnis: ut patet ex Plauti loco.
units.tr: Therefore even princes were held ridiculous who sought glory among the common people by false victories; for the crowd alone is deceived by such tricks. Hence, since the common people had the greatest power through votes and judgments, in a free commonwealth the laws took care that no one should become famous by such lies. Indeed a penalty was also set if any soldier falsely reported to a tribune or commander that he had done something brave. Polybius: If anyone, falsely professing bravery before the chiliarchs, should receive a reward... They called this crime properly concerning false battles, as is clear from the passage of Plautus.

units.la: Sic Tacitus Agric. cap. 39.
units.tr: So Tacitus, Agricola, chapter 39.

units.la: Inerat conscientia derisus fuisse nuper falsum è Germania triumphum, emtis per commercia, quorum habitus & crines in captivorum species formarentur: at nunc veram magnamque victoriam, tot millibus hostium cæsis, ingenti famâ celebrari.
units.tr: There was in them the awareness that the triumph recently celebrated from Germany was a false one, bought through trade, whose clothing and hair were fashioned into the appearance of captives. But now a true and great victory, with so many thousands of enemies slain, is celebrated with great fame.

units.la: Quo crimine postulatus à M. Catone Censorio Q. Thermus, Oratione, quæ inscripta: In Q. Minutium Thermum de falsis pugnis. Sic enim legendum apud Agellium & Nonium.
units.tr: For this charge Q. Thermus was prosecuted by M. Cato the Censor, in a speech entitled: Against Q. Minucius Thermus, concerning false battles. For so it is to be read in Agellius and Nonius.

units.la: MILITES plæriqueque gloriosi, jactabundi, spumantibus utuntur verbis, quadratis & sesquipedalibus. Mil. 1. 1. v. 13. Quem ego servavi in campis Gurgustidonijs, Ubi Bombomachides Cluninstarchysarchides Erat imperator summus
units.tr: Most soldiers are boastful and bragging, and they use swelling words, square and a foot and a half long. Mil. 1. 1. v. 13. Whom I saved on the Gurgustidonian plains, where Bombomachides Cluninstarchysarchides was the supreme commander.

units.la: Siculle Pœnol. 3. 3. ver. 49. E Spartâ se venisse ait, & militasse Regi Attalo.
units.tr: Sicilian. Poen. 3. 3. v. 49. He says he has come from Sparta, and served under King Attalus.

units.la: Et Pœn. 2. 1. v. 2 s.
units.tr: And Poen. 2. 1. v. 2 ff.

units.la: De pugnâ illâ pterornithicâ: quâ sexaginta millia hominum uno die volaticorum manibus occidimus. In fundas visci indebant grandiculos globos. Et illos volantes jussi funditarier. Quid multa verba? ut quemq; visco offenderant, Tam crebri ad terram accidebant, quàm pira. Ut quisq; acciderat, eum necabam illico per cerebrum primâ suâ sibi, quasi turturem.
units.tr: Concerning that bird-battle: in which we killed sixty thousand men in one day with the hands of winged creatures. They put large lumps of birdlime in the slings, and I ordered them to hurl those flying ones. Why say more? As soon as each one struck against the lime, they fell to the ground as often as pears. As each one fell, I at once killed him through the brain with my own hand, as if a turtle-dove.

units.la: Atque
units.tr: And

units.la: Atq; inde dicti ob arrogantiam illam per jocum Urbicapi: quia urbes capiunt. Bacch. 4.9. v.42. Mil. 4.2.v.64.
units.tr: And from that arrogance they were named, by way of joke, Urbicapi, because they capture cities. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 42. Mil. 4. 2. v. 64.

units.la: Nec tantum gloriosi & jactabundi sunt milites: verum etiam profani: impij, perjuri: mendaces. Poen. 2. 1. v. 20. Quid ei divini atque humani æquum est credere? Perge, optime hercle perjuras, Truc. 2.6, v.3. Scio ego multos memorasse milites mendacium.
units.tr: Soldiers are not only boastful and vainglorious, but also profane, impious, perjured and lying. Poen. 2. 1. v. 20. What is right, divine or human, is it proper to trust him? Go on, by Hercules, you are a very good perjurer. Truc. 2. 6. v. 3. I know that many soldiers have spoken of lying.

units.la: Quidvis etiam audacter dicere solent. Epid. 1, 1. v.14. Ubi Homo militaris opponitur Urbano scurrae: De quo vide Lexic.Plautinum.
units.tr: They are also accustomed to say whatever they like, boldly. Epid. 1. 1. v. 14. Here the soldierly man is set against the urbane buffoon; on this see the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: Optimi belli duces sunt, quorum ductu, imperio, & auspicio bellum geritur Reipublicae causâ. Amph. 1.1.v.41.
units.tr: The best generals of war are those by whose leading, command and auspices a war is waged for the sake of the commonwealth. Amph. 1. 1. v. 41.

units.la: Auxiliares socij eis libenter accedunt: ubi jus & æquum vigent: contra autem, ubi vis atq; affectus reliqui: ut patet ex Carthaginensibus, post finem belli Punici primi. Cist. 1.3. v.52. Sola namq; ea Virtus parit laudem & lauream.
units.tr: Allied auxiliaries gladly join them where justice and fairness prevail; but on the contrary, where force and selfish desire hold sway, as is clear from the Carthaginians after the end of the First Punic War. Cist. 1. 3. v. 52. For that virtue alone brings praise and the laurel.

units.la: In militiâ propius ad hostem accedentes, attollere solent signa. Caf. 2.6. v.5.
units.tr: Soldiers approaching the enemy more closely in war are accustomed to raise their standards. Caf. 2. 6. v. 5.

units.la: Postquam tempus operarum, quæ militi destinatæ erant, exactum erat, stipendia dabantur, ut emeritis. Bacch. 1.1. v. 9.
units.tr: When the time of the services due from the soldier had run out, the pay was given to the veterans. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 9.

units.la: Milites jubam & cæsariem ac cincinnos alebant. Mil. 1, 1. ver. 64. & 3.1. v.172. & 3 3. v.49.
units.tr: Soldiers grew a mane, hair and curls. Mil. 1. 1. v. 64, and 3. 1. v. 172, and 3. 3. v. 49.

units.la: Re bene gestâ, victimas, quas voverent, persolvebant. Men. 1.3.v.9. Turn. lib. 20. 27.
units.tr: When a campaign had gone well, they paid the victims they had vowed. Men. 1.3.v.9. Turn. lib. 20. 27.

units.la: Singulæ militiæ suâ habebant stipendia. Epid. 1.1. v.36.
units.tr: Each kind of soldiery had its own pay. Epid. 1.1. v.36.

units.la: Exuvias vivo hosti eripiebant. Epid. 1. 1. v. 36.
units.tr: They snatched the spoils from a living enemy. Epid. 1. 1. v. 36.

units.la: Virtute atque auspicio Imperatoris omnia dicuntur geri. Ep. 3.2.v.45.
units.tr: Everything is said to be done by the courage and auspices of the commander. Ep. 3.2.v.45.

units.la: Milites reversi e militiâ, solent memorare suas victorias, & spolia. Amph. Prol. v.136. & 1.1. v. 40.
units.tr: Soldiers returning from campaign are accustomed to recount their victories and spoils. Amph. Prol. v.136. & 1.1. v. 40.

units.la: Milites sub signum ducebantur, ne huc illuc vagarentur aut latrocinarentur. Caf 3.6.v.1. Pseud. 2.4. v.71.
units.tr: Soldiers were led under the standard, so that they would not wander here and there or go marauding. Caf 3.6.v.1. Pseud. 2.4. v.71.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: E BELLO redeuntes salvi, vota Deo vovebant. Amph. 3. 2. v. 66.
units.tr: Men returning safely from war used to make vows to God. Amph. 3. 2. v. 66.

units.la: ADSCRIPTIVI milites inermes adscribebantur, qui succederent armatis, si quis eorum deperiisset. Men. 1. 3. v. 2.
units.tr: Unarmed men were enrolled as reserves, who would take the place of the armed men if any of them had died. Men. 1. 3. v. 2.

units.la: OMNES ordines & legiones sub signis ducuntur in militiâ. Pseud. 2. 4. v. 71.
units.tr: All the orders and legions are led under their standards in war. Pseud. 2. 4. v. 71.

units.la: BELLO perpetua quoque laus & gloria comparatur. Epid. 3. 4. v. 6.
units.tr: Lasting praise and glory are also won by war. Epid. 3. 4. v. 6.

units.la: MILITES imperata promte exequi debent. Aul. 2. 1. v. 23. & 2. 2. v. 16. Cist. 4 2. v. 16. Bacch. 4 4. v. 74.
