units.tr: Soldiers ought to carry out orders promptly. Aul. 2. 1. v. 23. & 2. 2. v. 16. Cist. 4 2. v. 16. Bacch. 4 4. v. 74.

units.la: PUGNA velitaris levis erat contentio, Velitatio dicta. Inde Velites. Rud. 2. 6. v. 41.
units.tr: A skirmish was a light contest of the light troops, and was called a velitatio. Hence the Velites. Rud. 2. 6. v. 41.

units.la: PILUM catapultarium. Curc. 5. 3. v. 11. ἀλληγοερικῶς. Funes nervini: qui brachia catapultarum continebant. Ibid.
units.tr: A catapult-dart. Curc. 5. 3. v. 11. [allegorically: ἀλληγορικῶς]. Sinew cords: those which held the arms of the catapults. Ibid.

units.la: VETERES Romani solebant commeatum ad exercitum in colonia aliquâ positum, praesidij causâ impositum, auspicato portare: idq; auspicato faciebant, ne interciperetur. Epid. 3. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: The old Romans used to carry provisions to an army stationed in some colony, placed there as a garrison, always after taking the auspices; and they did this under the auspices so that it could not be intercepted. Epid. 3. 2. v. 7.

units.la: ARMA defendendi causâ induunt: ut ille loricam se induere ait, ut tutus sit ab insidijs ancillæ. Cas. 3. 5. v. 53.
units.tr: Men put on armour for the sake of defence, as when one says he puts on a breastplate so as to be safe from the tricks of a maidservant. Cas. 3. 5. v. 53.

units.la: SOCII militiæ, dicti Manipulares, qui prædam partipabant. Most. 1. 3. v. 153.
units.tr: Comrades in arms, called manipulares, who shared the booty. Most. 1. 3. v. 153.

units.la: CENTURIONES solebant circumferre tabellas, in quibus mercenariorum militum nomina conscribebant, ut scirent, quibus stipendia deberentur. Mil. 1. 1. v. 38.
units.tr: Centurions used to carry around tablets on which they wrote down the names of the mercenary soldiers, so that they would know to whom the pay was owed. Mil. 1. 1. v. 38.

units.la: IN bello rem bene gerentibus Rex Persarum pateram auream donodabat. Amph. 1. 1. v. 262. Vide Tit. Munerum.
units.tr: In war, the King of the Persians used to give a golden bowl to those who had fought well. Amph. 1. 1. v. 262. See the title Munerum.

units.la: UBI summus Imperator non adest ad exercitum, cujus quod facto non est usus, fit, quàm quod facto est opus. Amph. 1. 3. v. 6. Vide Tit. Praesentiæ - persona.
units.tr: When the supreme commander is not present with the army, what is not done is more often what needs doing. Amph. 1. 3. v. 6. See the title Praesentiae - person.

units.la: NOX solet bellum dirimere. Amph. 1. 1. v. 98.
units.tr: Night is wont to break off a battle. Amph. 1. 1. v. 98.

units.la: Sic Ennius:
units.tr: So Ennius:

units.la: ---- bellum,
units.tr: ---- the war,

units.la: Æquis de manibus non intempestà diremit. Livius 21.
units.tr: Not at an unseasonable time did it part from the hands of the Aequi. Livy 21.

units.la: Non accensum ingentibus animis pralium diremit. ARIETE oppugnabant muros. Perf. 1.2.v.22. ἀλληγορικῶς. GLADIIS capulum additum. Caf. 5.2. v.26. PEDITATUS equitatui additus. Mil. 1.1. v.54.
units.tr: The night parted the battle, which had not been kindled with great spirits. They attacked the walls with a battering ram. Perf. 1.2.v.22. [allegorically: ἀλληγορικῶς]. A hilt added to the sword. Caf. 5.2. v.26. Infantry added to cavalry. Mil. 1.1. v.54.

units.la: MILITES talis ludentes ciebant nomina suarum amicarum. Curc. 2.3.v.77.
units.tr: Soldiers playing at dice used to call out the names of their mistresses. Curc. 2.3.v.77.

units.la: PRÆDA & præmium hostibus eripi solet. Men. 1.2. v.25.26.
units.tr: Booty and reward are usually snatched from enemies. Men. 1.2. v.25.26.

units.la: TRAGULAM sive hastam inijcebant in hostem. Epid. 5.1. v.24. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: They threw a javelin or spear at the enemy. Epid. 5.1. v.24. See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: NEQUAM milites sunt, qui, alijs pugnantibus, ipsi fugiunt: ut Sofia Plautinus Amph. 1.1. v.44.
units.tr: Those soldiers are worthless who flee while others fight, as Plautus's Sosia says. Amph. 1.1. v.44.

units.la: IN balistario balistas servabant. Pœn. 1.1.v.73. ἀλληγορικῶς. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: In the ballista-room they kept the ballistae. Poen. 1.1.v.73. [allegorically: ἀλληγορικῶς]. See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: MANIPULARES centuriati dicebantur, qui sub centurione militabant. Mil. 3.2.v.3. ἀλληγορικῶς.
units.tr: Those who served under a centurion were called centuriati manipulares. Mil. 3.2.v.3. [allegorically: ἀλληγορικῶς].

units.la: MILITES plæriq; perjuri gloriarum pleni, Mil. 1.1.v.22.
units.tr: Most soldiers are perjured and full of boasting. Mil. 1.1.v.22.

units.la: MILITES magnum numerum meretricum secum ducebant. Ep. 2.2. v.29.
units.tr: Soldiers used to take a great number of prostitutes along with them. Ep. 2.2. v.29.

units.la: ARTE duellicâ divitiæ magnæ comparantur. Epid. 3.4.v.14.
units.tr: Great riches are won by the military art. Epid. 3.4.v.14.

units.la: BELLICOSIS hominibus solebant Martem propitium apprecari. Asin. Prol v.15.
units.tr: People who were warlike used to pray to Mars for his favour. Asin. Prol. v.15.

units.la: MILITIBUS scutum erat majus clypeo, & oblongæ formæ. Bacch. 1.1. v.39.
units.tr: Soldiers had a shield larger than the clipeus, and of oblong shape. Bacch. 1.1. v.39.

units.la: MACHÆRÆ militari veruina, seu verutum opponitur. Bacch. 4. 8.v.46. Turn.2.7.
units.tr: The military sword is set against the spear or javelin. Bacch. 4. 8.v.46. Turn. 2.7.

units.la: MILITES ferentarij laborantibus facilè auxiliantur. Trinum. 2.4. v.55.
units.tr: Light-armed soldiers readily assist those who are struggling. Trinum. 2.4. v.55.

units.la: MILITES censebantur. Rud. 4.8. v.9.&15. Qui militiæ nomen daturi erant, non minus, quàm coràm censoribus ordine alius post alium se sistebat, & ex omni numero tandem optimus quisque sumebatur.
units.tr: Soldiers were enrolled. Rud. 4.8. v.9. & 15. Those who were about to be given the name of soldier presented themselves in order, one after another, no less than before the censors, and from the whole number at last the best of each was chosen.

units.la: MILITES aurum praesentarium poscunt. Poen. 3. 3. v. 86.
units.tr: Soldiers demand ready money. Poen. 3. 3. v. 86.

units.la: PRÆDAM ex hostibus factam, ad quæstores urbanos deferebant. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 152.
units.tr: Booty taken from the enemy they used to carry to the urban quaestors. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 152.

units.la: MILITES jurabant per Martem, quem colebant; ut patrem suum. Poen. 3. 3. v. 31. Truc. 5. 1. v. 11. Mil. 5. v. 21.
units.tr: Soldiers swore by Mars, whom they worshipped as their father. Poen. 3. 3. v. 31. Truc. 5. 1. v. 11. Mil. 5. v. 21.

units.la: MILITES noctu in vigiliam eunt. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 84.
units.tr: Soldiers go out on night watch. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 84.

units.la: BENEFICIORUM. GRATITUDINIS. INGRATITUDINIS. BENEFICENTIÆ. BENEMERITI. STUDII. OFFICII. VIRTUTIS. LIBERALITATIS. GRATIÆ. AMORIS. FAVORIS. FAUTORUM.
units.tr: BENEFITS. GRATITUDE. INGRATITUDE. BENEFICENCE. DESERVING WELL. ZEAL. DUTY. VIRTUE. LIBERALITY. GRACE. LOVE. FAVOUR. PATRONS.

units.la: Vide etiam nonnulla Tit. Amicitiæ.
units.tr: See also some items under the title Friendship.

units.la: BENEFICIA non exprobranda sunt. Amphit. Prolog. 4. 47. Ubi Mercurius de Jove: Sed mos illic numquam fuit patri meo: Ut exprobraret quod bonis faceret bona.
units.tr: Benefits are not to be thrown in one's face. Amphit. Prolog. 4. 47. Here Mercury speaks of Jupiter: But it was never my father's custom to reproach good men for the good things he did for them.

units.la: BENEFICIA dignis merito dantur. Amph. Prol. v. 48.
units.tr: Benefits are rightly given to the worthy. Amph. Prol. v. 48.

units.la: Sic Mimus: Beneficium dando accipit, qui digno dedit.
units.tr: So the mime-writer: He who gives to a worthy man receives the benefit in the giving.

units.la: DUM alios servam nostris beneficiis, saepe nos impedimus interim. Rud. Prol. v. 37.
units.tr: While we keep others safe by our kindnesses, we often, in the meantime, hinder ourselves. Rud. Prol. v. 37.

units.la: Sic Curtius lib. 4. de Abdolomino: Causa ejus pauper tatis sicut plurimq; probitas erat.
units.tr: So Curtius, book 4, on Abdolominus: His poverty was as much the cause of his uprightness as it was of his fortune.

units.la: Isocrat. Parænes.
units.tr: Isocrat. Parænes.

units.la: μηδένα ζήλῳ τῶν ἐξ ἀδικίας κεκτημένων, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἀποδέχῃ τὸς μετὰ δικαιοσύνης ξυμπαθέντας.
units.tr: Do not envy those who have gained their possessions through injustice; rather, you should approve more of those who have joined in sympathy with justice. [μηδένα ζήλῳ τῶν ἐξ ἀδικίας κεκτημένων, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἀποδέχῃ τοὺς μετὰ δικαιοσύνης ξυμπαθέντας.]

units.la: NVLLVM beneficium duco esse id, quod, cui facias, non placet.Trin. 3. 2. v. 12.
units.tr: I consider that no benefit is one that does not please the person to whom it is done. Trin. 3. 2. v. 12.

units.la: Seneca l. 2. c. 19. de Benef.
units.tr: Seneca, book 2, chapter 19, On Benefits.

units.la: Si vis scire an velim, effice, ut possim nolle.
units.tr: If you want to know whether I am willing, make it so that I am able to be unwilling.

units.la: P. Syrus: Invitum qui servat, idem facit occidenti.
units.tr: Publilius Syrus: He who saves an unwilling man does the same as one who kills him.

units.la: Si quid benefacias, levior plumâ est gratia: si quid peccatum est, plumbeas iras gerunt. Poen. 3. 6. v. 17.
units.tr: If you do someone a good turn, gratitude is lighter than a feather; if you have done wrong, they bear grudges heavy as lead. Poen. 3. 6. v. 17.

units.la: Sic Herodianus in Oratione Pertinacis:
units.tr: So Herodian in the speech of Pertinax:

units.la: Καὶ τὰ μὲν δεινὰ τῶν ἔργων ἀεὶ μνημονεύεται· τὸ δὲ λυπῆσαι δυσεχέ- λεγτον· τὰ δὲ χρηστὰ, ἅμα τῇ ἀπολαύσει, ᾗ τὴν περὶ αὐτῶν μνή- μην σωσαναλίσκει. Hoc est: Injuriarum, si quæ facta sunt, semper est memoria: & quicquid offendit, egre eximitur: at beneficiorum, unà cum ipso fructu usuque, memoria perit.
units.tr: Dreadful deeds are always remembered; to have given offence is hard to forget; but good deeds, together with their enjoyment, the memory of them is used up and perishes. (Καὶ τὰ μὲν δεινὰ τῶν ἔργων ἀεὶ μνημονεύεται· τὸ δὲ λυπῆσαι δυσεχέλεγτον· τὰ δὲ χρηστὰ, ἅμα τῇ ἀπολαύσει, ᾗ τὴν περὶ αὐτῶν μνήμην σωσαναλίσκει.) That is: If any injuries have been done, there is always a memory of them; and whatever has given offence is hardly erased; but of benefits, the memory perishes along with the very enjoyment and use of them.

units.la: Tacitus lib. 1 v. Annal.
units.tr: Tacitus, book 1 of the Annals.

units.la: Proclivius est injuria, quàm beneficio vicem exsolvere: quia gratia oneri, ultio in quaestu habetur.
units.tr: It is easier to repay an injury than to repay a benefit, because gratitude is felt as a burden, while revenge is counted as a gain.

units.la: Seneca lib. 1. cap. 1. de Benefic.
units.tr: Seneca, book 1, chapter 1, On Benefits.

units.la: Ita naturâ comparatum est, ut altius injuria, quàm merita descendant, & illa citò defluant, hæc tenax memoria custodiat.
units.tr: It is so ordained by nature that injuries sink deeper than good deserts, and that the former quickly slip away, while the latter are kept by a tenacious memory.

units.la: IMPROBUS est homo, qui beneficium scit sumere, & reddere nescit. Pers. s. 1, v. 10.
units.tr: He is a wicked man who knows how to receive a benefit but does not know how to repay it. Pers. sat. 1, v. 10.

units.la: Cato:
units.tr: Cato:

units.la: Gratior officiis, quò sis mage carior esto:
units.tr: Be the more grateful for services, the dearer you are to be,

units.la: Ne nomen subeas, quod dicunt, officiperdi.
units.tr: Lest you incur the name that they call "destroyer of services."

units.la: Officiperda ἀλεσίχαρις est, apud quem omnia officia & beneficia pereunt: quiq;, ut ait Seneca:
units.tr: A "destroyer of services" (ἀλεσίχαρις) is one by whose hand all services and benefits perish; and, as Seneca says:

units.la: Officia haurit perforato animo.
units.tr: He drains away services with a perforated mind.

units.la: MAXIMA pars morem hunc homines habent, quod sibi volunt, dum id impetrant, boni sunt: sed id ubi penes se habent, ex bonis pessimi, & fraudulentissimi fiunt. Capt. 2. 1. v. 36. Tales sententiæ complures sunt apud alios Authores.
units.tr: Most men have this habit: while they seek something, they are good; but once they have it in their power, they become from good the worst and most treacherous. Capt. 2. 1. v. 36. There are many similar sayings in other authors.

units.la: Terent. Phorm. 3.3. v. 5.
units.tr: Terence, Phormio, 3.3, v. 5.

units.la: Quin cum opus est, beneficium rursum ei experimur reddere?
units.tr: When we need something, do we again try to repay the kindness to him?

units.la: Proverb. Δὸς λαβεῖν, ἢ λαβεῖν, ἄμα δίδως ἢ λάμβανε.
units.tr: Proverb: Give in order to receive, or receive while giving. (Δὸς λαβεῖν, ἢ λαβεῖν, ἄμα δίδως ἢ λάμβανε.)

units.la: Seneca lib. 4. Benef. c. 16.
units.tr: Seneca, book 4 On Benefits, chapter 16.

units.la: Quid tam laudabile, quid tam æqualiter in omnium animos receptum, quàm referre benemeritis gratiam?
units.tr: What is so praiseworthy, what is so equally welcomed into the minds of all, as to return thanks to those who have deserved well?

units.la: Ambros. lib. 1. Offic. c. 31.
units.tr: Ambrose, book 1 On Duties, chapter 31.

units.la: Imitandanobis est natura terrarum, quæ semen multiplicatum solet numero reddere.
units.tr: We should imitate the nature of the earth, which is accustomed to return the seed multiplied in number.

units.la: At vulgò contrà fit. Catullus:
units.tr: But in common practice it is the opposite. Catullus:

units.la: Omnia sunt ingrata, nihil fecisse benignè est,
units.tr: Everything is ungrateful; to have done a kindness is worth nothing,

units.la: Pindarus: τὰ λαμπρὰ χάρεις ἐυδει, ἀμνάμονες δὲ βροτοί Imò & benefactorem lædere solent: quod ait Nazianzenus: πρὶν τι λαβεῖν, τίου- σιν, ἀταρ συγγνωσι λαβόντες. Sic refertur Friderico Duce Albano, qui in Senatu Caroli V. dixit: Naturam hominum ita comparatam esse, ut summa beneficia, non nisi ingentibus maleficiis compensit.
units.tr: Pindar: "Bright deeds the Graces love, but mortals are forgetful." (τὰ λαμπρὰ χάρεις ἐυδει, ἀμνάμονες δὲ βροτοί.) Indeed they are accustomed even to injure their benefactor; as Nazianzen says: "Before they receive something they honour you, but once they have received it they take no account of you." (πρὶν τι λαβεῖν, τίουσιν, ἀταρ συγγνῶσι λαβόντες.) So it is reported of Frederick, Duke of Alba, who said in the Senate of Charles V: that human nature is so constituted that it repays the greatest benefits with nothing but the greatest injuries.

units.la: In hanc sententiam vide alia apud Richter. Axiom. Polit. c. 46.
units.tr: On this sentiment see also what is said in Richter, Axiomata Politica, chapter 46.

units.la: Beneficium homini, pprium quod datur, proprium sumseris. Trin. 5 2. v. 6. Men. 4.2. v. 93.
units.tr: A benefit given to a man, if it is his own, you will take as your own. Trin. 5. 2. v. 6. Men. 4. 2. v. 93.

units.la: Malo bene facere tantundem est periculum, quantum bono male facere. Poen. 3.3. v. 20. Qui verò? A D. scies: Malo si quid benefacias, id beneficium interit: Bono si quid malefacias, at tamen expetit.
units.tr: To do good to a bad man is as great a risk as to do evil to a good man. Poen. 3. 3. v. 20. But how so? You will know from what follows: if you do good to a bad man, the benefit is lost; if you do wrong to a good man, yet still he seeks (what is due to him).

units.la: Beneficia requirunt gratam duo, ἐν. Sic ait ille Capt. 2.2. v. 85. Is uti tu me hic habueris, proinde illum still curaverit. Bene merenti bene profuerit, male merenti par erit.
units.tr: Benefits require two things: a grateful recipient. So that man says in Captivi 2. 2. v. 85: "As you have treated me here, so let him take care of you. To one who deserves well, do well; to one who deserves ill, it will be equal." (Is uti tu me hic habueris, proinde illum still curaverit. Bene merenti bene profuerit, male merenti par erit.)

units.la: Stultum est in cum beneficium conferre, qui id neq; intelligat, neq; referre sciat. Aulular. 2. 5. v. 11. Stultum & sine gratia est tibi recte facere, quando quod faciat, perit.
units.tr: It is foolish to confer a benefit on one who neither understands it nor knows how to repay it. Aulularia 2. 5. v. 11. "It is foolish and without thanks to do right by you, since what he does, perishes."

units.la: Quod bonis benefit beneficium, gratia ac gravida est bonis. Capt. 2.2. v.
units.tr: A benefit that is well given to good men is pleasing and weighty to good men. Captivi 2. 2. v.

units.la: 2.2. v.108. Hoc est, ut ipse sese interpretatur Perf. 4. 5. ver. 3. Si quid bonis boni fit, esse idem & grave & gratum solet.
units.tr: 2. 2. v. 108. That is, as he himself explains it, Persa 4. 5. v. 3: If some good comes to good men, it is usually both weighty and welcome.

units.la: GRATIA aliorum insolescere solemus. Moft. 4.2, v.9. Ferocem facit, quia te heros tam amat.
units.tr: We are accustomed to grow proud of the favour of others. Mostellaria 4. 2. v. 9: It makes him proud, because the hero loves you so much.

units.la: SÆPE beneficijs nostris inimicos nobis paramus. Trin. 4.3. v. 45. Vide Tit. Creditorum: Mutui.
units.tr: Often by our kindnesses we make enemies for ourselves. Trin. 4. 3. v. 45. See the title Creditors: Loan.

units.la: BENE si amico feceris, ne pigeat fecisse: at potius pudeat, si non feceris. Trin. 2. 2.v.66. Vide etiam Avaritia.
units.tr: If you have done a kindness to a friend, do not regret having done it; rather be ashamed if you have not done it. Trin. 2. 2. v. 66. See also Avarice.

units.la: MISERUM est ingratum esse homini; id cp facias bene. Ep. 1:2.v.33.
units.tr: It is wretched to be ungrateful to a man, even when you have done him a good turn. Ep. 1. 2. v. 33.

units.la: BENEFICIUM cito datum, bis datur. Unde ancilla Caf. 4.1. v.7. 4.1.v.7. Quin datis, si quid datis.
units.tr: A benefit given quickly is given twice. Hence the maid in Casina 4. 1. v. 7: Indeed you give, if you give anything.

units.la: SAT habet fautorum semper, qui recte facit. Amph.Prol. v.79.
units.tr: He who does right always has enough patrons. Amphitruo, Prolog. v. 79.

units.la: QUI bene volunt, bene visitant. Pœn. 1,2.v.160.
units.tr: Those who wish well visit well. Poenulus 1. 2. v. 160.

units.la: PARS hominum multò mavult gratiam inire à potentibus paucio- ribus, quàm pluribus, h.e. Reip. prodesse. Trin. 1,1. v.15.
units.tr: Many men much prefer to gain favour with a few powerful people rather than with many, that is, to be of use to the commonwealth. Trin. 1. 1. v. 15.

units.la: NEQUAM hominis gratia non est magnifacienda. Bacch. 3.6.v.29.
units.tr: The favour of a worthless man is not to be valued highly. Bacchides 3. 6. v. 29.

units.la: POI meo quidem animo ingrato homine nihil impensius est. Bacch. 3.2.v.11.12. Malefactorem amitti satius quàm relinqui beneficium. Nimiò præstat impendisum te, quàm ingratum dicer. Illum laudabunt boni: hunc etiam ipsi culpabunt mali. Vide etiam Orat. Cic. post red. ad Quirites.
units.tr: In my own opinion, nothing is more troublesome than an ungrateful man. Bacchides 3. 2. v. 11, 12. It is better to lose a wrongdoer than to abandon a benefit. It is far better to be called wasteful than ungrateful. The good will praise the one; even the bad will blame the other. See also Cicero's speech After his Return to the Quirites.

units.la: DE nostro liberales esse convenit. Trin. 2.2.v.47. Quem locum imitatur Terent. De tuo largitor, puer.
units.tr: It is fitting to be generous with what is your own. Trin. 2. 2. v. 47. Terence imitates this passage: Boy, be generous with your own.

units.la: BENE facere præstantius est, quàm bene velle. Trin. 2.4.v.34.
units.tr: Doing good is more excellent than merely wishing well. Trin. 2. 4. v. 34.

units.la: MALE mereri de immerente inscitia est. Curc. 1.3.v.29.
units.tr: To deserve ill from one who has not deserved it is folly. Curculio 1. 3. v. 29.

units.la: UT acerbum est! cp benefactis cùm mali messem metas. Ep. 5.1.v.52.
units.tr: How bitter it is when, after good deeds, you reap the harvest of evil! Ep. 5. 1. v. 52.

units.la: ADDECET benemerenti bene ferre gratiam. Rud. 5.3.v.36.
units.tr: It is fitting for one who deserves well to receive thanks well. Rud. 5. 3. v. 36.

units.la: A quo beneficiũ non accepimº, ejus facile obliviscimur. Cap. 5.3 v.8
units.tr: We easily forget the one from whom we have received no benefit. Cap. 5. 3 v. 8.

units.la: BONUS bonis benefacere solet. Pœn. 5.4.v.44.
units.tr: A good man is accustomed to do good to good men. Poen. 5. 4. v. 44.

units.la: NUMQUAM est alienis gravis: qui suis se concinnat leyem. Trin. 3.2.v.56. Vide etiam Hit. Amicitia.
units.tr: He is never burdensome to others who adapts himself to his own. Trin. 3. 2. v. 56. See also the title Friendship.

units.la: BONIS quod bene fit, haud perit. Rud. 4.3.v.2.
units.tr: What is well done for good men does not perish. Rud. 4. 3. v. 2.

units.la: PROMERENTI optimè, non debet pretium reddi ingratum. Asin. 1.2.v.2.
units.tr: To one who deserves the very best, a reward should not be returned ungratefully. Asinaria 1. 2. v. 2.

units.la: BONA bonis ferri æquum est. Ut mala, malis; ut qui mali sunt, habeant mala: qui boni, bona. Pseud.Prol. v.2.3.
units.tr: It is right that good things be brought to good men, as bad things to bad men; let those who are bad have bad things, and those who are good have good things. Pseud. Prol. v. 2. 3.

units.la: DE bonis bene-partis liberales esse convenit: ideò, quia à DEO sunt. Trin. 2.2.v.74.
units.tr: From good things well acquired it is fitting to be generous, because they come from God. Trin. 2. 2. v. 74.

units.la: Deum virtute habemus, & qui nosmet utamur, & alijs qui comitati fimus bene volentibus.
units.tr: We have God as our virtue, and we use it for ourselves, and for others who are our companions and well-wishers.

units.la: BIBLIOTHECAE.
units.tr: LIBRARIES.

units.la: Vide supra Tit. Artium.
units.tr: See above, under the title Arts.

units.la: BONORUM. POSSESSIONUM. PROPRIETATIS. HAEREDITATIS.
units.tr: GOODS, POSSESSIONS, PROPERTY, INHERITANCE.

units.la: Vide plura Tit. Divitiarum.
units.tr: See more under the title Riches.

units.la: PROBAM mulierem nihil peculij habere addecet. Quicquid autem domi partum habet, duabus vijs consequitur: aut habet à viro, aut ab adultero. Caf. 2.2.v.26.27.
units.tr: An honest wife ought to have no private property of her own. Whatever she has acquired at home comes to her by two routes: either she has it from her husband, or from her lover. Cas. 2.2.v.26.27.

units.la: Plutarch. lib. de audiendis Poëtis:
units.tr: Plutarch, book on how young people should listen to poets:

units.la: Poliagrus est felix, calestem qui domi parantem alit capram.
units.tr: Happy is Poliagrus, who keeps at home a heavenly goat that bears.

units.la: Pomponius J C. lib. s. ad Q. Mutium:
units.tr: Pomponius the jurist, book 5 on Quintus Mucius:

units.la: Q. Mutius ait, cum in controversiam venit, unde ad mulierem quid pervenerit: & verum & honestius est, quod non demonstratur, unde habeas, existimari à viro, aut qui in potestate ejus esset, ad eam pervenisse. Evitandi autem turpis quaestus gratia circa uxorem videtur hoc Q. Mutius probasse.
units.tr: Quintus Mucius says that when it comes into dispute how something came to a wife, it is both true and more honourable that, where one cannot show where you got it, it be presumed to have come to her from her husband, or from someone under his power. Quintus Mucius seems to have approved this for the sake of avoiding shameful gain, in regard to a wife.

units.la: Vide Scip. Gentil. Parergalib.1.cap.19.
units.tr: See Scipio Gentilis, Parerga, book 1, chapter 19.

units.la: Bona propria sibi vendicabant hac formula: Hoc meum esse scio. Rud. 4.3. v. 86. Vide Briss. Form. lib. 5. pag. 374. Edit. Wech. in quarto.
units.tr: Goods that were one's own they claimed by this formula: I know this is mine. Rud. 4.3. v. 86. See Brisson, Formulae, book 5, p. 374, edition of Wechel, in quarto.

units.la: Propria dicebantur ea bona, quæ semper tenere licet. Trin. 5.2. v. 6. Vide Albericum Gentil. lib. 3. cap. 16. de jure belli.
units.tr: Those goods were called one's own which one may always hold. Trin. 5.2. v. 6. See Albericus Gentilis, book 3, chapter 16, on the law of war.

units.la: Quæ in manu nostra sunt, de ijs agere pro lubitu possumus. Merc. 2.3. v. 117.
units.tr: Those things which are in our hand, we may deal with at our pleasure. Merc. 2.3. v. 117.

units.la: Male partum male disperit. Pœn. 4.2. v. 22. Imitatus est Sallust. Male parta, male dilabuntur.
units.tr: What is badly gotten is badly lost. Poen. 4.2. v. 22. Sallust imitated this: Things badly gotten are badly dissipated.

units.la: Quod quis in publico accepit, & quasi casu invenit: id proprium est. Rud. 4.3. v. 33. & 4.4. v. 27.
units.tr: What someone has received in public, and as it were found by chance, is his own. Rud. 4.3. v. 33. and 4.4. v. 27.

units.la: Qui solvendo non erant, cedebant bonis jure Prætorio. Curc. 5.3. v. 44. Vide etiam Tit. Judiciorum : Prætoris : Solutionis.
units.tr: Those who were not able to pay used to surrender their goods by praetorian law. Curc. 5.3. v. 44. See also the title Judgments: Praetor: Payment of Debts.

units.la: C.
units.tr: C.

units.la: CALUMNIÆ. CONTUMELIÆ. INIURIÆ. OFFENSIONUM. CONVITIORUM. BACCHARUM. CONTEMTUS. CRIMINATIONIS. MALEDICTORUM. MALEDICENTIAE. SCURRARUM.
units.tr: SLANDERS. INSULTS. INJURIES. OFFENCES. REPROACHES. BACCHANTES. CONTEMPT. ACCUSATIONS. ABUSIVE WORDS. SLANDER. BUFFOONS.

units.la: ONVITIIS non semper respondendum : Quiæ Bacchæ bacchanti si velis adversarier, Exinsanâ facies insaniorem : fericet sæpius. Amph. 2.2. v.71. Hoc enim effet, quod in proverb.dicitur Irritare crabrones. Ibid. v.75. Suidas ait: Oblipidem excitare.
units.tr: Reproaches need not always be answered, for if you want to oppose a raving Bacchant, a madman becomes more insane; this happens quite often. Indeed, this would be what the proverb calls "to stir up hornets." Ibid. v. 75. Suidas says: "to rouse a wasp's nest."

units.la: T u contumeliam alteri facias? tibi non dicatur? Asin. 2.4. ver.82. Pseud. 4.7.v.77. Contumeliam si dicis, audies. Mostell. 4. 2. v.15. Tibi temperem : cum tu mihi nequeas?
units.tr: Do you insult another and expect no insult back? Asin. 2.4 v. 82. Pseud. 4.7 v. 77. If you speak an insult, you will hear one. Mostell. 4.2 v. 15. Should I spare you, when you cannot spare me?

units.la: Qui enim prior maledicit, tantundem audire debet. Perf. 2. 4. ver. 8. Maledicis majori. P. Prior promeritus perpetiare. Servam operam, linguam liberam herus meus me jussit habere. Ergo interdum re maledicere civile et fas est: uti de jurgio quodam Senatotis pronunciavit Vespasianus apud Suetonium c,9.
units.tr: For whoever abuses first ought to hear as much in return. Perf. 2.4 v. 8. "You abuse your superior." "P." "You earned it first, so bear it. My master ordered me to keep my tongue free while I do my slave's work." Therefore at times to revile in return is both proper and lawful, as Vespasian pronounced about a certain quarrel of senators, in Suetonius, ch. 9.

units.la: Terent. Phorm.
units.tr: Terence, Phormio.

units.la: Benedictus si certasset, audisset bene.
units.tr: Had Benedictus engaged in a contest, he would have heard good words.

units.la: Idem :
units.tr: The same author:

units.la: Si mihi pergit, quæ vult dicere, quæ non vult, audiet.
units.tr: If he goes on saying what he wishes, he will hear what he does not wish.

units.la: Euripides : ——ἐπεὶ τὰ μὴ κηλὰ φράσαειν ἐτόιμας, ταῦδι ἢ τὰ μὴ φίλα.
units.tr: Euripides: "Since you are ready to say things that are not pleasing, these or things not dear." [ἐπεὶ τὰ μὴ κηλὰ φράσαειν ἐτόιμας, ταῦδι ἢ τὰ μὴ φίλα.]

units.la: Homini amico decet potius bene dicere, q; male. Trin. 4.2.v.79.
units.tr: It befits a friend to speak well of a man rather than ill. Trin. 4.2 v. 79.

units.la: Nefas grande maledicere amico absenti. Trin.4.2. v. 81. Horat. Absen.
units.tr: It is a great wrong to speak ill of an absent friend. Trin. 4.2 v. 81. Horace, Satires:

units.la: *.-- Absentem qui rodit amicum,
units.tr: *"Whoever gnaws at an absent friend,

units.la: Hic niger est, hunc tu Romane caveto.
units.tr: he is black; you, Roman, beware of him."

units.la: Contumeliæ in ætatem puerilem excusantur. Perf. 2. 4. v. 5. Scio ego, quid ætatis sim: eò istuc maledictum impune auferes.
units.tr: Insults aimed at a child's age are excused. Perf. 2.4 v. 5: "I know how old I am; you will get away with that insult unpunished."

units.la: Convitium in servos erat Venefice, Vlmitriba, Cucule, Morticine. Perf. 2. 4. v. 7.
units.tr: Abuse hurled at slaves was: "Poisoner! Elm-thrasher! Hood! Carrion!" Perf. 2.4 v. 7.

units.la: Remedium petebant, & medicinam ad perferendas calumnias aliorum. Men. 5. 1. v. 42. Si scis monstra, quid bibam, Tuam qui possim perpeti petulantiam?
units.tr: They sought a remedy and medicine for enduring the slanders of others. Men. 5.1 v. 42: "If you know monsters, what should I drink? Who could endure your impudence?"

units.la: Calumniatores quidvis fingere solent. Men. 5. 5. v. 38. At ego te sacram Coronam surripuisse scio. Et ob eam rem in carcerem ted esse compactum scio. Tum patrem occidisse, & matrem vendidisse etiam scio. Similis locus est Trin. 1. 2. v. 47.
units.tr: Slanderers are wont to invent anything. Men. 5.5 v. 38: "But I know you stole the sacred crown, and I know you were thrown into prison for it; then I know you killed your father and sold your mother." A similar passage is Trin. 1.2 v. 47.

units.la: Insanit hic equidem, qui ipse maledicit sibi. Men. 2. 2. v. 3 5. 40.
units.tr: He is surely mad who curses himself. Men. 2.2 v. 35, 40.

units.la: Isthic est thesaurus stultis in lingua situs, ut quæstui habeant, male loqui melioribus. Pœn. 3. 3, v. 12. Vide Cæl. Rhod. lib. 15. Antiq. Lect. cap. 2 5.
units.tr: There is in the tongue of fools a treasure laid up for their profit: to speak ill of better men. Poen. 3.3 v. 12. See Caelius Rhodiginus, book 15, Antiquarian Lectures, ch. 25.

units.la: Ut ut calumniatores virus suum in nos evomant: innocentiæ conscientia præsto esse debet. Trin. 1. 2. v. 67. Est atq; non est mihi in manu, quin dicant, non est: merito ut ne dicant, id est.
units.tr: Although slanderers spew their poison upon us, consciousness of innocence ought to be at hand. Trin. 1.2 v. 67: "It is and it is not in my power to stop them saying it is not; so let them not say it, that is."

units.la: In hominum effeminatum & mollem, jaciebantur mira nomi na qualia vide Pœn. 5. 5. v. 25. & aliquot seqq.
units.tr: Against an effeminate and soft man, wonderful names were hurled; see Poen. 5.5 v. 25 and several following.

units.la: Qui alterum incusat probri, eum ipsum se intueri oportet. Truc. 1. 2. v. 57.
units.tr: One who accuses another of a fault ought to look at himself. Truc. 1.2 v. 57.

units.la: Cicero: Carere enim vitio debet, qui in alterum paratus est dicere.
units.tr: Cicero: "For he who is ready to speak against another ought himself to be free of fault."

units.la: Vanissimum hominum genus, Scurræ: Calumniatores: qui & curiosi: omnia se simulant scire, nec quicquam sciunt. Trinum. 1. 2. v. 162.
units.tr: The most vain kind of men are buffoons and slanderers, who are also busybodies; they pretend to know everything and know nothing. Trin. 1.2 v. 162.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Curiositatis.
units.tr: See also the title on Curiosity.

units.la: Sæpe ab eo convitijs excipimur, cui benedixi mus. Rud. 3. 2. v. 25.
units.tr: We are often met with insults from those to whom we have spoken well. Rud. 3.2 v. 25.

units.la: CALUMNIATORES non solent respicere se, cùm dicunt injustè alteri. Pseud. 2.2. v.18.
units.tr: Slanderers are not accustomed to look at themselves when they wrongly speak against another. Pseud. 2.2 v. 18.

units.la: INDIGNIS si malè dicitur, maledictum id esse dico. Verùm si dignis dicitur, benedictum est, meo quidem animo. Curc. 4. 2. v. 27.
units.tr: If ill is said to the unworthy, I call it a curse. But if it is said to the worthy, it is a blessing, at least in my opinion. Curc. 4.2 v. 27.

units.la: IN servos dictum herile convitium: Perjurij caput. Pseud. 1.1.v.120. & 1.2.v.1.
units.tr: Against slaves, the master's abuse: "Arch-perjurer!" Pseud. 1.1 v. 120 and 1.2 v. 1.

units.la: CALUMNIAS devitare non possumus :: modò præter nostrum meritum sint. Stich. 1.2.v. 58.
units.tr: We cannot avoid slanders, provided they are undeserved by us. Stich. 1.2 v. 58.

units.la: IN servos μάσιγας jaciebatur hoc convitium: Gymnasium flagri. Asi. 2.2. v.31. Item Cistos carceris ibid. Item Catenarum colonus. Et Virgarum lascivia Ibid.
units.tr: Against slaves this abuse was hurled, in Greek [μάσιγας] whips: "Gymnasium of the lash!" Asin. 2.2 v. 31. Likewise "jailers of the prison," ibid. Likewise "colonist of chains." And "wantonness of the rods," ibid.

units.la: Vide Calligraphiam Linguæ Latinæ Tit. Calumnia.
units.tr: See the Calligraphy of the Latin Tongue, title "Calumnia."

units.la: ETIAM suspicionem oportet adimere calumniatoribus. Ibi. Trin. 1.2.v. 470.
units.tr: One must also remove suspicion from slanderers. Trin. 1.2 v. 470.

units.la: MALA res frequenter pro dictis datur malis. Men. 3.2.v.31.
units.tr: A bad thing is often given in return for bad words. Men. 3.2 v. 31.

units.la: MALEDICTA ad lacrimas cogunt. Bacch. 4.9 v.17.
units.tr: Curses drive people to tears. Bacch. 4.9 v. 17.

units.la: IN cinædos hoc convitium conijcebatur: Cinæde calamistrate. Asin. 3.3. v.37.
units.tr: Against the effeminate this abuse was thrown: "Curl-haired catamite!" Asin. 3.3 v. 37.

units.la: IN forum & comitium trahebantur: qui convitijs alios lacerarent. Curc. 3.1.v.31.
units.tr: Those who tore others apart with abuse were dragged into the forum and the assembly. Curc. 3.1 v. 31.

units.la: CONVITIA improbi laudes suas censent. Pseud. 1.3. v.125 & sequentib.
units.tr: Reproaches: the wicked count their own praises. Pseud. 1.3 v. 125 and following.

units.la: Vide etiam Terent. Adelph. 2.1. & Aristophanem in Nubibus.
units.tr: See also Terence, Adelphi 2.1, and Aristophanes in the Clouds.

units.la: CONTEMNI & irrideri ab anu contumeliosum ducitur viro. Cist. 4 1. v.11.
units.tr: To be despised and mocked by an old woman is considered an insult to a man. Cist. 4.1 v. 11.

units.la: PESSIMUM est facinus, nequiter ferire malam maledicis. Amph. 1.1.v.158.
units.tr: It is a dreadful deed to strike with a wicked hand the one who slanders with a foul mouth. Amph. 1.1 v. 158.

units.la: CRIMINANTIBUS alios non temerè fides est adhibenda. Bacch. 4.3 v.15.
units.tr: One should not lightly give credence to those who accuse others. Bacch. 4.3 v. 15.

units.la: CALUMNIATORES furiosi : ut sacerdotes Isidis Deæ, qui in furofurore tympano usi. Poen. 5. 5. v. 38.
units.tr: Slanderers are frenzied, like the priests of the goddess Isis, who in their madness used the drum. Poen. 5.5 v. 38.

units.la: Contumeliae summae loco ducitur, si lotio perfundantur a-lij: quod est πλωΐς & frigida suffundi. Cist. 1. 1. v. 37.
units.tr: It is regarded as the greatest insult if others are drenched with urine, which is called [πλωΐς] in Greek, and cold water is poured over one. Cist. 1.1 v. 37.

units.la: Mali sunt homines, qui bonis dicunt male. Bacch. 1. 2. v. 10.
units.tr: Bad are the men who speak ill of good men. Bacch. 1.2 v. 10.

units.la: Quando ea dicuntur, quae vera sunt, calumniae crimen non habetur. Pers. 2. 2. v. 25.
units.tr: When things that are true are said, there is no charge of slander. Pers. 2.2 v. 25.

units.la: Mitte male loqui. P. Cum ut dignae es, dico: bene non male loquor.
units.tr: "Stop speaking ill." "P." "Since you are worthy, I say so: I speak well, not ill."

units.la: Contumeliosa verba etiam laedunt famam nostram: & aegrè faciunt. Truc. 2. 2. v. 10.
units.tr: Insulting words also harm our reputation and cause us pain. Truc. 2.2 v. 10.

units.la: CANITIEI. CAPILLORUM.
units.tr: GREYNESS OF HAIR.

units.la: Vide etiam Senectutis: Hominis: & Cultus.
units.tr: See also Old Age: of Man: and Adornment.

units.la: Calamistros alere cinaedorum erat. Asin. 3. 3. v. 37. Canities parentum debet liberis esse stimulus ad virtutes. Asin. 3. 1. v. 35.
units.tr: To keep curling irons in one's hair was the mark of effeminate men. Asin. 3. 3. v. 37. The grey hair of parents ought to be a spur to children towards virtue. Asin. 3. 1. v. 35.

units.la: Cantus. Musices. Tibicinum.
units.tr: Song. Music. Flute-players.

units.la: TIBIAE in Phrygia inventae. Inde tibicinae Phrygiae. Aul. 2. 5. v. 7.
units.tr: The FLUTE was invented in Phrygia. Hence Phrygian flute-girls. Aul. 2. 5. v. 7.

units.la: Tibull.
units.tr: Tibull.

units.la: nam turba jocosa obstrepit, & Phrygio tibia curva sono.
units.tr: for the merry crowd makes a din, and the curved flute sounds with a Phrygian tune.

units.la: TIBICINES, quia sacrificiis frequenter adhibiti, pingues fiebant. Aul. 2.5.v.6. Hinc Virgil. l.2.Georg.v.193.
units.tr: FLUTE-PLAYERS, because they were often employed at sacrifices, grew fat. Aul. 2.5.v.6. Hence Virgil, Georg. 2.193.

units.la: Inflavit cum pinguis ebur Tyrrhenus ad aras.
units.tr: When the Tyrrhenian player blew the full-toned ivory at the altars.

units.la: Vide ibi Servium & Philarg.
units.tr: See there Servius and Philargyrius.

units.la: TIBICINES si destituat anhelitus, ægrè tibias inflant. Quemadmodum jocatur Charin, ex nimio cursu vix suspirium trahens. Merc. l. 2. v.15.
units.tr: If the flute-players' breath fails them, they blow their pipes with difficulty, as Charinus jokes, drawing a gasp scarcely at all after running too hard. Merc. l. 2. v.15.

units.la: CANTU nocturno solebant se senes recreare apud concubinas. Stich. 4.1. v. 66.
units.tr: Old men were accustomed to refresh themselves with a song at night among their mistresses. Stich. 4.1. v. 66.

units.la: CANTIONES novae laudantur præ veteribus. Stich. 5. 5. v. 27.
units.tr: New songs are praised above the old. Stich. 5. 5. v. 27.

units.la: Pindarus Olymp. Od. 9.
units.tr: Pindar, Olympian Ode 9.

units.la: ---- αἱνει δὲ παλαιὸν μῆλοινον ἀνθεα δὲ ὑμνων νεωτέρων.
units.tr: He praises the old apple-song, but the flowers of newer hymns [αἰνεῖ δὲ παλαιὸν μῆλον, ἄνθεα δὲ ὕμνων νεωτέρων].

units.la: CAPTIVITATIS. EXILII. VINCULORUM. CARCERIS.
units.tr: CAPTIVITY. EXILE. CHAINS. PRISON.

units.la: Vide Tit. Suppliciorum.
units.tr: See the title Punishments.

units.la: QUI in vinculis sunt, rei causam dicere nequeunt: quia vincti dentur praedemnati. Truc. 4.3.v.63.
units.tr: Those who are in chains cannot plead their case, because the bound are handed over as already condemned. Truc. 4.3.v.63.

units.la: Vide Tit. Judicij plura.
units.tr: See the title Judgment, for more.

units.la: Qui sunt capti, aut exules patriae, perierunt. Capt. 3.4.v. 5.
units.tr: Those who have been captured, or who are exiles from their country, have perished. Capt. 3.4.v.5.

units.la: SERVI compingebantur in nervos, & arcas e robore factas poenae causa: itemque in catulos ferreos: & pila catapultaria. Curc. 5.3. v.11.12.13.42.45.
units.tr: Slaves were fastened in stocks and in chests made of oak, for punishment, and likewise in iron catuli (fetters) and catapult balls. Curc. 5.3.v.11.12.13.42.45.

units.la: CARBONUM.
units.tr: COALS.

units.la: Vide Tit. Artificum.
units.tr: See the title Artisans.

units.la: CARBONES vivi etiam ex aqua aridi exeunt. Rud. 2, 6. v. 50.
units.tr: Live coals come out dry even from water. Rud. 2.6.v.50.

units.la: CARNIS.
units.tr: FLESH.

units.la: CARNES suillae in delitijs olim praesertim die Natali. Pseud. 2. v.33. Men. 1.3. v.26. Mil. 2.6. v.104. Nimirum dapsilis est caro, & valde tenera, & hoc animal ad pastum natum; cui anima pro sale est, neputisset, ut Chrysippus ajebat teste Cicerone lib.2. de Nat.Deor. Vide Plutarch.lib.4.Sympos. Quaest.ult. Cur Judaei a carne Suilla abstineant. Vide etiam Tit. Ciborum.
units.tr: Pork was a delicacy in former times, especially on birthdays. Pseud. 2.v.33. Men. 1.3.v.26. Mil. 2.6.v.104. Indeed the flesh is rich and very tender, and this animal is born for food; its soul serves it as salt, so that it would not rot, as Chrysippus said, according to Cicero, book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods. See Plutarch, Table Talk book 4, last question, on why the Jews abstain from pork. See also the title Food.

units.la: APRUGNA caro callum obducit. Pers. 2.5.v.4. Poen. 3.2.v.2. Callum aprugnum callere aequè non sinam. Vide Lexicon Plautin. Callum.
units.tr: Boar's flesh grows a callus. Pers. 2.5.v.4. Poen. 3.2.v.2. "I will not allow the boar's callus to harden equally." See the Lexicon Plautinum, under Callum.

units.la: CENSIONIS. CIVIUM-ROMANORUM. QUIRITUM, LUSTRATIONUM.
units.tr: CENSUS; ROMAN CITIZENS; QUIRITES; LUSTRATIONS

units.la: Vide etiam Urbis: Civitatis.
units.tr: See also City: Citizenship.

units.la: Quinto anno lustrabantur cives Romani. Quorsum noster allusit. Capt. Prol. v.15.
units.tr: The Roman citizens were purified (lustrated) every fifth year. To this our author alludes: Captivi, Prologue, v. 15.

units.la: Vos qui ope vestra potestis censerier.
units.tr: You who by your help are able to be enrolled in the census.

units.la: CINERUM.
units.tr: OF ASHES.

units.la: Cinere eluebant vasa, quò allusit Mil. 4.2. v.10.
units.tr: They used to wash dishes with ashes, to which he alludes in Mil. 4.2. v.10.

units.la: CLAUDICATIONIS.
units.tr: LIMPING.

units.la: Claudi cum fuste incedere solent. Asin. 2.4. v.21.
units.tr: Lame men are accustomed to walk with a stick. Asin. 2.4. v.21.

units.la: CLIENTELÆ. PATROCINII. CLIENTUM. PATRONORUM.
units.tr: Clientela. Patronage. Clients. Patrons.

units.la: Clientes patronis suis in æde sacrâ convivium parabant: quod vocabant Cœnam popularem. Trin. 2.4. v.67. Vide Tit. Convivÿ.
units.tr: Clients used to prepare a banquet for their patrons in a sacred temple, which they called a popular dinner (cœna popularis). Plautus, Trinummus, act 2, scene 4, line 67. See the title "Convivium."

units.la: Patronos appellabant, quorū beneficijs utebantur. Mil. 3.3. v.41.
units.tr: They called patrons those whose benefits they enjoyed. Plautus, Miles gloriosus, act 3, scene 3, line 41.

units.la: Coloniæ.
units.tr: Colonies.

units.la: Vide etiam Urbis: Civitatis: Civium.
units.tr: See also City: State: Citizens.

units.la: QUI apud Romanos educendi erant in coloniam aliquam, in eam nomen dabant. Asin. 2. 2. v. O catenarum colone!
units.tr: Those who were to be led out among the Romans to some colony gave their name for it. Asin. 2. 2. v. O colonist of the chains!

units.la: Et Pseud. 4. 6. v. 38.
units.tr: And Pseud. 4. 6. v. 38.

units.la: Quid ego cesso Pseudolum facere, ut det nomen ad molarum coloniam.
units.tr: Why do I delay in having Pseudolus act, so that he may give his name to the colony of the millstones?

units.la: Vide etiam Parerga Scip. Gentil. lib. 1. cap. 35.
units.tr: See also Parerga Scip. Gentil. lib. 1, cap. 35.

units.la: Colorum.
units.tr: Of Colours.

units.la: COLOR alius purpureus, alius puniceus, alius luteus. Men. 5. 5. v. 19.
units.tr: One colour is purple, another is scarlet-red, another is yellow. Men. 5. 5. v. 19.

units.la: Subvolturius & subaquilus color: subniger est. Rud. 2. 4. ver. 9.
units.tr: A colour that is somewhat dark-brown and somewhat black, eagle-coloured. Rud. 2. 4. ver. 9.

units.la: COLOR aquilus est color fuscus, & subniger: ab aquâ, cujus color neq; albus, neq; niger, sed incertus, vel etiam nigrior. Poen. 5. 2. v. 152. Unde Aquily prænomen. Glossæ: Aquilum: μίλαν ὡς λευκίλιος.
units.tr: The colour aquilus is a dusky colour, and somewhat black; it is named from aqua (water), whose colour is neither white nor black, but indistinct, or even darker. Poen. 5. 2. v. 152. Hence the forename Aquilius. The glosses: Aquilum: dark, like the Leucilii.

units.la: Varro:
units.tr: Varro:

units.la: Atque Ægeus fluctum quam lavit ante aquilo,
units.tr: And Aegeus, which the eagle-coloured wave washes before it,

units.la: Sævus ubi posuit Neptuni filius urbem.
units.tr: Where the cruel son of Neptune founded the city.

units.la: Vide etiam Scalig. Notis ad Festum Pompejum.
units.tr: See also Scaliger, in his notes to Festus Pompeius.

units.la: COLOR niger comparatur Ægyptijs & Mauris hominibus: moris: seu merulis avibus. Poen. 5. 5. v. 10.
units.tr: The colour black is compared to Egyptians and Moors, or to blackbirds. Poen. 5. 5. v. 10.

units.la: COLOR balius est color tritici. Poen. 5. 5. v. 22.
units.tr: The colour balius is the colour of wheat. Poen. 5. 5. v. 22.

units.la: Color nauticus sive thalassicus, fluctibus marinis similis: qui & Venetus dicebatur: nautarum erat. Mil. 4. 4. v. 42.
units.tr: The nautical or sea colour, like the waves of the sea, which was also called Venetus, belonged to sailors. Mil. 4. 4. v. 42.

units.la: Creta sordes vestium extergebantur. Aul. 4. 9. v. 7.Vide Plin. lib. 35. v. 15. 17. Turn. l. 24. c. 23.
units.tr: With chalk (creta) the dirt of garments was wiped away. Aul. 4. 9. v. 7. See Plin. lib. 35, cc. 15, 17; Turn. l. 24, c. 23.

units.la: Color puniceus niger est. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 92.
units.tr: The colour puniceus is black. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 92.

units.la: Cras phaenicia corio invises pergulam.Rud. 4. 3. v. 59.
units.tr: Tomorrow you will make the porch hateful with Phoenician leather. Rud. 4. 3. v. 59.

units.la: Sunt aliy puniceo corio, magni item atq; alij.
units.tr: There are some with purple leather, great and likewise others.

units.la: COMITATUS.
units.tr: Escort.

units.la: MULIERES, matres-familias, virgines sine comite foras prodire impudicum erat. Amph. 3. 2. v. 48.Vide Tit. Pudicitia.
units.tr: For women, matrons and maidens, to go out of doors without an escort was shameless. Amph. 3. 2. v. 48. See the title Chastity.

units.la: COMITIORUM. JUDICII. ACCUSATIONIS. REORUM.
units.tr: ASSEMBLIES. JUDGMENT. ACCUSATION. DEFENDANTS.

units.la: IN forum & comitium vocabantur: qui couvitijs alios incessebant. Curc. 3. 1. v. 31.
units.tr: They were summoned into the forum and the comitium, those who assailed others with abuse. Curc. 3. 1. v. 31.

units.la: IN Comitijs agebatur de salute populi Rom. Aul. 4. 7. v. 19. ἀλληγο-εικῶς.Ibo intro, ubi de capite meo sunt comitia.Vide Ravard. c. 16. Protrib. & Nicol. Grucchium de Comitijs.
units.tr: In the assemblies the safety of the Roman people was debated. Aul. 4. 7. v. 19. Allegorically: Ibo intro, ubi de capite meo sunt comitia. See Ravard, c. 16, Protrib., and Nicolaus Grucchius, de Comitiis.

units.la: POSTQUAM praeco supremam dixerat, dimittebatur judicum consessus. Quo referendum censeo illud Plauti Asin. 3. 3. v. 4. Mater mihi mihi supremam dixit. Sed rectius forte refertur ad extremum. Vale in funeribus vide Tit. Funerum, & locum Turnebi.
units.tr: After the herald had pronounced the final words, the assembly of judges was dismissed. I think this is the place for that line of Plautus, Asin. 3. 3. v. 4: Mater mihi mihi supremam dixit. But it perhaps refers more rightly to extremum. Vale ("the last farewell"). For Vale at funerals, see the title Funerum and the passage in Turnebus.

units.la: In Comitijs ubi jus dicebatur, erant litigiosi. Curc. 4. 1. v. 9. Eò vocati quoq; homines perjuri; qui dicti Comitiales. Poen. 3. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: In the assemblies, where the law was declared, there were litigants. Curc. 4. 1. v. 9. Men who were perjured were also summoned there, and were called Comitiales. Poen. 3. 2. v. 7.

units.la: Rei in Comitijs cùm populum supplices Obsecraverant, ut eo periculo liberarentur, continuò Resecrare cogebantur à magistratu. Perf. 1. 1. v. 49.
units.tr: When defendants had entreated the people in the assemblies, begging to be freed from that danger, they were at once compelled by the magistrate to make the supplication again. Perf. 1. 1. v. 49.

units.la: Vide Tit. Obsecrationum.
units.tr: See the title Obsecrationum.

units.la: Comitia centuriata alia erant: Curiata; & Tributa. Aul. 4. 7. v. 12. De capite meo erunt comitia. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 131. Truc. 4. 3. v. 45. Vide Tractatum Nicolai Grucchij de Comitijs.
units.tr: There were other kinds of assemblies: the Curiata and the Tributa. Aul. 4. 7. v. 12: De capite meo erunt comitia. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 131. Truc. 4. 3. v. 45. See the treatise of Nicolaus Grucchius on the assemblies.

units.la: Conditionis. Gentis. Fortunæ. Vocationis. Status.
units.tr: Condition. Family. Fortune. Calling. Status.

units.la: Quisque suæ vocationis memor esse debet. Unde recte reprehenditur servus Plautinus Mil. 2. 6. v. 1.
units.tr: Everyone ought to remember his own calling. Hence the slave in Plautus is rightly rebuked, Mil. 2. 6. v. 1.

units.la: Satin' abiit ille, neque herile negotium Plus curat, quasi non servitute serviat?
units.tr: Has he really gone off, and cares no more for his master's business, as if he were not serving in slavery at all?

units.la: Qui ejusdem sunt conditionis, non debent insolescere. Perf. 3. 3. v. 24.
units.tr: Those of the same condition ought not to grow insolent. Perf. 3. 3. v. 24.

units.la: Qui ejusdem sunt conditionis & fortis, non possunt fortunam objicere alijs. Sic servus ille defendit contra meretriculam. Poen. 1. 2. v. 59. Tunc audes etiam servos[?] pernere? Propudium, quasi bella sit, quasi eampse Reges duclitent.
units.tr: Those of the same condition, and of the same spirit, cannot throw their fortune in the face of others. So that slave defends himself against the little courtesan. Poen. 1. 2. v. 59: "Do you dare, then, to pester even slaves? Shameful, as if it were a war, as if they were to lead off the very queens themselves."

units.la: Coniugii, Nuptiarum, Matrimonii, Sponsaliorum, Polygamiæ, Repudii, Divortii, Liberorum, Dotis, Connubii, Generationis, Nativitatis, Vxorum, Matris-familias, Viduitatis, Mulierum, Maritorum.
units.tr: Marriage, Nuptials, Matrimony, Betrothal, Polygamy, Repudiation, Divorce, Children, Dowry, Wedlock, Generation, Birth, Wives, Mother of the Family, Widowhood, Women, Husbands.

units.la: Vide etiam Titulo Nuptiarum.
units.tr: See also under the title Nuptiarum.

units.la: IN contrahendis matrimonijs voto utebantur, QUÆ RES BENEVORTAT! Trin. 2.4.v.100.
units.tr: In contracting marriages they used a vow: "WHAT A THING TO BRING GOOD FORTUNE!" Trin. 2.4 v.100.

units.la: In contrahendo matrimonio ratio quoque habenda similitudinis cõditionis: ne dispares conjungantur. Quod sensit Euclio senex Aul. 2.2. v.52. In mentem venit, te bovem esse, h. e. divitem: me asellum; hoc est, pauperem. Vbi tecum conjunctus fiem: Vbi onus nequeam ferre pariter, jaceam ego asinus in luto, &c. Vide integrum locum, ubi ἀλληγοεικῶς egregiè de hac re disserit. Similes sententias invenies apud Siraciden cap.13. & inibi Camerarium, nec non Drufium: & Lex. Conditio.
units.tr: In contracting marriage, account must also be taken of likeness of condition, so that unequals are not yoked together. Euclio the old man understood this, Aul. 2.2 v.52: "It came into my mind that you are an ox," that is, rich, "and I an ass," that is, poor. "Where I shall be joined with you; where I cannot bear the burden equally, I, an ass, shall lie in the mud," and so on. See the whole passage, where he discusses this matter excellently in allegory [ἀλληγορικῶς]. You will find similar sayings in Sirach ch. 13, and there Camerarius, and also Drusius; and the lexicon under Conditio.

units.la: Tribus modis uxor habebatur: Vsu: farre: Coëmtione. Confarratio tamen solis Pontificibus conveniebat. Minimum vero vinculi habuit illud matrimonium, quod usu tantum erat. Inde uxor Jovis Alcumena dicitur Vsuraria. Amph. Arg. 1.v.3. Vide Lex. Vsuraria. & Calligraphiam: Scortandi. Itemque J.Ctos B. Brissonium & Fr. Hottomannum de ritu Nuptiarum: nec non J. Lipsium ad 1 v. Annal. Taciti. Neque enim mei est instituti omnia huc congerere, quæ in rem sunt. Plauto soli servire cupio.
units.tr: A wife was held in three ways: by use, by spelt cake [farre], and by purchase [coemtione]. Confarreation, however, belonged only to the Pontiffs. The marriage that was merely by use had the least bond. Hence Jupiter's wife Alcmena is called usuraria (Amph. Arg. 1 v.3). See the lexicon under Vsuraria and under Calligraphiam and Scortandi; likewise the jurists B. Brisson and F. Hotman on the rite of marriage, and J. Lipsius on the first verse of Tacitus's Annals. For it is not my purpose to heap together here everything that bears on the matter. "I wish to serve Plautus alone."

units.la: Coniugum omnia sunt communia: inprimis vero liberi. Amph. 1.3.v.1.
units.tr: Everything between spouses is held in common, above all the children. Amph. 1.3 v.1.

units.la: Uxor dotata marito exprobrare solet dotem. Merc. 4. 3. ver. 3.
units.tr: A wife who has brought a dowry is wont to reproach her husband with it. Merc. 4.3 v.3.

units.la: Hem! cui decem talenta dotis detuli.
units.tr: "Hem! For whom I brought ten talents of dowry!"

units.la: Procreare liberos lepidum est onus. Mil. 3.1.v.87.
units.tr: Rearing children is a charming burden. Mil. 3.1 v.87.

units.la: Deum virtute, inquit senex, mihi propter divitias measLicuit uxorem dotatam genere summo ducere.Sed nolo mihi oblatratricem in aedes intromittere. Ibid.
units.tr: "By heaven," says the old man, "because of my riches I could have taken a wife with a dowry, of the highest birth. But I do not want a barking woman brought into my house." Ibid.

units.la: Bona uxor, si ea quidem deducta est usquam gentium,Ubi eam possim invenire? verum egone eam ducam domum?Quae mihi numquam hoc dicat; eme, mi vir, lanam, unde tibi palliumMalacum, & calidum conficiatur, tunicaeque hybernae bonae,Ne algeas hac hyeme, hoc numquam ex uxore audias.Verum priusquam galli cantent, quae me somno suscitet,Dicat: Da, mi vir, Kalendis mecam, quod matrem juverit,Da, qui faciat, condiatque; da, quod dem quinquatribusPraecantatrici, conjectrici, ariolae, atq; haruspicae.Flagitium est, si nihil mittetur, quo supercilio spicit!Tum patritam clementer non potest, quin munerem.Jam pridem quia nihil abstulerit, succensset geraria.Tum obstetrix expostulavit mecum, parum missum sibi.Quid? nutrici non missurus quicquam? quae vernas alit.Haec atque hujus similia alia damna multa mulierum.Me uxore prohibent, mihi quae hujus similes sermones ferat.Mil. 3.1.v.90. & seqq.
units.tr: "A good wife, if indeed she has been brought anywhere in the world, where could I find her? But shall I take her home, to tell me: 'Buy wool, my husband, so that a soft and warm cloak may be made for you, and good winter tunics, so you won't freeze this winter'? You will never hear such things from a wife. But before the cocks crow, so that she may rouse me from sleep, she says: 'Give me, my husband, money for the Kalends, to help my mother; give me money to hire someone to make and season the food; give me money to give at the Quinquatria to the enchantress, the diviner, the soothsayer and the haruspex. It is a disgrace if nothing is sent; see how haughtily she looks! Then the matron cannot possibly fail to receive a gift. The housekeeper is already angry, because for a long time nothing has been carried off for her. Then the midwife complained to me that too little was sent to her. What? Nothing to be sent to the nurse who raises the household slaves? These and many other such losses come from women. They keep me from taking a wife who might bring me talk like this." Mil. 3.1 v.90 and following.

units.la: Uxorem ducere est libertatem vendere. Mil 3.1.v.107.
units.tr: To marry a wife is to sell one's liberty. Mil. 3.1 v.107.

units.la: In contrarium, ducendam scil. esse uxorem, arguit alius eodem loco Mil 3.1.v.108.
units.tr: On the contrary, that a wife should be taken, another argues in the same place, Mil. 3.1 v.108.

units.la: At illa lam est magna in genere, & in divitijs maximis,Liberos hominem educare generi monumentum, & sibi.
units.tr: "But she is of great family and very great riches; to bring up children is a memorial to one's family and to oneself."

units.la: Graeci dicunt:
units.tr: The Greeks say:

units.la: Στύλοι δ᾽ οἶκον ἐσ᾽ παῖδες ἀγαπᾶνες.
units.tr: Children are the pillars of the house who are loved. [Στύλοι δ᾽ οἶκον ἐσ᾽ παῖδες ἀγαπᾶνες]

units.la: Caeterum disputationem integram: Num seni ducenda uxor operae pretium foret huc adscribere: sed non pigebit Lectorem adi-re ipsum. re ipsum contextum, ubi docte omnia differuntur versibus aliquot insequentibus. Neque enim sic nobis implendæ chartæ sunt, ut scilicet fiat liber: ubi in mundo Authoris nostri verba.
units.tr: To set out the whole discussion, "Whether an old man should take a wife," would be worth copying here; but the reader will not mind going to the passage itself, where everything is learnedly debated in the verses that follow. For we need not fill our pages so as to make a book, when the words of our author are in the world.

units.la: Quæ curæ parentes in liberorum generatione & educatione teneant, graphicè exponit senex Mil.3.1.v.123. Polsi habuissem, satis cepisse miseriarum liberis (enferem; a muro cecidissetne ebrius, aut de equo ʋspiam Metuerem, ne ibi defregisset crura, aut ceruices sibi. Tum uxor mihi insignitos pueros pariat: postea Aut varum, aut valgum, aut compernem, aut patum, aut brocchum filium.
units.tr: The old man vividly describes the cares parents bear in begetting and bringing up children, Mil. 3.1 v.123: "If I had had children, I would have had enough troubles: I would fear that he had fallen drunk from a wall, or somewhere from a horse, lest he had broken his legs or neck. Then let my wife bear me remarkable boys; afterwards a cross-eyed, bandy-legged, knock-kneed, squat, or buck-toothed son."

units.la: Qui inscijs parentibus filiam ducebant dolo & fraude; dote privabantur. Truc.4.3.v.70.
units.tr: Those who led away a daughter by trickery and fraud, without the knowledge of her parents, were deprived of the dowry. Truc. 4.3 v.70.

units.la: Haud mansisti, dum ego darem illam, tute sumsisti tibi. Nunc habeas, ut nactus: verum hoc ego te multabo bolo: Sex talenta magna a dote demam pro ista inscitia.
units.tr: "You did not wait while I gave her; you took her for yourself. Now keep her, since you have got her. But for this I will fine you: I will deduct six great talents from the dowry for that stupidity."

units.la: Divortium facientes: nuncium alteri remittere dicebantur, ut suas sibi res haberet. Truc.4.3.v.74.
units.tr: Those making a divorce were said to send a messenger back to the other party, so that he might have his own things for himself. Truc. 4.3 v.74.

units.la: Hoc facientes, jubebant aliam conditionem invenire sibi. Ibid. v.74.
units.tr: In doing this, they told him to find another arrangement for himself. Ibid. v.74.

units.la: Mariti ægrè ferant se observari ab uxoribus: præsertim si bene illis omnia præbeant: adeoq; sponte ruunt sæpe ad flagitia. Men. 1.2.v.12. & seqq.
units.tr: Husbands take it badly to be watched by their wives, especially if they provide everything well for them; and so they often rush of their own accord into disgraceful acts. Men. 1.2 v.12 and following.

units.la: Quæ male nuptæ sunt, domi & foris ægrè quod sit, satis semper est. Caf. 22.v.7.
units.tr: Those who are badly married have enough trouble, at home and abroad, always. Caf. 22 v.7.

units.la: Viri jus suum ad mulieres obtinere haud queunt. Caf. 2.2.v.21.
units.tr: Husbands cannot maintain their right over women. Caf. 2.2 v.21.

units.la: Peculii probam nihil habere addecet clam virum: & quæ habet partum, ei haud commodi est, quin vero aut subtrahat, aut flupro invenerit. Viri omne est, quod mulieres habent. Casin. 2.2. v.26.
units.tr: A respectable wife ought to have no savings hidden from her husband; and she who has a child should not be inclined to conceal it or steal it away, or to get something by adultery. "Everything that women have belongs to the husband." Casin. 2.2 v.26.

units.la: Patri aliquando licitum fuit dissolvere contracta se authore matrimonia. Stich. 1.1.v.44. & 1.2.v.73.
units.tr: At one time it was permitted for a father to dissolve marriages contracted on his authority. Stich. 1.1 v.44 and 1.2 v.73.

units.la: Sic Ennius apud Cic. lib.2.Rhet. ad Herenn. Injuria abs te afficior indigna, pater.
units.tr: So Ennius, in Cicero's Rhetorica ad Herennium, book 2: "I am treated with unworthy injury, father."

units.la: Nam si improbum Cresphontem existimaveras:
units.tr: "For if you had thought Cresphontes wicked,

units.la: (Cur me huic locabas nuptui? sin esi probus,
units.tr: (why were you giving me to him in marriage? But if he is good,

units.la: (Cur talem invitum invitam cogis linquere.
units.tr: (why do you compel such a man, against his will, to leave an unwilling woman?"

units.la: Et Affranius:
units.tr: And Afranius:

units.la: Indignum ò facinus! adolescentes optimos
units.tr: "Unworthy deed! Splendid young men,

units.la: Bene convenientes concordes q; cum viris
units.tr: well matched and harmonious with their wives,

units.la: Repente viduas faciat spurcitiis patris.
units.tr: are suddenly made widowers by the foul tricks of a father."

units.la: Vide hanc disputationem apud Alber. Gentilem J C. de Nupt. l. 4. c. 7.
units.tr: See this discussion in Albericus Gentilis, J.C., De Nuptiis book 4 ch. 7.

units.la: PAUPERTAS non tollit matrimonium*: neque facit divortium. Stich. 1. 2. v. 76.
units.tr: POVERTY does not abolish marriage, nor does it bring about divorce. Stich. 1.2 v.76.

units.la: Placet ille mihi mendicus suus rex Regina placet.
units.tr: "That beggar suits me as my king; the queen suits me."

units.la: Neque enim argento nuptum dantur mulieres: sed viro honesto.
units.tr: For women are not given in marriage for money, but to an honest man.

units.la: HONESTÆ & piæ conjuges suos maritos absentes non minus amant, honorant, quàm præsentes. Stich. 1. 2. v. 43.
units.tr: CHASTE and pious wives love and honour their absent husbands no less than present ones. Stich. 1.2 v.43.

units.la: Pudicitia est, eos magnificare, qui nos socias sumserunt sibi.
units.tr: "It is modesty to honour those who have taken us as partners."

units.la: Vide Hottom. de ritu Nupt. cap. 23.
units.tr: See Hotman, On the Rite of Marriage, ch. 23.

units.la: VIDUI parentes liberos consulere solent de secundis Nupt. Stich. 1. 2. v. 52. ubi senex sic alloquitur suas filias.
units.tr: WIDOWERS are wont to consult their children about a second marriage. Stich. 1.2 v.52, where the old man addresses his daughters thus:

units.la: Pol ego uxorem quaero: postquam vestra mater mortua est.
units.tr: "By Pollux, I am seeking a wife, since your mother is dead."

units.la: NUPTIÆ secundæ valdè ambiguæ. Raro enim meliorem accipimus. Stich. 1. 2. v. 53.
units.tr: SECOND marriages are very doubtful, for we rarely get a better one. Stich. 1.2 v.53.

units.la: UXOR secunda honestæ sit famæ. Stich. 1. 2. v. 37. Per urbem cum ambulet, omnibus os obturet: ne quis merito maledicat sibi.
units.tr: A second wife should be of honest reputation. Stich. 1.2 v.37. "When she walks through the city, she should stop everyone's mouth, so that no one may justly speak ill of her."

units.la: EA bona uxor est, cùm malefaciundi est potestas, quæ ne faciat, id temperat. Stich. 1. 2. v. 60.
units.tr: She is a good wife when she has the power to do wrong and refrains from doing it. Stich. 1.2 v.60.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Mulieres.
units.tr: See also under the title Mulieres.

units.la: VIRGINEM an viduam ducere expediat, ardua quæstio. Stich. 1. 2. v. 62. ubi soror ab parente ejus causâ in consilium adhibita sic respondet:
units.tr: Whether it is advantageous to marry a virgin or a widow is a difficult question. Stich. 1.2 v.62, where the sister, called into counsel on this by their father, answers thus:

units.la: E malis multis malum, quod minimum est, id minimè est malum. Qui potest mulieres vitare, vitet: ut quotidie pridie caveat, ne faciat, quod pigeat postridie.
units.tr: "Of many evils, the least is not evil at all. Let whoever can avoid women avoid them, so that each day he takes care beforehand not to do what he will regret afterwards."

units.la: Vide etiam Disputationem Socratis apud Val. Maximum lib. 7. cap. 2. pag. 311.
units.tr: See also Socrates' disputation in Valerius Maximus, book 7 ch. 2, p. 311.

units.la: INFELICES conjuges alter alterius mortem exoptat.
units.tr: UNHAPPY spouses each wish for the other's death.

units.la: Sic Megadorus ille de filiâ Euclionis Aul. 2. 1. v. 32.
units.tr: So Megadorus, concerning Euclio's daughter, Aul. 2.1 v.32:

units.la: Ut quidem emoriar priusquam ducam: Sed hic legibus, si quam dare vis, ducam, quae cras veniat, perendie foras feratur.
units.tr: "Would that I might die before I marry! But if you want to give me one here under the laws, I will take her; she who comes tomorrow and is carried out the day after."

units.la: Sic Hipponact. .
units.tr: So Hipponax.

units.la: Δύ' ἡμέραι γυναικὸς εἰσὶν ἡδίσται: ὅταν γαμῇ τις, κἀμφέρει ταθνηκυῖαν: Dies duo sunt conjugis suavissimi: quo nubit illa, quoq; fertur in rogum.
units.tr: Two days of a wife are most pleasant: when a man marries her, and when she is carried out to the pyre. [Δύ' ἡμέραι γυναικὸς εἰσὶν ἡδίσται: ὅταν γαμῇ τις, κἀμφέρει ταθνηκυῖαν]

units.la: Chæremon.
units.tr: Chaeremon.

units.la: γυναῖκα θάπτειν κρείττον ἐστὶν, ἢ γαμεῖν: Sepelire praestat uxorem, quàm ducere.
units.tr: It is better to bury a wife than to marry one. [γυναῖκα θάπτειν κρείττον ἐστὶν, ἢ γαμεῖν]

units.la: Si quis dotatam uxorem domi habet malè neminem sollicitat ire dormitum sopor. Most. 3. 2. v. 15.
units.tr: If someone has a dowered wife at home, sleep comes badly to anyone who goes to bed. Most. 3.2 v.15.

units.la: FEMINÆ apud Romanos jubebantur esse contentæ uno viro: ἀφ' ἑνὶ μίνυζαι.
units.tr: Among the Romans, women were required to be content with one husband: ἀφ' ἑνὶ μίνυζαι.

units.la: Sic Cist. 1. 1. v. 80. Matronæ magis conducibile est istuc, Silenium, Unum amare, & eum eo ætatem exigere, cui nupta est semel. Verùm animi meretrix fortunati est oppidi similima, Non potest suam rem obtinere sola sine multis viris.
units.tr: So in Cist. 1.1 v. 80: "It is more fitting for a matron, Silenium, to love one man and to spend her life with the one she has married. But a mind that is a whore is most like a prosperous town: it cannot keep its own property alone, without many men."

units.la: Et Merc. 4. 6. v. 8. Nam uxor contenta est, quae bona est, uno viro.
units.tr: And in Merc. 4.6 v. 8: "For a wife who is good is content with one man."

units.la: Horat. lib. 3. Od. 24. Dos est magna parentium Virtus, & metuens alterius viri Certo foedere castitas.
units.tr: Horace, Odes 3.24: "The great dowry of parents is virtue, and chastity that fears another man, bound by a sure pledge."

units.la: Affranius Epistolâ: Nam proba & pudica quod sum, consulo & parco mihi, Quoniam comparatum est, uno ut simus contenta viro.
units.tr: Afranius in a letter: "For being upright and chaste as I am, I take thought for myself and spare myself, since it has been arranged that we should be content with one husband."

units.la: Juvenal. Sat. VI. Unus Iberinae vir sufficit; ocyus illud Extorquebia, ut haec oculo contenta sit uno.
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire 6: "One husband is enough for the Spanish woman; you would sooner wrest from a woman that she be content with one eye."

units.la: Dicebantur & unum exspectare pudicæ: h.e. uni esse obedientes, atq; morem gerere.
units.tr: Chaste women were also said "to wait for one man," that is, to be obedient to one and to comply with him.

units.la: Mostell, 1.3. v. 31. Tu ecastor erras, quæ quidem illum exspectes unum, atq; illi Morem præcipuè sic geras, atq; alios asperneris.
units.tr: Mostellaria 1.3 v. 31: "Indeed you are wrong, for you would wait for that one man, and you would especially comply with him in this way, and spurn the others."

units.la: De eâdem copulâ continente & unicâ idem noster Mil. 4. 6. ver. 16. Spero ita futurum, quamquam illum multæ sibi expetiffant; Ille illas spernit segregatq; ab fe omnes, extra te unam.
units.tr: Our author, on the same faithful and single-minded woman, in Miles 4.6 v. 16: "I hope it will turn out so, although many women have sought him; he spurns them all and keeps them away from himself, except you alone."

units.la: Tales feminæ dicebantur habere bonum cupidinem.
units.tr: Such women were said to have "a good desire."

units.la: Propert. lib. 2. Eleg. 18. Quin ego deminuo curam, quod sæpè Cupido Huic malus esse solet, cui bonus ante fuit.
units.tr: Propertius, Elegies 2.18: "Indeed I lessen my care, because Cupid is often bad for the one for whom he was good before."

units.la: Quem noster sedatum Cupidinem vocat Amph. 2. 2. v. 210.
units.tr: Which our author calls "a calmed Cupid," Amphitryo 2.2 v. 210.

units.la: Similes sententias è Græcis collegit insignis Juvenis Janus Gebharius lib. 2. Crepundiorum cap. 14. Uti ex Euripide Androm. verf. 464. Iph. Aulid. v. 1158. Et Medeâ v. 549. & 627. Alia non injucunda reperies apud Crepundiorum minimè ludicrum illum authorem.
units.tr: Similar sayings from the Greeks were collected by the distinguished young man Janus Gebharius, Crepundiorum book 2, chapter 14: as in Euripides, Andromache v. 464, Iphigenia at Aulis v. 1158, and Medea vv. 549 and 627. You will find other not unpleasant things in that author of the Crepundia, who is by no means frivolous.

units.la: FIDES potiùs & virtus in matrimonio spectanda, quàm opes & divitiæ. Cist. 2.1. v. 16.18.
units.tr: In marriage, faith and virtue should be looked to rather than wealth and riches. Cist. 2.1 v. 16–18.

units.la: PATER puellæ propriè dicitur Spondere: adolescentisautem despondere: quamquam sæpè conscendi soleant. Cist. 2.1.v. 21.
units.tr: Properly, a father is said to betroth (spondere) a girl, but a young man is betrothed (despondere), although they are often used interchangeably. Cist. 2.1 v. 21.

units.la: Vide Alber. Gentilem de Nuptijs. lib. 2. c. 2.
units.tr: See Albericus Gentilis, On Weddings, book 2, chapter 2.

units.la: In matrimonij negotio plurimùm valent cognati, amici. Mil. 4. 3. v. 26.
units.tr: In the business of marriage, relatives and friends carry the most weight. Miles 4.3 v. 26.

units.la: Juris-consulti Matrimonium dicunt dissolvi bonâ gratiâ. ἀγαθῇ χάριτι [bonâ veniâ, amicabili separatione, μετ' εὐλόγου αἰτίας: sine querelâ ἀνευ μεμψεως.] Mil. 4. 3. v. 32.
units.tr: Jurists say that a marriage is dissolved by good grace [ἀγαθῇ χάριτι], that is, with good leave, by friendly separation, with a reasonable cause, without complaint [ἀνευ μεμψεως]. Miles 4.3 v. 32.

units.la: Filiæ demandatæ viro, solent perpetuas querimonias necterea[d] parentes: & virum accusare: cumq; observare. Parentes autem ut filias redigant in ordinem, sæpè approbant delicta virorum.
units.tr: Daughters handed over to a husband are accustomed to bring constant complaints to their parents, to accuse the husband and to keep watch on him. The parents, however, in order to bring their daughters back into line, often approve the offences of the husbands.

units.la: Vide totum locum Men. f. 2. v. 39.
units.tr: See the whole passage, Menaechmi, act 2 v. 39.

units.la: Mariti habitantes cum odiosâ uxore, Herculis labores se sustinere arbitrantur.
units.tr: Husbands who live with a hateful wife think they are enduring the labours of Hercules.
Epidicus 2.1 v. 9.

units.la: Hercules ego fui, dum illa mecum fuit, neq; sexta aerumna Acerbior Herculi, quàm illa mihi est objecta.
units.tr: "I was Hercules while she was with me, and the sixth labour was not more bitter for Hercules than she has been thrown at me."

units.la: Dos pulcra est pecunia: sed quæ non est marita. Epid. 2. 1. verf. 11. Nam dotatæ mactant & malo, & damno viros. Aulularia 3. 5. v. 62.
units.tr: A dowry is fine money, but the woman who brings it is not much of a wife. Epidicus 2.1 v. 11. "For dowered wives harass and damage their husbands." Aulularia 3.5 v. 62.

units.la: In conjuge dotatâ imperium solet vendi. Asin. 1. 1. v. 74. Argentum accepi, dote imperium vendidi.
units.tr: In a dowered spouse, power is wont to be sold. Asinaria 1.1 v. 74: "I took silver; I sold my authority for a dowry."

units.la: Sic Aul. 3. 5. v. 60. Quæ indotata est, ea in potestate est viri. Dotatæ mactant & malo & damno viros.
units.tr: So Aulularia 3.5 v. 60: "She who is undowered is in her husband's power. Dowered wives harass and damage husbands."

units.la: Arrogantes amatores & gloriosi solent jactare suas opes. Mil. 4. 2. v. 71.
units.tr: Arrogant lovers and boastful men are wont to boast of their wealth. Miles 4.2 v. 71.

units.la: PY. Non mihi avaritia inquam innata est, satis est divitiarum. Plus mihi auri mille est modiorum Philippei. PA. praeter thesaurum: Tum argenti montes, non massas habet: Ætna non æquè alta est.
units.tr: PY. "I am not, I say, born with avarice; there is enough wealth. I have more than a thousand measures of Philippic gold." PA. "Besides the treasure, he has mountains of silver, not lumps; Etna is not as high."

units.la: Juris-consulti alienarum nuptiarum temeratores, & sacrilegos nuptiarum quos vocant, graviter puniendos statuerunt. Et hoc designat noster Asin. 5. 2. verf. 23. Et Curc. 1. 1. v. 36.
units.tr: Jurists have decreed that violators of other people's marriages, whom they call sacrilegious toward marriages, are to be punished severely. Our author indicates this in Asinaria 5.2 v. 23, and Curculio 1.1 v. 36.

units.la: PLÆRUMQUE parentes sibi similes generant. Sic per jocum illu- ditur Militi. Mil. 4. 2. v.85.
units.tr: Very often parents beget children like themselves. This is mocked in jest in Miles 4.2 v. 85.

units.la: Meri bellatores gignuntur, quas hic pragnantes fecit, Et pueri annos octingentos qui vivunt. Quin mille annorum perpetuo vivunt, à sæculo ad sæculum.
units.tr: "Brave warriors are born, whom she has made pregnant here, and boys who live eight hundred years. Indeed they live for a thousand years in perpetuity, from age to age."

units.la: In conjugio mores mutandi sunt. Unde is Mil. 4.8. v.47. sic infit: Hau mihi! Cum venit in mentem, ut mores mihi mutandi sient, Discendi muliebres, obliviscendi stratiotici.
units.tr: In marriage, manners must be changed. Hence Miles 4.8 v. 47 begins thus: "Alas! When it comes into my mind that my manners must be changed, to learn women's ways and to forget soldierly ones."

units.la: More fit, inquit Pomponius: moriri suam quisq; uxorem, ut velit.
units.tr: "It is the custom," says Pomponius, "that each man may let his own wife die, as he wishes."
Asinaria 5.2 v. 37, 56. Casina 2.8 v. 70. Epidicus 2.1 v. 7, and 3.2 v. 27.

units.la: Sacrificas illico hostijs: neq; adeo injuriâ: quia licitum est, eam tibi vivendo vincere.
units.tr: "You sacrifice at once with victims, and not without injustice, since it is permitted to conquer her by living with her."

units.la: Trin.1.2.v.3.13. Et Caf.2.6.v.2. Illa adapol videre ardentem te extra portam Metiam velit.
units.tr: Trinummus 1.2 v. 3, 13. And Casina 2.6 v. 2: "Indeed she wishes to see you burning outside the Metian gate."

units.la: IMPERIUM natura non voluit esse penes feminam: quod sibi tamen sumit quandoque, Caf.2.6.v.57.
units.tr: Nature did not intend dominion to rest with the woman, though she sometimes claims it for herself. Casina 2.6 v. 57.

units.la: In malâ uxore atque inimico, si quid sumas, sumtus es. Mil.3. v.73.
units.tr: With a bad wife and an enemy, if you take anything, you are the one taken. Miles 3 v. 73.

units.la: MARITI quasi venatores sunt, nacti scilicet Canem, vel Hecubam aliquam. Caf.2.5.v.11. Mil.3.1.v.86. Rud.3 1. v.18.
units.tr: Husbands are like hunters, who have caught, of course, a dog or some Hecuba. Casina 2.5 v. 11. Miles 3.1 v. 86. Rudens 3.1 v. 18.

units.la: ORBÆ ex lege jubentur eis nubere, qui sunt genere proximi. Cist.1.1.v.102. & 1.3.v.26.
units.tr: By law, orphan girls are ordered to marry those who are nearest to them by kin. Cistellaria 1.1 v. 102, and 1.3 v. 26.

units.la: Terent. Phorm. & Adelph. hæc virgo orba est patre: Hic meus amicus illi genere est proximus: Huic leges cogunt nubere hanc.
units.tr: Terence, Phormio and Adelphoe: "This maiden is orphaned of her father; this friend of mine is nearest to her by kin; the laws compel her to marry him."

units.la: In dotem etiam ædes datæ, quæ soluto matrimonio revertebantur ad sponsam. Mil.4.4.v.30. Ædes dotales dicas tuas.
units.tr: Houses were also given into the dowry, which on the dissolution of the marriage returned to the bride. Miles 4.4 v. 30: "You may call your houses dowry houses."

units.la: OCCASIO bonæ conditionis non amittenda. Aul.2.2.v.71.
units.tr: The opportunity of a good match is not to be lost. Aulularia 2.2 v. 71.

units.la: PARENTES liberos elocantes: haud facilè indotatis locant. Trin.2.2.v.97.
units.tr: Parents giving their children in marriage rarely give them easily to the undowered. Trinummus 2.2 v. 97.

units.la: Verùm dos non semper quærenda, ubi & amicitia & gratia in familiâ allicitur. Ibid. v. 101.
units.tr: But a dowry is not always to be sought, where friendship and favour are won within the family. Ibid. v. 101.

units.la: Parentes adibant, poscebant filiam elocandam filio. Ibid. verf. 105. Scilicet propter authoritatem. Ibid.
units.tr: Parents went and asked that the daughter be given in marriage to their son. Ibid. v. 105. Clearly on account of authority. Ibid.

units.la: Coniugii maxima libertas: ad quod nemo invitus cogi potest. Stich. 1.2.v.82.
units.tr: The greatest freedom belongs to marriage: no one can be forced into it against his will. Stichus 1.2 v. 82.

units.la: Nusquam libertas tàm necessaria, quàm in matrimonio est: ait Quintil. Declamat. 257. Nam qui amare alieno animo potest? Omnes nuptiæ existimantur esse voluntas. l. 26. Cod. de Nupt. Propria hic debet esse voluntas. c. 16.32. Q.2.
units.tr: "Nowhere is liberty so necessary as in marriage," says Quintilian, Declamation 257. "For who can love with an alien mind? All marriages are judged to be by consent." Law 26, Code, On Marriages: "Here the consent must be one's own." c. 16.32, Q. 2.

units.la: In elocandâ filiâ hęc præcipuè spectanda sunt: Genus, Fides, Facta, Ætas: & tandem postremo loco Dos. Aul. 2.2.v.36.
units.tr: In giving a daughter in marriage, these matters are to be considered above all: birth, faith, conduct, and age; and finally, in the last place, the dowry. Aulularia 2.2 v. 36.

units.la: Ætas puellarum justa ad elocandum est annorum septemdecim. Cist. 4.2.v.92.
units.tr: The proper age for girls to be given in marriage is seventeen years. Cistellaria 4.2 v. 92.

units.la: Mediæ ætatis uxor ducenda. Aul. 2.1.v.37.
units.tr: A wife of middle age is to be taken. Aulularia 2.1 v. 37.

units.la: Vide Ætatis.
units.tr: See Age (Ætas).

units.la: Liberorum procreationem magnum mariti decus censent. Truc. 2.8.v.36.
units.tr: Husbands consider the procreation of children a great honour to them. Truculentus 2.8 v. 36.

units.la: Sponsalia constant mentione & repromissione nuptiarum futurarum: ut definit J C. Florentinus. Aul. 2.2.v.27.
units.tr: Betrothals consist in the mention and promise of future marriage, as the jurist Florentinus defines. Aulularia 2.2 v. 27.

units.la: Uxores absentes etiam amari à maritis suis volunt. Amphit. 1.3. v.30.
units.tr: Absent wives also wish to be loved by their husbands. Amphitryo 1.3 v. 30.

units.la: Fastidiosas querelas in suos maritos exprimit egregiè Men. 1.2.v.5. Quoties ire volo, me retines, revocas, Rogitas quò eam, quam rem ego agam, quid negotij geram, Quid petam, quid feram, quid foris egerim, &c.
