units.tr: He excellently expresses the tedious complaints against husbands: Menaechmi 1.2 v. 5: "As often as I wish to go out, you hold me back, call me back, ask where I am going, what business I am doing, what I am seeking, bringing, or doing outside, and so on."

units.la: Mariti irati suis uxoribus minabantur viduertatem. Men. 1.2. v. 4.
units.tr: Angry husbands threatened their wives with widowhood. Menaechmi 1.2 v. 4.

units.la: Uxor non tanti nobis debet esse: ut præ ejus amore negligamus RemRempublicam : aut partes muneris nobis demandati. Amph. 1.3. v.30.
units.tr: A wife should not be so dear to us that, for love of her, we neglect the commonwealth or the parts of the duty entrusted to us. Amphitryo 1.3 v. 30.

units.la: Leges iubent, ut is, qui virginem vitiavit, aut ut eam ducat, aut uxorem poscat. Aul. 4.10. v.63.
units.tr: The laws order that he who has violated a virgin must either marry her or ask for her as his wife. Aulularia 4.10 v. 63.

units.la: Dos imperiosa esse solet. Men. 5.2. v.16.
units.tr: A dowry is wont to be imperious. Menaechmi 5.2 v. 16.

units.la: Ita ista solent, qua viros subservire sibi postulant, dote freta feroces.
units.tr: "Thus such women are wont to be, who demand that husbands be subservient to them, proud in their dowry."

units.la: In matrimonio contrahendo non postrema cura debet esse familiae: & dotis amplioris. Cist. 2.3 v.18.57.
units.tr: In contracting marriage, the care of the family and of a larger dowry should not be the least consideration. Cistellaria 2.3 v. 18, 57.

units.la: Votum maritorum apud veteres fuit, uxoribus supervivere : uti & contra uxorum maritis. Asi. 1.1.v.630. Cas. 4.4.v.2. Cist. 1.1.v. 86. Epid. 2.1.v.8. Trin. 1.2.v.19.
units.tr: Among the ancients, husbands' wish was to outlive their wives, and conversely wives' wish to outlive their husbands. Asinaria 1.1 v. 630; Casina 4.4 v. 2; Cistellaria 1.1 v. 86; Epidicus 2.1 v. 8; Trinummus 1.2 v. 19.

units.la: Sic apud Terent. Hecyra act.2. sc.1.
units.tr: Thus in Terence, Hecyra, act 2, scene 1:

units.la: --- So. Non ita me Dii bene amant, mi Lache,
units.tr: --- So. "May the gods not love me so well, Laches,

units.la: Itaque una inter nos agere aetatem liceat. LA. Dii mala prohibeant!
units.tr: that we may be allowed to spend our lives together." LA. "May the gods forbid it!"

units.la: Parentes gaudent se fieri avos per elocationem filiarum. Aul. 4.10. v.67.
units.tr: Parents rejoice to become grandparents through the marrying off of their daughters. Aul. 4.10, v.67.

units.la: Uxores aegre ferunt absentiam maritorum. Amph. 1.3. v.15.31. Et Amph. 2.2.v.8.
units.tr: Wives find their husbands' absence hard to bear. Amph. 1.3, v.15.31. And Amph. 2.2, v.8.

units.la: In conjugio saepe litigia oriuntur: inprimis a morosulis uxoribus. Merc. 3.3.v.14. Senex queritur de uxore :
units.tr: Quarrels often arise in marriage, chiefly from peevish wives. Merc. 3.3, v.14. An old man complains about his wife:

units.la: Uxor me exspectat iamdudum esuriens domi
units.tr: "My wife has been waiting for me at home a long time, starving,

units.la: Iam iurgio enicabit, si intro redero.
units.tr: and now she will nag me to death if I go back inside."

units.la: Bonae matris-familias est diligenter curare rem communem, h. e. liberos & familiam : quia conjugum omnia sunt communia. Amph. 1.3. v.1.
units.tr: It is the task of a good mother of the family to take careful charge of the common property, that is, the children and the household, since all things belong in common to husband and wife. Amph. 1.3, v.1.

units.la: Vide Antonij Guiberti Costani Polyhistorem lib. 1.
units.tr: See Antonius Guibertus Costanus, Polyhistor, book 1.

units.la: Mater-familias gravida sibi parcere debet a laboribus. Amph. 1.3. v.2.
units.tr: A pregnant mother of the family ought to spare herself from labours. Amph. 1.3, v.2.

units.la: Purpura aetas occultari solet : auro turpe mulieris. Pulcra mulier nuda erit, quàm purpurata, pulcrior, Postea nequicquam exornata est bene: si morata est male. Pulcrum ornatum turpes mores pejus cæno collinunt. Most. 1.3. v. 130. & seqq.
units.tr: Beauty is commonly hidden under purple; gold is a disgrace to a woman. A beautiful woman is lovelier naked than dressed in purple. Afterwards she is adorned in vain, if her conduct is bad. Fine ornament smears ugly morals with filth, and worse than mud. Most. 1.3, v.130 and following.

units.la: Si commutare fas esset conjuges: utiq; crebræ essent istæ permutationes apud senes. Trin. 1.2.v.21. Vide Joh. Sarisber. lib. 8. Policrat. c. 9.
units.tr: If it were lawful to exchange spouses, such exchanges would surely be frequent among old men. Trin. 1.2, v.21. See John of Salisbury, Policraticus, book 8, ch. 9.

units.la: Matrimonio soluto dos tamen petebatur. Stich. 2.1.v.50. Vide Cod. Juris Tit. 3.l. 24. ff.
units.tr: Even when the marriage had been dissolved, the dowry was still demanded. Stich. 2.1, v.50. See the Codex Juris, title 3, law 24, Digest.

units.la: Soluto matrimonio quemadmodum Dos petatur.
units.tr: How a dowry is claimed when a marriage has been dissolved.

units.la: Generum etiam affinem vocabant. Aul. 3.4.v.14.
units.tr: They also called a son-in-law an affinis. Aul. 3.4, v.14.

units.la: Matrimonium inituri amicis aperiebant consilium suum de conditione, quam quærebant. Aul. 3.5. v.1.
units.tr: Those about to marry used to disclose their plans to their friends regarding the match they were seeking. Aul. 3.5, v.1.

units.la: Uxores iratæ suos maritos ne verbo dignantur compellare: quicquid etiam muneris donent. Truc. 2.6.v.61.
units.tr: Angry wives do not deign even to address their husbands with a word, however many gifts they give them. Truc. 2.6, v.61.

units.la: Mariti convivaturi clam uxoribus vix abeunt. Ib. 66.
units.tr: Husbands who are about to dine out slip away from their wives with difficulty, and secretly. Ib. 66.

units.la: Senes lascivi propudium erant populi. Cas. 3.1.v.4. Traducebantur enim his vocibus: Cano capite! ætate alienâ! Cas. 3.1.v.45.
units.tr: Lecherous old men were a disgrace to the people. For they were taunted with these words: "Grey-headed! Of another's age!" Cas. 3.1, v.4 and v.45.

units.la: Vtx honestè fieri potest, ut quis patiatur ire filiam in matrimonium sine dote. Trin. 3.3.v.3.
units.tr: It can scarcely be honourable for anyone to allow his daughter to go into marriage without a dowry. Trin. 3.3, v.3.

units.la: Mors uxoris grata maritis olim & hodie. Ideoq; Cist. 1.3.v.27. dicitur: Ea diem suum obiit, factă morigera est viro.
units.tr: The death of a wife has been welcome to husbands both in former times and today. Hence the saying: "She has met her day, she has become obedient to her husband." Cist. 1.3, v.27.

units.la: Magnum probrum erat, ante justas nuptias partum edere. Aul. 2.3.v.9.
units.tr: It was a great disgrace to bear a child before a lawful marriage. Aul. 2.3, v.9.

units.la: Parentes non producunt suos liberos in orbitatem, ut ijs pri-ventur iterùm: cóq; durum illis est, si decedant. Cist. 3.5.v.107.
units.tr: Parents do not raise their children so that they are bereaved and deprived of them again; and it is hard for them if the children die. Cist. 3.5, v.107.

units.la: Concubinis non dabatur dos. Inde distinguit à concubinatu matrimonium adolescens ille sororem alteri elocans. Tri. 3.2.v.25
units.tr: No dowry was given to concubines. Hence that young man who gives his sister to another man distinguishes marriage from concubinage. Trin. 3.2, v.25.

units.la: Uxoris est curare ancillas, non viri. Cas. 2.3.v.43.
units.tr: It is the wife's business to look after the maidservants, not the husband's. Cas. 2.3, v.43.

units.la: Multi parvi faciunt, quàm ducant, ingenuamne an libertinam, dummodò quæstuosa sit, quæ alat corpus corpore: & lepi-dissdissima, itemque adolescentula. Mil. 3. 1. v. 190.
units.tr: Many men care little whether they marry a freeborn woman or a freedwoman, so long as she is a earner who feeds her body with her body, and so long as she is most charming, and likewise a young girl. Mil. 3.1, v.190.

units.la: PLÆRUMQUE in contrahendis nuptijs virtus post numos quæri solet. Aul. 2. 2. v. 87.
units.tr: In arranging marriages, virtue is commonly sought only after money. Aul. 2.2, v.87.

units.la: MARITI magnam curam gerunt uxorum; adeò ut plurimùm eas metuant, si quid minus dextrè agant. Asin. 1. 1. v. 4.
units.tr: Husbands take great care of their wives, so much so that they mostly fear them if they do anything less adroitly. Asin. 1.1, v.4.

units.la: IN causâ matrimonij parentes non semper resistere debent filijs. Exemplo Philonis senis. Trin. 2. 3. v. 4.
units.tr: In matters of marriage, parents ought not always to oppose their sons. Example: old Philo. Trin. 2.3, v.4.

units.la: IN matrimonio non spectandæ opes æquiparabiles utrinque. Trin. 2. 4. v. 65.
units.tr: In marriage, wealth is not to be looked at; the parties should be equal on both sides. Trin. 2.4, v.65.

units.la: DOS emit sibi viros: & viri se dote vendunt. Most. 1. 3. v. 123.
units.tr: The dowry buys husbands for itself, and husbands sell themselves for a dowry. Most. 1.3, v.123.

units.la: DOTIS non habenda ratio: sive ea quidem certè non æstimanda ex divitijs. Aul. 2. 1. v. 45.
units.tr: No account is to be taken of the dowry; certainly it is not to be valued by the wealth it brings. Aul. 2.1, v.45.

units.la: Istias magnas factiones, animos, dotes dapsiles, Clamores, imperia, eburata vehicula, pallas, purpuram, Nihil moror; quæ in servitutem sumtibus redigunt viros.
units.tr: "Those great factions, those spirits, those lavish dowries, clamours, commands, ivory carriages, cloaks, purple: I make nothing of them; they reduce husbands to slavery by their expenses."

units.la: QUOTIES mulier dotem marito dabat, tum quæ ex suis bonis retinebat, neque ad virum transmittebat, ea recipere dicebatur: id est, excipere, ne in dominium mariti cum reliquâ dote venirent. Illam dotem uxor irata solebat servo suo donare, quem ea propter Dotalem nominabant. Alludit noster Asin. 1. 1. v. 72.
units.tr: Whenever a wife gave a dowry to her husband, what she kept back from her own goods and did not transfer to the husband was said to be "received back", that is, taken out, so that it would not pass into the husband's ownership with the rest of the dowry. An angry wife would often give that retained dowry to her slave, whom for this reason they called dotalis. Our author alludes to Asin. 1.1, v.72.

units.la: Idem etiam appellatus Receptitium.
units.tr: The same slave was also called receptitius.

units.la: Cato in suasione legis Voconiæ:
units.tr: Cato, in urging the Voconian law:

units.la: Principio nobis mulier magnam dotem attulit: tum magnam pecuniam recipit, quàm in viri potestate non committit, eam pecuniam viro dat mutuam: postea ubi irata facta est, servum receptitium scollari, atq; flagitare virum jubet.
units.tr: "At first a woman brought us a large dowry; then she takes back a large sum of money, which she does not entrust to her husband's power; she lends that money to her husband. Afterwards, when she has become angry, she orders her receptitius slave to be whipped and to demand the money from her husband."

units.la: Vide Tit. Servorum. & Lex.
units.tr: See the title Servorum, and the law.

units.la: ALCUMENA Amph 2.2.v.209. veram dotem sic depingit:
units.tr: Alcumena, in Amph. 2.2, v.209, portrays the true dowry thus:

units.la: Non ego illam mihi dotem duco esse, quæ dos dicitur: Sed pudicitiam & pudorem, & sedatum cupidinem, Deum metum, parentum amorem, & cognatum concordiam, Tibi (marito) morigera, atque ut munifica sim bonis, prosim probæ.
units.tr: "I do not count as my dowry what is called a dowry: but chastity and modesty, a calm desire, fear of God, love of parents, and harmony with kin; to you, my husband, may I be compliant, and generous with your goods, and a benefit to the good."

units.la: ADULTERÆ feminæ non domo solum exactæ, & dote privatæ fuerunt, sed etiam neccatæ. Alludit Amph 2.2.v.222.
units.tr: Adulterous women were not only driven out of the house and deprived of their dowry, but were even put to death. Alludes to Amph. 2.2, v.222.

units.la: Vide etiam Lipsium ad Annales Taciti lib. iv.
units.tr: See also Lipsius on the Annals of Tacitus, book 4.

units.la: DUMMODO morata recte veniat: dotata est satis. Aulular. 2. 2. v. 62.
units.tr: Provided she comes to her husband well-behaved, she is dowered enough. Aulul. 2.2, v.62.

units.la: MERETRICES Tuscæ dotem sibi quærebant ex corporis patien-tia. Cist. 1.3.v.20.
units.tr: Tuscan prostitutes used to win their dowries from the endurance of their bodies. Cist. 1.3, v.20.

units.la: Vide etiam Meretricum.
units.tr: See also under Meretrices.

units.la: Idem memorat Augustinus de Phænicibus.
units.tr: Augustine mentions the same custom of the Phoenicians.

units.la: MAGNA dos fuit accipere viginti talenta magna. Cist. 2.3.v.19.
units.tr: It was a great dowry to receive twenty great talents. Cist. 2.3, v.19.

units.la: NON semper dos quærenda. Aul 3.5.v.5.
units.tr: A dowry is not always to be sought. Aul. 3.5, v.5.

units.la: Opulentiores pauperiorum filias ut indotatas ducant Uxores domum: multo fiet civitas concordior. Et invidia nos minore utemur, quam utimur: Et illæ malam rem metuent, quam metuunt, magis, Et nos minore sumtu erimus, quam sumus.
units.tr: "If wealthier men took the daughters of poorer men as wives, without dowry, into their homes, the state would become much more harmonious. We would use less envy than we do, and they would fear the bad thing more than they fear it now, and we would be at less expense than we are."

units.la: Quæ quidem sententiam expresse è Platone lib. 6. de Rep. Apul. de Philosophia. Quare & dites inferiores nuptias non recusent, & locupletium consortium inopes consequantur.
units.tr: This opinion is expressly drawn from Plato, Republic, book 6, and from Apuleius, On Philosophy. Hence the rich should not refuse marriages with their inferiors, and the poor should obtain the partnership of the wealthy.

units.la: Hinc igitur Quæstio decidi facile potest: Utrum pauperem sine dote jungere matrimonio sit melius: an vero dotatam.
units.tr: From this, then, the question can easily be settled: whether it is better to join a poor woman to marriage without a dowry, or rather a dowered one.

units.la: Huic quæstioni nemo repugnabit, inquit Megadorus senex, nisi pauci aliqui locupletes, quorum animis avidis, atq; insatietatibus, neque lex, neque tutor capere est, qui possit modum.
units.tr: No one will oppose this question, says the old man Megadorus, except a few wealthy men, whose greedy and insatiable minds neither law nor guardian can restrain.

units.la: Illorum solvitur OBJECTIO. Namque hoc qui dicat? Quo illæ nubent divites dotatæ, si istud jus pauperibus ponitur? RESPON-
units.tr: Their objection is answered. For who would say this? Where would rich, dowered women marry if this right were established for the poor? REPLY:

units.la: RESPONDETUR. Quò lubeat, nubant, dum ne dos fiat comes: h.e. ne, quod plærumque fieri solet, dotatæ viris imperent: & sumtus viris faciant. Uxores enim dotatæ pilentis, alijsque vehiculis vehi volunt, quæ à mulis portantur.
units.tr: It is answered: let them marry wherever they please, provided the dowry does not become a companion; that is, lest, as usually happens, dowered wives command their husbands and make them spend. For dowered wives want to be carried in litters and other vehicles borne by mules.

units.la: Hoc ita si fiat, pergit philosophari senex: Mores meliores sibi parent pro dote, quos ferant, quàm nunc ferunt. Et faxim ego, ut muli, pretio qui superant equos, sient viliores Gallicis Canthe-rijs.
units.tr: If this were done, the old man goes on reasoning, they would procure for themselves better morals in place of a dowry, and such morals as they would bring would be better than those they now bring. And I would make mules, which now surpass horses in price, cheaper than Gallic cantherii.

units.la: Nulla igitur dicat:
units.tr: Let no woman therefore say:

units.la: Equidem dotem ad te attuli, majorem multò quàm tibi erat pecunia.
units.tr: "Indeed I brought you a dowry much greater than your money."

units.la: Enim mihi quidem æquum est, purpuram atque aurum dari, ancillas, mulos, muliones, pedisequos, salutigerulos pueros, vehicula, qui vehar.
units.tr: For it seems only fair to me that purple and gold be given to me, along with maidservants, mules, muleteers, footmen, boys to carry greetings, and carriages in which I may ride.

units.la: Nunc quoquò venias, plus plaustrorum in ædibus videas, quàm auri, quando ad villam veneris.
units.tr: Now, wherever you go, you see more wagons in the house than gold, when you come to the country villa.

units.la: Sed hoc etiam pulchrum est, pæquam ubi sumtus petunt: Stat fullo, phrygio, aurifex, lunarius, caupones, patagiarij, indusiarij, flammearij, violarij, carinarij, aut mantiliarij, murrobatharij, propolæ, linteones, calceonarij, sedentarij, sutores diabathrarij, solearij astant, astant semizonarij. Petunt fullones sarcinatores petunt, stropharij adstant, astant molochinarij. Jam hoscè absolutos censeas, cedunt, petunt. Trecenti cum stant phylacistæ in atrijs, textores, limborarij, arcularij, ducuntur, datur ės, jamq; hos absolutos censeas, cùm incedunt infectiores crocotarij, aut aliqua mala crux semper est, quæ aliquid petat. Ubi nugigerulis res soluta est omnibus, ibi ad postremum cedit miles, as petit, itur, putatur res cum argentario. Impransus miles astat, as censet dari. Ubi dispuncta est ratio cum argentario, etiam plus ipsius ultrò debet argentario, pro illis crocotis, stropbijs, sumtu uxorio. Spes prorogatur militi in alium diem.
units.tr: But this too is a fine thing, when they demand their expenses: the fuller stands there, the Phrygian embroiderer, the goldsmith, the moon-maker, the innkeepers, the makers of fancy trimmings, the shirt-makers, the makers of flame-coloured cloth, the violet-dyers, the keel-makers, the makers of hand-towels, the linen-workers, the shoemakers, the cobblers, the sitting-shoe makers, the sandal-makers and the half-belt makers stand by, all demanding payment. The fullers and the menders demand, the hairdressers stand by, the makers of mill-lifts stand by. Now you would think these had been paid off; they withdraw, and then they demand again. Three hundred weavers, border-makers and box-makers stand in the courtyards, and are led off; something is given them, and then you would think these too had been paid off, but then come the saffron-dyers, the dyers in pale yellow, and some other wretched cross always stands there to ask for something. When the trinket-bearers have all been settled, then at last the soldier gives way, asks for his penny, is taken off, and the account is reckoned with the banker. The soldier stands there unfed, thinking his penny should be given. When the account with the banker is settled, he even owes the banker more than before, on account of those saffron-dyers, those hairdressers, and the wife's expenses. The soldier's hope is postponed to another day.

units.la: Hæc sunt atque aliæ multæ in magnis dotibus incommoditates, sumtusque intolerabiles. Nam quæ indotata est, ea in potestate est viri. Dotatæ mactant, & malo, & damno viros.
units.tr: These and many other inconveniences, and intolerable expenses, come with large dowries. For a wife without a dowry is under her husband's power. Dowered wives ruin and damage their husbands.

units.la: X Ecce quid fit dotatam ducere. Similem describit Ep. 2.2. v. 41. 42. Tributus, cum imperatum est (wann man soll Schaßung geben) potesse pendi negant, illis quibus tributum major penditur (quales sunt artifices superius recitati) pendi potest. Quot ista, quae vestis quotannis nomina inveniunt nova?
units.tr: Here is what it means to marry a dowered woman. Horace describes a similar case, Ep. 2.2 vv. 41-42: when a tax is levied (when a levy is to be paid), they deny that it can be paid; by those from whom a larger tax is collected (such as the craftsmen mentioned above) it can be paid. How many new names does this clothing find every year?

units.la: Vide totum locum plane practicum, & geminum alteri in Aularia.
units.tr: See the whole passage, which is thoroughly practical, and its twin in the Aulularia.

units.la: Ubi tamen & hoc monebo, apud J Ctos, & in vita communi πα-ραδοξον plane videri, indotatam ducere: longeq; praestabilius esse, feminas esse dotatas: non solum ut viros reperiant: sed etiam, ut una cum liberis ab ijsdem alantur: ad quod merito serviunt fructus dotis: adeoque maritus dicitur decipi, si forte, cum dos ipsi esset promissa, cogatur indotatam habere uxorem. l. 9. si donaturus. §. 1 ff. de conditi caus. dat. Atque hinc non solum feminae interesse, & maxime quidem, ut habeat de dote actionem, scribit Cajus in l. 49. servo legato. §. si testator. 2. ff. de legat. 2. Verum etiam Reip. interesse, aut Paulus: mulieres dotes suas salvas habere. l. 2. ff. de jur. dot. & Pomponius in l. 1. ff. sol. matrim. publice interesse, dotes mulieribus conservari: & maxime necessarium esse, ut dotatae sint feminae ad sobolem procreandam, replendamque liberis civitatem. Mariti vero utilitas in dote versatur: ut tanto leviora ipsi fiant onera matrimonij, dum fructus ex dote percipit.
units.tr: Here I will also point out that among the jurists, and in ordinary life, it seems quite paradoxical to marry an undowered woman. It is far more advantageous for women to be dowered, not only so that they may find husbands, but also so that they may be supported, together with their children, by those husbands, for which purpose the fruits of the dowry rightly serve. Hence a husband is said to be deceived if, when a dowry had been promised to him, he is forced to have an undowered wife. l. 9. si donaturus. §. 1 ff. de conditi caus. dat. And so it concerns not only the woman, and especially so that she may have an action concerning her dowry, as Gaius writes in l. 49. servo legato. §. si testator. 2. ff. de legat. 2. It also concerns the Commonwealth, as Paulus says: that women should have their dowries safe. l. 2. ff. de jur. dot. And Pomponius, in l. 1. ff. sol. matrim., says that it is a public interest that dowries be preserved for women, and that it is most necessary for women to be dowered so that they may bear offspring and fill the state with children. The husband's advantage, however, lies in the dowry: the burdens of marriage become so much lighter for him, while he receives the fruits of the dowry.

units.la: Vide de dotis datione plura apud doctissimum J Ctum Conradum Rittershusium Ad L. xxxiii. de Reg. Jur.
units.tr: On the giving of dowries, see more in the most learned jurist Conrad Rittershusius, on Rule of Law 33.

units.la: Damnosi mariti clam suas uxores solent sibi bona facere: & Genio indulgere. Caf 2.8. v. 30. Men. 1.2. v. 43.
units.tr: Spendthrift husbands commonly make off with goods from their wives in secret and indulge their Genius. Cas. 2.8 v.30. Men. 1.2 v.43.

units.la: Damnosi mariti simulant se adire amicos, cum ad vinum eunt. Asin. 5.2. v. 10.
units.tr: Spendthrift husbands pretend they are going to visit friends when they are going to drink wine. Asin. 5.2 v.10.

units.la: Mariti damnosi velint uxores suas perisse. Caf. 2.6. v. 2. Ille adepol videre ardentem te extra portam Meliam velit. Item Caf. 2.3. v. 1. Uxor me excruciat, quia vivit.
units.tr: Spendthrift husbands wish their wives dead. Cas. 2.6 v.2: "By Pollux, I wish he could see you burning outside the Porta Melia." Likewise Cas. 2.3 v.1: "My wife tortures me because she is alive."

units.la: Mariti damnosi solent negligere familiam suam: & otio illam perdere. (Ury. 4.1. v. 11.)
units.tr: Spendthrift husbands tend to neglect their households and let them go to ruin through idleness. (Ury. 4.1 v.11.)

units.la: MARITI damnosi clam uxòrem alibi excubias solent quærere. Caf. Prol. v.54.
units.tr: Spendthrift husbands commonly look for night-time pleasures elsewhere, without their wives knowing. Cas. Prol. v.54.

units.la: UXORES dotatæ, adeóque moratæ etiam haud æquo animo ferunt maritos prodigos, adulteros: quin & parentibus hanc suam fortem queruntur. Merc. 4.4.v.45. Et Asin. 5.2.v.10.
units.tr: Dowered wives, and therefore spoiled ones, take it ill with good grace when their husbands are prodigal and adulterous, and they even complain of their lot to their parents. Merc. 4.4 v.45. And Asin. 5.2 v.10.

units.la: UXORES probæ per omnia volunt suos viros esse probos. Asin. 5. 2.v.10. Caf. 2.3.v.28. & seqq.
units.tr: Good wives in every respect want their husbands to be good. Asin. 5.2 v.10. Cas. 2.3 v.28 and following.

units.la: Ubi vide quei maritum suum senem excipiat uxor.
units.tr: Here see how a wife receives her husband when he is old.

units.la: UXORES ægrè ferunt, si mariti pellices in ædes introducant. Rud. 4.4.v.3.
units.tr: Wives take it badly when husbands bring their mistresses into the house. Rud. 4.4 v.3.

units.la: DIVORTIUM sine causâ non fiebat facilè. Men. 5.1.v.23.
units.tr: Divorce was not easily granted without cause. Men. 5.1 v.23.

units.la: DIVORTII formula fuit: It foràs mulier. Caf. 2.2.v.36.
units.tr: The formula of divorce was: Out you go, woman. Cas. 2.2 v.36.

units.la: Martial. lib. 11. Epigr. 105.
units.tr: Martial, book 11, epigram 105.

units.la: Uxor vade foras: aut moribus utere nostris.
units.tr: Wife, get out, or live by our customs.

units.la: Juvenal. 6.
units.tr: Juvenal, satire 6.

units.la: Collige sarcinulas, dicit libertus, & exi.
units.tr: "Gather up your little bundles," says the freedman, "and get out."

units.la: Videtiam Brissonij Formulas.
units.tr: See also Brisson's Formulas.

units.la: IN divortijs utebantur hac Formulâ: TIBI HABEAS RES TUAS. Amph. 3.2.v.47. Curc. 1.3.v.22. & Trin. 2.1.v.32.
units.tr: In divorces they used this formula: Take your own things for yourself. Amph. 3.2 v.47. Curc. 1.3 v.22. Trin. 2.1 v.32.

units.la: Vide Leges XII. Tabb. Tit. XVII. & inibi Interpretes Juris. Formulas itcm Brissonij lib. 8. pag. 722. Et Dempsteri Antiqq. lib. 5. c. 38.
units.tr: See the Laws of the Twelve Tables, Title XVII, and the legal commentators there. Likewise Brisson's formulas, book 8, p. 722, and Dempster's Antiquities, book 5, ch. 38.

units.la: REPUDIUM sive divortium fieri nequit, rebus omnibus paratis, atq; exornatis nuptijs. Aul. 4. 10. v. 53.
units.tr: Repudiation or divorce cannot take place once everything is prepared and the wedding is adorned. Aul. 4.10 v.53.

units.la: UXOR dotata, honesta, indicta causâ non poterat repudiari. Asin. 5.2.v.49. Faxo, ut scias, Quid periculi sit dotatæ uxori vitium dicere: h. e. exigere uxorem ædibus, nec causam palàm facere. Sic Merc. 4. 6. v.
units.tr: A dowered, respectable wife could not be repudiated without a stated cause. Asin. 5.2 v.49. "I will make you learn what danger there is for a dowered wife in calling her faulty, that is, in driving a wife out of the house without openly stating a cause." So Merc. 4.6 v.

units.la: UTRUM abscntia mariti aliquot annorum, nempe trium faciat legitimam causam divortij quæstio est apud JCtos. Stich. 1.1.v.25. 44. Vide Fr. Hottomann. De ritu Nupt. c. 24.
units.tr: Whether the absence of a husband for some years, namely three, makes a lawful ground for divorce, is a question among the jurists. Stich. 1.1 vv. 25, 44. See Fr. Hottoman, De ritu nuptiarum, ch. 24.

units.la: CONSCIENTIÆ.
units.tr: CONSCIENCE.

units.la: NIHIL est miserius, quàm animus hominis conscius. Mostell. 3. I. v. 13.
units.tr: NOTHING is more wretched than a human mind that is conscious of itself. Mostell. 3. I. v. 13.

units.la: Sallustius:
units.tr: Sallust:

units.la: Suum cuique animus ex conscientia spem prabet.
units.tr: Each man's mind gives him hope from his own conscience.

units.la: August. lib. 21. de Civ. Dei.
units.tr: Augustine, book 21, On the City of God.

units.la: Tranquillitate conscientiæ nihil excogitari quietius potest.
units.tr: Nothing can be imagined more quiet than the tranquillity of conscience.

units.la: Cicero pro Mil.
units.tr: Cicero, For Milo.

units.la: Magna vis est conscientiæ, Iudices, & magna in utramq; partem: ut neque timeant, qui nihil commiserunt, & poenam semper ante oculos versari putent, qui peccaverunt.
units.tr: Great is the power of conscience, judges, and great in either direction: so that those who have committed nothing do not fear, and those who have sinned think punishment always stands before their eyes.

units.la: Idem pro S. Rosc. Amer.
units.tr: The same, For S. Roscius Amerinus.

units.la: Sua quemq; fraus, & suus terror maximè vexat: suum quemq; scelus, amentiaq; afficit: suæ malæ cogitationes, conscientiaq; animi terrent. has sunt impiis assiduæ, domesticæq; Furiæ.
units.tr: Each man's own deceit and own terror torment him most; each man's own crime and madness afflict him; his own evil thoughts and the conscience of his mind frighten him. These are the constant and domestic Furies of the impious.

units.la: Videetiam Orat pro Sextio.
units.tr: See also the speech For Sextius.

units.la: Ovid lib. 1. Fast.
units.tr: Ovid, book 1, Fasti.

units.la: Conscia mens, ut cuiq; sua est, ita concipit intra Pectora, pro facto spemq; metumq; suo.
units.tr: The conscious mind, as each man's own is, so conceives within its breast, according to its deed, both hope and fear.

units.la: Qui sibi male conscij sunt, & qui culpam commeruerunt, turbare student, & res novas quærunt, & belli cupidiores sunt, quam pacis atq; otij. Most. 3. I. v. 15.
units.tr: Those who are badly conscious of themselves, and who have deserved blame, strive to create disturbance, seek new things, and are more eager for war than for peace and leisure. Most. 3. I. v. 15.

units.la: Exemplo fuit Pericles, qui cùm pecuniam publicam tractasset, eamque consumsisset, & conjecisset in propylæa illa præclara, & nominatissima, neque satis commodè se tantarum impensarum rationem referre posse videret: quo pacto rationem non referret potius, quàm quomodo referret, sibi videndum esse existimavit: atque ita bellum grave, magnum & difficile excitavit. q & nostrâ ætate à quibusdam ob eandem causam & eo dem consi- lio factum esse notissimum est.
units.tr: Pericles was an example. When he had handled public money and used it up, and had put it into those famous and renowned Propylaea, and saw that he could not give a sufficiently fitting account of such great expenses, he judged that he had to consider, not how to render the account, but how not to render it; and so he stirred up a serious, great and difficult war. It is very well known that in our own age, for the same reason and with the same purpose, something similar has been done by some people.

units.la: Cæterùm de stimulis malæ conscientiæ vide Bernartium ad Sta- tium Papinium : ut & Discursus politicos Gruteri ad Tacitum : nec non Commentarium nostrum ad Orationem Ciceronis pro Roscio Amerino.
units.tr: Concerning the goads of a bad conscience, see Bernartius on Statius Papinius, as well as Gruter's Political Discourses on Tacitus, and also our own commentary on Cicero's speech For Roscius Amerinus.

units.la: Semper cavere hoc sapientes aquissimum est, ne conscij sint ipsi maleficij sui. Red. 4. 7. v. 20.
units.tr: Wise men should always take the greatest care that they themselves are not conscious of their own wrongdoing. Red. 4. 7. v. 20.

units.la: Male conscij somniabant se teneri tædis Furiarum ardentibus. Men. 5. 2. v. 89.
units.tr: Those who were badly conscious dreamed that they were seized by the blazing torches of the Furies. Men. 5. 2. v. 89.

units.la: Consiliorum. Deliberationis. Prudentiæ.
units.tr: Counsels. Deliberation. Prudence.

units.la: Vide etiam Actionum.
units.tr: See also Actions.

units.la: CONSILIA non revelanda inimicis. Nam bonum consilium surripiuntur tibi sapissime, si minus cum curâ aut cauté locu loquendi lestus est. h. e. immunis ab arbitris ad decernendum.
units.tr: Counsels are not to be revealed to enemies. For a good plan is very often stolen from you, if one is not careful about it, or is not cautious about the place where he speaks, and so is not free from listeners when deciding.

units.la: Tum bene consultum, inconsultum est, si inimicis sit usui. Neq; potest, quin si id inimicis sui est, obsit tibi. Quippe si resciverint inimici consilium tuum, Quoque tibi consilio occludunt lu guam, & constringunt manus. Atque eadem quæ illi voluisti facere, faciunt tibi.
units.tr: A plan that is well considered becomes ill considered if it serves your enemies. Nor can it be that, if it is to their advantage, it does not harm you. Indeed, if enemies learn your plan, they close your mouth with your own counsel and bind your hands. And they do to you the very things you wanted to do to them.

units.la: Sero atque stultè, prius quod cautum oportuit, postquam com- edit rem, post rationem putat. Trin. 2. 4. v. 14.
units.tr: Too late and foolishly, a man thinks about what he should have guarded against first, after the thing has been eaten up. Trin. 2. 4. v. 14.

units.la: Consilia sedendo firmius concipiuntur. Most. 5. 1 v. 55.
units.tr: Plans are formed more firmly when we deliberate sitting down. Most. 5. 1 v. 55.

units.la: Consilii siliorum non semper resistere debent parentes. Trin. 2. 3. v. 4. Vide Tit. Parentum.
units.tr: Parents should not always resist the counsels of their children. Trin. 2. 3. v. 4. See the title Parents.

units.la: Ego o multos sæpè vidi Regionem fugere consilij, priusquam com- pertam haberent. Mil. 3. 3. v.12.
units.tr: Oh, I have often seen many men flee from a plan before they had found it out. Mil. 3. 3. v. 12.

units.la: Bene ubi quod consilium rescimus cccidisse, hominem cautum e- um esse declaramus: siultum autem illum, cui vertit male. Pseu. 2.3 v.15. Sic Plinius lib.5. Epist.21.
units.tr: Well, when we learn that a plan we devised has turned out well, we declare the man prudent; but the one for whom it turned out badly, we declare foolish. Pseud. 2. 3 v. 15. So Pliny, book 5, letter 21.

units.la: Est omnino iniquum, sed usu receptum, quod honesta consilia, vel turpia, prout male aut prosperè cedunt, ita vel probantur: vel re- prehenduntur.
units.tr: It is altogether unfair, yet customary, that honourable plans or shameful ones are approved or condemned according as they turn out badly or well.

units.la: Inde plærumque eadem facta modò diligentiæ, modò vanitatis, modò furoris nomen accipiunt.
units.tr: Hence the same deeds often receive now the name of diligence, now of vanity, now of madness.

units.la: Utriusq; rei documentum. Hinc Catti fuerint nobis, atqe inde Cherusci: de quorum dispari successu vide Tacit. in lib. de mo- ribus Germanorum.
units.tr: Proof of both: the Catti were hostile to us, and from there the Cherusci; on their unequal success see Tacitus in his book on the customs of the Germans.

units.la: Cicero pro Rabir.
units.tr: Cicero, Pro Rabirio.

units.la: Hoc plærumq; facimus, ut consilia eventus ponderemus: & cui be- ne quid processerit, multum illum providisse: cui secus, nihil sensisse dicamus.
units.tr: We generally do this: we weigh plans by their outcome, and we say that the one for whom something has gone well foresaw much, and the one for whom it went otherwise perceived nothing.

units.la: Idem ad Atticum lib. 9. Epist.10.
units.tr: The same, to Atticus, book 9, letter 10.

units.la: Etiam amplissimorum virorum consilia ex eventu non ex volun- tate à pluribus probari solent.
units.tr: Even the plans of the most distinguished men are usually approved by most people according to the outcome, not according to the intention.

units.la: Vide etiam Sallust. de Rep. ordinand. ad Cæsarem.
units.tr: See also Sallust, on ordering the state, addressed to Caesar.

units.la: Et hoc prudentiæ est, ut proximis ac certis utamur, relictis incer- tis. Certa enim amittimus, dum incerta petimus: atque hoc e- venit in labore, atq; in dolore, ut mors obrepat interim. Pseud. 2.3. v.19.
units.tr: And it is a mark of prudence to use what is near and certain, and leave aside what is uncertain. For we lose certain things while we seek uncertain ones; and this happens in toil and in grief, so that death creeps in meanwhile. Pseud. 2. 3. v. 19.

units.la: Vide Adagiorum Volum. col. 1545. Edit. Wech.
units.tr: See the Adagia, volume, column 1545, Wechel edition.

units.la: Consolationis.
units.tr: Consolation.

units.la: Consolantur se improbi juxta & probi societate malo-rum. Epid. i. i. v. 70. Solus perire nolo.
units.tr: The wicked console themselves, and the good too, with the company of evils. Epid. 1. 1. v. 70. I alone do not want to perish.

units.la: Symmachus lib. 9. Ep. 27.
units.tr: Symmachus, book 9, letter 27.

units.la: Et illa quidem adversa, quae cum pluribus pertulisti humani inge-nij haberi aliquid de societate solatium.
units.tr: And indeed, those adversities which you have borne along with many others, there is some comfort in the nature of man from sharing them.

units.la: Chrysost. Homil. 10. in 1. ad Timoth.
units.tr: Chrysostom, Homily 10 on 1 Timothy.

units.la: παραμυθίαν φέρει τὸ κοινωνὸς εἶναι τῶν συμφορῶν.
units.tr: Sharing in misfortunes brings consolation. [παραμυθίαν φέρει τὸ κοινωνὸς εἶναι τῶν συμφορῶν.]

units.la: Vide Rittershus. ad Guntherum.
units.tr: See Rittershus on Gunther.

units.la: χάρμα φέρει δειλοῖς ἀν ποιηῆς χρῶσιν ἐταίρευσι.
units.tr: It brings joy to cowards when they have comrades to share with. [χάρμα φέρει δειλοῖς ἀν ποιηῆς χρῶσιν ἐταίρευσι.]

units.la: Consolatio tutissima petitur à providentiâ Dei. Baccb. 4. 3. v. 24. Deus nos aliquis respicit.
units.tr: The surest consolation is sought from the providence of God. Bacch. 4. 3. v. 24. Some god looks upon us.

units.la: Constantiæ. Patientiæ.
units.tr: Constancy. Patience.

units.la: Ista virtus est, quando usus est, qui malum fert fortiter. Forti-ter malum qui patitur, idem post patitur bonum. Asin. 2. 2. v. 58.
units.tr: This is virtue, when it is exercised: he who bears evil bravely. He who suffers evil bravely afterwards also bears good. Asin. 2. 2. v. 58.

units.la: Cicero Philippica 11.
units.tr: Cicero, Philippics 11.

units.la: Sapientis est, quicquid homini accidere possit, id praemeditari fe-rendum modicè esse, si advenerit. Majoris omninò est consilij providere ne quid tale accidat: sed animi non minoris fortiter ferre, si venerit.
units.tr: It is the mark of a wise man to think beforehand about whatever can happen to a man, and to bear it moderately if it comes. It is certainly the mark of great counsel to foresee that nothing of the kind happens; but of no less a spirit to bear it bravely if it does come.

units.la: Pittacus: σωφρῶν ἀνδρῶν ἐστὶ πρὶν γενέσθαι τὰ δυσχερῆ, σφεσοῦσθαι, μὴ γίνεται· ἀνδρείων δὲ, γενόμενα εὖ φέρειν. Intelligentium est viro-rum, priusquam eveniunt incommoda, providere ne eveniant: Si evenerint, compositè & moderatè ferre.
units.tr: Pittacus: It is the mark of prudent men to foresee, before difficulties arise, that they do not arise; and of brave men, when they have arisen, to bear them well. [σωφρῶν ἀνδρῶν ἐστὶ πρὶν γενέσθαι τὰ δυσχερῆ, σφεσοῦσθαι, μὴ γίνεται· ἀνδρείων δὲ, γενόμενα εὖ φέρειν.] Intelligent men, before misfortunes happen, foresee that they will not happen; if they do happen, they bear them calmly and moderately.

units.la: CONSUETUDINIS. MORIS.
units.tr: CUSTOM. HABIT.

units.la: CONSUETUDINIS maxima vis: per quam habitum acquiri- mus cujuscunque rei. Marc. 5. 4. v. 41. Consuetudine rursus te animus huc inducet.
units.tr: The power of custom is very great: through it we acquire a habit of whatever thing we like. Marc. 5. 4. v. 41. Consuetudine rursus te animus huc inducet.

units.la: CONTAGII. PESTIS.
units.tr: CONTAGION. PLAGUE.

units.la: CONTAGIONE nocet, quod ab uno ad alium transit. Sic Mercurius se metuere dicit, co quod & pater ejus Jupiter metuat. Amph. Prol. v. 31.
units.tr: Harm comes by contagion, which passes from one to another. So Mercury says he fears, because his father Jupiter fears. Amph. Prol. v. 31.

units.la: Contagione mei patris metuo malum.
units.tr: I fear the evil from my father's contagion.

units.la: CONVIVII. TRICLINII. MENSARUM. POTUS. POTIONIS. CIBORUM. VICTUS. DIAETAE. CAENAE. PRANDII. LECTORUM. EPULARUM. COMMISSATIONUM. LIBATIONUM. JENTACULI. PANIS. OBSONIORUM. ESCARUM, AQUAE. LEGUMINUM. HILARITATIS. LAETITIAE.
units.tr: BANQUET. DINING-ROOM COUCH. TABLES. DRINK. DRAUGHT. FOOD. FARE. DIET. DINNER. LUNCHEON. COUCHES. FEASTS. REVELRY. LIBATIONS. BREAKFAST. BREAD. DELICACIES. DISHES, WATER. PULSE. MIRTH. GLADNESS.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Coquorum. & Tit. Ebrietatis pluscula.
units.tr: See also the title Cooks, and the several passages under the title Drunkenness.

units.la: FECUNDUS omninò, & uber est hic Locus Antiquitatis Romanæ, si quisquam. De eo non pauci viri docti scripserunt eruditè, & prolixè. Inter quos merito palmam obtinet Joh. Guilhelmus Stuckius Tigurinus, nobilis Theologus pariter & Philologus, non tàm frigidus Criticus: uti quidem arbitratur Thomas Dempsterus: qui ipse quàm caleat, nescio. Prodidit & multa primus litteratissimus Lipsius lib.3. Antiquarum Lectionum, quem quasi proprium destinavit huic loco. Eum secutus est Petrus Ciacconius Toletanus: cui Appendicem adjecit Fulvius Ursinus. Horum ego industriam hic compilare non constitui: sed ea duntaxat ex proprio nostro instituto huc conijcere, quæ ipse de hoc Romanorum more observavi ex PLAUTO nostro, cui soli nunc operam damus illustrando, in hoc volumine. Ea autem omnia in quatuor classes commodè distribuemus: in quarum PRIORE colligemus RITUS Accumbendi in Triclinijs. ALTERA continebit rationem VICTUS, & Ciborum. TERTIA Potûs, & Bibendi leges recitabit. QUARTA & ultima Ethicas & Oeconomicas doctrinas circa rationem convivandi describet.
units.tr: This topic is altogether rich and fruitful in Roman antiquity, if any is. Not a few learned men have written about it, learnedly and at length. Among them, the palm rightly belongs to Johann Wilhelm Stuck of Zurich, a noble theologian and philologist alike, not so much a cold critic, as Thomas Dempster thinks (though how warm he himself was I do not know). The most learned Lipsius also set out much in the third book of his Antiquarum Lectionum, which he designed as belonging especially to this place. Petrus Ciacconius of Toledo followed him, and Fulvius Ursinus added an appendix to him. I have not undertaken to compile their diligence here; but, from our own plan, I will throw in only those things which I myself have observed about this Roman custom from our PLAUTUS, whom alone we now labour to illustrate in this volume. All of these I will distribute conveniently into four classes: in the FIRST I will gather the RITES of reclining at the dining-couches; the SECOND will contain the system of FOOD and dishes; the THIRD will set out the laws of drink and drinking; the FOURTH and last will describe the ethical and domestic teachings concerning the manner of entertaining.

units.la: I. RITVS TRICLINII Romani.
units.tr: I. The Roman Triclinium Ritual

units.la: ROMANI Locum, in quo cœnabant, vocabant Cænaculum, teste Varrone lib. 4. L. L. sive Cœnationem, ut author est Seneca Epist. 90. & Suetonius in Nerone. In illâ cœnatione Lecti erant strati duo, vel tres. A duobus lectisternium dicebatur Biclinium: in quo plærumque amatores reclinabant: aut accumbebant; ut patet ex Bacch. 4.4.v.69. Ubi est Biclinium vobis strat um ? & ibid. v.102. Iam facite in biclinio: cum amica sua accumbitum eatis ita negotium est: atq; ibidem, ubi nunc sunt lecti strati potetis cito.
units.tr: The Romans called the room in which they dined the Cænaculum, as Varro says in Book 4 of the De Lingua Latina, or the Cœnatio, as Seneca in Letter 90 and Suetonius in his life of Nero report. In such a dining room there were two or three couches spread. A couch-arrangement for two was called a Biclinium, and on it lovers commonly reclined or reclined together. This is clear from Bacch. 4.4, v. 69: Where is the biclinium spread for you? and v. 102, ibid.: Now go and make the biclinium ready; with your sweetheart you are to recline; that is the arrangement: and right there, where the couches are now spread, drink quickly.

units.la: Ut plurimum autem Tres lecti strati: ut solemne est apud omnes Authores Triclinium. Cujus qualis fuerit forma, explicant Authores prius nominati: inprimis Fulvius Ursinus è marmoribus formam Triclinij promit: qualem & videas apud Hieron. Mercurialem. Nec possum, quin & ipse χ quoddam solidi filo elaboratum huc depingam: quo aliquo modo saltim repræsentem accubitionem & distinctionem lectorum. Illud igitur ecce quale sit.
units.tr: Usually, however, three couches were spread, and this is the usual term in all the authors, the Triclinium. The authors named above explain what its shape was. Above all, Fulvius Ursinus draws the form of the triclinium from marble reliefs, and you may see it also in Hieronymus Mercurialis. Nor can I refrain from sketching here myself a figure in the shape of a chi [χ], made with a solid line, by which I may at least in some measure represent the reclining and the arrangement of the couches. Here, then, is what it looks like.

units.la: SCHEMA TRICLINII Romani.
units.tr: The Diagram of the Roman Dining Couch (Triclinium).

units.la: VETE-
units.tr: THE ANCIENT

units.la: TRICLINIVM ROMANORVM.
units.tr: THE ROMAN DINING-ROOM.

units.la: Hinc Architriclinus apud Joan. cap. 2. v. 8.
units.tr: Hence Architriclinus, in John 2:8.

units.la: Refer ad pag. 170.
units.tr: See p. 170.

units.la: **** Hinc porrigebantur pedes.
units.tr: **** Hence the feet were stretched out.

units.la: Secunda seu media cline vel lectus.
units.tr: The second or middle couch or bed.

units.la: Hic stabant mensae ab orâ.
units.tr: Here the tables stood along the edge.

units.la: Hic versabantur Dapiferi, Pincernae, Psaltriae, Gelotopoei. Quidam, apud Plutarchum, ex convivis seu discumbentibus, jubet hinc discedere famulos, ut possit omnes convivas adspicere.
units.tr: Here the carvers, cupbearers, harpists and jesters moved about. In Plutarch someone orders the servants to withdraw from among the diners, so that he can see all the guests.

units.la: Hic stabant mensae ab orâ.
units.tr: Here the tables stood along the edge.

units.la: Eerni jacebant (apud Rom) in lectulis, secundum Horat. l.1. satyr. 4. & Juvenalem Satyr. 5.
units.tr: The Eerni reclined (among the Romans) on little couches, according to Horace, Satires 1.4, and Juvenal, Satire 5.

units.la: Lycurgus sanxit, ut in convivijs discumbentes subijcerent cubita, aut cavum lapidem, aut lignum. Suid.
units.tr: Lycurgus ordained that those reclining at banquets should prop themselves on the elbow, or on a hollowed stone, or on wood. Suidas.

units.la: Asinus Lucianicus accumbit ... Plutarch.
units.tr: Lucian's ass reclines... Plutarch.

units.la: Esth. 7. v. 8. Amanus supplicat Reginae super lectulo discubitorio.
units.tr: Esther 7:8. Haman begs the queen while lying on the couch where she reclined.

units.la: Luc Æ. 7. v. 38. Mulier peccatrix lavat pedes Domini stans. Ergò fuerunt sublimes; stans retrò. Ergò fuerunt porrecti in diversum à mensâ.
units.tr: Luke 7:38. The sinful woman washes the Lord's feet while standing. Therefore they reclined raised up; she stood behind. Therefore they were stretched out lengthwise, away from the table.

units.la: Joan. 13. v. 23. Recumbit in sinu Domini Discipulus quem diligebat. Unde intelligere licet, quàm incptè atq; impe- ritè Pictores depingant Johannem capite involutum in sinu Domini Jesu Christi.
units.tr: John 13:23. The disciple whom he loved reclined in the bosom of the Lord. From this one may understand how foolishly and unskilfully painters depict John with his head resting in the bosom of the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Zeno apud Diogenem Laertium cùm videret proximum apud se cubantem impellere inferiorem pede, impellit ipse hunc genu, ut quiesceat. Ergò itâ cubabant.
units.tr: Zeno, in Diogenes Laertius, when he saw his neighbour reclining beside him kicking the man below with his foot, pushed him with his knee to make him keep still. Therefore they reclined in this way.

units.la: Cicero lib. 9. Epist. ultimâ. Accubueram horâ nonâ, suprà me Atticus, infrà Verrius.
units.tr: Cicero, Letters to Friends (or to Atticus), book 9, last letter: "I had reclined at the ninth hour, Atticus above me, Verrius below."

units.la: Alexander jentabat sedens, coenabat cubans. Plutar.
units.tr: Alexander ate sitting, but dined reclining. Plutarch.

units.la: Cato post motum bellum civile semper sedens coenabat. Plutarch.
units.tr: Cato, after the civil war broke out, always dined sitting. Plutarch.

units.la: Martial. lib. 5. Omnia cum retro pueris obsonia tradas, Cur non mensa tibi ponitur ante pedes?
units.tr: Martial, book 5: "Since you hand all the delicacies back to the boys, why is no table set before your feet?"

units.la: Idem lib. 12. Bis Cottasoleas perdidisse se questus Dum negligentem ducit ad pedes vernam.
units.tr: Martial, book 12: Cotta complained that he had twice lost his sandals while the careless slave was led off by the feet.

units.la: Ovid. Metam. lib. 8. de Philemone & Baucide: in medio torus est de mollibus ulvis Impositus lecto, spondâ pedibusq; saligna Vestibus hunc velant, quas non nisi tempore festo, Accubuêre Dei. &c.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses book 8, on Philemon and Baucis: "In the middle is a couch of soft rushes, set upon a bed, with a frame and legs of willow; they cover it with cloths, which the gods reclined on only on festal days..." etc.

units.la: Hinc quoq; intelligitur, quid Luc. 22. v. 12. ἀνάγεον ἐστρωμένον, nempe coenaculum Lectis discubitorijs instructum.
units.tr: Hence it is also understood what Luke 22:12 means: anagaion estrōmenon [ἀνάγεον ἐστρωμένον], namely an upper room furnished with couches for reclining.

units.la: Hinc porrigebantur pedes. Tertia cline seu lectus. Hic 12. viri jacent cum sponsò medium locum tenente: apud Lucianum Lapith.
units.tr: Hence the feet were stretched out. Third couch or bed. Here twelve men recline, with the host occupying the middle place: in Lucian's Lapithae.

units.la: Prima cline seu lectus, sed non bonestus. Hinc porrigebantur pedes. Post lectos fuerunt spatia, unde per scabella ascendebant et cos, & ubi samuli servabant soleas vel calceos.
units.tr: First couch or bed, but not the most honoured. Hence the feet were stretched out. Behind the couches were spaces by which they climbed up onto the couches by footstools, and where the attendants kept the sandals or shoes.

units.la: VETERES autem Romani in Convivijs seu Triclinijs initiò non accumbebant, sed sedebant ad mensam, ut hodiè dum plæraque gentes. Sic Homerus Heroas suos, & procos Penelopes sedentes facit in convivio: & Catullus in Nuptijs Pelei. Servii item, & sordidi interdum Philosophi Cynici ad mensam non accumbebant: de quibus Plautus Stich. 5.4.v.21.
units.tr: The ancient Romans, however, did not at first recline at banquets or in dining-rooms, but sat at the table, as most nations still do today. So Homer makes his heroes, and Penelope's suitors, sit at the feast; and Catullus does so at the wedding of Peleus. Likewise servants, and sometimes filthy Cynic philosophers, did not recline at table: of whom Plautus says (Stichus 5.4 v. 21):

units.la: Potius in subsellio Cynicè accipiemur: quàm in lectis.
units.tr: I shall rather be received on a stool in the Cynic manner than on the couches.

units.la: Sic Tacitus lib. 13. Annal.
units.tr: So Tacitus, Annals book 13:

units.la: Mos habebatur Principum liberos sedentes vesci in aspectum propinquorum propriâ & parciore mensâ.
units.tr: It was the custom for the children of princes to eat sitting, in sight of their relatives, at a separate and more frugal table.

units.la: INPRIMIS verò in mulieribus, etiam posteris temporibus apud Romanos non minùs, quàm apud Græcos, turpis semper visus accubitus: quod patet ex illo loco Amph. 2. 2. v. 174. ubi Alcumena cum Jove in eodem lecto accumbens, sic reprehenditur à Sofia:
units.tr: Especially for women, even in later times among the Romans no less than among the Greeks, reclining was always regarded as shameful. This is clear from that passage in Amphitryon 2.2 v. 174, where Alcmena, reclining with Jove on the same couch, is rebuked by Sosia:

units.la: ALC. Cena apposita est: cenavisti mecum, ego accubui si-
units.tr: ALC. Dinner was served; you dined with me, I reclined—

units.la: AM. In eodem lecto? AL. In eodem. SOS.
units.tr: AM. On the same couch? AL. On the same. SOS.

units.la: Heu! non placet convivium.
units.tr: Alas! I do not like such a banquet.

units.la: Apud eundem nostrum Bacch. 4.4. v.103. & 4.8. v.18. Bacchidedes fororesin eodem cum amatoribus cænitant lecto.
units.tr: In the same author, Bacchides 4.4 v. 103 and 4.8 v. 18, the Bacchis sisters dine on the same couch as their lovers.

units.la: Probrosum autem id fuisse, etiam patet ex Cicerone in Verr. Accuf. 1.
units.tr: That this was disgraceful is also clear from Cicero, Verrine Orations, first speech:

units.la: Posteaquam satis calere ero Rubrio visa est: Quaeso, inquit, Philodame, cur ad nos intra filiam tuam non vocari jubes? homo, qui summa gravitate, & jam id ætatis, & parens esset, obstrepuit hominis improbo dicto. Instare Rubrius: tum ille, ut aliquid respondéret, negavit mores esse Græcorum, ut in convivio virorum accumberent mulieres. Hic tum alius ex alia parte: Enimvero ferendum hoc non est: vocetur mulier, & simul servis suis Rubrius, ut januam clauderent, & ipsi ad fores assisterent, imperat:
units.tr: When the wine seemed warm enough to Rubrius, "I ask you, Philodamus," he said, "why do you not order your daughter to be called in to us?" That man, who was of the greatest dignity, already of that age, and a parent, cried out against the wicked proposal of the fellow. Rubrius pressed on. Then the other, in order to answer something, said that it was not the custom of the Greeks for women to recline at a banquet of men. Then someone else from another side: "Indeed this cannot be endured; let the woman be summoned." And at the same time Rubrius orders his slaves

units.la: quod res assisterent, imperat: quod ubi ille intellexit, id agi, atque id parari, ut filia sua vis adferretur, servos suos ad se vocat: his imperat, ut ipsum negligant, filiam defendant.
units.tr: to shut the door and to station themselves at the doors. When Philodamus understood that this was being done and arranged, that violence was to be brought upon his daughter, he called his own slaves to himself and ordered them to disregard him and defend the daughter.

units.la: Eò quoque allusit Terentius Eunuch. 4. 1. ubi cum Thraso introduci jussisset Pamphilam, indignata Thais: Minimè, inquit, gentium. In convivium tu illam?
units.tr: Terence also alluded to this in Eunuchus 4.1, where, when Thraso had ordered Pamphila to be brought in, Thais indignantly said: "By no means, of all people! Would you bring her in to the dinner?"

units.la: Idem patet ex verbis Varronis Agath. apud Nonium voce Acerbum.
units.tr: The same is clear from the words of Varro's Agathon, cited by Nonius under the word Acerbum:

units.la: Virgo de convivio abdicaturideò, quod majores nostri virginis acerba aures Veneris vocabulis imbui noluerunt.
units.tr: A virgin is to be excluded from the banquet, because our ancestors did not want the bitter ears of a virgin to be steeped in the words of Venus.

units.la: Sic Ifaeus Orator nobilis in Oratione: quâ de Pyrrhi cujusdam hæreditate contenditur:
units.tr: So Isaeus, the noted orator, in the speech in which the inheritance of a certain Pyrrhus is disputed:

units.la: Καὶ τοὶ οὐδ᾽ πτυχα ὅτι γαμετὰς γυναῖκας οὐδεὶς ἂν κομίζειν τολμήσειεν, ἢ δὲ αἱ γαμεταὶ γυναῖκες ἐρχονται μετὰ τῶν ἀνδρῶν ὅτι τὰ δέιπνα, ἢ συνδειπνεῖν ἀξιοῦσι μετὰ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων, ἢ ταῦτα μετὰ τῶν ὀπτυχόντων.
units.tr: Translation: "For no one would dare to bring lawful wives to men's dinners; and lawful wives go with their husbands to dinners, or expect to dine with strangers, or they dine with those who are not their own." [Καὶ τοὶ οὐδ᾽ πτυχα ὅτι γαμετὰς γυναῖκας οὐδεὶς ἂν κομίζειν τολμήσειεν, ἢ δὲ αἱ γαμεταὶ γυναῖκες ἐρχονται μετὰ τῶν ἀνδρῶν ὅτι τὰ δέιπνα, ἢ συνδειπνεῖν ἀξιοῦσι μετὰ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων, ἢ ταῦτα μετὰ τῶν ὀπτυχόντων.]

units.la: Posterioribus tamen temporibus etiam feminæ unà accumbebant, & gremijs maritorum suorum inhærebant. Valerius Max. lib. 2. c. 1.
units.tr: In later times, however, women too reclined together with the men and leaned against their husbands' laps. Valerius Maximus, book 2, ch. 1.

units.la: Feminæ cum viris cubantibus sedentes canitabant: quæ consuetudo ex hominum convictu ad divina penetravit.
units.tr: Women, sitting while the men were reclining, sang; a custom which passed from human company into divine worship.

units.la: Cicero ad Attic. lib. 5. Ep. 1.
units.tr: Cicero, to Atticus, book 5, letter 1.

units.la: Sed prandimus in arcano, nostri hunc fundum, quò ut venimus, humanissimè Quinctius: Pomponia, inquit, tu invita mulieres, ego viros accivero.
units.tr: But we dined in a private place, at our estate, to which Quinctius, most courteously, brought us as soon as we arrived: "Pomponia," he said, "you invite the women, I shall summon the men."

units.la: Viros autem, quod initio cæperam dicere, longissimo tempore apud Romanos mensis assedisse tantum, non autem accubuisse in lectis, id verò ex multis Authoribus discimus.
units.tr: That for a very long time among the Romans men only sat at the tables and did not recline on couches, as I began to say, we learn from many authors.

units.la: Sic Virgilius lib. v 11. ubi de Pici Regiâ loquitur: Hoc illu Curia templum, Hæc sacris sedes epulis: hic arjete cæso Perpetim soliti patres consedere mensis.
units.tr: So Virgil, lib. v 11, where he speaks of the royal house of Picus: "This the temple of the Curia, this the seat of sacred feasts; here, the doorposts struck, the fathers were accustomed always to sit down at the tables."

units.la: Ubi Servius: Majores enim nostri sedentes epulabantur, quem morem morem habuerunt à Laconibus & Cretenses: ut Varro docet in libris De gente populi Romani, in quibus docet, quid à quâq; traxerit gente.
units.tr: Where Servius says: "For our ancestors feasted sitting, a custom which the Romans had from the Laconians and Cretans, as Varro teaches in his books On the Race of the Roman People, in which he shows what they derived from each race."

units.la: Διὰ φέρεας ajunt illos libros vocatos.
units.tr: They say these books are called Dia phereas [Διὰ φέρεας].

units.la: Juvenalis: —— ingens Cana sedet ——
units.tr: Juvenal: "...a great grey-haired man sits..."

units.la: Stantes autem prandisse constat ex hoc Afranij Fratrijs:
units.tr: That they dined standing is clear from this line of Afranius' Brothers:

units.la: Equidem prandere stantem nobiscum incinctam togâ.
units.tr: Indeed I dine standing with us, with my toga girded up.

units.la: Ubi male apud Nonium:
units.tr: Where Nonius wrongly has:

units.la: Incincta toga.
units.tr: Incincta toga.

units.la: Dehinc in lectis stratis accumbebant, coibant, epulabantur: quemadmodum etiamnum plaræque gentes in Oriente.
units.tr: Afterwards they reclined on spread couches, gathered together, and feasted, just as many nations in the East still do.

units.la: DICEBANTUR etiam in Triclinijs decumbere; non tantum discumbere. Asin. 5. I. V. I.
units.tr: In dining-rooms they were also said decumbere (to lie down), not only discumbere. Asinaria 5.1 v. 1.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut. nostrum contra vanitatem distinctionis, quam facit Acron ad Od. 27. lib. 1. Horat. inter Accumbere: quod sit Deorum: Discumbere: quod hominum: Recumbere: quod ferarum.
units.tr: See our Plautus Lexicon, against the vanity of the distinction Acron makes on Horace, Odes 1.27, between accumbere, said of gods; discumbere, said of men; and recumbere, said of wild beasts.

units.la: Exempla enim docent passim inter se permutari haec verba.
units.tr: For examples show everywhere that these verbs are used interchangeably.

units.la: LECTOS tàm cubiculares, quàm triclinares habebant ex ebore factos: cósq; ex Asiâ aut aliunde allatos. Stich. 2. 3. V. 52.
units.tr: They had couches, both for bedrooms and for dining-rooms, made of ivory, and brought from Asia or elsewhere. Stichus 2.3 v. 52.

units.la: Varro;
units.tr: Varro:

units.la: Cum in eborato lecto ac purpurei operis thoro cubare videas aegrotum.
units.tr: When you see a sick man lying on an ivory couch and a mattress of purple work.

units.la: Propert. lib. 2. Eleg. 10.
units.tr: Propertius, book 2, elegy 10.

units.la: Necmihi tunc fulcro sternatur lectus eburno:
units.tr: Nor let a couch be spread for me then with an ivory support,

units.la: Nec sit in Attalico mors mea nixa thoro.
units.tr: nor let my death lean upon an Attalic cushion.

units.la: Catullus Carm. 57.
units.tr: Catullus, poem 57.

units.la: O cubile, quot (o nimis Candido pede lectuli:)
units.tr: O couch, how many (O couches with feet too white!)...

units.la: Y 3
units.tr: Y 3

units.la: In Triclinijs magno luxo ostentabant aulæa, tapetia, peristromat, peregrina, Alexandrina, Persica, Babylonica. Stich. 2.3.v.53.
units.tr: In dining-rooms they displayed, with great luxury, hangings, carpets, coverlets, foreign ones: Alexandrian, Persian, Babylonian. Stichus 2.3 v. 53.

units.la: Lectos eburatos, auratos: accubabo regie. Tum Babylonica peri-stromata, solla, & tapetia advexit nimium bona rei ex Asia.
units.tr: Couches inlaid with ivory and gold: I shall recline like a king. Then he brought in Babylonian peristromata, rugs, and tapestries, very fine goods from Asia.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Vestium, Tapetiorum.
units.tr: See also the entry Vestium, Tapetiorum.

units.la: Mensas detergebant penicillis. Men.1.1.v.2. Rud.4.3.v.69.
units.tr: They wiped the tables with cloths. Men. 1.1 v.2. Rud. 4.3 v.69.

units.la: In triclinijs decumbebant unà cum pedibus. Curc.2.3.v.82.
units.tr: In the dining rooms they reclined with their feet and all. Curc. 2.3 v.82.

units.la: Accubituri deposuerunt pallia & annulos signatorios. Curc. 2.3.v.77.
units.tr: Those about to recline laid aside their cloaks and signet rings. Curc. 2.3 v.77.

units.la: Accubituri calceos & soccos deposebant. Most. 2.1.v.37.
units.tr: Those about to recline took off their shoes and sandals. Most. 2.1 v.37.

units.la: Vide Cicer. de Triclin. Andream Baccium de virorum historiâ lib.4.part.1. Scal. de Emend. Temp.lib.5.c.11.
units.tr: See Cicero, On the Dining Room; Andreas Bacchius, On the History of Men, lib. 4, part 1; Scaliger, On the Emendation of Time, lib. 5, c. 11.

units.la: Soleas induebant accubantes. Truc.25 v.25.& 2.8.v.1.
units.tr: They wore slippers while reclining. Truc. 2.5 v.25 & 2.8 v.1.

units.la: Ante discubitum autem excalceari solebant, ideò, ne lectum con-spurcarent: & soleas capiebant. Truc. 2.4.v.12.
units.tr: Before reclining they usually took off their shoes, so that they would not soil the couch, and they picked up their slippers. Truc. 2.4 v.12.

units.la: Martialis:
units.tr: Martial:

units.la: Deposui soleas.
units.tr: I have put off my slippers.

units.la: Horatius de Nasidieno inter cœnam surgente:
units.tr: Horace, of Nasidienus, when a guest got up during dinner:

units.la: Et soleas poscit.
units.tr: And he calls for his slippers.

units.la: Vide Lips.lib.3. Antiqq. Lect. & Tit. Cultus.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Antiquae Lectiones, lib. 3, and the entry Cultus.

units.la: Mensæ apponebantur apud veteres, & removebantur. Appone-bantur cibum capturis, & epulaturis: removebantur, ubi edendi & bibendi finem fecerant. Amph. 2.2. v.175.
units.tr: Tables were set before the ancients and taken away again. They were set for those about to eat and feast, and removed when they had finished eating and drinking. Amph. 2.2 v.175.

units.la: Te dormitare ajebas, mensa ablata est: cubitum hinc abijmus.
units.tr: You were saying you were nodding off, the table has been taken away: let us go off to bed from here.

units.la: Pueri mensam apponite.
units.tr: Boys, set the table.

units.la: Lecti discubitorij altiores fuerunt tricliniaribus. Men.1.1.v.27.
units.tr: The couches for reclining were higher than the couches of the triclinium. Men. 1.1 v.27.

units.la: Vide Lips. Antiq.Lect.lib.3.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Antiquae Lectiones, lib. 3.

units.la: Superiori loco accumbere dignitatis erat. Most. 1.1.v.42.
units.tr: To recline in the higher place was a mark of rank. Most. 1.1 v.42.

units.la: In tricliniari lecto, qui ad caput lecti decumbebat, Summus dice-batur: qui ad pedes Imus: qui inter istos, Medius, Sic opponit e-leganleganter Parasitus Stich. 3. 2. v. 32. Haud postulo equidem summa in lecto accumbere. Scis tu me esse imi subsellii virum. Sic enim locum illum ex vetustis editis libris legendum recte censuerunt viri docti.
units.tr: On the triclinium couch, the man who lay at the head of the couch was called Summus; the one at the feet Imus; the one between them Medius. The parasite puts it neatly like this, Stich. 3.2 v.32: I do not at all ask to recline at the top. You know I am a man of the lowest bench. For learned men have rightly judged that this passage should be read in this way, as in the old printed books.

units.la: ETIAM loci habebant rationem: quam tamen serviles negligebant. Perf. 5.1. v.15. & 5. 2. v.14.
units.tr: Places were taken into account too, though slaves neglected them. Persa 5.1 v.15 & 5.2 v.14.

units.la: Tu accumbe in summo. SA. At ego nihil morror.
units.tr: You recline at the top. SA. But I don't care at all.

units.la: AMANTES quoq; non habebant rationem loci in accumbendo. Stich. 5. 2. v.9.
units.tr: Lovers too took no account of place when reclining. Stich. 5.2 v.9.

units.la: IN convivijs honoris habebant rationem in collocandis convivis. Stich. 5.2. v. 14.
units.tr: At banquets they took account of honour in seating the guests. Stich. 5.2 v.14.

units.la: IN triclinijs locus medius honoratissimus. Asin. 5.2. v.42.
units.tr: In dining rooms the middle place was the most honoured. Asin. 5.2 v.42.

units.la: Vide Tit. Honorie. Et ea, quæ ex Lipsi & Duza compilavit Taubmanus pag. 136.
units.tr: See the entry Honorie, and what Taubmann gathered from Lipsius and Dousa, p. 136.

units.la: CERTUS fuit numerus convivarum: ac vix supra novem. Stich. 3.2. v.21. Varro in Satira, quæ inscribitur: NESCIS QUID SERUS VESPER VEHAT ait: Convivarum numerum incipere oportere à Gratiarum numero, & progredi ad Musarum; h.e. proficisci à tribus, & consistere in novem: ut cum paucissimi convivæ sunt, non pauciores sint, quàm tres: cùm plurima non plures, quàm novem. Vide Agell. lib. 13. c. 11.
units.tr: The number of guests was fixed, and scarcely more than nine. Stich. 3.2 v.21. Varro, in the satire entitled NESCIS QUID SERUS VESPER VEHAT, says that the number of guests ought to begin from the number of the Graces and proceed to that of the Muses; that is, start from three and stop at nine. So that when the guests are very few, they are not fewer than three; when they are most, not more than nine. See Gellius, lib. 13, c. 11.

units.la: ANTE convivium pilâ ludebant: dein lavatum ibant, tùm cænabant. Stich. 4.1. v.62. Ubi etiam senex id facit. & 4. 2. v.15. Sic apud Petron. Trimalcio ante lavationem pila sphærisa exercetur: Post demum se dat convivio.
units.tr: Before dinner they played at ball, then went to bathe, then dined. Stich. 4.1 v.62. Where the old man also does this. 4.2 v.15. So in Petronius: TRIMALCHIO ANTE LAVATIONEM PILA SPHAERISA EXERCETUR: POST DEMUM SE DAT CONVIVIO. (Trimalchio exercises himself with a ball before bathing; only afterwards does he give himself to the banquet.)

units.la: ANTE cœnam lavabant, non post cœnam, nisi qui lue essent perditi. Hi enim rem suam familiarem balneis & Venere & epulis absumebant: eóq; decoctores bonis clavisse dicebantur. Rud. 1, 2. v.63. Stich. 4.1. v.28. & 5.2. v.19 21.
units.tr: They bathed before dinner, not after dinner, except those who were ruined by vice. For these spent their property on baths, love and feasts, and so were said to have "closed their goods to their creditors" as bankrupts. Rud. 1.2 v.63. Stich. 4.1 v.28 & 5.2 v.19–21.

units.la: ACCUBITURI ad mensam manus & pedes lavabant. Perf. 1.3. v.ro & 5.1. v.17. & 5,2. v.14 Petronius: Discubuimus pueris Alexandrinis aquam in manus nivatam infundentibus, aliysq; insequentibus ad pedes.
units.tr: Those about to recline washed their hands and feet at the table. Persa 1.3 v.10 & 5.1 v.17 & 5.2 v.14. Petronius: We reclined, while Alexandrian boys poured water over our hands, and others followed to wash our feet.

units.la: Fab. Pictor :
units.tr: Fabius Pictor:

units.la: Aquam manibus pedibusq; dato.
units.tr: Give water for the hands and feet.

units.la: Vide etiam Briff. Form.
units.tr: See also Brisson, On Formulas.

units.la: GRÆCI & Romani priusquam accubitum irent, solebant in balneis sudare & inungi. Stich. 2.1.v.73. Bacch. 5.2.v 62.
units.tr: The Greeks and Romans, before they went to recline, used to sweat in the baths and be anointed. Stich. 2.1 v.73. Bacch. 5.2 v.62.

units.la: IN convivio accubantes, per puerum aquam manibus poscebant: Item mensulam ad ludum talorum: dehinc unguenta & flacten. Mostl. 1.3.v.149. Persf. 5.1.v.8.
units.tr: While reclining at dinner, they asked a boy for water for their hands; likewise a little table for the game of dice; then perfumes and garlands. Mostell. 1.3 v.149. Persa 5.1 v.8.

units.la: FLOREIS coronis redimiti, & unguentis delibuti cænabant, ubi se liberali invitare decreverant; tum voluptatis causa, tum quod crederent odoramentis ebrietatem impediri.
units.tr: Wreathed with flowery garlands and anointed with perfumes, they dined when they had resolved to invite guests generously, partly for pleasure, and partly because they believed that drunkenness was hindered by fragrances.

units.la: Nonnumquam etiam aviculas quasdam corollis suis alligabant, quarum e cantu assiduo, & crebris rostri unguiumque punctuiris efficeretur, ne ipsi inter potandum obdormiscerent. Amph. 3. 4.v.16. Men. 3 1.v.16. & 3.3.v.31, & 4.1.v.5. & 42.v.68. Asin. 5.2.v.30.
units.tr: Sometimes they also tied little birds to their garlands, whose constant singing and frequent pecking with beak and claws kept them from falling asleep while drinking. Amph. 3.4 v.16. Men. 3.1 v.16 & 3.3 v.31, & 4.1 v.5 & 4.2 v.68. Asin. 5.2 v.30.

units.la: IN triclinijs postquam lectos sternebant, odores & suffimenta incendebant. Men. 2.3.v.3.
units.tr: In dining rooms, after they had made up the couches, they lit incense and fumigations. Men. 2.3 v.3.

units.la: IN convivijs hilarioribus unguenta & odores adhibebant, lemniscos, & corollas dapsiles. Pseud. 5.1.v.21. & 5.2.v.2.
units.tr: At merrier banquets they used perfumes and ointments, ribbons and lavish garlands. Pseud. 5.1 v.21 & 5.2 v.2.

units.la: IN convivijs coronati erant, præsertim nuptijs. Caf. 4.1.v.9.
units.tr: At banquets they wore crowns, especially at weddings. Cas. 4.1 v.9.

units.la: AD mensam catellos quoque habebant. Stich. 4.2.v.39.
units.tr: They also kept little dogs at table. Stich. 4.2 v.39.

units.la: Accubabo vel inter cuneos ferreos. Tantillum loci ubi catellus cubet, id mihi sat est loci.
units.tr: I shall recline even among iron wedges. A tiny space where a little dog may lie is room enough for me.

units.la: INTER cænandum omnis generis acroamata adhibebantur. Nam aut symphoniâ personabat Triclinium, aut instrumenta varia organaque per tibicinas concinebant: aut Tragœdiæ vel Comœdiæ agebantur: incendebantur odores naribus gratissimi. De illis Stich. 2.3.v.55. Mostell. 4.2.v.25. De odoribus Men. 2.3. verf. 3.
units.tr: During dinner all kinds of entertainments were provided. For either a band of music sounded through the dining room, or various instruments and organs were played by flute-girls; or tragedies or comedies were performed; and fragrances most pleasing to the nose were burned. For these, Stich. 2.3 v.55. Mostell. 4.2 v.25. For the fragrances, Men. 2.3 v.3.

units.la: Vide paulò ante.
units.tr: See a little above.

units.la: Livius
units.tr: Livy.

units.la: Liwius lib. 29.
units.tr: Livy, lib. 29.

units.la: Tunc psaltria sambucistriaq; & cōvivalia ludionum obleƈlamenta addita epulis.
units.tr: Then harp-girls and sambuca-players, and the convivial jests of entertainers, were added to the feast.

units.la: Virgil. lib. i. Æneid in convivio Didonis:
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid book 1, at Dido's banquet:

units.la: ----- cithara crinitus Iopas Personat aurata.
units.tr: ...Iopas, long-haired, sounds on his golden lyre.

units.la: Vide Macrob. l. 2. c. 4. & Senec. de vitâ beatâ c. 11. & Ciaccon. de Triclin. Bapt. Pium Face Crit. Tom. 1. pag. 393.
units.tr: See Macrobius, lib. 2, c. 4, and Seneca, On the Happy Life, c. 11, and Ciaconius, On the Triclinium; Baptista Pius, Face Critica, vol. 1, p. 393.

units.la: Parasiti ad convivia admissi ridiculorum causâ. Capt. 3. i. v. 10, 17. Stich. 2. 3. v. 57. 63. & 3. 2. v. 1.
units.tr: Parasites were admitted to banquets for the sake of jokes. Capt. 3.1 v.10, 17. Stich. 2.3 v.57, 63 & 3.2 v.1.

units.la: In convivijs certis legibus vivebant. Quorsum alludit noster Asin. 3. 3. v. 11.
units.tr: At banquets they lived under certain rules. Our author alludes to this in Asin. 3.3 v.11.

units.la: Talis ludebant in convivijs, & quidem sub magisterio quodam forte enim cligebatur dominus seu magister convivij. Legem talariam noster vocat ἀλληγορικὰς.
units.tr: At banquets they played at dice, and indeed under a certain master; for a lord or master of the banquet was chosen by lot. Our author calls the dice-law allegorical [ἀλληγορικὰς].

units.la: In convivijs cūm more Græcorum solebant talis sortiri vices bibēdi: talos mittentes scorta invocabant, suasque amicas, fausti dominis causâ.
units.tr: At banquets, following the custom of the Greeks, they used to cast dice to decide their turns at drinking; throwing the dice they called upon courtesans and their own girlfriends, for the good luck of their masters.

units.la: Allusit noster Capt. 1. 1. v. 5. & Curc. 2. 3. v. 77.
units.tr: Our author alludes to this in Capt. 1.1 v.5 & Curc. 2.3 v.77.

units.la: Amantes meretriculæ in cōvivijs cantionem cynædicam & suavem cantabant suis amatoribus.
units.tr: Courtesans in love sang a lewd yet sweet song at banquets for their lovers.

units.la: In convivijs saltabant amantes. Stich. 5. 5. v. 13.
units.tr: Lovers danced at banquets. Stich. 5.5 v.13.

units.la: Amatores solebant amicarum fores spargere mero. Curcul. 1. 1. v. 89.
units.tr: Lovers used to sprinkle their mistresses' doors with wine. Curc. 1.1 v.89.

units.la: Vide Amatorum.
units.tr: See Amatorum.

units.la: Postquam cænati atque appoti erant, talos, h. e. quosvis ludos tractabant. Curc. 2. 3. v. 75.
units.tr: After they had dined and drunk well, they played at dice, that is, at any games. Curc. 2.3 v.75.

units.la: Vide Tit. Talorum.
units.tr: See the entry Talorum.

units.la: Qui inter amicos convivium sive cænam jubebatur parare erani-sta, accipiebat arrham sive symbolum, seu anulum, loco tesseræ. Quo forte allusum Bacch. 2.3.v.93. Pseud. 1.1.v.53.
units.tr: The man ordered to prepare a dinner or supper among friends, the eranista, received an earnest or token, a ring, in place of a tessera. Perhaps this is alluded to in Bacch. 2.3 v.93. Pseud. 1.1 v.53.

units.la: Terentius:
units.tr: Terence:

units.la: Heri aliquot adolescentuli coïimus in Piræeo. In hunc diem, ut de symbolis essemus: Chæream ei rei præfecimus: dati annuli, locum, tempus constitutum est.
units.tr: Yesterday several young men of us met in the Piraeus. For the contributions to this day we put Chaerea in charge of the business: rings were given, and a place and time fixed.

units.la: Vide amplius de istis symbolis Isaaci Casaub. Animadvers. ad Athenæum lib. 3. c.31.
units.tr: See more on these contributions in Isaac Casaubon's Animadversions on Athenaeus, lib. 3, c. 31.

units.la: Persæ & Romani sumtuosè admodum cænabant. Quod innuit Villicus ille Cas. 3.6.v.19.
units.tr: The Persians and Romans dined very sumptuously. The rustic in Cas. 3.6 v.19 hints at this:

units.la: Cœnare lepidè, nitidèq; volo: nihil moror barbarico ritu sanè esse jam.
units.tr: I want to dine elegantly and neatly; I care nothing for barbarian custom, certainly not now.

units.la: De Persis Horatius lib. 1. Odæ ultimæ:
units.tr: Horace on the Persians, in the last ode of book 1:

units.la: Persicos odi, puer, apparatus.
units.tr: Persian finery I hate, boy.

units.la: In Ædes sacra epulabantur. Mil. 3.1.v.117. Trin. 2.4.v.67. Clien-tes enim patronis suis ibi convivium parabant: quod vocabant Cænam popularem. Quod & siebat in triumphis, teste Suetonio. Item in sacris Herculis.
units.tr: They feasted in temples. Mil. 3.1 v.117. Trin. 2.4 v.67. For clients prepared a banquet there for their patrons, which they called the "popular dinner". This was also done at triumphs, as Suetonius testifies. Likewise at the rites of Hercules.

units.la: Vide Turneb. lib. 26. c.16. & inprimis P. Fabri Semestr. l.1 c.6.
units.tr: See Turnebus, lib. 26, c. 16, and especially P. Faber, Semestria, lib. 1, c. 6.

units.la: In sacris Herculis pollucibiliter vivebant. Stich. 5.2.v.6. Hodie pol-luctura præter nos jam dabitur nemini.
units.tr: At the rites of Hercules they lived lavishly. Stich. 5.2 v.6. Today, since the feast is to be lavish, nobody will be given anything except us.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut. Pollucere.
units.tr: See the Plautine lexicon, Pollucere.

units.la: Cereales cœnæ dicuntur à festo Cereris, quo omnes populariter indulgebant Genio Men. 1.1. v.25. Varro vocat Cerealem pompam: longum scil. ordinem ferculorum, quæ in Cereali epulo inferebantur.
units.tr: Cereal dinners are so called from the festival of Ceres, at which everyone, as the custom of the people was, gave themselves over to indulgence in honour of the Genius. Varro calls it a Cereal procession, that is, the long line of dishes that were brought in at the Cereal feast.

units.la: In dies singulas esculas edere solebant plærique: h.e. cænam, non prandium capiebant. Contra Parasitus. Men. 3.1.v.10.
units.tr: Most people were accustomed to eat a meal every single day; that is, they took a dinner, not a luncheon. Against this, see the parasite.

units.la: Mane solebant jentaculà vendi in usum puerorum. Unde adolescens ille Veneri manè vovet jentaculum. Curc. 1.1.v.72. & Truc. 2.7.v.38. Ubi pro jentaculo legitur spectaculo. Mart. l.14 Ep.223. Ibi vide Raderum: & Mercurialem Var. Lect. libr. 4. capit. 17. Ubi erudite disputat rarissimos fuisse Græcorum : qui sæpius die cibis implerentur. Romanos verò ita assuevisse cõfirmat, ut major hominum pars semel salutarentur: atq; id vespere ad cœnam: manè verò aut modicum quid, aut nihil omninò sumerent: rarissimè ter aut amplius efitarent. Quod verò hoc loco dicitur de Jentaculo, id de pueris accipiendum. Solebant enim pueri & senes valetudinis causâ uti manè jentaculo : & præter hos nemo alius. Quod si aliqui erant, qui uterentur, protinus tamquam incontinetes notabantur. Idem censendum de Merendâ. Sicut & illi non parvâ infamiâ affecti fuerunt, qui Comessationes, seu cibos post cœnam sumebant: atque Comessatores indecoro nomine vocabantur. Unde Clemens Alex. Pædag. 2. vehementer in pueris quoq; damnat prandiola, cœnas, epulas, atq; merendas. Aulus Vitellius Imperator luxuriosissimus, & incontinentissimus epulas sæpè trifariam, interdum quadrifariam dispertivit in jentaculum, prandium, cœnam, comessationem: quibus omnibus, teste Suetonio, vomitandi consuetudine suffecerat.
