units.tr: In the morning they used to sell breakfasts for the use of boys. Hence that young man vows a breakfast to Venus in the morning. Here, for breakfast, some read spectacle. See Rader there, and Mercurialis, Var. Lect. book 4, chapter 17, where he learnedly argues that the Greeks were very rarely filled with food more than once a day, while the Romans were so accustomed that most men were fed only once, and that in the evening at dinner; in the morning they took either a little something or nothing at all, and only very rarely ate three or more times. What is said here of the breakfast must be understood of boys. For boys and old men used to take a morning breakfast for reasons of health, and apart from these hardly anyone else did; and if there were any who did so, they were at once marked down as intemperate. The same must be thought of the afternoon snack. Just as those who took comessationes, that is, food after dinner, were also branded with no small disgrace, and were called comessatores by a disgraceful name. Whence Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 2, strongly condemns in boys also the little luncheons, dinners, feasts and snacks. The Emperor Aulus Vitellius, a most luxurious and intemperate man, often divided his feasts into three, sometimes four parts: breakfast, lunch, dinner and revel; and by all these, as Suetonius testifies, he was content with the habit of vomiting.

units.la: Etiam manè convivabantur luxuriosi. Perf.1.3.v.33.
units.tr: Even in the morning the luxurious used to feast together. Persius book 1, satire 3, line 33.

units.la: Sumebant quoq; merendam. Mostl.3.2.v.33.&4.2.v.50.
units.tr: They also took an afternoon snack. Plautus, Mostellaria 3.2, line 33, and 4.2, line 50.

units.la: Die mortuo cœnare solebant. Men. 1.2.v.43. & 3.2.v.27.
units.tr: On the day of a death they used to dine. Plautus, Menaechmi 1.2, line 43, and 3.2, line 27.

units.la: Post cœnam solebant comissari. Mostl.1.4.v.5.22. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: After dinner they used to revel. Plautus, Mostellaria 1.4, lines 5 and 22. See the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: Qui ibant comissatum, funalia, ac faces gestabant; sed quas exstinguebant, cùm ad fores erat ventum. Exemplum canticorum cujusmodi est Curc.1.2.v.57. Perf.4.4.v.20. Vide Lex. Plaut. & Scaligeri Notas ad Festum in Occentare. Et Horat. lib. 3. Od. 10.
units.tr: Those who went off to revel carried torches and lamps, but they put them out when they had reached the door. An example of such songs is in Plautus, Curculio 1.2, line 57, and Persa 4.4, line 20. See the Plautine lexicon, and Scaliger's notes on Festus under Occentare. Also Horace, book 3, Ode 10.

units.la: II. RATIO VICTVS & Ciborum.
units.tr: II. The Way of Life and Foods.

units.la: SERVORVM erat obsonari: h. e. obsonia emere: quos vocabant ὀψωνάς, obsonatores. Capt.3.1.v.14.
units.tr: It was the business of slaves to buy provisions, that is, to purchase delicacies; they were called ὀψωνάς, provision-buyers. Capt. 3.1.v.14.

units.la: Parasitorum haec fuit provincia quoq;.
units.tr: This was also the task of parasites.

units.la: Vide etiam Senecam Epist.47. & Athenaeum lib. 4.
units.tr: See also Seneca, Epist. 47, and Athenaeus, book 4.

units.la: Idem patet ex Terentio, ubi Gnatho parasitus se gratum ait esse cupediarijs, coquis, lanijs.
units.tr: The same is clear from Terence, where the parasite Gnatho says he is welcome to the sellers of dainties, the cooks and the butchers.

units.la: Inde quoque Phormioni nomen inditum, Nam φορμὶς vas est vimineum, ut sportula, quod ad macellum & torum cum irent, secum ferebant.
units.tr: Phormio also got his name from this, for φορμὶς is a wicker basket, like a sportula, which they carried with them when they went to the market and the bed.

units.la: IN convivijs solemnibus servorum distincta erant munia. Alij cado praeficiebantur.
units.tr: At solemn feasts the duties of the slaves were divided; some were put in charge of the wine-jar.

units.la: CIBVS cum sapit ac juvat, est quasi meritum.
units.tr: Food, when it is tasty and pleasing, is as it were a reward.

units.la: Ne quando esca una meruerit magis.
units.tr: Ne quando esca una meruerit magis.

units.la: Sic enim ibi retineri potest, propter consensum MSS. codicum, quamquam ευσὸχως μάλα Acidalius, ut caetera omnia: me iuverit, correxit.
units.tr: For so it can be retained there, on account of the agreement of the manuscripts, although Acidalius, who corrected all the rest very well, corrected it to me iuverit.

units.la: Vide etiam Capt. 1,2.v.26. Asin. 1.2. v.16.
units.tr: See also Capt. 1.2.v.26; Asin. 1.2. v.16.

units.la: Observavit aliquid in hanc rem Janus Gebhardus, ingeniosissimus ac modestissimus juvenis Crepund. lib.3.c.2.
units.tr: Janus Gebhardus, a very clever and modest young man, has noted something on this matter in his Crepundia, book 3, chapter 2.

units.la: Qui anxiè in convivijs cibum appetebant, dicebantur indecorè procumbere dimidiati, & se percellere. Mil. 3.1. v.166.
units.tr: Those who eagerly reached for food at dinners were said to lie down awkwardly, half-reclining, and to throw themselves about. Mil. 3.1. v.166.

units.la: Vide Casaub. ad Athen. pag. 551.
units.tr: See Casaubon on Athenaeus, p. 551.

units.la: IN convivijs varias herbas apposuerunt coqui: varia item condimenta.
units.tr: At dinners the cooks set out various herbs, and likewise various seasonings.

units.la: De quibus vide totam scenam 2. Act. 3. Pseud.
units.tr: On these see the whole scene, Act 2, Scene 3, of the Pseudolus.

units.la: Turtures, pisces, aves, opulentiorum cibi. Mostell. i. i. v. 44.
units.tr: Turtle-doves, fish and birds were the foods of the wealthier. Mostell. 1.1. v.44.

units.la: In delitijs erat sumen suis, τὸ ὑπερὸν ὑποκύλιον. Capt. 4. 3. v. 4.
units.tr: Among delicacies was the sow's belly, the upper part of the sow's flank. Capt. 4.3. v.4.

units.la: Itemq; glandia. Capt. 4. 4. v. 7.
units.tr: Likewise acorns. Capt. 4.4. v.7.

units.la: Pernæ item in delitijs. Capt. 4. 2. v. 70. & 4. 3. v. 4.
units.tr: Hams likewise were among the delicacies. Capt. 4.2. v.70 & 4.3. v.4.

units.la: Itemque Apri valdè æstimati: inprimis lumbus aprugnus & Callus. Capt. 4. 3. v. 4.
units.tr: Likewise the boar was highly prized, especially the loin and the hock of the wild boar. Capt. 4.3. v.4.

units.la: De quo pluribus vide Hier. Mercurial. lib. 2. c. 22. Var. nec non Lips. in Poliorc. lib. 4. Dial. 1.
units.tr: On this matter see more at Hieronymus Mercurialis, book 2, chapter 22, Var., and also Lipsius, Poliorcetica, book 4, Dial. 1.

units.la: In delitijs fuerunt omenta ifititia, glandula suilla, laridum, perna, pes suillus, sinciput, polimenta porcina.
units.tr: Among delicacies were the omenta, the pig's sausage, lard, ham, pig's trotter, pig's head and pork-jelly.

units.la: Perna, abdomen, sumen, suis glandium, assa bubula, in delitijs.
units.tr: Ham, belly, sow's belly, the acorn-fed pig, roast beef: these were delicacies.

units.la: Eaque solebant in carnario pro reliquijs asservari: ventris stabi- limenta.
units.tr: These were usually kept in the meat-larder as leftovers, to sustain the stomach.

units.la: Pro reliquijs frigidam pernam apponebant postridiè.
units.tr: For leftovers they set out cold ham the next day.
Perf. 1.3. v.2 ff.

units.la: Pernam quidem jus est apponi frigidam postridiè, Mil. 3. 1. v. 164. Et halecem. Ibid.
units.tr: "It is indeed fitting to serve cold ham the next day," Mil. 3.1. v.164. And a herring, ibid.

units.la: Delicatiores cibi erant olivæ, pulpamentum leporis, capparis. Curc 1. 1. v. 90.
units.tr: The more refined foods were olives, a hash of hare, and capers. Curc. 1.1. v.90.

units.la: Conger & offa penita in delitijs, Mil. 3. 1. v. 164.
units.tr: Conger eel and the belly of a fattened pig were among the delicacies. Mil. 3.1. v.164.

units.la: Conger & perna solebant frigidè asservari. Ibid.
units.tr: Conger eel and ham were usually kept cold. Ibid.

units.la: Inter bellaria habebant olim laterculos, sesamum, papaverem, triticum, frictas nuces. Pæn. 1. 2. v. 112.
units.tr: Among the sweetmeats they once had little tiles (cakes), sesame, poppy seed, wheat, and fried nuts. Poen. 1.2. v.112.

units.la: De singulis vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: On the individual items see the Lexicon Plautinum.

units.la: Cibus minimè lautus erat Epityrum Mil. 1. 1. v. 24.
units.tr: The food was by no means refined: epityrum. Mil. 1.1. v.24.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Lexicon Plautinum.

units.la: Collyram panificij genus madefaciebant: itemque Colliphia panes cum recenti caseo. Perf. 1. 3. v. 12.
units.tr: They soaked a kind of bread called collyra, and likewise colliphia, breads with fresh cheese. Perf. 1.3. v.12.

units.la: Item Collyricum jus è crassò cremore. Ibid.
units.tr: Likewise collyricum jus, made from thick gruel. Ibid.

units.la: Et Epicrocum pellucidum: Juream, Ibid.
units.tr: And epicrocum, transparent; Juream. Ibid.

units.la: De singulis vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: On the individual items see the Lexicon Plautinum.

units.la: In convivijs etiam sinapi usi sunt. Pseud. 3. 2. v. 28.
units.tr: At dinners they also used mustard. Pseud. 3.2. v.28.

units.la: Cicer frigi consuevit. Bacch. 4. 5. v. 7.
units.tr: Chickpeas were customarily fried. Bacch. 4.5. v.7.

units.la: Tam frixum ego illum reddam, quàm frixum est cicer.
units.tr: "I will make him as fried as a fried chickpea."

units.la: Horat. Arte Poët. v. 249.
units.tr: Horace, Ars Poetica, v.249.

units.la: Ne si quid frixi Ciceris probat, & nucis emptor.
units.tr: "Lest someone who buys fried chickpeas and nuts should approve of it."

units.la: In convivijs hospitibus peregrè adventantibus salem in mensâ apponebant. Curc. 4. 4. v. 6.
units.tr: At dinners they set salt on the table for guests arriving from abroad. Curc. 4.4. v.6.

units.la: Vide Tit. Peregrinationis.
units.tr: See the title Peregrinatio.

units.la: Struthea, & coluthea poma apponebant in scutris: ijsq; calamum inijciebant Perf. 1. 3. v. 7. De quibus omnibus vide Lex. Pl.
units.tr: They set out struthean and colutheal apples in baskets, and put a reed into them. Perf. 1.3. v.7. On all these see the Lexicon Plautinum.

units.la: Cibos frigidos postridiè in delitijs habebant. Perf. 1. 3. v. 30.
units.tr: They kept cold foods from the day before among their delicacies. Perf. 1.3. v.30.

units.la: Memini, ut murœna & conger ne calefierent. nam nimio melius oppesluntur frigida.
units.tr: "I remember that the moray and the conger were not to be warmed up, for cold things are preserved much better."

units.la: Rubido pane vescebantur, tosto in in furno: ij scilic. qui ruri vi-ctitabant villici. Caf. 2. 5. v. 2.
units.tr: They ate red bread, baked in an oven: namely, those who lived as farmhands in the country. Cas. 2.5. v.2.

units.la: Reliquias asservarunt incrastinum. Perf. 1. 2. v. 26. & 13. v. 25. Eas sectatur Parasitus:
units.tr: They kept leftovers until tomorrow. Perf. 1.2. v.26 & 1.3. v.25. The parasite pursues these:

units.la: Nunc huc introibo, visam hesternas reliquias: quierint rectè, nec ne, num infuerit febris. Men. 3. 1. v. 15. Stich 2 1. v. 90. & 3. 2. v. 50.
units.tr: "Now I will go in here, to see yesterday's leftovers: whether they have kept well or not, whether they have gone off. Men. 3.1. v.15. Stich. 2.1. v.90, & 3.2. v.50."

units.la: Frugaliores cænam asperam & terrestrem ex herbis & oleribus parabant. Capt. 1. 2. v. 80.
units.tr: The more frugal prepared a rough and earthy dinner of herbs and vegetables. Capt. 1.2. v.80.

units.la: Polenta seu farinâ hordeaceâ vescebantur Philosophi Stoici, qui scilicet tenui victu victitabant. Unde joculariter crepitus polentarius apud Plautum. Curc. 2. 3. v. 16. Perf. Sat. 3. v. 55.
units.tr: The Stoic philosophers fed on polenta, or barley meal, since they lived on a meagre diet. Hence the jesting phrase crepitus polentarius in Plautus. Curc. 2.3. v.16. Perf., Sat. 3. v.55.

units.la: Quibus & detonsa juventus
units.tr: "And the youth who have been shorn,

units.la: Invigilat, siliquis, & grandi pasta polentâ. Græci τὰ ἄλφιτα appellant victum tenuiorum: quali fere omnes Græci usi sunt.
units.tr: Keep watch on pods and on grain-porridge made of large barley." The Greeks call the food of the poorer sort τὰ ἄλφιτα [barley-meal]; almost all the Greeks used this kind of food.

units.la: Olera parasiti oderant in convivijs. Capt. 1.2. v.81.
units.tr: Parasites hated vegetables at dinners. Capt. 1.2. v.81.

units.la: Aridas ficus edebant tenuiores servi. Rud. 3.4.v.58.
units.tr: Poorer slaves ate dried figs. Rud. 3.4. v.58.

units.la: Allium & sal cibus servorum pauperum. Pers. 2.3.v.15.
units.tr: Garlic and salt were the food of poor slaves. Pers. 2.3. v.15.

units.la: Acetum seu posca, itemq; sal cibus servorum: & viliorum. Rud. 4.3.v.32. Hic Rex cum aceto pransurus est, & sale, sine bono pulmento. Pers. 3.3. v.24.
units.tr: Vinegar, or posca, and likewise salt, were the food of slaves and of the lowlier sort. Rud. 4.3. v.32. "This king is about to dine on vinegar and salt, without any good relish." Pers. 3.3. v.24.

units.la: Frugale erat convivium servorum: qui nucibus, fabis, siculis, aleo, lupillo contenti erant. Stich. 5.2. v.8. Vide Tit. Frugalitatis.
units.tr: The dinner of slaves was frugal: they were content with nuts, beans, figs, dry bread and lupin. Stich. 5.2. v.8. See the title Frugalitas.

units.la: Convivium servile describitur Asin. 5.1.v.2. Pers. 5.1. v.5.17.18. Lectulos ponebant: flores, corollam, panem, obsonia, vinum, aquam. Et hanc quidem calidam & frigidam: vel manibus, vel vino lymphando. Most. 1.3.v.148.
units.tr: A slave's dinner is described at Asin. 5.1. v.2; Pers. 5.1. v.5, 17, 18. They set out couches, flowers, a garland, bread, delicacies, wine and water; and this water was either warm or cold, and used either for washing the hands or for diluting the wine. Most. 1.3. v.148.

units.la: Vide Stuck. Antiqq. Conviv. lib.3. c.6. Lipsi lib. 1. Elect. c. 4.
units.tr: See Stuck, Antiquities, Banquets, book 3, chapter 6; Lipsius, book 1, Electa, chapter 4.

units.la: III. POTVS ET BIBENDI LEGES.
units.tr: III. The Laws of Drinking

units.la: Bacchus conviviorum præses. Stich. 5 2.v.13.
units.tr: Bacchus, president of the banquet. Stich. 5.2 v.13.

units.la: In convivijs magister bibendi erat. Stich. 5.2. v. 20. Strategum te facio huic convivio.
units.tr: At banquets there was a master of drinking. Stich. 5.2 v.20: I appoint you general of this banquet.

units.la: Vide Lambinum ad Horat. nec non Tractatum Æmylij Portii de priscâ Græcorum compotatione.
units.tr: See Lambinus on Horace, and also Æmilius Portus's treatise on the ancient Greek drinking-parties.

units.la: Pueros habebant ad cyathos. Men. 2.2. v.29.
units.tr: They had boys to serve the cups (cyathi). Men. 2.2 v.29.

units.la: Vetus Inscriptio pag. DLXX. 4
units.tr: An old inscription, p. DLXX, no. 4.

units.la: D. M.
units.tr: D. M.

units.la: DORYPHORO. CÆSARIS.
units.tr: To Doryphorus, of Caesar's household.

units.la: A. CYATHO.
units.tr: To A. Cyathus.

units.la: VIXIT. ANNOS. XX. D. XXIIII.
units.tr: He lived twenty years and twenty-four days.

units.la: HERRIA. VERECUNDA. MATER. FILIO. PIENTISSIMO. FECIT. ET. SIBI.
units.tr: Herria Verecunda made this for her most dutiful son, and for herself.

units.la: IN convivijs mulsum propinabant plenis cantharis. Perf. 5. 2. v. 40. Stich. 2. 1. v. 60.
units.tr: At banquets they drank mulsum from full cups. Pers. 5.2 v.40. Stich. 2.1 v.60.

units.la: IN bibendo modum quoq; adhibuerant. Interdum quinque cyathos biberunt, ut Stich 5. 4. v. 24. 37.
units.tr: In drinking they also observed a measure. Sometimes they drank five cyathi, as in Stich. 5.4 v.24, 37: As many as the fingers you have in your hand.

units.la: Tot quot digiti sunt tibi in manu.
units.tr: As many as the fingers you have in your hand.

units.la: Interdum septem. Perf 5. 1. v. 19.
units.tr: Sometimes seven. Pers. 5.1 v.19.

units.la: Septem cyathis committamus hos ludos.
units.tr: Let us commit these games to seven cups.

units.la: Et apud Mattialem:
units.tr: And in Martial:

units.la: ---- Septem Justina bibatur.
units.tr: Let seven be drunk for Justina.

units.la: Ad summum tamen decem: ut quidam colligunt ex Sticho 5. 1. v. 2 5.
units.tr: At most ten, however, as some gather from Stichus 5.1 v.25.

units.la: Καὶ ἡμιτέταρτα ἡ πέντε, ἡ τρεῖς.
units.tr: And a half-quartern, or five, or three [Καὶ ἡμιτέταρτα ἡ πέντε, ἡ τρεῖς].

units.la: Totidem enim litteris constabat nomen amicæ STEPHANIUM.
units.tr: For the name of his mistress, STEPHANIUM, had as many letters.

units.la: Sic enim ibi dicit servus: Cantio Græca est:
units.tr: For there the slave says: The song is Greek:

units.la: ἡ πέντε πὶν ἡ τρία πὶν ἡ μὴ τέτρακα.
units.tr: Five before three, or before not four [ἡ πέντε πρὶν ἡ τρία πρὶν ἡ μὴ τέτρακα].

units.la: De quâ cantione Eustathius Odyss. ὡσπερ. Et Casaub. ad Athen. lib.10. pag 545. Plutarch. Sympos.Quæst.lib.3. c.9. Scalig. Auson.Lect lib.2.c.27. Macrob lib. 1. c.6. Somn. Ubi vide Jf. Pontanum, Plin. lib. 28. c. 6, Numerum quoq; quaternarium prodidit Demetrius condito volumine: & quare quaterni cyathi, sextarijve non essent bibendi.
units.tr: On this song see Eustathius on the Odyssey [ὥσπερ]; and Casaubon on Athenaeus book 10, p. 545; Plutarch, Symposiacs book 3 ch. 9; Scaliger on Ausonius, Lectiones book 2 ch. 27; Macrobius, Saturnalia book 1 ch. 6. There see also J. Pontanus; Pliny book 28 ch. 6. Demetrius, in a published work, also gave the reason why four cups, or six, should not be drunk.

units.la: * sextarijve non essent bibendi.
units.tr: * or six cups should not be drunk.

units.la: Petronius:
units.tr: Petronius:

units.la: Excusare cæpit morem: quòd amica se non dimisisset, tribus nisi potionibus è lege siccatis.
units.tr: He began to excuse the custom: that his mistress had not let him go, unless three drinks had been drained according to the rule.

units.la: CONVIVIA veterum ita plærumque fuerant instituta, ut quilibet potum necesse habuerit poscere, nec semper prope cantharum accubarunt.
units.tr: Banquets of the ancients were mostly arranged so that each man had to ask for his own drink, and they did not always recline close to the bowl.

units.la: Unde apud Poëtas illud crebrò legimus:
units.tr: Hence in the poets we often read:

units.la: Da puer bibere. & id genus alia.
units.tr: Boy, give me something to drink. and other things of that kind.

units.la: Alludit noster Asin. 4.2. v.26. Tecum unà poscat: æquè pocula potitet.
units.tr: Our author alludes to this: Let him ask with you together, let him drink the cups on equal terms. Asin. 4.2 v.26.

units.la: Ubi simul alluditur ad morem amantum: qui in convivijs has sibi faciunt delitias, ut unà poscant, bibant: & talia: quæ Zeloty-pus amator caveri vult.
units.tr: Here there is also an allusion to the custom of lovers, who at banquets take pleasure in asking for drinks together, drinking together, and such things, which the jealous lover wants guarded against.

units.la: Pocula in convivijs circumibant à strophis ad antistrophas, velut in fabulis. Stich. 5.2. v.7. Monostrophe hoc convivium est: nem-pe in quo servi sibi ipsi ministrabant sine puerorum operâ.
units.tr: At banquets the cups went around from strophe to antistrophe, as in plays. Stich. 5.2 v.7: this banquet is a monostrophe, that is, one in which the slaves served themselves without the help of boys.

units.la: In convivijs circumferebatur phiala grandior, quam Dominus convivij jubebat ab uno in orbem per alios omnes convivas circumagi: quod est πεεισεβειν, & πεεισφέρω. Plauto: dare cantharum circum. Mostl. 1.3 v.33. Mep. 1.2.v.64. ἀλληλοεικῶς.
units.tr: At banquets a larger bowl was carried round, which the master of the banquet ordered to be passed from one man in a circle through all the other guests; this is called [περιπίνειν, περιφέρειν]. Plautus: to pass the cup around. Mostellaria 1.3 v.33; Menaechmi 1.2 v.64. [ἀλληλοεικῶς].

units.la: Vide Turn. lib. 19. c.13. J. Wowern. ad Sidonium: nec non Æmylium Portum de compotatione Græcorum.
units.tr: See Turnebus book 19 ch. 13; J. Wowern on Sidonius; and Æmilius Portus on Greek drinking-parties.

units.la: Bibentes vertebant poculum exhaustum. Stich. 3.4. v.39. Græci dicebant ἀμυσῶ.
units.tr: Drinkers turned the emptied cup over. Stich. 3.4 v.39. The Greeks called this [ἀμυσῶ].

units.la: Vide Lambin. ad Horat. nec non Æmyl. Portum de ratione Cõviv. apud Græcos.
units.tr: See Lambinus on Horace, and Æmilius Portus on the manner of banquets among the Greeks.

units.la: Ennius: & ex eo Virgil. lib. 9. Æneid.
units.tr: Ennius, and from him Virgil, Aeneid book 9:

units.la: Indulgent vino, & vertunt crateras ahenos.
units.tr: They indulge in wine, and turn the bronze mixing bowls over.

units.la: Et alius:
units.tr: And another:

units.la: Vertitur œnophorù fundus, sententia nobù.
units.tr: The bottom of the wine-jar is turned up, such is our opinion.

units.la: Quem morem Heroicum sc. in suis Francis laudat Taubmanus, ab eadem arte evacuandi culullos olim valde celebris:
units.tr: Taubmann praises this heroic custom among his own Franks, a practice once much celebrated for the same art of emptying cups:

units.la: Laudo meos Francos, qui se cervice supinant, Et fundo ex imo pocula summa bibunt.
units.tr: I praise my Franks, who tilt their necks back and drink the cups' contents from the very bottom.

units.la: Egregiam verò laudem tanti Mystagogæ!
units.tr: What an outstanding praise for so great a mystagogue!

units.la: Amatores potaturi de pleno poculo, aliquid Veneri libabant leviter defundentes guttulas vini: idque faciebant, vel in Aram, vel in mensam, quæ aræ loco erat, vel in focum, quisfacer habebatur, vel in mare, in honorem Deorum marinorum, vel in quemcumque locum pro re nata. De Amatoribus Curc. 1.2.v.31. Debrijs Amph.3.4.v.16. Virgil. lib.5. Æneid. --- vina liquentia fundam.
units.tr: Lovers, about to drink from a full cup, poured a little out as an offering to Venus, letting drop a few small drops of wine. They did this either on the altar, or on the table which served in place of an altar, or on the hearth, which was regarded as sacred, or into the sea in honour of the sea-gods, or in whatever place the occasion offered. On lovers, Curculio 1.2 v.31; on the Debrii, Amphitruo 3.4 v.16; Virgil, Aeneid book 5: I will pour out the flowing wine.

units.la: Vide Justum Lipsium Antiq.Lect.lib.3. Turneb.lib.11.c.7. & Janum Bernartium ad lib.1. Theb. Statij.
units.tr: See Justus Lipsius, Antiquae Lectiones book 3; Turnebus book 11 ch. 7; and Janus Bernartius on book 1 of Statius's Thebaid.

units.la: Convivæ exuno poculo bibebant: quod si forte mutarent, in multam incurrebant ex lege magistri. Stich.5.4.v.42.48.
units.tr: Guests drank from one and the same cup; if they changed cups, they incurred a fine under the master's law. Stich. 5.4 v.42-48.

units.la: Agedum, Stiche, uter demutassit poculo, multabitur.
units.tr: Come on, Stichus, whoever has switched cups shall be fined.

units.la: Et hoc illud est, quod est apud Horat.lib.2.Sat.2.v.123. Cuppa potare magistra.
units.tr: And this is what is meant in Horace, Satires book 2 v.123: to drink as the cup-master directs.

units.la: Ubi vide Notas nostras. Quamquam Turn. lib.7.c.9. aliter locum Plauti distinguat, sic nimirum: Agedum Stiche, uter demutassit, poculo multabitur. Nempe, inquit, excogitatum fuit ludi quoddam genus post cænam, quo non magistri imperio ad bibendum cogebantur, ne nimium ebrietati indulgeretur: sed ut ea coerceretur, nemo, nisi aliquâ in re peccarat, calicem ducebat: ut bibere, pænæ & dedecoris esset, non invitationis aut magistetrij.
units.tr: See our notes there. Although Turnebus, book 7 ch. 9, punctuates the passage of Plautus differently, thus: Come on, Stichus, whoever has switched, shall be fined with the cup. Indeed, he says, a certain kind of game was devised after dinner, in which people were not forced to drink by the master's command, lest drunkenness be indulged too much; rather, to restrain it, no one, unless he had erred in some matter, took up the cup. Thus to drink would be a punishment and a disgrace, not an invitation or a mark of office.

units.la: Vide etiam Villiomar. lib.8.c.15. contra Titium.
units.tr: See also Villiomarus book 8 ch. 15, against Titius.

units.la: Græci in convivijs solebant è poculo reliquias vini in terram elidere, ut sonum redderent, vel ut resonaret: quod Græci dicebant κοτταβίζειν: Facere cottabum.
units.tr: The Greeks at banquets used to flick the leftover wine from the cup onto the ground, so that it would make a sound or resound; the Greeks called this [κοτταβίζειν], that is, to make a cottabus.

units.la: Eò allusit Trin. 4.3.v.4. de cottabis bubulis. Morem autem illum videapud Lipf. Antiq.Lect.lib.3. & Jan. Parrhas. de Quæsitis per Epist.Athen.lib.10.&15.pag.666. Edit.Commelin.
units.tr: Plautus alludes to this in Trinummus 4.3 v.4, on the ox-hide cottabi. On that custom see Lipsius, Antiquae Lectiones book 3, and Janus Parrhasius, On Questions Put by Letter; Athenaeus books 10 and 15, p. 666, Commelin edition.

units.la: Propinandi mos in convivijs antiquissimus: ut patet ex Plauto. Curc.2.3.v.80. Stich.5.4.v.26.
units.tr: The custom of toasting at banquets is very ancient, as is clear from Plautus, Curculio 2.3 v.80 and Stichus 5.4 v.26.

units.la: Atque inter bibendum salutem propinabant. Stich. 3.2.v.16. Propino tibi salutem plenu faucibus.
units.tr: And during drinking they drank toasts to health. Stich. 3.2 v.16: I drink your health with full throats.

units.la: Inter propinandum autem hac ferè formulâ mutuam salutem vovebant.
units.tr: During the toasting they pledged mutual health with roughly this formula:

units.la: Bene. Mihi. Bene. Vobis. Bene. Amicæ. Meæ. Bene. Omnibus. Nobis. Bene. Ei. Qui, Non. invidet. Mihi. Et. Ei. Qui. Hoc. Gaudio. Gaudet.
units.tr: Good for me. Good for you. Good for my mistress. Good for all of us. Good for him who does not envy me, and for him who rejoices in this joy.

units.la: Sic Stich. ⁊. 4. v. 27.
units.tr: So Stichus 4 v.27.

units.la: Bene. Vos. Bene. Nos. Bene. Te. Bene. Me. Bene. Nostram. Stephanium.
units.tr: Good for you. Good for us. Good for you. Good for me. Good for our Stephanium.

units.la: In quâ formulâ hoc notandum: quod Amantes semper nominarint amicam suam: ut his locis patet. Necidamantes tantum observarunt: sed & alij conviuæ: qui in honorem vel Principis, vel benefactoris, Amici aut præceptoris sui, inter pocula & mensas secundas sibi invicem pocula aliquot propinabant: quod ostendit doctissimus Lipsius Dial. 10. l. 1. Poliorcet. nec non lib. 3. Antiq.Lect.
units.tr: In this formula it should be noted that lovers always named their mistress, as these passages show. Not only lovers observed this, but also other guests, who in honour of a prince, a benefactor, a friend or their teacher drank several toasts to one another between the cups and the second courses; as the most learned Lipsius shows in Dialogue 10 of book 1 of the Poliorcetica, and in book 3 of the Antiquae Lectiones.

units.la: Et prodijt nuper Francofurti libellus peculiaris De ratione propinandi.
units.tr: And recently a special booklet, On the Manner of Toasting, appeared at Frankfurt.

units.la: Quis hodiè abusus sit in hac propinandi ratione, id verò experientiâ omnibus notissimum est.
units.tr: How this custom of toasting is abused today is best known to everyone from experience.

units.la: Vide etiam Æmyl. Porti librum de Compotatione Græcorum.
units.tr: See also Æmilius Portus's book On the Drinking-Parties of the Greeks.

units.la: Semel iterumque bibebant, cùm quid eis odiosum & molestum accideraat: cùm è re laboriosâ emerserant, aut in câ versabantur, exemplo à cloacarijs aut fullonibus sumto, qui cùm perspiliant in stercore, in lotio, guttur sæpè proluunt. Asin. 5.2.v.58. Men. 5.1. v. 43. Et alibi.
units.tr: They drank once and again when something annoying and troublesome had befallen them, when they had emerged from hard labour or were still engaged in it, taking their example from sewer-cleaners or fullers, who, when they are covered in filth in the dung-pit or the urine-tub, often rinse their throats. Asin. 5.2 v.58; Menaechmi 5.1 v.43. And elsewhere:

units.la: Jam bis bibisse oportuit.
units.tr: Now it was necessary to drink twice.

units.la: Rud. 3.6 v.46. Claud. 1. in Eutrop. v. 270.
units.tr: Rudens 3.6 v.46; Claudian, In Eutropium 1 v.270:

units.la: Vix lassa resedit: & jam vina petit.
units.tr: Scarcely has she sat down, weary, and already she asks for wine.

units.la: In commissationibus quisque suum vinum conferebat, quasi in symbolam. Stich. 5.4. v. 4.
units.tr: In merry parties each man brought his own wine, as a contribution, as it were. Stich. 5.4 v.4.

units.la: In convivijs amatores postquam bibissent, savium dabant. Bacch. I.I.V.15.
units.tr: At banquets lovers, after they had drunk, gave kisses. Bacchides 1.1 v.15.

units.la: VINUM peregrè adventantibus dono dabatur. Stich. §.2.v.17.
units.tr: Wine was given as a gift to strangers arriving from abroad. Stich. 5.2 v.17.

units.la: AQUAM calidam puram putam, haud medicatam olim habebant in delitijs Græci & Romani. Vendebatur illa in thermopolijs. Trin. 4.3.v.6. Caf 2.3.v.37. Rud. 2.6.v.35. Pseud. 2,4.v.52. Curc. 2.3.v.13.
units.tr: The Greeks and Romans of old counted pure, hot water, not medicated, among their delights; it was sold in thermopolia. Trinummus 4.3 v.6; Casina 2.3 v.37; Rudens 2.6 v.35; Pseudolus 2.4 v.52; Curculio 2.3 v.13.

units.la: Ardua verò etiamnum agitur Quæstio inter Medicorum filios: Utrum calida an frigida Potio valetudini sit salutarior?
units.tr: A hard question is still being debated among the sons of physicians: Which drink is more beneficial to health, a warm one or a cold one?

units.la: Utrinque firmissima argumenta proferuntur ex intimâ antiquitate.
units.tr: Strong arguments are put forward on both sides from the most ancient times.

units.la: Pro Frigidâ pugnat Hieronymus Mercurialis lib.1. Variarum Lectionum cap. VIII. nec non Josephus Castalio lib. 1. Observat. cap.9. admodum prolixè.
units.tr: For the cold side Hieronymus Mercurialis fights, in Variae Lectiones book 1 ch. 8, and also Josephus Castalio, Observations book 1 ch. 9, at considerable length.

units.la: Pro Calidâ autem multò plures. Lipsius lib.1. Elector.c.4. Guilelmus Stuck.lib.3.c.6. Antiqq. Convivialium. Henric. Salmuth. ad Pancirollum lib. Memorabilium rerum deperditarum pagin. 541. Turn.in Joca Ciceronis: & deniq; Medicus Italus Antonius Perfius peculiari libro Italicè scripto: Del bever caldo costumato da gli antichi Romani: ubi multis firmamentis frigidam dissuadet, calidam commendat.
units.tr: For the warm side, however, there are far more: Lipsius, Electa book 1 ch. 4; Guilelmus Stuck, Antiquitates Convivialium book 3 ch. 6; Henricus Salmuth, on Pancirollus's Memorable Lost Things, p. 541; Turnebus, On the Jests of Cicero; and finally the Italian physician Antonius Persius, in a special book written in Italian, Del bever caldo costumato da gli antichi Romani, where by many arguments he dissuades from cold drink and commends warm.

units.la: Illi quoque accedit doctissimus vir Andreas Schottus ad Aurel. Victorium in Tiberio: & nuper lib.15. Observat. Human. cap. XXVIII. ubi insuper pro Calidâ hæc loca adduxit ex Arriano in Epictetum lib.1.cap.13. Eunapio Sardiano in Ædesio pag. 42.
units.tr: To these also add the very learned Andreas Schottus, on Aurelius Victor in Tiberius, and recently in book 15 of his Observationes Humanae, chapter 28, where he also adduced in favour of warm drink these passages: from Arrian on Epictetus, book 1, chapter 13; from Eunapius of Sardis in Aedesius, page 42.

units.la: Idem Proœresio pag.149.
units.tr: The same, in Proaeresius, page 149.

units.la: Julius Pollux lib.9.cap.6. pag. 433. Edit. Seberianæ:
units.tr: Julius Pollux, book 9, chapter 6, page 433, in the Seber edition:

units.la: Philo Judæus de Essæis :
units.tr: Philo the Jew, On the Essenes:

units.la: Vinum per illos dies non præbetur, sed aqua limpidissima, alijs qui-dem frigida : Σεμνὸν δὲ τῶν πρεσβυτάτων τοῖς ἀσεβεσιλαιτοις : calida autem his, qui inter seniores delicatum habentur.
units.tr: Wine is not offered to them on those days, but very clear water, cold for some; but it is a solemn thing among the most senior [Σεμνὸν δὲ τῶν πρεσβυτάτων τοῖς ἀσεβεσιλαιτοις], and warm water for those who are regarded among the elders as delicate.

units.la: In hac sententiarum diversitate, quid statuendum, difficile equi-dem est pronunciare. Ego, ut quid sentiam, aperiam : omnium maximè probo moderamen Magni Medici Mercurialis.
units.tr: On this divergence of opinions, it is indeed hard to pronounce what should be decided. For my part, to say what I think: I most of all approve the moderation of the great physician Mercurialis.

units.la: Nimirùm & calidâ, & frigidâ usi veteres: ut patet ex hoc loco Ju-venalis :.
units.tr: Certainly the ancients used both warm and cold drinks, as is clear from this passage of Juvenal:

units.la: ----quando ad te pervenit ille?
units.tr: When does that fellow come to you?

units.la: Quando vocatum adest calida, gelidaque minister?
units.tr: When is the attendant at hand, summoned, with warm and cold drink?

units.la: Et Martial. lib. ult.
units.tr: And Martial, in the last book:

units.la: Frigida non defit, non deerit calda petenti:
units.tr: Cold drink is not lacking, nor will warm be lacking to the one who asks for it,

units.la: Sed tu morosa ludere parce siti.
units.tr: But do not be so fussy as to trifle with a thirst.

units.la: Frigidâ quidem inter convivia ferè promiscuè omnes usi. Calidâ autem ad diluendum vinum merum. Calefactâ verò numquam utebantur, nisi ij, q' aliquâ valetudine affecti : aut qui vomere cupiebant, ut copiosius, & majori fame postmodum ingurgita-rent.
units.tr: Indeed, at banquets almost everyone used cold drink indiscriminately. Warm drink was used for diluting undiluted wine. Heated drink was never used except by those suffering from some illness, or by those who wanted to vomit, so that they could afterwards gorge more copiously and with greater appetite.

units.la: Potus enim calidæ contra naturam est, teste Plinio ; cùm & ipsa bruta frigida petsequantur. Ac non nisi ad ciendam vomitio-nem usurpari solcat calida.
units.tr: For drinking warm is contrary to nature, as Pliny testifies, since even brute animals seek cold water. And warm drink is customarily used only to provoke vomiting.

units.la: In Thermopolijs verò, quarum mentionem facit Plautus noster dulces potiones vendebantur : quas calidas sumebant: ita ut in-terdum guttures incenderentur. Illæ potiones dulces erant: Murrhina, passum, defrutum, melina, mel.
units.tr: In the thermopolia, which our Plautus mentions, sweet drinks were sold, and people took them warm, so that sometimes the throat was inflamed. Those drinks were sweet: murrhina, passum, defrutum, melina, honey.

units.la: De quibus Pseud. 2. 4. v. 51.
units.tr: On these see Pseud. 2. 4. v. 51.

units.la: De Murrhinâ vide Raderum ad Martialem. Turn.l.28.c.6.Mer-cur. l.5. Var.Lect.cap.1.
units.tr: On murrhina see Rader on Martial. Turnebus, book 28, chapter 6. Mercurialis, Variarum Lectionum book 5, chapter 1.

units.la: Atque hæc Mercurialis sententia mihi præ cæteris omnibus pla-cet. Displicet ea alijs. Quid tùm? Legantur Authores prædicti: quisquis autem probet, quod vult.
units.tr: And this opinion of Mercurialis pleases me more than all the others. It displeases others. So what? Let the authors named above be read, and let each approve what he wishes.

units.la: IV. MORALIA ET OECONOMICA de Conviviis.
units.tr: IV. MORALIA ET OECONOMICA: On Banquets.

units.la: CONVIVATORES de numero convivarum soliciti sunt: convivium ipsum curæ esse jubent coquis. Men. 1.4.v.6. Pseud. 3.1. v. 100.
units.tr: Hosts are anxious about the number of guests, and they tell the cooks that the banquet itself is their concern. Men. 1.4.v.6. Pseud. 3.1. v. 100.

units.la: Vide Apophoretum Martial. Obsonator.
units.tr: See the Apophoretum of Martial, Obsonator.

units.la: CONVIVÆ cum dulcedine apparatûs inducti plusculè aut comedunt aut bibunt, quàm satis est, prodi dicuntur. Rud. 2.7.v.31.
units.tr: Guests who, enticed by the delights of the spread, eat or drink rather more than is enough are said to be betrayed. Rud. 2.7.v.31.

units.la: Neptunus speravit nobis prodi alvum salsis poculis.
units.tr: Neptune hoped to betray our belly with salty drinks.

units.la: Terentius Eunuch.
units.tr: Terence, Eunuch.

units.la: Ætat data hercle verba mihi sunt.
units.tr: By Hercules, my age has played me false.

units.la: Vicit vinum quod bibi.
units.tr: The wine I drank has beaten me.

units.la: Et hinc illa nota:
units.tr: And hence that familiar saying:

units.la: Vino deponere, inescare.
units.tr: To lay low with wine, to bait.

units.la: Cicero lib. 7. Epist. Galli:
units.tr: Cicero, book 7 of the Letters to Gallus:

units.la: Lex sumtuaria, quæ videtur Nilbrutia attulisse, ea mihi fraudi fuit. Nam dum volunt isti lauti terrâ nata, quæ lege excepta sunt, in honorem adducere, fungos, helvellas, herbas omnes ita condiunt, ut nihil posset esse suavius, in eas cùm incidissem in cenâ Augurali apud Lentulum, tanta me διάβροια arripuit, ut hodie primum videar crepisse consistere.
units.tr: The sumptuary law, which Nilbrutius seems to have brought in, proved a disadvantage to me. For while those fine gentlemen want to bring into fashion the products of the earth that the law exempted, they season mushrooms, helvellae and all the herbs so well that nothing could be tastier. When I came across them at the augural dinner at Lentulus's house, such a diarrhoea [διάβροια] seized me that today, for the first time, I seem to have stopped bursting.

units.la: MULTI in convivijs comparebant non vocati. Trin. 2.4.v.67. De illis vide totum cap. 4. lib. 2. Antiq. Conviv. Gulielmi Stuckij. Et crebro apud Athenæum & Mart. Tales erant Parasiti, Adulatores.
units.tr: Many came to banquets uninvited. Trin. 2.4.v.67. On them see the whole of chapter 4 of book 2 of Wilhelm Stuck's Antiquities of Banqueting, and often in Athenaeus and Martial. Such were the parasites and flatterers.

units.la: De quibus vide infra Tit. Parasitorum.
units.tr: On whom see below, under the title Parasites.

units.la: PARASITI & ij, qui corpore merebant invocati ad convivia comparebant. Capt. 1.1.v.1. de Parasito. Idem de Myconijs tradi solet.
units.tr: Parasites, and those who earned their keep with their bodies, came to banquets when invited. Capt. 1.1.v.1. Concerning the parasite. The same is commonly reported of the Myconians.

units.la: Vide Athen. Casaub. Animadverf. lib. 8. cap. 7. & Athen. l. 1. de Philoxeno: alijsq;.
units.tr: See Casaubon's Animadversions on Athenaeus, book 8, chapter 7, and Athenaeus, book 1, on Philoxenus, and others.

units.la: Olim quos vellent invitatos, solemniter invitabant sic:
units.tr: Formerly they invited, with formal solemnity, those whom they wished to be guests, in these words:

units.la: Veni ad cenam: Volo fieri, non amittam: quin eas.
units.tr: Come to dinner. I want you there, I won't let you off; so come along!

units.la: Quiverò honoris saltim causâ vocabant, utebantur hac formulâ:
units.tr: Those who invited merely as a mark of honour used this formula:

units.la: Vocem te ad cenam, nisi egomet cenem foris.
units.tr: I invite you to dinner, unless I dine out myself.

units.la: Quam quidem formulam exsecratur Parasitus. Stich. 2. 1. v. 31. & seqq.
units.tr: The parasite curses this formula. Stich. 2.1. v. 31. and following.

units.la: Formula vocandi ad convivium erat: Ubi lubet, ire accubitum licet. Men. 2. 3. v. 16.
units.tr: The formula for inviting to dinner was: Whenever you like, you may go and recline. Men. 2.3. v. 16.

units.la: Vide Callig. Rom. Tit Convivij.
units.tr: See Callig. Rom., title Convivium.

units.la: Invitati ad convivium gaudere solent, ut navigantes secundo vento utentes. Cist. 1. 1. v. 15.
units.tr: Invited guests are wont to rejoice at a banquet, like sailors with a fair wind. Cist. 1.1. v. 15.

units.la: At ægrè ferunt, si non detur, quod bibant; inprimis si propinetur vinum non meracum, sed dilutum. Ibid. v. 20.
units.tr: But they take it badly if nothing is given them to drink, especially if the wine served is not neat but diluted. Ibid. v. 20.

units.la: Inter amicos tamen id fieri jus fasq; esse clamat puella meretrix. Cist. ib. v. 22.
units.tr: Among friends, however, the courtesan girl declares that this is right and lawful. Cist. ib. v. 22.

units.la: Mores convivarum simulantium se fastidire apparatum nimium: & strenuè interim convivantium: egregiè exprimuntur. Mil. 3. 1. v. 156.
units.tr: The manners of guests who pretend to find the spread excessive, yet meanwhile feast vigorously, are admirably portrayed. Mil. 3.1. v. 156.

units.la: Vide Tit. Hospitij.
units.tr: See the title Hospitality.

units.la: Hilare victuri brevitatem vitæ sibi proponebant. Mostell. 3. 2. v. 37.
units.tr: Those about to live set before themselves the brevity of life. Mostell. 3.2. v. 37.

units.la: Sic decet, ut homines sunt, ita morem geras:
units.tr: So it is fitting: since you are men, indulge your habit:

units.la: Vita quàm sit brevis, simul cogites.
units.tr: Think how brief life is.

units.la: Horatius lib. 2. Sat. 6. Et alibi sæpius:
units.tr: Horace, book 2, Satire 6, and elsewhere very often:

units.la: Dum licet in rebus jucundis, vive beatus.
units.tr: While it is allowed, live happily among pleasant things.

units.la: Vive memor, quam sis ævi brevis.
units.tr: Live mindful of how brief your span of life is.

units.la: Lucretius:
units.tr: Lucretius:

units.la: Brevis est hic fructus homullis.
units.tr: Short is this fruit for little men.

units.la: Tamquam jam moriturî bibebant, & tamquam numquam id sa-cturi. Stich. 5. 4. v. 38. Volo ego nos pro summo bibere: nullirei erimus postea.
units.tr: As if about to die they drank, and as if they would never do it again. Stich. 5.4. v. 38. "I want us to drink to the full; afterwards we shall be nothing."

units.la: Sic dicitur ἡδὺς βίῳ, τὸ ζῆν ταχύ: τὸ ϑανεῖν ὑποψία. Vide Scalig. Ausonn. Lect. l. 2. c. 26.
units.tr: Thus it is said: pleasant in life, quick is living; dying is a surmise [ἡδὺς βίῳ, τὸ ζῆν ταχύ: τὸ ϑανεῖν ὑποψία]. See Scaliger, Ausonian Lectures, book 2, chapter 26.

units.la: LIBENTER cœnare dicebantur, qui jucundè cœnabant. Capt. 3.1. v. 13.
units.tr: Those who dined pleasantly were said to dine gladly. Capt. 3.1. v. 13.

units.la: Sic Cic. lib. 2. de Finib.
units.tr: So Cicero, book 2 of De Finibus.

units.la: Ex quo illud efficitur: qui bene cænent, omnes libenter cænare: qui libenter, non continuo bene.
units.tr: From this it follows: all who dine well dine gladly; but those who dine gladly do not always dine well.

units.la: ETIAM decorum civile servandum est in convivijs, ne quidvis alijs præripiamus: quod parasitus ille fecit Trin. 2.4. v. 76.
units.tr: Even so, a civil decorum must be observed at banquets, so that we do not snatch anything from others, as that parasite did. Trin. 2.4. v. 76.

units.la: Sic Salomon Prov. cap. 23.
units.tr: So Solomon, Proverbs chapter 23.

units.la: Comede, ut homo, quæ apposita sunt tibi, neque devora, ne odio habeare.
units.tr: Eat, as a man, what is set before you, and do not gobble it up, lest you be hated.

units.la: IN convivijs arrogantiæ notam subit, qui publicas res clamat, & leges crepat. Mil. 3.1. v. 56.
units.tr: At a banquet a man incurs the mark of arrogance if he proclaims public affairs and rails against the laws. Mil. 3.1. v. 56.

units.la: Sic Varro in Menippeâ:
units.tr: So Varro in his Menippean satire:

units.la: Nec loquaces autem convivas, nec mutos legere oportet: quia eloquentia in foro, et apud subsellia, silentium vero non in convivio, sed in cubiculo esse debet.
units.tr: Neither talkative nor silent dinner companions ought to be chosen, because eloquence belongs in the forum and among the benches, but silence belongs not at a banquet but in the bedroom.

units.la: ALIAS convivij & boni convivæ virtutes enumerat idem senex Aul. 3.1. v. 17.
units.tr: Otherwise the same old man lists other virtues of a banquet and of a good dinner guest. Aul. 3.1. v. 17.

units.la: Neq; ego umquam alienum scortum subigito in convivio, Neq; præripio pulpamentum, neq; prævorto poculum: Neq; per vinum umquam ex me exoritur dissidium. Si quis ibi odiosus est, abeo domum, sermonem segrego, Venerem, amorem, amanitatem, accubans exerceo.
units.tr: I never poke my finger into another man's courtesan at a dinner, nor snatch the tidbit, nor push ahead for the cup; nor through wine does a quarrel ever arise from me. If anyone there is obnoxious, I go home, I keep my talk to myself, and I practise love, affection and friendliness while reclining.

units.la: IN convivijs non decet obloqui alteri: ait senex Mil. 3.1. v. 47.
units.tr: At a banquet one should not contradict another, says the old man. Mil. 3.1. v. 47.

units.la: --- neq; ego oblocutor sum alteri in convivio. Incommeditate abstinere me apud convivas commodè Commemini: & mea orationis justam partem persequi, Et meam partem itidem facere, cum altena est oratio.
units.tr: I am no contradicter of another at a banquet. I remember to refrain tactfully from awkward things among guests, to pursue my fair share of the conversation, and likewise to do my part when the talk is another's.

units.la: PARASITORUM hoc est decretum: Verecundari apud mensam nemineminem decet: ut in senatu nulla verecundia debet nos dimovere in sententia dicenda. Trin. 2.4.v 77.
units.tr: This is the decree of the parasites: no one should feel shame at table, just as in the senate no shame ought to keep us from giving our opinion. Trin. 2.4. v. 77.

units.la: Qui lautum & votivuum epulum pararent, pollucibiliter diceban- tur vivere. Rud. 5.3.v.63.
units.tr: Those who prepared a lavish and sumptuous feast were said to live in grand style. Rud. 5.3. v. 63.

units.la: Vide Lex. Pollucere.
units.tr: See the lexicon, under Pollucere.

units.la: Convivas decet hilaritas. Mil. 3.1.v.71.
units.tr: Cheerfulness befits guests. Mil. 3.1. v. 71.

units.la: Qui de die convivabantur, male audiebant ob intemperantiam, non expectato legitimo Cænæ tempore. Hinc nostER Asin. 4.2. v.15.
units.tr: Those who dined by daylight were ill spoken of for intemperance, since they did not wait for the proper hour of supper. Hence our Asin. 4.2. v. 15.

units.la: Tu ergo fac ut illi turbas, lites concias, Cum suo sibi gnato unà ad amicam de die Potare, illam expilare clam.
units.tr: So you, make them stir up trouble and cause quarrels, when with his own son he drinks by day with his mistress, secretly plundering her.

units.la: Non placet mihi cœna, quæ bilem movet: qualem scilic. dant inimici. Bacch. 3.6.v.8.
units.tr: I do not like a supper that stirs up bile, the sort, of course, that enemies provide. Bacch. 3.6. v. 8.

units.la: In convivijs sæpè ita excepti, & cibis impleti, ut nescirent quà irent domum. Rud. 3.5.v.30. de plagarum invitatione. ἀλληγοεικῶς.
units.tr: At banquets men were often so welcomed and filled with food that they did not know which way to go home. Rud. 3.5. v. 30. On the invitation of blows. [ἀλληγορικῶς], allegorically.

units.la: In convivijs adornandis admodùm soliciti fuerunt, præsertim natalitijs. De quibus vide solicitudinem Lenonis Pseud. 1.2.v.32.
units.tr: They were very anxious about arranging banquets, especially birthday banquets. On this see the anxiety of the pimp, Pseud. 1.2. v. 32.

units.la: Convivas etiam ad pompam instituuntur quandoq; : ut inde divitiæ eraniftæ alijs innotescant. Pseud. 1.2.v.34.
units.tr: Guests are sometimes also arranged for display, so that the wealth of the rich man becomes known to others. Pseud. 1.2. v. 34.

units.la: Inter urbanos & villicos discrimen observari debet victus. Most. 1.1.v.51.
units.tr: Between townsmen and country folk a difference in diet should be observed. Most. 1.1. v. 51.

units.la: In convivijs opulenti cum pauperibus: & vicissim mixti sunt, & convivantur. Trin. 2.4.v.72.
units.tr: At banquets the rich mingle with the poor, and in turn they are mixed together and dine together. Trin. 2.4. v. 72.

units.la: Cænam item nuptialem amicis apparatabant. Curc. 5.2.v.61.
units.tr: They also prepared a wedding supper for their friends. Curc. 5.2. v. 61.

units.la: Avari eos tantum vocant ad convivia: qui reddere possunt. Capt. 3.1.v.13.
units.tr: Misers invite to banquets only those who can repay them. Capt. 3.1. v. 13.

units.la: In convivijs etiam venefi cia adhibita. Pseud. 3.2.v.31.
units.tr: At banquets magic arts were also employed. Pseud. 3.2. v. 31.

units.la: Cænam dabant ob rem aliquam repertam. Curc. 5.2.v.61. Cænam sororiam.
units.tr: A supper was given for some discovered reason. Curc. 5.2. v. 61. A supper for sisters.

units.la: In convivio certabant cantharo. Men. 1.3.v.5. ἀλληγοεικῶς.
units.tr: At the banquet they contended over the cup. Men. 1.3. v. 5. [ἀλληγορικῶς], allegorically.

units.la: DE functo convivio dicitur Rud. 2. 6. v. 24. Scelestiorem canam, canavit tuam, quam quæ Thyesta quondam anteposita est, & Tereo.
units.tr: Of a finished banquet it is said: Rud. 2.6. v. 24. You have eaten a more wicked supper than yours, than that once set before Thyestes and Tereus.

units.la: COQUORUM. CUPPEDIARUM. DELITIARUM. POPINÆ. COQUINARUM. COQUINARIÆ.
units.tr: COQUORUM. CUPPEDIARUM. DELITIARUM. POPINÆ. COQUINARUM. COQUINARIÆ.

units.la: PRIVATÆ personæ coquos seu coctores non habebant familiares: sed in foro conducebant. Aul. 2.4.v.1.
units.tr: Private persons did not keep cooks or cooks' assistants as household servants; they hired them in the marketplace. Aul. 2.4.v.1.

units.la: Coqui ὡς ὅπῃ τὸ πρὸ fures, Pseud. 3.2.v.2. Non coquinum est sorum: verum furinum. Nam si ego juratus pejorem hominem quærerem, coquum non potui, quam hunc quem duco, ducere, multiloquum, gloriosum, insulsum, inutilem. Quin ob eam rem Orcus ad se recipere noluit, ut esset hic, qui mortuis cænam coquat. Aul. 2.4. v.47. & Aul. 2.5. v.20. Ubi si quid perierit, dicant: Coqui abstulerunt: comprehendite. Cas.3.6.v.1. De pœnâ Coquorum furum vide Tit. Supplicij: Pœna. Inde Rapacida dicti patronymica. Aul.2.7.v.8. Pseud.3.2.v.61.97. An invenire postulas quemquam coquum, nisi milvinus aut aquilinus unguis? Quaso hercle, priusquam quicquam convivis dabis, gustato tute priùs, & discipulis dato, ut prærodatis vestras furtificas manus.
units.tr: Cooks are thieves [ὡς ὅπῃ τὸ πρὸ]. Pseud. 3.2.v.2. It is not a kitchen job but a thieving one. For if I went looking under oath for a worse man, I could not have chosen a cook worse than the one I am bringing here: talkative, boastful, insipid, useless. Indeed, for this reason Orcus refused to admit him, so that there would be no one to cook dinner for the dead. Aul. 2.4. v.47, and Aul. 2.5. v.20. Where something has gone missing, they say: "The cooks took it; arrest them!" Cas. 3.6.v.1. On the punishment of cooks who steal, see the title Supplicij: Pœna. From this comes the derived name Rapacida. Aul. 2.7.v.8. Pseud. 3.2.v.61, 97. Do you expect to find any cook who doesn't have a kite's or eagle's claw? I beg you, by Hercules, before you serve anything to the guests, taste it yourself and give it to your apprentices, so that you may first pre-test your thieving hands.

units.la: Inde coqui rapaces, dum furantur, dicuntur Facere officium suum. Aul.2.9. v.8. Atque ideò etiam invocarunt Deam furum Lavernam. Aul. 3.2.v.31. Ita me bene amet Laverna!
units.tr: Hence rapacious cooks, while they steal, are said to "do their duty." Aul. 2.9. v.8. And for this reason they also invoked Laverna, the goddess of thieves. Aul. 3.2.v.31. So may Laverna love me!

units.la: Coquorum servi pisces desquamabant, ut congrum, exdorsuafuabant murenam: & cæteros exossabant. Aul.2.9.v.1.2.
units.tr: The cooks' servants scaled the fish, as with the conger; they flayed the eel from the back, and boned the rest. Aul. 2.9. v.1, 2.

units.la: Coqui in artoptâ vase panem tostum coquebant: gallum deplumabant: & glabrum reddebant. Aul.2.9.v.5. De pane tosto vide Turn.lib.14. cap.15. & Plin.lib.18 11. ibi Dalechamp.
units.tr: Cooks toasted bread in a vessel called an artopta, plucked the cock and made it bald. Aul. 2.9. v.5. On toasted bread see Turnebus, book 14, chapter 15, and Pliny, book 18, chapter 11, with Dalechamp's notes there.

units.la: Coqui arrogans & jactabunda natio. Pseud.2.2.v 21. Non item cænam condio, ut alij coqui. Ibid. vers. 40. & 55. 80. Nam vel ducenos annos poterunt vivere, meas qui esitabunt escas, quas condivero.
units.tr: Cooks are an arrogant and boastful tribe. Pseud. 2.2. v.21. I do not season the dinner as other cooks do. Ibid. vv. 40, 55, 80. For they will be able to live two hundred years, those who devour my dishes, which I season.

units.la: Sic coquus ille apud Alexidem : Δαυμαστὸν ἐμὸν εὕρεμα πάνυ, πο-λὺ δ' ἐγὼ ἐὰν παξαδῶ σοι, ᾧ σοσκατέθη τὰς ἀκτύλας σαυτῷ γε χαίρων.
units.tr: So that cook in Alexis: [Δαυμαστὸν ἐμὸν εὕρεμα πάνυ, πολὺ δ' ἐγὼ ἐὰν παραδῶ σοι, ᾧ σὺ κατέθηκας τὰς ἀκτύλους σαυτῷ γε χαίρων] — "My invention is truly marvellous; but if I hand it over to you, you who, delighting in yourself, have laid your fingers on it..."

units.la: Et alter apud Philemonem: ἅπαντες οἱ φαγόντες ἐχάνοντ' αὖ θεοί, Αθανασίαν εὕρηκα, τὰς ἡδὺ νεικεὺς, ὅταν ὀσφρανθῶσιν, ποιήσω ζῶν πάλιν.
units.tr: And another in Philemon: [ἅπαντες οἱ φαγόντες ἐχάνοντ' αὖ θεοί, Αθανασίαν εὕρηκα, τὰς ἡδὺ νεικεὺς, ὅταν ὀσφρανθῶσιν, ποιήσω ζῶν πάλιν] — "All who have eaten have perished again, and the gods too. I have found immortality; when they have smelled the sweet dish, I will make them live again."

units.la: Varia coquorum edulia: rationemque indendi, diluendi, condiendi, vide totâ scenâ 2. Act 3. Pseudolo.
units.tr: For the various cooks' dishes, and the method of seasoning, steeping and dressing them, see the whole scene, Act 2, Scene 3, of Pseudolus.

units.la: Coqui alebant discipulos. Pseud. 3.2.v.96.
units.tr: Cooks fed their apprentices. Pseud. 3.2.v.96.

units.la: Coqui subirascuntur, nisi convivæ maturè adsint: eò quòd cæna corrumpitur, Pseud. 3.2.v.102.
units.tr: Cooks grow angry unless the guests arrive promptly, because the dinner spoils. Pseud. 3.2.v.102.

units.la: Fartores cupediarij amatoribus delitias parabant. Trucul. 1. 2. v. 12.
units.tr: Pastry-makers and confectioners prepared delicacies for their lovers. Trucul. 1.2.v.12.

units.la: Coquorum coquarumve est scire, ut muriatica salsa sint maceranda. Pœn. 1.2.v.32.
units.tr: It is the business of cooks, male and female, to know how salted meats are to be soaked. Pœn. 1.2.v.32.

units.la: Pedissequi servi, alijque delicatiores nepotuli in popinis scribli-tas, & id genus cuppedias absumebaut. Pœn.Prob. v.42.
units.tr: Attendants, and more refined young nephews, used to consume pastries in taverns, and that kind of delicacy. Pœn. Prob. v.42.

units.la: Coqui condimentis varijs utuntur : & Amore tamen non utuntur condimento præstantissimo. Casin. 2.3.v.3.
units.tr: Cooks use various seasonings, yet they do not use the most excellent seasoning of all, which is love. Casin. 2.3.v.3.

units.la: Coqui aulas pervortunt; ignem reslinguunt aquâ. Caf. 4.1. v.16.
units.tr: Cooks overturn the kitchen pots and put out the fire with water. Caf. 4.1. v.16.

units.la: Coqui etiam inter fures. Aul. 2.4.v.47. Caf. 3.6.v.1.
units.tr: Cooks are even among the thieves. Aul. 2.4.v.47. Caf. 3.6.v.1.

units.la: Coquus novemdialis erat, qui mortuis in cænam pararet. Aulul. 2.4.v.50. Pseud. 3.2 v.7.
units.tr: A cook was a "novemdialis," that is, one who prepared the meal for the dead. Aulul. 2.4.v.50. Pseud. 3.2 v.7.

units.la: Coqui habebant servos discipulos. Aul. 3.1.v.4.
units.tr: Cooks had apprentice servants. Aul. 3.1.v.4.

units.la: Coqui solent sua jura confundere: & nidorem excitare. Mostt. 1. 3.v.119.
units.tr: Cooks are wont to confuse their broths and to stir up the smell. Mostell. 1.3.v.119.

units.la: Coqui jactabundi se hominum servatores jactant. Pseud. 3.2.v.84.
units.tr: Boastful cooks brag that they are the saviours of men. Pseud. 3.2.v.84.

units.la: Coqui sepijs oculos elidunt prius. Rud. 3.2.v.45.
units.tr: Cooks first gouge out the eyes of cuttlefish. Rud. 3.2.v.45.

units.la: Coquum decet habere cultrum. Aul. 3.2.v.3.
units.tr: A cook ought to have a knife. Aul. 3.2.v.3.

units.la: CURARUM. MEDITATIONIS. COGITATIONUM. SOLICITUDINIS.
units.tr: Of Cares, Meditations, Thoughts, and Anxieties.

units.la: CURAE maciem inducunt. Unde Græcis dictæ μελεδῶνες γυβέρνοι. Aul 3. 6. v. 27.
units.tr: Cares bring on emaciation. Whence the Greeks called them meledones [μελεδῶνες] and gyberni [γυβέρνοι]. Aul 3. 6. v. 27.

units.la: Agnus Curio, qui ossa atq; pellis totus est, ita curâ macet.
units.tr: "The lamb Curio, who is all skin and bones, is worn away by care."

units.la: Ubi tamen loci in nostrâ editione expressi crura. Quod quidem Wonsæsas homo in novissimâ editione alto naso despexit.
units.tr: Where, however, I have printed "crura" (legs) in our edition. The man Wonsaesas scorned this with a haughty nose in the latest edition.

units.la: Vide quid scripserim in Calligraphiâ Linguæ Latinæ Titulo Macies corporis, pagin. 761. Et sane nec dum mihi mea electio omnimodis displicet; cùm in allegoriâ persistat sermo. Quæ enim curæ macerarent agnum curionem? scil. ne scabie contabesceat agnus! Cæteroquin formulam alteram quando de hominibus usurpatur, nihil damno. Et exstat apud Plautum difertim Pseud. 1. v. 19.
units.tr: See what I wrote in the Calligraphia Linguae Latinae under the title Macies corporis, page 761. And indeed my choice does not yet displease me in every way, since the discourse keeps to the allegory. For what cares would waste away a lamb Curio? Namely, lest the lamb waste away from mange! Otherwise, when the other formula is used of human beings, I have no objection. And it occurs plainly in Plautus, Pseud. 1 v.19.

units.la: Miseria & cura me contabefacit.
units.tr: "Misery and care wear me down."

units.la: Vide dicto loco Calligr.
units.tr: See the passage cited in the Calligraphia.

units.la: CURAE corpus exedunt. Rud. 1. 4. v. 2. Inde dicuntur βιοφθόροι, λυχνολύτοροι.
units.tr: CARES consume the body. Rud. 1.4 v.2. Hence they are called biophthoroi [βιοφθόροι] and lychnolytoroi [λυχνολύτοροι].

units.la: COGITABUNDI pectus pultare solent digitis, quasi cor evocaturi foras. Mil 2. 2. v. 47. Merc. 3. 4. v. 15.
units.tr: THINKERS are wont to beat their breasts with their fingers, as if about to call the heart out. Mil. 2.2 v.47. Merc. 3.4 v.15.

units.la: Vide totum locum.
units.tr: See the whole passage.

units.la: CURAE sæpè impediunt somnum. Trin. 3. 1. v. 20.
units.tr: CARES often prevent sleep. Trin. 3.1 v.20.

units.la: CURAE etiam ætatem gravem reddunt. Trin. 2. 3. v. 8.
units.tr: CARES also make age burdensome. Trin. 2.3 v.8.

units.la: Qui cura & corde liberi sunt, aliena damna non facile æstimare possunt. Epid. 1. 2. v. 43.
units.tr: Those who are free of care and of heart cannot easily judge the losses of others. Epid. 1.2 v.43.

units.la: CURIARUM TRIBUUM. JUDICIORUM. CENTURIARUM.
units.tr: Curiae, Tribes, Courts, and Centuries.

units.la: Vide etiam Magistratus & Judiciorum litt. I.
units.tr: See also under Magistrates and Courts, letter I.

units.la: ROMÆ singulæ tribus habuerunt suos divisores, qui pecuniam populo viritim dividebant, singuli in suâ tribu: qui Magistri Curiarum dicti, & Curiones. Aul. I. 2. v. 29. & 2 2. v. 2. 3. Vide plura apud Asconium in 2. Verr. Rævardum lib. 2. Var. c. 16. Brod. Miscell. lib. 6. c. 11.
units.tr: At Rome each tribe had its own distributors, who divided money among the people by the head, each in his own tribe. They were called Masters of the Curiae and Curiones. Aul. I.2 v. 29 and II.2 v. 2, 3. See more in Asconius on the Second Verrine Oration; Raevardus, Varia, book 2, ch. 16; Brodaeus, Miscellanea, book 6, ch. 11.

units.la: CURIÆ erant pars tribûs Romanæ. Illarum curiarum præfectus dicebatur Magister curiæ. Aul. I. 2. v. 29. τεπιτάρχης.
units.tr: The curiae were a part of a Roman tribe. The prefect of such a curia was called Master of the curia. Aul. I.2 v. 29. [τεπιτάρχης]

units.la: CENTURIÆ ad suffragia conveniebant. Truculent. 4. 2. v. 160. ἀλ-λη-γοεικὸς.
units.tr: The centuries gathered for voting. Truculentus IV.2 v. 160. [ἀλληγοερικὸς]

units.la: SONTES reos condemnabant aperto capite. Capt. 3. 1. v. 16.
units.tr: They condemned guilty men with uncovered heads. Captivi III.1 v. 16.

units.la: CURIOSITATIS. ΠΟΛΥΠΡΑΓΜΟΣΥΝΗΣ.
units.tr: CURIOSITY. POLYPRAGMOSYNĒ [ΠΟΛΥΠΡΑΓΜΟΣΥΝΗΣ].

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Garrulitatis.
units.tr: See also the title Garrulitatis (Garrulity).

units.la: IN alieno si quis negotio imperiosior esset, dicebant cum sine suffragio populi ædilitatem gerere. Stich. 2. 3. v. 28.
units.tr: If someone was rather domineering in another's business, they used to say he was acting as aedile without the people's vote. Stich. 2. 3. v. 28.

units.la: Cicero:
units.tr: Cicero:

units.la: Sed quæro: quid hac re turpius, quàm sine provocatione senator, sine mandatis legatus.
units.tr: But I ask: what is more shameful than a senator without the right of appeal, or a envoy without instructions?

units.la: Suas quemque res curare addecet. Mil. 3.3. v. 55. 60. Alia cura. & Mil. 4.1. v. 5. & 4.2. v. 4.
units.tr: Everyone ought to look after his own affairs. Mil. 3.3. v. 55. 60. Alia cura. & Mil. 4.1. v. 5. & 4.2. v. 4.

units.la: Curiosi sunt hic quàm plures mali, alienas qui curant res studio maximo, quibus ipsis nulla est res, quam procurent sua. Stich. 2.1. v. 45.
units.tr: There are very many meddlers who, with the greatest zeal, look after other people's affairs, though they have no affairs of their own to attend to. Stich. 2.1. v. 45.

units.la: Sic Florilleg.
units.tr: So in the Florilegium:

units.la: Aliena curant evoluti propriis curiosi.
units.tr: Curious people, neglecting their own affairs, take care of others'.

units.la: Curiosus nemo est, quin sit malevolus. Stich 2.1. v. 34.
units.tr: No one is curious without also being malicious. Stich. 2.1. v. 34.

units.la: Plutarch. τὰς πολυπραγμονας ηχοιλθυς. Curiosi miseri ultrò suo labore. Ibid. Stich. v. 52.
units.tr: Plutarch, on the meddlesome [τὰς πολυπραγμονας]. Wretched meddlers, of their own accord and at their own cost. Ibid. Stich. v. 52.

units.la: HOMINES curiosi muscis comparantur ob impudentiam. Unde in proverb. Musca est: de homine curioso, & impudenti. Merc. 2.3. v. 26. Musca est meus pater: nihil potest clam illum habere, nec sacrum, nec tam profanum quicquam est, quin tibi illico aßit. Poen. 3.3. v. 76.
units.tr: Curious men are compared to flies because of their impudence. Hence the proverb Musca est ("He is a fly"), said of a curious and impudent person. Merc. 2.3. v. 26. Musca est meus pater: nihil potest clam illum habere, nec sacrum, nec tam profanum quicquam est, quin tibi illico adsit. Poen. 3.3. v. 76. ("My father is a fly: he can keep nothing hidden from him, nothing is so sacred or so profane that it is not at once on hand for you.")

units.la: Inde Ægyptij, ut est apud Horapollinem, impudentiam alicujus denotare volentes, Muscam pinxerunt.
units.tr: Hence the Egyptians, as Horapollo reports, when they wished to signify someone's impudence, painted a fly.

units.la: Curiosi plerumque calumniatores, maledici scurræ. Trin. 1. 2. v. 162.
units.tr: Meddlers are usually slanderers and malicious buffoons. Trin. 1. 2. v. 162.

units.la: Nihil est profectò stultius, neq; stolidius, neq; argutum magis, neq; confidentiloquius, neq; perjurius, quàm urbani assidui cives, quos Scurras vocant. Qui omnia se simulant scire, neq; quicquam sciunt. Quod Quod quiq; in animo habet, aut habiturus est, sciunt. Quod in au-rem Rex Regine dixit, id sciunt. Quod Juno fabulata est cum Jove, id sciunt. Qua neq; futura, neq; facta sunt, tamen id sciunt. Falsò' an vero laudent, culpent, quem velint, non floccifaciunt, dum illud quod lubet, sciant. Character hic est hominis curiosi.
units.tr: There is surely nothing more foolish, more stupid, more glib, more boastful or more perjured than the busy townsmen whom they call buffoons. They pretend to know everything and know nothing. They know whatever each man has in mind or is about to have in mind. They know what the king whispered in the queen's ear. They know what Juno chattered about with Jupiter. They know things that neither will be nor have been. Whether they praise or blame whomever they like, falsely or truly, they do not care, so long as they know what pleases them. This is the character of the curious man.

units.la: Stultitia magna, atque insipientia insulsitasque maxima hæc sit: Me ire in opus alienum, aut tibi meam operam pollicitari. Mil. 3.2.v.5. Sophoc. τὰ γὰρ περιττὰ πράγματα, ὑπ' ἐχρὴ τὰν ἀδύνα.
units.tr: This would be great folly, utter foolishness and the greatest silliness: to go into another's business or to offer you my services. Mil. 3.2. v. 5. Sophocles: "For superfluous business [τὰ γὰρ περιττὰ πράγματα] ..."

units.la: Curiosi & famigeratores olim supplicijs coërciti. Trin.1.2.v.182
units.tr: Meddlers and gossips were once restrained by punishment. Trin. 1.2. v. 182.

units.la: Qui tu scis? an tu forte fuisti meæ matri obstetrix? Meam rem non cures, si rectè facies, num ego curo tuam? Capt.3.4.v.99.
units.tr: How do you know? Were you perhaps midwife to my mother? If you behave properly, do not concern yourself with my affairs; do I concern myself with yours? Capt. 3.4. v. 99.

units.la: Tua quod nihil refert, ne cures. Stich. 2.2. v. 50.
units.tr: Since it makes no difference to you, don't bother about it. Stich. 2.2. v. 50.

units.la: Curiosum est, res novas inquirere. Most. 4.3. v.1.
units.tr: It is curious to inquire into new things. Most. 4.3. v. 1.

units.la: Cursus.
units.tr: Running.

units.la: Currendo ramices rumpi solent: hæc intestina, sive inguina: unde hernia oriri solet. Merc. 1.2.v.27.40. Pœn. 3.1. v.37. Tuâ causâ nemo nostram ruptarum est ramices.
units.tr: By running, the groins are wont to be ruptured; these are the intestines, or groins, from which a hernia usually arises. Merc. 1.2. v. 27. 40. Poen. 3.1. v. 37. No one has ruptured his groins on your account.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: In sterio-cursu quosvis oblivios velipsum Regem jubebantur per-vortebant. Stich. 2.2.v.1 4.
units.tr: In the stadium race they were ordered to outstrip all the others, even the king himself. Stich. 2.2. v. 1. 4.

units.la: Nimius cursus sudorem elicit. Marc.1.2.v.16.
units.tr: Excessive running draws out sweat. Merc. 1.2. v. 16.

units.la: Cyclopum.
units.tr: Cyclopes.

units.la: Cyclopes Cocsites Arimaspi Riphæos montes incolebant, & erant, ut fama ferebat, Unoculi. Curcul. 3.1.v.23. De Cocli-tum prosapiâ te esse arbitror. Nam ii sunt unoculi.
units.tr: The Cyclopes, the Cocsites and the Arimaspi inhabited the Riphaean mountains, and were, as report had it, one-eyed. Curcul. 3.1. v. 23. I think you are of the lineage of the Cocles, for they are one-eyed.

units.la: D.
units.tr: D.

units.la: DAMNI. MALI. MISERIÆ. INFORTUNII. PERICULORUM. CALAMITATUM. LÆSIONIS.
units.tr: DAMAGE. EVIL. MISERY. MISFORTUNE. DANGERS. CALAMITIES. INJURY.

units.la: LIQUID mali propter vicinum malum. Merc. 4. 4. v.32. In proverbio est. Vide Lex. Plaut. Proverbia. EMALIS multis, malum quod minimum est, id minimè est malum. Stich. 1.2. v.63.
units.tr: It is plainly an evil because of a nearby evil. Merc. 4. 4. v.32. It is a proverb. See the Plautine lexicon, Proverbia. Among many evils, the one that is least is least of all an evil. Stich. 1.2. v.63.

units.la: NOTA malares optima est. Trin. 1.2.v.25.
units.tr: A known evil is the best. Trin. 1.2.v.25.

units.la: Sic apud Livium:
units.tr: So in Livy:

units.la: Notissimum quodq; malum, maximè tolerabile est.
units.tr: The more familiar an evil is, the more bearable it is.

units.la: VICINIS damnum nullum inferendum. Mil. 2. 6. v.24.
units.tr: No harm is to be done to neighbours. Mil. 2. 6. v.24.

units.la: AN nocere inimico liceat, disputatur. Christianis ex decretis sacræ scripturæ minimè licet, Ratio humana interdum sibi id persuadet. Pœn. 5.2. v.130.
units.tr: Whether it is lawful to harm an enemy is debated. For Christians it is by no means lawful, according to the decrees of sacred Scripture; human reason sometimes persuades itself otherwise. Pœn. 5.2. v.130.

units.la: Inimico possum fieri subdolus, amico insipientia est. Inimico male faxim lubens.
units.tr: To an enemy I can be deceitful; to a friend that would be folly. To an enemy I would gladly do harm.

units.la: IN miserijs constituti semel atq; iterum bibebant. Rud 3.6. v.46.
units.tr: Placed in misery, they drank again and again. Rud 3.6. v.46.

units.la: Vide Tit. Convivij: Bibendi.
units.tr: See the title: Of Banquets: Of Drinking.

units.la: DAMNUM nullum solum. Pœn. 4. 2. v.97.
units.tr: No loss comes alone. Pœn. 4. 2. v.97.

units.la: Satin' ne primusquam unum est injectum telum, jam instat alterum?
units.tr: Is it not enough that, before one missile has been thrown, another is already upon us?

units.la: GAUDERE alienis malis improbum est. Cist. 4.2, v.13.
units.tr: To rejoice at others' misfortunes is wicked. Cist. 4.2, v.13.

units.la: Super malo mulicbri sunt lubentes.
units.tr: Women are glad to gloat over another's misfortune.

units.la: IMPROBI socios malorum quærunt. Epid. I.I.v.70.
units.tr: The wicked seek companions in their wickedness. Epid. 1.1.v.70.

units.la: Solus perire nolo.
units.tr: I do not want to perish alone.

units.la: Vide Tit. Consolationis.
units.tr: See the title: Consolation.

units.la: DECIMARUM.
units.tr: TITHES.

units.la: Vide infra Tit. Tributi.
units.tr: See below, under the title Tribute.

units.la: HERCULI pars decima de prædâ bonorum dabatur. Bacch. 4.4.v.15.
units.tr: A tenth part of the spoils of goods was given to Hercules. Bacch. 4.4.v.15.

units.la: Vide Plutarch. Ρομαϊνοῖς. & Diodorum Siculum.
units.tr: See Plutarch in the Roman Questions [Ρομαϊνοῖς], and Diodorus Siculus.

units.la: DEDICATIONIS. CONSECRATIONIS. MEMORIÆ. MONUMENTORUM.
units.tr: DEDICATION. CONSECRATION. MEMORIAL. MONUMENTS.

units.la: IN monumentum & memoriam rerum gestarum, solebant erigere statuas aureas. Curc. 3.I.v, 70. Ubi ridiculè exagitatur miles Thrasonicus.
units.tr: To serve as a monument and memorial of deeds done, people used to erect golden statues. Curc. 3.1.v. 70. Here the boastful soldier is ridiculed in comic fashion.

units.la: Vide ibi versûs memorabiles & jocosos.
units.tr: See there the memorable and jocular verses.

units.la: PANATHENAICIS magnis, quorum feriæ quinquennales erant, Peplus, seu Peplum Athenis Minervæ consecrabatur, cui intexta erat Titanomachia, & victoria Palladis de Encelado. Merc. Prol. v.67. Servius ad illud Virgil. lib.1. Æneid. Interea ad templum, non aquæ Palladis ibant (crinibus Iliades passis, peplumq; ferebant.
units.tr: At the great Panathenaic festival, whose celebrations came every fifth year, the peplos, or robe, was consecrated to Minerva at Athens. It was embroidered with the Titanomachy and with Pallas's victory over Enceladus. Merc. Prol. v. 67. Servius on that line of Virgil, Aeneid 1: "Meanwhile they went to the temple of Pallas, the Trojan women with their hair loose, carrying the robe."

units.la: Ubi Turneb. libr. 14. cap. 15. Peplum Trojanæ mulieres ferunt, ut câ vestè Minervæ simulacrum induant, & Deam propitiam habeant. Magnis enim in periculis Deorum fidem, & opem implorantes: eos vestibus etiam ornabant: illo cultu favorem, numinis emere se credentes.
units.tr: Here Turnebus, book 14, chapter 15: the Trojan women carry the peplos so that they may dress the image of Minerva in that garment and have the goddess favourably disposed. For in great dangers they implored the faith and help of the gods and also adorned them with garments, believing that by such honour they bought the favour of the divine power.

units.la: Vide Virgilij Cirin: & ibi Notas Scaligeri: ubi docet: Strenuorum quoq; Ducum Athenis gesta in peplo intexta Templo Minervæ impositā fuisse.
units.tr: See Virgil's Ciris, and there Scaliger's notes, where he teaches that the deeds of brave leaders at Athens were also woven into the peplos placed upon the temple of Minerva.

units.la: Vide etiam Marcelli Donati Dilucidationes pag. 999. & Lexic. nostrum Plautinum: Peplum.
units.tr: See also Marcellus Donatus, Dilucidationes, p. 999, and our Plautine lexicon, under Peplum.

units.la: IN Dedicationibus utebantur vocabulo statuendi. Curc.1.2.v.49.
units.tr: In dedications they used the word statuere (to set up). Curc. 1.2.v. 49.

units.la: Tibi ina ego vineam pro aurea statua statuam.
units.tr: "For you I will set up a vineyard in place of a golden statue."

units.la: Et Curc.3.1.v.69. Ibi nunc statuam vult dare. Rud. 4.2.v. Bacch. 4.4.v.1.
units.tr: And Curc. 3.1.v. 69: "There he now wants to give a statue." Rud. 4.2.v. Bacch. 4.4.v. 1.

units.tr: GODS. PROVIDENCE. TEMPLES. PIETY.

units.la: DIerant Majorum & Minorum gentium. Caf. 2 ȷ.v.24.27.
units.tr: There were the Greater and Lesser gods. Caf. 2 ȷ.v.24.27.

units.la: Ubi minuti Dij appellantur Humani Ioves, & Dij minores.
units.tr: Where the lesser gods are called human Jupiters and lesser gods.

units.la: DUODECIM DI Magni sunt. Epid. 5.1.v.4.
units.tr: There are twelve great gods. Epid. 5.1.v.4.

units.la: TOTUM manipulum Deorum colligit servus Bacch. 4.8.v.51.
units.tr: The slave gathers up the whole bunch of gods. Bacch. 4.8.v.51.

units.la: ---- Itame Iuppiter, Juno, Ceres, Minerva, Latona, Spes, Ops, Virtus, Venus, Castor, Pollux, Mars, Mercurius, Hercules, Sumanus, Sol, Saturnus, Dis omnes ament!
units.tr: ---- Thus may Jupiter, Juno, Ceres, Minerva, Latona, Hope, Ops, Virtue, Venus, Castor, Pollux, Mars, Mercury, Hercules, Summanus, the Sun, Saturn, all the gods love them!

units.la: TOTA cohors Deorum enumeratur Cist. 2.1.v.31. At itame DI Deæq., superi, atq; inferi, & medioxumi, Itaq; me Juno regina, & Jovis supremi filia. Itaq; me Saturnus patruus ejus. ME. Ecastor pater. AL. Itaq; me Ops opulenta illius avia. ME. immo mater quidem. AL. Juno filia, & Saturnus patruus, & summus Iuppiter.
units.tr: The whole troop of gods is enumerated. Cist. 2.1.v.31. And so, all gods and goddesses, above and below, and those in between! And so Juno the queen, and daughter of supreme Jupiter; and so Saturn, her uncle. ME. By Castor, father. AL. And so Ops the wealthy, her grandmother. ME. Nay, mother indeed. AL. Juno is the daughter, and Saturn the uncle, and highest Jupiter.

units.la: Medioxumos Græci Δαίμονες appellant. Vide Platonem in Symposio : & Apulejum de Genio Socratis. Ibidem tamen pergit adolescens Cist.2.1.v.45. Dei me omnes magni, minutiq; & patellarij Faxint, &c. Ubi Patellarij Dij sunt, quibus in patellis epulæ apponebantur, ut sunt Lares, Penates.
units.tr: The Greeks call the intermediate ones Daimones [Δαίμονες]. See Plato in the Symposium, and Apuleius on the Genius of Socrates. Yet in the same place the young man goes on: Cist. 2.1.v.45. May all the great and small gods and the patellarii favour me, etc. Here the patellarii gods are those at whose dishes (patellae) the feasts were set out, such as the Lares and Penates.

units.la: APOLLINEM ἀπόλλων Athenienses velut præsidem vicorum in vestibulo domus colebant. Bacch. 2.1.v.3.
units.tr: The Athenians worshipped Apollo [Ἀπόλλων] as the guardian, as it were, of the neighbourhoods (vici), in the vestibule of the house. Bacch. 2.1.v.3.

units.la: APOLLO ἀπόλλων, & ἀγυιεύς ante ædes ponebatur, eumq; invocabant in salutem, & sanitatem familiæ. Merc. 4.1. v.12.
units.tr: Apollo [Ἀπόλλων], and Agyieus, was placed before the houses, and they invoked him for the safety and health of the household. Merc. 4.1. v.12.

units.la: Vide Turn. l.7.cap.15.
units.tr: See Turnebus, book 7, chapter 15.

units.la: APOLLINEM ἀλεξίκακον quasi Apellinem, mala apellentem (ut ait Macrob. lib. 1. cap. 17.) invocabant in metu furtialiove periculo. Aul. 2.8.v.24.
units.tr: Apollo Alexikakos [ἀλεξίκακον], as if Apellinem, "calling evils away" (as Macrobius says, book 1, chapter 17), they invoked in fear of theft or other danger. Aul. 2.8.v.24.

units.la: APOLLO jaculator est. ἐκηβόλος, ἐκατηγεσλέτης, ἑκατος, ἐκάεργος. Aul. 2.8.v.28. Confige sagittis fures thesaurarios.
units.tr: Apollo is the archer: Hekebolos [ἐκηβόλος], Hekatēgeletēs [ἐκατηγεσλέτης], Hekatos [ἑκατος], Ekaergos [ἐκάεργος]. Aul. 2.8.v.28. Pierce the thieving treasurers with arrows.

units.la: Horl. 1. Sat. 9. ---- Sic me servavit Apollo.
units.tr: Horace, Satires 1.9: So Apollo saved me.

units.la: Cc
units.tr: Cc

units.la: LIBER vini pollens dicitur: à copiâ. Curc. i.2.v.21.
units.tr: LIBER is said to be powerful in wine, from abundance. Curc. 1.2.v.21.

units.la: INSANIENTES Bacchum invocant. Men. f.2.v.83.
units.tr: Madmen invoke Bacchus. Men. f.2.v.83.

units.la: CERERI annuo Ambarvaliorum festo vino sacrificabant: non item in nuptijs. Aul. 2.6. v.5.
units.tr: To Ceres, at her annual festival of the Ambarvalia, they sacrificed with wine; not so at weddings. Aul. 2.6. v.5.

units.la: Vide Tit. Nuptiarum.
units.tr: See the heading On Weddings.

units.la: CERERIS festo omnes populariter Genio indulgebant. Men. i.i. v. 25.
units.tr: At the festival of Ceres everyone indulged the Genius in the common way. Men. 1.1. v.25.

units.la: CLOACINÆ DRÆ sacra frequentabant mendaces & gloriosi homines: quia à Cluere: quod est κλυζειν nominare, dictum putant Venerem Cluacinam: quamquam alij à Cloacâ. Curcul. 4.i. v.19.
units.tr: Liars and boasters frequented the rites of Cloacina. They think Venus Cloacina was so named from cluere, which is κλύζειν, to name; though others derive it from cloaca (sewer). Curc. 4.1. v.19.

units.la: De situ ejus vide G. Fabricij Romam. pag. 127. Edit. Basil. Facit & ejus mentionem Lactantius lib.i.cap.20.
units.tr: On her site see G. Fabricius, Roma, p. 127, Basel edition. Lactantius also mentions her, book 1, chapter 20.

units.la: CUPIDO Deus amorum. Aul. 4.10. v.7. Deus mihi impulsor fuit.
units.tr: CUPID, god of loves. Aul. 4.10. v.7. The god was my instigator.

units.la: CLAVUS Cupidinis. Asin. i.3.v.4.
units.tr: The nail of Cupid. Asin. 1.3.v.4.

units.la: DIANÆ in templo sacerdos. Bacch. 2.3. v. 78.
units.tr: A priestess of Diana in the temple. Bacch. 2.3. v.78.

units.la: DIUS-FIDUS: est filius Jovis Hercules, per quem jurabant. Asin. i.i. v.8.
units.tr: DIUS FIDIUS is the son of Jupiter, Hercules, by whom they swore. Asin. 1.1. v.8.

units.la: IDEI fanum erat Romæ. Aul. 3.6.v.46.
units.tr: There was a shrine of Idaeus at Rome. Aul. 3.6.v.46.

units.la: FONTINALIS Deus fontibus præerat: ut Liber vino. Stich. 5.2.v.17.
units.tr: Fontinalis was a god who presided over springs, as Liber did over wine. Stich. 5.2.v.17.

units.la: FORTUNÆ Romæ juxta templum Jovis Victoris erat templum Respicientis Fortunæ.
units.tr: At Rome, near the temple of Jupiter the Victor, there was a temple of Fortune Looking Back.

units.la: Quò alluditur Captiv. 4.2. v.54. & Bacch. 4.3. verf.24. & Pœnol. 1, 2. v. 197.
units.tr: Alluded to at Captiv. 4.2. v.54, Bacch. 4.3. v.24, and Poenul. 1.2. v.197.

units.la: FORTUNA Dea incerti eventûs: culta, quæ posset prodesse, & obesse. Fors Fortuna, Dea prosperi eventûs: quæ tantùm prodesse.
units.tr: FORTUNE was a goddess of uncertain outcome, worshipped as one who could both help and harm. Fors Fortuna was a goddess of favourable outcome, who only helps.

units.la: Bacch. 4 8. v. 75. Illa Dubia dicta est: hæc etiam Fors absolutè nonnumquam legitur. Et colebatur ab infimæ fortis hominibus, operarijs, rusticis, servis: & omnibus, qui sine arte aliquâ viverent.
