units.tr: Bacch. 4.8. v.75. The former was called Dubia (the doubtful one); the latter is also sometimes read simply as Fors. She was worshipped by people of the lowest rank: labourers, country folk, slaves, and all who lived without any trade.

units.la: Invocatur à Comicis servis: ut Hecyr. Terent, 3.3.Phorm.1.2. & 5.6. Hinc Forte Fortuna. Eun.1.2 & 3.5.
units.tr: She is invoked by comic slaves, as in Terence, Hecyra 3.3; Phormio 1.2 and 5.6. Hence Forte Fortuna, Eun. 1.2 and 3.5.

units.la: Vide Lil. Giraldum in Historiâ Deorum.
units.tr: See Lilius Giraldus in his History of the Gods.

units.la: FORTUNA Obsequens Romæ olim colebatur. Asin. 3. 3 vers. 127.
units.tr: Fortune the Obliging was once worshipped at Rome. Asin. 3.3 v.127.

units.la: BONA Fortuna singulis invocata: & ominis causâ optata. Aul. 1.2. v. 22. inquit:
units.tr: Good Fortune is invoked for individuals and wished for as an omen. In Aul. 1.2 v.22 he says:

units.la: Si bona Fortuna venerit, ne intromittat: h.e. neminem.
units.tr: If Good Fortune comes, let her not come in: that is, no one.

units.la: Huic contra opponitur Mala Fortuna. Rud. 2 6.v.17.
units.tr: Opposed to this is Bad Fortune. Rud. 2.6.v.17.

units.la: GENIO DEO litabant præ cæteris homines luxuriosi. Pers. 1. 3. v. 28.
units.tr: Dissolute men sacrificed to the Genius Deus more than others. Pers. 1.3. v.28.

units.la: Sapis multum ad Genium.
units.tr: You are very wise about the Genius.

units.la: Genij virtutes graphicè depingit Arnob. lib. 4.
units.tr: Arnobius, book 4, vividly depicts the powers of the Genius.

units.la: Et quid quasi aut faciat, præsidatum focorum Deus ipse sortitur est? per humani generis coqui nas currit: inspiciens & explorans, quibusnam lignorum generibus suis ardor in foculo excitetur: habitudinem fictilibus contribuit vasculis, ne flammarum dissiliant vi victa: curat, ut ad sensum palati suis cum jucunditatibus veniant tecum incorruptarum saporum, & an ritè pulmenta condita sint, Pragustator fungitur atq; experitur officio.
units.tr: "And what, as it were, does the god himself take as his lot, the presiding over the hearths? He runs through the kitchens of the human race, inspecting and testing with what kinds of wood the fire is kindled in the hearth; he apportions the proportions among the earthen vessels, lest the flames burst out with overpowering force; he takes care that the flavours come to the sense of the palate uncorrupted and with their pleasures; and whether the dishes have been properly seasoned, the pre-taster discharges his office and tests them."

units.la: HERCULES unâ nocte non potuit creari. Jupiter enim eam noctem, quâ genuit Herculem, longiorem fecit. Amph Prol. v. 113.
units.tr: HERCULES could not be created in a single night. For Jupiter made the night in which he begot Hercules longer. Amph. Prol. v.113.

units.la: Et Amph. I.1.v.122. Pro quâ re explicandâ viri doĉti tales notas observarunt. Nimi-rùm inde dici à Lycophrone τρισέλνον, ὢ τρισσπεσον Λέοντα, & Αλκείδην τριέσπερον à Justino Martyre.
units.tr: And Amph. 1.1. v.122. To explain this, learned men have made such notes: namely, that from this Lycophron calls him "thrice-night" [τρισέλνον], the thrice-night lion [ὢ τρισσπεσον Λέοντα], and Justin Martyr calls Alcides "born of three evenings" [Αλκείδην τριέσπερον].

units.la: Statius lib. 12. vocat
units.tr: Statius, book 12, calls him:

units.la: Ternoĉtem Herculeam.
units.tr: The Herculean one of three nights.

units.la: Alij tamen duas duntaxat memorant. D. Hieronymus adversus Vigilantium :
units.tr: Others, however, mention only two. St Jerome, against Vigilantius:

units.la: Liberè proclamabit te esse aut Mercurium propter numorum cu-piditatem, aut Noĉturnum, juxta Plauti Amphit. quo dormiente in Alcumenæ adulterio duas noĉes Jupiter copulavit, ut magnæ fortitudinis Hercules nasceretur.
units.tr: He will freely proclaim that you are either Mercury, because of your greed for money, or Nocturnus, according to Plautus' Amphitryon, in whose sleeping, during the adultery with Alcmena, Jupiter joined two nights, so that Hercules of great strength might be born.

units.la: De eodem Seneca Tragœdus Agamemn. vers. 821,
units.tr: Of the same, Seneca the tragedian, Agamemnon v.821:

units.la: Violentus ille Noĉte non unâ potuit creari.
units.tr: That violent one could not be created in one night.

units.la: Sic Ovidius lib. 1. Amor.
units.tr: So Ovid, Amores book 1:

units.la: Ipse Deum genitrix, ne te tàm sæpè videret, Commisit noĉtes in sua vota duas.
units.tr: The very mother of the gods, so that she might not see you so often, gave two nights to her own wishes.

units.la: Propert. lib. 2. Eleg. 16.
units.tr: Propertius, book 2, elegy 16.

units.la: Juppiter Alcmenæ geminas requieverat Arĉtos: Et cœlum noĉtu bis sine rege fuit.
units.tr: Jupiter had rested through the two Bears for Alcmena, and heaven was twice without its king by night.

units.la: Arnobius lib. Advers. gentes novem noĉium meminit, si locus mendo caret, quâ de re videndi Authores commentarij ad illum locum.
units.tr: Arnobius, in Against the Nations, mentions nine nights, if the place is free of error; on this see the commentators on that passage.

units.la: Parasiti Herculem colebant. Curc. 2.2. v. 70. Invoco almam meam Nutricem Herculem. Et Stich. 2.1. v.70.80.
units.tr: Parasites worshipped Hercules. Curc. 2.2. v.70. I invoke my kindly nurse Hercules. And Stich. 2.1. v.70–80.

units.la: Herculi etiam decimam partem bonorum conferebant veteres. Stich. 2. 1. v. 80. & 5 2. v. 6. Most. 1.1. v. 23. & 4.2. v. 78. Bacch. 4. 4. v. 15. Truc. 2. 7. v. 11. Pars Herculana. Rud. 5. 3. v. 64. Causam reddit Plutarch. Q. Rom. & Diodorus Siculus.
units.tr: The ancients also gave Hercules a tenth part of their goods. Stich. 2.1. v.80, 5.2. v.6; Most. 1.1. v.23, 4.2. v.78; Bacch. 4.4. v.15; Truc. 2.7. v.11. Herculean share. Rud. 5.3. v.64. Plutarch in the Roman Questions and Diodorus Siculus give the reason.

units.la: Vide etiam Cafaub. ad Pers. Sat. 2. De Nativitate Herculis vide Titul. Noĉis.
units.tr: See also Casaubon on Persius, Satire 2. On the birth of Hercules, see the heading On Night.

units.la: Ara Herculis, cùm referta esset ijs, quæ imponi de ritu religionis priscæ solebant: tùm pollućlum dicebatur, quasi projećtum. TraTralatè nostèr de servo: polluštus virgis.
units.tr: The altar of Hercules, when filled with those things which were customarily placed upon it according to the rite of the old religion, was then called "polluted", as if "thrown forward". Our author uses it metaphorically of a slave: "thrashed with rods."

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut. Pollucero.
units.tr: See the Lexicon Plautinum, under pollucero.

units.la: HERCULIS labor sextus erat: quòd Hippolytam Amazonum reginam baltheo spoliavit.
units.tr: The sixth labour of Hercules was that he stripped the belt from Hippolyte, queen of the Amazons. Epid. 2.1. v.10. Men. 1.3. v.17.

units.la: HERCULEM invocabant à monstris infestati. Most. 2. 2. v. 94.
units.tr: Hercules was invoked by those troubled by monsters. Most. 2.2. v.94.

units.la: Vide Turn. lib. 10. 16.
units.tr: See Turnebus, book 10, chapter 16.

units.la: HERCULI sacrificabant peregrinaturi. Rud. 1. 2. v. 71.
units.tr: They sacrificed to Hercules when about to travel abroad. Rud. 1.2. v.71.

units.la: HERCULIS ærumnas recensèt Plautus Perf. 1. 1. v. 3.
units.tr: Plautus recounts the labours of Hercules. Persa 1.1. v.3.

units.la: De quibus vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: On these, see the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: HYMENÆUS Deus nuptiarum fuit. Cauf. 4. 3. v. 2. Vide de eo Cælium Rhodigin. lib. 15. cap. 34. Et interpretes Catulli Scal. & Muretum ad carmen Nuptiale, nec non Brissonium de ritu Nuptiarum.
units.tr: HYMENAEUS was the god of marriage. Cas. 4.3. v.2. On him see Caelius Rhodiginus, book 15, chapter 34, and the commentators on Catullus, Scaliger and Muretus on the wedding song, as well as Brisson on the rite of marriage.

units.la: INO uxor Jovis. Pæn. 5. 4. v. 47. Itame Di amabunt! ut ego, si im Jupiter, jam hercle ego illam uxorem ducam, & Junonem extrudam foras. Pæn. 5. 4. v. 47.
units.tr: INO, wife of Jupiter. Poen. 5.4. v.47. Thus may the gods love them! As I, if I were Jupiter, I would by Hercules take her as my wife and thrust Juno out of doors. Poen. 5.4. v.47.

units.la: JUNONEM Lucinam parturientes invocabant. Aul. 4. 7. v. 11.
units.tr: Women in labour invoked Juno Lucina. Aul. 4. 7. v. 11.

units.la: JUPITER Verspellis dicitur Amph. Prol. v. 123. propter varios concubitus, quorum duodecim potissimum enumerantur in Fabb. Quatuor recensentur Epig. Gr. Antholog. lib. 1. Taurus, Olor, Satyrus fit, & Aurum Jupiter ardens Euryopen, Ledin, Antiopen, Danaën. Et quosdam recitat Nazianzen carmine ad Nemesium. Seneca bis in Octavia. Nonnus Dionysl lib 7. 8. 16. 31. 4v. Observamus etiam Jovem nulli umquam puellarum vim intulisse: sed astu semper ijs potitum.
units.tr: Jupiter is called Shape-shifter (Amph. Prol. v. 123) because of his many amours, of which twelve are chiefly listed in the fables. Four are recounted in the Greek Anthology, book 1: He becomes a bull, a swan, a satyr, and gold; burning Jupiter loved Europa, Leda, Antiope, and Danaë. Gregory of Nazianzus recites some others in his poem to Nemesius. Seneca mentions them twice in the Octavia. Nonnus, Dionysiaca books 7, 8, 16, 31, 4v. We also observe that Jupiter never used force on any of the girls, but always got possession of them by trickery.

units.la: JOVEM decet vereri, ut equum esl. Amph. Prol. v. 23. Nulla enim gens sine Numine, teste Cicerone, & ipsâ scriptură sacrâ.
units.tr: One should reverence Jupiter, as is right. Amph. Prol. v. 23. For no nation is without a divinity, as Cicero testifies, and Holy Scripture itself.

units.la: Jupiter moechus : liber omnium nequitiarum fingitur à Poë-tis. Amph. Prol v. 105. 135.
units.tr: Jupiter the adulterer: the poets depict him as wholly unrestrained in every kind of wickedness. Amph. Prol. v. 105, 135.

units.la: Versipellem sæ facit, quando lubet. Ibid. v. 123.
units.tr: He makes himself a shape-shifter whenever he pleases. Ibid. v. 123.

units.la: Mart. Capella lib. 6. de Nupt. Philologiæ : Jupiter decentium puellarum versiformis cupitor.
units.tr: Martianus Capella, book 6, On the Marriage of Philology: Jupiter, the lover of graceful girls, who changes his form.

units.la: Et Tertull. de Pallio Versiformem appellat.
units.tr: And Tertullian, in On the Pallium, calls him one who changes form.

units.la: Cæterùm duodecim furtivi concubitus ac metamorphoses Jovis in fabulis narrantur.
units.tr: Moreover, twelve secret couplings and metamorphoses of Jupiter are narrated in the fables.

units.la: De quibus vide Rittershus. ad Oppianum.
units.tr: See Rittershusius on Oppian.

units.la: Isocrates in Encomio Helenæ negat Jovem ulli umquam ama-tarum puellarum vim attulisse, sed in earum amorem & fruitio-nem arte semper irrepisse: quod notavit Pimpontius in Para-lip. Virgil. adv. 198. lib. 1 v. Æneid.
units.tr: Isocrates, in the Encomium of Helen, denies that Jupiter ever used force on any girl he loved, but always crept into their love and enjoyment by craft. Pimpontius noted this in his Paralipomena on Virgil, on Aeneid 1, v. 198.

units.la: Jupiter in solio sedet in cælo. Trin. 4. 2. v. 98.
units.tr: Jupiter sits on a throne in heaven. Trin. 4. 2. v. 98.

units.la: De Jove quid sycophanta nugetur, memorabile est. Trin. 4. 2. verf. 101.
units.tr: It is memorable what the sycophant babbles about Jove. Trin. 4. 2. v. 101.

units.la: Eho! an etiam vidisti Jovem? S Y C. Alii Diî ipsè ad villam ajebant, servis deprom tum cibum.
units.tr: "Hey! Did you actually see Jupiter?" SYC. "Other gods themselves used to say he was at the villa, handing out food to the slaves."

units.la: Jupiter opulentus, inclytus: Opegnatus, supremus, validus, viripotens. Perf. 2. 3. v. 1.
units.tr: Jupiter rich, renowned, Opegnatus, supreme, strong, mighty in men. Perf. 2. 3. v. 1.

units.la: Jupiter dicitur Prodigialis Jupiter: quia prodigia depellit. Ἀ-ποτροπαῖος τέλεσιος. Amph. 2. 2. v. 107.
units.tr: Jupiter is called Prodigial Jupiter, because he drives off portents: the averter of evil, the perfecter [Ἀποτροπαῖος, τέλειος]. Amph. 2. 2. v. 107.

units.la: Jupiter Imperator Divûm atq; hominum. Rud. Prol. v. 9.
units.tr: Jupiter, commander of gods and men. Rud. Prol. v. 9.

units.la: Quadrigæ Jovis celerrimæ. Quia currus Jovis alatus fingitur apud Platonem. Amph. 1. 1. v. 292. Asin. 2. 2. v. 13. ubi quadrigas albas Turneb. lib. 24. cap. 31. Adversar. interpretatur quadrigas Jovis.
units.tr: The chariots of Jupiter are swiftest, because Plato imagines Jupiter's chariot to be winged. Amph. 1. 1. v. 292. Asin. 2. 2. v. 13, where Turnebus (Adversaria, book 24, ch. 31) interprets the white quadriga as Jupiter's.

units.la: Vide Jani Doufæ notas ad Tibull. cap. 7.
units.tr: See Janus Dousa's notes on Tibullus, ch. 7.

units.la: Jupiter, qui genus colis, alisque hominum, per quem vivimus vitaleævum. Poen. 5. 4. v. 14.
units.tr: Jupiter, who cherishes the race and nourishes men, through whom we live, giver of life. Poen. 5. 4. v. 14.

units.la: Jupiter Deûm regnator, architectus optimus. Amph. Pr. v. 45.
units.tr: Jupiter, king of the gods, the best architect. Amph. Pr. v. 45.

units.la: Jupiter ex Ope sive Cybele natus. Mil. 4.2. v. 90. Vide Vincent. Chartarium de Imaginibus Deorum Gallicè editum Lugduni, in quarto pag. 138.
units.tr: Jupiter born of Ops, or Cybele. Mil. 4. 2. v. 90. See Vincent's Chartarium de Imaginibus Deorum, published in French at Lyon, in quarto, p. 138.

units.la: Jupiter est vindex omnium scelerum. Rud. Prol. v. 16. Cottidie ille sciat, hic sibi quaerat malum. Qui hic litem apisci postulant, perjurio mali, res falsas, impetrant ad judicem: iterum ille eam rem judicatam judicat.
units.tr: Jupiter is the avenger of all crimes. Rud. Prol. v. 16. Every day he knows; this one seeks evil for himself. Those who here demand to win a suit by perjury obtain false things before the judge; again he judges that matter already judged.

units.la: Jupiter in Capitolio coronatus colebatur. Men. 5 5. v. 28. Trin. 1. 2. v. 47.
units.tr: Jupiter was worshipped crowned on the Capitol. Men. 5. 5. v. 28. Trin. 1. 2. v. 47.

units.la: LAR familiaris aedibus adjunctus fuit. Trin. 1.2. v. 1. Vide Tit. Ædium.
units.tr: The household LAR was attached to the house. Trin. 1. 2. v. 1. See the title Ædium.

units.la: LARES & aedibus, & saepè vicis integris praeficiebantur, atque itineribus etiam praesse credebantur. Ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος Aul. Prol. v. 2.
units.tr: The LARES were set over houses and often over whole streets, and were believed to preside over journeys too: the Good Spirit [Ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος]. Aul. Prol. v. 2.

units.la: Vide etiam Adversaria Heraldi lib. 1. cap. 7.
units.tr: See also Heraldus, Adversaria, book 1, ch. 7.

units.la: LARI sive foco solebant coronas floreas, & eas quidem inusitatâ magnitudine imponere. Aul. Prol. v. 25. Aut thure, aut vino, aut aliqui semper supplicat, Dat mihi coronas.
units.tr: Garlands of flowers, and of unusual size, were customarily placed on the LAR or on the hearth. Aul. Prol. v. 25. Either with incense, or with wine, or someone always entreats and gives me garlands.
The same: Aul. 2. 8. v. 15, and Trin. 1. 2. v. 1.

units.la: Juvenal. Sat. XII. Ite igitur pueri linguis animisque favente s, Sertaque debite, & farra imponite cultris.
units.tr: Juvenal, Sat. XII: Go therefore, boys, with tongues and minds favourable, and place the due garlands and spelt on the knives.

units.la: Idem: Inde domum repetam graciles ubi parva coronas Accipiunt fragili simulacra nitentia cera.
units.tr: The same: Thence I shall go home, where little shining images of fragile wax receive slender garlands.

units.la: Alius: Non ego thure modo, aut pictâ tua templa tabellâ Ornabo, & puris serta feram manibus.
units.tr: Another: I shall not adorn your temples with incense alone, or with a painted tablet, nor bring garlands in pure hands.

units.la: De hoc more vide Meursium ad Catonem. Imitatus est illum Justus Lipsius in Divâ suâ Sichemensi cap. 1. En coronam alteram ad te adfero àfloribus tuis plexam, è vicino tuo horto decerptam. Christiani hunc morem improbarunt. Arnobius adversus Gen. lib. 8.
units.tr: On this custom see Meursius on Cato. Justus Lipsius imitated it in his Diva Sichemensis, ch. 1: Behold, I bring you another garland, woven from your flowers, plucked from my neighbour's garden. Christians disapproved of this custom. Arnobius, Adversus Gentes, book 8.

units.la: Non floribus caput nectitis: coronas sepulchris denegatis.
units.tr: You do not bind flowers on your heads; you deny garlands to the tombs.

units.la: Tertullianus vocat sacrilegium de Coronis militum:
units.tr: Tertullian calls it sacrilege, in On the Garlands of Soldiers:

units.la: Tam contra naturam est, florem capite sectlari, quam cibum aure, quam sonum nare. Omne autem, quod contra naturam est, mon-stri meretur notam penes omnes: penes nos vero etiam eloquium sacrilegii in Deum, Natura Dominum & Autorem.
units.tr: It is as contrary to nature to cut a flower from the head as food from the ear, or sound from the nose. Whatever is against nature deserves the mark of monstrosity among all; among us, however, it is also a word of sacrilege against God, the Nature's Lord and Author.

units.la: PORCI sacri, sive sacres sinceri: h.e. puri & integerrimi, ad sacrifi-cium idonei Laribus immolabantur ab ijs, qui piaculum aliquod admiserunt, aut qui insani fuerant: immo etiam, quibus aucta erat liberorum prole familia. Men. 2. 2. v. 16. Rud. 4. 6. v. 4.
units.tr: Sacred pigs, or pure sacred pigs: that is, clean and wholly unblemished, fit for sacrifice, were offered to the Lares by those who had committed some offence, or who had been mad; indeed also by those whose family had been increased by a brood of children. Men. 2. 2. v. 16. Rud. 4. 6. v. 4.

units.la: Vide Lexicon Plaut.
units.tr: See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: PENATES Deos colebant, inprimis Larem, aedes deserentes. Merc. 5. 1. v. 5.
units.tr: PENATES: those who were leaving the house worshipped gods, especially the Lar. Merc. 5. 1. v. 5.

units.la: LARES viales sunt Dij, qui viae praesunt. quos invocare solent, qui peregre proficiscuntur, & ad viam se accingunt: quo etiam cognomento colebatur Mercurius. Merc. 5. 2. v. 24. Dicti etiam Dij Semitales. Vide etiam Aul. Prol. LAR.
units.tr: LARES viales are the gods who preside over roads, whom those setting out on a journey and girding themselves for the road are wont to invoke; under this surname Mercury too was worshipped. Merc. 5. 2. v. 24. The gods are also called Semitales. See also Aul. Prol., LAR.

units.la: Vide item Scalig. in Catalect. Virgil.
units.tr: See also Scaliger in the Catalecta of Virgil.

units.la: LARIUM sedes in privatis aedibus non una. Colebantur maximè in foco: item in cubiculo: sepè in parte aliquâ atrij, puta in compluvio adjuncta. Aul. 2. 8. v. 16.
units.tr: The seats of the LARES were not single in private houses. They were worshipped chiefly at the hearth, also in the bedroom, and often in some part of the atrium, namely in the adjoining compluvium. Aul. 2. 8. v. 16.

units.la: Hac imponentur in foco nostro Lari.
units.tr: Here on our hearth the Lar is placed.

units.la: LARIBUS familiaribus sacrificabant aucti liberis, vel generis, &c. Rud. 4. 6. v. 3.
units.tr: To the household LARES they sacrificed, those increased by children, or by family, etc. Rud. 4. 6. v. 3.

units.la: OFFEREBANT autem agnos & porcos sacres D I s Laribus. Ibid. v. 4. Errat igitur Lambinus, qui arbitratur nihil animatum ijs immolatum.
units.tr: They offered lambs and sacred pigs to the gods, the Lares. Ibid. v. 4. Therefore Lambinus is wrong, who thinks that nothing animate was sacrificed to them.

units.la: Horat. l. 2. Sat. 3.
units.tr: Horace, book 2, Sat. 3.

units.la: Immolet aquis hic porcum Laribus.
units.tr: Here let him sacrifice a pig to the Lares with water.

units.la: Ubi vide Notas Douzæ: & Turn.l.26.c.2. Quid sint porci sacres vide Lex, Plaut.
units.tr: See the notes of Dousa and the Turnebus, book 26, ch. 2. For what sacred pigs are, see the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: LAVERNAM invocabant coqui fures: scil. Deam furum. Aul.3.2.v.31.
units.tr: LAVERNA was invoked by thieving cooks, namely as the goddess of thieves. Aul. 3. 2. v. 31.

units.la: LUBENTIA Dea hilaritatis. Asin.2.2.v.2.
units.tr: LUBENTIA, goddess of cheerfulness. Asin. 2. 2. v. 2.

units.la: LUNA, Bacchus, Ceres, furoris Præsides credebantur: Unde Lunatici, Bacchi, Cerriti, pro furiosis. Amph.4.2.v.26.32.44. & 4.3.v.61.
units.tr: LUNA, Bacchus and Ceres were believed to be the presiders over madness; whence Lunatici, Bacchi, Cerriti for madmen. Amph. 4. 2. v. 26, 32, 44, and 4. 3. v. 61.

units.la: MARS belli præses. Asin. Prol. v,15.
units.tr: MARS, president of war. Asin. Prol. v. 15.

units.la: MARS Bellator dictus: & Pugnator. Mil. r.1. v.11. Notæ P. Diaconi: Dedicatus est hic locus Jovi Liberatori primum: deinde Marti Pugnatori: & Libero Patri.
units.tr: MARS is called Bellator and Pugnator. Mil. 1. 1. v. 11. Notes of P. Diaconus: This place was first dedicated to Jupiter the Liberator, then to Mars the Fighter, and to Liber Pater.

units.la: MARS curat milites. Mil.4.9.v.12.
units.tr: MARS takes care of soldiers. Mil. 4. 9. v. 12.

units.la: MARTI olim sacræ lupæ: & ipsi milites patrem suum colunt. Pœn.3.3.v.31. Truc.3.1.v.11.
units.tr: Wolves were formerly sacred to MARS, and soldiers themselves worship their father. Poen. 3. 3. v. 31. Truc. 3. 1. v. 11.

units.la: MARTIS uxor Neriene. Truc.2.6 v.34. Vide Agell. lib.13.c.21.
units.tr: Mars's wife is Neriene. Truc. 2. 6. v. 34. See Gellius, book 13, ch. 21.

units.la: MARTI lupi sacri: & in tutelâ ejus. Alluditur Pœn.3.3.v.31. & Truc. 3.1.v.11.
units.tr: Wolves are sacred to Mars and under his protection. This is alluded to in Poen. 3. 3. v. 31 and Truc. 3. 1. v. 11.

units.la: MERCURIUS: filius Jovis. Amph. Prol. v.20.
units.tr: MERCURY, son of Jupiter. Amph. Prol. v. 20.

units.la: Præerat lucris & fœnoribus. Amph. Prol. v.2.12. Stich. 3.v.1.3.
units.tr: He presided over gains and interest. Amph. Prol. v. 2, 12. Stich. 3. v. 1, 3.

units.la: Unde & ἑρμαιον dicebant, quod forte fortuna lucri aut boni obtigerat.
units.tr: Whence they also called a windfall hermaion [ἑρμαιον], what fortune by chance brought as gain or good.

units.la: Eustath. ad Odyss. π. v. 471. ὅτι διὰ ἑρμαιον τὸ εὐρημα ἐρμῆ ἢ αὐτῷ παρωνόμασε καὶ κερδῶν ἀνλασδὶ ὅθεν ἢ εὐρημέιν ῥῆμα τὸ εὐτυχεῖν, ἢ εὑρημία ἡ εὐτυχία, ἐν ἄλλοις λεδήλωται σαφῶς.
units.tr: Eustathius on the Odyssey, π, v. 471: because the discovery was named hermaion after Hermes himself, and gain was obtained; hence the verb "to find" means to be lucky, and "discovery" means fortune, as is clearly shown elsewhere [ὅτι διὰ τὸ ἑρμαῖον τὸ εὕρημα Ἑρμῆ ἢ αὐτῷ παρωνόμασε καὶ κερδῶν ἀνλασδὶ· ὅθεν ἢ εὐρημέιν ῥῆμα τὸ εὐτυχεῖν, ἢ εὑρημία ἡ εὐτυχία, ἐν ἄλλοις λεδήλωται σαφῶς].

units.la: Diodorus Siculus lib. v.
units.tr: Diodorus Siculus, book 5.

units.la: Λιὰ ἢ πολλοὶ τῶν Ιταλικῶν ἐμτόρων διὰ τὴν σωτηθ φιλαργυρίαν ἑρμαιον ἡγοῦνται πιὰ τῶν γαλατῶν φιλοτιμίαν.
units.tr: For many of the Italian merchants, through their excessive greed, count a windfall as the eager gain of the Gauls [Διὰ ἡ πολλοὶ τῶν Ἰταλικῶν ἐμπόρων διὰ τὴν σφοδρὰν φιλαργυρίαν ἑρμαῖον ἡγοῦνται τὴν παρὰ τῶν Γαλατῶν φιλοτιμίαν].

units.la: Eleganter quoq; Hierocles:
units.tr: Hierocles also says this elegantly:

units.la: Καλὸν μὲν τὰ ϑεῶ πειϑεσϑαι: καλὸν δὲ ἢ τοῖς γονεῦσιν, εἰ δὲ πρὸς ταῦτα ἡ ἀμφοτέρων ἀρα οἱ πειϑῶ, ἑρμαιον ἂν εἴη, ἢ ἀμαχον.
units.tr: It is good to obey God; good also to obey parents. But if one obeys both in these matters, it would be a windfall, and invincible [Καλὸν μὲν τὸ θεῷ πείθεσθαι· καλὸν δὲ καὶ τοῖς γονεῦσιν· εἰ δὲ πρὸς ταῦτα ἡ ἀμφοτέρων ἄρα οἱ πείθῃ, ἑρμαῖον ἂν εἴη, καὶ ἄμαχον].

units.la: Dicebatur & συνοντ ἐρμῆ.
units.tr: It was also said, "common Hermes" [κοινὸς ἑρμῆς].

units.la: Eūslach. Odyss. ν.
units.tr: Eustathius on the Odyssey, ν.

units.la: Φέρεται δὲ ἢ παροιμία: Σὺ κοινὸν ἐρμῆ: ἥγουν ἑρμαιον, ἢ εὔρημα ἐν- κείμενον ἀπ᾽ ὠφελεία τῷ ἐντυχόντι.
units.tr: The proverb runs: "Common Hermes is yours," that is, a windfall, or a find lying ready, to the benefit of whoever comes upon it.

units.la: Hesychius:
units.tr: Hesychius:

units.la: ἑρμαιον: εὕρημα ἢ κέρδος. Scd & κοινὸς ἑρμῆς partem e lucro forte fortuna oblato flagitantis vox erat.
units.tr: Hermaion: a find or a gain. But "common Hermes" was also the phrase for a share of gain that came by chance, a windfall, which someone demanded as his portion.

units.la: Theophrastus περὶ βλεδυρίας: ἢ τῶν ευεισκομένων χαλκῶν ἐν ᾧ ἐδοῖς ὑπὸ τῶν οἰκετῶν δεινὸς ἀπαυτῆζα τὸ μέρος, κοινὸν ἔναι φήσας τὸν ἑρμῆν.
units.tr: Theophrastus, in his work on bad manners: when, among the bronze vessels that had been found, a slave claimed an unfair share for himself, he said that Hermes was common property.

units.la: Diodorus Siculus lib. V.
units.tr: Diodorus Siculus, book 5.

units.la: τῷ ἀλ ἑρμῆ περστάπυσι τὰς ἐν τοῖς πολέμοις γμωμένας κηρυκέιας, ἢ διαλλαγᾶς ἀπ᾽ ἢ σκονδᾶς: ἢ τὸ τὸν σύστημον κυρηκεῖον, ὅ φορεῖν εἰώ- ϑασιν οἱ περὶ τῶν τοιούτων τὰς λόγως ποιούμενοι, ἢ διὰ τύτε τυγχά- νοντες, παρὰ τοῖς πολεμίοις ἀσφαλείας: ὅϑεν δὴ ἢ κοινὸν ἑρμῆν ωνο- μάζεσϑαι, διὰ τὸ τὴν ὠφέλειαν ἀμφοτέρους εἶναι κοινὴν τοῖς ἐν τῷ πο- λέμῳ τὴν εἰρήνην μετα λαμβάνυσι. Meminit & Aristotel. in Rhe- toricis.
units.tr: The heralds' staffs that were used in wars, for truces or treaties, were set up beside Hermes. Or the staff that men who negotiate such matters customarily carry, and by which they gain safety from the enemy. Hence Hermes was called "common," because both sides share in the benefit of the peace made in war. Aristotle also mentions this in his Rhetoric.

units.la: Cùm igitur quid boni, fortuitò obtigerat, id Mercurio appen- debatur.
units.tr: So whatever good happened by chance was credited to Mercury.

units.la: Æschylus ἐπτ. ὅπ ἅβ. Ἀνὴρ καὶ ἀνδρὶ τοῦτον ἡρέϑη δέλαν ἐξισορρῶ μοίραν, ἐνχείρα τύχης. κἀ εἰδ, ὅτε θυμὸν ὅπλων ῥέσιν μωμητος, ἑρμῆς δὲ εὐλόγως σωώγαγεν.
units.tr: Aeschylus, Seven against Thebes. A man was chosen to face a man, by the hand of fortune, to balance the lot. And when the rage of arms was quenched, Hermes rightly saved them.

units.la: Ubi Scholia: Ἰσῶν ὅτι πάντα τὰ ἐδαῖα, ἢ τὰ ἑρμεῖα, ἢ κατὰ τύχην συμβεβηκότα τοῖς βροτοῖς, τὸ ἑρμῆ ταῦτα ἀναπθέασινέλλυες. ἐ- πεὶ ἐν ἢ τύτοις σωέβη τυχηρῶς πῶς ἀλλήλοις ἀντπάξασϑω, τύτο εἰ- ρηκεν.
units.tr: The scholia: knowing that all the goods, or the gains, or whatever befell mortals by chance were attributed to Hermes. Since in these matters something happened by chance, however the lots fell to one another, he said this.

units.la: Indefactum, ut ἑρμᾶς ἐν τοῖς πεϑύροις τῶν οἴκων flatutos & collo- catos haberent, ἀγαϑῶ χάριν οἴων ἐ, scil. & ὅπ κέρδος ἐλπίδι.
units.tr: Indeed it was the custom to set up and place Hermae in the vestibules of houses, for the sake of good luck, as they did, and for the hope of gain.

units.la: Thucid. lib. v i.
units.tr: Thucydides, book 6.

units.la: ἐν δὲ τύτῳ ὅζοι ἑρμαῖ ἡζαν λίθινοι ἐν τῇ πόλει τῶν Αθηναίων (εισὶ δὲ κατὰ τὸ δημώδειον, ἢ τεταρτὸν ἐργασία, πολλοὶ ἐν ἰδίοις μεγάθυροις, ἐν ἱεροῖς) μιᾷ νυκτὶ οἱ πλεῖστοι πεπεσκότησαν τὰ πρόσωπα.
units.tr: In that time many stone Hermae stood in the city of the Athenians (there are many of them, as is common knowledge, the work of the later period, in private doorways and in temples); in one night most of them had their faces knocked off.

units.la: Ænylius Probus in Alcibiade: Id cùm apparetur, priusquam classis exiret, accidit, ut unâ nocte omnes Hermæ, qui in oppido erant Athenis, deiecerentur, præter unum, qui ante januam Andocidis erat, Andocidiq. Hermes vocatus est. Meminit & Plutarchus in Alcibiade.
units.tr: Aemilius Probus, in his Life of Alcibiades: When this was being prepared, before the fleet set out, it happened that in one night all the Hermae that stood in the town of Athens were thrown down, except one, which stood before the door of Andocides, and that one was called Andocides' Hermes. Plutarch also mentions this in his Alcibiades.

units.la: Atq; hinc est, quod Imago ejus sinistrâ virgulam, dextrâ faccu-lum nummarium gestans depingitur: qualis visitur in Inscriptio-nibus Romanis pag. 1. 1.
units.tr: Hence it is that his image is depicted holding a staff in the left hand and a purse in the right, as is seen in the Roman inscriptions, p. 1.1.

units.la: MERCURIO quoqu virga attributa, galerus, gallus & pinnulæ. Amph. Prol. v. 143.
units.tr: Mercury was also given a staff, a cap, a cock and little wings. Amphitruo, Prologue, v. 143.

units.la: Vide etiam Inscriptionem Romanam paulò ante dictam.
units.tr: See also the Roman inscription mentioned a little above.

units.la: MERCURIUS præerat quoque nuncijs. Amph. Prol. v. 12.
units.tr: Mercury also presided over messengers. Amphitruo, Prologue, v. 12.

units.la: Horat. lib. 1, Od. 10.
units.tr: Horace, book 1, Ode 10.

units.la: Te canam magni Jovis & Deorum nuncium.
units.tr: I will sing of you, messenger of great Jove and of the gods.

units.la: MERCURIUS lucris præest, & Mercatorum Deus est. Paxol. 1. 2. v. 114.
units.tr: Mercury presides over gains and is the god of merchants. Pseudolus, 1.2, v. 114.

units.la: MERCURIUS Jovis nuncius perhibetur. Stich. 2. 2. v. 1.
units.tr: Mercury is said to be the messenger of Jove. Stichus, 2.2, v. 1.

units.la: ATHENIS in Acropoli Ædes MINERVÆ erat. Bacch. 4. 8. v. 60.
units.tr: At Athens, on the Acropolis, there was a temple of Minerva. Bacchides, 4.8, v. 60.

units.la: MINERVÆ Panathenaicis Magnis Peplum consecrabatur, cui intexta Titanomachia, & victoria Palladis de Encelado. Innuit noster. Merc. Prol. v. 67.
units.tr: At the Great Panathenaic festival a peplum was consecrated to Minerva, on which were woven the Titanomachy and Pallas' victory over Enceladus. Our author alludes to this. Mercator, Prologue, v. 67.

units.la: Vide etiam Turneb. lib. 14. c. 15.
units.tr: See also Turnebus, book 14, ch. 15.

units.la: Vide supra Tit. Dedicationis: & Lex. Plaut. Peplum.
units.tr: See above, under the title Dedication, and the Plautine lexicon, under Peplum.

units.la: NEPTUNUS colebatur ijs, qui è naufragio incolumes evaserunt, Trin. 4. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: Neptune was worshipped by those who escaped unharmed from shipwreck. Trinummus, 4.1 and following.

units.la: NEPTUNO & Mercurio mercatores & navigationibus domum solvi reversi grates agebant. Stich. 3. 1. v. 3.
units.tr: Merchants and sailors, returning home safe from their voyages, gave thanks to Neptune and Mercury. Stichus, 3.1, v. 3.

units.la: NEPTUNUS maris Deus, Virtus, Victoria, Mars, Bellona in Tragoedijs introducti. Amph. Prol. v. 42.
units.tr: Neptune, the god of the sea; Virtue, Victory, Mars and Bellona are introduced in the tragedies. Amphitruo, Prologue, v. 42.

units.la: NEPTUNO gratiam habebant, si quando tuti evasissent. Most. 2.2. v.1.
units.tr: They gave thanks to Neptune whenever they had got safely away. Mostellaria, 2.2, v. 1.

units.la: NEPTUNUS piscatorum patronus. Rud. 4. 2. v.1.
units.tr: Neptune, patron of fishermen. Rudens, 4.2, v. 1.

units.la: NOCTURNINUS Deus praerat noctì. Amph. 1.1. v. 115. Hieronymus adversus Vigilantium: Liberè proclamabis te esse aut Mercurium propter numorum cupiditatem, aut Nocturninum juxta Plauti Amphitruonem, quo dormiente in Alcumenæ adulterio, duas noctes Jupiter copulavit, ut magnæ fortitudinis Hercules nasceretur. Meminit etiam hujus Semonis Martianus Capella de Nuptijs Philologiæ: Accitu Vejovis Dij publici Terquino ex limite convocantur, ex ultimâ regione Nocturninus, Janitoresq; terrestres similiter advocati sunt.
units.tr: Nocturnus was a god presiding over the night. Amphitruo, 1.1, v. 115. Jerome, against Vigilantius: "You will freely proclaim yourself either Mercury, because of your greed for money, or Nocturnus, after Plautus' Amphitruo, in whose sleep, during Alcmena's adultery, Jupiter lay with her for two nights, so that Hercules of great strength might be born." Martianus Capella also mentions this deity in his On the Marriage of Philology: "At the summons of Vejovis the public gods are called together from the Terquinian boundary; Nocturnus is summoned from the farthest region, and the earthly gatekeepers are likewise called."

units.la: PALÆMON sive PORTUMNUS Neptuni comes. Rud, 1.2. v.71.
units.tr: Palaemon, or Portumnus, the companion of Neptune. Rudens, 1.2, v. 71.

units.la: PIETAS Dea statuitur. Asin. 3.1, v.3. Piare Pietatem.
units.tr: Piety is set up as a goddess. Asinaria, 3.1, v. 3. "To propitiate Piety."

units.la: PILUMNUS & PICUMNUS Dij conjugales fuerunt: quibus parentes liberos suos elocaturi vota faciebant. Aul. 2.8. v.15.
units.tr: Pilumnus and Picumnus were gods of marriage, and parents who were about to marry off their children made vows to them. Aulularia, 2.8, v. 15.

units.la: De illis hoc adscribam, quod observat doctissimus Meursius l. 2. Animadv. Miscell. cap.1.
units.tr: On them I will add what the very learned Meursius observes, Animadversiones Miscellaneae, book 2, ch. 1.

units.la: Servius Ænëid. 1x. Fratres fuisse tradit; Picumnumque stercorandorum agrorum usum invenisse: indeque Sterquilinium dictum:
units.tr: Servius, on Aeneid 9, reports that they were brothers, and that Picumnus invented the manuring of fields, whence the word sterquilinium (dunghill) is derived;

units.la: Pilumnum verò pinsendi frumenti, ideoq; à Pisloribus cultum. Verba ejus haec sunt:
units.tr: while Pilumnus invented the pounding of grain, and for that reason was worshipped by millers. His words are these:

units.la: Pilumnus & Picumnus fratres fuerunt Dij. Horum Picumnus stercorandorum invenit usum agrorum: unde & Sterquilinius dictus est: Pilumnus vero pinsendi frumenti, & ab ipso pilumdictum est.
units.tr: Pilumnus and Picumnus were brothers, gods. Of these, Picumnus invented the use of manuring the fields, whence he was also called Sterquilinius; Pilumnus, indeed, of pounding grain, and the pestle (pilum) was named after him.

units.la: Ubi de Picumno certè mirum est, cùm Mythologi omnes Saturno id tribuant.
units.tr: Here it is indeed remarkable about Picumnus, since all the mythographers ascribe this to Saturn.

units.la: Deinde de Pilumno, etsi consentit Martianus Capella lib. 2. hoc valdè ineptum est, quòd dicat ab eo pilum dictum, cùm convenientius multò sit dicere, illum à pilo nomen habere.
units.tr: Then, about Pilumnus, although Martianus Capella agrees with Servius in book 2, this is very absurd: that he says the pestle (pilum) was named after him, whereas it is much more fitting to say that he had his name from the pestle.

units.la: Sunt autem nomina in vulgus minus nota Deorum notissimorum: Romuli & Martis.
units.tr: There are also names of the most famous gods that are less known to the common people: those of Romulus and Mars.

units.la: Pilumnum quidem Romulum esse, ex Saliorum carminibus cognosci potest: quibus Pilumni populi appellantur Romani: non quod pilis uti assueti, ut vult Festus (nam sic omnes Pileni Pilumni dicendi essent) nec quia praecipuè pellant hostes (tùm enim Pellumni nuncupari debebant) sed tamquam Romuli nepotes. Nam Pilumna ibi secundus casus est, numeri singularis, non primus pluralis: ut ille exstimavit.
units.tr: That Pilumnus is Romulus can be seen from the songs of the Salii, in which the Roman people are called Pilumni: not because they were accustomed to use javelins, as Festus holds (for then all the Pileni would have to be called Pilumni), nor because they especially drove off enemies (for then they ought to be called Pellumni), but as the grandsons of Romulus. For Pilumna there is the genitive singular, not the nominative plural, as he supposed.

units.la: Est verò Pilumnus idem cum Romulo Quirino. Ut enim Sabini suâ linguâ à Quiri Quirinum: ita Salij obscuritatis studiosissimi, vocumque ignotarum usurpatores & formatores Latinâ à pilo Pilumnum indigetabant. Jam Picumnum Martem esse, verum est. Nam ut picus: quia ei sacer, Martius vocabatur: ita vicissim ille à Pico Picumnus, ut Melicerta à Portu Portumnus, Romulus à pilo Pilumnus. Est autem idem cum Marte Sylvano. Inde intelligendus Æmylius Macer Theog. lib. 1.
units.tr: Pilumnus is indeed the same as Romulus Quirinus. For just as the Sabines called Quirinus from Quiris in their language, so the Salii, who were eager for obscurity and were users and coiners of unknown words, called Pilumnus from the Latin pilum. That Picumnus is Mars is true. For as the woodpecker (picus) was sacred to him and he was called Martius, so conversely he was called Picumnus from Picus, just as Portumnus was named from Portus, the Melicerta, and Romulus was called Pilumnus from the pilum. He is also the same as Silvanus, the Mars of the woods. Hence should be understood Aemilius Macer, Theogony, book 1: "And now among the rustic folk Picumnus is held in honour."

units.la: Et nunc agrestes inter Picumnum habetur.
units.tr: Picumnus is held in honour among the country folk.

units.la: Huc pertinet; quod Picus, à quo nomen accepit, etiam avis est sylvestris: quam Germani appellant Ein Specht.
units.tr: To this belongs the fact that Picus, from whom he took his name, is also a woodland bird, which the Germans call Ein Specht.

units.la: Convenit siquidem descriptio Pliniana lib. x. cap. xviii.
units.tr: Pliny's description, book 10, ch. 18, agrees.

units.la: Quo in genere arborum cavatores, scandentes in subrectum felium modo: illi verò & supini percussi corticis sono pabulum intelligunt.
units.tr: In this kind of tree the diggers climb upward like cats; but those lying on their backs perceive their food by the sound of the bark being struck.

units.la: Ovid. Metamorph. lib. xiv. Pennas in corpore vidit, Sequeque novem subitò Latijs accedere sylvis Indignatus avem, duro feraroboratoftro Figit, & iratus longu dat vulnera ramis.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 14: he saw wings on his body, and suddenly nine ... coming to the Latin woods; indignant at the bird, he pierces it with a hard oak spear, and in his anger he wounds the branches.

units.la: De Pilumno loquitur Inscriptio vetus, quæ Cumis pag. xcvi. 4.
units.tr: An ancient inscription, found at Cumae, p. xcvi. 4, speaks of Pilumnus.

units.la: Pilumno Sanctissimo Genio Municipi Sacrum
units.tr: To Pilumnus, the Most Holy Genius of the Municipality, Sacred

units.la: P. Jubentius Ancharius. i.i. Vir.
units.tr: P. Jubentius Ancharius, i.i. vir.

units.la: Picumnus verò, ut dictum, idem est cum Marte Silvano, sed domestico, non agresti, aut Orientali. Id ex eo apparet, quòd Romanis priscis cum filio Pilumno conjugij curam sit sustinere creditus. Atque causa, ob quam conjugij curam tribuerint Pilumno quidem, hæc quin sit, minimè dubitandum est: quia nimirùm civibus suis ad stabiliendum novum regnum, genusq; propagandum. Sabinas uxores dederit nobilissimâ illâ rapinâ.
units.tr: Picumnus, as I have said, is the same as Mars Silvanus, but the domestic form, not the rural or Eastern one. This is clear from the fact that the early Romans believed Picumnus, with his son Pilumnus, had charge of marriage. There is no doubt at all about why they gave the care of marriage to Pilumnus: it was so that he might provide wives for his citizens, to establish his new kingdom and propagate the race, by giving them the Sabine women in that most famous abduction.

units.la: Marti verò sive Picumno, quod is ejusce rapinæ Romulo auctor existimabatur.
units.tr: Or rather to Mars or Picumnus, because he was thought to have been the author of that abduction for Romulus.

units.la: Patet id ex Herfiliæ verbis, quæ ex Cn. Gellij Annal. iii. profert Agellius lib. xiii. cap. xx.
units.tr: This is clear from the words of Herfilia, which Gellius quotes from Gnaeus Gellius's Annals, book 3, in book 13, chapter 20.

units.la: Neria Martis te obsecro pacem dare, uti liceat nuptijs propitijs, & prosperis uti, quod de tui conjugii consilio contigit, uti nos itidem integras raperent: unde liberos sibi, suis posteris, patria parerent.
units.tr: Neria of Mars, I beg you to grant peace, so that we may enjoy happy and prosperous marriages, as has come about from your counsel on marriage, and so that they may likewise seize us unharmed, whence they might bear children for themselves, for their descendants, for the fatherland.

units.la: Utrique autem in Ædibus lectus sternebatur: cùm in terrâ infantem obstetrix statuisset, auspicatumq; esset, an rectus ac vitalis foret.
units.tr: A bed was spread in the house for both of them. When the midwife had set the infant on the ground, it was determined by augury whether it was upright and viable.

units.la: Varro de vitâ Pop. Rom. lib. 2.
units.tr: Varro, On the Life of the Roman People, book 2.

units.la: Puer sinatus erat, sublatus ab obstetrice, statuebatur in terrâ, ut auspicaretur vitalis ac rectus esse: Dis conjugalibus Pilumno & Picumno in ædibus lectus sternebatur.
units.tr: The boy had been allowed to live, lifted up by the midwife, and was set on the ground, so that the omen might be taken whether he would be viable and upright. For the conjugal gods Pilumnus and Picumnus a bed was spread in the house.

units.la: Eisdem mariti Kal. Martij: h. e. mensis Picumno sacrati pro conjugij conservatione vota faciebant.
units.tr: On the same Kalends of March the husbands made vows, that is, the month consecrated to Picumnus, for the preservation of marriage.

units.la: Sic Acron ad Od. viii. lib. 3.
units.tr: So Acron, on Horace, Odes 3.8.

units.la: Kalendis Martijs Matronalia diccbantur, co quòd mariti pro conservatione conjugij supplicabant, & erat dies proprie fe-stus matronis.
units.tr: On the Kalends of March the Matronalia were called, because husbands prayed for the preservation of marriage, and it was properly a festival day for matrons.

units.la: Numa etiam in lege suâ Pilumnum & Picumnum innuit: Sei. Puer. Parentem. Verberit. Ast. Ole. Plora Sit. Puer. Deiveis. Parentum. Sacer. Estod.
units.tr: Numa also, in his law, refers to Pilumnus and Picumnus: "If a son strikes his parent, and the parent has wept, let the boy be sacred to the gods of the parents."

units.la: Unde liquet statim post Ἀποθέωσιν collatum istum honorem.
units.tr: Whence it is clear that this honour was conferred immediately after the deification [Ἀποθέωσιν].

units.la: Plautus Mercatore s. 1. v. 5.
units.tr: Plautus, Mercator, s. 1, v. 5.

units.la: DI penates meum parentum familiaq,
units.tr: O household gods, of my parents and my family,

units.la: Lar pater, Vobis mando meum parentum rem bene ut tute-mini.
units.tr: Lar, father, I commend to you my parents' property, that you may keep it well.

units.la: Porrò Picumnus, sive Mars Silvanus, præstes Larum erat; ut Pluto Manium, Jupiter Deorum, Janus Geniorum. Id docent Inscriptiones veteres. pag. LXV. 2.
units.tr: Moreover, Picumnus, or Mars Silvanus, was the chief of the Lares, as Pluto was of the Manes, Jupiter of the gods, and Janus of the Genii. Ancient inscriptions teach this, p. LXV. 2.

units.la: Sylvano.
units.tr: To Silvanus

units.la: Sancto-Sacro. Larum. Cæsaris. N. Et. Collegi. Magni. Cn. Turpilius. Trophimus. Voto. Suscepto. Aram. De. Suo.
units.tr: To the holy and sacred Lares of Caesar, our lord, and of the Great College: Gnaeus Turpilius Trophimus, a vow having been undertaken, set up this altar at his own expense.

units.la: D. D.
units.tr: D. D.

units.la: Pag. LXIII. I. SILVANO, SACRUM. SODAL. EIUS. ET. LARUM. BONUM. POSUIT. TIB. CLAUDIUS. AUG. LIB. FORTUNATUS. A. CURA. AMICORUM.
units.tr: Page LXIII. 1. SACRED TO SILVANUS, HIS COMPANY AND THE GOOD LARES. TIBERIUS CLAUDIUS FORTUNATUS, FREEDMAN OF AUGUSTUS, SET THIS UP BY THE CARE OF FRIENDS.

units.la: Interdum κατ' ἐξοχὴν LAR vocabatur: parentesque eo nomine liberos in matrimonium elocaturi, ut bene nuptiæ cederent, sacra ei faciebant: cp patet ex loco Plauti Aul. quem initio citavi.
units.tr: Sometimes LAR was called par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], and parents who were about to marry off their children under that name made sacrifices to him so that the wedding might turn out well. This is clear from the passage of Plautus's Aulularia that I cited at the beginning.

units.la: Veteres etiam Laribus, quos Hostilios nominabant, sacrificabant, ut ab hostibus se defenderent: scilicet propter præsidem eorum Martem, penes quem bellorum arbitrium putabant. Festus: Hostilis Laribus immolabant, quod ab his hostes arceri putabant. Itaque formabantur cincta Gabino, qui militaris erat: unde à Perfio Sat. V. Succinctli appellantur: ubi vide Veterem interpretem. Atque ideo bullas nobiliores pueri his suspendebant ad omen & vota conciliandæ virtutis bellicæ tantæ, quanta erat in Tarquinij Prisci filio, qui annos agens XIV. hostem manu percusserat: quapropter & donatus est bulla, quæ id temporis triumphantium duntaxat habebatur. Hi ipsi quoq; Lares sunt: quibus Æmilius Rhegillus Prætor bello Antiochi Ædem vovit in Campo Martio, teste Macrob. lib. I. Satur. I.10. Pilumnum autem, de quo initio, mariti pro peculiari Genio suo colebant: ut patet ex inscriptione supra posita. Etiam Puerperæ post partum inter tres Deos custodes nnus adhibitus fuit, ne Silvanus per noctem ingrederetur, vexareturq; : & ejus significandi causâ constituebatur quidam, qui pilo limen feriret. Vide August. de Civ. Dei lib. VI. cap. IX. Ille Silvanus erat agrestis pastorum DEUS (neque enim confundi debent, qui diversi sunt) Dictus etiam Pan: & Incubus. Glossæ Πὰν ὁ Δαίμων Incubus Sylvanus.
units.tr: The ancients also sacrificed to the Lares whom they called Hostilii, so that they might be defended from enemies, namely because of their protector Mars, in whose power they thought the outcome of wars lay. Festus: They sacrificed to the Hostilian Lares, because they thought enemies were warded off by them. Hence they were portrayed girt in the Gabine fashion, which was military; whence Persius, Satire 5, calls them succincti; see the old commentator there. And for this reason boys hung nobler bullae on them, as an omen and a vow to gain such martial virtue as was in the son of Tarquinius Priscus, who, at the age of fourteen, had struck down an enemy with his own hand; for which reason he was also awarded the bulla, which at that time was held only by those celebrating triumphs. These too are Lares, to whom the praetor Aemilius Regillus vowed a temple in the Campus Martius during the war with Antiochus, as Macrobius witnesses, Saturnalia 1.10. But Pilumnus, with whom we began, husbands worshipped as their own peculiar Genius, as is clear from the inscription placed above. Also, for women after childbirth, one of three guardian gods was assigned, so that Silvanus might not enter during the night and harass them; and to signify this a certain figure was set up who struck the threshold with a pestle [pilum]. See Augustine, City of God 6.9. That Silvanus was the rustic god of the shepherds (for those who are different must not be confused). He was also called Pan and Incubus. Glosses: Pan is the Daemon; Incubus Silvanus.

units.la: Maximè autem hic Deus mulieres infestare credebatur. August. de Civ. Dei lib. XV. c. XXII. Et quoniam creberrima fama est, multiq; se expertos, vel ab eis, qui experti essent, de quorum fide dubitandum non est, audisse confirmant, Sylvanos, & Faunos: quos vulgo vulgò Incubos vocant, improbos sæpè extitisse mulieribus, & earum appetisse ac peregisse concubitum.
units.tr: Above all, this god was believed to harass women. Augustine, City of God 15.22: And since the report is very widespread, and many confirm that they have experienced it, or have heard it from those who experienced it, whose trustworthiness is not to be doubted, that Silvani and Fauni, whom commonly they call Incubi, have often been a burden to women and have sought and accomplished intercourse with them.

units.la: SALUS. Neque jam servare Salus, si volt, potest. Asin. 3. 3. v. 124. Capt. 3. 3. v. 14. Imitatus est Terentius Adelph. 4. 7. Ipsa si cupiat Salus, servare prorsus non potest hanc familiam.
units.tr: SALUS. Nor can Salus now save, even if she wishes. Asinaria 3.3 v. 124; Captivi 3.3 v. 14. Terence imitated this in Adelphi 4.7: Even if Salus herself should wish it, she absolutely cannot save this household.

units.la: SATURNO hostiæ humanæ immolabantur. Amph. 4. 2. v. 16. Vide Diodorum Siculum lib. x x. Cæl. Rhodig. lib. 13. Antiq. Lect. cap. 23. Monita Polit. Lipsij cap. 3.
units.tr: Human sacrifices were offered to Saturn. Amphitryon 4.2 v. 16. See Diodorus Siculus, book 20; Caelius Rhodiginus, Antiquae Lectiones 13, chapter 23; Lipsius, Monita et Exempla Politica, chapter 3.

units.la: SUMMANUS Deus est Manium summus: h. e. Pluto: qui omnes avarissimè rapit in suum thesaurū. Curc. 3. 1. v. 43. & 4. 3. v. 12. Inde fictum nomè Summanare, pro; avidè rapere & furari. Vide L. P.
units.tr: SUMMANUS is the highest god of the Manes, that is, Pluto, who most greedily snatches everything into his treasury. Curculio 3.1 v. 43 and 4.3 v. 12. From this comes the coined word summanare, meaning to snatch greedily and steal. See L. P.

units.la: SANCTA spes olim à Collatino consecrata. Cist. 4. 1. v. 18. Vide Spes
units.tr: SACRED HOPE, once consecrated by Collatinus. Cistellaria 4.1 v. 18. See Spes.

units.la: VENUS curat amores. Mil. 4. 9. v. 7.
units.tr: VENUS takes care of loves. Miles Gloriosus 4.9 v. 7.

units.la: VENUS dicitur Noctu-vigila: quà crebrà amat per vigilia. Nυκτι-λαμπις. Curc. 1 2 v. 4. Alias quoq; Noctiluca à quodam antiquo Poëta Lævino: de quo Scaliger ad Varronem, quem vide.
units.tr: VENUS is called Night-watcher, because she loves to be awake through the nights [Nυκτι-λαμπις]. Curculio 1.2 v. 4. She is also called Noctiluca by an ancient poet, Laevinus, about whom see Scaliger on Varro, which you should consult.

units.la: MERETRICES, puellæ corollas, serta, dedicabant Veneri: Asin. 4. 1. v. 58. Vide Tit. Res Venereæ. Vide Commentarium Isaaci Casauboni ad Sat. 2. v. 70. pag. 220. Edit. Parisiensis.
units.tr: PROSTITUTES offered garlands and wreaths to Venus. Asinaria 4.1 v. 58. See the title Res Venereae. See Isaac Casaubon's commentary on Satire 2 v. 70, p. 220 of the Paris edition.

units.la: VENERI litabant amantes, sub cujus imperio vivere se dicebant. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 13. Vide quæ notavimus ad Tit. Amoris.
units.tr: LOVERS sacrificed to Venus, under whose rule they said they lived. Pseudolus 1.1 v. 13. See what we have noted on the title Amoris.

units.la: VENERI ut Deo mundicianti initiabant Amatores. Caf. 2. 3. v. 9.
units.tr: LOVERS were initiated into the worship of Venus as the god of cleansing. Casina 2.3 v. 9.

units.la: VENERIS dies festi Aphrodisia erant. Poen. 1. 1. v. 63.
units.tr: The festival days of Venus were the Aphrodisia. Poenulus 1.1 v. 63.

units.la: IN gratiam Veneris totam noctem pervigilabant. Curc. 1 3. v. 2 f.
units.tr: IN FAVOUR OF VENUS they kept vigil through the whole night. Curculio 1.3 v. 2 f.

units.la: VENERI litabant lenones. Rud. Pæol. v. 60. & 1. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: PIMPS sacrificed to Venus. Rudens, Prologue v. 60, and 1.2 v. 7.

units.la: VENERIS fanum Aphrodisijs adierunt meretrices: aliæque illius Deæ clientæ. Poen. 5. 4. v. 6. Arabius, murrhinuq, odos omnia cō-plebat, haud sordere visum est Festus dies, Venus, nec tuum fanum: tantus ibi clientarum erat numerus, quæ ad Calydoniam venerant Venerem.
units.tr: PROSTITUTES, and other clients of that goddess, went to the temple of Venus at the Aphrodisia. Poenulus 5.4 v. 6. Arabian incense and myrrh filled everything; the festival day did not seem dirty, Venus, nor your temple: so great was the number of clients who had come there to the Venus of Calydon.

units.la: VULCANUS Veneris adversarius est. Rud. 3. 4. v. 55. Rationem vide Tit. Asyli.
units.tr: VULCAN is the enemy of Venus. Rudens 3.4 v. 55. For the reason, see the title Asylum.

units.la: EST profecto Deus: qui quae nos gerimus, audit q; & videt. Capt. 2. 2. v. 63.
units.tr: There truly is a God, who hears and sees what we do. Captivi 2.2 v. 63.

units.la: Theologica prorsus sententia ab homine Ethnico prolata.
units.tr: A wholly theological sentiment, uttered by a pagan man.

units.la: Sic Sophocles Electrâ:
units.tr: Thus Sophocles in Electra:

units.la: ἐστὶ μέγας ἐν ἠφανῇ Ζεὺς, ὡς ἑφορᾷ πάντα, ᾧ κρατύνεi.
units.tr: Zeus is great and hidden, who oversees all things, by whom he holds sway [ἐστὶ μέγας ἐν ἠφανῇ Ζεὺς, ὡς ἐφορᾷ πάντα, ᾧ κρατύνει].

units.la: Item: ἐστὶ δίκης ὀφθαλμὸς, ὅστις πάντ' ὁρᾷ.
units.tr: There is an eye of justice, which sees all things [ἐστὶ δίκης ὀφθαλμὸς, ὅστις πάντ' ὁρᾷ].

units.la: Homerus: Ζεὺς πάντα ἰδὼν, ᾧ πᾶσ' ἐπακούων.
units.tr: Homer: Zeus, who sees all and hears all [Ζεὺς πάντα ἰδὼν, ᾧ πᾶσ' ἐπακούων].

units.la: Juvencus lib. 1. Histor. Evangelicæ:
units.tr: Juvencus, Historia Evangelica, book 1:

units.la: Nil absente Deo loquimur: nil abdita clausum Pectoris antra tegunt. Cernit Deus omnia praesens.
units.tr: We speak nothing in the absence of God; no hidden caves of the breast conceal anything from him. God, present, sees all things.

units.la: Silius Ital. lib. 15.
units.tr: Silius Italicus, book 15.

units.la: Idem justitia cultor: quacumq; capesse, Testes factorum stare arbitrabere Divos.
units.tr: A worshipper of the same justice: wherever you go, you will think the gods stand as witnesses of your deeds.

units.la: Et hoc est, quod olim in formulâ dicebant, DEO SSE.
units.tr: And this is what they used to say in the formula, that there is a God.

units.la: Livius lib. 3.
units.tr: Livy, book 3.

units.la: Dum pro se quisque DEO SSE, & non negligere humana, fremunt.
units.tr: While each man, saying that there is a God and that human affairs are not neglected, grumbles.

units.la: Idem lib. 8. Manlius Torq. ait:
units.tr: The same author, book 8. Manlius Torquatus says:

units.la: Est caeleste Numen:
units.tr: There is a heavenly divinity:

units.la: Es Magne Jupiter.
units.tr: Great Jupiter, you are.

units.la: Sallustius ad Caesarem:
units.tr: Sallust to Caesar:

units.la: Namque mihi pro vero constat, omnium mortalium vitam divino Numine invisi: neq; bonum, neq; malum facimus cujusque pro nihilo haberi, sed ex naturâ diversa praemia bonos malosq.
units.tr: For I hold it as true that the life of all mortals is watched over by the divine power, and that the good and bad we do are not regarded as nothing, but that rewards for good and bad men follow according to their nature.

units.la: Eurip. Phryxo:
units.tr: Euripides, Phrixus:

units.la: ἐξὺς θεῶν ὀφθαλμῶν εἰς τὰ πάντα ἰδεῖν.
units.tr: It is for the eyes of the gods to see all things [ἐξὺς θεῶν ὀφθαλμῶν εἰς τὰ πάντα ἰδεῖν].

units.la: Basil. Magnus pag. 87.
units.tr: Basil the Great, p. 87.

units.la: ὅπωτες ἀν βασιλίζης, ὅπωτες ἀν ἀνεργῆς, καν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ὀδισκοπῶντα ἔχεις
units.tr: Wherever you sit, wherever you walk, even if you are in the dark, you have [God's eye, from a ready dwelling-place] [ὅπωτες ἀν βασιλίζης, ὅπωτες ἀν ἀνεργῆς, καν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ὀδισκοπῶντα ἔχεις].

units.la: Θεὸς ὀφθαλμὸν, ἐξ ἑτοίμων καταοικητηρίῳ αὐτῶ. ὑ πύλαι ἀνοίγονται ὑ παραπετάσματα σωμάγοντα. ἑτοιμόν ἐστιν εἰς θεὰν τὸ κατοικητήριον ἓ θεῶ. πάντας ἐφορᾷ τὰς γῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἰδὲ εἰς διαφεύγει ει ἑαυτὸ τὴν θέαν. ὑ σκότος, ὑ τοῖχοι παρακαλύπτοντες, ὑδὲν ἐμποδίον ἔστιν ὀφθαλμοῖς θεῶ.
units.tr: God's eye, from a dwelling-place prepared for him. The gates are opened and the veils drawn back. God's dwelling is ready to behold. He oversees all the lands of men. Nothing escapes his sight: darkness and walls that cover things do not stand in the way of God's eyes [Θεὸς ὀφθαλμὸν, ἐξ ἑτοίμων καταοικητηρίῳ αὐτῶ. ὑ πύλαι ἀνοίγονται ὑ παραπετάσματα σωμάγοντα. ἑτοιμόν ἐστιν εἰς θεὰν τὸ κατοικητήριον ἓ θεῶ. πάντας ἐφορᾷ τὰς γῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἰδὲ εἰς διαφεύγει ει ἑαυτὸ τὴν θέαν. ὑ σκότος, ὑ τοῖχοι παρακαλύπτοντες, ὑδὲν ἐμποδίον ἔστιν ὀφθαλμοῖς θεῶ].

units.la: Plutarch. in Sympos. Sept. Sapient.
units.tr: Plutarch, in the Banquet of the Seven Wise Men:

units.la: Ἡ ἐστιν εἰς τῆς δίκης ὀφθαλμὸς, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ὁπισκοπεῖ κύκλῳ τὸ περιτλό- μενα περὶ γῆν ἡ θάλασσαν.
units.tr: This is not the eye of Justice, but it looks around on all sides at whatever revolves about earth or sea. [Ἡ ἐστιν εἰς τῆς δίκης ὀφθαλμὸς, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ὁπισκοπεῖ κύκλῳ τὸ περιτλό- μενα περὶ γῆν ἡ θάλασσαν.]

units.la: Apud Achaeos Zeus παντόπτης fuit cultus, teste Hesychio.
units.tr: Among the Achaeans, Zeus was worshipped as Pantoptes (the All-seeing), according to Hesychius.

units.la: Cicero lib. 2. de LL.
units.tr: Cicero, book 2 of the De Legibus.

units.la: Homines existimare oportet, Deos omnia cernere.
units.tr: Men ought to suppose that the gods see all things.

units.la: Prudent. Cathemer.
units.tr: Prudentius, Cathemerinon.

units.la: Speculator adstat desuper; Qui nos diebus omnibus, actiuq; nostros prospicit a luce prima in vesperum. Hic testis, hic est arbiter, hic internetur, quicquid est, humana quod mens concipit: hunc nemo fallit judicem.
units.tr: A watchman stands on high, who looks over us and our deeds every day, from first light to evening. He is the witness, he is the judge; whatever the human mind conceives, he discerns it. No one deceives this judge.

units.la: In Constit. Imp. Leonis & Alexandri de Judicibus:
units.tr: In the Constitutions of the Emperors Leo and Alexander concerning judges:

units.la: Sed forte nos effugerit; pervigilem tamen, & insomnem oculum, cui nihil non, quamlibet occultum, effugere non poterit.
units.tr: But perhaps it will escape us; yet the ever-watchful and sleepless eye, from which nothing, however hidden, can escape.

units.la: Vide etiam Divi Ambros. lib. 1. Offic. cap. 14.
units.tr: See also Ambrose, De Officiis, book 1, chapter 14.

units.la: DIs iratis nihil feliciter geri eredebatur. Amph. I.I.v.236. Mil. 2.3. v. 43.
units.tr: It was believed that nothing could be carried through successfully if the gods were angry. Amphitryon 1.1 v.236; Miles Gloriosus 2.3 v.43.

units.la: Unde proverbium: DIs est natus iniquis: de homine invenusto ac misero, cui nihil bene succedit.
units.tr: Hence the proverb: Born under unkind gods, said of an unattractive and wretched man for whom nothing goes well.

units.la: Sic Persius:
units.tr: So Persius:

units.la: DIs iratus, Geniog; finistro.
units.tr: Angry with the gods and with a sinister genius.

units.la: Horat. Sat. 2. 3.
units.tr: Horace, Satires 2.3.

units.la: Iratus natum paries DIs, atq; Poëtis,
units.tr: Born of a father angry with the gods and with poets,

units.la: Contraria sunt:
units.tr: The opposites are:

units.la: DIs secundus: DIs hominibusq; plaudentibus.
units.tr: Favoured by the gods: with gods and men applauding.

units.la: Atq; adeò felicem denotare volentes ac venustum dicebant: Ipsi nascenti Deos risisse. Ipsum placido lumine vidisse.
units.tr: And wishing to describe someone fortunate and charming, they said: The gods smiled on his birth. They looked upon him with a gentle light.

units.la: Virg. 1. Æneid.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid 1.

units.la: ---- haud, credo, invisus cælestibus auras Vitales carpit.
units.tr: —surely not hateful to the heavenly powers, he draws the breath of life.

units.la: Dicebant: D I bonum nascenti sternutasse omen.
units.tr: They said: The gods gave a good omen by sneezing at his birth.

units.la: SOLEBANT Deos salutare, & quidem operto capite. Amph. 4. 3. v. 62. & 5. 1. v. 42. Curc. 1. 1 v. 70. & 3. 1. v. 19. Bacch 2. 1. v. 1. & 2. 3. v. 113. De ritu salutandi Deos vide Briss. Form. lib 1. pag. 33. 56. Lipsi lib. 2. Elect. c. 6. Muret. Var. lib. 10. cap. 1. Torrent. ad Suet. Vitell. cap. 2. Casaub. ad Perf.
units.tr: They used to greet the gods, and indeed with head covered. Amphitryon 4.3 v.62 and 5.1 v.42; Curculio 1.1 v.70 and 3.1 v.19; Bacchides 2.1 v.1 and 2.3 v.113. On the custom of greeting the gods see Brisson, De Formulis, book 1, pp. 33, 56; Lipsius, Electa, book 2, ch. 6; Muret, Variae Lectiones, book 10, ch. 1; Torrentius on Suetonius, Vitellius ch. 2; Casaubon on Persius.

units.la: DII non sunt similes hominibus nequam, & ebriosis. Amph. 1. 1. v. 127.
units.tr: The gods are not like worthless and drunken men. Amphitryon 1.1 v.127.

units.la: DI pauperibus magis parcere solent, quàm divitibus: quos solent damnare, & domare. Trin. 4. 1. v. 10.
units.tr: The gods are accustomed to spare the poor more than the rich, whom they are accustomed to condemn and subdue. Trinummus 4.1 v.10.

units.la: QUIDAM homines est sunt vesanię, ut dicant DEOS sibi esse obnoxios: & se metuere. Pœn. 5. 4. v. 18.
units.tr: Some men are so mad that they say the gods are bound to them and that they fear them. Poenulus 5.4 v.18.

units.la: SI Dij non protinus exaudiant, non desperandum: aut DIs insultandum: quod fecit impiè Anthemonides miles. Pœn. 2. 1. v. 13.
units.tr: If the gods do not hear at once, one must not despair, nor insult the gods, as the impious soldier Anthemonides did. Poenulus 2.1 v.13.

units.la: SOLEBANT veteres res carissimas & pretiosissimas, ipsasq; adeò opes, maximè in rebus dubijs, deponere in templis. Bacch. 2. 3. v. 78.
units.tr: The ancients were accustomed to deposit their most precious and valuable things, indeed their wealth, in temples, especially in times of uncertainty. Bacchides 2.3 v.78.

units.la: Cæsar. lib. 3. de bello Gall.
units.tr: Caesar, book 3 of the De Bello Gallico.

units.la: Ephesi à fano Dianæ depositas antiquitus pecunias Scipio tollijubebat.
units.tr: At Ephesus, Scipio ordered the money that had long been deposited in the temple of Diana to be taken away.

units.la: Et lib. 1. Bell. Civil.
units.tr: And book 1 of the De Bello Civili:

units.la: Arma imperantur, pecuniæ à municipijs exiguntur: & e fano tollantur.
units.tr: Arms are demanded, money is exacted from the towns, and let it be taken from the temple.

units.la: Herodianus in Commodo templum pacis commemorat de improviso incendio consumtum, ingenti multorum jacturâ, qui eò suas divitias congesserant.
units.tr: Herodian, in his account of Commodus, records that the temple of Peace was destroyed by a sudden fire, with great loss to many who had stored their riches there.

units.la: Cicero lib. 5. ad Att. Epist. ult.
units.tr: Cicero, book 5 of the Letters to Atticus, last letter:

units.la: Ut in fano deponerent C C. talenta non concessi.
units.tr: I did not allow them to deposit 200 talents in the temple.

units.la: Lib. de Legg.
units.tr: From the De Legibus:

units.la: Sacrum, sacrove commendatum, qui clepsit, rapseritve parrici-da esto.
units.tr: Whoever steals or carries off what is sacred, or what has been entrusted to a sacred place, shall be punished as a parricide.

units.la: Item: Sacrilego poena est, neq; ei soli, qui sacrum abstulerit, sed et-iam ei, qui sacro commendatum.
units.tr: Likewise: The penalty for sacrilege falls not only on the one who has carried off something sacred, but also on the one to whom something sacred has been entrusted.

units.la: Quod & nunc fit multis in Fanis. Vide etiam Broidæi Miscell. lib. 4. cap. 17. & Herald. Comm. ad Arnob. pag. 383. Edit. Parif.
units.tr: This is still done today in many temples. See also Broukhusius, Miscellanea, book 4, ch. 17, and Heraldus' commentary on Arnobius, p. 383, Paris edition.

units.la: SOLEBANT olim pietatis suæ præmia mercedemq; à Dis petere: & cùm in adversas res inciderant, se Deos læsisse arbitrabantur. Rud. 1.3. v.10.
units.tr: Men of old were accustomed to seek from the gods the rewards and wages of their piety; and when they fell into adverse circumstances, they thought they had offended the gods. Rudens 1.3 v.10.

units.la: Quid habebunt igitur impii posthac? si ad hunc modum est inno-xiis honor apud vos.
units.tr: What then will the impious have hereafter, if such is the honour paid among you to the innocent?

units.la: DEUS injustos iudices punit: & bonos habet in tabulis exscriptos: ne placatur donis hostijs. Rud. Prol. v.20.
units.tr: God punishes unjust judges and keeps the good written in his tablets; he is not appeased by gifts or sacrifices. Rudens, Prologue, v.20.

units.la: Vide Fab. De Diphtherâ Jovis.
units.tr: See Fabricius? On the Diphthera of Jupiter.

units.la: DII finguntur immortales, omnipotentes. Sic exclamat adolescens. Pæn. 1. 2, v. 63.
units.tr: The gods are imagined as immortal and almighty. So a young man exclaims. Poenulus 1.2 v.63.

units.la: Deos & amare & metuere dicebantur. Pæn. 1. 2. v. 70.
units.tr: It was said that the gods are both loved and feared. Poenulus 1.2 v.70.

units.la: Ovid. 1. Metam. v. 323. ---- aut illâ metuentur nulla Deorum.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1, v.323: or by her none of the gods will be feared.

units.la: PIETAS profanis hominibus ludibrio habetur. Pseud. 1.3. v.57. Ubi leno impiè deridet adolescentem pietatem prævortentem suo amori. Pietatem ergo istam amplexator nocta pro Phænicio.
units.tr: Piety is held up to ridicule by profane men. Pseudolus 1.3 v.57, where the pimp impiously mocks the young man who puts piety before his love: Therefore hold on to that piety, for Phoenicium.

units.la: QUI Deorum consilia culpet, stultus inscitusque sit, Quisq; eos vituperet, nunc jam istis rebus desisti decet. Mil. 3.1.v.140.
units.tr: Whoever criticises the counsels of the gods is foolish and ignorant; anyone who finds fault with them should now stop doing so. Miles Gloriosus 3.1 v.140.

units.la: ACTIONUM suarum successum folebant suspendere à nutu Deorum. Ideoq; addebant illud: Si DI volunt. Bacch. 2, 3. verf. 5. Et Capt. 2.3.v.94. Expedivi è servitute filium: SI DIS PLACET. Neq; enim ibi capi debet: ut aliàs vulgò.
units.tr: People used to make the success of their undertakings depend on the nod of the gods, and so they added: If the gods will. Bacchides 2.3 v.5; and Captivi 2.3 v.94: I have freed my son from slavery: IF IT PLEASES THE GODS. For the phrase should not be taken there in the sense commonly given to it elsewhere.

units.la: Catullus: Pauci, si tibi DI favent, diebus. Græci: Greek text.
units.tr: Catullus: Few days, if the gods favour you. The Greeks: [Greek quotation].

units.la: Xenophon Greek text.
units.tr: Xenophon: [Greek quotation].

units.la: Greek text.
units.tr: [Greek quotation].

units.la: Et iterùm:
units.tr: And again:

units.la: ἄμα δὲ δείξομεν τοῖς πολεμίοις, ἔνθα κρατῆζειν νομίζουσιν, ἐνταῦθα ἄλλως αὐτῶν κρείττως, ἢν Θεὸς θέλῃ.
units.tr: And at the same time we shall show the enemy that where they think they are strong, there we shall be stronger, if God wills it. [ἄμα δὲ δείξομεν τοῖς πολεμίοις, ἔνθα κρατῆζειν νομίζουσιν, ἐνταῦθα ἄλλως αὐτῶν κρείττως, ἢν Θεὸς θέλῃ.]

units.la: Julianus ὁ παραβάτης Epist. ad Libanium dixit: εἰ Θεοὶ θέλοιεν.
units.tr: Julian the Apostate, in his letter to Libanius, said: if the gods should will it. [εἰ Θεοὶ θέλοιεν.]

units.la: Frequenter étiam dicebant ξὺν Θεῷ.
units.tr: They also frequently said with God's help [ξὺν Θεῷ].

units.la: Sophocles Ajace: ζὼν Θεῷ πᾶς ἢ γὰρ ἂν ὠφελεῖ ἀδύνατα.
units.tr: Sophocles, Ajax: Everything lives by God's will, for nothing is impossible [ζὼν Θεῷ πᾶς ἢ γὰρ ἂν ὠφελεῖ ἀδύνατα].

units.la: Pind. Olymp. Od. 8.
units.tr: Pindar, Olympian Odes 8.

units.la: πολλαὶ δ᾽ ἀδοὶ σὺν Θεοῖς ἐντραγῶλαι.
units.tr: Many hopes are fulfilled along with the gods [πολλαὶ δ᾽ ἀδοὶ σὺν Θεοῖς ἐντραγῶλαι].

units.la: Herodotus ait Θεῶν τὰ ἰζα νεμόντων. Musavi.
units.tr: Herodotus says: the gods distributing equal shares [Θεῶν τὰ ἴσα νεμόντων]. Musavi.

units.la: Vide etiam Herald. Adverf. l.2.c.5.
units.tr: See also Heraldus, Adversaria, book 2, ch. 5.

units.la: Memorabile autem plane est, quod Ethnici, à veri Dei agnitio‑ne alieni, omnes tamen actiones à PROVIDENTIA DEI suspendebant. Quod ex Plauti nostri Comœdijs palàm conflat; Capt. 2.1.v.45.
units.tr: It is truly remarkable that the heathen, strangers to the knowledge of the true God, nevertheless made all their actions depend on the PROVIDENCE OF GOD. This is plainly clear from the comedies of our Plautus. Captivi 2.1 v.45.

units.la: Quoniam DIs immortales animium ostenderunt suum.
units.tr: Since the immortal gods have shown their will.

units.la: Indeq; consolationem certissimam hauriebant Bacch. 4.3. v.24.
units.tr: And from this they drew the most certain consolation. Bacchides 4.3 v.24.

units.la: Deus nos aliquùi respiciet.
units.tr: God will look upon us at some time.

units.la: Sic Senex Caf. 2.5. v.37.
units.tr: So the old man in Casina 2.5 v.37:

units.la: DIs fumfretus, Deos sperabimus.
units.tr: Relying on the gods, we shall hope in the gods.

units.la: Cui impius villicus impiè sic regerit: Non ego istud verbum emissim titivillitio. Nam omnes mortales Deis sunt freti, sed tamen Vidi ego DIs fretos saepè multos decipi.
units.tr: To this the impious bailiff impiously replies: I did not say that word in vain. For all mortals rely on the gods; but I have seen many who relied on the gods deceived.

units.la: Aliter Psaltes divinus suadet Psalmo 91.
units.tr: Otherwise the divine psalmist urges, in Psalm 91.

units.la: NIMIRUM solent homines cùm rerum suarum causam ignorant, aut verò cùm rebus adversis afflictantur, ideoq; Deos quodammodò accusant, ita se consolari: HOC DEO COMPLACITUM EST. Rud. 1.3, v.3. Sic Amph. 2.2.v.5. Ita DIs complacitum est, voluptatem ut mœror comes consequatur.
units.tr: Men commonly do this when they do not know the cause of their affairs, or when they are afflicted by adverse events; and so, in a way, they accuse the gods and console themselves: THIS HAS PLEASED GOD. Rudens 1.3 v.3. So Amphitryon 2.2 v.5: So it has pleased the gods that grief should follow pleasure.

units.la: Horatius l.1.Od.33. Sic Visum Veneri.
units.tr: Horace, Odes 1.33: So it seemed good to Venus.

units.la: Virgil. lib. 3. Æneid. Sic Visum Superis.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid 3: So it seemed good to the gods above.

units.la: Deo igitur & Providentiæ ipsius numquam resistendum. Pers. 1.1.v.24. Quid faciam? inquit servus: DIs ne adverser, quasi Titani, cum DIs belligerem, quibus sat esse non queam?
units.tr: Therefore one must never resist God or his providence. Persa 1.1 v.24: What shall I do? says the slave. Shall I set myself against the gods, like a Titan, and wage war with gods against whom I am no match?

units.la: Quin omnia Providentiæ Dei committenda, à quâ scil. nobis omnia bona - mala divitiæ - paupertas, proveniunt. Sic se solatur Euclio avarus. Aul. 1.2. v.10. Pauper sum, patior; quod DIdant sero.
units.tr: Indeed, all things must be committed to the providence of God, from whom all good and evil, riches and poverty, come to us. So the miserly Euclio consoles himself: Aulularia 1.2 v.10: I am poor and I endure it; yet the gods will give late.

units.la: Tantam Providentiæ vim agnoverant Ethnici: ut etiam probra sua, quamquam impiè illi adscripserint.
units.tr: The pagans recognised so great a power of Providence that they even ascribed their own disgraces to it, though they impiously attributed them to it.

units.la: Ita enim adolescens Lyconides Aul. 4.10.v.7.12. Deum mihi impulsor fuit, is me ad illam illexit: Factum est illud: fieri infectum non potest. Deos credo voluisse. nam ni vellent, non fierent, scio.
units.tr: So the young man Lyconides says in the Aulularia: "A god was my instigator; he lured me to her. It is done; what is done cannot be undone. I believe the gods willed it, for unless they had willed it, I know it would not have happened."

units.la: In salutandis & precandis Dijs dextrovorsum se vertere solebant.
units.tr: In greeting and praying to the gods they used to turn to the right.

units.la: Vide etiam Plin.lib.28.cap.2. Turn.lib.1.cap.17. & lib.22.cap.23. Itemq; Pithæi Advers.lib.1.cap.7. & Briss.lib.1.Form.
units.tr: See also Pliny, book 28, chapter 2; Turnebus, book 1, chapter 17, and book 22, chapter 23; likewise Pithoeus, Adversaria, book 1, chapter 7, and Brisson, book 1, De formulis.

units.la: Templa DIs in loco decoro consecrata. Rud. 1.4. v.35.
units.tr: Temples were consecrated to the gods in a fitting place. Rud. 1.4. v. 35.

units.la: Veteres ne errore laberentur, de nomine Dei alicujus certo dubitantes, dicere solebant: Quisquis es Deus. Rud. 1.4. v.37.
units.tr: Lest they fall into error, the ancients, uncertain of the name of some particular god, were accustomed to say: "Whoever you are, god." Rud. 1.4. v. 37.

units.la: Virgil.lib.4. Æn. v.577.
units.tr: Virgil, book 4 of the Aeneid, v. 577.

units.la: — sequimur te sanƈte Deorum,
units.tr: "We follow you, holy one of the gods,

units.la: Quisquis es.
units.tr: whoever you are."

units.la: Vide ibi interpretes, & Paullum Merulam Cosmogr.lib.1.cap.2.
units.tr: See the commentators there, and Paulus Merula, Cosmographia, book 1, chapter 2.

units.la: Pietas sæpè postponitur divitijs. Pseud. 1.3.v.120.
units.tr: Piety is often put after riches. Pseud. 1.3. v. 120.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Divitiarum.
units.tr: See also the title Divitiarum.

units.la: PIETAS majorum etiam posteris prodest beneficio Deum. Caf. 2.6. v. 66.
units.tr: The piety of ancestors is often of benefit to their descendants, by God's favour. Cas. 2.6. v. 66.

units.la: IN rebus angustis providentia Dei nos soletur. Capt. 2.1.v.1.
units.tr: In straitened circumstances the providence of God should comfort us. Capt. 2.1. v. 1.

units.la: QUI Deum honorant, ab eodem honorantur. Aul.Prol.v.20.
units.tr: Those who honour God are honoured by him. Aul. Prol. v. 20.

units.la: IN Deorum gratiam quidvis faciendum. Sic Mercurius Amph.Prol. v.57.
units.tr: Anything at all should be done for the favour of the gods. So Mercury says in the Amphitryon, prologue, v. 57: "—but I, being more shrewd,

units.la: —sed ego sultior,
units.tr: as if I did not know that you want it, I who am a god."

units.la: Quasi nesciam vos velle, qui Divos siem.
units.tr: Quasi nesciam vos velle, qui Divos siem.

units.la: SOLI Dij divites: homines autem & divites & mendici æquo censu mortiaccensentur. Trin. 2.4. v. 90.
units.tr: The gods alone are rich; men, both rich and beggars, are reckoned at the same valuation when they die. Trin. 2.4. v. 90.

units.la: DII Deæque habebant suos sacerdotes, & Antistitas. Rud.3.2.v.10.
units.tr: The gods and goddesses had their own priests and priestesses. Rud. 3.2. v. 10.

units.la: Venerea Antistita.
units.tr: "A priestess of Venus."

units.la: QUOI homini Dei sunt propitij, lucrum ei profecto obijciunt. Curc. 4.2 v.45.
units.tr: To the man to whom the gods are favourable, they surely present gain. Curc. 4.2. v. 45.

units.la: QUOI homini Dij sunt propitii, ei non iratos esse puto. Curc. 4.4. verf. 1.
units.tr: To the man to whom the gods are favourable, I think they are not angry. Curc. 4.4. v. 1.

units.la: CANDIDATI: h.e. albi, Deos Deasve accedebant. Rud. 1.5.v.12. Perf. Sat. 2.
units.tr: CANDIDATI: that is, the whitened ones, who approached the gods. Rud. 1.5. v. 12. Persius, Satire 2.

units.la: Negato Iuppiter hæc illi, quamvis te albata rogarit, Vide ibi Casaub.
units.tr: "Let Jupiter refuse him these things, though you ask him in white robes." See Casaubon there.

units.la: TALIS ludentes Deum aliquem propitium invocabant. Sic Parasitus Herculem. Curc. 2.3.v.79. Vide Tit. Talorum.
units.tr: Gamblers used to call upon some god to be favourable to them. So the parasite calls on Hercules. Curc. 2.3. v. 79. See the title Talorum.

units.la: QUI à Dijs aliquid petere cogitabant, cubabant in eorum, quorum ope indigebant, fanis: tamquam responsa ab ijs, vel vigilantes, vel in somnis accepturi. Sic ægroti in templo Æsculapij incubabant, ad remedia per somnium accipienda. Curc. 1.1.v.26. & 2.1.v.2. & 2.2.v.16. & 3.1.v.19.
units.tr: Those who meant to ask something of the gods lay down in the temples of those gods whose help they needed, as if to receive answers from them, either waking or in dreams. So the sick lay down in the temple of Aesculapius, to receive remedies through a dream. Curc. 1.1. v. 26; 2.1. v. 2; 2.2. v. 16; 3.1. v. 19.

units.la: Hic leno ægrotus incubat in Æsculapij fano.
units.tr: Here the sick pimp lies down in the temple of Aesculapius.

units.la: Vide Servium ad 7. Virg. Æneid.
units.tr: See Servius on Virgil's Aeneid, book 7.

units.la: Pellibus incubuit stratis.
units.tr: He lay down on the bedding of skins.

units.la: Et Turn lib.11. cap.7.
units.tr: And Turnebus, book 11, chapter 7.

units.la: Piu.
units.tr: Piu.

units.la: Prudent. Apotheos. verf. 254.
units.tr: Prudentius, Apotheosis, v. 254.

units.la: Ecquis in idolio recubans, inter sacra mille, Ridiculosq; Deos venerans sale, caspite, thure,
units.tr: "Who, reclining in an idol's shrine, amid a thousand sacred things, venerating ridiculous gods with salt, incense and frankincense,

units.la: Non putas esse Deum summum?
units.tr: does not think there is a supreme God?"

units.la: Hieron. ad Eustach. Tom. 1.
units.tr: Jerome, to Eustochium, vol. 1.

units.la: Nonne scandalizatur frater, si te viderit in idolio recumbentem?
units.tr: "Will not your brother be scandalised if he sees you reclining in an idol's temple?"

units.la: Patavij ajunt in Italia etiamnum in Templo Divi Antonij adolescentes & puellas rusticanas incubare.
units.tr: At Padua, in Italy, they say, young men and country girls still lie down in the temple of St Anthony.

units.la: Vide etiam Strabonem lib. 11.
units.tr: See also Strabo, book 11.

units.la: Μαντεῖον ἐγκοιμωμένων.
units.tr: [Μαντεῖον ἐγκοιμωμένων] An oracle for those who sleep in the temple.

units.la: Ubi Casaub. Not. nec non Inscriptionum Romanorum Indices.
units.tr: See Casaubon's notes there, and also the indexes of the Roman inscriptions.

units.la: DII qui lucem praebere solent, sunt: Vulcanus, Sol, Luna, Dies.
units.tr: The gods who are accustomed to give light are: Vulcan, the Sun, the Moon, the Day.

units.la: Bacch. 2 3. v. 21. Caesar de Germanis: Deorum numero eos solos ducunt, quos vident: Solem, Vulcanum & Lunam.
units.tr: Bacch. 2.3. v. 21. Caesar, on the Germans: They count as gods only those they can see: the Sun, Vulcan and the Moon.

units.la: PIETATIS invictae semper praemium est. Poen. 5. 4. v. 17.
units.tr: The reward of unconquered piety is always there. Poen. 5.4. v. 17.

units.la: SIBYLLA vaticinatrix divinare etiam potuit: quae legi non possunt. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 23. de litteris male scriptis.
units.tr: The Sibyl, a prophetess, could also foretell things which cannot be read. Pseud. 1.1. v. 23. Said of badly written letters.

units.la: DII caelum colunt. Perf. 4. 4. v. 32.
units.tr: The gods inhabit heaven. Persa 4.4. v. 32.

units.la: PIETAS parentum auxilio esse solet liberis. Poen. 5. 4. v. 105.
units.tr: The piety of parents is usually a help to their children. Poen. 5.4. v. 105.

units.la: MIRIS modis DI ludos faciunt hominibus, mirosq; exemplis somnia in somnis danunt. Merc. 2. 1. v. 1. 2. Rud. 3. 1. verf. 1. 2. Quae Plautus desumsit e Graeco Menandri, teste Nicol. Loensi. Misc. pag. 282. [Greek].
units.tr: In wondrous ways the gods make sport of men, and by wondrous examples they send dreams in sleep. Merc. 2.1. v. 1, 2. Rud. 3.1. v. 1, 2. Plautus took these from the Greek of Menander, as Nicolaus Loensis attests, Misc., p. 282.

units.la: DEUS est omnipotens. Sic Mercurius Amph. Prol. v. 53.
units.tr: God is almighty. So Mercury says in the Amphitryon, prologue, v. 53.

units.la: Deus sum: commutavero hanc si voltis.
units.tr: "I am a god; I would change this, if you wish."

units.la: RE bene gesta DIs supplicabant. Curc. 4. 2. v. 41. 46.
units.tr: After a successful undertaking they used to supplicate the gods. Curc. 4.2. v. 41, 46.

units.la: DIs bovis immolati. Asin. 3. 3. v. 124.
units.tr: Offering of an ox to the gods. Asin. 3.3. v. 124.

units.la: DIs non est maledicendum. Bacch. 1, 2. v. 11.
units.tr: One must not speak evil of the gods. Bacch. 1.2. v. 11.

units.la: DESIDERII. APPETITVS. CONCUPISCEN-TIÆ. CUPIDITATIS. PETITIONIS. APPETENTIAE.
