units.tr: DESIDERII. APPETITVS. CONCUPISCENTIÆ. CUPIDITATIS. PETITIONIS. APPETENTIAE.

units.la: EA est hominum indoles, ut sæpe incerta petant, certa amittant. Pseud. 2.3.v.17.
units.tr: Such is the nature of men: they often seek uncertain things and lose certain ones. Pseudolus, act 2, scene 3, verse 17.

units.la: Stulti haud scimus, frustrà ut simus, cum quid cupienter dari petimus nobis, quasi quid in rem sit, possimus noscere. Certa amittimus, dum incerta petimus. Atq; hoc evenit in labore, atq; in dolore, ut mors obrepat interim.
units.tr: Foolish as we are, we do not know that we are wrong when we eagerly ask for something to be given us, thinking we can tell whether it will be of use to us. We lose what is certain while we seek what is uncertain. And this happens in labour and in pain, so that death creeps upon us in the meantime.

units.la: Ita scil. homines ignorant, quid sibi vel prosit, vel obsit: & damnosa plærumq; exoptant.
units.tr: So, of course, people do not know what either benefits or harms them, and they very often desire what is ruinous.

units.la: Theognis:
units.tr: Theognis:

units.la: Ἄνθρωποι δὲ μάταια νομίζοντες εἰδότες ᾠδὲν Θεοὶ δὲ κατὰ σοφίαν πάντα τελεῖσι νοῦν.
units.tr: Men, thinking vain things, know nothing; but the gods accomplish all things with wisdom and mind. [Ἄνθρωποι δὲ μάταια νομίζοντες εἰδότες ᾠδὲν Θεοὶ δὲ κατὰ σοφίαν πάντα τελεῖσι νοῦν]

units.la: Seneca in Fragmento de otio Sapientis:
units.tr: Seneca, in the fragment from his work on the leisure of the wise man:

units.la: Fluctuamus, aliudq; ex alio comprehendimus: petita relinquimus: relicta repetimus: alternæ inter cupiditatem nostram, & pœnitentiam vices sunt.
units.tr: We waver, and we grasp one thing after another; we abandon what we have sought, and we seek again what we have abandoned; our desire and our repentance take turns.

units.la: Vide Adagia pag. 1545.
units.tr: See the Adagia, page 1545.

units.la: IMPETRARE oportet, qui æquum postulat. Stich. 5.4.v.44.
units.tr: One ought to obtain what he asks for who asks for what is fair. Stichus, act 5, scene 4, verse 44.

units.la: INIVSTA ab justis impetrare non decet. Justa autem ab injustis petere insipientia est. Amph.Prol. v. 35.
units.tr: It is not fitting to obtain unjust things from just men; to ask just things from unjust men is folly. Amphitryon, prologue, verse 35.

units.la: DVM nimis avidè quid expetimus, sæpè peccamus. Caf.2.6.v.18.
units.tr: When we desire something too eagerly, we often sin. Casina, act 2, scene 6, verse 18.

units.la: ISTVC fieri solet, quod in manu teneas, atq; oculis videas, id desideres. Trin. 4.2.v.69.
units.tr: It usually happens that when you hold something in your hand and see it with your eyes, you still long for it. Trinummus, act 4, scene 2, verse 69.

units.la: DIVITIARUM. OPUM. THESAURI. PECUNIAE. CRUMENAE. MARSUPII. FISCI.
units.tr: RICHES. WEALTH. TREASURE. MONEY. PURSE. WALLET. COFFER.

units.la: Vide etiam Titul. Bonorum : Mutui.
units.tr: See also the headings Goods and Loan.

units.la: DIVITIAE sæpè anteponuntur pietati. Quod fecit leno ille Pseud. 1. 3. v. 120. Ego scelestus nunc argentum promere possum domo: Tu qui pius es isfoc genere gnatus, nummum non habes. Vide etiam Senecam Epist. 115. ex Poët. Sine me vocari pessimum, ut dives vocer. &c.
units.tr: RICHES are often preferred to piety. The pimp does this in Pseudolus 1.3, v. 120: "I, a wretch, can now take money out of the house; you, who are so pious and born of such a family, have not a penny." See also Seneca, Epistle 115, quoting the poet: "Let me be called wicked, provided I am called rich, etc."

units.la: PLAERUMQUE divites sunt impij: ex sententiâ Piscatoris Plautini. Rud. 4. 7. v. 8. Isto tu pauper es, cum nimis sanctè pius.
units.tr: MOST rich men are wicked, according to the fisherman in Plautus's Rudens 4.7, v. 8: "You are poor on that account, because you are too exceedingly pious."

units.la: DEOS decet divitiæ & factiones, nos homunculi Salillum animæ: quam cum extemplo amisimus, æquo mendicus atque ille opulentissimus censetur censa ad Acherontem mortuus. Trin. 2. 4. v. 90. & seqq.
units.tr: Riches and high position befit the gods; we poor little men have only a little purse of breath. Once we have lost it, the beggar is judged equal to the richest man when he is dead and sent to Acheron. Trinummus 2.4, v. 90 ff.

units.la: Opes virtute Deum: & majorum obtingunt. Captiv. 2. 2. v. 74. &c.
units.tr: Wealth comes to those who are virtuous, and to those born of great men. Captivi 2.2, v. 74 etc.

units.la: Non ego omninò lucrum omne esse utile homini existimo. Est etiam, ubi profectò damnum præstet facere, quàm lucrum. Odi ego Aurum: Multa multìs suasit perperam.
units.tr: "I do not at all think that every gain is useful to a man. There is even a case where it is truly better to suffer loss than to make a gain. I hate gold: it has persuaded many men to do wrong."

units.la: Similes sententiæ passim reperiuntur apud authores.
units.tr: Similar sayings are found everywhere among the authors.

units.la: Phædrus lib. 5. Fab. 85.
units.tr: Phaedrus, book 5, fable 85.

units.la: Periculosum semper reputavi lucrum. Sed dicis: qui rapuere divitias, habent. Numeremus agedum, qui deprehensi perierint: Majorem turbam punitorum reperies.
units.tr: "I have always thought gain to be dangerous. But you say: those who have seized riches have them. Come, let us count those who were caught and perished: you will find a much greater crowd of the punished."

units.la: Hesiodus:
units.tr: Hesiod:

units.la: μὴ κρινὰ κεράδ αἰνειν, κρινὰ κέρδεα ἴσα ἀτησιν.
units.tr: "Do not praise shameful gains; gains are as good as ruin" [μὴ κακὰ κέρδεα αἰνεῖν, κέρδεα γὰρ ἴσα ἀτῇσιν].

units.la: Sophocles Antig.
units.tr: Sophocles, Antigone.

units.la: ἐν τῶν γὰρ αἰσχρῶν λυμάτων τὲς πλείονας ἀτωμένους ἴδοις ἂν ἢ σεσωσμένους.
units.tr: "For among shameful gains you would see more men ruined than saved" [ἐκ τῶν γὰρ αἰσχρῶν λυμάτων τοὺς πλείονας ἀτωμένους ἴδοις ἂν ἢ σεσωσμένους].

units.la: Ibidem:
units.tr: The same author:

units.la: τὰ δεινὰ κέρδη πημονὰς ἐργάζεται.
units.tr: "Terrible gains bring ruin" [τὰ δεινὰ κέρδη πημονὰς ἐργάζεται].

units.la: P. Sytus:
units.tr: Publilius Syrus:

units.la: Damnum appellandum est cum malâ famâ lucrum.
units.tr: Gain that comes with a bad reputation must be called loss.

units.la: Immundas fortunas & paupertatem æquum est squalorem sequi. Cist. 1. 1. v. 116.
units.tr: It is fitting that dirty fortunes and poverty should be followed by squalor. Cistellaria 1.1, v. 116.

units.la: Dives sum, si non reddo eis, quibus debeo: inquit argentarius. Curc. 3. 1. v. 3.
units.tr: "I am rich, if I do not pay those to whom I owe," says the banker. Curculio 3.1, v. 3.

units.la: Creditores aut debitores avari & nequam hunc habent morem, ut alius alium poscant, reddant nemini: quod faciebant olim argentarij: qui etiam ad prætorem accusati vix solvebant æs alienum. Curc. 3. 1. v. 7. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 61.
units.tr: Creditors and debtors who are greedy and worthless have this habit: each demands from the other, and neither pays anyone. Bankers used to do this too, and even when accused before the praetor they scarcely paid their debts. Curculio 3.1, v. 7; Pseudolus 1.3, v. 61.

units.la: Immò ad pugnos quandoq; res devenire solet. Ibid. v. 9.
units.tr: Indeed, matters often come to fisticuffs. Ibid., v. 9.

units.la: De collo gestabant crumenas, ut & nostrates rustici in primis-que degente Suevicâ institores, cænopolæ, alijq;. Truc. 3. 1. v. 7. & 5. v. 64. Asin. 3. 3. v. 67. Epid. 3. 2. v. Capt. 3. 1. v. 37. Pers. 4. 6. v. 9.
units.tr: They used to wear purses hung from the neck, as our country folk do too, especially in Swabia, as do pedlars, tavern-keepers and others. Truculentus 3.1, v. 7 and 5, v. 64; Asinaria 3.3, v. 67; Epidicus 3.2; Captivi 3.1, v. 37; Persa 4.6, v. 9.

units.la: Vide etiam Lex. Plaut. Decollare. Et Tit. Marsupij.
units.tr: See also the Plautine Lexicon under Decollare, and the heading Purse.

units.la: Pecunia multos habet inimicos: quia omnes insidias illi collocant. Aul. 3. 6. v. 43. Apophthegma est Euclionis avari.
units.tr: Money has many enemies, since everyone lays snares for it. This is a saying of the miser Euclio. Aulularia 3.6, v. 43.

units.la: Thesaurum collocabant in fano & templo alicujus Dei. Aul. 3. 6. v. 46. Ollam in Fidei fanum abstrudam. Vide supra Tit. Deorum.
units.tr: They used to deposit treasure in the shrine and temple of some god. "I will hide the pot in the shrine of Faith." Aulularia 3.6, v. 46. See above, under the heading Gods.

units.la: In pecuniâ elocandâ ratio accepti & expensi servari debet. Most. 1. 3. v. 145.
units.tr: When money is lent out, a record of receipts and expenses should be kept. Mostellaria 1.3, v. 145.

units.la: Gratior est nuncius, qui dicat se afferre, quàm petere pecuniam. Trin. 3. 3. v. 85.
units.tr: A messenger who says he is bringing money is more welcome than one who asks for it. Trinummus 3.3, v. 85.

units.la: Pecunia si detur adolescentibus: gladius datur, quo se occidant. Trin. 1. 2. v. 92. Vide Tit. Adolescentia: & Luxuria.
units.tr: If money is given to young men, a sword is given with which they may kill themselves. Trinummus 1.2, v. 92. See the headings Youth and Luxury.

units.la: Divitiæ etiam arte duellicâ comparantur. Epid. 3. 4. v. 14.
units.tr: Riches are also acquired by the art of war. Epidicus 3.4, v. 14.

units.la: Ita suntisti nostri divites: si quid benefacias, levior plumâ est gratia: si quid peccatum est, plumbeas iras gerunt. Pœn. 3. 6. v. 17.
units.tr: "That is what our rich men are like: if you do them a kindness, their gratitude is lighter than a feather; if you offend them at all, they nurse leaden anger." Poenulus 3.6, v. 17.

units.la: Divitiæ munere ac virtute Deorum dantur & majorum. Aul. 2. 1. v. 44. Ego virtute Deûm, & majorum nostrorum, divus sum satus.
units.tr: Riches are given by the gift and virtue of the gods and of ancestors. Aulularia 2.1, v. 44: "I was born divine, by the virtue of the gods and of our ancestors."

units.la: Pecunia nihil non potest. Asin. 3. 3. v. 46. Videtin' viginti minæ quid pollent? quidve possunt?
units.tr: Money can do anything. Asinaria 3.3, v. 46: "Do you see what twenty minae are worth, or what they can do?"

units.la: Stich. 3. 1. v. 9. Videte quæso, quid potest pecunia?
units.tr: Stichus 3.1, v. 9: "Please see what money can do!"

units.la: Quoniam re bene gestâ redîsti me videt, magnaque apportavisse divitias domum, in amicitiam atque in gratiam convertimus.
units.tr: "Since you have returned having done well, and see me, and have brought great riches home, we turn to friendship and favour."

units.la: Aul. 2. 2. v. 87. Dii immortales, obsecro, aurum quid valet?
units.tr: Aulularia 2.2, v. 87: "Immortal gods, I beg you, what is gold worth?"

units.la: Trin. 4. 2. v. 15. Ut ille me exornavit, ita sum ornatus. Argentum hoc facit.
units.tr: Trinummus 4.2, v. 15: "As he has adorned me, so am I adorned. Silver does this."

units.la: Aristoph. Ranis: φησί· ὡς μίγα λυλαδον πάντα χῦ τὰ ἀν ὀδολὸς.
units.tr: Aristophanes, Frogs: he says, "how great a thing everything is, all of it, even the smallest coin" [φησί· ὡς μέγα λυλαδὸν πάντα, χὼ τι ἂν ὀβολός].

units.la: Pecunia μεταφυμικῶς sumitur pro re emtâ pecuniâ.
units.tr: Money is taken metaphorically for a thing bought with money.

units.la: Asin. 3. 2. v. 43. Qui verberarem asinos, si forte occæperint clamare hinc ex crumenâ.
units.tr: Asinaria 3.2, v. 43: "I would beat the donkeys, if by chance they began to shout from the purse here."

units.la: Perf. 2. 3. v. 13. Nunc amico homini bobus domitiû meâ ex crumenâ largiar.
units.tr: Persa 2.3, v. 13: "Now I will generously give my friend oxen out of my purse, which I have tamed."

units.la: Perf. 2. 5. v. 16. Boves bini hic sunt in crumenâ. Mutuo, ut possim in bubile reti-cere, ne vagientur.
units.tr: Persa 2.5, v. 16: "Here in the purse there are two oxen. I will borrow, so that I can keep them in the stall and they do not bawl."

units.la: Truc. 3. 1. v. 8. Minas viginti mihi das.
units.tr: Truculentus 3.1, v. 8: "You give me twenty minae."

units.la: Mutuò cùm petimus pecuniam, respônsum hoc feré accipimus Non Est. Perf.1.1.v.6. & Trin.3.3.v.30.
units.tr: When we ask for money on loan, we usually get this answer: "There is none." Persa 1.1, v. 6, and Trinummus 3.3, v. 30.

units.la: Divites pauperes sæpè salutant ob spem prædæ. Aul. 2. 2. v. 3. 19. 69.
units.tr: The rich are often greeted by the poor because of the hope of gain. Aulularia 2.2, v. 3, 19, 69.

units.la: Thesaurum folebant in terrâ defodere. Trin.3.3.v.25.53.
units.tr: They used to bury treasure in the ground. Trinummus 3.3, v. 25, 53.

units.la: Dii pauperibus magis propitij, quàm ditioribus. Trin. 4.1.v.10.
units.tr: The gods are more favourable to the poor than to the rich. Trinummus 4.1, v. 10.

units.la: Quoad pecuniam damus, grati sumus. Absq; hac omnis gratia perit. Asin. 1.3.v.52.62. &c.
units.tr: As far as money goes, we are grateful; without it all gratitude perishes. Asinaria 1.3, v. 52, 62, etc.

units.la: Non tuto homini amico adcommodamus aliquid. Afinar. 2. 4. v. 39.
units.tr: We do not safely lend anything to a friend. Asinaria 2.4, v. 39.

units.la: Luxuriosi divitias suas habent pro stercore. Truc. 2. 7. v. 5.
units.tr: Spendthrifts regard their riches as dung. Truculentus 2.7, v. 5.

units.la: Pecunia in Zonâ gestabatur per urbem majoris securitatis causâ. Pœn. 5 2.v.48.
units.tr: Money was carried in a belt through the city for greater security. Poenulus 5.2, v. 48.

units.la: Pecuniæ caulâ quidvis homines mentiri solent. Trin. 4.2. verf. 132.
units.tr: For the sake of money men are wont to lie about anything. Trinummus 4.2, verse 132.

units.la: Pecunia fiscianima. Truc.Prol. v. 21.
units.tr: Money is the soul of the treasury. Truculentus, Prologue, v. 21.

units.la: Recte faciunt, qui diviti elocant aurum. Ab eo enim quamvis subitò licet sumere. Bacch. 2.3.v.105.
units.tr: They act rightly who lend gold to a rich man; for from him it may be taken even at short notice. Bacchides 2.3, v. 105.

units.la: Facinus audax incipit, qui cum opulento pauper homine cæpit habere negotium aut rem. Aul. 3.4.v.1.
units.tr: It is a bold undertaking when a poor man begins to have dealings or business with a wealthy man. Aulularia 3.4, v. 1.

units.la: Parentes liberis divitias, quærunt, non sine ærumnis. Trin. 4. 1. v.20.
units.tr: Parents seek riches for their children, not without toil. Trinummus 4.1, v. 20.

units.la: Divitiæ facilè Amicos inveniunt. Aul. 1.2.v.37.
units.tr: Riches easily find friends. Aulularia 1.2, v. 37.

units.la: Omnes me salutant benignum, quàm ante.
units.tr: "Everyone greets me kindly, more than before."

units.la: Picos divitijs superant divites, qui aureos montes dicuntur incolere. Aul. 4.8 v.1.
units.tr: The Pygmies surpass the rich in wealth, who are said to dwell on golden mountains. Aulularia 4.8, v. 1.

units.la: Huic homini dignum est divitias esse, & diu vitam dari, Qui & rem servat, & qui benè habet, suisq; amicis vult benè. Mil. 3.1.v.128.
units.tr: It is fitting for this man to have riches and to be granted a long life, he who both keeps his property and fares well, and wishes well to his friends. Miles Gloriosus 3.1, v. 128.

units.la: DIVITIÆ rarò cum virtute conjunctæ. Asin. 2.4.v.91.
units.tr: RICHES are rarely joined with virtue. Asinaria 2.4, v. 91.

units.la: Sic solatur se servus ille Asin. 2. 4. v. 91.
units.tr: Thus that slave consoles himself. Asinaria 2.4, v. 91.

units.la: Quamqnam ego sum sordidatus, Frugi tamen sum: nec potest pe-culium enumerari.
units.tr: "Although I am shabby, I am nonetheless thrifty; nor can my savings be counted."

units.la: DIVITIÆ virtuti præponi solent.
units.tr: RICHES are usually preferred to virtue.

units.la: Vide totam querelam Men. 4.2. verf.3. & seqq. & Titul. Patrem norum.
units.tr: See the whole complaint in Menaechmi 4.2, v. 3 ff., and the heading Father.

units.la: Qui homo maturè quæsivit pecuniam.
units.tr: A man who seeks money early.

units.la: Nisi eam maturè parsit, maturè esurit. Curc 3.1.v.10.
units.tr: Unless he saves it early, he hungers early. Curculio 3.1, v. 10.

units.la: Quoi homini Dei sunt propitij, lucrum ei profectò obijciunt. Curc. 4.2. v. 45.
units.tr: For the man to whom the gods are favourable, they surely throw gain in his way. Curculio 4.2, v. 45.

units.la: DIVITES tantas sæpè divitias habent, ut nesciant, quid faciant auro. Bacch. 2.3. v.100.
units.tr: Rich men often have such great riches that they do not know what to do with their gold. Bacchides 2.3, v. 100.

units.la: DIVITIAS vett. ut plurimùm fuisse in re pecuariâ non obscurè innuit nostér Capt. 2.2, v.31.
units.tr: The ancients for the most part had their wealth in livestock, as our author clearly hints. Captivi 2.2, v. 31.

units.la: Quid divitiæ? sunt ne opimæ? P H I. unde excoquat sevum?
units.tr: "What of riches? Are they plump? PHI. From where would he skim off the fat?"

units.la: DIVORTII.
units.tr: DIVORCE.

units.la: Vide Tit. Conjugij.
units.tr: See the title Marriage.

units.la: Gg -
units.tr: Gg -

units.la: DOTIS.
units.tr: DOWRY.

units.la: Vide Tit. Conjugy.
units.tr: See the title Marriage.

units.la: DUCIS.
units.tr: GENERAL (OF AN ARMY).

units.la: Vide Tit. Belli.
units.tr: See the title War.

units.la: DOLI. FRAUDIS. CAUTIONIS. ASTUTIÆ. STRATAGEMATIS.
units.tr: Guile. Fraud. Caution. Cunning. Stratagem.

units.la: DOLI non doli sunt, nisi astu coles. Capt. 2.1. v. 26.
units.tr: Guile is not guile unless you cultivate it with cunning. Capt. 2.1. v. 26.

units.la: In ætate hominum plurimæ fiunt transennæ, ubi decipiuntur dolis: h.e, varijs modis homines decipiuntur. Der Betrugist mancherley. Rud. 4.7.v.10.
units.tr: In human life many snares are set, where people are deceived by guile; that is, people are deceived in many ways. Deceit comes in many kinds. Rud. 4.7.v.10.

units.la: Cum ad summum deduxisti dolum: cum maximè cavendum, ne male rem geras. Mil. 4.4. v. 14.
units.tr: When you have brought your trick to its height, you must take the greatest care not to bungle the business. Mil. 4.4. v. 14.

units.la: OPPIDUM quodvis videtur posse expugnari dolis. Mil. 4.4.v.21. Vide Tit. Belli.
units.tr: Any town seems capable of being taken by guile. Mil. 4.4.v.21. See the title War.

units.la: QUI cavet, ne decipiatur, vix cavet, cum etiam cavet: Etiam cum cavisse ratus: sæpè is cautor captus est. Capt. 2. 2. v. 5.
units.tr: He who takes care not to be deceived scarcely takes care even when he does take care. Even when he thinks he has been cautious, the cautious man is often caught. Capt. 2. 2. v. 5.

units.la: NULLAM rem oportet dolose aggredi, nisi astutè, accuratèq; exequare, Truc. 2.5.v.10.
units.tr: No undertaking should be attempted by guile unless you carry it out with cunning and great care. Truc. 2.5.v.10.

units.la: Eborris.
units.tr: Eborris.

units.la: Bur suâ naturâ candidum frustra candefieret atramento. Most. 1.3. v. 101.
units.tr: In vain does what is white by its nature try to be made whiter with ink. Most. 1.3. v. 101.

units.la: Ebrietatis. Cauponæ. Vini. Potûs. Vomitûs. Cellarii. Thermopolii. Gulæ. Ciborum. Luxûs.
units.tr: Drunkenness. Taverns. Wine. Drinking. Vomiting. Cellar. Eating-house. Gluttony. Food. Luxury.

units.la: Vide supra plura Tit. Convivij: Triclinij.
units.tr: See above, under the heading Banquet; Dining-room, for more.

units.la: EBrii ore putido & fœtido ructu aliis molesti: eóq; ebrios, & vomiturientes fastidire solemus.
units.tr: DRUNKEN men, with their foul mouths and stinking belches, are a nuisance to others; therefore we are accustomed to loathe drunkards and those who are about to vomit.

units.la: Quid tu malum! ergo in os mihi ebrius irructas?
units.tr: What a curse you are! Are you going to belch drunkenly in my face?

units.la: Cas. 3.6. v. 7.10. Vide Tit. Senum.
units.tr: Cas. 3.6. v. 7.10. See the heading Old Men.

units.la: Turpe erat de die potare vel scortari. Pseud. 5.2.v.8. Asin. 4.2.v.17. Amph. 1.1. v.28.
units.tr: It was shameful to drink or to visit prostitutes by day. Pseud. 5.2.v.8. Asin. 4.2.v.17. Amph. 1.1. v.28.

units.la: Accius:
units.tr: Accius:

units.la: Nemo unquam vidit ebrium ire interdiu
units.tr: No one has ever seen a drunk man going out in the daytime

units.la: Neq; turbam facere, neq; fores exurere.
units.tr: Or making a disturbance, or setting fire to doors.

units.la: Ovidius lib. 7. Metamorph.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses book 7:

units.la: Lucis pars extrema mensæ
units.tr: The last part of the daylight

units.la: Est data. Vide etiam Prudent. Hymn. Cathemer. matut.
units.tr: Is given to the table. See also Prudentius, Hymn of the Cathemerinon, morning.

units.la: Huc referri potest Historia Pentecostes: quâ quidam Apostolos ebriosos clamarunt, cùm nondum esset quarta hora diei.
units.tr: To this may be referred the account of Pentecost, in which certain people called the Apostles drunk, although it was not yet the fourth hour of the day.

units.la: Vide etiam Terent. Adelph. 5. 9.
units.tr: See also Terence, Adelphi 5.9.

units.la: EBRII Baccho Bacchanal faciunt. Mil. 3.2.v.44.
units.tr: DRUNKEN men make a Bacchanal of Bacchus. Mil. 3.2.v.44.

units.la: DOLIA cùm replentur, dicuntur bacchari bac. Mil. 3.2.v.42.
units.tr: WHEN casks are filled, they are said to be Bacchic. Bac. Mil. 3.2.v.42.

units.la: Sic vetus Poëta de rustico ebrio:
units.tr: So an old poet describes a drunken countryman:

units.la: Percutit, & frangit vas, vinum defluit: ansa Stricta fuit: glut glut murmurat unda sonans.
units.tr: He strikes and breaks the jar; the wine runs out; the handle was tight; glut glut, the sounding wave murmurs.

units.la: Gluttus enim ἀρόχω, & ῥοόχω est vas vinarium: sic dictum à sorbo: unde gluttire. Ein Gutturoff Germanis.
units.tr: For gluttus is a wine vessel, from the Greek ἀρόχω and ῥοόχω [as printed], and so named from sorbing (sipping), whence gluttire. In German, a Gutturoff (throat-hole).

units.la: Vide Casaub. ad Sat. 5. Persij.
units.tr: See Casaubon on Persius, Satire 5.

units.la: VOMITUS magnoperè dehonestabat virum probum: adeò ut convitij loco in hominem impurum fuerit prolatum. Mosl. 3.1. v.115. Cas. 3.6.v.7.10.
units.tr: VOMITING greatly dishonoured an upright man, so that it was used as an insult against a disgusting person. Mosl. 3.1. v.115. Cas. 3.6.v.7.10.

units.la: Vide Tit. Senum.
units.tr: See the heading Old Men.

units.la: EBRIIS pes non facit officium: sed cadere cupiunt in via. Mosl. 1.4.v.11.13.16. Inde dormiunt. Ibid. v.30.
units.tr: WHEN men are drunk their feet do not do their duty, but they wish to fall down in the road. Mosl. 1.4.v.11.13.16. Hence they sleep. Ibid. v.30.

units.la: EBRII soluto somno redeunt ad pocula. Mosl. 2.1. v.26.
units.tr: DRUNKEN men, once their sleep is dispelled, return to the cups. Mosl. 2.1. v.26.

units.la: EBRII matulam poscebant, ut mejerent. Mosl. 2.1. v.39.
units.tr: DRUNKEN men were calling for a chamber-pot so that they might urinate. Mosl. 2.1. v.39.

units.la: EBRII coronati incedebant. Amph 3.4.v.16. Pseud 5.2.v.8.
units.tr: DRUNKEN men went about crowned with garlands. Amph. 3.4.v.16. Pseud. 5.2.v.8.

units.la: CIBUM sicciorem in ventrem, liquidiorem in vesicam descendere censebant. Perf. 1.3. v.
units.tr: They thought that drier food went down into the stomach, and more liquid into the bladder. Perf. 1.3. v.

units.la: Nolo in vesicam, quod eat in ventrem volo.
units.tr: I do not want what goes into the bladder; I want what goes into the stomach.

units.la: Sic Varro Satiram quandam suam inscripsit ESTMODUS MATULAE: quâ modum adhibendum monuit compotationi & ebrictati.
units.tr: So Varro entitled one of his satires What Measure for the Flask?, in which he advised that a measure be observed in drinking and drunkenness.

units.la: Idem Varro:
units.tr: Again Varro:

units.la: In quo nobilius est Philippeum, quod accipimus, quàm quod bibi-mus: mus: cum alterum addamus in bulgam, alterum in vesicam.
units.tr: In which that is nobler which we receive as a Philippeum, than that which we drink; when we add the one into the pouch, the other into the bladder.

units.la: EBRII crapulam amovere solent secedendo nonnihil. Pseud. 5. 1. v. 35.
units.tr: DRUNKEN men usually get rid of their hangover by withdrawing for a little while. Pseud. 5.1. v. 35.

units.la: AB ebrietate excusationem saepe facti quaerimus. Aulul. 4. 10. v. 15. Truc. 4. 3. v. 54.
units.tr: We often seek an excuse for what we have done from drunkenness. Aulul. 4.10. v. 15. Truc. 4.3. v. 54.

units.la: Mihi ignoscas, quod animi impos vini vitio fecerim.
units.tr: Forgive me, that I did it because, not being master of my mind, I was under the influence of wine.

units.la: Vide Tit. Excusationum plura.
units.tr: See the heading Excuses for more.

units.la: Sub vesperam plerumque erant ebrii illi, qui vino useri erant homines nihili. Trin. 3. 3. v. 82.
units.tr: Those drunkards who were addicted to wine and were worthless men were usually drunk towards evening. Trin. 3.3. v. 82.

units.la: Apul. Apolog.
units.tr: Apuleius, Apology.

units.la: Quid sit diei vides: dico crassum jam dudum ebrium stertere.
units.tr: You see what time of day it is: I say that the fat fellow has been snoring drunk for some time.

units.la: Vide etiam Curc. 1. 1. v.
units.tr: See also Curc. 1.1. v.

units.la: EBRII culpam vino adscribunt. Pseud. 5. 1. v. 4.
units.tr: DRUNKEN men lay the blame on wine. Pseud. 5.1. v. 4.

units.la: Si viandum mihi est hodie: magnum hoc vitium vino est: pedes captat primum, lictator dolosus est.
units.tr: If I must walk today, this great fault is due to wine: it catches my feet first; the lictor is treacherous.

units.la: EBRII edormiscebant crapulam. Rud. 2. 7. v. 28. Mil. 3. 2. v. 9. 13.
units.tr: DRUNKEN men sleep off their hangover. Rud. 2.7. v. 28. Mil. 3.2. v. 9. 13.

units.la: Ebho, an dormit Sceledrus intus?
units.tr: Hey, is Sceledrus asleep inside?

units.la: LV. Non nasoquidem. nam eo magnum clamat.
units.tr: LV. No, certainly not, for he shouts loudly.

units.la: Quilibitum est illi condormiscere.
units.tr: It is fitting for him to sleep alongside.

units.la: Terent. Adelph. 5. 2.
units.tr: Terence, Adelphi 5.2.

units.la: Dum edormiscam hoc villi
units.tr: While I sleep off this...

units.la: Laberius apud Nonium:
units.tr: Laberius, quoted by Nonius:

units.la: Homo ebriatus somno sanari solet.
units.tr: A drunken man is usually cured by sleep.

units.la: Eurip. Bacch.
units.tr: Euripides, Bacchae.

units.la: Athen. lib. 2. Eubulus τὸν τρίτον κρατῆρα τοῖς εὖ φρονοῦσιν ait esse ὕπνε, ὃν εἰσιόντες οἱ σοφοὶ κεκλημένοι, οὐκ ἀδὲ βαδίσασι.
units.tr: Athenaeus book 2: Eubulus says that the third mixing-bowl for the sensible is sleep, which the wise enter as invited guests, not as those walking away [τὸν τρίτον κρατῆρα τοῖς εὖ φρονοῦσιν ἔφη εἶναι ὕπνον, ὃν εἰσιόντες οἱ σοφοὶ κεκλημένοι, οὐκ ἀδὲ βαδίσασι].

units.la: Critias lib. 7. de vino:
units.tr: Critias, book 7, on wine:

units.la: ὁρᾷς δ' ὕπνον πέμοισαι, τὸν καμάτων λελυμένα. Vinum non parum confert ad somnum, qui laborum portus est.
units.tr: You see sleep sent by the gods, releasing us from our toils. Wine contributes not a little to sleep, which is the harbour of labours [ὁρᾷς δ' ὕπνον πέμψαισα τὸν καμάτων λελυμένα].

units.la: ETIAM feminæ, ancillæ se meraciore vino inebriabant. Unde percussæ flore Libyco dicebantur, & quæ sustentandæ erant, ne caderent. Caf. 3. f. v. 16.
units.tr: WOMEN too, and maidservants, made themselves drunk with stronger wine. Hence they were said to be struck by Libyan flower, and those who had to be supported lest they fall. Cas. 3.f. v. 16.

units.la: HOMINES gulosi in cauponis & Thermopolijs calidam bibebant infuso vino. Curc. 2. 3, v. 14. Ubi tanguntur mores Græculorum delicatiorum.
units.tr: GLUTTONOUS men in taverns and eating-houses drank hot wine with spices infused. Curc. 2.3, v. 14. Here the manners of the more pampered Greeklings are touched upon.

units.la: Vide etiam Lex. Plaut. Mil. 3. 2. v. 19. Trin. 4. 3 v. Vide quæ supra scripsi de thermopotandi ratione Tit. Convivij.
units.tr: See also the Plautine lexicon. Mil. 3.2. v. 19. Trin. 4.3 v. See what I have written above on the method of drinking hot wine, under the heading Banquet.

units.la: EBRIETAS omnes perturbat sensus. Amph. 2. 1. v. 24.
units.tr: DRUNKENNESS disturbs all the senses. Amph. 2.1. v. 24.

units.la: EBRIETAS insaniam parit. Men. 2. 3. v. 22.
units.tr: DRUNKENNESS brings forth madness. Men. 2.3. v. 22.

units.la: EBRII & saturi facti, petebant ἀφεδρῶνας. Curc. 2. 3. v. 84.
units.tr: DRUNK and sated, they sought the latrines [ἀφεδρῶνας]. Curc. 2.3. v. 84.

units.la: MERETRICES etiam ebrietati, & vino indulserunt apud lenones. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 50.
units.tr: PROSTITUTES too indulged in drunkenness and wine at the pimps' houses. Pseud. 1.2. v. 50.

units.la: EBRIETAS causa scortationis Aul. 4. 7. v. 8. Te eam compressisse vinolentum. Cist. 1. 3. v. 11.
units.tr: DRUNKENNESS is the cause of fornication. Aul. 4.7. v. 8. "That you had slept with her while drunk." Cist. 1.3. v. 11.

units.la: EBRIETAS facit, ut plus loquamur, quàm sat est. Cist. 1. 2. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: DRUNKENNESS makes us talk more than is enough. Cist. 1.2. v. 1. and following.

units.la: EBRIETAS amorem conciliat. Rud. 2. 7. v. 9.
units.tr: DRUNKENNESS wins love. Rud. 2.7. v. 9.

units.la: VINUM profundere nefas. Curc. 1. 1. v. 92.
units.tr: To pour out wine is an abomination. Curc. 1.1. v. 92.

units.la: VINUM recondebant in amphoras & urceum. Mil. 3. 2. v. 11. 18.
units.tr: They stored wine in amphorae and jugs. Mil. 3.2. v. 11. 18.

units.la: ID faciebat promus five cellarius. Ibid. v. 11. 24.
units.tr: The butler or cellarer did this. Ibid. v. 11. 24.

units.la: QUI habebat quoq; suppromum. Ibid. 12. 24.
units.tr: Whoever had one also had an under-butler. Ibid. 12. 24.

units.la: Calidum bibebant in prandio. Quod proinde non tam bibebant, quàm sorbendo absumserunt: ne amburerent guttur. Mil. 3.2. v.19. 22.
units.tr: They drank hot wine at lunch. Indeed they did not so much drink it as swallow it by sipping, so that it would not burn the throat. Mil. 3.2. v. 19. 22.

units.la: Vilioribus, ut servis, posca praebebatur, nempe levior potus seu vinum acidum, mixtum aquâ. Sic queritur serv° iniquè comparatum esse: Alij, inquit, ebrij sunt ex optimo vino: alij potiam potitant. Quae vera est ejus loci lectio. Mil. 3.2.v.23. Rud. 4. 3. v. 32.
units.tr: For cheaper people, such as slaves, posca was provided, namely a lighter drink, or sour wine mixed with water. So a slave complains that the arrangement is unfair: "Others," he says, "are drunk on the best wine; others drink the dregs." This is the true reading of that passage. Mil. 3.2. v. 23. Rud. 4.3. v. 32.

units.la: Vide Lipsium de Milit.Rom. Dial. 16. I.5. pag.235.
units.tr: See Lipsius, De militia Romana, Dialogue 16, book 1, p. 235.

units.la: Vinum
units.tr: Wine

units.la: Vinum vetus in laude & pretio. Aul. 3.6.v.34.
units.tr: Old wine, in praise and esteem. Aul. 3.6.v.34.

units.la: Ego jussero cadum vini veteris àme afferrier.
units.tr: I will order a jar of old wine to be brought here.

units.la: Flos veteris vini.
units.tr: The flower of old wine.

units.la: Cadum veteris vini tibi propino.
units.tr: I drink to you a jar of old wine.

units.la: Cas. Prol. v.5.
units.tr: Cas. Prol. v.5.

units.la: Qui utuntur vino vetere, sapientes puto.
units.tr: Those who drink old wine, I think, are wise.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Fabularum: & Antiquitatis.
units.tr: See also the headings Fabularum and Antiquitatis.

units.la: Vino convivas deponebant ... ut loquuntur Graeci. Aul. 3.6. v.36.
units.tr: Guests were laid down by wine, as the Greeks put it. Aul. 3.6. v.36.

units.la: Ego te hodie reddam madidum, si vivo, probe.
units.tr: I will make you thoroughly drunk today, if I live.

units.la: Te cui decretum est, bibere aquam.
units.tr: You, for whom it has been decided to drink water.

units.la: EV. Scio quàm rem agat, ut me deponat vino, eam affectat viam.
units.tr: EV. I know how he means to get me drunk; he is aiming for that route.

units.la: Quo loco sanè erubui, cùm viderem Taubmannum (D I boni! quem virum?) in postremâ suâ Editione terminos Mss. Codd. hic movere, & pro si vivo, rescribere, sed vino.
units.tr: At this point I blushed indeed when I saw Taubmann (O good man! what a man?) in his latest edition moving the terms of the manuscripts here, and rewriting si vivo as sed vino.

units.la: Quid quaeso ineptius? Nihil ad sensum illa lectio. Consídera, Lector, filum ac contextum totius loci: & mecum quoq; erubescés ad criticam hanc Taubmanni sapientiam. Mss. omnes pariter vulgatae edd. ipso quoq; attestante, legunt. si vivo. Ubi igitur Oraculum illud Gruterianum, quo toties triumphare solet?
units.tr: What, I ask, could be more absurd? That reading makes no sense. Consider, reader, the thread and context of the whole passage, and you will blush with me at this Taubmann wisdom. All the manuscripts, and the printed editions too, as he himself attests, read si vivo. Where, then, is that Gruterian oracle with which he is so often wont to triumph?

units.la: QUID INEPTIUS QUAM ABIRE A CONSENSU MSS.?
units.tr: WHAT IS MORE ABSURD THAN TO DEPART FROM THE AGREEMENT OF THE MANUSCRIPTS?

units.la: Ad hunc locum Gruterus noster in Excerptis sic adnotat: Vetus codex habet illud illud vivo inter lineas a manu secunda. Restat tamen in aliis Pall. Et ineptè id Pius mutat in, sed vino. Hem sic datur Taubmanè!
units.tr: On this passage our Gruter annotates thus in the Excerpts: An old codex has that "vivo" between the lines, in a second hand. It remains, however, in other Palatine manuscripts. And Pius foolishly changes it to sed vino. Lo, thus Taubmann is served!

units.la: MURRHINAM bibebant, suavem ac dulcem potum ad arcendam ebrietatem. Persi 1.3.v.8. Pseud. 2.4.v.51.
units.tr: They drank MURRHINE, a sweet and pleasant drink for warding off drunkenness. Persius 1.3. v.8. Pseud. 2.4. v.51.

units.la: Murrhinam, tum passum, defrutum, melinam, mel conjumedi:
units.tr: Murrhine, then passum, defrutum, melina, honey-wine of the mixed kind:

units.la: Qui in corde instruere quondam capit thermopolium.
units.tr: He who once undertakes to furnish a tavern in his heart.

units.la: Plin.lib.14. cap.13.
units.tr: Plin. lib.14. cap.13.

units.la: Vide de Murrhinâ Mercur.l. 5. cap. 1. Var. & inprimis Raderum ad Martialem.
units.tr: On Murrhine see Mercurialis lib.5 cap.1 Var., and especially Rader on Martial.

units.la: Varro de Vitâ P. R. lib. 1.
units.tr: Varro, de Vita P.R. lib.1.

units.la: Antiquae mulieres majores natu bibebant loram, aut sapam, aut defrutum, aut passum, quam murrhinam appellat Plautus
units.tr: Old women of rank used to drink lora, or sapa, or defrutum, or passum, which Plautus calls murrhine.

units.la: VINI egregia commendatio est in seqq. versibus: Flos veteris vini meis naribus objectus est. Ejus amos cupidam me huc e tenebris prolicit. Liberi lepos, ut veteris vetusti cupida sum! Nam omnium unguentum odos, praeluo nayтa est. Tu mihi stacte, tu cinnamomum, tu rosa, Tu crocinum & casia es, & bdellium. nam ubi Tu profusus, ibi ego pervelim me sipultam. Sed quum adhuc naso odos subsecutus es meo, Da vicissim meo gutturi gaudium, &c. Curcul. 1.2. verf. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: The wine is nobly commended in the following verses: The flower of old wine has been held up to my nostrils. Its scent lures me, eager, out of this darkness. Oh the charm of wine, how eager I am for old and aged wine! For the scent of all perfumes is nothing beside it. You are my storax, you my cinnamon, you my rose, you my saffron, cassia and bdellium. Wherever you are poured out, there I would gladly be buried. But since you have still followed the scent into my nose, give in return joy to my throat, etc. Curcul. 1.2. v.1 and following.

units.la: Sic Varro commendat Viunum: Vino nihil jucundius quicquam cluet. Hoc continet coagulum convivia. Hoc hilaritatis dulce seminarium. Hoc agritudinem ad medendum invenerunt. Aristophanes apud Athenæum vinum appellat Lac Veneris.
units.tr: Varro thus commends wine: Nothing is said to be more pleasant than wine. It holds banquets together. It is the sweet seed of cheerfulness. They discovered it as a remedy for sorrow. Aristophanes, in Athenaeus, calls wine the milk of Venus.

units.la: Apulejus:
units.tr: Apuleius:

units.la: Liber Veneris hortator & armiger.
units.tr: Bacchus, the encourager and armour-bearer of Venus.

units.la: Dicitur quoque Anima conviviorum.
units.tr: It is also called the soul of banquets.

units.la: Mulieres ex instituto majorum decebat esse sobrias & abste-mias. Tales sorores illæ, quæ patri osculum præbent in ejus rei argumentum. Stich. 1.2.v.32.
units.tr: By the custom of their ancestors, women ought to be sober and abstemious. Such were those sisters who give their father a kiss as proof of this. Stich. 1.2. v.32.

units.la: Vide Valer. Max.
units.tr: See Valerius Maximus.

units.la: Cauponæ semper male audierunt. Aut enim ibi lupanaria: aut introductæ, quæ in lupanari. Pæn. Prol. v.108.
units.tr: Taverns have always had a bad reputation. For either there are brothels there, or women are brought in who belong to a brothel. Poen. Prol. v.108.

units.la: Vinum præstat aquæ. Mil. 4.8.v.23.
units.tr: Wine is better than water. Mil. 4.8. v.23.

units.la: Nihil aquam moror, malo merum. Per jocum.
units.tr: I don't care for water; I prefer it neat. Said in jest.

units.la: Vini amphoris & patria & senectus inscripta ab vinarijs cœnopo-lis. Pæn. 4.2.v.14.
units.tr: The jars of wine bear inscribed both their place of origin and their age, from the wine-trading towns. Poen. 4.2. v.14.

units.la: Ibi tu videas litteratas fictiles epistolas, pice signatas: nomina insunt cubitum longis litteris. Ita vinariorum habemus nostra dile-ctum domi.
units.tr: There you may see letters on earthen vessels, sealed with pitch; the names are written in long letters a cubit high. Thus we have the wine-merchants' brand, dear to us, at home.

units.la: Vide Tit. Vasorum.
units.tr: See the heading Vasorum.

units.la: Blitea & lutea est meretrix, nisi quæ sapit in vino ad rem suam. Si alia membra vino madent, cor sit saltem sobrium. Trucul. 4.v.1.
units.tr: A whore is a sorry, muddy thing, unless she has her wits about her for her own business while drinking. If her other limbs are soaked in wine, let her heart at least be sober. Truc. 4. v.1.

units.la: Luxuriosi & gulosi in ventre habent suam confidentiam. Cap. 4.2.v.32. Eóq; recte à Clemente Alexandrino asino-pisci: quem Aristoteles dicit cor habere in ventre comparantur.
units.tr: Lecherous and gluttonous men place their confidence in their belly. Cap. 4.2. v.32. And so rightly Clement of Alexandria compares them to the donkey-fish, which Aristotle says has its heart in its belly.

units.la: Vide Mercurial. lib. 4. Var. Lect.
units.tr: See Mercurialis lib.4 Var. Lect.

units.la: Vinis Græcis, quæ travehebantur in titulum, solebant aquam marinam suffundere: præterquam Chijs.
units.tr: Greek wines, which were carried for sale, were accustomed to have sea water poured into them, except Chian wine.

units.la: Ad quem morem alludit Plautus Rud. 2.7.v.30.
units.tr: Plautus alludes to this custom, Rud. 2.7. v.30.

units.la: Quasi vinū Græcis Neptunus nobis suffudit mare.
units.tr: As if Neptune had poured the sea into our Greek wine.

units.la: Vide Athen. lib.1. Dipnosoph.
units.tr: See Athenaeus lib.1 Deipnosophists.

units.la: Plutarch. Διὰ τì τῷοἰνῳ θάλασσαν παραχέεσιν.
units.tr: Plutarch: "Why do they pour sea water into wine?" [Διὰ τί τῷ οἴνῳ θάλασσαν παραχέουσιν;]

units.la: Horat.l.2.Sat.8. Chium maris expers.
units.tr: Horace, lib.2 Sat.8: Chian, free of the sea.

units.la: Ibi vide Lamb. & Commentarium nostrum, quem in Horatij Satyras & reliqua opera confecimus.
units.tr: See there Lambinus, and our commentary, which we made on Horace's Satires and other works.

units.la: ANUM gulosam & ebriolam : lagenam dixerunt. Curc.I.1.v.78.
units.tr: A greedy and tipsy old woman they called a flask. Curc. I.1. v.78.

units.la: Sic Græci hominem ebriosum vocarunt ἀσκὸν, & Ϋλακον merum. Latini quoque Amphoram dixerunt: & Bicongium.
units.tr: So the Greeks called a drunken man a wineskin [ἀσκόν], and unmixed wine [ἄκρατον]. The Latins also called him an amphora, and a bicongium.

units.la: VINUM solebant aquâ diluere. Stich. 2.1.v.116. Vinum submeerum panxillulo poculo exanclavit sitissimè.
units.tr: They used to dilute wine with water. Stich. 2.1. v.116. He drained the lightly watered wine from a tiny cup, very thirstily.

units.la: VINUM solebant aromatis condire: ut docet Plinius lib. 14. c. 16. Dioscorides lib.5. c.64. Sic Vinum Nardinum, quod vel nardo vel unguento nardino conditum erat. Mil. 3,2.v.11. Turn. lib. 2. cap.2.
units.tr: They used to season wine with spices, as Pliny teaches, lib.14 c.16, and Dioscorides, lib.5 c.64. Thus nard wine, which was seasoned either with nard or with nard ointment. Mil. 3.2. v.11. Turnebus lib.2 cap.2.

units.la: VINI varia genera & præstantissima. Poen. 3.3. v.85. Ubi tu Leucadio, Coo, Thasio, Lesbio, vetustate vino edentulo ætatem irriges.
units.tr: Various kinds of wine, and the finest. Poen. 3.3. v.85: where you would water your old age, toothless with age, with Leucadian, Coan, Thasian and Lesbian wine.

units.la: QUÆDAM vineæ infelices uvas producunt. Quod sic fingit servus. Trin. 2.4. v.125.
units.tr: Some vineyards produce unlucky grapes, as a slave here pretends. Trin. 2.4. v.125.

units.la: Vinum priusquam coactum est, pendet putidum.
units.tr: Before wine is strained, it hangs there stinking.

units.la: ALBUM & atrum vinum erat veteribus. Men. 5.5.v.17. Album atrum vinum potas? inquit Medicus.
units.tr: The ancients had both white and black wine. Men. 5.5. v.17: "Do you drink white or black wine?" asks the doctor.

units.la: IN Massico monte optimum provenit, Pseud. 5.2.v.11.
units.tr: On Mount Massicus the best wine grows. Pseud. 5.2. v.11.

units.la: VINUM filia vitis. Amph. 1.1.v.274.
units.tr: Wine, the daughter of the vine. Amph. 1.1. v.274.

units.la: VINUM Chium præstans valde. Curc. 1.1. v.78.
units.tr: Chian wine, very excellent. Curc. 1.1. v.78.

units.la: Educationis. Filiorum. Liberorum. Parentum. Ætatis. Indolis. Disciplinæ. Adolescentiae. Literarum. Studiorum. Nativitatis. Generis. Juventutis. Infantum. Nutricis. Obstetricis. Praeceptorum. Paedagogi. Discipulorum. Scholarum.
units.tr: Education. Sons. Children. Parents. Age. Disposition. Discipline. Adolescence. Letters. Studies. Birth. Stock. Youth. Infants. Nurse. Midwife. Teachers. Tutor. Pupils. Schools.

units.la: Vide etiam particularibus Titulis, suis litteris.
units.tr: See also the particular headings, under their own letters.

units.la: EDucationis puerorum eadem est ratio, quæ novæ domus ædificatio. Hæc affligitur à tempestatibus sæpè: itidem adolescentia ignaviâ deturbatur, quæ omnem verecundiam, & virtutis modum prosternit. Mostl. 1.2. v. 16. Itemq; Amor imbri loco ingruit. Ibid. v. 61.
units.tr: The education of boys is governed by the same principle as the building of a new house. The house is often battered by storms; likewise youth is overthrown by idleness, which strips away all modesty and the measure of virtue. Mostell. 1.2. v.16. Likewise Love bursts in like a rainstorm. Ibid. v.61.

units.la: In educandis infantulis multa requiruntur. Truc. 5.v.10. Puero opus est cibo: opus est matre, quae puerum lavit: opus est nutrici, utrum ut habeat veteris vini largiter, ut dies, noctesq; potet: opus est igne: opus est carbonibus: fasciis opus est, pulvinis, cunis, incunabulis, oleum opus est, farina puero opus est, opus est totum diem.
units.tr: In bringing up little children many things are needed. Truc. 5. v.10: The boy needs food; he needs a mother to wash him; he needs a nurse, and she needs plenty of old wine, to drink day and night; he needs fire, he needs charcoal; he needs swaddling clothes, pillows, cradles, cribs; he needs oil, he needs flour; he needs it all day long.

units.la: Parentes liberos suos ad laborem exstimulare solent spe utilitatis propriæ: sic nimirum: Tibi arat, tibi occat, tibi serit, tibi eidem metet, Tibi deniq; ipse pariet lætitiam labos. Merc. Prol. v.73.
units.tr: Parents are wont to goad their children to labour by the hope of their own profit: "For you he ploughs, for you he hoes, for you he sows, for you he reaps; and finally, for you the toil itself will bring forth joy." Merc. Prol. v.73.

units.la: Parentum indulgentia corrumpit filios. Bacch. 4.10.v.4.
units.tr: Parental indulgence corrupts sons. Bacch. 4.10. v.4.

units.la: Exemplum parentum nullum est: si in eodem vitiorum genere peccarint ipsi adolescentes. Nihili igitur parens est Philoxemus: qui sic de filij luxu loquitur. Bacch. 4.10.v.5. Scio ego: fui illâ ætate, & feci illa omnia: sed modestò more. Duxi, habui scortum, potavi, edi, donavi, at enim id raro. Ergo dare me ludum meo nato instituit, ut animo obsequium suo mere possit: sed nimis nolo Desidia. Eum dare ludum.
units.tr: There is no example in parents if the young men themselves have sinned in the same kind of vices. So Philoxenus, who speaks thus of his son's dissipation, is worthless as a parent: Bacch. 4.10. v.5. I know; I was that age and did all those things, but in a moderate way. I took a mistress, I kept a harlot, I drank, I ate, I gave gifts, but rarely. So he has set me to give my son a school, so that he may be able to obey his own mind; but I very much do not want idleness. Let him have a school.

units.la: IN educatione liberorum diligenter opera danda, ut liberi ab otio ad labores assuefiant: exemplo senis illius Mercat. Prol. v. 65.
units.tr: In the upbringing of children, care must diligently be taken that they become accustomed to labour rather than idleness: take the example of that old man. Merc. Prol. v.65.

units.la: OLIM filios raro in urbem dimiserunt ad spectacula: sed ad rus ablegabant. Merc. Prol. v.68.
units.tr: Formerly they rarely sent their sons into the city to the shows, but sent them away to the country. Merc. Prol. v.68.

units.la: IMPROBORUM parentum nota est, jubere filios suos amare, bibere, &c. Most. 5.2.v.42.
units.tr: It is a mark of wicked parents to order their sons to love, to drink, and so on. Most. 5.2. v.42.

units.la: Immo me praesente amato, bibito, facito quod lubet.
units.tr: Indeed, while I am present, love, drink, and do whatever pleases you.

units.la: ÆQUUM est parentum vitijs ignoscere, illaque patienter tolerare.
units.tr: It is right to pardon the faults of parents and to bear them patiently.

units.la: Sic filius ille, quamquam patre haud paulo melior, inquit:
units.tr: Thus that son, though by no means worse than his father, says:

units.la: Pietas oculis dolorem prohibet.
units.tr: Piety keeps grief from the eyes.

units.la: NON decet discipulos obloqui praeceptoribus.
units.tr: It is not fitting for pupils to talk back to their teachers.

units.la: Nempe qui si decem habeant linguas, mutos esse addecet.
units.tr: Indeed, those who had ten tongues ought to be mute.

units.la: NON omnis aetas ludo convenit. Bacch. 1.2.v.20.
units.tr: Not every age suits play. Bacch. 1.2.v.20.

units.la: DEGENERES discipuli oblivisceuntur monita salutaria suorum magistrorum.
units.tr: Degenerate pupils forget the wholesome warnings of their masters.

units.la: Sic Lydus reprehendit adolescentem suum:
units.tr: Thus Lydus rebukes his young charge:

units.la: Iam perdidisti te atque me, atque operam meam,Quì tibi nequicquam saepè monstravi bene.
units.tr: Now you have ruined both yourself and me, and my effort too, since I have so often shown you the right way to no purpose.

units.la: Vide etiam versus seqq.
units.tr: See also the following verses.

units.la: DEGENERES discipuli non paedagogos aut praeceptores suos nominant magistros: sed nomine suo absolute, non sine contemtu. Bacch. 1.2.v.30.
units.tr: Degenerate pupils do not call their tutors or teachers "masters," but use their bare name, without respect. Bacch. 1.2.v.30.

units.la: DEGENERES discipuli minantur etiam suis paedagogis salutaria monentibus. Bacch. 1.2.v.43.
units.tr: Degenerate pupils even threaten their tutors when they give wholesome advice. Bacch. 1.2.v.43.

units.la: EÓ QUE paedagogos suae solet disiadere vitae: adeo quidem, ut mortem sibi exoptent. Bacch. 1.2.v.40.
units.tr: And so they are wont to vex the lives of their tutors, so much so that they wish death upon themselves. Bacch. 1.2.v.40.

units.la: PRAESERTIM si co prolabantur discipuli impietatis, ut praeceptores ptores interficere velint : quod Hercules fecit Lino præceptori suo, Bacch. 1. 2. v. 46.
units.tr: Especially if pupils fall into such impiety that they want to kill their teachers, as Hercules did to his teacher Linus. Bacch. 1. 2. v. 46.

units.la: Nimirum malè sic adolescentes collocant suam ætatem, cùm eò impudentiæ devenerunt, ut prorsus depuduerint, Bacch. 1. 2. v. 52.
units.tr: Surely young men spend their age badly when they have come to such shamelessness that they have utterly lost all sense of shame. Bacch. 1. 2. v. 52.

units.la: Furtum faciunt tales adolescentes & ætati, quum sua flagitia celant, & præceptores, & parentes. Bacch. 1 2. v. 52.
units.tr: Such young men commit theft against their age when they conceal their disgraceful deeds from both their teachers and their parents. Bacch. 1 2. v. 52.

units.la: Non bene parent im munus faciunt, qui cùm norint peccare suos filios, id patiantur. Qualis fuit Nicobulus Bacch. 5. 2. v. 72.
units.tr: Those who know that their sons sin and allow it do not do their duty well. Such was Nicobulus. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 72.

units.la: Utut est, etsi est decorum, patiar ; facere inducam animum.
units.tr: However it is, even if it is proper, I will endure it; I will bring my mind to it.

units.la: Parentes in educandis liberis nullis sumtibus parcunt : quin omnem dant operam, ut discant literas, jura ac leges. Mostell, 1. 2, v. 45.
units.tr: Parents spare no expense in raising their children; indeed they take every pains that they learn letters, law and statutes. Mostell. 1. 2, v. 45.

units.la: Ibi comparantur novo ædili, & fabris.
units.tr: There they are got ready for a new aedile and for smiths.

units.la: Ad militiam mittebantur primâ ætate cum custode è cognatis. Most. 1. 2. v. 49.
units.tr: For military service, in their early years they were sent off with a guardian from among their kin. Most. 1. 2. v. 49.

units.la: Parentes filijs dabant privos pædagogos, servos custodes. Bacch. 1. 2.
units.tr: Parents gave their sons private tutors, and slaves as guardians. Bacch. 1. 2.

units.la: Lydus erat pædagogus Pislocleri adolescentis : quem ob Amores vehementer redarguit. Pseud. 3. 2. v. 86. de coquis. Merc. Prol. v. 90. Epid. 3. 4. v. 54.
units.tr: Lydus was the tutor of the young man Pislocles, whom he sharply rebuked on account of his love affairs. Pseud. 3. 2. v. 86. On cooks: Merc. Prol. v. 90. Epid. 3. 4. v. 54.

units.la: Sicut autem adolescentibus servi custodes dati : ita puellis servulæ, quæ in lanificio unà essent, eas sectarentur, & curarent. Et dicebantur : Peculiares, quòd quasi in peculio essent.
units.tr: Just as slave guardians were assigned to young men, so slave girls who worked together at the wool-making were to follow and attend the girls. They were called "Peculiares," because they were, as it were, in a private fund (peculium).

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Litterarum : Studiorum.
units.tr: See also the title "Literarum: Studiorum."

units.la: Si liberi sint degeneres, magnus is mœror esse solet parentibus. Most. 4. 2. v. 70.
units.tr: If children turn out degenerate, this is usually a great grief to parents. Most. 4. 2. v. 70.

units.la: Adolescentes magnis parentibus nati plærumque degeneres & luxui dediti. Most. 5. 2. v. 20. 36.
units.tr: Young men born of great parents are mostly degenerate and given over to luxury. Most. 5. 2. v. 20. 36.

units.la: Num quid aliud fecit, nisi quod faciunt summis gnati generibus?
units.tr: Has he done anything other than what sons of the highest families do?

units.la: Degeneres filij & discipuli faciunt suos amicos, parentes, præceptores geruli-figulos flagitij infamiâ suâ. Bacch. 3. 1. v. 14. & 3.3. v. 95.
units.tr: Degenerate sons and pupils bring disgrace upon their friends, parents and teachers by their infamy. Bacch. 3. 1. v. 14. & 3.3. v. 95.

units.la: PARENTES liberos primùm natos, quos agnoscebant, tollebant. Alludit Mil. 2.3.v. 101.
units.tr: Parents used to lift up their firstborn children, whom they acknowledged. Alludes to Mil. 2.3.v. 101.

units.la: ÆTATE qui parés sunt: ingenio sæpè multùm distant; Bacch. 3.3. v. 57.
units.tr: Those who are equal in age often differ greatly in character. Bacch. 3.3. v. 57.

units.la: PUELLÆ crepundia gerebant in cistellulis suis. Rud. 4.4. v.37. In illis habebant icunculas, & nominasuorum parentum. Ibid. v.66.111.112.124.
units.tr: Girls carried baby trinkets in their little boxes. Rud. 4.4. v.37. In these they kept little images and the names of their parents. Ibid. v.66.111.112.124.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Lusus: Crepundiorum.
units.tr: See also the title "Lusus: Crepundiorum."

units.la: SI quem infantem educare nollent, & posuerant ad necem, & projecerant: quem verò educare cuperent, tollebant. Cist. 1.3.v.18. & 2.3.v.75.
units.tr: If they did not want to raise some infant, they set it out to die and threw it away; but whom they wished to raise, they lifted up. Cist. 1.3.v.18. & 2.3.v.75.

units.la: De infante ex stupro nato.
units.tr: On an infant born of illicit intercourse.

units.la: Vide infra Tit. Nativitatis plusucula in hanc rem.
units.tr: See below under the title "Nativitatis" for more on this matter.

units.la: JUVENTUS Attica noctu solebat graffationibus suis turbare publicam pacem. Amph. 1.1.v. 2.
units.tr: Attic youth used to disturb the public peace at night with their brawls. Amph. 1.1.v. 2.

units.la: Vide Tit. Graffationum.
units.tr: See the title "Graffationum."

units.la: PARENTES in educandis liberis admodum solliciti sunt: ne damnum illis inferatur, ne cadant, aut crura frangant, &c.
units.tr: Parents are very anxious in raising their children, lest any harm come to them, lest they fall or break their legs, etc.

units.la: Unde Tertullianus lib.1.cap.5. ad uxorem:
units.tr: Whence Tertullian, book 1, chapter 5, to his wife:

units.la: Liberos vocat amarissimam voluptatem.
units.tr: He calls children "the most bitter pleasure."

units.la: DISCIPLINA apud veteres fuit durior.
units.tr: Discipline was harsher among the ancients.

units.la: HONESTA & libera educatio etiam liberam formam conservat, præsertim puellis.
units.tr: An honest and free upbringing preserves even a free bearing, especially in girls.

units.la: Si quidem ita eris, ut volo, numquam Hecata fies.
units.tr: If indeed you turn out as I wish, you will never become a Hecate.

units.la: DISCIPLINA Attica præ cæteris bene audijt. Cas. 3.5. v. 24. 28.
units.tr: Attic discipline had a better reputation than the rest. Cas. 3.5. v. 24. 28.

units.la: FILIÆ à matribus ita educandæ sunt, ut ne foris versentur crebrò. Cist. 1.1. v.92.
units.tr: Daughters must be brought up by their mothers so that they do not often go about outside. Cist. 1.1. v.92.

units.la: Vide Tit. Virginum: Pudicitiæ.
units.tr: See the title "Virginum: Pudicitiæ."

units.la: LACONES plagipatidæ nominantur à Plauto, ob patientiam disci-plinæ. Capt. 3.1. v.12.
units.tr: The Laconians are called "beaten-patients" by Plautus, because of the patience of their training. Capt. 3.1. v.12.

units.la: Petron. Ego quidem tres plagas Spartanâ nobilitate concoxi.
units.tr: Petronius: "I indeed have digested three blows with Spartan nobility."

units.la: Equitationis.
units.tr: Horse-riding.

units.la: Duobus quandoq; equis utebantur absq; ephippijs: ex uno desiliebant, & in alterum mirâ celeritate insiliebant. Dicti inde Desultores. Mil. 2.3, v. 9. ἀλλὴ οεινὰς.
units.tr: Sometimes they used two horses without saddles: they would leap down from one and mount the other with remarkable speed. Hence they were called Desultores. Mil. 2.3, v. 9. ἀλλὴ οεινὰς. [the Greek is as printed in the source]

units.la: Exemplorum.
units.tr: Examples.

units.la: ALIENIS exemplis sæpè sapimus. Perf. 4.3 v.70.
units.tr: We often grow wise from other people's examples. Perf. 4.3 v.70.

units.la: Te de aliys, quàm aliòs de te, suavius esse fieri doctos.
units.tr: It is more pleasant to be made wise by others' experiences than for others to be made wise by yours.

units.la: Plin. lib.18. cap. 15.
units.tr: Plin. lib.18. cap. 15.

units.la: Optimum est, ut vulgo dixere, alienâ insaniâ frui.
units.tr: It is best, as people commonly say, to enjoy another man's madness.

units.la: Terent. Scitum est, periculum ex aliys facere, tibi quod ex usu fiet.
units.tr: Terent. It is well known that one should make the trial on others, and what will turn out to your advantage will come from experience.

units.la: IMPROBIA ad sui defensionem solent exemplis uti. At jam ante alij fecerunt idem. Epid. 1.1, v. 30. Terent. Adelph. 4.5.
units.tr: Wicked men usually use examples to defend themselves: "But others have already done the same." Epid. 1.1 v.30. Terent. Adelph. 4.5.

units.la: EXEMPLIS errores solemus excusare. Merc. 2.2. v.47.
units.tr: By examples we are accustomed to excuse our errors. Merc. 2.2 v.47.

units.la: Nihil est jam, quod tu mihi succenseas: Fecere tale ante alij spectatí viri.
units.tr: There is now nothing for which you should be angry with me: other men of standing have done such a thing before.

units.la: EXEMPLA veteres pro gravissimis pœnis usurpabant. Mosl. 5.1. v. 67. Terent. Eun. 5.5.
units.tr: The ancients used examples in support of the gravest punishments. Mostell. 5.1 v.67. Terent. Eun. 5.5.

units.la: In quem exempla sient.
units.tr: Against whom examples will be made.
And 5.7.

units.la: Uterq, in te exempla edet.
units.tr: Each of them will make an example of you.

units.la: Agell. lib. 6. cap. 14.
units.tr: Gell. lib.6. cap. 14.

units.la: Ut apud te exemplum experiundi habeas, ne petas foris.
units.tr: So that you may have an example of trying in your own case, do not look for one abroad.

units.la: EXCUSATIONIS.
units.tr: Excuses.

units.la: EXcusatio ab ebrietate infirma admodum est. Trucul. 4. 3. verf. 54.
units.tr: An excuse based on drunkenness is quite weak. Truc. 4.3 v.54.

units.la: Mihi ignoscas, quod animi impos vini vitio fecerim. CA. Non placet: in mutum confers culpam, quod nequit loqui. Nam vinum si fabulari posset, se defenderet. Non vinum hominibus moderari, sed vino homines solent: Qui quidem probi sunt, verum qui improbus est, si bibit, sive adeo caret temeto, tamen ab ingenio est improbus.
units.tr: "Forgive me, that I did it through the fault of wine, not being master of my mind." CA. "That does not please me: you lay the blame on a dumb thing, which cannot speak. For if wine could talk, it would defend itself. It is not men who govern wine, but wine that governs men. Honest men are honest even when they drink; but a wicked man, whether he drinks or even lacks wine altogether, is wicked by nature."

units.la: Excusatio ab vino & amore non habet locum.
units.tr: An excuse from wine and love has no place.

units.la: Cum istac te oratione huc ad me adire ausum, impudens? Nam si istuc jus esset, ut sic tu istuc excusare posses, Luce claro depipiamus aurum matronis palam: postid prehensi si sumus, excusemus ebrios nos fecisse, amoris causa.
units.tr: "With that speech, how dare you, shameless fellow, come up to me here? For if that were a legal right, that you could excuse yourself in that way, we could rob matrons of their gold openly in broad daylight; and if we were caught afterwards, we would excuse ourselves by saying we were drunk, for love's sake."

units.la: Excusatio amore & consuetudine inepta est.
units.tr: An excuse based on love and habit is foolish.

units.la: More hoc fit, atq; stultè, meâ sententiâ: si quem hominem exspectant, eum solent provisere: qui hercle illâ causâ nihilo citius venit.
units.tr: "This is done out of habit, and foolishly, in my opinion: if they are waiting for some man, they usually look out for him; yet, by Hercules, for that reason he comes not a whit the sooner."
Stich. 5.1 v.1.

units.la: Excusamus errores exemplis: & quod inviti fecerimus.
units.tr: We excuse our errors by examples, and by saying that we did what we did unwillingly.

units.la: Huc non voluntas me impulit.
units.tr: "It was not my will that drove me to it."

units.la: Excusatio à Providentiâ divinâ non habet semper locum.
units.tr: An excuse from divine Providence does not always hold good.

units.la: Aul. 4.10. v.12. adolescens amator sic excusat scortationem:
units.tr: Aul. 4.10 v.12. The young lover excuses his fornication thus:

units.la: Deos credo voluisse, nam ni vellent, non fieret, scio.
units.tr: "I believe the gods wished it; for if they had not wished it, I know it would not have happened."

units.la: Respondet Euclio:
units.tr: Euclio replies:

units.la: At ego Deos credo voluisse, ut apud te me in nervom enicem.
units.tr: "But I believe the gods wished that I be beaten to death with a whip at your place."

units.la: Qui homo culpam admisit in sese, nullus est tàm parvi pretij, quin pudeat, quin purget sese.
units.tr: Whoever has committed a fault is of so little worth that there is no one who is not ashamed of it, and who does not clear himself.

units.la: Excusatio vitiorum fit multis modis, per vinum, imprudentiam, adolescentiam, seu aetatem.
units.tr: Excuses for faults are made in many ways: through wine, through thoughtlessness, through youth or old age.

units.la: F. FABULARUM. HISTRIONUM. ACTORUM. MIMORUM. SCENÆ. THEATRI. COMOEDIÆ. TRAGOEDIÆ. VERSUUM. POEMATUM.
units.tr: FABLES. ACTORS (HISTRIONES). MIMES. SCENE. THEATRE. COMEDIES. TRAGEDIES. VERSES. POEMS.

units.la: Vide etiam Titulo Ludorum: Theatri, & Spectaculorum. Ubi non pauca huc spectantia.
units.tr: See also under the title Games, Theatre and Spectacles. There are not a few things there that bear on this.

units.la: AEquum est placere veteres fabulas: Nam nunc nova quæ prodeunt Comœdia Multo sunt nequiores, quàm numml novi. Cas. Prol. v. 7.
units.tr: It is right to please the old plays: For the new comedies that come out now are much worse than the new coins. Cas. Prol. v. 7.

units.la: Horatius tamen Epistola ad Augustum docet, non ut vina, sic & poëmata, quæ sunt antiquissima, esse optima.
units.tr: Horace, however, teaches in his Epistle to Augustus that poems are not, as wines are, best when they are oldest.

units.la: Pindarus recentissimum quodq; carmen ait esse laudabile: αἶνει ἀλλ᾽ ἀκλεῶν ῥήσω οἶνον, ἄνθεα δ᾽ ὑμνων νεωτέρων: h. e. Laus da vinum quidem vetus, flores autem hymnorum recentiorum.
units.tr: Pindar says that the most recent song is always the most praiseworthy: "αἶνει ἀλλ᾽ ἀκλεῶν ῥήσω οἶνον, ἄνθεα δ᾽ ὑμνων νεωτέρων" [praise the old wine, but the flowers of newer hymns]; that is, praise the old wine indeed, but the flowers of the newer hymns.

units.la: In proscenio fabularum non licebat sedere scortis exoletis. Pœn. Prol. v. 17.
units.tr: In the forepart of the stage at plays, worn-out prostitutes were not allowed to sit. Pœn. Prol. v. 17.

units.la: In theatris: ut & fabularum scenis Dissignatores sive Locarÿ constituti: quos sectabantur lictores majoris securitatis ergò. Pœn. Prol. v. 19.
units.tr: In the theatres, as also on the stages of plays, dissignatores or locarii were appointed, whom lictors attended for greater security. Pœn. Prol. v. 19.

units.la: Idem quoq; Martialis lib. 5. Epist. 25. Germanicè dicas Platz-meister. Pretium dicebatur locarium.
units.tr: Martial too, book 5, epigram 25. In German you would say Platz-meister. The fee was called locarium.

units.la: Vide etiam Lipsium de Amphit cap. 15. ubi docetin Funeribus quoq; adhibitos dissignatores.
units.tr: See also Lipsius, On the Amphitheatre, ch. 15, where he shows that dissignatores were also employed at funerals.

units.la: SINGVLARE artificium Comicum Plautus in Amphitruonis ser-vo Sosiâ usurpavit Amph. 1.1.v.48. Nam (Verba sunt Lambini) quia Fabulae recitantur spectatorum causâ, non solùm autem simplex, & artis expers erat futurum, si ista Alcumenae narraren-tur à Sosiâ in proscenio, sed etiam inutile ad Poëtae consilium, fa-bulaeq; argumentum: quia tolleretur occasio venustissimae rixae inter Sosiam & Mercurium, Alcumenae interventu: multoque magis, si haec eadem Sosia Alcumenae narraret, aut narrare intel-ligeretur in postscenio, seu post siparium, spectatoribus non au-dientibus: iccircò Poëta facit Sosiam ea coram populo, ante-quam ad Alcumenam perveniat, meditantem, audiente Mercu-rio, qui eodem tempore in proscenium processit.
units.tr: A SINGULAR comic device Plautus used in the slave Sosias in the Amphitruo, Amph. 1.1 v. 48. For (these are Lambinus's words), if the story of Alcmena were told by Sosias on the stage in the forepart, it would not only be plain and without art, but also useless for the poet's purpose and the plot, because the occasion for the most delightful quarrel between Sosias and Mercury, brought about by Alcmena's intervention, would be lost. Much more so if Sosias told this same story to Alcmena, or were understood to tell it in the backstage, or behind the curtain, where the spectators could not hear. For this reason the poet makes Sosias, before he reaches Alcmena, rehearse these things in front of the people, with Mercury listening, who at the same time came forward onto the stage.

units.la: <bl>SPECTATORES</bl> finitâ fabulâ ad caenam vocabantur, sed in cras-tinum: joculariter.
units.tr: <bl>THE SPECTATORS</bl>, when the play was finished, were invited to dinner, but for the next day: jokingly.

units.la: Vos hic comissatum omnes venitote ad me ad annos sedecim.
units.tr: You all come here to me to a revel, for sixteen years.
Stich. 5.5 v. 54.

units.la: <bl>SUB</bl> finem Fabularum plausu exceperunt Actores.
units.tr: <bl>AT</bl> the end of the plays the actors were received with applause.
Truc. 5 v. 76.

units.la: Et passim in Fabb. Plautinis, Terentianis legitur <bl>PLAUDITE</bl> atq; <bl>VALETE.</bl>
units.tr: And throughout the Plautine and Terentian plays one reads <bl>PLAUDITE</bl> and <bl>VALETE</bl>.

units.la: Quae Formula pronunciabatur à grege, vel à persona, quae ulti-ma in scenam producebatur.
units.tr: This formula was pronounced by the troupe, or by the character who was brought on to the stage last.

units.la: Caf. Grex. v.4. Cist. Grex. v.6. Epid. Grex. v.2. Poen. 5.6. v.33.
units.tr: Caf. Grex. v. 4. Cist. Grex. v. 6. Epid. Grex. v. 2. Poen. 5.6 v. 33.

units.la: Plausus ducitur condimentum totius Fabulae.
units.tr: Applause is regarded as the seasoning of the whole play.

units.la: Plausus autem quomodo fieret, docet Horatius lib. 2. Epist.1. --- quibus oblitus actor
units.tr: How applause was made Horace shows in Epistles book 2, epistle 1: ... by which the forgetful actor,

units.la: Cùm stetit in scenâ, concurrit dextera laevâ.
units.tr: When he has stood on the stage, the right hand strikes the left.

units.la: Seneca Nat. Quaest. lib.2.c.27. & 28.
units.tr: Seneca, Natural Questions book 2, chs. 27 and 28.

units.la: Non quemadmodum illisa manus inter se plausum edunt.
units.tr: Not as hands struck against each other make applause.

units.la: Ibid.
units.tr: Ibid.

units.la: Sed palma cum palmâ collata plausum fecit.
units.tr: But palm brought together with palm made applause.

units.la: Adhibebatur in plausu dando etiam ratio, & quasi ars quædam: quam primùm nullam fuisse Ovidius in Arte testatur:
units.tr: In giving applause there was also a method, and as it were an art, which Ovid in the Ars attests was not present at first:

units.la: In medio plausu (plausus tunc arte carebat)
units.tr: In the midst of applause (applause then lacked art)

units.la: Rex populo ---
units.tr: The king to the people ...

units.la: Quintilianus lib. 6. cap 1. –
units.tr: Quintilian, book 6, ch. 1.

units.la: Tunc esl commovendum Theatrum, cum ventum est ad ipsum illud, quo veteres Tragœdiæ Comœdiæq; claudantur: PLAUDITE.
units.tr: Then the theatre is to be stirred when one comes to that very thing with which the old tragedies and comedies used to end: PLAUDITE.

units.la: Vide etiam Joseph. Castalionem Observ. Decad. 10. cap 1 & Lælium Biscioìam de Societate Jesu Horarum Subsceciv. lib. 8. c. 2. Ingolstad edit. Brissoniùm lib. v i i i. Formul. pag. 748.
units.tr: See also Joseph Castalio, Observations, decade 10, ch. 1; and Lelius Biscioia, On the Society of Jesus, Hours of Leisure, book 8, ch. 2, Ingolstadt edition; Brissonius, book 8, Formulae, p. 748.

units.la: OPORTET Histriones peritos esse: & Fabulam simul edidicisse, antequam in Proscenium prodeant.
units.tr: Actors must be skilled, and must have learned the whole play by heart before they come forth onto the stage.

units.la: Conditiorfum, quàm Tragœdi aut Comici.
units.tr: Better trained than tragic or comic actors.
Pers. 4.2 v. 8.

units.la: Tragici atq; Comici numquam æquè sunt meditati.
units.tr: Tragic and comic actors have never studied so well.

units.la: IN scenâ erat choragus, qui scenici apparatûs præscriptus ac præbitor erat. Inde choragium locus, unde omnia necessaria ad ludum promuntur.
units.tr: On the stage there was a choragus, who was the appointer and provider of the stage equipment. Hence choragium is the place from which everything necessary for the play is brought out.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut. Trin. 4. 2, v. 16. Curc. 4. 1. v. 3. Persi 3. v. 79.
units.tr: See the Plautine lexicon: Trin. 4.2 v. 16; Curc. 4.1 v. 3; Pers. 3 v. 79.

units.la: SERVI potantes, amantes, atq; ad cænam condicentes in scenam, raro inducebantur: eòque se excusat Plautus, quòd in palliatâ seu Græcâ Comœdiâ hoc tolerari queat.
units.tr: Slaves who were drinking, in love, or invited to dinner were rarely brought onto the stage; and Plautus excuses himself on the ground that in the palliata, or Greek comedy, this could be tolerated.
Stich. 3.1 v. 37.

units.la: LUDORUM & Fabularum actiones in religionis parte numerabantur.
units.tr: The performances of games and plays were counted among the parts of religion.

units.la: Pœn. Prol. v. 128.
units.tr: Pœn. Prol. v. 128.

units.la: Et Asin. Prol. v. 15.
units.tr: And Asin. Prol. v. 15.

units.la: Ut vos item alias, pariter nunc Mars adjuvet! Vide etiam Prol.Caf.Rud. v. 81. Cist. Turn.lib. 19.cap.10.
units.tr: So may Mars now help you, as he helps the others. See also Prol. Caf., Rud. v. 81; Cist.; Turn. book 19, ch. 10.

units.la: POST peractam fabulam, quaedam intus fiebant, non palam. Caf. Grex. v. 1.
units.tr: After the play was finished, certain things were done inside, not in public. Caf. Grex. v. 1.

units.la: SERVI aliquid pro loco in theatris pendebant. Poen. Prol. v. 23.
units.tr: Slaves paid something for places in the theatres. Poen. Prol. v. 23.

units.la: Servi ne obsideant, liberi ut sit locus, vel as pro capite dent.
units.tr: Slaves are not to occupy seats, so that there may be room for free men; or they give an as for their head.

units.la: Graeci appellarunt σατηρίαν: h. e. ut Scholiastes Calim. interpretatur, τὰ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἰδίων λώρα.
units.tr: The Greeks called it satēria [σατηρίαν], that is, as the scholiast on Callimachus explains, the payments made on behalf of one's own (slaves) [τὰ ὑπὲρ τῶν ἰδίων λώρα].

units.la: Nec vero in servis tantum: sed receptum hoc etiam in aliis é plebe, qui Locarijs nescio quid pro sede pendebant.
units.tr: Nor was this confined to slaves: this practice was also received for others from the common people, who paid the locarii something or other for a seat.

units.la: Merces autem Histrionum ac saltatorum, quam Editor: h. e. Praetor, aut magistratus dabat, proprie Lucar dicebatur: Gloss. σεατρικὸν, & μισθὸς ἀπὸ ζίννι.
units.tr: The payment to actors and dancers, which the editor (that is, the praetor or magistrate) gave, was properly called lucar. The glossary has [σεατρικὸν] and [μισθὸς ἀπὸ ζίννι].

units.la: Vide de hac mercede Tacit. lib. 1. Annal. cap. 77. & ibi Marcell. Donatum, & Lipsium: nec non Scaligerum ad Festum: itemq; Inscriptionum volum.pag.329. & 636.
units.tr: On this payment see Tacitus, Annals book 1, ch. 77, and there Marcellus Donatus and Lipsius; likewise Scaliger on Festus; also the Inscriptions volume, pp. 329 and 636.

units.la: Vide etiam Muret.lib.17. Var.Lect.cap.14.
units.tr: See also Muretus, Variae Lectiones book 17, ch. 14.

units.la: HISTRIONES, si quid deliquerant in actione, vapulabant: caeteri autem, qui nihil deliquerunt, haustum vini acceperunt. Cist. Grex. v. 4.
units.tr: Actors, if they had made a mistake in their performance, were beaten; the others, who had made no mistake, received a drink of wine. Cist. Grex. v. 4.

units.la: QUID differat Comoedia ab Tragoedia: quid item sit Tragico-Comoedia fere explicat Prolog. Amph. v. 54. & 60. Videndus etiam proprie Julius Scaliger de Re poetica lib. 1. cap. 7.
units.tr: What comedy differs from tragedy, and what tragicomedy is, the prologue of the Amphitruo, vv. 54 and 60, roughly explains. Julius Scaliger, On the Poetic Art, book 1, ch. 7, should be consulted in particular.

units.la: Vide etiam Lex. Plaut. Tragico-Comoedia.
units.tr: See also the Plautine lexicon, under Tragicomoedia.

units.la: IN Comoedia pro aureis nummis numerantur lupini, ob duritiem. Poen. 3.2. v.20.
units.tr: In comedy, lupins are counted out instead of gold coins, because of their hardness. Pœn. 3.2 v. 20.

units.la: Vide Tit. Monetaria.
units.tr: See the title Monetaria.

units.la: CENSORES fabularum erant spectatores: qui Juratores dicebantur. Poen.Prol. v. 58. & Trin. 4.2. v. 30.
units.tr: The censors of the plays were the spectators, who were called jurors. Pœn. Prol. v. 58; Trin. 4.2 v. 30.

units.la: IN Comœdijs & Mimis servuli fugitivi conjecto in humeros pallio, & capite velato exprimebantur.
units.tr: In comedies and mimes, runaway slaves were represented with a cloak thrown over their shoulders and their head veiled.
Capt. 4.1 v. 9; Epid. 2.2 v. 10.

units.la: Vide Lipf. Epist. Quæst. lib. c. 23. & Tit. Habitus: Cultus.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Epistolicae Quaestiones book ..., ch. 23, and the title Habitus: Cultus.

units.la: FABB. etiam optimæ, si ab ineptis actoribus agantur, tædio sunt.
units.tr: Even excellent plays, if performed by inept actors, are tedious.
Bacch. 2.2 v. 35.

units.la: ÆDILES jurabant se ei daturos palmam, qui omnium optime agebant fabulas.
units.tr: The aediles swore that they would give the palm to whoever acted the plays best of all.

units.la: Amph. Prol. v. 72.
units.tr: Amph. Prol. v. 72.

units.la: Ibi innuitur Ædiles etiam persidiose suas partes egisse.
units.tr: There it is hinted that the aediles also played their parts treacherously.

units.la: PALMA ferè tribus modis solebat obtineri: Per literas, per internuncium, & ex compacto Histrionum. Omnes tangit Plautus Amph. Prol. v. 71.
units.tr: The palm was usually won in roughly three ways: through letters, through a messenger, and by agreement with the actors. Plautus touches on all of them, Amph. Prol. v. 71.

units.la: Omnes autem modi illegitimi sunt, ut patet ibidem.
units.tr: All these methods are illegitimate, as is clear from the same passage.

units.la: Tales enim delegati fautores spoliabantur ornamentis: & loris cædebantur.
units.tr: For such hired supporters were stripped of their ornaments and beaten with thongs.

units.la: IN fabulis actoribus victoriam adjudicabant cum palmâ & acclamatione.
units.tr: In the plays, the judges awarded victory to the actors with a palm and acclamation.

units.la: Euge, Euge, vicit tua Comœdia.
units.tr: Well done, well done! Your comedy has won.

units.la: Qui enim bene egerant histriones, secundùm actionem præmio asficiebantur: contra mulctabantur.
units.tr: Actors who had performed well were rewarded according to their acting; on the contrary, they were fined.

units.la: Vide etiam Cist. in fine fabulæ Caterv.
units.tr: See also Cist. at the end of the play, Caterv.

units.la: Ne exspectetis, &c.
units.tr: Do not expect, etc.

units.la: COMICI sapienter dicta proferunt ad applausum, cùm sunt in scenâ: at domum reversi, nullus est illo pacto, ut illi jusserant.
units.tr: Comic actors deliver wise sayings for applause while they are on the stage; but when they have returned home, nothing happens in that way as they had ordered.

units.la: IN Fabulis erant histrionum præfecti.
units.tr: In the plays there were prefects of the actors.

units.la: Poen. Prol. v. 4.
units.tr: Pœn. Prol. v. 4.

units.la: Audire jubet vos imperator histricus. Ibidem per præconem imperabatur silentium: & audientia. Ibid. v. II.
units.tr: The histrionic imperator bids you listen. In the same place silence and attention were ordered by a herald. Ibid. v. 11.

units.la: HISTRIONUM fuerunt familiæ, ut & Gladiatorum. Men. Prol. v. 74.
units.tr: There were troupes of actors, as there were of gladiators. Men. Prol. v. 74.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: IN fabulis scenicis Chorus musicus circumibat strophas ad antistrophas canendo. Stich. 5.2. v.7. ἀπὸ ἀεικῶς de Convivio.
units.tr: In scenic plays a musical chorus went around, singing strophes and antistrophes. Stich. 5.2 v. 7. [ἀπὸ ἀεικῶς], of the banquet.

units.la: LICET interdum Deum in fabulis introducere, teste Ariftotele, & Horatio: Nec Deus intersit, nisi dignus vindice nodus Incideritt ----
units.tr: Although, as Aristotle and Horace testify, it is sometimes permissible to introduce a god into plays: Nor should a god intervene, unless a knot worthy of a deliverer has arisen ----

units.la: Sic Lar adhibebatur Aululariæ Prologo.
units.tr: So the Lar was brought on at the prologue of the Aulularia.

units.la: ORNAMENTA scenica chorago commendata: qui ab Ædili illa accipiebat. Perf. 1.3. v. 79.
units.tr: The stage ornaments were entrusted to the choragus, who received them from the aedile. Pers. 1.3, v. 79.

units.la: PER præconem solebant silentium petere in fabulis. Asin. Prol. v. 4.
units.tr: In plays a herald would ordinarily call for silence. Asin. Prologue, v. 4.

units.la: SPECTATORES in theatris sedebant. Pœn. 5.4. v. 52. Sitiunt, qui sedent.
units.tr: The spectators sat in the theatres. Poen. 5.4, v. 52. Those who sit are thirsty.

units.la: SOCCIS utebantur Comici actores. Cist. 4.2. v. 29. Socci video vestigium in pulvere.
units.tr: Comic actors wore socci. Cist. 4.2, v. 29. I see the track of a sock in the dust.

units.la: QUI scrius, quàm oportebat proscenium ingrederetur, vapulabat. Trin. 4.2. v. 148.
units.tr: Whoever came onto the stage later than he should was beaten. Trin. 4.2, v. 148.

units.la: COMOEDIÆ aguntur choragio Comico: Tragœdiæ Comico. Capt. Prol. v. 61.
units.tr: Comedies are performed with a comic chorus, and tragedies with a tragic chorus. Capt. Prologue, v. 61.

units.la: HISTRIONUM est, partes suas defendere. Mil. 3.1. v. 215.
units.tr: It is the part of actors to defend their roles. Mil. 3.1, v. 215.

units.la: FACTI.
units.tr: FACTI.

units.la: Vide supra Tit. Actionum.
units.tr: See above, under the title Actionum.

units.la: QUANDO non poenitere se facti dicerent, sed voluptatem ex eo capere: usurpabant hanc formulam:
units.tr: When people said they did not regret a deed but took pleasure in it, they used this formula:

units.la: Gaudeo factum, si quid tibi feci, quod placet.
units.tr: I am glad of the deed, if I have done you something that pleases you.

units.la: FAMAE. INFAMIAE. EXISTIMATIONIS. RUMORIS.
units.tr: FAME. INFAMY. ESTEEM. RUMOUR.

units.la: FAMAE τεχέτον est plurimùm mendi secum trahere. Quod apparet ex illâ fabulâ Medeae de Æsone, & Peliâ.
