units.tr: Fame [τεχέτον] is wont to bring a great deal of harm with it. This appears from that story of Medea about Aeson and Pelias.

units.la: Quod τεχέτον pluribus explicat Marq. Freherus J.C. lib. 1. de Fama pag. 67. quem vide & lege.
units.tr: Marquard Freher, J.C., explains this word [τεχέτον] at length in book 1 of his work on Fame, p. 67, whom you should consult and read.

units.la: Interim teste Corn. Tacito:
units.tr: Meanwhile, the testimony of Cornelius Tacitus:

units.la: Fama non semper errat, interdum seligit.
units.tr: Fame does not always err; sometimes it chooses.

units.la: RUMOR non negligendus.
units.tr: RUMOUR is not to be disregarded.

units.la: Nec tuis depellor dictis, quin rumori serviam.
units.tr: Nor am I turned aside from your words, so that I should not yield to rumour.

units.la: Pomponius tamen Poëta inquit per jocum:
units.tr: Yet the poet Pomponius says in jest:

units.la: Ego rumorem parvifacio, dum sit, rumen qui impleam.
units.tr: I make little of rumour, so long as there is something to fill my gullet.

units.la: De Famâ & Rumore vide exactissimum Tractatum ejusdem Marquardi Freheri.
units.tr: On Fame and Rumour, see the most exact treatise of the same Marquard Freher.

units.la: Infamia hominum est immortalis: etiam tùm vivit, cùm esse credas mortuam. Perf. 3. 1. v. 27.
units.tr: The infamy of men is immortal: it is still alive even when you think it dead. Perf. 3. 1. v. 27.

units.la: Gunth. lib. 4. v. 527.
units.tr: Gunther, book 4, v. 527.

units.la: Fadaq, mansuræ fugio commercia linguæ.
units.tr: Fadaq, I flee the dealings of a tongue that will endure.

units.la: Claudius Imperator, cùm cuidam notam appositam, deprecantibus familiaribus, ademisset: Litura tamen, inquit, exstat: sententiens remissâ culpâ, infamiæ prioris vestigia manere. Docent namque JCti varijs modis infamiam inuri: imprimis hominum opinione. Nam is qui apud bonos & graves tiros male audit, infamis dicitur: licet ei jure & legibus nulla irrogetur infamia.
units.tr: When the Emperor Claudius, at the entreaty of his friends, had removed a mark that had been placed upon someone, he said: "Yet the erasure remains," meaning that although the fault was pardoned, traces of the former infamy remain. For the jurists teach that infamy is branded in various ways, chiefly by men's opinion. For one who is ill spoken of among good and serious men is called infamous, even though no infamy is imposed on him by law or statute.

units.la: Vide Franc. Duaren. lib. 1. cap. 42. & Frcherum de Infamiâ.
units.tr: See Franciscus Duarenus, book 1, chapter 42, and Freher on Infamy.

units.la: Qualis est hominum de aliquo existimatio, talis ei apud illos fides est.
units.tr: Whatever men's estimation of someone is, such is the trust they place in him.
Mostell. 1. 3. v. 70.

units.la: P. Syrus:
units.tr: Publius Syrus:

units.la: Bona opinio hominis tutior est pecunia. Et Honestus rumor alterum est patrimonium.
units.tr: A good opinion of a man is safer than money. And an honest reputation is a second inheritance.

units.la: Probro & infamiâ alios notare volentes, ad ostium carmen occentabant Quod proprie dicebant Occentare:
units.tr: Those wishing to brand others with disgrace and infamy used to sing a song at their doors, which they properly called occentare (to serenade with abuse).

units.la: De quo verbo vide Lex. Plaut. & Notas Scaligeri ad Pompejum: pag. CXVII.
units.tr: On this word see the Lexicon of Plautus and Scaliger's notes on Pompeius, p. CXVII.

units.la: Maledicentes nihil non solent calumniari, recte-perverse facta, dicta. Ibid.
units.tr: Slanderers are wont to calumniate everything, whether deeds or words, whether right or wrong. Ibid.

units.la: Nihil pretiosius famâ: cujus tamen jacturam prætulit Leno ille, jacturæ rei familiaris.
units.tr: Nothing is more precious than reputation; yet that pimp preferred to suffer its loss rather than a loss of his household property.

units.la: Vide Tit. Pudoris.
units.tr: See the title Of Shame.

units.la: Famæ non semper credendum. Trin. 1. 2. v. 175.
units.tr: One should not always believe rumour. Trin. 1. 2. v. 175.

units.la: Famigeratores olim supplicijs coërciti.
units.tr: Rumour-mongers were once restrained by punishments.

units.la: FAMÆ discrimen subit etiam luxuria, & ingratitudo. Quisque autem bene audire cupit. Exemplo est adolescens luxuriosus.
units.tr: Luxury and ingratitude also put one's fame at risk, and everyone wishes to be well spoken of. An example is the dissolute young man.

units.la: FAMA majorum virtute ante parta, non est per flagitium perdenda. Trin. 3.2.v. 16. & seqq.
units.tr: The fame of ancestors, won earlier by virtue, must not be lost through disgrace. Trin. 3. 2. v. 16. and following.

units.la: Vide totum locum.
units.tr: See the whole passage.

units.la: OMNES famæ suæ rationem habent, ut monumentum aliquod sui post se relinquant.
units.tr: All men have regard for their reputation, so that they may leave some memorial of themselves behind.

units.la: NON negligendum quid alii de nobis sentiant.
units.tr: It is not to be neglected what others think of us.

units.la: Avaritia nomen infame est.
units.tr: Avarice is an infamous name.

units.la: PROBI scelera nolunt fieri nobiles.
units.tr: Honest men do not want their crimes to make them notorious.

units.la: RUMOR velocissimus. Si quid factum vel bene, vel perperam, per vias omnes fabulantur.
units.tr: Rumour is very swift. If anything has been done, whether well or badly, they gossip about it on every street.

units.la: PRÆSTAT damnum ferre, quàm famæ facere jacturam.
units.tr: It is better to bear a financial loss than to suffer a loss of reputation.

units.la: FAMAM nostram lædi ægerrimè ferre solemus.
units.tr: We are wont to take it very badly when our reputation is harmed.

units.la: FAMILIÆ. OECONOMIÆ. SERVITII. PEDISSEQUII. FAMULITII. ANCILLARUM. OPERÆ. OPERARUM. ÆDIUM. MUNDITIEI. REI DOMESTICÆ. MATRUM-FAMILIAS. PATRUM-FAMILIAᵉs. PEDISSEQUARUM. FAMULARUM. REI-SUPELLECTILIS. CONJUGUM. MULIERUM.
units.tr: FAMILY. HOUSEKEEPING. SERVANTS. ATTENDANTS. MENIAL SERVANTS. MAIDSERVANTS. WORK. WORKERS. HOUSES. CLEANLINESS. HOUSEHOLD AFFAIRS. MISTRESSES OF THE FAMILY. MASTERS OF THE FAMILY. FEMALE ATTENDANTS. MAIDSERVANTS. HOUSEHOLD GOODS. WIVES. WOMEN.

units.la: Vide etiam infra Tit. Gynaecéi: & Servorum. Ubi plura in hanc rem invenies.
units.tr: See also below under the title Gynaeceum, and Servants, where you will find more on this subject.

units.la: Vide item Tit. Habitús : de ornatu mulierum.
units.tr: See also the title Dress, on the adornment of women.

units.la: BONI mariti est vestire feminam, ancillas, & penum recte praehibere.
units.tr: It is the duty of a good husband to clothe his wife and maidservants, and to provide their food properly.

units.la: DAMNOSI mariti suam rem ad meretrices deferunt.
units.tr: Wasteful husbands carry their property over to prostitutes.

units.la: FRUMENTUM olim appendebatur servis. Stich. 1.2. v.3. Vide Tit. Servorum.
units.tr: Grain was once weighed out to slaves. Stich. 1.2. v. 3. See the title Servants.

units.la: Et legg. xii. Tab. & Horat. l. 1. Sat. 5. — cui satis una Farris libra foret, gracili sic, tamq; pusillo.
units.tr: And the Twelve Tables, and Horace, Satires 1.5: for whom a single pound of spelt would be enough, so slender and so small.

units.la: ALIA erant Rustica Cibaria; alia Urbana. Vide Colv.lib.9. Apul. Asin. & Bud.ff.priorib.& Rævard.lib.5.c.20.Var. Et Cafaub. ad Idyll.17. Theocr. ἁμαλλίη ἐμμνῶν. Dimensum.
units.tr: There were rustic foods and urban foods. See Columella book 9, Apuleius' Golden Ass, Budé on the Pandects earlier, and Rævard book 5 chapter 20 on Varro; and Casaubon on Theocritus Idyll 17: a bundle of sheaves [ἁμαλλίη ἐμμνῶν]. Dimensum.

units.la: IN ÆDIBUS omnia mundè à servis & ancillis componebantur.
units.tr: In the house everything was kept neatly in order by the male and female slaves.

units.la: Nisi erit mihi quidq; supellectilis in suo loco situm, cum ego revortar vos monumentis commonefaciam bubulis. Non homines habitare mecum mihi hic videtur, sed sues.
units.tr: Unless every item of household equipment is in its place, when I come back I will remind you of it with cowhide thongs. It seems to me that I am living here not with men but with pigs.

units.la: Transfcidi loris omnes domi: ita supellex squalet, atque ædes mea.
units.tr: You have all been flogged at home: the furniture is in such a mess, and so is my house.

units.la: VILISSIMA quæq; utensilia annulo signatorio seu sigillaricio clau- sa: ne quid furto aut negligentia periret.
units.tr: The cheapest utensils were sealed with a signet ring, or seal, so that nothing would be lost through theft or carelessness.

units.la: Plin. lib. 33. cap. 1.
units.tr: Pliny, book 33, chapter 1.

units.la: At nunc cibi quoq; & potus annulo vindicantur a rapina.
units.tr: But now even food and drink are guarded from robbery by a signet ring.

units.la: Martial. lib. 9.
units.tr: Martial, book 9.

units.la: Nunc signat meum annulus lagenam.
units.tr: Now my ring seals the flask.

units.la: Q. Frater ad Tironem:
units.tr: Quintus, the brother, to Tiro:

units.la: Sicut olim matrem nostram facere memini, quia lagenas etiam ina- nes obsignabat, ne diceretur inanes aliqua fuisse, quia furtim ef- fent exsiccata.
units.tr: Just as I remember our mother used to do in the old days, for she sealed even empty flasks, so that no one could say there had been something in them which had been secretly drained out.

units.la: LANIFICIUM decet mulieres, & matres-familias.
units.tr: Wool-working befits women and matrons.

units.la: Possisne tu, si ipsus venerit, subtemen tenue nere? P A. Possim. LY. Si tenue scis, scio te uberius posse nere. P A. De lanificio nemi- nem metuo, una âtate quæ sit.
units.tr: Could you, if he came, spin a fine thread? P A. I could. LY. If you know how to spin a fine thread, I know you can spin a good deal more. P A. I have no fear of anyone in wool-working, whatever her age.

units.la: Postulas viros? dare unâ illi operâ pensum postulas inter ancillas sedere jubens, lanam carere.
units.tr: Do you ask for men? You are asking for a task to be done at the same time, ordering her to sit among the maidservants and card wool.

units.la: Ergò id non virorum est, sed puellarum, & feminarum.
units.tr: Therefore this is not men's work, but the work of girls and women.

units.la: MATRES-familias in ancillas eligebant deformes & vetulas.
units.tr: Matrons chose ugly and old women as maidservants.

units.la: Eóque pithecia dicebantur. Secus lenocinia facere credebantur.
units.tr: And for that reason they were called pithecia (apes). Otherwise they were believed to be running brothels.

units.la: IN Oeconomiâ decet vigere bonam disciplinam, ut domestici nimirùm fores pultantibus promtè aperiant. Eo nomine queritur Acanthio Merc. 1. 2. v. 23.
units.tr: In household management good discipline ought to flourish, so that servants promptly open the doors to those who knock. On this account Acanthio complains. Merc. 1. 2. v. 23.

units.la: PARENTES filijs addebant custodes, qui illos asservarent.
units.tr: Parents assigned guardians to their sons to keep watch over them.

units.la: Vide supra Tit. Educationis.
units.tr: See above under the title Education.

units.la: PEDISSEQUAS decet sollicitas esse de suis dominabus: earumque infortunium suum ducere. Quod fecit Bromia ancilla Alcumenæ. Amph. 5.1. v.9.
units.tr: Attendant maidservants ought to be anxious about their mistresses and to count their misfortunes as their own. Bromia, the maidservant of Alcmena, did so. Amph. 5. 1. v. 9.

units.la: ANCILLÆ plærumq; segniores sunt, & socordes, ac securæ rerum suarum, eóq; ab dominabus suis sæpè magnum sibi inveniunt infortunium.
units.tr: Maidservants are for the most part lazier and more careless, unconcerned with their own affairs, and so they often incur great misfortune from their mistresses.

units.la: ANCILLÆ non debent nimis curiosè formam suam curare, sed rei œconomicæ studere.
units.tr: Maidservants ought not to take too much trouble over their looks, but should attend to household management.

units.la: Talem senex describit Mero. 2.3.v.61.79.81.
units.tr: An old man describes such a one in Mero. 2. 3. v. 61. 79. 81.

units.la: Non nostra forma habet dignam domo. Nihil opus est nobis ancilla, nisi quæ texat, quæ molat lignum cædat, pensum faciat, ædes verrat, vapulet, quæq; habeat cotidianum familiæ collum cibum: h.e. quæ sit bona coqua.
units.tr: Our looks are not fit for a household. We have no need of a maidservant, except one who weaves, grinds, chops wood, makes her daily quota of yarn, sweeps the house, takes a beating, and eats each day the household's bread from the neck: that is, one who is a good cook.

units.la: MATRES-familiâs ancillam pedisequam seu comitem alebant.
units.tr: Matrons kept a maidservant as attendant or companion.

units.la: Ibid. v. 69.
units.tr: Ibid. v. 69.

units.la: PEDISSEQUÆ non nimis comtæ erant.
units.tr: Attendants were not to be too elegant.

units.la: Ibid. v. 71.
units.tr: Ibid. v. 71.

units.la: Tales enim si alantur formosulæ, occasio calumniarum præbetur amatoribus: & herum heramque suspectos faciunt lenocinij.
units.tr: For if such pretty girls are kept, an occasion for slander is given to admirers, and they make master and mistress suspected of procuring.

units.la: Quia illa forma matrem-familiâs flagitium fit, si sequatur, quando incedat per vias, contemplent, conspiciant omnes, nutent, nictent, sibilent, vellicent, vocent, molesti sint, occentent ostium: impleantur foros elogiorum carbonibus, atq; ut nunc sunt maledicentes homines, uxori meæ, mihiq; objectet lenocinium facere.
units.tr: For that beauty becomes a disgrace to the matron if the girl follows her when she walks through the streets: everyone gazes, stares, nods, winks, hisses, plucks at her, calls out, makes a nuisance of himself, and sings at the door. Let the forum be filled with the charcoal of insults; and, since men are now so slanderous, let them accuse my wife and me of running a brothel.

units.la: Vide etiam paulò ante ex eodem Mercatore.
units.tr: See also a little earlier in the same Mercator.

units.la: BONÆ matris-familiâs est curare domum: & æstatæ tractare lanam, pro necessitate mariti, suâ, & liberorum, ad bene transfigundam hyemem.
units.tr: It is the duty of a good matron to look after the house, and in summer to work wool, for the needs of her husband, herself and the children, so as to get through the winter well. Mil. 3. 1. v. 92.

units.la: Usæ mulieres aquarijs servis. Pæn. 1. 2. v. 14. Vide Tit. Aquarierum.
units.tr: Women used water-carrying slaves. Pæn. 1. 2. v. 14. See the title Water-carriers.

units.la: Boni patris-familiâs est priusquàm galli cantent, ad labores accedere. Mil. 3. 1. v. 95.
units.tr: It is the duty of a good householder to be at work before the cocks crow. Mil. 3. 1. v. 95.

units.la: Ministerium vilissimum erat, latrinam lavare: h. e. in privatum balneum aquam ferre. Curc. 4. 4. v. 24.
units.tr: The meanest service was washing the latrine, that is, carrying water to the private bath. Curc. 4. 4. v. 24.

units.la: Quamquam ibi sermo potius est de latrinâ, ubi excrementa corporis.
units.tr: Although there the talk is rather of a latrine, where the excrement of the body is.

units.la: Etiam culcitas habebant: sic dictas, ab inculcando. Mil. 4. 4. v. 42. Vide Scaligerum ad Varronem.
units.tr: They also had mattresses, so called from stuffing them (inculcando). Mil. 4. 4. v. 42. See Scaliger on Varro.

units.la: Famis. Inediæ.
units.tr: Hunger. Fasting.

units.la: Inedia & fames varijs humoribus opplent corpus humanum. Quod medicè admodùm disputat Parasitus Curc. 2. 3. v. 39.
units.tr: Fasting and hunger fill the human body with various humours. The parasite in Curc. 2.3 v.39 discusses this quite medically.

units.la: Os amarum habeo, dentes blennos, lippiunt faucesfame: Ita cibi vacivitate venio laxis lachtibus.
units.tr: I have a bitter mouth, my teeth are dull, my jaws are sore with hunger; so, through the emptiness of food, I come with slack gums.

units.la: De famis autem incommodis vide quæ differat doctissimus Cælius Rhodiginus lib. 13. c. 24. Antiqq. Lect.
units.tr: On the discomforts of hunger, see what the most learned Caelius Rhodiginus discusses in book 13, chapter 24 of his Antiquae Lectiones.

units.la: Fames omnia contemnit. Cafin. 4. 3. v. 5. Nihil facio tibi amator, pericli; mihi inanitate jamdudum intestina murmurant.
units.tr: Hunger despises everything. Cas. 4.3 v.5. I make nothing of danger for you, lover; my intestines have long been rumbling with emptiness.

units.la: Fames & mora bilem in nasum conciunt. Amph. 4. 3. v. 40. Seneca de Ira lib. 3. c. 10. Apud Theocr. Idyll. 15. v. 148. muliercula de marito. — Esurienti haud obvius esto. Prov. Latrant stomacho omnia mora bilem movet.
units.tr: Hunger and delay stir up bile in the nose. Amph. 4.3 v.40. Seneca, De Ira 3.10. In Theocritus, Idyll 15 v.148, a little woman speaks about her husband. Do not come across a hungry man. Proverb: Everything barks at an empty stomach; delay stirs bile.

units.la: Præ fame dentes solent dentire. Mil. 1. 1. v. 34. Vide Lex. & Dentium. Offa memorem facit ventrem. Ibid. v. 49.
units.tr: From hunger the teeth tend to chatter. Mil. 1.1 v.34. See the Lexicon under Dentium. A morsel makes the belly mindful. Ibid. v.49.

units.la: Fames mater parasitorum fingitur eleganter. Stich. 2. 1. v. 1. Vide seqq.
units.tr: Hunger, the mother of parasites, is elegantly imagined. Stich. 2.1 v.1. See what follows.

units.la: Fames mansuetum facit. Asin. 1. 2. v. 19.
units.tr: Hunger makes a man tame. Asin. 1.2 v.19.

units.la: Ferri. Rubiginis.
units.tr: Iron. Rust.

units.la: FErrum facile rubigine inficitur. Rud. 5.2. v.13. Hoc quidem pol è rubigine, non è ferro factum est, ita quanto magis extergeo, rutilum atq; tenuius fit. Nam quidem hoc verè natum est verum: ita in manibus consenescit.
units.tr: Iron is easily infected with rust. Rud. 5.2 v.13. Indeed, by Pollux, this was made from rust, not from iron; so the more I scour it, the redder and thinner it grows. For this is truly born of rust, and thus it grows old in the hands.

units.la: Feriarum. Festorum.
units.tr: Holidays. Festivals.

units.la: Vide etiam Deorum : Sacrificiorum.
units.tr: See also Gods: Sacrifices.

units.la: ELeutheria erant festa, quæ celebrantur in honorem Jovis eleutherij, qui & Σωτὴρ dictus. Perf. I.I. v.29.
units.tr: The Eleutheria were festivals celebrated in honour of Jupiter Eleutherius, who was also called Soter [Σωτὴρ]. Perf. 1.1 v.29.

units.la: Cereri Ambarvaliorum annuo festo sacrificabant vino, nonitem in nuptijs. Aul. 2.6. v. 5.
units.tr: At the Ambarvalia, the yearly festival of Ceres, they sacrificed with wine; not so at weddings. Aul. 2.6 v.5.

units.la: Vide Tit. Nuptiarum.
units.tr: See the title Weddings.

units.la: Ad dies festos conveniebant quoq; contractuum dissolvendorum causâ.
units.tr: On festival days people also gathered for the sake of dissolving contracts.

units.la: Pseud. I.I. v.57.
Ad Dionysia præstituta erat dies militi exsolvendi as pro puella.
units.tr: On the Dionysia a day had been appointed on which the soldier was to pay the as on behalf of the girl.

units.la: Diebus festis omnia ornatè fiebant, in delubris : varij odorcs accensi.
units.tr: On festival days everything was done splendidly in the shrines, and various perfumes were burned.

units.la: Cereris vigiliæ celebratæ.
units.tr: The vigils of Ceres were celebrated.

units.la: Dionysia in honorem Bacchi solemniter celebrata : spectaculo edito. Curc. 5.2. v. 45.
units.tr: The Dionysia were solemnly celebrated in honour of Bacchus, with a spectacle provided. Curc. 5.2 v.45.

units.la: PER festa Dionysia matres suas filias deduxerunt spectatum pompam. Cist. I.I.V.92.
units.tr: During the festival of the Dionysia, mothers led their daughters to watch the procession. Cist. 1.1 v.92.

units.la: Vide Tit. Mulierum: Virginum.
units.tr: See the title Women: Virgins.

units.la: FESTO Matronalium matronæ Junoni sacrificabant Calendis Martijs. Mul. 3.I.V.96.
units.tr: At the festival of the Matronalia, matrons sacrificed to Juno on the Kalends of March. Mul. 3.1 v.96.

units.la: Vide Tit. Strenarum.
units.tr: See the title New Year's Gifts.

units.la: Quinquatribus præcantatrici, quæ carminibus & incantamentis mala ab hominibus amoliri se posse profitebatur, munera offerebant. Mul. 3.I.V.96.
units.tr: At the Quinquatria they offered gifts to the enchantress, who professed that by songs and incantations she could drive evils away from men. Mul. 3.1 v.96.

units.la: De Quinquatribus vide Hospinianum pag. 83. de Festis Ethnicorum. Itemq; Manutium Comment. Epist. Ciceron. lib. 2. Epist. 12.
units.tr: On the Quinquatria see Hospinian, p. 83, On the Festivals of the Heathens; likewise Manutius, commentary on Cicero's Letters, book 2, letter 12.

units.la: PANATHENAICA Magna quinto quoquo anno celebrata: in quibus peplum Minervæ consecrabatur. Merc. Prol. V.67.
units.tr: The Great Panathenaea, celebrated every fifth year, at which the robe of Minerva was consecrated. Merc. Prol. v.67.

units.la: Vide Tit. Deorum: Dedicationis, & copiosum authorem Hospinianum de Festis Ethnicorum in Mense Junio.
units.tr: See the title Gods: Dedication, and the copious author Hospinian, On the Festivals of the Heathens, under the month of June.

units.la: FESTA erant vel publica, vel privata: & hæc quidem transferebantur de familiâ in familiam, de agro in agrum: immò impetrabantur à sacerdotibus & Impp.
units.tr: Festivals were either public or private, and these were indeed transferred from family to family and from field to field; indeed they were obtained from priests and emperors.

units.la: APHRODISIA dies festi & sacri Veneri Aphrodisiæ.
units.tr: The Aphrodisia were a festal and sacred day for Venus Aphrodite.

units.la: Pæn. I.I. v.63.
FESTIS diebus hilarius vixerunt, quàm profestis.
units.tr: People lived more cheerfully on festival days than on ordinary days.

units.la: Fidei. Benignitatis. Beneficen- tiæ. Credulitatis.
units.tr: Faith. Kindness. Beneficence. Credulity.

units.la: AB ijs qui nullius fidei, pignus accipiebatur. Rud. 2.7.v.23.
units.tr: From those of no trustworthiness a pledge was taken. Rud. 2.7 v.23.

units.la: NERVI & artus sapientiæ sunt, nemini temere credere, inquit Epicharmus apud Cicer. de petit. Consul. Unde Pamphilippus adolescens in re etiam levis momenti, Antiphoni, quamvis socero, non aliter, quàm satisfactione acceptâ fidem habituram se dicit, nisi sciret sibi amicum esse. Stich. 4.1. v. 4.
units.tr: Sinews and joints of wisdom are: to trust no one rashly, says Epicharmus, cited by Cicero in De Petitione Consulatus. Whence the young Pamphilus, in a matter even of slight importance, says of Antipho, though his father-in-law, that he will not otherwise have trust unless he receives security, unless he knows him to be a friend. Stich. 4.1 v.4.

units.la: Satis abs te accipiam, nisi videam mihi te amicum esse Antipho: nunc quia te amicum mihi experior esse, creditur tibi.
units.tr: I shall take sufficient security from you, unless I see that you are a friend to me, Antipho; now, since I find you to be a friend to me, credit is given to you.

units.la: MANUS vetat prius, quàm penes sese habeat, quicquam credere. Asin. 1.3.v.50.
units.tr: The hand forbids entrusting anything before it has it in its own possession. Asin. 1.3 v.50.

units.la: Manus nostrae oculatae sunt, credunt quod vident.
units.tr: Our hands have eyes; they believe what they see.

units.la: Truc. 5.v. 5.
units.tr: Truc. 5 v.5.

units.la: FIDE omninò digni esse debent, quibus Respublica & privata geritur.
units.tr: Those by whom the public or private business is conducted must be entirely worthy of trust.

units.la: TESTIMONIUM hominis improbi, quales olim lenones, non admittitur.
units.tr: The testimony of a dishonest man, such as the pimps of old, is not admitted.

units.la: ÆQUUM est tenere per fidem, quod creditum est.
units.tr: It is fair to hold by good faith what has been entrusted.

units.la: Ne bene merenti fit malo benignitas.
units.tr: Let kindness not turn into harm for one who has deserved well.

units.la: FIDEI fanum erat exstructum Romæ. Aul. 3.6. v.46.
units.tr: A temple of Faith was built at Rome. Aul. 3.6 v.46.

units.la: MULIEBRIS fides suspecta. Mil. 2.5. v. 46.
units.tr: A woman's faith is suspect. Mil. 2.5 v.46.

units.la: FOEDERUM. FACTORUM. CONVENTUUM. CONTRACTUUM.
units.tr: Of Treaties, Deeds, Agreements, and Contracts.

units.la: IN fœderibus sanciendis victimæ saxo feriebantur : quò allusit proverbium :
units.tr: In sanctioning treaties, victims were struck against a stone; to which the proverb alludes:

units.la: Intra sacrum: saxum q; sta.
units.tr: Within the sacred precinct, and the stone also stands.

units.la: Ritus in fœderibus sanciendis solemnis tangitur à Suetonio in Claudio cap. 25.
units.tr: The ritual solemnly observed in sanctioning treaties is touched on by Suetonius in Claudius, chapter 25.

units.la: Fœdus in foro icit, porcâ cæsâ, ac veterum Fetialium præfatione adhibitâ.
units.tr: He made a treaty in the forum, a sow being slain, and with the preface of the ancient Fetiales employed.

units.la: De porcâ cæsâ vide ibi Comment. Torrentij, & Festum in Fedus & Fetialis. At Præfatio qualis fuerit, luculenter deducitur apud Livium lib. 1. de Federe inter Tullum Hostilium, & Albanos. Fetialis Regem Tullum ita rogavit: Jubesne me Rex &c.
units.tr: On the sow slain, see the commentary of Torrentius there, and Festus under Fedus and Fetialis. But what the preface was like is clearly set out in Livy, book 1, on the treaty between Tullus Hostilius and the Albans. The Fetialis asked King Tullus thus: Do you command me, King, etc.

units.la: Quem locum iterum laudat Livius lib. 9.
units.tr: Livy praises this passage again in book 9.

units.la: Quod enim sponsionibus in fœdere opus esset, aut obsidibus, ubi precatione res transigitur, per quem populum fiat, quo minus legibus dictis stetur, ut eum ita Jupiter feriat, quemadmodum a fetialibus porcus feriatur.
units.tr: For since sponsions in a treaty, or hostages, are needed, where the matter is concluded by prayer, by whatever people it is done, so that they do not stand by the terms spoken, let Jupiter strike that people just as a pig is struck by the fetiales.

units.la: Nec non lib. 30.
units.tr: Nor indeed in book 30 as well.

units.la: Fetialis cum in Africam ad fœdus feriendum ire juberentur, ipsis postulantibus S C. in hæc verba sactum est; ut privos lapides, silices, privasq; verbenas secum ferrent, ut Prætor Romanus hoc imperaret, ut fœdus ferirent.
units.tr: When the Fetiales were ordered to go to Africa to strike a treaty, at their own request a decree of the Senate was passed in these words: that they should carry with them sacred stones, flint stones, and sacred verbena, so that the Roman praetor might give this order, that they should strike the treaty.

units.la: Ubi videtur evincere locus hic posterior, non semper porcum intervenisse, sed abjectum modo lapidem: cui favent illa Polybij lib. 3. de fœdere item icto cum Pœnis : Fetialis lapidem tenens ita ait: Si sine dolo malo ago, bonis afficior: si sciens fallo, cæteris omnibus salvis in suis civitatibus, legibus, Laribus, delubris, sepulcris, pulcris, solus ego concidam; ut lapis è manibus meis decidet, nec plura loquetur Lapidem abjiciet.
units.tr: Here this later passage seems to prove that a pig did not always intervene, but a stone alone was thrown down; and to this agree those words of Polybius, book 3, about a treaty likewise struck with the Carthaginians: The Fetialis, holding a stone, says thus: If I act without evil intent, may good things befall me; if knowingly I deceive, then, all others being safe in their own states, laws, household gods, shrines, tombs, and fair things, may I alone be cast down, just as this stone falls from my hands, and he said no more, and cast down the stone.

units.la: Quibus paria videantur apud Festum in Lapidem Silicem. Dealijs quibusdam verbis solemnibus in Fœdere Romanorum cum Latinis consulendus Dionysius lib. 6. Antiquitatum circa finem planè.
units.tr: Similar things appear in Festus under Lapidem Silicem. For other solemn words in the treaty of the Romans with the Latins, Dionysius, book 6 of the Antiquities, near the end, is plainly to be consulted.

units.la: SOLEBANT Græci in pactis conventis uti quibusdam tesseris, quæ συμβολα vocabantur, quæ loco tabularum, & syngrapharum erant: atque ex his jus dicebatur. Bacch. 2.3.v.29. Pseud. 2.1.v.12. Turn. Adv. lib. 2. cap. 30.
units.tr: The Greeks used to employ in agreed pacts certain tokens, which were called symbola, and which took the place of tablets and written contracts; and by these law was declared. Bacch. 2.3.v.29. Pseud. 2.1.v.12. Turnebus, Adversaria, book 2, chapter 30.

units.la: ROMANI post meridiem nihil soliti sunt pacisci. Most. 3.1.v.114. Turn. lib. 16. 10.
units.tr: The Romans were accustomed to make no bargains after midday. Most. 3.1.v.114. Turnebus, book 16, chapter 10.

units.la: FOETORIS. ODORIS.
units.tr: Stench. Smell.

units.la: ALITER longè catuli olent, aliter sues. Epid. 4.2.v.9.
units.tr: Puppies smell quite differently from pigs. Epid. 4.2.v.9.

units.la: FOETIDI homines abigebantur hac formulâ: Fi fi fetet! Cas. 3.6.v.7.
units.tr: Foul-smelling men were driven away with this formula: "Phew, phew, how it stinks!" Cas. 3.6.v.7.

units.la: ALLIUM qui comederent, maximè fœtebant: & erant odiosi. Most. 1.1.v.38.
units.tr: Those who ate garlic stank the most, and they were disliked. Most. 1.1.v.38.

units.la: Fue! obolusti allium.
units.tr: "Ugh! You've been eating garlic for a halfpenny."

units.la: Vide etiam versus seqq. de fœtidis animalibus.
units.tr: See also the following verses about foul-smelling animals.

units.la: FORMÆ. SIMILITUDINIS. DEFORMITATIS. FUCI. FUCATIONIS. PIGMENTI. IMAGINIS.
units.tr: FORMS. LIKENESS. DEFORMITY. PAINT. PAINTING. PIGMENT. IMAGE.

units.la: Vide infra Tit. Mulierum: Feminarum. Ubi aliquid de ornatu mulierum.
units.tr: See below under the title Women: Females. There is something there on the adornment of women.

units.la: FABULOSUM quidem est exemplum Amphitruonis & Sosiæ apud Plautum nostrum, qui ob formæ similitudinem in tantum discrimen adducti sunt: tota Comœdia primore: at in veris historijs non omnino inusitatum aut infrequens. Legatur totum caput 14. lib. 9. apud Valerium Maxim. inprimis vero insignis historia Martini Guerræ & Arnoldi Tilij, quæ recensetur à Corrasio J C. & integrè cum Notis describitur ab Michaële Neand. lectu dignissima.
units.tr: The example of Amphitruo and Sosia in our Plautus, who were brought into such peril by the likeness of their form, is indeed a fable, and the whole comedy turns on it. In true histories, however, it is not altogether unusual or rare. Let the whole fourteenth chapter of book 9 of Valerius Maximus be read. Especially notable is the story of Martin Guerra and Arnold Tilly, which is recounted by the jurist Corrasius and described in full, with notes, by Michael Neander; it is most worth reading.

units.la: Alia Exempla passim obvia, & ad hunc Titulum referenda.
units.tr: Other examples are found everywhere and are to be referred to this title.

units.la: FORMÆ præstantioris puellas pictoribus in exemplum proponebant.
units.tr: Painters used to set girls of outstanding beauty before them as models.
Pæn. 5. 4. v. 99 and following.

units.la: MAGNA vis est formæ.
units.tr: Great is the power of beauty.

units.la: Apulejus:
units.tr: Apuleius:

units.la: Virgo formosa, etsi sit oppido pauper, tamen abundè dotata est.
units.tr: A beautiful girl, even if she is quite poor, is nonetheless richly dowered.

units.la: Affranins:
units.tr: Afranius:

units.la: Formosa virgo est. Dotis dimidium vocant Isti, qui dotes negligunt uxorias.
units.tr: The girl is beautiful. Those who despise wifely dowries call it half the dowry.

units.la: Ovid. 11. Metamorph.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses book 11.

units.la: Potissima formâ.
units.tr: Chiefly by beauty of form.

units.la: Forma puellarum illicium adolescentium: & seditiosa valde. Vide Tit. Familia: Oeconomia.
units.tr: The beauty of girls is an allurement to young men, and very seditious. See the title Family: Household Management.

units.la: Forma simili saepe nascuntur peccari, ut mater vix agnoscat, quae mammam dat.
units.tr: Children are often born so much like their parents that the mother can hardly recognise the one at her breast. Likeness of form

units.la: Men. Prol. v.19. Et Men. 5.9. v 29.
units.tr: Men. Prol. v. 19. And Men. 5. 9. v. 29.

units.la: Namque ego hominem homini similiorem numquam vidi alte-rum.
units.tr: For I have never seen one man more like another man.

units.la: Neq; aqua, aquae: neq; latte est latti usquam similius, Quam hic tui est: tuq; hujus.
units.tr: Nor is water more like water, nor milk more like milk anywhere, than this one is like yours, and yours like this one.

units.la: Proh Dii immortales! similiorem mulierem magis quam eandem, utpote quae non sit eadem, non reor Deos facere posse.
units.tr: Good heavens! I do not think the gods can make a woman more like the same woman, since she is not the same.

units.la: Ad fucandam faciem cerussam, stibium, melinum, pigmentum, purpurissum, rubricetam, & id genus offucias alias adhibebant.
units.tr: To paint the face they used white lead, antimony, melinum, rouge, purple dye, red ochre and other cosmetics of that kind.

units.la: Most. 1.3. v. 100. Vide Tit. Gynaeceum.
units.tr: Most. 1. 3. v. 100. See the title Women's Quarters.

units.la: Frustra tamen id saepe faciunt puellae: quae nova pictura inter polare solent opus lepidissimum: h. e. formam honestam: quasi cburatramento candefacere postulantes.
units.tr: Yet girls often do this in vain: they apply a fresh coat of paint over the polish, as it were, wanting to whiten with white lead a most charming work, that is, an honest face.

units.la: Pigmentum & alium quemvis fucum allinebant ijs, quos alijs deridendos propinare volebant: idque turpiculis puellis potissimum, quas hoc contumeliae genere a procaci juventute affici mos erat: ut hac censione quasi deformitatis suae memoriam recarentur.
units.tr: They daubed paint and any other colouring on those whom they wished to offer to others for mockery. This was done especially to ugly girls, whom wanton youth customarily treated with this kind of insult, so that by such a censure they would be reminded, as it were, of their deformity.

units.la: Deformes mulieres comparantur pithecio, & spinturnici. Mil. 4.1. v. 42. Truc. 2. 5. v.24. Ubi Ancilla nomen Pithecij accepit. Ein heßliche Aff.
units.tr: Ugly women are compared to a monkey and a spinturnix. Mil. 4. 1. v. 42. Truc. 2. 5. v. 24. Where the maid receives the name Pithecium. An ugly ape.

units.la: Nimia est miseria, pulchrum esse hominem nimis: inquit Pyrgopolinices Mil. 11. v. 68.
units.tr: It is too great a misery to be too handsome a man, says Pyrgopolynices. Mil. 11. v. 68.

units.la: Formosa satis est, quae morata est.
units.tr: A woman is beautiful enough if she is well-mannered.

units.la: Vide Tit. Conjugy.
units.tr: See the title Marriage.

units.la: FORMAM puellae laudantes, cum Junone comparabant.
units.tr: When they praised a girl's beauty, they compared her with Juno.

units.la: ALEXANDRI seu Paridis Trojani forma prae caeteris laudata.
units.tr: The beauty of Alexander, or of Paris of Troy, was praised above all others.

units.la: CUIUS quis imitatur formam, ejusdem quoq; imitari debet mores
units.tr: Whoever one imitates in form, one ought to imitate in character as well.

units.la: EX uno puteo similior numquam potest
units.tr: From one well no water can be more like water.

units.la: Aqua aquae sumi, quam haec est atque ista hospita.
units.tr: Water is taken for water; no one is more alike than this woman and that stranger.

units.la: LACTE lacti similimum.Men. v. 9. v. 30. Mil. 2. 2. v. 85.
units.tr: Milk most like milk. Men. 5. 9. v. 30. Mil. 2. 2. v. 85.

units.la: Sic ova ovis, apes apibus.
units.tr: So egg to egg, bee to bees.

units.la: FORTITUDINIS.
units.tr: OF COURAGE.

units.la: ROMANI eum demum bonum & formosum putarunt, qui effet fortis.
units.tr: The Romans judged that only the man who was brave was good and handsome.

units.la: FORTUNÆ. EVENTUS. CASUS. PROVIDEN-TIÆ. CALAMITATIS. INFORTUNII, REI-ADVERSÆ. FELICITATIS. PROSPERITATIS.
units.tr: FORTUNE. EVENT. CHANCE. PROVIDENCE. CALAMITY. MISFORTUNE, ADVERSITY. HAPPINESS. PROSPERITY.

units.la: Vide etiam infra Tit. Voluptatis: & Hominis.
units.tr: See also below, under the heading Pleasure and Man.

units.la: FORTUNA humana fingit, aptatq; ut subet.Capt. 2.2. v. 54.
units.tr: Human fortune shapes things and fits them to its will. Capt. 2.2. v. 54.

units.la: CENTUM doctum hominum consilia sola hæc devincit Dea Fortuna: atq; hoc verum est: proinde ut quisq; eâ utitur, Ita præcellet: atq; exinde sapere eum omnes dicimus.
units.tr: The goddess Fortune alone overcomes the plans of a hundred learned men. This is true: whoever makes use of her excels accordingly, and from then on we all say he is wise.

units.la: Egregia sententia: quam explicat Plinius Secundus Epist. 2. l. 5. Est omnino iniquum, ait, sed usu receptum, quod honesta consilia, velturpia, prout male aut prospere cedunt: ita vel probantur vel reprehenduntur.
units.tr: This is an excellent saying, which Pliny the Younger explains in Epist. 2, book 5: "It is altogether unjust, but customary, that honourable plans or shameful ones are then either approved or condemned, according as they turn out badly or well."

units.la: Inde plærumque eadem facta modò diligentiæ, modò vanitatis, modò libertatis, modò furoris nomen accipiunt.
units.tr: Hence the same deeds often receive now the name of diligence, now of folly, now of freedom, now of madness.

units.la: Et Livius recte ait lib. 44.
units.tr: And Livy rightly says in book 44:

units.la: Fortuna plus humanū consilijs pollet.
units.tr: Fortune has more power than human plans.

units.la: Sallustius:
units.tr: Sallust:

units.la: Fortuna plerasq; res libidine suâ agitat.
units.tr: Fortune drives most things according to her own whim.

units.la: NULLUM bonum sine malo.
units.tr: NO GOOD WITHOUT EVIL.

units.la: Dic mihi, an boni quid unquam est, quod qui quam uti possit
units.tr: Tell me, is there any good that a man can use

units.la: Sine malo omni, aut ne laborem capies, cum illo uti velis.
units.tr: without some evil, or else you will not take the trouble to want to use it?

units.la: Ego bonum malum cui accedit, haud mihi dari desidero.
units.tr: I do not want a good to be given to me to which evil is attached.

units.la: In rebus prosperis constituto solebant boni ominis causâ apprecari hac formulâ DI Deaque te adjuvant: Cui homini omnes res suppetunt prosperè.
units.tr: Those standing in prosperous circumstances were accustomed, for the sake of a good omen, to pray with this formula: May the gods and goddesses help you. To the man for whom all things go well.

units.la: FORTUNA mala abominationi: ut bona Fortuna religioni.
units.tr: Bad Fortune is an abomination, as good Fortune is a matter of religion.

units.la: Vide Tit. Deorum.
units.tr: See the title Of the Gods.

units.la: TUM demûm homines nostra intelligimus bona, Cùm quæ in potestate habuimus, ea amisimus.
units.tr: Only then do men understand our goods, when we have lost what we had in our power.

units.la: Expressit quoque elegantem hanc sententiam Horatius lib. 3. Od. 23.
units.tr: Horace also expressed this elegant saying, in book 3, Ode 23:

units.la: Virtutem incolumem odimus: Sublatam ex oculis quærimus invidi.
units.tr: We hate virtue while it is unharmed; once it is removed from sight, we envious people seek it.

units.la: Et Sophocles Ajace:
units.tr: And Sophocles in the Ajax:

units.la: οἱ δ' κακοὶ γνώμαισι τ' ἀγαθὸν χερσοῖν' ἐχοντες, ὡς ἰσασιν, πρὶν τις ἐμβάλῃ.
units.tr: The base, holding the good in their hands, do not know what it is until someone throws it at them. [οἱ δὲ κακοὶ γνώμαισι τ' ἀγαθὸν χερσοῖν ἔχοντες, ὡς ἴσασιν, πρὶν τις ἐμβάλῃ.]

units.la: FORTUNA Divûm atque hominum spectatrix atq; Hera eadem hominibus.
units.tr: Fortune, the watcher of gods and men, and the same to men as a mistress.

units.la: Sic Ennius apud Cic. lib. 1. offic.
units.tr: So Ennius, quoted by Cicero in book 1 of the De Officiis:

units.la: Vosne velit, an me regnare Hera.
units.tr: Whether she wishes me or you to rule as mistress.

units.la: Græci Δὶ ἀπούναν vocant.
units.tr: The Greeks call her [Δὶ ἀπούναν].

units.la: Vide H. Columnam ad lib. 5. & 8. Annal. Ennij.
units.tr: See H. Columna on books 5 and 8 of the Annals of Ennius.

units.la: EX prospera fortunâ incidere in adversam, miserum est.
units.tr: To fall from prosperous fortune into adverse is a wretched thing.
Stich. 1.2. v. 68.

units.la: Difficile est æquo animo pati sibi esse pejus quàm fuit.
units.tr: It is hard to bear with an even mind that one's lot is worse than it once was.

units.la: Cicero:
units.tr: Cicero:

units.la: Tum ubi non sis, qui fueris, non esses cur vivere velis.
units.tr: Since you are no longer what you were, you have no reason to wish to live.

units.la: Utramque fortunam æquo animo ferre non tantum difficile est feminis: verum etiam viris.
units.tr: To bear either fortune with an even mind is difficult not only for women but even for men.

units.la: De feminis vide Stich. 1. 2. v. 67.
units.tr: On women see Stich. 1.2. v. 67.

units.la: Multa evenient homini, quæ vult, quæ nevult.
units.tr: Many things happen to a man that he wants and that he does not want.

units.la: Quam sententiam senex refutare conatur his verbis:
units.tr: The old man tries to refute this saying with these words:

units.la: Mentire adepol gnate. Nam sapiens quidem pol ipse fingit Fortu-nam sibi. Eo ne multa, quæ nevult evenient, nisi fictor malus est. L. Y. Multa est operâ opus fictura, qui se fictorem probum vitæ agendæ esse expetit: h. e. Opus est ei multâ operâ ac curâ fingendi ac liberandi, qui rationem vitæ rectè degendæ sibi fingere cogitat.
units.tr: Do not lie, by Pollux, my son. For indeed a wise man makes his own fortune. Therefore, that many things happen which he does not want is only because he is a bad craftsman. L. Y. It takes much work to shape the one who seeks to be an upright craftsman of his own life: that is, he needs much labour and care to shape and free himself, who intends to fashion for himself a rule for living rightly.

units.la: Cicero in Paradoxis:
units.tr: Cicero in the Paradoxa:

units.la: Nec est ulla res, quæ plus apud sapientem polleat, quam ipsius voluntas atq; judicium. Cui quidem etiam, quæ vim habere maximam dicitur, Fortuna ipsa cedit: sicut sapiens Poëta dixit: Suis ea cuiq; fingitur moribus.
units.tr: There is nothing that has more power with the wise man than his own will and judgment. To this even Fortune herself, which is said to have the greatest force, yields, just as the wise poet said: "Each person's fortune is shaped by his own character."

units.la: Sic Appius in Sall. oratione ad Cæs.
units.tr: So Appius in Sallust's speech to Caesar:

units.la: Sed res docuit id verum esse, quod in Carminibus Appius ait: F A-BRUM esse SuÆ QuEMQUE FORTUNÆ.
units.tr: But events have taught that what Appius says in his songs is true: that each man is the smith of his own fortune.

units.la: Nepos in vita Attici:
units.tr: Nepos in the life of Atticus:

units.la: Sui cuiq; mores fortunam fingunt.
units.tr: Each man's own character shapes his fortune.

units.la: Fulgentius è Carniadis libro Telesiaco:
units.tr: Fulgentius, from the Telesian book of Carneades:

units.la: Πάσα τύχη αἰσθησιν φρονῦντ' ἀ καταικεῖ. Omnis fortuna in sensu Sa-pienti habitat.
units.tr: All fortune dwells in the sense of the wise man. [Πᾶσα τύχη αἰσθήσει φρονοῦντος ἐνοικεῖ.] Omnis fortuna in sensu sapienti habitat.

units.la: Utique Prudentia ars & norma est totius vitæ, quemadmodum Cicero inquit lib. 5. de Finibus:
units.tr: Indeed prudence is the art and rule of the whole of life, as Cicero says in book 5 of De Finibus:

units.la: Artem vivendi esse Prudentiam, ut Medicinam valetudinis.
units.tr: Prudence is the art of living, as medicine is the art of health.

units.la: Huic igitur rectè subjectam quoque ipsam Fortunam docet Plautus prædicto loco. Menander:
units.tr: Plautus, in the passage cited, therefore rightly teaches that Fortune herself is subject to this. Menander:

units.la: Ἀπαντα δὲ λα, τῷ φρονεῖν κατίσατα.
units.tr: All things that are rightly accomplished come from good sense. [Ἅπαντα δὲ τὰ τῷ φρονεῖν κατορθούμενα.]

units.la: Mm
units.tr: Mm

units.la: Plato: νῦς ἀνθρώπῳ θεὸς, ὕτω ἐαν ἀγαθὸς, θεὸς.
units.tr: Plato: mind is man's god; if it is good, it is a god. [νοῦς ἀνθρώπῳ θεός, οὗτος ἐὰν ἀγαθὸς ᾖ, θεός.]

units.la: Actutum solet Fortuna mutarier: varia vita est. Nos divites eum meminimus, atq; iste pauperes nos. Vertit sese rota vicissim.
units.tr: Fortune is wont to change suddenly: life is varied. We who were once rich become poor, and those poor become rich. The wheel turns in turn.

units.la: Qualis est Fortuna, talis est hominum vultus, oratio.
units.tr: As Fortune is, so is the look and speech of men.

units.la: Felicitatis perpetuus comes Invidia.
units.tr: Envy is the constant companion of happiness.

units.la: Vide Tit. Invidia.
units.tr: See the title Envy.

units.la: Centum doctum hominum consilia sola haec devincit Dea Fortuna: atque hoc verum est: proinde ut quisq; cã utitur, ita praecellet, atque exinde sapere eum omnes dicimus.
units.tr: The goddess Fortune alone overcomes the plans of a hundred learned men. This is true: whoever makes use of her excels accordingly, and from then on we all say he is wise.
Pseud. 2.3. v. 13.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Consilij.
units.tr: See also the title Counsel.

units.la: Qui homo timidus erit in rebus dubijs, nauci non erit.
units.tr: A man who is timid in doubtful matters will be worth nothing.

units.la: Fortunam prosperam vix ferre æquo animo possumus: quod ostendit exemplum Parasiti.
units.tr: We can scarcely bear prosperous fortune with an even mind, as the example of the Parasite shows.

units.la: Capt. 4.1. per totam scenam.
units.tr: Capt. 4.1, throughout the whole scene.

units.la: In summa felicitate constitutus cavere debet, ne fortuna inclinet.
units.tr: One who is placed in the highest happiness ought to take care that fortune does not turn.

units.la: Idem animus esse debet in paupertate, qui olim in divitijs fuit.
units.tr: The mind should be the same in poverty as it once was in riches.
Stich. 1.2. v. 77.

units.la: Nimio hominum Fortunæ minus miseræ memorantur, quàm reapse experiundo ijs datur acerbum.
units.tr: Men's fortunes are recorded as less wretched than they really find them to be through experience, which gives them a bitter taste.

units.la: Eventus rebus in omnibus, velut in horreo horna messis, magnifit. Most. i. 3. v. 3.
units.tr: In all matters, events, like the harvest in a granary, are plentiful. Most. 1.3. v. 3.

units.la: Quod Dij dant boni, nostra culpa non amittendum.
units.tr: What the gods give as good things must not be lost through our fault.
Bacch. 5.2. v. 69.

units.la: Bonus animus in mala re, dimidium est mali.
units.tr: A good mind in a bad situation is half of the evil.
Pseud. 1.5. v. 37.

units.la: Bonum fere semper commixtum est malo. Asin. 2. 2. v. 44.
units.tr: Good is almost always mixed with evil. Asin. 2.2. v. 44.

units.la: Malis saepe bene esse solitum est. Merc. 3. 1. v. 13. Quod tamen in joco dictum videri potest.
units.tr: It has often been the custom for those in trouble to be well off. Merc. 3.1. v. 13. Yet this may seem to be said in jest.

units.la: Fortuna Obsequens olim Romae colebatur.
units.tr: Fortune, who is compliant, was once worshipped at Rome.

units.la: Fortuna homines saepe frustratur.
units.tr: Fortune often deceives men.

units.la: Fortunas secundas decent superbiae.
units.tr: Prosperous fortunes suit pride.
Stich. 2.2. v. 28.

units.la: Nulli est homini perpetuum bonum. Voluptati enim plærumque adjunctum odium. Curc. 1. 3. v. 33.
units.tr: No good is lasting for any man, for hatred is generally attached to pleasure. Curc. 1.3. v. 33.

units.la: Aequus animus optimum est aerumnae condimentum.
units.tr: An even mind is the best seasoning for hardship.

units.la: FRIGORIS
units.tr: COLD

units.la: Frigus parit trepidationem, & dentium crepitationem.
units.tr: Cold produces trembling and chattering of the teeth.

units.la: FRUGALITATIS. DIVITIARUM. MEDIOCRITATIS. SUMTUUM. PARSIMONIÆ. VICTUS.
units.tr: FRUGALITY. RICHES. MODERATION. EXPENSE. THRIFT. FARE.

units.la: PArsimoniæ veteres operam dabant. Mostell. I.2.v.74.
units.tr: Men of old devoted their efforts to thrift. Mostell. I.2.v.74.

units.la: MOdice & modestè melius est vitam vivere. Nam si ad paupertatem admigrant infamiæ, gravior paupertas fit, fides subleslior.
units.tr: To live sparingly and modestly is better. For if people fall into poverty through disgrace, the poverty becomes heavier and their credit more fragile.

units.la: Varro Satyram inscripsit Modius: quo in victu & vestitu reprehendit τὰ πλέον τε, ἢ τὸ ἐλαττον. E luxu enim nimio oritur & paupertas & infamia.
units.tr: Varro entitled a satire Modius, in which he criticises in food and clothing both the excess and the deficiency [τὰ πλέον τε, ἢ τὸ ἐλαττον]. For both poverty and disgrace arise from excessive luxury.

units.la: CUM modo obsona, nec magno sumtu: mihi QUIDVIS SAT EST.
units.tr: When the provisions are cheap and not at great cost, ANYTHING IS ENOUGH for me.

units.la: Turpilius: Profecto ut quùq; minimo contentus fuit, Ita fortunatam vitam vixit maximè: Ubi Philosophi ajunt isti, quis QUIDVIS SAT EST.
units.tr: Turpilius: "Truly, the less a man is content with, the more fortunately he lives, most of all; whence those philosophers of yours say, ANYTHING IS ENOUGH."

units.la: Lucilius: Cum telum est, QUIDVIS SAT EST.
units.tr: Lucilius: "Since it is a weapon, ANYTHING IS ENOUGH."

units.la: Vide Prov. Caseum & Salem edo.
units.tr: See the proverb: "I eat cheese and salt."

units.la: QUI parvo contenti sunt, alijs supplices fieri non habent necesse: De suo enim victitant.
units.tr: Those who are content with little have no need to become suppliants to others, for they live on what is their own.

units.la: Quicquid est pauxillulum illuc, nostrum illud omne intus est. Neque nos quemquam flagitamus, neq; nos quisquam flagitat.
units.tr: Whatever little there is there, all of it is ours at home. We demand nothing from anyone, and no one demands anything from us.

units.la: QUOD quis habet, id satest: dummodò benedictio Dei adsit.
units.tr: Whatever a man has is enough, provided God's blessing is present.

units.la: DI faciant, uti diu sint! plus plusq; sospitent istuc, quod nunc habes.
units.tr: May the gods grant that you have it long! May they keep safe, and increase, what you now have.

units.la: Quisque pro opibus suis frugaliter debet vivere: ut servi, more servorum.
units.tr: Each person ought to live thriftily according to his means, like slaves, in the manner of slaves.
Stich. 5.2.v.10.

units.la: Servo homini modeste melius facere sumtum, quam ampliter.
units.tr: For a servant it is better to spend modestly than lavishly.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Conjugij.
units.tr: See also the title On Marriage.

units.la: De magnis divitiis si quid demas, non fit plus, sed minus. Parsimoniae igitur studendum.
units.tr: If something is taken away from great riches, they do not grow but shrink. Therefore one must pursue thrift.

units.la: Pauxillo contentos esse jubet natura.
units.tr: Nature bids us be content with little.

units.la: Veteres parsimoniae in laude.
units.tr: Old-time thrift is praised.

units.la: FRUGUM. FRUMENTI. MESSIS. PAPAVERIS.
units.tr: OF FRUITS OF THE EARTH. OF GRAIN. OF THE HARVEST. OF THE POPPY.

units.la: PAPAVEREM comedunt formicae.
units.tr: Ants eat the poppy-seed.

units.la: FRUGES mergis sive furculis compingebantur.
units.tr: The fruits were gathered together in sheaves or bundles of twigs.

units.la: FRUMENTUM demetiebantur modio, trimodio, & ipso horreo.
units.tr: The grain was measured out by the peck, the three-peck measure, and even by the whole granary.

units.la: Men. Prol. v.15.
units.tr: Men. Prol. v.15.

units.la: FULLONUM. FULLONIÆ.
units.tr: FULLERS. FULLING.

units.la: VEstes dicebantur apud fullones consiliari, quando cogebantur. Ejusmodi coacta vestimenta vocabantur Feltra. τὰ ἀπ τεγχαν σωπεσμενα.
units.tr: Garments that were pressed together were called consiliari among fullers. Such pressed garments were called Feltra. [τὰ ἀπὸ τεγχαν σωπεσμενα]

units.la: Pseud. 1.2. v. 13. Consiliata tapetia.
units.tr: Pseud. 1.2, v. 13: pressed rugs.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut. Consiliare: quod est σημπιχὼν, πιέζειν, ἢ συμπάτησαν.
units.tr: See the Plautus lexicon under Consiliare: which means to press together, to squeeze, or to trample down [σημπιχὼν, πιέζειν, ἢ συμπάτησαν].

units.la: Vide Scalig. ad Varronem, & Isidor. lib. 6. cap. 16. & Plin. lib. 8. cap. 48.
units.tr: See Scaliger on Varro, Isidore book 6 chapter 16, and Pliny book 8 chapter 48.

units.la: Et Laur. Pignorium Tract. De Servis, pag. 182.
units.tr: And Lorenzo Pignorio, De Servis, p. 182.

units.la: Fullonum duo erant officia. Vestem eluere, & cogere: quae sic elota, & coacta incretataq; indurescit. Unde formula illa Comicorum petita: Nequeo durare.
units.tr: Fullers had two tasks: to wash clothes and to press them. Clothes that were washed and pressed in this way, and stiffened with chalk, become hard. Hence the phrase borrowed from the comic poets: "I cannot hold out" (Nequeo durare).

units.la: Fullones in dealbandis pannis & expurgandis, eos manibus pedibusq; calcabant & percutiebant. Quo allusit puer lenonius Pseud. 3.1. v.16.
units.tr: Fullers, when whitening and cleaning cloths, trampled and beat them with hands and feet. The pimp's slave in Pseud. 3.1, v. 16, alludes to this.

units.la: Fullones vestes cogendo illas dicebantur durare, obdurare.
units.tr: Fullers, by pressing garments, were said to harden them (durare, obdurare).

units.la: Asin. 2.2. v. 56. μεταφορικῶς.
units.tr: Asin. 2.2, v. 56: used metaphorically.

units.la: Unde id verbum translate postmodum fuit usurpatum.
units.tr: Hence that word was afterwards used in a transferred sense.

units.la: Asin. 2.2. v.56. μεταφορικῶς.
units.tr: Asin. 2.2, v. 56: used metaphorically.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut. Durare: & Jani Gulielmij Verisimil. lib. 2. c. 8. Coleri Parerg. c. 34. Fullones, ut & cloacarij in luto & stercore constituti guttur sæ- pè proluunt.
units.tr: See the Plautus lexicon under Durare: and Janus Gulielmius, Verisimilia, book 2 chapter 8; Coler, Parerga chapter 34. Fullers, like sewer-workers standing in mud and dung, often rinse their throats.

units.la: Rud. 3.6. v.46. ἀλλὰ γοερὰς.
units.tr: Rud. 3.6, v. 46: "but mournful ones" [ἀλλὰ γοερὰς].

units.la: Vide Tit. Convivy: Bibenda.
units.tr: See the title Convivy: Bibenda (Drinking).

units.la: Fulminis. Tonitru. Cæli. Meteororum.
units.tr: Of Lightning. Of Thunder. Of the Sky. Of Meteors.

units.la: Fulmina arboribus infesta in agris.
units.tr: Lightning hostile to trees in the fields.

units.la: In scenis machinæ fuerunt, quibus tonitrua excitata, dictæ Ἀστραπαὶ, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀστράπτειν.
units.tr: On the stage there were machines by which thunder was produced; they were called Astrapae [Ἀστραπαὶ], from the verb to lighten [ἀστράπτειν].

units.la: Vide Cæl. Rhodig. lib. 8. cap. 8. & P. Crin. lib. 2. c. 10. & Jul. Cæs. Bulenng. de Theatro.
units.tr: See Cael. Rhodig. lib. 8. cap. 8, and P. Crin. lib. 2. c. 10, and Jul. Caes. Bulenger, de Theatro.

units.la: Funeris. Sepulchri. Sepulturæ. Luctus.
units.tr: Funerals. Sepulchres. Burial. Mourning.

units.la: Vide infra plura in hanc rem Tit. Mortis.
units.tr: See below, under the title Death, for more on this subject.

units.la: APud veteres cadaver albâ veste indutum post efflatam animam, cubiculo efferebant, & ablutum, unctum, coronatum, in vestibulo ædium ad januam ipsam collocabant: ita ut pedes in viam spectarent: hoc situ abitionem illam postremam significantes: idq; dicebatur Collocatio, εἰς ὕπνον. Illudit Plautus Aul. 5.6. v.30. Tum tu idem optimum est, loces ss. rendum. nam jam credo mortuus est. Rud. 3.2.v.46. Porrigite hoc pedibus hominem, stem quasi occisam suem.
units.tr: Among the ancients, the corpse, clothed in white after the soul had breathed out, was carried out of the bedroom. Once washed, anointed and garlanded, it was laid in the vestibule of the house, right at the door, with the feet turned toward the street. By this posture they signified that final departure. This was called collocatio, and [εἰς ὕπνον, into sleep]. Plautus makes sport of this in the Aulularia 5.6, v. 30: "Then you too, it's best to have him laid out for the funeral, for now I believe he is dead." In the Rudens 3.2, v. 46: "Stretch this man out feet first; he is like a pig just slaughtered."

units.la: Hunc morem quoq; tangit Seneca Ep. 99.
units.tr: Seneca also touches on this custom, Epistle 99.

units.la: Quàm multis cum maximè funus locatur ? quàm multis vitalia eruuntur ? quàm multi post luctum tuum lugent ?
units.tr: "How many people are hired for funerals just now? How many have their vitals torn out? How many weep after your mourning?"

units.la: Val. Antias lib. 75.
units.tr: Valerius Antias, book 75.

units.la: Deinde funere locato, ad forum descendit.
units.tr: "Then, the funeral having been contracted, he went down to the forum."

units.la: Apul. lib. 3. Florid.
units.tr: Apuleius, Florida book 3.

units.la: Frenum nigens locatum, scil. efferendum, & urendum à Libita-rijs.
units.tr: "A funeral let out," namely, to be carried out and burned by the Libitinarii.

units.la: Allusum quoq; quidam putant ad ritum hunc in joco Amph. I. I. v. 147.
units.tr: Some think this also alludes in jest to this custom, in the Amphitryo 1.1, v. 147.

units.la: Ego vix affirmarim, cùm sensus inibi aliter constet.
units.tr: I could hardly assert it, since the sense there stands otherwise.

units.la: Vide Kirchmannum de Funeribus Romanorum: nec non Meurfium: de eodem argumento.
units.tr: See Kirchmann on Roman funerals, and also Meursius on the same subject.

units.la: SOLEBANT etiam veteres cum ijs, qui Libitinam exercebant, certo pretio contrahere, ut omnem funeris apparatum suis sumti-bus præstarent.
units.tr: The ancients also used to contract, for a fixed price, with those who ran the Libitina, so that they would supply the whole funeral equipment at their own expense.

units.la: Quò referri quoq; potest locus Plauti paulò ante nominatus.
units.tr: The passage of Plautus named a little earlier may also be referred here.
Aulularia 3.6, v. 30.

units.la: Cedundum ego illum conduxi. EV. Tum tu idem, optimum est, loces efferendum.
units.tr: "I have hired that man for the burial." EV. "Then you too, it's best to have him laid out for the funeral."

units.la: IN funere imagines præferri solitæ mortuis.
units.tr: At funerals, the images of the dead were customarily carried in front.

units.la: Quo allusit Sofia Amph. I. 1. v. 301.
units.tr: Sosia alludes to this in the Amphitryo 1.1, v. 301.

units.la: Ubi tamen alij ad Ludos funebres illud referunt, quod dicit Sofia:
units.tr: Others, however, refer to funeral games what Sosia says:

units.la: Vivofit, quod numquam quisquam mortuo faciet mihi: h. e. Nunc mihi ludi fiunt: h. e, nunc ego ludificor probè, cui nullus postea ludos facere volet in morte. Fortassis referri quoq; possit ad morem illum, cujus meminit Dionysius Halicarnasseus lib. VII. pag. 477.
units.tr: "It is a living thing, which no one will ever do for me when I am dead," that is, now games are made for me; now I am properly made a fool of, since no one will want to hold games for me after my death. Perhaps it may also be referred to that custom which Dionysius of Halicarnassus mentions in book 7, p. 477.

units.la: Greek line: ἐδἰοr διὰ ἡ ἀνδρῶν ὅπα ἰμάων ταφαῖς ἅμα ἕ ἄλλαις πομπαῖς σεσημ-μένης μένες τῆς κλίνης τὲς σατυρικὰς χορὺς κινουμένας τῷ σικίννῳ ὀρχη-σιν, μάλιςα ἢ ἐν τοῖς ἐκδημίοις κήδεσι. Hoc est: Quin &c in il-lustriam virorum funebribus pompis inter cateros feretrum præcedentes vidi Choros Satyricos, qui ficinnen saltarent maximè in divitum exequiis.
units.tr: [Greek passage, Dionysius of Halicarnassus.] "Indeed, I have seen at the funerals of illustrious men, among the other pomps that preceded the bier, satyr choruses dancing the [σικίννῳ ὄρχησιν, sikinnis] dance, especially at the funerals of the rich."

units.la: Tangit eundem morem Suetonius Tiberio cap. 57. & Vespasia-no cap. 19.
units.tr: Suetonius touches on the same custom in Tiberius 57 and Vespasian 19.

units.la: Cadavere jam ustulato, cæterisq; omnibus ritè peractis præfi-ca altâ voce pronunciabat Ilicet. Ad quem ritum omninò illud referendum, quod dicitur Asin. 3.3.v.4.
units.tr: When the body had been burned and all the other rites duly performed, the praefica pronounced "Ilicet" in a loud voice. To this rite must certainly be referred what is said in the Asinaria 3.3, v. 4:

units.la: Mater mihi supremum tua dixit.
units.tr: "Your mother has spoken the last words to me."

units.la: Virgil. lib 6. teste Servio, nominat novissima verba, quibus pro-latis, tùm demùm cuncti, qui comitati funus ad se redituri ex-tremum Vale clamant.
units.tr: Virgil, book 6, according to Servius, names the novissima verba, the last words. When these had been uttered, all who had accompanied the funeral, about to return home, at last cried out the final "Farewell."

units.la: Idem Virgil. lib. 11. supremum vocat:
units.tr: The same Virgil, in book 11, calls it supremum:

units.la: Condimus & magnâ supremum voce ciemus.
units.tr: "We also gather together and call out the last words with a loud voice."

units.la: Quintil. Declamat. 8.
units.tr: Quintilian, Declamations 8.

units.la: Vidimus frequenter ad vitam post conclamata suprema re-deuntes.
units.tr: "We have often seen men return to life after the last rites had already been cried over them."

units.la: Aliter tamen Turneb. lib. 3. c. 2. interpretatur locum Plauti re-ferens omnia ad supremam sententiam in judicijs.
units.tr: Turnebus, however, in book 3, chapter 2, interprets the passage of Plautus differently, referring everything to the final sentence in judgments.

units.la: Vide Turnebum: & Jani Doufæ Fil. Notas ad Catullum cap. 6. pag. 39.
units.tr: See Turnebus, and the notes of Janus Dousa's son on Catullus, chapter 6, p. 39.

units.la: In funeribus ab amicis & propinquis ossa collecta: quorsum allu-ditur Capt. 4.2.v.18.
units.tr: After funerals, the bones were gathered up by friends and relatives. This is alluded to in the Captivi 4.2, v. 18:

units.la: Dentilegos omnes mortalės faciam.
units.tr: "I will make all mortals tooth-gatherers."

units.la: Simile est illud Martialis lib. 8. Epigr. 57.
units.tr: Similar is the epigram of Martial, book 8, epigram 57:

units.la: Tres habuit dentes: &c.
units.tr: "He had three teeth," etc.

units.la: Vide Kirchman. de funeribus Romanorum lib. 3. c. 6. De ossi le-gio veterum.
units.tr: See Kirchmann on Roman funerals, book 3, chapter 6, on the gathering of the bones among the ancients.

units.la: Cadavera mortuorum per pollinctores sepulturæ mandaban-tur.
units.tr: Corpses of the dead were handed over to the undertakers (pollinctores) for burial.

units.la: Alludit noster Afin. 5.2. v. 61.
units.tr: Our author alludes to this in the Asinaria 5.2, v. 61:

units.la: Ecquis currit pollinctorem arcessere ?
units.tr: "Is there anyone who will run to fetch the undertaker?"

units.la: Q. d. Dæmenetus jam metu exanimatus est, ut pænè mortuus fit: eóq; pollinctore opus habeat.
units.tr: That is: Demaenetus has been struck lifeless with fear, so that he is almost dead and therefore needs an undertaker.

units.la: De pollinctore vide Lexicon. Plaut.
units.tr: On the pollinctor, see the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: Mortui dicebantur efferri. Epid. 2.1. v. 6. Aul. 2.1. v. 34.
units.tr: The dead were said to be carried out (efferri). Epidicus 2.1, v. 6; Aulularia 2.1, v. 34.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut. Efferre. Afin. 3.3. 4.25. Ter. And. Effertur: imus.
units.tr: See the Plautine lexicon, under efferre. Asinaria 3.3; 4.2.5. Terence, Andria: "He is being carried out; let us go."

units.la: Formula antiqua indictivorum funerum talis erat: TITIUS. VIXIT. L. TITIO. EXEQUIAS. IRE. CUI. COMMODUM, EST. HEM. TEMPUS. OLLUS. ECFERTUR.
units.tr: The old formula for announcing funerals ran thus: TITIUS LIVED. TO TITIUS THE FUNERAL RITES. LET WHOEVER IT SUITS COME; IT IS TIME. HE IS CARRIED OUT.

units.la: ORCO etiam hostias immolabant. Epid. 2.1. v. 7.
units.tr: They also sacrificed victims to Orcus. Epidicus 2.1, v. 7.

units.la: IN funeribus ab exequijs convivium funebre dabatur, neq; fas fuit degustare quicquam ex eo, qui intulissent: sed tantum cernere silentio: unde silicernium dictum. Qui vero lucri causa nefanda omnia subire non verebantur, Bustirapi convitio audiebant.
units.tr: At funerals, after the rites, a funeral banquet was given. Those who had carried the body might not taste anything from it, but could only look on in silence; hence it was called silicernium. Those, however, who for gain were not ashamed to undertake all these unholy things, were given the insulting name bustirapi, grave-robbers.
Pseudolus 1.3, v. 126.

units.la: Vide Jani Guliel. Verisim.lib.3.c.12. & Kirchm. de Funer. Rom. lib. 4. cap. 12.
units.tr: See Janus Gulielmus, Verisimilia book 3, chapter 12, and Kirchmann on Roman funerals, book 4, chapter 12.

units.la: AD sepulcra demortuorum præficæ næniam lugubrem edebant. Illa carmina Præficarum, Nugæ dictæ; & Mortalia.
units.tr: At the tombs of the dead, the praeficae sang a mournful dirge. Their songs were called nugae and mortalia.
Asinaria 4.1, v. 63.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut. Nænia.
units.tr: See the Plautine lexicon, under naenia.
Bacchides 3.4, v. 22; Truculentus 2.1, v. 3.

units.la: Tralatè de muribus confossis in muscipulâ Plautus Bacch. 4. 8. v. 48.
units.tr: Figuratively, of mice pierced in a trap, Plautus, Bacchides 4.8, v. 48.

units.la: IN funeribus eædem præficæ mulieres alios collaudabant, se verò non poterant. Truc. 2.8. v. 14.
units.tr: At funerals the same praeficae women praised others, but could not praise themselves. Truculentus 2.8, v. 14.

units.la: Vide de his Authores eos, qui de Funeribus Rom. scripserunt: Meursium & Kirchmannum.
units.tr: On these matters, see the authors who wrote about Roman funerals: Meursius and Kirchmann.

units.la: Qui moriebantur, dicebantur Abire in locum communem: itemq; ἀπελθεῖν εἰς τὸς πλείονας.
units.tr: Those who died were said "to go to the common place," and likewise [ἀπελθεῖν εἰς τοὺς πλείονας, to go to the many].

units.la: Dicebantur etiam Absintes: quemadmodum Vivi superstites: præsentes.
units.tr: They were also called absentes, just as the living were called superstites and praesentes.

units.la: Casin. Prol. v. 19. Trin. 2.2.v.14.
units.tr: Casina, Prologue v. 19; Trinummus 2.2, v. 14.

units.la: Me ad plures penetravi.
units.tr: "I have gone to join the many."

units.la: Sic autem loquebantur καὶ ἐυφημισμὸν. Et sepulchretum vocabant πολυάνδειον. Dicebantur quoq; μακάριοι, Felices.
units.tr: They spoke in this way, [καὶ εὐφημισμόν, by euphemism]. They also called a burial ground [πολυάνδειον, a common grave]. The dead were also called [μακάριοι, blessed], that is, happy.

units.la: Horat. lib. 1. Sat. 9.
units.tr: Horace, Satires book 1, satire 9.

units.la: Omnes composui felices: nunc ego resto: Confice.
units.tr: "I have laid all the happy ones to rest; now I remain. Finish it off."

units.la: Plaut. Pœn. 5.1.v.25. Eum fecisse ajunt, sibi quod faciundum fuit.
units.tr: Plautus, Poenulus 5.1, v. 25: "They say he did what had to be done for himself."

units.la: Et 5.2.v.125. Si quid me suat.
units.tr: And 5.2, v. 125: "If anything should happen to me."

units.la: Vide etiam Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: See also the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: Viri uxoribus suis, quarum obitu tamen delestati, justa facie-bant. τὰ δεῖα νόμιμα.
units.tr: Husbands performed the proper rites for their wives, though they were glad of their death: [τὰ θεῖα νόμιμα, the divine customs].
Cistellaria 1.3, v. 28.

units.la: Cadavera demortuorum cremabantur in rogo extra portam Metiam, sive Esquilinam. Cas. 2.6. v.2.
units.tr: The bodies of the dead were burned on a pyre outside the Metian gate, or the Esquiline gate. Casina 2.6, v. 2.

units.la: Inde cineres in sepulchrum & urnam recondebant. Men. 1. 2. v.43 & 3.2. v. 27. ἀλλην οεικῶς.
units.tr: From there they put the ashes into a tomb and an urn. Menaechmi 1.2, v. 43 and 3.2, v. 27.

units.la: In sepulchris veteres thesauros condebant, partim luxûs, partim majoris securitatis ergò.
units.tr: In tombs the ancients stored away treasures, partly for luxury and partly for greater security.

units.la: Pseud. 1.4. v.20. ἀλλην οεικῶς.
units.tr: Pseudolus 1.4, v. 20.

units.la: Vide etiam Freheri Parerga lib.1.c.4. & Kirchm.de Funer.Rom. lib.3. c.24.
units.tr: See also Freher, Parerga book 1, chapter 4, and Kirchmann on Roman funerals, book 3, chapter 24.

units.la: Unde & hoc liquet, aliam fuisse rationem sepulchrorum apud veteres, atq; hodie est. Illa enim fornicata fuêre: neq; obrüeban-tur terrâ. Idem ex historiâ Evangelicâ non est obscurum..
units.tr: From this it is also clear that the ancients had a different way of building tombs from ours today. For those were vaulted, and were not buried under earth. The same point is not obscure from the Gospel history.

units.la: Cæterum de sepulchris egregiè commentatus est doctissimus Me-ursius lib. 3. Exerc. Crit, cap. 20. quæ non pigebit huc addere.
units.tr: Otherwise, the most learned Meursius has discussed tombs admirably in Exercitationes Criticae book 3, chapter 20, which I will not be sorry to add here.

units.la: Sepulchra Romanos juxta vias habuisse satis constat: ut & Græ- cos. Patet ex Idyll. Theocr. v i i.
units.tr: It is well established that the Romans, like the Greeks, had tombs beside the roads. This is clear from Theocritus, Idyll 7.

units.la: κεῖπω τὰν μεζάτων ὁδὸν ἀνυμες, ὃς ἐς τὸ σῆμα ἀμὶν τῷ Βρασίλα κατεφαίνετο --
units.tr: [Greek verse from Theocritus, Idyll 7: "Let us go by the great road, which at the tomb of Brasilas appears to us..."]

units.la: Primitus tamen in ædibus ea constituebant.
units.tr: At first, however, they set them up in their houses.

units.la: Isidorus Orig. x v. cap. i i.
units.tr: Isidore, Origines book 15, chapter 11.

units.la: Sepulchrum a sepulto dictum est. Prius autem in domo sua quis- que sepeliebatur.
units.tr: "A tomb is so named from the one buried (sepultus). Formerly, however, each person was buried in his own house."

units.la: Inde Lares coli cæperunt.
units.tr: Hence the Lares began to be worshipped.

units.la: Servius Æneid. v i.
units.tr: Servius on the Aeneid book 6.

units.la: Apud majores omnes homines in suis domibus sepeliebantur. un- de ortum est, ut Lares colerentur in Ædibus.
units.tr: Among the ancients, all men were buried in their own houses, whence it came about that the Lares were worshipped in the homes.

units.la: Atq; erant cellæ isti usui, quæ postea translatæ etiam extra urbem.
units.tr: And those cells, which served this purpose, were afterwards moved outside the city as well.

units.la: Petronius Satyrico:
units.tr: Petronius, in the Satyricon:

units.la: In conditorium etiam profequuta est defunctum, positumq; in Hypogeo Græco more corpus custodire ac flere totis noctibus diebusq; capit.
units.tr: "She followed the dead man even to the burial vault, and, with the body placed in a hypogeum in the Greek manner, she began to keep watch over it and weep through whole nights and days."

units.la: Origo earum Græca, quod satis etiam declarat Petronius: & con- stat ex Phlegonte Tralliano περὶ θαυμ. ἡ μακρόβ. cujus hæc sunt verba:
units.tr: Their origin is Greek, as Petronius also sufficiently shows, and it is established from Phlegon of Tralles, On Marvels, whose words are these:

units.la: Ἀναχθέισης δὲ ὑφ' ἡμῶν τῆς καμάρας εἰς ἣν πάντες οἱ οἰκεῖοι μετα- κάσοντες ἐτίθεντο, ὅτι μὴ τῶν ἄλλων κλινῶν ἐφάνη τὰ σώμα- τα κείμενα.
units.tr: When the vault into which all the relatives were carrying and laying out their dead was opened by us, the bodies were seen lying apart from the other couches [Ἀναχθέισης δὲ ὑφ' ἡμῶν τῆς καμάρας εἰς ἣν πάντες οἱ οἰκεῖοι μετακομίζοντες ἐτίθεντο, ὅτι μὴ τῶν ἄλλων κλινῶν ἐφάνη τὰ σώματα κείμενα].

units.la: Sciendum itaque sepulcra aut fuisse privis hominibus facta, vel conjugibus, aut omni familiæ posterisq;. Privorum appellaban- tur Requietoria.
units.tr: It should be understood that tombs were made either for private individuals, or for spouses, or for an entire family and its descendants. Those made for private individuals were called Requietoria (resting-places).

units.la: Inscriptio vetus: pag. 954. i.
units.tr: Ancient inscription: p. 954, no. 1.

units.la: P. Scantius. Philetus. Fecit. Sibi. Et Scantiæ. Nice. Lib. Requietorium.
units.tr: P. Scantius Philetus made this for himself and for Scantia Nice, his freedwoman: a resting-place.

units.la: Vide etiam alias Inscriptiones pag. 883.4. 1030.8. 1094.8. Lycophron ἐυαςήειον. Loci apud J C. & Inscriptionibus. Augustinus de Civitate Dei lib. i.c.i. Testantur hoc martyrum loca, & basilicæ Apostolorum. Item Ossuaria. In veteri Inscriptione JULIA. FUSCINIA. OSSUARIUM. VIVA. SIBI. FECIT. Et Cineraria in alia Inscriptione. Unde Cinerarij, qui cineraria, & reliquias martyrum honorabant, apud Hieronymum Epistolam quadam ad Riparium:
units.tr: See also the other inscriptions at p. 883.4, 1030.8 and 1094.8. Lycophron [ἐυαςήειον]. Places mentioned by the jurists and in inscriptions. Augustine, City of God, bk 1, ch. 1, testifies to this, as do the places of the martyrs and the basilicas of the Apostles. Likewise ossuaries: in an old inscription, JULIA FUSCINIA MADE THIS OSSUARY FOR HERSELF WHILE ALIVE. And cinerary urns in another inscription. Hence the Cinerarii, who honoured the ashes and relics of the martyrs, are mentioned by Jerome in a letter to Riparius.

units.la: Au Vigilantium osfœtidum vursus aperire, & putorem spurcissimum contra Sanctorum proferre reliquias, & nos qui eas suspicimus appellare Cinerarios, & idololatras, qui mortuorum hominum ossa veneremur.
units.tr: You open your foul-smelling mouth, Vigilantius, and pour out the most filthy stench against the relics of the saints, and you call us, who venerate them, Cinerarii and idolaters, who worship the bones of dead men.

units.la: Toti familiæ & posteris facta sepulchra notum est ex solemni illa formulâ Inscriptionum veterum:
units.tr: That tombs were made for the whole family and its descendants is clear from that formula, so common in ancient inscriptions:

units.la: FECIT SIBI POSTERISQUE SUIS.
units.tr: MADE THIS FOR HIMSELF AND HIS DESCENDANTS.

units.la: Ovidius Metamorph. lib. xiii.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses, bk 13.

units.la: At puto funeribus dotabere regia virgo, (condeturq; tuum monimentis corpus avitis.
units.tr: But I think, royal maiden, you will be honoured with funeral rites, and your body will be laid in your ancestors' tombs.

units.la: Lapis vetus: TERNOS. CINERES. EX. HISPANIA EXPORTATE. COMMUNIQUE SEPULCRO. CONDITE. QUO AVITIS. CINERIBUS. IMMIXTI SACRO. GAUDEANT. ANNIVERSARIO. PARENTARI.
units.tr: Old stone: "Carry three urns of ashes out of Spain, and bury them in the common tomb, where, mixed with ancestral ashes, they may rejoice in the sacred annual parentalia."

units.la: Solinus cap. v.
units.tr: Solinus, ch. 5.

units.la: Quorum reliquiæ in Conditorio Salustianorum videntur.
units.tr: Their remains are seen in the Conditorium of the Sallustii.

units.la: Quintil. Declam. xi.
units.tr: Quintilian, Declamations, no. 11.

units.la: Miser ego nec ad cadaver accessi, non in sepulcra majorum meis manibus intuli.
units.tr: Wretched that I am, I did not even approach the corpse, nor did I carry it with my own hands into my ancestors' tombs.

units.la: Dicebantur autem ea Loci Communes.
units.tr: These were called common places.

units.la: Artemidorus lib.i. cap. LXXX. vide paulò ante ex Cafinâ: & Lexic. Plautin.
units.tr: Artemidorus, bk 1, ch. 80; see above from Casina, and the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: Cicer. Verr. VI.
units.tr: Cicero, Verrines, bk 6.

units.la: Dico nihil istum ejusmodi rerum in provincia reliquisse: nihil in aedibus cuiusquam ne in oppidis quidem, nihil in Locis communibus, ne in fanis quidem.
units.tr: I say that he left nothing of that kind in the province: nothing in anyone's house, not even in the towns; nothing in the common places, not even in the temples.

units.la: Iustinianus Instit. l. 2. Titul. 1. In communem autem locum purum invito socio inferre non licet. Etiam familiaria sepulcra.
units.tr: Justinian, Institutes, bk 2, tit. 1: "But it is not lawful to bring a body into a common place against the will of a partner." Also family tombs.

units.la: Item hereditaria. ff. lib. 11. Tit. 7. Familiaria sepulcra dicuntur, quae quis sibi familiaeq; suae constituit. Hereditaria autem, quae quis sibi haeredibusq; suis constituit.
units.tr: Likewise hereditary tombs. Digest, bk 11, tit. 7: Family tombs are those which someone has established for himself and his family. Hereditary tombs are those which someone has established for himself and his heirs.

units.la: Qui alibi sepeliebantur, ἀπόταφοι nominabantur. Harpocration. ἀπόταφοι ἀντὶ τῶν ἀπισεφημένων τῶν ἀγοραίων τάφων. Erant praeterea publica sepulcra, in quibus nimirum ij locabantur, qui honoris ergò de publico sepeliebantur.
units.tr: Those who were buried elsewhere were called apotaphoi [ἀπόταφοι]. Harpocration: apotaphoi are those denied burial in the public tombs of the market-place [ἀπόταφοι ἀντὶ τῶν ἀπεσφημένων τῶν ἀγοραίων τάφων]. There were also public tombs, in which, of course, those were placed who were buried at public expense as a mark of honour.

units.la: Mentio eorum apud Siculum Flaccum lib. de Conditionibus agrorum.
units.tr: Siculus Flaccus mentions them in his book on the conditions of fields.

units.la: Auctores divisionis assignationisque leges quasdam coloniis describunt, ut qui agri delubris sepulcrisq; publicis, qui solis itineris viae actus ambitus ductusq; aquarum, qui publicis utilitatibus servierint: ad id usq; tempus, quo agri divisiones fierent, in eadem conditione esse, quā ante fuerant.
units.tr: The authors of the division and assignment describe certain laws for the colonies: that the fields which belong to shrines and public tombs, and those which serve the road of the sun, the paths, roads, drives, courses of the aqueducts, and public uses, should remain in the same condition they were in before, until the time when the fields were divided.

units.la: Solita autem strui sepulcra in finibus agrorum juxta vias, nisi si steriles aut saxuosi essent, quippe tùm etiam in eorum meditullio fiebant. Testatur idem Flaccus loco citato.
units.tr: Tombs were usually built on the boundaries of fields beside the roads, unless the land was barren or rocky; indeed, they were then made even in the middle of the fields. Flaccus testifies to this in the passage cited.

units.la: Huc addenda & illa loca, quae loquuntur de sepulchris in Praedijs Haereditarijs.
units.tr: To this should be added those passages which speak of tombs on hereditary estates.

units.la: Ulpianus lib. xxv. ad Edictum:
units.tr: Ulpian, bk 25, on the Edict:

units.la: Si venditor fundi exceperit locum sepulchri, ad hoc, ut ipse, posteriq; ejus illo inferrentur.
