units.tr: If the seller of an estate has reserved a place for a tomb, so that he himself and his descendants may be carried into it.

units.la: Celsus lib. iii. Digestorum:
units.tr: Celsus, bk 3 of the Digest:

units.la: Defundo alieno, quem imprudens emerat, in eoq; aedificaverat: sin- gepan. gepauperem, qui si reddereid cogatur, laribus, sepulcris avitis carendum habeat.
units.tr: A man who unknowingly bought another's land and built on it, if he is compelled to give it back, must be left without his household gods and ancestral tombs, a poor man, that is.

units.la: In Lege Solonis apud Cajum lib. iv. ad xii. Ἐὰν τις αἱμαςίαν παρ᾽ ἀλλοτρίῳ χωρίῳ ὀρύξῃ, τὸν ὅρον μὴ παρααβαίνειν. ἐὰν τείχιον, πόδα ἐπολίπειν. ἐὰν δὲ οἰκίημα, δύο πόδας. ἐὰν δὲ τάφου, ἢ βόθρου ὀ- ςύτλη, ὃ ζῶν τὸ βάθος ἤ, τοσοῦτον ἐπολίπειν.
units.tr: From Solon's law, cited by Gaius, bk 4, on the Twelve Tables: "If anyone digs a stone fence on another's land, he shall not cross the boundary. If a small wall, he shall leave a foot; if a building, two feet; and if a tomb or a pit, he shall leave as much as the depth of the excavation" [Ἐὰν τις αἱμασίαν παρ' ἀλλοτρίῳ χωρίῳ ὀρύξῃ, τὸν ὅρον μὴ παραβαίνειν. ἐὰν τείχιον, πόδα ἀπολείπειν. ἐὰν δὲ οἴκημα, δύο πόδας. ἐὰν δὲ τάφου ἢ βόθρου ὀρύγματα, ὅ ζῶν τὸ βάθος ἦ, τοσοῦτον ἀπολείπειν].

units.la: Apulejus lib. ix. Milesi.
units.tr: Apuleius, bk 9, Metamorphoses (the Milesian tales).

units.la: Iam q; totum frugalitate spoliatum, ipsis etiam glebulis exterminare gestiebat: siniumq; inani commotā quæstione, terram totam sibi vendicabat. Tunc agrestis, verecundus alioquin, avaritia divitiæ jam spoliatus, ut suo saltim sepulcro paternum retineret solum, amicos plurimos ad demonstrationem finium, trepidans eximiè corrogarat.
units.tr: Now, having stripped him of all his thrift, he was eager to drive him off even from his little clods; and, raising a pointless dispute over the boundary, he claimed the whole land for himself. Then the countryman, otherwise modest but already robbed of his wealth by avarice, anxiously gathered very many friends to point out the boundaries, so that at least he might keep his ancestral soil for his own tomb.

units.la: Meminit & Quintilianus lib. vii. cap. ix.
units.tr: Quintilian also mentions it, bk 7, ch. 9.

units.la: Ambrosius Sermone de Passione S. Agnetis:
units.tr: Ambrose, sermon on the Passion of St Agnes:

units.la: Parentes vero ejus nullam penitus tristitiam habentes, cum omni gaudio abstulerunt corpus ejus, et posuerunt illud in prædiolo suo, non longè ab Urbe, in viâ, quæ dicitur Numentana.
units.tr: Her parents, having no sadness at all, carried away her body with every joy and placed it on their little estate, not far from the city, on the road called Nomentana.

units.la: Unde & hæ notæ apud Valer. Probum: In Fr. P. vi. In Ag. P. x. In fronte pedes sex, in agro pedes decem, quæ totics in Epitaphijs lapidibus. Qui verò tàm pauperes, ut nec prædiolum, nec locum sepulturæ avitum haberent, extra portam Metiam, quæ & Esquilina, sepeliebantur, vel comburebantur. Plautus Casin. 2. 6. v. 2. Illum adepol videre ardentem te extra portam Metiam credo ecasftor te velle. Vel etiam abijciebantur, tàm tenuiq; terrâ ingerebantur, ut insepulti viderentur.
units.tr: Hence also these notations in Valerius Probus: "In Fr. P. vi. In Ag. P. x. Six feet at the frontage, ten feet in depth," which is how it is on epitaph stones so many times. Those who were so poor that they had neither a little estate nor an ancestral burial place were buried or burned outside the Metian gate, also called the Esquiline. Plautus, Casina 2.6: "I think you want to see him burning outside the Metian gate, by Castor." Or they were even thrown away and covered with so thin a layer of earth that they seemed unburied.

units.la: Horatius: Post in sepulta membra different lupi, Et Esquilinæ alites.
units.tr: Horace: Afterwards the wolves and the Esquiline birds tear the unburied limbs.

units.la: Ubi & nocentes divexabantur, Cornel. Tacit. lib. xi. Annal. Hic feræ & puticuli.
units.tr: Here also the guilty were dragged off, as Cornelius Tacitus says, Annals, bk 11. Here were the wild beasts and the pauper pits.

units.la: De quibus vide Festum Pompejum.
units.tr: On these, see Festus Pompeius.

units.la: FRUSTRA lugemus ea, quæ præteriére. Truc. 4. 2. v. 17.
units.tr: It is in vain that we lament what has gone by. Truculentus 4.2, v. 17.

units.la: Thetis lamentando lessum fecit filio frustra.
units.tr: Thetis, lamenting, made a lessus for her son in vain.

units.la: De Lesso vide Authores de Funeribus Roman. & Lexicon Plautinum.
units.tr: On the lesso, see the writers on Roman funerals and the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: IN funere lugubrem ejulationem emittebant, quam lessum appellarunt.
units.tr: At funerals they uttered a mournful wailing, which they called the lesso.
Aulularia 4.9, v. 17.

units.la: Horat. Eppd. 10.
units.tr: Horace, Epodes 10.

units.la: Et illa non-virilis ejulatio.
units.tr: And that unmanly wailing.

units.la: IN Funeribus adhibiti Locarij, sive Dissignatores.
units.tr: At funerals there were employed the locarii, or dissignatores.

units.la: Pœn. Prol. v. 19.
units.tr: Poenulus, prologue, v. 19.

units.la: Vide Tit. Fabularum. Et Lipsius de Amphit. cap. 15.
units.tr: See the title Fabularum. And Lipsius, On the Amphitheatre, ch. 15.

units.la: IN funeribus proximi hæredes aderant.
units.tr: At funerals the nearest heirs were present.

units.la: Men. 3. 2. v. 8. ἀλληγοεικῶς.
units.tr: Menaechmi 3.2, v. 8: allegorically [ἀλληγορικῶς].

units.la: FURUM. FURTI. RAPINÆ. ZONARIORUM.
units.tr: THIEVES. THEFT. ROBBERY. OF THE ZONARII.

units.la: QUI dolo malo aliena bona eripiebant, damnabantur ad quadruplum pretium solvendum.
units.tr: Those who by wicked fraud snatched away other people's goods were condemned to pay four times the price.

units.la: Perf. 1. 2. v. 10. de Parasito:
units.tr: Persa 1.2 v.10, on the Parasite:

units.la: Neque quadruplari me volo. nam enim decet sine meo periculo aliena bona ereptum ire.
units.tr: I do not want to be made to pay fourfold, for it is right to walk away with other people's goods snatched away without risk to myself.

units.la: Sic Plinius Paneg.
units.tr: So Pliny, Panegyricus:

units.la: Ereptum alienas pecunias eunt? perdent quas habent.
units.tr: Do they go off having snatched other people's money? They will lose what they have.

units.la: MULTI alienorum bonorum iniquissimi sunt captatores sub specie æqui: attamen malos illos cives esse egregie docet Parasitus ille Perf. 1.2. v.10. Neq; quadruplari me volo: neq; enim decet sine meo periculo aliena bona ereptum ire. Nam q; illi, qui faciunt, mihi placent: nam publica rei causa, qui non id facit magis, quam sui quaesti, animus haud inducti potest, cum & fidelem & civem esse & virum bonum: sed legirupam quidem, ni duit in publicum diminuum; atq; etiam mea lege adscribitor, ubi quadruplator cupiam injexit manum, tantidem ille illi rursum injiciat manum, ut aequa parte prodeant ad Treviros.
units.tr: Many are the most unjust seekers of other people's goods under the appearance of fairness. Yet that parasite in Persa 1.2 v.10 clearly shows that such men are bad citizens: I do not want to be quadrupled, for it is not right to walk away with others' goods snatched without risk to myself. For I am pleased with those who do so: for a man who does not act for the public good but only for his own gain cannot be persuaded that he is at once faithful, a citizen and a good man. But let the law of the quadrupler be... and by my law it is written that when the quadrupler lays hand on someone, let the other in turn lay hand on him, so that both go forth to the Treviri with an equal share.

units.la: Si id fiat, ne isti faxim nunquam appareant, Qui hic albo ariete aliena oppugnant bona.
units.tr: If that should happen, may those men never appear who here with the white ram attack other people's goods.

units.la: Quo in loco aliud est Quadruplari, & Quadruplatorem agere: quam vulgò apud JCtos accipitur, teste Asconio Paediano, pro accusatoribus sive Delatoribus criminum publicorum sub poena quadrupli: sive quòd ipsi ex damnatorum bonis, quos accusaverant, quartam partem consequebantur.
units.tr: In this place quadruplari and quadruplatorem agere mean something other than what is commonly understood by the jurists, as Asconius Pedianus testifies: namely accusers or informers of public crimes under penalty of fourfold, or because they themselves received a quarter of the goods of the condemned whom they had accused.

units.la: De quibus vide Turn. lib.3.c.9. Lipsi ad Tac. lib.4. Ann. & Marcell. Donat. Dilucid. in Capitolinum pag. 873. Edit. Franc. in 8. ubi ex JCtis l. 2. §. in hac actione. ff. de vi bon. rapt. docet Quadruplari pretium alicujus rei dici, cùm ejus pretium in quadruplum est.
units.tr: On these see Turnebus, book 3, ch. 9; Lipsius on Tacitus, Annals book 4; and Marcellus Donatus, Dilucidatio on Capitolinus, p. 873, ed. Francf. in 8vo, where, from the jurists (l. 2, §. in hac actione, ff. de vi bonorum raptorum), he teaches that quadruplari pretium is said of a thing when its price is quadrupled.

units.la: Sic Ulpianus:
units.tr: So Ulpian:

units.la: Intra annum utile verum pretium rei quadruplatur.
units.tr: Within the year of action, the true price of the thing is quadrupled.

units.la: Fures balneatii capitali supplicio affecti sunt, cùm caeteris dupli tantùm poena propositta esset. Rationem reddunt hanc ICti, q; propter frequentiam hominum licet furtum factum esset, tamen furem cognoscere erat difficile, & siniistrâ suspicione multis notari accidebat.
units.tr: Bath thieves were punished with capital punishment, whereas for other thieves a double penalty alone was set. The jurists give this reason: because of the crowd of people, even when a theft had been committed, it was hard to identify the thief, and it happened that many men were marked by unfounded suspicion.

units.la: Qui it lavatum in balneas, ibi cùm sedulo sua vestimenta servat, tamen surripiuntur. Fur facile quem observet, videt: custos qui fur fit, nescit.
units.tr: Whoever goes to the baths to wash, though he carefully keeps watch over his clothes, they are nevertheless stolen. The thief easily sees whom to watch; the custodian, who is himself the thief, does not know.

units.la: De his furibus vide varios Authores: Alciat. Parerg. l. 2. c.38. P. Victor. Var. Lect. l.7.17. Muret. ad Catull.carm.30. Steph. Forcatulum Necyom. Dial,28. Tertull. vocat lavantium praedones.
units.tr: On these thieves see various authors: Alciatus, Parerga l. 2, c. 38; P. Victorius, Variae Lectiones l. 7, c. 17; Muretus on Catullus, carm. 30; Stephanus, Forcatulus, Necyomantia, Dialogue 28. Tertullian calls them robbers of bathers (lavantium praedones).

units.la: Furum manus celeres sunt.
units.tr: The hands of thieves are quick.

units.la: Aul. 2.4. v. 47. Uter vestrorum est celerior?
units.tr: Aul. 2.4 v.47. Which of you is quicker?

units.la: De cocis sermo: quia & cocì inter fures.
units.tr: The discussion is about cooks, because cooks too are among the thieves.

units.la: Plaut. Fragm. Cornicularia:
units.tr: Plautus, Fragments, Cornicularia:

units.la: Litaveram, Laverna mi ne furis scelerascit manu.
units.tr: I have made my offering, Laverna; let not my hand be made criminal by theft.

units.la: Fures sunt quasi sentes: quia quicquid tangunt, secum auferunt, aut scindunt: ideoq; sub signis sunt ducendi, ut milites, ne latrocinentur.
units.tr: Thieves are like thorns: whatever they touch they carry off or tear. Therefore they must be led under standards, like soldiers, lest they commit robbery.
Casina 3.6 v.1.

units.la: Furti accusari nemo potest, nisi manifesto deprehensus. Sic adolescens se à furto liberat coram Euclione.
units.tr: No one can be accused of theft unless he is caught in the act. So the young man clears himself of theft before Euclio.

units.la: Fures sunt de genere Geryonaceo. Geryon enim Rex Hispaniarum Tricorpor, terna habuit capita, senos pedes, totidemq; manus.
units.tr: Thieves are of the Geryon kind. For Geryon, king of Spain, had three bodies, three heads, six feet, and as many hands.

units.la: Furum genus fuit: Parietum perfossores. Pseud. 4.2. v. 23. Ut vestitus est, perfossor parietum!
units.tr: There was a class of thieves: wall-borers. Pseud. 4.2 v.23. Dressed as he is, a wall-borer!

units.la: Vide Langl. Otij Semestr. pag. 488.
units.tr: See Langl., Otium Semestre, p. 488.

units.la: In metu furti aliove periculo invocabant Apollinem ἀλεξίκακον, ut Euclio Aul. 2.8. v. 24.
units.tr: In fear of theft or other danger they invoked Apollo the warder-off-of-evils (alexikakos), as Euclio does, Aul. 2.8 v.24.

units.la: Apollo quaeso subveni mihi, atq; adjuva, confige sagittis fures thesaurarios.
units.tr: Apollo, I beg you, help me and aid me; pierce the treasure-thieves with your arrows.

units.la: Hor. l.1. Sat. 9.
units.tr: Hor. l. 1, Sat. 9.

units.la: Sic me servavit Apollo.
units.tr: So Apollo saved me.

units.la: Jurisconsulti disputant, an furtum fiat in Hominibus.
units.tr: The jurists dispute whether theft can be committed against men.

units.la: Fures estis ambae: quia annos multos filias meas celavistis clam me.
units.tr: You two are thieves, for you have for many years secretly hidden my daughters from me.

units.la: Fur manifestus dici non potest, postrem in destinatum locum perlatam: latam: quamvis cum ipsâ re deprehendatur: immò ne fur quidem est, cùm dolo malo rem aliquam non contrectarit.
units.tr: A manifest thief cannot be said to be one who, though caught with the thing itself, has carried it to a designated place. Indeed he is not even a thief if he has not handled the thing with wicked intent.

units.la: Vide Francisc. Hotoman. in lib. 3. Instit. Comment.
units.tr: See Franciscus Hotomanus, commentary on Institutes book 3.

units.la: MORIS fuit, ut quem quis furem esse sciret, eum testibus præsentibus interrogaret: numquid illa res apud illum esset, aut: numquid eam contrectassei: Si negaret, res testibus ijsdem præsentibus comperiebatur.
units.tr: It was the custom that whoever someone knew to be a thief, he would ask in the presence of witnesses whether such and such a thing was with him, or whether he had handled it. If he denied it, the thing would be found in the presence of the same witnesses.

units.la: ITA versuti sæpè sunt fures, ut unus alteri inter currendum surripuerit soleam calceamenti.
units.tr: Thieves are so often crafty that, while running, one steals a shoe from another.

units.la: Sic Plauti Querol.
units.tr: So in Plautus' Querolus:

units.la: Ubinam illa est cohors fuliginosa, Vulcanosa, atra, quæ de die sub terras habitant, noctu in tectis ambulant.
units.tr: Where is that sooty, smoke-black, Vulcan's troop, which lives under the earth by day and walks about the roofs by night?

units.la: ROMÆ olim in Suburrâ majore vesperi furtivæ res venundabantur: & solé occidente mercatus illarum rerum incipiebat. Inde noster dixit:
units.tr: Long ago at Rome, in the Suburra Major, stolen goods were sold in the evening, and when the sun set the trade in those goods began. Hence our author said:

units.la: Vesperi suo vivere. h. e. furtis suis vitam sibi parare.
units.tr: To live one's evening, that is, to make a living for oneself by thefts.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Urbis Romæ.
units.tr: See also the title Urbis Romae.

units.la: FURTI suspectis excutiebant pallium, & vestes.
units.tr: Suspected thieves were searched, shaking out their cloaks and clothes.

units.la: FURES manifestarij deprehensi obtruncari poterant sine periculo.
units.tr: Manifest thieves who were caught could be clubbed to death without danger.

units.la: Aul. 3. 4. v. 10. ἀλλαγοεικός.
units.tr: Aul. 3.4 v.10. allegorically [ἀλληγορικῶς].

units.la: Capio fustem, obtrunco gallum furem manifestarium.
units.tr: I take a club and kill the cock, the manifest thief.

units.la: JURISCONSULTI disquirunt: an ædium & fundi furtum committatur.
units.tr: The jurists inquire whether theft of a building and of land can be committed.

units.la: Sic Euclio reprehenditur ab anu:
units.tr: So Euclio is rebuked by the old woman:

units.la: Quippini ego intus servem? anne quis ædes auferet?
units.tr: Why should I not keep watch indoors? Or will someone carry off the house?

units.la: Vide Scip. Gentil. lib. singulari Origin.
units.tr: See Scipio Gentilis, the separate book Origines.

units.la: Fures exploratores omnia loca contemplantur, circumspectant omnia, aedes observant, ut noctu veniant furatum.
units.tr: Thieves, spying out, survey all places, look around at everything, and watch the houses, so that they may come by night to steal.

units.la: In manifesto furto deprehensi flagris, & loris caesi.
units.tr: Those caught in manifest theft were beaten with rods and thongs.

units.la: Furtum facit, qui alterius nomen invadit.
units.tr: He commits theft who usurps another's name.

units.la: Sic matrem furtivam innuit Cistell. 2. 3. v. 15. & filias furtivas.
units.tr: So he hints at a stolen mother, Cistell. 2.3 v.15, and stolen daughters.

units.la: Furem insequentes clamabant Tene, Tene, prehende furem.
units.tr: Those pursuing the thief cried: Stop him, stop him, seize the thief!

units.la: Vide Briss. Formulas ex Petronio.
units.tr: See Brissonius, Formulae, from Petronius.

units.la: Sacrilegium maximum furtum.
units.tr: Sacrilege is the greatest theft.

units.la: Iovi surripere coronam.
units.tr: To steal the crown from Jupiter.
And Trin. 1.2 v.47.

units.la: Plagii convicti in vincula conjecti.
units.tr: Kidnappers, when convicted, were put in chains.

units.la: Fur dici nequit, nisi qui aliquid alieni abstulerit.
units.tr: One cannot be called a thief unless he has taken away something of another's.

units.la: In foro Zonariorum furum copia.
units.tr: In the Forum of the Zonarii there is a plenty of thieves.

units.la: In furto manifesto deprehensi, quadruplicem pecuniam reddere tenebantur reddere.
units.tr: Those caught in manifest theft were bound to restore the money fourfold.

units.la: Fures omnia clam faciunt.
units.tr: Thieves do everything in secret.

units.la: Coqui furaces in puteum conditi.
units.tr: Cooks who steal, hidden away in a well.

units.la: Vide Tit. Supplicij.
units.tr: See the title Supplicij.

units.la: FURTUM quoq; est celare rem alienam ad se allatam.
units.tr: Theft is also the concealing of another's property that has been brought to oneself.

units.la: FURES noctu furatum venientes loca omnia in aedibus vestigant.
units.tr: Thieves who come by night to steal search all places in the houses.

units.la: PIETAS prohibet quicquam surripere parentibus.
units.tr: Piety forbids stealing anything from parents.

units.la: SPARTANI furtis suis nobiles.
units.tr: The Spartans, famous for their thefts.

units.la: FURES Vulcano dicuntur studere.
units.tr: Thieves are said to be devoted to Vulcan.

units.la: G.
units.tr: G.

units.la: Garrulitatis. Loquacitatis. Susurrionum.
units.tr: Garrulity. Loquacity. Whispering.

units.la: OMINES otiosi garruli versabantur crebrò in medicinis, tonstrinis, &c. Amph. 4.1. v.5. Epid. 2.2. v.13. Vide Tit. Locorum.
units.tr: ALL idle chatterers were constantly loitering in doctors' rooms, barbershops, etc. Amph. 4.1. v.5. Epid. 2.2. v.13. See the title Locorum.

units.la: Mulieres garrulæ. Pœn. 4.2. v.54. Rud. 4. 4. v.70.
units.tr: Garrulous women. Pœn. 4.2. v.54. Rud. 4.4. v.70.

units.la: HOMINES garruli, curiosi, calumniatores, solent plærumq; in locis suspectis versari otiosi, & curiosi de rebus alienis. Curc. 4.1. v.10. Vide Tit. Roma.
units.tr: MEN who are garrulous, nosy and slanderous usually loiter in suspicious places, idle and prying into other people's affairs. Curc. 4.1. v.10. See the title Roma.

units.la: GARRULI, Sycophantæ in foro sedebant: & id genus hominum nihili. Trin. 3.3. v.86.
units.tr: CHATTERERS and sycophants sat in the forum, and that kind of men is worthless. Trin. 3.3. v.86.

units.la: HOMINES qui gestant, quiq; auscultant crimina, si meo arbitratu liceat, omnes pendeant: Gestores linguis, auditores auribus. Pseud. 1.5. v.12.
units.tr: MEN who carry tales and who listen to accusations, I wish, if it were up to me, all of them hanged: carriers of gossip with their tongues, listeners with their ears. Pseud. 1.5. v.12.

units.la: Inde Plauto nostro dicuntur Famigeratores: & Famigeratio in Trinum: 3.2. v.66. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: Hence in our Plautus they are called tale-mongers, and tale-mongering in the Trinummus 3.2. v.66. See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: Sic Seneca Epist. 123.
units.tr: So Seneca, Epistle 123.

units.la: Pessimum genus hominum videbatur: qui verba gestarent: sunt quidam, qui vitia gestant.
units.tr: They seemed to be the worst kind of men, those who carried words about; there are some who carry vices.

units.la: GARRULI suâ importunitate tantùm non enecant.
units.tr: GARRULOUS people almost kill with their importunity alone.
Miles Gloriosus 4.2. v.92.

units.la: Sinite abeam, si possum, viva à vobis.
units.tr: Let me go, if I can, alive, away from you.

units.la: Exemplum seu χαρακτῆρα Garruli hominis exprimit Horatius lib. 1. Sat. 9.
units.tr: Horace, Satires book 1, satire 9, expresses the example or character (χαρακτήρ) of the garrulous man.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Molestia.
units.tr: See also the title Molestia.

units.la: Multiloquium amatorum proprium.
units.tr: Much talking is characteristic of lovers.

units.la: Merc. Prol. v. 31.
units.tr: Mercator, Prologue, v. 31.

units.la: P. Syrus: Lingua est multiloquax mentis indicium mala.
units.tr: Publius Syrus: A tongue that talks too much is a sign of a bad mind.

units.la: Loquaces sunt importuni.
units.tr: Talkers are tiresome.
Mercator 1.2. v.45.

units.la: Lassitudinem hercle verba tua mihi addunt: enicas.
units.tr: Your words really wear me out, by Hercules; you are killing me.

units.la: Gestuum.
units.tr: Gestures.

units.la: Vide Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See the title Hominis.

units.la: Gestus hominis cogitabundi exprimitur. Mil. 2 2. v. 47. Vide totum locum.
units.tr: The gesture of a man lost in thought is portrayed. Miles Gloriosus 2.2. v.47. See the whole passage.

units.la: Gladiatorum. Pugilum. Gymnastices, Athletarum.
units.tr: Gladiators. Boxers. Gymnastics, Athletes.

units.la: Vide etiam infra Tit. Theatri.
units.tr: See also below, the title Theatri.

units.la: PILA ludebant coriaceâ vento repletâ: quam pugno, non palmâ percutiebant.
units.tr: They played at ball, filled with wind, which they struck with the fist, not the open palm.
Rudens 3.4. v.86.

units.la: Ego te faciam follem pugillatorium.
units.tr: I will make you into a punching bag.

units.la: Pugiles enim follem suspensum pugnis insectabantur.
units.tr: For boxers used to attack a bag hung up with their fists.

units.la: Gladiatores vulnerati audiebant hanc formulam: Hoc habet. Mostl. 3.1. v. 26.
units.tr: Wounded gladiators heard this formula: He has it. Mostellaria 3.1. v.26.

units.la: Terent. And. 1.1. certè captus est: Habet.
units.tr: Terence, Andria 1.1: certainly he is caught: He has it.

units.la: Virgil. 12. Æneid. Hoc habet: h. e. lethali ictu percussus est.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid 12: He has it, that is, he was struck by a deadly blow.

units.la: Prudentius: Hoc habet, exclamat victrix regina.
units.tr: Prudentius: He has it, cries the victorious queen.

units.la: Seneca Agamemn.
units.tr: Seneca, Agamemnon.

units.la: Habet: peractum est: quas petis, poenas dedit.
units.tr: He has it: it is done; you have paid the penalty you sought.

units.la: Turn. lib. 7. c. 10. Lipf. Saturn. lib. 2. cap. 21.
units.tr: Turnebus, book 7, ch. 10. Lipsius, Saturnalia, book 2, ch. 21.

units.la: Pugiles, & athletas validos lacertos decet habere. Unde forma illa: pugllicè, & athleticè: item pancraticè valere apud Plaut. Epid. 1.1. v. 18. & Bacch 2.3. v. 14.
units.tr: Boxers and athletes ought to have strong arms. Hence the expressions in boxer fashion and in athlete fashion; likewise to be strong in the pancratium in Plautus, Epidicus 1.1. v.18 and Bacchides 2.3. v.14.

units.la: Gladiatores dicebantur captare ictus adversarij.
units.tr: Gladiators were said to seek out the blows of their opponent.
Mostellaria 5.1. v.21 and 5.2. v.21.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut. Captare.
units.tr: See the Plautine Lexicon, Captare.

units.la: Dirempta praelusione, abiectisq; lusorijs armis transfibant ad vera, quod dicebant versis gladijs depugnare.
units.tr: When the preliminary play was over and the playful weapons laid aside, they passed on to real fighting, which they called fighting with reversed swords.
Casina 2.5. v.35.

units.la: Vide Lipf. in Saturnal. lib. 2. cap. 19.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Saturnalia, book 2, ch. 19.

units.la: Gladiatores magna curā & arte se componebant, & colligebant in arma, utpote quibus haec propositā sors est (teste Agellio) aut occidere, si occupaverit, aut occumbere si cessaverit. Hanc posituram vocabant Statum.
units.tr: Gladiators would take up their positions with great care and skill, and gather themselves for arms, since the fate set before them is (as Agellius witnesses) either to kill, if they seize the chance, or to be killed, if they hesitate. This stance they called the Status.

units.la: Allusit noster Mil. 4.9. v. 12.
units.tr: Our author alludes to it: Miles Gloriosus 4.9. v.12.

units.la: Vide Lipf. Saturn. l. 2. cap. 20.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Saturnalia, book 2, ch. 20.

units.la: GLADII.
units.tr: SWORDS.

units.la: GRÆCI ut & Romani in urbe non gerebant gladium. Marc. 5. 2. v. 86.
units.tr: The Greeks, as well as the Romans, did not carry swords in the city. Mercator 5.2. v.86.

units.la: GRASSATIONUM. NOCTURNARUM.
units.tr: NIGHT ASSAULTS.

units.la: UVENTUS Attica luxu perdita grassationibus nocturnis infice-re solita erat publicam pacem. Quod è Plauto patet. Amph. 1. 1. v. 2. Stich. 4. 2. v. 33. Trin. 2. 2. v. 34.
units.tr: The Attic youth, ruined by luxury, used to disturb public peace with night assaults. This is clear from Plautus: Amphitryon 1.1. v.2; Stichus 4.2. v.33; Trinummus 2.2. v.34.

units.la: Et forte Plautus noster primo re loco Amph. alludit ad legem aliquam populi Romani, quâ cautum fuit, ne cui noctis conticinio per urbem iter facere liceret, praesertim temporibus belli Punici secundi, quibus Plautum nostrum vixisse, dixi in Dissertatione de vitâ Plauti.
units.tr: And perhaps our Plautus, at the very beginning of the Amphitryon, alludes to some law of the Roman people, by which it was provided that no one might travel through the city at dead of night, especially in the times of the Second Punic War, in which, as I said in my Dissertation on the life of Plautus, our Plautus lived.

units.la: Lege sis historiam de Socrate apud Ælianum lib. 9. Variæ Histor. cap. 29.
units.tr: Please read the story of Socrates in Aelian, Varia Historia, book 9, ch. 29.

units.la: Neque alienum est ab hac juvenum petulantiâ, quod exstat apud Apulejum lib. 2. Milef.
units.tr: Not unlike this youthful wantonness is what is found in Apuleius, Metamorphoses, book 2.

units.la: Sed heus tu, caveregrediare cænâ maturius. Nam vesana facti-o nobilissimorum juvenum pacem publicam infecit: & passim trucidatos per medias plateas videbis jacere.
units.tr: But hey you, take care you leave dinner early. For the mad deed of most noble youths has infected the public peace, and everywhere you will see men slaughtered and lying in the middle of the streets.

units.la: Et quid quaeso magis solemne nostrae juventuti, in publicis Academijs Dianae potius & Selinae litantibus, quàm Apollini & Musis? Ibi quisque ferocem Ajacem se ostentat, bellum cum lapidibus gerens, & fenestras civium expugnans. Sed sic Arx Honoris non superatur. GRASSATORES nocturni carcere olim mancipati per trium-viros. Amph. I. 2. v.3.
units.tr: And what, I ask, is more customary for our youth than sacrificing in public academies to Diana and Selene rather than to Apollo and the Muses? There each one shows himself a fierce Ajax, waging war with stones and storming the windows of citizens. But thus the Citadel of Honour is not overcome. Nocturnal brawlers were once consigned to prison by the triumvirs. Amphitryon I.2. v.3.

units.la: Ausón. Pervigila ante fores: noƈte capi metuo.
units.tr: Ausonius: I keep watch before the doors; I fear being caught by night.

units.la: De istis grassatoribus nocturnis vide prolixè apud Joh. Langlæum lib.8.cap.10. Otij semestris: ubi consuetudinem Gallorum, Italorum, & Anglorum exponit: qui in nocturnos ambulones severissimas semper pœnas statuerunt.
units.tr: On these nocturnal assailants see at length John Langlaeus, Otium semestre, book 8, ch. 10, where he sets out the customs of the French, Italians and English, who always decreed the most severe punishments against nocturnal loiterers.

units.la: GRATULATIONUM.
units.tr: CONGRATULATIONS.

units.la: Vide Tit. Votorum.
units.tr: See the title Vows.

units.la: AMICI gratulabantur suis amicis, si quando familiæ suæ causâ, captivos redemissent. Capt. 3.2. v. 5.
units.tr: Friends used to congratulate their friends whenever they had ransomed captives for the sake of their family. Capt. 3.2. v. 5.

units.la: GYNÆCEI. MULIERUM.
units.tr: THE WOMEN'S QUARTERS. WOMEN.

units.la: Vide etiam Titul. Habitus: & Rei Oeconomicæ: Familiæ: Matronarum: Puellarum: Pedissequij: Pudicitiæ.
units.tr: See also the titles Dress, Household Management, Family, Matrons, Girls, Attendants, and Chastity.

units.la: HABEBANT mulieres suas puellas à formâ: h.e. ornatrices.
units.tr: Women kept girls chosen for their looks, that is, hairdressers.

units.la: Vide Woweri notas ad illud Petronij: Dic Chrysis, numquid in compta sum?
units.tr: See Wower's notes on that passage of Petronius: "Tell me, Chrysis, am I well groomed?"

units.la: SOLEBANT itidem sese ungere: maximè vetulæ, edentulæ, quæ vitia corporis fuco occultant. Ubi sese autem sudor cum unguentis consociavit, illico Itidem olent, quasi cum una multa jura confundit coquus. Quid oleas nescias, nisi id unum, ut male olire intelligas. Most. 1.3. v.119. & seqq.
units.tr: They likewise used to anoint themselves, especially old women and toothless ones, who hide the defects of their bodies with cosmetics. When sweat has mixed with the unguents, they at once smell just the same, as when a cook mixes many sauces together. Why do you not know what you are smelling, except this one thing, that you realise you smell bad. Most. 1.3. v.119 and following.

units.la: Ancillas non decebat annulus aureus, neq; soleæ. Caf. 3. 5. v. 63.
units.tr: A maidservant was not allowed to wear a gold ring, or slippers. Caf. 3. 5. v. 63.

units.la: In Gynæceo præfectum mulierum habebant: quem nos appella-mus Frawenzimmer Hofmeister. Aul. 3. 5. v. 30.
units.tr: In the women's quarters they had a supervisor of the women, whom we call the ladies' steward (Frawenzimmer Hofmeister). Aul. 3. 5. v. 30.

units.la: Erant ancillæ vestispicæ, quæ vestes inspicerent: & quæ flabella ferebant flabelliferæ: item quæ dominæ sandalia portarent sandaligeræ: quæ cistulas observarent cistellariæ. Trin. 2. 1. v. 22.
units.tr: There were maidservants who inspected garments (vestispicae), those who carried fans (flabelliferae), those who carried their mistress's sandals (sandaligerae), and those who looked after the little boxes (cistellariae). Trin. 2. 1. v. 22.

units.la: Terent. Eun. 3. 5. Cape hoc flabellum: Ventulum huic sic facito.
units.tr: Terence, Eunuchus 3.5: "Take this fan, and fan him gently like this."

units.la: Vide Turneb. 29. 8. P. Victor. lib. 14. cap. 15.
units.tr: See Turnebus 29.8; P. Victorius, lib. 14, cap. 15.

units.la: Virgines aut matronæ honestiores numquam sine assectatorum pedisequo prodibant in publicum, nesi in proximum quidem diverterent: quo videlicet & culpam & suspiciones evitarent.
units.tr: Unmarried girls and more respectable matrons never went out in public without a retinue of attendants, unless they were going to the house next door; clearly this was so that they might avoid both blame and suspicion.

units.la: Amph. 3. 2. v. 48. Caf. 2. 2. v. 1. Cist. loco amisso. Astat ea in via sola: Prostibulum sane est.
units.tr: Amph. 3. 2. v. 48. Caf. 2. 2. v. 1. Cist., lost passage. "She stands alone on the road: she is certainly a prostitute."

units.la: Nævius: Subito famam tollunt, si quam solam videre in via.
units.tr: Naevius: "If they see any woman alone on the road, they at once spread a rumour."

units.la: Hic comitatus fere e spadonibus constabat.
units.tr: This retinue usually consisted mostly of eunuchs.

units.la: Vide Rævard, Var. lib. 4. cap. 17.
units.tr: See Rævard, Var. lib. 4, cap. 17.

units.la: Virgines & matronæ honestæ debent ad colum sedere: & quidem ad eam sæpius somnus calvitur manus.
units.tr: Unmarried girls and honourable matrons ought to sit at the distaff; and indeed sleep often steals upon their hands while they do so.

units.la: Feminæ circumferebant virorum suorum imagines in tabulis cereis.
units.tr: Women carried around images of their husbands in wax tablets.

units.la: Vide Tit. Pictura: Imaginum.
units.tr: See the title Painting: Images.

units.la: ꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏ
units.tr: ꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏꝏ

units.la: H.
units.tr: H.

units.la: Habitūs. Cultūs. Calceorum. Amictūs. Vestium. Rei-Vestiariæ. Ornatūs.
units.tr: Dress. Adornment. Shoes. Garments. Clothing. Wardrobe. Ornaments.

units.la: EMINÆ, etiam ancillæ fictos, compositos, crispos & unguentatos cincinnos alebant, & purpurissatas buccas. Truc. 2.2.v.32. Sic Varro formosam & ornatam puellam pingit: Ante aures nodo ex subolib̊ parvuli intorti demittebantur cincinni: sed & oculi suppetuli, nigellis pupulis quandam hilaritatem significantes animi, risus parvissimus: ore frenato, risu rosco.
units.tr: WOMEN, even maidservants, wore curled, styled, crimped and perfumed ringlets, and cheeks painted with rouge. Truc. 2.2 v.32. Thus Varro paints a beautiful and well-adorned girl: Before the ears, little curls hung down, twisted into a knot from the hair at the back; and eyes rather prominent, with small dark pupils signifying a certain cheerfulness of spirit, a very slight smile; mouth restrained, lips in a smile.

units.la: Solebant etiam intortos crispos cincinnos demittere ante aures: & in nodum cogere: ut patet ex priore loco Trucul.
units.tr: They also used to let curled ringlets hang down before the ears and gather them into a knot, as is clear from the former passage in Truculentus.

units.la: De purpurissâ sic Apul. Apolog. Quis non disciplinam matris agnovit: cum in puellâ videret immedicatum os, & purpurissatas genas, & illices oculos?
units.tr: On rouge, thus Apuleius in the Apology: Who did not recognise the training of the mother, when he saw in the girl an unmedicated mouth, rouged cheeks and alluring eyes?

units.la: Tertull. de cultu feminarum:
units.tr: Tertullian, on women's dress:

units.la: Quæ autem medicaminibus ungunt, genas rubore maculant.
units.tr: Those who anoint themselves with cosmetics stain their cheeks with redness.

units.la: Item:
units.tr: Likewise:

units.la: An cum cerussâ, purpurissò, & croco, & in illo ambitu capitis resurgatis?
units.tr: Or do you rise again with white lead, rouge and saffron, and in that circuit of the head?

units.la: Plautus eodem loci v. 39.
units.tr: Plautus, in the same place, v. 39.

units.la: Buccas rubrica, cera omne corpus intinxit tibi.
units.tr: Rouge on your cheeks; wax has coloured your whole body.

units.la: Caput operiebant in re turpi deprehensi: summo pudore affecti, in rebus desperatis, vitam projicere parantes.
units.tr: They covered their head when caught in a shameful act, overcome by utmost shame, or in desperate situations, preparing to throw away their life.
Mostellaria 2.1 v.76 and 2.2 v.89.

units.la: Horat. lib. 2. Sat. 3.
units.tr: Horace, Satires, book 2, sat. 3.

units.la: Nam male re gestâ, tum nollem mittere operto Me capite in flumen---
units.tr: For when I had done badly, I would not wish to be sent with covered head into the river...

units.la: Livius lib. 1. Ann.
units.tr: Livy, book 1.

units.la: I lictor, colliga manus, caput obnubito, arbori infelici suspendito.
units.tr: Go, lictor, bind his hands, cover his head, and hang him on the unlucky tree.

units.la: Socrates quoque apud Plat. Phædr. de amore verba facturus caput operiebat.
units.tr: Socrates too, in Plato's Phaedrus, covered his head when he was about to speak of love.

units.la: MULIERES aureum spinther, ἀκροχείλιον, fibulam, aut armillam in humeris gerebant.
units.tr: Women wore a golden spinther, an akrocheilion [ἀκροχείλιον], a clasp, or an armlet on their shoulders.

units.la: HABEBANT quoq; armarium, in quo vestes recondebant, aliaq; ornamenta sua.
units.tr: They also had a cupboard in which they stored their clothes and other ornaments.

units.la: INAURES quoq; oblongas, quas stalagmia vocabant auribus infi-xerunt.
units.tr: They also thrust long earrings, which they called stalagmia, into their ears.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: CINÆDI cauponij cum longis manicatis tunicis incedebant.
units.tr: Cinaedi, the tavern boys, walked about in long-sleeved tunics.

units.la: Quis hic est, cum tunicis longis puer cauponium?
units.tr: Who is this tavern boy in long tunics?

units.la: Vide plura in hanc rem apud Meursium Comment. in Cassan-dram Lycophr. pag. 291.
units.tr: See more on this subject in Meursius, Commentary on Lycophron's Cassandra, p. 291.

units.la: Et inprimis eruditissimum Martinum de Roa lib. 3. Singul. cap. 15 pag. 327.
units.tr: And especially the most learned Martín de Roa, book 3 of Singularities, ch. 15, p. 327.

units.la: Ubi prolixè disputat de hoc cinædorum cultu: itemq; de cæterâ vanitate vestiariâ.
units.tr: There he discusses at length this dress of the cinaedi, and likewise other vanity in clothing.

units.la: TEMPORE hyberno pallium & tunicas gestabant.
units.tr: In winter they wore a cloak and tunics.

units.la: MILITES cæsariati fuerunt.
units.tr: Soldiers were dressed in the Caesarian fashion.

units.la: CHLAMYS vestis viatoria : itemq; militaris : nec non servorum aulicorum.
units.tr: The chlamys was a travelling garment, also a military one, and was worn by court servants.

units.la: Ubi de homine gloriosò loquitur, qui quassando undantem facit chlamydem : h.e. quasi undatim crispantem ob nimiam commotionem, & quassationem : quod est jactabundorum & arrogantium.
units.tr: Where he speaks of a boastful man who shakes a billowing chlamys, that is, one rippling as in waves from excessive agitation and shaking; this is characteristic of braggarts and the arrogant.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: See Lex. Plaut.

units.la: IMMODERATÆ sunt mulierum munditiés : ut explicant ipsæ mulieres.
units.tr: Women's attention to cleanliness is immoderate, as the women themselves explain.

units.la: Lavari, aut fricari, aut tergeri, aut ornari, poliri, expoliri, pin-gi, fingi.
units.tr: To be bathed, or rubbed, or dried, or adorned, polished, thoroughly polished, painted, moulded.

units.la: BONO ingenio ornatum esse, quàm auro, multò satius est, inquit puella Pœn. 1. 2. v. 88.
units.tr: To be adorned with a good character is much better than with gold, says the girl. Poen. 1.2 v.88.

units.la: Aurum in fortunâ invenitur, naturâ ingenium bonum. Bonam ego, quàm beatam me esse nimió dici mavolo. Virginem pudo-rem magis gerere decet, quàm purpuram : magisque virginum pudorem, quàm aurum gerere condecet. Pulcrum ornatum tur-pes mores pejus cæno collinunt. Lepidi mores turpem ornatum facile factu comprobant.
units.tr: Gold is found in one's fortune, a good character by nature. I would rather be called good than very rich. A maiden should bear modesty rather than purple, and it becomes maidens to bear modesty rather than gold. Bad morals smear fine ornament with filth, worse than mud. Charming morals easily make an ugly ornament look good.

units.la: CALCEAMENTA clavis fixa fuerunt, & quandoque clavis aureis ex luxu divitum : quod constat ex Bacch. 2. 3. v. 98. Et Antiochi exercitus magna ex parte aureos clavos crepidis subjectos habuit. Plinius l. 33. c. 3. de Agnone Tejo Alex. Magni purpurato narrat, quòd aureis clavis suffigere solitus fit crepidas. Quandoque etiam æneis usi sunt : quod ait Lucill. Fulmentas clavis æneis subcudere.
units.tr: Shoes were fastened with nails, and sometimes with golden nails, out of the luxury of the rich; this is clear from Bacch. 2.3 v.98. And the army of Antiochus largely had golden nails set under their sandals. Pliny, book 33, ch. 3, tells of Agnon of Teos, the purple-clad favourite of Alexander the Great, who was accustomed to fasten his sandals with golden nails. Sometimes they also used bronze, as Lucilius says: "to hammer soles on with bronze nails."

units.la: Et Trin. 3. 2. v. 92. Jubeam fulmentas suppingi soccis : quod est Græcè ἐγκόπτειν ἥλως ἐγκρύειν.
units.tr: And Trin. 3.2 v.92: "I will order soles to be fastened under the socks"; in Greek this is to drive in nails [ἐγκόπτειν ἥλως ἐγκρύειν].

units.la: Rustici vilissimis sculponeis calceis usi sunt. Caf. 2.8.v. 61. quibus interdum os sibi batuebant. Ibid.
units.tr: Country folk used very cheap wooden-soled shoes, Caf. 2.8 v.61, with which they sometimes struck their own mouths. Ibid.

units.la: Romani non folebant in publico uti soleis: sed vel in triclinio, vel in cubiculo: verum foris calceis. Truc. 2.8. v.1. Idcoq; Cicero Verri crimini ducit, quod soleatus fuerit.
units.tr: Romans did not customarily wear slippers in public, but only at dinner or in the bedroom; outdoors they wore shoes. Truc. 2.8 v.1. Hence Cicero counts it as a charge against Verres that he went about in slippers.

units.la: Vide Turneb. lib. 24. cap. 17.
units.tr: See Turnebus, book 24, ch. 17.

units.la: Sed mulieres potius soleis usæ quàm calceis. Catull. de Lesbia: Argutâ constitit in soleâ.
units.tr: But women used slippers rather than shoes. Catullus, about Lesbia: she stood on the elegant slipper.

units.la: Mulieres, inprimis amasiæ, ornamenta sua muliebria, ut speculum, & id genus alia recondita habebant in arculâ. Most. 1.3. v.90.
units.tr: Women, especially mistresses, kept their feminine ornaments, such as a mirror and things of that kind, hidden in a little chest. Most. 1.3 v.90.

units.la: Peristromata Campanica: & tapetia Alexandrina, Persica, Babylonica, in delitiis: & famâ passim.
units.tr: Campanian carpets, and Alexandrian, Persian and Babylonian tapestries, in luxury, and renowned everywhere.

units.la: Unde in joco apud Plautum de servis flagritribis Pseud. 1.2. v.13.
units.tr: Hence the joke in Plautus about the slave-whippers. Pseud. 1.2 v.13.

units.la: Ita ego vestra latera lorís faciam, ut valide varia sient, ut ne peristromata quidem aque pitta sint Campanica: neq; Alexandrina belluata consiliata tapetia.
units.tr: So I will make your sides with whips, so that they become well striped, so that even Campanian carpets are not as painted, nor Alexandrian tapestries, embroidered with beasts, so well counselled.

units.la: De Persicis vide Brissonium lib. 2. de Regno Persico pag. 225.
units.tr: On Persian work see Brisson, book 2, On the Persian Kingdom, p. 225.

units.la: Vide item Tit. Triclinj: Lectorum.
units.tr: See also the title Couches (Triclinium: Lectorum).

units.la: Toga nivea principiò: posteà, ubi sordes contraxit, cretâ inficiebatur.
units.tr: The toga was at first snow-white; later, when it had gathered dirt, it was whitened with chalk.

units.la: Per dies autem festos talem non ferebant.
units.tr: On festival days they did not wear such a toga.

units.la: Inde Candidati dicti.
units.tr: Hence the candidates were so named.

units.la: Capillorum maximam elegantuli elegantulæve curam gerunt: an recte & commodè comtæ sint.
units.tr: A very elegant young man or woman takes the greatest care of the hair, whether it is combed properly and becomingly. Most. 1.3 v.96.

units.la: Vide Tit. Gynacei.
units.tr: See the title Gynaeceum.

units.la: Et Notas Woweri ad illud Petronij:
units.tr: And the notes of Wower on that line of Petronius:

units.la: Dic, Chrysis, numquid incomta sum?
units.tr: Tell me, Chrysis, am I not dressed up?

units.la: Ubi explicat puellas Ornatrices fuisse: quæ tali cultui servirent.
units.tr: Where he explains that the girls called ornatrices were those who served such adornment.

units.la: Vide etiam loco supra dicto apud Martinum Roa: nec non Declamationem nostram De cultu eruditorum. Quæ est in volumine peculiari Declamationum Oratoriarum, propediem à nobis edendo.
units.tr: See also the passage of Martín de Roa cited above, and our declamation On the dress of the learned, which is in a separate volume of Oratorical Declamations that we shall soon publish.

units.la: Cerussam pro fucanda facie adhibebant.
units.tr: They used white lead to make up the face.
Mostellaria 1.3 v.100.

units.la: Vide Tit. Gynæcei.
units.tr: See the title Gynaeceum.

units.la: Creta sordidæ vestes nititabantur.
units.tr: Dirty garments were made bright with chalk.

units.la: Qui vestitu & creta se occultant, & sedent, quasi sint frugi.
units.tr: Those who hide themselves with clothing and chalk, and sit about as if they were honest.

units.la: Et Poen. 5. 2. v. 8. ἀλληγορικῶς.
units.tr: And Poen. 5.2 v.8, allegorically:

units.la: Creta est professio mihi horum hominum oratio.
units.tr: Chalk is my profession, the speech of these men.

units.la: Vide Plin. lib. 35. cap. 15. & 17.
units.tr: See Pliny, book 35, chs. 15 and 17.

units.la: Isidorus:
units.tr: Isidore:

units.la: Fit toga addito quodam creta genere candidior.
units.tr: A toga is made whiter by adding a certain kind of chalk.

units.la: Persius: quem ducit hiantem (Creta ambitio
units.tr: Persius: whom gaping ambition drives on (chalk, ambition...).

units.la: Non tantum rusticitatis, sed etiam impudentiæ nota est, calceis inconcinnis uti.
units.tr: To wear ill-fitting shoes is a mark not only of rusticity but also of impudence.
Trinummus 4.2 v.52.

units.la: Vide Agell. lib. 13. cap. 20. & Casaub. Charact. Theophrast.
units.tr: See Gellius, book 13, ch. 20, and Casaubon on the Characters of Theophrastus.

units.la: Vestes meretricum erant auratæ, & regiæ. Inducula regilla, impluviata: quæ scilicet nomina è suis vestimentis faciunt.
units.tr: The garments of prostitutes were gilded and royal: an inducula regilla, an impluviata; these names are clearly derived from their clothing.

units.la: Vide locum integrum.
units.tr: See the whole passage.

units.la: PALLIUM extrema vestis apud Græcos, ut Toga apud Romanos: & tunicam tegebat: ideoq; tunica propior corpori, quàm pal- lium.
units.tr: The pallium was the outermost garment among the Greeks, as the toga was among the Romans; and it covered the tunic. Hence the tunic lies closer to the body than the pallium does.

units.la: Tunica propior pallio est.
units.tr: The tunic is nearer to the body than the pallium.

units.la: ERANT servi vestipici: & ancillæ vestipicæ: quæ aliàs dictæ à veste in Antiqq. Inscript.
units.tr: There were slaves who were menders of clothing (vestipici), and maidservants (vestipicae), who are otherwise called after their garment in ancient inscriptions.

units.la: PÆNULA servilis, & viatoria vestis.
units.tr: The penula was a slave's garment and a traveller's garment.

units.la: SEDENDO prudentiores efficimur.
units.tr: By sitting we become wiser.

units.la: Vide Tit. Judicÿ.
units.tr: See the title Judges.

units.la: LIBERTI noviiih togâ apparebant.
units.tr: Freedmen appeared in a new toga.

units.la: Vide Tit. Libertorum.
units.tr: See the title Freedmen.

units.la: TUNICAM, zonam, chlamydem, & caufiam sumebant peregri- naturi.
units.tr: Those about to travel took a tunic, a belt, a chlamys and a caussia.

units.la: PENICULO extergebantur baxeæ seu crepidæ.
units.tr: Baxeae or crepidae were wiped clean with a penicle.

units.la: PALLA vestimentum muliebre: pallium, virile.
units.tr: The palla was a woman's garment; the pallium, a man's.

units.la: MATRONÆ promissos crines alebant, scorta breviores.
units.tr: Matrons let their hair grow long; prostitutes wore it shorter.

units.la: Vide Tit. Conjugÿ.
units.tr: See the title Marriage.

units.la: ADOLESCENTES cinĉiculis inducbantur.
units.tr: Young men were dressed in little belts (cinciculi).

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: CUM pallâ saltabant. Men. 1.3. v.14.
units.tr: They danced with a cloak. Men. 1.3. v.14.

units.la: SUCCINGULUM, baltheus erat muliebris. Men. 1.3. v.17.
units.tr: The SUCCINGULUM was a woman's belt. Men. 1.3. v.17.

units.la: SOLEAS domi & pallium inducebant accubantes puerperæ. Truc. 2.5. v.25.
units.tr: At home, women lying at table in childbed would put on slippers and a cloak. Truc. 2.5. v.25.

units.la: Vide Tit. Triclinij.
units.tr: See the title Triclinium.

units.la: PALLIOLATIS tunicis usi cinædici saltatores. Pseud. 5.1. v. 29.
units.tr: Effeminate dancers wore tunics with little cloaks. Pseud. 5.1. v. 29.

units.la: VETERES Græci & Romani subligaculis, uti nos hodie, extra stadium aut scenam non utebantur. Itaque illi pallium, hi togam ad calceos demittebât. Quod si quid illis, qui gnavi & actuosi haberi volebant, diligentius faciundum esset: vel pallium pone-bant, vel in humeros reijciebant, & velato capite incedebant. Atque hic servorum fere habitus fuit in Comœdijs.
units.tr: The ancient Greeks and Romans did not wear undergarments outside the stadium or the stage, as we do today. So the Greeks let the cloak hang down to the ankles and the Romans let the toga do so. If anything had to be done more diligently by those who wished to be seen as active and energetic, they either put the cloak aside or threw it back over their shoulders and walked with their heads uncovered. This was almost the usual dress of slaves in comedies.

units.la: Eodem pacto, ut Comici servi solent, conjiciam in collum pallium.
units.tr: In the same way, as comic slaves usually do, I will throw the cloak around my neck.

units.la: Sic Geta Phorm. properans apud Terent. Humerum sibi onerat pallio.
units.tr: So Geta in Terence's Phormio, in a hurry: He loads the cloak onto his shoulder.

units.la: Idq; faciebant, vitandi solis causâ: cùm pilei usus ijs non esset.
units.tr: They did this only to avoid the sun, since they had no use for the hat.

units.la: Seneca Epist. 115. de mollitie Mæcenatis: Hunc esse, qui in tribunali, in rostris, in omni publico catu sic apparuerit, ut pallio velaretur caput, exclusis utringue auribus, non aliter, quam in Mimo divitis fugitivi solent.
units.tr: Seneca, Epistle 115, on the effeminacy of Maecenas: He who appeared on the tribunal, on the rostra, in any public gathering, with his head covered by a cloak, with his ears hidden on both sides, was no different from the rich runaway slaves in the mime.

units.la: Vide etiam Lipsi Epist. Quæst.l.3. cap.23. & Casaub. ad Charact. Theophrast.
units.tr: See also Lipsius, Epistolicae Quaestiones 3.23, and Casaubon on the Characters of Theophrastus.

units.la: Vide quoq; Fit. Fabularum.
units.tr: See also the title Fabulae.

units.la: AMICULUM superinduebant reliquis vestibus. Εἰν ὑπένδυμα. Ein Bergzug. Cist. 1.1. v. 117.
units.tr: The AMICULUM was worn over the other garments. Εἰν ὑπένδυμα [an under-garment]. A German gloss: Ein Bergzug. Cist. 1.1. v. 117.

units.la: MASTRUGA scortea vestis: quâ Sardi pelliti utebantur.
units.tr: The MASTRUGA was a leather garment, which the pelted Sardinians used to wear.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: MILITES jubam & cæsariem alebant.
units.tr: Soldiers grew a mane and long hair.

units.la: TUNICA & pallium Græcorum fuit.
units.tr: The tunic and the cloak were Greek dress.

units.la: Ex cultu & ornatu, quod quis velit, colligi potest.
units.tr: What someone wishes to be taken from dress and adornment can be gathered.

units.la: VESTIS muliebris palla fuit.
units.tr: The woman's garment was the palla.

units.la: PILLEUS signum libertatis.
units.tr: The PILLEUS was a sign of freedom.

units.la: Vide Tit. Servorum.
units.tr: See the title Servorum.

units.la: NON tàm vestis, quàm farctum: h. e. corpus in veste, observari debet: quod faciunt amatores.
units.tr: Attention should be paid not so much to the clothing as to the body beneath it, that is, the person inside the clothes, as lovers do.

units.la: Ubi tu commoda es, capillum commodum esse credito.
units.tr: Where you are charming, believe that the hair is charming too.

units.la: MANICATÆ tunicæ probro vertebantur. Tales habebat Pœnus ille Hanno.
units.tr: Sleeved tunics were regarded as disgraceful. The Carthaginian Hanno had such a tunic.

units.la: Sed quænam illac auh est?
units.tr: But what bird is that over there?

units.la: Ita eum appellat Avem, ob manicas alarum instar utrinque pensiles liberèq: fluentes.
units.tr: He calls him a bird in this way, because of the sleeves, which hang on both sides like wings and flow freely.

units.la: CARTHAGINENSES tunicati. Pœn. 5.3. v.2.
units.tr: The Carthaginians wore tunics. Pœn. 5.3. v.2.

units.la: Ennius lib.7. Ann. Tunicata juventus.
units.tr: Ennius, Annals book 7: the tunicked youth.

units.la: TIARA utebantur Persæ & Chaldæi. Quò allusum Perf. 4.2. verf. 2.
units.tr: The Persians and Chaldeans wore the tiara. Perf. 4.2. v.2 alludes to this.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut, & Briffon. de Regno Persarum.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus and Brisson, On the Kingdom of the Persians.

units.la: CAUSIA ferruginea, itemque pallium ferrugineum colore thalassico seu Veneto, vestis erat nauclerica.
units.tr: The CAUSIA was rust-colored, and the rust-colored cloak had the sea-colour or Venetian hue; it was the dress of sailors.

units.la: PALLIUM erat vestis cænatoria, sive synthefin: quo usi sunt amatores. Bacch. I.I. v. 38.
units.tr: The PALLIUM was a dinner garment, or synthesis, which lovers used. Bacch. 1.1. v. 38.

units.la: PALLA vestis muliebris è Græciâ. Truc. 2. 8. v. 55.
units.tr: The PALLA was a woman's garment from Greece. Truc. 2.8. v. 55.

units.la: Purpura ex Sarâ sive Tyro in magno pretio. Ibid.
units.tr: Purple from Sarra or Tyre was held in great esteem. Ibid.

units.la: Et induviæ vestium ex Ponto. Ibid.
units.tr: And garments from Pontus. Ibid.

units.la: NIMIA elegantia nonillum modò qui amat, sed quemcumq; attigit, magno atque solido mactat infortunio. Nec pol profectò quisquam sine grandi malo, præ quam res patitur, studuit elegantiæ. Merc. Prol. v. 20.
units.tr: Excessive elegance does not merely destroy the one who loves, but whoever it touches, with great and solid misfortune. Indeed, by Pollux, no one has ever pursued elegance without great harm, beyond what the situation allows. Merc. Prol. v. 20.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Amoris.
units.tr: See also the title Amoris.

units.la: TEGILLUM erat cuculiunculus è scirpo factus. Ein Schauben-hut: quo utebantur plebeij in pluviis. Rud. 2. 7. v. 18.
units.tr: The TEGILLUM was a little hood made of rush. Ein Schauben-hut (a straw hat), which common people used in the rain. Rud. 2.7. v. 18.

units.la: PATRICII splendidius cæteris amiciebantur. Cas. 3. 6. v. 4.
units.tr: Patricians dressed more splendidly than others. Cas. 3.6. v. 4.

units.la: Magnificè patriceq; amiciri.
units.tr: Dressed magnificently, as befits a patrician.

units.la: POENI veste distincta utebantur. Pœn. 5. 2. v. 48.
units.tr: The Carthaginians wore garments of distinct colour. Pœn. 5.2. v. 48.

units.la: INFRA pallium tunicas habebant. Aul. 4. 4. v. 21.
units.tr: Beneath the cloak they had tunics. Aul. 4.4. v. 21.

units.la: PAUPERTAS squalorem parit, & immunditiem. Cist. I. I. v. 116.
units.tr: Poverty brings squalor and filth. Cist. 1.1. v. 116.

units.la: ROMANI plærumq; capite aperto incedebant. Curc. 2. 3. v. 9. 14.
units.tr: Romans for the most part walked with their heads uncovered. Curc. 2.3. v. 9, 14.

units.la: Vide Tit. Populorum.
units.tr: See the title Populorum.

units.la: HÆREDITATIS. BONORUM. FORTUNA- RUM. TESTAMENTI.
units.tr: INHERITANCE. GOODS. FORTUNES. WILL.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Diuitiarum: Opum.
units.tr: See also the title Riches: Wealth.

units.la: AMICI, cognati, hæreditatis hercisçundæ gratia munera solent mittere.
units.tr: Friends and kinsmen are wont to send gifts for the sake of an inheritance to be divided.

units.la: HÆREDEM faciebant eum, qui laudes decantaret viui.
units.tr: They used to make heir the one who would sing the praises of the living.

units.la: Mira sunt, nisi herus hunc hæredem facit. Nam is quidem illi, ut meditatur, verba facit emortuo.
units.tr: They are marvellous, unless the master makes this man his heir. For he talks to him, as he plans, as to a dead man.

units.la: PATRUELES suos nepotes sæpè hæredes faciunt.
units.tr: Cousins often make their nephews their heirs.

units.la: FILIIS bona paterna restituebantur.
units.tr: Paternal goods were restored to sons.

units.la: Paterna oportet reddi filio bona. Æquum est habere hunc bona, quæ possedit pater.
units.tr: The paternal goods ought to be given back to the son. It is fair that he have these goods which his father possessed.

units.la: PARTUS etiam illegitimè-natus bonorum paternorum hæres est. Sic miles meretriculæ promittit.
units.tr: A child born out of wedlock is also heir to the paternal goods. So the soldier promises the harlot:

units.la: Bona sua me habiturum omnia.
units.tr: I shall have all his goods.

units.la: FRATER fratris inhiat sæpè hæreditatem, quasi esuriens lupus.
units.tr: A brother often gapes after his brother's inheritance, like a hungry wolf.

units.la: IN hæreditate decimam partem bonorum Herculi consecrabant.
units.tr: From the inheritance they used to consecrate a tenth part of the goods to Hercules.

units.la: Vide Tit. Auctionis: Bonorum.
units.tr: See the title Auction: Goods.

units.la: SOLI cives Romani habebant sacra hæreditaria ex lege xii. Tabb. Sacra. Privata. Perpetuo. Habento: quà cavebatur, ut pater, filiusq; hæres eadem sacra colerent. Unde cum de potestate filius exibat, non amplius paternis sacris astringebat. Capt. 4.1. v. 8. Trin. 2.4. v. 83.
units.tr: Only Roman citizens had hereditary sacred rites under the Law of the Twelve Tables. Sacred Rites: Private. Perpetual. Let them hold: by which it was provided that father and son, as heir, should observe the same sacred rites. Hence, when a son went out from paternal power, he was no longer bound by the paternal sacred rites. Capt. 4.1. v. 8. Trin. 2.4. v. 83.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Sacrorum.
units.tr: See also the title Sacred Rites.

units.la: Diem suum obituri testamentum condebant. Men. Prol. v. 62.
units.tr: Those about to die made their will. Men. Prol. v. 62.

units.la: Bona parentis sunt bona filij: & vicissim. Trin. 2.2. v. 48. Quod tuum est, meum est: omne meum est autem tuum.
units.tr: The goods of a parent are the goods of the son, and vice versa. Trin. 2.2. v. 48. What is yours is mine, and all that is mine is yours.

units.la: Divitiæ & bona virtute Deûm : & sedulitate hominum acquiruntur. Trin. 2. 2. v. 65.
units.tr: Riches and goods are acquired by the favour of the gods and the diligence of men. Trin. 2. 2. v. 65.

units.la: Si fratres sororibus patrimonium absumserint: odio illis sunt: & vicissim. Trin. 3.2. v. 57.
units.tr: If brothers have consumed the patrimony of their sisters, they are hateful to them, and vice versa. Trin. 3.2. v. 57.

units.la: Hæreditas sine sacris non erat. Trin. 2. 4. v.83.
units.tr: There was no inheritance without sacred rites. Trin. 2. 4. v. 83.

units.la: Æquum est parentes morituros bona tradere filijs suis. Curc. 5.2. v.39.
units.tr: It is fair that dying parents hand their goods down to their sons. Curc. 5.2. v. 39.

units.la: Herbarum.
units.tr: Herbs.

units.la: Vide Tit. Plantarum.
units.tr: See the title Plants.

units.la: Hominis: & partium ejus. Humanæ Vitæ. Animi. Aurium. Barbæ. Bilis. Cordis. Crepitus-Ventris. Cutis. Dentium. Digiti. Facieì. Genua. Jecur. Lien. Manus. Naris. Oculi. Pollex. Sputi. Staturæ. Supercilii. Vultus.
units.tr: Of man and his parts. Human life. Mind. Ears. Beard. Bile. Heart. Belching of the stomach. Skin. Teeth. Finger. Face. Knees. Liver. Spleen. Hand. Nostril. Eyes. Thumb. Spittle. Stature. Eyebrow. Countenance.

units.la: AB homine homini quotidianum periculum, inquit Seneca Epist. 103. Asin. 2.4. v. 88. Lupus est homo homini, non homo, cum qualis sit, non novit. Anacharsis Scytha interrogatus, τί ἐστι τὸ πολέμιον ἀνθρώποις; respondit, αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοῖς. Contrarium est illud Caecilij: Homo hominis Deus est, si suum officium sciat.
units.tr: Daily danger from man to man, says Seneca, Epist. 103. Asin. 2.4. v. 88. A man is a wolf to a man, not a man, since he does not know what sort he is. Anacharsis the Scythian, when asked "What is the enemy to men?" [τί ἐστι τὸ πολέμιον ἀνθρώποις;] answered, "They themselves to themselves" [αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοῖς]. Contrary to this is the saying of Caecilius: Man is a god to man, if he knows his duty.

units.la: ANIMUS hominis saepe alibi est, ubi non est corpus. Perf. 4.6. v. 27. Animus est in navi.
units.tr: The mind of a man is often elsewhere, where the body is not. Perf. 4.6. v. 27. The mind is in the ship.

units.la: MALE audiebant apud Romanos barbari, praesertim Poeni, qui AURES perforatas habebant: neq; mediocriter eos aversabantur. Poen. 5.2.v.21. Incedunt cum annulatis auribus: h.e. perforatis. Lucillius: Nequam est, aurum aures cujus vehementius ambit. Unde jocus Ciceronis in Afrum: Atq; aurem foratam habes. Apud Sygeum Achillis statuam fuisse notat Servius Fuld. lib. 1. Aeneid. q in imâ parte auris elenchum more femineo habuerit.
units.tr: Barbarians, especially the Carthaginians, who had pierced EARS, were badly regarded among the Romans, and they were not moderately despised. Poen. 5.2.v.21. They walk with ringed ears: that is, pierced. Lucilius: Worthless is the man whose ears gold courts more eagerly. Hence Cicero's joke against Afer: And you have a pierced ear. Servius notes that at Sigeum there was a statue of Achilles which, in the lower part of the ear, had an earring in the womanish manner (Fuld. lib. 1 Aeneid).

units.la: BARBA hirquina in cōvitio. Pseud. 4.2.v.12. Etiam apud Germanos. Gilsbart / Bocksbart. Graece: ἀιγοπώγων. Apuleius lib. 11. Milef. Qui pallio baculoq; & baxeu & hirquino barbitio Philosophum fingeret. Ammianus Marcell. lib. 22. de Juliano: Barbam prasefe ferens hirquinam. Idem lib. 25. Hirsutâ barbâ in acutum definente vestitu. Inde Julianus dictus Capella.
units.tr: GOAT-like BEARD as an insult. Pseud. 4.2.v.12. Also among the Germans: Gilsbart / Bocksbart. In Greek: [ἀιγοπώγων] "goat-bearded". Apuleius, Metamorphoses book 11: who with cloak, staff, sandals and a goatish beard would feign a philosopher. Ammianus Marcellinus, book 22, on Julian: bearing a goatish beard. The same, book 25: with a hairy beard coming to a point, and clothing. Hence Julian was called Capella.

units.la: BARBA fœtosa & horrida labra compungit. Caf. 5.2. v. 40.
units.tr: A filthy and bristly beard pricks the lips. Caf. 5.2. v. 40.

units.la: BILIS atrai irae sedes. Amph. 2.2. v. 95.
units.tr: Bile is the seat of anger. Amph. 2.2. v. 95.

units.la: COR sedes prudentiae. Perf. 4.4. v.72. Ita cauta est, & callida: habet cor.
units.tr: The heart is the seat of prudence. Perf. 4.4. v. 72. She is so cautious and clever: she has a heart.

units.la: COR dicitur salire in summa hilaritate: eoque objurgat Captivus cor suum, ɋ etiam in maximo periculo exsultet. Capt. 3.4. v.103. Quin quiescis dierectum cor meum! i, ac suspende te: Tu assultas, ego miser vix asto praeformidine.
units.tr: The heart is said to leap in the highest cheerfulness; hence the captive scolds his heart for exulting even in the greatest danger. Capt. 3.4. v. 103. Why do you not keep still, my upright heart! Go on, hang yourself! You leap about, while I, wretch, can hardly stand for dread.

units.la: Qui versus expressi fortassis ex Comico Alexandride apud Athenaeum lib. 5. ὦ πόρνη καὶ δία, ὀπηχαιφόμακον ὡς ἓι μόνον τὸ σῶμα τῷ· ὀρχῆ δ᾽ εὐθὺς, ἣν ἰδῆς ἀληθινόν.
units.tr: These verses, perhaps, are taken from the comic poet Alexandrides, in Athenaeus book 5: [ὦ πόρνη καὶ δία, ὀπηχαιφόμακον ὡς ἓι μόνον τὸ σῶμα τῷ· ὀρχῆ δ᾽ εὐθὺς, ἣν ἰδῆς ἀληθινόν.] (roughly: "O harlot and goddess... you have only the body for the ... but straightaway, when you see it truly, it is a dance.")

units.la: Vide etiam Mureti Varia lib.19, cap.9.
units.tr: See also Muretus, Varia, lib. 19, cap. 9.

units.la: Cor lienosum dicitur palpitare præ metu instar lienis: impropriè, cùm cor morbo lienis non soleat tentari.
units.tr: A spleen-heart is said to palpitate from fear like the spleen; improperly, since the heart is not usually affected by disease of the spleen.

units.la: Præ dolore pectus tundit.
units.tr: He beats his breast from grief.

units.la: Cor salire solet in amore.
units.tr: The heart is wont to leap in love.

units.la: Tristitia & timore ita afficitur cor, ut dicatur pectus pulsare.
units.tr: The heart is so affected by sadness and fear that the breast is said to pound.

units.la: Cor saltat, & facit rem ludicram præ metu.
units.tr: The heart dances and makes the matter ludicrous from fear.

units.la: Continuò mecum cor cœpit artem facere ludicram, atque in pectus micare.
units.tr: At once my heart began to make a playful art within me, and to flutter in my breast.

units.la: Caf. 2.6. v. 9. Turn. l.24. cap.5. & l.19. cap.22. Brod. Miscell. lib. 3. cap. 27. Æschylus: λέγοις ἀν· ὀρχεῖται δὲ ηαρδία φόβῳ.
units.tr: Caf. 2.6. v. 9. Turn. l.24 cap. 5 & l.19 cap. 22. Brod. Miscell. lib. 3 cap. 27. Aeschylus: "You would say the heart dances from fear" [λέγοις ἂν· ὀρχεῖται δὲ καρδία φόβῳ].

units.la: In pectore sedes consilij & sapientiæ est: Eaq; propter prætextatis bulla pendebat pro pectore.
units.tr: The seat of counsel and wisdom is in the breast; and for this reason a bulla hung on the breast of boys wearing the toga praetexta.

units.la: Vide Alex. ab Alex. lib. 2. 19. & Macrob. lib. 1. Sat. cap. 6.
units.tr: See Alexander ab Alexandro, lib. 2 cap. 19, and Macrobius, lib. 1 Sat. cap. 6.

units.la: CRepitus ventris cibum comestum redolere solet. Inde crepitus polentarius Græcorum Philosophorum Stoicorum, è polentâ comestâ.
units.tr: A belch of the stomach is wont to smell of the food eaten. Hence the "polenta belch" of the Greek Stoic philosophers, from eaten barley-meal.

units.la: Eos ego si offendero, ex utroque eorum excutiam crepitum polentarium.
units.tr: If I catch them, I shall shake out of both of them a polenta belch.

units.la: Crepitus ventris flagitiosè editur in cœtu hominum, præsertim in convivio.
units.tr: A belch of the stomach is shamefully let out in company, especially at a dinner.

units.la: Cepitum ventris emittere flagitium est.
units.tr: To let out a belch of the stomach is a disgrace.

units.la: Pœn.
units.tr: Poen.

units.la: Fores hæ fecerunt magnum flagitium.
units.tr: These doors have made a great disgrace.

units.la: AD. Quid id est flagitij?
units.tr: AD. What is that disgrace?

units.la: COL. (repuerunt clarè.
units.tr: COL. (They cracked loudly.)

units.la: Claudius tamen Imperator permittere in animo habuit. Sueton. cap. 32.
units.tr: Yet the Emperor Claudius intended to permit it. Suetonius, cap. 32.

units.la: Dicitur etiam meditatus edictum, quo veniam daret efflatum, crepitumq; ventris in convivio emittenti, cum periclita- tum quendam præ pudore ex continentia reperisset.
units.tr: He is also said to have contemplated an edict by which he would pardon one who let out a breath, and a belch of the stomach, at a dinner, when he had found someone endangered by shame through his restraint.

units.la: Nec infamis tantùm crepitus,sed etiam religione turbans. Nam auspicia vitiabat, comitia prohibebat.
units.tr: Nor was a belch merely shameful, but it also disturbed religion. For it spoiled the auspices and prevented the assemblies.

units.la: Cato Orat. de sacrilegio commisso:
units.tr: Cato, in his speech on the sacrilege committed:

units.la: Domi cùm auspicamur, honorem me Deùm immortalium velim habuisse. Servi, ancilla, si quis eorum sub centone crepuit, quod ego non sensi, nullum mihi vitium facit. Si cui ibi- dem servo, aut ancillæ dormienti evenit, quod comitia prohibere solet, ne id quidem mihi vitium facit.
units.tr: When we take the auspices at home, I would wish to have shown honour to the immortal gods. If a slave or a maidservant under a patched cloak has belched, which I did not notice, it does me no harm. If it happens to a slave or maidservant sleeping there, which is wont to prevent the assemblies, that too does me no harm.

units.la: Interdum ex metu emissus.
units.tr: Sometimes it is let out from fear.

units.la: Aristoph. Pluto:
units.tr: Aristophanes, Plutus:

units.la: Καπέκειτο ἀ̓ ἀυτὴν ἐντυλίξας ἠσυχῇ ὑπὸ Ϝ Δεὺς βδέυςα Δειμύτε- ςον γαλῆς.
units.tr: [Καπέκειτο ἀ̓ ἀυτὴν ἐντυλίξας ἠσυχῇ ὑπὸ Ϝ Δεὺς βδέυςα Δειμύτε-ςον γαλῆς.] (roughly: "He lay there, wrapping it up quietly... Zeus, farting... the weasel.")

units.la: Idem Nubibus:
units.tr: The same, Clouds:

units.la: ἢ σέβομαι γ᾽ ὠπολυτίμητοι. ἢ βούλομαι ἀνταπαραδεῖν ἐαῖς τὰς βεοντὰς. ὕτως αὐτὰς ἡ ἐεμαίνω ἢ πεφόβημαι.
units.tr: [ἢ σέβομαι γ᾽ ὠπολυτίμητοι. ἢ βούλομαι ἀνταπαραδεῖν ἐαῖς τὰς βεοντὰς. ὕτως αὐτὰς ἡ ἐεμαίνω ἢ πεφόβημαι.] (roughly: "Either I revere them, the most honoured ones, or I wish to exchange the sacred things with them; so either I am mad or I am frightened.")

units.la: Horat. lib. 1. Sat. v I I. Priapus inquit:
units.tr: Horace, Satires, book 1, sat. 8, v. 11. Priapus says:

units.la: ---- ut non testis inultus
units.tr: ---- so that, not an unavenged witness,

units.la: Horruerim voces Furiarum, & factaduarum.
units.tr: I should shudder at the voices of the Furies and the deeds of the witches.

units.la: Nam disslosa sonat, quantum vesica pepedi
units.tr: For it sounds, split open, as much as I let fly from my bladder,

units.la: Dississá nate ficu.
units.tr: split with a split fig-wood.

units.la: Atqui asinorum diversa est natura, qui præ gaudio crepant.
units.tr: But the nature of asses is different, since they bray from joy.

units.la: Aristophanis Scholiastes ad illa verba εἰρήνης:
units.tr: The scholiast of Aristophanes on the words of Eirene (Peace):

units.la: ἥδομαι δὲ ἢ γέγηθα, ἢ πέποςδα, ἢ γελῶ.
units.tr: [ἥδομαι δὲ ἢ γέγηθα, ἢ πέποςδα, ἢ γελῶ.] (I rejoice, or I exult, or I have farted, or I laugh.)

units.la: Sic adnotat:
units.tr: He annotates thus:

units.la: ἡ μεταφορὰ ἀπὸ τῶν ὀνων.
units.tr: [ἡ μεταφορὰ ἀπὸ τῶν ὀνων.] (The metaphor is from the asses.)

units.la: χαίροντες γὰ πέρδοντεu.
units.tr: [χαίροντες γὰρ πέρδονται.] (For they fart rejoicing.)

units.la: Lege etiam Tractatum de Physiologiâ Crepitus ventris Marpurgi editum.
units.tr: Read also the tractate on the physiology of belching of the stomach (Crepitus Ventris), published at Marburg.

units.la: CUTIS mollis comparatur nebulæ molli. Cas. 4. 4 v. 21.
units.tr: Soft skin is compared to soft cloud. Cas. 4.4. v. 21.

units.la: PARTES aliæ corporis in affectu quodam dicuntur prurire, salire. Idq; vel prosperi, vel adversi quid portendere credebant. Amph. 1.1. v. 139. Et Pœn. 5.5. v. 36. Dentes pruriunt. Et Mil. 2. 4. v. 44. Dorsus prurit. Persf. 1. 1. v. 32. Scapulæ pruriunt. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 74. Caput prurit. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 105. Supercilium salit.
units.tr: Other parts of the body are said, in a certain affection, to itch or to leap; and they believed this portended something favourable or adverse. Amph. 1.1. v. 139. And Poen. 5.5. v. 36. The teeth itch. And Mil. 2.4. v. 44. The back itches. Persius 1.1. v. 32. The shoulder-blades itch. Bacch. 5.2. v. 74. The head itches. Pseud. 1.1. v. 105. The eyebrow twitches.

units.la: Vide Tit. Omini: Superstitioni.
units.tr: See the heading Omina: Superstitions.

units.la: DENTES septuennipuero excidunt. Merc. 3. 1. v. 44. Men. 5. 9. v. 57.
units.tr: The teeth fall out in the seventh year of a boy's life. Merc. 3. 1. v. 44. Men. 5. 9. v. 57.

units.la: DENTES dicuntur dentire, cùm dolent, vel grandescunt.
units.tr: Teeth are said to teethe when they hurt or come through.

units.la: De ista dentitione vide Turneb. lib. 7. cap. 6. & Scalig. ad Catal. Virgil. ad illud Fameq; genuini crepant. Pag. 232.
units.tr: On this teething see Turnebus, book 7, chapter 6, and Scaliger on the Catalepton of Virgil, on the line about the jaws of the starving that gnash, page 232.

units.la: DIGITORUM varià commotione solebant dolorem & trististiam innuere.
units.tr: By a varied movement of the fingers people were accustomed to signal pain and sadness.

units.la: Epid. 4. 1. versf. 33. vide Omini: Superstitioni. Vide Meursium Exerc. Crit, part. 1. cap. 5.
units.tr: Epid. 4. 1. vers. 33. See Omina: Superstitions. See Meursius, Exercitationes Criticae, part 1, chapter 5.

units.la: FACIEI color immutatus designat dolorem: aut alium asse-ctum.
units.tr: A change of colour in the face marks pain or some other affection.

units.la: Sed istuc quid est, quod tibi commutatum est color? Numquid tibi dolet? C H. Nescio, quid meo animo est, pater.
units.tr: "But what is it that has changed your colour? Is something hurting you?" "C H. I don't know what is in my mind, father."

units.la: Ex facie colliguntur mores hominis. Pseud. 2.4. v.35. & 2.1. v.17.
units.tr: A person's character is gathered from his face. Pseud. 2. 4. v. 35. & 2. 1. v. 17.

units.la: PER genua obtestabantur: quòd in illis sedes misericordiæ. Most. 3.2. v. 57. Rud. 3.2. v.13. Truc. 4.3. v.52.
units.tr: They used to entreat by the knees, because the seat of pity is there. Most. 3. 2. v. 57. Rud. 3. 2. v. 13. Truc. 4. 3. v. 52.

units.la: Vide Tit. Obsecrationum.
units.tr: See the heading Entreaties.

units.la: JEGUR omnis concupiscentiæ sedes. Poen. 1.2. v. 178.
units.tr: The liver is the seat of all desire. Poen. 1. 2. v. 178.

units.la: De affectu LIENIS, HEPATIS, distractione PULMONUM & cordis, medicè admodum disputat Leno. Curc. 2.1. v.21. & seqq. Ubi lieni ambulationem utilem esse dicit.
units.tr: On the condition of the spleen and liver, and the disturbance of the lungs and heart, Leno discourses quite medically. Curc. 2. 1. v. 21 and following. There he says that walking is useful for the spleen.

units.la: LIEN nimio cursu inquietatur.
units.tr: The spleen is disturbed by too much running.

units.la: Seditionem facit lien: præcordia occupat.
units.tr: The spleen causes sedition: it occupies the midriff.

units.la: LÆVA Manus soror dextera: per quam obtestabantur. Poen. 1.2. v. 9.
units.tr: The left hand is the sister of the right, by which people used to entreat. Poen. 1. 2. v. 9.

units.la: HOMINI tantùm duæ, non tres manus.
units.tr: A man has only two hands, not three.

units.la: Euclio avarus tertiam manum servi cupit excutere. Nempe Avaritia ei sensum quoq; communem ademit.
units.tr: Euclio the miser wants to shake a third hand out of his slave. Indeed avarice has also taken away from him his common sense.

units.la: IN dextris fuit religio: ijsq; amicitiæ firmatæ.
units.tr: Religion was in right hands, and by them friendships were confirmed.

units.la: Vide Tiraquell. ad Alex. ab Alex. l.1. c.19.
units.tr: See Tiraquellus on Alexander ab Alexandro, book 1, chapter 19.

units.la: OCULI vitio qui laborabant, laneum panniculum oculis prætendebant: dicebanturq; Lanoculi apud Festum Pomp. Unde is Mil. 4.4 v.42. jubet oculi vitium simulare: Habeas culcitam ob oculos laneam.
units.tr: Those who suffered from a weakness of the eyes held a woollen rag before their eyes, and they were called Lanoculi in Festus Pompeius. Hence in Mil. 4. 4. v. 42 he orders them to feign an eye ailment: "Have a woollen cushion over your eyes."

units.la: GLAUCOMA vitium oculorum: Græcis γλαύκωμα. Celsus lib.6. vocat suffusionem.
units.tr: Glaucoma is a disease of the eyes; in Greek γλαύκωμα. Celsus, book 6, calls it suffusion.

units.la: Nostler μεταφορικῶς de dolis usurpat.
units.tr: Our author uses it metaphorically [μεταφορικῶς] of tricks.

units.la: Glaucomam ob oculos obýciemus.
units.tr: "We shall throw a glaucoma over their eyes."

units.la: PER oculos & caput suum jarabant. Men. 5.9. v. 1.
units.tr: They rubbed their eyes and their head. Men. 5. 9. v. 1.

units.la: Vide Tit. Juramenti.
units.tr: See the heading Oath.

units.la: LIMI oculi proprie amatorum dicuntur.
units.tr: Sidelong eyes are properly said of lovers.

units.la: Vide Tit. Amoris.
units.tr: See the heading Love.

units.la: OCULORUM testimonium certissimum.
units.tr: The testimony of the eyes is most certain.

units.la: Vide Tit. Testimonij.
units.tr: See the heading Witness.

units.la: OCULI in furore luridi sunt, & virent. Men. 5.2. v. 76.
units.tr: In fury the eyes become livid and green. Men. 5. 2. v. 76.

units.la: Vide Tit. Iracundiæ: Furoris.
units.tr: See the heading Anger: Fury.

units.la: QUÆ carissima erant, Oculorum nomine indigetabant.
units.tr: Things that were most dear were called by the name of eyes.

units.la: OCULI in Amore duces.
units.tr: The eyes are the leaders in love.

units.la: Vide Tit. Amoris.
units.tr: See the heading Love.

units.la: OCULORUM sensus præfertur Auditui.
units.tr: The sense of sight is preferred to hearing.

units.la: Vide Tit. Testium.
units.tr: See the heading Witnesses.

units.la: LOLIUM oculis pernitiosum.
units.tr: Darnel is harmful to the eyes.

units.la: Luscitiosi dicuntur, qui clarius vespertino tempore vident, quàm matutino: qualis fuit Tiberius.
units.tr: Those are called luscitiosi (blear-eyed) who see more clearly in the evening than in the morning, as Tiberius did.

units.la: Oculis signum damus nictando.
units.tr: We give a signal to the eyes by winking.

units.la: Id quod praecipuè observant Amantes.
units.tr: Which lovers especially observe.

units.la: Naevius de quâdam impudicâ apud. Isid. l. 1. c. 25.
units.tr: Naevius, about a certain unchaste woman, in Isidore, book 1, chapter 25.

units.la: Quasi in choro pilâ ludens datatim dat sese & communem facit. Alium tenet, aliy adnutat: alibi manus est occupata: aliy pervellit pedem: aliy dat anulum spectandum: & àlabrum alium invocat: cum alio cantat: attamen aliys dat digito litteras.
units.tr: As if playing ball in a dance, she gives herself to each and makes herself common to all. She holds one, nods to another, elsewhere her hand is busy, she tugs at another's foot, she shows a ring to another to look at, she calls another from the side, she sings with another; yet to another she gives letters with her finger.

units.la: Salomon:
units.tr: Solomon:

units.la: Annuit oculo, terit pede, digito loquitur.
units.tr: He winks with his eye, treads with his foot, speaks with his finger.

units.la: De ejusmodi nictibus multa Poetae.
units.tr: Poets have much to say about such winks.

units.la: Musaeus:
units.tr: Musaeus:

units.la: Λοξὰ δ' ὀπιπτεύων ὀλεγεὰς ἐλέλιζεν ὀφθαλμούς, νεύματι ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ψαφαπαλάζων φρένα κηδεμών.
units.tr: Looking sidelong, he kept winking his eyes a little, stirring his anxious mind with nods of his eyes. [Λοξὰ δ' ὀπιπτεύων ὀλεγεὰς ἐλέλιζεν ὀφθαλμούς, νεύματι ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ψαφαπαλάζων φρένα κηδεμών.]

units.la: Idem:
units.tr: Again:

units.la: Νεύμασι λαθεῖδιοισιν ὑπαγγέλλων ἀλλήλοις.
units.tr: Signalling to one another with secret nods. [Νεύμασι λαθεῖδιοισιν ὑπαγγέλλων ἀλλήλοις.]

units.la: Ovidius de Arte 1.
units.tr: Ovid, Art of Love, book 1.

units.la: Nil opus est digitis, per quos arcana loqueris, Nec tibi per nutus accipienda nota est.
units.tr: You have no need of fingers, by which you speak secrets, nor must a sign be received by you through nods.

units.la: Proximus ad dominam nullo prohibente sedeto, Junge tuum lateri, quam potes usq; latus.
units.tr: Sit next to your mistress, with no one forbidding it, and press your side against hers as closely as you can.
