units.la: Idem Amor. l. 1. Eleg. 1 v.
units.tr: The same, Amores, book 1, elegy 1, verse.

units.la: Cum premit ille torum, vultu comes ipsa modesto Ibis, ut accumbas, clam mihi tange pedem.
units.tr: When he presses the couch, you will go with a modest face as his companion, so that you may recline; secretly touch my foot.

units.la: Mespicta, nutu usq; meos, vultumq; loquacem Excipe, furtivas & refer ipse notas.
units.tr: Watch my nods and my face, which speaks; receive the secret signs and return them yourself.

units.la: Tibullus: Illa viro coram nutus conferre loquaces, Blandaq; compositis addere verba notis.
units.tr: Tibullus: She can exchange eloquent nods in front of her husband, and add flattering words with arranged signs.

units.la: Propertius: Nec lacrimis oculos lingua esse sedare loquaces.
units.tr: Propertius: Nor can the tongue, with tears, quiet eyes that are so talkative.

units.la: NIL magis amamus quàm oculos. Unde proverbium variè natum.
units.tr: We love nothing more than our eyes. Whence a proverb arose in various forms.

units.la: Tamquam oculos amare. Oculitus amare. Ocellus. In oculis habere, &c. Mil. 4. 1. v. 37.
units.tr: Like loving one's eyes. To love with the eyes. Ocellus. To have in one's eyes, etc. Mil. 4. 1. v. 37.

units.la: OCULIS meretrices venaturam faciunt.
units.tr: With their eyes, harlots make a hunt.

units.la: OCULI lippi manu perpetuò attrectantur, neq; quin attingas, abstinere queas.
units.tr: Sore eyes are constantly handled by the hand, nor can one refrain from touching them.

units.la: OCULORUM epulæ sunt spectacula.
units.tr: The feast of the eyes is spectacles.

units.la: Chrysost. προφὴ ὀφθαλμῶ : θεωρία.
units.tr: Chrysostom: the food of the eyes is contemplation. [τροφὴ ὀφθαλμῶν: θεωρία.]

units.la: FUMUS oculis molestus. Most. 4. 2. v. 10.
units.tr: Smoke is annoying to the eyes. Most. 4. 2. v. 10.

units.la: VETERUM opinio fuit, ut frontem Pudoris, Risus lienem, sic & iræ sedem esse NARES.
units.tr: Among the ancients the opinion was that the nostrils are the seat of anger, just as the forehead is the seat of shame and the spleen the seat of laughter.

units.la: Vide egregia in hanc rem apud Casaub. Lect. Theocr. cap. 1.
units.tr: See excellent discussion of this in Casaubon, Lectiones Theocriteae, chapter 1.

units.la: PODEX jocosè dicitur guttur inferius à Coro.
units.tr: The anus is jokingly called the lower throat, by Corus.

units.la: Etiamne obturat inferiorem gutturem? tum ne quid animæ forte amittat dormiens.
units.tr: "Does he even stop up the lower throat? Then lest he perhaps lose some of his breath while sleeping."

units.la: PULMO etsi perpetuò monet, tamen loco numquam promo-vet. Inde proverbialis sermo: pedibus pulmoneis esse, de tardio-ribus, & ad itineris laborem ineptis.
units.tr: The lung, though it constantly gives warnings, never moves from its place. Hence the proverbial saying "to have lungs for feet," said of slower people, unfit for the labour of a journey.

units.la: Dicitur etiam proverbio: pulmo prius venisset.
units.tr: It is also said proverbially: "the lung would have come first."

units.la: SPUERE signum eminentiæ, & vanitatis fuit.
units.tr: Spitting was a sign of self-importance and vanity.

units.la: Vide Casaub. ad Charact. Theophrast.
units.tr: See Casaubon on the Characters of Theophrastus.

units.la: NIMIS magna STATURA non ponitur in laude.
units.tr: Excessive height is not praised.

units.la: Rud. 2. 2. v. 11. de sene:
units.tr: Rud. 2. 2. v. 11, of an old man:

units.la: Ecquam recalvum, ac silonem senem, statutum, ventriosum: tortis supercilijs, contractâ fronte.
units.tr: Some bald, flat-nosed, short and paunchy old man, with twisted eyebrows and a knitted brow.

units.la: USITATA hominis statura erat pedum fere sex: pondus Romanarum librarum centum plus minus.
units.tr: The usual height of a man was about six feet, and his weight about a hundred Roman pounds, more or less.

units.la: Vide Casaub. in Suet.
units.tr: See Casaubon on Suetonius.

units.la: SUPERCILIUM tollere signum est hominis iracundi. Mil. 3. 1. v. 99. & Catull. Alij eadem notâ tristem hominem significare volunt.
units.tr: Raising the eyebrow is a sign of an angry man. Mil. 3. 1. v. 99. and Catullus. Others want the same mark to signify a sad man.

units.la: Vide Petri Vict. Var. lib. 8. cap. 1.
units.tr: See Petrus Victorius, Variae Lectiones, book 8, chapter 1.

units.la: Petronius: Postquam se amari sensit, supercilium altius sustulit.
units.tr: Petronius: After he felt that he was loved, he raised his eyebrow higher.

units.la: Vide etiam Plin. lib. 11. cap. 37.
units.tr: See also Pliny, book 11, chapter 37.

units.la: Juvenalis: Frontis nulla fides.
units.tr: Juvenal: There is no trust in the forehead.

units.la: Martial. lib. 1. Epist. 25. Nolito fronti credere.
units.tr: Martial, book 1, Epist. 25: Do not trust the forehead.

units.la: VULTUS trepidationem arguit. Epid. 1. I. v. 59.
units.tr: The face reveals trepidation. Epid. 1. 1. v. 59.

units.la: VULTUS etiam arguit hominis indolem.
units.tr: The face also reveals a person's character.

units.la: VITA
units.tr: LIFE

units.la: VITA hominum lusus quasi Deorum est.
units.tr: Human life is like a game played by the gods.

units.la: Capt. Prol. v. 22.
units.tr: Capt. Prol. v. 22.

units.la: DI nos quasi pilas homines habent.
units.tr: The gods hold us men like balls.

units.la: Et v. 51.
units.tr: And v. 51.

units.la: Homunculi quanti sunt, cum recogito.
units.tr: How small men are, when I think about it.

units.la: Sic Graeci:
units.tr: So the Greeks say:

units.la: θεῶν παίγνια ἄνθρωποι.
units.tr: Men are the playthings of the gods [θεῶν παίγνια ἄνθρωποι].

units.la: Herod. lib. 1.
units.tr: Herodotus, book 1.

units.la: ὁ ἄνθρωπινὸν ἐνδαιμονίη ἐδαμάσεν τῷ ὧυτῷ μένει.
units.tr: Human prosperity never remains in the same place [ὁ ἀνθρώπινος ὄλβος οὐδαμοῦ μένει].

units.la: Plato homines propterea dicebat θεῶν ἀθύρματα.
units.tr: Plato therefore called men the playthings of the gods [θεῶν ἀθύρματα].

units.la: Æsopus interrogatus, quid ageret Juppiter, respondit: τὰ μὲν οἰκοδομεῖν, τὰ δὲ καταβάλλειν.
units.tr: When Aesop was asked what Jupiter was doing, he replied: building some things, pulling down others [τὰ μὲν οἰκοδομεῖν, τὰ δὲ καταβάλλειν].

units.la: Hinc est, quod in Antiquis monumentis Lares Penatesq; cum pilis depicti spectantur: quas in manibus gestantes versent, quo pacto lubet: quò forte allusit noster loco dicto.
units.tr: Hence it is that in ancient monuments the Lares and Penates are seen depicted with balls, which they turn about in their hands however they please. Our author perhaps alluded to this in the passage cited.

units.la: Vide Festum in Pila.
units.tr: See Festus under Pila.

units.la: Et amplius de miserâ rerum humanarum conditione Muretum lib. 16. c. 15. Variarum Lectionum.
units.tr: On the wretched condition of human affairs in more detail, see Muretus, Variae Lectiones, book 16, chapter 15.

units.la: IN vitâ humanâ paucæ & raræ voluptates sunt, si cum molestijs comparentur.
units.tr: In human life pleasures are few and rare, if they are set against troubles.

units.la: Amph. 2.2. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: Amph. 2.2. v. 1. & seqq.

units.la: Satin' parva res est voluptatum in vitâ, atque in ætate agundâ: præquàm, quod molestum est: ita cuiq; comparatum est in ætate hominum. Ita Dis placitum, voluptatim ut maeror comes consequatur. Quin incommodis plus maliq; illicò assit, boni si obtigit quid.
units.tr: Is it a small thing, the pleasures of life and of the age we live through, compared with what is troublesome? That is how each man's lot is cast in his age. So the gods have decreed: grief follows pleasure as its companion. Indeed, troubles and evils are at hand at once, if any good thing has come our way.

units.la: Querela est Alcumenæ.
units.tr: This is a complaint of Alcmena.

units.la: Vide similem sententiam de Amore ex Cistell. 1. 1. v. 72. Titul. Amoris.
units.tr: See a similar saying about love from Cistell. 1. 1. v. 72. Title Amoris.

units.la: IN hominum ætate multa eveniunt ejusmodi: Capiunt voluptates, tes, capiunt rursus miserias. Amph. 3. 2. v. 57.
units.tr: In the lives of men many such things happen: they gain pleasures, and then again they gain miseries. Amph. 3. 2. v. 57.

units.la: Vide Tit. Amicitia.
units.tr: See title Amicitia.

units.la: De iis, qui post longas & gravissimas iras in solidam & firmam amicitiam coaluerunt iterum.
units.tr: Concerning those who, after long and very grave quarrels, have grown together again into a solid and firm friendship.

units.la: Vide etiam infra Tit. Voluptatis.
units.tr: See also below, title Voluptatis.

units.la: Et supra Tit. Fortuna.
units.tr: And above, title Fortuna.

units.la: NIHIL magis caducum, quàm homo.
units.tr: Nothing is more fleeting than man.

units.la: Rud. 1, 2. v. 66. de Naufragis:
units.tr: Rud. 1, 2. v. 66. On shipwrecked men:

units.la: Hui homunculi quanti estis! ejecti ut natant.
units.tr: Oh, what little men you are! Tossed out, how they swim!

units.la: Sic Petron. pag. 149. Edit. Gold.
units.tr: So Petronius, p. 149, ed. Gold.

units.la: Haec sunt consilia mortalium, haec vota magnarum cogitationum. En homo quem admodum notat! Itenunc mortales, & magnis cogitationibus pectora implete.
units.tr: These are the plans of mortals, these the wishes of great minds. Behold how man is marked! Go now, mortals, and fill your hearts with great thoughts.

units.la: Vide ibi plura.
units.tr: See there for more.

units.la: Vetus Poeta de Fortunae inconstantiâ:
units.tr: An old poet on the inconstancy of Fortune:

units.la: Ite nova in tperra conquirite mundo,
units.tr: Go, seek out new lands across the wide world, for surely no land is fit to hold great leaders.

units.la: Nempe manet magnos par vulla terra Duces.
units.tr: Surely no other land remains equal to its great leaders.

units.la: ITA me DI Deaq, amenti! aequum fuit
units.tr: So help me gods and goddesses, it was only fair

units.la: Deos parasse, uno exemplo ne omnes vitam viverent.
units.tr: that the gods should have arranged things so that not everyone lives his life after one and the same pattern.

units.la: Sicuti mercipretium stat, uti pro virtute vaneat,
units.tr: Just as the price of goods is fixed, so that each sells for its worth,

units.la: Qua in proba est merces, pro vitio dominum precio pauperet:
units.tr: so that for good merchandise the price enriches the owner, while a defect impoverishes him.

units.la: Itidem divos dispertisse vitam humanam aequum fuit.
units.tr: In the same way it was right that the gods should have distributed human life.

units.la: Qui lepide ingeniatus esset, vitam longinquam darent:
units.tr: Those who were charming and clever they would grant a long life;

units.la: At qui improbi & scelesti, ijs adimerent animam citò.
units.tr: but those who were wicked and criminal they would quickly deprive of life.

units.la: Si hoc paravissent, homines essent minus multi mali,
units.tr: If they had arranged this, there would be fewer wicked men among men,

units.la: Et minus audaciter scelesta facerent facta, & postea
units.tr: and they would commit criminal deeds less boldly, and afterwards

units.la: Qui probi homines essent, esset his annona vilior.
units.tr: those who were honest men would have grain at a cheaper price.

units.la: HOMO hominem debet deridere: quia uterq; homo.
units.tr: A man ought to mock a man, because both are men.

units.la: HOMINES sunt ludus Deorum.
units.tr: Men are the sport of the gods.

units.la: Vide Tit. Deorum.
units.tr: See title Deorum.

units.la: HOMINIS ea est indoles, ut incerta petat: certa autem amittat.
units.tr: Man's nature is such that he seeks uncertain things, but loses certain ones.

units.la: Vide Tit. Prudentia & Cupiditatis.
units.tr: See titles Prudentia and Cupiditatis.

units.la: HOMO novarum aedium similis quomo do sit, explicatur Most. 1. 2. v. 8. & seqq. quos vide.
units.tr: How a man is like a new house is explained in Most. 1. 2. v. 8. & seqq., which see.

units.la: HOMINES Salus frustratur, & Fortuna.
units.tr: Safety and Fortune frustrate men.

units.la: HOMINES aequales & divites, & mendici: omnes morti obnoxij.
units.tr: Men are equal, rich and beggars alike: all are subject to death.

units.la: Soli Dij divites.
units.tr: Only the gods are rich.

units.la: HOMINIS Anima pro sale est illi. Ibid. Salillum anima.
units.tr: A man's soul is worth as much to him as a pinch of salt. Ibid. (the phrase about the little salt-cellar of the soul).

units.la: INAURES dono dabant die natali.
units.tr: They used to give earrings as gifts on birthdays.

units.la: METEMΨΥΧΩΣΙΣ aut μεταμψύχωσις realis nulla est. Per jocum tamen dicitur Rud. 3. 6. v. 48.
units.tr: Metempsychosis, or transmigration of souls, is not real at all. Yet it is said in jest in Rud. 3. 6. v. 48.

units.la: (redo alium in aliam belluam hominem vortier.
units.tr: (I will change a man into another beast.

units.la: VETUSTAS tradidit, quamquam fallo, homines mutatos in lupos & feras. Amph. 4.3. v.3.
units.tr: Antiquity has handed down, though falsely, that men were changed into wolves and wild beasts. Amph. 4.3. v.3.

units.la: Legatur Plin. lib. 8. cap. 22.
units.tr: Let Pliny, book 8, chapter 22, be read.

units.la: FABULOSE memorant ex dentibus serpentis, quem interfecit Cadmus, natos fuisse homines armatos.
units.tr: Fabulously, people record that men, armed, were born from the teeth of the serpent which Cadmus killed. Amph. 4. 3. v. 15. From Ovid's Metamorphoses, book 3.

units.la: Amph. 4. 3. v. 15. Ex Metamorphosi Ovidiana lib. 3.
units.tr: Amph. 4. 3. v. 15. From Ovid's Metamorphoses, book 3.

units.la: CORPUS hominis non potest esse, aut ubiq; , aut pluribus in locis. Intellexit id Leno Plautinus Rud 5.2. v.41. Si hercle abiero hinc: hic non ero: inquit ibi Leno.
units.tr: A man's body cannot be everywhere at once, or in several places. The Plautine pimp understood this: "If, by Hercules, I go away from here, I shall not be here," says the pimp there. Rud. 5.2. v.41.

units.la: Magis id liquet ex loco Amph. 2.1.v.11.16.41.46.
units.tr: This is clearer from the passage Amph. 2.1. v.11.16.41.46.

units.la: Nemo umquam homo antehac vidit: NEC POTEST FIERI, tempore uno Homo idem duobus locis ut simul siet.
units.tr: No man has ever seen this before: IT CANNOT HAPPEN that one man, at one time, should be in two places at once.

units.la: Sic Mostl. 3. 2. v. 106.
Ego hic esse, & illic simul haud potui.
units.tr: I could not be here and there at the same time.

units.la: Vide etiam infra Tit. Praesentia loci.
units.tr: See also below, title Praesentia loci.

units.la: NEC verisimile loquere, nec verum, comisse quemquam ut quisquam absentem possiet.
units.tr: You say nothing likely, nor true, that anyone could bring it about that a person who is absent could be present.

units.la: Mostl. I.I. v. 13.
units.tr: Mostl. I.I. v. 13.

units.la: Nimirùm proprie id fieri nequit. Quod mihi notentij, qui in sacrisillud ἀχώρητον statuunt; Corpus Christi absens in calo proprie comedi posse ore corporali. Quin & comeditur: sed modo sacramentali: ut obiter hoc quoq; innuam.
units.tr: Clearly this cannot happen in the proper sense. I say this to those who, in sacred matters, hold that the body of Christ is uncontainable [ἀχώρητον]: "The absent body of Christ in heaven can properly be eaten with the bodily mouth." Indeed it is eaten, but only in a sacramental way, as I hint in passing here too.

units.la: Mirùm sanè è Plauto Ethnico homine, qui aliquot saecula ante Christum natum vixit, portentum UBIQUITATIS, & ORALIS MANDUCATIONIS Corporis CHRISTI, posse refutari. Apage igitur naenias istas absurdas, & planè futiles. Sed nunc non ago Theologum.
units.tr: It is remarkable that from the heathen Plautus, who lived some centuries before Christ was born, the portent of UBIQUITY and of ORAL MANDUCATION of the body of Christ can be refuted. Away, then, with those absurd and altogether trifling lullabies. But now I am not acting as a theologian.

units.la: HONORIS. HONESTATIS. DIGNITATIS. LOCI. FAMAE. EXISTIMATIONIS. GLORIAE, LAUDIS. PRAEMIORUM.
units.tr: HONOUR. HONESTY. DIGNITY. PLACE. REPUTE. ESTEEM. GLORY, PRAISE. REWARDS.

units.la: HONORIS causa pulvinum praebebant assidentibus. Stich. 1.2. v. 37. Filia parenti.
units.tr: For the sake of honour they offered a cushion to those seated beside them. Stich. 1.2. v. 37. Filia parenti.

units.la: NUMQUAM nimis curare possunt suum parentem filiae. Stich. 1.2. v. 40.
units.tr: Daughters can never take too much care of their parent. Stich. 1.2. v. 40.

units.la: FILIAE honestae & piae patris honorem praeferunt mariti. Stich. 1.2. v. 40.
units.tr: Honest and dutiful daughters put their father's honour before that of their husbands. Stich. 1.2. v. 40.

units.la: SUBSELLIUM imum minus erat honestum.
units.tr: The lowest bench was less honourable.

units.la: Sic Parasiti dicuntur viri imi subsellij. Capt. 3. 1. v. 11.
units.tr: Thus parasites are called men of the lowest bench. Capt. 3.1. v. 11.

units.la: Locus medius semper honorificentissimus habitus.
units.tr: The middle place was always regarded as the most honourable.

units.la: Hic patri concessus a filio. Asin. 5.2. v. 42.
units.tr: This was granted to the father by the son. Asin. 5.2. v. 42.

units.la: Da puer ab summo, ago tu interibi ab infimo da savium.
units.tr: Boy, give the kiss from the top; and you, meanwhile, give one from the bottom.

units.la: Pater scilicet medius inter illos.
units.tr: The father, of course, in the middle between them.

units.la: Illustrabo hoc ex alijs Authoribus.
units.tr: I will illustrate this from other authors.

units.la: Seneca de Injurijs cap. 10.
units.tr: Seneca, On Injuries, ch. 10.

units.la: Sermonem meum aut superbe aversatus est, aut palam risit, & non in medio me loco, sed imo collocavit.
units.tr: He either disdainfully turned away from my speech or openly laughed, and placed me not in the middle place but at the bottom.

units.la: Idem Seneca lib. 3. de Ira cap. 37.
units.tr: The same Seneca, On Anger, book 3, ch. 37.

units.la: Minus honorato loco positus, irasci capisti convivatori ipsi, qui tibi praeferebetur. Demens quid interest, quam lecti premau partem.
units.tr: Placed in a less honoured position, you began to be angry with the host himself, who was preferred over you. Madman, what difference does it make which part of the couch you press?

units.la: Cicero lib. 9. Epist. ad Pætum.
units.tr: Cicero, book 9, Letters to Paetus.

units.la: Accubueram horânonâ. Vbi? apud Eutrapelum; & quidem supra me Atticum, infra Verrium familiares tui.
units.tr: I was reclining at the ninth hour. Where? At Eutrapelus's; and indeed above me Atticus, below Verrius, your friends.

units.la: Medius scilicet erat Cicero.
units.tr: Clearly Cicero was in the middle.

units.la: Virgil. lib. 1. Æncid.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid book 1.

units.la: — Aulæis jam se regina superbisAurea composuit sponda, mediumq; locavit.
units.tr: Now the queen, reclining on embroidered hangings, took her place on a golden couch and placed herself in the middle.

units.la: Ovid. lib. 2. Amor. Eleg. 16. v. 13.
units.tr: Ovid, Amores book 2, elegy 16, v. 13.

units.la: Non ego si medius Pollux & Castore ponar,In cœli sine te parte fuisse velim.
units.tr: If I were placed in the middle between Pollux and Castor, I would not wish to be in heaven without you.

units.la: Suetonius de Tiberio cap. 17.
units.tr: Suetonius, Tiberius ch. 17.

units.la: Nihilominus urbem prætextatus, & laurea coronatus intra-vit: positumque in septis tribunal, senatu adstante, con-scendit: ac medius inter duos Coss. cum Augusto simul se-dit.
units.tr: Nevertheless he entered the city in a purple-bordered toga and crowned with laurel; and, having mounted the tribunal placed in the enclosure, with the senate standing by, he sat down in the middle between the two consuls, with Augustus seated at the same time.

units.la: Idem Calig. cap. 22.
units.tr: Suetonius, Caligula ch. 22.

units.la: Atq; ade Castoris & Pollucis in vestibulum transfigurata, con-sistens sæpe inter fratres Deos medium se adorandum ad-euntibus exhibebat.
units.tr: And indeed, standing often in the vestibule of the temple of Castor and Pollux, transformed, between the brother gods, he showed himself in the middle to those approaching, to be worshipped.

units.la: Quo loco vide Comment. Beroald. ubi exemplis idipsum evin-cit.
units.tr: See the commentary of Beroaldus, where he proves this very point by examples.

units.la: Val. Max. lib. 8. c. 15. de Mario:
units.tr: Valerius Maximus, book 8, ch. 15, on Marius:

units.la: Imperator Africanus ipsum respiciens supra se cubantem, vel hunc dixit: &c.
units.tr: The commander Africanus, looking up at him reclining above himself, said this, or that: etc.

units.la: Minutius Octavio:
units.tr: Minucius, to Octavius:

units.la: Et cum dicto ejus assedimus: ita ut & me ex tribus medium lateris ambitione protegerent.
units.tr: And at his word we sat down, so that they protected me in the middle, out of three, by surrounding my sides.

units.la: Huc quoque referri potest illud Christi Salvatoris:
units.tr: To this may also be referred that saying of Christ the Saviour:

units.la: Vbi duo aut tres in nomine meo congregati fuerint: ibi ego ero Medius inter illos.
units.tr: Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the midst of them.

units.la: Cæterum inter eruditos vehementer disceptari solet, utrum dexter an sinister locus honoratior sit habitus.
units.tr: Otherwise, among the learned, it is much debated whether the right or the left place was regarded as the more honourable.

units.la: Pro dextro verè pugnat Justus Lipsius lib. 2. Electorum cap. 2. inibique refutat Goropium Becanum popularem suum sinistri honorem asserentem.
units.tr: Justus Lipsius, Electorum book 2, ch. 2, truly argues for the right, and there refutes Goropius Becanus, his fellow countryman, who asserts the honour of the left.

units.la: Eundem sinistrum adprobat quoque Robert. Bellarminus lib. 1. de Pontifice Romano c. 27. Inspiciantur hi duo Authores. Mihi probabilior fit sententia pro Dextro.
units.tr: Robert Bellarmine, On the Roman Pontiff, book 1, ch. 27, also approves the left. Let these two authors be consulted. To me the opinion favouring the right seems more probable.

units.la: Eandem adstruit quoq; idem Lipsius Centur. III. Epist. ad Johann. Baptist. Hansenium Epist. x c. Et argumenta in eam rem in mundo sunt: quæ nunc jam differo in alium Tractatum.
units.tr: The same Lipsius also supports it in Centuria III, in his letter to Johannes Baptista Hansenius, Epist. x c. There are also arguments on this point in the world, which I now defer to another treatise.

units.la: IN ludis curatores cavebant ne injuriâ palma daretur cuiquam: ne, ambitionis causâ boni extruderentur foras: sed quisq; virtute suâ dignum acciperet præmium: neve deteriores anteponerentur bonis.
units.tr: In the games the overseers took care that no palm was given to anyone by favour, lest the good be thrust out through ambition; but each should receive a prize worthy of his virtue, and the worse should not be placed before the good.

units.la: Poen. Prol. v. 37.
units.tr: Poen. Prol. v. 37.

units.la: HONORIFICUM est alteri obvianti in viâ, aut semitâ cedere.
units.tr: It is an honour to yield the way to another who meets you on the road or path.

units.la: Vide Tit. Via.
units.tr: See the title Via.

units.la: PARENTIBUS male suadentibus contra bonos mores, & pietatem, vix obtemperandum.
units.tr: Parents who advise badly, against good morals and piety, are hardly to be obeyed.

units.la: Nunc placet pater, cum recte monstras: nunc tibi anscultabimus.
units.tr: Now I like you, father, since you advise rightly: now we shall obey you.

units.la: Vide totum Dialogum parentis cum duabus filiabus suis.
units.tr: See the whole dialogue of the parent with his two daughters.

units.la: GLORIOSORUM hi sunt mores, ut non satis habeant summatim sua facinora recensere: nisi etiam ordine id fiat.
units.tr: Boasters have this habit: they are not content to recount their deeds in summary, unless this is also done in order.

units.la: Vide Casaub. in Charact. Theoph. [Greek: περὶ ἀλαζονείας].
units.tr: See Casaubon on Theophrastus's Characters, [περὶ ἀλαζονείας] (On Boastfulness).

units.la: MAGISTRIS olim sub disciplinâ parebant usq; ad id tempus ætatis, quo petere magistratus liceret. Bacch. 3.3. v. 35.
units.tr: Formerly pupils were under discipline to their teachers until the age at which it was permitted to seek magistracies. Bacch. 3.3. v. 35.

units.la: In summâ ac profulâ hilaritate cor solet salire: itidemque in pavore.
units.tr: In sheer and pure merriment the heart is wont to leap; likewise in fear.

units.la: Vide Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See the title Man.

units.la: Viri fortes, strenui in honoribus saepè negliguntur ob malos saeculi mores. Ita virtuti omnis adimitur quandoq; honos.
units.tr: Brave and vigorous men are often neglected in honours because of the bad morals of the age. Thus honour is sometimes taken away from virtue.

units.la: Alii ob virtutem, gloriam assequuntur immortalem: alij ob malefacta.
units.tr: Some attain immortal glory on account of virtue; others on account of wicked deeds.

units.la: Ad utramq; rationem alludit noster Capt. 3. f. v. 31. 32.
units.tr: Our author alludes to both reasons: Capt. 3.f. v. 31. 32.

units.la: Qui ex imis sordibus ad summas dignitates evehuntur; lumbrici appellantur.
units.tr: Those who are raised from the lowest filth to the highest dignities are called lumbrici (earthworms).

units.la: Alias etiam Terræ filij.
units.tr: Elsewhere also sons of the earth.

units.la: Præmia dabantur ob virtutem.
units.tr: Prizes were given on account of virtue.

units.la: Vide Tit. Virtutis.
units.tr: See the title Virtue.

units.la: Alexander Magnus & Agathocles, ob res maximas gloriam immortalem sunt consecuti.
units.tr: Alexander the Great and Agathocles attained immortal glory on account of very great deeds.

units.la: Virgo mala est, quæ sapit præter quàm placet parentibus.
units.tr: A girl is bad who is wiser than pleases her parents.

units.la: Honores distribuendi virtute præditis tantum.
units.tr: Honours are to be distributed only to those endowed with virtue.

units.la: Amph. Prol. v. 78.
units.tr: Amph. Prol. v. 78.

units.la: Parentes verberare piaculare nefas: abominabile prorsus occidere.
units.tr: To beat one's parents is an impious crime; to kill them is utterly abominable.

units.la: ornament
units.tr: ornament

units.la: HORTORUM.
units.tr: GARDENS.

units.la: HORTI fodiebantur palis.
units.tr: The gardens were dug up with stakes.

units.la: ÆDIBUS hortos plærumq; veteres habebant additos.
units.tr: The ancients usually had gardens attached to their houses.
Casina 3. 4. v. 23.
Mostellaria 5. 1. v. 4.
Persa 3. 3. v. 41.

units.la: HOSPITII. HOSPITALITATIS.
units.tr: HOSPITALITY. HOSPITALITAS.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Convivij.
units.tr: See also the heading Banquets.

units.la: FUIT antiqui moris tesseram dimidiatam dari hospitibus, quam quicumque attulisset ad hospitem, continuò agnosci posset, & hospitio excipi tamquam amicus & vetus hospes. Hoc autem jus ad posteros transibat: propterea tesseram hospitalem diligenter asservabant.
units.tr: It was an ancient custom to give guests a halved tessera, and whoever brought it to the host could at once be recognised and received into his house as a friend and an old guest. This right also passed down to their descendants, so people carefully kept the hospitality tessera.

units.la: Qui autem jus hospitij violabat, is tesseram hospitalem confregisse dicebatur.
units.tr: Someone who violated the right of hospitality was said to have broken the hospitality tessera.

units.la: Deum hospitalem, ac tesseram mecum fero.
units.tr: I carry with me a god of hospitality and a tessera.

units.la: Deus Hospitalis Jupiter Xenius dictus fuit: quem invocabant, quemadmodum Amici Philium Jovem: & Sodales Hetærium: & gentiles seu cognati Homognium. Si quem igitur contracti hospitij pœnituisset, renunciare hospitium solebat: ne hospitij jus violaret.
units.tr: The god of hospitality was called Jupiter Xenius, whom they invoked as friends invoked Jupiter Philius, comrades invoked Hetaerius, and kinsmen or clansmen invoked Homognius. So if someone regretted a hospitality he had entered into, he would usually renounce the hospitality, so that he did not violate its right.

units.la: Vide Budæum in Pandectas.
units.tr: See Budaeus on the Pandects.

units.la: Qui jus hospitalitatis inter se colebant tesseram seu symbolum hospitalitatis monumentum relinquebant post se.
units.tr: Those who kept the right of hospitality between themselves left behind a tessera, or symbol of hospitality, as a memorial.

units.la: Vide de his symbolis Isaac. Casaub. Animad Athen. lib. 3. cap.31. Ubi dictum locum Plauti eò quoq; trahit. Sed mihi non videtur illuc pertinere: cùm de arrhâ emtionis ibi sit sermo. Inspiciatur locus paulò diligentius: & quod dixi, patebit verum esse.
units.tr: On these symbols see Isaac Casaubon, Animadversions on Athenaeus, book 3, chapter 31, where he also draws the passage of Plautus cited there into this context. But it does not seem to me to belong there, since the discussion there concerns the earnest money of a purchase. Let the passage be examined a little more carefully, and the truth of what I have said will become clear.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Convivij & Annulorum.
units.tr: See also the headings Banquets and Rings.

units.la: Proletarius est sermo eorum, qui quando hospitio excepti, & quando accubuere, ubi cœna apposita est, dicere:
units.tr: This is the language of those who, when they are received as guests and when they recline at the table where the dinner has been laid, say:

units.la: Quid opus fuit hoc hospes sumtu tanto nostrâ gratiâ?
units.tr: Why did you need, host, to spend so much on our account?

units.la: Insanivisti hercle: nam idem hoc hominibus sat erat decem.
units.tr: You have gone mad, by Hercules! For this same amount would have been enough for ten men.

units.la: Quod eorum causâ obsonatum est, culpant, & comedunt tamen.
units.tr: They find fault with what was bought for their sake, and yet they eat it.

units.la: Sed ydem homines numquam dicunt, quamquam appositum est ampliter:
units.tr: But these same men never say so, although the food has been served lavishly:

units.la: Jube illud demi: tolle hanc patinam, remove pernam, nihil mo- ror.
units.tr: Tell them to take that away; remove this dish, take away the ham, I don't care for it at all.

units.la: Auffer illam offam penitam, probum hic conger frigidum.
units.tr: Take away that piece of fat, here is a cold conger, not good.

units.la: Remove, abi, aufer: neminem eorum hac asseverare audias.
units.tr: Remove it, take it away, carry it off: you will not hear any of them say such things.

units.la: Sed percellunt se, & procumbunt dimidiati, dum appetunt.
units.tr: But they knock themselves over and fall half-dead while they reach for it.
Mil. 3. 1. v. 156 and following.

units.la: Hospitii jus violare nefas.
units.tr: To violate the right of hospitality is an impiety.

units.la: Hospites enim debent custodire depositum: non furari: qualis infidelis hospes fuit Antolycus.
units.tr: For guests ought to guard a deposit, not steal it; such an unfaithful guest was Autolycus.

units.la: TRANSEUNTEM hospitio excipere, magna est comitas.
units.tr: To receive a traveller into one's home as a guest is a great courtesy.

units.la: HOSPES nullus tàm in amici hospitium divorti potest,Quin ubi triduum continuum fuerit, jam odiosus fiet.Verùm ubi dies decem continuos ire ad eundem instat,Tametsi dominus non invitus patitur, servi murmurant.
units.tr: No guest can be so welcome in a friend's house that he does not become tiresome once he has stayed three days in a row. But when he is set to come to the same house for ten days running, then, although the master may not mind, the slaves grumble.

units.la: HOSPITEM peregrinum non decet esse importunum in alienâ domo.
units.tr: A foreign guest ought not to be a nuisance in another man's house.

units.la: In bono hospite, atq; amico quæstus est, quod sumitur.
units.tr: From a good guest and friend, what is taken is a gain.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Ignis. Flammæ. Incendii.
units.tr: Fire. Flames. Conflagration.

units.la: Gnis Vulcani pater. Aul. 2. 6. v. 10.
units.tr: Fire is the father of Vulcan. Aul. 2. 6. v. 10.

units.la: Ignem parcè accendebant avari, neædes comburerent. Aul. 2. 6. v. 12.
units.tr: Misers kindled fire sparingly, lest they burn their houses. Aul. 2. 6. v. 12.

units.la: Ignis datur, tamenetsi ab inimicis petas. Trin. 3. 2. v. 53. Igitur inhumanus prorsus Euclio, qui vicinis ignem negavit Aul. 1. 2. v. 12. Nam veteres non semper domi suæ ignem excitabant: neque eum facilè negare petenti licebat.
units.tr: Fire is given, even if you ask it of enemies. Trin. 3. 2. v. 53. Therefore Euclio was utterly inhuman, who refused fire to his neighbours. Aul. 1. 2. v. 12. For the ancients did not always kindle fire at home, and it was not easy to refuse it to one who asked.

units.la: Videbatur enim hoc valdè alienum esse ab ipsâ humanitate, & vitâ hominum, atq; naturâ, quæ aquâ & igni carere non potest.
units.tr: For this seemed very alien to humanity itself, to human life and to nature, which cannot do without water and fire.

units.la: Sic Enniusapud Ciceronem lib. 1. Ut homo, qui erranti comiter monstrat viam, Quasi lumen de suo lumine accendat, faciat, Ut nihilominus ipsi luceat, cum illi accenderit.
units.tr: So Ennius, in Cicero, book 1: "As a man who kindly shows the way to one who has gone astray, lights a torch from his own torch, so that it shines for himself too, once he has lit it for the other."

units.la: De flammâ tamen Deûm: h. e. de igne sacrificiorum, non licebat ignem accendere, vel lumen mutuari, ne scilicet sacra profanarentur: quâ de re Phædrus lib. 4. Fabb. 68. ad quem locum vide Rittershusium.
units.tr: But of the flame of the gods, that is, of the fire of sacrifices, it was not permitted to kindle a fire or borrow a light, lest sacred things be profaned. On this matter see Phaedrus, book 4, fable 68; on that passage see Rittershusius.

units.la: Ignem veteres non semper domi suæ excitabant: sed à vicinis plærumque petebant: neque eum negare facilè petenti licebat.
units.tr: The ancients did not always kindle fire at home, but mostly asked their neighbours for it, and it was not easy to refuse one who asked.

units.la: Videbatur enim valdè alienum esse ab ipsâ humanitate, & vitâ hominum, atq; naturâ, quæ aquâ & igni carere non potest.
units.tr: For this seemed very alien to humanity itself, to human life and to nature, which cannot do without water and fire.

units.la: Vide paulò ante.
units.tr: See a little above.

units.la: IGNIS quicquid contingit, amburit.
units.tr: FIRE burns whatever it touches.

units.la: Ille quidem Vulcani irati est filius: Quaqua tangit, omne amburit. Tralatè.
units.tr: That one is indeed the son of angry Vulcan: wherever he touches, he burns everything. Used figuratively.

units.la: FLAMMA fumo est proxima. (Curc. 1. 1. v. 53.
units.tr: FLAME is next to smoke. (Curc. 1. 1. v. 53.

units.la: IGNI vita comparatur. Aul. 1. 2. v. 15.
units.tr: Life is compared to fire. Aul. 1. 2. v. 15.

units.la: IMITATIONIS.
units.tr: IMITATION.

units.la: EXEMPLA improborum trahuntur in imitationem. Epid. 1. 1. v. 30.
units.tr: Examples of the wicked are drawn into imitation. Epid. 1. 1. v. 30.

units.la: Vide Tit. Exemplorum.
units.tr: See the title Examples.

units.la: INDULGENTIÆ.
units.tr: INDULGENCE.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Educationis & Parentum.
units.tr: See also the title Education and Parents.

units.la: INSIGNE exemplum indulgentiæ paternæ est Dæmenetus, qui ad lustra & meretrices tantum non deduxit suum filium.
units.tr: A striking example of paternal indulgence is Demaenetus, who all but led his son to the brothels and the courtesans.

units.la: Contra laudat Chremetem Lucilius lib. 28. apud Nonium in Ire.
units.tr: By contrast, Lucilius, book 28, praises Chremes, as cited in Nonius under Ire.

units.la: In medium Chremes, in summum ire Dæmenetus: h. e. Chremes in indulgendo filio, medium tenuit: Dæmenetus verò summum: eóq; medium excessit.
units.tr: "Chremes kept to the middle, Demaenetus went to the extreme": that is, Chremes kept the middle course in indulging his son, but Demaenetus went to the extreme, and so overshot the middle.

units.la: Vide etiam Asin. 5. 1. v. 3.
units.tr: See also Asin. 5. 1. v. 3.

units.la: PLUS semper indulgent filijs matres, quàm patres. At contra Asin. 1. 1. v. 64. Vide Tit. Parentum.
units.tr: Mothers always indulge their sons more than fathers do. But on the contrary, Asin. 1. 1. v. 64. See the title Parents.

units.la: INIURIARUM.
units.tr: INJURIES.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Asyli: Templorum: Vis: Violen-tia: Ara.
units.tr: See also the titles Asylum, Temples, Violence, Force, Altar.

units.la: SI quis quem re, aut verbo læserat, interpositione jurisjurandi, quò cum, qui læsus erat, adjurabat indignum eâ injuriâ esse, & ei nolle factam; satis faciebat, atque purgabat.
units.tr: If anyone had wronged another by word or deed, he made amends and cleared himself by the interposition of an oath, by which the one who had been wronged swore that he deserved the injury and did not want it done to him.

units.la: Alludit huc Amph. 3. 2. 1. 8. 50. & Rud. 5. 3. v. 28.
units.tr: This alludes to Amph. 3. 2. 1. 8. 50. & Rud. 5. 3. v. 28.

units.la: De quâ consuetudine satisfaciendi pro injuriâ illatâ videndus in-primis præstantissimus JC. Janus Langlæus lib.10. Semest. cap.1. pag. 596. Itemq; Petrus Nannius Misc. lib.2. c.7. Turneb.lib.18. c.25. Scipio Gentil.ad Apul. Apolog. notâ 943. pag. 548. & Tit. Juramenti.
units.tr: On this custom of making amends for an injury inflicted, see above all the most distinguished jurist Janus Langlaeus, book 10 Semest. ch. 1, p. 596; likewise Petrus Nannius, Misc. book 2 ch. 7; Turnebus book 18 ch. 25; Scipio Gentilis on Apuleius' Apology, note 943, p. 548; and the title Oath.

units.la: Vide etiam Terent. Adelph. 2.1. v.
units.tr: See also Terence, Adelphi 2. 1. v.

units.la: INIURIA puellis infertur, si violetur earum pudicitia.
units.tr: An injury is done to girls if their chastity is violated.

units.la: Cistell. 1.3. v.32.
units.tr: Cistell. 1. 3. v. 32.

units.la: Injuria lib. 1 v. ad Herenn. definitur: Quæ aut pulsatione corpus, aut convitio aures, aut aliquâ turpitudine vitam alicujus vio-lat.
units.tr: Injury is defined in the first book of the Herennius: That which violates a person's body by blows, his ears by abuse, or his life by some disgrace.

units.la: Te alloquor vitij probriq, plena, quæ circum vicinos vagas.
units.tr: I address you, full of vice and reproach, you who wander about the neighbours.

units.la: Propert. lib.4. Eleg.8.
units.tr: Propertius, book 4, Elegy 8.

units.la: Cum fieret nostra totiens injuria lectlo.
units.tr: Since our bed was so often the scene of injury.

units.la: Idem. lib. 2. Eleg. 24.
units.tr: The same, book 2, Elegy 24.

units.la: Nec si per totam infamiâ traduceret urbem.
units.tr: Nor if she carried infamy through the whole city.

units.la: Idem lib. 2. Eleg. 20.
units.tr: The same, book 2, Elegy 20.

units.la: Cum de me & de te compita nulla tacent.
units.tr: Since no crossroads keep silent about me and you.

units.la: Tt 3
units.tr: Tt 3

units.la: Idem lib. 3. Eleg. 25.
units.tr: The same, book 3, Elegy 25.

units.la: Risus eram positus inter convivia mensis.
units.tr: I was made a laughingstock at the tables among the feasts.

units.la: Iniuriarum & offensionum semper est memoria: beneficiorum non item.
units.tr: There is always a memory of injuries and offences; of benefits, not so.

units.la: Vide Tit. Beneficiorum.
units.tr: See the title Benefits.

units.la: Stultus est, qui illi male aegre patitur dici, qui facit.
units.tr: He is a fool who is ill pleased to be told what he himself does.

units.la: Iniuria etiam rebus inanimatis inferri potest.
units.tr: Injury can also be inflicted on inanimate things.

units.la: Quia est, qui tam protervè nostris foribus facit injuriam?
units.tr: Who is it that so insolently does injury to our doors?

units.la: Vim facere in oppido pacato, & quidem luce, in via, & libero homini, nefas.
units.tr: To use force in a peaceful town, and indeed by daylight, in the street, against a free man, is wrong.

units.la: In eos à quibus accepimus beneficia, non debemus esse injurij.
units.tr: Towards those from whom we have received benefits we ought not to be injurious.

units.la: Praesertim in pauperes. Ibid.
units.tr: Especially towards the poor. Ibid.

units.la: Graeci moris fuit, ad vim, injuriamq; arcendam, confugere ad templa, statuas, aras.
units.tr: It was the custom of the Greeks, to ward off force and injury, to flee to temples, statues and altars.

units.la: Vide Taub. Comm. pag. 572. 1011.
units.tr: See Taubmann's commentary, pp. 572, 1011.

units.la: Iniurias illatas vindicabant avidè.
units.tr: They eagerly avenged the injuries inflicted on them.

units.la: INGENII,
units.tr: OF WIT,

units.la: Vide Tit. Morum.
units.tr: See the title Manners.

units.la: Ingenii hebetudinem arguit crassities cutis. Unde de homine stupido dicitur Mil. 2. 2, v. 80.
units.tr: A thick skin indicates dullness of wit. Hence of a stupid man it is said, Mil. 2. 2. v. 80.

units.la: Hermo Herus meus elephanti corio circumtentus est, non habet plus sapientiam, quam lapis.
units.tr: Hermo, my master, is wrapped in an elephant's hide; he has no more wisdom than a stone.

units.la: Rationem hujus rei vide apud Cæl. Rhodig. lib. 6. c. 1. Antiqq. Lect.
units.tr: For the reason of this, see Caelius Rhodiginus, book 6 ch. 1 of the Antiquae Lectiones.

units.la: UT sæpe summa ingenia in occulto latent! Capt. 1. 2. v. 56.
units.tr: How often great talents lie hidden in obscurity! Capt. 1. 2. v. 56.

units.la: Simile est illud: Sæpe sub sordido palliolo latet sapientia.
units.tr: A similar saying is: Often wisdom lies hidden under a shabby cloak.

units.la: Innocentiæ.
units.tr: Innocence.

units.la: DECET innocentem qui sit, atq; innoxius, Servum superbum esse apud herum potissimum. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 45.
units.tr: It befits a man who is innocent and blameless to be proud, especially before his master, a slave should be. (Pseud. 1. 5. v. 45.)

units.la: Innocentia facit confidentem. Capt. 3. 5. v. 7.
units.tr: Innocence makes a man confident. (Capt. 3. 5. v. 7.)

units.la: Insaniæ. Furoris.
units.tr: Madness. Fury.

units.la: Vide etiam paulò post Tit. Iræ: Iracundiæ: Nam Ira furor brevis est. Ideoq; Tituli affines sunt.
units.tr: See also a little later under the title Wrath: Irascibility: For anger is a brief madness. Hence these titles are related.

units.la: IRATUS & insanis oculi solent ardere. Capt. 3. 4. v. 62. Men. 5. 2. v. 76. Virgil. 12. Æneid, Ardentes oculorum orbes ad mænia torsit Turbidus.
units.tr: Angry men's eyes and mad men's eyes are wont to blaze. Captivi 3.4 v.62. Menaechmi 5.2 v.76. Virgil, Aeneid book 12: Blazing eyeballs he turned, wild, toward the walls.

units.la: Insani & furiosi, mente impotes in vinculis habiti sunt. Capt. 3. 4. v. 62. Men. 5. 2. v. 76.
units.tr: Madmen and furious men, impotent in mind, have been kept in chains. Captivi 3.4 v.62. Menaechmi 5.2 v.76.

units.la: Cicero in Pisonem: Si familiam tuam dim, &c.
units.tr: Cicero against Piso: If your household ... &c.

units.la: Philipp. II. Tu mentis es compos? tu non constringendus?
units.tr: Philippics II: Are you in possession of your mind? Are you not to be bound?

units.la: De Divinat. II. Quod sic ita natura paratum esset, &c.
units.tr: On Divination II: Because it was so prepared by nature, &c.

units.la: Melancholia saepe furorem conciliat.
units.tr: Melancholy often produces madness.
Captivi 3.4 v.82.

units.la: Ubi servus captivus comparatur Ajaci, cujus furor ex melancholia manavit, quâ de re Celsus Medicus sic ait lib. 6. cap. 18.
units.tr: Here the captive slave is compared to Ajax, whose madness arose from melancholy. On this matter Celsus the physician says as follows, book 6, chapter 18.

units.la: Quidam imaginibus, non mentefalluntur: qualem insanientem Ajacem vel Orestem Poëtarum fabulæ ferunt.
units.tr: Some are deceived by images, not in their minds: such as the raving Ajax or Orestes that the fables of the poets tell of.

units.la: INSANIENTEM vox est: Evoe! Evoe! Bromie!
units.tr: A RAVING MAN's cry: Evoe! Evoe! Bromius!
Menaechmi 5.2 v.83.

units.la: HELLEBORUM insaniæ curandæ perutilem esse tradunt Medici.
units.tr: Physicians report that hellebore is very useful for curing madness.
Pseudolus 4.7 v.89.
Rudens 4.3 v.67.

units.la: Horat. lib. Sat. 3.
units.tr: Horace, Satires, book 3.

units.la: Danda est hellebori multo pars maxima avaro.
units.tr: The greatest part of the hellebore must be given to the miser.

units.la: INSANI nomen suum ignorant, neque sciunt, qui sient: uti jocatur captivus Tyndarus Capt. 3. 4. v. 28. Ubi tres insani commemorantur, Alcmæo, Orestes, & Lycurgus.
units.tr: MADMEN do not know their own name, nor do they know who they are, as the captive Tyndarus jokes in Captivi 3.4 v.28, where three madmen are mentioned: Alcmaeon, Orestes and Lycurgus.

units.la: Ab insanis porci sacres immolabantur,
units.tr: Pigs were sacrificed to madmen,
Menaechmi 2.2 v.16; 3.2 v.51.
Rudens 4.6 v.4.

units.la: Vide Tit. Sacrificiorum: & Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: See the title Sacrifices, and the Plautus lexicon.

units.la: INSANIT hic equidem, qui ipse maledicit sibi.
units.tr: Truly he is mad who curses himself.
Menaechmi 2.2 v.35, 40.

units.la: NEMO sanus insanit.
units.tr: NO SANE MAN GOES MAD.
Menaechmi 5.3 v.2.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Morborum.
units.tr: See also the title Diseases.

units.la: INSANI à servis pluribus retinebantur.
units.tr: MADMEN were restrained by several slaves.
Menaechmi 5.5 v.50.

units.la: INSANI larvas sumebant.
units.tr: MADMEN put on masks.

units.la: Aul. 4. 4. v. 15. IN furore sæpè fiunt, quæ minus recta sunt. Cist. 2.1. v.54.
units.tr: Aulularia 4.4 v.15. IN madness people often do what is not right. Cistellaria 2.1 v.54.

units.la: FURIBUNDI Bacchum inclamarunt. Cas. 5.4. v.10.
units.tr: RAVING MEN called upon Bacchus. Casina 5.4 v.10.

units.la: INSULARUM.
units.tr: ISLANDS.

units.la: INsulæ fortunatorum erant, quò cunêti, qui ætatem egerunt caste suam, conveniebant. Trin. 2.4. v.148.
units.tr: There were the Islands of the Blessed, to which all who had lived their lives chastely used to gather. Trinummus 2.4 v.148.

units.la: De ijsdem vide Muretum lib.5. cap.1. Var. Lect. Isaac. Casaub. ad Strabonem lib.1. pag. 2.
units.tr: On the same, see Muretus, book 5, chapter 1, Variae Lectiones; Isaac Casaubon on Strabo, book 1, page 2.

units.la: INVIDIÆ. LIVORIS. ODII.
units.tr: ENVY. SPITE. HATRED.

units.la: INvidi res secundas aliis obtingere invident. Bacch. 3.6. v.14. Truc. 4.2. v.30. Mavelim mihi inimicos invidere, quàm me inimicis meis. Nam invidere aliy bene esse, tibi male esse, miseria est. Qui invident, egent: illi quibus invidetur, rem habent.
units.tr: Envious men grudge that good fortune falls to others. Bacchides 3.6 v.14. Truculentus 4.2 v.30. I would rather have my enemies envy me than envy my enemies. For to envy others their well-being, while you are ill, is misery. Those who envy are needy; those who are envied have wealth.

units.la: QUONIAM æmulari non licet, nunc invides. Mil. 3.2. v.21.
units.tr: Since you may not rival him, now you envy him. Miles 3.2 v.21.

units.la: FELICITAS alterius invidiam patitur. Most. 1.1. v.48.
units.tr: Another's happiness suffers envy. Mostellaria 1.1 v.48.

units.la: EST miserorum, ut malevolentes sint, atque invideant bonis. Capt. 3.4. v.51.
units.tr: It is the lot of the wretched to be malicious and to envy the good. Captivi 3.4 v.51.

units.la: Pindarus: ὁ φθόνῳ ὀιχπρμῶ ἐσὶν ἀμείνων.
units.tr: Pindar: He who is better than envy [ὁ φθόνῳ ... ἐσὶν ἀμείνων].

units.la: AMICI sublesti invident alteri bene esse.
units.tr: Sycophantic friends envy another's well-being.
Bacchides 3.6 v.14.

units.la: INVIDIA dolorem oculis conciliat.
units.tr: Envy brings pain to the eyes.
Mostellaria 4.2 v.10.

units.la: DUMMODO propitium habeamus Jovem, supremum Numen, si quando odio aliorum premimur, minutos alios Deos floccifacere possumus.
units.tr: Provided we have Jupiter, the supreme Divinity, favourable to us, if at any time we are oppressed by the hatred of others, we can think nothing of the lesser gods.
Casina 2.5 v.23.

units.la: FELICITATIS perpetuus comes Invidia. Ideoq; adolescens inquit Most. 1. 3. v. 147. de suis amoribus:
units.tr: Envy is the constant companion of good fortune. Therefore the young man says, Mostellaria 1.3 v.147, about his loves:

units.la: Hæc qui gaudent, gaudeant perpetuo suo semper bono.
units.tr: Let those who rejoice in these things rejoice forever in their good fortune.

units.la: Qui invident, ne umquam eorum quisquam invideat prorsus commodis.
units.tr: Let those who envy never envy these advantages at all.
And Persa 5.1 v.23.

units.la: Bene ei, qui non invidet mihi.
units.tr: Well for him who does not envy me.

units.la: Sic P. Syrus:
units.tr: Thus Publilius Syrus:

units.la: Sint infelices, quibus nemo invidet.
units.tr: Let them be unhappy, whom no one envies.

units.la: Miserrima est fortuna, quæ caret inimico.
units.tr: Most wretched is the fortune that lacks an enemy.

units.la: Martial. lib. 1. Epig. 41.
units.tr: Martial, book 1, epigram 41.

units.la: Omnibus invideas, livide, nemo tibi.
units.tr: You envy everyone, envious man; no one envies you.

units.la: IRÆ. IRACUNDIÆ.
units.tr: ANGER. IRASCIBILITY.

units.la: NON temerè irascendum: potius blandis verbis agendum. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 34.
units.tr: Do not be angry rashly; rather deal with him in gentle words. Pseudolus 1.5 v.34.

units.la: Jam istæc insipientia est, sic iram in promtu gerere: quanto satius est Adire blandè verbis?
units.tr: Now this is folly, to carry anger ready to hand: how much better to approach with gentle words?

units.la: IRÆ sedes bilis atra putatur. Amph. 2. 2. v. 95.
units.tr: The seat of anger is thought to be black bile. Amphitruo 2.2 v.95.

units.la: ARES irę sedes. Amph. 4.3. v.40.
units.tr: Ares, the seat of anger. Amphitruo 4.3 v.40.

units.la: Vide Casaub. ad Theocrit. cap.1.
units.tr: See Casaubon on Theocritus, chapter 1.

units.la: IRA solet etiam sensus turbare. Amph. 4.3. v.47.
units.tr: Anger is wont also to disturb the senses. Amphitruo 4.3 v.47.

units.la: Vix video prę irā.
units.tr: I can scarcely see for anger.
Asinaria 2.4 v.45.

units.la: VANUM est illi irasci, à quo contemneris.
units.tr: It is vain to be angry at one by whom you are despised.
Truculentus 4.2 v.55.

units.la: Si stimulos pugnis cædis, manibus plus doles.
units.tr: If you strike goads with your fists, you hurt your hands more.

units.la: Proverbialiter: De nihilo est irasci, quae te non flocci facit.
units.tr: Proverbially: It is nothing to be angry at one who does not care a fig for you.

units.la: STULTITIA est, ex te esse tristem: cujus potestas plus potest.
units.tr: It is folly to be sad on your own account at one whose power is greater than yours.
Casina 2.4 v.4.

units.la: Hesiodus:
units.tr: Hesiod:

units.la: ἄρχων ὃς ἂν ἐθέλῃ πρὸς χρέιστονας ἀντιφερίζειν.
units.tr: A ruler who wishes to set himself against his betters [ἄρχων ὃς ἂν ἐθέλῃ πρὸς χρέιστονας ἀντιφερίζειν].

units.la: Et vulgò dici solet: Vana est sine viribus ira.
units.tr: And it is commonly said: Anger without strength is vain.

units.la: LENITER qui sæviunt, sapiunt magis.
units.tr: THOSE who rage gently are wiser. Bacchides 3.3 v.

units.la: Bacch. 3.3. v.
units.tr: Bacchides 3.3 v.

units.la: IRÆ fervor, seu furor resident: & leniter; non durat semper.
units.tr: The heat or fury of anger subsides, and gently; it does not last forever.

units.la: HOMINES irati quassanti capite incedere solent.
units.tr: Angry men are wont to walk about shaking their heads.
Asinaria 2.3 v.23.

units.la: IRA hominis orationem intercipit, & imperfectam reddit.
units.tr: Anger interrupts a man's speech and leaves it unfinished.
Persa 5.2 v.9.

units.la: HOMINIS iracundi signum est, supercilium tollere.
units.tr: It is a sign of an angry man to raise his eyebrows.
Miles 3.1 v.99.

units.la: Vide Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See the title Man.

units.la: JUDICII. FORI. ACTIONIS. JURIS. CAUSSIDICORUM. CITATIONIS. VADIMONII.
units.tr: Of Judgment, the Forum, Action, Law, Advocates, Summons, and Bail (Vadimonium)

units.la: QUI judex olim captus vel datus erat, is sibi qui in consilio essent, amicos advocabat, ut verius & melius de re cognosceret, & judicaret: ijq; subsellijs ijsdem considebant, ut & in tribunali, qui à magistratibus adorabantur. Merc. 4. 3. v. 34. Is judex sequester dictus fuit. Ibid.
units.tr: A judge who had once been chosen or appointed would summon friends to sit with him as his council, so that he might know the matter more truly and better and so judge it. They sat on the same benches, as on the tribunal, and were honoured by the magistrates. Merc. 4. 3. v. 34. Such a judge was called a sequester. Ibid.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: ETIAM Homines apud sequestros depositi fuerunt.
units.tr: Even men were deposited with sequesters.

units.la: Vide Rævard. ad L. xii. Tabb. cap. 6.
units.tr: See Rævard on the Twelve Tables, chapter 6.

units.la: SI reus non latitaret, sed agendi secum Actori faceret potestatem, solebat postulationum die in jus sequi adversarium: cùmq; citatus respondisset, statim Actor causam dicebat, suamq; reo sedente pro tribunali Prætore, actionem edebat. Antequam autem in jus ventum esset, reo actionem edere Actor non cogebatur.
units.tr: If the defendant did not hide, but gave the plaintiff the chance to pursue him, the plaintiff would on the day of the hearings follow his opponent into court. When the defendant had been summoned and answered, the plaintiff at once made his case, and with the praetor sitting on the tribunal and the defendant seated, he set out his action. Before they came into court, however, the plaintiff was not compelled to set out his action to the defendant.

units.la: HOMINES infames & intestabiles, ut sunt fures, aut lenones etiam sine antestatione injectâ manu invitos in jus habere licebat.
units.tr: Infamous and incompetent men, such as thieves or pimps, could be brought into court against their will, even without a call to witness and with a hand laid on them.

units.la: Solos autem liberos fas erat antestari: servi testes esse non poterant.
units.tr: Only free men could be called as witnesses; slaves could not be witnesses.

units.la: De verbo Antestari: & antestandi totâ ratione vide Lexicon nostrum Plaut.
units.tr: On the word antestari and the whole practice of calling to witness, see our Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: LEGE agere dicebantur illi, qui causam habebant suspectam & lubricam: seu quorum intentio, ut loquitur Donatus Phorm. 5. 7. contemtibilis adversario videbatur.
units.tr: Those were said to proceed by law (lege agere) who had a suspicious and slippery case, or whose claim, as Donatus says on Phorm. 5. 7., seemed contemptible to their opponent.

units.la: Aul. 3. 3. v. 20. Lege agito mecum, molestus ne sis.
units.tr: Aul. 3. 3. v. 20. Lege agito mecum, molestus ne sis.

units.la: AD Prætorem ducere, & in jus vocare, licebat: rapere non licebat, nisi ei qui antestatus esset. Itaq; perturbatus Euclio sic alloquitur adolescentem Aul. 4. 10. v. 30.
units.tr: It was allowed to lead a man before the praetor and summon him to court; it was not allowed to seize him, unless he had been called as a witness. So the troubled Euclio addresses the young man: Aul. 4. 10. v. 30.

units.la: Jam quidem hercle ad Prætorem te rapiam, & tibi scribam dicam.
units.tr: Now indeed, by Hercules, I will drag you to the praetor, and I will tell a clerk to write it down for you.

units.la: IN judicijs dies actus constituebatur causis agendis, qui status dicebatur.
units.tr: In lawsuits a fixed day was appointed for pleading the cases, which was called the status.

units.la: Si status conditus cum hoste intercedit dies.
units.tr: If a day of hearing has been fixed with the enemy, it intervenes.

units.la: ADVOCATOS conducebant pretio.
units.tr: They hired advocates for a fee.

units.la: PERICULOSA res ire ad judicem.
units.tr: A dangerous thing, to go before a judge.

units.la: JUDICUM & Prætorum est sedere: co quod judex animo constante, sedato, & bene composito esse debet.
units.tr: Sitting is the business of judges and praetors, because a judge ought to have a steady, calm and well-composed mind.

units.la: Propert. lib. 3.
units.tr: Propertius, book 3.

units.la: Minos sedet arbiter Orci,
units.tr: Minos sits as judge of the underworld,

units.la: Idem lib. 4.
units.tr: The same, book 4.

units.la: --- posita judex sedet ÆAcus urnâ.
units.tr: --- Aeacus sits as judge, with his urn placed before him.

units.la: Cicero pro Rabior:
units.tr: Cicero, for Rabirius:

units.la: Modo vos ijdem in A. Gabinium judices sedistis.
units.tr: Only just now you yourselves sat as judges in the case against Aulus Gabinius.

units.la: Apul. Apol.
units.tr: Apuleius, Apology:

units.la: Quod si modo judices, de causa ista sederent. C. Fabricium, Cn. Pompejum,
units.tr: If judges were sitting on this case: Gaius Fabricius, Gnaeus Pompeius,

units.la: PRÆTOR in privatis controversijs, quacumq; de re ageretur, da-bant bant Recuperatores, per quos suum quisq; jus recuperare posset. Nunc dicuntur Judices Delegati & Commissarij. Bacch. 2.3. v.37. Rud. 5.1. v. 2.
units.tr: In private disputes, whatever the matter, the praetor gave recuperatores, through whom each man could recover his right. Now they are called Judices Delegati and Commissarij. Bacch. 2. 3. v. 37. Rud. 5. 1. v. 2.

units.la: Vide Corraf. Miscell. lib. 3. 18. Torrent. in Sueton. Neron. c.17. Ræuard. lib. 3. c. 20. Pollet. Foro Romano lib. 3. cap. 15.
units.tr: See Corraf., Miscellanea book 3, chapter 18; Torrentius on Suetonius, Nero chapter 17; Rævard, book 3, chapter 20; Pollet, Forum Romanum, book 3, chapter 15.

units.la: IN judicijs dicebantur ad Prætorem abduci: à quo addicebantur. Bacch. 5.2. v. 86. Pœn. 3.4. v.10. & 5. 6. v. 24.
units.tr: In lawsuits people were said to be led away to the praetor, by whom they were assigned (addicebantur). Bacch. 5. 2. v. 86. Poen. 3. 4. v. 10. & 5. 6. v. 24.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut. Addicti.
units.tr: See the Plautine Lexicon, Addicti.

units.la: REBUS jam judicatis, ni judicatum facerent, ac sententiæ parerent, in privatum carcerem, ac vincula conijciebantur.
units.tr: Once the matters had been adjudged, if they did not carry out the judgment and obey the sentence, they were thrown into a private prison and chains.

units.la: Ubi senex amator Philoxenus ad Bacchides:
units.tr: Where the old lover Philoxenus says to the Bacchides:

units.la: Ducite nos, quo lubet, tamquam quidem addictos.
units.tr: Lead us where you like, as if we were indeed assigned to you.

units.la: Et Men. 1. 1. v. 21. Ubi Parasitus inquit de seipso:
units.tr: And Men. 1. 1. v. 21., where the Parasite says of himself:

units.la: Nam ego Menachmum nunc eo, quo jam diu sum judicatus, nitro eo, ut me vinciat.
units.tr: For now I go to Menaechmus, to whom I have long been adjudged; I make my way there so that he may put me in chains.

units.la: Sic Terent. Phorm. 2. 2. v. 20.
units.tr: So Terence, Phorm. 2. 2. v. 20.

units.la: Discent damnatum domum.
units.tr: They will lead the condemned man home.

units.la: Vide etiam Lexic. Plaut. Addicti. Et Cic. lib. 2. de Orat. Livium lib. 6. Cajum Manlium apud Sallustium in Epistola quadam.
units.tr: See also the Plautine Lexicon, Addicti. And Cicero, De Oratore, book 2; Livy, book 6; Gaius Manlius in a certain letter in Sallust.

units.la: Idem olim sanxerunt Decem-viri in Legg. XII. Tabb. ÆRIS. CONFESSI. REBUSQUE. JURE. JUDICATIS. XXX. DIES. JUSTI. SUNTO. POST. DEINDE. MANUS. INJECTIO. ESTO. IN. JUS. DUCITO. NI. JUDICATUM. FACIT. AUT. QUIPS. ENDO. EO. IN. JURE. VINDICIT. SECUM. DUCITO. VINCITO. AUT. NERVO. AUT. COMPEDIBUS. XV. PONDO. NE. MAJORE. AT. SI. VOLET. MINORE. VINCITO.
units.tr: The Decemvirs decreed the same in the Twelve Tables: "For money confessed and matters adjudged at law, thirty days are granted. After that, a hand may be laid on the debtor; let him be led into court. If he does not satisfy the judgment, or no one stands surety for him before the court, let the creditor take him home and bind him with a thong or with fetters of fifteen pounds, not heavier; or lighter if he wishes."

units.la: Vide etiam supra Tit, Ærù alieni: pag. 42.
units.tr: See also above, under the title Aes alienum, p. 42.

units.la: Mos veterum fuerat (Verba sunt Asconij) ut si quis in judiciis absolvendus effet, statim absolveretur, si damnandus, statim damnaretur; si causa non effet idonea ad damnationem, absolvi tamen nō posset A M P L I U S pronunciaretur. Ad quem morem noster alludit Amph. 4. 3. v. 65. quando dicit: Judicium silet.
units.tr: It was the custom of the ancients (these are the words of Asconius) that if someone was to be acquitted in a judgment, he was acquitted at once; if to be condemned, condemned at once. If the case was not suitable for condemnation, yet could not be acquitted, it was pronounced amplius (adjourned for further hearing). Our author alludes to this custom in Amph. 4. 3. v. 65., where he says: Judicium silet.

units.la: De hoc more Judiciorum videndi amplius Marcellus Donatus Dilucid. Liv. Pag. 106. Cæl. Rhodig. lib. 23. cap. 19. Franc. Pol- letus Hist. Fori Romani lib. 4. cap. 15. Rosin. Antiq. lib. 9. cap. 24. & Lexic. Juris: alijq;.
units.tr: On this custom of judgments, see further Marcellus Donatus, Dilucidationes Livianae, p. 106; Caelius Rhodiginus, book 23, chapter 19; Francis Pollet, History of the Roman Forum, book 4, chapter 15; Rosinus, Antiquities, book 9, chapter 24; the Lexicon Juris; and others.

units.la: Qui judicio contenderent, invicem sacramento soliti sunt provocare, & certum aliquem pecuniæ conspectum deponere, malo ejus, qui damnaretur.
units.tr: Those who contended in a lawsuit were accustomed to challenge one another to a sacramentum, and to deposit a certain sum of money, which would be lost by the one who was defeated.

units.la: Pro câ pecuniâ, si forte dare damnas effet, prædem dabant sæpè, & porrò quanti alterius interesset.
units.tr: For that money, if he happened to be condemned to pay, they often gave a surety (praes), and in addition as much as the other party's interest was.

units.la: Si honestior effet persona, quàm uteam rapiin jus cōveniret, diem ei dicebant, eamq; promissâ pœnâ (quam nosterm multam appellat) datisve, nī prædia possiderent, vadibus: vel pignore dimittebat. Eò allusum ab Parasito Capt. 3. 1. v. 34.
units.tr: If the person was of higher standing than the one he was dragged into court by, they set a day for him and released him on a promised penalty (which our poet calls a fine), or on sureties if they possessed estates, or on a pledge. The Parasite alludes to this in Capt. 3. 1. v. 34.

units.la: VADIBUS accepti in jus vocabantur.
units.tr: Those received on sureties were summoned to court.

units.la: Indeque se fisterejussi. Ibid. Edicto enim publicè latitantes citabantur.
units.tr: And from there they were bound to appear, fisterejussi. Ibid. For those who were publicly hiding were summoned by edict.

units.la: Vide Rævardum J C. in Protrib. cap. 9.
units.tr: See Rævard, the jurist, in Protrib. chapter 9.

units.la: NEFASTO die jus non dicebatur. Pœn. 3. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: On a nefastus day law was not declared. Poen. 3. 2. v. 7.

units.la: Vide Tit. Dierum.
units.tr: See the title Dierum.

units.la: CAUSIDICI lites emunt, si non habent.
units.tr: Pleaders buy lawsuits if they have none.

units.la: Iidem comparantur canibus.
units.tr: The same are compared to dogs.

units.la: Jus dicebat Prætor.
units.tr: The praetor declared the law.

units.la: Pœn. I. I. v. 58.
Qui vadimonium obibant, ultrò se in judicio sistębant.
units.tr: Those who attended a vadimonium presented themselves in court of their own accord.

units.la: In jus alios vocantes solebant alios prehensâ auriculâ antestari, additâ hac formulâ Memento.
units.tr: In summoning others to court they used to call them as witnesses by seizing the ear, adding this formula: Memento (Remember).

units.la: De vocabulo Antestari vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: On the word Antestari, see the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: A D Prætorem trahebantur obtorto collo : nempe fauces & gulam prehendebant vestæ ad collum injectâ.
units.tr: They were dragged before the praetor with necks twisted; namely, they seized the throat and gullet, with a garment thrown round the neck.

units.la: Vide Turn. l. 26. cap. 2.
units.tr: See Turnebus, book 26, chapter 2.

units.la: PRÆTER actionem & judices dabat. Qui actionem habebat, ex quâ cum alio experiretur, hostem in jus vocaturus, primùm à Prætore petebat, ut liceret eum, quem libello descripserat, vadari.
units.tr: Besides the action, the praetor also gave judges. The one who had an action by which he was to contest with another, and who was about to summon an enemy to court, first asked the praetor for leave to have bail (vadari) taken for the man he had named in the petition.

units.la: Prætor autem libello subscribebat.
units.tr: The praetor, however, signed the petition.

units.la: Ubi tu es, qui me libello Venereo citavisti?
units.tr: Where are you, who summoned me with your amorous petition?

units.la: Euclioni pridem milvus deripuit. Homo ad prætorem plorabundus devenit, infit ibi postulare plorans, ejulans, ut sibi liceret milvium vadarier.
units.tr: The kite long ago snatched Euclio's prize. The man came weeping to the praetor, and there began to demand, crying and wailing, that he be allowed to have the kite bailed.

units.la: Plin. lib. 1. Epist.
units.tr: Pliny, Letters, book 1.

units.la: Sedeo pro tribunali, subnoto libello, conficio tabulas.
units.tr: I sit before the tribunal, I take down the petition, I draw up the records.

units.la: Vadari autem dicebantur, quando in jus citarent die dicta.
units.tr: But they were said to be bailed (vadari) when they summoned men to court on a set day.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: CREDITORES tenebantur nexos, ni suo viverent, alere.
units.tr: Creditors were bound to feed their debtors who had been bound over (nexi), unless the debtors could support themselves.

units.la: Terent. Phorm.
units.tr: Terent. Phorm.

units.la: Mihi sciunt nihil esse, dices: duces damnatum domum.
units.tr: They know I have nothing, you will say; you will lead the condemned man home.

units.la: Alere nolunt hominem edacem.
units.tr: They refuse to feed a greedy man.

units.la: Vide Rævard. ad l. xii. Tabb. cap. 8.
units.tr: See Rævard. on the Law of the Twelve Tables, chap. 8.

units.la: IN controversijs adhibendus arbiter & sequester.
units.tr: In disputes an arbiter and a sequestrer are to be employed.

units.la: Non probare pernegando mihi potes, nisi pars datur, aut ad arbitrum reditur, aut sequestro ponitur.
units.tr: You cannot prove to me by flat denial; unless a share is given, or the matter is referred to an arbiter, or it is placed in the hands of a sequestrer.

units.la: JURE civili extra suum forum nemo judicium accipere cogitur: in suo autem debet. Et, Actor rei, non reus actoris forum sequitur.
units.tr: By civil law no one is compelled to accept a trial outside his own jurisdiction, but within his own he must. And: the plaintiff follows the forum of the defendant, not the defendant the forum of the plaintiff.

units.la: JUDICES reos dicuntur à vita abjudicare, & morti adjudicare. Quorsum alludit noster. Asin. 3. 3. v. 17.
units.tr: Judges are said to take away the lives of the accused and to hand them over to death. To this our author alludes. Asin. 3. 3. v. 17.

units.la: JURE potius lites definiendæ, quàm jurgio.
units.tr: Lawsuits should be settled by law rather than by wrangling.

units.la: ADVOCATI modò tristes & jracundi sunt: modò lenes.
units.tr: Advocates are now grim and angry, now mild.

units.la: INANTESTATI non facilè rapiebantur in jus: nisi homines improbi, quales erant lenones.
units.tr: Those not summoned as witnesses were not easily dragged into court, except wicked men, such as pimps.

units.la: Ubi nec indemnati judicabantur. Ibid.
units.tr: Where not even the unconvicted were tried. Ibid.

units.la: REUS non nisi solutus ex vinculis causam dicere poterat. Vincti enim videntur prædamnati.
units.tr: A defendant could not plead his case unless he was released from chains, for the bound seem already condemned.

units.la: JUS fiebat per prætorem.
units.tr: Law was made through the praetor.

units.la: PRÆTORES male solventium bona adjudicabant creditoribus.
units.tr: Praetors assigned the goods of those who could not pay to their creditors.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Paupertatis: & Possessionum.
units.tr: See also the title Poverty and Possessions.

units.la: IN jus vocaturi dicam scribebant adversarijs.
units.tr: Those about to summon an adversary to court used to write him a notice.

units.la: IN Comitio patroni & amici dicebantur suis adesse.
units.tr: In the Comitium, patrons and friends were said to stand by their own.

units.la: PRÆTORIS erat addicere rem.
units.tr: It was the praetor's office to award the thing to a claimant.

units.la: IN foro fures Zonarij metuebantur.
units.tr: In the forum, Zonarian thieves were feared.

units.la: IN judicijs res proferri dicebantur, quando erat jurisdictionis silentium, & justitiam. Et hoc fiebat vel temporibus belli: vel ferijs & vacationibus. Captiv. 1. 1. v. 10. De Parasitis usurpatur ἀλληγο- εἰκῶς.
units.tr: In trials, matters were said to be deferred when there was a suspension of jurisdiction and of justice. This happened either in time of war or on holidays and vacation days. Captiv. 1. 1. v. 10. Of Parasites it is used allegorically [ἀλληγορικῶς].

units.la: Sic Lucan. in Pison.
units.tr: So Lucan against Piso:

units.la: --- si quando judice festo
units.tr: --- if ever, when the judge was on a festal day,

units.la: Turbida prolatiu tacuerunt jurgia rebus.
units.tr: the turbulent disputes fell silent, the matters being deferred.

units.la: Minutius Felix:
units.tr: Minucius Felix:

units.la: Sane ad vindemiam feriæ judiciariam curam relaxaverant.
units.tr: Surely, at the time of the vintage, the holidays had relaxed the judicial concern.

units.la: Contra, Res agi dicebantur, quando εἰσὶ ἀὶ δίκαι, ut loquitur Demosthenes. Unde etiam Rerum actus dicebantur apud Suetonium.
units.tr: On the contrary, matters were said to be acted (res agi) when the lawsuits were in progress, [εἰσὶ αἱ δίκαι], as Demosthenes puts it. Hence also "acts of affairs" (rerum actus) were so called in Suetonius.

units.la: IN judicijs advocato sibi sumebant rei.
units.tr: In trials the accused took an advocate for themselves.

units.la: REI accusati, damnati & convicti abducebantur. Asin. 5. 2. v. 87. Ubi Dæmenetus à Parasito delatus, accusatus, & ab uxore convictus, tandem judicatus abducitur domum. Ubi tamen Fr. Polletus Histor. Fori Rom. lib. 4. cap. 11. pag. 373. legit Indicatum.
units.tr: The accused, condemned and convicted men were led away. Asin. 5. 2. v. 87. Where Demaenetus, denounced by a Parasite, accused, and convicted by his wife, is at last judged and led home. Yet Fr. Pollet, History of the Roman Forum, book 4, chap. 11, p. 373, reads Indicatum.

units.la: Vide locum plenum omnis eruditionis Juridicæ.
units.tr: See the passage, full of all juridical learning.

units.la: INTERDVM rei quoq; dicuntur lites judicio disceptare, & perage-re : quod proprie est judicum.
units.tr: Sometimes the accused too are said to dispute their suits in trial and carry them through, which properly belongs to judges.

units.la: ORATOR stat; Judex sedet, Inde Sessiones Judicum.
units.tr: The orator stands; the judge sits. Hence the Sessions of Judges.

units.la: Vide Historiam Polleti lib. 1. cap. 5. & 7.
units.tr: See Pollet's History, book 1, chaps. 5 and 7.

units.la: DEVS injustos judices punit.
units.tr: God punishes unjust judges.

units.la: Rud. Prol. v. 20.
units.tr: Rud. Prol. v. 20.

units.la: ADVOCATI, dum causam agebant, stabant. Caf. 3. 3. v. 5.
units.tr: Advocates, while they pleaded the case, stood. Caf. 3. 3. v. 5.

units.la: Vide Langlæum lib. 1. Semeftr. cap. 3.
units.tr: See Langlaeus, book 1, Semestr., chap. 3.

units.la: ACCVSATORES dicuntur primarij, viri in judicio, qui rem alteri facessunt.
units.tr: Accusers are called the leading men, the men in court, who bring trouble upon another.

units.la: LITES discutiuntur, aut in Comitijs pro rostris ad populum: aut in Basilica apud Prætorem in jure: aut in fori area apud Judices. Men. 4. 2. v. 18. 19.
units.tr: Lawsuits are argued either in the Comitia, from the rostra before the people; or in the Basilica before the praetor in court; or in the open space of the forum before the judges. Men. 4. 2. v. 18. 19.

units.la: Vide Rævard. JC. in Protrib. cap. 7. & Hiftor. Polleti cap. 4.
units.tr: See Rævard, JC, on the Protribunal, chap. 7, and Pollet's History, chap. 4.

units.la: IN judicium vocati, si Vades deesscnt, in carcerem compingebantur.
units.tr: If those summoned to court lacked sureties (vades), they were thrown into prison.

units.la: Vide Rævard. JC. ad Legg. xii. Tabb. cap. 5.
units.tr: See Rævard, JC, on the Law of the Twelve Tables, chap. 5.

units.la: IN judicijs dies litibus dicebatur, ad quam indictionem rei mœsti erant.
units.tr: In trials a day was announced for the lawsuits, and at this summons the accused were in mourning.

units.la: JURAMENTI. JURISJURANDI. PERJURII.
units.tr: OF OATHS. OF SWEARING. OF PERJURY.

units.la: JURABANT per Fidem: & Bonam fidem: quod quidem jura-mentum erat sanctissimum. Plutarch. in Numâ. Dionys. Halic. lib. 9. & 11.
units.tr: They swore by Faith and by Good Faith, which indeed was a most sacred oath. Plutarch, Life of Numa. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, books 9 and 11.

units.la: Petronius:
units.tr: Petronius:

units.la: Per fidem, pater, cujus hæc navis est, aut quos vehat, dicere potes?
units.tr: "By Faith, father, whose ship this is, or whom it carries, can you say?"

units.la: Aul. 4. 10. v. 42. Dic bonâ fide.
units.tr: Aulularia 4.10 v. 42. "Say it in good faith."
(Captivi 4.2 v. 110.

units.la: GRÆCI jurabant per μὰ, & νὴ: sicut Latini per ME, & E.
units.tr: The Greeks swore by mē and nē, just as the Latins swore by ME and E.
Captivi 4.2 v. 100.

units.la: μὰ τὸν Διόλλω! νὴ τὰν Σόςαν!
units.tr: "No, by Diollo! Yes, by Sosas!" [μὰ τὸν Διόλλω! νὴ τὰν Σόςαν!]

units.la: Ubi Parasitus per Urbes jurat.
units.tr: Where the parasite swears by the cities.

units.la: JURISJURANDI religio apud veteres plurimùm valebat.
units.tr: Among the ancients, the sanctity of an oath carried very great weight.
Bacchides 4.9 v. 119.

units.la: Vide Cicer. lib. 3. de Officijs, de dictis M. Atilij Reguli, & M. Pomponij Tribuni plebis.
units.tr: See Cicero, On Duties, book 3, on the sayings of M. Atilius Regulus and of M. Pomponius, tribune of the plebs.

units.la: JURANDI formula fuit: ID. EGO. SI. FALLO. tàm te summe Juppiter Quafo Amphitruoni ut semper iratus sies.
units.tr: The formula of swearing was: "If I deceive in this, I ask you, highest Jupiter, so may you always be angry with Amphitryo."
Amphitryo 3.2 v. 52.

units.la: Ubi Juppiter jurat per seipsum.
units.tr: Where Jupiter swears by himself.

units.la: JURAMENTUM constabat conceptis verbis.
units.tr: An oath consisted of set words.
Cistellaria 1.1 v. 100. Asinaria 3.2 v. 16. Truculentus 4.2 v. 54. Pseudolus 1.3 v. 118 and 4.5 v. 5. Bacchides 4.9 v. 105.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut. Et Turn. lib. 3. cap. 10.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus, and Turnebus, book 3, chapter 10.

units.la: IN religiosissimo jurejurando aras tenebant. Rud. 5. 2. v. 49.
units.tr: In the most solemn oath they held the altars. Rudens 5.2 v. 49.

units.la: Tene aram hanc Veneris. L.A. Teneo. G.R. Per Venerem hanc jurandum est tibi.
units.tr: "Hold this altar of Venus." L.A.: "I hold it." G.R.: "By this Venus you must swear to me."

units.la: Virg. lib. 12. Æneid.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid, book 12.

units.la: Tango aras, mediosq; ignes, & Numina testor.
units.tr: "I touch the altars and the midst fires, and call the divinities to witness."

units.la: Fiebat jusjurandum hoc corporaliter præstitum conceptis verbis, & adversario præeunte, Ara tacta.
units.tr: This oath was made in a physical manner, with the words set down, the opponent speaking first, and the altar being touched.

units.la: Cicero pro Flacco:
units.tr: Cicero, For Flaccus:

units.la: Is si aram tenens juraret, crederet nemo.
units.tr: "If he swore while holding the altar, no one would believe him."

units.la: Juvenal. Sat. 14.
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire 14.

units.la: Falsus erit testis: vendet perjuria summâ Exiguâ, Cereris tangens aramq; pedemq;
units.tr: "He will be a false witness: he sells perjuries for a small sum, touching the altar and the foot of Ceres."

units.la: Ovid. Amor.
units.tr: Ovid, Amores.

units.la: Tange manu mensam, tangunt quo more precantes Optatâ merito cum mala multa viro.
units.tr: "Touch the table with your hand, as those do who pray, with the customary words, for the many evils that they rightly wish upon a desired husband."

units.la: Etiam sacramentum dicturi & precaturi aras tangebant, vel tenebant. Habebant enim Aræ ansulas quasdam, ut notat Scalig. lib. 5. cap. 3. Poët.
units.tr: Even those about to swear an oath and to pray touched or held the altars. For the altars had certain little handles, as Scaliger notes, Poetics, book 5, chapter 3.

units.la: GRATIA jurisjurandi solet, aut addelatum & susceptum, aut ad præstitum jusjurandum referri. Qui jusjurandum remittit, gratiam jurisjurandi facere dicitur: qui præstiti jurisjurandi religione aliquem liberat, is etiam jurisjurandi gratiam facit.
units.tr: The grace of an oath is usually referred either to an oath that has been deferred and taken up, or to an oath already rendered. He who remits an oath is said to grant grace of the oath; and he who releases someone from the obligation of an oath already rendered also grants grace of the oath.

units.la: Sic ex loco Plauti Rud. 5. 3. verf. 58. Jurisjurandi volo gratiam facias: apparet evidenter, cùm id, quod juramento promissum est ultro, sive pactione aliquâ remittitur: tunc etiam jurisjurandi gratiam fieri.
units.tr: Thus, from the passage of Plautus, Rudens 5.3 v. 58: "You should grant me grace of the oath." It clearly appears that when what was promised by oath is remitted, either voluntarily or by some agreement, then grace of the oath is granted as well.

units.la: Cæterum de formulâ istâ Gratiam facere: vide Lexicon Plautin. Litt. G.
units.tr: As for the phrase "to grant grace" itself, see the Plautine Lexicon, under G.

units.la: MULIERUM solum erat juramentum Mecastor, teste Macrobio & Donato, itemq; Agellio lib. 11. cap. 6.
units.tr: The oath Mecastor belonged to women alone, according to Macrobius and Donatus, and likewise Gellius, book 11, chapter 6.
Asinaria 5.2 v. 50. Aulularia 1.1 v. 29.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: Neque viris per Castorem, neq; per Herculem feminis jurare licuit: per Pollucem autem commune utrisq; fuit.
units.tr: Men were not allowed to swear by Castor, nor women by Hercules; but by Pollux it was common to both.
