units.la: Jusjurandum servandæ rei, non perdendæ conditum est. Rud. 5. 3. v. 18. Verè inquit perjurus Leno: sed Sophisticè.
units.tr: An oath was established for keeping a thing, not for losing it. Rudens 5.3 v. 18. The perjured pimp speaks truly, but sophistically.

units.la: Pacuvius:
units.tr: Pacuvius:

units.la: Jusjurandum esse mantile, quo quotidiana noxa extergentur.
units.tr: "An oath is a towel with which daily harms are wiped clean."

units.la: Laberius:
units.tr: Laberius:

units.la: Quid est Jusjurandum? Emplastrum æris alieni.
units.tr: "What is an oath? A plaster for debt."

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Injuriarum.
units.tr: See also the title "Of Injuries."

units.la: Qui consultò per Deos arasq; Deorum pejerabant, Pontificibus pœnas dabant, qui per Genium Principis, qui aliâ ratione Censoribus. Pontifices enim de omnibus causis ad sacra pertinentib° judicarunt; & ideò etiam de perjurio, quod per Jovem, per Dium Fidium, aut per aras Deorum solemni modo præstabatur, cognoverunt.
units.tr: Those who knowingly swore falsely by the gods and the altars of the gods paid penalties to the pontiffs; those who swore by the genius of the prince, or by some other means, paid them to the censors. For the pontiffs judged all cases pertaining to sacred matters, and therefore they also took cognizance of perjury committed by Jupiter, by Dius Fidius, or by the altars of the gods, in the solemn manner.
Rudens 5.3 v. 21.

units.la: Tun' meo Pontifex perjurio es? inquit perjurus Leno.
units.tr: "Are you a pontiff over my perjury?" says the perjured pimp.

units.la: Vide Ræv ard. l. 2. Var. c. 3. Alex. ab Alex. Doufam ad illud Horatij l. 5. Od. ult. Et Esquilini Pontifex Venefici.
units.tr: See Ravardus, book 2, Variae, chapter 3; Alexander ab Alexandro; and Dousa on that passage of Horace, last ode of book 5: "and the pontiff of the Esquiline witch."

units.la: Juramenti formula præconceptis verbis repetebatur singillatim ab ijs qui præstarent juramentum: quotquot etiam essent. Vide integram jurandi Formulam Rud. 5. 2. v. 51.
units.tr: The formula of the oath was repeated word by word, set out beforehand, by those who gave the oath, however many of them there were. See the whole formula of swearing, Rudens 5.2 v. 51.

units.la: Multi linguâ solùm jurant; nihilq; præstant: ut perjurus ille Leno Rud. 5. 2. v. 68.
units.tr: Many swear only with the tongue and perform nothing, like that perjured pimp. Rudens 5.2 v. 68.

units.la: Meus arbitratus est, lingua quod juret mea.
units.tr: "It is my decision: whatever my tongue swears."

units.la: In juramenti formulâ pœnam addebant:
units.tr: In the formula of the oath they added a penalty:

units.la: Tunc me faciat, quod vult magnus Jupiter!
units.tr: "Then may great Jupiter do to me what he wishes!"
Aulularia 4.10 v. 46.

units.la: Jurabant per oculos, & caput suum.
units.tr: They swore by their eyes and their head.
Menaechmi 5.9 v. 1.

units.la: Vide Brisl. lib. 8. Formul. Jurabant per Jovem, & ejus matrem-familiâs Junonem. Amph. I. I. v. 277. & 2. 2. v. 201. Jurare quandoq; solebant per omnes Deos. Bacch. 4. 8. v. 51.
units.tr: See Brisson, book 8, Formulae. They swore by Jupiter and by his wife, Juno, the matron of the household. Amphitryo 1.1 v. 277 and 2.2 v. 201. They sometimes swore by all the gods. Bacchides 4.8 v. 51.

units.la: Milites per Martem jurabant: Amatores per Venerem seu Dionam. Mil. 5. v. 21.
units.tr: Soldiers swore by Mars; lovers by Venus or Dione. Miles, 5 v. 21.

units.la: Jurabant etiam per Herculem Dium Fidium: hoc est, filium Jovis. Asin. 1. 1. v. 8.
units.tr: They also swore by Hercules Dius Fidius, that is, the son of Jupiter. Asinaria 1.1 v. 8.

units.la: Per se & vitam suam jurabant, sic: Non hercle ita sum, qui sum, nisi, &c. Men. 3. 2. v. 6.
units.tr: They swore by themselves and their own life, thus: "No, by Hercules, I am not who I am, unless, etc." Menaechmi 3.2 v. 6.

units.la: L.
units.tr: L.

units.la: LABORIS. OFFICII. STUDII. NEGLIGEN-TIÆ. DESIDIÆ, ASSIDUITATIS. INDUSTRIÆ.
units.tr: LABOUR. DUTY. STUDY. NEGLECT. IDLENESS. DILIGENCE. INDUSTRY.

units.la: LAborì & quibuscumque honestis officijs debetur præmium. Sic recte indignantur Advocati.
units.tr: Reward is owed to labour and to every honourable duty. So advocates rightly complain.

units.la: Injuriam illic insignitè postulat: Nostro sibi servire nos censet cibo.
units.tr: He demands compensation outright; he thinks we ought to serve him with our food.

units.la: Sic Trucul. 1. 2. v. 34.
units.tr: Thus Trucul. 1. 2. v. 34.

units.la: Tuo vestimento & cibo alienis rebus curas.
units.tr: You take care of other people's goods with your clothing and food.

units.la: Contrarium est, quod dicit Terent. Eun. 2. 2. v. 34.
units.tr: The opposite is what Terence says, Eun. 2. 2. v. 34.

units.la: Viden' otium & cibus quid faciat alienus?
units.tr: Do you see what idleness and another man's food can do?

units.la: Quo loco mira monstra fingunt Critici. Nobis vulgata arridet, quam modò protulimus.
units.tr: Here the critics invent strange monsters. I prefer the reading we have just given, the Vulgate.

units.la: Langius ad Officia Ciceronis legit Viden' os suum: & videtur probare magnus JCtus Franc. Hotomannus: cujus propriâ manu adscriptum id habeo ad marginem Langianarum Notarum.
units.tr: Langius, in his notes on Cicero's Offices, reads "Do you see his own mouth?", and the great jurist Francis Hotman seems to approve it; I have his own handwriting noting this in the margin of my copy of Langius's notes.

units.la: LABORI assuefaciendum liberos à teneris.
units.tr: Children should be accustomed to labour from their earliest years.

units.la: Merc. Prol. v. 68.
units.tr: Merc. Prol. v. 68.

units.la: IN malâ uxore, atque inimico si quid sumas, sumtus es.In bono hospite atque amico quæstus est, quod sumitur.Et quod in divinis rebus sumas, sapienti lucro est.
units.tr: If you take anything from a bad wife or an enemy, it is spent; what is taken from a good host or friend is profit. And what you take in divine things is gain to the wise.
Mil. 3. 1. v. 78 and following.

units.la: SINE labore DI nihil dant mortalibus.
units.tr: Without labour the gods give nothing to mortals.

units.la: Videndum Proverb. Θεοὶ τ' ἀγαθὰ τοῖς πόνοις πωλοῦνται : ex sententiâ Epicharmi.
units.tr: See the proverb: the gods sell good things for toil [Θεοὶ τ' ἀγαθὰ τοῖς πόνοις πωλοῦνται], in the sense of Epicharmus.

units.la: NIMIS homo nihili est, qui piger est (inquit diligens Piscator Rud. 4. 2. v. 14.)
units.tr: A man who is lazy is worth very little, says the diligent fisherman (Rud. 4. 2. v. 14).

units.la: Vigilare decet hominem, qui vult sua tempori conficere officia. Non enim illum exspectare oportet, dum horas se ad suum sei-scitet officium. Nam qui dormiunt dibenter, sine lucro, & cum malo quiescunt. Nam ego nunc mihi, qui piger fui, reperi, ut piger si velim, siem.
units.tr: A man who wants to get his duties done in time ought to be awake. He should not wait for the hours to summon him to his duty. For those who sleep willingly rest without profit and to their loss. For I now, who was lazy, have found that if I wish to be lazy, I may be.

units.la: LACTIS.
units.tr: MILK.

units.la: NIHIL lactu similius, quàm lac. Men. 5. 9. v. 30.
units.tr: Nothing is more like milk than milk. Men. 5. 9. v. 30.

units.la: LACRIMARUM. FLETUS. PLORATUS.
units.tr: TEARS. WEEPING. LAMENTATION.

units.la: LACRIMÆ oculos corrumpunt. Mero. 3. 1. v. 3.
units.tr: Tears ruin the eyes. Mero. 3. 1. v. 3.

units.la: PRÆ lætitiâ lacrumas effundere solemus. Stich. 3. 2. v. 13.
units.tr: We are accustomed to shed tears for joy. Stich. 3. 2. v. 13.

units.la: LANIONUM.
units.tr: BUTCHERS.

units.la: LANII solebant interdum agninam vendere pro aricinâ: quo- rum dolus reprehenditur à Parasito. Capt. 4. 2. v. 39. Ubi ta- men diversa est illius loci interpretatio.
units.tr: Butchers sometimes used to sell lamb as aricina (a kind of mutton); their trickery is rebuked by the Parasite. Capt. 4. 2. v. 39. Yet the interpretation of that passage is different there.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut. Duplex.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus, Duplex.

units.la: LANII lenonum æmuli: quos sectabantur Parasiti. Capt. 3 1. v. 15. Ubi tamen lenones ex MSS. Pall. retinendum, non laniones. Et Capt. 4. 2. v. 38. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 63. & 1. 3. v. 97. Trin. 2. 4. v. 6.
units.tr: Butchers were rivals of the procurers, and the Parasites ran after them. Capt. 3 1. v. 15. Yet here lenones is to be retained from the Palatine manuscript, not laniones. Also Capt. 4. 2. v. 38. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 63 and 1. 3. v. 97. Trin. 2. 4. v. 6.

units.la: LANII non minus atque lenones jurejurando malo quaerunt rem. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 63.
units.tr: Butchers seek gain by evil oaths no less than procurers do. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 63.

units.la: LAPIDUM. PUMICIS.
units.tr: STONES. PUMICE.

units.la: LAPIDE veterior: h. e. durior, in proverbio Bacch. 5. 2. v. 31. Tibi dedo veteriorem lapide, lenitum, ut reddas.
units.tr: "Harder than stone": that is, more stubborn, as in the proverb in Bacch. 5. 2. v. 31: I give you someone harder than a stone, to be softened, so that you may give him back.

units.la: PUMEX lapis aridus, non continens aquam. Unde Proverb. Aul. 2. 4. v. 18. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 73. Ubi servus ait: Pumiceos oculos habeo: non quo lachrymam exorare. Pers. 1. 1. v. 42. Tu aquam a pumice nunc postulas, qui ipsus sitiat.
units.tr: PUMICE is a dry stone that does not hold water. Hence the proverb in Aul. 2. 4. v. 18 and Pseud. 1. 1. v. 73, where a slave says: I have pumice eyes, not to be coaxed into shedding a tear. Pers. 1. 1. v. 42: Now you ask water from a pumice, which is itself parched.

units.la: IN lapide nulla sapientia. Unde dicitur proverbio de homine stu- pido: Non habet plus sapientiam, quam lapis. Mil. 2. 2. v. 81.
units.tr: There is no wisdom in a stone. Hence the proverb about a stupid man: He has no more wisdom than a stone. Mil. 2. 2. v. 81.

units.la: LATERNARUM. LUCERNARUM.
units.tr: LANTERNS. LAMPS.

units.la: Fiebant olim laternæ ex cornu, & quandoque ex vesicâ. Amph. 1. 1. v. 184. Vulcanum in cornu conclusum geris. Martial lib. 14. Epig. 62. vocantur duces viarum : & Noctilucæ. Lycophronis interpres Zezes tradit Prometheum fuisse primum Authorem laternarum è cornu factarum. De laternis surdis videndus Isaacus Casaubonus Animadversiones in Sueton. pag. 26. Et prolixè Martinus de Roa de omni usu Laternarum lib. 2. Singular. Locor. cap. 22.
units.tr: Once lanterns were made of horn, and sometimes of bladder. Amph. 1. 1. v. 184: You carry Vulcan shut up in a horn. Martial, book 14, epigram 62. They are called guides of the roads and Noctilucae. Tzetzes, the interpreter of Lycophron, relates that Prometheus was the first maker of lanterns made of horn. On deaf lanterns see Isaac Casaubon, Animadversiones in Suetonium, p. 26. At greater length, Martín de Roa, On All Uses of Lanterns, book 2, Singularia Loca, ch. 22.

units.la: Lucerna filinteum unctum defit, exstinguitur. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 42.
units.tr: A lamp, when its linen wick has run short of anointing oil, goes out. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 42.

units.la: Laternæ Africanæ supra cæteros erant pellucidæ, propter cornu, quod erat lucidius, & nitidius. Aul. 3. 6. v. 29. Ita is pellucet, quasi laterna Punica.
units.tr: African lanterns were more transparent than all others, because of the horn, which was brighter and more lustrous. Aul. 3. 6. v. 29: He shines through like a Punic lantern.

units.la: LATRINÆ. CLOACÆ. SECESSUS.
units.tr: LATRINES. SEWERS. PRIVIES.

units.la: Ebrii & saturi facii petebant secessus. Curc. 2. 3. v. 84.
units.tr: Drunk and full, they made for the privies. Curc. 2.3, v. 84.

units.la: Laudis. Encomii. Gloriæ. Victoriæ.
units.tr: Praise. Eulogy. Glory. Victory.

units.la: PERICULUM putabatur olim, si quis vel se ipsum impensius laudaret, vel praesens ab alio laudaretur. Ideoque utebantur vocabulo Præfiscine. De quo vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: It was once thought dangerous if someone praised himself too eagerly, or if he were praised to his face by another. For this reason they used the expression Praefiscine. On this see the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: SI quid olim laude dignum, vituperiove, carbonibus notabant ad parietes: appellabantque elogiorum carbones. Alludit huc Demipho senex Merc. 2. 3. v. 74. Idque Græcis quoq; in usu fuisse demonstrat Martinus de Roa lib. 6. singularium c. 17. Aristophanes de Demo Pyrilampis filio, qui valdè pulcher habebatur, scribit januas elogijs pulchritudinis inscriptas:
units.tr: If anything worthy of praise or blame happened, they used to mark it with charcoal on the walls, and they called these charcoal eulogies. The old man Demipho alludes to this in Merc. 2. 3. v. 74. That this was also in use among the Greeks is shown by Martinus de Roa, book 6 of Singularia, chapter 17. Aristophanes writes about Demos, son of Pyrilampes, who was considered very handsome, that doorways were inscribed with eulogies of his beauty:

units.la: Si viderit alicubi scriptum in janua: Δῆμου καλὸν.
units.tr: If one saw written somewhere on a door: "Demos is beautiful" [Δῆμου καλὸν].

units.la: Item: Pasicompsa formosa.
units.tr: Likewise: "Pasicompsa is beautiful."

units.la: Idem fecit Phidias apud Clement. Alexand. PANTARCES PULCHER. Nec ad januas solùm; sed etiam arbores elogia scribebant. Theocr. in Epithalamio Helenæ Eydill. 18. Et Ovidius Epist. 9. Oenone Paridi.
units.tr: Phidias did the same, according to Clement of Alexandria: "PANTARCES IS BEAUTIFUL." And not only on doorways, but people also wrote eulogies on trees. Theocritus in the Epithalamium of Helen, Idyll 18; and Ovid, Epistle 9, Oenone to Paris.

units.la: Interdum etiam ad columnas pingebant ejusmodi elogia. Vide plura dicto loco apud doctissimum de-Roa Hispanum.
units.tr: Sometimes such eulogies were also painted on columns. See more at the place cited above in the learned de Roa the Spaniard.

units.la: IMMODERATÆ arrogantiæ exemplum insigne est Miles Gloriosus.
units.tr: The Braggart Soldier is a notable example of immoderate arrogance.

units.la: Vide Titul. Militiæ.
units.tr: See the title Militia.

units.la: ETIAM bello gloria comparatur.
units.tr: Glory is also won by war.

units.la: STRENUIORI deterior si prædicat suas pugnas, de illius ore fiunt sordidæ. Nam propria laus sordet.
units.tr: If a weaker man boasts of his battles, which the stronger man has fought, they become shameful from his mouth. For self-praise is shameful.

units.la: Epid. 3. 4. v. 10. 21. Vide Cic. lib. 5. Epist. ad Lucejum. Et Plutarch. in lib. Quâ quis ratione seipsum laudare queat.
units.tr: Epid. 3. 4. v. 10. 21. See Cicero, book 5, Letters to Lucceius; and Plutarch in the work on how one may praise oneself.

units.la: Non placent, quem scurræ laudant, manipulares mussitant: Neq; illi, quorum linguaˇ gládiorum aciem præstringit domi : ut sunt Rhetores demagogi.
units.tr: Those whom buffoons praise are not pleasing; the common soldiers mutter; nor are those pleasing whose tongues blunt the edge of swords at home, such as the demagogic rhetoricians.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Virtutis.
units.tr: See also the title Virtus.

units.la: Laus propria sordet.
units.tr: Self-praise is shameful.

units.la: Malum istuc aliis videatur; quàm uti te collaudes.
units.tr: Let that be a fault in others, rather than that you should praise yourself.

units.la: Nemo seipsum contemnere debet.
units.tr: No one ought to despise himself.

units.la: LECTORUM.
units.tr: Of Couches.

units.la: Lectri sternebantur, sulciebantur, molliebantur, ut somno & amoribus essent aptiores.
units.tr: The couches were strewn, sprinkled, and softened, so that they would be more suited to sleep and love.

units.la: Yy
units.tr: Yy

units.la: Legationis.
units.tr: Of Embassies.

units.la: QUis in legationibus usurpandus, videndum. Pyrgopolinices ad Regem Seleucum misit Parasitum.
units.tr: It must be considered who should be employed in embassies. Pyrgopolinices sent a parasite to King Seleucus.

units.la: LEGATI cum publico imperio mittebantur.
units.tr: Envoys were sent with public authority.

units.la: Truc. I. I. V. 74.
LEGATI publicè mittuntur ij, qui gratiâ & authoritate publicâ valent.
units.tr: Those are sent publicly as envoys who have favour and public authority.

units.la: Legum.
units.tr: Of Laws.

units.la: LEGES sæpè cedunt malis moribus.
units.tr: Laws often yield to bad morals.

units.la: Mores leges perduxerunt jam in potestatem suam: magis quoâ sunt obnoxiosi, quàm parentes liberis: ea misera etiam ad paristem sunt fixa clavis ferreis: ubi malos mores affigi nimio fuerat æquius.
units.tr: Morals have now brought laws into their power, so that they are more subject to them than parents are to their children; those wretched laws are fixed to the post with iron nails, where it would have been more fitting to fix bad morals.

units.la: LEGES moriserviunt. Ibid.
units.tr: Laws become slaves to morals. Ibid.

units.la: Mores autem rapere properant, quàsacrum, quàpublicum. Ibid. V. 37.
units.tr: Morals hasten to seize things, as sacred as they are public. Ibid. v. 37.

units.la: AQ. Vario lata est lex in eos, qui in Rempub. conspirassent, inito consilio, quò populum Romanum vita ac victu prohibe-rent.
units.tr: AQ. A law was passed by Varius against those who had conspired against the Republic, having formed a plan by which they would keep the Roman people from life and sustenance.

units.la: Alludit Parasitus ille Capt. 3. I. V. 32.
units.tr: That parasite alludes to this in Capt. 3. 1. v. 32.

units.la: IMPROBI quasi aquam fervDentem frigidam esse, ita putant Leges. ges. Curc. 4. 2. v. 25. Ut enim aquam ferventem, quamdiu fervet, nemo tangere audet: ubi refrixit, nemo tangere dubitat: ita leges cum primum latæ sunt, valent, & metuuntur: cum tempore obsolescunt, & negliguntur.
units.tr: Wicked men think that laws are like cold water boiled hot. For as no one dares to touch boiling water while it boils, but when it has cooled, no one hesitates to touch it: so laws, as soon as they are passed, have force and are feared; but with time they grow obsolete and are neglected.

units.la: Mali mores pariunt varias leges.
units.tr: Bad morals produce various laws.

units.la: Leguminum. Cæparum. Fabarum.
units.tr: Pulses. Onions. Beans.

units.la: Lupinum aquâ maceratum amarorem deponit: ideoque bobus propositum fuit in pabulum, & ex eo etiam in Comœdiâ numi facti.
units.tr: Lupine soaked in water loses its bitterness; for this reason it was set before oxen as fodder, and from it coins were also made in comedy.
Poenulus 3. 2. v. 20. Stichus 5. 4. v. 9.

units.la: In fabis nascuntur vermiculi, quos Midas appellant, eos dum pueri inveniunt, rem magnam se gloriantur invenisse.
units.tr: In beans there are born little worms, which the Midas call; while boys find them, they boast that they have found a great thing.
Aulularia 5. v. 11.

units.la: Pisa vilissima legumina: & allium ulpicum sive punicum.
units.tr: Peas are the cheapest pulses; and garlic, the ulpicum or Punic kind.
Poenulus 5. 5. v. 35.

units.la: Libationum.
units.tr: Libations.

units.la: Vide Tit. Conviviorum.
units.tr: See the title Banquets.

units.la: LIBERORUM. FILIORUM. INDOLIS.
units.tr: CHILDREN. SONS. DISPOSITION.

units.la: FIlii nepotes, prodigi, convitium sunt familiae paternae. Merc. Prol. v. 59.
units.tr: Sons, grandsons and spendthrifts are a disgrace to the paternal family. Merc. Prol. v. 59.

units.la: Iidemq; probrum sunt familiae.
units.tr: And they are also a shame to the family.

units.la: Mercat. I. I. v. 59.
units.tr: Mercat. I. I. v. 59.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut. Convitium.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus, under Convitium.

units.la: LIBERI debent canitie suorum parentum commoveri ad virtutes.
units.tr: Children ought to be moved to virtue by the grey hair of their parents.

units.la: LIBERORUM conspectus non minus charus nobis esse solet, quam vita.
units.tr: The sight of one's children is usually no less dear to us than life itself.

units.la: LIBERI omnino debent dicto audientes esse parentum suorum, inprimis filiae suarum matrum.
units.tr: Children ought above all to be obedient to their parents, and daughters especially to their mothers.

units.la: Asin. 3. I. v. I. 6.
units.tr: Asin. 3. I. v. I. 6.

units.la: Multo autem minus parentes objurgare. Ibid. v. 10.
units.tr: But much less should they scold their parents. Ibid. v. 10.

units.la: LIBERTORUM. LIBERTATIS. MANU-MISSIONIS.
units.tr: FREEDMEN. FREEDOM. MANUMISSION.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Servorum plura.
units.tr: See also the entry Servorum for more.

units.la: LIBERTI novi in togâ apparebant, h. e. communi civium veste, quæ erat alba. Quò forte referendum illud Caf. 2. 8. v. 10. de Olympione villico, qui libertus fuit: & sponsus.
units.tr: Freedmen appeared in the toga, that is, the common dress of citizens, which was white. Perhaps the passage in Casina 2.8 v. 10 about Olympio the steward, who was a freedman and also a fiancé, should be referred here.

units.la: Vide Lipf. lib. 1. Elect. cap. 13.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Electorum book 1, chapter 13.

units.la: LIBERALI causâ suum manu asserere popularem cuilibet olim licuit.
units.tr: In a freeborn cause, anyone among the people could once claim a person as free by hand.
(Truculentus 5.2 v. 23.)

units.la: Qui scias mercari furtivas atq; ingenuas virgines.
units.tr: You know how to buy stolen girls and freeborn ones alike.
And Poenulus 5.2 v. 5.

units.la: Tuum flagitium est, tuas populares te pati servire ante oculos, domi quæ fuerint liberæ.
units.tr: It is your disgrace that your countrywomen, who were free at home, you let be enslaved before your eyes.

units.la: Vide Rævardum J C. lib. 1. cap. 18. Var.
units.tr: See the jurist Rævardus, book 1, chapter 18, Var.

units.la: SERVI servæq; liberali judicio natalibus restituebantur. Quod erat liberali causâ asserere: καρπίζεσθαι.
units.tr: Slaves, men and women, were restored to their birth by a judgment of freedom. To assert someone in a freeborn cause was καρπίζεσθαι [to claim as one's own].
Persa 1.3 v. 83. Rudens 4.3 v. 34. Poenulus 5.2 v. 142, and 4.2 v. 84, and 5.2 v. 4.

units.la: Vide Jurisconsultos: & Interpretes XII, Tabb.
units.tr: See the jurists, and the commentators on the Twelve Tables.

units.la: LIBERTATE nihil lepidius aut charius.
units.tr: Nothing is more charming or dearer than liberty.
Miles gloriosus 3.1 v. 88. Persa 4.4 v. 107.

units.la: LIBERTAS cælibatûs aurea prorsus.
units.tr: Freedom from marriage is altogether golden.
Miles gloriosus 3.1 v. 106.

units.la: Si istam semel amiseris libertatem, haud facile te in eundem rursus restitues locum.
units.tr: If you have once lost that freedom, you will not easily be restored to the same position again.

units.la: IN libertinis non vindicabantur furta Veneris: atq; ex eo ordine multæ meretrices erant. Cistell. I.I. v. 40. Vide Turn. I. 29. cap. 31. Et Lipsi ad Tacitum.
units.tr: Among freedmen, the thefts of Venus were not punished, and from that class there were many prostitutes. Cistellaria 1.1 v. 40. See Turnebus, book 29, chapter 31, and Lipsius on Tacitus.

units.la: <bl>LIBERTATIS</bl> maximam semper habuerunt rationem: nec eam facilè prostituebant.
units.tr: They always held liberty in the highest regard, and did not readily sell it.
Rudens 2.6 v. 5.

units.la: <bl>PRO</bl> capite numerare dicebantur: quando in libertatem asserebant: ob pactionem libertatis.
units.tr: They were said to count money "per head" when they asserted someone into liberty, on account of the agreement for freedom.

units.la: Pseud. 1. 2. v. 88. Poen. 3. 1. v. 16. Perf. 1. 1. v. 37. Brisson. lib. 3. de Verborum signif. & Gruter. ad Senecam.
units.tr: Pseudolus 1.2 v. 88. Poenulus 3.1 v. 16. Persa 1.1 v. 37. Brisson, book 3, De Verborum significatione, and Gruter on Seneca.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: MORIS erat, nomen manumissii in Acta referri, causâ etiam seu Titulo manumissionis adscripto. Quod colligimus ex loco Perf. 4. 3. v. 17.
units.tr: It was the custom for the name of the person manumitted to be entered in the public records, with the cause or title of the manumission added. We gather this from the passage in Persa 4.3 v. 17.

units.la: MANUMISSIO fiebat festucâ sive virgâ (quam Vindictam appellabant) Prætoris per Lictorem.
units.tr: Manumission was effected by a rod or staff (which they called vindicta) from the praetor, through the lictor.
Miles gloriosus 4.1 v. 15. Pseudolus 1.3 v. 123. Rudens 4.2 v. 123. Curculio 1.3 v. 56.

units.la: De Vindictâ vide Lexicon nostrum Plaut. lit. F. Festuca.
units.tr: On the vindicta, see our Plautine lexicon, under the letter F, Festuca.

units.la: <bl>INGENUI</bl> etiam fiebant, qui non nati tales, prorsus uti liberi, sed non nisi ante liberi. Post libertatem indultam, quidam & in ingenuitatem asserebantur: neque hæc est autem plena & justa libertas, ut alij opinantur. Non enim ingenuitatis jus datum omnibus qui manumissi etiam justâ libertate.
units.tr: Some were also made ingenui, who were not born such, but became altogether like freeborn persons, though only after being freed. After liberty had been granted, some were also asserted into full freeborn status; yet this is not, as others think, complete and lawful freedom. For the right of freeborn status was not given to all who were manumitted, even with lawful freedom.

units.la: Vide Justi Lipsij Comment. ad Annal. Tac. lib. 13. Ingenuos & Libertinos clarè Seneca discriminat de vitâ beatâ cap. 24. & Suetonn. August. cap. 74. Ad quem locum vide etiam Comm. Casauboni.
units.tr: See Justus Lipsius's commentary on Tacitus's Annals, book 13. Seneca clearly distinguishes freeborn persons and freedmen in De vita beata chapter 24, and Suetonius, Augustus chapter 74. On that passage see also the commentary of Casaubon.

units.la: Præter hos autem viros doctos operæ pretium est legere Oratio-nem doctissimi viri Michaelis Piccarti: Philologiæ & Antiquitatis scientissimæ: quam proprie de hac re publice dixit. Ex eâ huc non pigebit quædam appingere: Quia Locos Communes conscribere, nostri instituti id esse initio præscripsi.
units.tr: Besides these learned men, it is worth reading the oration of the most learned Michael Piccartus, most skilled in philology and antiquity, which he delivered publicly on this subject. I will not hesitate to add some things from it here, since at the outset I laid down that it belongs to my plan to write common-place notes.

units.la: PRINCIPIO notum est omnibus: Alios ingenuos fuisse sive liberos: alios servos: atq; hos quidem ex servitute in libertatem, interveniente Manumissione, assertos.
units.tr: At the beginning it is known to all that some were ingenui, or free, and others slaves; and of these, some were asserted from slavery into liberty by manumission.

units.la: Manumissionis autem modi ac rationes varij fuerunt, attestante Jaboleno JC. l. ult. ff. de manum.
units.tr: The modes and methods of manumission were various, as the jurist Javolenus attests in the last law of the Digest, De manumissionibus.

units.la: Servum, ait, furiosum omni genere manumissum ad libertatem perduci posse putat Labeo.
units.tr: Labeo thinks, he says, that a slave who is insane can be brought to liberty by any kind of manumission.

units.la: Tacitus lib. xiii. Annal. duas ait institutas esse manumittendi species: quarum upa à J C. appellatur Manumissio Justa: altera Manumissio Latina.
units.tr: Tacitus, Annals book 13, says that two kinds of manumission were instituted: one of which the jurists call Justa manumission, the other Latina manumission.

units.la: De Justa agit Seneca de Vita Beata:
units.tr: Seneca deals with the Justa kind in De vita beata:

units.la: Hominibus prodesse natura, jubet servi liberive sint hi, ingenui an libertini, justa libertatis, an secus, quid refert? ubicumque homo est, beneficio locus est.
units.tr: Nature bids us to do good to men, whether they are slaves or freeborn, freeborn or freedmen, with full lawful freedom or otherwise; what does it matter? Wherever there is a human being, there is room for kindness.

units.la: De eadem Sueton. Aug. cap. 40. Eadem libertas dicitur legitima & plenissima. § ult. Institut. de libertinis: & l. 1. § sin autem scias. C. de Com. serv. manumiss.
units.tr: Suetonius, Augustus chapter 40, speaks of the same. The same liberty is called legitima and plenissima [lawful and fullest]. Last section of the Institutes, De libertinis; and law 1, section sin autem scias, Code, De commercio servorum manumissorum.

units.la: Item Libertas Major à Theophilo d. §. ult. institutis de libertinis. Item Perfecta Libertas à Plutarcho in Valerio. Latina & Juniana dicitur ex lege Junia. D. Augustus tertiam introduxit, quae Deditinia solet appellari.
units.tr: Likewise, Libertas Major [greater liberty] is so called by Theophilus, in the last section of the Institutes, De libertinis. Likewise Perfecta [perfect] liberty is so called by Plutarch in his life of Valerius. It is called Latina and Junian from the Junian law. The deified Augustus introduced a third kind, which is usually called Dediticia.

units.la: Justa qui manumissii, plane plenéq; erant liberi: altera, vinculo adhuc (ut loquitur Tacitus) quodam attinebantur Servitutis: ut vel poenitentiae locus foret, vel novo beneficio. Hos igitur licebat in servitutem retrahere. Quod patet ex hoc loco Plauti Men. f. 9. v. 88. Ibi Mesenio à fratribus Men. manumissus, non contentum se ait eo beneficio: Meliore, inquit, opus est auspicio, liber ut siem.
units.tr: Those manumitted by the Justa kind were entirely and fully free; the others were still bound, as Tacitus puts it, by a certain tie of servitude, so that there might be room for repentance or for a new kindness. These, therefore, it was lawful to draw back into servitude. This is clear from this passage of Plautus, Menaechmi act 9 v. 88. There Mesenio, manumitted by the brothers Menaechmi, says he is not content with that benefit: A better omen is needed, he says, for me to be free.

units.la: Unde constat, Manumissos manumissione Latina, ut plene fierent liberi, Justa etiam manumissos fuisse. Quò pertinet locus Plinij lib. 7. Epist.
units.tr: Hence it is established that those manumitted by Latin manumission were also manumitted by the Justa kind, so that they might become fully free. To this belongs the passage of Pliny, book 7, Letters.

units.la: Facile deflectent ad te, si Vindicta volu liberare, quos proxime inter amicos manumisisti.
units.tr: They will easily turn to you, if you wish to free by the vindicta those whom you have just manumitted among your friends.

units.la: Caterum utraq; Manumissio, tres habuit rursum manumittendi modos: Iusta videlicet Vindicta: Censum & Testamentum. Latina vel inter amicos fiebat; vel Adhibitione Convivij: vel deniq; per Epistolam.
units.tr: Moreover, each manumission had three further modes of manumitting: namely, the Justa vindicta, the census, and the testament. The Latina kind was done either among friends, or by the presence of a dinner gathering, or finally by letter.

units.la: De Justæ manumissionis modis perspicuè Cicero in Topp.
units.tr: Cicero, in the Topica, clearly describes the modes of lawful manumission.

units.la: Si neq; Censu, neq; Vindicta, neq; Testamento liber factus est, non est ergo liber jure Quiritium.
units.tr: If someone has been made free neither by the census, nor by the vindicta, nor by testament, then he is not free by the law of the Quirites.

units.la: Per Vindictam manumitti Servus dicebatur, cùm Dominus Romæ apud Prætorem vel Consulem primo consulatûs die in provincijs velut apud Præsidem vel Proconsulem allatis manumissionis causis, caput aut aliud membrum servi tenens, & solemnia quædam verba pronuncians, Alapam ei infligebat, inq; gyrum eum torquens & circumagens è manu tandem emittebat: quibus peractis Prætor vindictâ, quæ & Festuca dicebatur, servi qui manumittendus erat, capitiim posità, certâ formulâ liberum eum pronunciabat.
units.tr: A slave was said to be manumitted by the vindicta when the master, at Rome before the praetor or consul on the first day of his consulship, or in the provinces before the governor or proconsul, having presented the grounds for manumission, holding the slave's head or another part of his body, and pronouncing certain set words, struck him with a slap, turned him around in a circle, and at last released him from his hand. When these were done, the praetor, with the vindicta, which was also called festuca [staff], placed it on the head of the slave who was to be freed, and by a fixed formula declared him free.

units.la: 1. Dominos caput manumittendi tenere solitos, docet Festus:
units.tr: 1. Festus teaches that masters were accustomed to hold the head in manumitting.

units.la: 2. Itemq; Alapam impingere.
units.tr: 2. Likewise, to deal a slap.

units.la: Justinianus has Alapas vocat βλεις ... ἀπισματα.
units.tr: Justinian calls these slaps blows [βλεῖς] ... strokes [ῥαπίσματα].

units.la: Tertull. lib. de Spectaculis Alaparum Contumelias. Claudianus Gratum ictum, & felices injurias.
units.tr: Tertullian, in his book De spectaculis, speaks of the insults of slaps. Claudian speaks of a welcome blow and happy injuries.

units.la: Basilius τελευταῖαν τῶν δούλων πληγήν: h. e. novissima Servorum verbera.
units.tr: Basil calls it τελευταίαν τῶν δούλων πληγήν [the last blow of slaves], that is, the last beatings of slaves.

units.la: 3. Alapas sequebatur in gyrum actio. Persius vocat vertiginem: & Turbinem. Clemens Alex, Strom. 5. Quintil. Declam 342. Epictet. Arrian, cap. 2. Seneca Epist. 9. & Juriscon-sulti sæpè.
units.tr: 3. The slap was followed by a turning in a circle. Persius calls it vertigo [whirling] and turbo [whirlwind]. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 5; Quintilian, Declamationes 342; Epictetus, Arrian, chapter 2; Seneca, Letter 9; and the jurists very often.

units.la: 4. Sic circumactum Dominus è manu mittebat: significans istâ & conversione, & è manu missione datam isti servo facultatem abeundi in omnes partes, sive quò vellet, ea enim facultas libertas erat.
units.tr: 4. Having been turned around in this way, the slave was released by the master's hand, signifying by both the turning and the release from the hand that the slave was given the power to go away in whatever direction he wished; for that power was liberty.

units.la: Itaque Epictetus c. 26. l. 3. dicere volens, Liber sum; προσἐνομαι, inquit, ὅπερ θέλω : ἔρχομαι ὅθεν θέλω. Inde Suidas ἐλεύθερος di-ctus, quasi ὁ ἐλεύθων ὅπω ἐρᾷ.
units.tr: Hence Epictetus, chapter 26, book 3, wishing to say I am free, says: I am allowed what I wish; I come and go whence I wish [προσένομαι ὅπερ θέλω· ἔρχομαι ὅθεν θέλω]. Hence Suidas calls someone ἐλεύθερος, as if it were ὁ ἐλεύθων ὅπου ἐρᾷ [one who goes where he wishes].

units.la: 5. Solemnia Domini erant: Liber esto: atq; abito. Livius lib. 9. & 10. Cic. Phil. 3. Plautus Menæch. dicto loco. Nobilior tamen formula fuit, & communior: Hunc Hominem Libe-rum Esse. Volo. De aliis Formulis vide Formularium Brissonij.
units.tr: 5. The master's formula was: Be free, and go away. Livy, books 9 and 10; Cicero, Philippics 3; Plautus, Menaechmi, in the passage cited. The more noble and more common formula, however, was: I wish this man to be free. On other formulas see Brisson's formulary.

units.la: 6. His ita peractis Lictor Vindictâ Prætoris caput servi feriebat: quod ex annotatis locis Plauti patet.
units.tr: 6. When these things were done, the lictor struck the slave's head with the praetor's vindicta; this is clear from the cited passages of Plautus.

units.la: Vide supra Hermog. l. 23. ff. de Manum.
units.tr: See above, Hermogenianus, law 23, Digest, De manumissionibus.

units.la: Ambrof. lib. 2. Epist.
units.tr: Ambrose, book 2, Letters.

units.la: Libertas, inquit, quam manumissus accipit, & lictoris palmâ donatus acquirit.
units.tr: Liberty, he says, which the freed slave receives, and gains when he is touched by the lictor's hand.

units.la: Postea verò ipse prætor impositâ capiti vindictâ, pronunciabat: Ajo te liberum more Quiritium.
units.tr: Afterwards the praetor himself, laying the rod on the man's head, pronounced: "I declare you free according to the custom of the Quirites."

units.la: Allusit eleganter Lipsius Centur. I v. Miscell. ad Wowerium: Nondum te vindictâ manumisi.
units.tr: Lipsius alludes to this cleverly in Centuria I of his Miscellanea, in the letter to Wower: "I have not yet freed you with the rod."

units.la: 7. Quamprimum manumissi essent: Patrone. Salve, exclamabant: ut notat Festus ex Plauto.
units.tr: 7. As soon as they had been freed, they would cry out: "Patron, hail!" as Festus notes from Plautus.

units.la: 8. Postea rasum caput ibant: in quo erat sedile lapideum: cui versus hic inscriptus: Bene. Meriti. Servi. Sedeant. Surgant. Liberi.
units.tr: 8. Afterwards they went about with shaved heads. On a stone seat was inscribed this verse: "Let the well-deserving slaves sit; let the free rise."

units.la: Sic Sofia Servus Amph. I.I. v. 304.
units.tr: So the slave Sosia in the Amphitryon, Act 1, scene 1, verse 304.

units.la: Utinam ego raso capite calvus hic pileum capiam!
units.tr: "Would that I, here bald with my head shaved, could take a cap!"

units.la: Vide etiam infra Tit. Servorum, alia loca.
units.tr: See also below, under the title Servorum, and other passages.

units.la: Plutarch. in Flam. pag. 377.
units.tr: Plutarch, in Flamininus, p. 377.

units.la: ἐϑ' τοῖς οἰκέταις ὅταν ἐλευθερωθῶσιν ξύεσθω τε τὰς κεφαλὰς ἐς πιλία φορεῖν.
units.tr: When slaves are set free, let them have their heads shaved and wear caps. [ἐπὶ τοῖς οἰκέταις ὅταν ἐλευθερωθῶσιν ξύεσθω τε τὰς κεφαλὰς ἐς πιλία φορεῖν.]

units.la: Livius lib. 34.
units.tr: Livy, book 34.

units.la: Præbuerunt speciem triumphi capitibus rasis: qui servitute ex-emti fuerunt. Causa Calvitij describit apud Nonium: Ut enim naufragi caput item radebant, quod procellas maris superassent: ita hi, quod tempestatem servitutis. Hinc factum, ut pileus pro libertate caperetur Suet. in Tib. Servis frustra ad pileum vocatis in Siciliam profugit.
units.tr: They presented the appearance of a triumph, with shaved heads, those who had been released from servitude. Nonius describes the cause of the baldness: just as shipwrecked men likewise shaved their heads because they had survived the storms of the sea, so these men did so because they had survived the tempest of slavery. Hence the cap came to be taken as the sign of liberty. Suetonius, in Tiberius: "Having vainly summoned the slaves to the cap, he fled into Sicily."

units.la: Seneca lib. 6. Epist. Dicet nunc aliquis, me vocare ad pileum servos, & Dominos de fastigio suo deijcere.
units.tr: Seneca, letter 6: "Someone will now say that I am calling slaves to the cap and casting masters down from their high station."

units.la: 9. Usurpabant etiam Togam, caligas, & calceos, quæ ornamenta aliàs civium, teste Servio ad 1. Æneid. Polybius de Prusiâ scribit, eum legatis Romanis occurrisse raso capite, pileatum, togatum, & caligatum, omniq; adeò ornatu, quo illi, qui nuper à Romanis manumissi, quos libertos nominant.
units.tr: 9. They also adopted the toga, the military boots and the shoes, which were otherwise the ornaments of citizens, as Servius attests on the first book of the Aeneid. Polybius writes of Prusias that he met the Roman envoys with a shaved head, wearing a cap, a toga and boots, and with all the dress of those who had lately been freed by the Romans, whom they call freedmen.

units.la: Calceorum in Prusiâ meminit Appianus principio belli Mithridatici, & Diodorus Siculus. Plutarch. in Pompejo: quà de pyratarum crudeli joco.
units.tr: Appian, at the beginning of the Mithridatic War, and Diodorus Siculus mention Prusias' shoes. Plutarch, in Pompey, tells of the pirates' cruel joke.

units.la: De Coronâ Tertull. de Coron. mil. Plautus Pseud. Pseudolo cum corollâ venienti inquit herus: Liberè hoc quidem hercle. q. d. coronatus tu? quasi jam manumissus.
units.tr: On the garland, Tertullian, On the Crown of the Soldier. In Plautus' Pseudolus, when the slave comes in with a garland, the master says: "Free indeed, by Hercules!" that is, "Are you crowned? As if already freed."

units.la: Hac coronâ pileus erat redimitus, quæ oleagina visitur in Iconio Numi Cordi Russi Trium - viri monetalis. Vestis eorum alba erat, Cujacio observante, lib. 3. Obser. c. 24. & Borchold. JC. ad Tit. Manum. Justin.
units.tr: This garland was wrapped around the cap, which is seen in olive-coloured form on the coin of Cordus Rufus, moneyer. Their clothing was white, as Cujas observes in book 3 of his Observations, chapter 24, and Borchold, jurist, on the title De manumissionibus in Justinian.

units.la: Tertull. lib. de Resurr. carn.
units.tr: Tertullian, in his book On the Resurrection of the Flesh.

units.la: Si famulum tuum libertate mutaveris, & albæ vestis nitore.
units.tr: "If you have changed your servant's status for freedom, and for the brightness of white clothing."

units.la: Denique nomen geminabant. Usurpabant enim Domini, sive Patroni nomen, ut innuit Persius in Marco Dama: & Cicero Rosc. Amer. de L. Chrysogono liberto Syllæ.
units.tr: Finally they doubled the name. For masters or patrons used their own name, as Persius hints in the case of Marcus Dama, and Cicero in Pro Roscio Amerino concerning Lucius Chrysogonus, freedman of Sulla.

units.la: Atque hæc de primâ specie Manumissionis: quæ consequentibus temporibus migravit è foro & curiâ in Ecclesiam: à Consulibus & Prætoribus ad sacerdotes: idque Constantini Constitutione: ut passim videre est Codice & Jure Canonico. Niceph. l. 7. cap. 16. Histor. Eccles. de Constantino loquens: Libertatem quoque, inquit, Ecclesiæ lege latâ concessit, & ut libertate sacerdotiidotibus testibus donati Civium Romanorum numero adscribe- rentur.
units.tr: And this is what we have on the first kind of manumission. In later times it passed from the forum and the senate-house to the Church, from consuls and praetors to priests, and this by a constitution of Constantine, as can be seen everywhere in the Code and in Canon Law. Nicephorus, book 7, chapter 16 of his Ecclesiastical History, speaking of Constantine: "He also granted freedom to the Church by a law passed, and that those endowed with the liberty of priesthood, having witnesses, should be enrolled in the number of Roman citizens."

units.la: Citantur Constitutiones istæ lib.I. cap.9. Historiæ Tripartitæ, & visuntur etiamnum C. lib. I, Tit. I.
units.tr: These constitutions are cited in book 1, chapter 9 of the Tripartite History, and they are still to be seen in the Code, book 1, title 1.

units.la: Meminit hujus manumissionis etiam Concilium Carthaginien- se. Atque in hac notandum venit, quod sicut in manumissione per Vindictam nomen & causa manumissi in Acta referebantur, ita hic ut lapidibus inscribebantur, & elogium conficiebatur, quod testamentum ingenuitatis vocabant. Videatur Guli- elmus Fornerius Aurelianensis JC. in libb. Opin.
units.tr: The Council of Carthage also mentions this manumission. Here it should be noted that just as in manumission by the rod the name and cause of the freed man were recorded in the acts, so here they were inscribed on stones, and an inscription was drawn up, which they called the testament of freeborn status. See William Fornier of Orléans, jurist, in his books of Opinions.

units.la: De altera specie Manumiss. quæ per censum fiebat, sciendum est: moris apud Romanos fuisse, ut lustris singulis: hoc est, singulo quinquennio singuli cives Romani censum profiterentur: hoc est, apud Censores in Campo Martio declararent, quantum quisque in bonis haberet.
units.tr: Concerning the other kind of manumission, which was done by the census, it must be known that it was the custom among the Romans that at each lustrum, that is, every five years, individual Roman citizens made their census declaration, that is, declared before the censors in the Campus Martius how much property each one had.

units.la: Profitebantur autem primum nomen, quod deferebatur in ta- bulas censuales. Deinde Bona, hac formula:
units.tr: They first declared their name, which was entered on the census tables. Then they declared their goods, in this form:

units.la: Ego. L. Titius. Profiteor. Mihi. A. Patre. Legata. Hs. XX.
units.tr: "I, Lucius Titius, declare: to me, from my father, left by legacy, 20 sesterces."

units.la: Manumittere ergo per censum, nihil aliud erat, quàm cùm Do- minus servo imponeret nomen civis Romani: hoc est, suum, servo imponebat, manumittebat, & in censum deferre cogebat. Quod patet ex Cicer. pro Cæcinn. loco, cùm is, qui in servitute justâ fuerit, censu liberetur, eum qui cùm liber esset, censeri no- luerit, ipsum sibi libertatem abjudicasse indicat.
units.tr: To manumit by the census, therefore, was nothing other than when the master gave the slave the name of a Roman citizen, that is, his own name; he thereby manumitted him and compelled him to be entered in the census. This is clear from Cicero, Pro Caecina, where he says that one who has been in lawful servitude is freed by the census, and indicates that one who, though free, has refused to be enrolled has himself renounced his liberty.

units.la: Tertius manumittendi modus per Testamentum est, cùm quis testamento condito servum liberum esse jubebat: quæ manu- missio, quod valere Ulpianus lib.12. Tabb. facere ait.
units.tr: The third mode of manumitting is by testament, when someone, having made his will, ordered that a slave be free. Ulpian says that this manumission is valid, in book 12 on the Tables.

units.la: Dabatur libertas hoc modo dupliciter: vel directò, vel per fidei commissum. Directò quidem his verbis: Stichum. Ser- vum. Meum. Liberum. Esse. Jubeo. Vel. Liber. Esto. Fidei commisso hoc modo: Rogo. Fidei. Com- misso. Hæredis. Mei. Ut. Stichum. Servum. Manumittat. Priori modo manumissus Horcinus libertus dicebatur, ut videre est Cod. l. 9. de testam. manum.
units.tr: Liberty was given in this way in two ways, either directly or by trust. Directly, with these words: "I order that my slave Stichus be free", or "Be free". By trust, in this way: "I ask my heir, by trust, to manumit my slave Stichus." A slave freed in the former way was called an Orcinian freedman, as can be seen in Code 9, on testamentary manumission.

units.la: A Theophilo in Tit. de sing. reb. per fidei commiss. Vel Charonis dicitur, quasi à Plutone, vel Charonte manumissus. Atque talis pileo assumto, funus Domini praecedebat: ut videre est apud Justin. l. 1. Cod. de Lat. libertate tollenda. Quem ipsum etiam familiae libertum dicebant.
units.tr: From Theophilus, on the title on single things, by trust. Or he is called a freedman of Charon, as if freed by Pluto or Charon. And such a man, with his cap put on, used to go before the funeral of his master, as can be seen in Justinian, Code book 1, on the removal of Latin freedom. Such a man they also called a freedman of the household.

units.la: Posteriori modo ficbat haeredis libertus. Quod erat servum ab haerede manumittere,
units.tr: The latter way made a freedman of the heir, when the heir manumitted a slave.

units.la: Latinae sive Junianae manumissionis tres quoq; species fuerunt: Una, quae inter amicos fieret: altera, quae adhibitione convivij: tertia, quae per Epistolam. De prima Val. Maxim. l. 2. cap. 8. Convivium olim solemne Romanos instituere solitos, illud χαρισιον appellasse, cui praeter cognatos & amicos nemo interponebatur. Finis is erat, ut si qua inter necessarias personas quaerela esset orta apud Sacra mensae, & inter hilaritatem animorum, fautoribus concordiae adhibitis, tollerentur. Inter hujusmodi conviviaaliquos plerumque manumitti consuevisse, testes sunt omnes Comici: & apud Plautum exempla compluria. Memini & Seneca loco supra dicto.
units.tr: There were also three kinds of Latin or Junian manumission. One was done among friends; another by the invitation to a banquet; the third by letter. Concerning the first, Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 8: the Romans were accustomed to hold a solemn banquet, which they called charision [χαρισιον], to which no one was admitted except relatives and friends. Its purpose was that if any quarrel had arisen between close persons, it might be removed at the sacred table, amid the cheerfulness of minds, with friends of concord present. At such banquets slaves were generally freed; all the comic writers attest this, and Plautus has many examples. I also recall Seneca in the passage cited above.

units.la: Alter modus erat, cum Dominus servum mensae adhibitum, inter edendum manumitteret. Adhibere autem Domini servos diebus festis mensae solebant, sine tamen manumissione: id quod è Columella liquet. Theophilus & Cajus hanc speciem appellant Manumissionem per mensam. Tertullianus de Resurr. carnis honorari mensa appellat.
units.tr: The other mode was when the master, while a slave was admitted to the table, manumitted him during the meal. Masters used to admit their slaves to the table on feast days, but without manumission; this is clear from Columella. Theophilus and Gaius call this kind manumission by the table. Tertullian, in On the Resurrection of the Flesh, calls it the honour of the table.

units.la: Ultima denique species est Manumissio per Epistolam, cujus fit mentio L. qui absent. ff. de acquir. posse. Quando videlicet Dominus absentem servum per Epistolam jubebat esse liberum.
units.tr: The last kind is manumission by letter, mentioned in the law Qui absentem, Digest, on acquiring possession. This is when the master, by letter, ordered that an absent slave be free.

units.la: His igitur omnib' modis Manumissi liberi quidem fiebant, non tamen ingenui. Nam hic aliud opus ratione. A Principe enim jus aureorum annulorum petendum erat: hoc est, equestris dignitas, permanente tamen salvo jure patronatus. Qua impetrata annulum mutabant. Servis enim apud Romanos interdictum ctum erat aureis annulis: solùm ferreis uti licebat teste Isid. lib. 19. cap. 22. & Statio lib. 3. Sylvarum. Atque hæc ferè collegerat vir ille doctus, cujus supra memini.
units.tr: By all these ways the manumitted were indeed made free, but not freeborn; for that required another process. The right of the gold rings had to be sought from the Prince, that is, equestrian rank, the right of patronage remaining intact. When this was obtained, they changed their ring. For slaves were forbidden by the Romans to use gold rings; they were permitted only iron ones, as Isidore, book 19, chapter 22, and Statius, book 3 of the Silvae, attest. These things the learned man I mentioned above has gathered for the most part.

units.la: Cæterùm & hoc observatione dignum est: servos manumissos, Quiritcs appellatos apud Persium Sat. v. ---- quibus una Quiritem Vertigo facit ----
units.tr: Moreover, this too is worth noting: manumitted slaves were called Quirites, as in Persius, Satire 5: "whom a single Vertigo makes Quirites."

units.la: Livius lib. 2. cùm de Vindicio agit, rationem sic videtur reddere:
units.tr: Livy, book 2, when he treats of Vindicius, seems to give the reason thus:

units.la: Ille primùm dicitur Vindicta liberatus: quidam Vindicta quoque nomen tractum ab illo putant: Vindicio ipsi nomen fuisse: post illum observatum, ut qui ita liberati essent, in civitatem accepti viderentur.
units.tr: "He is said to have been first freed by the rod. Some think that the name of the rod was also derived from him, Vindicius himself having been the name. After him it was observed that those who were so freed seemed to be received into the citizenship."

units.la: Ita quoq; docebantur Servi testamento facti liberi.
units.tr: So too were slaves taught to become free by will.

units.la: Perf. Sat. iii. ---- ast illum
units.tr: Persius, Sat. iii. ---- but that one

units.la: Hesterni capite induto subiere Quirites.
units.tr: Yesterday, with the cap put on their heads, the Quirites came under.

units.la: Hinc factum, ut qui libertate donati essent: & civitate viderentur.
units.tr: Hence it came about that those who had been granted liberty were also regarded as having citizenship.

units.la: Unde M. Cicero pro Balbo:
units.tr: Whence Marcus Cicero, in the speech for Balbus:

units.la: Servos deniq;, quorum jus & fortuna conditio infima est, bene de Rep. meritos, perfepe libertate, h.e. civitate publicè donari videamus.
units.tr: Indeed we often see slaves, whose right and condition are lowest but who have deserved well of the commonwealth, granted freedom publicly, that is, citizenship.

units.la: Hoc ex Tullij Regis sanctione apud Halicarnas. lib. 4. Antiq. Rom.
units.tr: This comes from the decree of King Tullius, in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities, book 4.

units.la: ὁ ἀπὸ Τύλλιος ἐν τοῖς ἐλευθερωμένοις τῶν δεσπότων, μετέχειν τῆς ἰσοπολιτείας ἐκέλευσεν.
units.tr: Tullius ordered that those freed by their masters should share in equal citizenship [ὁ ἀπὸ Τύλλιος ἐν τοῖς ἐλευθερωμένοις τῶν δεσπότων, μετέχειν τῆς ἰσοπολιτείας ἐκέλευσεν.]

units.la: Quod ita deinceps habitum est.
units.tr: This was afterwards maintained in this way.

units.la: Pomponius l. 5. §. Captivus. ff. de Capt. & postl. reversf.
units.tr: Pomponius, book 5, section Captivus, Digest, On captives and those returned by postliminy.

units.la: Captivus autem si a nobis manumissus fuerit, & pervenerit ad suos, ita demum postliminio reversus intelligitur, si malit eos sequi, quàm in nostrà civitate manere. Imperator l. 1. §. Sin autem. Cod. de Communi servo manumiss. plenissimam eam libertatem vocat: & sic habere facultatem servum libertate donare: & eum habere plenissimam libertatem: & civitate Romana perfrui.
units.tr: But if a captive has been manumitted by us, and has reached his own people, he is understood to have returned by postliminy only if he chooses to follow them rather than remain in our state. The emperor, in book 1, section Sin autem, Code, On the manumission of a common slave, calls that liberty the fullest: and so the slave has the power to grant freedom, and he has the fullest liberty, and enjoys Roman citizenship.

units.la: Vide Adrian. Bchotij Apophoret. l. 2. c. 7.
units.tr: See Adrian Bachotius, Apophoreta, book 2, chapter 7.

units.la: Lignorum. Postium.
units.tr: Of Wood. Of the Posts.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Ædium.
units.tr: See also the title Of Buildings.

units.la: LIGNA nisi tempestive: h. e. suo tempore excindantur cariosa fiant. Moft. 3. 2. v. 144.
units.tr: Logs, unless they are cut down in their proper season, that is, at the right time, become rotten. Moft. 3. 2. v. 144.

units.la: POSTES pice solebant induci. Moft. 3. 2. v. 145.
units.tr: Doorposts used to be smeared with pitch. Moft. 3. 2. v. 145.

units.la: IN foribus ornamento varia appicta. Ibid. v. 147. & 150.
units.tr: On doors, various decorations were painted. Ibid. v. 147. & 150.

units.la: LIGNATUM ituri ferebant securim & lora. Capt. 3. 4. v. 125.
units.tr: Those who were about to go out for wood used to carry an axe and a rope. Capt. 3. 4. v. 125.

units.la: Cato lib. II. Orig.
units.tr: Cato, book II of the Origines.

units.la: Quin aquatum, ut lignatum, jubentur ire: securim atq; lorum ferunt.
units.tr: For they are ordered to go to the water as they go to the wood: they carry an axe and a rope.

units.la: Vide Lipf. Epist. Quaest. lib. 1. 13.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Epistolicae Quaestiones, book 1, letter 13.

units.la: Linguarum.
units.tr: Of Languages.

units.la: LINGUA patrona perjurij. Asin. 2. 2. v. 26.
units.tr: The tongue is the patron of perjury. Asin. 2. 2. v. 26.

units.la: SICULORUM lingua neque plane Græca, neq; plane Latina fuit, sed cinnus quidam ex utroq; mistus. Mer. Prol. v. 12. Inde Siculi trilingues Apulejo dicuntur lib. 11. Milef. quod Græcè, Latinè, & Siculè loquerentur. Vide Lexic. Plaut. Logi Siculi.
units.tr: The Sicilian language was neither plainly Greek nor plainly Latin, but a certain mixture of both. Mer. Prol. v. 12. Hence Apuleius, in book 11 of the Metamorphoses, calls the Sicilians trilingual, because they spoke Greek, Latin and Sicilian. See the Plautine Lexicon, under Logi Siculi.

units.la: POENI, sive Carthaginienses erant. Utebantur enim lingua Tyriorum & Afrorum. Pœn. 5. 2. v. 74.
units.tr: The Poeni, or Carthaginians, used the language of the Tyrians and Africans. Pœn. 5. 2. v. 74.

units.la: Hanno Poenus dicitur Migdilybs.
units.tr: Hanno the Carthaginian is called Migdilybs.

units.la: Virgil. lib. 1. Æneid.
units.tr: Virgil, book 1 of the Aeneid.

units.la: Quippe domum timet ambiguam Tyriosq; bilingues.
units.tr: For he fears the ambiguous house and the Tyrians, who speak two tongues.

units.la: Qui autem duplici utuntur lingua, infideles & veteratores improbique habentur. Unde idem Hanno dicitur bisulci-lingua, quasi proserpens bestia.
units.tr: Those who use a double language are regarded as faithless, deceitful and wicked. Hence the same Hanno is called forked-tongued, as if a creeping beast.

units.la: RUSTICI κατ' ἀφαίρεσιν saepe pronunciant dictiones. Trucul. 3. 2. v. 20. 21. 22. 23. Cauliator, pro cavillator : Rabo, pro arrhabo : Conia, pro ciconia.
units.tr: Country people often pronounce words by aphaeresis [κατ' ἀφαίρεσιν]. Trucul. 3. 2. v. 20. 21. 22. 23. Cauliator for cavillator; Rabo for arrhabo; Conia for ciconia.

units.la: VERBA Attica Siculis sunt multò lectiora. Perf. 3. 1. v. 67.
units.tr: Attic words are far more choice for Sicilians. Perf. 3. 1. v. 67.

units.la: Cicero:
units.tr: Cicero:

units.la: Si litteras Græcas Athenis, non Lilybæi; Latinas Romæ, non in Siciliâ didicisse.
units.tr: If he had learned Greek letters at Athens and not at Lilybaeum, and Latin at Rome and not in Sicily.

units.la: Asconius Pædianus:
units.tr: Asconius Pedianus:

units.la: Dicit illum Græcas litteras simul latinas in Siciliâ didicisse: in eâ insulâ, quæ neutrâ linguâ bene utatur.
units.tr: He says that he learned Greek letters together with Latin in Sicily, on that island which uses neither language well.

units.la: Inde Plautus dixit Sicilissitare. Men. Prol. v. 12.
units.tr: Hence Plautus said Sicilissitare. Men. Prol. v. 12.

units.la: POENORUM linguam alij è Syriacâ tractam putant : ut Isaac. Casaub. ad Sueton. alij ipsam Hebraicam, quâ sacra Biblia descripta sunt, Phæniciam esse existimant, ut Joseph. Scalig. & Guilh. Postellus.
units.tr: Some think the Punic language was derived from Syriac, as Isaac Casaubon on Suetonius; others think it was Hebrew itself, in which the holy Bibles were written, that is, Phoenician, as Joseph Scaliger and Guillaume Postel.

units.la: Vide etiam Caninij Grammaticam Græcam.
units.tr: See also Caninius's Greek Grammar.

units.la: LITIUM. CONTROVERSIÆ. DISCOR-DIÆ. CONTENTIONUM.
units.tr: Strife. Controversies. Dissensions. Contentions.

units.la: STultitia est eum prævorti litibus, cui benè esse licet. Perf. 5. 2. v. 20.
units.tr: Folly it is to be drawn into quarrels by one who is permitted to be well off. Perf. 5. 2. v. 20.

units.la: Vide Plin. lib. 7. cap. 32.
units.tr: See Pliny, book 7, chapter 32.

units.la: Adeò quidam lites amant: ut si nihil sit litium, lites emant. Pœn. 3. 2. v. 10.
units.tr: Some people so love lawsuits that, if there were no lawsuits, they would buy them. Pœn. 3. 2. v. 10.

units.la: LITTERARUM. SCRIBENDI. SCRIPTURÆ.
units.tr: Letters. Writing. Script.

units.la: LITTERA I dicitur littera longa, quia exporrecta est in longitudinem: non item T. vel L. Aul. 1. 1. v. 4.
units.tr: The letter I is called a long letter, because it is stretched out lengthwise, but not T or L. Aul. 1. 1. v. 4.

units.la: Videndus Lipsius de Pronunc. L. L. cap. 8. Cælius Rhod. lib. 10. cap. 8. Joh. Cast. lib. 2. cap. 9. Observat.
units.tr: See Lipsius, On the Pronunciation of Latin Letters, chapter 8; Caelius Rhodiginus, book 10, chapter 8; Johannes Castellanus, Observations, book 2, chapter 9.

units.la: De littera V vide supra Tit. Artium. pag. 105.
units.tr: On the letter V, see above, under the title Artium, p. 105.

units.la: Si quid observatione dignum notabant, longis litteris utebantur. Pœn. 4. 2. v. 15. Aul. 1. 1. v. 39. Rud. 5. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: If they noted something worthy of attention, they used long letters. Pœn. 4. 2. v. 15. Aul. 1. 1. v. 39. Rud. 5. 2. v. 7.

units.la: ANTE Chartæ & membranarum usum, in dolatis ex lingno codicillis Epistolarum colloquia scribebantur: teste Isidoro lib. 7.
units.tr: Before the use of paper and parchment, conversations by letter were written on wooden writing tablets of planed wood, as Isidore testifies in book 7.

units.la: Fiebant autem istæ Tabulæ inductâ cerâ è fago, abiete, buxo, tiliâ, sive philyrâ, acere, citro, ebore. Easdem obsignare soliti cerâ, & lino obligare. Vestigia hujus moris plura sunt in nostro Authore Plauto. Asin. 4. 1. v. 22.
units.tr: These tablets were made by coating wood from beech, fir, box, linden or philyra, maple, citron or ivory with wax. They were accustomed to seal them with wax and bind them with thread. Traces of this custom are many in our author Plautus. Asin. 4. 1. v. 22.

units.la: Ne illi sit cera, ubi facere possit litteras. Bacch. 4. 4. v. 64. Efferstylum, ceram, & tabellas & linum. Et v. 81. 96. Ne interturba, jam imperatum in cerâ inest. Cedò tu ceram ac linum aclutum. Et 4. 6. v. 19. Nosce signum. Et 4. 9. v. 60. 62. 63. Tacitus conscripsit tabellas: obsignatas has dedit mihi. Nosco signum. Cera quidem haud parsit, neq; stylo. Et 4. 7. v. 10. Hæ tabellæ te arguunt.
units.tr: Let him not have wax on which he could make letters. Bacch. 4. 4. v. 64. Bring out the stylus, the wax, the tablets and the thread. And v. 81. 96. Don't make a fuss, the order is already written in the wax. Now hand me the wax and the sharp thread. And 4. 6. v. 19. Know the seal. And 4. 9. v. 60. 62. 63. He wrote the tablets in silence and gave me these sealed. I know the seal. The wax, at least, did not spare, nor the stylus. And 4. 7. v. 10. These tablets convict you.

units.la: Pseud. 1. 1. v. 40. 45. Lignea salus.
units.tr: Pseud. 1. 1. v. 40. 45. Wooden safety.

units.la: Pers. 2. 2. v. 66. Ego hanc ad heram tuam obsignatam abiitem.
units.tr: Pers. 2. 2. v. 66. I went off to your mistress with this one sealed.

units.la: Pers. 4. 3. v. 59. Postquam recitasti, quod erat cera creditum.
units.tr: Pers. 4. 3. v. 59. After you read aloud what had been entrusted to the wax.

units.la: Pseud. 1. 4. v. 8. Quasi Poëta tabulas cum capit sibi.
units.tr: Pseud. 1. 4. v. 8. As when a poet takes up his tablets for himself.

units.la: De hac consuetudine videndus Lipsius Epist. Institut. cap. 1. & 2. Turneb. 24. 31. Suspiciones Gruteri. Mercerus Opinionum lib. 2. cap. 23. Salmuth. ad Pancirollum. Taubm. ad locum Asin. & Bacch. Ubi nonnulla in hanc rem compilavit ex Recentioribus.
units.tr: On this custom, see Lipsius, Epistolica Institutio, chapters 1 and 2; Turnebus, 24, 31; Gruter's Suspiciones; Mercerus, Opinionum, book 2, chapter 23; Salmuth on Pancirollus; Taubmann on the passages in the Asinaria and the Bacchides. Here he has gathered some material on this subject from recent writers.

units.la: SCRIBEBANT autem stylo sive graphio in tabellas. Mil. 1. 1. v. 38.
units.tr: They wrote, however, with a stylus or graphium on tablets. Mil. 1. 1. v. 38.

units.la: Habes tabellas? AR. Habeo & stylum.
units.tr: Have you tablets? AR. I have a stylus too.

units.la: Pseud. 1. 5. v. 131. de servis:
units.tr: Pseud. 1. 5. v. 131. concerning slaves:

units.la: Quasi in libro cum scribuntur calamo litteræ. Stilis me totum, mag, almeis conscribito.
units.tr: As when letters are written in a book with a reed pen. Write me all down with the stylus, my master, in full.

units.la: Eratque graphium illud ferè ferreum, sive æreum, atque acutum valdè, cōq; ad cædem aptum.
units.tr: And that graphium was mostly of iron or bronze, very sharp, and so suited to killing.

units.la: Sueton. Julio cap. 82.
units.tr: Suetonius, Julius, chapter 82.

units.la: Cæsar Cassii brachium arreptum graphio trajecit.
units.tr: Caesar pierced the seized arm of Cassius with a stylus.

units.la: Idcoq; theeis fuerunt impositæ graphia. Suet. Claud. cap. 35.
units.tr: Hence styluses were placed in cases. Suetonius, Claudius, chapter 35.

units.la: Ne cuivis comiti aut librario calamaria aut graphiaria theca adimerentur.
units.tr: That neither the ink-case nor the stylus-case be taken away from any companion or secretary.

units.la: Martialis lib. 14.
units.tr: Martial, book 14.

units.la: Sortitus thecam calamis armare memento.
units.tr: Be sure, once you have drawn your lot, to arm your pens from the case.

units.la: Figuram ejus repræsentavit geminam Laurentius Pignorius Patavinus: quam huc apponam ex libro De Servis pag. 118.
units.tr: Laurentius Pignorius of Padua has represented its figure twice; I will set it here from his book On Slaves, p. 118.

units.la: Sympolius Ænigm. I. Graphium.
units.tr: Symposius, Riddle 1: The Stylus.

units.la: De summo planus: sed non ego planus in imo.
units.tr: Flat at the top, but I am not flat at the bottom.

units.la: Versor utrimq; manu, diversò & munere fungor.
units.tr: I am turned about by either hand, and I serve in two different offices.

units.la: Altera pars revocat, quicquid pars altera fecit.
units.tr: The one part recalls whatever the other part has done.

units.la: Appositè sanè. nam si in imo acumen graphij digitis complectamur, ut poscit usus, eiusdem planities, seu latitudo erit in summo.
units.tr: Aptly indeed: for if we grasp the point at the lower end with our fingers, as use requires, its flatness, or breadth, will be at the top.

units.la: Althelmus in Heptasticbis.Aenigm. de Elementis.
units.tr: Aldhelm, in the Heptasticha, Riddle on the Elements.

units.la: Nascimur ex ferro, rursus ferro moribunda,
units.tr: We are born of iron, and dying we are restored by iron,

units.la: Necnon & volucris penna volitantis ad æthram.
units.tr: And also by the wing of a bird flying up into the air.

units.la: Idem Ænigm. de Pugill.
units.tr: The same, Riddle on the Writing Tablets.

units.la: Melliguris apibus mea prima processit origo,
units.tr: My first origin came forth from honey-bearing bees,

units.la: Sed pars exterior crescebat cætera sylvis.
units.tr: But my outer part grew among the other woods.

units.la: Calceamenta mihi tradebant tergora dura.
units.tr: Hard hides handed over footwear to me.

units.la: Nunc ferri stimulus faciem proscindit amænam.
units.tr: Now the goad of iron cuts open my pleasant face.

units.la: Flexibus, & sulcis obliquat ad instar aratri.
units.tr: With bends and furrows it slants, like a plough.

units.la: Eleganter vocat ferri stimulum : quia mucrone scribebant : planitie scriptum abradebant. Columella in Horto: Nomine tum Grajo ceu littera proxima prima Pangitur in cerâ doêli mucrone magistri. Sic & humi pingui ferrata cuspidû illâ Deprimitur, folio viridis, pede candida Beta.
units.tr: He aptly calls the iron point a goad, because they wrote with the point and scraped off the writing with the flat end. Columella, in the Garden: "Then with the Greek name, as the letter next after the first, it is traced in wax with the point of the skilled teacher. So too on the rich soil the white beet, green in leaf and white in stalk, is pressed down with that iron-tipped point."

units.la: LITTERARUM. EPISTOLARUM. TABULARUM.
units.tr: LETTERS. EPISTLES. TABLETS.

units.la: TABULAS obsignabant, præsertim amantes imagine suâ: & annulis signatorijs.
units.tr: TABLETS they sealed, especially lovers, with their own image, and with signet rings.

units.la: Signum autem annuli imprimebatur in ceram. Dehinc in Epistolarum usum successit creta.
units.tr: The impression of the ring was pressed into wax. Later, clay (creta) came into use for letters.

units.la: Cicero 1 v. in Verrem;
units.tr: Cicero, first speech against Verres:

units.la: Signum iste animadvertit in cretulâ.
units.tr: This man noticed the seal on the clay tablet.

units.la: Et pro Flacco:
units.tr: And in the speech for Flaccus:

units.la: Hæc quæ est ànobis prolata laudatio, obsignata erat cretâ illâ Asiaticâ, quæ est ferè omnibus nota nobis.
units.tr: This praise which has been delivered by us was sealed with that Asian clay, which is almost universally known to us.

units.la: Nec procul abluduntunt illa S. Leonrij lib. v. contra Judæos:
units.tr: Not far from these is that passage of St Leontius, book 5, against the Jews:

units.la: Greek passage, a quotation from Leontius, printed in Greek letters, with the Latin sentence: Quem locum ideò adscripsi, q- rarior author, & non in omnium manibus.
units.tr: A passage of Leontius in Greek follows. I have added it here because this author is rarer and not in everyone's hands.

units.la: ANTEQUAM litteras recitarent, jubebant, adversus quos facerent, ne postea dicerent fictas, cognoscere signum. Bacch. 4. 6. v. 19. Pseud. 4. 2. v. 45. Vide P. Victorium lib. 14. cap. 4.
units.tr: BEFORE they read out letters, they ordered that the seal be recognised by those against whom they were to be used, so that they could not afterwards say the letters were forged. Bacch. 4. 6. v. 19. Pseud. 4. 2. v. 45. See P. Victorius, book 14, chapter 4.

units.la: ÆQUUM est Tabellis consignatis credere.
units.tr: IT IS fair to trust sealed tablets.

units.la: TABULÆ erant syngrapha, quâ cavebatur ob acceptam pecuniam: Ex constabant ex ceris, in quibus dicebatur Scribi.
units.tr: TABLETS were also a bond, by which a debt was secured on money received. They were made of wax, on which it was said that things were written.

units.la: LITTERARUM ϲηπʒ continebat nomen scribentis: & ejus ad quem scribebatur: addita salutatione. Ut: Phanicium Callidoro amatori suo salutem mittit.
units.tr: The opening of a letter (the greeting formula [χαίρειν]) contained the name of the writer and of the one to whom it was written, with a salutation added. For example: Phoenicium sends greetings to Callidorus, her lover.

units.la: IMPUDENS est Epistola, quæ initio caret salute.
units.tr: A LETTER is impudent if it lacks a greeting at the beginning.

units.la: SOLEMNIS formula in Epistolis fuit:
units.tr: A set formula was used in letters:

units.la: Si vales, gaudeo: ego valeo.
units.tr: If you are well, I am glad; I am well.

units.la: IN Epistolis si læta essent scribenda, utebantur genere litterarum contractiore, & accuratiore. Sic Bacch. 4. 9. v. 68. Nicobulus cùm resignasset epistolam, quæ tamen magnis erat litteris conscripta, utpote tristia nuncians, ait exultans, tamquam læta foret lecturus:
units.tr: IF the letters were to announce happy news, they used a more compressed and precise style. So in Bacch. 4. 9. v. 68, when Nicobulus had unfolded a letter, which was nevertheless written in large characters because it announced sad things, he said, exulting, as if he were about to read good news:

units.la: Euge litteras minutas.
units.tr: Hurrah, small letters!

units.la: Chrysalus autem servus, de miseriâ filij certus, subijcit: qui quidem videat parum.
units.tr: But the slave Chrysalus, who was certain of his son's misfortune, adds: which, indeed, one may see but little of.

units.la: EPISTOLA claudebatur hac formulâ: VALE, atq; hac cura.
units.tr: A LETTER was closed with this formula: FAREWELL, and take care of this.

units.la: LITTERÆ & scriptura etiam loquitur.
units.tr: LETTERS and writing also speak.

units.la: Bacch. 4. 7. v. 3. Quid hæ loquuntur litteræ? Et 4. 9. v. 6. Metuo ne idem canten, quod priores.
units.tr: Bacch. 4. 7. v. 3. What do these letters say? And 4. 9. v. 6. I fear they sing the same song as the earlier ones.

units.la: Antea dixerat 2. 3. v. 51. Ne idem clament.
units.tr: He had said earlier, 2. 3. v. 51: Let them not cry the same thing.

units.la: Pseud. 1. 1. v. 97. Litterarum sermo.
units.tr: Pseud. 1. 1. v. 97. The speech of letters.

units.la: Rud. 2. 5. v. 21. Urna hæc litterata est: ab se cantat, cuja sit.
units.tr: Rud. 2. 5. v. 21. This urn is lettered: it sings of itself whose it is.

units.la: Perf. 4.3.v.30. Quid isthaec narrant? To. Percunctare ex ipsis: ipse tibi narrabunt.
units.tr: Pers. 4.3.v.30. What do those things tell? Answer: Question them, and they themselves will tell you.

units.la: Cic. lib. 1. de Legg.
units.tr: Cicero, book 1 of the Laws.

units.la: Dum latina loquentur litterae.
units.tr: As long as Latin letters speak.

units.la: Idem pro Deniot.
units.tr: The same, in the speech for Deiotarus.

units.la: Ut annales P. R. & monumenta vetustatis loquuntur.
units.tr: As the annals of the Roman people and the monuments of antiquity speak.

units.la: Symmach. lib. 1. Epist. 13.
units.tr: Symmachus, book 1, letter 13.

units.la: Monumenta Curiae nostrae plenius tecum loquentur.
units.tr: The monuments of our Senate will speak to you more fully.

units.la: Idem lib. 9. Epist. 102. dixit Litteras loqui.
units.tr: The same, book 9, letter 102, said that letters speak.

units.la: Et Epist. 67. Historias loqui.
units.tr: And letter 67: histories speak.

units.la: Agellius lib. 9. cap. 3.
units.tr: Gellius, book 9, chapter 3.

units.la: Demosthenis incluta illa Orationes, concionesq; vocificant.
units.tr: The famous orations and speeches of Demosthenes cry out.

units.la: Apul. Apolog.
units.tr: Apuleius, Apology.

units.la: Si litterae, ita ut partim vocales dicuntur, etiam propriam vocem usurparent.
units.tr: If letters, as some of them are called vowels, could also take on a voice of their own.

units.la: Sic etiam Sidon. Apoll. in Panegyr. dixit sidera clamare, & aves loqui.
units.tr: Likewise Sidonius Apollinaris, in the Panegyric, said that the stars cry out and the birds speak.

units.la: Cassiodorus lib. 8. Var. Epist 10.
units.tr: Cassiodorus, book 8, Variae, letter 10.

units.la: Vulnera corporis vocat praeconium sine assertore, propriamque linguam Virtutis.
units.tr: He calls the wounds of the body a herald without a spokesman, and the proper language of Virtue.

units.la: Ammian. lib. 25. de Juliano:
units.tr: Ammianus, book 25, on Julian:

units.la: Si nocturna lumina inter quae lucubrabat, potuissent vocem ullā testari.
units.tr: If the night lamps by which he was working late could have borne witness with any voice.

units.la: Quod notandum ideo duxi: quia inter Theologos disceptari video: S. Scripturam Controversias Fidei non posse dirimere ideo, quod loqui nesciat. Videatur Colloquium Ratisbonense. Certè in Novo Testamento: quoties illud occurrit? Λέγει ὁ χεαφὴ. Sed haec ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ. Non enim nunc ago Theologum. Nec tamen me cohibeo: quoties in his litteris quid occurrit ad Arcem illam Pietatis illustrandam, aut muniendam.
units.tr: I thought this worth noting, because I see it disputed among theologians that Scripture cannot settle controversies of faith because it does not know how to speak. See the Colloquy of Regensburg. Surely in the New Testament, how often does it occur: Scripture says [Λέγει ἡ γραφή]? But these things are said in passing; for I am not now acting as a theologian. Yet I do not restrain myself: whenever something occurs in these letters that serves to illustrate or fortify that stronghold of piety.

units.la: LITTERÆ in perniciem illius scriptæ, qui eas defert, dicuntur Bellerophontéæ: & Uriæ.
units.tr: LETTERS written for the ruin of the man who carries them are called Bellerophontic, and Uriah's letters.

units.la: LATOR Epistolæ sæpè suspectus est, cùm etiam non est.
units.tr: The bearer of a letter is often suspected, even when he is not guilty.

units.la: LITTERAS peregre latas, portitoribus committebant; qui eas deinde curarent.
units.tr: Letters carried from abroad they entrusted to porters, who then took care of them.

units.la: Sic Terent. Phorm. I. 2.
units.tr: So Terence, Phormio, I. 2.

units.la: Sed Epistolam ab eo allatam esse, audivi modòEt ad portitores esse delatam: hanc petam.
units.tr: But I have just heard that a letter was brought from him, and was delivered to the porters: I shall seek it.

units.la: Neque enim licebat cuiq; litteras obsignatas, vel aperire & legere, vel alteri legendas tradere. Secus enim Falsum committebatur: quod egregiè docet Magnus Jurisconsultus Aremoricus Janus Langlæus lib. 8. Otij Semestr. cap. 12. Cujus quidem sententiam, cùm liber ejus in Germania raro prostet, non pigebit huc adscribere.
units.tr: For it was not permitted for anyone to open and read a sealed letter, or to hand it over for another to read. Otherwise a forgery was committed; this is taught admirably by the great French jurist Janus Langlaeus, book 8, Otium Semestre, chapter 12. Since his book is seldom to be found in Germany, I shall not hesitate to quote his opinion here.

units.la: Falsum, inquit, committit, non tantùm qui depositâ apud se cujusquam instrumenta adversario prodit (l. 1. §. It qui ff. ad l. Cornel. de Fals.) sed & qui cujusvis litteras improbè legit, resignat, recludit, alijve legendas & inspiciendas tradit (l. si quis aliquod. §. qui uni & duobus seqq. ff. de pæn.) si modò ejus, qui scripserit, vel ad quem scriptæ fuerint, interfit lectas non fuisse. (l. 1. ff. de fals. ubi Bartol. gloss. & doct. l. damus. C. eodem Bald. consil. 14.) Quamobrem & Augustum scribit Tranquillus (Aug. cap 67) Thallo amanuensi suo crurifragij supplicium ideò indixisse: qu secretiorem quandam suam Epistolam, pretio corruptus, cuidam cujus forte intererat eam inspicere legendam subjecisset, vel recitasset: Thallo (inquit) amanuensi, quod pro Epistolâ prodita denarios quingentos accepisset, crura effregit.
units.tr: He says: he commits forgery not only who betrays to an adversary the instruments deposited with him by someone (l. 1. §. It qui ff. ad l. Cornel. de Fals.), but also he who improperly reads, unseals, opens, or hands over another's letter to be read and inspected (l. si quis aliquod. §. qui uni & duobus seqq. ff. de pæn.), provided it was in the interest of the writer, or of the one to whom it was written, that it not be read. (l. 1. ff. de fals., where Bartolus, the gloss and the doctors; l. damus. C. eodem; Baldus, consilium 14.) For this reason Suetonius also writes (Aug. cap. 67) that Augustus ordered his secretary Thallus to be punished by having his legs broken, because, bribed for money, Thallus had submitted a certain private letter of his to someone who happened to have an interest in inspecting it, or had read it aloud. Thallus, he says, as secretary, because he had received five hundred denarii for betraying a letter, had his legs broken.

units.la: Id autem ita accipiendum, si dolum eâ in re adhibitum fuisse constare posset.
units.tr: But this must be understood as applying if it could be shown that fraud was employed in the matter.

units.la: ° CatèCæterùm si vel per errorem, aut simplicitatem quisquam alicu- jus Epistolam legerit, aut aperuerit, cùm forte crederet, indedam- mnum nemini illatum iri, vel quia ad scriptam putaret: quod ejusdem nominis, cujus & is, ad quem mittebatur, esset: nullius criminis reum eum existimaverim (l. nec exemplum. C. de dolo. §. item. l. Corn. de falf. instit. de pub. jud.) Loquitur enim lex de eo, qui improbè legerit, aut aperuerit.
units.tr: But if anyone, by mistake or simplicity, reads or opens another's letter, because he happened to believe that no harm would come to anyone, or because he thought it was written to himself, namely to one of the same name as the person to whom it was sent, I should judge him guilty of no crime (l. nec exemplum. C. de dolo; §. item; l. Corn. de falsis; Instit. de publicis iudiciis). For the law speaks of one who has read or opened it improperly.

units.la: Proinde etsi quis vinculum tantùm Epistolæ solverit, neque illam legerit, vel amplius quidquam fecerit, crediderim eum falsi crimine non teneri: neque poenæ ulli obnoxium esse.
