Nam & Ulpianus Edicto, quo cautum est, ne quis sciens, aperiendum, recitandum, describendumque curet occisi Testamentum, priusquam de familiâ habita quæstio fuerit, sumtumq; de noxiis supplicium, cum non teneri dixit, qui dolo non aperuerit: sicut nec illum, qui tabulas naturaliter non reseravit, quamvis linum incideriit, sed excusatione dignum esse, quia dolo caret, qui ipse tabulas omninò non aperuerit (l.3 §. quod ad causam. & §. si quis tabulas ff. ad Syllan.)
units.tr: Accordingly, even if someone has only loosened the fastening of a letter without reading it, or done nothing further, I should think he is not liable to the charge of forgery, nor subject to any penalty. For Ulpian, in his Edict, in which it is provided that no one knowingly should take care to open, read out or copy the will of a murdered man before an inquiry had been held among the household and the punishment of the guilty had been carried out, said that one is not liable who has not opened it with fraud; just as one is not liable who did not unseal the tablets in the ordinary way, even though he cut the thread, but is deserving of pardon, because he is free of fraud who did not open the tablets at all (l. 3 §. quod ad causam; §. si quis tabulas; ff. ad Syllan.).

units.la: Unde non inscitè colligit Bartholus Antistitis constitutione, quâ sacer, abominatúsque sit, quisquis obsignatis alterius litteras aperuerit, non ligarit illam, qui vinculum id ruperit, quò occlusæ sint, eas modò nec aperuerit, legerit, aut alij legendas tradiderit. (Bart. d. §. si quis tabulas.) Illud in confesso reseraverit, legerit, aut alij inspiciendas dederit, civili etiam indicio conveniri posse, neque in eum depositi tantùm agi, verùm etiam in facti & injuriarum, si injuriæ faciendæ animum habuerit.
units.tr: Hence Bartolus rightly infers from the constitution of the bishop, by which whoever opens another's sealed letters is cursed and abominable, that it does not bind the one who breaks the fastening by which they were closed, provided he has neither opened nor read them, nor handed them over to another to be read (Bartolus, on the same §. si quis tabulas). It is agreed that if he has unsealed, read, or given them to another to inspect, he can be sued in a civil proceeding, and not only on a charge of deposit, but also for the wrong of the act and for injury, if he had the intention of doing an injury.

units.la: Ait enim Ulpianus: Si quis tabulas Testamenti apud se depositas pluribus præsentibus legerit, utilius esse in factum, & injuriarum agi: si injuriæ faciendæ causâ secreta judiciorum publicavit, (l. si quis testam. §. 1. ff. ad l. Aquil.) hocque animo recitatum est testamentum, quibusdam præsentibus, ut judicia secreta ejus, qui testatus est, divulgarentur. (l.1. § si quis tab. ff. de po.)
units.tr: For Ulpian says: If someone reads aloud, in the presence of several people, the testament deposited with him, it is more useful to bring an action on the case and for injury, if he made the secrets of the courts public with the intention of doing an injury (l. si quis testam. §. 1. ff. ad l. Aquil.); and the testament was read out in the presence of certain people with this intention, that the private affairs of the one who made the testament should be divulged (l.1. § si quis tab. ff. de po.).

units.la: Uniuscujusque enim non mediocriter interest, arcana sua nemini pandi. (l.2. C. quando & qui quar. par. deb. lib. 10.)
units.tr: For it is of no small concern to anyone that his private affairs should be revealed to no one (l.2. C. quando & qui quar. par. deb. lib. 10.).

units.la: Daturq; ideò laudi Friderico Cæsari: quòd cum Casparis Solli- chij litteræ in manus ejus venissent: quæ nonnullis Hungaris in- scribebantur, essentque qui eas aperiendas diceren, quod in ijs aliquid proditionis scriptum esse putarent, quod sciri expediret: dixit Fridericus Caspar em se probum virum, suique amantem exi stimare: quod si fallleretur, malle se per sese errorem patére, quàm suâ diligentiâ investigari: neque adduci potuit, ut amici Epistolam ad se non spectantem aperiret, tametsi quibusdam vi- deretur inde sibi periculum imminere: quod profecto plærique facturi non fuissent. Nam & Cicero quâdam Epist. ad Att. lib.9. fatetur, cùm litterarum quidem falsiculus in manus suas incidis- set, quamvis ad se scriptum nihil esset, quasdam tamen resignasse, quod suspicaretur ijs famam suam proscindi: ut & alijs, quas sibi legendas hi dederant, ad quos missæ erant. Vide totam Epist.
units.tr: Emperor Frederick is therefore praised for this: when the letters of Caspar Sollitius came into his hands, which were addressed to some Hungarians, and there were people who urged that they be opened, since they thought something treacherous was written in them that it would be useful to know, Frederick said that he judged Caspar to be an upright man and a lover of himself; and if he were deceived, he preferred that the error be exposed by itself rather than sought out by his own diligence. Nor could he be persuaded to open a letter of a friend that did not concern him, although some thought that danger was threatening him from it; which most people would certainly not have refrained from doing. For Cicero too, in a certain letter to Atticus (book 9), admits that when a bundle of letters had fallen into his hands, although nothing was written to him, he nevertheless unsealed some of them, because he suspected that his reputation was being torn apart in them; and likewise others which those who had sent them had given him to read. See the whole letter.

units.la: Unde patet, non magnoperè culpandum Ciceronem, quem ju- stus dolor ad hujusmodi litterarum resignationem impulerit, quasq; nihilominus reddi fideliter curaverit.
units.tr: From this it is clear that Cicero is not to be greatly blamed, since a just grief drove him to unseal letters of this kind, and yet he took care that they were nonetheless faithfully delivered.

units.la: Illud receptissimum est, tabellarium, qui litteras ad aliquem per- ferendas receperit, nec eas, aut non satis fideliter reddiderit, ut quia sciens alij restituerit, quàm cui restituere mandatum fusce- perat, aut illi ipsi, sed resignatas, ab alioque inspectas, falsi quo- que criminis reum fieri posse. l. Titio. ff. ad municip. l.1. ubi Bar- tol. de sal. non item si imprudens.
units.tr: It is most generally accepted that a courier who has undertaken to deliver letters to someone, and either does not deliver them faithfully enough, as when he knowingly hands them over to another than the one to whom he had been commanded to deliver them, or to that very person but unsealed, and after they have been inspected by someone else, can also be made liable for the crime of forgery (l. Titio. ff. ad municip.; l.1. ubi Bartol. de sal.); not so, however, if he acted without knowledge.

units.la: Tritum enim est, quod dicitur, falsum absq; dolo non commit- ti. l. nec exemplum. C. ad l. Cornel. de falf. Nam & Augustinus cùm de falso testamento quæreretur, omnesque signatores lege Cornelia tenerentur, non tantùm duas tabulas damnatoriam & absolutoriam simul cognoscentibus dedit, sed tertiam quoque quâ ignoscereturijs, quos ad signandum fraude vel errore indu- ctos constitisset.
units.tr: For it is a commonplace, as the saying goes, that no forgery is committed without fraud (l. nec exemplum. C. ad l. Cornel. de falsis). Indeed Augustus too, when a false testament was being investigated and all the witnesses were bound by the Cornelian law, did not only give two tablets, one condemning and one acquitting, to those examining the case together, but also a third, by which he pardoned those whom it was established had been led into signing by fraud or error.

units.la: Quamobrem si tabellario ipsi in viâ litteræ excideriut, vel à ma- gistratibus, aut alijs in itineris (quod frequenter evenit) inter- ceptæ fuerint, æquum non est, ob id illud damnum aliquod, vel supplicium subire, ut cujus dolus nullus argui possit. Fit autem crebrius, per belli maximè tempus, ut tabellarij excutiantur, litteræque intercipiantur, neque ijs, qui perferendas eas susceperint, prius reddantur, quàm lectæ inspectæque fuerint à magistratib°, limenarchis, portitoribus, aut alijs, quibus id negotium datum fuerit, & nonnumquam etiam à latronibus & hostibus: quod ex pluribus Epist. Ciceronis colligi potest: ut lib.10. Ep. Asinij Pollionis. Et lib.2. Ep.Caij Cassij. Et ad Attic. lib.1. Ep.10. Et supra in Plauti nostri Trinum.
units.tr: Therefore, if the letters have fallen from the courier himself on the road, or have been intercepted by magistrates or others on the journey (which happens often), it is not fair that he should suffer any loss or punishment on that account, since no fraud on his part can be charged. Moreover, it happens more often, especially in time of war, that couriers are searched and letters intercepted, and are not returned to those who undertook to carry them until they have been read and inspected by magistrates, customs officers, harbour-masters, or others to whom the business has been assigned, and sometimes even by brigands and enemies. This can be gathered from many letters of Cicero: as in book 10, letter of Asinius Pollio; and book 2, letter of Gaius Cassius; and to Atticus, book 1, letter 10; and above in our Plautus, in the Trinummus.

units.la: Ammian. Marcell. lib. 21.
units.tr: Ammianus Marcellinus, book 21.

units.la: Capto à stationarijs militibus notario, quem miserat ad Constantinum, scrutatoq; si quid portaret, epistola ejus reperta est, in quâ, praeter alia multa, id quoq; scripserat: Cæsar tuus disciplinam non habet.
units.tr: After the soldiers on guard had seized a secretary whom he had sent to Constantine, and searched him to see whether he was carrying anything, a letter of his was found, in which, among many other things, he had also written this: Your Caesar has no discipline.

units.la: Sed etsi tabellarij ipsius, vel Reip. interfit, litteras, quas perferendas suscepit, inspici: putarim ipsum nullo supplicio afficiendum, quòd eas aperuerit, legerit, aut alij legendas tradiderit. Quid enim si Bellerophontis, aut Uriæ sint litteræ, quas quis velut commendatitias perfert, cùm contra eum sint scriptæ? quid item si in Reip. perniciem scriptas appareat? nemo certè recti judicij dixerit, eum idcò deliquisse, quod obsignatas, ut acceperat, non reddiderit.
units.tr: But even if it is in the interest of the courier himself, or of the state, that the letters he has undertaken to deliver be inspected, I should think he ought not to be punished at all for having opened them, read them, or given them to others to read. For what if the letters are those of Bellerophon or Uriah, which someone carries as though they were letters of recommendation, when in fact they are written against him? What if, likewise, they are shown to have been written for the ruin of the state? No one of sound judgment would say that he had done wrong merely because he did not return them sealed, as he had received them.

units.la: Nam ex Thucid. & Diod. Siculo constat, tabellarium, qui à Pausaniâ Lacedæmonio Epistolam ad Xerxen Persarum Regem perferendam acceperat, cùm eam aperuisset, ephorisque deinde, obsignaculis referatis, legendam dedisset, nullam poenam subiisse: cùm per eam proditorium Pausaniæ consilium detectum fuisset, eademque compertum fuisset, mandasse Pausaniam à Persis necari.
units.tr: For it is established from Thucydides and Diodorus Siculus that a courier who had received from Pausanias the Spartan a letter to be carried to Xerxes, King of the Persians, when he had opened it and then, having broken the seals, given it to the ephors to read, suffered no punishment; yet through it the treacherous plan of Pausanias was disclosed, and it was learned from the same letter that Pausanias had ordered that he be put to death by the Persians.

units.la: Atque hæc hactenus è Langlæo J C. de litterarum resignatorib°. Docet ibidem lib. 8. cap.13. Falsi quoq; crimine teneri eum qui alienum chirographum vel signum effinxerit: quod caput lectu jucundissimum huc quoque referre animus erat, sed cùm ejus rei nullum vestigium in Plauto nostro, nisi forte per aliquam consequentiam, omisi: & in alium locum commodius recensendum interea distuli.
units.tr: So far from Langlaeus, the jurist, on those who unseal letters. He teaches in the same place, book 8, chapter 13: Whoever has counterfeited another's handwriting or seal is also held liable for the crime of forgery. I intended to bring this most pleasant chapter in here too, but since I find no trace of this matter in our Plautus, except perhaps by some consequence, I have omitted it, and for the time being have put off reviewing it in a more suitable place.

units.la: LOCORUM. PRÆSENTIÆ-LOCI. HABITATIONIS.
units.tr: PLACE: PRESENCE OF PLACE: DWELLING.

units.la: POssum us animo esse, ubi corpore non sumus. Aul, 2.2. v.4. Egomet sum hic, animus domi est.
units.tr: I can be in spirit where I am not in body. Aul. 2.2 v.4: I am here myself; my mind is at home.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Hominis: Corporis.
units.tr: See also the title Man: Body.

units.la: Certè Plauto nostro portentum illud Ubiquitatis, quod hodie irrepsit in Ecclesias, ex lacunis Nestorianorum & Eutychianorum hæreticorum nequicquam persuaderi potuisset: quò statim Corpus Christi in pluribus locis simul esse. Refutavit illud in Amphitruone. Vide Titulos modò dictos. Dehinc ex hoc loco Aululariæ liquet communem & vulgatam esse synecdochen, quam vocant ἀλλοίωσιν, sive κοινωνίαν ἰδιωμάτων, itemque ἐπιζευξιν. Ait enim Senex: Egomet (totum suppositum intelligens) sum hic: animus (ut pars suppositi) domi est. Quod obiter attingere libuit.
units.tr: Certainly that monstrosity of ubiquity, which today has crept into the Churches, could never have been persuaded out of the pits of the Nestorian and Eutychian heretics, for it holds at once that the body of Christ is in many places at the same time. Plautus refutes it in the Amphitryon (see the titles just mentioned). Moreover, from this passage of the Aulularia it is clear that the synecdoche is common and familiar, which they call alloiosis [ἀλλοίωσιν], or the communication of properties [κοινωνίαν ἰδιωμάτων], and likewise epizeuxis [ἐπιζευξιν]. For the old man says: I myself (understanding the whole person) am here; my mind (as a part of the person) is at home. I was pleased to touch on this in passing.

units.la: Sic enim litteræ humaniores tractandæ sunt, ut ad gnomonem sacrarum litterarum dirigantur.
units.tr: For humane letters must be handled in this way: they are to be directed by the rule of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Loca impudica & probrosa adeuntes: operiebant caput. (apt. 3. I.V. 1f.
units.tr: Those who go to shameless and disreputable places cover their heads. (Apt. 3, I.V. 1f.)

units.la: Petron. Ascyltus caput operuit, ut se vidit in lupanar deductum.
units.tr: Petronius: Ascyltus covered his head when he saw that he had been taken into a brothel.

units.la: Divus Chrysostomus Homil. xi. ad Thessal. pag. 1478. Edit. Commel.
units.tr: Divus Chrysostom, Homily 11 on Thessalonians, p. 1478, ed. Commelin.

units.la: In civitate ubi mores mali, amici infidi & improbi, non est commoda habitatio. Merc. 5. I.V. 9.
units.tr: In a city where morals are bad and friends are faithless and wicked, the dwelling is not pleasant. Merc. 5, I.V. 9.

units.la: In locis suspectis versari solent homines otiosi, garruli; qui alijs dicunt contumeliam, & ipsi sat habent, quod in se posset vere dicier. Curc. 4. I. V. 10.
units.tr: Idle, talkative men are wont to loiter in suspicious places; they heap insults on others, and yet have enough to do with what could truly be said of themselves. Curc. 4, I.V. 10.

units.la: Vide Tit. Roma.
units.tr: See the title Rome.

units.la: Homines garruli, otiosi luxui dediti & gulæ, versabantur in medicinis, in tonstrinis, gymnasijs, in foro per myropolia & lanienas. nas. Amph. 4. 1. v. 5. Epid. 2. 2. v. 13. Loci qui nusquam est, meminit sycophanta. Trin. 4. 2. v. 83. Illum reliqui ad Rhadamantem in Cercopiâ insulâ. Arabia non est in Ponto. Trin. 4. 2. v. 89. In Arabiâ thus gignitur. Ibid. Loca latebrosa vitanda adolescentibus. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 22. & 3. 3. v. 26.
units.tr: Talkative, idle men given over to luxury and gluttony spent their time at doctors' surgeries, barbers' shops, gymnasia, and in the forum, among the perfume shops and the butchers' stalls. Amph. 4.1 v.5; Epid. 2.2 v.13. The parasite speaks of a place that is nowhere. Trin. 4.2 v.83: I left him with Rhadamanthus on the island of Cercopia. Arabia is not in Pontus. Trin. 4.2 v.89. Incense is produced in Arabia. Ibid. Hidden, shadowy places are to be avoided by young men. Bacch. 1.1 v.22 and 3.3 v.26.

units.la: Lucri. Quæstus.
units.tr: Gain. Profit.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Usura: Fenoris.
units.tr: See also the title Usury: Interest.

units.la: Lucrum præponi solet sopori & quieti. Rud. 4. 2. v. 11.
units.tr: Gain is usually put before sleep and rest. Rud. 4.2 v.11.

units.la: Ad suum quemque hominem quæstum esse æquum est callidum. Asin. 1. 3. v. 34. Truc. 2. 4. v. 62. & 5. v. 40.
units.tr: It is fair and clever for every man to make a profit. Asin. 1.3 v.34; Truc. 2.4 v.62, and 5 v.40.

units.la: Non potest quæstus consistere, si eum sumtus superat. Poen. 1. 2. v. 74.
units.tr: Profit cannot last if expense outstrips it. Poen. 1.2 v.74.

units.la: Necesse est facere sumtum, qui quærit lucrum. Asin. 1. 3. v. 65.
units.tr: He who seeks gain must necessarily spend. Asin. 1.3 v.65.

units.la: LUDIBRII. CONTEMTUS. CONTUMELIÆ.
units.tr: MOCKERY. CONTEMPT. INSULTS.

units.la: Vide Convivij: Calumniæ: Injuriarum.
units.tr: See: Banquet; Calumnies; Injuries.

units.la: LUDIBRIO alios afficientes digitum medium infamem & impudicum intendebant in illum.
units.tr: Those inflicting mockery on others would thrust the middle finger, the infamous and shameless one, at him.

units.la: Vide Laërtium in Diogene. Et est proverbium: Digitum medium intendere.
units.tr: See Laertius on Diogenes. And there is the proverb: to thrust out the middle finger.

units.la: HOMO hominem non debet ludibrio afficere: quia uterq; homo.
units.tr: A man ought not to subject a man to mockery, because each is a man.

units.la: Quos alijs deridendos propinare volebant, allinebant fuco: & fuligine.
units.tr: Those whom they wished to make a laughing-stock for others, they daubed with paint and soot.

units.la: LUDORUM CIRCENSIUM. THEATRI. AMPHITHEATRI. GYMNASTICES. AGONUM. CERTAMINUM. PUGILUM.
units.tr: CIRCUS GAMES. THEATRE. AMPHITHEATRE. GYMNASTICS. CONTESTS. COMBATS. BOXING.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Gladiatorum.
units.tr: See also the title Gladiators.

units.la: ROMANA juventus varijs ludis exercebatur. Most. 112. v. 72. Rud. 2. 1. v. 7.
units.tr: The Roman youth trained in various games. Most. 112. v. 72. Rud. 2. 1. v. 7.

units.la: Vide P. Fabrum Agonist. H. Mercur. JC. Scal. de Poët. lib. 1. cap. 22. & Hippol. Palat. pag. 91.
units.tr: See P. Faber's Agonisticon, H. Mercurialis, and J. C. Scaliger, De poetica, lib. 1, cap. 22, and Hippolytus Palatinus, p. 91.

units.la: In Circensib9 erant seni sole perusti, qui vas aquâ plenum circumferrent, ut equos cursu defessos frigidâ aspergerent. Illud vas vocabant nasiternam, à ternis nasis, vel ansis.
units.tr: In the Circus games there were old men, burnt by the sun, who carried around a vessel full of water to sprinkle cold water on horses worn out by the race. They called that vessel a nasiterna, from its three nozzles or handles.

units.la: Poen. 5. 5. v. 12. Qui cortinam ludis per circumferunt.
units.tr: Poen. 5. 5. v. 12. Who carry the curtain around through the games.

units.la: De Cortinâ & Nasiternâ vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: On the cortina and the nasiterna, see the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: Ludi Olympiæ cursurâ fiebant ad metam cum curru. Stich. 2. 2. v. 34.
units.tr: The Olympic games were run as a race around the turning-post with a chariot. Stich. 2. 2. v. 34.

units.la: Ludorum curatores palmam distribuebant actoribus fabularum: studiosèq; cavebant, ne injuriâ cuiquam artifici darent. Poen. Prol. v. 37.
units.tr: The managers of the games awarded the palm to the actors of plays, and took care not to give it unjustly to any performer. Poen. Prol. v. 37.

units.la: In hippodromo exercebantur currendo. Cist. 2. 3. v. 7.
units.tr: They trained in the hippodrome by running. Cist. 2. 3. v. 7.

units.la: In Circo portæ ad bestias emittendas erant. Perf. 3. 3. v. 31. Citius extemplo aforo fugiunt, quàm exportâ ludis, cum emissus est lepus.
units.tr: In the Circus there were gates for releasing the wild beasts. Perf. 3. 3. v. 31. They flee from the gate faster than they run out of the games when the hare is let loose.

units.la: Vide Lipf. de Amph. c. 9. pag. 29.
units.tr: See Lipsius, De amphitheatro, c. 9, p. 29.

units.la: Lepores etiam in theatris emissi. Perf. 3. 3. v. 31.
units.tr: Hares were also released in the theatres. Perf. 3. 3. v. 31.

units.la: In Amphitheatro ultimus locus, in quo populus sedebat Cavea dicebatur, à formâ, quia erat excavatus.
units.tr: In the amphitheatre the highest place, where the people sat, was called the cavea, from its shape, because it was hollowed out.

units.la: Ibidem erant subsellia, quæ nominabantur Cunei. Tangit Plautus Amph. Prol. v. 65.
units.tr: In the same place there were benches called cunei. Plautus alludes to them. Amph. Prol. v. 65.

units.la: Videndus amplius Lipsius in libello de Amphitheatro.
units.tr: See Lipsius's little book on the amphitheatre for more.

units.la: Ibidem histriones fabulas suas ludebant: ut ex eodem loco liquet.
units.tr: There the actors performed their plays, as is clear from the same passage.

units.la: Prohibebantur infantes vagientes in theatrum adducere. Poen. Prol. v. 28.
units.tr: Crying infants were forbidden to be brought into the theatre. Poen. Prol. v. 28.

units.la: Nutrices pueros infantes minutulos domi procurent, neve spectatum afferant, ne & ipsæ sitiant: & pueri peritent fame: neve esurientes hic quasi hædi obvagiant.
units.tr: Nurses should keep the little infants at home and not bring them as spectators, lest they themselves go thirsty and the children perish of hunger, and lest, hungry, they bawl here like kids.

units.la: In ludis circumferebatur manducus, sive μορμολυκεῖον inter cæteras ridicularias & formidolosas personas, magnis malis latéq; deterrens hiscens & clarè crepitans dentibus, in Atellanis præsertim fabu-lis. Rud. 2. 6. v. 51.
units.tr: At the games a bogeyman, or mormolykeion [μορμολυκεῖον], was carried around among the other comic and frightening masks, terrifying with great evils, gaping and loudly clacking its teeth, especially in the Atellan farces. Rud. 2. 6. v. 51.

units.la: Juvenal. Satyr. 3. tandemq; redit ad pulpita notum Exodium; cum persona pallentis hiatum In gremio matris formidat rusticus infans.
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire 3: At last the familiar exodium returns to the stage; the rustic infant, in his mother's lap, fears the gaping mask of the pale man.

units.la: Dentes enim magnos, & voracitatem attribuebant noctur-nis il-lis terriculamentis. Quo nomine factum, ut Lamiam puero-rum infantium deglutricem fingerent. Etiam Pythonem pro terriculamento, & Gorgonium pro manduco dixerunt: quia γοργόνες cum magnis dentibus pingebantur.
units.tr: They gave those nocturnal bugbears large teeth and voracity. Hence they imagined the Lamia as a devourer of infant children. They also called a bugbear a Python, and a bogeyman a Gorgonius, because the gorgones [γοργόνες] were painted with large teeth.

units.la: Lucillius: Illo quid fiet Lamia, & Pytho oxiodontas?
units.tr: Lucilius: What will become of Lamia, and of the Python with sharp teeth [oxiodontas]?

units.la: NEMÆEI & Olympij ludi, qui Herculi & Archemoro fiebant, celebres apud Græcos. Caf. 4. 1. v. 1.
units.tr: The Nemean and Olympic games, which were held in honour of Hercules and Archemorus, were famous among the Greeks. Caf. 4. 1. v. 1.

units.la: Vide Pindarum.
units.tr: See Pindar.

units.la: CIRCENSIUM quadrigæ maximâ concitatione ferebantur. Aul. 4. 1. v. 14.
units.tr: Chariots in the Circus were driven at the greatest speed. Aul. 4. 1. v. 14.

units.la: COEUNTES in Circensibus prælium dicebantur committere. Perf. 1. 3. v. 32.
units.tr: Those who met in the Circus games were said to engage in battle. Perf. 1. 3. v. 32.

units.la: IN Circo ludi fiebant. Mil. 4. 2. v. 1. ἀλλὰ ηγοεικ. Jam est ante ædes circus, ubi sunt Ludi faciendi mihi.
units.tr: The games were held in the Circus. Mil. 4. 2. v. 1. [ἀλλὰ ηγοεικ.] Now there is the circus before the house, where the games are to be held for me.

units.la: ROMÆ quotannis Dij ipsi ludis Circensibus traducebantur in car-pentis. Quò forte allusum Mil. 1. 1. v. 67. Ut te quasi pompam illac praeterducerem.
units.tr: At Rome, every year, the gods themselves were conveyed in carriages at the Circus games. Perhaps the allusion is to Mil. 1. 1. v. 67: So that I might lead you past there as if in a procession.

units.la: Vide Lipsi lib. 2. Antiq. c. 16. & ad Tacitum lib. 12. Annal. p. 258. Suum quoq; fastigium Agrippina extollere altius, carpento Capitolium ingredi: qui mos sacerdotibus, & sacris antiquitus concessus.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Antiquities, lib. 2, c. 16, and his note on Tacitus, Annals 12, p. 258: Agrippina also raised her own status higher, entering the Capitol in a carpentum, a custom once granted to priests and sacred rites.

units.la: Ibi Notas vide.
units.tr: See the notes there.

units.la: IN Circensibus & theatralibus pompis Ludij adolescentes erant tunicisniculas insignes induti, galeati & ensiferi, peltatiq; in versum incedebant, ipsis Salijs veluti pompæ duces similes. Quorum si qui grandiusculi & jam vesticipes erant, vellebantur, glabriq; reddebantur.
units.tr: In the Circus and theatrical processions the young men called Ludii wore tunics with striking embroidery, and went helmeted, sword-bearing and shielded, marching in order, very like the leaders of the Salian procession. If any of them were somewhat older and already wore the toga, they were plucked and made smooth.

units.la: Gallum glabriorem reddes mihi, quàm Volsius Lydius est.
units.tr: You will make me a cock smoother than Volsius the Lydian is.

units.la: Lydij autem dicti, quòd à Lydis hoc genus ludicri inventum videretur.
units.tr: They were called Lydians because this kind of game seemed to have been invented by the Lydians.

units.la: Vide Turn. lib. 6. c. 26. ex Dion. Halicarnasseo. & Lex. Plautin. lit. L. Lydij, Ludij, Ludiones, ὀρχησταὶ, χορευταὶ, σατυεισταὶ σκηνι-κοὶ. Curc. 1.2. v. 63. Bacch. 1.2. v. 13.
units.tr: See Turnebus, lib. 6, c. 26, from Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and the Plautine lexicon under L: Lydii, Ludii, Ludiones: dancers [ὀρχησταί], chorus-dancers [χορευταί], satyr-actors [σατυρισταί], stage performers [σκηνικοί]. Curc. 1. 2. v. 63. Bacch. 1. 2. v. 13.

units.la: In Curulibus ludis olim apud Græcos non septimo, sed duodecimo spatio finitum: apud Romanos autem septimo. Perf. 3.1. v. 19. ἀλληγοεικῶς.
units.tr: At the Curule games, the course among the Greeks was once finished not at the seventh lap but at the twelfth; among the Romans it was the seventh. Perf. 3. 1. v. 19. [ἀλληγορικῶς] allegorically.

units.la: In ijsdem ludis, cùm factiones quadrigarum è carceribus emittebantur, dicebantur committi. Perf. 5.1. v. 19. ἀλληγοεικῶς.
units.tr: In the same games, when the chariot factions were released from the starting-gates, they were said to be sent into battle. Perf. 5. 1. v. 19. [ἀλληγορικῶς] allegorically.

units.la: Prostibula per ludos publicos in scenam introduci solebant. Caf. Prol. v. 14, 15. Pœn. Prol. v. 17. Vide Tit. Scortorum.
units.tr: Prostitutes were customarily brought onto the stage during public games. Caf. Prol. v. 14, 15. Poen. Prol. v. 17. See the title Harlots.

units.la: Ædilis erat indicere ludos. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 133.
units.tr: It was the duty of the aedile to announce the games. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 133.

units.la: In Comœdijs tibicines adhibiti. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 160.
units.tr: Flute-players were employed in comedies. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 160.

units.la: Vide etiam Artem Poët. Horat. & Epist. 1. lib. 2. & Proleg. Donatii in Horat. itemque inscriptiones Fabb. Terentij.
units.tr: See also Horace's Art of Poetry and Epistle 1, book 2, the prolegomena of Donatus on Horace, and likewise the inscriptions to the plays of Terence.

units.la: Gymnasia etiam ante Neronem fuerunt: quia Plautus eorum mentionem facit. Epid. 2. 2. v. 14.
units.tr: There were gymnasia even before Nero, since Plautus mentions them. Epid. 2. 2. v. 14.

units.la: Contrasentit P. Faber in Agonisticis.
units.tr: P. Faber disagrees in his Agonisticon.

units.la: Gymnastæ & magistri exercitores erant in ludis. Trin. 4. 3. v. 9. ἀλληγοεικῶς.
units.tr: There were gymnasts and trainers in the games. Trin. 4. 3. v. 9. [ἀλληγορικῶς] allegorically.

units.la: In ludo Circensium citis quadrigis currebant. Perf. 3. 3. v. 38.
units.tr: In the Circus games they ran with swift chariots. Perf. 3. 3. v. 38.

units.la: AURIGÆ in Circensibus solent identidem respectare eos, qui pone sequuntur. Men. 1. 2. v. 50.
units.tr: Charioteers in the Circus are accustomed to look back again and again at those who follow behind. Men. 1. 2. v. 50.

units.la: PILA dicebantur ludere datatim, raptim, & expulsim. De primo Curcul. 2. 3. v. 17.
units.tr: People were said to play ball in three ways: datim, raptim and expulsim. On the first, see Curcul. 2. 3. v. 17.

units.la: Alludit Poëta Nævius de meretrice lascivíore apud Isid. lib. 1. Orig. cap. 25.
units.tr: The poet Naevius alludes to a rather wanton prostitute, as cited in Isidore, Origines, lib. 1, cap. 25.

units.la: quasi in choro pila
units.tr: As if in a dance, the ball.

units.la: Ludens datatim dat se: & communem facit: Alium tenet: alij nutat: alibi manus est occupata.
units.tr: Playing datim, she gives herself and makes herself common; she holds one, nods to another, and elsewhere her hand is busy.

units.la: Pomponius Adelph.
units.tr: Pomponius, Adelphi.

units.la: Cum datatim in lectô tecum lusi.
units.tr: When I played datim with you on the couch.

units.la: De cæteris vide Turneb. lib. 7. c. 4. & Hier. Mercurial. lib. 1. c. 5. Gymnast.
units.tr: For the rest see Turnebus, lib. 7, c. 4, and Hieronymus Mercurialis, lib. 1, c. 5, Gymnastica.

units.la: TENUIORES sub dies ludorum togulam suam incretabant Aul. 4. 9. v. 7. de furibus Euclionis:
units.tr: The poorer people, during the days of the games, would whiten their little togas with chalk. Aul. 4. 9. v. 7, about the thieves of Euclio:

units.la: Complures hic vestitu & creta occultant sese.
units.tr: Many here hide themselves with clothing and chalk.

units.la: Vide Lipsi. lib. 1. Elect. cap. 13.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Electa, lib. 1, cap. 13.

units.la: ADOLESCENTES sese exercebant in palæstra disco, & cursura. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 33. 34. & 3. 3. v. 26. & Most. 1. 2. v. 72.
units.tr: Young men exercised themselves in the palaestra with the discus and running. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 33, 34, and 3. 3. v. 26; Most. 1. 2. v. 72.

units.la: Item macherâ, cestu, galeâ cum crissâ, hastâ, loricâ, scuto, equis. Ibidem. Vide elegantem locum ex oppositis: ubi opponitur palæstra meretricum & adolescentum.
units.tr: Likewise with the sword, the cestus, the helmet with its plume, the spear, the cuirass, the shield and horses. Ibidem. See the elegant passage that sets the palaestra of the harlots against that of the young men.

units.la: Vide Disciplina: Educatio.
units.tr: See Discipline: Education.

units.la: LUDI scenici in theatro agebantur: in Amphitheatro gladiatorij ac venatorij. Theatrum et dictum spectaculum. Curc. 5. 2. v. 47. Mulieres co deducebant suos quoq; infantes. Ibid.
units.tr: Scenic games were performed in the theatre; gladiatorial and beast fights in the amphitheatre. The theatre was also called a spectaculum. Curc. 5. 2. v. 47. Women brought their little infants there too. Ibid.

units.la: IN pompis ludis q; Circensibus juvenes ibant in numerum saltantes & subsilientes: qui Ludy & Ludiones dicti. Alludit noster Curc. 1. 2. v. 63.
units.tr: In processions and at the Circus games young men went about in a troop, dancing and leaping, and they were called Ludii and Ludiones. Our author alludes to them. Curc. 1. 2. v. 63.

units.la: Pessuli, site causa mea Lydi barbari, subsilite obsecro.
units.tr: Pessulus, sit for my sake, you Lydian barbarians, leap up, I beg you.

units.la: Ludimagistri olim Floralibus & alijs diebus dabant ludos, h.e. ferias. Inde formula Ludos dare.
units.tr: Schoolmasters once gave games on the Floralia and other days, that is, holidays. Hence the formula ludos dare, "to give games."

units.la: Cas. Prol. v. 25.
units.tr: Cas. Prol. v. 25.

units.la: In ludo fidiciniofe exercebant fidibus.
units.tr: In the school of the lyre-players they trained with the lyre.

units.la: Rud. Prol. v. 43.
units.tr: Rud. Prol. v. 43.

units.la: Lustrationum.
units.tr: Lustrations.

units.la: Vide Tit. Sacrificiorum.
units.tr: See the title Sacrifices.

units.la: Lusus. Ludorum. Oblectationis. Ludicri. Ridiculi. Talorum. Tesserarum. Aleæ.
units.tr: Play. Games. Amusement. Sport. Jesting. Knucklebones. Dice. Gambling.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Pueritiæ de Crepundijs.
units.tr: See also the title Childhood, on rattles.

units.la: Oblectamenta puerilia erant pulli, passeres, anseres, monedulæ, anates, coturnices. Quò allusit olim servus. Capt. 5. 4. v. 5. & Cas. 1. 1. v. 50.
units.tr: Children's playthings were chicks, sparrows, geese, jackdaws, ducks and quails. A slave once alluded to these. Capt. 5.4 v.5 and Cas. 1.1 v.50.

units.la: Meus pullus passer, mea columba, mi lepus. in blanditijs amantum.
units.tr: My chick, my sparrow, my dove, my little hare, in the endearments of lovers.

units.la: Arnob. lib. 7.
units.tr: Arnobius, book 7.

units.la: Ut parvuli pusiones, quò lacrimis parcant, abstinentq; plorations, passerculos, pupulos, oculos, panes accipiunt, quibus se avocare possint.
units.tr: As little boys, to spare their tears and stop their crying, receive little sparrows, little chicks, little eyes and little breads, with which they can distract themselves.

units.la: Plin. lib. 4. Epist. 2.
units.tr: Pliny, book 4, letter 2.

units.la: Habeat puer mannulos multos junctos, et solutos, habeat cares majores, minores, habeat lescintas, p sittacos, merulas.
units.tr: Let the boy have many little toys, joined and loose; let him have larger and smaller carts; let him have hoops, parrots and blackbirds.

units.la: Erat ludus puerorum, qui ducebant sparteam restem, aut tam diu trahebant, donec aut rumperent, aut alteruter omisså funis prehensione in nates caderet. Alludit Plautus Pœn. Prol. v. 116. & 5. 4. v. 54.
units.tr: There was a game of boys who pulled a rope of esparto grass, or dragged it for so long until either they broke it or one of them, letting go of the rope, fell on his backside. Plautus alludes to this in Poen. Prol. v.116 and 5.4 v.54.

units.la: Jam ne hoc tenetis? si tenetis, ducite.
units.tr: Now don't you have this? If you have it, pull.

units.la: Tertullianus:
units.tr: Tertullian:

units.la: Sed non decet ultrà de authoritate scripturarum ejusmodi su- nem contentiosum alterno ductu in diversa distendere car- men liberum: Prendam te tamen, & tenebo prensum.
units.tr: But it is no longer fitting, concerning the authority of such Scriptures, to stretch a free song in opposite directions with a contentious pulling back and forth. Yet I will seize you, and hold you seized.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut. Tenere.
units.tr: See the Plautine lexicon, under Tenere.

units.la: CALCULORUM ludus jucundus. Stich. 5.4.v.52.
units.tr: The game of pebbles is pleasant. Stich. 5.4 v.52.

units.la: Lucret.
units.tr: Lucretius.

units.la: At catulos blandè jam linguâ lambere tentant,Aut ubi eos jactant pedibus morsuq; petentes,Suspensos teneros imitantur dentibus haustus:Longè alios pallo gannitu vocis adulant.
units.tr: But now they try to lick the puppies gently with their tongues, or when they toss them about with their feet and seek to bite them, they imitate with their teeth the tender holds, hanging on; and they fawn with a far different whining of voice.

units.la: APUD Græcos Tabula calculorum quinque erat linearum. In me- diâ autem tabulâ erant inciti calculi. Quare cùm alteruter ex lu- forib ad incitam lineam cogeretur, tunc movebat calculum ab eadem mediâ lineâ, hoc dicto: κινῶ τὸν ἀρ' ἱσῶς. Sic enim linea illa dicta.
units.tr: Among the Greeks the pebble board had five lines. In the middle of the board were the pebbles set in motion. So when one of the players was forced to the line in motion, he then moved a pebble from that middle line, saying: [κινῶ τὸν ἀρ' ἱσῶς] "I move the one from the level." For that line was called thus.

units.la: Et inde proverbium: Ad incitas redire: Ciere calcem.
units.tr: Hence the proverb: to return to the lines; to stir the pebble.

units.la: Vide Turn. 27.3. & 15.
units.tr: See Turnebus 27.3 and 15.

units.la: NOCTU dormientibus ridiculi causa ora solebant pingere.
units.tr: At night, for the sake of a joke, people used to paint the faces of those sleeping.

units.la: Stulta soror es, quàm volo, an verò pulcra videre obsecro, si tibi illic non os oblitum est fuligine.
units.tr: You are a foolish sister, as I wish you to be; or indeed, I beg you, a beautiful one to look at, if your face there is not smeared with soot.

units.la: Idem Pœn 5.5. v. 11. Ita illum replebo atritate, atrior multò ut fiet, quàm Ægyptij.
units.tr: The same, Poen. 5.5 v.11. So I will fill him with blackness; he will become far blacker than the Egyptians.

units.la: Petronius:
units.tr: Petronius:

units.la: Cùm Ascyltos gravatus tot malis in somnum laberetur, illa quæ injuriâ depulsa fuerat ancilla, totam faciem ejus fuligine lonlongâ perfricuit, & non sentientis labra humerosq; sublitio-nibus pinxit. Ita enim locum illum restituit Martinus de Roâ lib. 6. Sing. cap. 17.
units.tr: When Ascyltos, weighed down by so many troubles, was sliding into sleep, the maid who had been put out for her offence rubbed his whole face with soot, and painted his lips and shoulders with smears, while he did not notice. For so Martinus de Roa restored that passage in book 6 of Singularia, chapter 17.

units.la: POSTQVAM cænati, atque appoti erant Talos sibi poscebant; amantes inprimis: quibus cum luderent, Deum aliquem propitium invocabant: Milites Martem: Amatores Venerem, aut p Venere, Amasiam suam, quod fecit senex Demænetus, Philenium suam invocans. Asin. s.2. v.60. & 4.1. v.35. Capt. 1.1. v.s. Bacch. 1.1. v.38.
units.tr: After they had dined and drunk, they called for knucklebones for themselves, lovers above all. While they played, they invoked some propitious god: soldiers invoked Mars, lovers Venus, or, through Venus, their sweetheart, as the old man Demaenetus did, invoking his Philenium. Asin. 5.2 v.60; 4.1 v.35; Capt. 1.1 v.8; Bacch. 1.1 v.38.

units.la: Parasiti Herculem Nutricem. Curc 2.3. v.79.
units.tr: Parasites [invoked] Hercules the Nurturer. Curc. 2.3 v.79.

units.la: LUDEBANT autem Talis tàm liberi, quàm servi. Mil. 2.2. v.9. Nelegi fraudem faciant talaria accuratote, ut sine talis domi agitent convivium. Stich. 5.4. v.20.
units.tr: Both free men and slaves played knucklebones. Mil. 2.2 v.9. Let them make the cheating with the dice very careful, so that they may conduct the banquet at home without dice. Stich. 5.4 v.20.

units.la: Quoniam verò creberrima mentio hujus Ludi in Authore nostro Plauto, in gratiam Philologiæ & Antiquitatis studiosorum conjiciam huc, quæcumq; ex variâ lectione olim mihi observata in Noctibus Palatinis.
units.tr: Since mention of this game is very frequent in our author Plautus, for the benefit of philologists and students of antiquity I will set down here whatever I once observed from various readings in the Noctes Palatinae.

units.la: Ac primùm sciendum, in cõvivijs per magistrum conviviorum, quem συμποσίαρχον appellabant, Talos fuisse depromtos, quibus & ipse electus fuit ad leges convivij: ut suprà quoque ex Plauto & alijs Authoribus ostendi. Inde Tali illi quadrati, vel ex auro vel argento, vel ebore facti, vel etiam revera tali ex animali, in fritillum fuerunt conjecti, h. e. in fimum, pyrgum, turriculam, orcam, sive pyxidem corneam, quæ gradus intus habebat. Concusså illâ orcâ ex angusto collo in tabulam fundebantur tali non sine aliquo strepitu, & risu.
units.tr: First, it should be known that at banquets the knucklebones were brought out by the master of the feast, whom they called symposiarch, and by him too was he chosen to lay down the rules of the drinking, as I have shown above from Plautus and other authors. Then those knucklebones, squared and made of gold, silver or ivory, or indeed really of the bones of animals, were thrown into a fritillus, that is, into a dice-box, a tower, a little turret, a jar, or a horn cup, which had steps inside. When the jar was shaken, the knucklebones were poured out from its narrow neck onto the board, not without some clatter and laughter.

units.la: Et fuerunt numero quatuor, ut patet ex illo Martialis: Non sum talorum numero par tessera, cum sit Major quàm talis, alea sæpè mihi.
units.tr: There were four of them, as is clear from that line of Martial: I am not a tessera equal to the number of the knucklebones, since the throw is greater than the knucklebone; often the gamble is against me.

units.la: Nam tesseris tantùm tribus utebantur. Numerorum autem figuram supplebant certæ figuræ. Sic unitatis figura significabatur per CANEM.
units.tr: For they used only three dice. The figures of the numbers were supplied by certain figures. Thus the unit was signified by the DOG.

units.la: Persius Sat. III. vocat Caniculam:
units.tr: Persius, Satire III, calls it the little dog:

units.la: Scire erat in voto, damnosa canicula quantum Raderet.
units.tr: It was in the wish to know how much the ruinous little dog would scrape away.

units.la: Propertius:
units.tr: Propertius:

units.la: Semper damnosi subsiluere canes.
units.tr: The ruinous dogs always leapt up.

units.la: Ovid. lib. 2. Trist. Eleg. 1.
units.tr: Ovid, Tristia, book 2, elegy 1.

units.la: Quid valeant tali, quo possit plurima jactu Figere, damnosos effugiasque canes.
units.tr: What the knucklebones can do, by which throw one may hit the many and escape the ruinous dogs.

units.la: Martial. lib. 13. Epigr. 1.
units.tr: Martial, book 13, epigram 1.

units.la: Senio nec nostrum cum cane quassat ebur.
units.tr: Nor does the ivory shake our old age with the dog.

units.la: Hic Jactus, seu Manus, sive bolus (ita enim vocabant τὰς πλώ- σεις Curc. 5. 2. v. 13. Rud. 2. 3. v. 30.) vocatur Damnosus: quia qui canem jecerat, nihil tollebat, sed aliquid conferebat: ut patet ex Suetonio Aug. c. 71.
units.tr: This throw, or "hand," or "bolus" (for so they called the throws [τὰς πλώσεις]), is called ruinous, because whoever had thrown the dog took nothing up, but contributed something. This is clear from Suetonius, Augustus, chapter 71.

units.la: Talis jactatis, ut quisque Canem, aut Senionem miserat in singulos talos, singulos denarios in medium conferebat.
units.tr: When the knucklebones were thrown, as each had sent the Dog or the Senio on the single knucklebones, he contributed a single denarius to the pool.

units.la: Atque ut hic Jactus canis erat infelicissimus: ita Jactus Veneris, qui fuit oppositus cani, omnium fuit fortunatissimus. Notabat enim senarium numerum. Quaternarius dicebatur Senio. Trinarius Chius. Ubi tamen mirifice video variare Authores: quos studiosus Antiquitatis ipse consulat.
units.tr: Just as this throw of the dog was the most unlucky, so the throw of Venus, opposed to the dog, was the most fortunate of all. It marked the number six. Four was called Senio, three Chius. Here the authors vary remarkably, and the student of antiquity should consult them himself.

units.la: De Talis autem scripserunt varij: Cælius Rhodig. lib. 20. cap. 27. Interpretes ad Suetonium Augustt. cap. 71. Beroaldus, Sabellicus, Torrentius, Casaubonus. M. Antonius Delrio ad Senecæ Herculem Furentem. Thomas Dempsterus Supplemento Antiquitatum Rosini. Guilhel. Stuckius Antiquitatib. Conviviali-bus: alijque.
units.tr: Those who have written on knucklebones include: Caelius Rhodiginus, book 20, chapter 27; the commentators on Suetonius, Augustus, chapter 71; Beroaldus, Sabellicus, Torrentius, Casaubon; M. Antonius Delrio on Seneca's Hercules Furens; Thomas Dempster in the supplement to Rosinus's Antiquities; Wilhelm Stuck in his Antiquitates Conviviales; and others.

units.la: Luxûs. Luxuriæ. Voluptatis. Gulæ. Prodigalitatis. Libidinis.
units.tr: Extravagance. Luxury. Pleasure. Gluttony. Prodigality. Lust.

units.la: Improbi adolescentes, Veneris alumni, lucrifugæ, damni cupidi, se suamque ætatem benè curant, edunt, bibunt, luxurian-tur, lustrantur, scortantur.
units.tr: Wicked young men, nurslings of Venus, who shun profit and crave loss, look after themselves and their youth well: they eat, drink, indulge in luxury, bathe, and frequent brothels.

units.la: Luxuriosis & dissolutis adolescentibus uxor dabatur in poe-nam.
units.tr: Dissolute young men in luxury were given a wife as a punishment.

units.la: Vide Tit. Matrimon: Nuptiarum: & paulò post.
units.tr: See the title Matrimony: Marriage, and a little after.

units.la: Inter alia instrumenta perditi luxûs & matulas in triclinia infer-re solebant: quas sæpè ubi incaluissent in capita sibi invicem illi-serint.
units.tr: Among the other equipment of reckless luxury, they used to bring flasks into the dining room, which they often hurled at one another's heads once they had grown heated.

units.la: Vide Tit. Parasitorum.
units.tr: See the title Parasites.

units.la: Luxus vestiarius in mulieribus tantus sæpe est, ut publica officia impediat: ita ut tributus imperatus est, potesse pendi negent. Epid. 2. 2. v. 39.
units.tr: Women's extravagance in clothing is often so great that it hinders public duties: when a tax has been imposed, they refuse to pay it. Epid. 2. 2. v. 39.

units.la: Vide etiam Aul. 3. 5. pænè per totam scenam de hoc sumtu mu-liebris ornatûs. Inspice Lectorem utrumque locum.
units.tr: See also Aul. 3. 5., where almost the whole scene concerns this expense on women's dress. Let the reader consult both passages.

units.la: Propertius lib. 3. Matrona incedit censu induta nepotum Et spolia opprobrij nostra per ora trahit.
units.tr: Propertius, book 3: The matron walks about dressed in her grandchildren's wealth, and drags our spoils of shame through the streets.

units.la: Ovidius lib. 3. de Arte: Quid de veste loquar? non jam segmenta requiro: Nec quae bis Tyrio murice lana rubet. Cum tot prodierint pretio leviore colores: Quis furor est censu corpore ferre suos?
units.tr: Ovid, book 3 of the Art of Love: Why should I speak of clothing? I no longer ask for embroidered borders, nor for wool reddened twice with Tyrian purple. Since so many colours have appeared at a lower price, what madness is it to carry one's fortune on one's body?

units.la: Luxuriosi ubi rem suam comederunt, & cofregerunt omnem in militiam solent abire latrocinatum.
units.tr: Spendthrifts, when they have eaten up their property and squandered all of it, usually go off to the army to plunder.

units.la: Luxuriosi omnes vitæ momentum ponunt in luxu ac voluptatibus, amoribus.
units.tr: Spendthrifts all put the whole purpose of life in extravagance, pleasures, and love affairs.

units.la: Hoc est, quamobrem cupiam vivere.
units.tr: That is, why I should wish to live.

units.la: Hoc est, homini, quamobrem vitam amet: hic omnes voluptates, in hoc omnes venustates sunt: Deis proximum esse arbitror.
units.tr: That is, why a man should love his life: here are all pleasures, here all charms; I think this is closest to the gods.

units.la: Vide reliquos versus.
units.tr: See the remaining verses.

units.la: Per luxum etiam maximæ divitiæ diffluunt.
units.tr: Through extravagance even the greatest riches run away.

units.la: Comesum, expotum, exunctum, elotum in balneis: Piscator, piscator abstulit, lanij, coqui, olitores, myropolæ, aucupes: confite citò, quasi si obyciat formicis papaverem.
units.tr: Eaten, drunk, anointed, washed in the baths: the fishmonger, the fishmonger has carried it off; butchers, cooks, greengrocers, perfumers, fowlers: quickly consumed, as if one were to throw poppy seed to ants.

units.la: Ita varia genera sunt luxûs juvenilis. Decoctionibus, compotationibus, unctionibus, balneis, varijsque aliis delitijs & cupedijs rem perdere solebant in ganeis & popinis.
units.tr: Thus there are various kinds of youthful extravagance: by debauchery, drinking parties, anointing, baths, and other kinds of delights and dainties, they were accustomed to ruin their property in brothels and taverns.

units.la: Vide singulis Titulis.
units.tr: See the individual titles.

units.la: Luxum sequitur Inopia: quæ filia luxuriæ fingitur à Trin. Prolog. v. 1. & seqq. & 2. 1. v. 24. Fit ille, dum illu comis est, inops amator. Rud. Prol. v. 37.
units.tr: Want follows extravagance, which is imagined as the daughter of luxury. Trin. Prol. v. 1 and following, and 2. 1. v. 24. He becomes a poor lover while he is busy with his mistress. Rud. Prol. v. 37.

units.la: Sic Claud. Ruff.
units.tr: So Claudian says:

units.la: Et luxus populator opum: cui semper adhærens Infelix humili gressu comitatur Egestas.
units.tr: And luxury, the plunderer of wealth, whom wretched Want always follows with a humble step.

units.la: Sic Paulinus Epist ad Amand. pedissequam pigrorum dixit esse Inopiam. Vide Marq. Freheri de Famâ lib. 2. pag. 227. Lege etiam cap. 19. Cent. 1. Philippi Camerarij de fugâ Lascivia & voluptatum.
units.tr: So Paulinus, in his letter to Amandus, called Want the attendant of the lazy. See Marquard Freher, On Fame, book 2, p. 227. Read also chapter 19 of the first century of Philipp Camerarius, On Flight from Wantonness and Pleasures.

units.la: Claudiani præterea elegantes hi sunt versus in luxuriam:
units.tr: Moreover, these are Claudian's elegant verses against luxury:

units.la: Luxuries prædulce malum, quæ dedita semper Corporis arbitrijs habebat caligine sensus,
units.tr: Luxury, a very sweet evil, which, given over always to the whims of the body, kept the senses in darkness,

units.la: Membraq, Circéis effeminat acrius herbis.
units.tr: and effeminates the limbs more fiercely than Circe's herbs.

units.la: Blanda quidem vultu, sed quâ non tetrior ulla
units.tr: Charming indeed in appearance, yet no one is more foul,

units.la: Interius fucata genas, & amicta dolosis
units.tr: painting her cheeks within, and wrapped in deceitful

units.la: Illecebris, torvos auro circumlinit hydros,
units.tr: enticements; she smears gold on the grim serpents,

units.la: Illi voluptatum multos intexuit hamos.
units.tr: and has woven many hooks of pleasures for them.

units.la: Mulieres eftrices, cibo sese ingurgitantes dicuntur corvitare.
units.tr: Women who gorge themselves with food are said to gorge themselves.

units.la: Vide Lexic. & Tit. Corvorum.
units.tr: See the lexicon and the title Crows.

units.la: Prodigi adolescentes interdum redire solent ad frugem: & vi-cem suam deplorare: quod facit Adolescens Dinarchus.
units.tr: Prodigal young men are sometimes accustomed to return to thrift and lament their own fate, as the young man Dinarchus does.

units.la: Truc. 2. 3. v. 22. & seqq. & Trin. 2. 1. v. 34. Lysiteles.
units.tr: Truc. 2. 3. v. 22 and following, and Trin. 2. 1. v. 34. Lysiteles.

units.la: Luxuriosi omnibus bonis profusis ex urbe in militiam ausu-giunt.
units.tr: Spendthrifts, once all their goods are squandered, flee the city to join the army.

units.la: Multæ sunt rationes perdendi rem suam. Vel enim quis publi-cis negotijs implicando se; vel mercaturam exercendo; vel libe-ralitate nimia sua profundendo, ad egestatem redigi potest.
units.tr: There are many ways of losing one's property. For one may be reduced to poverty either by becoming entangled in public business, or by engaging in trade, or by pouring it away through excessive generosity.

units.la: Trin. 2. 2. v. 50. & seqq.
units.tr: Trin. 2. 2. v. 50 and following.

units.la: Qui nimis magnos sumtus faciunt, insanire dicuntur.
units.tr: Those who spend far too much are said to be mad.

units.la: Et Græcis μαίνεσθαι, & μανία.
units.tr: And among the Greeks, to be mad and madness [μαίνεσθαι, μανία].

units.la: Ditiores aureos clavos calceis suffigebant.
units.tr: Richer men used to fasten golden nails to their shoes.

units.la: Filii luxu perditi mortem parentum in votis habent.
units.tr: Sons ruined by extravagance wish for their parents' death.

units.la: Luxuriosi amatores comedunt pecuniam parentum suorum in lustris.
units.tr: Spendthrift lovers squander their parents' money in brothels.

units.la: Servi infideles solent bona dominorum comedere.
units.tr: Unfaithful slaves are accustomed to consume their masters' goods.

units.la: Vide hic Compilatorem Taubmannum.
units.tr: See here the compiler Taubmann.

units.la: Luxus veterum magnus circa unguenta, & balnea, compotationes: ut de amatoribus dicitur.
units.tr: The extravagance of the ancients was great in perfumes, baths, and drinking parties, as is said of lovers.

units.la: Luxu & amoribus adolescentes etiam optimi corrumpuntur.
units.tr: Even the best young men are corrupted by extravagance and love affairs.

units.la: Most. 1. 1. v. 20. & seqq.
units.tr: Most. 1. 1. v. 20 and following.

units.la: Luxuriosis in frænum luxûs dabatur uxor.
units.tr: A wife was given to spendthrifts as a curb on their extravagance.

units.la: Vide Tit. Conjugÿ.
units.tr: See the title Marriage.

units.la: Luxuriosi divitias suas habent pro stercore.
units.tr: Spendthrifts regard their riches as dung.

units.la: Per luxuriam ad egestatem redacti impudentes redditi.
units.tr: Those reduced to poverty through extravagance become shameless.

units.la: M.
units.tr: M.

units.la: Macelli. Carnium. Lanionum.
units.tr: Macelli. Carnium. Lanionum.

units.la: IN macello etiam pisces venditi. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 36. IN macello vendebant præter carnes, agninam, bubulam, vitulinam, porcinam, etiam pisces. Aul. 2. 8. v. 3.
units.tr: In the market (macellum) fish were also sold. Pseud. 1.2, v. 36. In the market they sold, besides meats, lamb, beef, veal, pork, and also fish. Aul. 2.8, v. 3.

units.la: Maciei.
units.tr: Maciei.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See also the title Hominis.

units.la: MACIES seu macritudo proprè circa ossa. Unde natum proverbiale illud: Ossa atque pellis sunt miserâ macritudine. Capt. 1. 2. v. 26.
units.tr: Emaciation, or leanness, properly concerns the bones. Hence the proverbial saying: Ossa atque pellis sunt miserâ macritudine. Capt. 1.2, v. 26.

units.la: Magistratus. Ædilium. Tribunï-Plebis. Prætoris. Triumviri. Lictorum.
units.tr: Magistrates. Aediles. Tribunes of the Plebs. Praetor. Triumvirs. Lictors.

units.la: MINORES magistratus, ut sunt Tribuni, Triumviri, Quæstores, & hujusmodi minora exercentes, sedebant non in sellis Curulibus, aut Tribunalibus: sed in subsellijs: teste Asconio
units.tr: The lesser magistrates, such as the tribunes, triumvirs, quaestors and others who held minor offices, did not sit in curule or tribunal chairs but on benches, as Asconius attests

units.la: Ddd Pædiano in Verrem. Inde Parasitus dicit se esse imi subsellij vi-rum. Stich. 3.2. v. 33.
units.tr: Pedianus on Verres. Hence the parasite says he is a man of the lowest bench. Stich. 3.2. v. 33.

units.la: TRIBUNI plebis dicebantur δήμαρχοι.
units.tr: Tribunes of the plebs were called δήμαρχοι [dēmarchoi].

units.la: Apud Dorienses dicti δημιοργοί. Turneb. lib. 14. cap. 11. Adver.
units.tr: Among the Dorians they were called δημιοργοί [dēmiourgoi]. Turneb. lib. 14. cap. 11. Adver.

units.la: TRIBUNI nascentibus malis moribus cogitationes sciscunt bo-nas.
units.tr: Tribunes, when evil morals are springing up, resolve upon good intentions.

units.la: ERANT & certi Comarchi, κώμαρχοι, qui vicos curarent. Plau-tus scr.
units.tr: There were also certain village chiefs, κώμαρχοι [kōmarchoi], who looked after the villages. Plautus writes:

units.la: MAGISTRATUM ambitione adipisci nefas.
units.tr: It is wrong to attain magistracy through ambition.

units.la: Amph. Prol. v. 74.
units.tr: Amph. Prol. v. 74.

units.la: Virtute oportet. Ibid.
units.tr: One must attain it by virtue. Ibid.

units.la: ÆDILES erant ἀγορανόμοι, quorum erat habere rationem annonæ & fori. Marcellmeister.
units.tr: The aediles were the ἀγορανόμοι [agoranomoi], whose duty was to oversee the grain supply and the market. Marcellmeister.

units.la: De his vide Authores de Magistratibus Romanis: inprimis Historiam Fori Romani Polleti lib. 3. c. 2.
units.tr: On these see the authors on Roman magistrates, especially Pollet's History of the Roman Forum, book 3, chapter 2.

units.la: ÆDILIBUS cura erat viarum: & publicæ munditici. Alluditur Truc. 2.7. v. 6. de Amatoribus: Puras sibi vult esse ÆDes: domi quicquid habet, verritur.
units.tr: The aediles had charge of the streets and public cleanliness. There is an allusion to this in Truc. 2.7. v. 6, about lovers: She wants her house to be clean; whatever is in the home gets swept out.

units.la: ÆDILES sine suffragio populi non fiebant. Stich. 2.3. v. 28.
units.tr: Aediles were not made without the vote of the people. Stich. 2.3. v. 28.

units.la: ÆDILES Curules erant Ordinis senatorij: & dicti Majores: Nam Minores dicti ἀγορανόμοι. Men. 4. 2. v. 23.
units.tr: Curule aediles were of senatorial rank and were called Greater; the Lesser were called ἀγορανόμοι [agoranomoi]. Men. 4.2. v. 23.

units.la: ÆDILIS erat indicere ludos. Pseud. 1.5. v. 133.
units.tr: It was the aedile's duty to announce the games. Pseud. 1.5. v. 133.

units.la: MERETRICES apud Ædilem nomina sua profitebantur. Poen. 5.3. v. 20.
units.tr: Prostitutes declared their names before the aedile. Poen. 5.3. v. 20.

units.la: SOLEBANT Ædiles improbas merces in profluentem interdum jactare, ut edulia, quæ putebant.
units.tr: Aediles sometimes used to throw bad goods into the flowing water, such as foodstuffs they judged to be rotten.

units.la: Rud. 2.3. v. 43. de naufragio. Neptunus ædilis est fastidiosus, si quæ improbæ sunt merces, ja-ctat omnes.
units.tr: Rud. 2.3. v. 43, of a shipwreck: The aedile of the sea is fastidious: if any goods are bad, he throws them all overboard.

units.la: De mensuris etiam cognoscebant, quâ æquæ: iniquas frange-bant.
units.tr: They also inspected measures, and broke those that were unfair.

units.la: Pers. Sat. 1. Juven. Sat. 10. Ulpian. c. 13. ff. locati.
units.tr: Pers. Sat. 1. Juven. Sat. 10. Ulpian, c. 13, ff. locati.

units.la: Hieronymus:
units.tr: Jerome:

units.la: ἐΑb Ædilibus, quos ἀγορανόμους Græci appellant, vendentium coërcebatur rabies.
units.tr: By the aediles, whom the Greeks call ἀγορανόμους [agoranomous], the frenzy of sellers was restrained.

units.la: Vide Furneb. l. 29. cap. 20. Colv. ad Apulejum. & Fr. Duar. lib. 1. cap. 26.
units.tr: See Furneb. l. 29, cap. 20. Colv. on Apuleius, and Fr. Duar. lib. 1, cap. 26.

units.la: ÆDILIS erat curare ornamenta scenica.
units.tr: The aedile's duty was to take care of the stage decorations.

units.la: DICTATOR magistratus fuit Romanus: non Atheniensis.
units.tr: The dictator was a Roman magistrate, not an Athenian one.
Pseud. 1. 5. v. 2.

units.la: DICTATURA summus honos. Trin. 3. 2. v. 69.
units.tr: The dictatorship is the highest honour. Trin. 3. 2. v. 69.

units.la: Is est Honos homini pudico, meminisse officium suum. Ibid.
units.tr: That is the honour of a modest man: to remember his duty. Ibid.

units.la: PRÆFECTI in suis Præfecturis jus dicebant. Quò alludit Parasi-tus. Capt. 4. 3. v. 7.
units.tr: Prefects gave judgment in their own prefectures. The parasite alludes to this. Capt. 4. 3. v. 7.

units.la: Nunc ibo, ut præfecturam s jus dicam larido: Et quæ pendent indemnatæ, pernù ut auxilium feram.
units.tr: Now I will go and give judgment in Laridus's prefecture, and bring help to the ham that hangs there uncondemned.

units.la: Vide Fr. Polleti Hist. Fori Rom. lib. 3.
units.tr: See Fr. Pollet's History of the Roman Forum, book 3.

units.la: PRÆTORIS erat jus dicere. Epid. 1. 1. v. 23. Pœn. 1. 1. v. 58. Truc. 4. 3. v. 66. Vide Manut in Ep. ad Q. Fratrem: & Corasium in Epist. Quæst. cap. 2.
units.tr: It was the praetor's duty to give judgment. Epid. 1. 1. v. 23. Poen. 1. 1. v. 58. Truc. 4. 3. v. 66. See Manutius on the Letter to Quintus his Brother, and Corasius, Epistolary Questions, chapter 2.

units.la: PRÆTORIBUS erant lictores, & viminei sasces virgarum: sive teretes bacilli ex ulmo præcipuè aut betullâ loco colligati in modum sascis. Ejusmodi sasces scx Prætori, ut & Magistro Equitum: Consuli autem xii. Dictatori x xi v. præferebantur a totidem lictoribus, qui non gregatim, nec item biniternive, sed singuli, & in lineam ibant. Epid. 1,1,v. 26. Vide Lips. lib. 1. Electorum c. 23. Vide etiam Censorinum de die Natali c. 17. ubirecitatur Plebiscitum à M. Pletorio Tribuno plebis. De numero lictorum variant authores. Vide etiam Lipf. Cent. 1. Epist. 5.
units.tr: Praetors had lictors and fasces of wicker rods, or slender rods, chiefly of elm or birch, bound together in the manner of fasces. Six such fasces went before the praetor, as before the master of horse; the consul had twelve, and the dictator twenty-four, each preceded by as many lictors, who went not in a crowd nor two by two, but singly, in a line. Epid. 1, 1, v. 26. See Lipsius, book 1 of the Electa, chapter 23. See also Censorinus, On the Birthday, chapter 17, where a plebiscite of M. Pletorius, tribune of the plebs, is cited. Authors differ about the number of lictors. See also Lipsius, Cent. 1, Epist. 5.

units.la: PRAETORIS erat cognoscere causas: & addicere rem. Poen. 3. 1. v. 61.
units.tr: The praetor's duty was to hear cases and to adjudge the matter. Poen. 3. 1. v. 61.

units.la: A comitijs publicis non licebat abesse praetori. Poen. 3. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: The praetor was not permitted to be absent from the public assemblies. Poen. 3. 2. v. 7.

units.la: PRAETORIS erat manumissos in Acta referre. Perf. 4. 3. v. 17.
units.tr: The praetor's duty was to enter freedmen in the records. Perf. 4. 3. v. 17.

units.la: PRAETORIS officium fuit creditoribus aeris alieni jus dicere. Curc. 3. 1. v. 6.
units.tr: It was the praetor's office to give judgment to creditors concerning debts. Curc. 3. 1. v. 6.

units.la: A praetore syngraphum petebant milites ad bellum abituri; hoc est, diploma quoddam ad salvum conductum. Capt. 2. 3. v. 90. & 3. 2. v. 6.
units.tr: Solders about to go to war used to ask the praetor for a syngraphum, that is, a written pass for safe conduct. Capt. 2. 3. v. 90, and 3. 2. v. 6.

units.la: PRAETOR ubi jus cognovit, addixit rem solemniter his tribus verbis: Do. Dico. Addico. Poen. 1. 1. v. 58.
units.tr: When the praetor had heard the case, he solemnly adjudged the matter in these three words: Do. Dico. Addico. Poen. 1. 1. v. 58.

units.la: Vide Rævard. in Protrib. cap. 6.
units.tr: See Ravardus in Protrib. chapter 6.

units.la: QUAESTORES urbani aerarium curabant: & manubias hostium praedesq; vendebant. Capt. Prol. v. 34. & 1. 2. v. 2.
units.tr: The urban quaestors looked after the treasury, and sold the spoils of the enemy and the sureties. Capt. Prol. v. 34, and 1. 2. v. 2.

units.la: TRESVIRI sive Triumviri, alias Judices capitales dicti, prorsus idem erant Romae, qui Athenis Undecimviri. Munus illorum fuit: praesse carceri, punire damnatos: itemque, cognoscere de furtis admissisque servorum, aut ejusmodi viliorum capitum ad Maeniam columnam: quod adnotavit Lipsius ad lib. V. Ann. Taciti pag. 233. Edit. Lugd.
units.tr: The triumvirs, otherwise called capital judges, were exactly the same at Rome as the Undecemvirs were at Athens. Their duty was to preside over the prison and to punish the condemned; likewise to inquire into thefts and offences of slaves, or of such base persons, at the Maenian column. Lipsius noted this on book 5 of Tacitus's Annals, p. 233, Lyon edition.

units.la: Idem docet Rævardus J C. lib. 2. Var. cap. 18. ex nostro Rud. 3. 6. v. 19. Aul. 3. 2. v. 2.
units.tr: Ravardus, J.C., book 2, Var., chapter 18, teaches the same, citing our Rudens 3. 6. v. 19, and Aulularia 3. 2. v. 2.

units.la: Vide Tit. Supplicíorum.
units.tr: See the title "Punishments" (Supplicia).

units.la: Tresviri etiam sacramenta exigebant judicabantque. Asinar. 1. 2. v. 5. Aul. 3. 2. v. 2. Perf. 1. 2. v. 20.
units.tr: The triumvirs also exacted oaths and passed judgment. Asinaria 1. 2. v. 5; Aul. 3. 2. v. 2; Perf. 1. 2. v. 20.

units.la: OCTO habebant lictores validissimos, qui eorum iussu in damna- tum animadvertebant. Amph. i. i. v. 7. Asin. 3. 2. v. 118.
units.tr: The eight had very strong lictors who, at their order, carried out the punishment on the condemned. Amph. 1. 1. v. 7; Asin. 3. 2. v. 118.

units.la: Vide etiam Fr. Hotomani lib. de Magistratibus Romanis: nec non Rosini Antiqq. qui varia e variis de Triumviris capitalibus collegit lib. 7. Antiq. cap. 27.
units.tr: See also Fr. Hotoman's book on Roman magistrates, and Rosinus's Antiquities, who gathered various accounts of the capital triumvirs from various sources, book 7, chapter 27.

units.la: AD Tresviros res graves delatæ. Perf. 1. 2. v. 20.
units.tr: Serious matters were referred to the triumvirs. Perf. 1. 2. v. 20.

units.la: REI solebant nomen apud magistratum deferre ante accusatio- nem datis tabellis. Asin. 1. 2. v. 6.
units.tr: Defendants used to lodge their name with the magistrate before the accusation, with tablets given. Asin. 1. 2. v. 6.

units.la: LICTORES palam monebant populum, ut magistratibus adven- tantibus viam darent. Aul 3. 1. v. 2. Curc. 2. 3. v. 1.
units.tr: Lictors used to warn the people publicly to make way for magistrates as they approached. Aul. 3. 1. v. 2; Curc. 2. 3. v. 1.

units.la: Vide etiam Formulas Briss. pag. 271. & 272. Edit. Francof. in 4. DATE VIAM CONSULI.
units.tr: See also the formulas of Brisson, pp. 271 and 272, Frankfurt edition in quarto. MAKE WAY FOR THE CONSUL.

units.la: MANDATI. DOMINII. EDICTI. IMPERII. NUTUS. OFFICII.
units.tr: ORDERS. LORDSHIP. EDICT. COMMAND. NOD. DUTY.

units.la: IMPERATUR bene bonis: & facile est imperium in bonos. Bacch. 4. 4. v. 74. Mil. 3. 1. v. 16.
units.tr: Good things are commanded well to the good, and command over the good is easy. Bacch. 4. 4. v. 74. Mil. 3. 1. v. 16.

units.la: IMPERIA heri non decet somniculosè persequi. Amph. 2. 1. v. 75.
units.tr: Yesterday, orders should not be carried out drowsily. Amph. 2. 1. v. 75.

units.la: REI mandatæ omnes sapientes primùm prævorti decet. Merc. 2. 3. v. 72.
units.tr: All wise men should first take care to anticipate the tasks entrusted to them. Merc. 2. 3. v. 72.

units.la: Locum communem de mandatis pertractat Cicero in Ro- sciana.
units.tr: Cicero treats this commonplace about commands in the Pro Roscio.

units.la: Ibi vide: & huc adnota.
units.tr: See there, and note this here.

units.la: HERI divites duriores sunt servis suis, quàm egeni. Amph. I. I. v. 12.
units.tr: Yesterday, the rich were harsher to their slaves than the needy are. Amph. I. I. v. 12.

units.la: Vide Tit. Servitutis.
units.tr: See the title Servitude.

units.la: IN omnibus edictis boni ominis causâ præmittebant hanc formulam: BONUM FACTUM. Poen. Prol. v. 16, 45. Græci κάλὰς ἔχει apud Josephum.
units.tr: In all edicts, for the sake of a good omen, they began with this formula: GOOD OUTCOME. Poen. Prol. v. 16, 45. The Greeks use "it goes well" [κάλὰς ἔχει] in Josephus.

units.la: Vide Formularum authorem locupletissimum Barnabam Brissonium.
units.tr: See the most learned author of the formulas, Barnabas Brisson.

units.la: OTIM solo nutu aut crepitu digitorum, si quid vellent, poscebant, aut significabant. Aul. 4. I. v. 13.
units.tr: Formerly, if they wanted something, they demanded it or signalled it by a nod alone or a snap of the fingers. Aul. 4. I. v. 13.

units.la: Herile imperium edisçat, ut quod frons velit, oculi sciant.
units.tr: Let the slave learn his master's command so that his eyes know what his brow wishes.

units.la: Petronius:
units.tr: Petronius:

units.la: Trimalcio lautissimus homo, digitos concrepuit, ad quod signum matellam stado ludenti suppositum.
units.tr: Trimalchio, that most refined of men, snapped his fingers, and at that signal a chamber pot was set under the playing boy.

units.la: Martial. lib. 14. Matelia fictilis.
units.tr: Martial, book 14. An earthenware chamber pot.

units.la: Dum poscor crepitu digitorum, ac verna moratur, O quoties pollex culcita falsa mea est!
units.tr: While I am summoned by the snapping of fingers and the slave dawdles, O how often my pillow is a false one!

units.la: Idem Martial.
units.tr: Martial again.

units.la: Cum peteret feram media jam nocte matellam Arguto madidum pollice Panarettus.
units.tr: When Panaretus, drenched with wine, called for the chamber pot in the middle of the night, with a shrill snap of his thumb.

units.la: Idem:
units.tr: The same:

units.la: Digiti crepantis signa novit Eunuchus Et delicatæ suscitator urinæ Domini bibentis ebrium regit penem.
units.tr: The eunuch knows the signal of the snapping finger, and the rouser of the pampered bladder; the drunken lord's penis he guides with his hand.

units.la: MARIS. FLUVIORUM.
units.tr: Sea. Rivers.

units.la: QUISNAM istic fluvius est, quem non recipiat mare? Curc. I. I. v. 86.
units.tr: What river is there here that the sea does not receive? Curc. I. 1. v. 86.

units.la: MARITIMI morus à maris inconstantiâ dicti. Cist. 2. I. v. 11. Lucret. lib. 5.
units.tr: Maritime (the sea) is so called from the sea's inconstancy. Cist. 2. 1. v. 11. Lucretius, book 5.

units.la: Nec poterat quemquam placidi pellacia ponti Subdola pellicere in fraudem ridentibus undis.
units.tr: Nor could the deceitful wiles of the calm sea, with its laughing waves, entice anyone into treachery.

units.la: MARE dicitur tranquillum, cùm caret tempestatibus. Stich. 4. 1. v. 25. Pœn. 1.2. v. 143.
units.tr: The sea is called calm when it is free from storms. Stich. 4. 1. v. 25. Poen. 1. 2. v. 143.

units.la: MARE mutum dicitur ob lenitatem fluctuum. Mil. 3. 1. v. 69.
units.tr: The sea is called mute on account of the gentleness of its waves. Mil. 3. 1. v. 69.

units.la: MARE quidem certè commune est omnibus. Rud. 4. 3. v. 36.
units.tr: Certainly the sea is common to all. Rud. 4. 3. v. 36.

units.la: AQUAE omnes abeunt, & derivantur in mare. Truc. 2. 7. v. 15.
units.tr: All waters flow away and are carried off into the sea. Truc. 2. 7. v. 15.

units.la: AQUA marina sordes omnes abluit. Rud. 2. 1. v. 12.
units.tr: Salt water washes away all filth. Rud. 2. 1. v. 12.

units.la: Salsi lautiâ, purè domum redimus.
units.tr: Having bathed in the salt water, we return home clean.

units.la: MARSUPII. CRUMENÆ. PECUNIÆ.
units.tr: Purse, Money-Bag, Money

units.la: SOLEBANT Veteres de collo sibi crumenam suspendere, quæ decollabat, cùm in collo nusquam erat. Inde translata ista forma loquendi: Stipes decollabit. Epid. 3. 2. v. 24. Capt. 3. 1. v. 37.
units.tr: The ancients used to hang a purse from their necks, which was "beheaded" (decollabat) even though it was nowhere on the neck. From this the expression was transferred: Epid. 3. 2. v. 24. Capt. 3. 1. v. 37. "The purse will be beheaded."

units.la: De collo autem in sinum demittebant crumenam. Unde sinus frequens mentio in condendâ pecuniâ. Apulejus lib. 8. Milef.
units.tr: But they also let the purse down from the neck into the bosom. Hence the frequent mention of the bosom in storing money. Apuleius, Metamorphoses, book 8.

units.la: Stipes æreas, imò verò & argenteas multùm certatim offerentibus sinu recepere patulo.
units.tr: They received the coins, and even silver ones, into their wide bosoms while many eagerly offered them.

units.la: Martial. Epigr. 16. lib. 5.
units.tr: Martial, Epigrams, book 5, epigram 16.

units.la: Et fiet vario sordidus are sinus.
units.tr: And the bosom will become filthy with assorted bronze.

units.la: Ovidius lib. 1. Amor. Eleg. 10.
units.tr: Ovid, Amores, book 1, elegy 10.

units.la: Quid puerum Veneris pretio prostare jubetis? Quo pretium condat, non habet ille sinum. Idem lib. 3. Amor. Eleg. 7. Sed postquam sapiens in munera venit adulter; Prabuit ipsa sinu, & dare jussa dedit. Juvenal. Sat. 14. Si nondum implevi gremium ——— Idem Sat. 1. Major avaritia patuit sinus ——— Seneca 1. Non recipit sordidum virtus amatorem: soluto ad eam sinu veniendum est.
units.tr: Why do you order the boy of Venus to sell himself for a price? He has no bosom in which to store the price. Ovid, Amores, book 3, elegy 7: "But when the clever adulterer came with gifts, she herself offered her bosom and gave what she was asked to give." Juvenal, Satires 14: "If I have not yet filled my lap..." Juvenal, Satire 1: "Greater avarice has opened its bosom..." Seneca, Epistle 1: "Virtue does not receive a filthy lover; one must come to her with a loosened bosom."

units.la: Sic enim intelligendus locus Senecæ ex hac consuetudine.
units.tr: Seneca's passage must be understood in this way, in light of this custom.

units.la: Budæus exponit: Effusa copia, & liberalitate.
units.tr: Budaeus explains it as: "with lavish abundance and generosity."

units.la: At virtus mercenaria non est.
units.tr: But mercenary virtue is no virtue at all.

units.la: Vide eundem Senecam de vita beata cap. 23.
units.tr: See the same Seneca, On the Happy Life, chapter 23.

units.la: Propertius lib. 2. Eleg. 16. Semper amatorum ponderat illa sinum.
units.tr: Propertius, Elegies, book 2, elegy 16: "She always weighs the bosom of her lovers."

units.la: MEDICORUM. MEDICINÆ. ÆGRORUM.
units.tr: Physicians. Medicine. The Sick.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Morborum.
units.tr: See also the title Of Diseases.

units.la: MEDICI plærumque arrogantes. Plærumque enim nimis morantur, ut magis ægros inveniant. Sic ille Men. 5. 3. v. 9. ait, Se obligasse crus fractum Æsculapio: Apollini autem brachium, h. e. occupatum fuisse in medicina Deorum.
units.tr: Physicians are for the most part arrogant. For they usually delay, so that they may find more patients. Thus that man in the Menaechmi (5.3, v. 9) says that he had bound up a broken leg for Aesculapius, but the arm for Apollo; that is, he was busy with the medicine of the gods.

units.la: Seneca lib. 6. cap. 36. Gravissima infamia est medici, opus quaerere.
units.tr: Seneca, letter 6, ch. 36: It is the gravest disgrace for a physician to go looking for work.

units.la: Philemon:
units.tr: Philemon:

units.la: Τίς ἐστιν ὕτ© ἰατρὸς. ὰς κακῶς ἔχει ἅπας ἰατρὸς, ἂν καλῶς μηδὲις ἔχει!
units.tr: Τίς ἐστιν ἰατρός; ὃς κακῶς ἔχει ἅπας ἰατρός, ἂν καλῶς μηδεὶς ἔχῃ! [Who is a physician? Every physician fares badly, if no one fares well!]

units.la: Ubi morbus incidit, medicum accersebant.
units.tr: When sickness struck, they would send for the physician.

units.la: Nemo sanus insanit.
units.tr: No one who is sane goes mad.

units.la: Oleribus ægri curati olim.
units.tr: The sick were formerly cured with vegetables.

units.la: Vide librum 20. Plinij.
units.tr: See the twentieth book of Pliny.

units.la: Paulus Apostolus Rom. 14.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul, Rom. 14.

units.la: ὁς μὴ πιστεύει φαγεῖν πάντα, ὁ δὲ ἀσθενὴς λάχανα ἐσθίει.
units.tr: ὁ μὲν πιστεύει φαγεῖν πάντα, ὁ δὲ ἀσθενὴς λάχανα ἐσθίει. [One believes he may eat all things, but the weak man eats herbs.]

units.la: Medici quoque de somno inquirunt.
units.tr: Physicians also inquire about sleep.

units.la: Sani medicum non expetunt.
units.tr: The healthy do not seek out physicians.

units.la: Pol sanum si sim, non te medicum mihi expetam.
units.tr: By Pollux, if I were healthy, I would not be seeking you as my physician.

units.la: Mediocritatis Modi.
units.tr: The Measure of Moderation.

units.la: Mediocritatis ubique sua laus: non item nimietatis. Sic ridiculè ait Miles:
units.tr: Moderation everywhere has its own praise, but excess does not. So the soldier says wittily:

units.la: Nimia est miseria, pulchrum esse hominem nimis.
units.tr: Excessive is the misery of being a man too handsome.

units.la: Modus omnibus in rebus optimum est habitu. Nimia omnia nimium exhibent negotium hominibus ex se.
units.tr: Measure is best to have in all things. Excessive things all bring too much trouble on men of their own accord.

units.la: Poeta:
units.tr: The poet:

units.la: Est modus in rebus: sunt certi denique fines:
units.tr: There is a measure in things; there are certain limits at last,

units.la: Quos ultra citraque nequit consistere rectum.
units.tr: Beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.

units.la: Varro Modio:
units.tr: Varro in Modius:

units.la: Quid aliud est, quod Delphice canat columna litteris suis: μη- δὲν ἄγαν: quam nos facere ad mortalem modum medioxu- mè, ut quondam patres nostri loquebantur.
units.tr: What else is it that the Delphic column proclaims in its letters, nothing in excess [μηδὲν ἄγαν], which we render to mortal measure as medioxumè, as our forefathers once used to say?

units.la: Seneca Oedipo vers. 909.
units.tr: Seneca, Oedipus, verse 909.

units.la: Quicquid excessit modum, pendet instabili loco.
units.tr: Whatever exceeds the measure hangs on an unstable footing.

units.la: Constantinus Manass. Annal.
units.tr: Constantine Manasses, Annals.

units.la: Præclare sapientérq; dixerunt priscilli homines: Nihil ultrà modum. Et præclara res est Mediocritas.
units.tr: Wisely and well did the men of old say: nothing beyond the measure. And moderation is an excellent thing.

units.la: Memoriæ. Recordationis. Reminiscentiæ. Oblivionis. Monumenti.
units.tr: Of Memory. Recollection. Reminiscence. Forgetfulness. Monument.

units.la: MEMORIA optima memorat ea, quæ longinquo facta sunt. Mil. 1.1. v. 49.
units.tr: Memory best recalls what happened long ago. Mil. 1.1. v. 49.

units.la: MEMORIA juvari sæpè solet similium repetitione, præsertim in aliorum nominibus memorandis. Trin. 4.2.v.77.
units.tr: Memory is usually aided by the repetition of like things, especially in remembering names. Trin. 4.2.v.77.

units.la: Vide Jul. Cæs. Scal. l 3.cap.90. Poët.
units.tr: See Julius Caesar Scaliger, book 3, chapter 90, Poetics.

units.la: Si male quid faciendum est, immortalis est memoria. Sin bene quid oblivio est perpetua. Mil. 3.3.v.14. De mulieribus.
units.tr: If something bad is to be done, memory is immortal; but if something good, forgetfulness is perpetual. Mil. 3.3.v.14. On women.

units.la: MEMORIA magis vigetante sumtum cibum. Sic Sofia Amph. 1. 1. v. 97. Hoc adeo hoc commemini magis: quia illo die impransus fui.
units.tr: Memory is sharper when food has been taken. Thus Sophia: Amph. 1.1. v. 97. I remember this all the better, because I had not eaten breakfast that day.

units.la: MEMORIA fugax & labilis est. Bacch. 1.1. v. 2. Igitur ei subveniendum. Ibid.
units.tr: Memory is fleeting and slippery. Bacch. 1.1. v. 2. Therefore it must be helped. Ibid.

units.la: STATUAS statuebant in memoriam bene meritorum. Bacch. 4.4 v. 1.
units.tr: People used to set up statues in memory of those who deserved well. Bacch. 4.4 v. 1.

units.la: MENDACII.
units.tr: Of Lying.

units.la: SCELUS videtur parenti proloqui mendacium. Mero, I.2.v. 96.
units.tr: It seems a crime to tell a lie to a father. Mero, I.2.v. 96.

units.la: MENDACEM oportet esse memorem. Mil 2.4.v.1. Trin. 4.2.v. 50. & seqq. quos vide de Sycophantæ mendacijs.
units.tr: A liar ought to have a good memory. Mil 2.4.v.1. Trin. 4.2.v. 50. & seqq.; see these on the lies of the sycophant.

units.la: Quintil.
units.tr: Quintilian.

units.la: Mendacia plærumq; confutari solent inconstantia sermonis.
units.tr: Lies are usually refuted by inconsistency of speech.
