units.la: MENDACI non creditur etiam verum dicenti. Bacch 4.4. v.46, 49.
units.tr: A liar is not believed even when he tells the truth. Bacch 4.4. v.46, 49.

units.la: MENDACIUM officiosum sæpè prodest. Capt. 3.5. v. 47.
units.tr: A kindly lie often does good. Capt. 3.5. v. 47.

units.la: MENDACIUM officiosum, ut servetur amicus, quandoque dici potest. Bacch. 3.4. v. 31.
units.tr: A kindly lie may sometimes be told, so that a friend may be saved. Bacch. 3.4. v. 31.

units.la: MENDACIUM in tempore prolatum utile esse solet. Pseud. I.3. v. 23.
units.tr: A lie told at the right time is usually useful. Pseud. I.3. v. 23.

units.la: DI immortales, aurichalco contra non carum fuit Mendacium, hic modo quod subito commentum fuit.
units.tr: Good heavens, a lie was not dear even at the price of orichalc, this one, just what was invented on the spur of the moment.

units.la: MENDACIUM dignum plagis. Amph. I.I. v. 213.
units.tr: A lie deserves blows. Amph. I.1. v. 213.

units.la: Nunc vapula ob mendacium.
units.tr: Now be beaten for lying.

units.la: Germ. Auff ein Lügen gehört ein Maul-Tasch.
units.tr: German: For a lie, a slap in the mouth is due.

units.la: CALIDUM herclè audivi esse optimum mendacium h. e. Mendacium ex tempore natum. Mostl. 3.1. v. 131.
units.tr: I have indeed heard that a hot lie is the best lie, that is, a lie made up on the spur of the moment. Mostl. 3.1. v. 131.

units.la: MENSURÆ.
units.tr: MEASURES.

units.la: HEMINA fuit mensura liquidorum. Mil. 3. 2. v. 18. Vide Casp. Waseri Tigurini eruditissimum Tractatum de Mensuris lib. 3. cap. 2. §. 6.
units.tr: The hemina was a measure of liquids. Mil. 3. 2. v. 18. See the most learned treatise on measures by Caspar Waser of Zurich, book 3, chapter 2, §. 6.

units.la: UNCIA pondo dicebant. Rud. 4. 2. v. 9.
units.tr: They called the uncia a weight. Rud. 4. 2. v. 9.

units.la: MERETRICUM.
units.tr: OF PROSTITUTES.

units.la: Vide plura supra Tit. Adulteriš & Amorum.
units.tr: See more above under the title Adulteries & Loves.

units.la: MERETRICES ut plurimùm Romæ erant libertinæ condi-tionis. Cistell. 1. 1. v. 40. Nos libertinæ sumus & ego & tua mater amba meretrices fuimus. Livius lib. 39. Scortum nobile libertina Hispala Fecenia. Sic Horat. lib. 1. Satyr. 2. notat Sallustium in libertinarum amore insanivisse, non minus, quàm qui mæcharetur.
units.tr: PROSTITUTES at Rome were for the most part of freed condition. Cistell. 1. 1. v. 40. We are freedwomen, and both I and your mother were prostitutes. Livy, book 39: A noble prostitute, the freedwoman Hispala Fecenia. So Horace, Satires 1. 2, observes that Sallust went mad for love of freedwomen, no less than a man who commits adultery.

units.la: MESSIS. HORREI.
units.tr: The Harvest. The Granary.

units.la: FRUMENTUM metebatur mergis. Pœn. 5. 2. v. 58.
units.tr: FRUMENT was being reaped with sickles. Pœn. 5. 2. v. 58.

units.la: Meteora. Iridis. Coeli.
units.tr: Meteors. The Rainbow. The Heavens.

units.la: CRedidit vetustas Iridem demissis in terram cornibus a- quam è fontibus haurire. Inde per jocum noster deanu Cur c. 1.2. v.41.
units.tr: ANTIQUITY believed that the rainbow, with its horns lowered to the earth, drew water from springs. Hence our friend jokingly says: Cur c. 1.2. v.41.

units.la: Ecce, bibit arcus, pluet credo hercle hodie.
units.tr: Look, the bow is drinking; I believe it will rain today, by Hercules.

units.la: Sic Virgil. lib. 1. Georg. v. 380.
units.tr: So Virgil, Georgics book 1, verse 380:

units.la: Et bibit ingens Arcus.
units.tr: And the huge bow drinks.

units.la: Propert. lib. 3.
units.tr: Propertius, book 3:

units.la: Purpureus pluvias cur bibit arcus aquas?
units.tr: Why does the purple bow drink the rain waters?

units.la: Vitruvius lib. 9. cap. 4.
units.tr: Vitruvius, book 9, chapter 4:

units.la: Per calorem videmus non minus aquæ vapores à fontibus ad nu- bes per arcus excitari.
units.tr: In the heat we see that vapours of water are drawn up from springs to the clouds by the bow, no less than by other means.

units.la: Martial.
units.tr: Martial:

units.la: Casuras altè sic rapit Iris aquas.
units.tr: Thus Iris snatches the waters that would otherwise fall from on high.

units.la: Vide etiam Cælium Rhodig. lib. 22. c. 29. Antiq. Lectt. Turneb. lib. 22, c. 23. & lib. 29. cap. 31.
units.tr: See also Caelius Rhodiginus, book 22, chapter 29, Antiquae Lectiones; Turnebus, book 22, chapter 23, and book 29, chapter 31.

units.la: Minarum.
units.tr: Threats.

units.la: VETERES cùm minarentur, aut significarent, quod quis di- ceret, aut faceret, impunè non habituram, malo id eius futu- rum ajebant.
units.tr: WHEN the ancients threatened, or signified that whoever said or did something would not go unpunished, they used to say that this would be to his harm.
Amphitryo 1.1. v. 165. Asinaria 1.2. v. 4 and 2.4. v. 65. Rudens 3.4. v. 69.

units.la: MINISTERII.
units.tr: MINISTRY.

units.la: Vide Tit. Familia.
units.tr: See the title Familia.

units.la: MISERATIONIS. MISERICORDIÆ. COMMISERATIONIS.
units.tr: PITY. MERCY. COMPASSION.

units.la: Συμπαθείας.
units.tr: Of sympathy [συμπαθείας].

units.la: PLACULUM est misereri nos hominum rem malè gerentum. Trinc. 2.1. v.13.
units.tr: It is a nuisance to pity men who have got themselves into a bad way. Trinc. 2.1. v.13.

units.la: NEMINIS misereri certum est: quia mei miseret neminem. Capt. 3.5. v. 107.
units.tr: It is settled that one should pity no one, since no one pities me. Capt. 3.5. v. 107.

units.la: Minus id quidem piè dictum est.
units.tr: Indeed, that is not said very piously.

units.la: Simile vide de mendicis Tit. Egestatis.
units.tr: See something similar under the title Egestatis, on beggars.

units.la: MOLESTIÆ. IMPORTUNITATIS.
units.tr: ANNOYANCE. IMPORTUNITY.

units.la: MOLESTIAM summam creant homines importunè-garru-li: cóque tantùm non enecant. Mil. 4. 2. v. 92.
units.tr: Chattering, importunate people cause the greatest annoyance, and almost kill with it. Mil. 4. 2. v. 92.

units.la: Sic Græci Θάνατον, sive morbum sibi esse dicunt rem auditu molestam ac tædiosam.
units.tr: So the Greeks say that death [θάνατον], or sickness, is a thing unpleasant and tedious to hear.

units.la: Sophocles; ὦ μοι θάνατος μὴ τάδ' ἀκούειν.
units.tr: Sophocles: "Oh, may I not have to hear these things, death!" [ὦ μοι θάνατος μὴ τάδ' ἀκούειν.]

units.la: MONETÆ. REI-MONETARIÆ. NUMMORUM. METALLORUM. AURI. ARGENTI. AURICHALCI.
units.tr: COINS. MONETARY MATTERS. COINAGE. METALS. GOLD. SILVER. ORICHALCUM.

units.la: NUMMUS notat nummum aureum Romanum: & discernebatur à sestertio. Pseud. 3.2.v.19. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: NUMMUS denotes a Roman gold coin, and it was distinguished from the sestertius. Pseud. 3.2.v.19. See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: NUMUS aureus valebat duobus noftratibus aureis: uti quidem Lambinus sentit. Ego verò æquasse Ungaricum ducatum puquemadmodum exposui in Lexico Plautino lit. N. Ibi vide.
units.tr: The gold NUMMUS was worth two of our gold florins, as Lambinus holds. But I have equated it with the Hungarian ducat, as I explained in the Plautine Lexicon under the letter N. See there.

units.la: NUMUS interdum didrachmum valet, seu duas drachmas. Vulgò Sestertius. Truc. 2. 7. v. 11. De hoc legendi Authores Rei-Monetariæ: Matthæus Hoftus, Budæus de Asse, Hottomannus, Marq. Freherus, Waserus Tigurinus: qui toti in hac materiâ accuratè pertractandâ.
units.tr: NUMMUS sometimes means a didrachm, or two drachmas, commonly called a sestertius. Truc. 2. 7. v. 11. On this subject read the writers on monetary matters: Matthaeus Hostus, Budaeus On the As, Hottomannus, Marquard Freher, and Waserus of Zurich, who all treat this material with care.

units.la: NUMMI novi nequiores, quàm veteres. Cas. Prol. v. 10.
units.tr: NEW coins are worse than old ones. Cas. Prol. v. 10.

units.la: NUMI Philippéi quondam fuerunt aurei, insigniti nomine & imagine Philippi, Regis Macedonum. Iidem dicuntur Philippi apud Plautum nostrum. Vide Lexicon Plaut. Trin. 1.2. v. 115.
units.tr: The PHILIPPIC coins were once gold, marked with the name and image of Philip, king of the Macedonians. In our Plautus they are called philippi as well. See the Plautine Lexicon. Trin. 1.2. v. 115.

units.la: ETSI nihil sit tàm simile, quàm solidus solido, inquit Gildas Sapiens in Querolo, tamen distantia quæritur in auro. Epid. 5.1. v. 4. Vide Freherum Parerg. lib. 1. cap. 14.
units.tr: ALTHOUGH nothing is so like one solidus to another solidus, says the wise Gildas in the Querolus, yet a difference is sought in gold. Epid. 5.1. v. 4. See Freher, Parerga, book 1, chapter 14.

units.la: PLUMBEI numi nullius valoris. Mostell. 4.2.v.11. Trin. 2.4.v.120. Plumbeos numos cudere solet: in Proverbio.
units.tr: LEADEN coins of no value. Mostell. 4.2.v.11. Trin. 2.4.v.120. Plumbeos numos cudere solet: a proverb, "he is in the habit of striking leaden coins."

units.la: ALIUD alijs in locis drachmarum fuit pretium: secundum quas & æstimatio Talenti varia fuit. Trin. 2.4.v.23.
units.tr: In different places the drachma had different values, and the valuation of the talent varied accordingly. Trin. 2.4.v.23.

units.la: Drachma Philippica.
units.tr: Philippic drachma.

units.la: Vide Agell. lib. 1. cap. 16.
units.tr: See Gellius, book 1, chapter 16.

units.la: LIBELLA erat minutus argenteus, decima denarij pars. Proinde As, libra, libella argenti Plauto: & libella Ciceroni, & Assis pro eodem accipiuntur. Pseud. 1.1.v.96.
units.tr: The LIBELLA was a small silver coin, the tenth part of a denarius. Hence Plautus uses as, libra, libella of silver, and Cicero takes libella and as in the same sense. Pseud. 1.1.v.96.

units.la: E LUPINO conficiebant numos, quos in Comœdijs distribuebant: quos vocabant aurum Comicum. Pœn. 3.2.v.20. ob duritiem. Stich. 5.4.v.9. Lupilli comminuto crustulo.
units.tr: From LUPINE seed they made coins, which they distributed in comedies; these they called comic gold, Pœn. 3.2.v.20, because of their hardness. Stich. 5.4.v.9: Lupilli comminuto crustulo.

units.la: Idem faciunt etiamnum pueri in Italiâ, qui inter æs & lupinum parum distinguunt: teste Turneb. l. 1. c. 15. & lib. 19. c. 7. Sed Aliatus lib. 7. Parerg. c. 3. ex naporum sive raporum rotulis confectos fuisse contendit. Quicquid sit: Aurum Philippeum; præstat Comico.
units.tr: Children in Italy still do the same, scarcely distinguishing between bronze and lupine: witness Turnebus, book 1, chapter 15, and book 19, chapter 7. But Aliatus, Parerga book 7, chapter 3, contends that they were made from slices of turnips or radishes. Whatever the case, Philippean gold is better suited to comedy.

units.la: AURICHALCUM nostrer pluris facit, quàm talentum auri. Curc. 1.3.v.46.
units.tr: Our man values ORICHALCUM above a talent of gold. Curc. 1.3.v.46.

units.la: De Aurichalco vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: On orichalcum see the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: TALENTA à minis discerni debent. Mostell. 4.2.v.57.
units.tr: TALENTS must be distinguished from minae. Mostell. 4.2.v.57.

units.la: <bl>QUID</bl> sit Talentum magnum, vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: For what the great talent is, see the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: ARGENTUM commodum erat, non adulteratum, sed integrum. Rud. 5.2.v.31. Talentum argenti commodum. Asin. 3.3.v.136. Merc. 2.3.v.101. Pseud. 4.7.v.50.
units.tr: SILVER was good: not debased, but sound. Rud. 5.2.v.31. A good talent of silver. Asin. 3.3.v.136. Merc. 2.3.v.101. Pseud. 4.7.v.50.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: MINA & numus discernuntur. Pseud. 3.2. v.87.
units.tr: The MINA and the nummus are distinguished. Pseud. 3.2. v.87.

units.la: TALENTUM in viaticum sumsit cacula. Trin. 3.2. v.101.
units.tr: The cacula took a talent as travelling money. Trin. 3.2. v.101.

units.la: Numus est servorum: talentum dominorum. Epid. 5.1. v. 35.
units.tr: The coin belongs to slaves, the talent to masters. Epid. 5.1. v. 35.

units.la: MONSTRI.
units.tr: MONSTERS.

units.la: ASPECTRIS & monstris infestati, Herculem invocabant, monstrorum domitorem. Most. 2.2. v. 94. Vide Turn. lib. 16.10.
units.tr: Infested by apparitions and monsters, they invoked Hercules, the tamer of monsters. Most. 2.2. v. 94. See Turnebus, book 16, chapter 10.

units.la: MONTIUM.
units.tr: MOUNTAINS.

units.la: AETNA altissimus mons. Mil. 4.2. v. 73.
units.tr: AETNA, the highest mountain. Mil. 4.2. v. 73.

units.la: AUREOS montes colunt Pici. Aul. 4.3. v.1.
units.tr: The Picene mountains are inhabited by golden ones. Aul. 4.3. v. 1.

units.la: PERSARUM montes aurei perhibentur. Stich. 1.1. v. 22.
units.tr: The mountains of the Persians are said to be golden. Stich. 1.1. v. 22.

units.la: MORAE.
units.tr: MORAE.

units.la: MORAE mulierum in proverbio. Mil. 4.7. v.9. Vide Tit. Mulierum.
units.tr: MORAE mulierum: a proverb. Miles Gloriosus 4.7, verse 9. See the title Mulierum.

units.la: MORA & fames bilem in nasum concient. Amph. 4.3. v.40. Vide Tit. Famis. Et Senec. de Ira lib. 3. cap.10.
units.tr: Mora and hunger stir up bile in the nose. Amphitryon 4.3, verse 40. See the title Famis. And Seneca, On Anger, book 3, chapter 10.

units.la: MORBORUM. ÆGRITUDINIS. VALETUDINIS. PALLORIS. VULNERIS.
units.tr: Of Diseases, Sickness, Health, Pallor, and Wounds.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Medicorum.
units.tr: See also the title Physicians.

units.la: MORBUS Comitialis, seu Herculaneus, Morbus sacer, Morbus caducus: & ἐπιληψία, erat is morbus, qui insputabatur mali ominis causâ.
units.tr: The comitial disease, also called Herculean, the sacred disease, or the falling sickness, is the disease that was spat upon to avert an evil omen. The Greek name is ἐπιληψία [epilēpsia].

units.la: Quæ autem insputandi fuerit ratio, videndum apud Hier. Mercurialem lib. 5. c. 11. variarum Lectionum.
units.tr: On the method of spitting, see Hieronymus Mercurialis, Variae Lectiones, book 5, chapter 11.

units.la: Plin. lib. 28. cap. 4.
units.tr: Pliny, book 28, chapter 4.

units.la: Despuimus Comitialem morbos, h.e. contagia regerimus.
units.tr: We spit at the comitial disease, that is, we ward off contagion.

units.la: Cæterùm hujus sontici morbi συμπτώματα quamplurima alia egregiè explicat ad Aposogiam Apuleij Ocellus ille Jurisconsultorum Scipio Gentilis: quem vide sis; quicunque de Chironiâ cupis esse familiâ.
units.tr: Moreover, that little eye of the jurists, Scipio Gentilis, explains many other symptoms of this sacred disease excellently in his commentary on Apuleius' Apology. See it, if you wish to belong to Chiron's family.

units.la: Vide item Senecam lib. 3. de Irâ cap. 10.
units.tr: See also Seneca, On Anger, book 3, chapter 10.

units.la: CÙM ramices rumpuntur ex nimio cursu, hernia oritur.
units.tr: When the ramices (the sinews in the groin) burst from excessive running, a hernia arises.

units.la: Ibidem herniosi jubentur bibere resinam Ægyptiam cum melle v. 28. At Medici repugnant, qui per solam chirurgicam herniam curari affirmant. Vide Dioscor. lib. 1. c. 93. Plin. lib. 24. c. 6. Vide etiam Mercur. Var. lib. 1. c. 20. De Ramice vide Lex. Plaut. & Dalecamp ad Plin. lib. 20. c. 13.
units.tr: In the same place, people with hernia are ordered to drink Egyptian resin with honey, v. 28. But physicians disagree, who maintain that a hernia can be cured only by surgery. See Dioscorides, book 1, chapter 93; Pliny, book 24, chapter 6. See also Mercurialis, Variae Lectiones, book 1, chapter 20. On the ramex, see the Plautine lexicon and Dalechamps on Pliny, book 20, chapter 13.

units.la: Ex ramicum ruptione sanguinis exsputatio oritur: quin potius sanguinis exsputatio signum est ramices esse ruptos.
units.tr: Spitting of blood arises from a rupture of the ramices; indeed, spitting of blood is rather a sign that the ramices have burst.

units.la: Ægri salutem quidem anhelant: sed cruciatum aversantur.
units.tr: The sick indeed gasp for health, but shrink from the torment.

units.la: Sicille Mereat. 1.2.v.33.
units.tr: Likewise, Mercator 1. 2. v. 33.

units.la: Apage istiusmodi salutem cum cruciatu quæ advenit.
units.tr: Away with health of that kind, which comes with torment.

units.la: Homines ex febre, aut ex longo jejunio interdum delirare: & mentis errore affici solent.
units.tr: Men sometimes rave from fever or from a long fast, and are wont to be affected by a disturbance of the mind.

units.la: Quò allusum Curc. 1.1. v. 17.
units.tr: Alluded to here: Curc. 1. 1. v. 17.

units.la: Melancholia sæpè furorem conciliat.
units.tr: Melancholy often brings on madness.

units.la: Vide Tit. Insanie.
units.tr: See the title Insanity.

units.la: Quis morbus solstitialis: disputant authores.
units.tr: Authors dispute what the solstitial disease is.

units.la: Vide Mercur. Var. 1. f. c. 3. Turn. 1. 24. c. 38. Best quivis pravus & lethalis. Solstitium enim periculosum atque morbosum, ut docet Hippocrates & Aristoteles.
units.tr: See Mercurialis, Variae Lectiones, 1, f., chapter 3; Turnebus, book 24, chapter 38. Almost any illness is wicked and deadly, for the solstice is dangerous and morbid, as Hippocrates and Aristotle teach.

units.la: Vomicæ ægrè præstantur. Nam ubi quis malâ tetigit manu, dolores cooriuntur.
units.tr: Abscesses are hard to lance, for when someone touches one with an unskilled hand, pains arise.

units.la: Vomicæ immaturè non secandæ.
units.tr: Abscesses must not be lanced prematurely.

units.la: A morbo valere possumus, ab animo autem ægri esse.
units.tr: We can be well in body but sick in mind.

units.la: Insanis potio dabatur.
units.tr: A drink was given to the insane.

units.la: Medici garruli occidunt ægros suis fabulis.
units.tr: Chattering physicians kill their patients with their tales.

units.la: Medici de intestinis rogant, an crepent, quia scil. eorum quos atra bilis agitat, corpora flatuosa sunt.
units.tr: Physicians ask about the intestines, whether they rumble, because the bodies of those troubled by black bile are flatulent.

units.la: Insanis ac biliosis oculi duri fiunt ob intemperiem & abundantiam atræ bilis.
units.tr: In the insane and the bilious the eyes become hard, owing to the disorder and excess of black bile.

units.la: Sic Suetonius de Nerone moribundo:
units.tr: So Suetonius, of Nero dying:

units.la: Atq; in eâ voce defecit, exstantibus, rigentibúsq; oculis, usq; ad horrorem, formidinemq; visentium.
units.tr: And in that utterance he failed, with eyes staring and stiff, to the horror and dread of those who looked on.

units.la: Vide P. Vict. var. lect. lib. 25. 16.
units.tr: See P. Victorius, Variae Lectiones, book 25, chapter 16.

units.la: ANGINA est inflammatio faucium.
units.tr: Quinsy is an inflammation of the throat.

units.la: In anginam ego nunc me velim verti, ut veneficæ illi Fauces prehendam, & enicem.
units.tr: Now I would wish to be turned into quinsy, so that I might seize that poisoner's throat and strangle her.

units.la: De hoc morbo videndi Medici. Et Scal. ad Festum. Turn. l. 12. cap. 16. & Jacobus Nicolaus Loënsis Miscell. lib. 9. c. 22.
units.tr: On this disease, see the physicians; and Scaliger on Festus; Turnebus, book 12, chapter 16; and Jacobus Nicolaus Loënsis, Miscellanea, book 9, chapter 22.

units.la: ANGINA potissimum affligit fuces.
units.tr: Quinsy chiefly afflicts the throat.

units.la: Trin. 2. 4. [illegible, ~4 letters] 9.
units.tr: Trin. 2. 4. [illegible] 9.

units.la: VOMITUS sæpè morbi medicina.
units.tr: Vomiting is often a remedy for disease.

units.la: Perij! animo male sit: contine quaso caput. C H. Pulmoneum edepol nimis velim vomitum vomas.
units.tr: I am lost! I feel sick: please hold my head. CH. By Pollux, I would very much like you to vomit up your lungs.

units.la: ÆGROTI in templo Æsculapij incubabant ad remedia per somnium accipienda.
units.tr: The sick used to lie down in the temple of Aesculapius to receive remedies in a dream.

units.la: Vide Tit. Deorum.
units.tr: See the title Gods.

units.la: INSANI elleboro curabantur.
units.tr: The insane were cured with hellebore.

units.la: Non potest hac res ellebori jugere obtinerier. Elleb. potabit aliquos viginti dies.
units.tr: This matter cannot be achieved without hellebore. He will drink hellebore for some twenty days.

units.la: NON quodvis vinum ægro conducit.
units.tr: Not every wine suits a sick person.

units.la: Album, an atrum vinum potas.
units.tr: Do you drink white wine or black?

units.la: ANIMI deliquio correptis, aquula adspergi solebat.
units.tr: Those seized by a swoon were wont to be sprinkled with a little water.

units.la: LARVATI, cerriti, quos veternus habebat, aut aqua intercus, à Medicis curabantur.
units.tr: Those with larvae, the cerriti (those held by lethargy), or with dropsy, were treated by physicians.

units.la: OPTIMÆ & corroboratæ valetudinis & temperamenti signum est numquam ægrotasse.Men. 5.5.v.56.
units.tr: The best and most robust health and constitution is shown by never having been sick. Men. 5. 5. v. 56.

units.la: PODAGROSI tardè incedunt, ut cochleæ.Pœn. 3.1.v.29.
units.tr: Gouty people walk slowly, like snails. Pœn. 3. 1. v. 29.

units.la: CORLIENOSUM improprie dicitur: cùm affectu lienis non tangatur.Cas. 2.6.v.62.
units.tr: "Splenetic" is improperly used, since a person is not touched by an affection of the spleen. Cas. 2. 6. v. 62.

units.la: IN deliquio animæ aquâ utsi.Truc. 2, 4.v.15.
units.tr: In a swoon of the spirit, use water. Truc. 2. 4. v. 15.

units.la: PALLOR nota invaletudinis: & oritur ab amore quandoq; non tamen semper.Perf. 1.1. v.24.
units.tr: Pallor is a mark of poor health, and sometimes arises from love, though not always. Perf. 1. 1. v. 24.

units.la: TRAGULAM dicebantur decidere: cum vulnere latius inciso telum evellebant.Cas 2.3.v.18. ἀπληγοεικὼς de fallacijs.Vide Lexicon Plaut.
units.tr: They used to say the spear fell out: after cutting the wound wider, they pulled out the weapon. Cas. 2. 3. v. 18. On deceits, the Greek term [ἀπληγοεικὼς] (apleogeikōs). See the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: MORTIS. SUSPENDII. INFERNI. ORCI.
units.tr: DEATH. HANGING. HELL. ORCUS.

units.la: Vide suprà plura in hanc rem Tit. Funeria.
units.tr: See above, under the title Funerals, for more on this subject.

units.la: MORTUOS credebant continuò Orco tradi.Capt. 2.2.v.33. Vivat, nec ne, id Orcum scire oportet scilicet.
units.tr: They believed that the dead were at once handed over to Orcus. Capt. 2.2.v.33. Whether he lives or not, Orcus must surely know it.

units.la: ORCUS receptor mortuorum dictus.Most. 2.2.v.67,76. Me Acherunt em recipere Orcus noluit.
units.tr: Orcus was called the receiver of the dead. Most. 2.2.v.67,76. Orcus would not receive me into Acheron.

units.la: CADAVERA mortuorum pollingebantur à pollinctoribus: nempe varijs odoribus & aromatis adspersa fuerunt, & peruncta, ad putorem illum lethalem abigendum.Pœn.
units.tr: Corpses were anointed by undertakers, that is, they were sprinkled and smeared with various perfumes and spices, to drive away that deadly stench. Poen.

units.la: Pœn. Prol. v. 63.
units.tr: Poen. Prol. v. 63.

units.la: Pollinctor mihi dixit, qui eum pollinxerat.
units.tr: The undertaker who had anointed him told me.

units.la: Tertullianus de Resurrect. carnis:
units.tr: Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh:

units.la: Proinde & corpora medicata condimentis sepultura: mausa-leis, & monumentis sequestrantur.
units.tr: Accordingly, bodies treated with seasonings are set apart for burial, in mausoleums and tombs.

units.la: Persius: tandem, beatulus alto Compositus lecto, crassisq; lutatus amomo.
units.tr: Persius: at last, the rich little man, laid on a high bed and smeared with thick amomum.

units.la: Ennius:
units.tr: Ennius:

units.la: Tarquini corpus bona femina lavit & unxit.
units.tr: A good woman washed and anointed the body of Tarquin.

units.la: Virgilius: corpusq; lavant frigentis & ungunt.
units.tr: Virgil: they wash and anoint the cold body.

units.la: Vide de hac pollinctura Lexic. Plaut. nec non Authores Funer. Rom. Meursium & Kirchmannum: itemque Ræverd. ad l. xii. Tabb. cap. 12. & P. Colvium lib. iii. Florid. Apulei.
units.tr: On this anointing see the Lexicon of Plautus, and also the authors on Roman funerals, Meursius and Kirchmann; likewise Raeverdus on the Twelve Tables, chapter 12, and P. Colvius, book 3 of Apuleius's Florida.

units.la: SOLEBANT etiam tumbis mortuorum imponere viaticum, aurum & pretiosa vasa: putantes sine his animas nusquam posse diverti.
units.tr: They also used to place provisions for the journey, gold and precious vessels, on the tombs of the dead, believing that souls could not be lodged anywhere without these.

units.la: Pœn. Prol. v. 71.
units.tr: Poen. Prol. v. 71.

units.la: Ipse abiit ad Acheruntem sine viatico.
units.tr: He went off to Acheron without provision for the journey.

units.la: Fortassis respectum ad antiquum illum gentilium ritum, quo nummum Ναύλον in os mortuis imponebant, Charonti portorium & naulum.
units.tr: Perhaps this refers to the ancient pagan custom of placing a coin in the mouths of the dead, as Charon's toll and fare.

units.la: Aristophanes in Ranis duorum obolorum meminit, qui essent Χαρόντιον Charontis: postea ad triobulum excrevit. Vide Gol-dastum Not. ad Columbanum.
units.tr: Aristophanes in the Frogs mentions two obols, which were Charon's fee (Charontion); later it grew to three obols. See Goldastus's notes on Columbanus.

units.la: NULLÆ herbæ, nulli delicati cibi mortem præpedire possunt: si vel Coquus ille cicilendrum, sive polindrum aut mæacidem: vel cæptidem condiat: quod tamen frustra jactitat.
units.tr: No herbs and no delicate foods can prevent death, even if that cook seasons it with cicilendrum, or polindrum, or maeacis, or ceptis, which he vainly boasts of.

units.la: Hominem quando animam efflavit, quid eum quæras, qui fuit? Perf. 4. 4. v. 42.
units.tr: When a man has breathed out his soul, why do you ask who he was? Persius 4.4 v. 42.

units.la: MORTUI dicebantur proprie Efferri. Moft. 4. 3. v. 8.
units.tr: The dead were properly said to be carried out (efferri). Most. 4.3 v. 8.

units.la: DUM ne ob malefacta pereamus, patientur ferre debemus mala. Nam qui per virtutem peritat, non interit. Capt. 3. 5. v. 24, 32.
units.tr: Provided we do not perish through our misdeeds, we ought to bear evils patiently. For he who perishes through virtue does not perish. Capt. 3.5 v. 24, 32.

units.la: MORTUI nullius sunt pretij. Bacch. 4. 3. v. 17.
units.tr: The dead are of no value. Bacch. 4.3 v. 17.

units.la: OMNES morti obnoxij. Trin. 2. 4. v. 92.
units.tr: All are subject to death. Trin. 2.4 v. 92.

units.la: Æquo mendicum, atq; ille opulentissimus censetur censu ad Acherontem mortuum.
units.tr: The beggar is reckoned equal to the richest man, once both are dead and gone to Acheron.

units.la: Quodvis ibi genus hominum videas, quasi Acherontem venire. Loquitur de Lenone.
units.tr: You may see every kind of man there, as if they were coming to Acheron. He is speaking of a pimp.

units.la: Tales sententiæ passim apud authores obviæ & huc referendæ. Plinius lib. 19. cap. 4.
units.tr: Such sayings are met with everywhere among the authors and belong here. Pliny, book 19, chapter 4.

units.la: Etiamne herba aliqua divitijs tantum nascitur? Nemo sacros Aventinosq; montes, & irate plebis secessu etiam spexerit? Mors enim certè æquabit, quos pecunia superaverit. Horat. l. 1. Od. 4.
units.tr: Is any herb born only for the rich? Does no one look upon the sacred and Aventine hills, and the secession of the angry plebs? For death will surely level those whom money has surpassed. Horace, Odes, book 1, ode 4.

units.la: Pallida mors æquo, &c.
units.tr: Pale death, with impartial foot, etc.

units.la: TANTUS fuit apud Veteres interni & proprij spiritus contemt, ut sæpè alia omnia externa præillo insuper haberent. Ejusq; rei variæ causæ in Plauto nostro leguntur.
units.tr: So great was the contempt among the ancients for what is external, compared with inner and personal spirit, that they often held all other external things in scorn. Various causes of this are read in our Plautus.

units.la: Primum enim, quoties non ex animi sententia res succederent: mortem sibi exoptabant: ut Præceptor ille ob infelicem disci-plinam & institutionem. Bacch. 1. 2. v. 40.
units.tr: First, whenever things did not turn out as they wished, they longed for death for themselves, like that teacher because of his unhappy training and instruction. Bacch. 1.2 v. 40.

units.la: Deinde, mortem & suspendium meditabantur in ægritudine aut calamitate alijs rebus desperatis constituti.
units.tr: Second, they contemplated death and hanging when placed in sickness or calamity, or when other hopes had been abandoned.

units.la: Sic Charinus adolescens Mercat. 2.4. v. 3.
units.tr: Thus the young man Charinus: Merc. 2.4 v. 3.

units.la: Cur ego vivo? cur non morior? quid mihi est in vitâ boni? Cer-tum est, ibo ad medicum: atque ibi me toxico morti dabo: Quando mihi adimitur quâ causâ vitam cupio vivere.
units.tr: Why do I live? Why do I not die? What good is there in life for me? Certainly I will go to the doctor, and there I will give myself to death with poison, since the one reason I have for wanting to live is taken from me.

units.la: Omnibus amicis meis idem unum convenit, ut me suspendam, ne addicar Agoraštocli.
units.tr: One thing is agreed by all my friends: that I should hang myself, lest I be handed over to Agorastocles.
And Poen. 3.5 v. 50.

units.la: Nunc ibo, amicos consulam, quo me modo suspendere æquum censeant potissimum.
units.tr: Now I will go and consult my friends, as to how they think it best for me to hang myself.

units.la: Ut res fortunæq; nostræ ferunt, par est moriri, neq; melius mor-te in malis rebus miseris.
units.tr: As our fortunes and circumstances bear, it is fitting to die; nor is there anything better than death in wretched misfortunes.

units.la: Rud. 1.3. v.27. de muliere naufragâ:
units.tr: Rud. 1.3 v. 27, of a shipwrecked woman:

units.la: Quæ mihi est ipsa? quâ me nunc vivere velim?
units.tr: What is my life to me? For what reason would I now wish to live?
And Rud. 1.4 v. 1.

units.la: Quid mihi est melius? quid magis in rem est? quàm corpore vi-tam secludam? ita male vivo: atq; ita multa in pectore mihi sunt curæ exanimales. Nunc dein vitæ haud parco: perdidi ipsem, quâ me obleƈtabam.
units.tr: What is better for me? What is more to the purpose than to shut life out of my body? So badly do I live, and so many lifeless cares are in my breast. Now I spare my life no longer: I have ruined the very self in which I used to delight.

units.la: Sic in temporibus calamitosis spontaneam quærebant mortem, uti se subtraherent longis ærumnis, neque inciderent in manus tyrannorum aut hostium. Sueton. Neron. cap.11. Tacitus plu-ries. Valer. Maximus lib.11.cap.vi. Itemque constituti in pericu-lis è bello profugi. Sueton. Calig. cap.1.
units.tr: So in times of calamity men sought a voluntary death, so that they might withdraw from long troubles and not fall into the hands of tyrants or enemies. Suetonius, Nero, chapter 11. Tacitus, several times. Valerius Maximus, book 11, chapter 6. Likewise those placed in dangers who fled from war. Suetonius, Caligula, chapter 1.

units.la: Tertiò, impotentiâ amoris & desiderij, quò etiam referri potest exemplum Charini adolescentis Merc.2.4.v.3. Item Mil 4 6. v, 26. Pseud. 1.1. v.88. Cist. 3.1. v.9.
units.tr: Third, from the powerlessness of love and desire, to which the example of the young man Charinus, Merc. 2.4 v. 3, may also be referred. Likewise Mil. 4.6 v. 26. Pseud. 1.1 v. 88. Cist. 3.1 v. 9.

units.la: Accipe me ad te Mors, amicum & benevolum.
units.tr: Take me to you, Death, a friend and well-disposed.

units.la: Quò pertinet fabula de Thisbe & Pyramo apud Ovid. Sueto-nius in Otthone non dissimiliter narrat.
units.tr: To this belongs the tale of Thisbe and Pyramus in Ovid. Suetonius in Otho relates something not unlike it.

units.la: Quarto, quòd morbos incurabiles doloresq; infandos aliter curare nequirent, quàm extremâ illâ novacula mortis, sibi manus violentas quandoque inferebant. Sic Gallus Tetrinius senator repentè oculis captus inediâ mori destinavit. Suet. Aug. c. LIIII. De Proculejo idem recitat Plinius lib. x I. c. ult. & Plin. Jun. lib. I. Epist. XII. Val. Max. lib. II. cap. VI.
units.tr: Fourth, because they could not otherwise cure incurable diseases and unspeakable pains, they sometimes laid violent hands on themselves, using that final razor of death. So Gallus Tetrinius, a senator, suddenly blinded, resolved to die by starvation. Suetonius, Augustus, chapter 54. Pliny relates the same of Proculeius, book 11, last chapter; and Pliny the Younger, book 1, letter 12. Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 6.

units.la: Quinto, famæ studio Empedocles in ferventem Æthnam insilijt. Sic per suspendium immortales se fieri arbitrabantur. Rud. 5. 3. v. 59.
units.tr: Fifth, from desire for fame, Empedocles leapt into burning Etna. Thus they thought that by hanging they would become immortal. Rud. 5.3 v. 59.

units.la: Sexto, conscientia justitiæ innocentiam suam aliter ostendere non potuit, quàm propriâ internecione, ut Severianus apud Dion. Hadrian. priusquam jugularetur, ignem poposcit, atque incenso thure: Vos, inquit, ô Dij testor innoxium me esse.
units.tr: Sixth, conscience of justice could not show his innocence otherwise than by his own destruction. So Severianus, in Dio's account of Hadrian: before he was throttled, he asked for fire, and with incense burning he said: I call the gods to witness that I am innocent.

units.la: Sic de L. Æmilio Victore vetus Inscriptio: D. M. L. ÆMILI. VICTORIS. Qui. Pridie. Natalem. Suum. Vicesimum. Et. Secundum. Pruna. In. Pensili. Posita. Urgente. Fato. Sanum. Ipse. Necavit. Se. L. ÆMILIUS. VICTOR. Principalis. Et. Ælia. Veneria. Filio. Pientissimo. Et. Sibi.
units.tr: So an old inscription concerning L. Aemilius Victor: To the divine spirits. L. Aemilius Victor, principalis, and Aelia Veneria, to their most dutiful son and to themselves. On the day before his twenty-second birthday, hung up while fate pressed upon him, he himself, though sound, killed himself.

units.la: Simile quid legimus de Juliano in Musopogone. Is namq; cùm Lutetiam Parisiorum venisset, ibidemque cænacula per fornaces calefieri solita frequentasset, illatis in cubiculum prunis, præ nidore illo molesto pænè extinctus est.
units.tr: Something similar we read of Julian in the Misopogon. For when he had come to Lutetia of the Parisians, and had often frequented the upper rooms there, which were usually heated by furnaces, he had coals brought into his bedroom, and was almost suffocated by the troublesome fumes.

units.la: Postremo, quod mirum omninò videri possit, Fortunam prosperam Morte volebant terminare, ne forsan adversa recurreret. Et sic omninò intelligendus locus apud Terentium Eunucho Act. 3. Scen. v. ubi Chærea sic loquitur:
units.tr: Lastly, what may seem altogether strange, they wished to end a prosperous fortune by death, lest adversity perhaps return. The passage in Terence's Eunuch, Act 3, scene 5, must be understood in this way, where Chaerea speaks thus:

units.la: Janne erumpere hoc licet mihi gaudium? Proh Jupiter! nunc est profecto interfici, cum perpeti me possum: ne hoc gau- diuṁ dium contaminet vita aegritudine aliquâ. Atque hæc è No-ctibus nostris Palatinis.
units.tr: Can this joy burst out for me? O Jupiter! Now it is surely right to be killed, while I can still bear it, lest life with some sickness contaminate this joy. And these are from our Palatine Nights.

units.la: Qui moriuntur, non redeunt. Fœn. 1. 2. v. 131. Quando ? Quo die Orcus ab Acheronte mortuos amiserit. h. e. Numquam.
units.tr: Those who die do not return. Poen. 1.2 v. 131. When? On what day has Orcus let the dead slip from Acheron? That is, never.

units.la: MORTEM gentiles designarunt per Orcum: & Acherunt em. Poen. 1. 2. v. 131. & 4. 2. v. 9. Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: The Gentiles designated DEATH by Orcus and Acheron. Poen. 1.2 v. 131 and 4.2 v. 9. See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: Sic Ennius: Acherunte m obibo, ubi Mortis thesauri objacent.
units.tr: Thus Ennius: I shall go to Acheron, where the treasures of Death lie before me.

units.la: Eaberius: Tollet bona fide vos Orcus in Charonium.
units.tr: Laberius: Orcus will carry you in good faith to Charon's.

units.la: Ennius: Acherusia templa salvete infera.
units.tr: Ennius: Hail, Acherusian temples, lower regions.

units.la: Næwius Poëta: Orcivum thesaurum vocat.
units.tr: The poet Naevius calls it the Orcan treasure.

units.la: MORTEM omnes extimescimus: præsertim mulieres. Rud. 3. 3. v. 23. Sed multebri animo sum tamen, misera ubi venit in mentem, mihi mortis metus membra occupat adepol.
units.tr: We all fear DEATH, especially women. Rud. 3.3 v. 23. But I am of brave spirit nevertheless; yet when, wretched me, the thought of death comes to mind, fear of death seizes my limbs, by Pollux.

units.la: MORS sive Acheruns nihil eorum, quæ accepit, reddit. Truc. 4. 2. v. 36. Item ut Acherunti, hic ratio accepti scribitur. de meretricib.
units.tr: DEATH, or Acheron, gives back nothing of what it has received. Truc. 4.2 v. 36. Likewise, as with Acheron, the account of what was received is written here. Concerning courtesans.

units.la: FILII luxu perditi mortem parentum in votis habent. Bacch. 4. 4. v. 80. & 5. 2. v. 85. Most. 1. 3. v. 76.
units.tr: Sons ruined by debauchery have their fathers' and mothers' deaths in their prayers. Bacch. 4. 4. v. 80. & 5. 2. v. 85. Most. 1. 3. v. 76.

units.la: CAPUT operiebant summo pudore affecti, in rebus desperatis vitam projicere parantes. Most. 2. 1. v. 76. Vide Cultus: Habitus.
units.tr: They covered their heads, affected with the utmost shame, preparing to throw away their lives in desperate circumstances. Most. 2. 1. v. 76. See Cultus: Habitus.

units.la: QUEM DI diligunt, adolescens moritur. Bacch. 4. 7. v. 19.
units.tr: Whom the gods love dies young. Bacch. 4. 7. v. 19.

units.la: Sic Menander:
units.tr: Thus Menander:

units.la: ἔνγε φιλεῖ ὁ θεὸς, ἀποθνήσκειν νέους.
units.tr: Whom the god loves dies young [ἔνγε φιλεῖ ὁ θεὸς, ἀποθνήσκειν νέους].

units.la: Moriturus ad Orcum abituri credebantur.
units.tr: Those about to die were believed to be going away to Orcus.

units.la: Post mortem in morte nihil est, quod metuam mali.
units.tr: After death there is nothing in death of evil that I should fear.

units.la: MORUM. CONSUETUDINIS. CONVERSATIONIS. NATURÆ. INGENII. INDOLIS. IMPROBORUM-HOMINUM.
units.tr: Morals. Custom. Conversation. Nature. Disposition. Character. Of wicked men.

units.la: UT esse addecet nequam homines, ita sunt.
units.tr: As worthless men ought to be, so they are.

units.la: MORUM contagio pessima.
units.tr: The contagion of morals is most deadly.

units.la: Seneca:
units.tr: Seneca:

units.la: Definit esse remedio locus, ubi quae fuerant vitia, MORES sunt.
units.tr: Where what were vices have become customs, there is no longer any room for a remedy.

units.la: Tacitus de moribus Germanorum:
units.tr: Tacitus, on the customs of the Germans:

units.la: Nemo illic vitiaridet: nec corrumpere, & corrumpi SAECULUM vocatur.
units.tr: No one there laughs at vices, and to corrupt and be corrupted is not called the way of the age.

units.la: Nullus frugi esse potest homo, nisi qui bene & male facere tenet. Improbus cum improbis fit, harpaget, furibus furetur, quod quoniam, versipellem frugi convenit esse hominem, pectus cui sapit. Bonus sit bonis: malus sit malis, utrumque res sit, ita animum habeat.
units.tr: No man can be honest unless he knows how to do both good and evil. A wicked man becomes wicked with the wicked; he plunders with plunderers, and he robs with thieves. Since an honest man must be a man of two faces and have a mind that understands this, let him be good to good men, bad to bad men, and let him have a disposition that adapts to either.

units.la: Baech, 4. 4. v. 10. & seqq. ex sententia servi Chrysali.
units.tr: Bacch. 4. 4. v. 10 and following, in the words of the slave Chrysalus.

units.la: Ex nostro ingenio alios plerumque æstimamus, sive boni, sive malisumus.
units.tr: We usually judge others by our own disposition, whether we are good or bad.

units.la: RARA messis bonorum morum.
units.tr: A thin harvest of good morals.

units.la: Nam hic nimium morbus mores invasit bonos: Itaque, plerumque omnes jam sunt intermortui. Sed dum illi aegrotant, interim mores mali, quasi herba irrigua succrevere uberrime. Neque quicquam hoc vile nunc est, nisi mores mali: eorum licet jam messem metere maximam.
units.tr: For this disease has taken hold of good morals here so greatly that almost all of them are now dead. But while they lie sick, bad morals have sprung up most abundantly, like a weed in irrigated ground. Nothing here is now cheap except bad morals; of these one may now reap the greatest harvest.

units.la: Trin. I. I. v. 9.
MORES maritimi in proverbium abierunt. Dolosi enim sunt, & incerti.
units.tr: Seafaring morals have passed into a proverb, for they are deceitful and unreliable.

units.la: Cist. 2. I. v. II.
Vide Tit. Mare.
units.tr: See the title Mare.

units.la: MORES rusticorum merum rus sapiunt. Sic Servus ille rusticus, cum salutaretur ab urbana ancilla: quam infice te respondet?
units.tr: The manners of country people smack of nothing but the countryside. So that rustic slave, when greeted by a city maidservant, answers: "How are you?"

units.la: Nihil moror, non salveo: aegrotare malum, quam tua salute esse sanior. Tantum facit educatio.
units.tr: "I care nothing for it, I do not greet you; may it be a curse to be ill rather than to be healthier than you." Only education makes such a difference.

units.la: NATURAE mores non facile mutantur. Naturam enim expellas furcā, tamen usque recurret.
units.tr: Natural dispositions are not easily changed. For though you drive nature out with a pitchfork, she will still keep coming back.

units.la: Aul. 2. 4. v. 49. Sic sum, ut vides.
units.tr: Aul. 2. 4. v. 49. "I am as you see me."

units.la: Amphitruo 2. 4. v. 57. Aulular. 2. 4. v. 49. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 61. Perf. 2. 4. v. 13. Ita sum. Rud. Prol. v. 3. Cist. 2. 1. v. 7. Ita est ingenium meum. Stich. 4. 2. v. 46. Amph. 3. 2. v. 18.
units.tr: Amphitruo 2. 4. v. 57. Aulularia 2. 4. v. 49. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 61. Pers. 2. 4. v. 13. "So I am." Rud. Prol. v. 3. Cist. 2. 1. v. 7. "So is my nature." Stich. 4. 2. v. 46. Amph. 3. 2. v. 18.

units.la: Terentius:
units.tr: Terence:

units.la: Ita sum, si placeo utere.
units.tr: "This is what I am; if you like me, use me."

units.la: Theocr. Idyll. 22.
units.tr: Theocritus, Idyll 22.

units.la: ἀγρῷ ἐι, ὡς ταύτα ταλίγκοτος, ἡ ὑπεξέπλης.
units.tr: You are a rustic, and as harsh as these things, or as ... [ἀγρῷ εἶ, ὡς ταῦτα ταλίγκοτος, ἠὲ ὑπεξέπλης.]

units.la: Amycl. τοῖς δ' ἰᾶ ὀφᾶς.
units.tr: To those who ... [τοῖς δ' ἰᾶ ὀφᾶς.]

units.la: Memini dictum hoc saepius in ore quondam Doctoris mei, viri Clarissimi Lamberti Ludolphi Helmij Pithopaei: Professoris Philologi in Inclyta Heidelbergā celeberrimi. Cum n. non omnibus Carmina sua, & Asiaticam, quam à naturā habebat, in dicēdo tolutiloquentiam probaret: facetè, ut omnia, respondit:
units.tr: I remember this saying often on the lips of my teacher, the most distinguished Lambert Ludolph Helmius Pithopaeus, professor of philology at the famous university of Heidelberg. Since not everyone approved of his poems or of the Asiatic, bombastic fluency in speaking that he had by nature, he replied, wittily as he did everything: I am what I am; if you like me, make use of me.

units.la: Ita sum, si placeo, utere. CUM probis potius, quàm cum improbis vanidicis est vivendum: quod rectè sentit adolescens. Trin. 2.1. v.37. & 2.2. v.5,33. & seqq. quos lege.
units.tr: One should live with the upright rather than with the wicked and boastful. The young man rightly thinks so. Trin. 2.1, v. 37, and 2.2, vv. 5, 33 and following. Read them.

units.la: BONI sibi expetunt rem, fidem, honorem, gloriam & gratiam. Ibid.
units.tr: Good men seek for themselves property, good faith, honour, glory and favour. Ibid.

units.la: NOVI ego hoc saeculum moribus quibus sit, malus bonum, malum esse vult, ut sit sui similis: turbant, miscent mores mali. Trin. 2.2. v. 8. & seqq. quos lege.
units.tr: I know what manners this age has: the bad man wants the good to be bad, so that he may be like himself; bad men upset and corrupt morals. Trin. 2.2, v. 8 and following. Read them.

units.la: MORIBUS Antiquis est vivendum. Capt. 1.1. v. 37. Trin. 2.2. v.16.
units.tr: One must live by the old customs. Capt. 1.1, v. 37. Trin. 2.2, v. 16.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: ADOLESCENTES debent animum suum vincere, non vinci ab animo. Trin. 2.2. v. 25. & seqq.
units.tr: Young men ought to conquer their own minds, not be conquered by their minds. Trin. 2.2, v. 25 and following.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Adolescentia.
units.tr: See also the title Adolescentia.

units.la: FILII plerumque studia parentum sectantur. Sic Senex de filio suo jocatur Most. 3.1. v. 104. Euge Philolaches patrissat. Iam homo in mercaturâ vortitur.
units.tr: Sons for the most part follow their fathers' pursuits. So the old man jokes about his son in Most. 3.1, v. 104: Bravo, Philolaches is playing the father! Now he is busy in trade.

units.la: MORES deteriores increbrescunt indies. Merc. 5.1. v. 9. Trin. 1.2. v. 54.
units.tr: Bad customs grow stronger every day. Merc. 5.1, v. 9. Trin. 1.2, v. 54.

units.la: UTINAM Veteres mores, veteresque parsimoniae potius majori honori hic esset, quàm mores mali. Trin. 4.3. v. 22.
units.tr: Morals have brought the laws into their own power. Ibid. v. 30.

units.la: MORES leges perduxerunt in potestatem suam. Ibid. v.30.
units.tr: By indulgence we corrupt young people. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 9. Trin. 1. 2. v. 98.

units.la: INDULGENTIA corrumpimus adolescentes. Bacch. 3.3. v.9. Trin. 1.2. v.98.
units.tr: See both passages, and the title Adolescentia.

units.la: Vide utrumque locum: & Tit. Adolescentia.
units.tr: Urban manners distinguish men from country folk. Merc. 4. 15. v. 3.

units.la: URBANI moribus distinguuntur ab rusticis. Merc. 4.15. v. 3.
units.tr: See both passages, and the title Adolescentia.

units.la: MULIERUM. FEMINARUM.
units.tr: WOMEN. FEMALES.

units.la: Vide etiam supra Tit. Forma: & Habitus.
units.tr: See also above, under the title Form and Dress.

units.la: NEGOTII sibi qui volet vim parare, Navem & Mulierem, hæc duo comparato.
units.tr: If anyone wants to gain power in business, let him acquire these two things: a ship and a woman.

units.la: Nam nulla magis res dua negotij habent: ea forte si ornare occeperis, neq; unquam satis ha duaru ornantur. Neque ea ulla ornandi satietas est.
units.tr: For no things have more business than these two. If you begin to adorn them, perhaps, they are never adequately adorned, and there is no satiety of adorning them.

units.la: Pœn. 1. 2. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: Poen. 1.2 v.1 and following.

units.la: Sic P. Syrus:
units.tr: Thus Publius Syrus:

units.la: Feminarum curam gerere, desperare est otium.
units.tr: To take care of women is to despair of leisure.

units.la: Miserius nihil est, quàm mulier.
units.tr: Nothing is more wretched than a woman.
Bacch. 1.1 v.4.

units.la: Mulieres ex instituto majorum erant abstemiæ.
units.tr: Women, by the custom of their ancestors, were abstinent.

units.la: Vide Tit. Ebrietatis.
units.tr: See the title Drunkenness.

units.la: Mulieres creduntur esse excordes. Cist. 1.1. v. 68.
units.tr: Women are believed to be foolish. Cist. 1.1 v.68.

units.la: Mulieres non habent cor: eoq; parum sapiunt.
units.tr: Women have no heart, and therefore they have little sense.

units.la: FORMOSULÆ meretrices, ut frontem tegerent, nimbis eam imminuebant: quia frons parva in honore reputabatur: ut patet ex Horat. lib.1. Od. 33. & lib.1. Epist.7. Inde Nimbata dicebantur. Pœn. 1.2. v.135. Vide Lex. Plaut. Nimbus.
units.tr: Beautiful courtesans, to cover their brow, reduced it with nimbi (false hair-pieces), because a small brow was considered a mark of beauty, as is evident from Horace, Odes 1.33 and Epistles 1.7. Hence they were called Nimbatae. Poen. 1.2 v.135. See the Plautine Lexicon, under Nimbus.

units.la: Alij tñ aliam rationem frontis imminuendæ fuisse autumant: sicuti Laurentius Ramirez explicat ex consuetudine Hispanarum mulierum his verbis, quæ apponam: Capillos, inquit, à vertice in faciem demittunt: fasciolâ deinde serica vel lineâ frontem ligant, comprehensis subtus capillis, quos deinde retrò flectunt: & fasciolâ interiore eos detinente frons brevior videtur.
units.tr: Others, however, think there was another method of diminishing the brow, as Laurentius Ramirez explains from the custom of Spanish women, in these words, which I shall add: "They let the hair fall from the crown onto the face; then they bind the forehead with a silk or linen band, the hair being gathered beneath and turned back; and with an inner band holding it in place, the forehead appears shorter."

units.la: Petronius de Circe: Frons minima, & quæ radices capillorum retro retro flexerat: ne scilicet existimaret invidus aliquis minimam il-lam frontem a nimbo esse, & capillos non a radicibus, sed a fascio-la recta retro flexos.
units.tr: Petronius, on Circe: "A very small forehead, and one whose roots of hair had been bent back; lest, of course, some envious person should think that the small brow came from a nimbus, and that the hair was bent back not from the roots but from a straight band."

units.la: Arnobius lib. 2.
units.tr: Arnobius, book 2.

units.la: Laminas pertunderent aurium: imminuerent frontes nimbi.
units.tr: They pierced the lobes of their ears; the nimbi diminished their foreheads.

units.la: Sed vide quæ præter hæc notavi de hoc Nimbo Lexico Plautino.
units.tr: But see what I have noted besides these things about this Nimbus in the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: GEREBANT etiam amiculum, quod verrebat suo syrmate hu-mum.
units.tr: They also wore a little cloak, which swept the ground with its train.

units.la: Pœn. 1. 2. v. 136. Age sustolle hoc amiculum.
units.tr: Poen. 1.2 v.136. "Come, lift up this little cloak."

units.la: ITA est ingenium muliebre: Bene cum lauto est, tersa, ornata, fi-cta est, infixta est tamen: nimioque sibi mulier repperit odium ocyus suâ immunditiâ. Stich. 5. 5. v. 3.
units.tr: Such is the female disposition: when she is well bathed, polished and adorned, she is painted; yet she is fixed, and by her own filthiness a woman quickly finds hatred, to her great harm. Stich. 5.5 v.3.

units.la: MULIER ornatu suo multum morae insumunt, Stich. 5. 2. v. 19.
units.tr: Women spend much time on their adornment. Stich. 5.2 v.19.

units.la: Sic Terentius:
units.tr: Thus Terence:

units.la: Dum moliuntur, dum comuntur annum est:
units.tr: While they are struggling, while they are adorning themselves, it is a year.

units.la: Sic ex hoc loco ibi legendum; non, conantur, aut comantur.
units.tr: So in this passage one should read there, not conantur or comantur.

units.la: MULIER profecto nata est ex ipsâ morâ, Nam quæ vis alia, quæ mora est æque, mora, Minor ea videtur, quàm quæ propter mulierem est. Mil. 4. 7. v. 9.
units.tr: A woman is truly born from delay itself. For what other force, what delay is equal to it? Delay seems smaller than that which is caused by a woman. Mil. 4.7 v.9.

units.la: MULIER rectè olet, ubi nihil olet. Solebant autem unguentis se-se unclitare. Mostell. 1. 3. v. 116.
units.tr: A woman smells sweet when she smells of nothing. They used to anoint themselves with unguents. Most. 1.3 v.116.

units.la: Inprimis veteres edentulæ, quæ vitium corporis fuco occulunt. Ibidem. Vide Ginaecei.
units.tr: Especially the old toothless women, who hide a bodily defect with paint. Ibid. See Ginaecei.

units.la: MULTA sunt mulierum vitia, sed hoc è multis maximum est, cum sibi nimis placent, nimisque operam dant, ut placeant viris. Pœn. 5. 4. v. 31.
units.tr: Women have many vices, but the greatest of these is that they please themselves too much, and take too much pains to please men. Poen. 5.4 v.31.

units.la: MOS est mulierum: Omnes id faciunt, cum se amari intelligunt. Numquam ab amatore suo postulant, id quod datum est; sed relliquum dant operam, ne sit reliquum. Truc. Prol. v. 14.
units.tr: It is the custom of women: all do this when they understand they are loved. They never demand from their lover what has been given, but take care for what remains, lest there be anything left. Truc. Prol. v.14.

units.la: SI quid faciendum est mulieri malè, atque malitiolè.
units.tr: If something is to be done by a woman badly and maliciously...

units.la: Ejus illi immortalis memoria est meminisse, & sempiterna: Sin bene quid, aut fideliter faciendum est, eò deveniunt, Obliviosè extemplò uti fiant, meminisse nequeunt. Mil. 3.3. v. 14.
units.tr: Her memory of that is immortal and everlasting; but if something good or faithful is to be done, they come to the point where, at once forgetful, they cannot remember. Mil. 3.3 v.14.

units.la: OPTIMA nulla potest eligi : alia alia pejor est. Aul. 2.1. v. 19.
units.tr: No best can be chosen: one is worse than another. Aul. 2.1 v.19.

units.la: MULIERES cunctatrices esse solent.
units.tr: Women are wont to be dilatory.

units.la: PYR. Propera, stando excrucior.
units.tr: PYR. Hurry, I am tormented by waiting.

units.la: PA. Pedetentim, tute haec scio, tractari solere hujusmodi merces. Mil. 4.2. v. 32.
units.tr: PA. Slowly; I know all these goods are usually handled in this way. Mil. 4.2 v.32.

units.la: MULIERES eftrices, cibo nimio se ingurgitantes dicuntur corvitare. Caf. 4.1. v. 20.
units.tr: Women who are gluttonous, stuffing themselves with too much food, are said to "corvitare" (to gorge like ravens). Cas. 4.1 v.20.

units.la: Vide Lexic. & Vit. Corvorum.
units.tr: See the Lexicon and Vit. Corvorum.

units.la: MULIEBRIS fides in proveibium abijt ob lubricitatem. Sic Mil. 2. 5. v. 46. Muliebri fecisti fide.
units.tr: Women's faith has passed into a proverb because of its slipperiness. So Mil. 2.5 v.46: "You have acted with womanly faith."

units.la: MULIEREM vocari contumeliosum fuit. Amph. 2.2. v. 182. & v. 206.
units.tr: To call someone a woman was an insult. Amph. 2.2 v.182 and v.206.

units.la: MULIEREM ducere, est miseriam ducere. Trin. 2. 2. v. 61.
units.tr: To take a woman is to take on misery. Trin. 2.2 v.61.

units.la: MATRES suas filias deducebant ad solemnes festos dies cum pompâ & morâ spectatum, ut spectarentur, & ipsæ. Cist. 1.1.v.92. Mil. 1.1. v.67.
units.tr: Mothers used to take their daughters to solemn festal days with pomp and delay, to be seen, and themselves to be seen too. Cist. 1.1 v.92. Mil. 1.1 v.67.

units.la: MULIERES male audiunt nomine ignavie, adeo ut militem ignavum Mulierem dicant. Bacch. 4.8. v.2.
units.tr: Women are badly spoken of with the name of cowardice, so much so that they call a cowardly soldier a woman. Bacch. 4.8 v.2.

units.la: Et Proverb. Mulier ignavior: Et, Mulier Imperator: Et, Mulier miles. Mil 2. 6. v.
units.tr: And the proverbs: A woman more cowardly; A woman commander; A woman soldier. Mil. 2.6 v.

units.la: MULIERES impudicæ comparantur navi, quòd domi instar navis instructæ & paratæ stabant, exspectantes donec vocarentur. Caf. 3.2. v. 27.
units.tr: Unchaste women are compared to a ship, because at home they stood equipped and ready, like a ship, waiting until they were called. Cas. 3.2 v.27.

units.la: MULIERES mari comparantur. Truc. 2.2. v. 9.
units.tr: Women are compared to the sea. Truc. 2.2 v.9.

units.la: Sic es tu ἂλς mera.
units.tr: Thus you are pure brine [ἅλς].

units.la: NEQUE eques, neque pedes profecto quisquam tantâ audaciâ, Qui æquè faciat confidenter quicquam, quàm quæ mulieres faciunt. Mil. 2. 5. v. 54.
units.tr: Surely neither horseman nor foot soldier does anything with such boldness, nor does anything as confidently, as women do. Mil. 2.5 v.54.

units.la: MULIERES dololæ & fraudulentæ naturâ. Truc. 2. 5. v. 17.
units.tr: Women are deceitful and fraudulent by nature. Truc. 2.5 v.17.

units.la: Mulieri nimiò malefacere melius est onus, quàm bene.
units.tr: For a woman, to do much wrong is a lesser burden than to do well.

units.la: Vide etiam aliquot præcedentes versus.
units.tr: See also some of the preceding verses.

units.la: ECASTOR lege durâ vivunt mulieres, multóq; iniquiore miseræ, quàm viri. Merc. 4. 6. v. 1.
units.tr: Truly women live under a harsh law, and wretched ones, far more unfairly than men. Merc. 4.6 v.1.

units.la: Vide rationem Tit. Nuptiarum.
units.tr: See the reason under the title Marriage.

units.la: MULIERIBUS est eordolium, si alias videant se melius ornatas. Pœn. 1. 2. v. 86.
units.tr: For women it is a source of vexation if they see themselves better adorned than others. Poen. 1.2 v.86.

units.la: ÆDEPOL nunc nos tempus est malas pejores fieri. Mil. 4. 6. v. 3.
units.tr: By Pollux, now is the time for us to become worse than bad women. Mil. 4.6 v.3.

units.la: EA mulier multò videtur esse sapientissima, quæ tùm, cùm res secundæ sunt, se poterit noscere: & illa, quæ æquo animo patictur sibi esse pejus, quàm fuit. Stich. 1. 2. v. 67.
units.tr: That woman will seem by far the wisest who is able to know herself when things go well; and she who bears with equanimity that her lot is worse than it was. Stich. 1.2 v.67.

units.la: FEMINÆ muscis comparantur. Truc. 2. 2. v. 30.
units.tr: Women are compared to flies. Truc. 2.2 v.30.

units.la: MEMINI malas mulieres, ut sint malæ: mihi illa ego supersum: inquit Philocomasium. Mil. 2. 4. v. 3.
units.tr: "I remember bad women, that they are bad; I am left to myself with that," says Philocomasium. Mil. 2.4 v.3.

units.la: MULIER mala merx est: & callida, quæ imitatur bestiam damnificam Involvulum, quæ in pampini folio intorta, implicat se. Cist. 4. 2. v. 61,63. Perf. 2. 2. v. 56.
units.tr: A woman is a bad commodity, and a crafty one, who imitates the harmful beast Involvulus (bindweed), which, twisted about a vine leaf, entangles itself. Cist. 4.2 v.61, 63. Persa 2.2 v.56.

units.la: FEMINA dicax, rabiosa canis dicitur. Men. 5. 2. v. 85.
units.tr: A chattering woman is called a rabid dog. Men. 5.2 v.85.

units.la: MULIERES præsertim anus, sunt rimis plenæ: & garrulæ. Aul. 2. 3. v. 1.
units.tr: Women, especially old ones, are full of cracks and garrulous. Aul. 2.3 v.1.

units.la: Jam deblaterasti vicinis omnibus mea me filiae daturum dotem.
units.tr: Now you have babbled to all the neighbours that I will give my daughter a dowry.

units.la: NIL pejus muliere, neque audacius. Mil. 2. 3. v. 34.
units.tr: Nothing is worse than a woman, nor more audacious. Mil. 2.3 v.34.

units.la: MULIER malares. Cas. 2 3. v. 12. Merc. 3. 1. v. 16. in joco. Trin. 1. 2. v. 25.
units.tr: A woman, a bad thing. Cas. 2.3 v.12. Merc. 3.1 v.16. In jest: Trin. 1.2 v.25.

units.la: Mimus:
units.tr: A mime:

units.la: Mulier tùm demum est bona, cùm apertè est mala.
units.tr: A woman is then at last good, when she is openly bad.

units.la: Hhh
units.tr: Hhh

units.la: MULIER ex sententia Poëtæ antiqui, per se & naturâ suâ est res mala. Sic dicit noster: Mulieres duas peiores esse, quam unam. Curc. 5.1. v.2. & v.8. Apage istam caniculam. Inde est in proverbio: Mulier bis malitia. Epid. 3.4. v.19.
units.tr: A woman, according to the opinion of an ancient poet, is by herself and by her nature an evil thing. So our author says: "Two women are worse than one." Curc. 5.1 v.2 and v.8. "Away with that little bitch!" Hence the proverb: "A woman is double malice." Epid. 3.4 v.19.

units.la: MULIERES latratus similes scævæ caninæ. Cas. 5.4. v.4.
units.tr: Women's barking is like the snarling of a vicious bitch. Cas. 5.4 v.4.

units.la: VIRGO atque mulier nulla erit, quin sit mala: quæ præter sapiet, quàm placet parentibus. Perf. 3.1. v.37. Item quæ reticet, si quid fieri pervorsè videt.
units.tr: There will be no virgin or woman who is not bad, who knows better than to please her parents. Likewise, she who keeps silent when she sees something going wrong. Persa 3.1 v.37.

units.la: MULIER sæpè ex voce cognoscitur. Rud. 1.4. v.12.
units.tr: A woman is often recognised by her voice. Rud. 1.4 v.12.

units.la: ETIAM mulieres tonstrices dictæ: forte ab arte mariti. Truc. 2.4. v.51.
units.tr: Even women have been called tonstrices (shearers), perhaps from the trade of the husband. Truc. 2.4 v.51.

units.la: MULIERES garrulæ. Trin. 3. 3. v. 72. Pol tacere numquam quicquam est, quod queat. Pæn. 4. 2. v.54. Tacitium tacitius tibi rem istam ; quàm quod dictum est mala mulieri.
units.tr: Women are garrulous. Trin. 3.3 v.72. By Pollux, there is never anything that can be kept quiet. Poen. 4.2 v.54. Keep that matter quieter than what was said to a bad woman.

units.la: MULIERES garrulæ comparantur lingulacis piscibus. Cas. 2, 8. v. 64.
units.tr: Garrulous women are compared to the lingulacae fish (tongue-fish). Cas. 2.8 v.64.

units.la: MULIERI numquam desunt verba, ut nec lusciniæ cantio. Bacch. 1.1. v. 4.
units.tr: A woman never lacks words, any more than the nightingale lacks song. Bacch. 1.1, v. 4.

units.la: MULTILOQUACES merito omnes habemur. Nec mutam profiteor repertam ullam esse. Hodie dicunt mulierem ullo in seculo. Aul. 2.1. v. 5. Et tamen malæ reperiuntur nominibus atque viri. Igitur de joco est, quod dicit Plautus. Feminæ namque loquacissimæ.
units.tr: We are all rightly counted talkative. I profess that no mute woman has ever been found. Today they say there is no woman in any age who is not talkative. Aul. 2.1, v. 5. And yet bad women are found by name and by husband. So what Plautus says is said in jest, for women are most talkative.

units.la: MULIERIS supellex est clamor immodestus. Pæn. 5. 3. v.26. Tace, atque parce mulieribus supellectili. Salt dein clappertbüchs gu.
units.tr: A woman's furniture is uncontrolled clamour. Poen. 5.3, v. 26. Be quiet, and spare the women's household goods. Shut your clapper-box.

units.la: TACITA bona est mulier semper, quàm loquens. Rud. 4.4. v.70.
units.tr: A silent woman is always better than a talking one. Rud. 4.4, v. 70.

units.la: MULIERES garrulæ, & domi & foris molestæ sunt viris. Pæn. Prol. v.35.
units.tr: Talkative women are a nuisance to men, both at home and abroad. Poen. Prol., v. 35.

units.la: MULIERES mordaces Hecubæ similes, quæ in canem conversa. Men. 5. 1. v. 14.
units.tr: Scolding women are like Hecuba, who was changed into a dog. Men. 5.1, v. 14.

units.la: MULIERES imprægnatæ ærumnam suam quæri solent. Epid. 4.1. v.30.
units.tr: Pregnant women are wont to complain of their troubles. Epid. 4.1, v. 30.

units.la: MUNERUM. DONORUM.
units.tr: GIFTS AND PRESENTS.

units.la: VIRTUTE bellicâ præditi donabantur paterâ aureâ. Sic Amphitruo, ob virtutem bellicam, donat aurea paterâ: qui Pterela Rex potitare est solitus. Amph. I.I. v,103,261. Sic Vopiscus Aureliano:
units.tr: Men distinguished by military valour were rewarded with a golden bowl. Thus Amphitryon, on account of his military valour, gives a golden bowl, the kind King Pterelas was accustomed to possess. Amph. I.1. v. 103, 261. Thus Vopiscus of Aurelian:

units.la: Data est ei prætereâ, cum legatus ad Persas iisset, patera, qualis solet Imperatoribus dari à Rege Persarum, in quâ insculptus erat Sol.
units.tr: Moreover, when he had gone as envoy to the Persians, he was given a bowl, such as the King of the Persians customarily gives to commanders, on which the Sun was engraved.

units.la: Muneribus ac donis placantur puellæ inprimis. Cist. I.I. v.95. Vide plura in hanc rem sup. pag. 53. Tit. Amatorum.
units.tr: Girls are above all appeased with gifts and presents. Cist. I.1. v. 95. See more on this subject above, p. 53, under the title Lovers.

units.la: MUNDICIEI.
units.tr: CLEANLINESS.

units.la: Vide Tit. Familia.
units.tr: See the title Family.

units.la: MUNDICIEI studere oportet in ædibus: nisi velint fucs haberi. Stich. I.2. v.6.
units.tr: One ought to take care of cleanliness in the house, unless they want to be taken for drones. Stich. I.2. v.6.

units.la: MUTATIONIS. PERMUTATIONIS.
units.tr: OF CHANGE; OF EXCHANGE.

units.la: PERICULOSA est omnis permutatio: præsertim rei notæ, cum ignotâ. Trin. I.2. v.25.
units.tr: Every exchange is dangerous, especially of a known thing for an unknown one. Trin. 1.2. v.25.

units.la: NATA-
units.tr: NATA-

units.la: N. NATALIS. NATALITIORUM.
units.tr: N. NATALIS. Birthdays.

units.la: VETERES anxiè admodùm, & cùm magnâ devotione ac solemnitate diem suum Natalem celebrare solebant. Quod non uno loco apparet ex Plauto nostro. Cui Authori illustrando nunc omnem operam impendimus. Itaq; nonnullam me gratiam initurum confido apud Antiquitatis studiosos: si quæcumq; de die Natali mihi in Adversarijs meis, cùm è scriptis veterum, tùm recentiorum olim collegi in hunc Locum Communem satis celebrem, quasi sub unum adspectum repræsentarem. E recentioribus duo doctissimi viri hanc materiam ex professo, quod ajunt, meditati sunt. Alter Martinus de Roa Hispan° in libb. Singularium: Alter Michael Piccartus Germanus: Professor Academiæ Noricæ in Altorff solertissimus: peculiari Oratione. Ex hisce Authoribus quasi palantibus depromam, quæ in rem nostram facient: multa ex Noctibus meis Palatinis illis additurus.
units.tr: The ancients were extremely careful, and celebrated their birthdays with great devotion and solemnity. This appears in more than one place in our Plautus. In illustrating this author I now devote all my effort to it. I trust I shall win some favour with lovers of antiquity if I set out, as it were at a single glance, whatever I once gathered on birthdays in my Adversaria, from the writings of both the ancients and the more recent authors, for this fairly well-known commonplace. Of recent writers, two very learned men have made this subject their special study, as they say: one is Martin de Roa, a Spaniard, in his books Singularium; the other is Michael Piccart, a German and a most skilful professor at the Academy of Altdorf, in a separate oration. I shall draw from these authors, who are scattered about, what will serve my purpose, adding much from my Palatine Nights.

units.la: Die igitur Natali suo sibi demum nasci videbantur: ut patet ex Plauto nostro Pseud. 3. v. 14.
units.tr: On their birthdays, then, people believed that they were only now truly born, as our Plautus shows in Pseudolus 3, line 14.

units.la: Hodiè - nate, heus! heus hodiè - nate, tibi ego dico.
units.tr: Today, birthday boy, hey! Hey, birthday boy today, I am talking to you.

units.la: Appetentem cùm rogabant, uti candidus veniret, vovebant ex Thraciæ gentis ritu: quæ candidis & atris lapillis dies lætos à tristibus distinguere solebat.
units.tr: When they asked the one approaching whether he would come bright, they made vows, following the custom of the Thracian people, who used to distinguish happy days from sad ones with white and black pebbles.

units.la: Virgilius: Clarus inoffenso procedat lumine Titan Lætificú q; dies eat omnibus æthere puro.
units.tr: Virgil: Let the bright Titan advance with unobstructed light, and let the day pass for all in pure air.

units.la: Frequenter id occurrit in Tibullo, Propertio, & Ovidio. Vide etiam Formularium Brissonij.
units.tr: This occurs often in Tibullus, Propertius and Ovid. See also Brisson's Formularium.

units.la: Postquam illuxisset Genio viri, Junoni natalitiæ fæminæ litabant: non quidem hostiâ: sed mero, h.e. vino non diluto, aut aquâ macerato: sed puro & sacrificijs apto. Ita enim ex sententiâ Varronis, æquum vid batur, ut cùm die natali mûn° annale Genio solveretur, manus à cæde ac sanguine abstinerent: ne die quâ ipsi lucem accepissent, alijs demerent.
units.tr: After the genius of the man had been honoured, women offered sacrifice to Juno of birth; not indeed with a victim, but with undiluted wine, that is, wine not mixed with water, but pure and fit for sacrifice. For according to Varro's opinion it seemed fitting that when the yearly offering was made to the genius on the birthday of the husband, they should abstain from slaughter and blood, so that on the day on which they themselves had received the light they might not take it from others.

units.la: Plautus Persa 5.1. v.17.
units.tr: Plautus, Persa 5.1, line 17.

units.la: Age, accumbe; hunc diem suavem meum Natalem agitemus amanum date aquam manibus: apponite mensam. Age puere, asummo septenu Cyathis committte hos ludos, &c.
units.tr: Come, recline; let us celebrate this sweet and lovely birthday of mine. Give water for the hands, set out the table. Come, boy, mix these games with cups of the highest seven, etc.

units.la: Tibullus lib. 1 Eleg. 7.
units.tr: Tibullus, Book 1, Elegy 7.

units.la: Huc ade & centum ludis Geniumq; choréis Concel bra, & multo tempora sunde mero.
units.tr: Come hither and celebrate the genius with a hundred games and dances, and pour wine copiously over your temples.

units.la: Hæc vini libatio seu fusio, trina erat in caput Genij: quod liquet ex eodem Tibullo lib. 4. Eleg. 3.
units.tr: This libation or pouring of wine was threefold, made over the head of the genius; as is clear from the same Tibullus, Book 4, Elegy 3.

units.la: Adhibebant quoque libum, seu placentam de farre, melle, & oleo item thus, præsertim divites.
units.tr: They also brought a cake, or flat loaf, of spelt, honey and oil, and likewise incense, especially the wealthy.

units.la: Tibullus:
units.tr: Tibullus:

units.la: Genio dum thuris honorem Libabã, Mopsopio dulcia melle feram.
units.tr: While I pour out the honour of incense to the genius, I shall bring sweet honey for the Mopsopian one.

units.la: Neque unguenta negligebant: & serta de vario flore gerebant.
units.tr: Nor did they neglect perfumes, and they wore garlands of many flowers.

units.la: Tibullus:
units.tr: Tibullus:

units.la: Ipse sups adsit Genius vt surum honores Cùm decorant sanctum florea serta comas. Illius & puro destillent tempora nardo.
units.tr: May the genius himself be present, as the garlands of flowers adorn your holy hair, and may your temples drip with pure nard.

units.la: Ad hæc sacrificia accedebant εὐχαριστίαι, sive gratiarum actiones pro tutelâ & vitâ in eum usque diem prorogatâ. Et vota concipiebantur. Optabant enim dari sibi à Genio Bonam Mentem, Bonam Famam, Bonam Fidem: ut est apud Persium Satirâ 11. Ubi vide integrum locum. Vota illa siebant voce clarâ, ut palàm ab omnibus exaudiri possent.
units.tr: To these sacrifices were added thanksgivings [εὐχαριστίαι], or acts of gratitude for protection and for life prolonged up to that day. Vows were also made. For they prayed that a good mind, good repute and good faith might be given them by the genius, as in Persius, Satire 11, where see the whole passage. These vows were made in a clear voice, so that they could be heard plainly by all.

units.la: Dè hinc post sacra illa peracta: splendidè exornabant domum: ut ibi omnia munda essent: uti colligimus ex hoc loco Plauti.
units.tr: Then, after those rites had been completed, they lavishly adorned the house, so that everything there was clean; as we gather from this passage of Plautus.

units.la: Pseud. 1. 2. v. 28. & seqq.
units.tr: Pseudolus 1.2, line 28 and following.

units.la: Tibi hoc praecipio; ut niteant aedes: habes, quod facias, propera citò: abi intro. Tu esto lecti sterniator: tu argentum eluito, sidem exstruito. Hæc cùm ego à foro revertor, facite, ut offendam parata, vorsa, sparsa, tersa, strata, lauta, strulaq, omnia, ut sint. Nam mihi hodie dies natalis est: decet eum vos omnes concelebrare.
units.tr: I order you this: let the house shine. You have something to do, hurry up quickly, go inside. You be the bed-maker, you wash the silver, you build up the hearth. When I come back from the forum, see that I find everything ready, turned, swept, scrubbed, spread, washed and tidy. For today is my birthday, and it is fitting that you all celebrate it.

units.la: Eundem apparatum exprimit quoque Augustinus Orat. 1. de Adventu:
units.tr: Augustine also expresses the same preparation, in his first Oration On the Advent:

units.la: Considerate, quando aliquis homo potens, aut Nobilis Natalem suum, aut filij sui celebrare desiderat: quanto studio ante plures dies, quicquid in domo suâ sordium invenerit, ordinet emunda-ri, quicquid ineptum, & incongruum projecit: quicquid utile & necessarium, praecipit exhiberi. Domus etiam si obscura fuerit dealbatur: pavimenta scopis mundantur: & diversis respersa floribus adornantur: quicquid etiam ad laetitiam animi, & corporis deliciàs pertinet omni solicitudine providetur.
units.tr: Consider how, when some powerful or noble man wishes to celebrate his birthday or that of his son, with what eagerness, many days beforehand, he orders everything in his house to be cleaned of filth, throws out whatever is unfit and out of place, and has whatever is useful and necessary brought forward. Even if the house is dark, it is whitewashed; the floors are swept clean and adorned, sprinkled with various flowers; and every care is taken for whatever pertains to the delight of mind and body.

units.la: Sequebatur opiparum convivium: cui adhibiti, propinqui, amici, clientes. Res notissima ex Plauto nostro locis praedictis. In illis convivijs sedebant Albati togis candidis, recentibus: & usu nondum sordidis aut obsoletis: coque vestes intactas vocat Ovidius.
units.tr: A sumptuous banquet followed, to which were invited relatives, friends and clients. This is well known from our Plautus in the passages mentioned. At those banquets people sat dressed in white togas, fresh, and not yet soiled or worn by use; Ovid calls such garments untouched.

units.la: Principes & qui lautiori fortunâ epulum publicum instituebant, ut de Augusto narrat Tacitus & Dio. Apud Ægyptios Pharao epulum publicum dedit.
units.tr: Rulers, and those of greater fortune, gave a public feast, as Tacitus and Dio tell of Augustus. Among the Egyptians Pharaoh gave a public feast.

units.la: Legimus quoque de Herodis festivitate, sed Tragicâ planè. De Persis scribit Athenæus lib. 4. natali die boves integros aliaque animantiâ majora in fornacibus assata apposuisse.
units.tr: We also read of Herod's festivity, but one that was wholly tragic. Athenaeus, Book 4, writes that the Persians set out on birthdays whole oxen and other larger animals roasted in furnaces.

units.la: Memorabile & hoc est, quòd in natalitio isto convivio in delitijs praecipuè habuerint carnem suillam: ut patet ex loco Pseud. 1. 2. v. 33.
units.tr: It is also worth remarking that at this birthday banquet they especially delighted in pork, as is clear from Pseudolus 1.2, line 33.

units.la: Pernam, callum, glandinem, sumen, facito in aquâ jaceant.
units.tr: Let the ham, the trotter, the sow's belly, and the sow's udder lie in water.

units.la: Meminit & Juvenalis Sat. x 1.
units.tr: Juvenal also mentions it, Satire 11.

units.la: Mores erat quondam festis servare diebus Et natalitium cognatis ponere lardum,Accedente nota, si quam dabat hostia, carne.
units.tr: It was once the custom to keep festive days and to serve bacon at a birthday to one's kinsmen, with the meat of the sacrificial victim added as a mark of distinction.

units.la: Eădem die Munera varia missa ab amicis & clientibus: etiam à parentibus.
units.tr: On the same day various gifts were sent by friends and clients, and also by parents.

units.la: Rud. 4. 4. v. 127.Et bulla aurea est, pater quam dedit mihi natali die.
units.tr: Rudens 4.4, line 127: And it is a golden bulla which my father gave me on my birthday.

units.la: Pseud. 3. 1. v. 9,15.Nunc nisi lenoni munus hodie misero, cras mihi potandum est flu- -ctus fullonium. Vide Tit. Fullonum.
units.tr: Pseudolus 3.1, lines 9, 15: Now unless I must give a present today to the wretched pimp, tomorrow I must drink the flood of the fullers. See the title Fullonum.

units.la: Curc. 5. 2. v. 56.Hic est annulus, quem ego tibi misi natali die.
units.tr: Curculio 5.2, line 56: This is the ring which I sent you on your birthday.

units.la: Epid. 5. 1. v. 33.Non meminisli me in aurem ad te adferre natali die?
units.tr: Epidicus 5.1, line 33: Do you not remember that I whispered to you on your birthday?

units.la: Pseud. 1. 3. v. 2,5.Mittam hodie huic suo die natali malam rem magnam & maturam.
units.tr: Pseudolus 1.3, lines 2, 5: Today, on his birthday, I shall send him a great and ripe misfortune.

units.la: Morem hunc illustrant varij authores. Symmachus lib. 1. Ep. 5. Cùm jam filiæ vestræ dies natalis appeteret, cómodum adrant, qua muneri miseratis.
units.tr: Various authors illustrate this custom. Symmachus, Book 1, Letter 5: When your daughter's birthday was approaching, you were at leisure to consider what gift you should send.

units.la: Et lib. v 1. Epist. 49.Natalitiè munere, quod frequentari à vobis communis felicitas faciet, nostrum hilaritas animum, vestrum probasti.
units.tr: And Book 7, Letter 49: By the birthday gift, which the common happiness will make to be celebrated by you, our cheerfulness has approved your feeling and ours.

units.la: Et lib. 6. Epist. 80. Lineas margaritarum feminis mittebant.
units.tr: And Book 6, Letter 80: they used to send strings of pearls to women.

units.la: Juvenalis Sat. 9.En cui tu viridem umbellam, cui succina mittasGrandia, natalis quotiès redit
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire 9: See, to whom you send a green parasol, to whom large amber, whenever the birthday returns.

units.la: Vide etiam Casaubonum ad Perf. Sat. 1. de Sardon. natalitiâ.
units.tr: See also Casaubon on Persius, Satire 1, on the Sardonian natalitia.

units.la: Poëtæ carmina miserunt: ut constat ex Tibullo Propertio.
units.tr: Poets sent poems, as is clear from Tibullus and Propertius.

units.la: Apulejus Apol. ad Critiam:Florea serta meum mel: & hæc tibi carmina dono.Carmina dono tibi: serta tuo genio.Carmina, uti Critia lux hæc optata canaturQuæ bis septeno verè tibi remeat.
units.tr: Apuleius, Apology, to Critias: Flowery garlands, my honey, and these songs I give you as a gift. Songs I give you, garlands to your genius. Songs, that this day, desired, may be sung for Critias, which returns to you truly twice seven times.

units.la: Serta autem, ut læto tibi tempore, tempora verrunt:Ætatis florem floribus ut decoret.
units.tr: Garlands, moreover, sweep the temples for you on a happy occasion, so that flowers may adorn the flower of your age.

units.la: NATATIONUM.
units.tr: SWIMMING.

units.la: PUERIS qui nare discunt, scirpea induitur ratis, qui laborent minus, facilius ut nent, & moveant manus.Aul. 4. 1. v. 10.
units.tr: For boys who are learning to swim, a raft of rushes is put on, so that those who struggle less may swim more easily and move their hands. Aulularia 4.1, line 10.

units.la: NATIONUM. POPULORUM. GENTIUM. URBIUM. INSULARUM. REGIONUM.
units.tr: NATIONS. PEOPLES. NATIONS. CITIES. ISLANDS. REGIONS.

units.la: ROMANI, immò plæræque olim gentes capite nudo fuerunt, neque pileo usi sunt, nisi in certis casibus. Unde delicati illi, & molles tanguntur Græci palliati. Curc. 2.3. v.9,14,15. & 3.1.v.19. Vide amplius Lipsi. Amphit. cap. 20. & lib. 1. Electorum cap. 23. Itemque Ant. Guibertum in Polyhistore.
units.tr: The Romans, and indeed most of the ancient peoples, went bareheaded and did not wear a cap except in certain circumstances. Hence the effeminate and soft Greeks in cloaks are mocked. Curc. 2.3. vv. 9, 14, 15, and 3.1. v. 19. See more in Lipsius, Amphitheatre, ch. 20, and Electorum book 1, ch. 23. Likewise Antonius Guibertus in Polyhistor.

units.la: PARVAM Græciam Italiam appellabant ipsam magnam Græciam. Merc. 3.1.v.27. Truc. 2.6. v.55,
units.tr: They called Italy Lesser Greece, and Greater Greece was Italy itself. Merc. 3.1. v. 27. Truc. 2.6. vv. 55.

units.la: ISTRI, Hispani, Massilienses, Illurij: finitimi. Mare superum est Adriaticum. Græcia exotica est Italia. Men. 2.1.v.10. Vide Cosmographos, & Scalig. ad Festum.
