units.tr: Istrians, Spaniards, Massilians, Illyrians: neighbours. The upper sea is the Adriatic. Italy is a foreign Greece. Men. 2.1. v. 10. See the cosmographers, and Scaliger on Festus.

units.la: VITIA sæpe derivantur in totam familiam. Pseud. 1.1.v.75. Genus nostrum semper siccoculum fuit.
units.tr: Vices are often passed down to the whole family. Pseud. 1.1. v. 75. Our race has always been dry-eyed.

units.la: POENI perfidi. Inde Punica perfidia.Pœn. Prol. v.113. Pœnus plane est.
units.tr: The Carthaginians are faithless. Hence Punic faith. Poen. Prol. v. 113. He is a Carthaginian through and through.

units.la: Et 5. 2. v. 31. Pœno nullus est Punior.
units.tr: And 5.2. v. 31. No one is more Punic than a Carthaginian.

units.la: Cicero Orat. 2. in Rull. Pœni fraudulenti ac mendaces.
units.tr: Cicero, Orations, book 2, against Rullus: The Carthaginians are deceitful and lying.

units.la: Idem de Arusp. resp.
units.tr: The same, in the speech on the haruspices.

units.la: Nos necnumero Hispanos, nec robore Gallos, nec calliditate Pœnos, nec artibus Græcos superavimus.
units.tr: We have not surpassed the Spaniards in numbers, the Gauls in strength, the Carthaginians in cunning, or the Greeks in the arts.

units.la: Syrorum natio quasi nata servituti. Trin. 2. 4. v. 141.
units.tr: The Syrian nation, as if born for slavery. Trin. 2.4. v. 141.

units.la: Umbri & Appuli habiti fuerunt rustici, illepidi & subidi homines: adeoque etiam luxus & delitiarum infamia flagrarunt: nec non crapulæ dediti. Innuit hoc Senex Mil. 3. 1. v. 52.
units.tr: The Umbrians and Apulians were regarded as rustic, uncouth and boorish people; and so they were also notorious for luxury and self-indulgence, and given over to gluttony. The old man in the Miles hints at this, 3.1. v. 52.

units.la: Post Ephesi natus sum, non in Apulia, non sum in Umbria.
units.tr: I was born after Ephesus, not in Apulia, I am not in Umbria.

units.la: Ephesus vero urbs ab elegantijs & facetijs bene audijt: ut pleni fuerunt inficetiarum Umbri. Alludit quoque Gallus ad Egnatium:
units.tr: Yet the city of Ephesus was well spoken of for its elegance and wit, whereas the Umbrians were full of boorishness. Gallus also alludes to Egnatius:

units.la: Aut porcus Umber, aut obesus Ethruscus.
units.tr: Either an Umbrian pig or a fat Etruscan.

units.la: Vide etiam Plutarch. Sympos. lib. 2. cap. 10.
units.tr: See also Plutarch, Symposiacs, book 2, ch. 10.

units.la: Campani molles & libidinosi. Trin. 2. 4. v. 144.
units.tr: The Campanians are soft and lustful. Trin. 2.4. v. 144.

units.la: Lemnii rustici inficeti. Truc. 2. 4. v. 4. Cist. 2. 1. v. 58.
units.tr: The Lemnians are rustic and uncouth. Truc. 2.4. v. 4. Cist. 2.1. v. 58.

units.la: Attica disciplina bene audijt. Cas. 3. 5. v. 24, 28.
units.tr: Attic culture has a good reputation. Cas. 3.5. vv. 24, 28.

units.la: Populares jure gentium sibi obstricti sunt ad omnia humanitatis & amicitiæ officia. Pœn. 1. 2. v. 81.
units.tr: Fellow citizens are bound to one another by the law of nations to perform all the duties of humanity and friendship. Pœn. 1.2. v. 81.

units.la: Dic quæso & impera popularitatis causa.
units.tr: Tell me, please, and give your command, for the sake of popularity.

units.la: Thessalia veneficijs infamis. Amph. 4. 5. v. 10.
units.tr: Thessaly is notorious for witchcraft. Amph. 4.5. v. 10.

units.la: Thessalus veneficus.
units.tr: A Thessalian poisoner.

units.la: Horat. l. 1. Od. 27.
units.tr: Horace, book 1, Odes 27.

units.la: Thessala venena.
units.tr: Thessalian poisons.

units.la: Propert. lib. 3. Eleg. 24.
units.tr: Propertius, book 3, Elegies 24.

units.la: Thessala saga.
units.tr: Thessalian witch.

units.la: Prov. [Greek]
units.tr: Proverb. [Greek]

units.la: Vide etiam Passeratij Prælectiones in Propertium lib 1. Eleg. 5. vers. 6.
units.tr: See also Passerat's Lectures on Propertius, book 1, Elegy 5, verse 6.

units.la: Massiliensium mores traducuntur, ut molles, & servi
units.tr: The customs of the Massilians are described as effeminate and servile

units.la: simul, sed diversis saeculis: adeoque ut potissimum ob mollitiem in proverbium abierint. Caf 5. 4. v. 1.
units.tr: at the same time, but in different ages; so that they became proverbial, chiefly for their softness. Cas. 5.4. v. 1.

units.la: De iis videndi Authores hi: Athenaeus lib. 12. pag. 523. Editionis Commelinianae Casaub. Lipsii in Comment. ad Germaniam Taciti. Cael. Rhodig. lib. 16. c. 8. Brod. Miscell. lib. 3. c. 27.
units.tr: On these matters the following authors should be consulted: Athenaeus, book 12, p. 523, in the Commelin edition; Casaubon; Lipsius in his commentary on Tacitus's Germania; Rhodiginus, book 16, ch. 8; Brodaeus, Miscellanies, book 3, ch. 27.

units.la: POENI male audiebant apud Romanos, ob aures perforatas. Poen. 5. 2. v. 21.
units.tr: The Carthaginians had a bad reputation among the Romans for their pierced ears. Poen. 5.2. v. 21.

units.la: Vide Tit. Hominum: Aurium.
units.tr: See the title Of Men: Ears.

units.la: AEGYPTII & Mauritatri. Poen. 5. 5. v. 12. Petron. Tinctli colore noctis.
units.tr: The Egyptians and Moors. Poen. 5.5. v. 12. Petronius: dyed with the colour of night.

units.la: Apul. l. 1. Horid. Quibus in corpore color est noctis.
units.tr: Apuleius, book 1, Florida: those whose bodies have the colour of night.

units.la: PRAENESTINI infulsi & barbari judicati. Trin. 3. 1. v. 7. Vide Jul. Caes. Scalig. lib. 7. Poët. c. 6. p. 905.
units.tr: The Praenestines were judged foolish and barbarous. Trin. 3.1. v. 7. See Julius Caesar Scaliger, Poetics, book 7, ch. 6, p. 905.

units.la: LYDI barbari dicti in Proverb. Bacch. 1. 2. v. 13.
units.tr: The Lydians are called barbarians in a proverb. Bacch. 1.2. v. 13.

units.la: HOMINUM natio Epidamnia, voluptarii: potatores maximi. Men. 2. 1. v. 34.
units.tr: The people of Epidamnus: pleasure-seekers and the greatest drinkers. Men. 2.1. v. 34.

units.la: POENI pultiphagi. Mostl. 3. 2. v. 146. Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: The Carthaginians are pulse-eaters. Mostell. 3.2. v. 146. See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: PICI aureos montes colunt. Aul. 4. 8. v. 1.
units.tr: The Picentes dwell on the golden mountains. Aul. 4.8. v. 1.

units.la: FILII: Nepotes non debebant honorem majorum suorum contaminare: atque ita vindices fieri honori illorum: quam illis tradiderunt. Trin. 3. 2. v. 17.
units.tr: Sons and grandsons ought not to defile the honour of their ancestors, and so become avengers of that honour which they handed down to them. Trin. 3.2. v. 17.

units.la: POENI fuerunt Pultiphagi. Unde Plautus dictus Parvus Pultiphagonides. Poen. Prol. v. 54.
units.tr: The Carthaginians were pulse-eaters. Hence Plautus was called the little son of a pulse-eater. Poen. Prol. v. 54.

units.la: Apud Catonem legitur plus punica.
units.tr: In Cato we read more Punic.

units.la: LACONES plagipatidae appellantur ob patientiam plagarum, & disciplinae. Capt. 3. 1. v. 12.
units.tr: The Laconians are called flogging-men, because of their endurance of blows and their discipline. Capt. 3.1. v. 12.

units.la: Horat. lib. 1. Od. 7. Nec me tam patiens Lacedaemon.
units.tr: Horace, book 1, Odes 7: nor Lacedaemon, so patient of me.

units.la: LYDORUM seu Tuscorum filiae ex quaestu meretricio sibi dotem quaerebant, ut author est Herodotus.
units.tr: The daughters of the Lydians, or Tuscans, earned a dowry for themselves by prostitution, as Herodotus records.

units.la: Lemnia pessimè audijt rusticitatis & inscitiæ nomine. Cist. 2. 1. v. 15. True. 2. 4. v. 4.
units.tr: Lemnos had a very bad name for rusticity and ignorance. Cist. 2.1. v. 15. Truc. 2.4. v. 4.

units.la: Arcadia abundabat asinis. Asin. 2. 2. v. 67.
units.tr: Arcadia abounded in asses. Asin. 2.2. v. 67.

units.la: Nativitatis. Generationis. Imprægnationis. Puerperii. Educationis. Partûs. Foetûs. Superfoetationis.
units.tr: Birth. Generation. Impregnation. Childbirth. Upbringing. Parturition. Foetus. Superfetation.

units.la: Infantes olim, simul ac nati forent, humi deponebantur. Ab humo pater tollebat, & in sinum recipiebat, si infantem nutriri & educari cuperet. Secus exponi voluit, & proijci. Amph. 1. 3. v. 3. Caf. Prol. v. 42, 79. True. 2. 4. v. 5.
units.tr: In former times infants, as soon as they were born, were laid on the ground. The father lifted them from the ground and took them into his bosom if he wished the infant to be nursed and reared. Otherwise he chose to have it exposed and cast out. Amph. 1. 3. v. 3. Caf. Prol. v. 42, 79. True. 2. 4. v. 5.

units.la: Si quod peperissem, id educarem, & tollerem, Bona sua me habituram omnia.
units.tr: If I had borne a child, I would have reared it and lifted it up; I would have all her goods.

units.la: Ac quia occasio est explicandi hunc quà Græcorum, quà Latinorum barbarum & immanem morem, libet huc cõijcere, quicquid olim è variijs Authoribus in Noctibus nostris Pa- latinis obnoxiè admodùm adnotaramus. Ecce igitur singulis testibus, quà pote, sua firmemus puncta. Humi collocatos fuisse infantes, suo exemplo docet Magnus ille infans Augustus, apud infantiæ, & ulterioris curriculi sui diligentissimum scriptorem Tranquillum c. 5.
units.tr: Since there is an occasion to explain this custom, barbarous and monstrous among both Greeks and Latins, I am pleased to set down here whatever I once noted, with great care, from various authors in my Palatine Nights. Behold, then, I will confirm our points with individual witnesses, as far as I can. That infants were laid on the ground is shown by the example of that great infant Augustus, according to Tranquillus, the most diligent writer of his infancy and later course, c. 5.

units.la: Cum C. Lœtorius adolescens patricij generis, in deprecandâ gravere adulterij pœnâ, prater ætatem, atq; natales, hoc quoq; Patribus Consc. allegaret se esse possessorem ac velut ædituum soli, quod primum D. Augustus nascens tetigisset : decretum est, &c.
units.tr: When Gaius Loetorius, a young man of patrician birth, pleading against the severe penalty for adultery, alleged to the Conscript Fathers, besides his age and birth, that he was the owner and, as it were, the guardian of the ground which the divine Augustus first touched when he was born: it was decided, etc.

units.la: Idem Nerone cap. 6.
units.tr: The same, Nero, ch. 6.

units.la: Neronatus est Antij ante novem menses, quàm Tiberius excessit 8. Kal. Jan. tantum quod exoriente sole, pane ut radys prius, quàm terra contingeretur.
units.tr: Nero was born at Antium nine months before Tiberius died, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, just as the sun was rising, so that he touched the earth with his rays almost before the earth could touch him.

units.la: Statius lib. 1. Thebaid. v. 60. ——— simé de patre cadentem Fovisti gremio.
units.tr: Statius, Thebaid, book 1, v. 60: ...you cherished in your lap him who fell at once from his father's side.

units.la: Tertullianus:
units.tr: Tertullian:

units.la: Dum prima etiam constitutio infantis super terram, statim ei Dea sacrum est.
units.tr: While the infant is first set upon the earth, the goddess is at once consecrated to him.

units.la: Dein humo infantem sustulit pater & in sinum recepit, pro suo-que agnovit. Iterum Tranquillus in Julio c. 11. de filio è Cleo-patra:
units.tr: Then the father lifted the infant from the ground, received it into his bosom, and acknowledged it as his own. Again Tranquillus, in Julius, c. 11, concerning the son by Cleopatra:

units.la: M. Antonium agnitum etiam ab eo Senatui affirmavit.
units.tr: He affirmed to the Senate that Marcus Antonius had also acknowledged him.

units.la: Agnitum tolli jubebat, educariqué: ut patet ex nostro, loco su-pradicto.
units.tr: Having been acknowledged, he ordered him to be lifted up and reared, as is clear from our passage cited above.

units.la: Terentius Andriâ:
units.tr: Terence, Andria:

units.la: Quodquid peperisset, decreverunt tollere.
units.tr: Whatever she had borne, they decided to raise.

units.la: Ibidem: Nam quod peperisset, jussit tolli.
units.tr: In the same place: "For whatever she had borne, he ordered it to be raised."

units.la: Idem Heaut. 4. 1.
units.tr: The same, Heautontimorumenos, 4. 1.

units.la: Meministi me esse gravidam, & mihi te magnopere intermi-natum, si puellam parerem, nolle tolli. CH Scio, quid fe-ceris. Sustulisti. SY Sic est factum, domina.
units.tr: You remember that I am pregnant, and that you strictly warned me that if I bore a girl you would not want her raised. CH: I know what you did. You raised her. SY: So it was done, mistress.

units.la: Ex quibus locis & hoc amplius perspicuum fit, sublationem pa-tri ac matri communem fuisse. Sed ecce, consonant & hi autho-res.
units.tr: From these passages it becomes still clearer that the lifting up was common to father and mother. But see, these authors agree as well.

units.la: Statius Epicéd. in filium:
units.tr: Statius, Epicedion on his son:

units.la: ——— meus ille, meus, tollere cadentem Excepit, & vinclum genitali carmine fovi.
units.tr: "That one was mine, mine: as he fell, I took him up, and I cherished the bond with a song of begetting."

units.la: Idem Epicéd. in Glauciam:
units.tr: The same, Epicedion on Glaucias:

units.la: ——— raptum sed protinus alvo Sustulit exultans, ac primâ lucida voce Astra salutantem Dominum sibi mente dicavit, Amplexu ǵ sinu, tulit, & genuisse putavit.
units.tr: "But straightway, exulting, she lifted him, snatched from the womb, and with her first bright voice dedicated him in mind to the Lord who greets the stars; with embrace and bosom she bore him, and thought she had begotten him."

units.la: Claudian. in Rufin. 1.
units.tr: Claudian, Against Rufinus, book 1:

units.la: ——— quem prima meo de matre cadentem Suscepi gremio.
units.tr: "Whom I received in my lap, as he first fell from my mother's womb."

units.la: Juvenal. Sat. 9.
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire 9:

units.la: Tollis enim & libris actorum spargere gaudes Argumenta viri, foribus suspende coronas: Jam patere.
units.tr: "For you lift him up, and you delight to scatter in the books the deeds of the man; hang up the garlands on the doors: now open."

units.la: Terentius Adelph.
units.tr: Terence, Adelphi:

units.la: Qui sine ac jurabat se unum numquam victurum diem: Qui in suo gremio positurum puerum dicebat.
units.tr: "He who swore that he would never live another day; he who said that he would place the boy in his own lap."

units.la: Seneca libb. de morali Philos.
units.tr: Seneca, books of moral philosophy:

units.la: Quid ergo est? quare apud Poetas falacissimus Jupiter desierit tollere liberos.
units.tr: "What then is it? Why has the most deceitful Jupiter among the poets ceased to lift up his children?"

units.la: Quos vero nollent alere, eos exponebant, & pro abdicatis habebant.
units.tr: But those whom they were unwilling to rear, they exposed and held to be disowned.

units.la: Apud Græcos quidem hic exponendi mos fuit, ut liberos in vasis fictilibus ad compita exponerent, quo magis obvij inventu, & faciliores absportatu essent: si quis forte illos educare non gravaretur.
units.tr: Among the Greeks this custom of exposing existed: they set their children in earthen vessels at crossroads, so that they would be more easily found by passers-by and more easily carried off, if perhaps someone was not unwilling to rear them.

units.la: Hunc morem tangit Aristophanes in Ranis de Oedipode exposito:
units.tr: Aristophanes, in the Frogs, alludes to this custom, speaking of Oedipus exposed:

units.la: Πῶς γὰρ ὅτε λὴ πρῶτον μὲν αὐτὸν γενόμενον χειμῶν᾽ ὀντ᾽ ἐξέδε-σαν ἐν ὀσφάχῳ.
units.tr: "For how, when he was first born, they exposed him in a potsherd, as a babe in swaddling clothes" [Πῶς γὰρ ὅτε λὴ πρῶτον μὲν αὐτὸν γενόμενον χειμῶν᾽ ὀντ᾽ ἐξέδε-σαν ἐν ὀσφάχῳ.]

units.la: Et Terentius Andr. 4. 4.
units.tr: And Terence, Andria, 4. 4:

units.la: M. O hominem audacem! D. Verum vidi cantharum suf-farcinatum.
units.tr: "M. O bold man! D. Indeed, I saw a pot stuffed full."

units.la: Athenis tale quid fuisse, meminit Suidas:
units.tr: Suidas records that something of this kind existed at Athens:

units.la: Κυνὸσαργες τόπος ἐν τῇ Ἀττικῇ, ἐν ᾧ τὰς νόθους τῶν παίδων ἐτίθεσαν.
units.tr: "Kynosarges, a place in Attica, where they used to place the illegitimate children" [Κυνὸσαργες τόπος ἐν τῇ Ἀττικῇ, ἐν ᾧ τὰς νόθους τῶν παίδων ἐτίθεσαν.]

units.la: Cynosargas locus in Attica, ubi spurios infantes ponebant.
units.tr: Cynosarges, a place in Attica, where they placed spurious infants.

units.la: Causa hæc additur: quia nimirum Herculis ibi templum, qui & ipse inter spurios fuit.
units.tr: The reason given is that there was a temple there of Hercules, who himself was among the spurious.

units.la: Romæ Lactariam Columnam fuisse in foro olitorio, ait Festus: quòd ibi infantes lacte alendos deferebant.
units.tr: At Rome, says Festus, there was a Milk Column in the Forum Olitorium, because there they brought infants to be nourished with milk.

units.la: Victor in descriptione Urbis:
units.tr: Victor, in his description of the City:

units.la: Forum olitorium. In eo columna lactaria, ad quam infantes lac-te alendos deferunt.
units.tr: The Forum Olitorium. In it is a milk column, to which they bring infants to be fed with milk.

units.la: Kkk Eos Eos Græci Θερσίτης & χαμαιζευτὴς, humi-repentes. Latini Altel-los vocarunt.
units.tr: The Greeks called such children Thersites and chamaizeutes, "crawlers on the ground" [Θερσίτης, χαμαιζευτὴς]; the Latins called them Altellos.

units.la: At cur sic expositi? Caussam invenio non unam.
units.tr: But why were they exposed in this way? I find not one cause.

units.la: Aristoteles lib. 7. cap. Polit. Vult numerum prolium definiri, & si cui is augeatur, ac duplicetur, priusquam in vitam veniant, abortum esse procurandum.
units.tr: Aristotle, Politics, book 7: he wants the number of children to be fixed, and if anyone's number is increased and doubled, abortion should be brought about before they come into life.

units.la: Abortus igitur mitior loco Expositionis fuit.
units.tr: Abortion, therefore, was milder than exposure.

units.la: Romulus (teste Dionysio Halicarnasseo lib. 11. p. 88.) lege quadam omnem masculam prolem voluit educari, & è fœmellis primogenitas. Nihil autem, quod natum esset, occidere ante tricanij tempus, nisi aliquid mutilum aut monstrosum statim à partu esset. Hæc enim talia non vetuit exponi, sic tamen, ut parentes prius è vicinià ostenderent, si & ijs ita videretur.
units.tr: Romulus (according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 11, p. 88) by a certain law wished every male child to be reared, and of females the firstborn. Nothing that was born was to be killed before the age of three, unless it was maimed or monstrous from birth. Such children he did not forbid to be exposed, provided however that the parents first showed them to their neighbours, if these also judged it right.

units.la: Apulejanus tamen pater Milef. x. peregrè proficiscens, sine dissimine, mandavit uxori suæ, ut si sexus sequioris edidisset fœtus, protinus quod esset natum, necaretur. Idem videas apud Terent. Heaut. 4. 1.
units.tr: Yet the father in Apuleius (Milesian Tales, book 10), setting out abroad without delay, ordered his wife that if she brought forth a child of the weaker sex, whatever was born should at once be killed. See the same in Terence, Heautontimorumenos, 4. 1.

units.la: Expositi etiam mutili, debiles, monstrosique liberi. Seneca Pater lib. 4. Controv. 33. Debilitans expositos. Et Seneca filius de Irâ lib. 1. c. 15.
units.tr: Maimed, weak and monstrous children were also exposed. Seneca the Elder, Controversies, book 4, 33: "maiming the exposed." And Seneca the Younger, On Anger, book 1, ch. 15.

units.la: Alij expositi ob paupertatem parentum, quo alendo non essent. Vide Lactant. lib. 6. c. 20. Præsertim verò calamitosis temporibus, si fames, bellum, & id genus alia familiam urgerent. Vide Suet. Calig. cap. 5. & Claud. cap. 27. Invenies forte alias causas, quas è lectione sedulà Authorum huc transferes.
units.tr: Others were exposed because of their parents' poverty, since they could not feed them. See Lactantius, book 6, ch. 20. Especially in calamitous times, when famine, war and that kind of thing pressed upon the family. See Suetonius, Caligula, ch. 5, and Claudius, ch. 27. You will perhaps find other causes, which you may carry over here from diligent reading of the authors.

units.la: Sed quid tamen Expositis factum? Etiam hic non unum institutum parentum video. Plerumque Gladiatoribus traditi, qui ad artem suam aluerunt, puta si formâ essent vulgarià. At si venustâ nimis, oculos eripuerunt, Eunuchumque Reginæ alicui tradiderunt, quod alibi in Tranquillo meminime legere.
units.tr: But what, after all, became of the exposed? Here too I see no single practice of parents. Mostly they were handed over to gladiators, who reared them for their art, if they were of ordinary appearance. But if they were very beautiful, they put out their eyes and gave them to some queen as eunuchs, which I recall reading nowhere else in Tranquillus.

units.la: Alij itidem servi facti eorum, qui illos suscepuerunt, monente id Senecâ Patre Controversiâ modò dictâ. Et Trajano ad Plinium lib. 10. Epist. 72.
units.tr: Others likewise became the slaves of those who took them up, as Seneca the Elder advises in the controversy just mentioned, and as Trajan writes to Pliny, book 10, letter 72.

units.la: Item l. 1. Cod. Theodof. de Infant. Expositione: ac præterea ex lege 8. de Pignoribus & hypoth. junêtâ lege 6. ejusdem Tit. utraque ex lib. 73. Ulpiani ad Edictum. De hoc tamen jure antiquato vide Cujacium ad Tit. 1. lib. 1. Sent. Pauli: nec non Guil. Ranchinum Var. lib. 1. c. 2. Omnium tamen immanissimum, qp Expositos in solitudinem abjecerunt feris in prædam.
units.tr: Likewise law 1 of the Theodosian Code, on the exposure of infants; and besides, law 8 on pledges and hypothecs, joined with law 6 of the same title, both from book 73 of Ulpian on the Edict. On this right, now abolished, see Cujas on title 1 of book 1 of the Sentences of Paul, and also Guillaume Ranchin, Variae Lectiones, book 1, ch. 2. Yet the most savage of all were those who cast the exposed into solitude to become prey for wild beasts.

units.la: Suidas: Ἐκπθέναι τὸ βρέφος: ἀντὶ δὲ εἰς Coɛἀν θηρίοις, ἢ ἡ ἄλλοις εἰς ἀσαφθο- ρὰν παραπθέναι ἀπ' ἐρημίας.
units.tr: Suidas: "To expose the infant: either to set it down for wild beasts in a solitary place, or to abandon it to destruction from desolation" [Ἐκτιθέναι τὸ βρέφος: ἢ εἰς θηρία ἐν ἐρημίᾳ, ἢ εἰς ἀφθαρσίαν ἐκ τῆς ἐρημίας παραθεῖναι.]

units.la: Quintilianus Declamator.
units.tr: Quintilian, Declamations:

units.la: Velut expositos in aliquâ solitudine, aut in mariâ projectos.
units.tr: As if exposed in some solitude, or cast out into the sea.

units.la: Solebant etiam strangulare.
units.tr: They also used to strangle them.

units.la: Arnobius lib. 8.
units.tr: Arnobius, book 8:

units.la: Vos enim (Roman.) video procreatos filios, nunc feris & avibus exponere, nunc adstrangulatos misero mortis genere illidere.
units.tr: "For I see, Romans, that you, having begotten sons, now expose them to wild beasts and birds, now dash them down, strangled, in a wretched kind of death."

units.la: Lactant. lib. 6. c. 20.
units.tr: Lactantius, book 6, ch. 20:

units.la: Non possunt innocentes existimari, qui viscera sua in prædam canibus objiciunt, & quantum in ipsis est, crudelius necant, quàm si strangulassent.
units.tr: "Those cannot be thought innocent who throw their own flesh to dogs as prey, and who, so far as in them lies, kill more cruelly than if they had strangled them."

units.la: Idem lib. 5. cap. 9.
units.tr: The same, book 5, ch. 9:

units.la: Qui natos ex se pueros, aut strangulant, aut si nimium pý fuerint, exponunt.
units.tr: "Those who either strangle the children born of them, or, if they are too many, expose them."

units.la: Tertull. ad uxorem lib. 1. cap. 5.
units.tr: Tertullian, To His Wife, book 1, ch. 5.

units.la: Querenda nobis onera sunt (liberorum) quæ & à gentilium profanis vitantur, quæ legibus locantur, quæ parricidiis expugnantur.
units.tr: The burdens of children are to be lamented: they are avoided even by the profane heathen, they are put out under the terms of laws, and they are carried out by parricides.

units.la: Cæterùm, istam immanitatem à Christianis Principibus postmodùm coercitam, docet Lipsius Centur. primâ Epist. ad Belgas LXXXV.
units.tr: Moreover, that savagery was afterwards restrained by Christian princes, as Lipsius teaches in the first Century, Epistle 85 to the Belgians.

units.la: Ac primi quidem vetuerunt Valentinianus, Valens, & Gratia-nus: quorum lex in utroque Codice Theodosij & Justiniani ex-stat ad Legem Corneliam de Sicarijs:
units.tr: And the first to forbid it were Valentinian, Valens and Gratian, whose law stands in both the Codex of Theodosius and the Codex of Justinian, under the Lex Cornelia on assassins.

units.la: Si quis necandi infantis piaculum aggressus, aggressave sit, erit capitale istud malum.
units.tr: If anyone has undertaken the crime of killing an infant, whether man or woman, that shall be a capital crime.

units.la: Atque haec sufficiant illustrando barbaro huic Ethnicorum mo-ri. Plura huc e quotidiana lectione Authorum, quà Graecorum, quà Latinorum adscribet Humanitatis & Antiquitatis indaga-tor.
units.tr: Let these suffice to illustrate this barbarous custom of the heathens. An investigator of humanity and antiquity will add more from his daily reading of authors, both Greek and Latin.

units.la: Vide etiam Bernartium ad Statij lib. II. & somnium Astyagis apud Justinum lib. I. & Val. Max. lib. I. c. 7.
units.tr: See also Bernartius on Statius, Book II, the dream of Astyages in Justin, Book I, and Valerius Maximus, Book I, chapter 7.

units.la: Olim non statim, ut erat natus infans aliquis, & tolli jussus, pro vitali & γονίμῳ partu habebatur: sed aliquam multi expectaban-tur dies, qui fidem facerent vitalis foetus. Dehinc ubi plena fides, lustrabatur, atque nomen ei imponebatur. Illos dies appellabant Lustricos.
units.tr: In former times a newborn child was not at once regarded as a viable and legitimate birth [γονίμῳ] merely because it had been born and ordered to be exposed. Instead, several days were awaited, to give assurance that the offspring was viable. Then, when full confidence was had, the child was purified and given its name. They called those days the Lustric days.

units.la: Festus:
units.tr: Festus:

units.la: Lustrici dies infantum appellantur: puellarum Octavus: Pue-rorum Nonus: quia his lustrantur, atque eis nomina impo-nuntur.
units.tr: The Lustric days of infants are so called: for girls the eighth, for boys the ninth, because on these days they are purified and given their names.

units.la: In diebus discrimen ponunt, & observant Authores.
units.tr: Authors draw a distinction between the days and observe them.

units.la: Plutarch. Quaest. Rom. c 11.
units.tr: Plutarch, Roman Questions, chapter 11.

units.la: Διὰ πῶν μὲν παίδων τοῖς ὀρφεσιν ἐναπαίοις, ταῖς δὲ θήλεσιν ὀγ-δοαίως τὰ ὀνόματα τίθενται.
units.tr: For boys the names are given on the ninth day, for girls on the eighth [Διὰ πῶν μὲν παίδων τοῖς ὀρφεσιν ἐναπαίοις, ταῖς δὲ θήλεσιν ὀγδοαίως τὰ ὀνόματα τίθενται].

units.la: Macrobius lib. I. Saturn. cap. 16.
units.tr: Macrobius, Saturnalia, Book I, chapter 16.

units.la: Est enim Nundina Romanorum Dea, a nono die nascentium nuncupata, qui Lustricus dicitur. Est autem lustricus dies, quo lustrantur, & nomen accipiunt: sed iis in maribus no-nus, octavus est feminis.
units.tr: For Nundina is the goddess of the Romans, named from the ninth day after birth, which is called the lustric day. The lustric day is the day on which they are purified and receive their name: for males it is the ninth day, for females the eighth.

units.la: M. Antonius Imperator videtur mutasse, ac tricesimum diem prafinisse.
units.tr: The Emperor Marcus Antoninus seems to have changed this and fixed the thirtieth day.

units.la: Ita enim Capitolinus de eo:
units.tr: For Capitolinus says of him:

units.la: Jussit apud Praefectos aerarij Saturni nnumquemq; civium na-tos li. tos liberos profiteri, intra tricesimum diem nomine impositô. Vbi etiam legitur intra tertium diem.
units.tr: He ordered that each of the citizens should register his born children with the prefects of the treasury of Saturn within thirty days, with the name given. Elsewhere it is read "within the third day."

units.la: Apud Græcos modò septimâ, modò decimâ die id factitatum legimus: quando scilic. propinquos convocabant, & amicos: atque tum etiam sacrificabant: & nomen infanti imponebant: illisque omnibus convivium celebrabant. Id patet ex multis Authoribus.
units.tr: Among the Greeks we read that this was done sometimes on the seventh day, sometimes on the tenth: when they summoned relatives and friends, and then also sacrificed, gave the infant its name, and held a feast for them all. This is clear from many authors.

units.la: Polyænus Stratag. lib. 6. in Jasone:
units.tr: Polyaenus, Stratagems, Book 6, on Jason:

units.la: Καὶ διὰ ποτὲ παιδίον γεννηθέντος αὐτῷ μέλλοντι ὄνομα τίθεσθαι τὰς ἀδελφὰς Στρατονίκας καλέσας, παρεκάλεσε τὸν ἀδελφὸν προσῆναι τῆς ὑποδοχῆς.
units.tr: And once, when a child had been born to him and he was about to give it a name, he called his sisters Stratonice and asked his brother to attend the reception [Καὶ διὰ ποτὲ παιδίον γεννηθέντος αὐτῷ μέλλοντι ὄνομα τίθεσθαι τὰς ἀδελφὰς Στρατονίκας καλέσας, παρεκάλεσε τὸν ἀδελφὸν προσῆναι τῆς ὑποδοχῆς].

units.la: Ibidem:
units.tr: Likewise:

units.la: Μετὰ ἀπυδῆς ὅτι τὸ δέπνον ἦλθε, ἡ τῷ ἀδελφῷ ἀπουδῶν κατάσχειν ἐπεμψεν, ἡ κύριον ἂν εἶναι τῆς θέσεως ἕ ὀνόματος ἕ παιδίου.
units.tr: After a quarrel arose over the dinner, he sent for his brother so that he might either hold back the dispute or be the one who decided the placing of the child's name [Μετὰ ἀπυδῆς ὅτι τὸ δέπνον ἦλθε, ἡ τῷ ἀδελφῷ ἀπουδῶν κατάσχειν ἐπεμψεν, ἡ κύριον ἂν εἶναι τῆς θέσεως ἕ ὀνόματος ἕ παιδίου].

units.la: Suidas:
units.tr: Suidas:

units.la: Ἐὰν ἦν παιδῶν συγγενομένων τοῖς Ἀθηναίων ἀσοῖς τὴ δεκάτη τῶν νυκτῶν ὑπὸ τῆς γενέσεως συγκαλεῖσθαι τὰς ὠρὰς πατρὸς ἡ μητρὸς οἰκείας, ἡ τὰς ἐγγύτατα φίλης, ἡ παρόντων ἐκείνων τὰ ἑ ὀνόματα τοῖς παισὶ τίθεσθαι, ἡ χαλλιερεῖσθαι τοῖς θεοῖς, ἔπειτα ἐυαγχεῖσθαι τὰς συγγενυθόντας.
units.tr: If, when children were born to Athenian citizens, on the tenth day after the birth the father's or mother's kin, or those closest friends, were summoned together, and in their presence the names were given to the children, and they sacrificed to the gods, and then feasted those who had gathered [Ἐὰν ἦν παιδῶν συγγενομένων τοῖς Ἀθηναίων ... ἔπειτα ἐυαγχεῖσθαι τὰς συγγενυθόντας].

units.la: Illud sacrificium & convivium vocabatur Δεκάτη.
units.tr: That sacrifice and feast was called the Dekate (the tenth).

units.la: Inde δεκάτην θύειν, & δεκάτην ἐστιάσαι dicebantur parentes.
units.tr: Hence parents were said to "sacrifice the tenth" and "feast the tenth."

units.la: Aristophanes Avibus:
units.tr: Aristophanes, Birds:

units.la: Οὐκ ἄρα θύω τὴν δεκάτην ταύτης ἐγώ;
units.tr: Do I not, then, sacrifice the tenth day for this one [Οὐκ ἄρα θύω τὴν δεκάτην ταύτης ἐγώ;]?

units.la: ἡ τούνομα ὥστερ παιδίῳ νῦν δὴ τέμνειν.
units.tr: Or cut its name, just as for a child now [ἡ τούνομα ὥστερ παιδίῳ νῦν δὴ τέμνειν].

units.la: Vbi Scholiastes:
units.tr: Where the scholiast says:

units.la: Σαφὲς ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν παίδων ἐτίθεσαν τῇ δεκάτῃ.
units.tr: It is clear that they gave the names of children on the tenth day [Σαφὲς ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν παίδων ἐτίθεσαν τῇ δεκάτῃ].

units.la: Hesychius:
units.tr: Hesychius:

units.la: Δεκάτην θύσειν τῇ δεκάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ, ὅτε τὰ ὀνόματα ἕ βρέφεσιν ἐτέθεσαν.
units.tr: To sacrifice the tenth on the tenth day, when they gave names to the infants [Δεκάτην θύσειν τῇ δεκάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ, ὅτε τὰ ὀνόματα ... ἐτέθεσαν].

units.la: Euripides Electrâ:
units.tr: Euripides, Electra:

units.la: Ἡκω ζας, εἶμαι, τῶν ἐμῶν λοχευμάτων. τούτων ὑπὲρ μυθύσσον. ὑ δ' οἷσί ἐγώ, Δεκάτῃ σελήνῃ παιδὸς, ὡς νομίζεται.
units.tr: I have come, as I am, of my own childbirths, and I speak about these. For the child's tenth moon, as is customary [Ἡκω ζας, εἶμαι, τῶν ἐμῶν λοχευμάτων ... Δεκάτῃ σελήνῃ παιδὸς, ὡς νομίζεται].

units.la: Interdum id septimâ quoque die factitatum : ut colligimus ex Aristotele Hist. Animal. lib. 7. c. ult.
units.tr: Sometimes this was also done on the seventh day, as we gather from Aristotle, History of Animals, Book 7, last chapter.

units.la: Τὰ πρὸς τοῖς διὰ παιδία ἀναιρεῖται τοῖς τῆς ἀβδομῆς. Διὸ ἢ τὰ ὀρθμα- τα τότε τίθενται, ὡς πισέυοντες ἤδη μέλλον τῆς σωτηρίας.
units.tr: Those who are born ... are destroyed on the seventh day. Therefore names are then given, as if they were now trusted to be safe [Τὰ πρὸς τοῖς διὰ παιδία ἀναιρεῖται τοῖς τῆς ἀβδομῆς. Διὸ ... τίθενται, ὡς πισέυοντες ἤδη μέλλον τῆς σωτηρίας].

units.la: Harpocration :
units.tr: Harpocration:

units.la: Τοῖς ἀποτυθεῖσι παιδίοις τὰς ἐβδομάδας ἢ τὰς δεκάδας ἤγον, ἡ τάγε ὀνόματα ἐτίθεντο ἀβροῖς οἱ μὲν ἐλάδομ, ὡς ἢ ὁ ῥήτωρ, οἱ δὲ τῆ δε- κάτῃ.
units.tr: For infants who had been exposed they observed the seventh or the tenth day, and they gave names either on the seventh day, as the orator did, or on the tenth [Τοῖς ἀποτυθεῖσι παιδίοις τὰς ἐβδομάδας ἢ τὰς δεκάδας ἤγον ... οἱ μὲν ἐλάδομ, ὡς ἢ ὁ ῥήτωρ, οἱ δὲ τῆ δεκάτῃ].

units.la: Luftrandi autem partes illo die proprie erant piatricum mulier- cularum : quæ anus recoctæ fuerunt ; dicebanturque σωμά- κτειαι vel περιμάκτειαι Milite 3. 1. v. 100.
units.tr: The duty of purifying on that day properly belonged to the midwives, the old women who had nursed; they were called sōmaktriai or perimaktriai. Plautus, Miles Gloriosus 3.1, v. 100.

units.la: Tum piatricem clementer non potest, quin munerem.
units.tr: "Then the midwife, being kindly, cannot but give a gift."

units.la: Ubi tamen sequi malim vestigia lectionis : quæ est in MSS. Ca- merario - Palatinis : patritam. Nec parùm miror, cur Coleria- nam hariolationem Taubmannus prætulerit lectioni ei, quæ MSS. codd. maximè affinis erat. Sed omnes nobis videmur esse belli & saperdæ : cùm simus copri.
units.tr: Here I would rather follow the reading found in the Camerarius and Palatine manuscripts, "patritam." I am rather surprised why Taubmann preferred Colerus's guess to the reading that is closest to the manuscripts. But we all seem to be fine fellows and salted fish, since we are all dung-beetles.

units.la: Cæterùm diem illum Gregorius Nazianzenus appellat ὀνομα- σίαν : alij ἑορτὴν ὀνομάτων. Glossæ : Nominalia : ὀνομασία.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen calls that day onomasia, others call it "the feast of names." The glosses: Nominalia = onomasia.

units.la: Symmachus Epist. ad Flavianum fratrem lustralem solemnita- tem nominat generatim. Tertullianus Nominalia vocat libro de Idololatria c. 17. Circa officia verò privatarum & communium, ut togapura, ut sponsalium, ut nuptialium, ut nominalium.
units.tr: Symmachus, in his letter to his brother Flavianus, names the lustral festival in general terms. Tertullian, in On Idolatry chapter 17, calls it Nominalia: "Concerning the duties of private and public life, such as the toga, betrothals, weddings, and namings."

units.la: Nomina autem proximi dare solent : qui ritus etiamnum hodiè observatur.
units.tr: The parents usually give the names, and this custom is still observed today.

units.la: Suetonius Nerone cap. 6.
units.tr: Suetonius, Nero, chapter 6.

units.la: Futuræ felicitatis signum evidens : lustrico die exstitit. Nam C. Cæsar, rogante sorore, ut infanti ei quod vellet, nomen da- ret, intuens Claudium, ejus darefe dixit.
units.tr: A clear sign of future good fortune appeared on the lustric day. For when his sister asked Gaius Caesar to give the infant whatever name he liked, he looked at Claudius and said it should be given his name.

units.la: Ubi nomen pro pronomine capiendum : quia ipsa gentilia no- mina certa semper eademque erant : at pronomina modò mu- tabant.
units.tr: Here "nomen" must be taken as a pronoun, because the Gentile names were always fixed and the same, whereas the pronouns alone changed.

units.la: Porrò, quinto die à partu Græcæ mulieres sacrificabant, & infantem circa aram curriculo gestant: & obstetrices purgabant manus suas: eoúne τὰ ἀμφιδρόμια dicta.
units.tr: Moreover, on the fifth day after birth, Greek women sacrificed and carried the infant in a circuit round the altar, and the midwives cleansed their hands; hence the rite is called the amphidromia.

units.la: Meminit Plautus noster in fabulâ palliatâ Truc. 2. 4. v. 30.
units.tr: Our Plautus mentions it in the comedy in Greek dress, Truculentus 2.4, v. 30.

units.la: Quin DIs sacrificare hodiè pro puero volo.
units.tr: "Indeed, I want to sacrifice to the gods today for the boy."

units.la: Quinto die quod fieri oportet, DIN. Censeo.
units.tr: "On the fifth day, what ought to be done. I think so."

units.la: Auctor Proverbiorum:
units.tr: The author of the Proverbs:

units.la: Ἀ μφιδρομίαν τὴν πέμπτην ἀγυνιν ὅπ᾽ τοῖς βρέφεσιν, ἐν ᾗ ἀποκαλεῖ- γοντα τὰς χεῖρας ἀὶ σωα-λαμενα τῆς μιώσεως: τὸ δὲ βρέφος παραφέρυσι τε, ἰ τὴν ἀσίαν προέχοντες, ᾧ δῶρα πέμπουσιν οἱ ᾿Αεσ-σήκοντς ὡς ὅπι τὸ πλεῖσον πολύποδας ᾗ σπλίας τῇ λεκάνῃ, ὅτε τὸ ὄνομα τίθεται.
units.tr: The amphidromia is the fifth festival for infants, on which they wash their hands and are kept safe from harm; the infant is carried around, and relatives send gifts, mostly octopus and entrails for the bowl, when the name is given [Ἀμφιδρομίαν τὴν πέμπτην ἑορτὴν ἐπὶ τοῖς βρέφεσιν ...].

units.la: Ephippus in Geryone:
units.tr: Ephippus, in Geryon:

units.la: Οὐ κνίσα κρύει ῥινὸς ὑπερσχὰς ἄκρας Ἀμφιδρομίων ὄντων.
units.tr: The savour of fat does not rise over the top of the nose, since there are amphidromia [Οὐ κνίσα κρύει ῥινὸς ὑπερσχὰς ἄκρας Ἀμφιδρομίων ὄντων].

units.la: Eodem die munera quoque obtulerunt matri puerperæ.
units.tr: On the same day they also offered gifts to the mother who had given birth.

units.la: Plautus ibidem Truc. 2. 4. v. 72.
units.tr: Plautus, in the same play, Truculentus 2.4, v. 72.

units.la: Non audes aliquod mihi dare munusculum?
units.tr: "Do you not dare give me some little gift?"

units.la: Æschylus Eumen. primis vocat γαιδλιον δόσιν.
units.tr: Aeschylus, Eumenides, calls the first of these the gift of the birthday [γενέθλιον δόσιν].

units.la: Terentius Phorm. 1. 1. v. 12.
units.tr: Terence, Phormio 1.1, v. 12.

units.la: Porrò autem Geta ferietur alio munere: ubi erit puero natalis dies: ubi initiabunt, omne hoc mater auferet: puer caussa erit mittundi.
units.tr: "Moreover, Geta will be struck with another gift, when the boy has his birthday, when they will initiate him; the mother will take all of this away; the boy will be the reason for the sending."

units.la: Utrum autem puer vitalis esset nec ne, Pilumni lectum contulebant.
units.tr: Whether the child was viable or not, they used to bring in the couch of Pilumnus.

units.la: Servius:
units.tr: Servius:

units.la: Varro Pilumnum & Picumnum infantium Deos esse ait, ei q. pro puerperâ lectum in atrio sterni, dum exploretur, an vitalis sit, qui natus est.
units.tr: Varro says that Pilumnus and Picumnus are gods of infants, and that a couch is spread in the atrium for the woman in childbirth, while it is examined whether the child that has been born is viable.

units.la: Eodem spectabat mensa Junonis: quae per totam hebdomadam proponebatur.
units.tr: To the same purpose belonged the table of Juno, which was set out throughout the whole week.

units.la: Tertullianus de Anima c. 39.
units.tr: Tertullian, On the Soul, chapter 39.

units.la: Cui hominum non adhaerebit spiritus nequam, ab ipsa etiam jam nata nativitatis animas aucupabundus, vel qua invitatus, tota illa puerperii superstitione? Ita omnes idololatriae obstetrice nascuntur, dum ipsi adhuc uteri infulis apud Idola confectu redimiti, genimina sua daemoniorum candidata profitentur: dum in partu Lucina & Diana ejulatur: dum per totam hebdomadam Junoni mensa proponitur: dum ultima die fata scribunda advocantur.
units.tr: Which of men does not have an evil spirit clinging to him, hunting for souls even from the moment of their birth, or invited by that whole superstition of childbirth? Thus all are born with the midwifery of idolatry: while they themselves are still wrapped in the fillets of the womb, dedicated before the idols, they profess their offspring consecrated to demons; while in labour Lucina and Diana are invoked; while a table is set out for Juno throughout the week; while on the last day the fates are summoned to be written.

units.la: Eadem die omina captabant ex nomine: vel ex ijs omnibus, quae ab ejus horoscopo ad eum diem usque contigerant. Idque vocabant Fata.
units.tr: On the same day they took omens from the name, or from all the events that had befallen the child from his horoscope up to that day. This they called the "fates."

units.la: Ausonius Parental. de Aemylio Magno Arborio:
units.tr: Ausonius, Parentalia, on Aemilius Magnus Arborius:

units.la: Me tibi, me patribus, charum decus esse profitsum, Dictasti fatu verba notanda mea.
units.tr: You declared me a dear ornament to you and to my fathers, and by my fate you bade my words be noted.

units.la: Illa Fata videntur in Tabula quadam descripsisse. Potest id colligi ex Chrysost. in Epist. ad Galatas: ubi conqueritur de nefario eorum usu, qui tabellas impietatis plenas, cum infantes nascentur, scribere sunt soliti:
units.tr: Those Fates seem to have been written down on a certain tablet. This can be gathered from Chrysostom on the Epistle to the Galatians, where he complains of the wicked practice of those who used to write out tablets full of impiety when children were born:

units.la: Ἁλλίνων ἐθη παραπιστι των ἡμετέρων φυλάττεται κλησονισμοῖ ἡ διώ- νισμοῖς ἡ συμβολαι, ἡ ἡμεραις παρεστηκοσεις, ἡ ἡ ἀσελ των ἐνα- σιν απωλια ἡ τα πασης ασεβειας γραμμα τεια, ἀ τικτο- μενων των παιδιων ἐιθεως ἐπι κακω τοις εαυτων σωπησαι κε- φαλης.
units.tr: Pagan customs are kept among us: incantations, invocations or binding charms, contracts, the days that stand by, the ... of the stars, and written records of all impiety, which they are wont to inscribe on the heads of newborn children, to their own harm. [Ἁλλίνων ἐθη παραπιστι των ἡμετέρων φυλάττεται κλησονισμοῖ ἡ διώ- νισμοῖς ἡ συμβολαι, ἡ ἡμεραις παρεστηκοσεις, ἡ ἡ ἀσελ των ἐνα- σιν απωλια ἡ τα πασης ασεβειας γραμμα τεια, ἀ τικτο- μενων των παιδιων ἐιθεως ἐπι κακω τοις εαυτων σωπησαι κε- φαλης.]

units.la: In electione nominum itidem captabant omen futurae felicitatis: teste eodem Chrysostomo in c. 4. prioris ad Corinthios: ubi ait, moris fuisse adhuc sua a tate nonnullorum, qui pro Christianis haberi volebant, ut infanti nomen imposituri, lumina multa accenderent, suum cuique nomen assignantes: puta uni lumini Zosimi appellationem indebant: alteri Stephani: tertio Procopij: & ita in caeteris: atque ejus demum, quod caeteris exstinctis supervixerat, nomen arripiebant: ac puero imponebant.
units.tr: In the choice of names, too, they sought omens of future happiness. The same Chrysostom testifies on chapter 4 of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, where he says that in his own time it was the custom among some who wished to be regarded as Christians, when they were about to give a name to an infant, to light many lamps, assigning each one a name: for example, they gave one lamp the name Zosimus, another Stephen, a third Procopius, and so on for the rest. Then they seized the name of whichever lamp had outlasted the others when they were extinguished, and gave it to the boy.

units.la: QUIBUS ex animi sententiâ res minimè succederent, DIs inimi-cis se natos dictitabant. Mostell. 3. 1. v. 32. Mil. 2. 3. v. 20.
units.tr: Those for whom things did not turn out as they wished used to say that they had been born to hostile gods. Mostell. 3. 1. v. 32. Mil. 2. 3. v. 20.

units.la: ORSTETRICES & nutrices dona accipiebant à parentibus. Mil. 3. 1. v. 102, 103.
units.tr: Midwives and nurses received gifts from the parents. Mil. 3. 1. v. 102, 103.

units.la: LIBERI parentibus plærumque similes nascuntur. Truc. 2. 6. v. 24.
units.tr: Children for the most part are born like their parents. Truc. 2. 6. v. 24.

units.la: Eóque mores & artes parentum maturè imitantur. Ibid. Ubi natus est, jam macharam & clypeum posc̄ bat sibi Filius: scil. militis.
units.tr: And so they early imitate the morals and pursuits of their parents. Ibid. As soon as he was born, the son was already demanding a sword and shield, namely a soldier's.

units.la: DIE natalitio solebant convivium adornare amicis. Capt. 1. 2. v. 65.
units.tr: On the birthday they used to prepare a feast for their friends. Capt. 1. 2. v. 65.

units.la: PARTURIENTES fœminæ solebant filium potius, quàm filiam exoptare. Amph. 2. 2. v. 86.
units.tr: Women in labour used to pray for a son rather than a daughter. Amph. 2. 2. v. 86.

units.la: PRÆGNANTIBUS dabantur mala Punica, contra malaciam: te-ste Plinio & Dioscoride. Amph. 2. 2. v. 91. ambiguo & joculari sensu: Prægnanti oportet & malum, & malum dari, ut quod obrodat sit, animo si male esse occaperit.
units.tr: Pomegranates were given to pregnant women against miscarriage, as Pliny and Dioscorides testify. Amph. 2. 2. v. 91, in an ambiguous and joking sense: a pregnant woman ought to be given both an apple and a pomegranate, so that if she begins to feel ill, what is going off may be dealt with.

units.la: PARTUS nullus sine doloribus facilè: adeóque uxores propterea maritos accusant. Truc. 2. 6. v. 37.
units.tr: No birth is easy without pains, and for that reason wives accuse their husbands. Truc. 2. 6. v. 37.

units.la: Tu me pane interfecisti vitâ, & lumine: vimq; magni doloris per voluptatem tuam condidisti in corpus: quo nunc etiam morbo misera sum.
units.tr: You killed me with bread, with life and with light; and through your pleasure you stored up in my body the force of great pain, by which disease I, wretched, am now also afflicted.

units.la: Sic Homerus Iliad ϛ. Agamemnonis vulneratí dolorem cum parturientis ὠδίνας confert. Quos versus Græcæ mulieres non ab Homero, sed ab alio scriptos esse dicebant, teste Plutarcho. Ita Medea Euripidis apud Ennium: Ter sub arma malim vitam cernere, Quàm semel modo parere.
units.tr: So Homer in Iliad 11 compares the pain of Agamemnon's wound to the pangs [ὠδίνας] of a woman in labour. Greek women used to say, according to Plutarch, that these verses were written not by Homer but by someone else. So Medea in Ennius: I would rather face life thrice under arms than give birth once.

units.la: Scriptura sacra istas mulierum ὠδίνας sæpè in similibus & exem-plis usurpat. Quæ loca huc coacervanda erunt.
units.tr: Holy Scripture often uses these pangs of women [ὠδίνας] in similar contexts and examples. These passages will have to be gathered together here.

units.la: Et tamen de meretrice illa dicitur. Truc. 4. 3. v. 32. Ut facilius alia, quam illa, unde est, puerum alienum parit! Haec labore alieno puerum peperit sine doloribus.
units.tr: And yet it is said of that harlot: Truc. 4. 3. v. 32. She would more easily bear another's child than the one from whom she came! She bore a child by another's labour, without pains.

units.la: Alcumena quoque fingitur peperisse sine doloribus. Amph. 3. 1. v. 19. & 5. 1. v. 40, 48. Quod secus fit aliis mulieribus ex prima comminatione Dei ob peccatum: Cum dolore paries liberos tuos.
units.tr: Alcmena, too, is pictured as having given birth without pains. Amph. 3. 1. v. 19, and 5. 1. v. 40, 48. For other women it happens otherwise, from God's first threat because of sin: In pain you shall bring forth your children.

units.la: Mulieres impraegnatae aerumnam suam queri solent. Epid. 3. 4. v. 30.
units.tr: Pregnant women are wont to complain of their hardship. Epid. 3. 4. v. 30.

units.la: Elephantus gravida esse solet perpetuos decem annos. Stich. 2, 1. v. 25. In proverbio.
units.tr: An elephant is wont to be pregnant for ten full years. Stich. 2. 1. v. 25. This is a proverb.

units.la: A partu lavationibus multum utebantur. Amph. 2. 2. v. 37. & 5. 1. v. 50. Mil. 3. 1. v. 191. Truc. 1. 2. v. 94. Terent. Andr. Facisthac, ut lavet. Vide Jan. Parrhas. de Quaesitis, per Epistolam pag. 121. & Meursium de Puerperio.
units.tr: After childbirth they made frequent use of baths. Amph. 2. 2. v. 37, and 5. 1. v. 50. Mil. 3. 1. v. 191. Truc. 1. 2. v. 94. Terence, Andria: You are doing this so that she may bathe. See Janus Parrhasius, On Things Sought, in his letter, p. 121, and Meursius, On the Puerperium.

units.la: Legitima nativitas & partio fermè decimi mensis ingressus est, inquit Tertullianus de anima, & confirmat noster Amph. 2. 2. v. 38. ubi Turneb. lib. 4. c. 15. interpretatur mensem Lunarem, qui menses nostris breviores.
units.tr: Lawful birth and delivery usually comes at the start of the tenth month, says Tertullian in his book On the Soul, and our author confirms this at Amph. 2. 2. v. 38, where Turnebus (book 4, chapter 15) interprets the month as a lunar month, which is shorter than ours.

units.la: Sic Cist. 1. 3. v. 15. & Stich 2. 1. v. 6. joculariter de Fame. Illa me in alvo gestavit menses decem. Truc. 2. 4. v. 48. Jam decumus menses adventat prope. Mil. 4. 10. v. 68.
units.tr: Thus, jokingly, of Hunger: Cist. 1. 3. v. 15, and Stich. 2. 1. v. 6. She carried me in her womb for ten months. Truc. 2. 4. v. 48. Now the tenth month is drawing near. Mil. 4. 10. v. 68.

units.la: Puerperae in partu solebant Deos invocare, inprimis Junonem Lucinam, ad opem ferendam. Amph. 5, 1. v. 9. & 40. Aul. 4. 7. v. 11.
units.tr: In labour, women used to call upon the gods, especially Juno Lucina, to bring help. Amph. 5. 1. v. 9, and 40. Aul. 4. 7. v. 11.

units.la: Terent. Andr. Act 3. Scen. 1. Juno Lucina fer opem, serva me obsecro.
units.tr: Terence, Andria, Act 3, Scene 1: Juno Lucina, bring help, save me, I beg you.

units.la: Horat. Carm. secul. Lenis Ilithyia fuere matres.
units.tr: Horace, Carmen Saeculare: The mothers called upon gentle Ilithyia.

units.la: Catull. Carm. 31. Tu Lucina Juno dicta puerperis. Vide etiam Festum Pompejum in Supercilia. Et Turn. lib. 20. c. 31. Meursf. de Puerperio.
units.tr: Catullus, Carm. 31: You, called Juno Lucina by women in childbirth. See also Festus Pompeius under Supercilia, and Turnebus, book 20, chapter 31, and Meursius, On the Puerperium.

units.la: SINGULARIS Deorum benevolentiæ habebatur, & pietatis pudicitiæque puerperæ, si geminos peperisset. Amph. 5. 1. v. 38.
units.tr: It was regarded as a singular sign of the goodwill of the gods, and of the piety and chastity of the woman in childbirth, if she had borne twins. Amph. 5. 1. v. 38.

units.la: Vide Meursium de Puerperio. cap. 2.
units.tr: See Meursius, On the Puerperium, chapter 2.

units.la: MAGNI ominis fuit, si infantes magni essent nati. Amph. 5. 1. v. 51. Truc. 2. 6. v. 24.
units.tr: It was a great omen if the infants were born large. Amph. 5. 1. v. 51. Truc. 2. 6. v. 24.

units.la: ETIAM munera offerebant puerperæ: quæ sibi reservabant. Truc. 2. 4. v. 71.
units.tr: Women in childbirth also made offerings, which they kept for themselves. Truc. 2. 4. v. 71.

units.la: Non audes aliquod mihi dare munus ?
units.tr: Do you not dare to give me some gift?

units.la: ALIENOS etiam fœtus solebant supponere lucri causâ. Truc. 2. 5. v. 8.
units.tr: They also used to substitute other people's offspring for the sake of gain. Truc. 2. 5. v. 8.

units.la: MULIEREM superfœtari posse, patet ex loco Plauti Amphit. 1. 2. v. 19. Et Plin. lib. 7. c. 11. refert mulierem quandam septem mensium edito puerperio, in seculis aliquot mensibus, geminos eixam.
units.tr: That a woman can superfetate is clear from a passage of Plautus, Amphitryon 1. 2. v. 19. Pliny, book 7, chapter 11, also reports a certain woman who, after giving birth at seven months, bore twins some months later.

units.la: Paullus quoq; J C. scribit, Mulierem ab Alexandriâ perductam, ut D. Hadriano ostenderetur cum quinque liberis, ex quibus quatuor eodem tempore enixa dicebatur, quintum post quadragesimum diem.
units.tr: Paulus the jurist also writes that a woman was brought from Alexandria so that she might be shown to the Emperor Hadrian with five children, of whom four were said to have been born at the same time and the fifth after forty days.

units.la: MERETRICES plærumque sine obstetricis operâ, & sine doloribus pariunt. Cist. 1. 2. v. 22.
units.tr: Prostitutes for the most part give birth without a midwife's help and without pains. Cist. 1. 2. v. 22.

units.la: Vide paulò ante, & Tit. Meretricum.
units.tr: See a little above, and the title Of Prostitutes.

units.la: IN partione difficili periculum mortis esse solet. Truc. 1. 2. v. 92.
units.tr: In a difficult delivery there is usually danger of death. Truc. 1. 2. v. 92.

units.la: PRÆGNANTES uterum sæpè celant: ut ne extumeat: ne scil. amatorum culpâ abortioni operam cogantur dare, & fœtum necare. Truc 1. 2. v. 97.
units.tr: Pregnant women often conceal their bellies, so that they do not swell, namely so that through their lovers' fault they are not forced to procure an abortion and kill the foetus. Truc. 1. 2. v. 97.

units.la: MULTI infantes nascuntur insigniti: hoc est, vitio aliquo notati: aut vari, aut valgi, aut compernes, aut brocchi, &c.
units.tr: Many infants are born marked, that is, noted with some defect: squinting, or bow-legged, or knock-kneed, or with protruding teeth, and so on.

units.la: Terentius Adelph. 5. 4.
units.tr: Terence, Adelphi 5. 4.

units.la: MULIERES à partione filiorum plærumque animis fiunt elatiores. Truc. 2.8. v.10.
units.tr: Women are for the most part made more haughty in spirit by bearing sons. Truc. 2. 8. v. 10.

units.la: Postquam filiolum peperit, animos sustulit.
units.tr: After she bore a little son, she lifted up her spirits.

units.la: PUERPERAM salutabant: eique gratulabantur. Truc. 2.6. v.31.
units.tr: They greeted the woman in childbirth and congratulated her. Truc. 2. 6. v. 31.

units.la: A puerperio plærumque ægræ sunt. Truc. 2.5. v. 11.
units.tr: After childbirth women are for the most part sickly. Truc. 2. 5. v. 11.

units.la: PUERPERÆ flactâ, & igni super aram sacra faciebant Junoni Lucinæ. Truc. 2.5. v. 23.
units.tr: Women after childbirth used to make sacrifices to Juno Lucina, with a torch and fire upon the altar. Truc. 2. 5. v. 23.

units.la: Vide Tit. Sacrificiorum.
units.tr: See the title Of Sacrifices.

units.la: PUERPERÆ post partum pallent. Truc. 2.7. v.22.
units.tr: After childbirth women grow pale. Truc. 2. 7. v. 22.

units.la: Pallida est, ut peperit puerum.
units.tr: She is pale, since she has borne a boy.

units.la: NAVIS. NAVIGATIONIS. MARIS. FLUCTUUM. NAUFRAGII. NAUTARUM. URINATORUM. PORTORII.
units.tr: SHIPS. NAVIGATION. THE SEA. WAVES. SHIPWRECK. SAILORS. DIVERS. TOLL.

units.la: HABEBANT naves lusorias sive cubiculatas, quas vocat Seneca. Iis animi causâ utebantur Rud. 4.2. v. 27.
units.tr: They had pleasure boats or cabin boats, which Seneca calls by that name. They used these for amusement Rud. 4.2 v. 27.

units.la: Post animi causâ mihi navim faciam, atque imitabor stratonicum, atq; oppida circumvectabor.
units.tr: After this, for amusement, I will make myself a ship, and I will imitate the stratonicus, and I will sail round the towns.

units.la: De tali loquitur Suetonius Cæsare. cap. 52.
units.tr: Suetonius speaks of such a boat in his Life of Caesar, ch. 52.

units.la: Cum Cleopatrâ eadem nave thalamego pene Æthiopia tenus Ægyptum peragravit.
units.tr: With Cleopatra, in the same thalamegus boat, he travelled through Egypt almost as far as Ethiopia.

units.la: Ejusmodi Ægypti Reges 800. paratas habebant teste Appiano initio.
units.tr: According to Appian at the beginning, the kings of Egypt had 800 such boats ready.

units.la: Similes fuerunt Gallorum Parade: & illa Neronis, de quâ Plutarchus περὶ δοξ-ασίας pag. 461.
units.tr: The Gallic parades were similar, and so was Nero's, of which Plutarch writes in his work On Opinions [περὶ δοξασίας], p. 461.

units.la: Vide & Athen. pag. 204. lib. 5. & Joseph. Scalig. Ausonius. Lect. lib. 2. lib.2. cap. 14. Parada est genus navigij Vibisci voluptarij, undi-que tecti, quo æstu ultrò citróque reciprocante, per Garumnam molliter ferebantur, eeque toris & culcitris insternebantur, ne a-gitatio ulla sentiretur.
units.tr: See also Athenaeus p. 204, book 5, and Joseph Scaliger. Ausonius, Lectiones, book 2, ch. 14: the parada is a kind of pleasure boat of the Vibisci, roofed on all sides, in which, as the tide flowed back and forth, they were gently carried along the Garonne; and it was spread with cushions and mattresses so that no jolting could be felt.

units.la: UNDE navis maritima confecta fuerit, vide Trin, 4.1. v.17.
units.tr: On how a sea ship was built, see Trinummus 4.1 v. 17.

units.la: E navigatione tuti cum evasissent, Neptuno & Mercurio vota fa-ciebant, gratiam habentes: & simul quasi omnem dehinc navi-gationem ejurantes.
units.tr: When they had come safely through a voyage, they made vows to Neptune and Mercury, giving thanks; and at the same time they renounced, as it were, all further voyaging.

units.la: Most. 2.2. v.1. Mil.2.5.v.1. & sequentib. Rud. 2.6.v.1. Stich.3.1. v. 3. 4.
units.tr: Most. 2.2 v. 1. Mil. 2.5 v. 1 and following. Rud. 2.6 v. 1. Stich. 3.1 v. 3, 4.

units.la: Cum bene re gesta salvus convorter domum, Neptuno grates ha-beo & tempestatibus; simul Mercurio, qui me in mercimo-niis juvit, lucruq; quadruplicavit, rem meam.
units.tr: When, my business well done, I return home safe, I give thanks to Neptune and the storms; and at the same time to Mercury, who helped me in my trading and multiplied my property fourfold.

units.la: Trin. 4.1.v.1. & seqq. de Charmide sene, qui salvus domum e Seleucia redijt.
units.tr: Trin. 4.1 v. 1 and following, concerning the old man Charmides, who returned home safe from Seleucia.

units.la: Navigatio quippe nihil aliud est, q; mortis quædam professio:
units.tr: For navigation is nothing other than a kind of profession of death.

units.la: Phædrus lib. 4.
units.tr: Phaedrus, book 4.

units.la: Nec ad profisse mortis audacem viam
units.tr: Nor had Argus built a ship with Palladian skill for the bold path to death

units.la: Fabricasset Argus opere Palladio ratam.
units.tr: Nor had Argus built a ship with Palladian skill for the bold path to death.

units.la: Anacharsides apud Plutarchum:
units.tr: Anacharsis, in Plutarch:

units.la: Odi vitam, quæ pendet a funibus, ubi navigantes vix tribus digitis absunt a morte.
units.tr: I hate a life that hangs by ropes, where sailors are scarcely three fingers from death.

units.la: Juvenal. Sat. 12.
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire 12.

units.la: I nunc. & ventis animam committe, dolato
units.tr: Go now, and entrust your life to the winds, relying on a plank of wood,

units.la: Confisus ligno, digitis a morte remotus
units.tr: removed from death by four fingers

units.la: Quattuor; aut septem, si sit latissima tada.
units.tr: or seven, if the pitch-pine plank is very broad.

units.la: Terentius Hecyrā:
units.tr: Terence, Hecyra:

units.la: Nescis, quid malæ praeterieris, qui numquam es ingressus mare.
units.tr: You do not know what evils you have escaped, you who have never set foot on the sea.

units.la: Ovidius:
units.tr: Ovid:

units.la: Et prope tam letum, quam prope cernit aquam.
units.tr: and he sees death as near as the water.

units.la: Laertius:
units.tr: Laertius:

units.la: Πῆσον γῆ, ἄπισον ἢ Θάλασσα
units.tr: Land is a cubit away; the sea is untrustworthy [Πῆσον γῆ, ἄπισον ἢ Θάλασσα].

units.la: Hora-
units.tr: Horace

units.la: Horat. lib. 1. Od. 3. Illi robur et aes triplex Circa pectus erat, qui fragilem truci Commisit pelago ratem Primus.
units.tr: Horace, book 1, Odes 3: "He had a heart of oak and triple bronze about his breast, who first committed a fragile raft to the savage sea."

units.la: Quis nauclerorum fuerit ornatus explicatur. Mil. 4. 4. v. 41. Facito ut venias ornatus huc ornatu nauclerico, Causiam habeas ferrugineam, culcitam ob oculos lineam, Palliolum habeas ferrugineum (nam is colos thalassicus est) Id erit connexum in humero laevo: exaffilato brachio Pracinctius: atque assimulato quasi gubernator sis.
units.tr: What the dress of sailors was like is explained in Miles 4.4 v. 41: "See that you come here dressed as a sailor: have a rust-coloured cap, a linen cloth over your eyes, and a rust-coloured cloak (for that is the sea colour), fastened on the left shoulder, with your arm bared and your belt tightened, and pretend to be a steersman."

units.la: NAVIGANTES gaudent in tranquillo mari, si vento secundo utantur. Cist. 1. 1. v. 15.
units.tr: Sailors rejoice in a calm sea if they have a favourable wind. Cistellaria 1.1 v. 15.

units.la: NAVIS res est plena negotij, ut mulier. Pœn. 1. 2. v. 1.
units.tr: A ship is a matter full of trouble, like a woman. Poenulus 1.2 v. 1.

units.la: Vide Tit. Mulierum.
units.tr: See the title On Women.

units.la: Qui e naufragio servati erant, radebant caput in signum liberationis. Rud. 5. 2. v. 16.
units.tr: Those who had been saved from shipwreck shaved their heads as a sign of their deliverance. Rudens 5.2 v. 16.

units.la: UT CUMQUE in alto ventus est, exinde velum vortitur. Epid. 1. 1. v. 47. Pœn. 3. 5. v. 9.
units.tr: Whenever there is wind on the deep, the sail is turned about. Epidicus 1.1 v. 47; Poenulus 3.5 v. 9.

units.la: IN naufragio naves periculose ad unum saxum fluctus ferunt. Most. 3. 1. v. 143. ἀλληγορικῶς.
units.tr: In a shipwreck, ships are carried by the waves dangerously against a single rock. Most. 3.1 v. 143, allegorically.

units.la: IN navi erat & proreta, & gubernator. Rud. 4. 3. v. 75.
units.tr: There was both a prow-man and a steersman on the ship. Rudens 4.3 v. 75.

units.la: Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: E navigationibus aurum, argentum: aliosque pretiosos ornatus vestiar os, e peregrinis regionibus importabant.
units.tr: From voyages they imported gold, silver, and other precious ornaments and clothing from foreign regions.

units.la: Stich 2. 3. v. 53.
units.tr: Stichus 2.3 v. 53.

units.la: IN naufragio homines piscibus præbent pabulum.
units.tr: In a shipwreck men provide food for the fishes.
Rudens 2.6 v. 29.

units.la: Piscibus in alto, credo, præbent pabulum.
units.tr: They provide food for the fishes in the deep, I suppose.

units.la: Petronius:
units.tr: Petronius:

units.la: ——— Regnum Neptuni pavit Ulysses.
units.tr: "Ulysses fed the kingdom of Neptune."

units.la: Maris aqua salsa est. Rud. 2.6. v.33,46. & 2.7.v.31.
units.tr: The water of the sea is salt. Rud. 2.6 v. 33, 46, and 2.7 v. 31.

units.la: In navi habebant funem nauticum, qui ob strepitum Rudens dicti Rud. 4.3. v.1.
units.tr: On the ship they had a nautical rope, which, from its noise, was called rudens Rud. 4.3 v. 1.

units.la: Naufragium etiam poenam impiorum ducebant. Rud. 2.6. v.21.
units.tr: They also regarded shipwreck as the punishment of the wicked. Rud. 2.6 v. 21.

units.la: Arcturus cum oritur, naufragium nautis minatur. Rud. Prol. v.68.
units.tr: When Arcturus rises, it threatens sailors with shipwreck. Rud. Prol. v. 68.

units.la: Portitori solvebant portorium pro navigatione. Trin. 4.4. v.15. & Asin. 1.3. v.7.
units.tr: They paid the toll to the toll-collector for the voyage. Trin. 4.4 v. 15, and Asin. 1.3 v. 7.

units.la: Navibus scaphae additae, in quas tempore periculi insiliebant. Rud. 2.3. v.36. & Rud. Prol. v.74.
units.tr: Small boats were added to the ships, into which they leapt in time of danger. Rud. 2.3 v. 36, and Rud. Prol. v. 74.

units.la: Navigationibus mercaturam exercebant. Merc. Prol. v.76.
units.tr: They carried on trade by means of voyages. Merc. Prol. v. 76.

units.la: Naves dicuntur conferri, quando concurrunt. Bacch. 4.6. v.27. ἀλληγοεικῶς de fallacijs.
units.tr: Ships are said to be brought together when they meet. Bacch. 4.6 v. 27, allegorically, concerning deceits.

units.la: Cum ventus navim deserit, periculum est naufragij. Most. 3.2. v.49. ἀλληγοεικῶς.
units.tr: When the wind deserts the ship, there is danger of shipwreck. Most. 3.2 v. 49, allegorically.

units.la: Vide Locum.
units.tr: See Locus.

units.la: Naufragium passi pro uvidis vestimentis sumebant arida. Rud. 2.7. v.15.
units.tr: Those who had suffered shipwreck took dry clothes in place of wet ones. Rud. 2.7 v. 15.

units.la: Ubi bonus est architectus, facile est navem bonam facere. Mil 3.3. v.41.
units.tr: Where there is a good architect, it is easy to make a good ship. Mil. 3.3 v. 41.

units.la: Nulla est voluptas navitis major, quam quando ex alto procul terram conspiciunt. Men. 2.1. v.1.
units.tr: There is no greater pleasure for sailors than when they see the land from afar across the deep. Men. 2.1 v. 1.

units.la: Tranquillitas evenit quasi navi in mari: utcunque est ventus: exin velum vortitur. Poen. 3.5. v.8.
units.tr: Calm comes as it does to a ship at sea: whatever the wind, then the sail turns. Poen. 3.5 v. 8.

units.la: NAUTÆ allium ulpicum edebant: & inde turpiter fœtebant.
units.tr: Sailors ate pungent garlic, and from it they stank foully.

units.la: Pœn. 5. 5. v. 35. Plenior allÿ ulpici, quàm sunt Romani remiges.
units.tr: Poenulus 5.5 v. 35: "Fuller of garlic than the Roman rowers are."

units.la: NAVES corbitæ in tranquillo mari lentè progrediuntur.
units.tr: Merchant ships move slowly forward on a calm sea.
Poenulus 3.1 v. 4.

units.la: SI quid in naufragio perijssset, urinatores quæsiverunt.
units.tr: If anything had been lost in a shipwreck, divers were sought.
Rudens 2.3 v. 66.

units.la: PORTUMNUS portubus præerat. Rud. 1. 2. v. 71.
units.tr: Portumnus presided over the harbours. Rudens 1.2 v. 71.

units.la: NAUTÆ hortatores in navi solent hortari remiges.
units.tr: On a ship, sailors as exhorters usually encourage the rowers.
Mercator 4.2 v. 5.

units.la: NAUTÆ suo remigio rem gerentes, beati sunt.
units.tr: Sailors who carry on their business by rowing are happy.
Miles 3.1 v. 151.

units.la: NAVES longæ compingebantur multis clavis. Rud. 3. 4. v. 48.
units.tr: Long ships were fastened together with many nails. Rudens 3.4 v. 48.

units.la: NAVIGATIO senibus molesta. Bacch. 2. 3. v. 109.
units.tr: Voyaging is troublesome for old men. Bacchides 2.3 v. 109.

units.la: NAUFRAGIUM vitæ humanæ fragilitatem ostendit.
units.tr: Shipwreck shows the fragility of human life.
Rudens 1.2 v. 66.

units.la: Vide Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See the title On Man.

units.la: NECESSITATIS.
units.tr: NECESSITY.

units.la: NECESSITAS non habet legem.
units.tr: Necessity has no law.

units.la: NOBILITATIS. GENERIS. STIRPIS. PROSAPIÆ. FAMILIÆ.
units.tr: NOBILITY. BIRTH. STOCK. LINEAGE. FAMILY.

units.la: PATRITII magnificè vestiebantur ex dignitate sui ordinis.
units.tr: Patricians dressed magnificently in keeping with the dignity of their order.

units.la: QUI bono sunt genere nati, si sunt ingenio malo, suopte culpam genere capiunt: genus iugenio improbant. Merc. 5. 4. v. 8.
units.tr: Those born of good birth, if they have a bad nature, bring the blame upon their own birth; by their conduct they discredit their lineage. Merc. 5. 4. v. 8.

units.la: Linea recta in familiâ hæc est: Pater, Avus, Proavus, Abavus, Atavus, Tritavus. Perf. 1.2. v. 5.
units.tr: The direct line in a family is this: father, grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather, great-great-great-grandfather, great-great-great-great-grandfather. Perf. 1.2. v. 5.

units.la: Nobilitas generis ad virtutem debet esse cæteris omnibus propensior. Pæn. 5. 4. v.12.
units.tr: The nobility of birth ought to be more inclined to virtue than all other things. Pæn. 5. 4. v.12.

units.la: Eo sumus genere gnatæ: ut decet nos esse à culpâ castas.
units.tr: We are born of such a stock that it befits us to be chaste and free from fault.

units.la: NOMINUM.
units.tr: NAMES.

units.la: Culi Regis dicuntur præcipui in Aulâ. Pœn. 3.3. v.80. Vide Tit. Aulæ.
units.tr: The leading men in a royal court are called by this name. Poen. 3.3 v.80. See the entry on Court.

units.la: Meretrices nomina mutabant. Pœn. 5.3. v. 20. Vide Tit. Meretricum.
units.tr: Prostitutes changed their names. Poen. 5.3 v.20. See the entry on Prostitutes.

units.la: Ex nomine de moribus conjecturâ fieri sæpè potest: eóque veteres nomina vitabant. Bacch. 2.3. v.49. & 4.4. v. 53. Pœn. Prol. v. 92.
units.tr: From a name one can often guess a person's character, and for this reason the ancients avoided certain names. Bacch. 2.3 v.49; 4.4 v.53; Poen. Prol. v.92.

units.la: Sic ex nomine Verris augurabantur homines fore, ut ab eo Sicilia verteretur. Cicero pro Roscio Amer. Venio nunc ad nomen illud aureum Chrysogoni. Vide Hieron. Column. ad Enn. P. 370. & Martialis Epigramma de nominibus funestis.
units.tr: So from the name Verres people predicted that Sicily would be overturned by him. Cicero, Pro Roscio Amerino: "I come now to that golden name, Chrysogonus." See Hieronymus Columna on Ennius, p. 370, and Martial's epigram on ill-omened names.

units.la: Veteres olim mala nomina vitabant. Asin. 3. 3. v. 155. Inprimis quando à cognatis pronunciarentur: quod dicebant Obscevare. Asin. 2. 1. v. 18. & omen vituperare. Caf. 2.6.v.58. & Mil. 4. 8. v. 31.
units.tr: The ancients long avoided ill-omened names, especially when they were spoken by relatives; this they called "speaking ill-omened" and "blaming the omen." Asin. 3.3 v.155; Asin. 2.1 v.18; Capt. 2.6 v.58; Mil. 4.8 v.31.

units.la: Nomina trium litterarum διφωνικῶς dicebantur de ijs, qui ingenuî videri affectabant: ut, Nomen, pronomen, agnomen: ut, Q. V. M. Quintus, Valerius, Maximus.
units.tr: Names of three letters were said diphōnikōs [διφωνικῶς] of those who wished to seem freeborn, such as nomen, praenomen and agnomen, as in Q. V. M., Quintus Valerius Maximus.

units.la: Ausón. in Grypho: Tres equitum turmæ: trianominanobiliorum.
units.tr: Ausonius, in Gryphus: "Three troops of knights: three-named nobles."

units.la: Juven. Sat. 5. Tamquam habeas tria nomina.
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire 5: "As if you had three names."

units.la: Sed Plautus hominem trium litterarum vocavit Furem. Aul. 2.4. v. 51.
units.tr: But Plautus called a thief a man of three letters. Aul. 2.4 v.51.

units.la: ARROGANTIÆ est sibi longa nomina adsciscere : quod hodiè nimis quàm solemne est. In illos convenit illud Curc. 3. 1. v. 40. Novi edepol nomen militis Theropontigeni platagidori, nam mi- hi stoc nomine, Dum scribo, explevi totas ceras quatuor· Trin. 4. 2. v. 43. Si ante lucem abire occipias ā meo primo nomine concubium sit noctis, priusquam ad postremum perveneris. Est minusculum alterum, quasi vas vinarium, C H. Opus est facullā & viatico ad tuum nomen.
units.tr: ARROGANCE is to assume long names for oneself, which today is all too common. Against such people fits that line: "By Pollux, I know the name of the soldier, Theropontigenus Platagidorus; for while I write this name I have filled four whole wax tablets." Trin. 4.2 v.43: "If you begin to leave before dawn, from my first name it will be night before you reach the last. There is another, a small one, like a wine-jar, C.H. You need resources and provisions for your name."

units.la: PERSARUM mores ita sunt : longa nomina & contortuplicata habere. Pœrs. 4.6. v.27.
units.tr: It is the custom of the Persians to have long and convoluted names. Pers. 4.6 v.27.

units.la: DE nominibus servorum in Comœd. Vide Tit. Servorum.
units.tr: On the names of slaves in comedy. See the entry on Slaves.

units.la: FURTUM facit, qui nomen alterius invadit. Sic matrem furtivam innuit Cist. 2. 3. v.15. & filias furtivas. Poen. 5.4. v. 66.
units.tr: He commits theft who takes up another's name. So Plautus hints at a "stolen" mother (Cist. 2.3 v.15) and "stolen" daughters (Poen. 5.4 v.66).

units.la: NOMINA sæpè sortiebantur ex re ipsâ. Stich, 2. 1. v. 21. 88. Horat. l. 2. Sat. 2.
units.tr: Names were often drawn from the thing itself. Stich. 2.1 v.21, 88; Horace, Satires 2.2.

units.la: Cui canis ex vero duœlum cognomen adhæret.
units.tr: To whom a nickname sticks, drawn from the truth.

units.la: Sic Ovidius in Tibulli mortem: Flebilis indignos, Elegia, solve capillos: Acnimis ex vero nunc tibi nomen erunt.
units.tr: So Ovid, on the death of Tibullus: "Elegy, loosen your hair, unworthy of tears; now your name will be true to you."

units.la: NOMINA in historicis & fabulis sæpè permutantur, & confun- duntur. Ut Pseud. 3.2. v.8. Pelias pro Æsone positus.
units.tr: Names in histories and fables are often exchanged and confused, as with Pelias put in place of Aeson. Pseud. 3.2 v.8.

units.la: Sic Ovidius: Sive quis Antilochum narrabit ab Hectore vislum.
units.tr: So Ovid: "Or if anyone shall tell that Antilochus was seen by Hector."

units.la: Cùm tamen à Memnone sit occisus. Talia multa præsertim in Poëtis.
units.tr: Yet he was killed by Memnon. Many such things occur, especially in the poets.

units.la: Vide Meurs. ad Cassandr. pag. 176. & Taubmann. in Bucolica Virgilij.
units.tr: See Meursius on Cassandra, p. 176, and Taubmann on Virgil's Bucolics.

units.la: FILII heriles, qui hæreditatem ac dominum habebant in spe, di- ẽti fuerunt heri Minores: Patres autem Majores. Asin. 2.2. v.63. Sic & de feminis & filiabus. Truc. 4.3. v. 22, 23. Mulierem vocari, contumeliosum fuit. Amph. 2. 2. v. 182.
units.tr: Sons who were heirs, and who had the inheritance and lordship in prospect, were called the lesser ones, while the fathers were the greater. Asin. 2.2 v.63. So also with women and daughters. Truc. 4.3 v.22-23. To be called a "woman" was an insult. Amph. 2.2 v.182.

units.la: Ex nomine saepe omina captabant. Pers. 4. 4. v. 74.
units.tr: From a name they often took omens. Pers. 4.4 v.74.

units.la: Vide Tit. Augur: Omin:
units.tr: See the entries on Augury and Omens.

units.la: NOTITIÆ. SCIENTIÆ.
units.tr: KNOWLEDGE. SCIENCE.

units.la: QUI se in utraque fortunâ novit, multò videtur esse sapientissimus tàm vir, quàm femina. Stich. 1. 2. v. 67.
units.tr: He who knows himself in both kinds of fortune seems far the wisest, man or woman alike. Stich. 1.2 v.67.

units.la: Ut cognosci quis possit, signa docent varia. Men. 5. 9. v. 51.
units.tr: Various signs teach how a person may be recognized. Men. 5.9 v.51.

units.la: Vix decumus est quisque, qui ipsus sese noverit: ex dicto Thalet is: per jocum. Pseud. 4. 2. v. 17.
units.tr: Scarcely one in ten knows himself: a saying of Thales, spoken in jest. Pseud. 4.2 v.17.

units.la: Quid opus nota noscere? Mil. 3. 1. v. 41.
units.tr: Why need one learn what is already known? Mil. 3.1 v.41.

units.la: Scientia maxima nihil scire: secundum Socratem Bacch. 2. 3. v. 90. & 4. 6. v. 21.
units.tr: The greatest knowledge is to know nothing, according to Socrates. Bacch. 2.3 v.90; 4.6 v.21.

units.la: NOVERCÆ.
units.tr: STEPMOTHERS.

units.la: NOVERCÆ durities in proverbio. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 79. Non esse argentum tibi, apud novercam quaerere. Vide Dilucidationes Donati in Tacitum p. 121.
units.tr: The hardness of a stepmother is proverbial. Pseud. 1.3 v.79: "It is pointless to seek money from a stepmother." See Donatus's Dilucidationes on Tacitus, p. 121.

units.la: Nucis.
units.tr: NUTS.

units.la: QUI è nuce nucleum esse vult, frangit nucem. Curc. 1. 1. v. 55.
units.tr: He who wants the kernel out of a nut must crack the nut. Curc. 1.1 v.55.

units.la: Nuncii, Evangelii.
units.tr: Messengers, Good News.

units.la: TAlthybius & Eurybates nuncij & præcones in Græco-rum exercitu. Inde omnes nuncij lætiores cum illis compa-rati, si εὐαγγέλιον attulissent. Stich 2.2. v.33. Contundam facta Talthybij, contemnamq; omnes nuncios.
units.tr: Talthybius and Eurybates were the messengers and heralds in the Greek army. Hence all other messengers, compared with them, would have been happier if they had brought good news [εὐαγγέλιον]. Stich. 2.2 v.33. I will crush the deeds of Talthybius, and I will despise all messengers.

units.la: Coniuges maritorum suorum adventum qui nunciarent, præ-mio affecerunt. Stich. 2. 2. v.27.
units.tr: Wives rewarded those who brought news of their husbands' return. Stich. 2.2 v.27.

units.la: Ob bonum nuncium præmium dari solitum, quod item εὐαγγέλιον dictum. Capt. 4. 1. v.10.
units.tr: A reward was customarily given for good news, which was also called euangelion [εὐαγγέλιον]. Capt. 4.1 v.10.

units.la: Mos erat veteribus vinum læta nunciantibus propinare. Quò al-lusit noster Pœn. 1. 2. v. 47.
units.tr: It was the custom among the ancients to pour out wine for those announcing happy news. Our author alludes to this in Poen. 1.2 v.47.

units.la: Aristoph. Plut. 3. 2. Servus Cario Plutum recepisse visum nun-cians à Chremyli uxore id efflagita:
units.tr: Aristophanes, Plutus, act 3, scene 2. The servant Carion, announcing that Plutus has recovered his sight, demands this from Chremylus's wife:

units.la: Ταχέως, ταχέως φέρ' οἶνον ὦ δέσποινα, ἵνα καὶ τὴν πῖᾶς, φιλεῖς διὰ δρᾶς αὐτῷ σφόδρα. ὡς ἀγαθὰ συλλήβδην ἀπαντά σοι φέρω.
units.tr: Quickly, quickly bring wine, mistress, so that you too may drink; you love him very much. Since I bring you all good things in a word. [Ταχέως, ταχέως φέρ' οἶνον ὦ δέσποινα, ἵνα καὶ τὴν πῖᾶς, φιλεῖς διὰ δρᾶς αὐτῷ σφόδρα. ὡς ἀγαθὰ συλλήβδην ἀπαντά σοι φέρω.]

units.la: Ubi Scholiastes:
units.tr: Where the scholiast says:

units.la: ἰνίκα ἦν ἐπαγγελία, ἐθῶ· ἦν πίνειν οἶνον.
units.tr: When there was a good report, it was the custom to drink wine. [ἰνίκα ἦν ἐπαγγελία, ἐθῶ· ἦν πίνειν οἶνον.]

units.la: Nuncium aliò missuri: aut per nuncium aliquid curaturi, ar-gentum solvebant. Men. Prol. v. 51, 52, 53. Pœn. Prol. 81, 82.
units.tr: Those who were about to send a messenger elsewhere, or to have something attended to through a messenger, used to pay money in advance. Men. Prol. vv. 51, 52, 53. Poen. Prol. 81, 82.

units.la: Nuptiarum.
units.tr: Nuptiarum.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Conjugii. Ubi plura de Dote: Divor-tijs & Repudijs.
units.tr: See also the title Conjugii (Marriage), where more is said about Dowry, Divorces and Repudiations.

units.la: NUptiæ quandóque fiebant per sortitiones: ut illæ Cas. 2. 6. v. 36. In quâ sortitione sæpè devotationes, h. e. diræ & imprecationes obligabant novos nuptos. Ibidem: Credo hercle hæc devotabit sortes, si attigerit. Quid sit devotare: vide in Lex. Pl.
units.tr: Weddings were sometimes made by lot, as in Cas. 2.6, v. 36. In that drawing of lots, curses and imprecations, that is, dire oaths, often bound the newly married. In the same place: "I believe, by Hercules, she will curse the lots if she touches them." For what devotare means, see the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: Exprimit autem admodùm diserte Author libri de Herbis : qui Apuleij habitus est, his verbis cap. 7. Si quis devotatus defixusque fuerit in suis nuptijs: sic eum resolvas. Ecce devotatum defixum, ait.
units.tr: The author of the book On Herbs, thought to be Apuleius, states this quite clearly in chapter 7: "If anyone has been cursed and bound in his marriage, loose him in this way." Notice, he says, "cursed and bound."

units.la: Sic enim dicebant Defigere dirù.
units.tr: For this is how they spoke of "binding with curses" (defigere diris).

units.la: Virgil. Ciri: Regis Iolchiacù animum defigere votis.
units.tr: Virgil, Ciris: "to bind the mind of the king of Iolcos with vows."

units.la: Et Glossæ veteres: Defictiones: νεκυομαντεῖαι, καταδέσμω.
units.tr: And the old glosses: Defictiones: necromancies, bindings [νεκυομαντεῖαι, καταδέσμω].

units.la: Virgil. Eclog. 8. Veneris dic vincula nectlo.
units.tr: Virgil, Eclogue 8: "Tell me, I tie the bonds of Venus."
