units.la: Nuptiæ serviles Jure civili non sunt justæ: neque servorum mulieres dicuntur uxores: sed conjunctæ. Caf. Prol. v. 68. Varro l. i. Rei Ruft. c. 17. At in Apuliâ, ut dicit Prolog. Nuptiæ similes majori operâ curari solent, quàm liberales. Vide Alex. ab Alex. lib. 2. c. 5. & ibi Tiraquellum.
units.tr: Servile marriages are not lawful under civil law, and the women of slaves are not called wives but companions. Cas. Prol. v. 68. Varro, Rust. bk. 1, ch. 17: "But in Apulia, as the prologue says, weddings of slaves are usually arranged with greater care than those of free men." See Alexander ab Alexandro, bk. 2, ch. 5, and Tiraqueau there.

units.la: Aruspicum curæ olim erat nubentes profiteri, se liberorum quærendorum causâ convenire. Caf. Prol. v. 86. Vide Fr. Hotomannum de veteri ritu Nupt. c. 2.
units.tr: It was once the business of the haruspices to have brides declare that they came together for the sake of begetting children. Cas. Prol. v. 86. See Francis Hotman, On the Ancient Rite of Marriage, ch. 2.

units.la: Novis nuptis bene precabantur, & spem sobolis vovebant hac formulâ: QUOD TIBI SEMPITERNUM SALUTARE SIT LIBERIS PROCREANDIS. Aul. 2. 1. v. 26. Vide Tit. Actionum: Omini.
units.tr: People blessed new brides well and wished them hope of offspring in this formula: "MAY IT BE LASTING SALVATION TO YOU FOR THE BEGETTING OF CHILDREN." Aul. 2.1, v. 26. See the title Actions: Omens.

units.la: Mos erat Romanis, in domum mariti novas nuptas, & quidem velatas traducere, quod fiebat vespere, tædis ac facibus præeuntibus. noctu enim nubebant. Aul. 2. 1. v. 28. & 3. 5. v. 6. & Trin. 2. 2. v. 97. Alia loca παραλλαξ. Lexico nostro Plautino petes. De ipso autem ritu hoc nuptiali adeundus tibi Brissonius J C. lib. 1. c. 18. de Select. Antiq.
units.tr: It was the Roman custom to lead new brides, and indeed veiled, into the husband's house. This was done in the evening, with torches and flaming brands going before, for they married at night. Aul. 2.1, v. 28; 3.5, v. 6; and Trin. 2.2, v. 97. Other passages are cited parallel; you will seek them in our Plautine Lexicon. For the rite itself, consult Brisson, J.C., bk. 1, ch. 18, On Selected Antiquities.

units.la: Partus ante nuptias probrum erat. Aul. 2. 3. v. 9. Nunc nobis prope adest exitium, mihi atque herili filiæ. Nam probrum atque partitudo prope abest, ut fiam palàm, quod celatum est, atq; occultatum muq; adhuc, nunc non potest.
units.tr: Giving birth before marriage was a disgrace. Aul. 2.3, v. 9: "Now the ruin is nearly upon us, I and my master's daughter. For the disgrace and the childbirth are close at hand, so that what has been hidden and concealed until now cannot be kept secret any longer."

units.la: Lege dura vivunt mulieres, multòque iniquiore miseræ quàm viri. Nam si vir scortum duxit clam uxorem suam, id si resciuit uxor, impune est viro. Uxor viro, si clam domo egressa est foras, viro sit causa, exigitur matrimonio. Utinam lex esset eadem, quae uxori est, viro: qui minus vir una uxore contentus sit.
units.tr: Women live under a harsh law, and far more unjustly, poor things, than men. "For if a husband has secretly taken a mistress, and the wife learns of it, it is unpunished for the husband. A wife who has gone out of the house secretly gives her husband grounds, and she is put away from the marriage. Would that the law were the same for husband as for wife: then the husband would be less content with one wife."

units.la: Merc. 4. 6. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: Merc. 4.6, v. 1 and following.

units.la: De hac lege dura vide Discursum Alberici Gentilis de Nupt. l. 6. c. 21. p. 696.
units.tr: On this harsh law see the discourse of Alberico Gentili, On Marriage, bk. 6, ch. 21, p. 696.

units.la: In repudijs causam adjecerunt. Merc. 4. 6. v. 6.
units.tr: In cases of divorce they added a cause. Merc. 4.6, v. 6.

units.la: Cicero Phil. 2.
units.tr: Cicero, Philippics 2.

units.la: Mimam suas sibi res habere jussit: & XXII. Tabb. causam addit: exegit.
units.tr: "She ordered the mime to keep her own things," and the Twelve Tables add a cause: "he demanded it."

units.la: Ostendit idipsum Repudij Etymon apud Festum: Repudium, Veniusait dictum, quod sit ob rem pudendam.
units.tr: Festus shows the same thing in the etymology of repudium: Verrius says it was so called "because it is on account of a shameful thing" (ob rem pudendam).

units.la: Uxor contenta est, quae bona est, uno viro. Merc. 4. 6. v. 8.
units.tr: The wife is content who is good and has one husband. Merc. 4.6, v. 8.

units.la: Sic Hor. lib. 3. Od. 24.
units.tr: So Horace, Odes bk. 3, ode 24.

units.la: Dos est magna, parentiumVirtus, & metuens alterius viriCerto foedere castitas.
units.tr: "Dowry is great, the virtue of parents, and chastity, fearing another's husband, under a sure covenant."

units.la: In nuptijs contrahendis sponsio praecedebat: & nominatio Dotis. Trin. 5. 2. v. 34. Curc. 5. 2. v. 74. Aul. 2. 2. v. 77.
units.tr: In contracting marriages, the betrothal came first, and the naming of the dowry. Trin. 5.2, v. 34; Curc. 5.2, v. 74; Aul. 2.2, v. 77.

units.la: Nuptis novis omnia fausta apprecabantur. Trin. 5. 2. v. 31.
units.tr: For new marriages they prayed for every good omen. Trin. 5.2, v. 31.

units.la: Si placet sponsa, placenda quoque dos est. Ibid. v. 35.
units.tr: "If the bride is pleasing, the dowry must also be made pleasing." Ibid. v. 35.

units.la: Promissio & dotes multum differunt: ut docent J Cti. Trin. 5. 2. v. 38. Vide Ravardum.
units.tr: A promise and a dowry differ greatly, as the jurists teach. Trin. 5.2, v. 38. See Ravardus.

units.la: Per sponsalia etiam contrahuntur affinitates ex jure civili. Trin. 5. 2. v. 39.
units.tr: Through betrothals, too, affinities are contracted under civil law. Trin. 5.2, v. 39.

units.la: Vide Alb. Gentil. l. 5. c. 12. de Nuptijs. & Scip. Gent. Parerg.
units.tr: See Alberico Gentili, bk. 5, ch. 12, On Marriages, and Scipio Gentili, Parerga.

units.la: Sine Cerere & Baccho friget Venus. Caf. 4. 3. v. 5.
units.tr: Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold. Cas. 4.3, v. 5.

units.la: Nova nupta non tangebat limen domus: sed levabatur manibus aliorum. Caf. 4. 4. v. 1.
units.tr: A new bride did not touch the threshold of the house but was lifted over it by the hands of others. Cas. 4.4, v. 1.

units.la: Vide Turneb. lib. 8. c. 11. Muretum ad illud Catulli: Transfer omine cum bonoLimen aureolos pedes.
units.tr: See Turnebus, bk. 8, ch. 11, and Muretus on that line of Catullus: "Carry her across the threshold with good omen, on golden feet."

units.la: Item Hottoman. de ritu Nupt. c. 19. Briffon. Formul. pag. 529. Isid. lib. 9. c. ult. Plutarch. in Quæstionib. Romanis: & Servius ad 8. Eclog.
units.tr: Likewise Hottoman, On the Rite of Marriage, ch. 19; Brisson, Formulae, p. 529; Isidore, bk. 9, last chapter; Plutarch, Roman Questions; and Servius on Eclogue 8.

units.la: IN nuptijs vovebant longam vitam novæ nuptæ: ut viro semper sit superstes. Caf. 4. 4. v. 2.
units.tr: At weddings the new bride prayed for a long life, that she might always outlive her husband. Cas. 4.4, v. 2.

units.la: MULIERES suis viris debent esse morigeræ: neque illis imperare: Idcoque malè monstrant illæ malæ ancillæ. Caf. 4. 4. v. 3, 4.
units.tr: Wives ought to be obedient to their husbands and not to command them; hence those bad maids show badly. Cas. 4.4, v. 3, 4.

units.la: IN primo conflictu venereo jubebantur sponsi impercere novæ nuptæ. Caf. 4. 4. v. 11.
units.tr: At the first venereal conflict, bridegrooms were ordered to spare the new bride. Cas. 4.4, v. 11.

units.la: AN compressio justa causa sit matrimonij, disputant JCti. Aul. 4. 7. v. 7.
units.tr: The jurists dispute whether compression (sexual violation) is a just cause of marriage. Aul. 4.7, v. 7.

units.la: Confido istuc me à fratre impetrassere: & causa justa est, si quidem ita est, ut prædicas, te eam compressisse virginem.
units.tr: "I trust I obtained that from my brother; and the cause is just, if indeed it is as you say, that you have lain with that maiden."

units.la: MATRONÆ ut peculiari habitu incedebant, nempe duplici vitâ, stolâ, &c. ita quoque promissos alebant capillos: non item scorta, quibus ut eò commodius se modò in pueros, modò in puellas transformare possent crines erant breviores. Ita ancilla suadet Philematio, ut capiat crines matronæ instar, atq; uni morem gerat. Sic enim recte ibidem explicari puto illud capere crines. Most. 1. 3. v. 69. Mil. 3. 1. v. 196.
units.tr: Matrons walked about in a distinctive dress, namely the double-length robe, the stola, and so on; likewise they let their hair grow for betrothed women. Courtesans did not, since shorter hair let them transform more easily into boys or girls. So the maid persuades Philematium to take up her hair in the manner of a matron and to obey one man. For thus I think that phrase capere crines ("to take up the hair") is rightly explained here. Most. 1.3, v. 69; Mil. 3.1, v. 196.

units.la: Vide Lips. Antiq. Lect. lib. 3. pag. 65.
units.tr: See Lipsius, Antiquae Lectiones, bk. 3, p. 65.

units.la: PICUMNUM sive Martem Silvanum domesticum, Præstitem Larum parentes liberos in matrimonium elocaturi, ut benè Nuptiæ cederent, invocarunt. Aul. 2. 8. v. 15.
units.tr: Parents about to marry off their children invoked Picumnus or Mars Silvanus, the household god, and the Praestites and Lares, so that the wedding would turn out well. Aul. 2.8, v. 15.

units.la: Nunc tusculum emi, & has coronas floreas: hæc imponentur in foco nostro Lari, ut fortunatas faciat gnatæ Nuptias.
units.tr: "Now I have bought a garland and these floral wreaths: these will be placed on our hearth for our Lar, so that he may make my daughter's wedding fortunate."

units.la: Dij Penates meum parentum, familiaq; Lar pater, vobis mando parentum meum rem benè tutemini.
units.tr: "Penates of my parents, and Lar of the family, father, I entrust to you: see that my parents' affairs are well kept."

units.la: Stipulationis in sponsalibus formula erat: Etiam mihi desponsa fuerit filiam. Aul. 2. 2. v. 77. Sponsa autem dicebatur, non qui sponderet, sed quod sponderetur à patre videl. vel alio. Lege enim cautum fuit, ne quis uxorem duceret priusquam aliquis filii eam despondisset. Vide quæso Hotoman. de veter. Nupt. ritibus. c. 9. & Brisf. de Ritu Nuptiarum,
units.tr: The formula of stipulation in betrothals was: "Has he promised me his daughter in marriage?" The bride was called sponsa not because she made the promise, but because she was promised (sponderetur) by her father or another. For by law it was provided that no one should take a wife before someone had betrothed her to him. See, please, Hottoman, On Ancient Marriage Rites, ch. 9, and Brisson, On the Rite of Marriage.

units.la: Facta sponsione nuptiis dies constituebatur. Trin. 2. 4. v. 180. Solebant etiam novæ nuptæ gratulari. Ibidem.
units.tr: Once the betrothal was made, a day was fixed for the wedding. The new brides were also accustomed to receive congratulations. Trin. 2.4, v. 180; ibid.

units.la: In conjugiis multi dotem, non virtutem spectant. Perf. 3. 1. v. 57. Non tu nunc hominum mores vides? cuju modi hic cum fama facile nubitur, dum dos fit, nullum vitium, vitio vortitur.
units.tr: In marriages many look to the dowry, not to virtue. "Do you not see the morals of men now? Of what kind is the one who is easily married despite her reputation, provided there is a dowry; no fault is turned into a fault."

units.la: In dotem sæpè non pecunia datur: sed aliud quidvis, quod magno æstimatur. Sic Parasitus filiæ suæ dotem promittit ex artis suæ libris sexcentos logos. Perf. 3. 1. v. 66. Ridiculè: sed Homeri exemplo, qui suæ quoque filiæ propter inopiam Cypria sua carmina dedisse in dotem perhibetur. Vide Ælian. lib. 9. Variæ Histor. cap. 15.
units.tr: In place of a dowry, often money is not given but some other thing of great value. Thus the parasite promises his daughter a dowry of six hundred logs from the books of his art. This is ridiculous; yet it follows the example of Homer, who is said to have given his Cypria poems as a dowry to his own daughter because of his poverty. See Aelian, Varia Historia, bk. 9, ch. 15.

units.la: Sponsi candidati incedebant. Caf. 2. 8. v. 10. & 14. v. 9.
units.tr: Candidate bridegrooms walked about. Cas. 2.8, v. 10; 2.14, v. 9.

units.la: Quinque facibus utebantur in Nuptijs: quòd is numerus quasi symbolum quoddam fit nuptiarum, ut qui ex primo impari, & primo pari, tamquam ex mare & femina constat. Quin & ominosum habitum fuit, creditumque, qui novæ nuptæ luxissent facem, eos postea nihil fore.
units.tr: Five torches were used at weddings, because that number is in a way a symbol of marriage, as it consists of the first odd and the first even number, as of male and female. Moreover it was an omen, and was believed, that those who had let the torch of a new bride burn out would afterwards come to nothing.

units.la: Allusum Caf. 1. 1. v. 30.
units.tr: Alluded to: Caf. 1. 1. v. 30.

units.la: Vide Hotomannum de Ritu Nuptiarum cap. 1. Muretum ad Catullum:
units.tr: See Hotomann, de Ritu Nuptiarum, ch. 1, and Muretus on Catullus:

units.la: Tollite o pueri faces.
units.tr: Lift up the torches, O boys.

units.la: Brissonium de Nuptijs.
units.tr: Brissonius, de Nuptiis.

units.la: Ante nuptias sacrificabant. Aul. 3. 6. v. 42.
units.tr: They sacrificed before weddings. Aul. 3. 6. v. 42.

units.la: Cereri in nuptijs vinum adhiberi erat nefas, quæ Orci nuptiæ dicebantur, quas præsentiâ sui Pontifices ingenti solemnitate celebrabant. Aul. 2. 6. v. 5.
units.tr: At weddings it was forbidden to serve wine to Ceres, and these were called the nuptials of Orcus, which the pontiffs celebrated with great solemnity in their presence. Aul. 2. 6. v. 5.

units.la: Cererine has nuptias sunt facturi. Qui?
units.tr: Are they going to hold these nuptials for Ceres? How so?

units.la: Quia temeti nihil allatum intelligo.
units.tr: Because I understand that no wine has been brought.

units.la: Vide Servium Danielis lib. 1. Georg. ver. 343. pag. 87. C. No-cturnæ enim Ἀσιμοφοξία abstemiæ prorsus erant solemnitates ac sine temēto: Unde Græcis dictæ θυσίαι νηφάλιοι.
units.tr: See Servius Danielis on Georgics 1, line 343, p. 87 C. For the nocturnal rites were entirely abstemious and without wine: hence they were called by the Greeks sober sacrifices [θυσίαι νηφάλιοι], and the abstinence [ἀσιμοφοξία].

units.la: Vide Centur. Doufæ. Alexand. ab Alex. & Tiraquell.
units.tr: See Centuria Doufae, Alexander ab Alexandro, and Tiraquellus.

units.la: Uxores luxuriosis filijs in poenam datæ. Hac enim solâ habenâ uxoriâ castigari & coërceri solet dissoluta juventus.
units.tr: Wives were given to wanton sons as a punishment. For a wild youth is usually checked and restrained by this one rein alone, a wife.

units.la: Continuò arbitretur uxor tuo gnato: h. e. prospiciatur ei de uxore.
units.tr: Let a wife be provided for your son at once: that is, let a wife be found for him.

units.la: C A. Miseria una quasi homini est affatim. C H. immò huic parum est.
units.tr: CA. One misery is, as it were, enough for a man. CH. Nay, for this one it is not enough.

units.la: Nam si pro peccatis centum ducat uxores, parum.
units.tr: For even if he takes a hundred wives as the penalty for his sins, it is still too little.

units.la: Suadet idem Plutarch. περὶ παίδων ἀγωγῆς extremo libelli: φειγάτεον δὲ τὰς τῶν ἡδονῶν πῖλυς, ᾗ πεῖς τὰς δαπμήσεις δυσπόνον, γάμῳ καταζεύξαι. Δεσμὸς δ' ἐπ᾿ ἐπ᾿ ἔτι τῆς νεότητος ἀσφαλέστατος.
units.tr: Plutarch urges the same at the end of his treatise On the Education of Children: one must flee the pursuit of pleasures, which makes the faults hard to correct, by yoking the young man in marriage; for a bond is the most secure of youth [φειγάτεον δὲ τὰς τῶν ἡδονῶν πῖλυς, ᾗ πεῖς τὰς δαπμήσεις δυσπόνον, γάμῳ καταζεύξαι. Δεσμὸς δ' ἐπ᾿ ἐπ᾿ ἔτι τῆς νεότητος ἀσφαλέστατος.].

units.la: Metu poenæ matrimonia non obstringi, docent JCti: & eò referendum Pseud. 1. 1. v. 110. Satin' est, si hanc hodiè mulierem effigio tibi, tuaque sit, aut si tibi do viginti minas
units.tr: The jurists teach that marriages are not bound by fear of punishment, and to this should be referred Pseud. 1. 1. v. 110. Is it enough if I give you this woman today to be yours, or if I give you twenty minas?

units.la: Vide de hoc contractu clarissimum JCtum Albericum Gentilem lib. 3. c. 13. pag. 329.
units.tr: On this contract see the most distinguished jurist Albericus Gentilis, book 3, ch. 13, p. 329.

units.la: Neque enim huc omnia velim exscribere, quæ inibi prolixè & crudite, tractat JCtus.
units.tr: For I do not wish to copy out here everything that the jurist treats there at such length and learning.

units.la: Matrimonium, liberorum procreandorum causâ, susceptum: idque per Auspices edicebatur. Capt. 4. 2. v. 109.
units.tr: Marriage was undertaken for the sake of procreating children, and this was proclaimed through the augurs. Capt. 4. 2. v. 109.

units.la: Vide Fr. Hotomannum de Ritibus Nupt. cap. 3. & Desid. Herald. ad Arnob. lib. 7.
units.tr: See Fr. Hotomann, de Ritibus Nuptiarum, ch. 3, and Desiderius Heraldus on Arnobius, book 7.

units.la: In Nuptijs contrahendis stipulatio sæpè fit post pactum & ratam conditionem. Pœn. 5. 3. v. 34. Trin. 2. 4. v. 174.
units.tr: In contracting marriages a stipulation is often made after the agreement and the settled terms. Poen. 5. 3. v. 34. Trin. 2. 4. v. 174.

units.la: Vide Tit. Stipulationum.
units.tr: See the title Of Stipulations.

units.la: Vasa supellectilia in sponsalibus purè eluerunt. Aul. 2. 2. v. 3.
units.tr: Household vessels were thoroughly washed at betrothals. Aul. 2. 2. v. 3.

units.la: Novum maritum, & novam nuptam, solebant prosequi ad loca, in quis habitabat. Caf. 4.2. v.3.
units.tr: They used to escort the new husband and the new bride to the place where they lived. Cas. 4. 2. v. 3.

units.la: In solemni Nuptiarum festivitate etiam tibicines adhibiti fuerunt, qui suavi cantu cöcelebrarunt plateam omnem Hymenæo, Deo Nuptiarum: cum hacclamatione: Io hymen! Hymenæe, Io hymen! Aul. 2.4. v.2. Caf. 4.3. v. 1,2,3. Terent. Adelph. 5. 7.
units.tr: At the solemn festivity of the wedding, flute-players were also engaged, who with sweet song made the whole street resound with Hymenaeus, the god of marriage, with the cry: Io Hymen! Hymenaee, Io Hymen! Aul. 2. 4. v. 2. Cas. 4. 3. v. 1, 2, 3. Ter. Adelph. 5. 7.

units.la: Verum hoc mihi mora est Tibicen, & hymenæum, qui canat.
units.tr: But this is a delay for me: the flute-player and the hymenaeus, who is to sing.

units.la: Nuptiis appropinquantibus ante omnia vasa diligenter eluebant: & sacrificabant Junoni, Veneri, & Gratijs. Aul. 2.3. v.3.
units.tr: As the nuptials drew near, they first washed all the vessels carefully, and sacrificed to Juno, Venus and the Graces. Aul. 2. 3. v. 3.

units.la: Vasculaintus pure propera: atq; elue.
units.tr: Quickly wash the little vessels thoroughly and cleanly.

units.la: Desponsatæ jam sibi arrham dabant. Rud. Prol. v. 45. Desponsatio autem fiebat corde, ore, opere: ut docet eruditus JC. Albericus Gentilis lib. 2. de Nupt. c. 22. quem vide sis.
units.tr: Those already betrothed gave each other a pledge (arrha). Betrothal was made by heart, mouth and deed, as the learned jurist Albericus Gentilis teaches in book 2, de Nuptiis, ch. 22, which you may consult.

units.la: Nuptias paraturi, varia obsonia emebant: escas molliculas, sepiolas, lepadas, lolligiunculas hordejas: de quibus vide Lexicon Plaut. Caf. 2. 8. v. 57.
units.tr: Preparing for the wedding, they bought various delicacies: soft dishes, cuttlefish, limpets, and little barley-squids. On these see the Lexicon of Plautus. Cas. 2. 8. v. 57.

units.la: Neque parcebant sumtibus. Ib. v. 67.
units.tr: Nor did they spare expense. Ib. v. 67.

units.la: De dote filiæ dandâ admodum soliciti fuerunt veteres. Trin. 1. 2. v. 120.
units.tr: The ancients were very anxious about giving a dowry with a daughter. Trin. 1. 2. v. 120.

units.la: Quærebant etiam conditionem suis filiabus dignam. Trin. 1. 2. v. 122.
units.tr: They also sought a match worthy of their daughters. Trin. 1. 2. v. 122.

units.la: In Nuptijs novam nuptam præcedebat ἅμαξα, h. e. puer cum cereo. Curc. 1.1. v.9. Caf. 1.1. v.30.
units.tr: At weddings the new bride was preceded by a wagon [ἅμαξα], that is, a boy with a wax torch. Curc. 1. 1. v. 9. Cas. 1. 1. v. 30.

units.la: Adeoque ἅμαξοι illi non fuerunt usque adeo bonæ famæ, ut apparet ex Luciani Lexiphane. Martial. 12. Ep. 42. Præluxére faces. Vide etiam Langlæi Semestr. Otij libb.
units.tr: And those wagon-men [ἅμαξοι] were not held in such good repute, as appears from Lucian's Lexiphanes. Martial 12, Ep. 42: the torches have shone forth. See also Langlaeus, Semestria Otii, books.

units.la: Ad nuptias coquebant: eoque coqui conducti. Aul. 3.2 .v. 15.
units.tr: For the wedding they cooked, and cooks were hired for this purpose.

units.la: Dos attrahit procos. Quod deplorat Euclio senex. Aul. 2.2.v.87.
units.tr: A dowry attracts suitors, which old Euclio laments. Aul. 2. 2. v. 87.

units.la: Di immortales obsecro, Aurum quid valet! Credo ego jam illum inaudijse, mihi esse thesaurum domi: Id inhiat, ea affinitatem hanc obstinavit gratiâ.
units.tr: Immortal gods, I beg you, what is gold worth! I believe he has already heard that I have a treasure at home. He gapes after that; this is why he has bound himself to this marriage for the sake of favour.

units.la: Sperata erant sponsæ: quam procus sibi dari sperabat. Pœn. 5. 4. v.
units.tr: The bride was hoped for: the one the suitor hoped would be given to him. Poen. 5. 4. v.

units.la: 4. v. 9. Germani dicunt: Meine Zukünftige. Vide lex. Plaut.
units.tr: 4. v. 9. The Germans say: Meine Zukünftige, "my future one." See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: Sponsi in nuptijs soliciti erant de officio suo: ne quis sc. eos devotaret, ut alibi loquitur Plautus: aut illis occentaret: eoque ipsi offenderent Hymenæum. Caf. 4. 3. v. 8. Ubi oës Mss. Lamb. Camerarij: & Palatini: omnesque editi Frisin. Carpent. Argentorat. Pap. Venet. versum eum sic legunt:
units.tr: Bridegrooms at weddings were anxious about their duty, lest anyone should curse them, as Plautus says elsewhere, or sing to them, and so offend Hymenaeus. Cas. 4. 3. v. 8. Where all the manuscripts (Lambinus, Camerarius and Palatine) and all the printed editions (Frisingen, Carpentras, Strasbourg, Pap., Venice) read that line thus:

units.la: O L. Quid si etiam offendam Hymenæum.
units.tr: O L. What if I should also offend Hymenaeus?

units.la: Et cur Taubmannus novissimus Editor mutavit in occentem? Vah sapientiam hominis! O Criticum novo sæculo dignum! Veterem lectionem confirmat inibi ipse Senex versu 11. Dirupi cantando Hymenæum licet: illo morbo, quo dirumpi cupio, non est topia.
units.tr: And why did Taubmann, the latest editor, change it to occentem? Oh, the wisdom of the man! O critic worthy of a new age! The old reading is confirmed there by the old man himself, in verse 11: I may burst from singing Hymenaeus; that illness by which I long to burst is not out of place.

units.la: Consuetudo proprie de stupro. Cist. 1. 1. v. 89. In jure tamen pro consuetudine honesta, & maritali usurpatur. Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: The word is properly used of illicit intercourse. Cist. 1. 1. v. 89. In law, however, it is used of an honourable, marital cohabitation. See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: In nuptijs peregrè advenientibus cæna dabatur. Curc. 5. 3. v. 51.
units.tr: At weddings a meal was given to those arriving from abroad. Curc. 5. 3. v. 51.

units.la: Avari dotem metuunt in elocandâ filiâ. Aul. 2. 2. v. 80.
units.tr: Misers fear the dowry when a daughter is given away in marriage. Aul. 2. 2. v. 80.

units.la: Patre mortuo frater sororis pupillæ legitimus tutor est: eique merito dotem dat. Curc. 5. 2. v. 63.
units.tr: When the father has died, a brother is the lawful guardian of an unmarried sister, and he rightly gives her a dowry. Curc. 5. 2. v. 63.

units.la: Novæ nuptæ facere debent officium nuptiale. Caf. 5. 4. v. 32. Ubi tamen profligata utitur sententiâ prostibulum servi.
units.tr: New brides ought to perform the nuptial duty. Cas. 5. 4. v. 32. Where, however, the shameless prostitute-slave uses a cynical sentence.

units.la: Vicini maximè ad nuptias vocabantur. Caf. 2. 8. v. 6.
units.tr: Neighbours were especially invited to weddings. Cas. 2. 8. v. 6.

units.la: Ludi nuptiales quoque celebrati. Caf. 5. 1. v. 2.
units.tr: Nuptial games were also celebrated. Cas. 5. 1. v. 2.

units.la: Viri etiam dicebantur nubere. Caf. 5. 1. v. 5. Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: Men too were said to marry (nubere). Cas. 5. 1. v. 5. See the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: Eadem potest esse & nupta & vidua. Mil. 4. 1. v. 19. Vidua, quatenus non experiê Venerem. Nupta, quatenus habet maritum.
units.tr: The same woman can be both bride and widow. Mil. 4. 1. v. 19. Widow, insofar as she has not experienced Venus; bride, insofar as she has a husband.

units.la: Cænam nuptialem dabant amicis. Curc. 5. 2. v. 61. Rud. 4. 6. v. 11. Vide Fabr. Sem. l. 1. c. 6. v. 27.
units.tr: They gave a wedding dinner to friends. Curc. 5. 2. v. 61. Rud. 4. 6. v. 11. See Fabricius, Semestria, book 1, ch. 6, v. 27.

units.la: Nuptiale verbum est conditio. Stich 1. 2. v. 81.
units.tr: Conditio is a nuptial term. Stich. 1. 2. v. 81.

units.la: Quin vos capitis conditionem ex pessumâ primariam?
units.tr: Come, do you rank the condition of your life, from the worst, as first?

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut. loca.
units.tr: See the passages in the Lexicon of Plautus.

units.la: In nuptijs lautè vestiti, exornatiqúe erant: & candidè incedebant cum coronâ & lampade. Cas. 2.8.v.10. & 4.1.v.9. & 4.2.v.17. & 4.4.v.26.
units.tr: At weddings they were dressed and adorned splendidly, and walked brightly with a garland and torch. Cas. 2. 8. v. 10, and 4. 1. v. 9, and 4. 2. v. 17, and 4. 4. v. 26.

units.la: In nuptijs hilariter vivendum. Quod & avarus agnovit Euclio. Aul. 2.8.v.1.
units.tr: At weddings one ought to live cheerfully, as even the miser Euclio acknowledged. Aul. 2. 8. v. 1.

units.la: In eloc andis liberis familiæ non postrema semper habita ratio. Trin. 5.2.v.9.
units.tr: In giving children in marriage, the standing of the family was not always regarded as the least consideration. Trin. 5. 2. v. 9.

units.la: NUTRICUM.
units.tr: NURSES.

units.la: NUTRICES à pueris variè maculantur. Unde in Proverbio Nutricis Pallium.
units.tr: Nurses are variously stained by their charges. Hence the proverb The nurse's cloak.

units.la: O.
units.tr: O.

units.la: Oblivionis.
units.tr: Oblivion.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Memoriæ.
units.tr: See also the heading Memory.

units.la: MOs est hominibus oblivisci, neque novisse, cujus nihil sit faciunda gratia.Capt. 5. 3. v. 8.
units.tr: It is the custom of people to forget, and not to know, anyone for whose sake they have done nothing. Capt. 5. 3. v. 8.

units.la: Obsecrationum. Obtestationum. Resecrationum.
units.tr: Entreaties. Adjurations. Releasings.

units.la: QUi obsecrabatur, ne religione teneretur, subijciebat Resecro: quo verbo religionem solvebat. Aul. 4. 7. v. 4. Perf. 1. 1. v. 9. Si quis enim antiquitus diceret obsecro, eum quem alloquebatur, obstringere quodam sacramento & jurejurando videbatur: & si ea persona erat, cui pudorem deberet, cuique omnia liberè in utramque partem esse vellet, ut eam religione solveret subijciebat Resecro. In ejusmodi obtestationibus sæpè etiam utebantur hac formulâ Potin es: ut loco Persæ: Facere amicum me tibi potis es sempiternum? Sic Terentius: Si tibi placere potis es, mihi ut respondeas. Idem: Potin' es verum dicere? Persius Sat. 1. Et verum, inquis, amo: verum mihi dicito de me: Qui pote?
units.tr: When someone was entreated, so that he would not be bound by religious obligation, he would reply "I release you" [Resecro], and by that word he loosed the obligation. Aul. 4. 7. v. 4. Perf. 1. 1. v. 9. For if in ancient times someone said "I beg you" [obsecro], he seemed to bind the person he addressed by a kind of sacred oath and sworn pledge. And if that person was one to whom he owed respect, and whom he wanted to be free to answer either way, he would reply "I release you" [Resecro] to free him from the obligation. In such entreaties they also often used this formula, "Can you?" [Potin es], as in the passage from the Persa: "Can you make me your everlasting friend?" So Terence: "If you can be pleasing to me, answer me." Again: "Can you tell the truth?" Persius, Satire 1: "And you say you love the truth; tell me the truth about myself. How can you?"

units.la: Atque hæc sic explicarunt Diaconus ex Festo Pomp. Turneb. l. 18. cap. 25. Pithæus lib. 1. Adverf. cap. 10.
units.tr: These matters have been explained thus by Diaconus from Festus, Pomponius, Turnebus book 18 chapter 25, and Pithou book 1 Adversaria chapter 10.

units.la: PER varia corporis membra fiebant obtestationes. Per genua. Mil. 2. 6. v. 61. Cist. 2. 3. v. 45. Curc. 5. 2 v. 31. Moss. 3. 2. v. 57.
units.tr: Entreaties were made by various parts of the body: by the knees. Mil. 2. 6. v. 61. Cist. 2. 3. v. 45. Curc. 5. 2 v. 31. Moss. 3. 2. v. 57.

units.la: Mil. 4. 6. v. 24. Rud. 4. 3. v. 13. Truc. 4. 3. v. 52. Quia scil. in illis sedes misericordiae credebatur esse. Turn. l. 11. c. 22. Quintil. l. 6. c. 2. Gruterus ad Senecam de Brevitate vitae cap. 8.
units.tr: Mil. 4. 6. v. 24. Rud. 4. 3. v. 13. Truc. 4. 3. v. 52. Because, namely, the seat of mercy was believed to be in those parts. Turnebus book 11 chapter 22. Quintilian book 6 chapter 2. Gruter on Seneca, On the Shortness of Life, chapter 8.

units.la: OBTESTATIO fiebat per dextram: h. e. fidem alicujus. Amph. 3. 2. v. 42. Capt. 2. 3. v. 82. Poen. 1. 3. v. 8.
units.tr: An adjuration was made by the right hand, that is, by someone's pledge of faith. Amph. 3. 2. v. 42. Capt. 2. 3. v. 82. Poen. 1. 3. v. 8.

units.la: ETIAM Deos inclamabant hac formulâ: Servate me DI obsecro? Ibid. v. 31.
units.tr: They also called upon the gods with this formula: "Save me, gods, I beg you!" Ibid. v. 31.

units.la: SOLEBANT obtestari alios non tantum per Divos: sed per omnia ea, quae illis chara esse noverant. Asin. 1. 1. v. 3. Obtestor te per senectutem, & uxorem tuam.
units.tr: They used to adjure others not only by the gods but by all those things they knew to be dear to them. Asin. 1. 1. v. 3. "I adjure you by your old age and your wife."

units.la: Sallustius in Catilinar. Per liberos tuos rogatus.
units.tr: Sallust in the Catiline: "Asked by your children."

units.la: Idem in Jugurth. Adherbalem inducit in extremâ ad Senatum Oratione: P. C. Per vos, per liberos, atque parentes vestros, per majestatem populi Rom. subvenite misero mihi. Ite obviam injuriae.
units.tr: The same author, in the Jugurtha, has Adherbal, in his final speech to the Senate, say: "Conscript Fathers, by yourselves, by your children and your parents, by the majesty of the Roman people, help me in my wretchedness. Go and meet the injustice."

units.la: Cornificius ad Herenn. Rhetor. lib. 4. Parce, & per ea, quae tibi dulcissima sunt in vita, miserere nostri.
units.tr: Cornificius to Herennius, Rhetoric book 4: "Spare us, and by those things which are sweetest to you in life, have pity on us."

units.la: Caelius lib. 8. Epist. 15. Ciceronem obsecrat: Per fortunas tuas, per liberos te oro, & obsecro.
units.tr: Caelius, Letters book 8 letter 15, entreats Cicero: "By your fortunes, by your children, I beg you and entreat you."

units.la: Cicero pro Quint. Obsecravit Quintus Naevium, per fratris sui mortui cinerem, per nomen propinquitatis, per ipsum conjugem, & liberos.
units.tr: Cicero, For Quinctius: "Quintus entreated Naevius by the ashes of his dead brother, by the name of kinship, by his very wife and children."

units.la: Et lib. 14. ad Famil. Epist. 1. Terentiae conjugi de Tullio filio: Per fortunas miseras nostras, vide ne puerum perditum eamus.
units.tr: And in book 14 of the Letters to Friends, letter 1, to his wife Terentia about their son Tullius: "By our wretched fortunes, take care that we do not lose the boy."

units.la: Seneca Controv. 1. Porcius Latro pro filio: Ergo fame morientem videbo patrem, per cuius cineres juraturus sum?
units.tr: Seneca, Controversies 1, Porcius Latro for a son: "So shall I see my father dying of hunger, by whose ashes I am about to swear?"

units.la: Et Praefat. lib. 3. Controv. L. Albutius Silo: Jura per patris tui cineres, qui inconditi jacent. Jura per patrus memoriam.
units.tr: And in the preface to book 3 of the Controversies, L. Albutius Silo: "Swear by your father's ashes, which lie unburied. Swear by the memory of your father."

units.la: Vide Briffon. lib. 8. Form. & Andr. Schotti lib. 3. Observ. c. 39.
units.tr: See Brisson book 8 On Formulas, and Andreas Schott book 3 Observations chapter 39.

units.la: OBTESTABANTUR etiam per pietatem suam.
units.tr: They also swore by their own piety.

units.la: OCCASIONIS. TEMPORIS. MATURITATIS.
units.tr: OCCASION. TIME. OPPORTUNITY.

units.la: OCcasio bona non prætermittenda: quia post hæc calva; ք recte ait servus ille Asin. 2. 2. v. 12. si huic occasioni tempus se subduxerit Numquam ædepol quadrigis albis indipiscet postea.
units.tr: A good opportunity is not to be let slip, because afterwards it is bald; rightly does that slave in the Asinaria say: "If time has drawn itself away from this opportunity, never afterwards will he attain it, even with white horses."
And in the Aulularia:

units.la: Quando illac occasio perit, post sero cupit.
units.tr: "When that opportunity has perished, afterwards he desires it too late."

units.la: MIserum est rem necessariam providere, cùm tempus parandi non datur. Most. 2. 1. v. 32. Miserum est opus Igitur demum foderePuteum, ubi sitis fauces tenet. Inquit adolescens nepos, qui adventum patris nimis sero prævertit.
units.tr: It is a wretched thing to provide for a necessary matter when the time for preparing is not given. In the Mostellaria: "It is a wretched thing to do the work then, namely to dig the well, when thirst already grips the throat." So says the young man, the nephew, who anticipates his father's arrival far too late.

units.la: VIrtus est, ubi occasio admonet, dispicere. Perf. 2. 3. v. 16.
units.tr: It is a virtue, when opportunity gives warning, to look carefully about.

units.la: OFFICII. MUNERIS. FUNCTIONIS.
units.tr: OF DUTY. OF OFFICE. OF FUNCTION.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit, Honoris: Magistratus.
units.tr: See also Tit., under Honour: Magistrate.

units.la: OFficium faciendum est sine ἀσθαλμοδυλία. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 1. & seqq. quos lege de malis servis.
units.tr: ADuty is to be performed without ἀσθαλμοδυλία [self-conceit]. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 1 and following. Read on concerning bad slaves.

units.la: Officium suum meminisse, magnus est honos homini pudico. Trin. 3 2. v. 71.
units.tr: To remember one's duty is a great honour for an upright man. Trin. 3. 2. v. 71.

units.la: Sapientis officium suum æquum est colere & facere. Stich. 1. 1. v. 33.
units.tr: It is fitting for a wise man to cultivate and perform his duty. Stich. 1. 1. v. 33.

units.la: Quem honoramus, ab eo honoramur. Aul. Prol. v. 20.
units.tr: Whom we honour, by him we are honoured. Aul. Prol. v. 20.

units.la: Qui manet, nt moneatur semper servus homo officium suum, nec voluntate id facere meminit: servus is habitu haud probus est. Stich. 1. 2. v. 1.
units.tr: He who remains, that a slave may always be reminded of his duty and does not remember to do it of his own will: such a slave is not of good character. Stich. 1. 2. v. 1.

units.la: OLEI. VNGVENTI. VNCTIONIS. ODORUM.
units.tr: OF OIL. OF OINTMENT. OF ANOINTING. OF SCENTS.

units.la: OLEO amatores se inungebant: qp in culleis venditum in pergulis. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 77. Etiam pulmenta inde fiebant. Ibid.
units.tr: Lovers used to anoint themselves with oil; it was sold in flasks, in the stalls. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 77. Also relishes were made from it. Ibid.

units.la: NIHIL oleo tranquillius. Pæn. 5. 4. v. 84.
units.tr: Nothing is more soothing than oil. Poen. 5. 4. v. 84.

units.la: ELEGANTIORES homines odoratis unguentis caput perfundere solebant. Caf. 2. 3. v. 19. Mart. lib. 8. Ep. 77.
units.tr: Fashionable people were accustomed to pour scented ointments over their heads. Cas. 2. 3. v. 19. Mart. book 8, epigram 77.

units.la: Si sapis, Assyrio semper tibi crinis amomo
units.tr: If you are wise, let your hair always shine with Assyrian amomum.

units.la: Splendeat.
units.tr: Shine.

units.la: Juvenal. Hirsuto spirant opobalsama collo. Vide plura apud Bernartium ad lib. 1. Sylvarum Statij.
units.tr: Juvenal: Balsam of opobalsamum breathes from a hairy neck. See more in Bernartius on the first book of the Silvae of Statius.

units.la: UNGUENTA exotica fragrantissima erant. Moft. 1. 1. v. 41.
units.tr: Exotic ointments were most fragrant. Most. 1. 1. v. 41.

units.la: Non omnes possunt olere unguenta exotica.
units.tr: Not everyone can smell of exotic ointments.

units.la: UNGEBANTUR prius veteres, deinde fricabantur. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 92.
units.tr: The ancients were first anointed, then rubbed. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 92.

units.la: UNGUENTA ex peregrinis regionibus advehebant. Stich. 2. 3. v. 58.
units.tr: They brought ointments from foreign regions. Stich. 2. 3. v. 58.

units.la: MAGNUM luxus instrumentum cottidianæ unctiones. Trin. 2. 4. v. 5. Rud. 2. 7. v. 22.
units.tr: Daily anointings are a great instrument of luxury. Trin. 2. 4. v. 5. Rud. 2. 7. v. 22.

units.la: Eluas tu, an exungare: ciccum non interdum.
units.tr: You may wash yourself, or be rubbed down; not sometimes with a little cloth.

units.la: IN convivijs unguentis & odoribus usi. Pseud. 5. 1. v. 21.
units.tr: At banquets they used unguents and perfumes. Pseud. 5. 1. v. 21.

units.la: GRÆCI unctionibus abundabant propter unguentorum copiam. Stich. 2. 1. v. 73.
units.tr: The Greeks abounded in anointings because of their plenty of ointments. Stich. 2. 1. v. 73.

units.la: UNGUENTA vendebant myropolæ. Caf. 2. 3. v. 10. Vide Lexicon Plautin.
units.tr: Perfumers sold ointments. Cas. 2. 3. v. 10. See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: SERVOS unctores alebant. Trin. 2. 1. v. 22.
units.tr: They kept slaves as anointers. Trin. 2. 1. v. 22.

units.la: OPILIONUM. OVIUM.
units.tr: SHEPHERDS. SHEEP.

units.la: OPILIONES mordaces canes alunt. Bacch. f. 2. v. 27.
units.tr: Shepherds feed biting dogs. Bacch. act 2. sc. 1. v. 27.

units.la: ORATIONUM. PRECUM. SUPPLICATIONUM.
units.tr: Of Orations, Prayers, and Supplications.

units.la: MAGNATES non rogati suppliciter exorantur. Rud. 2. 4. v. 18. Basilicus sum, quem nisi oras, nihil auferes.
units.tr: Great men are not humbly entreated unless they are asked. Rud. 2. 4. v. 18. "I am a king; unless you beg me, you will get nothing from me."

units.la: SUPPLICANTES orabant manibus velatis. Amphit. 1.1 v. 100. Velati autem dicebantur, teste Scaliger, qui caput cinctum licio laneo habebant.
units.tr: Suppliants prayed with their hands veiled. Amphit. 1.1 v. 100. Scaliger holds that those called "veiled" were those who had their heads bound with a woollen band.

units.la: Virgil. lib. 12. Æn. vers. 120.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid book 12, verse 120.

units.la: Velati lino, & verbenis tempora cincti.
units.tr: "Veiled with linen, and their temples bound with sacred herbs."

units.la: Livius lib. 1.
units.tr: Livy, book 1.

units.la: Legatus, ubi ad fines eorum venit, unde res repetuntur, capite velato:
units.tr: "The envoy, when he came to the borders of those from whom the things are demanded back, with his head veiled:"

units.la: AUDI JUPITER, inquit, &c.
units.tr: "Hear, Jupiter," he says, etc.

units.la: Sic supplicia, & velamenta dicebant τὴν ἱκετηρίαν, quòd nimirum filo laneo velatum erat caduceum. Vide etiam Turn. lib. 4. c. 15. Adverf. & Servium Danielis lib. 8. p. 494. Edit. Parif.
units.tr: Thus they called supplications and veils the suppliant's branch [τὴν ἱκετηρίαν], because the caduceus was wrapped with woollen thread. See also Turnebus, Adversaria book 4, chapter 15, and Servius on Daniel, book 8, p. 494, Paris edition.

units.la: SUPPLICABANT attrectatis genibus. Asin. 3. 3. v. 80, 88. Truc. 2. 7. v. 30.
units.tr: Suppliants touched their knees. Asin. 3. 3. v. 80, 88. Truc. 2. 7. v. 30.

units.la: IN blandiore supplicatione frictio genuum adhibita, Asin. 3. 3. v. 80, 88. Truc. 2. 7. v. 30.
units.tr: In a more coaxing supplication, the knees were rubbed. Asin. 3. 3. v. 80, 88. Truc. 2. 7. v. 30.

units.la: IMPII putant se posse placare Deum donis: sed & operam & sumtum perdunt: ideo fit: quia nihil ei acceptum est à perjuris supplicij. Facilius namque si qui pius est, à DIs supplicans, quàm qui scelestus est, inveniet veniam sibi. Rud. Prol. ver. 2 2. & sequentibus.
units.tr: The impious think they can placate God with gifts, but they lose both their effort and their expense. This happens because nothing is acceptable to God from perjured suppliants. For a man who is pious, supplicating the gods, will more easily find pardon than one who is wicked. Rud. Prol. v. 22 and following.

units.la: Cic. lib. 2. de Legg.
units.tr: Cicero, book 2 of the Laws.

units.la: Impius ne audero placare donis iram Deorum.
units.tr: "The impious man will not dare to placate the anger of the gods with gifts."

units.la: Æschylus:
units.tr: Aeschylus:

units.la: Λιτὰς δικαίως θεὸς κλύει.
units.tr: "Justly God hears entreaties" [Λιτὰς δικαίως θεὸς κλύει].

units.la: Demosthen.
units.tr: Demosthenes.

units.la: Τοσούτῳ πλείους ἀφορμὰς ὥστε τὴν ἕ ... (Greek text, partly illegible)
units.tr: "So much more grounds, so that ..." [Τοσούτῳ πλείους ἀφορμὰς ὥστε τὴν ἕ ...] (the Greek is partly illegible in the scan).

units.la: SOLEBANT veteres orare per Deos, per sacra, per liberos: per res charissimas: per ipsam Precem Jovis filiam: h. e. per τὰς Λιτὰς, Capt. 2. 1. v. 47, 48.
units.tr: The ancients were accustomed to pray by the gods, by sacred things, by their children, by their dearest possessions, and by Prayer herself, the daughter of Jupiter, that is, by the Litae [τὰς Λιτὰς]. Capt. 2. 1. v. 47, 48.

units.la: ORDINIS.
units.tr: Order.

units.la: PRIUS potest esse posterius: posterius prius, καὶ ἀντίγραφα: quod solvitur. Cist. 2. 3. v. 71.
units.tr: What is first can be last, and what is last first, and counterparts [καὶ ἀντίγραφα]: which is resolved. Cist. 2. 3. v. 71.

units.la: OSCULORUM. BASII. SUAVII.
units.tr: KISSES: BASIUM, SUAVIUM

units.la: Vide Tit. Amoris.
units.tr: See the title Love.

units.la: INTER cæteras antiquæ vetustatis blanditias hoc quoque osculi genus observatum est: quo solebant pueri parentes, aut alios, vel amantes inter se, alterius auribus apprehensis, osculari: idque ollam sive χύτρεαν appellabant: quòd in eo gesta, ut caput ollæ, ita aures arifarum formam referre videbantur. Asin. 3. 3. v. 78. Poen. 1. 2. v. 163.
units.tr: Among the other endearments of ancient times, this kind of kiss was also practised: children would kiss their parents, or others, or lovers would kiss one another, having taken hold of the other's ears. They called this "kissing the jar" (ollam) or "kissing the handle" (χύτρεαν), because, just as the mouth of a jar has handles, so the ears seemed to resemble the shape of the handles of a jar. Asin. 3. 3. v. 78. Poen. 1. 2. v. 163.

units.la: Sine te exorem, sine te prendam auriculis, sine dem savium.
units.tr: Let me beg you, let me take you by the ears, let me give you a kiss.

units.la: Vide ibi, quæ Taubmann. exscripsit. pag. 872. Et Turneb. Adverf. lib. 29. cap. 32.
units.tr: See there what Taubmann copied out, p. 872, and Turnebus, Adversaria, book 29, chapter 32.

units.la: Pollux lib. 10. Λαβὼν (sic) τὰν ὦτων φιλησοντην χύσιν. Ollam prehensis osculator auribus.
units.tr: Pollux, book 10: taking the ears, the pouring out of kisses [Λαβὼν τὰν ὦτων φιλησοντην χύσιν]. Kissing the jar by taking hold of its ears.

units.la: Tibullus lib. 2. Eleg. 5.
units.tr: Tibullus, book 2, Elegy 5.

units.la: Et fœtus matrona dabat, natuq̄, parenti
units.tr: And the mother gave her offspring, and the child to its parent,

units.la: Oscula comprensis auribus eripuit.
units.tr: Snatched kisses from the ears it had seized.

units.la: Osculum amicitiæ signum. Pœn. 1. 2. v. 192.
units.tr: A kiss is a sign of friendship. Poen. 1. 2. v. 192.

units.la: Non sum iratus. A G. Da ergò, ut credam, faviam.
units.tr: I am not angry. — Then give me a kiss, so that I may believe you; I will kiss you.

units.la: Osculantes capita inter inter fe nectere solent: & ferrumina- re labra labellis. Mil. 4. 8. v. 25.
units.tr: Kissing people are accustomed to entwine their heads together, and to weld lip to lip. Mil. 4. 8. v. 25.

units.la: Erat genus osculi, quod vocabant κατα λάττισμα, quodque lingua exserta fiebat. Asin. 3. 3. v. 105. Pseud. 5. 1. v. 15.
units.tr: There was a kind of kiss which they called katalattisma [κατα λάττισμα], and which was done with the tongue thrust out. Asin. 3. 3. v. 105. Pseud. 5. 1. v. 15.

units.la: In amore basium dantes notam imprimebant. Men. 1. 3. v. 12.
units.tr: In love, those giving kisses left a mark. Men. 1. 3. v. 12.

units.la: Filiæ patri adventanti osculum offerebant. Stich. 1. 2. v. 32.
units.tr: Daughters offered a kiss to their father when he arrived. Stich. 1. 2. v. 32.

units.la: Oscula in senibus salsura sunt animæ. Ibid.
units.tr: Kisses on old men are a salty seasoning for the soul. Ibid.

units.la: Amantes pignus dabant in savium : uter utri daret. Pœn. 5. 4. v. 70.
units.tr: Lovers gave a pledge in kisses, each in turn giving to the other. Pœn. 5. 4. v. 70.

units.la: Peregre advenientes salutabant osculo. Epid. 4. 2. v. 2.
units.tr: Those arriving from abroad greeted people with a kiss. Epid. 4. 2. v. 2.

units.la: Otii. Ignaviæ. Desidiæ. Negligentiæ.
units.tr: Leisure. Idleness. Sloth. Negligence.

units.la: Otiosi homines in basilicâ & Rostris olim obambulabant rumorum alienorum aucupes. Capt. 4. 2. v. 35. Unde Subbasilicani dicti, & Subrostrani.
units.tr: Idle men once strolled about in the basilica and on the Rostra, hunters after other people's rumours. Capt. 4. 2. v. 35. Whence they were called Subbasilicani and Subrostrani.

units.la: Desidia adolescentibus pernitiosissima. Bacch. 4. 10. v. 8.
units.tr: Sloth is most destructive to young people. Bacch. 4. 10. v. 8.

units.la: Homines otiosi in locis suspectis habitare, & versari solent. Curc. 4. 1. v. 10. Vide Tit. Urbis Romae.
units.tr: Idle people are accustomed to live and loiter in suspicious places. Curc. 4. 1. v. 10. See the title Rome.

units.la: Ignaviae precia sunt verbera. Men. 5. 6. v. 11.
units.tr: Beatings are the wages of idleness. Men. 5. 6. v. 11.

units.la: Ignavi milites mulieres dicti. Vide Tit. Mulier.
units.tr: Lazy soldiers are called women. See the title Woman.

units.la: Ignavia ad omne vitium impellit adolescentes. Trin. 3. 2. v. 24, 29, 32.
units.tr: Idleness drives young people to every vice. Trin. 3. 2. v. 24, 29, 32.

units.la: Chrysost. πᾶσαν ἡσυχίαν ἐπιδἀξειν ἡ ἀργία.
units.tr: Chrysostom: idleness shows itself as every kind of quiet [πᾶσαν ἡσυχίαν ἐπιδἀξειν ἡ ἀργία].

units.la: Diem sermone terere, segnities mera est. Trin. 3. 3. v. 67.
units.tr: To waste the day in talk is pure sloth. Trin. 3. 3. v. 67.

units.la: Ignavia non secus ac tempestas adobruit juvenilem ætatem. Most. 1. 2. v. 56. & seqq. ἀλλὰ γοεικὰς.
units.tr: Idleness, no less than a storm, overwhelms youthful age. Most. 1. 2. v. 56 and following. [ἀλλὰ γοεικὰς].

units.la: Multa damna secum apportat huic ætati.
units.tr: It brings many losses with it to this time of life.

units.la: Pigri stimulis sunt fodiendi. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 40.
units.tr: Lazy people must be prodded with goads. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 40.

units.la: P.
units.tr: P.

units.la: POENITENTIÆ. RESIPISCENTIÆ.
units.tr: REPENTANCE. RESIPISCENCE.

units.la: ERò atque stultè, prius quod cautum oportuit, postquam comedit rem, post rationem putat. Trin. 2. 4. v. 14.
units.tr: Rashly and foolishly, he thinks about reasoning only after he has eaten the thing, when he should have been careful beforehand. Trin. 2. 4. v. 14.

units.la: Palloris.
units.tr: Of Pallor.

units.la: PALLIDI mortuis similiores, quàm vivis. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 33.
units.tr: Pale men, more like the dead than the living. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 33.

units.la: PARASITORUM. SYCOPHANTARUM. SCURRARUM. ADULATORUM. ASSENTATIONUM. BLANDITIARUM.
units.tr: PARASITES. SYCOPHANTS. BUFFOONS. FLATTERERS. FAWNING. FLATTERY.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Calumnia.
units.tr: See also the title Calumny.

units.la: PARASITI comparantur cochleis. Capt. 1,1. v. 12. Item parasiti rebus prolatis latent In occulto miseri: victitant succo suo, Dum ruri rurant homines, quos ligurriant. Vide reliquos versus.
units.tr: Parasites are compared to snails. Capt. 1. 1. v. 12. Likewise, parasites lie hidden in secret, wretched, living on their own juice, while the men they lick are busy in the country. See the remaining verses.

units.la: PARASITI etsi non servi, maximè tamen servi les erant, qui libertatem offa venalem habebant, ejusque gratia præter irrisum, dicteria, colaphos, etiam ollas sibi in caput cöfringi permittebant: quæ scilic. ollæ cinere erant oppletæ, ut nimirum eo per totum corcorpus effuso majorem risum Præbitoribus suis exhiberent.
units.tr: Parasites, although not slaves, were nevertheless for the most part slaves who had sold their freedom for a bit of food, and for its sake they put up with mockery, insults and blows, and even allowed pots to be broken over their heads. Those pots, of course, were filled with ash, so that when the ash spilled over their whole body they might provide their patrons with greater laughter.

units.la: Curc. 3. v. 26. Nam quid id refert mea, An aula quasâ cum ci-nere effossus oculus fiet.
units.tr: Curc. 3. v. 26. For what does it matter to me whether my eye is gouged out with a pot full of ashes?

units.la: Perf. 1.2. v.8. Duri capitones inde dicti.
units.tr: Perf. 1. 2. v. 8. Hence they were called thick-heads.

units.la: Et Perf. 5. 2. & 16. Capt. 1.1. v. 20. Nisi qui colaphos perpeti potis parasitus, frangi aulas in caput.
units.tr: And Perf. 5. 2. & 16. Capt. 1. 1. v. 20. Unless a parasite is able to endure blows, let pots be smashed on his head.

units.la: Quintil. Parasitorum vita est, contumelias in quastu habere: & injuria pasci. Vide Cafaub. ad Athen. lib. 1. cap. 14.
units.tr: Quintilian: "The life of a parasite is to make a living from insults and to feed on injury." See Casaubon on Athenaeus, book 1, chapter 14.

units.la: PARASITI solebant advocari quoque ad epulum, cùm Herculi decimas pollucerent: ideoque Parasitus ille Herculem Nutricem suam invocat. Curc. 2, 3. v. 79.
units.tr: Parasites were also invited to the feast when they paid the tithe to Hercules; therefore that parasite calls on Hercules, his nurse. Curc. 2. 3. v. 79.

units.la: TRIPLEX genus fuit Parasitorum: Derisores. Plagipatidæ, five Lacones, & Adulatores. De derisoribus agitur Capt. 1.1. v.3.
units.tr: There were three kinds of parasites: jesters, blow-takers (or Laconians), and flatterers. The jesters are discussed at Capt. 1. 1. v. 3.

units.la: PARASITI quos numquam quisq̃, neq; vocat, neque invocat, Quasi mures semper edunt alienum cibum. Capt. 1.1. v. 8, 9.
units.tr: Parasites whom no one ever invites or summons, like mice, always eat other people's food. Capt. 1. 1. v. 8, 9.

units.la: PARASITORUM olim provincia fuit, obsonare. Capt. 3.1. v. 14. Vide Tit. Convivij.
units.tr: It was once the business of parasites to buy provisions. Capt. 3. 1. v. 14. See the title Feast.

units.la: Quæ fuerit suppellex & disciplina parasitica, explicat Parasitus ipse. Stich. 2.1.v. 74.
units.tr: What the parasitic equipment and discipline were, the parasite himself explains. Stich. 2. 1. v. 74.

units.la: Cavillationes malacas ampullarias, ampullam rubidam: rubigino-sam strigilem: perjuratiunculas parasiticas Vide inf. ex Persa.
units.tr: "Soft flatteries of the flask, the red flask, the rusty strigil, little parasitic perjuries." See below, from the Persa.

units.la: Sic Cicer. lib. 4. de Finibus: Si ad illam vitam, quæ cum virtute degitur, ampulla aut strigilis accedat, sumturum sapientem eam vitam potius, cui hæc adjeċta.
units.tr: So Cicero, book 4 of De Finibus: "If a flask or a strigil were added to that life which is lived with virtue, the wise man would rather choose that life to which these things were added."

units.la: PARASITI sunt microtrogi: qui ut mures aliena rodunt. Ibid. v. 88. Vide paulò post.
units.tr: Parasites are nibblers, who gnaw at other people's goods like mice. Ibid. v. 88. See shortly after.

units.la: PARASITORUM est mensas divitum attondere, & divitib° semper aliquid abradere: eoque à Phocyllide appellautur ῥαπιζοκό-ρoι. Epid. 2.3. v.6.
units.tr: It is the business of parasites to scrape the tables of the rich and always to take something off the rich; hence Phocylides calls them table-scrapers [ῥαπιζοκόροι]. Epid. 2. 3. v. 6.

units.la: PARASITI perpetuò cum fame confligantur. Stich. 2.1.v.1. Famem fuisse suspicor matrem mihi. Nam post quam natus sum, satur numquam fui.
units.tr: Parasites are constantly at war with hunger. Stich. 2. 1. v. 1. I suspect Hunger was my mother, for since I was born I have never been full.

units.la: PARASITI Herculè colebant. Curc. 2.2.v.79. Stich.2.1.v. 70,80.
units.tr: Parasites worshipped Hercules. Curc. 2. 2. v. 79. Stich. 2. 1. v. 70, 80.

units.la: PARASITI apud regem aliquem, seu patronum, saginam quære-bant. Trin. 3.2.v.96. Most. 1.1.v.62.
units.tr: Parasites at the court of some king or patron sought out fattening feasts. Trin. 3. 2. v. 96. Most. 1. 1. v. 62.

units.la: PARASITI muribus comparantur. Perf. 1.2.v.6.
units.tr: Parasites are compared to mice. Perf. 1. 2. v. 6.

units.la: Numquam quisquam meorum majorum fuit, quin parasitando paverint ventres suos: pater, avus, proavus, abavus, atavus, tritavus, quasi mures semper edere alienum cibum: neque eda-citate eos quisquam poterat vincere. Sic Capt. 1.1.v. Quasi mures semper edimus alienum cibum.
units.tr: There was never any of my ancestors who did not fill his belly by parasitism: father, grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather, and so on, always eating other people's food like mice; nor could anyone outdo them in gluttony. Thus Capt. 1. 1. v.: "Like mice, we always eat other people's food."

units.la: Diogenes cum videret mures ad mensam subrepentes: Ecce tibi, inquit, etiam Diogenes Parasitos alit.
units.tr: When Diogenes saw mice creeping up to the table he said: "Look, even Diogenes feeds parasites!"

units.la: PARASITI ridiculi causâ adhibiti in convivijs. Stich. 2.3.v.57,63. & 3.2.v.1.
units.tr: Parasites were brought in at dinners for the sake of amusement. Stich. 2. 3. v. 57, 63, & 3. 2. v. 1.

units.la: PARASITI Sanctam colebant Saturitatem, quæ illis eratinstar omnium Deorum. Capt. 4.2.v.97.
units.tr: Parasites worshipped holy Satiety, who for them stood in place of all the gods. Capt. 4. 2. v. 97.

units.la: PARASITI divites, sub quorum clientelâ vivebant, Genios suos appellabant. Capt. 4.2.v.99. Curc. 2.3.v.22. & 5.2.v.29. Men. 1.2.v.20. Bacch. Teneo dextrâ Genium.
units.tr: Parasites called their wealthy patrons, under whose clientage they lived, their Genii. Capt. 4. 2. v. 99. Curc. 2. 3. v. 22, & 5. 2. v. 29. Men. 1. 2. v. 20. Bacch.: "I hold the Genius with my right hand."

units.la: ITEMQUE Reges appellarunt, quorum lautitias sectabantur. Asin. 5.2.v.69. Stich. 3.2.v.2. Men. 5.5.v.4. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: Likewise they called kings, whose luxuries they pursued, by that name. Asin. 5. 2. v. 69. Stich. 3. 2. v. 2. Men. 5. 5. v. 4. See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: VOCABANT etiam Jove terrestres. Perf. 1.3.v.20.
units.tr: They even called them earthly Jupiters. Perf. 1. 3. v. 20.

units.la: PARASITORUM exercitum, & milites ἀλληγορικῶς & jocuları-ter explicat noster Capt. 1.2.v.50. Opus est tibi multigeneribus militibus, Primodum opus est pistorensibus. Opus paniceis, opus polentinis, Opus turdetanis, opus ficedulensibus: Jam maritimi omnes milites opus sunt tibi, etc.
units.tr: Our author explains the parasites' army and soldiers allegorically and in jest. Capt. 1. 2. v. 50. You need soldiers of many kinds: first of all you need bakers, you need bread-men, you need porridge-men, you need thrush-men, you need fig-pecker men. Now all the sea-men are needed by you, etc.

units.la: PARASITI species cibarias sectantur. Curc. 2.3.v.28.
units.tr: Parasites pursue the dishes of food. Curc. 2. 3. v. 28.

units.la: NIHIL parasitus est, cui argentum domi est: lubido extemplò cepere est convivium. Perf. 1.3.v.40. Nam quis probus esse velit parasitus, cum Cynica gentis esse oportet. Ibid. v.43.
units.tr: A man has no parasite if he has money at home; desire at once takes him to a banquet. Perf. 1. 3. v. 40. For who would wish to be an honest parasite, since he must be of the Cynic breed? Ibid. v. 43.

units.la: DISCIPLINA parasitorum à parasito graphicè depingitur Perf. 1.3.v.44. & seqq.
units.tr: The discipline of parasites is vividly portrayed by a parasite. Perf. 1. 3. v. 44 and following.

units.la: Ampullam, strigilem, scaphium, soccos, pallium, marsupium habeat: inibi paulum prasidij: qui familiarem suam vitam oble-ret domi. Vide supra ex Stich.
units.tr: "Let him have a flask, a strigil, a bowl, slippers, a cloak, a purse; there a little support, for one who would ruin his own life at home." See above, from the Stichus.

units.la: VENTER parasitorum profundum est mare. Capt. 1.2. v. 73.
units.tr: The belly of parasites is a deep sea. Capt. 1. 2. v. 73.

units.la: PARASITI nullis rationibus abigi possunt à cænis. Capt. 1. 2. v. 78.
units.tr: No reasons can drive parasites away from dinners. Capt. 1. 2. v. 78.

units.la: PARASITI quasi lupus esuriens irruunt in aedes domos. Capt. 4. 4. v. 4.
units.tr: Parasites rush into houses like hungry wolves. Capt. 4. 4. v. 4.

units.la: PARASITI etiam Scorta dicti. Capt. 1. 1. v. 1. Truc. 3.2. v. 12. Quia impudenter cænas captabant, & invocati aderant.
units.tr: Parasites were also called "whores" (scorta). Capt. 1. 1. v. 1; Truc. 3. 2. v. 12. Because they shamelessly hunted for dinners and were present when invited.

units.la: PARASITI ima subsellia occupabant. Capt. 3.1. v. 11.
units.tr: Parasites occupied the lowest seats. Capt. 3. 1. v. 11.

units.la: PARASITI genus non tantum vorax, sed & adulatorium. Mil. 1.1. v. 16,31. & seqq. Omnia autem ventris causa faciunt.
units.tr: The parasitic kind is not only greedy but also flattering. Mil. 1. 1. v. 16, 31, and following. "They do everything for the sake of the belly."

units.la: PARASITI etiam linguam habent venalem. Stich. 2.1. v. 103.
units.tr: Parasites also have a tongue for sale. Stich. 2. 1. v. 103.

units.la: PARASITORUN est nugas garrire: propter quas scilicet vivunt. Curc. 5.2. v. 6.
units.tr: The business of parasites is to chatter about trifles, and for these very things they live. Curc. 5. 2. v. 6.

units.la: PARASITI tametsi capital fecerint, non aufugiunt, dum habent, quod edant; aut potent. Men. 1.1. v. 16.
units.tr: Even if parasites have endured a dreadful hunger, they do not run away while they have something to eat or drink. Men. 1. 1. v. 16.

units.la: PARASITI avidum genus hominum, nescium satiari, ut etiam furfures subus excutere gestiant. Capt. 4.2. v. 30, & 32.
units.tr: Parasites are a greedy race of men, never knowing satiety, so that they even eagerly pick bran out of the pigs' swill. Capt. 4. 2. v. 30 and 32.

units.la: PARASITI impuri homines. Most. 4. 2. v. 5.
units.tr: Parasites are impure men. Most. 4. 2. v. 5.

units.la: PARASITI comparantur muscis ob impudentiam. Pæn. 3.3. v. 76.
units.tr: Parasites are compared to flies for their impudence. Poen. 3. 3. v. 76.

units.la: PARASITI palpum obtrudebant uxoribus herorum suorum. Stich. 2.3. v. 47.57.
units.tr: Parasites used to thrust their palms, that is, fawn upon, the wives of their masters. Stich. 2. 3. v. 47, 57.

units.la: PARASITI invocati veniebant ad convivia. Unde scorta appellabantur: quia & hæc comparere solebant etiam non vocata. Capt 1.1. v. 1.
units.tr: Invited parasites came to banquets, whence they were called "whores," because these also used to turn up even when not invited. Capt. 1. 1. v. 1.

units.la: PARASITI penicillis comparantur, quibus mensas detergebant. Men. 1.1. v. 2.
units.tr: Parasites are compared to the wiping-cloths with which they cleaned the tables. Men. 1. 1. v. 2.

units.la: PARASITI edaces, voraces. Men. 1. 3. v. 5.
units.tr: Parasites are greedy and voracious. Men. 1. 3. v. 5.

units.la: PARASITIS divinæ & humanæ res, est Esca, & Mensa senatus. Trin. 2. 4. v. 77.
units.tr: For parasites, divine and human matters are food and the table of the senate. Trin. 2. 4. v. 77.

units.la: Verecundari apud mensam neminem decet.
units.tr: No one ought to be ashamed at the table.

units.la: Nam ibi de divinis atq; humanis cernitur.
units.tr: For there, matters both divine and human are decided.

units.la: Sic enim locus ille intelligendus, ex sententia Parasiti. In senatu dicitur, nulla verecundia nos debet dimovere à sententia dicendâ, ubi de rebus divinis aut humanis agitur.
units.tr: That passage is to be understood thus, according to the parasite's opinion: in the senate it is said that no shame should keep us from giving our opinion when matters divine or human are under discussion.

units.la: PARASITI impudentes in convivijs: etiam quidvis præripiunt convivis. Trin. 2.4. v. 76.
units.tr: Shameless parasites at banquets snatch up whatever they can from the guests. Trin. 2. 4. v. 76.

units.la: ÆGRE ferunt se non vocari crebrò ad cænas. Trin. 2. 4. v. 83.
units.tr: They take it badly that they are not invited often to dinners. Trin. 2. 4. v. 83.

units.la: PARASITIS religio est denegare cænam. Curc. 2. 3. v. 71.
units.tr: For parasites it is a matter of conscience to refuse a dinner. Curc. 2. 3. v. 71.

units.la: PARASITI escis alienis student. Perf. 3.1. v. 9.
units.tr: Parasites strive after other people's food. Perf. 3. 1. v. 9.

units.la: SYCOPHANTÆ solent vanissimè multa jactare. Trin. 4.2.v.3. Advenio ex Seleucia, Macedonia, Asia, atq; Arabia: quas ego neque pedibus unquam usurpavi meis.
units.tr: Sycophants are wont to boast very vainly of many things: "I come from Seleucia, Macedonia, Asia and Arabia, places I have never set foot in." Trin. 4. 2. v. 3.

units.la: SYCOPHANTÆ & id genus nauci hominum, in foro versaban-tur, tamquam in comitijs. Pæn. 3. 2. v. 7. Trin. 3.3. v. 86.
units.tr: Sycophants and that worthless kind of men used to haunt the forum as if it were the assemblies. Poen. 3. 2. v. 7. Trin. 3. 3. v. 86.

units.la: PARENTUM. FILIORUM. LIBERORUM.
units.tr: PARENTS. SONS. CHILDREN.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Conjugy. Item Tit. Educationis.
units.tr: See also the title Marriage. Likewise the title Education.

units.la: MATRES miserè sunt solicitæ de suis infantulis: eóque luben-tes illis mammas dant. Truc. 2. 5. v. 1.
units.tr: MOTHERS are anxiously concerned for their little infants, and so, wanting to please them, they give them the breast. Truc. 2. 5. v. 1.

units.la: NON rectam instant viam parentes illi, qui filijs frænum laxant ad ad libidines: quod Demenætus senex fecit. Asin. 1. 1. v. 50. Omnes parentes, Libane, liberis suis, Qui mihi auscultabunt, facient obsequentiam: Quippe qui mage amico utantur gnato atq; benevolo.
units.tr: Those parents do not walk the straight path who loosen the reins on their sons' desires, as the old man Demaenetus did. Asin. 1. 1. v. 50. All parents, Libanus, who will listen to me, will show obedience to their children, since they treat a son as a friend and a well-wisher.

units.la: At nulli parentes auscultabunt Demænetum nauci parentem.
units.tr: But no parents will listen to Demaenetus, the worthless parent.

units.la: PARENTUM exemplum pravum, depravat quoque filios. Asin. 1.1. v. 55. Præter morem matres solent esse filijs duriores, quàm patres. Talis est mater Argyrippi Asin. 1. 1. v. 64. Quæ filium artè continuè habet, Patres ut consueuerunt.
units.tr: A parent's bad example also corrupts the sons. Asin. 1.1. v. 55. Contrary to custom, mothers tend to be harsher toward their sons than fathers. Such is the mother of Argyrippus: Asin. 1. 1. v. 64. She keeps her son under constant restraint, as fathers usually do.

units.la: Seneca eleganter: Non vidu, quanto aliter patres, aliter matres indulgeant? Illi exercitari iubent liberos ad studia obeunda maturè, feriatis quoq; diebus non patiuntur esse otiosos, & sudorem illis, & interdum lacrimas excutiunt. At matres continere in sinu, fouere in umbrâ volunt.
units.tr: Seneca nicely says: Do you not see how differently fathers and mothers indulge? The former order their children to be trained early for their studies, do not allow them to be idle even on holidays, and wring out sweat and sometimes tears. But mothers want to keep them in their bosom and cherish them in the shade.

units.la: Nihil parentibus magis in voto, quàm relinquere suos sibi hæredes: h.e. liberos superstites. Asin. 1. 1. v. 1.
units.tr: Nothing is more desired by parents than to leave their own as heirs, that is, surviving children. Asin. 1. 1. v. 1.

units.la: Quem morem sic illustrant alij Authores. Cicero lib. 2. de Natura Deorum: Nam qui totos dies precabantur & immolabant, ut sui liberi sibi superstites essent, superstitiosi sunt appellati, quod nomen postea latius patuit.
units.tr: Other authors illustrate this custom. Cicero, book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods: For those who prayed and sacrificed all day that their children might survive them were called superstitious, a name which later spread more widely.

units.la: Et maximum illud votum Martialis lib. 7. Epigr. 95. Sic ad Lethaeas nisi Nestore sirior undas. Non eat, optabis quem superesse tibi.
units.tr: And there is Martial's great wish, book 7, epigram 95: So that you do not go to the Lethean waters before Nestor, you will wish for the one whom you want to survive you.

units.la: Item querela parentis apud Quintilianum Declamat. corporis projecti:
units.tr: Likewise the complaint of a parent in Quintilian's declamation of the cast-out body:

units.la: Ille est filius noster, cujus ipsas amavimus, quem apud omnia templa, & surdos Deos superstitem precati sumus: a quo sepeliri optavimus.
units.tr: He is our son, whom we loved above all, whom we prayed for in every temple, and to deaf gods, to survive us; by whom we wished to be buried.

units.la: Et optio apud Sylonem Pompejum citante Senecâ lib. 9. Controv. 4.
units.tr: And the prayer of Sylo Pompeius, cited by Seneca, book 9 of the Controversies, chapter 4:

units.la: Ita mihi superstite filio mori liceat, ut ego illum, qui mori maluit parricidam vocavi.
units.tr: May it be granted to me to die with my son surviving, as I called the one who preferred to die a parricide.

units.la: Et ibidem Mento:
units.tr: And in the same place, Mento:

units.la: Ita oculos meos filij manus operiant, ut ego inter liberos meos fortior steti.
units.tr: May my son's hands close my eyes, just as I stood firm among my children.

units.la: Arellius Fuscus pater lib. 2. Contr. 4. Quid tibi, optime socer, pro ista misericordia tua, quam mihi & patri peperisti, precer? nisi superstitem filium?
units.tr: Arellius Fuscus the father, book 2 of the Controversies, chapter 4: What, best father-in-law, should I pray for in return for that kindness of yours, which you showed to me and to my father, except a surviving son?

units.la: Respexit huc Seneca c. 3. de Consolatione ad Marciam: Eligite itaq; itaque utrum exemplum putas probabilius. Si illud prius sequi vis; eximie tot numero viverorum. Aversaberis & alienos liberos, & tuos, ipsumq; desiderabis triste matribus agmen occurrere.
units.tr: Seneca looked to this in chapter 3 of the Consolation to Marcia: Choose then which example you think more worthy. If you wish to follow the first, you will be outstanding among so many living. You will shun other people's children and your own, and you will long for the sad line of mothers to meet you.

units.la: Hoc est: Libitinarios, & hujusmodi genus hominum, quorum vel occursus parentum oculis gravior. Et merito suggillatur ab Suetonio cap. 62. Tiberij illud: quod identidem Priamum feliicem vocaret, quia superstes omnium suorum exstitisset, tamquam inhumanum, & dirum, quippe inducit Lucanus lib. 3. Argi patrem ideo se interficientem, ne filio superviveret, qui jam tamen animam agebat; hisce metris: Ille caput labens, & jam labentia colla Viso patre levat. Vide caetera.
units.tr: That is: undertakers and this kind of men, whose very sight is more grievous to parents' eyes. And rightly Suetonius, chapter 62, branded the remark of Tiberius that he repeatedly called Priam happy, because he had outlived all his own, as inhuman and dreadful. Indeed Lucan, book 3, introduces Argus's father killing himself so as not to outlive his son, who was still breathing, in these verses: He lifts his sinking head and sinking neck when he sees his father. See the rest.

units.la: Et pari de causa apud Tacitum legimus lib. 16. Annal.
units.tr: And for the same reason we read in Tacitus, Annals book 16:

units.la: Tunc eodem cubiculo eodem ferro abscindunt venas, properiq; & in singulis vestibus ad verecundiam velati, balneis inferuntur. Pater filiam, avia neptem. illa utroq; intuens, & certatim precantes labenti animae celerem exitum, ut relinquerent suos superstites & morituros. Servavitq; ordinem fortuna, ac senior prius, tum cui prima aetas extinguuntur.
units.tr: Then in the same room, with the same blade, they cut their veins; and hurrying, veiled in their garments for modesty, they were carried into the baths. The father looked at his daughter, the grandmother at her granddaughter, and both, vying with each other in prayer, asked for a swift end for the failing life, so that they might leave their survivors to die. Fortune kept the order, and the older died first, then the one of the first age.

units.la: Narratio est de L. vetere socruque ejus Sextia & Pollutia filia. Scilicet inde etiam JC. Jabolenus lib. 5. ex Cassio: Cum pubere filio mater naufragio periit: cum explorari non posset, uter prior exstinctus sit, humanius est credere, filium diutius vixisse.
units.tr: This is the account of L. Vetus, his mother-in-law Sextia, and his daughter Pollutia. Thus also the jurist Javolenus, book 5, from Cassius: When a mother perished in a shipwreck with her adult son, and it could not be determined which of them died first, it is more humane to believe that the son lived longer.

units.la: Ad quem locum videndus est JC. Hugo Donellus.
units.tr: On this passage the jurist Hugo Donellus is to be consulted.

units.la: Vide etiam Plutarch. in Cat. Majore pag. 340. Edit. Wechelia-nâ. D.
units.tr: See also Plutarch in the Life of Cato the Elder, page 340, Wechel edition, D.

units.la: Quin etiam nefas fuisse legimus ipsis liberis optare sibi parentes superstites. Seneca de Consol. ad Marciam: Non est ignotum, qualem te in persona patris tui geseris, quem non minus, quam liberos dilexisti: excepto eo, quod non optabus superstitem: nec scio, an & optaverit. Permittit enim sibi quaedam, & contra bonum morem magna pietas.
units.tr: Indeed we read that it was even wicked for the children themselves to wish their parents to survive them. Seneca, On Consolation to Marcia: It is not unknown what sort of son you showed yourself to be in the case of your father, whom you loved no less than your children, except that you did not wish him to survive you; nor do I know whether he did wish it. For great affection permits itself some things, even against good custom.

units.la: His consentaneum illud Valerij Maximi lib. 5. c. 9. ubi proponit filium, qui insidias nectere videbatur suo parenti. Vide locum.
units.tr: Consistent with this is the passage of Valerius Maximus, book 5, chapter 9, where he presents a son who seemed to lay snares for his parent. See the passage.

units.la: PARENTIBUS omnia condonanda sunt, quæcumque fecerint: ut egregiè disserit cum sorore suâ soror. Stich. 1. 1. v. 20.
units.tr: Everything is to be pardoned to parents, whatever they have done; as a sister argues well with her sister. Stich. 1. 1. v. 20.

units.la: Spes est melius eum factarum, novi ego illum: istaec joco dicit: neq; ille mereat Persarum sibi montes, qui esse perhibentur aurei, s-studut faciat quod tu metuis: & si faciat, tamen minimè irasci decet. Faciendum est nobis, quod parentes imperant. Ib. v. 46.
units.tr: There is hope he will be the better for it; I know him: he says this in jest. Nor would he deserve the mountains of the Persians, which are said to be golden, to do what you fear; and even if he did, it is not fitting to be angry at all. We must do what parents command. Ib. v. 46.

units.la: PARENTES non semper liberorum consilijs resistere debent. Trin. 2.3. v. 4.
units.tr: Parents ought not always to resist their children's counsels. Trin. 2.3. v. 4.

units.la: Qui qui nihil aliud, nisi quod sibi sibi placet consulit, adversum si-lium, nugas agit. Miser examino sit: selius nihilo facit: suæ se-netluti so acriorem hyemem parat: cum illam, importunam tempestatem conciet.
units.tr: He who consults nothing but what pleases himself, and opposes his son, is playing the fool. Poor fellow, he is no better off: he prepares for his old age a harsher winter, when he stirs up that troublesome storm.

units.la: PIETAS prohibet quicquam surripere parentibus. Pseud. 1.3. v. 56.
units.tr: Piety forbids taking anything from parents by stealth. Pseud. 1.3. v. 56.

units.la: PROBUM patrem esse oportet: qui gnatum suum esse probiorem, quàm ipsus fuerit, postulet. Pseud. 1.5. v. 23.
units.tr: A father ought to be upright: he who demands that his son be more upright than he himself was. Pseud. 1.5. v. 23.

units.la: Id ne tu miraris, si patrissat filius Ibid. v. 27.
units.tr: So do not be surprised if the son imitates his father. Ibid. v. 27.

units.la: PARENTES si ijs pædagogos alebant, qui eorum progressus actiones, aut mores observarent. Pseud. 1.5. v. 32.
units.tr: Parents, if they maintained pedagogues to watch over the progress, actions, or morals of their children. Pseud. 1.5. v. 32.

units.la: ETIAM duro parenti obtemperandum. Stich. 1. 2. v. 11.
units.tr: Even a harsh parent must be obeyed. Stich. 1. 2. v. 11.

units.la: Quid agimus soror, si offirmabit pater adversum nos?
units.tr: What shall we do, sister, if our father sets himself against us?

units.la: PA. Pati nos oportet, quod ille faciat, cujus potestas plus potest.
units.tr: PA. We must endure what he does, since his power is the greater.

units.la: Gratiam à patre, si petimus, spero ab eo impetrassere: Adversa-sari sine dedecore, & scelere snmmo haud possumus. Neque ego factura sum: neque tu, ut facias, consilium dabo. Verùm ut exoremus. Novi ego nostros: exorabilis est.
units.tr: If we ask our father for a favour, I hope we shall obtain it from him; we cannot oppose him without dishonour and the greatest wickedness. Nor will I do it, nor will I advise you to do it. But let us try to win him over. I know our father: he is easily swayed.

units.la: PARENTES decurso ætatis spacio in senectâ pacem, non turbas amant in familiâ. Stich. 1.2. v. 16.
units.tr: Parents, when the span of life has run its course, love peace in old age, not disturbance in the household. Stich. 1.2. v. 16.

units.la: PARENTUM loco censentur quoque ij, qui ex aliquo magno malo alios liberant: & quasi pariunt. Capt. 5. 4. v. 11.
units.tr: Those also are counted in the place of parents who free others from some great evil, as if they had given birth to them. Capt. 5. 4. v. 11.

units.la: Sic qui patriam conservant PARENTES PATRIÆ dicuntur.
units.tr: So those who save their country are called Fathers of the Country.

units.la: Tanta est patrum sedulitas: ut pretio nihil parcant: dum modò filijs rectè consultum eant: præsertim si eos amiserint. Capt. Prol. v. 32. Exemplo Hegionis senis.
units.tr: So great is the diligence of fathers that they spare no expense, provided they act well for their sons, especially if they have lost them. Capt. Prol. v. 32. Example: old Hegio.

units.la: Filii luxu perditi mortem parentum in votis habent. Bacch. 4.4. v. 80. & 5.2. v. 85.
units.tr: Sons ruined by luxury wish for their parents' death. Bacch. 4.4. v. 80. and 5.2. v. 85.

units.la: Parentes senes non debent indulgere peccatis filiorum: quia idem forte in adolescentiâ commiserunt. Malè igitur argumentatur pater senex Periphanes Epid. 3 3. v. 9, 10.
units.tr: Old parents ought not to indulge their sons' sins, because perhaps they committed the same in their youth. So old Periphanes argues badly. Epid. 3.3. v. 9, 10.

units.la: Scelus videtur, parentibus proloqui mendacium. Merc. 1. 2. v. 96.
units.tr: It seems wicked to tell parents a lie. Merc. 1. 2. v. 96.

units.la: Parentum imprecationes omnis aliquid habent. Asin. 3.3. v. 155.
units.tr: A parent's curses always have some effect. Asin. 3.3. v. 155.

units.la: Liberi, nisi indulgentiâ parentum fruantur, mortem sæpè ijs imprecantur. Merc. 3. 4. v. 6.
units.tr: Children, unless they enjoy their parents' indulgence, often wish death upon them. Merc. 3. 4. v. 6.

units.la: Parentes liberis bono exemplo præire par est. Inde Dæmenetus à conjuge suâ rectè reprehenditur. Isloscine patrem æquum mores est liberûs largirier?
units.tr: Parents ought to go before their children with a good example. Hence Demaenetus is rightly reproached by his wife: Is it fitting for a father to give his sons free rein in their morals?

units.la: Filium bonum decet patri morem gerere. Amph. 3.4. v. 9.
units.tr: A good son ought to comply with his father's wishes. Amph. 3.4. v. 9.

units.la: Liberos amissos ex crepundijs agnoscebant. Cist. 3.1.v.5. Vide Tit. Crepundiorum.
units.tr: They recognised their lost children by their keepsakes (crepundia). Cist. 3.1, v. 5. See the title Crepundiorum.

units.la: Filii filiæque patris ingenioferè sapere solent: h. e. patrissare. Pœn. 5.4. v. 26.
units.tr: Sons and daughters usually take after their father in disposition, that is, they act like their father. Poen. 5.4, v. 26.

units.la: Parentum vitia corruptelæ sunt liberis. Asin. 5.2. v. 17.
units.tr: The vices of parents are a corruption to their children. Asin. 5.2, v. 17.

units.la: Parentum est, filijs thesauros congerere. Trin. 4.1. v. 20.
units.tr: It is the duty of parents to heap up treasures for their children. Trin. 4.1, v. 20.

units.la: Parentum diræ in filios immorigeros non sunt vanæ, aut irritæ. Asin. 3.3. v. 155. Vide supra Tit. Abominationis.
units.tr: The curses of parents against disobedient sons are not empty or ineffectual. Asin. 3.3, v. 155. See above under the title Abominationis.

units.la: PARRICIDII.
units.tr: PARRICIDE.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Sceleris.
units.tr: See also the title Crime.

units.la: PARRICIDIUM crimen omnium atrocissimum. Men. 5. 5. v. 41.
units.tr: PARRICIDE is the most atrocious of all crimes. Men. 5. 5. v. 41.

units.la: Quæ poena fuerit Parricidij, docui in Commentario ad Orat. Cicer. pro Roscio Amerino.
units.tr: What the punishment for parricide was, I have set out in my commentary on Cicero's speech for Roscius of Ameria.

units.la: PATIENTIÆ.
units.tr: Of Patience

units.la: PATIENTER ferendum, si quid secus accidit, quàm volumus. Caf. 2. 6. v. 25.
units.tr: Whatever happens otherwise than we wish must be borne patiently. Caf. 2. 6. v. 25.

units.la: Nimiò id, quod pudet, facilius fertur, quàm illud, quod piget, h. est, facilius est id ferre, quod pudorem affert, quàm quod damnum importat. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 46.
units.tr: That which causes shame is borne more easily than that which causes distress; that is, it is easier to bear what brings shame than what brings loss. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 46.

units.la: Mala patienter ferenda. Sic Lorarij solantur captivos. Capt. 2. 1. v. 1.
