units.tr: Evils are to be borne patiently. So the jailers console the captives. Capt. 2. 1. v. 1.

units.la: Si DI immortales id voluere, vos hanc ærumnam exequi, Decet id pati æquo animo: si id facietis, levior labos erit. Ibid. v. 8. In re malâ, animo si bono utare adjuvat. Et Pseud. 1. 5. v. 51. Bonus animus in re malâ dimidium est mali. Et Rud. 2. 3. v. 71. Animus æquus optimum est ærumnæ condimentum.
units.tr: If the immortal gods have willed that you undergo this distress, it is fitting to bear it with an equal mind; if you do so, the labour will be lighter. Ibid. v. 8. In a bad situation, a good mind helps you when you use it. And Pseud. 1. 5. v. 51: a good mind in a bad situation is half the evil. And Rud. 2. 3. v. 71: an equable mind is the best seasoning of distress.

units.la: Terent. And. 5. 1. v. 13. Incepi dum res tetulit, nunc non fert, feras. Et Adelph. 4. 7. v. 10. Nunc cum non queo, æquo animo fero.
units.tr: Terence, Andria 5. 1. v. 13: "I began when circumstances allowed; now they do not, so bear it." And Adelphi 4. 7. v. 10: "Since now I cannot help it, I bear it with an equal mind."

units.la: P. Syrus: Feras non culpes, quod mutare non potes.
units.tr: Publilius Syrus: Bear what you cannot change; do not blame it.

units.la: Horat. lib. 1. Od. 24.
units.tr: Horace, Odes book 1, ode 24.

units.la: Durum: sed levius fit patientiâ,
units.tr: Hard, but it is made lighter by patience,

units.la: Quicquid corrigere est nefas.
units.tr: Whatever it is unlawful to correct.

units.la: Sic Græci: Ἀνάγκα δὲ ... θεοί, φασὶ, μάχονται.
units.tr: So the Greeks: "But against necessity, they say, even the gods fight." [Ἀνάγκα δὲ ... θεοί, φασὶ, μάχονται.]

units.la: Plato lib. 7. de Legg. & Synef. Ep. 103. Et Eurip. ... ἀνάγκη.
units.tr: Plato, Laws book 7, and Synesius, Epistle 103. And Euripides: "necessity" [ἀνάγκη].

units.la: PATIENTER mala adeoque mortem ferre decet, dum ne ob mala facta. Capt. 3. 5. v. 24, 32.
units.tr: One ought to bear evils patiently, and even death, provided it is not on account of wicked deeds. Capt. 3. 5. v. 24, 32.

units.la: Patronorum. Clientum.
units.tr: Of Patrons and Clients

units.la: PATRONI suorum clientium tenebantur causam dicere. Men. 4. 2. v. 16. Vide Ræv. ad LL. 12. Tabb. c. 4.
units.tr: Patrons were bound to plead the cause of their clients. Men. 4. 2. v. 16. See Rävardus on the Twelve Tables, c. 4.

units.la: OPTUMI maximi morem habent hunc: Clientes sibi omnes volunt esse multos, Boni nean mali sint, id haud quæritant. Æs quæritur magis, quàm clientum Fides cujusmodi clueat. Men. 4. 2. v. 3. & sequent. vide. De ejusmodi leguleijs vide Fr. Polleti Fori Rom. Hist. lib. 2. c. 3. & 9.
units.tr: The best and greatest men have this custom: they want to have many clients, whether good or bad, and do not inquire into that. Money is sought more than the kind of loyalty the clients show. Men. 4. 2. v. 3 and following. On such lawyers see Francesco Poleti's History of the Roman Forum, book 2, chapters 3 and 9.

units.la: Patriæ. Popularium.
units.tr: Of the Fatherland, of Fellow Citizens

units.la: NIHIL chatius patriâ. Stich. 5. 2. v. 2. Bacch. 2. 1. v. 1.
units.tr: Nothing is dearer than one's fatherland. Stich. 5. 2. v. 2. Bacch. 2. 1. v. 1.

units.la: POPULARIUM cura & amor nos vehementer tenet & afficit. Rud. 3. 1. v. 13.
units.tr: Concern for and love of our fellow citizens grip us and move us powerfully. Rud. 3. 1. v. 13.

units.la: Paupertatis. Egestatis. Inopiæ. Famis. Mendicitatis. Stipis.
units.tr: Of Poverty. Want. Indigence. Hunger. Beggary. Alms.

units.la: PAUPERTAS homines facit ridiculos. Stich. 2. 1. v. 23, 64. Nam illa omnes artes perdocet, ubi quem attigit, inquit Parasitus. Juvenal. Sat. 3.
units.tr: Poverty makes men ridiculous. Stich. 2. 1. v. 23, 64. For it teaches every art thoroughly, says the Parasite, wherever it has laid hold of someone. Juvenal, Satire 3.

units.la: Nil habet infelix Paupertas durius in se, Quàm quòd ridiculos homines facit.
units.tr: Wretched poverty has nothing harder in it than that it makes men ridiculous.

units.la: Perfius:
units.tr: Persius:

units.la: Quis expedivit Psittaco suum χαίρε,
units.tr: Who taught the parrot to say his "chaire"?

units.la: Picasq; docuit nostra verba conari?
units.tr: Who taught the magpies to try our words?

units.la: Magister artis ingeniq; largitor
units.tr: The master of art and the giver of talent

units.la: VENTER est, negatas artifex sequi voces.
units.tr: Is the belly, the craftsman that makes denied voices follow.

units.la: Seneca Epist. 15. Quos nova artificia Fames docuit. Apulejus: Quemcumq; cum aliqua laude miramur, eum paupertas ab incunabulis nutricata est. Paupertas inquam prisca apud fæcula omnium civitatum conditrix, omnium artium repertrix. D. Hieronymus: Litteræ marsupium non sequuntur: Laboris comites sunt, & sudoris.
units.tr: Seneca, Epistle 15: hunger taught new arts. Apuleius: whomever we admire with any praise, poverty has nursed from the cradle; poverty, I say, the ancient founder of the dregs of all states, the discoverer of all arts. St Jerome: letters do not follow the purse; they are companions of toil and sweat.

units.la: Vide alia in hanc sententiam apud Casaubonum ad Prol. Persium p.25. Et apud Petron. in Satirico.
units.tr: See other sayings to this effect in Casaubon on the Prologue of Persius, p. 25, and in Petronius' Satyricon.

units.la: PAUPERTAS nihil detrahit virtuti. Sic ait Servus ille Asin. 2. 4. v. 91. Quamquam ego sum sordidatus,
units.tr: Poverty takes nothing away from virtue. So that slave in Asinaria 2. 4. v. 91 says: "Although I am shabbily dressed,"

units.la: Frugi tamen sum: Nec potest peculium enumerari.
units.tr: "Yet I am honest, and my savings cannot be counted."

units.la: Seneca Epist. 2.
units.tr: Seneca, Epistle 2.

units.la: Cui cum paupertate bene convenit, dives est. Non qui parum habet, sed qui plus cupit, pauper est. Modus divitiarum primus est; habere quod necesse est.
units.tr: For one who lives well with poverty is rich. It is not the man who has little, but the man who wants more, who is poor. The first measure of riches is to have what is necessary.

units.la: Hesiodus:
units.tr: Hesiod:

units.la: ψευδῆ μαχάρων δόσις αἰὲν ἐόντων.
units.tr: The gift of the ever-existing blessed ones [ψευδῆ μαχάρων δόσις αἰὲν ἐόντων].

units.la: SALEM lingere dicebantur, qui tenui victu victitabant.
units.tr: Those who lived on a meagre diet were said to lick salt.
Curculio 4. 4. v. 6.

units.la: Hodie apud me numquam delinges salem.
units.tr: "Today you will never lick salt at my house."

units.la: Vide Tit. Peregrinat.
units.tr: See the title Peregrinatio.

units.la: MISER homo est, qui ipse sibi, quod edat, quærit, & id ægre invenit.
units.tr: A man is wretched who must seek for himself what he eats, and finds it with difficulty.

units.la: Sed ille est miserior, qui & ægre quærit, & nihil invenit.
units.tr: But he is more wretched who seeks with difficulty and finds nothing.

units.la: Ille miserrimus est, qui cum esse cupit, quod edit, non habet.
units.tr: He is most wretched who, when he wishes to eat what he has, does not have it.

units.la: OMNIBUS modis qui pauperes sunt homines, miserè vivunt, præsertim quibus nec quæstus est, nec artem didicere ullam. Necessitate sitate quicquid est domi, id sat est habendum. Rud. 2. 1. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: All men who are poor in every way live miserably, especially those who have no income and have learned no trade. Out of necessity, whatever there is at home must be considered enough. Rud. 2. 1. v. 1 and following.

units.la: PAUPERTAS æquo animo ferenda.
units.tr: Poverty must be borne with an equal mind.

units.la: Pauper sum, patior. Quod DI dant, fero.
units.tr: I am poor, I suffer. What the gods give, I bear.
Aulularia 1. 2. v. 10.

units.la: Non est verisimile hominem pauperem Pauxillum parvi facere, quin numum petat.
units.tr: It is not likely that a poor man would make so little of a small sum as not to ask for a coin.

units.la: Qui è re lautâ ob sua vitia in paupertatem inciderunt: civibus ludibrio habiti: & ad infamiam redacti. Trin. 3. 2. v. 28.
units.tr: Those who fell from a comfortable situation into poverty through their vices were held up to ridicule by their fellow citizens and reduced to infamy. Trin. 3. 2. v. 28.

units.la: Mos fuit pulcherrimus, & verè pius apud Græcos, sublevandi amicos pauperes, si non essent solvendi. Quò allusum Curc. 5. 3. v. 7. Vide Casaub. ad Theoph. Characteres.
units.tr: Among the Greeks it was a most beautiful and truly pious custom to help poor friends, if they could not repay. Curc. 5. 3. v. 7 alludes to this. See Casaubon on Theophrastus' Characters.

units.la: Ad paupertatem per luxuriam redacti, impudentes fiebant. Truc. 4. 2. v. 50. 51.
units.tr: Those reduced to poverty through luxury became shameless. Truc. 4. 2. v. 50, 51.

units.la: Fio impudens: perdidi omne, quod fuit: nec mihi adeo est hillum, pensi, jam quos capiam calceos.
units.tr: "I become shameless; I have lost everything I had; nor have I so much as a penny left, so which shoes am I to put on now?"

units.la: Mendici stipem rogabant in saccum ad portam tergeminam Ostiensem. Capt. 1. 1. v. 22.
units.tr: Beggars asked for alms in a bag at the Ostian Triple Gate. Capt. 1. 1. v. 22.

units.la: In ponte mendicantes sedebant. Trin. 2. 4. v. 21.
units.tr: Beggars sat on the bridge. Trin. 2. 4. v. 21.

units.la: In sublicium pontem me transfer, & inter egentes abige: non ideo tamen me dispiciam, quod in illorum numero consideo, qui manum ad stipem porrigunt.
units.tr: "Carry me across to the Sublician bridge and drive me among the needy; yet I shall not be despised for sitting among those who stretch out their hands for alms."

units.la: FLAGITATORES usque; à mani ad vesperum adstabant ad ostium. Most. 3 2. v. 82.
units.tr: Persistent beggars; from morning until evening they stood at the door. Most. 3. 2. v. 82.

units.la: De mendico male meretur, qui ei dat, quod edit, aut quod bibat.
units.tr: He does a bad turn to a beggar who gives him what he eats or drinks.

units.la: Nam & illud, quod dat, perdit, & illi producit vitam admise- riam. Trin. 3. 2. v. 58.
units.tr: For what he gives, he also loses, and prolongs the wretched life of the other. Trin. 3. 2. v. 58.

units.la: Sic apud Plutarchum Mendicus à Lacone stipem petebat: hic vero: Si darem, inquit, tibi, eò magis mendicares. Nam huic tuæ deformitati causam præbuit is, qui primus tibi dedit, eoque te ignavuum reddidit. Hæc verò omnia abluduntur à vero Christianismo, ut patet ex scriptura sancta.
units.tr: So in Plutarch a beggar asked alms of a Spartan, who replied: "If I gave you something, you would beg all the more. For the man who first gave you alms caused this deformity of yours, and so made you idle." But all these things are rejected by true Christianity, as is clear from holy Scripture.

units.la: Qui à paupere poscit argentum, nudo detrahere vestimenta po-stulat. Asin. I.I. v. 79.
units.tr: He who demands silver from a poor man demands that a naked man be stripped of his clothes. Asin. 1. 1. v. 79.

units.la: Nam sine pennis nemo potest volare. Ibid.
units.tr: For no one can fly without wings. Ibid.

units.la: Item piscari in aëre: Et avem venari in medio mari. Ibid.
units.tr: Likewise, to fish in the air, and to hunt a bird in the middle of the sea. Ibid.

units.la: EGESTAS saepè cogit extrema pati: quod secus nemo faceret, si in re esset. Trin. 4.2. v. 5.
units.tr: Want often compels people to endure extremes, which no one would do if he were well off. Trin. 4. 2. v. 5.

units.la: DII pauperibus magis propitij, quàm ditioribus. Trin. 4.1. v. 10.12.
units.tr: The gods are more favourable to the poor than to the rich. Trin. 4. 1. v. 10, 12.

units.la: PAUPERTATIS causa saepè est nimia beneficentia. Rud. Prol. v.37. Vide Tit. Beneficentiae.
units.tr: Excessive generosity is often the cause of poverty. Rud. Prol. v. 37. See the title Beneficence.

units.la: ITEM QUE luxus paupertatem parit. Ibid.
units.tr: Likewise, luxury produces poverty. Ibid.

units.la: NON temerarium est, ubi dives blandè appellat pauperem. Aul. 2.2. v. 7,69,
units.tr: It is not rash when a rich man addresses a poor man kindly. Aul. 2. 2. v. 7, 69.

units.la: IDEM animus esse debet in paupertate, qui olim in divitijs fuit. Stich. 1.2. v. 77.
units.tr: The same spirit ought to be in poverty as once was in riches. Stich. 1. 2. v. 77.

units.la: INOPIA filia Luxuriae elegantèr fingitur à Prol. Trin. v. 1. & sequentib.
units.tr: Want, the daughter of Luxury, is elegantly fashioned by the Prologue of Trinummus, v. 1 and following.

units.la: PAUPERI cum divite non datur aequâ lege experiri: ideoque saepè perdenda est causa. Aul. 2.2. v.50. Cist. 2.1. v.55.
units.tr: The poor man is not given the chance to contend with the rich under an equal law, and so the cause is often lost. Aul. 2. 2. v. 50. Cist. 2. 1. v. 55.

units.la: QUIDVIS egestas imperat. Asin. 3.3. v.81.
units.tr: Want commands anything whatever. Asin. 3. 3. v. 81.

units.la: PECCATI. ERRORIS. DELICTI. VITIORUM, NÆVI.
units.tr: SIN. ERROR. OFFENCE. FAULTS, BLEMISHES.

units.la: QUI peccarunt per impudentiam veniam deprecari decet culpæ. Aul. 4.10.v.8,22,62. Fateor me peccavisse (inquit adolescens amator) me hanc culpam commeritum scio: Eo ultrò tibi supplicatum venio ob stultitiam meam. Recte igitur Euclio sentit, quando sic adolescentem affatur: Non mihi homines placent, qui quando male fecerunt, purgitant.
units.tr: Those who have sinned out of shamelessness ought to beg pardon for their fault. Aul. 4.10.v.8,22,62. I confess that I have sinned (says the young lover). I know I have deserved this fault. So I have come to you of my own accord as a suppliant, because of my folly. Euclio rightly feels this way when he addresses the young man thus: I don't like men who, when they have done wrong, make excuses.

units.la: VITIA domare grandis labor. Trin. 2.1.v.35. Persius Sat. 5. Et premitur ratione animus, vincit, laborat. Ibi vide Commentar. Casaub.
units.tr: Taming vices is a great labour. Trin. 2.1.v.35. Persius, Sat. 5: And the mind is restrained by reason, conquers, and labours. See there the commentary of Casaubon.

units.la: LAUS maxima ducitur, si ad frugem redeant adolescentes corrupti. Trin. 2.1.v.35.
units.tr: Great praise is won if corrupted young men return to decency. Trin. 2.1.v.35.

units.la: VITIA sæpè in totam familiam propagantur. Pseud. 1.1.v.73. Genus nostrum semper siccoculum fuit.
units.tr: Vices often spread through the whole family. Pseud. 1.1.v.73. Our race has always been dry-eyed (unweeping, shameless).

units.la: CULPAM quidam in Deum transferunt peccatorum suorum. Aul. 4.10.v.7,12. Deos credo voluisse, nam ni vellent, non fieret, scio.
units.tr: Some transfer the blame for their sins onto God. Aul. 4.10.v.7,12. I believe the gods wished it, for if they did not wish it, I know it would not happen.

units.la: CUIVIS homini, vel optumo, vel pessumo Quamvis desubitò, facilè est facere nequiter. Verùm id videndum est, id viri docti opus est, Quæ designata sunt, & facta nequiter. Most. 2.1.v.62.
units.tr: Any man, whether the best or the worst, can easily do wrong on the spur of the moment. But this must be considered: it is the task of a learned man to look into what has been planned and done wickedly. Most. 2.1.v.62.

units.la: VETERES, ut melius in officio continerentur homines, & à sceleribus absterrerentur, cruciatus infernales, quos imminere ijs credebant, in tabulis depingebant, ut quasi præsentes intuerentur. Unde illud Capt. 5.4.v.1. Vidi ego multa sæpè picta, quæ Acheruntii fierent cruciamenta.
units.tr: The ancients, so that people might be better kept in their duty and turned away from crimes, painted in pictures the infernal torments that they believed hung over such men, so that they might look upon them as if present. Hence that line in Capt. 5.4.v.1: I have often seen many pictures of the tortures that go on in Acheron.

units.la: IN innocente culpa non est transferenda. Amph. 3.1.v.12. & 3.2.v.14.
units.tr: Fault must not be transferred onto the innocent. Amph. 3.1.v.12. and 3.2.v.14.

units.la: QUI homo culpam admisit in se, nullus est tàm parvi pretij, quin pudeat, quin purget sese. Aul. 4.10.v.60.
units.tr: No man who has committed a fault is of so little worth that he is not ashamed of it and does not clear himself of it. Aul. 4.10.v.60.

units.la: Ab ætate sæpè veniam impetramus culpæ. Merc. 5. 4. v. 37.
units.tr: By reason of youth we often obtain pardon for a fault. Merc. 5.4.v.37.

units.la: Virginem atque puellam non decet reticere, si quid videt fieri pervorlè. Perf. 3. 1. v. 40.
units.tr: A maiden and a girl ought not to keep silent if she sees something going seriously wrong. Perf. 3.1.v.40.

units.la: Errores & peccata solemus excusare exemplis. Merc. 2. 2. v. 47.
units.tr: We are wont to excuse errors and sins by examples. Merc. 2.2.v.47.

units.la: Pecuniæ.
units.tr: Money.

units.la: Vide supra Tit. Ærù - alieni : & Marsupij.
units.tr: See above under the titles Debt and Purse.

units.la: Peregrinationis. Viæ. Platearum.
units.tr: Of Journeys. Roads. Streets.

units.la: Peregre redeuntes, uxori nuncios de suo adventu præmiserunt. Amph. 1. 1. v. 40.
units.tr: Returning from abroad, they sent word ahead to their wives of their arrival. Amph. 1. 1. v. 40.

units.la: Plutarchus libello Romanarum Quæstionum p. 266. A. Tomo 11. Edit. Wechel. has huic rei assignat causas.
units.tr: Plutarch, in his little book of Roman Questions, p. 266 A, vol. 11, Wechel edition, gives the following reasons for this custom.

units.la: 1. Quia hoc est probitati uxoris suæ confidentis viri (nam ex improviso, & subitò supervenire, speciem insidiarum, & infensæ observationis habet) ideò dant operam, ut desiderantibus se, atque expectantibus uxoribus lætum sui adventûs nuncium afferant.
units.tr: (1) Because it is a sign of a husband's trust in his wife's goodness. For to arrive unannounced and suddenly has the look of an ambush and of hostile spying. So they take care that the wives, who are longing for them and waiting, receive the joyful news of their coming.

units.la: 2. Quia ipsi rescire cupiunt, salvasne, & desiderio sui affectas uxores domi sint offensuri.
units.tr: (2) Because they themselves want to learn whether their wives at home are safe and still affected by longing for them.

units.la: 3. Vel quia plura sunt mulieribus domestica negotia, & rei familiaris occupationes plures, mariti ubi absunt, variæque curæ & discursus: ideò adventus nuncium accipiunt, ut omissis istis negotijs absque tumultu ac suaviter maritum excipiant.
units.tr: (3) Or because women have many domestic affairs, and there are many concerns of the household; when husbands are away, there are various cares and comings and goings. So they send word of the arrival, so that, with those tasks set aside, the wives may greet their husbands quietly and pleasantly, without bustle.

units.la: Occurrentes devia, de semita, decedere solent alijs: idque honoris causâ. Trin. 2. 4. v. 80.
units.tr: Those who meet one another on an out-of-the-way path usually step aside for the other, and this as a mark of honour. Trin. 2. 4. v. 80.

units.la: Vide
units.tr: See

units.la: Vive Alex. ab Alex. l. 2. c. 19.
units.tr: See also Alexander ab Alexandro, bk. 2, ch. 19.

units.la: Sic Seneca Epist.
units.tr: So Seneca, in an Epistle:

units.la: Si Consulem video, aut prætorem, omnia quibus honor haberi solet, faciam: equo descendam, caput adaperiam, semitâ cedam.
units.tr: If I see a consul or a praetor, I will do everything by which honour is usually shown: I will dismount from my horse, uncover my head, and give way on the path.

units.la: Vide etiam Agell. lib. 2. c. 2.
units.tr: See also Gellius, bk. 2, ch. 2.

units.la: Uxores ad adventum maritorum operam dabant, ut omnia in ædibus munda essent. Stich. 5. 3. v. 4, 5.
units.tr: Wives were busy, before their husbands arrived, so that everything in the house was clean. Stich. 5. 3. v. 4, 5.

units.la: Peregre adventantes salutabant. Trin. 4. 4. v. 5. Et salve, & salvum te advenisse gaudeo.
units.tr: They greeted those arriving from abroad. Trin. 4. 4. v. 5. And hail; I rejoice that you have arrived safe.

units.la: Peregrinationibus varijs exerciti, solent esse arrogantes, ex sententiâ Sycophantæ Trin. 4. 2. v. 104. Pudicum neminem manere oportet, qui abs terrâ ad cœlum pervenerit.
units.tr: Men who have been exercised by various journeys tend to be arrogant, in the words of the sycophant: Trin. 4. 2. v. 104. No chaste man ought to stay, who has come from earth to heaven.

units.la: Peregre advenientes solebant Deos salutare, ijsque gratias agere: dein amicos suos: uxores. Amph. 1. 1. v. 26. Epid. 3. 3. v. 34. Stich. 4. 1. v. 29. Mil. 2. 5. v. 1. & seqq. Bacch. 2. 2. v. 8. & 2. 3. v. 113.
units.tr: Those arriving from abroad used to greet the gods first and give them thanks, then their friends and their wives. Amph. 1. 1. v. 26. Epid. 3. 3. v. 34. Stich. 4. 1. v. 29. Mil. 2. 5. v. 1 and following. Bacch. 2. 2. v. 8. and 2. 3. v. 113.

units.la: Filiæ parentibus: aut propinquæ honoratiori cognato domum revertenti advorsum ibant. Amph. 2. 2. v. 43. Men. 5. 2. v. 25. Stich. 1. 2. v. 32.
units.tr: Daughters went out to meet their parents, or relatives went to meet a more honoured kinsman returning home. Amph. 2. 2. v. 43. Men. 5. 2. v. 25. Stich. 1. 2. v. 32.

units.la: Peregrinaturi Herculi sacrificabant: qui Sancus Hercules dictus. Rud. 1. 2. v. 71.
units.tr: Those about to travel abroad sacrificed to Hercules, who was called Sancus Hercules. Rud. 1. 2. v. 71.

units.la: Mos erat, ut qui primùm ingrederentur regionem aliquam, ad eamve ex intervallo reverterentur: religiosè eam salutarent: idque quoniam suo cuíque loco suum quendam Genium præesse arbitrantur. Bacch. 2. 1. v. 1. Stich. 5. 2. v. 1.
units.tr: It was the custom that those who first entered some region, or returned to it after an absence, greeted it with reverence, because they believed that a certain guardian spirit (Genius) presides over each place. Bacch. 2. 1. v. 1. Stich. 5. 2. v. 1.

units.la: Sic Menand. in Senariolis:
units.tr: So Menander, in the Senarii:

units.la: Χαῖρε, ὦ φίλη γῆ ἀλλ' χρόνα πολλῶν σ' ἰδὼν λαπάζομαι.
units.tr: Hail, dear land! For I rejoice, having seen you after many years. [Χαῖρε, ὦ φίλη γῆ· ἀλλ' ἐπὶ χρόνον πολλῶν σ' ἰδὼν χαίρω.]

units.la: Vide etiam Muret. ad Catull. Meurs. Cassand. Heinf. ad lib. 13. Silij.
units.tr: See also Muretus on Catullus; Meursius; Casaubon; Heinsius on book 13 of Silius.

units.la: Hospitibus peregrè adventantibus post gratulationem, & salutationem salem in mensâ apponebant, eo concordiam inter se mutuò optantes,ut ex aquâ & terrâ illa constat. Cure. 4. 4. v.5,6. Hodie apud menumquam delingū salem. Vide Cassand. Meurs. p.132. & Notas Casaub. ad Laërt. ἄλα λέιχειν.
units.tr: To guests arriving from abroad, after congratulation and greeting, they set salt on the table, thereby wishing one another mutual harmony, as that is made of water and earth. Curc. 4. 4. v. 5, 6. Today at my house you will never lick salt. See Cassander, Meursius, p. 132, and Casaubon's notes on Diogenes Laertius, on to lick salt [ἄλα λείχειν].

units.la: PEREGRE abituri chlamydem, aliasque vestes viatorias usurpabant. Merc. 5.2. v.70. Sumebant etiam Zonam, in quâ condebant pecuniam. Ibid. v. 85. Itemque Ampullam secum portabant, in quâ oleum servabant ad ingendos pedes antequam calceos induerent. Hesychius: ἠλείφοντο τὺς ποδὰς οἱ ἀχχαῖοι, πρὶν τὸ ὑποδήσασθαι. Inde λιτραῖοι πόδες, dicti apud Poëtas.
units.tr: Those about to leave abroad put on a cloak and other travelling clothes. Merc. 5. 2. v. 70. They also took a belt, in which they stored money. Ibid. v. 85. Likewise they carried a flask with them, in which they kept oil for anointing their feet before putting on their shoes. Hesychius: the Achaeans anointed their feet before putting on their shoes [ἠλείφοντο τοὺς ποδὰς οἱ Ἀχαιοὶ πρὶν τὸ ὑποδήσασθαι]. Hence the poets speak of anointed feet [λιτραῖοι πόδες].

units.la: PEREGRE reversi Deos salutabant primùm: dein uxores suas. Stich. 4.1. v.29.
units.tr: Those returning from abroad greeted the gods first, then their wives. Stich. 4. 1. v. 29.

units.la: SOLEB ANT honoris causâ hospitio excipi peregrini, & illis dari cœna, quæ nominabatur Viatica, Adventitia, Adventoria. Amph. 1.1. v.8,139, 140. & 2.2.v.33. Epid. 1.1 v.6. Pœn. 5.3.v.51. Trac. 1.2. v.25. & 2.4.v.8. Most. 5.2.v.8. Merc. 5.2.v.107. Stich 4.1. v.8. Pers. 4.3.v.43. Stich 5.2.v.6. & 5.3.v.7. Bacch. 1.1.v.61. & & 2.2.v.8. & 3.6.v.8. Most. 4.3.v.12. Rud. 2.4.v.4. Vide Turn. lib.2.c.30. & lib.30.c.26. & Scalig. ad Aufon. lib.2. c.19. & 24.
units.tr: Travellers were customarily received as guests with honour, and a meal was given them, called Viatica, Adventitia, Adventoria. Amph. 1. 1. v. 8, 139, 140; 2. 2. v. 33. Epid. 1. 1. v. 6. Poen. 5. 3. v. 51. Truc. 1. 2. v. 25; 2. 4. v. 8. Most. 5. 2. v. 8. Merc. 5. 2. v. 107. Stich. 4. 1. v. 8. Pers. 4. 3. v. 43. Stich. 5. 2. v. 6; 5. 3. v. 7. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 61; 2. 2. v. 8; 3. 6. v. 8. Most. 4. 3. v. 12. Rud. 2. 4. v. 4. See Turnebus, bk. 2, ch. 30, and bk. 30, ch. 26, and Scaliger on Ausonius, bk. 2, chs. 19 and 24.

units.la: MAGNA est voluptas ijs, qui postquam diu peregrè abfuerunt, terram suam: h.e. patriam, videant. Men. 2.1.v.4.
units.tr: It is a great pleasure for those who, after being long abroad, see their own land, that is, their homeland. Men. 2. 1. v. 4.

units.la: PEREGRE abeuntes Lares viales invocabant. Merc. 5.2.v.24. Vide Tit. Deorum.
units.tr: Those leaving abroad invoked the Lares viales (guardians of the road). Merc. 5. 2. v. 24. See the title Gods.

units.la: PEREGRINANTES rerum visarum historiam domum reversi conscribere solebant. Men. 2.1.v.23.
units.tr: Those who travelled abroad used to write, on returning home, an account of the things they had seen. Men. 2. 1. v. 23.

units.la: VIATICUM sumebant peregrinaturi. Men. 2.1.v.30. Viaticati hercle astivè sumus. Vide Turn. lib.18.c.15. Cæl. Rhod. lib.6. c.12.
units.tr: Those about to travel took the viaticum (travel provision). Men. 2. 1. v. 30. Truly, we have taken our viaticum in summer. See Turnebus, bk. 18, ch. 15, and Caelius Rhodiginus, bk. 6, ch. 12.

units.la: CURRERE per vias insaniæ indicium. Pœn. 3.1. v.25. Haud quisquam nostrum currset per vias, neque nos populus pro-cerritis insectabit lapidibus.
units.tr: Running through the streets was a sign of madness. Poen. 3. 1. v. 25. None of us will run through the streets, nor will the people, struck mad, hunt us with stones.

units.la: PEREGRINANTES habebant vidulum five bulgam è corio, & melinam, in quâ res suas recondebant. Epid. 1. 1. v. 20. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: Travellers carried a travelling bag or pouch of leather, and a linen bag, in which they stored their belongings. Epid. 1. 1. v. 20. See the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: UXORES maritis peregrè absentib°, obviam mittunt servos suos. Stich. 1.2. v. 94.
units.tr: Wives, whose husbands were away abroad, sent their servants to meet them. Stich. 1. 2. v. 94.

units.la: VINUM peregrè adventantibus dono dabatur. Stich. 5. 2. v. 17. Germani dicunt: Den Wein verehren.
units.tr: Wine was given as a gift to those arriving from abroad. Stich. 5. 2. v. 17. The Germans say: to honour with wine (Den Wein verehren).

units.la: PEREGRE advenientes solebant salutari & osculo excipi; lavari; cænâ excipi. Amph. 2.2.v.84,99,168,170,172. Epid. 4. 2. v. 2. & 5.1.v.58. Bacch. 1. 1. v.61. & 72. Etiam in lectum admitti ad sedandam lassitudinem. Ibid. v.75.
units.tr: Those arriving from abroad were customarily greeted and received with a kiss; they were bathed and given a meal. Amph. 2. 2. v. 84, 99, 168, 170, 172. Epid. 4. 2. v. 2; 5. 1. v. 58. Bacch. 1. 1. v. 61 and 72. They were even admitted to the couch to ease their weariness. Ibid. v. 75.

units.la: PEREGRE adventantes mariti uxoribus suis solebant præmij locoaliquod munus peregrinum adferre. Truc. 2. 6. v. 55.
units.tr: Husbands arriving home from abroad used customarily to bring their wives some foreign gift as a reward. Truc. 2. 6. v. 55.

units.la: PEREGRE abituri vicinis credebant Thesaurum suum. Trin. 1.2, v.117.
units.tr: Those about to leave abroad entrusted their treasure to neighbours. Trin. 1. 2. v. 117.

units.la: PEREGRE abeuntes extremum Vale dicebant omnibus familiaribus. VALETE & VIVITE. Mil. 4. 8. ver. 30. Rogabantque, ut absentibus benedicant. Ibid.
units.tr: Those leaving abroad said a final farewell to all their family: Farewell and live! Mil. 4. 8. v. 30. And they asked that those who stayed behind should bless them. Ibid.

units.la: PEREGRINI ubi in civitatem recens veniunt, solent inquirere in ædes eorum, quos cupiunt convenire. Asin. 2.3. v. 1.
units.tr: Strangers, when they newly come into a city, usually make inquiries at the houses of those whom they wish to meet. Asin. 2. 3. v. 1.

units.la: PEREGRINI postponendi civibus. Trin. 1. 2. v.65.
units.tr: Strangers are to be placed after citizens. Trin. 1. 2. v. 65.

units.la: NEMO ire quemquam publicâ viâ vetat. Curc. 1.1. v. 35.
units.tr: No one forbids anyone to use the public road. Curc. 1. 1. v. 35.

units.la: PEREGRE adventantibus gratulabantur salvum reditum. Stich. 4. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: Those arriving from abroad were congratulated on their safe return. Stich. 4. 2. v. 7.

units.la: PEREGRE adventantes de salute suorum liberorum inquirere solent: & si salvos omnes reperiant, admodum sibi gratulantur. Trin. 4.3. v.67.
units.tr: Those arriving from abroad usually ask after the safety of their children, and if they find them all safe, they greatly rejoice. Trin. 4. 3. v. 67.

units.la: PEREGRE abituri commendabant res suas amicis. Trin. 1.2.v.78.
units.tr: Those about to leave abroad entrusted their possessions to friends. Trin. 1. 2. v. 78.

units.la: PERICULI.
units.tr: PERICULI.

units.la: Non tu scis, cum ex alto puteo sursum ascenderis, Maximum periculum inde esse ab summo, ne rursum cadas. Mil. 4. 4. v. 14.
units.tr: Do you not know that when you climb up out of a deep well, the greatest danger is from the top, that you may fall back again? Mil. 4. 4. v. 14.

units.la: PERIURII. PERFIDIÆ.
units.tr: PERJURY. FAITHLESSNESS.

units.la: Vide etiam Iuramenti.
units.tr: See also Oath.

units.la: LINGUA patrona perjurij. Asin. 2. 2. v. 26.
units.tr: The tongue is the patron of perjury. Asin. 2. 2. v. 26.

units.la: PERFIDIÆ summæ nota est, si quis & hominum & Dei fidem fallit. Amph. 2. 2. v. 40. Asin. 5. 2. v. 4. Bacch. 3. 4. v. 6.
units.tr: It is the mark of great faithlessness if someone deceives both men and God. Amph. 2. 2. v. 40. Asin. 5. 2. v. 4. Bacch. 3. 4. v. 6.

units.la: PERIURI vocabantur in convitium ad Puteal Libonis: ad quod solebat jurari. Curc. 4. 1. v. 9.
units.tr: Perjurers were called, as an insult, those at the Puteal of Libo, where people used to swear oaths. Curc. 4. 1. v. 9.

units.la: SI quidem incubare velint, qui perjuraverint, Locus non præberi potis est in Capitolio. Curc. 2. 2. v. 18. De Incubatione religiosa vide Tit. Deorum.
units.tr: If perjurers wished to lie down for incubation, there could be no place for them in the Capitol. Curc. 2. 2. v. 18. On religious incubation see the title Gods.

units.la: PICTURÆ. IMAGINUM. PICTORUM.
units.tr: PICTURES. IMAGES. PAINTERS.

units.la: APELLES, Zeuxis, magni pictores. Poen. 5. 4. v. 20. Epid. 5. 1. v. 20.
units.tr: APELLES and Zeuxis, great painters. Poen. 5. 4. v. 20. Epid. 5. 1. v. 20.

units.la: O Apella, o Zeuxis pictor, cur numero estis mortui: hinc exemplum, ut pingeretis. Nam alios pictores nihil moror huiusmodi tractare exempla.
units.tr: O Apelles, O Zeuxis the painter, why are you counted among the dead? Here is an example for you to paint. For I take no interest in other painters handling examples of this kind.

units.la: TABELLAS conficiebant ex cera amantes, in quibus picturam & imaginem depingebant eorum, quos amabant: utriusque scilicetsexus. Quacumq; alterius sexus imitata figuram est. Meminit nostier. Asin. 4.1. v.23.
units.tr: Lovers used to make tablets of wax on which they painted a picture and likeness of those they loved, of either sex. Whatever figure of the other sex it imitated... Our author mentions it: Asin. 4.1. v. 23.

units.la: Sic Propert. lib. 2. Eleg. 6.
units.tr: So Propertius, book 2, elegy 6.

units.la: Me juvenum facies pictæ, me nomina ledunt,
units.tr: The painted faces of young men hurt me, and their names hurt me,

units.la: Nempe, quia subscripta tabulis nomina eorum, quorum pictæ facies.
units.tr: Namely, because the names of those whose faces were painted were written beneath the tablets.

units.la: Idem Propert. lib. 3. Eleg. 8. v.16.
units.tr: The same Propertius, book 3, elegy 8, verse 16.

units.la: Seu miseram in tabulâ pictâ puella movet.
units.tr: Or a girl on a painted tablet moves the wretched man.

units.la: Unde scilicet Zelotypia orta utrique sexui.
units.tr: Whence jealousy arose in both sexes.

units.la: Solebant itidem heroinæ virorum, seu quos pro viris haberent, effigies ex cerâ domi habere.
units.tr: Heroines likewise used to keep wax effigies at home of men, or of those whom they regarded as their husbands.

units.la: Ovid. lib. 2. de Remed. Amor.
units.tr: Ovid, book 2 of the Remedia Amoris.

units.la: Si potes & ceras removere: quid imagine mutâ
units.tr: If you can also remove the wax, why are you wounded by a silent image?

units.la: Carperis? hoc periit Laodamia modo.
units.tr: Did Laodamia perish in this way?

units.la: Eadem scilicet Laodamia contabuit viri effigiem assiduo foven-do. In Epist. Heroid.
units.tr: Laodamia, of course, wasted away by constantly cherishing her husband's effigy. In the Epistulae Heroidum.

units.la: Apud Virgilium quoque legimus Didonem Sichæi viri sui imaginem domi habuisse.
units.tr: In Virgil too we read that Dido kept the image of her husband Sichaeus at home.

units.la: Cæterum de ratione scribendi in cerâ apud antiquos, lege Tit. Litterarum: Scribendi.
units.tr: On the manner of writing on wax among the ancients, read the title Litterarum: Scribendi.

units.la: PICTURAS habebant in pariete: etiam spurcas: & rei Venereæ: aliasque. Men. 1. 2. v. 34.
units.tr: They had pictures on their walls, even obscene ones, and pictures of love affairs, and others. Men. 1. 2. v. 34.

units.la: PIGNORIS. HYPOTHECÆ.
units.tr: PLEDGE. MORTGAGE.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Auctionis sup. pag. 106.
units.tr: See also the title Auctionis above, p. 106.

units.la: ARRHABONEM auferebant: si quid alij darent mutuò. Pœn 5.6, v. 22.
units.tr: They took earnest money if they lent something to someone else. Poen. 5. 6. v. 22.

units.la: PISCIUM. PISCATORIS.
units.tr: FISH. FISHERMAN.

units.la: PISCES recentes optimi. Asin. 1.3.v.28. Prov. Græc. ἰδεῖς σα-πεὸς μέγας ἰχθύς Omnis piscis quantumvis magnus, nullus est, si putidus.
units.tr: Fresh fish are the best. Asin. 1. 3. v. 28. Greek proverb: [ἰδεῖς σαπρὸς μέγας ἰχθύς] Every fish, however large, is nothing if it is rotten.

units.la: Seneca Quæst. Natur. 3. Quò pervenere deliciæ? ut pro putrido jam piscis effertur, qui non hodie ednli ... hodie occisus est. Vide Rittersh. in Oppiani Halieut. & Brod. lib.7. c.6. Miscell.
units.tr: Seneca, Quaestiones Naturales 3: "To what have luxuries come? A fish is now carried out as stale that was not eaten today... was killed today." See Rittershusius on Oppian's Halieutica, and Brodaeus, book 7, chapter 6, Miscellanea.

units.la: NEPTUNI pecudes quomodo à coquis condientur, explicat coquus Pseud. 3.2.v.45.
units.tr: How the sheep of Neptune are seasoned by cooks, the cook explains. Pseud. 3. 2. v. 45.

units.la: IN piscinam qui retejaculum parat, quando abijt rete pessum, tum adducit sinum: sin icit rete, pisces ne effugiant, cavet. Tum hic tum illic ii retitos impedit pisces usque adeò donicum eduxit foràs. Itidem est Amator. Truc. 1.1.v.14.
units.tr: A man who prepares a net for a fishpond, when the net has sunk to the bottom, then draws up the bag; if he has cast the net, he takes care that the fish do not escape. Then, here and there, he hinders the fish caught in the mesh, until at last he has drawn them out. Likewise there is the lover in Truc. 1. 1. v. 14.

units.la: QUICQUID habet squamas, piscium nomine venit. Et piscatores nihil piscari decet, nisi pisces. Rud. 4.3. v.53.
units.tr: Whatever has scales is called a fish. And it is not fitting for fishermen to catch anything but fish. Rud. 4. 3. v. 53.

units.la: POLYPUS piscis, ut tenerior esset & melius coqueretur, solebat adterram affligi: quemadmodum hodiè asellus, sive salpa fustibus mitigatur. Rud. 4.3, v. 71.
units.tr: The polypus, so that it may be more tender and cook better, used to be beaten against the ground, as the little donkey, or salpa, is softened with clubs nowadays. Rud. 4. 3. v. 71.

units.la: PASSER marinus sive struthiocamelus ita volat in mari, ut à terrâ se non tollat, sed alarum passis velis unà currens remiget. Pers. 2.2. v.17. Vola curriculo. P. istuc marinus passer per circum solet.
units.tr: The sea sparrow, or struthiocamelus, flies over the sea without lifting itself from the land; running along with its wings spread like sails, it rows. Pers. 2. 2. v. 17. "Fly like a racehorse. P. The sea sparrow usually goes that way round the circus."

units.la: PISCES elixi suaviores, quàm assi. Most. 5.1. v. 66.
units.tr: Boiled fish are more pleasant than grilled. Most. 5. 1. v. 66.

units.la: PISCATORES nasså utuntur, quâ escam petant. Mil 4.2. v.98.
units.tr: Fishermen use a net with which to seek bait. Mil. 4. 2. v. 98.

units.la: PISCES usque dum vivunt, lavant in aquis. Trin. 2.3. v. 1.
units.tr: Fish wash themselves in water as long as they live. Trin. 2. 3. v. 1.

units.la: PISCES lineâ capiebantur. Most. 5, 1. v. 22. ἀλιηγευικῶς.
units.tr: Fish were caught with a line. Most. 5. 1. v. 22. In the manner of fishermen [ἀλιηγευικῶς].

units.la: MURIATICA salsa macerantur aquâ. Pœn. 1.2.v.32. Græci τὰ τα-ρίχη. Vide Lex. Plaut. Muriatica.
units.tr: Pickled meats are soaked in salt water. Poen. 1. 2. v. 32. The Greeks [τὰ ταρίχη]. See the Plautine lexicon under Muriatica.

units.la: Anguilla piscis glaber: qui citò elabitur. Pseud. 2.4. v.57.
units.tr: The eel is a smooth fish that quickly slips away. Pseud. 2. 4. v. 57.

units.la: Nepæ cancri vel scorpiones recessim, seu retrocessim incedunt. Cas. 2.8. v. 7.
units.tr: Crabs, or scorpions, walk sideways or backwards. Cas. 2. 8. v. 7.

units.la: Pisces marini sunt echini, lepades, ostrea, balani, conchæ, marina urtica, musculi, pelagusiæ striatæ. Rud. 2.1. v.8. Vide de singulis Lexic. Plaut. nec non Casaubonum ad Athenæum: Dalecampium & Rondeletium Medicos: nec non Aldrovandum, & Gesnerum.
units.tr: Sea fish are sea urchins, limpets, oysters, barnacles, shells, sea nettles, mussels and striped pelagusiae. Rud. 2. 1. v. 8. On each, see the Plautine lexicon, as well as Casaubon on Athenaeus, Dalechamps and Rondelet the physicians, and also Aldrovandi and Gesner.

units.la: Piscatores fures maritimi, conchitæ, hamiotæ, famelica hominum natio: pereunt fame, siti, speque. Rud. 2.2. v.7.
units.tr: Fishermen are sea thieves, shell-gatherers, hook-fishers, a starving race of men who perish with hunger, thirst and hope. Rud. 2. 2. v. 7.

units.la: In scopulis olim piscatum exercuerunt. Rud. 2.1. v. 10.
units.tr: Once they practised fishing on the rocks. Rud. 2. 1. v. 10.

units.la: Piscatum hamatilem & saxatilem aggredimur.
units.tr: We take up fishing with hook and rock-fishing.

units.la: Vide Meurs. ad Caffand. pag. 109.
units.tr: See Meursius on Cassander, p. 109.

units.la: Pisces in macello divenditi. Rud. 4.3. v.40. Cùm extemplò in macellum pisces prolati sient.
units.tr: Fish sold in the market. Rud. 4. 3. v. 40. When fish were at once brought out into the market.

units.la: De nocte abierunt piscatum ad mare: ubi tamen cùm tempestas erat, nulla spes capturæ fuit. Rud. 4.1. v. 7.
units.tr: They went out by night to fish at sea, but since there was a storm, there was no hope of a catch. Rud. 4. 1. v. 7.

units.la: Neptunus piscatorum patronus Rud. 4.2. v.1.
units.tr: Neptune, patron of fishermen. Rud. 4. 2. v. 1.

units.la: Navicula piscatoria Horia dicebatur. Ibid. v.5.
units.tr: A fishing boat was called a horia. Ibid. v. 5.

units.la: Sepiis dum coquuntur, prius oculi eliduntur.
units.tr: Cuttlefish: while they are being cooked, their eyes are first plucked out.

units.la: Cancri non prorsus: sed ex transverso incedunt.
units.tr: Crabs do not walk straight, but sideways.

units.la: Piscatores solebant fœtidos pisces vendere.
units.tr: Fishermen used to sell stinking fish.

units.la: Muræna à coquo facilè exossantur totæ. Pseud. 1.3. v.147.
units.tr: The cook can easily bone whole murenae. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 147.

units.la: PISTORUM.
units.tr: BAKERS.

units.la: OLIM Romæ Pistoris nulli usque ad annum v c. ıɔlxxx. sed unusquisque civium pinsebat, quantum sibi suisque usui esset, & erat mulierum opus; posteà verò in urbem intrarent Pistores: qui vocabantur Pinsores, teste Servio ad Æneid. lib. i.
units.tr: FORMERLY at Rome there were no bakers until the year 580 from the founding of the city. Instead, each citizen ground grain for his own household's needs, and this was women's work. Afterwards, bakers came into the city, who were called Pinsores, according to Servius on Aeneid book 1.

units.la: Plinius lib. 18. c. 11.
units.tr: Pliny, book 18, chapter 11.

units.la: Pistores Romæ non fuerunt ad Persicum usque bellum, annis ab v. c. ıɔlxx. Ipsi panem faciebant Quirites, muliarumq; id erat opus: sicut etiam nunc in plurimis gentibus.
units.tr: There were no bakers at Rome until the Persian war, in the year 570 from the founding of the city. The citizens made their own bread, and this was the work of women, as it still is among very many peoples.

units.la: Docet idem Plautus noster Mercatore 2.3. v.60.
units.tr: Our Plautus teaches the same in Mercator, act 2, scene 3, line 60.

units.la: Nihil opus nobis ancilla, nisi quæ texat, quæ molat.
units.tr: We need no maidservant except one who weaves and grinds.

units.la: Et paulò post v. 81.
units.tr: And a little later, line 81.

units.la: Ea molet, conficiet pensum.
units.tr: Let her grind and finish her task.

units.la: Manserunt itaque Pistores longo tempore, quoad sub Imperatoribus, collabente paullatim maximo illo imperio, iterùm à fœminis fieri panes soliti. Ulpianus l. Quæsitum est. 12. ff. de instit. vel instrum. leg. Item fabrum, qui villæ reficiendæ causa paratus sit, & mulieres, quæ panem coquant, quaq; villam servent: & Panicoctoria nominabantur vulgò.
units.tr: So the bakers remained for a long time, until under the emperors, as that great empire gradually declined, bread was again commonly made by women. Ulpian, law Quaesitum est, 12, Digest, on instruments or legacies: Likewise a carpenter, who is provided for the repair of a farm, and women who bake bread and keep the farm. They were commonly called panicoctoriae.

units.la: Chrysologus Serm. xcix.
units.tr: Chrysologus, sermon 99.

units.la: Sic dicendo apprendit animos auditorum, & attonitos reddit stupore toto quid regno Dei, quid imperio divino valeat comparari: atq; illa mente per multa & magna pervagantibus, cœli Dominus in hospitio pauperis in manu Panicoctoriæ mulieris regni sui invenit & formať exemplum.
units.tr: By speaking in this way he captures the minds of his hearers and leaves them astonished, struck with wonder at what can be compared with the kingdom of God and the divine rule. While their minds wander over many great things, the Lord of heaven finds his kingdom in the hospitality of a poor woman, in the hand of a bread-baking woman, and shapes an example.

units.la: Locus dicebatur Panificium.
units.tr: The place was called the panificium.

units.la: Glossæ: Ἀρτοποιεῖον. Panificium. & Panificium Ποπαγεῖον.
units.tr: Glosses: bakery [Ἀρτοποιεῖον]. Panificium. And panificium [ποπαγεῖον].

units.la: Vide Meurs. Exerc. Crit. part. 2. c. 32. pag. 181. Et eund. ad Lycorph. Cassand.
units.tr: See Meursius, Exercitationes Criticae, part 2, chapter 32, page 181. And the same author on Lycophron's Cassandra.

units.la: PISTORES furfure solent sues alere. Capt. 4. 2. v. 27.
units.tr: Bakers usually feed their pigs on bran. Captivi, act 4, scene 2, line 27.

units.la: PISTRINI. MOLETRINÆ.
units.tr: MILLS. MILLHOUSES.

units.la: DUÆ rationes molendi fuerunt: Una s cùm suspensà molâ fruges frangimus, ut cùm in fabâ fresâ, &in polentâ crassiusculâ: Altera, cùm molæ non suspenduntur, sed lapis lapidem terit, id est, mola molam, cùm tenuior farina & minutior elicitur. Utramque indicat Plautus Asin. I. I. v. 16.
units.tr: There were two ways of grinding. One was when we crushed the grain with the millstone suspended, as when beans are crushed and in thicker porridge. The other was when the millstones are not suspended, but one stone wears down another, that is, one millstone against another, and a finer and smaller meal is produced. Plautus indicates both in Asinaria, act 1, scene 1, line 16.

units.la: Cæterùm de Moletrinis videndus Pancirollus in Novis Repertis, cum Notis Henrici Salmuthi Tit. xxii.
units.tr: Otherwise, on mills, see Pancirollus in Novae Reperta, with the notes of Henricus Salmuth, title 22.

units.la: ANTE repertum usum Aquæ-molarum, servi adhibiti ad eam rem.
units.tr: Before the invention of water-mills, slaves were used for this task.

units.la: Illis autem quandoque machina ad collum appensa, quæ Polluci παυσιγὴν dicta, ne inter molendum polentam comesse, neve manus ori admovere possent. Asin. I. I. v. 18.
units.tr: Sometimes a contrivance was hung from their necks, which Pollux calls [παυσιγὴν], so that they could not eat the porridge while grinding or bring their hands to their mouths. Asinaria, act 1, scene 1, line 18.

units.la: PISTRINUM mulcta servorum erat. Asin. 3. 3. v. 120. Vide Tit. Servorum.
units.tr: Being sent to the mill was a punishment for slaves. Asinaria, act 3, scene 3, line 120. See the title Servorum.

units.la: PLANTARUM. HERBARUM. ARBORUM, FRUTICUM. AROMATUM. RADICUM. STIRPIUM.
units.tr: PLANTS. HERBS. TREES, SHRUBS. SPICES. ROOTS. STALKS.

units.la: SIRPE & laserpitium & maguderim ex Libyâ exportabant ad rem faciendam. Rud. 3. 2. v. 16. Vide de singulis Lexic. Plaut. Nec non ea, quæ Pseudo-Villiomarus disputat contra Robertum Titium. Item Robertum Constantinum in Supplemento Linguæ Latinæ.
units.tr: Sirpe, laserpitium and maguderis they used to export from Libya for the purpose of making money. Rud. 3.2 v. 16. See the individual entries in the Lexica of Plautus. Also what Pseudo-Villiomarus argues against Robertus Titius, and Robertus Constantinus in the Supplement to the Latin Language.

units.la: Neque enim lubet ea exscribere: quod fecit Taubmannus pagin. 1011.
units.tr: For I do not wish to copy them out: which Taubmann has done, page 1011.

units.la: HELLEBORUM insanis dabatur in medicinam. Rud. 4. 3. v. 67.
units.tr: Hellebore was given to the insane as a medicine. Rud. 4.3 v. 67.

units.la: HELLEBORUM insaniæ curandæ, & bili expurgandæ adhibe-bant. Men. 5. 5. v. 15, 47. Vide Tit. Insaniæ.
units.tr: Hellebore they used for curing madness and purging bile. Men. 5.5 v. 15, 47. See the title "Insanity."

units.la: HERBÆ solstitiales paulisper sunt, nec diu durant: quando nimi-rum tempore solstitij, nocte præsertim frigidiuscula & rorulenta subnascitur, & postea à calore Solis diurni exuritur. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 36. Ad quem locum vide Interpretes apud Centones Taub-manni.
units.tr: Summer herbs last only a little while and do not endure long: namely because they sprout up at the time of the solstice, especially at night when it is rather cold and dewy, and afterwards are scorched by the heat of the daytime sun. Pseud. 1.1 v. 36. On this passage see the commentators collected in Taubmann's Centones.

units.la: RUMICEM, brassicam, betam, blitum, atrum olus apposuerunt coqui in convivijs. Pseud. 3. 2. v. 26.
units.tr: Cooks at banquets served radish, cabbage, beet, blite and black herbs. Pseud. 3.2 v. 26.

units.la: SINAPIS scelerata teritur, cùm illis, qui terunt, priusquam terue-runt, oculi ut exstillent, facit. Pseud 3. 2. v. 28.
units.tr: Wicked mustard, when it is ground, makes the eyes of those who grind it, before they have ground it, stream with tears. Pseud. 3.2 v. 28.

units.la: FUNGI & citò crescunt, & facilè ab imbribus prosternuntur. Stich. 5. 5. v. 32.
units.tr: Mushrooms also grow quickly, and are easily flattened by the rains. Stich. 5.5 v. 32.

units.la: LOLIUM ob acres vapores, quos in cerebrum tollit, non solùm ebrietatis speciem quandam creat, sed etiam oculos vitiat & ob-tundit. Mil. 2. 3. v. 50. Ovid. lib. 1. Fast Et careant lolijs oculos vitiantibus agri. Vide Polit. Miscell. c. 66. & Dalechampium ad Livium.
units.tr: Darnel, because of the sharp vapours it sends up into the brain, not only creates a certain semblance of drunkenness but also injures and dulls the eyes. Mil. 2.3 v. 50. Ovid, Fasti book 1: "and let the fields be free of darnel, which injures the eyes." See the Polit. Miscell. ch. 66, and Dalechamps on Livy.

units.la: THUS in Arabia gignitur. Trin. 4. 2. v. 89.
units.tr: Frankincense is produced in Arabia. Trin. 4.2 v. 89.

units.la: CUNILA gallinacea, & absynthium ubi crescat, enarrat nugator sycophanta. Trin. 4. 2. v. 90.
units.tr: The braggart sycophant describes where hen's cunila and wormwood grow. Trin. 4.2 v. 90.

units.la: ALLIUM qui comederent fœtebant, & odio alijs erant. Most. 1. 1. v. 38.
units.tr: Those who ate garlic made people stink, and were hateful to others. Most. 1.1 v. 38.

units.la: FUNGUS putidus nullius momenti. Bacch. 4. 7. v. 23.
units.tr: A rotten mushroom of no account. Bacch. 4.7 v. 23.

units.la: PLUVIÆ. IMBRIS. TEMPESTATIS. VENTORUM.
units.tr: Rain. Shower. Storm. Winds.

units.la: TEMPESTAS liquida, tranquilla est. Most. 3. 2. v. 65. de ho-mine tranquillo: Tàm liquidus est, quàm liquida esse tempestas solet.
units.tr: A storm that is clear and calm. Most. 3.2 v. 65, said of a calm man: "He is as clear as a storm usually is clear."

units.la: Favonius ventus liquidiusculus. Mil. 3. 1. v. 70.
units.tr: The west wind is a rather clear breeze. Mil. 3.1 v. 70.

units.la: Pluvia facilimè fungos prosternit. Stich. 5. 5. v. 32.
units.tr: Rain very easily lays low mushrooms. Stich. 5.5 v. 32.

units.la: Ventus leviter dissilat folia, & panniculam tectoriam. Mil. 1. 1. v. 18.
units.tr: The wind gently scatters the leaves and the plaster cloth. Mil. 1.1 v. 18.

units.la: Favonius serenus est, isthic auster imbricus: Hic facit tranquillitatem: iste omnes fluctus conciet. Merc. 5. 2. v. 35.
units.tr: The west wind is calm here; the south wind there brings rain. The one makes calm; the other stirs up all the waves. Merc. 5.2 v. 35.

units.la: Venti detexunt domos. Rud. 1. 1. v. 2.
units.tr: The winds have stripped the houses bare. Rud. 1.1 v. 2.

units.la: Neptunus nobis tempestatem misit.
units.tr: Neptune has sent us a storm.

units.la: Talis tempestas describitur à Varrone: Repente noctu circiter meridiem: Cum pictum aer fervidus late ignibus Coeli choreas astricas ostenderet: Nubes aquales frigido velo leves Coeli cavernas aureas subduxerant, Ventus, frigido se ab axe eruperant Phrenetici septemtrionum filij, Secum ferentes tegulas, ramos, sirus. At nos caduci naufragij ciconia Quarum bipennis fulminis plumas vapos Percussit alte, mæstè in terram cecidimus.
units.tr: Such a storm is described by Varro: "Suddenly, at night, about midday, when the fiery air, spreading far and wide with its fires, showed the starry dances of heaven, the clouds, equal and light with their cold veil, had drawn down the golden hollows of the sky. From the cold axis the frenzied sons of the north winds had burst out, carrying with them roof tiles, branches and rubbish. But we, like the storks of a fallen shipwreck, whose plumes were struck by the double-edged axe of lightning, fell sadly to the ground."

units.la: Vide etiam apud Senec. Agamemn. Act. 3.
units.tr: See also Seneca, Agamemnon, Act 3.

units.la: Poetarum. Comicorum. Versuum.
units.tr: Of the Poets. Of the Comics. Of the Verses.

units.la: POETÆ vanitatis saepè convicti: quales jocosè nostèr vocat Homeronidas Poëtillas: h. e. Homeri posteros, & imitatores, qui de falsis pugnis heroum convicti sint. Truc. 2. 6. v. 4.
units.tr: Poets are often convicted of falsehood, such as our author jokingly calls the little Homerids, that is, the descendants and imitators of Homer, who have been convicted of false battles of heroes. Truc. 2.6 v. 4.

units.la: Poetæ fallaces & astuti dicuntur. Cas 5. 1. v. 7.
units.tr: Poets are said to be deceitful and crafty. Cas. 5.1 v. 7.

units.la: Poetæ Comici omnes res gestas esse Athenis autumant, Quò ad Græcum videatur magis. Men. Prol. v. 7. Interdum tamen in alia urbe Græciæ fingitur esse scena. Vide Casaub. Athen. lib. 3. cap. 34.
units.tr: All comic poets claim that their plots are set at Athens, so that they may seem more Greek. Men. Prol. v. 7. Sometimes, however, the scene is feigned to be in another city of Greece. See Casaubon, Athenaeus, book 3, chapter 34.

units.la: POETA tabulas cum cæpit sibi, quærit quod nusquam est gentium, reperit tamen. Facit illud verisimile, quod mendacium est. Nunc ego Poeta fiam: inquit servus mendax Pseud. 1. 4. v. 8.
units.tr: When the poet has taken up his tablets, he seeks something that exists nowhere in the world, yet he finds it. He makes probable what is a lie. "Now I will become a poet," says the lying slave. Pseud. 1.4 v. 8.

units.la: VERSUS hexametros sæpe usurpant Comici. Nostep quatuor habet. Trin. 4. 1. v. 14.
units.tr: Comic poets often use hexameter verses. Our author has four of them. Trin. 4.1 v. 14.

units.la: Etiam alij authores in prosa sæpe imprudentes posuerunt: quod tamen Cicero putat vitiosum.
units.tr: Other authors writing in prose have also often unintentionally put in verses, which Cicero, however, thinks faulty.

units.la: PRÆCONUM.
units.tr: OF HERALDS.

units.la: PER præconem solebant silentium petere in scenis & fabulis. Asin. Prol. v. 4.
units.tr: Through a herald they were accustomed to ask for silence in the stage-plays and comedies. Asin. Prol. v. 4.

units.la: PRÆCONIBUS opus erat voce contentiosâ: per quam sibi vi-ctum & cultum parabant. Pœn. Prol. v. 13.
units.tr: Heralds needed a loud, strong voice, by which they gained their food and clothing. Pœn. Prol. v. 13.

units.la: Seneca Epist. 47. Vocem præco experitur.
units.tr: Seneca, Epist. 47: He tries his voice as a herald.

units.la: IN conquirendis res amissas præconibus olim utebantur. Mirc. 3. 4. v. 78. Vide Tit. Rei - Amissæ.
units.tr: In seeking out lost goods they formerly made use of heralds. Mirc. 3. 4. v. 78. See the title Rei - Amissæ.

units.la: PRÆSENTIÆ. PERSONÆ.
units.tr: PRESENCE. PERSONS.

units.la: PRÆSENTIA in omnibus negotijs prævalet: inprimis in militiâ. Amph. 1. 1. v. 9.
units.tr: Presence prevails in all affairs, especially in war. Amph. 1. 1. v. 9.

units.la: Ubi summus Imperator non adest ad exercitum, cujus quod non facto est usus fit, quàm quod facto est opus.
units.tr: Where the supreme commander is not present with the army, what is done without his presence is more needed than what is done with it.

units.la: Gemina dicta Authorum hæc sunt:
units.tr: These are the paired sayings of authors:

units.la: Livius:
units.tr: Livy:

units.la: Non satis feliciter procedunt, qua oculis agis alienis.
units.tr: Those things go not very successfully which you do with other people's eyes.

units.la: Æschylus in Persis : ὄμμα δόμων ῥομίζω δεαπότης παςυσίαν. Lumen edium puto domini præsentiam.
units.tr: Aeschylus in the Persians: "I consider the eye of the house to be the presence of the master" [ὄμμα δόμων νομίζω δεσπότου παρουσίαν].

units.la: Aristot. lib. 1. Oecon. c. 6. Oculus Domini est, qui maximè pinguefacit equum.
units.tr: Aristotle, Oeconomica bk. 1, ch. 6: The master's eye is what fattens the horse most.

units.la: Plin. lib. 18. c. 6. Majores fertilissimum in agro oculum domini esse dixerunt.
units.tr: Pliny, bk. 18, ch. 6: The ancients said that the master's eye is the most fertile thing in a field.

units.la: Symmachus lib. 9. Epist. 6. Procul positis nullus dominorum terror incurrit.
units.tr: Symmachus, bk. 9, letter 6: When masters are far away, no fear of them reaches the servants.

units.la: Et huc pertinet Apologus ille Phædri lib. II. Fab. xxxix. Cervi ad boves : οὑμὸς ὀπμύθιον est: Dominum videre plurimum in rebus suis.
units.tr: This also pertains to the fable of Phaedrus, bk. II, fable xxxix, The stags and the oxen, whose moral is: [οὗτος ὁ μῦθος] The master sees most in his own affairs.

units.la: Itemque Æsopi de cassitâ & pullis ejus, descriptus ab Agellio lib. 2. c. 29. & Gabr. Faerno. Nec non Ennianum illud: Hoc erit tibi argumentum semper in promtu situm, Ne quid expectes amicos, quod tute agere possies.
units.tr: So too Aesop's fable of the cassita and her chicks, recorded by Agellius, bk. 2, ch. 29, and by Gabriel Faernus. Nor should we omit that line of Ennius: This will always be a ready argument for you, not to expect friends to do what you can do yourself.

units.la: PRINCIPII.
units.tr: OF THE BEGINNING.

units.la: Vide Tit. Actionis.
units.tr: See the title Of the Action.

units.la: OMNE principium felix, omen erat bonum. Stich. 5. 2. v. 23.
units.tr: Every beginning is happy; the omen was good. Stich. 5. 2. v. 23.

units.la: PRINCIPIS. REGUM. MAGNATUM. IMPERATORUM.
units.tr: OF PRINCES. KINGS. NOBLES. EMPERORS.

units.la: CUM suspicamur Principem bonâ fide nobis se amicum præbere: vultu inquam & voce: sed corde aliud volatare: hoc versu uti possumus; Quoi homini Dij propitij sunt, ei non iratos esse puto. Curc. 4. 4. v. 1.
units.tr: When we suspect that a prince is showing himself to us as a friend in good faith, in face and voice, but that his heart is set on something else, we may use this line: "The man whom the gods favour, I think they are not angry with." Curculio, act 4, scene 4, line 1.

units.la: REX Persarum per Epistolam aut per nuncium adiri voluit. Mil. 4. 5. v. 10.
units.tr: The King of the Persians wished to be approached by letter or through a messenger. Miles Gloriosus, act 4, scene 5, line 10.

units.la: ACCESSUS, Aditus Principum difficiles sunt.
units.tr: Access to princes, their approaches, are difficult.

units.la: PROMISSIONUM. STIPULATIONUM. OBLIGATIONUM. SPONSIONUM.
units.tr: PROMISSIONUM. STIPULATIONUM. OBLIGATIONUM. SPONSIONUM.

units.la: IN stipulatione est adstipulator plærumque, ut in promissione adpromissor. Stipulator rogat: adstipulator arrogat. Sic dicitur Rud. ƒ. 2. v. Venus hæc volo arrogatte.
units.tr: In a stipulation there is usually an adstipulator, just as in a promise there is an adpromissor. The stipulator asks; the adstipulator joins in the asking (arrogat). So it is said in Rudens, act 2, scene 3: "Venus, I want you to join in this request."

units.la: SCITUM est, atque elegans, cùm quid promisisti, ne exspectare dum rogeris: sed suo tempore occurrere, atque obviam ire, & promissa patrare. Ita proverbium hoc explicat Pæn. Prol. ver. 7. Muretus. Alij aliter.
units.tr: It is a witty and elegant saying that when you have promised something, you should not wait to be asked, but should anticipate the request, go to meet it, and carry out what you promised. Plautus's Poenulus, prologue, line 7, explains this proverb in this way. Muretus; others differently.

units.la: Si quis per jocum aliquid promiserit, Paulus J.C. negat nasci obligationem l. ob ig. §. ult. de oblig. servorum. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 123. Auferetur id pramium ame, quod promisi per jocum?
units.tr: If someone has promised something in jest, the jurist Paulus denies that an obligation arises (law "ob ig.", §. last, de oblig. servorum). Pseudolus, act 4, scene 7, line 123: "Shall that reward be taken from me which I promised in jest?"

units.la: Vide etiam Rævard. lib. 2. cap. ƒ. Var.
units.tr: See also Rævardus, book 2, chapter ... Var.

units.la: SPONSIONUM & stipulationum formulas certis verbis concipiebant, & ferè ordiebantur à Si, Sive: Ni, Nive, Curc. 1. 1. v. 4. Si medianox est, sive est prima vespera, &c. Rud. 3. 4. verf. 9. Pseud. 4. 6. v. 9. Vide etiam Lex. Plaut. Si: pro Sive.
units.tr: Sponsions and stipulations they framed in fixed words, and usually began with Si, Sive, Ni, Nive. Curculio, act 1, scene 1, line 4: "If it is midnight, or if it is early evening, etc." Rudens, act 3, scene 4, line 9; Pseudolus, act 4, scene 6, line 9. See also the Plautine Lexicon under Si: used for Sive.

units.la: STIPULATIONUM Formula erat: SPONDEN' Tu istud? Capt. 4. 2. v. 118.
units.tr: The formula of stipulation was: "Do you promise that?" (SPONDEN' Tu istud?) Captivi, act 4, scene 2, line 118.

units.la: Ex jure sibi quisque tantum, non autem alteri stipulari potest. §. alteri, inst. de inutil. stipul. Most. 3. 2. v. 113. Vide Lexic. Plautin. Redhibere.
units.tr: By law one can stipulate only for oneself, not for another. Institutes, §. alteri, de inutilibus stipulationibus. Mostellaria, act 3, scene 2, line 113. See the Plautine Lexicon under Redhibere.

units.la: STIPULATIO interdum post pactum adhibebatur. Pœn. 5. 3. v. 34.
units.tr: A stipulation was sometimes added after the agreement had been made. Poenulus, act 5, scene 3, line 34.

units.la: Vide Hottomannum J.C. & supra Tit. Nuptiarum.
units.tr: See the jurist Hotman, and above under the title Marriages.

units.la: PUDORIS. VERECUNDIÆ. PUDICITIÆ. CASTITATIS. VIRGINUM. PUELLARUM. VIRGINITATIS.
units.tr: PUDORIS. VERECUNDIÆ. PUDICITIÆ. CASTITATIS. VIRGINUM. PUELLARUM. VIRGINITATIS.

units.la: PLÆRIQUE omnes, quos quum nihil réfert, pudet: ubi pudendum est, ibi eos deserit pudor, quum usus est, ut pudcant. Epid. 2. I. v. 1, 2. Ter. Andr. 4. I. v. 13. Ubi fides sirogus, nihil pudet: hic ubi opus est, non verentur: illic ubi nihil opus est, ibi verentur.
units.tr: Most people are ashamed when it does not matter, and where shame is called for, shame deserts them; they are without shame where it is needed, and they feel shame where there is no need for it. Epidicus, act 2, scene 1, lines 1–2; Terence, Andria, act 4, scene 1, line 13: "Where loyalty is lacking, they feel no shame: where it is needed, they do not hesitate; where nothing is needed, there they hesitate."

units.la: VIRGINES & puellæ male-cavent suæ pudicitiæ, quæ in publicum prodeunt ad festas solemnitates, &c. Cist. I. I. v. 92. Exemplum quoq; in sacris est Dina, quæ à Sichemitis corrupta.
units.tr: Virgins and girls take great care of their chastity when they go out in public to festive celebrations, etc. Cistellaria, act 1, scene 1, line 92. There is also an example among the sacred writings in Dinah, who was violated by the Shechemites.

units.la: Quos pudet, rubore suffunduntur. Capt. 5. 2. v. 9.
units.tr: Those who are ashamed are suffused with a blush. Captivi, act 5, scene 2, line 9.

units.la: VIRGINES integræ dicuntur corrumpi. Truc. 4. 3. v. 47. Augustinus: Obstetrix virginis cujusdam integritatem manu velut explorans perdidit.
units.tr: Virgins are said to be corrupted when they are intact. Truculentus, act 4, scene 3, line 47. Augustine: a midwife, by feeling a certain virgin's integrity with her hand, destroyed it.

units.la: PUDOR & verecundia pœnæ loco subrogari solet, & culpam, si levis sit, exstinguere, Most. 5. 2. v. 43. Vide Langl. Semestr. lib. 10. cap. 1.
units.tr: Shame and modesty are often substituted in place of punishment, and can extinguish a fault if it is slight. Mostellaria, act 5, scene 2, line 43. See Langlois, Semestria, book 10, chapter 1.

units.la: PUDORIS & metus signum est, non audere alicui ἀντιβλέπειν, h. e. contra oculos adspicere: addo etiam, malæ conscientiæ. Caf. 5. 3. v. 2. Vide Def. Herald. lib. 2. c. 4.
units.tr: Not daring to look someone in the face, that is, to look them straight in the eyes (ἀντιβλέπειν), is a sign of shame and fear; I add also of a guilty conscience. Cásina, act 5, scene 3, line 2. See Dès Hérault, Herald, book 2, chapter 4.

units.la: IMPUDICITIA non decet servum herilem: qui heri fidelis esse cupiat. Perf. 2. 2. v. 11.
units.tr: Shamelessness does not befit a household slave who wishes to be faithful to his master. Persa, act 2, scene 2, line 11.

units.la: INIURIA puellis infertur, si violetur earum pudicitia. Bacch. 11. v. 25.
units.tr: Wrong is done to girls if their chastity is violated. Bacchides, act 1, line 25.

units.la: VERECUNDIÆ est abstinere à verbis nuptis. Caf. 5. 2. v. 19, 22.
units.tr: It is a mark of modesty to abstain from words unbecoming to a bride. Cásina, act 5, scene 2, lines 19, 22.

units.la: DECET verecundum esse adolescentem. Asin. 5. 1. v. 6.
units.tr: It becomes a young man to be modest. Asinaria, act 5, scene 1, line 6.

units.la: EGO illum perijsse duco, cui quidem perijt pudor. Bacch. 3. 3. v. 81.
units.tr: I consider him lost who has lost his sense of shame. Bacchides, act 3, scene 3, line 81.

units.la: POL pudere quàm pigere præstat, totidem litteris. Trin. 2. 2. v. 64.
units.tr: Indeed, it is better to feel shame than regret, with the same number of letters (pudere, pigere). Trinummus, act 2, scene 2, line 64.

units.la: Sff
units.tr: Sff

units.la: PUDORIS jactura gravior, quàm rei familiaris: contra quàm sen-tit Leno. Pseud. 1.3.v.46.
units.tr: The loss of one's shame is more serious than the loss of one's property; contrary to what the pimp thinks. Pseudolus, act 1, scene 3, line 46.

units.la: Sophocles: τὸ αἰσχύνεσθαι ἡδύ, καὶ ἀπὸ ἀ- ... In Prov. αἰσχύνη ἀλλ' ... ἀμεινον. Lucrum pudori praestat.
units.tr: Sophocles: "To feel shame is sweet" [τὸ αἰσχύνεσθαι ἡδύ]. ... In the proverb, "shame is better" [αἰσχύνη ... ἀμεινον]. Profit is preferable to shame.

units.la: VIRGINES ægerrimè ferunt, si propudij insimulantur. Mil. 2.4.v.11.43.
units.tr: Virgins take it very badly if they are accused of unchastity. Miles Gloriosus, act 2, scene 4, lines 11, 43.

units.la: CAPUT operiebant in returpi deprehensi: summo pudore affecti, in rebus desperatis: vitam projicere parantes. Most. 2.1.v.76. Vide Tit. Cultus: Habitus.
units.tr: Women caught in adultery covered their heads, overcome by the deepest shame, when they were in desperate straits and prepared to throw away their lives. Mostellaria, act 2, scene 1, line 76. See the title Dress: Attire.

units.la: PUDICITIÆ mulierum, matrum-familias, virginum, puellarum est; non prodire domo sine comitatu, aut pedisequio. Amph. 3.2. ver.48. Caf. 2.2.v.1. Ciftell. loco amisso: Astat ea in via sola: Prostibulum sane est. Nævius: Subitò famem tollunt, si quam solam videre in via. Hic comitatus ferè è spadonibus constabat. Vide Ravard. Var. lib. 4.c.17.
units.tr: It is a mark of the chastity of women, of married matrons, virgins and girls, not to go out of the house without an escort or attendant. Amphitryon, act 3, scene 2, line 48; Casina, act 2, scene 2, line 1. Cistellaria, lost passage: "To stand alone in the street: that is certainly a prostitute." Naevius: "They quickly satisfy their hunger if they see any woman alone in the street." Such an escort usually consisted of eunuchs. See Rævardus, Var., book 4, chapter 17.

units.la: VIRGINI per stuprum injuria infertur. Aul. 4.10: v.64.
units.tr: Wrong is done to a virgin through rape. Aulularia, act 4, scene 10, line 64.

units.la: VERECUNDIA adolescentum deturbatur ignaviâ. Most. 1.2.v.58.
units.tr: The modesty of young men is undermined by idleness. Mostellaria, act 1, scene 2, line 58.

units.la: PUERITIÆ.
units.tr: PUERITIÆ.

units.la: PUERI patricij in delitijs habebant passeres, anseres, anates, & alias aviculas. Capt. 5.4.v.5. Bacch. 1.1. v.35. Vide Tit. Lusus: Ludicri: Avium.
units.tr: Patrician boys kept sparrows, geese, ducks and other small birds among their pets. Captivi, act 5, scene 4, line 5; Bacchides, act 1, scene 1, line 35. See the title Play: Sport: Birds.

units.la: LIBEROS amissos, tùm aliunde, tùm etiam ex crepundijs agnoscebant: unde γνωρίσματα quoque dicta. Cist. 3.1.v.5. Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: Lost children they recognised by other means, and even by their baby-rattles; hence these were also called tokens of recognition (γνωρίσματα). Cistellaria, act 3, scene 1, line 5. See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: Cicero in Bruto: Nunc quoniam totum me, non navo aliquo, aut crepundijs, sed corpore omni videri velle cognoscere. Vide Meurs. Exerc.Crit.part.1.c.3. ad Cist.& Taubm. ad Mil. 5. v.6. p.724.
units.tr: Cicero, in the Brutus: "Now since I wish to be recognised as a whole, not by some mark or baby-rattles, but by my whole body..." See Meursius, Exercitationes criticae, part 1, chapter 3, on the Cistellaria; and Taubmann on Miles Gloriosus, act 5, line 6, p. 724.

units.la: PUE-
units.tr: PUE-

units.la: PURPURÆ.
units.tr: PURPURÆ.

units.la: PVRPVRA ætatem vetulæ feminæ occultabant. Most. 1. 3. v. 129.
units.tr: Purple concealed the age of an elderly woman. Mostellaria, act 1, scene 3, line 129.

units.la: Vide Bernart. ad lib. 1. Sylv. Statij.
units.tr: See Bernartius on book 1 of the Silvae of Statius.

units.la: REFRIGERII.
units.tr: COOLING

units.la: VENTULUM pallio faciebant. Cas. 3. 5. v. 15.
units.tr: They made a little breeze with their cloaks. Cas. 3. 5. v. 15.

units.la: REI-AMISSÆ. REI-PERDITÆ. AMISSIONIS.
units.tr: THINGS LOST. THINGS PERISHED. LOSS.

units.la: AN res amissa & inventa ab alio, debeat ostendi, disputatur. Rud. 4. 4. v. 52.
units.tr: Whether a lost thing, once found by another, ought to be shown (to the owner) is disputed. Rud. 4. 4. v. 52.

units.la: AD conquirendas res amissas præconibus olim utebantur. Merc. 3. 4. v. 78. Rud. 5. 3. v. 1.
units.tr: Heralds were once used to search out lost things. Merc. 3. 4. v. 78. Rud. 5. 3. v. 1.

units.la: Si neq; per præconem recipere potuissent, à prætore Conquisitores impetrabant. Ibid. Apulejus: Si quis à fuga retrahere, vel occultam demonstrare potuerit regis filiam, Veneris ancillam nomine Psychen, convenit retrò metas Murcias Mercurium prædicatorem. Moschus Idyll. 1.
units.tr: If they could not recover the thing through a herald, they obtained searchers from the praetor. Ibid. Apuleius: If anyone could bring back from flight, or disclose where it is hidden, the king's daughter, Venus's maidservant named Psyche, let him come to the Murcian turning-post, to Mercury the herald. Moschus, Idyll 1.

units.la: ἄ κύπρις ἡ ἐφωτα ἡ ψέα μακρὸν ἐβώσγει, ἐι πς ἐνί τειδδοισι πλανώμενον εἴδεν.
units.tr: ἄ κύπρις ἡ ἐφωτα ἡ ψέα μακρὸν ἐβώσγει, ἐι πς ἐνί τειδδοισι πλανώμενον εἴδεν. [Aphrodite long cried out, if anyone had seen him wandering among the thickets.]

units.la: Inscribebant etiam columnæ alicui in publicis porticibus & rem amissam, & nomen cujus ea esset: item ubi habitaret, promissâ quoque inventori stipe, ut redderet. Propertius lib. 3. Eleg. ante-penult. de amissis tabellis.
units.tr: They also inscribed on columns in public colonnades both the lost thing and the name of its owner, and also where he lived, with a reward promised to the finder for returning it. Propertius, book 3, elegy second from the last, on the lost tablets.

units.la: Quas si quis mihi retulerit, donabitur auro: Quæ pro divitiis ligna retenta velit? I puer, & citius hæc aliquâ propone columnâ; Et dominum Exquilijs die habitare tuum.
units.tr: If anyone brings them back to me, he shall be given gold. What wood would she prefer kept in exchange for riches? Go, boy, and quickly post this on some column, and say that your master lives on the Esquiline.

units.la: Petronius: Si quis Gyton a reddere aut commonstrare voluerit accipiet numos mille. Vide etiam Lucian. in vitâ Demonactis.
units.tr: Petronius: If anyone is willing to return Gyton, or to point him out, he shall receive a thousand coins. See also Lucian, in the Life of Demonax.

units.la: Fortunatianus lib. 1. Rhet. E edicto, vel præco iso quomodo fit? Cujus servus fugerat, libello proposito, vel per præconem nuncians dixit daturum se denarios mille et, q ui se servum perduxisset.
units.tr: Fortunatianus, book 1 of the Rhetoric: By edict, or how is it done by a herald? Whose slave had fled; a notice being posted, or by a herald announcing, he said he would give a thousand denarii to whoever brought the slave back.

units.la: Ulpianus in l. falsus creditos §. solent. ff. de furtis. Tit. 2. lib. 47. Solent plerique etiam hoc facere, ut libellum proponant, continentem invenisse, & redditurum ei, qui desideraverit.
units.tr: Ulpian, in the law "falsus creditos" §. solent, Digest, title on theft, book 47: Many people also customarily do this: they post a notice stating that the thing was found, and that it will be returned to whoever claims it.

units.la: Vide etiam Petri Pithæi Adversf. lib. 1. c. 2. & lib. 2. cap. 19. Gold. ad Petron. p. 668.
units.tr: See also Pierre Pithou, Adversaria, book 1 chapter 2 and book 2 chapter 19; Gold. on Petronius, p. 668.

units.la: Eadem inquisitio facta in furtis: ubi munitissima quæque quamvis obsignata loca solet perscrutari, quod vocabant per licium & lancem. Pretium dicebatur ἐυρέτηρον. Indicium, pro præmio indicij.
units.tr: The same search was made in cases of theft, where they would commonly search even the most secure places, however sealed, which they called searching "with a licium and a lanx" (a loincloth and a dish). The reward was called euretron; "indicium" was used for the reward for information.

units.la: Si quid perditum esset, publicis litteris majoribus affigebant, idq; faciebant tenuiores: ut Stich. Gelasimus. Et Rud. 5. 2. v. 6. Cubitum hercle longü litteris signabo jam usquequaq;, si quis perdiderit vidulum cum argento & argento multo, ad Gripum ut veniat. Alij opulentiores ad eam rem usi præcone. Qui mos etiamnum viget: ut vel basilicis vel portis affigatur: vel per præconem verbi Dei pro concione id fiat. Vide l. falsus cred. 43. §. proinde 8. ff. de furtis.
units.tr: If anything had been lost, they fixed public notices on large boards, and the poorer people did this. So in Stichus, Gelasimus; and Rud. 5. 2. v. 6: Indeed, I will mark it with letters a full cubit long, everywhere, if anyone has lost a little chest with silver and much gold, to come to Gripus. Others, who were wealthier, used a herald for this purpose. This custom still flourishes: notices are posted on the public halls or gates, or else the thing is announced by a herald before the congregation, as the word of God is proclaimed. See the law "falsus cred." 43, §. proinde 8, Digest, on theft.

units.la: REM perditam anxiè requirebant, & quasi cum augurio mentis.
units.tr: They sought a lost thing anxiously, and almost with a sense of foreboding.

units.la: Ille nunc lætus est, qui eam habet: quæ neq; illa illi quicquam usui est. Solabantur se in re perditâ hac formulâ: Quod perijt, periit: Alium est. Cist. 4. 2. v. 36. & Trin. 4. 3. v. 19. Quin tu, quod periit, perisse ducas.
units.tr: He who has it now is glad, but it is of no use to him at all. In losing a thing they comforted themselves with this formula: What has perished has perished; it belongs to another. Cist. 4. 2. v. 36. And Trin. 4. 3. v. 19: Come now, consider what has perished as already lost.

units.la: Omnes ego pro nihilo esse ducto, quod fuit, quando fuit, tamquam hominem, quando animam efflavit, quid eum, qui fuit? Persa. 4. 4. v. 86.
units.tr: I consider all things to be nothing, what was, when it was, like a man, once he has breathed out his soul: why should we care about what has been? Persa 4. 4. v. 86.

units.la: Pro re perditâ, ij, qui repererunt, mercedem postularunt. Cist. 4. 2. v. 71.
units.tr: For a lost thing, those who had found it demanded a reward. Cist. 4. 2. v. 71.

units.la: REIPUBLICÆ. CIVITATIS.
units.tr: THE COMMONWEALTH. THE CITIZEN.

units.la: CIVES anteponendi hostibus, seu peregrinis. Trin. 1. 2. v. 65.
units.tr: Citizens are to be preferred to enemies, or to foreigners. Trin. 1. 2. v. 65.

units.la: RESPUBLICA nobis potiordebet esse, quàm amor uxoris. Amph. 1. 3. v. 40.
units.tr: The commonwealth ought to be dearer to us than love of a wife. Amph. 1. 3. v. 40.

units.la: REIPUBLICÆ gerendæ ratio belli domíque summæ fuit curæ. Amphit. 1. 1. v. 41. Vide Phras. Respublicæ: ubi formula GERE RE REMP. Vide Formulas Brissonij lib. 11. pag. 206. Edit. Wechel.
units.tr: The management of the commonwealth, in war and at home, was a matter of the greatest concern. Amphit. 1. 1. v. 41. See the phrase under Respublica, where the formula GERE RE REMP. is given. See the formulas of Brisson, book 11, p. 206, Wechel edition.

units.la: PROLETARII in Republicâ ducebantur, qui præter prolem Reipublicæ nihil exhibebant: contra Assidui. Mil. 3. 1. v. 156. Proletarius sermo.
units.tr: Proletarians were counted in the commonwealth as those who contributed nothing to the state beyond their offspring; by contrast the assidui. Mil. 3. 1. v. 156. The expression proletarius sermo.

units.la: CIVITATEM cive augere: & majore facere summæ laudi ducitur. Persa. 4. 3. v. 5.
units.tr: To increase the state by the citizen, and to make it greater, is held to be a matter of the highest praise. Persa. 4. 3. v. 5.

units.la: QUID est suavius, quàm bene rem gerere bono publico? Capt. 3. 2. v. 1.
units.tr: What is sweeter than to manage affairs well for the public good? Capt. 3. 2. v. 1.

units.la: REIPUBLICÆ causâ quidvis faciundum. Curc. 3. 1. v. 19. Vide Tit. Belli.
units.tr: Anything whatever is to be done for the sake of the commonwealth. Curc. 3. 1. v. 19. See the title Belli.

units.la: REI-SUPELLECTILIS.
units.tr: Household Furniture

units.la: Vide Tit. Familia.
units.tr: See the title Familia.

units.la: ROMÆ. VRBIS.
units.tr: Rome. The City.

units.la: HOMINES otiosi solebant olim Romæ sub Basilica, & Ro- stris obambulare. Unde in convitio fuerunt subrostrani: subbasilicani, homines ἀργόμοι, qui & ordinarij dicti fuerunt, Capt. 4.2. v. 35. Vide Lex. Plaut. Subbasilicanum.
units.tr: Idle men used long ago in Rome to stroll about under the Basilica and the Rostra. Hence in abuse they were called subrostrani and subbasilicani, idlers [ἀργόμοι], who were also called ordinarii. Capt. 4.2. v. 35. See the Plautine lexicon, Subbasilicanum.

units.la: ITEMQUE scorta exoleta. Mariti damnosi In foro piscario symbolarum collectores sedebant otiosi. In foro infimo boni homines atque dites ambulant. In medio propter canalem ibi ostentatores meri, Confidentes, garrulique: & malevoli supra lacum, &c. Curcul. 4.1.ver.10. & seqq. Vide locum elegantem de variis locis Romæ. Caf 3.3. v. 2.
units.tr: Likewise, worn-out prostitutes. Spendthrift husbands. In the fish market, idle collectors of shares for dinners sat about. In the lowest forum, good and wealthy men walk about. In the middle, by the canal, there are mere showoffs, braggarts and chatterers, and the ill-disposed above the pool, etc. Curcul. 4.1. ver. 10 and following. See the elegant passage on the various places of Rome. Caf. 3.3. v. 2.

units.la: ITEM coqui, tibicinæ, in foro conducebantur. Aul. 2.3. v. 2.
units.tr: Likewise cooks and flute-girls were hired in the forum. Aul. 2.3. v. 2.

units.la: ALIIQUE homines nihili, garruli, sycophantæ, vitilitigatores: qui inde Comitiales dicti per jocum. Trin. 3.3.v. 86. Pseud. 3.2. v. 11. Poen. 3.2.v.7.
units.tr: Some worthless men, gossips, sycophants and petty litigants, who were called Comitiales in jest. Trin. 3.3. v. 86. Pseud. 3.2. v. 11. Poen. 3.2. v. 7.

units.la: AD tergeminam portam Horatiorum & Curiatiorum, quæ & Ostiensis dicta, egentes stipem rogabant in sacculum. Plin. lib. 35. cap. 5. Capt. 1.1. v. 22.
units.tr: At the triple gate of the Horatii and Curiatii, which was also called the Ostian gate, beggars asked for alms into a little bag. Pliny, book 35, chapter 5. Capt. 1.1. v. 22.
