units.la: ROMÆ in Saburra majore vesperi res furtivæ venundabantur. Mil. 4.2. v. 5. Vide Commentatores ad Horat. lib.1.Sat.1. Fallacem circum vespertinum, pererro Sæpe forum. Vide etiam Durantij Var.lib.1, c.5. & Tit. Furti.
units.tr: At Rome in the Subura, at evening, stolen goods were sold. Mil. 4.2. v. 5. See the commentators on Horace, book 1, Satire 1: Fallacem circum vespertinum, pererro Sæpe forum. See also Durantius, Variae lectiones, book 1, chapter 5, and the title Furti.

units.la: VELABRUM locus Romæ juxta Aventinum montem, ubi tabernæ Oleariorum. Capt. 3.1. v.29.
units.tr: The Velabrum, a place in Rome near the Aventine hill, where the shops of the oil-sellers were. Capt. 3.1. v. 29.

units.la: EXTRA portam Metiam habitabant carnifices. Pseud. 1.3. v.97. Extra portam erant tabernae: in quas fæx populi diverti solebat. Pseud. 2. 2. v. 63. de Caculâ militis servo.
units.tr: Outside the Metian gate lived the executioners. Pseud. 1.3. v. 97. Outside the gate there were taverns, where the dregs of the people used to turn aside. Pseud. 2.2. v. 63, concerning Caculus the soldier's slave.

units.la: S.
units.tr: S.

units.la: Sacerdotum. Vatum. Ariolorum. Haruspicum. Religionis.
units.tr: Priests. Prophets. Soothsayers. Haruspices. Religion.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Deorum.
units.tr: See also the title Gods.

units.la: ARIOLI furiosi se ipsos verberare solent. Trucul. 2. 7. ver. 41. Vide de sacerdotibus Isidis apud Apulejum lib. 8. Metamorph.
units.tr: Frenzied soothsayers are wont to beat themselves. Trucul. 2. 7. ver. 41. See on the priests of Isis in Apuleius, book 8 of the Metamorphoses.

units.la: Bonus vates poteras esse, cùm quæ sunt futura, videas. Mil. 3. 3. v. 37.
units.tr: You could have been a good prophet, since you see what is to come. Mil. 3. 3. v. 37.

units.la: Sacerdotieus genuaampleͤtebantur sacrificaturi. Rud. 1. 5. v. 16,22.
units.tr: Those about to sacrifice used to embrace the knees of the priests. Rud. 1. 5. v. 16, 22.

units.la: Aruspices, similè abominabantur, odio erant, & invisi. Poen. 3. 5. v. 1.
units.tr: Haruspices were likewise held in abhorrence, hated and disliked. Poen. 3. 5. v. 1.

units.la: Pontifices de omnibus causis ad sacra pertinentibus, adeò de ipso perjurio cognoscebant. Rud. 5. 3. v. 21. Vide Tit. Juramenti.
units.tr: The pontiffs took cognizance of all causes pertaining to sacred matters, even of perjury itself. Rud. 5. 3. v. 21. See the title Oath.

units.la: Sacerdos Herculis imperitus & barbarus dicebatur Potitius. Bacch. 1. 2. v. 15. Vide Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: A priest of Hercules was called unskilled and barbarous, Potitius. Bacch. 1. 2. v. 15. See Lex. Plaut.

units.la: Aruspices exta consulebant: & futura inde prædicebant. Amph. 5. 1. v. 76.
units.tr: Haruspices consulted the entrails and from them foretold the future. Amph. 5. 1. v. 76.

units.la: Fanaticorum mos erat, ut capillum funderent, ac promitterent. Rud. 2. 3. v. 46.
units.tr: It was the custom of frenzied worshippers to let their hair fall loose and grow long. Rud. 2. 3. v. 46.

units.la: Vide Turn. lib. 11. c. 10. Tibull. l. 2. Eleg. 5. Fallavit fusa, sed ca- put ante comâ.
units.tr: See Turnebus, book 11, chapter 10. Tibullus, book 2, elegy 5: "She deceived with her hair flowing loose, but her head was in front of her hair."

units.la: In re dubiâ solebant vates, & conjectores arcessere. Amph. 5. 1. v. 76.
units.tr: In doubtful matters, prophets and interpreters were wont to be summoned. Amph. 5. 1. v. 76.

units.la: Aruspices ex inspectione extorum augurabantur bene, male. Poen. 5. 4. v. 34.
units.tr: Haruspices augured from the inspection of the entrails whether omens were good or bad. Poen. 5. 4. v. 34.

units.la: Sacrificiorum. Sacrorum. Lustrationum.
units.tr: Sacrifices. Sacred Rites. Lustrations.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Deorum: Religionis.
units.tr: See also the title Gods: Religion.

units.la: Veteres arbitrabantur in sacrificijs Deos delectari, si sibi res divina multa fieret: & eâ re felicitate eorum augere. Unde natæ formulæ Maclare Deos victimis: Augere Deos extis. Amph. 4. 2. v. 14.
units.tr: The ancients believed that the gods were delighted by sacrifices, and that if a rite was performed for them often, they were increased in their good fortune by it. Hence the formulas to slaughter victims for the gods, to increase the gods by entrails. Amph. 4. 2. v. 14.

units.la: Ante sacrificia, & rem divinam, lavabant aquâ calidâ. Amp h. 5. 1. v. 8. Aul. 3. 6. v. 42. & 4. 2. v. 5. Rud. 1. 2. v. 63. & 23. v. 80.
units.tr: Before sacrifices and sacred rites, they washed with warm water. Amph. 5. 1. v. 8. Aul. 3. 6. v. 42, and 4. 2. v. 5. Rud. 1. 2. v. 63, and 2. 3. v. 80.

units.la: Vide Tit. Balnei: Lotionum. Ubi plura in hanc rem invenies.
units.tr: See the title Baths: Washings. There you will find more on this matter.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Convivij.
units.tr: See also the title Feast.

units.la: Ante sacra lavabantur etiam virgines, & mulieres: quas proinde tangere nefas erat. Poen. 1. 2. v. 137. Sic capiendum illud Papinij lib. 1. v. 678.
units.tr: Before sacred rites, virgins and women were also washed, and it was therefore unlawful to touch them. Poen. 1. 2. v. 137. In this way that line of Papinius, book 1, v. 678, must be understood:

units.la: quis defluat ordo
units.tr: what order flows down

units.la: Sanguinis antiqui, piget inter sacra fateri.
units.tr: Of ancient blood, it is a shame to confess among sacred things.

units.la: Sacrificaturi lavabant manus, & quidem in vivo flumine. Amph. 5. 1. v. 42. Aul. 3. 6. v. 42. & 4. 2. v. 5. Rud. 3. 3. v. 37. Truc. 2. 5. v. 28.
units.tr: Those about to sacrifice washed their hands, and indeed in running water. Amph. 5. 1. v. 42. Aul. 3. 6. v. 42, and 4. 2. v. 5. Rud. 3. 3. v. 37. Truc. 2. 5. v. 28.

units.la: Et memorabile est, quod scribit Servius in III. Æneid. Virg. Apud Veteres neq; uxor duci, neq; ager arari sine sacrificijs perac- ti poterat.
units.tr: And what Servius writes on the third book of Virgil's Aeneid is worth noting: Among the ancients, neither a wife could be led home nor a field ploughed without the performance of sacrifices.

units.la: In sacris oves minæ lectæ numerari solebant. Pseud. 4.7.v.50. ἀλ-ληγοεικῶς.
units.tr: In sacred rites, the sheep and lambs chosen were usually counted. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 50. [allegorically]

units.la: In sacrificijs exta lustralia reservabant, quorum partem Dijs reddebant: partem in epulatione comedebant: ad quam adhibebant charissimos: vel etiam si nollent convivium celebrare, è vi-ctimâ partem ad amicos mittebant. Mil. 3.1.v.116. Vide Turn. l. 7.c.6. & 23. & Casaub. ad Characteres Theophrast.
units.tr: In sacrifices they kept the lustral entrails, part of which they gave back to the gods, and part they ate at a feast, to which they invited their dearest friends; or even, if they did not wish to hold a banquet, they sent a portion of the victim to their friends. Mil. 3. 1. v. 116. See Turnebus, book 7, chapters 6 and 23, and Casaubon on the Characters of Theophrastus.

units.la: Puerperæ Junoni sacra facientes verbenam & thus offerebant. Trin. 2.5.v.27.
units.tr: Women after childbirth, performing sacred rites for Juno, offered verbena and incense. Trin. 2. 5. v. 27.

units.la: Lenones Veneri immolarunt hostiam. Pœn. 2.1.v.2. Et thuris grana sacrificarunt. Ib. v. 3.
units.tr: Pimps sacrificed a victim to Venus. Poen. 2. 1. v. 2. And they offered grains of incense. Ib. v. 3.

units.la: Exta cocta solebant profecare: & aruspici inspicienda offerre. Pœn. 2.1.v.8. Partem autem aliquam eorum adolebant, partem consecrabant, sacerdotibus qui dabant: partem sibi apponebant.
units.tr: They used to cut off the boiled entrails and offer them to the haruspex to be inspected. Poen. 2. 1. v. 8. Some part of them they burned on the altar, some they consecrated and gave to the priests who made the offering, and some they set before themselves.

units.la: In sacrificijs aliæ hostiæ primò cædebantur, quæ Præcidanea dicta: Alij secundò, quæ Succidanea nominata. Alludit noster Asin. 2.4.v.89. Jam nunc mihi secunda facis: quamquam aliquid mimos hoc referant, qui secundas facere dicebantur, quum alterì cederent, & abblandirentur. Et Pœn. 4.2.v.27. Meretrices nostræ Venerem placavère primis hostijs extemplo. Vide Scalig. ad Festum Pompejum, & Taub. ad Asin. ex Palmerio.
units.tr: In sacrifices, some victims were struck first, and these were called Praecidanea; others second, and these were named Succidanea. Our author alludes to this in Asin. 2. 4. v. 89: Now you are making me second, though some think this refers to mimes, who were said to "make second" when they yielded to another and flattered him. And in Poen. 4. 2. v. 27: Our prostitutes have at once appeased Venus with the first victims. See Scaliger on Festus Pompeius, and Taubmann on the Asinaria, drawn from Palmerius.

units.la: Sacrificaturi petebant aquam, ignem, cultrum, veru, olam extarem, aliaque vascula. Rud. 1.2.v.46.
units.tr: Those about to sacrifice asked for water, fire, a knife, a spit, a pot for the entrails, and other small vessels. Rud. 1. 2. v. 46.

units.la: Sacrificia etiam propter viam fiebant, in quibus sc. id quod ex epulis superfuisset, igne consumebatur. Rud 1.2.v.62. Vide Macrob. lib.2.cap.2. Turneb. lib.9.cap.4. Muret. ad Tibull. l.1. Eleg.1.
units.tr: Sacrifices were also made beside the road, in which whatever was left over from the feast was consumed by fire. Rud. 1. 2. v. 62. See Macrobius, book 2, chapter 2; Turnebus, book 9, chapter 4; Muretus on Tibullus, book 1, Elegy 1.

units.la: Et tempestatibus & fluctibus Neptunijs servati, ignem indebant in aram: & odore Arabico fumificabant. Mil. 2.5.v.1. & seqq.
units.tr: And those saved from storms and Neptune's waves put fire on the altar and fumigated it with Arabian perfume. Mil. 2. 5. v. 1 and following.

units.la: Thura aris dabantur primoribus digitis, Bacch. 4.4.v.24.
units.tr: Incense was given to the altars with the tips of the fingers. Bacch. 4. 4. v. 24.

units.la: Lactant. lib. 1. c. 20.
units.tr: Lactantius, book 1, chapter 20.

units.la: Colunt enim thure, ac summis digitis, quae sensibus intimis colere debuerunt.
units.tr: For they worship with incense and with the tips of their fingers what they ought to worship with their innermost senses.

units.la: Idem lib. 5. cap. 19. Hieron. in Epist. ad Heliodorum. Et Prud. Hymno Eulal.
units.tr: The same, book 5, chapter 19. Jerome, in his letter to Heliodorus. And Prudentius, in the hymn to Eulalia.

units.la: Si modicum salis eminulis Thuris & exiguum digitis Tangere velis
units.tr: If you wish to touch a little salt with your small fingers, and a little incense.

units.la: In sacrificijs vasa pura adhibita fuerūt. Aul. 2. 3. v. 3. Capt. 4. 2. v. 81.
units.tr: In sacrifices, pure vessels were used. Aul. 2. 3. v. 3. Capt. 4. 2. v. 81.

units.la: In sacrificijs aliena DIs immolare nefas fuit. Capt. 4. 2. v. 82.
units.tr: In sacrifices it was unlawful to sacrifice what belonged to others to the gods. Capt. 4. 2. v. 82.

units.la: In sacrificijs libis utebantur, quae fratres dicebantur, Mil. 1. 1. v. 8. Macchera miserè gestit fratrem facere ex hostibus, joculariter. Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: In sacrifices they used cakes called brothers. Mil. 1. 1. v. 8: Macchaerus is miserably eager to make a brother out of enemies, said jokingly. See the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: Urbes & agri lustrabantur hostijs in orbem circumlatis, id quod proprie vocabant circumferre. Amph. 2. 2. v. 144. Vide etiam Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: Cities and fields were purified with victims carried round in a circle, which they properly called carrying round. Amph. 2. 2. v. 144. See also the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: In sacrificijs volentes propitios Deos, Deasve invocabant.
units.tr: In sacrifices they invoked the gods or goddesses, wishing them to be propitious.

units.la: Curc. 1. 1. v. 89. Fite mihi volentes propitiæ.
units.tr: Curc. 1. 1. v. 89: Be willing and propitious to me.

units.la: Cato: Mars pater, te precor, quæsoq; uti sies volens propitius mihi, domo, familiæq; nostræ.
units.tr: Cato: Father Mars, I pray you, and beg that you be willing and propitious to me, to my house and to my family.

units.la: Horat. lib. 3. Od. 30. Et mihi Delphicâ Lauro cinge volens Melpomene caput.
units.tr: Horace, book 3, Ode 30: And, willing, Melpomene, bind my head with Delphic laurel.

units.la: Livius: Pacem precibus exposcunt, uti volens propitius suam semper sospitet progeniem.
units.tr: Livy: They ask for peace with prayers, that the Father, willing and propitious, may always keep his offspring safe.

units.la: Quintil. lib. 4. c. 1. Dexterq; ac volens adsit.
units.tr: Quintilian, book 4, chapter 1: And let him be present, right-handed and willing.

units.la: Sallustius: Munificas nemo putabatur, nisi pariter volens.
units.tr: Sallust: No one was thought generous unless he was equally willing.

units.la: In sacrificijs vasa erant litterata: & utplurimùm effigie Dei vel Deæ inscripta, cui fiebat res divina. Rud. 2. 5. v. 21. Vide Tit. Vasorum.
units.tr: In sacrifices the vessels were inscribed with letters, and most often with the image of the god or goddess to whom the sacred rite was being performed. Rud. 2. 5. v. 21. See the title Vessels.

units.la: Genio suo sacrificare solebant: & peracto sacrificio epulum ad-ornare. Capt. 2. 2. v. 40. Et plærumque Samijs: h. e. fictilibus vasis utebantur tenaciores: alij vero opulentiores aureis. Ib. v. 41.
units.tr: They used to sacrifice to their own Genius, and when the sacrifice was done they prepared a feast. Capt. 2. 2. v. 40. And for the most part, those of Samos, that is, the more frugal used earthenware vessels, while others, the wealthier, used gold ones. Ib. v. 41.

units.la: Victimæ piaculares aliena mala excipiebant, & in poenam fuc-cede. cedebant, Epid. 1. 2. v. 36. Plin. lib. 3. Epist. 9.
units.tr: Expiatory victims took on the evils of others and went in as substitutes for punishment. Epid. 1. 2. v. 36. Pliny, book 3, letter 9.

units.la: Ne potentissimi, vilissimo quoque quasi piaculari dato, elabe-rentur.
units.tr: Lest the most powerful escape, when the most worthless of men is given as a sacrificial victim.

units.la: Vide Lipsi Com. in Plin. Paneg. Si hostia, seu jumentum ipsum, quod immolari debuit, fugisset, vel non volens ad peregendum sacrificium accessisset, ista reprobata alia insuper adducebatur, eamque succedaneam victimam appellabant: quod quasi secundo loco caederetur. Epid. 1. 2. v. 37. ἀλλητοεικῶς: Ut meum tergum flultitia tua subdas succedaneum.
units.tr: See Lipsius's commentary on Pliny's Panegyric. If the victim, or the animal itself that ought to have been sacrificed, had fled, or had not come willingly to the completion of the sacrifice, that one was rejected and another was brought in besides, and they called it the substitute victim, because it was struck second, as it were. Epid. 1. 2. v. 37. [allegorically]: That you may put your back under my folly as a substitute.

units.la: Vide Agellium lib. 4. c. 6.
units.tr: See Aulus Gellius, book 4, chapter 6.

units.la: E sacrificijs pingues fiebant tibicinæ: scil. è convivijs, Aul. 2. 5. v. 6.
units.tr: From the sacrifices, fat flute-girls were made; that is, from the feasts. Aul. 2. 5. v. 6.

units.la: Re divinâ factâ convivium de reliquijs extorum & libationum instituebant. Curc. 4. 2. v. 46. Amph. 3. 3. v. 20. Mil. 3. 1. v. 4. Poen. 2, 1. v. 44. & 3. 3. v. 4. & 3. 6. v. 9. Stich. 2. 1. v. 96.
units.tr: When the sacred rite was done, they set up a banquet from the leftovers of the entrails and libations. Curc. 4. 2. v. 46. Amph. 3. 3. v. 20. Mil. 3. 1. v. 4. Poen. 2. 1. v. 44, and 3. 3. v. 4, and 3. 6. v. 9. Stich. 2. 1. v. 96.

units.la: Summo Jovi sacrificantes & extra in manibus tenentes, diceban-turilli porricere, & Dis offerre. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 31. Vide Lex. Plaut. Porricere.
units.tr: Those sacrificing to supreme Jupiter, and holding the outer parts in their hands, were said to porrigere them and offer them to the gods. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 31. See the Plautine lexicon, under porricere.

units.la: Hostia ante sacrificia solebat conspergi molâ salsâ, hoc est, frugibus molitis: seu moliturâ salsâ: per metonymiam. Amph. 2. 2. v. 108. Horat. lib. 3. Od. 23. Farre pio & saliente mica. Ubi vide interpretes Vide etiam Tit. Somniorum.
units.tr: Before sacrifices, the victim was usually sprinkled with salt meal, that is, with ground grain, or with salted flour, by metonymy. Amph. 2. 2. v. 108. Horace, book 3, Ode 23: With holy spelt and crackling salt. On this see the commentators. See also the title Dreams.

units.la: Quoties serio in rem aliquam serio, ac non perfunctorie, aut oscitanter incumbebant, inclamabant Hoc age. Quâ formulâ attentionem imperabant, & silentium in sacrificijs. Asin. Prol. v. 1. De quâ consuetudine inprimis legendi Brisson. Form. lib. 1. pag. 11. & Jani Gruteri Animadv. in Senecam lib. 1. de clementia. c. 12. Alia Plauti loca (cui soli Authori nunc operam damus) Vide in Lex. Plaut.
units.tr: Whenever they set seriously to some matter, and not carelessly or half-heartedly, they called out Hoc age ("Do this"). By this formula they commanded attention and silence in sacrifices. Asin. Prol. v. 1. On this custom, see especially Brisson, Formulae, book 1, p. 11, and Janus Gruterus's Animadversions on Seneca, book 1, On Clemency, chapter 12. Other passages of Plautus (to whom alone we are now devoting our effort) see in the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: VICTIMÆ in fœderibus sanciendis saxo feriebantur: quorsum allusit proverbialis illa dictio: Intra sacrum, saxumq; sto. Capt. 3.4.v.84.
units.tr: In making covenants, victims were struck with a stone, to which that proverbial expression alludes: I stand between the sacred thing and the stone. Capt. 3. 4. v. 84.

units.la: VESTÆ sacrificabant mulieres. Stich. 2.3. v.72.
units.tr: Women sacrificed to Vesta. Stich. 2. 3. v. 72.

units.la: IN sacrificijs Herculis omnia exponebantur obvijs. Alludit noster Rud. 2.4.v.11. Non ego sum pollucta pago: h. e. non omnibus me prostituo. Hanc enim lectionem defendo cum Turnebo. Vide etiam Doufæ Centurionatum lib.4.c.13.
units.tr: In the sacrifices of Hercules, everything was exposed to whoever came by. Our author alludes to Rud. 2. 4. v. 11: I am not a polluted girl for the village, that is, I do not prostitute myself to everyone. For I defend this reading with Turnebus. See also Doujat's Centuriae, book 4, chapter 13.

units.la: IN ijsdem sacris pollucibiliter vivebant. Stich. 5.2.v.6. Vide Lex. Pollucere.
units.tr: In the same rites they lived in a lavish, feasting way. Stich. 5. 2. v. 6. See the lexicon under pollucere.

units.la: POST rem divinam prandium apparabant. Rud. 2.3. v.13.
units.tr: After the sacred rite they prepared a dinner. Rud. 2. 3. v. 13.

units.la: MULSUM sacrificabant DIs, Deabusve. Aul. 4.2.v.15. Mulsi congialem plenam faciam tibi fideliam.
units.tr: They sacrificed mead to the gods and goddesses. Aul. 4. 2. v. 15: I will make you a full gallon of mead, faithful one.

units.la: CERERI Ambarvaliorum annuo festo sacrificabant vino, nonitem in nuptijs. Aul. 2. 6. v.5.
units.tr: To Ceres, at the annual festival of the Ambarvalia, they sacrificed with wine, and sometimes at weddings. Aul. 2. 6. v.5.

units.la: DIs boves immolati. Asin. 3.3.v.124.
units.tr: Oxen were sacrificed to the gods. Asin. 3.3.v.124.

units.la: DIs etiam argento sacrificabant. Most. 1.3. v.84.
units.tr: They even sacrificed silver to the gods. Most. 1.3. v.84.

units.la: DIIS minoribus, & heroibus ture, & vino supplicabant. Aul. Prol. v.24. Sallust. Tum venienti (Metello) ture, quasi Deo, supplicant. Sen. lib.3. de Ira c.18. Mario thure & vino supplicabant. Vide ibi Lipsi.
units.tr: To the lesser gods and the heroes they offered supplication with incense and wine. Aul. Prol. v.24. Sallust: When Metellus was approaching, they supplicated him with incense, as though he were a god. Seneca, book 3 of De Ira, c.18: They supplicated Marius with incense and wine. See Lipsius there.

units.la: CERERIS sacra στομοφέια celebrabantur à mulieribus jejunantibus noctu: ad quæ scilicet multa scelera admissa. Aul. Prol. v.36.
units.tr: The rites of Ceres, called stomophegia [στομοφέια], were celebrated at night by women who fasted; at these, of course, many crimes were committed. Aul. Prol. v.36.

units.la: SACRA familiaria, quæ pecuniam, h. e. hæredem sequebantur, aliquo cum sumtu fieri necesse erat. Capt. 4.1. v.8. Trin. 2.4. v.83.
units.tr: The household rites, which followed the money, that is, the heir, had to be performed at some expense. Capt. 4.1. v.8. Trin. 2.4. v.83.

units.la: De his sic loquitur Cicero lib. 2. de Legg. De sacris autem, qui locus patet latius, hæc sit una sententia: ut conserventur semper, & deinceps familiis prodantur, & ut in leg posita, perpetua sint sacra.
units.tr: Cicero speaks on this in book 2 of De Legibus: As for sacred rites, which field extends more widely, this is the one principle: that they are always to be preserved and handed down to families in succession, and that, as laid down in the law, the sacred rites be perpetual.

units.la: Et quæ in hanc sententiam plura ibi egregiè habet Cicero. Erant autem familijs sacra sua privata: atque ea quidem, quasi pro notâ erant, & vinculo. Inde formulæ illæ: Transfire in gentem & sacra. Hæreditas cum sacris, sine sacris.
units.tr: Cicero there has many excellent points to this effect. Families had their own private sacred rites, and these served as it were as a mark and a bond. Hence those formulae: to pass into the clan and its sacred rites; inheritance with the sacred rites, without the sacred rites.

units.la: In sacris Bacchi omnia reconditissima erant. Mil. 4. 2. v. 25.
units.tr: All things in the rites of Bacchus were most secret. Mil. 4.2. v.25.

units.la: Cedo mihi signum, si harum Baccharum es. Sic ibi ex Mss. legendum. Apul. Apol. Si quis forte adesse eorundem solemnium mihi particeps, signum dato. Arnob. vocat symbolam. Clemens Alex. συνθήματα. Apul. Memoracula. Nulli autem nisi ijsdem sacris initiato cognita erant illa sacra.
units.tr: Give me the sign, if you are one of these Bacchae. So it is to be read there from the manuscripts. Apuleius, Apology: If by chance anyone is a sharer with me in these same solemnities, give the sign. Arnobius calls it symbola; Clement of Alexandria calls it synthemata [συνθήματα]; Apuleius calls them memoracula. But those rites were known only to those initiated into these same sacred rites.

units.la: In sacrorum renovatione commovebantur simulacra. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 107. Scis tu quidem hercle, mea si commovi sacra, quo pacto quantas soleam turbelas dare. ἀλληγορικῶς.
units.tr: In the renewal of the sacred rites the images were moved. Pseud. 1.1. v.107: You certainly know, by Hercules, how great and what sort of disturbances I am accustomed to cause, if I have stirred up the sacred rites. Allegorically [ἀλληγορικῶς].

units.la: Virgil. Æn. 4.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid 4.

units.la: qualis commotis excita sacris
units.tr: Such as a Thyas roused by the stirred rites

units.la: Thyas, ubi audito. Ibi vide Servium.
units.tr: Thyas, when she heard. See Servius there.

units.la: Horat. l. 1. Od. 18.
units.tr: Horace, book 1, Ode 18.

units.la: non ego te candide Bassareu
units.tr: I, bright Bassareus,

units.la: Invitum quatiam. Intelligendum hoc de triennalibus Bacchi: quæ sacra tertio quoque anno renovabantur. Dicebantur etiam struem in sacris commovere, piaculo aliquo commisso: quò aliqui viri docti referunt dictum Plaut. ex Pseud. verbi causâ: Priusquam porcum feminam immolabis. JANO struem commoveto, sic: JANE PATER TE HAC STRUE COMMOVENDA BONAS PRECES PRECOR. Et mox: Fertum Jovi moveto, & mactato sic: JUPPITER, TE HOC FERCTO OBMOVENDO, &c.
units.tr: would not shake you against your will. This is to be understood of the triennial rites of Bacchus, which were renewed every third year. It was also said that the struem was stirred in sacred rites when some expiatory offence had been committed. To this some learned men refer the saying of Plautus from the Pseudolus, for example: Before you sacrifice a female pig. Janus, stir the struem, thus: Father Janus, by stirring this struem I pray for good prayers. And soon after: Move the fertum to Jupiter and slaughter it, thus: Jupiter, by moving this fertum to ward off evil, and so on.

units.la: Vide Tur. L. 21. c. 21. & Scaligeri Notas ad Festum in Struferta-rios. pag. 145. ubi omnia ea ad hunc locum de sacris gentilium referenda erunt.
units.tr: See Turnebus, book 21, chapter 21, and Scaliger's notes to Festus under Struferta-rios, p.145, where all of these are to be referred to this passage on the sacred rites of the Gentiles.

units.la: GENUS quoddam Venerationis erat, & ceremoniæ superstitiosque Terram tangere: sed non nisi in his rebus, quæ ad Deos inferos ac mortuos pertinent usurpari consuetum.
units.tr: Touching the earth was a certain kind of veneration and superstitious ceremony, but it was customarily used only in those matters which pertain to the gods below and to the dead.

units.la: Macrob. lib. 3.
units.tr: Macrobius, book 3.

units.la: Cum tellurem dicit, manibus terram tangit.
units.tr: When he names the earth, he touches the earth with his hands.

units.la: Cic. de Aruspicum responsis:
units.tr: Cicero, On the Responses of the Haruspices:

units.la: Aut puer ille patrimus aut matrimus, si terram non tenuit.
units.tr: Either that boy is a patrimus or a matrimus, if he did not hold the earth.

units.la: Turneb. lib. 16. cap. 10.
units.tr: Turnebus, book 16, chapter 10.

units.la: OFFICIA religiosa antelucana erant. Pœn. I. 2. v. 105.
units.tr: Religious duties before dawn were customary. Poen. 1.2. v.105.

units.la: Iam nondum ante lucem ad ædem Veneris venimus.
units.tr: Now, not yet before dawn, we have come to the temple of Venus.

units.la: Vide Casaub. ad lib. 2. Sueton. in Augusto pag. 134.
units.tr: See Casaubon on book 2 of Suetonius, Augustus, p.134.

units.la: QUIS homo est tantâ injuriâ, qui sacerdotem audeat violare?
units.tr: What man is there who would dare to violate a priest with such an injury?

units.la: QUOD in rebus divinis sumas, sapienti lucro est.
units.tr: What you take in divine matters is a profit to the wise.

units.la: SALIS.
units.tr: SALT.

units.la: SAL modijs vendebatur vili pretio. Ejus igitur annonæ ratio quoque habita. Caf. 3. 2. v. 8.
units.tr: Salt was sold by the peck at a cheap price. Therefore the price of this commodity was also taken into account. Cas. 3. 2. v. 8.

units.la: SAL ab aquâ consumi solet. Merc. 1. 2. v. 93.
units.tr: Salt is usually dissolved by water. Merc. 1. 2. v. 93.

units.la: SALTATIONIS.
units.tr: DANCING.

units.la: IONICA saltatione usi cinædi: & amatores. Pseu. 5. 1. v. 29. Stich. 5. 7. v. 6. Eâque sludebant placere amicæ.
units.tr: Catamites and lovers used the Ionian dance, and Pseu. 5. 1. v. 29. Stich. 5. 7. v. 6. they strove to please their mistresses by it.

units.la: AMANTES saltabant in convivijs, ut libidinem accenderent. Stich. 5. 5. v. 15.
units.tr: Lovers danced at banquets to kindle desire. Stich. 5. 5. v. 15.

units.la: SALTUS Jonici & Cynædici à meretricibus saltati. Stich. 4. 4. v. 28.
units.tr: Ionian and Cinaedic dances were danced by prostitutes. Stich. 4. 4. v. 28.

units.la: Horat. 1. 3. Od. 6. Motus doceri gaudet Ionicos.
units.tr: Horace, Odes 1.3.6: He delights to be taught Ionian movements.

units.la: Vide Turn. l. 4. c. 21. & Bulenq. de Theatro lib. 43. & Taubm. ad Perf. 5. 2. v. 43. p. 975.
units.tr: See Turnebus, bk. 4, ch. 21, and Bulenger, On the Theatre, bk. 43, and Taubmann on Persius 5.2.43, p. 975.

units.la: Cum
units.tr: With

units.la: Cùm pallâ saltabant. Men. 1. 3. v. 14.
units.tr: They danced with a cloak. Men. 1. 3. v. 14.

units.la: SALTARE cinædorum malacorum est. Mil. 3. 1. v. 73.
units.tr: To dance is the mark of effeminate, debauched men. Mil. 3. 1. v. 73.

units.la: SALUTIS.
units.tr: SALUTIS.

units.la: NIHIL homini melius salute. Asin. 3. 3. v. 128.
units.tr: NOTHING is better for a man than health. Asin. 3. 3. v. 128.

units.la: SALUS Dea fingitur. Capt. 3. 3. v. 14. Vide Tit. Deorum.
units.tr: Health (Salus) is imagined as a goddess. Capt. 3. 3. v. 14. See the title Gods (Deorum).

units.la: SALUTATIONUM. COMITATIS. VALEDICTIONIS. Vide etiam Peregrinat. Patronorum: Clientum. SALUTANTES addebant jusjurandum, ut serió hoc fecisse putarentur. Trin. 1. 2. v. 11. Tu ædepol salve. Donatus ad illud Hecyr. 1. 2. Salve mecastor. Vide Brissonum in Formulis. NON temerarium est, si divites salutent pauperes. Faciunt enim id ob spem prædæ alicujus. Aul. 2. 2. v. 7, 69. DISCEDENTES ab ijs, quos numquam visuri essent, sic salutabant: VALE atque SALVE. Capt. 3. 5. v. 86. COMITATIS & benevolentiæ signum maximè apud Græcos fuit, salutare peregrinos prehensâ dextrâ. Curc. 2. 3. v. 60. CLIENTES Romæ patronos suos observabant: ad ædes frequenteraderant, salutabant. Amph 4. 3. v. 22. Vide sis herus salutator oppessulatas ante foras graditur. Quo de more plusicula Doufa Pater in Centurionatu Plautino lib. 1. c. 3. p. 27. nec non Gasper Scioppius Verisimil. lib. 1. c. 8. alijque. Est enim res obvia in omnibus Authoribus Romanis. Exempla huc colligantur à studiosis humanitatis.
units.tr: OF GREETINGS (SALUTATIONUM), OF COURTESY, OF FAREWELL. See also Peregrinat., Patrons: Clients. Those greeting others added an oath, so that they might be thought to have done so in earnest. Trin. 1. 2. v. 11: "Indeed, by Pollux, greetings to you." Donatus on that line of the Hecyra, 1. 2: "Greetings, by Castor." See Brisson on Formulas. It is not rash for the rich to greet the poor, for they do it in hope of some reward. Aul. 2. 2. v. 7, 69. Those departing from people whom they would never see again used to take leave of them in this way: "Farewell and hail." Capt. 3. 5. v. 86. Among the Greeks, a sign of courtesy and goodwill was especially to greet strangers by taking their right hand. Curc. 2. 3. v. 60. At Rome clients honoured their patrons: they crowded to their house and greeted them. Amph. 4. 3. v. 22: "See, the master's greeter goes out before the locked doors." On this custom see several things in Doufa Pater, Centurionatus Plautinus, lib. 1, c. 3, p. 27, and also Gaspar Scioppius, Verisimilia, lib. 1, c. 8, and others. For it is a matter found in all Roman authors. Examples for this are gathered by students of humanity.

units.la: Qui aliorum patrocinio uterentur, salutabant suos patronos: Patrone salve. Most. 3. 2. v. 59.
units.tr: Those who enjoyed the patronage of others greeted their patrons: "Hail, patron." Most. 3. 2. v. 59.

units.la: CONSALUTANTES dexteram tenebant. Men. 1. 2. v. 29.
units.tr: Those greeting one another held out their right hands. Men. 1. 2. v. 29.

units.la: SALUTANTIBUS manuum porrigebant. Truc. 1. 2. v. 23.
units.tr: To those greeting them they gave their hands. Truc. 1. 2. v. 23.

units.la: PEREGRE advenientes salutabant osculo. Epid. 4. 2. v. 2.
units.tr: Those arriving from abroad they greeted with a kiss. Epid. 4. 2. v. 2.

units.la: ETIAM inimici sunt salutandi: ejusque dicendum Vale, atque Salve. Capt. 3. 5. v. 86.
units.tr: Even enemies are to be greeted, and to them one must say "Farewell" and "Hail." Capt. 3. 5. v. 86.

units.la: SANGUINIS.
units.tr: OF BLOOD (SANGUINIS).

units.la: Vide Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See the title Of Man (Hominis).

units.la: PRÆ METU sanguis dicitur emigrare e corpore. Most. 2. 2. v. 75. Guttam haud habeo sanguinis.
units.tr: From fear, the blood is said to flee out of the body. Most. 2. 2. v. 75: "I have not a drop of blood."

units.la: SAPIENTIÆ. PRUDENTIÆ. PHILOSOPHIÆ.
units.tr: OF WISDOM. OF PRUDENCE. OF PHILOSOPHY.

units.la: DICTUM Sapienti sat est. Persa 4. 7. v. 19.
units.tr: A saying: "For a wise man, enough is said." Persa 4. 7. v. 19.

units.la: SOCRATES Sapientiæ nomine clarus. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 50.
units.tr: Socrates, famous for the name of wisdom. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 50.

units.la: SAPIENTIS officium suum æquum est colere, & facere. Stich. 1. 1. v. 33.
units.tr: It is right for a wise man's duty to be to cultivate fairness and to act accordingly. Stich. 1. 1. v. 33.

units.la: NEMO solus satis sapit. Mil. 3. 3. v. 12.
units.tr: No one is wise enough alone. Mil. 3. 3. v. 12.

units.la: SAPIENTIÆ sedes pectus est. Trin. 1. 2. v. 53.
units.tr: The seat of wisdom is the breast. Trin. 1. 2. v. 53.

units.la: OMNES sapientes decet conferre, & fabulari. Rud. 2. 3. v. 8.
units.tr: It befits all wise men to confer and to talk together. Rud. 2. 3. v. 8.

units.la: Prudentia est formatrix vitæ nostræ: cui & ipsa Fortuna subjacet. Trin. 2. 2. v. 80. Vide plura Tit. Fortunæ.
units.tr: Prudence is the shaper of our life, and Fortune herself is subject to it. Trin. 2. 2. v. 80. See more under the title Fortune (Fortunæ).

units.la: Sapientia non semper annis acquiritur: sed ætate. Trin. 2. 2. v. 86. Vide plura Tit. Ætatis.
units.tr: Wisdom is not always acquired with years, but with age. Trin. 2. 2. v. 86. See more under the title Age (Ætatis).

units.la: Satietatis.
units.tr: Of Satiety.

units.la: Eò illud satius est, satiū, quod satis est, habitu, quàm quod plus sat est: h. e. Quam ob causam habitu satius est, sive melius habetur haberive potest illud satis, quod est satis, quàm illud, quod plus sat est. Pæn. 1. 2. v. 75.
units.tr: Hence the saying "that is more agreeable (satius), which is enough, to have than what is more than enough": that is, for this reason it is better, or it is more fittingly held or can be held, to have that which is enough, which is sufficient, than that which is more than enough. Pæn. 1. 2. v. 75.

units.la: Sceleris. Criminis. Facinoris. Improbitatis.
units.tr: Of Wickedness. Of Crime. Of Villainy. Of Wrongdoing.

units.la: Facinorosorum prosapia ferè ijsdem fatis duc solet. Inde Servus ille Mil. 2. 4. v. 19. Noli minitari, scio crucem futuram mihi sepulchrum. Ibi mei majores sunt siti, pater, avus, proavus, abavus.
units.tr: The lineage of criminals is generally led by the same fates. Hence that slave in Mil. 2. 4. v. 19: "Do not threaten me; I know the cross will be my tomb. There my forefathers are laid: father, grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather."

units.la: Improbi scelerati convitia laudes suas ducunt. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 125. Vide Tit. Convitiorum.
units.tr: The wicked and criminal count abuse as their praises. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 125. See the title Of Abuse (Convitiorum).

units.la: Ubi crimen admisissent, de expiatione soliciti erant. Most. 2. 2. v. 34.
units.tr: Once they had committed a crime, they were anxious about atonement. Most. 2. 2. v. 34.

units.la: In scelere manifesto mendacijs amplius tegere scelera non possunt. Cas. 5. 4. v. 13.
units.tr: In a manifest crime they cannot conceal their wrongdoings any further by lies. Cas. 5. 4. v. 13.

units.la: SCHOLARUM. GYMNASIORUM.
units.tr: Schools. Gymnasia.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Artium.
units.tr: See also the title Artium.

units.la: GYMNASIA loca erant variis exercitiis destinata. Aul. 3. 1. v. 5. ἀλληγορικῶς.
units.tr: The gymnasia were places set aside for various exercises. Aul. 3. 1. v. 5. allegorically [ἀλληγορικῶς].

units.la: LUDOS habebant litterarios, in quibus litteras discebant. Quorsum alludit senex amator. Merc. 2. 2. v. 32.
units.tr: They had schools for letters, where they learned their letters. The old man in love alludes to this. Merc. 2. 2. v. 32.

units.la: PUERIS in ludum itantibus paedagogi addebantur custodes. Merc. Prol. v. 90.
units.tr: When boys went to school, attendants called paedagogi were assigned to them. Merc. Prol. v. 90.

units.la: Vide Tit. Educationis.
units.tr: See the title Educationis.

units.la: Sic Appollonius: εἰς διδάσκειν ἐξηγήσει. Γεγονέναι δὲ τὸ καταρχὰς δῆλον, ᾧ παῖδας ἔχοντα διδάσκειν γράμματα ὡς τὴν θησεῖφ.
units.tr: Thus Apollonius: "for teaching, in explanation. That it arose at the beginning is clear, when a man having children taught them letters, as in the case of Theseus" [εἰς διδάσκειν ἐξηγήσει. Γεγονέναι δὲ τὸ καταρχὰς δῆλον, ᾧ παῖδας ἔχοντα διδάσκειν γράμματα ὡς τὴν θησεῖφ.]

units.la: Unde & hoc apparet, publicas fuisse Scholas.
units.tr: From this it also appears that the schools were public.

units.la: SENATUS.
units.tr: Senate.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Comitiorum: & Magistratus.
units.tr: See also the title Comitia and Magistrates.

units.la: QUI aberat à Senatu pignoribus captis multabatur. Ibidem sortiebantur provincias. Mil. 2. 6. ver. 112. Men. 3. 1. v. 9. ubi pignoribus captis parasitus coërceri vult eam, qui non venerit in concionem.
units.tr: Whoever was absent from the Senate was fined by seizing his pledges. Provinces were also allotted there. Mil. 2. 6. v. 112. Men. 3. 1. v. 9. where the parasite wants the one who has not come to the assembly coerced by seizing his pledges.

units.la: Vide Cicer. de Oratore lib. 3. & lib. 2. de leg. Itemque Philipp. 1.
units.tr: See Cicero, On the Orator, book 3, and On the Laws, book 2. Likewise Philippics 1.

units.la: AD Senatum non venientes citabantur. Men. 3. 1. v. 9.
units.tr: Those who did not come to the Senate were summoned. Men. 3. 1. v. 9.

units.la: Senectutis.
units.tr: Old Age.

units.la: SEnectus onus Ætnâ gravius. Men. 5. 2. v. 5. Consitus sum senectute: onustum gero corpus, virus reliquêre. Ut atas mala, mala merx est ergò?
units.tr: SOld age is a burden heavier than Mount Etna. Men. 5. 2. v. 5. I have been sown with old age; I carry a loaded body; they have left behind the poison. Since age is an evil, is it therefore an evil merchandise?

units.la: Merc. 4. 1. v. 6. ——— quin is ocyus?
units.tr: Merc. 4. 1. v. 6. ——— Why not go more quickly?

units.la: SY. Neque mecastor: tantum hoc oneris est, qui fero.
units.tr: SY. Indeed, by Castor, no; this is burden enough, the load I bear.

units.la: DOR. Quid oneris? SY. annos octoginta & quatuor.
units.tr: DOR. What burden? SY. Eighty-four years.

units.la: Senes plærumque sunt molles: eóque vitio vertitur senì Stalino-ni, quod unguentatus per vias incesserit. Caf. 2. 3. v. 23. Eoque comparantur canalicolis, hominibus nihili & nauci. Ibid. v. 22.
units.tr: Old men are generally soft, and so the old Stalino is reproached for walking through the streets perfumed. Cas. 2. 3. v. 23. For this reason they are compared to canal-dwellers, men of no worth and no value. Ibid. v. 22.

units.la: Senes salaces, ebrios, vomiturientes fastidire solebant. Caf. 3. 6. v. 7, 10.
units.tr: Old men, lecherous, drunken and vomiting, used to be looked down upon. Cas. 3. 6. v. 7, 10.

units.la: Sic Cæcilius in Plotio apud Agell. lib. 2. c. 23.
units.tr: So Caecilius in Plocium, in Gellius, book 2, ch. 23.

units.la: S. Sed tua morosane uxor quaso est? M. Vah, rogas? S. Qui tandem? M. tadet mentionis: quæ mihi, Ubi domum adveni, ac sedi, extemplo savium Dat jejunâ animâ. S. nil peccat de savio, Ut devomas vult, quod forte potaverit.
units.tr: S. But is your wife morose, I ask? M. Vah, do you ask? S. Why, pray? M. I am sick of mentioning it: she, when I come home and sit down, at once gives me a kiss on an empty stomach. S. She does no wrong with the kiss; she wants you to vomit up whatever you may have drunk.

units.la: Senectutis summa authoritas in omnibus negotijs.
units.tr: The highest authority of the old lies in all affairs.

units.la: Sic Trin. 2. 2. v. 106. in causâ matrimonij inquit filius adolescens, patri seni:
units.tr: So in Trin. 2. 2. v. 106. in a matter of marriage a young son says to his old father:

units.la: Gravius erit tuum unum verbum ad eam rem, quàm centum mea.
units.tr: One word of yours on that matter will weigh more than a hundred of mine.

units.la: Senes etiam historiarum veterum periti. Trin. 2. 2. v. 101.
units.tr: Old men are also skilled in ancient histories. Trin. 2. 2. v. 101.

units.la: Turpe est senes amare, osculari. Merc. 3. 3. v. 12. & 5. 4. v. 23, 25. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 44. Caf. 3. 2. ver. 5, 8, 20. Ubi etiam salacibus hircis comparantur edentuli & salaces senes. Et Hircis salvis, fœtidis. Men. 5. 2. v. 86. Nec non Leoni Getulo. Ibid. & Asin. 5. 2. v. 43. Ideoque lascivi senes sic à populo traducebantur: Cano capite! ætate alienâ! Ey deß alten Gecken! Caf. 3. 1. v. 4, 5.
units.tr: It is disgraceful for old men to love and to kiss. Merc. 3. 3. v. 12, and 5. 4. v. 23, 25. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 44. Cas. 3. 2. v. 5, 8, 20. Here toothless and lustful old men are also compared to lustful he-goats. And with the goats safe, foul-smelling. Men. 5. 2. v. 86. Nor the Getulian lion. Ibid. and Asin. 5. 2. v. 43. Therefore lascivious old men were thus mocked by the people: "Grey head! Age not your own! Ah, the old fop!" Cas. 3. 1. v. 4, 5.

units.la: Vide Tit. Amoris. Sunt enim ad Venerem inepti: eoque Verve-ces dicti. Ibid.
units.tr: See the title Love. For they are unfit for Venus, and so they were called Vervices (rams). Ibid.

units.la: SENES æquum est se molliter curare. Merc. 3. 2. v. 6.
units.tr: OLD MEN it is right that they take care of themselves gently. Merc. 3. 2. v. 6.

units.la: SENES petulci insano pruritu indomabiles prorsus sunt. Cas. 4. 3. v. 12. Ne ædepol, tu si sis equus, esses indomabilis. Nimis enim tenax est: h. e. laboras tentiginoso ψιλαπισμῷ. Ibid. v. 13. Vide Horat. lib. 1. Od. 25.
units.tr: OLD MEN, wanton with mad itching, are altogether unmanageable. Cas. 4. 3. v. 12. Indeed, by Pollux, if you were a horse you would be unmanageable. For he is too tenacious: that is, you suffer from a lustful [ψιλαπισμῷ] tickling. Ibid. v. 13. See Horace, book 1, Ode 25.

units.la: SAPERE iflac ætate oportet, qui sunt capite candido. Most. 5. 2. v. 27.
units.tr: WISDOM ought to belong to that age, to those whose heads are white. Most. 5. 2. v. 27.

units.la: SENES ob ætatem imbecilliori visu. Most. 3. 2. v. 157. Epid. 5. 1. v. 28. Mala ætatis vitio senes minus sincere utilitatem oculis obtinent.
units.tr: OLD MEN, because of their age, have weaker sight. Most. 3. 2. v. 157. Epid. 5. 1. v. 28. By the fault of age, old men less sincerely obtain benefit for their eyes.

units.la: Poen. Senes ætate tardiores.
units.tr: Poen. Old men are slower because of their age.

units.la: SENES parentes non semper resistere debent consilijs filiorum. Trin. 2. 3. v. 4.
units.tr: OLD MEN, as parents, ought not always to resist the counsels of their sons. Trin. 2. 3. v. 4.

units.la: SENECTUS hyemis vitæ. Trin. 2. 3. v. 4. ex sententiâ Eratosthenis.
units.tr: OLD AGE is the winter of life. Trin. 2. 3. v. 4. according to the opinion of Eratosthenes.

units.la: SENUM vitium est plærumque male olere sub axillis: fœtidamque habere animam. Unde Hircosi senes dicti. Merc. 3. 3. v. 14. Vide Cujac. Observ. lib. 11. c. 10. & Laur. Ramirez in Mart. E-pig. lib. 3. & Joh. Savaro in Sidonium Apollinar. l. 9. Ep. 13.
units.tr: It is a fault of old men generally to smell bad under the armpits and to have a foul breath. Hence they were called goat-smelling old men. Merc. 3. 3. v. 14. See Cujacius, Observations, book 11, ch. 10, and Laurentius Ramirez on Martial, Epigrams, book 3, and Joannes Savaro on Sidonius Apollinaris, book 9, letter 13.

units.la: PUERILIA facinora, ut amores aliaque id genus, turpe est seni-bus posse obijci. Mil. 3. 1. v. 23. 27.
units.tr: It is shameful for old men to be charged with childish misdeeds, such as love affairs and others of that kind. Mil. 3. 1. v. 23, 27.

units.la: SENES scipione innituntur. Asin. 1. 1. v. 111. Caf. 5. 4. v. 6. Men. 5. 2. v. 103. Tremuli sunt. Et Men. 5. 2. v. 101. Barbatum, tremulum, Titanum.
units.tr: OLD MEN lean on a staff. Asin. 1. 1. v. 111. Cas. 5. 4. v. 6. Men. 5. 2. v. 103. They are trembling. And Men. 5. 2. v. 101. bearded, trembling, a Titan.

units.la: SENES avari servis edacitatem tectè, aperte objiciunt. Trin. 4. 3. v. 9. Curculio est exercitor: is hunc hominem curDuram docet.
units.tr: OLD MEN, being greedy, openly and covertly reproach their slaves for gluttony. Trin. 4. 3. v. 9. Curculio is the overseer; he teaches this man to be a hard master.

units.la: SENES cùm satis partum habent, debent se otio dare. Trin. 4. 1. v. 19.
units.tr: OLD MEN, when they have enough property, ought to give themselves to leisure. Trin. 4. 1. v. 19.

units.la: SENES exangues & Acheruntici, mortuis quàm vivis sunt similiores. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 33. Odiosum est mortem amplexari.
units.tr: OLD MEN, bloodless and like Acheron, are more like the dead than the living. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 33. It is hateful to embrace death.

units.la: SENES uxores suas perire volunt. Trin. 1. 2. v. 13. Quid agit tua uxor? ut valet? C A. plusquam ego volo.
units.tr: OLD MEN want their wives to die. Trin. 1. 2. v. 13. "What is your wife doing? Is she well?" "More than I would like."

units.la: SENES interdum repuerascunt, acutum cernunt, amant. Merc. 2. 2. v.25,28,35.
units.tr: OLD MEN sometimes become boys again, see sharply, and fall in love. Merc. 2. 2. v. 25, 28, 35.

units.la: SENES ægrè ferunt se eâ ætate ludificari, cùm sunt capite cano, barbâ albâ. Bacch. 5. 1. v. 15.
units.tr: OLD MEN take it badly that at that age they are made fools of, when they have grey hair and white beards. Bacch. 5. 1. v. 15.

units.la: SENES deridentur nomine Ovium detonsarum & palitantium. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: OLD MEN are mocked with the name of shorn and straying sheep. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 7.

units.la: SENES exercitijs & lotionibus fovebant senectutem suam. Stich. 4. 1. v. 62. Vide Tit. Conviv.
units.tr: OLD MEN used exercises and baths to cherish their old age. Stich. 4. 1. v. 62. See the title Banquets.

units.la: SENES etiam nuptias inhiant, & plærumq; libidinosi. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 93. Stich. 4. 1. v. 65. Vide de Nuptijs senum Albericum Gentilem l. 5. c. 3. p. 485.
units.tr: OLD MEN also gape after marriages, and are mostly lustful. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 93. Stich. 4. 1. v. 65. On the marriages of old men see Alberico Gentili, book 5, ch. 3, p. 485.

units.la: SENES albis capillis, sæpe ingenio non sunt senes, sed moribus adolescentes: & sæpe ut pueri peccant. Mil. 3. 1. v. 36,67. & seqq. Trin. 1. 2. v. 5.
units.tr: OLD MEN with white hair are often not old in mind but young in their behaviour, and often sin like boys. Mil. 3. 1. v. 36, 67, and following. Trin. 1. 2. v. 5.

units.la: In fabulis Medea recoxit Æsonem: & ex sene adolescentulum fecit. Pseud. 3. 2. v. 80. Sic Catull. Tibi & Suffetio seni recoctio.
units.tr: In the fables Medea boiled down Aeson and made a young man out of an old one. Pseud. 3. 2. v. 80. So Catullus: For you and for Suffetius, an old man to be reboiled.

units.la: VEGETA senectus est anno ætatis 54. Quod de se gloriatur senex ille Mil. 3. 1. v. 34.
units.tr: VIGOROUS old age is at the age of fifty-four. The old man in Mil. 3. 1. v. 34 boasts of this about himself:

units.la: Clarè oculis video, pernix sum manibus, sum pedes mobilis.
units.tr: I see clearly with my eyes, I am nimble with my hands, I am agile on my feet.

units.la: BENIGNITAS senum sæpe major, quàm adolescentum. Ibid. v. 39.
units.tr: KINDNESS of old men is often greater than that of young men. Ibid. v. 39.

units.la: SENES plærumque sunt sputatores, sternutatores, & muccidi. Mil. 3. 1. v. 51.
units.tr: OLD MEN are generally spitters, sneezers, and snufflers. Mil. 3. 1. v. 51.

units.la: SENES non deladendi. Aul. 2. 2. v. 75.
units.tr: OLD MEN are not to be deceived. Aul. 2. 2. v. 75.

units.la: SENES comparantur sepulchro veteri. Pseud. 5. 4. v. 19.
units.tr: OLD MEN are compared to an old sepulchre. Pseud. 5. 4. v. 19.

units.la: SENSUUM. VISUS. AUDITUS. ODORIS.
units.tr: SENSES. SIGHT. HEARING. SMELL.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See also the title Man.

units.la: OCULORUM sensus certissimus testis. Rud. 4. 4. v. 23.
units.tr: The sense of the eyes is the most certain witness. Rud. 4. 4. v. 23.

units.la: Negas quod video?
units.tr: Do you deny what I see?

units.la: NASO odoramur quandoq; praesentiam alterius: ut jocatur meretrix. Mil. 4. 6. v. 41. Odore nasum sentiat, si intus siet. Et v. 44. Naso pol jam hac quidem videt plus, quam oculis.
units.tr: We sometimes smell the presence of another with the nose, as the courtesan jokes. Mil. 4. 6. v. 41. Let him feel it with his nose by the smell, if he is inside. And v. 44. Indeed, by Pollux, this nose now sees more than the eyes.

units.la: OCULORUM sensus praefertur Auditui. Truc. 2, 5. v. 8. Vide Tit. Testium. Aristoteles l. 1. Met. 1. contra Auditum profert: quifons omnis scientiae.
units.tr: The sense of the eyes is preferred to hearing. Truc. 2, 5. v. 8. See the title Witnesses. Aristotle, Metaphysics 1, puts sight against hearing, as the source of all knowledge.

units.la: OCULI mores hominum indicant: praesertim amantium. Mercat. 1. 2. v. 97.
units.tr: The eyes indicate the characters of men, especially of lovers. Mercat. 1. 2. v. 97.

units.la: Ego illic aspicio formam eximiam mulierem, quam ego postquam adspexi, non ita amo, ut sani solent. Vide Titul. Amoris. & Dilucid. Marcelli Donati ad Suetonium p. 567. Edit. Rofanae, in 8.
units.tr: There I look at a woman of exceptional beauty, whom, after I have looked at her, I do not love as sane men usually do. See the title Love, and the Elucidations of Marcellus Donatus on Suetonius, p. 567, Rosenthal edition, in octavo.

units.la: OCULORUM sensus nobis omnium est carissimus. Ideo in expri-mendâ vi amoris crebrò utitur Plautus. Homo oculissimus est carissimus. Curc. 1. 2. v. 28. & 1. 3. v. 47. Ostium oculissimum: est carissimum. Curc. 1. 1. v. 17.
units.tr: The sense of the eyes is the dearest of all to us. Therefore Plautus often uses this in expressing the force of love: The man is the dearest to the eyes. Curc. 1. 2. v. 28, and 1. 3. v. 47. The door is dearest to the eyes. Curc. 1. 1. v. 17.

units.la: Catullus: Ambobus mihi, quae charior est oculis.
units.tr: Catullus: Of both of them to me, who is dearer than my eyes.

units.la: SENTENTIARUM, PROVERBIORUM.
units.tr: MAXIMS, PROVERBS.

units.la: PLAUTUS noster sententias saepè contrarias ita enunciat, ut idem videatur esse subjectum & praedicatum, quemadmodum Logici loquuntur: quod Aristoteles tradit Epicharmum quoq; fecisse. Tale est illud Curc. 4. 4 v. 1. Quos homines Dii non sunt propitii: eos non esse iratos puto.
units.tr: Our Plautus often expresses contrary maxims in such a way that the same thing seems to be both subject and predicate, as the logicians put it. Aristotle reports that Epicharmus also did this. An example is that in the Curculio 4.4 v.1: Those men to whom the gods are not favourable, I think are not angry.

units.la: Sic Capt. Prolog. v. 1. Hos quos videtis stare hic captivos duos Illi qui adstant, qui stant ambo, non sedent.
units.tr: So too in the Captivi Prologue v.1: These two captives whom you see standing here; those who stand beside them, who both stand, do not sit.

units.la: Vos vos mihi testes estis, me verum loqui loqui.
units.tr: You yourselves are my witnesses that I speak the truth, speak, speak.

units.la: Simile est illud Stich. 1.2. v.65.
units.tr: A similar one is that in the Stichus 1.2 v.65.

units.la: E malis multis, malum quod minimum est, id minimum est malum.
units.tr: Of many evils, the least evil is the least evil.
Rudens 1.4 v.8 and Rudens 4.3 v.105.

units.la: Etsi ignotus est, notus est: si non notus, ignotissimus est.
units.tr: Though he is unknown, he is known; if he is not known, he is most unknown.

units.la: Ter. Andr. 1.3. v.9.
units.tr: Ter. Andr. 1.3 v.9.

units.la: Quo jure, quaeso, injuria precipientem mihi pistrinum dabo.
units.tr: By what right, I ask, do you wrongly give me the mill, when I am giving the orders?

units.la: In hoc genere facetissimum est illud Ciceronis ad Att. Noli putare pigritiam facere me, quod non manu mea scribam: sed mehercle pigritia. nihil enim habeo aliud, quod dicam: & tamen in tuis quoque Epistolis Alexin videor agnoscere. Vide Mureti Var. lect. lib. 14. c. 5.
units.tr: In this kind the most witty is that of Cicero to Atticus: Do not think it is idleness that keeps me from writing with my own hand; but by Hercules, it is idleness. For I have nothing else to say; and yet in your letters too I seem to recognise Alexis. See Muretus, Variae lectiones, book 14, ch. 5.

units.la: VERBA vetera, & sententiae: si tempestative usurpentur, multum venustatis habent. Poen. 1.1. v.7. Turn. lib. 15. c. 6.
units.tr: Old words and maxims, if they are used at the right moment, have much charm. Poenulus 1.1 v.7. Turnebus, book 15, ch. 6.

units.la: SERMONIS. COLLOQUII. LOQUELAE. ORATIONIS. VERBORUM, DISPUTATIONIS. ORATORUM. RHETORUM. GRAMMATICES.
units.tr: SPEECH. CONVERSATION. TALK. ORATION. WORDS, DISPUTATION. ORATORS. RHETORIC. GRAMMAR.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Artium.
units.tr: See also the title Arts.

units.la: MAGNA vis verborum. Trin. 1.2. v.123. Dij immortales, verbis paucis, quàm cito alium fecisti me?
units.tr: Great is the power of words. Trin. 1.2. v.123. Immortal gods, in how few words you have quickly made me into someone else!

units.la: ODIOSA est oratio; cùm rem aveas, longinquum loqui. Merc. 3.4. v.23.
units.tr: Speech is hateful when, though you want the thing, you talk at length. Merc. 3.4. v.23.

units.la: SERMO honestus est ille, qui cum re consentit. Stich. 2. 2. v.7. Honesta dicta factis.
units.tr: That speech is honourable which agrees with the deed. Stich. 2. 2. v.7. Let words match deeds.

units.la: CUM aliena est oratio, praesertim in convivijs, decet tacere: maximè adolescentem. Mil. 3.1.v.50.
units.tr: When the talk is about another's affairs, especially at dinner parties, it is fitting to be silent, above all for a young man. Mil. 3.1.v.50.

units.la: XXX
units.tr: XXX

units.la: Sic Cicero lib. 1. Off. Sit igitur sermo, in quo Socratici excellunt, lenis, minimeque pertinax: insit in eo lepos, nec vero tamquam in possessionem suam venerit, excludat alios: sed cum reliquis in rebus, tum in sermone communi vicissitudinem non iniquam putet.
units.tr: So Cicero, On Duties, book 1: Let conversation be, in which the Socratics excel, gentle and least obstinate; let it have charm, but let it not, as if it had taken possession of its own property, shut others out; let him think that in conversation, as in other things, a fair give and take is right.

units.la: ORATORUM est, cogere ad lacrimas. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 57.
units.tr: It is the mark of orators to draw forth tears. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 57.

units.la: LOQUELA tantum homini competit: coque prodigium est, si brutaloquantur. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 22.
units.tr: Speech belongs to man alone, so it is a marvel if beasts talk. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 22.

units.la: DICTUM sapienti sat est. Pers. 4. 7. v. 19.
units.tr: A word is enough for the wise. Pers. 4. 7. v. 19.

units.la: OMNES sapientes decet conferre & fabulari. Rud. 2. 3. v. 8.
units.tr: It becomes all wise men to converse and talk together. Rud. 2. 3. v. 8.

units.la: STRENUI nimió plus prosunt populo, quàm arguti& cati. Facile sibi facunditatem virtus argutam invenit. Truc. 2. 6. v. 13. & v. 14. Sine virtute argutum civem mihi habeam pro pratica: quae alios collaudare, eapse vero se non potest.
units.tr: Brave men do far more good to the people than clever talkers. Virtue easily finds for itself a sharp and fluent eloquence. Truc. 2. 6. v. 13. & v. 14. Without virtue, I would count a clever citizen as a mere worthless fellow: one who can praise others but cannot praise himself.

units.la: SERPENTUM.
units.tr: SERPENTS.

units.la: Vide etiam Animal. Brutorum.
units.tr: See also Animals, Brutes.

units.la: ANGUES quos Hercules infans confecit, fuerunt jubati. Amph. 5. 1. v. 56.
units.tr: The snakes which the infant Hercules strangled were crested. Amph. 5. 1. v. 56.

units.la: SERPENTES duplices linguas putantur habere. Asin. 3. 3. v. 105. Plinius tamen facit trisulci-linguas. lib. 11. c. 37.
units.tr: Serpents are thought to have double tongues. Asin. 3. 3. v. 105. Pliny, however, makes them three-forked tongues. Book 11, chapter 37.

units.la: SERVORUM. SERVITUTIS. MINISTERII. SERVITII. FAMULORUM. DOMINORUM. HERORUM. MANCIPII. OPERARUM.
units.tr: SLAVES. SERVITUDE. MINISTRY. SERVICE. ATTENDANTS. MASTERS. OWNERS. BONDSERVANTS. PURCHASED MEN. HIRED LABOURERS.

units.la: Vide plura supra Tit. Libertorum: Manumissionis. Et, Supplicij: Captivitatis: Ergastuli.
units.tr: See more above under the titles Freedmen: Manumission. And Punishment: Captivity: Workhouse.

units.la: De Ancillis & Pedissequis vide Tit. Gynaecei.
units.tr: On maidservants and attendants see the title Women's Quarters.

units.la: Item de variis ministerijs vide Tit. Familiae.
units.tr: Likewise, on the various kinds of service, see the title Household.

units.la: LOCUS Servorum latissime quoque patet in antiquitate Romana. Tractarunt illum ex professo duo viri docti: Laurentius Pignorius, Patavinus; cujus Tractatus de Servis editus Augustae Vindelicorum: nec non Ausonius Popma, Frisius. Nos e Plauto seligemus: quaecumque de Servis inibi leguntur.
units.tr: The subject of slaves is also very broad in Roman antiquity. Two learned men have treated it expressly: Laurentius Pignorius of Padua, whose treatise on slaves was published at Augsburg; and Ausonius Popma of Frisia. From Plautus I shall select whatever is read there about slaves.

units.la: OMNIS servitus dura est. Capt. I.I. v.18. Omnes profecto liberi ludentes summa, quam servimus.
units.tr: Every servitude is harsh. Capt. 1.1 v.18. Surely all free men, playing for the highest stakes, are in the same position as we slaves who serve.

units.la: SERVITUS juncta cum turpitudine, res aerumnosa valde. Pseud. 3.1. v.1. & seqq.
units.tr: Servitude joined with disgrace is a very wretched condition. Pseud. 3.1 v.1 and following.

units.la: SERVITUS alia privata, alia publica erat: quod colligimus e Capt. 2. 2. v. 84. Publici autem servi nominantur, qui licet servitute liberati, manuque missi fuerint, ministerium tamen publicum, aut magistratibus, aut sacerdotibus exhibent. Qui quidem ex libertinorum corpore plurimque sumebantur.
units.tr: Servitude was of two kinds, private and public, as we gather from Capt. 2.2 v.84. Public slaves are those who, though released from servitude and manumitted, nevertheless provide public service either to magistrates or to priests. These were very often taken from the body of freedmen.

units.la: Servi publici mentio quoque fit in Inscriptione antiqua, quae exstat Romae in domo Alberini: quam vide in Opere Inscriptionum pag. DCVII.1.
units.tr: Mention of public slaves also occurs in an ancient inscription which exists at Rome in the house of Alberini; see it in the work on inscriptions, p. DCVII.1.

units.la: Vide etiam Petri Fabri Semestr. lib.2. Et Justi Lipsij Elect. lib.1. cap. 2 2.
units.tr: See also Petrus Faber's Semestria, book 2, and Justus Lipsius's Electa, book 1, chapter 22.

units.la: Usu fiebant servi. Amph. 1.1. v.218. Pugnis me usu fecisti tuum.
units.tr: Slaves were made by use. Amph. 1.1 v.218. You have made me yours by your fists.

units.la: GREGEM venalium servorum mango circumducebat. Aul. 3.3. v 4. Rud.2.7. v.26.
units.tr: A dealer was leading a flock of slaves for sale about the market. Aul. 3.3 v.4. Rud. 2.7 v.26.

units.la: IN mancipijs vendendis vadem paciscebatur venditor, ne fugitivum aut erronem praestaret. Et hoc dicebant suo periculo emere, & vendere. Perf.4.3.v.55.
units.tr: In selling slaves, the seller gave security by stipulation that he would not answer for a runaway or a wanderer. They also said they bought and sold at their own risk. Perf. 4.3 v.55.

units.la: SERVORUM vestimenta separatim vendita. Stich. 2.1. v.16. Ad quem locum vide Taub. p. 1062. Et Perf. 4.4. v.118.
units.tr: Slaves' clothing was sold separately. Stich. 2.1 v.16. On this passage see Taubmann, p. 1062. And Perf. 4.4 v.118.

units.la: SERVI utplurimum Syri: & erant patientissimi ad labores. Trin. 2.4.v,141.
units.tr: Slaves were mostly Syrians, and they were very enduring of labour. Trin. 2.4 v.141.

units.la: SERVITUS opulento homini dura est. Divitis servus miser est. Noctes, diesque assiduo satis supe que est, Quo facto aut dicto adest opus, quietus ne sis. Amph. 1.1.v.12.
units.tr: Slavery is hard for a wealthy man; the servant of a rich man is wretched. Nights and days there is more than enough constant work; whatever deed or word is needed, you may not be at rest. Amph. 1.1 v.12.

units.la: IN servitute accidunt multa iniqua: habendum & ferendum est hoc onus cum labore. Ib. v.21.
units.tr: Many unjust things happen in servitude; this burden must be borne and endured with toil. Ib. v.21.

units.la: VILIORES erant servi nati, quan facti. Amph. 1.1. veif. 23. Val. Max. lib 3. c 4. Vernam natum huic urbi regem dando. Cicero de Prov. Consularibus: Judaei & Syri nationes servituti natae. De qua Israelitarum miserâ fortunâ Moses Deuteron. cap.28.
units.tr: Born slaves were held in lower esteem than those made slaves. Amph. 1.1 verse 23. Val. Max. book 3, chapter 4. Giving the king of this city a home-born slave. Cicero, On the Consular Provinces: Jews and Syrians are nations born for servitude. Of the wretched fortune of the Israelites Moses speaks in Deuteronomy 28.

units.la: ETSI pari jure habebantur servi bello capti, atque ij, qui vernae essent: hoc illis tamen quasi miseriae suae solatium ac levamen erat, quod exprobrare servitutem non liceret: cum idipsum minime honestum exis timarent. Capt. 3.4. v.59.
units.tr: Although captives of war and home-born slaves were held under the same law, this was nevertheless a kind of consolation and relief for their misery: they could not be reproached with servitude, since they themselves thought that very thing not at all honourable. Capt. 3.4 v.59.

units.la: SERVORUM Atticorum major licentia Athenis, quam Romae. Stich. 3.1. v. 37.
units.tr: Attic slaves had greater licence at Athens than at Rome. Stich. 3.1 v.37.

units.la: Vide Joh. Brodaei Misc.lib.3 cap.12. Casaub.ad Sueton. & Athenaeum lib. 6. c.19.
units.tr: See John Brodaeus, Miscellanea, book 3, chapter 12; Casaubon on Suetonius; and Athenaeus, book 6, chapter 19.

units.la: SERVI dominos suos patronos vocabant. Men. 5.7. v. 42.
units.tr: Slaves called their masters patrons. Men. 5.7 v.42.

units.la: NOMINA servorum unde imponi solita sint, docet Helladius Bi-santifantinous apud Photium Biblioth. pag. 544. Edit. Andr. Schotti: Comici plerumq; servis nomina a natali solo indunt, ut Syrum, Carionem, Mydam, Getam, & similia: partim ex adjunctis, ut a colore quidam Pyrrian, & Xanthian: a moribus Parmenonem, Pistum, Dromonem: item a die, quo emtus est servus: unde & Numenias vocant.
units.tr: Helladius of Bisanthe, in Photius's Bibliotheca, p. 544, ed. Andreas Schottus, shows whence names were commonly given to slaves: Comic poets mostly gave slaves names from their native land, such as Syrus, Carion, Midas, Geta, and similar; partly from accompanying features, as Pyrrias and Xanthias from colour, Parmeno, Pistus, and Dromo from manners; also from the day on which the slave was bought, whence they are also called Numenias.

units.la: Bacch. 4.4.v.7. Non mihi isti placent Parmenones, Syri: qui duas aut tres minas auferunt heris.
units.tr: Bacch. 4.4 v.7. I do not like those Parmenos, the Syrians, who take two or three minae from their masters.

units.la: Sic Trin. 4.3.v.13. exadjunctis eorum moribus: Occulteripida, Cruricrepida, Masligia.
units.tr: Thus, Trin. 4.3 v.13. names are taken from their manners: Occulteripida, Cruricrepida, Masligia.

units.la: Docet etiam Athenæus Comica nomina duarum syllabarum: Tragica vero plurium fuisse antiquitus: immò vel unius etiam syllabæ: ut Mu, Servus Epicuri.
units.tr: Athenaeus also records that comic names were of two syllables, while tragic names were of more syllables in antiquity, even of a single syllable, as Mu, slave of Epicurus.

units.la: Vide Frid. Lindenb. ad Terent. Andr. 2.1. & Isaac Casaubon. Animad. lib. 14. c. 1. ad Athen.
units.tr: See Fridericus Lindenbrog on Terence, Andria 2.1, and Isaac Casaubon, Animadversions, book 14, chapter 1, on Athenaeus.

units.la: SERVI, servæ, peculium sibi habebant. Sic Anus ancilla Euclionis gallum gallinaceum habuit peculiarem. Aul. 3.4.v.6. Asin. 2.2.v 11. ἀλλη̃οεικω̃ς. Et 2.4.v91. Most.1.3. v.95. Pseud.4.7.v.91. Ambigue. Pœn. 4.2.v.21. Crucior pretijs emtos maximis apud vos servos fieri expeculiatos suis heris. Trin. 2 4. v.33.
units.tr: Male and female slaves had their own property (peculium). Thus the old woman, the maid of Euclio, had her own cockerel. Aul. 3.4 v.6. Asin. 2.2 v.11. Greek word [ἀλληοεικῶς]. And 2.4 v.91. Most. 1.3 v.95. Pseud. 4.7 v.91. Ambiguous. Poen. 4.2 v.21. I am grieved that slaves bought among you at the highest prices are stripped of their property by their masters. Trin. 2.4 v.33.

units.la: SERVI olim histrioniam faciebant in scena. Amph. Prol. v. 31. Seneca Epist. 81.
units.tr: Slaves once performed pantomime on the stage. Amph. Prol. v.31. Seneca, Epist. 81.

units.la: Ille qui in scena elatus incedit, servus est, quinq; modios accipit, & quinq; denarios.
units.tr: He who struts on the stage, raised high, is a slave; he receives five modii and five denarii.

units.la: Petron. pag. 32. Edit. Wower. Grex (servorum) agit in scena mimum.
units.tr: Petronius, p. 32, ed. Wower: The troupe of slaves performs a mime on the stage.

units.la: PATREM vocabant herum majorem: filium, minorem, & filium herilem. Bacch. 4. 4. v.2.
units.tr: They called the father the greater master (herus), and the son the lesser, the young master. Bacch. 4.4 v.2.

units.la: HERI suis filijs conducebant servos peculiares: qui ijdem & Vicarij dicti. Capt. Prol.
units.tr: Masters hired out personal slaves to their sons, who were also called substitutes (vicarii). Capt. Prol.

units.la: SERVIS honos nullus debebatur: multò minus supplicatio aliqua honestior. Asin. 3.3. v.80,88. Truc. 2.7.v.30.
units.tr: No honour was owed to slaves, and much less any more honourable tribute. Asin. 3.3 v.80, 88. Truc. 2.7 v.30.

units.la: Servorum confervi dicebantur Collegæ. Asin. 3. 2. v. 10. & 30.
units.tr: Slaves were called fellow-slaves (confervi), that is, colleagues. Asin. 3.2 v.10 and 30.

units.la: S E R V I T I I pars erat januam observare, seu custodire. Asin. 2. 2. v. 7. Mil. 2. 3. v. 57.
units.tr: Part of servitude was to watch over the door, or to guard it. Asin. 2.2 v.7. Mil. 2.3 v.57.

units.la: Inde puto vocari fores conservas, & amicas servorum: à custodia scilicet. Asin. 2. 3. v. 7. Dicti enim Servi Ostiarij.
units.tr: Hence, I think, doors are called fellow-servants and friends of the slaves, clearly from their guarding. Asin. 2.3 v.7. For slaves who served as door-keepers were called ostiarii.

units.la: S E R V I erant calatores. Pseud. 4. 2. v. 52. Rud. 2. 3. v. 5. Vide Lex. Plaut. & Scaligerum ad Festum. Item Laur. Pignorij: nec non Ausonij Pompæ de Servis.
units.tr: Slaves served as messengers (calatores). Pseud. 4.2 v.52. Rud. 2.3 v.5. See the Plautine lexicon and Scaliger on Festus. Likewise Laurentius Pignorius, and Ausonius Popma's work on slaves.

units.la: SERVIS variæ dabantur provinciæ in re familiari.
units.tr: Slaves were assigned various duties in the management of the household.

units.la: Alij aquæ hauriundæ præfecti: alij lignis secandis, sive provinciæ caudicali: alius ædibus expurgandis: & exornandis: alius lacisternijs: alius poculis & vasis eluendis.
units.tr: Some were put in charge of drawing water; others of cutting wood, or of the woodshed; another of cleaning and decorating the house; another of the cisterns; another of washing cups and vessels.

units.la: Vide Pseud. 1. 2. v. 24. & seqq.
units.tr: See Pseud. 1. 2. v. 24 and following.

units.la: Alij Atrienses erant Principes tricliniares. Pœn. 5. f. v. 4. Asin. 2. 2. v. 69. Alij promi-condi, procuratores peni. Pseud. 2. 2. v. 14. Vide Lex. Atriensis.
units.tr: Some slaves were called atriensēs, the chief attendants of the dining-room. Poen. 5. f. v. 4. Asin. 2. 2. v. 69. Others were promi-condi, stewards of the storeroom. Pseud. 2. 2. v. 14. See the Lexicon under Atriensis.

units.la: S E R V I atrienses habebant servos vicarios, qui illis subservirent. Asin. 2. 4. v. v. 26, 28.
units.tr: Slaves who were atrienses had slaves under them to act as their deputies. Asin. 2. 4. v. 26, 28.

units.la: S E R V I atriensis in alios servos habebant imperium. Asin. 2. 3. v. 10.
units.tr: The slave who was atriensis had authority over the other slaves. Asin. 2. 3. v. 10.

units.la: Quæ potestas atriensium: quodque munus aliorum servorum, eleganter exprimitur. Asin. 2 3. v. 18.
units.tr: The power of the atriensēs, and the office of the other slaves, is expressed elegantly. Asin. 2. 3. v. 18.

units.la: S E R V I atrienses aliorum servorum operas locare solebant. Asin. 2. 4. v, v. 37.
units.tr: Slaves who were atrienses used to hire out the labour of other slaves. Asin. 2. 4. v. 37.

units.la: S E R V I atrienses cæteris servis poterant colaphum impingere. Asin. 2. 2. v. 104.
units.tr: Slaves who were atrienses could strike the other slaves with a blow of the fist. Asin. 2. 2. v. 104.

units.la: S E R V I atrienses heris suis argentum elocabant in fenus. Asin. 2. 4. v. 23.
units.tr: Slaves who were atrienses lent their masters' silver out at interest. Asin. 2. 4. v. 23.

units.la: Servi fuerunt clavigeri: & clavatores. Rud. 3. 5. v. 25. Vide Turn. l.13. Adv. cap.6.
units.tr: Slaves were key-bearers and key-keepers. Rud. 3. 5. v. 25. See Turnebus, book 13, Adversaria, chapter 6.

units.la: Servi vinarij vendebant vinum. Asin. 2.4. v. 30. Vide Lexic. Plautinum.
units.tr: Wine-slaves sold wine. Asin. 2. 4. v. 30. See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: Aquarii servi mulierum: earumque amorum internuntij. Poen. 1.2. v. 14.
units.tr: Water-carrying slaves were go-betweens for women and their love affairs. Poen. 1. 2. v. 14.

units.la: Baiuli servi omnia collo suo efficiunt. Poen. 5.6.v.17.
units.tr: Porter slaves carry everything on their necks. Poen. 5. 6. v. 17.

units.la: Servi unctores erant quoque, qui unguenta curabant, quos ungebant amantes. Trin. 2.1. v. 22.
units.tr: There were also slave anointers, who looked after perfumes, and whom lovers anointed. Trin. 2. 1. v. 22.

units.la: Servi erant vestispici: & vestispicæ ancillæ. Trin. 2.1. v.22.
units.tr: There were slave clothes-inspectors, male and female. Trin. 2. 1. v. 22.

units.la: Salutigeruli pueri apud parum pudicas mulieres. Aul. 3.4. v.28. Pignorius pag. 214. Vide eundem de aliis omnibus servis.
units.tr: Greeting-bearing boys were kept by women who were not very chaste. Aul. 3. 4. v. 28. Pignorius, p. 214. See the same author on all the other kinds of slaves.

units.la: Mulliones servi ex urbano erant ministerio: & pedissequi in Gynæceo. Aul. 3 5. v.27. Vide Laur. Pignor. de Servis pag. 214.
units.tr: Slaves called mulliones were drawn from urban service, and there were attendants in the women's quarters. Aul. 3. 5. v. 27. See Laurentius Pignorius, On Slaves, p. 214.

units.la: Servi accipiebant dimensum cibum quot-calendis, seu in mensem. Stich. 1. 2. v. 3.
units.tr: Slaves received a measured allowance of food on the calends, or for the month. Stich. 1. 2. v. 3.

units.la: Sic Donatus: Servi quaternos modios accipiebant frumenti in mensem: & id dimensum dicebatur: utrum à Mense, an à metiendo, incertum est.
units.tr: Thus Donatus: Slaves used to receive four measures of grain a month, and this was called dimensum; whether from the month or from measuring, it is uncertain.

units.la: Juvenal: Servorum ventres modio castigat iniquo Ipse quoque esuriens,
units.tr: Juvenal: "He keeps the bellies of slaves in check with an unfair measure, himself hungry too."

units.la: Seneca Epist. 20. Servus est: quinq; modios accipit.
units.tr: Seneca, Epistle 20: "He is a slave: he receives five measures."

units.la: Forteinde: quia honestiores plusculum acceperunt. Vide etiam Tit. Oeconomiæ.
units.tr: Perhaps because the more respectable ones received a little more. See also the title Oeconomia.

units.la: Servorum cibus salfuit. Perf. 3.3. v.24.
units.tr: The slaves' food was salted fish. Pers. 3. 3. v. 24.

units.la: Servorum potus fuit acetum, sive posca. Rud. 4.3.v.32. Hic rex cum aceto pransurus est, & sale sine bono pulmento. Vide Tit. Vini.
units.tr: The slaves' drink was vinegar, or posca. Rud. 4. 3. v. 32. "Here the king is about to dine on vinegar and salt, without a good relish." See the title Vinum.

units.la: Heri avari allium cum sale suis servis obsignabant, magna tamen suo damno: quia tanto nequiores inde servi facti. Perf. 2. 3. v.14.
units.tr: Some stingy masters sealed garlic with salt for their slaves, though to their own loss, because the slaves became all the more wicked from it. Pers. 2. 3. v. 14.

units.la: Id demum lepidum est, triparcos homines, vetulos, avidos, aridos, benè admordere, qui allium cum sale servo obsignant. Sal namque & allium, cibus pauperum servorum.
units.tr: This is indeed witty: to bite well at tight-fisted, old, greedy, dry men who seal up garlic with salt for a slave. For salt and garlic were the food of poor slaves.

units.la: Juvenal. Sat. 3. quis tecum sectile porrum Sutor, & elixi vervecis labra comedit?
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire 3: "Who eats a sliced leek with you, the cobbler, and the lips of boiled mutton?"

units.la: Pers. Sat. 4.
units.tr: Persius, Satire 4.

units.la: Tunicatum cum sale mordens eapé.
units.tr: "Biting the man in the tunic with salt..."

units.la: SERVI corrupti maleficium, non primùm Prætoris edicto coercitum fuit: sed lege Aquilia: cui Prætoris edictum successit.
units.tr: The punishment of a slave corrupter was first established not by the praetor's edict but by the Aquilian law, which the praetor's edict later followed.

units.la: Sic Poen. 1. 1. v. 57. Milphio servus Agorastoclis domino persuadet, ut si lenonem perdere velit, trecentos Philippeos nummos Collibisco villico suo det, quos ad lenonem deferat, simulans se peregrinum: & ait:
units.tr: Thus Poen. 1. 1. v. 57. Milphio, slave of Agorastocles, persuades his master that, if he wishes to ruin the pimp, he should give three hundred Philippean coins to his bailiff Collibiscus, to carry to the pimp, pretending to be a foreigner. And he says:

units.la: Leno ad se accipiet auri cupidus: unde efficiat habet. Et act. 3. scen. 4. v. 13.
units.tr: "The pimp will take it, greedy for gold; he will find a way to bring it about." And in act 3, scene 4, v. 13:

units.la: Vidistis leno cum aurum accepit? AD. Vidimus. AG. Eum vos esse servum meum scitis. AD. Scivimus. AG. Rem adversus populi sæpe leges? AD. Scivimus.
units.tr: "Did you see the pimp when he took the gold? AD. We saw. AG. You know he is my slave. AD. We knew. AG. Do you often break the laws of the people? AD. We knew."

units.la: Ubi ad secundum legis Aquiliæ caput respexit Plautus, quo servi corruptor aut receptator ex inficiatione tenebatur in duplum.
units.tr: Here Plautus looked to the second chapter of the Aquilian law, by which a corrupter or receiver of a slave was liable, on denial, for double damages.

units.la: Populi enim leges etiam Plebis scita dici, non est absurdum: cùm populi appellatione Plebs contineatur: & viciissim populus plebem notet apud Martial. l. 12. Ep. 3.
units.tr: For it is not absurd to call the leges populi also plebis scita, since the term populus includes the Plebs, and conversely populus denotes the plebs, as in Martial, book 12, epigram 3.

units.la: Ille dabit populo, patribus, equitibus, legendum.
units.tr: Martial: "He will give it to be read to the people, the senators, the knights."

units.la: Nec Prætoris edictum intellexit Plautus, nam edicta numquam Populi leges dici consueverunt: & ex edicto corruptor etiam sine inficiatione duplo multabatur.
units.tr: Nor did Plautus have the praetor's edict in mind, for edicts were never customarily called laws of the people; and by edict a corrupter was fined double even without denial.

units.la: SERVI litteris notabantur in fronte: eoque dicti Litterati, Stigmatiæ.
units.tr: Slaves were branded with letters on the forehead, and so were called litterati and stigmatiae.

units.la: Vide, quæ scripsi in Plautino Lexico voce Litteratus.
units.tr: See what I have written in the Plautine Lexicon under the word litteratus.

units.la: Videndus item Lipsius lib. 2. Elect. cap. 15. Dousa ad Petron. lib. 2.c.6. Cælius Rhod. lib. 7. c. 31. Tit. Popma de Operis Servorum.
units.tr: See also Lipsius, book 2 of Electa, chapter 15; Dousa on Petronius, book 2, chapter 6; Caelius Rhodiginus, book 7, chapter 31; and Titus Popma, On the Work of Slaves.

units.la: Servorum olim pabulum, plagæ & flagra fuere: unde Flagritribæ dicti, & Ulmitribæ. Perf. 2.4. v. 7. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 5. Ubi graphicè eorum mores describit Poeta:
units.tr: Once the fodder of slaves was blows and whips, whence they were called flagritribae and ulmitribae. Pers. 2. 4. v. 7. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 5. Where the poet vividly describes their character:

units.la: Qui hæc habent consilia: Ubi data occasio est: Rape, clepe, tene, harpaga, Bibe, es, fuge, hoc est eorum opus, ut mavelis lupos apud oves linquere, quam hos domi custodes.
units.tr: "Those who have these plans: when the chance is given, snatch, steal, grab, seize, drink, eat, flee; this is their work, so that you would sooner leave wolves among sheep than these as guards at home."

units.la: At faciem cùm adspicias eorum, haud mali videntur, operâ fallunt. Ergò hominum genus rapacissimum, fallacissimum Servi.
units.tr: But when you look at their faces they seem not bad; they deceive by their work. Therefore slaves are the most rapacious and deceitful race of men.

units.la: Sic Trin. 2.2. v.12. Caeterarapae, trahe, fuge, late.
units.tr: Thus Trin. 2. 2. v. 12. "Snatch, drag, flee, hide away."

units.la: Ex Diphilo:
units.tr: From Diphilus:

units.la: ἁρπάζ᾽ ἀπελθὼν, κλέπ᾽, ἀποσέγει, κύκα, μηδὲν πλαινθῆς.
units.tr: "Snatch and be off, steal, hide yourself, do not wander about for nothing." [ἁρπάζ᾽ ἀπελθὼν, κλέπ᾽, ἀποσέγει, κύκα, μηδὲν πλαινθῆς]

units.la: Magistratus virgis in noxios utebatur: Domini loris in servos domi. Pœn. Prol. v. 26.
units.tr: Magistrates used rods against wrongdoers; masters used thongs against slaves at home. Poen. Prol. v. 26.

units.la: Ne& hic sclic. in publico theatro servi varientur virgis: & loridomi.
units.tr: Here too the scholiast notes that in the public theatre slaves are flogged with rods, and beaten with the thong at home.

units.la: Eâque de causâ audiebat servus; Crux stimulorum, tritor compedum. Perf. 5.2. v.17.
units.tr: Hence the slave heard: "Cross of goads, grinder of fetters." Pers. 5. 2. v. 17.

units.la: Servorum pœna erat ulmi, stimuli, laminæ, cruces, compedes, nervi, catenæ, carceres, numellæ, pedicæ, bojæ. Amph. Prol. v. 31. Men. 1.1. v. 4. Capt. 1.2. v. 3.
units.tr: The punishments of slaves were the elm rod, goads, plates, crosses, fetters, sinews, chains, prisons, numellae, pedicae, and bojae. Amph. Prol. v. 31. Men. 1. 1. v. 4. Capt. 1. 2. v. 3.

units.la: Servis captivis manicæ injectæ. Capt. 3.5. v. 1. Mostl. 5.1. v. 17.
units.tr: Captive slaves had manacles put on them. Capt. 3. 5. v. 1. Most. 5. 1. v. 17.

units.la: Servi ferreis catenis vinciebantur in mancipia. Truc. 2.2. v.17.
units.tr: Slaves were bound in iron chains as chattel. Truc. 2. 2. v. 17.

units.la: Mancupium qui accipias, cape eccos ahenos annulos.
units.tr: "If you take a mancipium, take these bronze rings."

units.la: Legatum servorum testamento est, τὸ Va!
units.tr: A legacy of slaves by will [τὸ Va!]

units.la: Servi in quæstionibus vinciebantur.
units.tr: Slaves were bound during examinations.

units.la: Yyy Inde ἀλλησοεικῶς servus Merc. 1. 2. v. 54. Dissolve jam me, obse-cro, nimis diu animi pendeo.
units.tr: Hence the slave, [ἀλλησοεικῶς]. Merc. 1. 2. v. 54. "Release me now, I beg you; I have hung in suspense far too long."

units.la: SERVIS puniendis lora poscebantur. Capt. 3. 4. v. 125. Most. 4. 3. v. 44.
units.tr: Straps were demanded for punishing slaves. Capt. 3. 4. v. 125. Most. 4. 3. v. 44.
