units.la: SERVIS compedes impositi: virgis & restibus quando caederentur. Pers. 2. 3. v. 18. & 2. 4. v. 11.
units.tr: Fetters were put on slaves when they were to be beaten with rods and cords. Pers. 2. 3. v. 18, and 2. 4. v. 11.

units.la: SERVI suo tergo male metuunt. Most. 4. 1. v. 11.
units.tr: Slaves fear for their backs with good reason. Most. 4. 1. v. 11.

units.la: PLAGAE, servorum cibus erant. Asin. 3. 3. v. 38.
units.tr: Blows were the food of slaves. Asin. 3. 3. v. 38.

units.la: SERVI flagris & verberibus nati & destinati. Inde verberea statua dictus servus Pseudolus. Pseud. 4. 1. v. 7.
units.tr: Slaves were born and destined for whips and blows; hence the slave Pseudolus was called a "beaten statue." Pseud. 4. 1. v. 7.

units.la: SERVI ita verberibus erant malacissati, ut Statua verberea nomen meruerint. Capt. 5. 1. v. 31.
units.tr: Slaves were so softened by beatings that they earned the name "beaten statue." Capt. 5. 1. v. 31.

units.la: SERVIS crura & tali confringebantur: & tergum ulmeam sensit virgidemiam. Rud. 3. 2. v. 21.
units.tr: Slaves' legs and ankles were broken, and their backs felt the elm-rod beating. Rud. 3. 2. v. 21.

units.la: SERVI a plagis dicti plagipatidae, & ferritribaces. Most. 2. 1. v. 9. Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: From their blows slaves were called plagipatidae and ferritribaces. Most. 2. 1. v. 9. See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: SERVI in pistrinum dati. Asin. 3. 3. v. 120. Bacch. 4. 6. v. 11. Most. 1. 1. v. 6.
units.tr: Slaves were given to the mill. Asin. 3. 3. v. 120. Bacch. 4. 6. v. 11. Most. 1. 1. v. 6.

units.la: SERVIS nihili, ignavis, & improbis dantur verba, compedes, molae, fames, lassitudo, frigus durum. Men. 5. 6. v. 10, 16. Asin. 3. 2. vers. 4.
units.tr: For worthless, lazy and wicked slaves there are words, fetters, millstones, hunger, weariness and hard cold. Men. 5. 6. v. 10, 16. Asin. 3. 2. v. 4.

units.la: Ulmea virgae, stimuli, lamina, cruces, compedes, nervi, carceres, numellae, pedicae, boja.
units.tr: Elm rods, goads, metal plates, crosses, fetters, thongs, prisons, little chains (numellae), stocks (pedicae), and collars (boja).

units.la: SERVI nequam & fontes ad columnam fortiter adstricti. Bacch. 4. 7. v. 25.
units.tr: Worthless slaves and brazen rogues, tightly bound to the pillar. Bacch. 4. 7. v. 25.

units.la: SERVI in longum exporrecti pendebant, & flagris caedebantur.
units.tr: Slaves were stretched out at full length, hanging, and beaten with whips.

units.la: Unde jocus de uva pensili, & litteră longa Aul. 1. 1. v. 40. de Staphylā anu servā. Aul. 4. 4. v. 16. Capt. 3. 4. v. 103. Caf. 2. 6. v. 38. & 5. 4. v. 25. Most. 3. 2. v. 166. & 5. 2. v. 45. Men. 5. 5. v. 48. Merc. 1. 2. v. 72. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 79. Poen. 1. 1. v. 32. & 1. 2. v. 134. Truc. 4. 3. v. 3.
units.tr: Hence the joke about the hanging grape, and the long letter. Aul. 1. 1. v. 40, concerning Staphyla the slave-woman. Aul. 4. 4. v. 16. Capt. 3. 4. v. 103. Caf. 2. 6. v. 38 and 5. 4. v. 25. Most. 3. 2. v. 166 and 5. 2. v. 45. Men. 5. 5. v. 48. Merc. 1. 2. v. 72. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 79. Poen. 1. 1. v. 32 and 1. 2. v. 134. Truc. 4. 3. v. 3.

units.la: AD pedes autem servorum pendentium alligabatur pondus aliquod, ne inter vapulandum calcitrarent, neve pedibus ,aut calcibus eos, à quibus verberabantur peterent. Ac quidem adeò crudele à servis sumtum supplicium, ut totam sepè noctem pendentes flagris exagitati fuerint. Amph. 1. 1. v. 123. Asin. 2. 2. v. 35. & 3. 3. v. 27. Mil. 2. 6. v. 23.
units.tr: To the feet of hanging slaves a weight was attached, so that they could not kick during the beating, nor strike with their feet or heels those by whom they were beaten. The punishment inflicted on slaves was indeed so cruel that they were often hung and lashed for nearly the whole night. Amph. 1. 1. v. 123. Asin. 2. 2. v. 35 and 3. 3. v. 27. Mil. 2. 6. v. 23.

units.la: Huic diutinae servitiae, qui pares essent, carnifices lecti fuerunt oco. Amph. 1. 1. v. 7. Asin. 3. 2. v. 18. & 28.
units.tr: For this prolonged torment, executioners who were equal to it were chosen, eight in number. Amph. 1. 1. v. 7. Asin. 3. 2. v. 18 and 28.

units.la: SERVI olim ita se ac scapulas suas frequente ac paene quotidiana virgidemiâ ad sufferendas plagas assuefecerant, induraverantq;, ut jam adversus quaevis etiam suppliciorum genera examussim patientissimi ac firmissimi usus diuturnitate & cõsuetudine reddidi viderentur, callo humeris scil. tergoque ac lateribus obducto, praegnantium plagarum multitudine. Fatentur id de se servi, ac quasi sibi exprobrant hanc callorum duritiem. Asin. 3. 2. v. 28.
units.tr: Slaves in former times so accustomed their shoulders and backs to bear blows by frequent and almost daily flogging, and so hardened them, that through long practice and habit they seemed perfectly patient and steadfast under any kind of punishment, a callus being spread over the shoulders, back and sides by the multitude of blows they had received. The slaves themselves confess this about themselves, and as it were reproach themselves for this hardness of calluses. Asin. 3. 2. v. 28.

units.la: Quo pertinet cõvitium illud Titinnij apud Festum in Reduvia. Lassitudo conservum reduviae flagri. H. e. qui delassare consuetus valentissimos virgatores, conservos tuos.
units.tr: To this belongs the taunt of Titinnius in Festus, in Reduvia: "The weariness of my fellow slave, the reduvia whip." That is, one who is accustomed to wear out the strongest whip-men, your fellow slaves.

units.la: Solebant namque servi olim inter se flagellare, ut de Atriensibus paulò ante memoravi ex nostro. Reduviae flagri, inquit: quasi circa verberonem illum ulmeae virgae & flagra se resolvant, tergi ejusdem firmitudine contritae ac dissipatae. Reduviae namque à resolvendo dictae. Unde à Comico nostro haec nomina acceperunt servi: Ulmitribae, Bucedae, Restiones, Subicula flagri, Tribuni vapulares, &c.
units.tr: For slaves used formerly to flog one another, as I mentioned a little while ago about the Atriensians, from our author. "Reduviae flagri," he says, as if the elm rods and whips loosened themselves around that thong-beating, worn down and scattered by the toughness of the same back. For the reduviae are named from resolving (resolvendo). Whence our Comic poet gave slaves these names: Ulmitribae, Bucedae, Restiones, Subicula flagri, Tribuni vapulares, &c.

units.la: SERVI ad lautumias & pistrina damnabantur. Poen. 4. 2. v. 8. Vel in lautumijs, vel in pistrino mavelim agere aetatem, praeditus mea latera forti ferro. Capt. 3. 5. v. 65. & 5. 4. v. 3.
units.tr: Slaves were condemned to the stone quarries and the mills. Poen. 4. 2. v. 8. Rather would I spend my life either in the quarries or at the mill, with my sides provided with strong iron. Capt. 3. 5. v. 65 and 5. 4. v. 3.

units.la: A quae hauslio, ut & molitura, & lapidum caesura servis fuit in poenam. Caf. 1. 1. v. 34. Vide Lipsij Elect. lib. 2. cap. 15. Ubi explicat quoque, quid sit Fenestra ergastularis. Caf. 1. 1. v. 44.
units.tr: From this, drawing water, grinding at the mill, and cutting stone were a punishment for slaves. Caf. 1. 1. v. 34. See Lipsius, Elect. book 2, chapter 15, where he also explains what an ergastulum window (fenestra ergastularis) is. Caf. 1. 1. v. 44.

units.la: Servis quandoque ferreum est negotium: quando scil. in ergastulis sunt compacti. Perf. 1. 1. v. 21. Pluriculum annum fui prae ferratus apud molas tribunus vapularis. Unde & ferratile genus dicuntur Moftell. 1. 1. v. 17.
units.tr: For slaves the business is sometimes made of iron, namely when they are bound in workhouses. Perf. 1. 1. v. 21. For many years I have been a chained slave, a flogged tribune at the mills. Whence they are also called a ferratile genus, an "ironed kind." Moftell. 1. 1. v. 17.

units.la: De Ergastulis vide prolixe apud Lipsium lib. 2. Elect.
units.tr: On the workhouses see at length Lipsius, book 2 of the Electa.

units.la: Adeo crudele a servis sumtum fuit supplicium, ut totam noctem imo diem, saepe pendentes exagitati fuerint. Amph. 1. 1. ver. 123. Mil. 2. 6. v. 22.
units.tr: The punishment inflicted on slaves was so cruel that they were often hung and tormented through the whole night, indeed the whole day. Amph. 1. 1. v. 123. Mil. 2. 6. v. 22.

units.la: Et quidem lictores virgatores, aut carnifices, quitantae saevitiae, & tam diutinae pares essent, lecti fuerunt octo. Amph. 1. 1. v. 7. Asin. 3 2. v. 18, 19, 28. Ubi lenta virga dicuntur: quia totam noctem, & diem verberabant. Sed & certa tempora ad ista servilia supplicia elegerunt, quae Carnisicum dies fuerunt appellata. Asin. 2. 2. verf. 45. quos carnifices celebrabant, cum muneri suo varent.
units.tr: And indeed the lictors who were whip-men or executioners, and who were equal to such great savagery and such long duration, were chosen eight in number. Amph. 1. 1. v. 7. Asin. 3. 2. v. 18, 19, 28. Where they are called lenta virga, "slow rods," because they beat through the whole night and day. But they also chose fixed times for these servile punishments, which were called Carnisicum dies, "the executioners' days." Asin. 2. 2. v. 45, which executioners observed when they were free for their duty.

units.la: Servi primum in catenis, carcere, chordâ ac ferro detenti: deinde in crucem acti. Moft. 3. 2. v. 56.
units.tr: Slaves were first held in chains, prison, cord and iron, and then brought to the cross. Moft. 3. 2. v. 56.

units.la: Servi latii in crucem. Moft 5. 2. v. 12.
units.tr: Slaves led to the cross. Moft 5. 2. v. 12.

units.la: Servi Cane & Furcâ puniti. Caf. 2. 6. v. 36.
units.tr: Slaves punished with the cane and fork. Caf. 2. 6. v. 36.

units.la: Furriferi servi sub furcâ plectebantur: & in exemplum traducebantur. Caf. 2. 8. v. 2. Vide etiam Carbonarij. Vide item Lipf. lib. 3. cap. 4. de Cruce. Turn. 13. 3. Casaubon. ad Suetou. lib. 6.
units.tr: Fork-bearing slaves were punished under the fork, and led about as an example. Caf. 2. 8. v. 2. See also Carbonarii. See likewise Lipsius, book 3, chapter 4, on the cross; Turnebus 13. 3; Casaubon on Suetonius, book 6.

units.la: Servorum supplicium fuit, talifragium, ut & crurifragium. Mil. 2. 2. v. 1.
units.tr: A punishment for slaves was talifragium, as also crurifragium, the breaking of the ankles or legs. Mil. 2. 2. v. 1.

units.la: Moribus receptum, ut servus interdum cum Domino quasi pacisceretur in certum pretium: quod si exsolvisset, liber esset. Id pretium fuit e peculio servi, veladventitio aliquo lucro. Aul. 5. v. 8, 15. Caf. 2. 5. v. 5.
units.tr: By custom it was accepted that a slave sometimes made a bargain with his master for a fixed price, and if he paid it, he would be free. This price came from the slave's savings (peculium) or from some chance gain. Aul. 5. v. 8, 15. Caf. 2. 5. v. 5.

units.la: Seneca Epist. 80.
units.tr: Seneca, Epist. 80.

units.la: Mancipia quoq; conditionis extrema, & in his sordibus nata omni modo exuere conantur servitutem: peculium suum, quod comparaverunt fraudato ventre, pro capite numerant.
units.tr: Chattels of the lowest condition, born in such squalor, try in every way to cast off servitude: they count as their capital the savings they have gained by defrauding their bellies.

units.la: Virgilius:
units.tr: Virgil:

units.la: Nec spes libertatis erat, nec cura peculii.
units.tr: There was neither hope of liberty nor care for savings.

units.la: Vide etiam Rud. 4. 2. v. 22. Caf. 2. 5. v 8.
units.tr: See also Rud. 4. 2. v. 22. Caf. 2. 5. v. 8.

units.la: Frugi autem servi, raro servierunt ultra quinquennium, teste Cicer. Philipp. 8.
units.tr: Thrifty slaves, however, seldom served beyond five years, as Cicero witnesses, Philippics 8.

units.la: Etenim P.C. cum non in spem libertatis sexennio postquam ingressi, diutius, servitutem perpeti quam captivi frugi, & diligentes solent, quas vigilias, quas solicitudines, quot labores, liberandi populi R. causa recusare debemus?
units.tr: For, Conscript Fathers, when slaves who have entered service after six years do not hope for freedom, they usually endure servitude longer than captives who are thrifty and diligent. What vigils, what anxieties, what labours ought we to refuse for the sake of freeing the Roman people?

units.la: Idem quoque apud Turcas hodie obtinet, ut mancipium recensemtum, herum cogat, vel ut praescribat certum servitutis terminum, vel pretium statuat, quo soluto liber abeat.
units.tr: The same custom still holds among the Turks today: a registered slave may compel his master either to fix a definite term of servitude or to set a price, and on payment of which he goes free.

units.la: Vide Lipsium ad lib. 14. Tac. Annal. & Ravard. lib. 19. Tit. de Reg. Jur. Briss. lib. 6. Form.
units.tr: See Lipsius on book 14 of Tacitus' Annals, and Ravard, book 19, title "De Regulis Juris"; Brisson, book 6, "Formulae."

units.la: Servi ut liberos mentirentur cretam addebant in vestem, ut fallerent alijs permixti.
units.tr: Slaves, to pass themselves off as freemen, added chalk to their clothing, so that they might mingle among others and deceive them.

units.la: Aul. 4. 9. v. 7. de furibus Euclionis:
units.tr: Aul. 4. 9. v. 7. Concerning the thieves of Euclio:

units.la: Complures hic vestitu & creta occultant se, & sedent quasi frugi.
units.tr: Several here hide themselves with clothing and chalk, and sit as if they were honest.

units.la: Servum dotalem (inquit Papinianus) vir, qui solvendo est, constante matrimonio manumittere potest: si autem solvendo non est, licet alios creditores non habet, libertas servi impeditur, ut constante matrimonio deberi dos intelligatur. Alludit nostrer Asin. 1. 1. v. 72.
units.tr: A dotal slave (Papinian says) may be manumitted during marriage by a husband who is solvent. But if he is not solvent, even though he has no other creditors, the slave's liberty is hindered, so that the dowry is understood to remain owed during the marriage. Our author alludes to this, Asin. 1. 1. v. 72.

units.la: Vide Tit. Dotis. Et Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: See the title on dowry (Tit. Dotis), and the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: Servi pileo donati, sive etiam ancillae, post manumissionem, DIs supplicatum ibant, quorum virtuti ac benignitati potissimum libertatem acceptam referrent suam: magno religionis ac pietatis argumento. Perf. 3. 3. v. 42.
units.tr: Slaves who were presented with the cap (pileus), or maidservants too, after manumission went to offer supplication to the gods, to whose virtue and kindness they chiefly credited the freedom they had received: a great proof of religion and piety. Perf. 3. 3. v. 42.

units.la: Cum servi manumittebantur, raso capite pilleum accipiebant, idque in què in templo Feroniæ, libertatum Deæ, quasi Fidonia Varro-ni. Amph. i. i. v. 304. Inde pilleus erat signum libertatis. Vide Laz. Bayf. de revestiariâ c. 20. & Schott. ad c. 69. Aurel. Victo-ris, aliosque.
units.tr: When slaves were manumitted, they received a cap with a shaven head, and this in the temple of Feronia, goddess of freedmen, as in Varro's Fidonia. Amph. 1. 1. v. 304. Hence the pileus was a sign of liberty. See Lazarus Bayfius, De re vestiaria, chapter 20, and Schott on chapter 69 of Aurelius Victor, and others.

units.la: LIBER captivus avis ferœconsimilis est: Semel fugiendi si data est occasio, Satis est: numquam postillâ possis prendere. Capt. i. i. v. 7.
units.tr: A free man is like a captive wild bird: once the chance to flee is given, that is enough; afterwards you can never catch it again. Capt. 1. 1. v. 7.

units.la: Qui servi à Domino manumittebantur, dicebantur à Domino Abire. Amph. 2. 2. v. 227.
units.tr: Those slaves who were manumitted by their master were said to be dismissed (abire) by him. Amph. 2. 2. v. 227.

units.la: MANUMISSI fiebant liberti. Asin. 2. 3. v. 5.
units.tr: Manumitted slaves became freedmen. Asin. 2. 3. v. 5.

units.la: SERVI libertatem consecuti, per omnia insolescebant. Pers. 5. 2. v. 57.
units.tr: Slaves who had gained their freedom grew insolent in every way. Pers. 5. 2. v. 57.

units.la: Sed ita pars libertinorum est: nisi patrono, qui adversatus est, ni illi offuit, ni eimaledixit, ni grato ingratus repertus est, nec sa-tis liber sibi videtur, nec satis frugi: nec satis honestus.
units.tr: But such is the character of the freedmen: unless the patron, whom they opposed, unless they injured him, unless they spoke ill of him, unless they are found ungrateful to a benefactor, they seem neither free enough to themselves, nor thrifty enough, nor honest enough.

units.la: De his libertinorum moribus lege Casaub. ad Satir. v. Persiij pa-gin. 415.
units.tr: On the manners of freedmen, see Casaubon on Persius, Satire 5, p. 415.

units.la: SERVI non debent esse ὀφθαλμόδουλοι. Pers. i. i. v. 7. Qui hero suo servire vult bene servus servitutem, nam adepol illum multa in pe-store suo collocare oportet, quæ hero placere censeat præsenti, atque absenti suo.
units.tr: Slaves should not be ὀφθαλμόδουλοι [eye-servants]. Pers. i. i. v. 7. He who wants to serve his master well as a slave must indeed lay up in his breast many things which he thinks will please his master, both when present and when absent.

units.la: ETIAM servis nequam sæpè carere non possumus. Sic ipse servus improbus Pers. i. i. v. 10. Ego neq; libenter servio, neq; satis sum-hero ex sententiâ, sed quasi lippo oculo herus meus manum abstine-re haut quit tamen. Ita Bacch. 4. 8. v. 7 z. Lippi oculi servus ille est similimus: Si non est, nolu esse, neq; desideres: Si est, abstinere, quin attingas, non queas.
units.tr: We cannot often do without even good slaves. So the wicked slave himself, Pers. i. i. v. 10: I serve neither willingly nor to my master's liking, but my master, as if with a bleary eye, still cannot keep his hands off me. So Bacch. 4. 8. v. 7: That slave is very like one with bleary eyes. If he is not, he does not want to be, and you do not want him to be; if he is, he cannot refrain from touching you.

units.la: SERVI nil nisi plagis coacti recte faciunt: sicuti asini. Pseud. i. 2. v. 4.
units.tr: Slaves do nothing right unless they are forced by blows, like donkeys. Pseud. i. 2. v. 4.

units.la: Neque ego homines magis asinos unquam vidi, ita plagis costæ callent. Quos dum feriàs, tibi plus noces: eo enim ingenio sunt hi flagitribæ. Ita vos estis perditi, negligentes, ingenio improbo, effi-cium. cium vestrum, ut vos malo cogatis commonerier. Nempe ita animati estis, vos vincere hoc duritia tergi: plagigera genera hominum.
units.tr: I have never seen men more like donkeys; their ribs are so hardened by blows. If you strike them, you harm yourself the more, for these whipping-boys are made that way. So you are lost, careless, of wicked disposition; you make it so that you force them to be warned by punishment. Indeed you are so spirited that you think you can overcome this with the toughness of your hide, you race of men made for the lash.

units.la: SERVORUM epitheta, ex moribus desumta, varia sunt. Perf. 3.3. v.13.
units.tr: The epithets of slaves, taken from their habits, are various. Perf. 3.3. v. 13.

units.la: Vtri summa populi, stabulum servitricium, sortorum liberator, subiculum flagri, compedum contritor, pistrinorum civitas, perenni-serve, lurco, edax, furax, fugax.
units.tr: You, the rabble of the people, stable of slave-women, liberator of lots, cushion of the whip, grinder of fetters, city of the mill, ever-slave, glutton, gobbler, thief, runaway.

units.la: SERVUM decet herum amantem retinere, ne eo quo incumbit, compellat: ita ut quasi ratis sit hero amanti, ut toleret, ne pessum abeat. Aul. 4.1. v. 6.
units.tr: A slave ought to hold back a master who is in love, so that he does not drive him onward to where he is leaning; so that he becomes, as it were, a raft for his amorous master, to keep him afloat and stop him from sinking. Aul. 4.1. v. 6.

units.la: SERVI frugi officium est, sine mora exequi herile imperium. Nam qui hero ex sententia servire servus postulet, in herum maturā, nisi sera conderet capescere. Sin dormitet, servum sese ut cogitet. Aul. 4.1. v.1. & seqq.
units.tr: It is the duty of a good slave to carry out his master's orders without delay. For a slave who wants to serve his master to his liking must be quick to grasp his wishes, and not slow to store them up. But if he dozes, let him think of himself as a slave. Aul. 4.1. v. 1 and following.

units.la: SERVORUM est obtemperare heris, non heros servis. Mil. 3.1. v. 150. inquit Senex:
units.tr: It is the business of slaves to obey masters, not of masters to obey slaves. Mil. 3.1. v. 150. The old man says:

units.la: Strvienteu servitutem ego introduxi servos mihi, Hospes, non qui mihi imperarent, quibus ego essem obnoxius: Si illis agre est, mihi quod volupe est, meo remigio rem gero. Tamen id, quod odiosum est, faciundum est cum magno malo, atq; ingratis.
units.tr: I have introduced slaves for myself, guest, who would not command me, and to whom I should be bound. If they are displeased, I manage my affairs with my own oar, with what pleases me. Yet what is hateful must be done, with great pain and against their will.

units.la: SERVI, qui cum culpa carent, tamen malum Metuunt, hi solent heris esse utibiles. Nam qui nihil metuunt, postquam sunt malum Meriti, multa sibi consilia expetunt. Exercent sese ad cursuram, fugiunt. Most. 4.1. v. 1. & seqq. Men. 5.6. v.22. Guntherus Ligur. lib. 2. verf. 33.
units.tr: Slaves who are free of fault yet fear punishment are usually useful to their masters. For those who fear nothing, once they have deserved punishment, devise many schemes for themselves. They train themselves to run; they flee. Most. 4.1. v. 1 and following. Men. 5.6. v. 22. Guntherus Ligur. lib. 2, v. 33.

units.la: SPECTAMEN bono servo id est, qui rem herilem Procurat, videt, collocat, cogitatque, Ut absente hero, rem heri diligenter Tutetur, quam si ipse adsit, aut rectius: Tergum, quàm gulam, crura, quàm ventrem oportet Potiora esse, cui cor modestè situm est. Men. 5. 6. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: The mark of a good slave is one who manages his master's property, watches over it, arranges it, and thinks how, while his master is away, he may guard his master's property as carefully as if he were present, or even more so. The back rather than the belly, the legs rather than the stomach, ought to be the first concern of one whose heart is modestly disposed. Men. 5.6. v. 1 and following.

units.la: Hominem servum suos Domitos habere oportet oculos, & manus, Orationem Mil. 2. 6. v. 80.
units.tr: A slave ought to have his eyes and hands tamed. Mil. 2.6. v. 80.

units.la: Quod olim de Prætore dixit Pericles: Prætorem decet non solum manus, sed etiam oculos abstinentes habere. Apud Ciceron. lib. 1. Offic. pag. 57. Edit. Robert. Steph.
units.tr: What Pericles once said of the praetor: "A praetor ought to have restrained not only his hands but also his eyes." Cicero, Off. lib. 1, p. 57, ed. Robert Stephanus.

units.la: Servi nutum sui heri scire debent: ut quod frons velit, oculi sciant. Aul. 4. 1. v. 13. Quod jubeat herus, citius quadrigis citius properet prosequi.
units.tr: Slaves ought to know their master's nod, so that what the brow wills, the eyes perceive. Aul. 4.1. v. 13. What the master commands, let him hasten to carry out more quickly than a chariot.

units.la: Servorum peculium sunt doli, astutiæ, sycophantiæ perjuria, &c. Asin. 3. 2. v. 2. Vide totum locum. Erant Perfossores parietum, fures, sacrilegi. Ibid.
units.tr: The slaves' perquisites are tricks, cunning, false accusations, perjuries, etc. Asin. 3.2. v. 2. See the whole passage. They were wall-breakers, thieves, and sacrilegious men. Ibid.

units.la: Satis spectatum est, Deos atque homines ejus negligere gratiam, cui herus est perjurus: & nauci. Poen. 4. 2. v. 1.
units.tr: It is well enough known that gods and men disregard the favour of one whose master is a perjurer, and it is not worth a nut. Poen. 4.2. v. 1.

units.la: Es ist kein Stern dabey / wann einer so ein losen Meister hat.
units.tr: There is no star in it when one has such a loose-living master.

units.la: Servi boni metuunt, ut à culpa abstineant. Men. 5. 6. v. 20.
units.tr: Good slaves fear, so that they keep away from fault. Men. 5.6. v. 20.

units.la: Par est, servum se instituere ad mores heri sui, & vultum ex vultu heri comparare. Amph. 3. 3. v. 5.
units.tr: It is right that a slave should train himself to his master's ways and shape his looks from his master's face. Amph. 3.3. v. 5.

units.la: Servorum est obedire heris etiam duris: quos Apostolus Petrus. 1. Pet. 2. 18. vocat οἰκέτας. Captiv. 2. 1. v. 6. Indigna digna habenda sunt, herus quæ facit. Et Capt. 2. 3. v. 44.
units.tr: It is the slave's duty to obey even harsh masters, whom the Apostle Peter, 1 Pet. 2.18, calls οἰκέτας [household servants]. Things undeserved must be counted as deserved, when the master does them. Capt. 2.1. v. 6. And Capt. 2.3. v. 44.

units.la: Æschylus:
units.tr: Aeschylus:

units.la: Ἀτλὰ δεσπότας ἀχνυ, χὴ δίκαια, ἢ ἀδίκα.
units.tr: Ἀτλὰ δεσπότας ἀχνυ, χὴ δίκαια, ἢ ἀδίκα. [But the sufferings of masters, whether just or unjust.]

units.la: Servi etiam cum periculo & damno suo fideles esse debent heris suis. Mil. 2. 4. v. 55. Merito reprehenditur Palæstrio, qui ita servum alloquitur:
units.tr: Slaves ought to be faithful to their masters even at their own risk and loss. Mil. 2.4. v. 55. Palaestrio is rightly rebuked, for he addresses his slave thus:

units.la: P A. Nate edepol stultitia tua pene perdidit, Dum te fidelem facere hero voluisti, pene absumtus es.
units.tr: P.A. Son, by Pollux, your folly has nearly ruined you. While you wished to make yourself faithful to your master, you were nearly destroyed.

units.la: Servus qui benè servijt spectatus satis dicebatur. Men. 5. 6. v. 1. Terent. Adelph. 5. 6.
units.tr: A slave who serves well was considered sufficiently tested. Men. 5.6. v. 1. Terence, Adelph. 5.6.

units.la: Servus probus officium suum sponte facere debet. Stich 1.2. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: A good slave ought to do his duty of his own accord. Stich. 1.2. v. 1 and following.

units.la: Plus oportet scire servum, quàm loqui. Mil. 2:5. v. 67. Tide Tit. Silentij.
units.tr: A slave ought to know more than he says. Mil. 2.5. v. 67. See the title "Of Silence".

units.la: Servorum est, quæ secius fiunt in familiâ, significare. Mil. 3. 2. v. 46.
units.tr: It is for slaves to report what is done otherwise in the household. Mil. 3.2. v. 46.

units.la: Ut servi volunt esse herum, ita solet esse. Bonus cum probis est, malus cum malis. Most. 4. 1. v. 17.
units.tr: As slaves wish their master to be, so he tends to be. A good master is with good people, a bad one with bad. Most. 4.1. v. 17.

units.la: Servitutis causæ, sæpè sunt casus & pericula varia. Rud. 1. 3. v. 37. Vide Jos. Merceri Opin. lib. 1. c. 9.
units.tr: The causes of slavery are often chance and various dangers. Rud. 1.3. v. 37. See Jos. Mercer's Opinions, lib. 1, c. 9.

units.la: Servi in expediundis negotijs utebantur hac formulâ: Si quid mevis, imperat. Capt. 5. 3. v. 1.
units.tr: In carrying out business, slaves used this formula: "If you want anything, command." Capt. 5.3. v. 1.

units.la: Herorum officium est, servis de se benè meritis benefacere. Mil. 4. 8 v. 54.
units.tr: It is the duty of masters to do good to slaves who have deserved well of them. Mil. 4.8. v. 54.

units.la: Servis non est obijcienda edacitas ab avaris heris. Trin. 4. 3. v. 9.
units.tr: Slaves should not be reproached with greed by greedy masters. Trin. 4.3. v. 9.

units.la: Frugi servorum est, onus herorum in se suscipere. Asin. 3. 3. v. 70.
units.tr: It is the mark of a good slave to take upon himself his master's burdens. Asin. 3.3. v. 70.

units.la: Iniquum est, servos heris succensere. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 57.
units.tr: It is unfair to be angry with slaves. Pseud. 1.5. v. 57.

units.la: Servi; qui culpâ carent, & metuunt, ij solent esse heris utibiles. Men. 5. 6. v. 22.
units.tr: Slaves who are free of fault and yet fear, these are usually useful to their masters. Men. 5.6. v. 22.

units.la: Servi etiam annulos in digitis gesserunt: Condalium. Trin. 4. 3. v. 7.
units.tr: Slaves also wore rings on their fingers: a condalium. Trin. 4.3. v. 7.

units.la: Miserrima isthæc miseria est servo bono, Apud herum, qui vera loquitur, si id vi verum vincitur. Amph. 2. 1. v. 43.
units.tr: This is the most wretched misery for a good slave, before a master, when he speaks the truth and the truth is overcome by force. Amph. 2.1. v. 43.

units.la: Decet innocentem servum atque innoxium, confidentem esse, suum apud berum potissimum. Capt. 3. 5. v. 7. Pseud. 1. 5. v. 45.
units.tr: It befits an innocent and blameless slave to be confident, especially before his master. Capt. 3.5. v. 7. Pseud. 1.5. v. 45.

units.la: Nequius nihil est, quàm egens consilij servus, nisi habet Multipatens pectus, ubicumque usus fiet, pectore expromat suo. Bacch. 4.4. v. 8. & seqq.
units.tr: Nothing is more wicked than a slave who lacks counsel, unless he has a broad breast, and wherever the need arises, he should bring it forth from his breast. Bacch. 4.4. v. 8 and following.

units.la: SERVI
units.tr: SERVANTS

units.la: SERVI sæpè importuni esse solent: aliisque imperare suâ importunitate. Curc. 2. 3. v.20.
units.tr: Slaves are often wont to be troublesome, and by their troublesomeness to command others. Curc. 2.3. v. 20.

units.la: IN servos vulgò convitium herile hoc factum: Perjurii caput ob summam perfidiam eorum. Pseud. 1.1. v.129. & 1. 2. v.1. Rud. 4.4. v.55.
units.tr: Commonly the master's reproach against slaves is this: "Head of perjury!" on account of their great faithlessness. Pseud. 1.1. v. 129, and 1.2. v. 1. Rud. 4.4. v. 55.

units.la: SERVI ad fraudandum herum callidi. Asin. 2, 1. v. 9.
units.tr: Slaves are clever at cheating their master. Asin. 2.1. v. 9.

units.la: NON decet superbum esse hominem servum. Asin. 2.4. v.64.
units.tr: It is not fitting for a slave to be proud. Asin. 2.4. v. 64.

units.la: QUI nequam & improbis servis utitur, & se & illos in diserimen adducit. Rud. 4. 7. v. 32.
units.tr: He who uses wicked and dishonest slaves brings both himself and them into danger. Rud. 4.7. v. 32.

units.la: SERVI ad comminiscendas fraudes aptissimi. Trin. 2.4.v.115.
units.tr: Slaves are most apt for devising frauds. Trin. 2.4. v. 115.

units.la: SERVI & famuli improbi domo fugiunt, quando verbera metuunt. Cas. 5.3. v.10.
units.tr: Wicked slaves and servants run away from home when they fear beatings. Cas. 5.3. v. 10.

units.la: Sic Symmach. l. 10. Ep. 13. Plurimi enim de familiâ domûs meâ per fugam elapsi.
units.tr: So Symmachus, lib. 10, Ep. 13: For many of the household of my house have escaped by flight.

units.la: Idem lib. 4. Ep. 48. Rebellem servum sibi adduci poscit, ad cujus investigationem, nec præcepti cœlestis auctoritas, nec Africani Comitis vigor potuit pervenire.
units.tr: The same author, Letter 48 of Book 4: he demands that a rebel slave be brought to him, for whose tracking down neither the authority of the heavenly command nor the vigour of the Count of Africa could prevail.

units.la: Ab Imperatore in leg. 8. de Jurisdict. & ubi quis deb. con. Cod. Theod. dicitur Servum fugax. Inde in venditionibus Servorum cautiones istæ: Servum non esse fugitivum: furem non esse. Salvianus lib. 4. de Gubernat. Dei: Multi à Dominis suis fugiunt, dum conservos timent.
units.tr: From the Emperor, in law 8, on jurisdiction and where a person ought to be sued, in the Theodosian Code, it is said a fugitive slave. Hence in the sale of slaves come those guarantees: that the slave is not a runaway, that he is not a thief. Salvian, Book 4 of On the Government of God: Many flee from their masters because they fear their fellow slaves.

units.la: SERVI solebant corrumpere filios heriles. Mostell. 1.1. v. 20. Præsertim heris suis absentibus peregrè. Ibid. v. 26, 27.
units.tr: Slaves used to corrupt their masters' sons, especially when their masters were away abroad. Mostellaria 1.1 vv. 20; 26, 27.

units.la: IMPROBUM par servorum introducit Plautus Asin. 2. 2. in quo malitiam, audaciam, astutiam servilem agnoscas prorsus admirabilem.
units.tr: Plautus introduces a wicked pair of slaves in the Asinaria 2.2, in whom you may recognise a thoroughly remarkable servile wickedness, audacity and cunning.

units.la: SERVI mendax hominum natio. Amph. 1. 1. v. 43. Si dixero mendacium, solens meo more fecero.
units.tr: Slaves are a lying race of men. Amphitruo 1.1 v. 43: If I tell a lie, I shall do it as I usually do.

units.la: SERVI furtes multiplici damno afficiunt heros. Caf. 3. 6. v. 3.
units.tr: Slaves burden their masters with losses in many ways through theft. Casina 3.6 v. 3.

units.la: SERVI leves & luxuriosi erant: nihil pensi habentes tergum suum, dummodò hilarè viverent. Pfeud. 1. 1. v. 126. Nunc edico amicis meis in hunc diem âme, ut caveant, me credant mihi.
units.tr: Slaves were frivolous and dissolute, caring nothing for their backs, so long as they lived merrily. Pseudolus 1.1 v. 126: Now I bid my friends to be on their guard until this day; believe me.

units.la: SERVI folebant esse astuti, versuti: & dominorum suorum imperia callidè perficere. Asin. 1. 1. v. 106.
units.tr: Slaves were accustomed to be clever and shrewd, and to carry out their masters' commands skilfully. Asinaria 1.1 v. 106.

units.la: SERVI iufideles sunt herilis pernicies. Moft. 1. 1. v. 2.
units.tr: Unfaithful slaves are the ruin of their masters. Mostellaria 1.1 v. 2.

units.la: SERVI mendaces Poëtis comparantur. Pseud. 1. 4. v. 8.
units.tr: Lying slaves are compared to poets. Pseudolus 1.4 v. 8.

units.la: MALUS & nequam est homo, qui nihili imperium heri sui servus facit: nihili est autem, suum qui officium facere immemor est, nisi adeò monitus. Pseud. 4. 7 v. 1. & seqq. De servorum ὀφδαλ- μοδυλείᾳ eadem praecipit Apostolus Paulus passim in suis Epistolis.
units.tr: He is a bad and worthless man who makes light of his master's command and treats it as nothing; and he who forgets to do his duty is worthless indeed, unless he is reminded. Pseudolus 4.7 v. 1 and following. On the eye-service [ὀφθαλμοδουλεία] of slaves. The Apostle Paul gives the same instruction throughout his Epistles.

units.la: SILENTII. TACITURNITATIS.
units.tr: SILENCE. TACITURNITY.

units.la: QUID quis scit, nescire debet. Baech. 2. 3. v. 90. & 4. 6. v. 21.
units.tr: What someone knows, he ought to pretend not to know. Baech. 2. 3. v. 90. & 4. 6. v. 21.

units.la: POSTHAC etiam illud, quod scies, nescieris. Ne videris, quod videris. Mil. 2. 6. v. 89. & Terent. Eunuch. 4. 4. v.
units.tr: Henceforth, too, you should act as if you did not know even what you do know. Do not seem to see what you have seen. Mil. 2. 6. v. 89. & Terent. Eunuch. 4. 4. v.

units.la: TACITURNITAS decet viros. Mulieres enim garrulae. Foen. 4. 2. v. 54.
units.tr: Taciturnity becomes men, for women are chatterboxes. Foen. 4. 2. v. 54.

units.la: CVM sermo est alterius, praesertim in convivijs, decet tacere adolescentem. Mil. 3. 1. v. 50. Vide Tit. Sermonis.
units.tr: When another is speaking, especially at a banquet, a young man should keep quiet. Mil. 3. 1. v. 50. See the title Speech.

units.la: PLUS oportet scire servum, quàm loqui. Epid. 1. 1. v. 57. Mil. 2. 5. v. 67.
units.tr: A slave ought to know more than he says. Epid. 1. 1. v. 57. Mil. 2. 5. v. 67.

units.la: Vegetius lib. 2. cap. 14. Centurio magis ad facienda, quae et imperarantur, quàm ad loquendum paratus sit.
units.tr: Vegetius, book 2, chapter 14: A centurion should be more ready for doing what is commanded than for speaking.

units.la: Julianus: Plus mehercle audire, quàm loqui militarem hominem decet, actibus coalitum gloriosis.
units.tr: Julianus: A soldier ought to hear much more than he speaks, being made up of glorious deeds.

units.la: Infidos celamus, non eos, qui sunt firmâ fide. Mil. 4. 2. v. 24, 25. Cedo mihi signum, si harum Baccharum es. In sacris enim Bacchi omnia reconditissima erant.
units.tr: We hide things from the unfaithful, not from those who have firm faith. Mil. 4. 2. v. 24, 25. Give me the password, if you are one of these Bacchae. For in the rites of Bacchus all things were most closely hidden.

units.la: Vide Tit. Sacrorum: Deorum.
units.tr: See the headings Sacred Rites: Gods.

units.la: Taciturnitas summa virtus, commendatur etiam ab muliere. Cist. 1. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: Taciturnity is the highest virtue; it is commended even by a woman. Cist. 1. 2. v. 7.

units.la: Quae tamen per ebrietatem violatur. Ibid.
units.tr: Yet it is violated by drunkenness. Ibid.

units.la: Res serias cum silentio audire decet. Trin. 1. 2. v. 110.
units.tr: Serious matters one should hear in silence. Trin. 1. 2. v. 110.

units.la: Societatis. Vicinia. Communionis.
units.tr: Of Fellowship. Neighbourhood. Communion.

units.la: Malis & improbis χάρμα ἐστιν ἐπὶ δεικνῦς ἔχειν ἐταίρας. Semper enim socios malorum quaerunt. Caf. 2. 6. v. 45. Epid. 1. 1. v. 70. Solus perire nolo. Vide Tit. Consolationis.
units.tr: For the wicked and the dishonest, it is a joy to have a companion in their wrongdoing [χάρμα ἐστιν ἐπὶ δεικνῦς ἔχειν ἐταίρας]. For they always seek out partners in crime. Caf. 2. 6. v. 45. Epid. 1. 1. v. 70. I alone do not want to perish. See the title Consolationis.

units.la: Flamma fumo proxima est. Curc. 1. 1. v. 53.
units.tr: The flame is next to the smoke. Curc. 1. 1. v. 53.

units.la: Solitudinis.
units.tr: Solitude.

units.la: De locis solitarijs proverbialiter dicitur: Neque magis sola terra sunt sola, quàm haec loca, atque hae regiones. Rud. 1. 4. v. 8.
units.tr: Of solitary places it is said proverbially: These places and these regions are no more lonely than the desolate land itself. Rud. 1. 4. v. 8.

units.la: Qui soli in umbrâ vitam degunt: Umbraticola dicti, per convitium. True. 2. 7. v. 48. de moechis amatoribus. Ut & Curc. 4. 3. v. 34. Vide Lex. Plaut. Lit. V.
units.tr: Those who live their lives alone in the shade are called umbraticola, "shade-dwellers," as a term of abuse. True. 2. 7. v. 48. is said of adulterous lovers. Likewise Curc. 4. 3. v. 34. See the Lexicon of Plautus, under the letter V.

units.la: SOMNI. SOMNIORUM. CORPORIS. VIGILIÆ.
units.tr: SLEEP. DREAMS. THE BODY. WAKEFULNESS.

units.la: SOMNUS homini necessarius. Merc. 2. 3. v. 36.
units.tr: Sleep is necessary for man. Merc. 2. 3. v. 36.

units.la: SOMNUS indicium valetudinis bonæ. Men. 5. 5. v. 29.
units.tr: Sleep is a sign of good health. Men. 5. 5. v. 29.

units.la: EQUI cantherij stantes somniant. Men. 2. 3. v. 44.
units.tr: Standing horses dream. Men. 2. 3. v. 44.

units.la: NON bonus somnus est homini de prandio. Most. 3. 2. v. 8. Pseud. 2. 2. v. 69.
units.tr: Sleep after dinner is not good for a man. Most. 3. 2. v. 8. Pseud. 2. 2. v. 69.

units.la: Ubi prandero, dabo operam somno.
units.tr: When I have dined, I will give myself to sleep.
And ibid. 4. 1. v. 14.

units.la: Scilicet mos erat veteribus, adeoque hodie quoque, æstivo tempore meridiè somnum leviusculum capere: quod dicebant, meridiare.
units.tr: Clearly it was the custom of the ancients, and so it still is today, to take a light sleep at midday in summer; they called this meridiating.

units.la: Varro de Re rustica lib. 1. c. 2. somnum insititium vocat.
units.tr: Varro, in De Re Rustica book 1, chapter 2, calls it insititius somnus, an added sleep.

units.la: Ego hic, ubi nox & dies modicè redit, & abit, tamen æstivo die, si non diffinderem meo insititio somno meridiem, vivere non pos-sem.
units.tr: I here, where night and day return and depart only moderately, could not live through a summer day if I did not split the midday with my added sleep.

units.la: Plæriq; Authores hunc somnum meridianum parùm probant.
units.tr: Most authors do not greatly approve of this midday sleep.

units.la: Oppianus lib. 5. de piscatorib. v. 616. ὕπνω τ' ὐχ ἁλίευσιν ἐοικότι μαλθάσσονται. Somno non conveniente piscatoribus effeminantur.
units.tr: Oppian, On Fishing book 5, v. 616: they are softened by sleep, which does not suit fishermen [ὕπνῳ τ' οὐχ ἁλιεῦσιν ἐοικότι μαλθάσσονται]. They are made effeminate by sleep unsuited to fishermen.

units.la: Homerus Iliad. 2. in viro Principe & Rege, itidem improbat: quod sicad litteratum iuflectas: ὐ χρὴ παννύχιον μισῶν δεδάπονται καθέυδειν, ᾧ βίλλοι ὅτι τετράφατα σοφιῶ μέμηλε.
units.tr: Homer, Iliad book 2, likewise disapproves of this in a prince and king: a man entrusted with counsel should not sleep all night, when the people depend on him and he has many cares [οὐ χρὴ παννύχιον εὕδειν βουληφόρον ἄνδρα].

units.la: Xenophon de militibus lib. 2, Cyripæd. ἀποκοιμηθῆναι ὥσον μέτριον. Vide extremo libri.
units.tr: Xenophon, On the Cyropaedia, book 2 on soldiers: to fall asleep only as much as is moderate [ἀποκοιμηθῆναι ὅσον μέτριον]. See the end of the book.

units.la: Democritus apud Stobæum: ἡμερήσιοι ὕπνοι σώματος ὀχλησιν, ἡ ψυχῆς ἀδημοσωνην, ἡ ἀργίην, ἡ ἀταιδευσίην σημαίνοντι
units.tr: Democritus, in Stobaeus: daytime sleeps indicate weakness of the body, or distress of the mind, or idleness, or lack of education [ἡμερήσιοι ὕπνοι σώματος ὄχλησιν, ἢ ψυχῆς ἀδημοσύνην, ἢ ἀργίην, ἢ ἀπαιδευσίην σημαίνουσι].

units.la: Antequam cubitum irent, lucernam prius exstinguebant. Mostell. 2. 2. v. 56.
units.tr: Before they went to bed, they first put out the lamp. Mostell. 2. 2. v. 56.

units.la: Nimis diu dormire, estignavorum. Rud. 42. v. 14. Vide Tit. Laboris.
units.tr: To sleep too long belongs to lazy men. Rud. 42. v. 14. See the title Laboris.

units.la: Solebant deprecari somnia thure aut mola falsa a prodigiali Jove, alijsq; Dis Averruncis. Id uno verbo dicebant comprecari. Amph. 2. 2. v. 108. Vide locum seq.
units.tr: They used to avert dreams with incense or salted meal, by the prodigy-averting Jove and the other averting gods. They called this in one word comprecari. Amph. 2. 2. v. 108. See the following passage.

units.la: Cum triste quid in somnijs viderant, prodigiali Jovi, ᾧ Σεῶς ἀπο-τροπαίοις sacrificabant. Quod vocabant Comprecari. Sic Palaestrio post somnij narrationem, jubet amicam herilem intro abire, & comprecari. Mil. 2.4.v.41. Amph. 2, 2. v. 106. Curc. 2. 1. v. 32. Vide Centurionatum Doufae pag. 253. Et Desid. Herald. Adverf. pag. 94.
units.tr: When they had seen something sad in their dreams, they sacrificed to Jove the averter of prodigies [Ζεὺς ἀποτροπαῖος], which they called comprecari. So Palaestrio, after the telling of a dream, bids his master's mistress go inside and comprecari. Mil. 2. 4. v. 41. Amph. 2. 2. v. 106. Curc. 2. 1. v. 32. See the Centurionatus of Doufa, p. 253, and Desiderius Heraldus, Adversaria, p. 94.

units.la: Somnia non semper fallunt: sed saepe praesentia omnia faciunt. Mil. 2.4. v. 41. Stich. 4.1. v. 38.
units.tr: Dreams do not always deceive, but often bring about everything they present. Mil. 2. 4. v. 41. Stich. 4. 1. v. 38.

units.la: Somnia in somnis immittunt Dij. Merc. 2. 1. v. 12. Vide Tit. Deorum.
units.tr: The gods send dreams within dreams. Merc. 2. 1. v. 12. See the title Deorum.

units.la: Somnia pro nihilo ducuntur. Men. 5.7. v. 57. Haec nihilo mihi esse videntur fecium, quam somnia.
units.tr: Dreams are counted as nothing. Men. 5. 7. v. 57. These things seem to me worth no more than dregs, than dreams.

units.la: In somno stertentes dicuntur sorbere. Mil. 3. 2. v. 6.
units.tr: Those who snore in sleep are said to sorbere. Mil. 3. 2. v. 6.

units.la: Sorbet dormiens? P A. Quid sorbet? L V. Illud stertit, volui dicere. Sed quia consimile est, quod stertat, quasi sorbeas. P A. Eho! an dormit? L V. Nonnaso quidem. Nam te magnum clamat.
units.tr: PA. Does he sorb while sleeping? LV. What does he sorb? Ah, he snores, I meant to say. But since it is similar, "stertat" is like "sorbeas." PA. Hey! Is he asleep? LV. Indeed he is snoring. For he is calling you loudly.

units.la: De Sopore sorbili vide Mercur. lib. 1. cap. 10.
units.tr: On sopor sorbilis see Mercurialis, book 1, chapter 10.

units.la: Somnus non capitur commode sine curis. Trin. 3. 1. v. 20.
units.tr: Sleep is not easily had without cares. Trin. 3. 1. v. 20.

units.la: SORTIS. SORTITIONIS.
units.tr: LOTS. CASTING OF LOTS.

units.la: SORTES mittebantur in sitellam plenam aquâ. Caf. 2. 4. v. 17. & 2. f. v. 33, 42. & 2. 6. v. 7, 11, 28. Suet. Neronec. 11, & Livius lib. 25.
units.tr: Lots were put into a bucket full of water. Cas. 2. 4. v. 17, and 2. 5. v. 33, 42, and 2. 6. v. 7, 11, 28. Suetonius, Nero 11, and Livy book 25.

units.la: Ex ligno populno vel abiegno, imò querno durissimo, ne in aquâ subsiderent, conficiebantur sortilegia: ijsque aliquid inscriptum. Caf. 2. 6. v. 26, 32, 61, 63.
units.tr: Divinations were made with lots of poplar or fir, or even very hard oak, so that they would not sink in the water; something was written on them. Cas. 2. 6. v. 26, 32, 61, 63.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Nuptiarum.
units.tr: See also the title Nuptiarum.

units.la: CRESPHONTES Messeniam sibi vultassignari. Itaque ut res componatur Temenum rogat, rem ut forti committat. Ille in situlam aquâ plenam fortes mittit: re ita constitutâ, ut utra sors prior exijsset, illi Messenia adjudicaretur. At ille Aristodemi quidem liberum fortem ex argillâ sole indurată: Cresphontis verò è cocţili laterculo fecit. Inde factum, ut illâ soluta hæc constituit: atque ita Cresphonti Messenia obtigerit. Hanc historiam tangit Plautus Caf. 2. 6. verf. 46. Recitatur autem integra apud Pausaniam.
units.tr: Cresphontes wanted Messenia assigned to himself. So, to settle the matter, he asks Temenus to entrust it to the chance of a lot. Temenus put lots into a bucket full of water, arranged so that whichever lot came out first would award Messenia to that man. But he made the lot of Aristodemus's son from clay hardened in the sun, and that of Cresphontes from a brick of unfired clay. Hence, when the lots were drawn, the clay one dissolved, and so Messenia fell to Cresphontes. Plautus touches on this story in Cas. 2. 6, v. 46; the full account is given by Pausanias.

units.la: Vide etiam P. Victor. Var. lib. 25.
units.tr: See also P. Victorius, Variae Lectiones book 25.

units.la: SPECTACULORUM.
units.tr: SPECTACLES.

units.la: Vide supra Tit. Ludorum: Fabularum: Scenæ.
units.tr: See above, the titles Ludorum, Fabularum, Scenae.

units.la: SERVI olim histrioniam faciebant. Vide Tit. Servorum.
units.tr: Slaves once performed as actors. See the title Servorum.

units.la: HISTRIONES inter se de victoriâ certarunt, & ei cui victoria adjudicata esset, præmium tributum est per Ædilem. Illa autem Victoria interdum non virtute, neque jure, sed ambitione & favore parabatur.
units.tr: Actors competed among themselves for victory, and the prize was awarded to the one judged victorious by the aedile. Yet that victory was sometimes won not by merit or justice, but by ambition and favour.

units.la: Amph. Prol. v. 65,76,85. Petron. Arbiter: Neve plausor in scena sedeat redemtus histrionis additus.
units.tr: Amph. Prol. v. 65, 76, 85. Petronius, Arbiter: "Let no applauder sit on the stage, bought off, added to the actor."

units.la: Plautus Poen. Prol. v. 37. Suetonius Nerone: Adversarios quasi plane conditionis ejusdem observare, captare, infamare, secreto numquam ex occursu maleficii incessere, acsi, qui arte praecellerent, corrumpere etiam solebat.
units.tr: Plautus, Poen. Prol. v. 37. Suetonius, Nero: he used to watch his rivals, who were of the same rank, to lie in wait for them, to slander them, and secretly, whenever they met, to attack them with harm; and as if to corrupt those who excelled in the art, he was accustomed to do so.

units.la: HISTRIONES Artifices dicti. Amph. Prol. v. 70.
units.tr: Actors were called artists. Amph. Prol. v. 70.

units.la: PALMA sive Victoria per Ædiles distributa. Amph. Prol. v. 72.
units.tr: A palm, or victory, was awarded by the aediles. Amph. Prol. v. 72.

units.la: IN fabulis omnia spectatorum causâ fiunt. Amph. I.1. v. 48.
units.tr: In plays everything is done for the sake of the spectators. Amph. 1. 1. v. 48.

units.la: SPECTACULORUM tempore, neque libellos dare, neque in jus vocare homines, fas erat. Caf. Prol. v. 27.
units.tr: During the time of the spectacles it was not lawful to hand out petitions or to summon people to court. Cas. Prol. v. 27.

units.la: OLIM parentes non facile filios dimiserunt ad spectacula. Merc. Prol. v. 67.
units.tr: In former times parents did not readily let their sons go to the spectacles. Merc. Prol. v. 67.

units.la: SPECULORUM.
units.tr: SPECULA (MIRRORS).

units.la: NON oris causâ modò homines æquum fuit Sibi habere speculum, ubi os contemplarent suum, Sed qui perspicere possent cor sapientiæ: Ubi id inspexissent, cogitarent postea Vitam ut vixissent olim in adolescentiâ. Epid. 3.3. v. 1, 2. & seqq.
units.tr: It was right for men to have a mirror not only for the sake of their face, where they might look at their own appearance, but also one that could show them the heart of wisdom. Having looked into it, they should then think about how they had lived in their youth. Epid. 3.3. v. 1, 2. & seqq.

units.la: De Speculi utilitate vide Apol. Apul. & inibi Scipionem Gentilem. Senec. Natur. Quæst. lib. 1. cap. 17. Martial. l. 9. 17. Phædri Fab. 47. & 6. ibique Rigaltium. & Plaut. Mostel. 1.3. v. 110. & ad illum locum Meurs. Part. 2. Exerc. Crit. c. 6.
units.tr: On the usefulness of the mirror, see the Apology of Apuleius and, there, Scipio Gentilis. Seneca, Natural Questions book 1 chapter 17. Martial book 9, epigram 17. Phaedrus, Fables 47 and 6, with Rigaltius there. And Plautus, Mostellaria 1.3, v. 110, & on that passage Meursius, Part 2 of Critical Exercises, chapter 6.

units.la: SPECULA etiam ex argento facta. Mostel. 1. 3. v. 110. Epid. 3. 3. v. 1.
units.tr: Mirrors were also made of silver. Mostellaria 1.3. v. 110. Epidicus 3.3. v. 1.

units.la: SPECULIS usi ad dignoscendas imagines ac formas. Men. 5. 9. v. 3.
units.tr: People used mirrors to distinguish images and shapes. Menaechmi 5.9. v. 3.

units.la: Mulier, quæ se suamque ætatem spernit, speculo ei usus est. Mostell. 1. 3. v. 92. Vide Meurs. part. 2. Crit. Exerc. c. 6.
units.tr: A woman who despises herself and her age used a mirror. Mostellaria 1.3. v. 92. See Meursius, Part 2, Critical Exercises, chapter 6.

units.la: Amasiæ placituræ suis amatoribus, ad speculum sese exornabant. Mostell. 1. 3. v. 90.
units.tr: Lovers who were about to please their suitors adorned themselves before the mirror. Mostellaria 1.3. v. 90.

units.la: Eædem speculum, & omnia ornamenta sua habebant recondita in arculis. Mostell. 1. 3. v. 90.
units.tr: The same women kept their mirror and all their ornaments stored away in little chests. Mostellaria 1.3. v. 90.

units.la: Speculi æquor, & planities clara esse debet. Mostell. 3. 1. v. 107. de Ædibus: Speculo claras, clarorem merum.
units.tr: The surface and flat plane of a mirror ought to be clear. Mostellaria 3.1. v. 107, concerning the house: "bright as a mirror, pure brightness."

units.la: Spectrorum.
units.tr: SPECTRA (APPARITIONS).

units.la: Vbi scelus in ædibus perpetratum, monstris & spectris illas infestari credebant. Mostell. 2. 2. v. 73.
units.tr: Where a crime had been committed in a house, people believed the house was haunted by monsters and specters. Mostellaria 2.2. v. 73.

units.la: In ludis circumferebantur spectra, seu terriculamenta, μορμολυκεῖα. Rud. 2. 6. v. 51.
units.tr: In the games, specters, or bugbears, were paraded about: mormolykeia [μορμολυκεῖα]. Rudens 2.6. v. 51.

units.la: Vide Tit. Ludorum: Mimorum.
units.tr: See the heading Games: Mimes.

units.la: Spei. Exspectationis. Eventūs.
units.tr: SPES (HOPE). EXSPECTATIO (EXPECTATION). EVENTUS (OUTCOME).

units.la: Spes olim à Collatino Romæ fuit consecrata, teste Cicer. lib. 2. de Leg. Cist. 4. 1. v. 18. Sancta spes mihi subveni!
units.tr: Hope was once consecrated at Rome by Collatinus, as Cicero reports in book 2 of On the Laws. Cistellaria 4.1. v. 18. "Holy Hope, come to my aid!"

units.la: Insperata accidunt magis sæpè, quàm quæ speres. Mostell. 1. 3. v. 40. MULTA praeter spem scio multis bona evenisse. AM. At ego etiam qui speraverint, spem decepisse multos. Rud. 2.3.v.70.
units.tr: Unexpected things happen far more often than the things you hope for. Mostellaria 1.3. v. 40. "I know that many good things have happened to many people beyond their hope." AM. "But I also know that many who did hope have been disappointed by their hope." Rudens 2.3. v. 70.

units.la: STULTUM est exspectare ea, quae nusquam sunt. Curc.1.2.v.56.
units.tr: It is foolish to expect things that are nowhere to be found. Curculio 1.2. v. 56.

units.la: SPONGIAE. PENICILLI.
units.tr: SPONGIAE. PENICILLI (SPONGES. BRUSHES).

units.la: SPONGIAE plenae aquâ aut humore alio exurgentur. Rud. 4.3. v. 71.
units.tr: Sponges full of water or other moisture are squeezed out. Rudens 4.3. v. 71.

units.la: SPONSIONIS.
units.tr: SPONSIONIS (OF SURETYSHIP).

units.la: REDEMTORES datis sonsoribus, & factis syngraphis suo periculo opus aliquod faciundum conduxerunt. Bacch. 4.4. v. 100. Meâ fiducia opus condnxi: & meo periculo rem gero. ἀλλ᾽ γοεικῶς.
units.tr: Contractors, having provided sureties and drawn up bonds, undertook some work at their own risk. Bacchides 4.4. v. 100. I have undertaken the work on my own confidence, and I carry out the business at my own risk. But, as the saying goes [ἀλλ᾽ γοεικῶς].

units.la: PRO alio spondere periculosum. Rud. Prol. v.37.
units.tr: To stand surety for another is dangerous. Rudens, Prologue, v. 37.

units.la: Dum alios servat, se impedivit interim.
units.tr: While he keeps others safe, he has in the meantime hindered himself.

units.la: SPUTI. SPUTATIONUM. INSPUTATIONUM.
units.tr: SPUTI. SPUTATIONUM. INSPUTATIONUM (SPITTING. SPITTINGS. SPITTING UPON).

units.la: AD omnia dira & horribilia arcenda, solebant exspuere: ut si rabiosum, si comitiali morbo correptum vidissent, &c. Capt. 3.4.v.21. Vide Morborum: & Abominationis.
units.tr: To ward off all dire and horrible things, people used to spit: for example, when they saw someone mad with rabies or seized by the falling sickness, and so on. Captivi 3.4. v. 21. See the headings Diseases and Abomination.

units.la: STATURÆ.
units.tr: STATURA (STATURE).

units.la: Vide Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See the heading Man.

units.la: STATURA commoda seu justa censebatur olim septem pedum: vel utalij, sex. Asin. 2. 3. v. 21. Vide quaeso Commentarium Isaaci Casauboni in Suetonium pag. 226. Item Godefch. Stewechium in Veget. lib. 1. c. 5. nec non Brodaei Miscell. lib. 4. cap. 19.
units.tr: A convenient or proper stature was once reckoned to be seven feet, or, according to others, six. Asinaria 2.3. v. 21. Please see Isaac Casaubon's commentary on Suetonius, p. 226. Likewise Godefridus Stewechius on Vegetius book 1, chapter 5, and also Brodaeus's Miscellanies book 4, chapter 19.

units.la: STELLARUM. SIDERUM. ASTRORUM. CÆLI.
units.tr: STELLARUM. SIDERUM. ASTRORUM. CAELI (STARS. CONSTELLATIONS. HEAVENLY BODIES. SKY).

units.la: ARCTOPHYLAX seu Arcturus ad femur seu coxam Bootæ, stella splendens, candida: oritur diebus 11. ante æquinoctium autumnale. Noctu in cælo clarus est Arctur° inter Deos, inter mortales ambulat interdius. Rud. Prol. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: Arctophylax, or Arcturus, a bright, shining, white star at the thigh or hip of Boötes, rises eleven days before the autumnal equinox. At night Arcturus shines bright in the sky among the gods; by day he walks among mortals. Rudens, Prologue v. 1 and following.

units.la: ARCTURUS signum omnium accerrimum, vehemens cum exoritur: vehementius cum occidit. Rud. Prol. v. 70. Horat. lib. 3. Od. 1.
units.tr: Arcturus is the most keen of all signs, violent when it rises, and more violent when it sets. Rudens, Prologue v. 70. Horace, book 3, Odes 1.

units.la: NEQUE se Septemtriones quoquam in cælo commovent, Neque se Luna quoquam motat, Neque Jugula, neque Vesperugo, neque Vergiliæ occidunt. Amph. 1,1. v. 116.
units.tr: Neither do the Septentriones move anywhere in the sky, nor does the moon move anywhere, nor do the Hyades, the Evening Star, or the Pleiades set. Amphitruo 1.1. v. 116.

units.la: Vide Lex. Plaut. Jugula.
units.tr: See the Plautine lexicon, under Jugula.

units.la: STELLÆ Jovi facinora hominum annunciant. Rud. Prol. v. 10. Is non per gentes alium aliutà disparat, hominum qui facta, mores, pietatem, & fidem noscamus, ut quemque adjutet opulentia: qui falsas lites falsis testimonijs petunt: quíque in jure abjurant pecuniam, eorum referimus nomina exscripta ad Jovem.
units.tr: The stars announce men's deeds to Jove. Rudens, Prologue v. 10. He does not sort people by nation or by tribe, so that we may know men's deeds, morals, piety and good faith, and how wealth helps each one. Those who seek false lawsuits by false testimony, and who swear falsely in court about money, we record their names, written out, for Jove.

units.la: Stomachi. Cibi.
units.tr: Stomach. Food.

units.la: Vide Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See the heading Man.

units.la: Stomachi ἀνομοξίαν sæpè sedat mutatio loci: ubi cibi melius beant, aut juvant. Capt. 1. 2. v. 27. Vide etiam Asin. 1. 2. v. 16. & Most. 3. 1. v. 2.
units.tr: A change of place often relieves stomach complaints [ἀνορεξίαν] where the food agrees better or does more good. Capt. 1. 2. v. 27. See also Asin. 1. 2. v. 16, and Most. 3. 1. v. 2.

units.la: Strenarum. Præmiorum. Munerum. Donorum.
units.tr: Strenae, Gifts, Presents, Donations.

units.la: Calendis Martijs Matronæ Junoni sacrificabant, ut is annus ab exordio totus eis esset felix & faustus, & in partu & in amore conjugali: atq; etiam munera sibi missitare solebant. Mil. 3. 1. v. 96. Atque hæc festa Matronalia dicebantur.
units.tr: On the Calends of March matrons used to sacrifice to Juno, so that the whole year from its beginning might be happy and fortunate for them, both in childbirth and in married love; and they also used to send one another presents. Mil. 3. 1. v. 96. These festivals were called Matronalia.

units.la: Juvenal.
units.tr: Juvenal.

units.la: Munera femineis tractat secreta Calendis.
units.tr: The secret gifts of women are handled on the Calends.

units.la: Martial. lib. 8. Ep. 86. Saturnalia muliebria appellat.
units.tr: Martial, book 8, epigram 86. He calls them the Saturnalia of women.

units.la: Vide Macrob. lib. 1. c. 9. Tibull. Eleg. 1. l. 3. & l. 4. Eleg. 2. Item Comment. Cruq. ad Horat. lib. 3. Od. 8. nec non Servium ad 8. Æneid. Virg.
units.tr: See Macrobius, book 1, chapter 9; Tibullus, Elegies 1, line 3, and Elegy 4, 2; likewise the commentary of Cruquius on Horace, book 3, Ode 8; and also Servius on the 8th book of Virgil's Aeneid.

units.la: Stultitiæ. Nugarum. Sycophantiæ. Scurrarum.
units.tr: Foolishness. Trifles. Sycophancy. Buffoonery.

units.la: Qui cum stulto agit, stultior est.
units.tr: Whoever deals with a fool is the greater fool.

units.la: Graphicum sycophantæ characterem vide totâ illâ scenâ 2. act. 4. Trin.
units.tr: For a vivid picture of the sycophant, see the whole scene of Trin. 2. act 4.

units.la: Et stultè facere, & stultè fabulari utrumq; interdum haud est bonum. Trin. 2. 4. v.61.
units.tr: To act foolishly and to talk foolishly, both at once, is at times not good. Trin. 2. 4. v. 61.

units.la: Stulti saxo comparantur. Mil. 4. 2. v. 33. Nullum est hoc stolidius saxo.
units.tr: Fools are compared to a stone. Mil. 4. 2. v. 33. "Nothing is more stupid than a stone."

units.la: Stulti comparantur sui occisæ, quæ plus sapit, quàm stulti. Mil. 2. 6. v. 104.
units.tr: Fools are compared to those who have killed themselves; the one who is wiser than fools. Mil. 2. 6. v. 104.

units.la: Cum insanis fabulari stultum. Mil. 2. 4. v. 18.
units.tr: To talk with madmen is foolish. Mil. 2. 4. v. 18.

units.la: Successus.
units.tr: Success.

units.la: Successus in omnibus rebus animos parat. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 18. & Mil. 4. 1. v. 1.
units.tr: Success puts spirit into everything. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 18, and Mil. 4. 1. v. 1.

units.la: Volupe est, quod agas, si id procedat lepidè ex sententiâ.
units.tr: It is a pleasure to do what you do, if it turns out nicely as you wished.

units.la: Sudoris.
units.tr: Sweat.

units.la: Qui sudat, tremit. Asin. 2. 2. v. 23. alluditur ad sudiculum flagelli genus Festo, dictum quod vapulantes sudantes facit. Alius quippe sudor est ab externo calore, alius ab æstu animi & tremore. Hippocrates: ἐπὶ ἱδρῶτι φύσιν ἡ χρησίν. Propert. Eleg. 2. 2. lib. 2.
units.tr: He who sweats, trembles. Asin. 2. 2. v. 23. It alludes to the sudiculum, a kind of whip, which Festus says is so called because it makes those who are whipped sweat. For one sweat comes from external heat, another from the agitation and trembling of the mind. Hippocrates: in the case of sweat, the nature or the use [ἐπὶ ἱδρῶτι φύσιν ἡ χρησίν]. Propertius, Eleg. 2. 2, lib. 2: "If perhaps she has harshly refused me anything with her face, cold water grew warm over my whole brow."

units.la: Quæ si forte aliquid vultu mihi dura negavit, Frigida de totâ fronte calebat aqua.
units.tr: On this sweat and its causes, Passeratius, in his Prælectiones, p. 333, has gathered many other remarks, in other passages.

units.la: Ad quem locum multa παρὰ λλα de hoc sudore, & ejus causâ procreante collegit magnus Passeratius. pag. 333. Prælect.
units.tr: See also Caelius Rhodiginus, lib. 6, c. 4, Antiq. Lect.

units.la: Vide etiam Cæl. Rhodig. lib. 6. c. 4. Antiq. Lect.
units.tr: See also Caelius Rhodiginus, book 6, chapter 4, Antiquae Lectiones. ## Of Suspicion.

units.la: Suspicionis.
OMnes bonos bonasque accurare addecet, suspicionem & culpam, ut ab se segregent. Trin. 1. 2. v. 41. Ausonius:
units.tr: All good men, both men and women, ought to take care to keep suspicion and blame away from themselves. Plautus, Trinummus, act 1, scene 2, line 41. Ausonius:

units.la: nec vero crimine ladar,
units.tr: Nor stained by doubt; they seem to differ a little,

units.la: Nec maculer dubio. paulum differre videntur
units.tr: Suspected and perhaps guilty." And Trin. 3. 3. v. 54.

units.la: Suspectus vereq; reus. Et 3. 3. v. 54.
units.tr: "Suspected, and perhaps a defendant." And act 3, scene 3, line 54.

units.la: Caesar apud Suetonium:
units.tr: Caesar, as quoted by Suetonius:

units.la: Tam suspicione, quam crimine carere oportet.
units.tr: "A man ought to be free of suspicion as well as of crime."

units.la: UTRUM vitari possit suspicio, disputat Senex Trin. 1. 2. v. 45. Rationem addit:
units.tr: Whether suspicion can be avoided, the old man discusses in the Trinummus, act 1, scene 2, line 45. He adds a reason:

units.la: Ne admittam culpam, ego meo sum promtu pectori. Suspicio est in pectore alieno sita. Exemplo etiam illustrat sententiam suam. Quis prohibebit, quo minus suspicer te Jovi surripuisse coronam? An tu propterea surripuisti?
units.tr: "I am ready in my own heart not to commit a fault. Suspicion lies in another's heart." He also illustrates his opinion with an example: "Who will prevent me from suspecting that you stole the crown from Jupiter? Or did you steal it for that reason?"

units.la: VEL suspicio probri, nobis gravis esse solet. Amph. 1. 2. v. 27.
units.tr: Even the suspicion of disgrace is usually grievous to us. Amphitruo, act 1, scene 2, line 27.

units.la: Suspicio saepe fallit. Mil. 2. 4. v. 48.
units.tr: Suspicion often deceives. Miles Gloriosus, act 2, scene 4, line 48.

units.la: Suppliciorum. Carnificum. Carceris. Crucis. Tortorum. Lorariorum. Quaestionis. Suspendii. Mortis.
units.tr: Punishments. Executioners. Prison. Cross. Torturers. Lorarii. Questioning. Hanging. Death.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Servorum.
units.tr: See also the title Servorum.

units.la: SUPPLICII genus apud Carthaginenses fuit, sub cratim supponere, & lapides multos imponere, ut necetur.
units.tr: One kind of punishment among the Carthaginians was to place a hurdle over a man and pile many stones on it, so that he was crushed to death.

units.la: Tacitus lib. de mor. Germ.
units.tr: Tacitus, in his book on the manners of the Germans.

units.la: Proditores & profusos arboribus suspendunt: ignavos & imbecilles, & corpore infames, caeno ac palude, injecta insuper crate, mergunt.
units.tr: They hang traitors and deserters from trees; the cowardly and feeble, and those infamous in body, they drown in mud and marsh, with a hurdle thrown on top.

units.la: Livius
units.tr: Livy.

units.la: Ad vociferationem eorum, quos sub crate necari jusserat concur-fusfatio.
units.tr: At the cries of those whom he had ordered to be killed under the hurdle, there was a running together.

units.la: Vide Stewech ad Veget. lib. 3. & Miscell. Brodæi lib. 1. c. 28.
units.tr: See Stewech on Vegetius, book 3, and Brodaeus' Miscellanies, book 1, ch. 28.

units.la: SUPPLICIUM servorum virgæ & stimulus erant. Mil. 2. 6. v. 22, 31.
units.tr: For slaves, the rod and the goad were the punishment.

units.la: LOCUS pœnæ coquis furibus destinatus, dicebatur Puteum: sive hypogæum, & barathrum, in quod conditi. Græci λάκκος vocabant.
units.tr: The place of punishment set aside for thieving cooks was called the Puteum, the Well; or it was an underground pit and cesspit into which they were put. The Greeks called it lakkos [λάκκος].

units.la: Ulpianus appellat malam mansionem. Aul. 2. 5. v. 20. Coqui abstulerunt, comprehendite, vincite, verberate, in puteum condite.
units.tr: Ulpian calls it a bad dwelling. Aul. 2. 5. v. 20. The cooks have taken him; seize him, bind him, beat him, shut him down in the well.

units.la: Vide Parerg. Scip. Gentil. lib. 1. c. 39. Turn. l. 6. c. 24.
units.tr: See Parergon of Scipio Gentilis, book 1, ch. 39; Turnebus, book 6, ch. 24.

units.la: ROBUR in carcere est is locus, quo præcipitatur maleficorum genus: quod ante arcis robustis includebatur. Plautus appellat robustum codicem. Pœn. 5. 3. v. 53. & Custodem ligneam. Pœn. 5. 6. v. 28.
units.tr: The robur in prison is the place into which a class of criminals is thrown down; formerly they were shut up in strong towers. Plautus calls it a robust block, Poen. 5. 3. v. 53, and a wooden guard, Poen. 5. 6. v. 28.

units.la: Livius Decad. 4. l. 8. Ut in carcere inter fures nocturnos vir clarissimus Scipio includatur; in robore ac in tenebris exspiret. Hor. l. 2. Od. 13. Ilalum robur appellat. Vide Lipsij Cpmment. Tacit lib. 4. Ann. & Turneb. l. 23. cap. 21. nec non Lex. Plaut. Et Colvium ad Apul. Apol. & Aufon. Popm. ad Catonem. Habebant etiam antiqui in carceribus Arcas, in quas maleficos includebant. In earum locum successit Robur. Curc. 5. 3. v. 14.
units.tr: Livy, Decad. 4, book 8: That the most distinguished man, Scipio, be shut up in prison among the night thieves, and expire in the oak and in darkness. Horace, book 2, Odes 13, calls it the Italian oak. See Lipsius' commentary on Tacitus, Annals book 4; Turnebus, book 23, ch. 21; also the Plautine lexicon; and Colvius on Apuleius' Apology and Ausonius; Pompeius on Cato. The ancients also had in prisons arcae, chests in which they enclosed criminals. The robur succeeded to their place. Curc. 5. 3. v. 14.

units.la: OB crimen in carcerem compacti: & post sub furcâ virgâ cæsi. Men. 5. 5. v. 40.
units.tr: For a crime, shut up in prison, and afterwards beaten with rods under the fork. Men. 5. 5. v. 40.

units.la: SUB furcâ non omninò occisi. Ibid. vide Lipf. de Cruce. lib. 3. cap. 2.
units.tr: Beaten under the fork, but not wholly killed. Ibid. See Lipsius, de Cruce, book 3, ch. 2.

units.la: DIERECTI suspendebantur. Capt. 3. 4. v. 103.
units.tr: Those directi were hanged. Capt. 3. 4. v. 103.

units.la: Vide Tit. Servorum prolixè. Moft. 1. 1. v. 8.
units.tr: See the title Servorum at length. Most. 1. 1. v. 8.

units.la: Vide etiam Lex. Plaut. Dierectus.
units.tr: See also the Plautine lexicon, under Dierectus.

units.la: NERVUS supplicij genus. Aul. 4. 10. v. 13. At ego credo Deos voluisse, ut apud te me in nervum eniceus.
units.tr: The nervus was a kind of punishment. Aul. 4. 10. v. 13. But I believe the gods wanted me to be thrown into the nervus at your house.

units.la: S E R V I proprie in malis constituti, ad suspendium solebant confugere, tamquam ad extremum remedium malorum suorum. Caf. 2. 7. v. 1. & 3. 4. v. 9. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 88.
units.tr: Slaves, properly placed in misfortune, were accustomed to flee to hanging as the last remedy for their troubles. Cas. 2. 7. v. 1, and 3. 4. v. 9; Pseud. 1. 1. v. 88.

units.la: M O R S iuimicis solet voluptatem creare. Caf. 2. 7. v. 1. Sic Petron. Attulissem mihi damnatas manus: si non inimici victoria invidissem.
units.tr: Death is wont to give pleasure to enemies. Cas. 2. 7. v. 1. So Petronius: I would have brought the condemned hands upon myself, if I had not begrudged my enemy his victory.

units.la: S U P P L I C I O adjudicati, jubebantur duci, & rapi sublimes. Mil. 5. v. 1.
units.tr: Those adjudged to death were ordered to be led away and dragged up aloft. Mil. 5. v. 1.

units.la: S U P P L I C I O affecti, jurabant de non referenda vindicta. Mil. 5. v. 17.
units.tr: Those subjected to death swore not to take revenge. Mil. 5. v. 17.

units.la: S U P P L I C I U M Crucis vile fuit apud Romanos, maxime servorum. Mil. 2. 4. v. 19. Noli minitari, scio, inquit Servus ipse, crucem futuram mihi sepulchrum.
units.tr: Crucifixion was a cheap punishment among the Romans, especially for slaves. Mil. 2. 4. v. 19. Don't threaten me, I know, says the slave himself; the cross will be my tomb.

units.la: I N poenam elinguabantur. Aul. 2. 2. v. 72.
units.tr: As punishment they were tongue-cut. Aul. 2. 2. v. 72.

units.la: I T E M Q U E. & castrabantur. Aul. 2. 2. v. 73.
units.tr: And also they were castrated. Aul. 2. 2. v. 73.

units.la: S E R V I in crucem acti, fractis pedibus, & brachijs. Mosl. 2. 1. v. 11. Vide Taub. pag. 537. Et Scalig. ad Eusch. pag. 110.
units.tr: Slaves put on the cross, with legs and arms broken. Most. 2. 1. v. 11. See Taubmann, p. 537; and Scaliger on Eusebius, p. 110.

units.la: I N crucis medio stipite erat tabella prominentior, cui insistebant fontes. Unde eo dicuntur excurrere. Mosl. 2. 1. v. 12. Vide Lipf. de Cruce lib. 2. cap. 7, 9, 10. & P. Molinaeum Notis in Epistolas Gregorij Nisseni, ubi docetur, quatuor clavis cruci affigi solitos.
units.tr: In the middle upright of the cross there was a small projecting board on which the feet rested; hence they are said to run out. Most. 2. 1. v. 12. See Lipsius, de Cruce, book 2, chs. 7, 9, 10; and P. Molinaeus' notes on the letters of Gregory of Nyssa, where it is shown that four nails were customarily fixed to the cross.

units.la: E T I A M in sedes sceleratorum animadversum. Mil 2. 3. ver. 39. Truc. 2. 8. v. 8. Vide Val. Max. lib. 6. c. 3. Quintil. lib. 3. c. 7. Vide etiam Ravard. lib. 1. c. 7. Var.
units.tr: Even the seats of the wicked were used for punishment. Mil. 2. 3. v. 39; Truc. 2. 8. v. 8. See Valerius Maximus, book 6, ch. 3; Quintilian, book 3, ch. 7. See also Ravardus, book 1, ch. 7, Var.

units.la: D I S P E S S I S & expansis manibus servi gerebant patibulum crucifigendi extra portam Metiam sive Esquilinam. Mil. 2. 4. v. 7. Omnia enim supplicia apud Romanos fumi solita extra portas, ne frequenti caede ac sanguine contaminari oculi civium, aut delibari videretur libertas. Atque in eum finem carnifex domum habuit extra urbem. Caf. 2.6.v.2. Pfeud. 1.3.v.96. Vide etiam Muret. Var. lib.9. c.13. & Isiac. Casaub. ad Charact. Theophrafti Vide Lipf. de Cruc. lib.3. cap.7. & Schoppij Suspect. lib. 5. Epift. 3.
units.tr: With their hands stretched out and spread, slaves carried the crossbeam for crucifixion outside the Metian or Esquiline gate. Mil. 2. 4. v. 7. For all the Romans' customary punishments were carried out outside the gates, so that the eyes of citizens should not be polluted by frequent slaughter and blood, nor liberty seem to be violated. And to this end the executioner kept his house outside the city. Cas. 2. 6. v. 2; Pseud. 1. 3. v. 96. See also Muretus, Var. book 9, ch. 13; Isaac Casaubon on the Characters of Theophrastus; Lipsius, de Cruce, book 3, ch. 7; and Schoppius, Suspectae lectionis, book 5, letter 3.

units.la: CARNIFICES fuerunt carceris custodes, non triumviri capitales.
units.tr: The executioners were the jailers of the prison, not the capital triumvirs.

units.la: Inde eodem modo dicebant: In carcerem: & ad carnificem trahere. Triumviri autem curam custodiæ carceris habuerunt: non fuerunt autem ipsi custodes. Rud. 3.6.v.19.
units.tr: Hence they said in the same way: to prison, and to drag to the executioner. The triumvirs, however, had charge of the prison's custody, but were not themselves the jailers. Rud. 3. 6. v. 19.

units.la: SERVI à carnifice stimulis fodicbantur, ut tergum perforatum videretur,& quasi cribrum. Unde natum illud convitium: Carnificum cribrum! Moft. 1.1.v.52. Vide Taub. p.518.
units.tr: Slaves were pricked with goads by the executioner, so that their back seemed pierced through, like a sieve. Hence that insult: Executioner's sieve! Most. 1. 1. v. 52. See Taubmann, p. 518.

units.la: PER vias ferebant furcam sive patibulum. Inde Patibulatus servus, & furcifer. Moft. 1.1.v.53. 66.
units.tr: Through the streets they carried the fork, or crossbeam. Hence a slave with a crossbeam and fork-bearer. Most. 1. 1. v. 53, 66.

units.la: COLUMBAR genus vinculi. Rud. 2.6. v.49.
units.tr: Columbar, a kind of fetter. Rud. 2. 6. v. 49.

units.la: Illic in columbum credo leno vortitur. nam in columbari collum haud multo post erit. In nervum hodie mille nidamenta conge-ret.
units.tr: There, I believe, the pimp will turn into a dove; for soon there will be a neck in the dovecote. Today he will gather a thousand nests into the nervus.

units.la: SERVIS crura fracta. Inde crurifragium. Pfeud. 1.1.v.178. Afin. 2. 4.v.68. Vide Lipf. de Cruce lib.2.c.14. Mil. 2.3.v.23. Rud. 4. 4.v.15.
units.tr: Slaves had their legs broken. Hence leg-breaking. Pseud. 1. 1. v. 178; Asin. 2. 4. v. 68. See Lipsius, de Cruce, book 2, ch. 14. Mil. 2. 3. v. 23; Rud. 4. 4. v. 15.

units.la: GENUS quoddam tormenti sunt, cum ferventi pice instillatu corpora hominum urebantur. Capt. 3.4.v.65. Atra pix agitet apud carnificem, tuoq; capiti illuceat. Lucretius: Verbera, carnifices, robur, pix lamina, teda.
units.tr: There was a certain kind of torture: human bodies were burned by having boiling pitch dripped onto them. Capt. 3. 4. v. 65. May black pitch stir at the executioner's place, and shine upon your head. Lucretius: Lashes, executioners, the rack, pitch, the plate, the torch.

units.la: In urbe non sumebatur supplicium de fontibus: sed extra urbem: quo quidem trahit illud Caf. 2.6.v.2. Turneb.in Comment. Orat. pro C. Rabirio. p.25. quando servus sic de suo hero queritur ad heram: Ille edepol videre, ardentem te extra portam Metiam vult. Sed fortassis eo non trahendum, ob summam indignitatem.
units.tr: In the city, punishment was not inflicted by torches but outside the city; and this is indeed the sense of Cas. 2. 6. v. 2, see Turnebus' commentary on Cicero's oration for C. Rabirius, p. 25, where a slave complains of his master to the mistress: He, by Pollux, wants you burned outside the Metian gate. But perhaps this is not to be drawn in here, on account of the extreme indignity.

units.la: SUPPLICII genus fuit, tædas ardentes applicare corpori. Quò forte allusum. Mero. 3.4. v.32. Montes tu quidem mali ardentes in me jacta. Vide Dalech, ad Plin. lib. 14. c 20. & Brodæi Misc. lib 2 c. 10.
units.tr: One kind of punishment was to apply burning torches to the body. Perhaps there is an allusion to this: Mer. 3. 4. v. 32. You indeed throw burning mountains of evil upon me. See Dalechamps on Pliny, book 14, ch. 20; and Brodaeus, Miscellanies, book 2, ch. 10.

units.la: Qui capita tecerant, fugere solebant. Men. 1. 1. v. 16.
units.tr: Those who had covered their heads used to flee. Men. 1. 1. v. 16.

units.la: CONFESSIONIS per tormenta expressæ, lubrica est fides. Ideoque Callicles ille Truc. 4 3 v. 8 ancillarum confessioni non ante fidem habuit, quam aliam rursum abijt post tormenta exegisset. Ibid. v. 5. & 6. Vide Taub p. 1219. Et Langl. Otij Semest. libb. p. 582. Et Tit. Servorum.
units.tr: Faith in confessions extracted by torments is slippery. So that Callicles in the Truculentus 3. 4? Truc. 4. 3. v. 8 did not give credence to the confession of the maidservants until, after he had tortured them, he had gone off and extracted another one. Ibid. v. 5 and 6. See Taubmann, p. 1219; Langius, Otium Semestre, p. 582; and the title Servorum.

units.la: ETIAM ancillæ aloratijs vinctæ sunt: & pendentes quæstioni dadæ. Ibid. v. 4.
units.tr: Even maidservants were bound with thongs and, hung up, were given over to questioning. Ibid. v. 4.

units.la: TORTURA interdum extrudit veritatem: ob dolorem. Ibid. v. 9.
units.tr: Torture sometimes forces out the truth, through pain. Ibid. v. 9.

units.la: IN quæstione diversi stare debent, ut eliciatur veritas. Ibid v. 14.
units.tr: In questioning, those under examination must be kept apart, so that the truth may be drawn out. Ibid. v. 14.

units.la: CARNIFICES extra portam Metiam habitabant Romæ. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 97. Ubi appellantur per jocum Lanij cum tintinnabulis.
units.tr: Executioners lived in Rome outside the Metian gate. Pseud. 1. 3. v. 97. There they are called, in jest, butchers with bells.

units.la: DAMNATI ad supplicium, duci jubebantur. Capt. 3. 5. v. 63. Vide Lex. Ducere.
units.tr: Condemned persons were ordered to be led off to execution. Capt. 3.5, v. 63. See the lexicon, under "Ducere".

units.la: VINCULI ferrei genus erat præter furcam, Canis in pœnâ servorum. Caf. 2. 6. v. 36.
units.tr: The iron fetter was a kind of punishment for slaves, besides the fork-shaped stocks (canis). Cas. 2.6, v. 36.

units.la: PUDOR pœnæ loco subrogari solet. Most. 5. 2. v. 43. Vide Tit. Pudoris.
units.tr: Shame is commonly substituted in place of punishment. Most. 5.2, v. 43. See the title "Pudoris".

units.la: MALEFICIS oculos exurebant. Men. 5. 2. v. 89.
units.tr: They burned out the eyes of malefactors. Men. 5.2, v. 89.

units.la: TALIFRAGIUM inter supplicia servilia. Mil. 2. 2. ver. 1. ut & Crurifragium: paulo ante.
units.tr: Talifragium (breaking of the ankles) was among the servile punishments, as also crurifragium (breaking of the legs), mentioned a little earlier. Mil. 2.2, ver. 1.

units.la: SYLVARUM. LUCORUM.
units.tr: GROVES AND SACRED WOODS.

units.la: SYLVANUS præses lucorum. Aul. 4. 6. v. 8. Ubi apparet, in lucis quoq; salicta fuisse. Nam quod Taubmannus legere ibi malit: lacus Sylvani, ineptum est.
units.tr: Sylvanus, the overseer of groves. Aul. 4. 6. v. 8. Here it appears that there were also willow thickets in the groves. For Taubmann's preference to read "the lake of Sylvanus" in that place is absurd.

units.la: TEM.
units.tr: TEM.

units.la: T.
units.tr: T.

units.la: Templi. Aræ. Asyli.
units.tr: Temples. Altars. Asylum.

units.la: Vide plura supra Tit. Injuriarum.
units.tr: See more above under the title Injuriarum.

units.la: IN templis consilia capiebant sedendo. Most. 5. 1. v. 55.
units.tr: In temples they took counsel while seated. Most. 5. 1. v. 55.

units.la: IN templis perpetuò ædituus collocatus. Curc. 1. 3. v. 48.
units.tr: In temples a sexton was always stationed. Curc. 1. 3. v. 48.

units.la: JURANTES Aræ ansulas tangebant, & tenebant. Rud 5. 2. v. 49. Vide Tit Juramenti.
units.tr: Those swearing an oath touched and held the little rings of the altar. Rud 5. 2. v. 49. See the title Juramenti.

units.la: AB ara neminem licebat vi abripere: ut tamen arcerentur inde, admovebant ignem, atq; ita non ab hominibus, sed à Deo Vulcano amoveri credebantur. Most. 5. 1. v. 65. & 5. 2. v. 14. Rud. 3. 4. v. 55. Turn. lib. 9. c. 12.
units.tr: No one was permitted to drag someone away from the altar by force. Yet to keep them from it, people brought fire near, and so they were believed to be driven off not by men but by the god Vulcan. Most. 5. 1. v. 65. & 5. 2. v. 14. Rud. 3. 4. v. 55. Turn. lib. 9. c. 12.

units.la: Temporis. Dierum. Auroræ. Noctis.
units.tr: Time. Days. Dawn. Night.
