units.la: PER tempus obviam ire scitum est. Pœn. 1. 1. v. 7.
units.tr: It is proverbial to meet time halfway. Pœn. 1. 1. v. 7.

units.la: TEMPORIS pretiosa parsimonia, præsertim ætate juvenili. Most. 1. 2. v. 70. & seqq.
units.tr: A precious thrift of time, especially in youthful years. Most. 1. 2. v. 70. & seqq.

units.la: ITANE quod tu occæperis negotium agere, id totum procedit diem. Pers. 1. 3. v. 35.
units.tr: So that whatever business you have begun turns out well all day long. Pers. 1. 3. v. 35.

units.la: DIERUM alij fasti erant, alij nefasti. Aul. 2. 8. v. 10. Pœn. 3. 2. v. 7. Varro lib. 5. de L L. Dies fasti, per quos Prætoribus omnia verba sine piaculo licet fari. Comitiales dicti, quod tum esset populus constitutus ad suffragium ferendum. Contrarij horum vocantur dies nefasti: per quos dies nefas fari Praetorem Do, Dico, Addico. Vide Tit. Praetoris.
units.tr: Some days were fasti, others nefasti. Aul. 2. 8. v. 10. Pœn. 3. 2. v. 7. Varro, book 5 of De Lingua Latina: Dies fasti, days on which the praetors may speak all formulas without sin, are so called. They were called comitiales because the people were then assembled to cast their votes. The opposite of these are called dies nefasti, days on which it is unlawful for the praetor to say Do, Dico, Addico. See the title Praetoris.

units.la: Dies senex dicitur contabescere. Stich. f. 1. v. 8.
units.tr: A day is said to grow old and waste away. Stich. f. 1. v. 8.

units.la: Jupiter fingitur noctem longiorem fecisse, cum Alcumenam uxorem Amphitruonis comprimeret. Amph. Prol. v. 113.
units.tr: Jupiter is imagined to have made the night longer when he lay with Alcmena, the wife of Amphitryon. Amph. Prol. v. 113.

units.la: Non solet bellum dirimere. Amph. 1. 1. v. 98. Vide Tit. Belli.
units.tr: It does not usually bring an end to war. Amph. 1. 1. v. 98. See the title Belli.

units.la: Ad concubium noctis vesperi faces accensae. Trin. 4. 2. v. 44. Vide Joh. Lalamantij Tractatum.
units.tr: At the coming on of night, torches are lit in the evening. Trin. 4. 2. v. 44. See the treatise of Joh. Lalamantius.

units.la: Juventus Attica noctu solebat graffationibus suis turbare publicam pacem. Amph. 1. 1. v. 2. Vide Tit. Graffationum.
units.tr: Attic youth used to disturb the public peace at night with their assaults. Amph. 1. 1. v. 2. See the title Graffationum.

units.la: Noctu milites in vigiliam eunt. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 84.
units.tr: At night soldiers go on watch. Pseud. 4. 7. v. 84.

units.la: Prima pars noctis dicebatur Conticinium, νυκτὸς ἀρχὴ. Der erste Schlaf. Asin. 3. 3. v. 95.
units.tr: The first part of the night was called Conticinium, [νυκτὸς ἀρχὴ], the beginning of the night; the first sleep. Asin. 3. 3. v. 95.

units.la: Noctu scortatores cubare solebant in cellis meretricum: ita, ne viderentur. Amph. 1. 1. v. 132. Et si quando quis à lenone scorti alicujus noctem conduxerat, primo diluculo abeundum illi fuisse, docet Juvenalis Sat. 6.
units.tr: At night whoremongers used to lie in the cells of prostitutes, so that they would not be seen. And if anyone had hired a prostitute's night from her pimp, he had to leave at first daybreak, as Juvenal teaches in Satire 6. Amph. 1. 1. v. 132.

units.la: Nox ea, quâ Hercules est gemitus omnium longissima fuisse fingitur. Amph. 1. 1. v. 122. Nam ut Seneca ait: Violentus ille nocte non unâ potuit creari. Unde & Lycophroni τρισέλνν, item λέων, leo trinox: & τρίσωμος Αλκείδης vocatur. Statius lib. 12. Ternoctem Herculeam dixit. Alij tamen duas memorant Ovid. lib. 1. Eleg. 13. Amor. Ipse Deum genitor, ne te tam sepe videret, commisit noctes in sua vota duas.
units.tr: That night in which Hercules' groaning is said to have been longest is imagined. Amph. 1. 1. v. 122. For, as Seneca says: That violent man could not have been conceived in one night. Hence Lycophron calls it a [τρισέληνον] three-moon night, and also a three-night lion, and Alcides is called [τρίσωμος] three-bodied. Statius, book 12, spoke of the Ternoctem Herculeam, Hercules' three-night. Others, however, mention two nights; Ovid, book 1, Elegy 13 of the Amores: The father of the gods himself, so that he would not see you so often, granted two nights to his desires.

units.la: Propertius lib. 2. Eleg. 22.
units.tr: Propertius, book 2, Elegy 22.

units.la: Juppiter Alcmenae geminas requieverat Arctos: Et calum noctu bis sine rege fuit.
units.tr: Jupiter had let the twin Arctics rest for Alcmena, and the sky was twice without a king by night.

units.la: Ad quem locum vide Prælectiones Passeratij, ubi egregia in hancrem. pag. 335.
units.tr: On this passage see the Lectures of Passerat, where there is an excellent discussion of this matter, p. 335.

units.la: De nocturnis grassatoribus: vide Tit. Graffationum.
units.tr: On nocturnal robbers, see the title Graffationum.

units.la: Testium. Testimonii.
units.tr: Witnesses. Testimony.

units.la: Pluris est oculatus testis unus, quàm auriti decem. Qui audiunt, audita dicunt: qui vident planè sciunt. Truc. 2. 6. v. 8. Vide Taub. pag. 1199. Philo: Qui auritos testes accipit, is vanè, non sanè accipit. Herodotus: Aures minus sunt fida hominibus, quàm oculi. Seneca Epist. 6. Plus homines oculis, quàm auribus credunt. Joannes Chrysostomus Homil. 14. Epist. ad Hebr. ἡ ἀκοὴ ἡμῶν ἀμαθεστέρα τῆς ὄψεως ἐστιν. ὃ γὰρ ὤτως, ἄπερ ἀν ἰδωμεν αὐτ ὀφθεῖν.
units.tr: One eyewitness is worth more than ten earwitnesses. Those who hear report what they have heard; those who see know for certain. Truc. 2. 6. v. 8. See Taub. p. 1199. Philo: He who accepts ear-witnesses accepts them rashly, not soundly. Herodotus: Ears are less trustworthy to men than eyes. Seneca, Epist. 6: Men trust their eyes more than their ears. John Chrysostom, Homily 14 on the Epistle to the Hebrews: Our hearing is more ignorant than sight [ἡ ἀκοὴ ἡμῶν ἀμαθεστέρα τῆς ὄψεως ἐστιν]. For what we see, we see with our own eyes.

units.la: Sic in Jure civili non creditur testi se audisse dicenti, sed se vidisse. Quomodo hæc applicet ad testimonium in concubitu duorum, vide Albericum Gentil. de Nupt. l. 7. c. 10. pag. 786.
units.tr: So in the civil law, a witness who says he heard something is not believed; he must say he saw it. On how this applies to testimony about the intercourse of two people, see Albericus Gentilis, De Nuptiis, bk. 7, ch. 10, p. 786.

units.la: Plautus Pœn. 3. 3. v. 93. Quid si evocemus huc foràs Agorastoclem, ut ipse sit testis certissimus.
units.tr: Plautus, Poen. 3. 3. v. 93: What if we call Agorastocles out here, so that he himself may be the most certain witness?

units.la: Sic Priapeja: Ludens hæc ego, teste te, Priape, Scripsi non nimium laboriose.
units.tr: So in the Priapeia: I wrote these playful lines, with you as witness, Priapus, and not very laboriously.

units.la: Testimonium sensuum & inprimis oculorum certissimum. Rud. 4. 4. v. 23. Hic ejus eccillum vidulum. G R. Non habeo. T R. Negas quod oculis video?
units.tr: The testimony of the senses, and above all of the eyes, is most certain. Rud. 4. 4. v. 23: Here is his little trunk. G: I haven't got it. T: Are you denying what I can see with my own eyes?

units.la: Qui de eo testimonium perhibet, quod pono parietem, vel aulæum, aut conopeum constitutus audiverit, vel cùm ad ostium staret, vel per rimam seu fissuram inspexerit, in jure fidem facere creditur. Quò pertinet illud Caf. 2. 8. v. 7. ubi Chalinus servus retrocedit ad parietem nepam imitaturus ad captandum domini cum villico sermonem. Quod autem ibi de nepa dicitur: ferè sic exprimit alius servus Pseud. 4. 1. v. 45.
units.tr: A person who bears witness to something he heard while standing behind a wall, a curtain, or a canopy, or while standing at the door, or who looked through a crack or chink, is believed in law. To this belongs that passage in Cas. 2. 8. v. 7, where the slave Chalinus steps back against the wall, imitating a viper, in order to catch the conversation of his master with the farm overseer. What is said there about the viper, another slave expresses in much the same way in Pseud. 4. 1. v. 45.

units.la: Non prorsus: verum ex transverso cedit, quasi cancer solet. Poen. 3.3. v.67. & 3.5. v.22.De hoc testimonij genere pluribus agit Janus Langl. JC. lib. 4. Otij Semestr. c.2. Vide caput hoc.
units.tr: Not at all; rather it moves sideways, as a crab usually does. Poen. 3. 3. v. 67, and 3. 5. v. 22. Janus Lanclius, Otium Semestre, bk. 4, ch. 2, treats this kind of testimony at more length. See this chapter.

units.la: INTESTABILES erant, qui nefasti fuerant, quibus non licebat in jus aut comitium venire. Poen. 3.2. v.7. Vide Rævard. Conject. lib.2.c.20.
units.tr: The intestabiles were those who were unlawful (nefasti) and were not permitted to come into court or to the assembly. Poen. 3. 2. v. 7. See Revardus, Conjectures, bk. 2, ch. 20.

units.la: TESTIMONIUM sensuum praesertim oculorum, certum, & infallibile. Sic ille Mil.2.3.v. 60,74,75. & 2.4 v.15. Mihi ego video, mihi ego sapio, mihi ego credo plurimum: Me homo nemo deterruerit, quin ea sit in his aedibus. Sic Amph. II. v.290.
units.tr: Testimony of the senses, especially of the eyes, is certain and infallible. So that man in Mil. 2. 3. vv. 60, 74, 75, and 2. 4. v. 15: I see for myself, I know for myself, I believe very much for myself: no man will talk me out of it, that she is in this house. So also in Amph. 2. v. 290.

units.la: Novi herum, novi adeo nostras, sane sapio et sentio: Non ego illi obtempero, quod loquitur.
units.tr: I know my master, I know our people, indeed I understand and feel it well: I do not obey what he says.

units.la: HOMINES infames & intestabiles, ut fures, lenones, & id genus hominum, sine ante testatione in jus trahere licebat. Curc. 4.4. v.9. Ne facias testes.
units.tr: Men who were infamous and disqualified as witnesses, such as thieves, pimps, and that kind of person, were permitted to be dragged into court without a prior summons. Curc. 4. 4. v. 9: Don't make them witnesses.

units.la: UNUS testis poterit quandoque testari. Amph. 2.2. v.193.
units.tr: A single witness can sometimes give testimony. Amph. 2. 2. v. 193.

units.la: IN regraviori testes requirebant. Poen. 1.2. v.15. & 3.1.v.61. Adduce testes tecum: aurum scil. & servum tuum.
units.tr: In more serious cases they required witnesses. Poen. 1. 2. v. 15, and 3. 1. v. 61: Bring witnesses with you, namely gold and your slave.

units.la: RES ipsa quoque testatur. Aul. 3.2.v.7. Etsi taceas, palam id quidem est, res ipsa testis est.
units.tr: The thing itself also bears witness. Aul. 3. 2. v. 7: Even if you keep silent, it is plain enough; the thing itself is the witness.

units.la: ABSENTES testes nominare nefas. Merc. 3.4. v.42. Deos absentes testes memoras: qui ego istuc credam tibi?
units.tr: It is wrong to name absent witnesses. Merc. 3. 4. v. 42: You cite gods who are absent as witnesses; why should I believe you in that?

units.la: AD rem constabiliendam testibus utebantur. Poen. 5.2. v.12.
units.tr: They used witnesses to confirm a matter. Poen. 5. 2. v. 12.

units.la: TESTIMONIUM sensus oculorum ita certum putatur, ut etiam alienis fides habeatur. Mil. 4.2. v.14.
units.tr: The testimony of the sense of sight is considered so certain that even another's word is believed. Mil. 4. 2. v. 14.

units.la: TESTUDINUM. OSTREARUM.
units.tr: TESTUDINES. OYSTERS.

units.la: OSTEARUM testae scruposae sunt, & rimosae, seu cavernosae. Poen. 1.2. v.186. ἀλληγοεικῶς. Testudinum gradus, tardus in proverbium abijt. Amph. DI vostram. v. 52. Cui opponitur Grallatorium. Aul. I. I. v. 10.
units.tr: Oyster shells are rough and fissured, or hollow. Poen. 1.2. v.186. Allegorically. The gait of tortoises has passed into a proverb, slow as a tortoise. Amph. DI vostram. v. 52. Opposed to this is the Grallatorium. Aul. I. I. v. 10.

units.la: Timoris. Metus. Pavoris.
units.tr: Of Fear. Dread. Terror.

units.la: PER metum multa male agimus. Aul. 2. 2. v. 70.
units.tr: Through fear we do many things badly. Aul. 2. 2. v. 70.

units.la: IN pavore cor solet salire, non minus atque in hilaritate profusa. Capt. 3. 4. v. 103. Caf. 2. 6. v. 9, 62. Vide Tit. Hominis : Cordis.
units.tr: In terror the heart is wont to leap, no less than in overflowing joy. Capt. 3. 4. v. 103. Cas. 2. 6. v. 9, 62. See the title Man: Heart.

units.la: HORAE hybernae breviores aestivis. Pseud. 5. 2. verf. 11. Vide Coel. Rhod. lib. 12. c. 9. Antiq. Lect.
units.tr: Winter hours are shorter than summer ones. Pseud. 5. 2. verse 11. See Coel. Rhod. lib. 12. c. 9, Antiq. Lect.

units.la: PRAE metu sanguis dicitur emigrare e corpore. Most. 2. 2. v. 75. Guttam haud habes sanguinis.
units.tr: From fear, the blood is said to flee from the body. Most. 2. 2. v. 75. You have not a drop of blood.

units.la: METUS a culpa abstinere solent. Men. 5. 6. v. 20.
units.tr: Through fear people are wont to abstain from fault. Men. 5. 6. v. 20.

units.la: QUEM metuimus, eundem & amare possumus. Poen. 1. 2. v. 70. Vide Tit. Religionis.
units.tr: Whom we fear, we are also able to love. Poen. 1. 2. v. 70. See the title Religion.

units.la: METUS saepe nos facit ea reticere, quae ex re nostra sunt. Aul. 2. 1. v. 12.
units.tr: Fear often makes us keep silent about things that concern our own affairs. Aul. 2. 1. v. 12.

units.la: NON tantum mulieres, sed etiam viri armati, quandoque extimescunt. Mil. 4. 6. v. 58.
units.tr: Not only women, but even armed men sometimes tremble. Mil. 4. 6. v. 58.

units.la: TIMOR solet praepedire dicta linguae. Caf. 3. 5. v. 25. 59.
units.tr: Fear is wont to hinder the words of the tongue. Cas. 3. 5. v. 25, 59.

units.la: IN summo metu caput operiebant. Most. 2. 1. v. 76. Vide Cultus : Habitus.
units.tr: In great fear they covered their heads. Most. 2. 1. v. 76. See Dress: Habit.

units.la: METUS & pudoris signum est, non audere contra oculis adspicere. Caf. 5. 3. v. 2. Vide Def. Herald. lib. 2. c. 4.
units.tr: Not to dare to look straight at someone in the face is a sign of both fear and shame. Cas. 5. 3. v. 2. See Def. Herald. lib. 2. c. 4.

units.la: Tonsorum. Tonstrinæ.
units.tr: Barbers. Barber-shops.

units.la: IN tonstrinis solebant sedere, & quasvis nugas expiscari. Asin. 2. 2. v. 76. Unde natum Proverb. Lippis & tonsoribus notum.
units.tr: In barber-shops people used to sit and pick up all sorts of trifles, Asin. 2.2 v.76. Hence the proverb: "Known to the bleary-eyed and to barbers."

units.la: Duo tonsorum genera tondendi: unum strictim: alterum per pectinem, injiciendo involucrum, quod Græci ὑμόλινον vocant. Strictim autem tondere: est tondere ad cutem ἐν χεφὶ κείειν. Glatt hinweg. Per pectinem est paulo longius à cute interposito pectine tondere: Über den Kamp scheren. ἀλληγοϊκῶς illa de fallacijs effert noster Capt. 2. 2. v. 18.
units.tr: There are two ways of shaving. One is strictim (close shaving); the other is per pectinem (with a comb), where a covering is put on, which the Greeks call ὑμόλινον. To shave strictim is to shave right down to the skin, [ἐν χερὶ κείειν]: "glatt hinweg" (smooth off). To shave per pectinem is to shave somewhat further from the skin, with a comb interposed: "über den Kamm scheren" (shear over the comb). Our author uses the word [ἀλληγοϊκῶς] of deceits in that sense, Capt. 2.2 v.18.

units.la: Etiam tonstrices mulieres, sive ancillæ, erant in familia, Truc. 4. 2. v. 59.
units.tr: Women barbers, or maidservants, were also kept in a household, Truc. 4.2 v.59.

units.la: Tonsores etiam ungues demserunt: unde præsegmina collecta ab avaro Euclione. Aul. 2. 4. v. 33.
units.tr: Barbers also cut nails, and so the clippings were gathered up by the miserly Euclio, Aul. 2.4 v.33.

units.la: Tributi. Censûs.
units.tr: Tribute. Census.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Vectigalis. Et sup. Tit. Decimarum.
units.tr: See also the title Vectigalis, and above, the title Decimarum.

units.la: MULIERES etiam tributum pendebant magistratui. Epid. 2. 2. v. 41. 42. Tributum, cum imperatum est, pendi posse negant. Illis quibus tributus major penditur, pendi potest.
units.tr: Women too paid tribute to the magistrate, Epid. 2.2 vv.41-42. "When a tribute is imposed, they deny that it can be paid. Those on whom a larger tribute is levied can pay it."

units.la: Tutelæ. Pupillorum.
units.tr: Guardianships. Of wards.

units.la: PATRE mortuo, frater sororis pupillæ legitimus tutor est: eiq; dotem dat. Curc. 5. 2. v. 63.
units.tr: When the father has died, the brother of the ward's sister is her lawful guardian, and he gives her a dowry, Curc. 5.2 v.63.

units.la: VASO-
units.tr: VESSEL-

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: VASORUM. TESTARUM. AMPHORÆ. OLARUM. INSTRUMENTORUM. CRIBRI. ARMORUM.
units.tr: Of vessels, pots, amphorae, jars, instruments, sieves, and arms.

units.la: VASA vinaria habebant varia: sinum, epichysin, cantharum, gaulum, cyathum. Rud. 5.2. v. 32. Vide de singulis Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: Vessels for wine they had in various kinds: the sinus, the epichysis, the cantharus, the gaulus, and the cyathus. Rud. 5.2, v. 32. See each in the Plautine lexicon.

units.la: VASA, Arma, Testas, seu amphoras litteris inscriptas habebant: unde Epistolæ fictiles dicuntur. Poen. 4.2.v.14. & 2.5. v.21. Litterata urna. & 4.4. v.iii. de Crepundijs: Ensiculum litteratum est: in quo nomen patris inscriptum est. Post altrinsecus est scouricula ancipes. Item litterata aurea: ibi matris nomen est. & 5. 2. v.7. Urna litterata: & ensiculum litteratum.
units.tr: They had vessels, urns, tiles, or amphorae inscribed with letters, whence they are called letter-tiles [Epistolæ fictiles]. Poen. 4.2, v. 14, and 2.5, v. 21: a lettered urn. And 4.4, v. 3, on children's toys: the little sword is lettered, having the father's name inscribed on it. Afterwards, on the other side, there are two-edged scourges. Likewise a golden lettered thing, where the mother's name is. And 5.2, v. 7: a lettered urn and a lettered little sword.

units.la: Petronius:
units.tr: Petronius:

units.la: Statim allatæ sunt amphoræ vitreæ diligenter gypsatæ, quarum in cervicibus pittacia erant affixa: cum hoc titulo: FALERNUM. OPIMIANUM. ANNORUM. CENTUM.
units.tr: Immediately there were brought glass amphorae, carefully plastered with gypsum, on whose necks labels were attached, with this inscription: FALERNIAN, OPIMIAN, ONE HUNDRED YEARS OLD.

units.la: Idem Schidium affixum ampullis, cui inscripta ætas vini. Crebra hujus moris mentio apud Horatium. Loca igitur ταξάλνλα huc pertinent.
units.tr: The same author mentions a placard attached to the flasks, on which the age of the wine was written. Frequent mention of this custom is found in Horace. The passages on the ταξάλνλα [taxalyla] therefore belong here.

units.la: VASA, pocula ex Samio luto, vilioris erant pretij. Stich. 5 2. v. 12.
units.tr: Cups made of Samian clay were of cheaper value.

units.la: OMNIA vasa, ut & marsupia diligenter obsignabant. Men. 5.7.v. 47. & salvis signis, si quid asservatum fuit, reddebant.
units.tr: They sealed up all vessels, as also purses, carefully; and if anything had been kept, they returned it with the seals intact.

units.la: VASA, ut & cistulæ, solebant signis herorum obsignari. Amph. I, v. 263. & 2.2. v.142.
units.tr: Vessels, as also little boxes, were accustomed to be sealed with the seals of the masters. Amph. 1, v. 263, and 2.2, v. 142.

units.la: VASA Samia citò confringi solent. Bacch 2.2. v 24.
units.tr: Samian vessels are often quickly broken. Bacch. 2.2, v. 24.

units.la: VASA obsignabantur. Perf. 2. 3. v. 15. Vide paulò ante.
units.tr: Vessels were sealed. Perf. 2.3, v. 15. See a little above.

units.la: CRIBRO nihil pellucidius. Rud 1. 2. v. 14.
units.tr: Nothing is more transparent than a sieve. Rud. 1.2, v. 14.

units.la: MATULA abjectissimum vas in domo. Perf. 4. 3. v. 64.
units.tr: A matula is the most worthless vessel in a house. Perf. 4.3, v. 64.

units.la: VECTIGALIS. PORTUS.
units.tr: Customs duties. Harbour.

units.la: AD portus maris portitores sunt, qui exquisitè omnia indagant. Men. 1. 2. v. 2.
units.tr: At the harbours of the sea are the tax-collectors, who inquire into everything with care. Men. 1.2, v. 2.

units.la: POPULI Romani vectigalia erant è portubus: quæ Portoria dicebantur: è pascuis: quæ Scripturæ (quia publicanus scribendo rationem cum pastore conficiebat: ob quod & ager scripturarius dicitur) ex arationibus, quæ Decimæ. Truc. 1. 2. v. 40.
units.tr: The public revenues of the Roman people came: from the harbours, and these were called portoria; from the pastures, and these were called scripturae (because the publican made his account by writing with the herdsman, and for this reason land too is called scripturarius); and from the ploughed fields, and these were called decimae. Truc. 1.2, v. 40.

units.la: Cicero pro Leg. Man. Neque ex portu, neq; ex Decumis, neque ex scriptura vectigal conservari potest.
units.tr: Cicero, pro Lege Manilia: "Revenue cannot be preserved neither from the harbour, nor from the tithes, nor from the pasture-tax."

units.la: Et Verr. 4. Qui sit iste Verrutius Mercator an arator, an pecuarius.
units.tr: And in the Verrines, book 4: "What sort of man is that Verrutius: a merchant, or a ploughman, or a herdsman?"

units.la: Vide Turneb. lib. 1. cap. 5. & Festum Pomp.
units.tr: See Turnebus, book 1, chapter 5, and Festus Pompeius.

units.la: VENATIONIS.
units.tr: Of hunting.

units.la: IN saltibus capiuntur apri. Unde proverbium illud: Uno in saltu lepidè apros capiam duos. Caf. 2. 8. v. 42.
units.tr: Boars are caught in the woods. Hence that proverb: "In one wood I shall neatly catch two boars." Cas. 2.8, v. 42.

units.la: VENATORES lupum & feras reliquas in plagas per canes agunt. Pœn. 3. 3. v. 34.
units.tr: Hunters drive the wolf and the other wild beasts into the nets with dogs. Poen. 3.3, v. 34.

units.la: STULTITIA est, venatum ducere invitas canes. Stich. 1. 2. v. 82.
units.tr: It is folly to lead unwilling dogs out to hunt. Stich. 1.2, v. 82.

units.la: VENATORES plagis utuntur. Rud. 3. 1. v. 13.
units.tr: Hunters use nets. Rud. 3.1, v. 13.

units.la: VEHICULORUM. PLAUSTRORUM. CURRUUM. LECTICÆ.
units.tr: Vehicles, Wagons, Chariots, Litters.

units.la: VEHICULORUM duo erant genera. Sirpea, & Tintinnabulum. Pseud. 1 3. v.97. Vide Scalig. ad Varronem.
units.tr: There were two kinds of vehicles: the sirpea and the tintinnabulum. Pseud. 1.3, v. 97. See Scaliger on Varro.

units.la: Mulis mulabusque plurimum usi sunt veteres ad carrucas trahendas, quibus plærumque insidebant honestiores matronæ. Aul. 3.4.v.20.31. Scævola: Quæsitum est, an carruca dormitoria cum mulie, cum semper uxor usa sit, debeatur. Respondit, si ejus usus causa habita esset, deberi. Paullus JC. lib. 9. de Legat. lib. 3.
units.tr: The ancients used mules and mule-drawn teams very much for pulling carriages, in which for the most part the more distinguished matrons rode. Aul. 3.4, vv. 20–31. Scaevola: "It was asked whether a sleeping-carriage with its mule is owed, since the wife had always used it. He answered that if it had been kept for her use, it is owed." Paulus, jurist, Book 9 on Legacies, Book 3.

units.la: Muliones de urbano ministerio erant.
units.tr: The muleteers belonged to the urban service.

units.la: Martial. lib. 3 Epigr. 63.
units.tr: Martial, Book 3, Epigram 63.

units.la: Aurea quod fundi pretio carruca paratur:
units.tr: "Since a gilded carriage is bought for the price of an estate,"

units.la: Quod pluris mula est, quam domus emta tibi.
units.tr: "and the mule costs more than the house bought for you."

units.la: De Lecticis vide Lipsium in Electis.
units.tr: On litters see Lipsius in the Electa.

units.la: VENEFICII. VENEFICARUM. VENENI.
units.tr: POISONING. POISONERS. POISON.

units.la: VENEFICÆ in convivijs condicrunt condimenta, quæ intestina exederent. Pseud. 3.2.v.31.
units.tr: Poisoners at banquets prepared seasonings that would eat away the entrails. Pseud. 3.2.v.31.

units.la: Mulieres olim veneficæ, dictæ Sagæ, Simulatrices, Fictrices, Veratrices μοφοωτρίαι. Aul. 1.2.v.8. Trivenefica.
units.tr: Women who were once poisoners, called witches, deceivers, fabricators, enchantresses (pharmacists of magic) [μοφοωτρίαι]. Aul. 1.2.v.8. Trivenefica.

units.la: Venenum & cicutam bibebant in periculis constituti. Rud. 2. 3. v. 31.
units.tr: They drank poison and hemlock when placed in danger. Rud. 2. 3. v. 31.

units.la: Veneni haustum imprecabantur inimicis. Pers. 5.2. v.42.
units.tr: They wished a draught of poison upon their enemies. Pers. 5.2. v.42.

units.la: Toxicum mortiferum est. Merc. 2. 4. v. 4.
units.tr: Poison is deadly. Merc. 2. 4. v. 4.

units.la: VENIÆ: Vide supra Tit. EXCUSATIONIS.
units.tr: PARDON (VENIA): See above, under the title EXCUSATION.

units.la: AB ætate sæpè veniam impetramus culpæ. Mere 5. 4. v. 37.
units.tr: From youth we often obtain pardon for our faults. Mere 5. 4. v. 37.

units.la: VERITATIS.
units.tr: TRUTH.

units.la: VERITAS vi interdum extorquetur. Truc. 4. 3. v. 9.
units.tr: Truth is sometimes extorted by force. Truc. 4. 3. v. 9.

units.la: VERMIUM. LUMBRICORUM.
units.tr: WORMS. EARTHWORMS.

units.la: LUMBICI è terrâ erépunt. Aul. 4. 4. v. 1. Foràs lumbrice, quì sub terrâ crepsti modò, qui modò nunquam comparebas: nunc cum compares, perit. Ita Græcis dicuntur ἔντερα γῆς.
units.tr: Earthworms crawl out of the ground. Aul. 4. 4. v. 1. Come out, you earthworm, who only just now were creeping under the ground, and sometimes were never seen: now that you are seen, you are dead. So the Greeks call them [ἔντερα γῆς], the bowels of the earth.

units.la: LUMBRICI terrâ pascuntur. Cas. 1. 1. v. 39.
units.tr: Earthworms feed on earth. Cas. 1. 1. v. 39.

units.la: VICISSITUDINIS-RERUM.
units.tr: THE VICISSITUDE OF THINGS.

units.la: Vide Tit. Hominis: & Fortunæ.
units.tr: See the title Of Man and of Fortune.

units.la: VICISSITUDO rerum humanarum est, ut quod quis habet, paulò post alius possideat. Truc. 2. 1, v. 8. De bonis amato-rum. Vide etiam Tit. Fortunæ.
units.tr: THE vicissitude of human affairs is that what one man holds, a little later another possesses. Truc. 2. 1, v. 8. Concerning the goods of lovers. See also the title Of Fortune.

units.la: VICTORIÆ. TRIUMPHI.
units.tr: VICTORIES. TRIUMPHS.

units.la: VICTORIÆ signum, palma. Most. 1. 1. v. 31.
units.tr: The sign of victory is the palm. Most. 1. 1. v. 31.

units.la: VIRTUTIS vera est victoria. Cist. 1. 3. v. 46. Ea parit laudem & lauream.
units.tr: The victory of virtue is a true one. Cist. 1. 3. v. 46. It brings forth praise and the laurel.

units.la: In victoriâ & triumpho insultabant inimicis per hanc formulam: VÆ VICTIS! Pseud. 5. 2. v. 19. Et sic Varro Satiram suam inscripsit. Vide Proverb. Quid nisi victis dolor?
units.tr: In victory and triumph people insulted their enemies with this formula: WOE TO THE CONQUERED! Pseud. 5. 2. v. 19. Varro also entitled his satire in this way. See the proverb: What is left for the conquered but grief?

units.la: VICTORIBUS acclamabant: Euge! Euge! palmam habes. Trin. 3. 2. v. 80.
units.tr: To the victors they shouted: "Well done! Well done! You have the palm." Trin. 3. 2. v. 80.

units.la: VICTOR victorum cluet; qui animum vincit. Trin. 2. 2. v. 28. Sic Plato 1. de legg: τὸ νικᾶν ἑαυτὸν πασῶν νικῶν πρώτη ἀρίστη. τὸ δὲ ἡττᾶσθαι αὐτὸν ὑφ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ, πάντων αἰσχίστον καὶ κάκιστον. Val. Max. lib. 3. Multò seipsum, quàm hostem superasse operosius est. P. Syrus: Bis vincit, qui se vincit in victoriâ. Idem: Effugere cupiditatem, regnum est vincere. Alius: Fortior est, qui se, quàm qui fortissima vincit Mœnia, nec virtus altius ire potest.
units.tr: The victor of the conquered is he who conquers his own mind, and he is celebrated as such. Trin. 2. 2. v. 28. So Plato in the first book of the Laws: To conquer oneself is the first and best of all victories; but to be conquered by oneself is the most shameful and worst of all. Valerius Maximus, book 3: It is far more laborious to have conquered oneself than an enemy. Publilius Syrus: He conquers twice who conquers himself in victory. The same: To escape from desire is to reign; to conquer it is to be a king. Another: He who conquers himself is stronger than he who conquers the strongest walls, nor can virtue rise higher.

units.la: VICINITATIS.
units.tr: NEIGHBOURS.

units.la: VICINIS damnum nullum inferendum. Mil. 2. 6. v. 24.
units.tr: No harm is to be done to neighbours. Mil. 2. 6. v. 24.

units.la: VICINIS nihil denegandum. Quod fecit nequiter avarus Euclio, qui ignem, aquam, vasa, & id genus supellectilia denegavit vicinis. Aul. 1. 2. v. 18.
units.tr: Nothing is to be refused to neighbours. What miserly Euclio did wickedly, when he refused fire, water, vessels, and that kind of household goods to his neighbours. Aul. 1. 2. v. 18.

units.la: VICINI maximè ad nuptias vocabantur. Caf. 2. 8. v. 68.
units.tr: Neighbours were especially invited to weddings. Caf. 2. 8. v. 68.

units.la: VICINÆ etiam mulieres absentibus maritis cubabant cum vicinis. Caf. 2. 8. v. 50.
units.tr: Neighbouring women, too, while their husbands were away, used to sleep with neighbours. Caf. 2. 8. v. 50.

units.la: VIDUITATIS. VIDUERTATIS,
units.tr: WIDOWHOOD. WIDOWHOOD,

units.la: Vide Tit. Conjugij.
units.tr: See the title Marriage.

units.la: VIDUERTAS grave mulieribus malum. Stich. 1. 1. v. 1. Exemplo Penelopæ.
units.tr: WIDOWHOOD is a grievous evil for women. Stich. 1. 1. v. 1. Example: Penelope.

units.la: Cccc VIDUERTATEM in magno malo censebant. Men. 5. I. v. 20.
units.tr: They considered WIDOWHOOD a great evil. Men. 5. 1. v. 20.

units.la: VIGILUM.
units.tr: WATCHMEN.

units.la: IN benè constituta Republica vigiles nocturni locandi. Amph. I. I. v. 149.
units.tr: In a well-ordered commonwealth, night watchmen should be posted. Amph. 1. 1. v. 149.

units.la: VINDICTAE. ULTIONIS.
units.tr: REVENGE. VENGEANCE.

units.la: SUPPLICIO aut poenâ affecti, jurabant de non referendâ vindictâ. Mil. 5. v. 17.
units.tr: Those who were subjected to punishment or penalty swore not to seek revenge. Mil. 5. v. 17.

units.la: ULTIO altera vita. Perf. 5. I. v. 4.
units.tr: Vengeance awaits in the other life. Perf. 5. 1. v. 4.

units.la: VIRIUM. ROBORIS. FORTITUDINIS.
units.tr: POWERS. STRENGTH. FORTITUDE.

units.la: PLUS potest, qui plus valet. Truc. 4. 3. v. 38.
units.tr: He who is stronger has more power. Truc. 4. 3. v. 38.

units.la: Vetus Poëta:
units.tr: An old poet:

units.la: Qui potest, plus urget: pisces ut sæpe minutos
units.tr: He who has the power presses harder: as the big fish often devours the small, / as the hawk kills the birds.

units.la: Magnum comest: ut aves enecat accipiter.
units.tr: (see unit 13)

units.la: Virtutis Justitiæ, Probitatis. Pietatis. Impietatis. Laudis. Honoris. Honestatis. Humilitatis. Modestiæ. Existimationis.
units.tr: Virtue. Justice, Uprightness. Piety. Impiety. Praise. Honour. Honesty. Humility. Modesty. Esteem.

units.la: Virtus præmium est optimum. Virtus omnibus rebus anteit profecto. Libertas, salus, vita, res, parentes, Patria & prognati tutantur, servantur. Virtus omnia in se habet, omnia assunt bona, quem penes est virtus. Amph. 2.2. v.17. & seqq. Jamblichus Chalcedonensis: Virtus velut sanctam delubrum.
units.tr: Virtue is the best reward. Virtue certainly surpasses all things. Liberty, safety, life, property, parents, country and children are protected and preserved by it. Virtue holds all things within itself; all good things are at hand for him in whose possession virtue is. Amph. 2. 2. v. 17 and following. Jamblichus of Chalcedon: Virtue is like a holy shrine.

units.la: Virtuti debetur præmium. Amph. 1.3. v.30.
units.tr: Reward is owed to virtue. Amph. 1. 3. v. 30.

units.la: Virtutis vera est victoria. Cist. 1.3. v. 46. Ea parit laudem & lauream.
units.tr: The true victory belongs to virtue. Cist. 1. 3. v. 46. It brings forth praise and the laurel.

units.la: Qui multùm se posse aliquâ in restudioque putant, atque id aliquando factis usuque antea demonstrarunt, cavent quicquam facere, quod à parta jam laude degeneret. Ita enim intelligunt, se existimationem perdituros, ac quod summis laboribus, periculisque decus acquisiverint, subitò amissuros. Sic Parasitus Aden. 3. 2. v. 6. iniquo animo fert, sibi impositum esse. Non hercle ut sum, &c.
units.tr: Those who think they are very capable in some matter, and have sometimes shown it earlier by their deeds and experience, take care not to do anything that would fall away from the praise already won. For they understand that they would lose their reputation and suddenly forfeit the honour they gained by the greatest labours and dangers. Thus the parasite in Adelphoe 3. 2. v. 6 bears it with ill will that it has been imposed on him: "Not by Hercules, as I am," etc.

units.la: Sic Theseus apud Euripidem Hippol. v.976. εἰ γὰρ παθὼν γε σιγᾷ δὲ πασηθήσομαι, ὁ μαρτυρήσει Γῶμι Σίννις ποτὲ κτανεῖν ἑαυτὸν, ἀλλὰ κομπάζειν μάτην.
units.tr: So Theseus in Euripides, Hippolytus v. 976: "For if I suffer and keep silent, shall I not be... will anyone testify that Sinis once killed himself? No, I boast in vain." [εἰ γὰρ παθὼν γε σιγᾷ δὲ πασηθήσομαι, ὁ μαρτυρήσει Γῶμι Σίννις ποτὲ κτανεῖν ἑαυτὸν, ἀλλὰ κομπάζειν μάτην.]

units.la: Is probus est, quem non poenitet, quàm probus sit, & frugi bonæ. Qui ipsus sibi satis placet, nec probus est, nec frugi bonæ. Trin. 2.2. v.39. Cyprianus Serm. III. de Patientiâ: Qui nec humiles sunt, nec miles, sed sibi multùm placent, hoc ipso, quod sibi placent, Deo displicent.
units.tr: He is upright who is not ashamed of how upright and honest he is. He who is well pleased with himself is neither upright nor honest. Trin. 2. 2. v. 39. Cyprian, Sermon III on Patience: Those who are neither humble nor gentle, but are very pleased with themselves, by that very fact displease God.

units.la: Qui se ipsus contemnit, in eo est indoles industriæ. Trin. 2.2. v. 42.
units.tr: In one who despises himself there lies the disposition for diligence. Trin. 2. 2. v. 42.

units.la: Qui seipsus contemnit, in eo est indoles industriae. Trin. 2. 2. v. 42.
units.tr: In one who despises himself there lies the disposition for diligence. Trin. 2. 2. v. 42.

units.la: Qui per virtutem peritat, non interit: h. e. non separatur prorsus a vivis: sed remanet in fama hominum. Capt. 3. 5. v. 32. Sall. Catil. Nonne mori per virtutem praestat? Justin. Qui pro Rep. ceciderunt, in perpetuum per gloriam vivere intelliguntur.
units.tr: He who perishes through virtue does not perish; that is, he is not wholly separated from the living, but remains in the fame of men. Capt. 3. 5. v. 32. Sallust, Catiline: "Is it not better to die through virtue?" Justin: Those who fell for the Republic are understood to live forever through glory.

units.la: VIRTUTE ambire oportet, non fautoribus. Sat habet fautorum semper, qui recte facit. Amph. Prol. v. 78.
units.tr: One should seek office by virtue, not by supporters. He who acts rightly always has enough supporters. Amph. Prol. v. 78.

units.la: VIRTUS longe postponi solet divitiis. Men. 4. 2. v. 3. & seqq. Vide Tit. Patronorum.
units.tr: Virtue is commonly valued far below riches. Men. 4. 2. v. 3 and following. See the title Patrons.

units.la: VIRTUTI nihil detrahit virtus. Asin. 2. 4. v. 9.
units.tr: Virtue takes nothing away from virtue. Asin. 2. 4. v. 9.

units.la: VIRTUS sibi facile argutam facunditatem invenit. Truc. 2. 6. v. 13. & v. 14. Vide etiam Fit. Eloquentia.
units.tr: Virtue easily finds for itself a lively eloquence. Truc. 2. 6. v. 13 and v. 14. See also the title Eloquence.

units.la: VIRTUS semper inimicos habet. Itaque si quam rem adversus multorum, suorum inprimis sententiam essent aggressi, dicebant se omnes inimicos reperisse. Epid. 1. 2. v. 6.
units.tr: Virtue always has enemies. Therefore, whenever they attacked some matter against the opinion of many, especially of their own people, they all said they had found enemies. Epid. 1. 2. v. 6.

units.la: VIRTUTEM multi docent, parum interim virtuosi ipsi: quod de Comicis dicit Plautus Rud. 4. 7. v. 23. ubi senex: Spectavi ego pridem Comicos ad istum modum Sapienter dicta dicere, atque ijs plaudier, Cum illos sapientes mores monstrabant populo: Sed cum inde suam quisque ibant divorsi domum, Nullum erat illo pacto, ut illi jusserant.
units.tr: Many teach virtue while being themselves little virtuous. Plautus says this of the comic poets, Rud. 4. 7. v. 23, where an old man says: "I have long watched the comic poets speak wise sayings in that manner and be applauded for them, when they showed the people those wise morals; but when each went off separately to his home, nothing was done in that way that they had commanded."

units.la: Sententia plane ex tripode. Idem de Pharisaeis passim queritur Christus. Et annon hodie de praeconibus quibusdam verbi Dei idem dici queat?
units.tr: A sentiment plainly from the tripod. Christ complains of the same about the Pharisees throughout. And can the same not be said today of certain heralds of the Word of God?

units.la: Qui nimis sancte pius est, pauper est. Wann einer gar zu fromb ist, so wird vnd bleibt er arm. Rud. 4. 7. v. 8.
units.tr: He who is too holy is poor. "If someone is too pious, he becomes and remains poor." Rud. 4. 7. v. 8.

units.la: Persi Sat. v. 138. Varro regustatum digito terebrare salinum Contentus perages, si vivere cum Iove tendis.
units.tr: Persius, Sat. v. 138. Varro: "Content to bore the salt-cellar with a rubbed finger, if you strive to live with Jove."

units.la: PLAERUMQUE divites sunt impij, ex sententia Piscatoris Plauti-ni Rud. ni. Rud. 4. 7. v. 8. Isto tu pauper es, cum nimis sanctè pius.
units.tr: Mostly the rich are wicked, according to the sentiment of the fisherman in Plautus' Rudens: Rud. 4. 7. v. 8. "You are poor for that very reason, since you are too pious."

units.la: SEMPER tu hoc facito cogites, id optimum esse, tute ut sis optimus: si id nequeas, saltem ut optimis sis proximus. Trin. 2. 4. v. 85. Consilium senis patris, quod dat filio suo.
units.tr: Always make this your thought: that it is best for you to be the best yourself; if you cannot manage that, at least be next to the best. Trin. 2. 4. v. 85. The advice of an old father to his son.

units.la: VIRTUTI debetur praemium. Probi enim ab improbis discernendi. Rud. 3. 2. v. 6. Statuite exemplum impudenti, date pudori praemium.
units.tr: Reward is owed to virtue, for the good must be distinguished from the wicked. Rud. 3. 2. v. 6. "Set an example for the shameless, give a reward to modesty."

units.la: Sic Amphitruo ornatus paterâ aurea ob virtutem bellicam. Amph. I. I. v. 103.
units.tr: So Amphitryon, adorned with a golden bowl for martial virtue. Amph. 1. 1. v. 103.

units.la: VIS. VIOLENTIÆ.
units.tr: FORCE. VIOLENCE.

units.la: Vide supra Tit. Injuriarum.
units.tr: See above, under the title Injuriarum.

units.la: VIS publica major utique est, quàm privata: ejusque criminis convictus majore poenâ affici solet. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 49. Ubi publica via dicitur, quòd meretrix filium parentis detinuerit. Vide Tit. Meretricum. Et Langl. Otij Semestr. libb. p. 502.
units.tr: Public force is certainly greater than private force, and a person convicted of this crime is usually punished more severely. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 49. Here publica via is said because the prostitute had detained the parent's son. See the title Meretricum. And Langl. Otij Semestr. libb. p. 502.

units.la: VISUS.
units.tr: SIGHT.

units.la: Vide Tit. Sensuum: & Hominis.
units.tr: See the titles Sensuum and Hominis.

units.la: PUDORIS & metûs signum est, non audere contra oculis adspicere. Cas. 5. 3. v. 2. Vide Def. Herald. Adverf. lib. 2. c. 4.
units.tr: Not daring to look directly into someone's eyes is a sign of shame and fear. Cas. 5. 3. v. 2. See Def. Herald. Adverf. lib. 2. c. 4.

units.la: OCULIS hiantibus optimè cernitur: ut est in joco. Mer. 1. 2. v. 71.
units.tr: Things are seen best with gaping eyes, as in the joke. Mer. 1. 2. v. 71.

units.la: VITÆ. LONGÆVITATIS. MORUM. ADOLESCENTIÆ. IUVENTUTIS.
units.tr: LIFE. LONGEVITY. MORALS. ADOLESCENCE. YOUTH.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Hominis.
units.tr: See also the title Hominis.

units.la: VITA comparatur Igni. Aul. 1. 2. v. 15.
units.tr: Life is compared to fire. Aul. 1. 2. v. 15.

units.la: IN vitâ humanâ paucæ & raræ sunt voluptates, si cum molestijs comparentur. Amph. 2. 2. v. 1, 2. & seqq.
units.tr: In human life pleasures are few and rare, if they are weighed against troubles. Amph. 2. 2. v. 1, 2 and following.

units.la: Dddd PROIN-
units.tr: Dddd PROIN-

units.la: PROINDE ut diu vivitur, bene vivitur: h. e. optima est vita illa, cui adsueveris. Trin. 1.2.v.27. Philosophica plane sententia: quam illustrat passim Seneca.
units.tr: Therefore, the longer one lives, the better one lives: that is, that life is best to which you have grown accustomed. Trin. 1. 2. v. 27. A plainly philosophical saying, which Seneca illustrates everywhere.

units.la: MORES ANTIQUI ob simplicitatem & virtutem in proverbio sunt. Moribus antiquis. Quod scito vir Antiquis Moribus justus Lipsius superbijt. Capt. 1.1.v.37.
units.tr: Ancient manners are proverbial for their simplicity and virtue. Moribus antiquis. This is what Justus Lipsius, a man of ancient manners, took pride in knowing. Capt. 1. 1. v. 37.

units.la: IN vita humana nihil est perpetuum datum. Cist. 1.3.v.46.
units.tr: Nothing in human life is given as lasting. Cist. 1. 3. v. 46.

units.la: QUORUM parentes longævi sunt, & ipsi longævi futuri existimantur. Mil. 4.2.v.88.
units.tr: Those whose parents are long-lived are themselves thought likely to be long-lived. Mil. 4. 2. v. 88.

units.la: HILLO sunt homines miserè miseri. Cist. 4.2.v.2.
units.tr: There, men are wretchedly miserable. Cist. 4. 2. v. 2.

units.la: VITAM nostram ante-actam debemus tamquam in speculo contemplari. Epid. 3.3.v.5. Idem namque peccare in adolescentiâ soliti sunt senes, quod nunc adolescentes: eoq; illis venia danda.
units.tr: We ought to contemplate our past life as in a mirror. Epid. 3. 3. v. 5. For old men were accustomed to sin in youth just as young men do now, and so indulgence must be granted to them.

units.la: IN hominum ætate multa eveniunt hujusmodi: capiunt voluptates, capiunt rursus miserias. Amph. 3.2.v.57.
units.tr: Many such things happen in the course of human life: people take up pleasures, and again they take up miseries. Amph. 3. 2. v. 57.

units.la: VMBRÆ.
units.tr: SHADOWS.

units.la: VMBRA grata ædificiis. Most. 3.2.v.83.
units.tr: Shade is pleasing to buildings. Most. 3. 2. v. 83.

units.la: UMBRA in puteis. Most. 3.2.v.83. Lucret. Aer lumine cassu. Vide egregiam orationem Jani Doufæ Fil. de Umbrâ.
units.tr: Shade in wells. Most. 3. 2. v. 83. Lucretius: air deprived of light. See the excellent oration of Janus Dousa the son on the shadow.

units.la: UMBRA sequitur corpus: nec procul à corpore abest. Perf. 2.4.v.27. Caf. 1.1.v.4.
units.tr: The shadow follows the body and is not far from it. Perf. 2. 4. v. 27. Caf. 1. 1. v. 4.

units.la: VOCIS.
units.tr: OF THE VOICE.

units.la: VOx etiam corvorum est: sed ἀκυρολόγως. Physici etiam tradunt, vocem tantùm hominis esse. Aul 4.3.v.2.
units.tr: Crows too have a voice, but improperly [ἀκυρολόγως]. Physicians also teach that only man has a voice. Aul. 4. 3. v. 2.

units.la: VOCE bonâ prædití, victum inde sibi quærere possunt, ut olim præcones. Poen. Prol. v.14.
units.tr: Those gifted with a good voice can earn their living by it, as heralds did formerly. Poen. Prol. v. 14.

units.la: VOCE sæpe vir à muliere discernitur. Rud. 1.4.v.12.
units.tr: A man is often told apart from a woman by his voice. Rud. 1. 4. v. 12.

units.la: NIMIA contentio vocis, ravim conciliat & raucedinem. Aul. 2. 5. v. 10. Poen. 3. 5. v. 33.
units.tr: Excessive straining of the voice brings on hoarseness and roughness. Aul. 2. 5. v. 10. Poen. 3. 5. v. 33.

units.la: Volatûs.
units.tr: OF FLYING.

units.la: SINE pennis volare, haud facilè est: meæ alæ pennæ. Poen. 4. 2. v. 49.
units.tr: Flying without wings is not easy: my wings are feathers. Poen. 4. 2. v. 49.

units.la: Voluntatis. Coactionis.
units.tr: OF THE WILL. OF COMPULSION.

units.la: VOLUNTAS hominis variat, prout sunt tempora: atq; ex eventu quoque subitò immutant: ut ventus in mari vortitur. Epid. 1. 1. v. 47. Poen. 3. 5. v. 9.
units.tr: A man's will varies with the times, and is also suddenly changed by the outcome, as the wind turns about at sea. Epid. 1. 1. v. 47. Poen. 3. 5. v. 9.

units.la: INVITI quod facimus, minus feliciter succedit. Stich. 1. 2. v. 82.
units.tr: What we do unwillingly turns out less successfully. Stich. 1. 2. v. 82.

units.la: Voti. Apprecationum.
units.tr: OF VOWS. OF PRAYERS.

units.la: BENE-PRECARI ac vovere solebant per has formulas: Dii tibi dent, quæcunq; optes! Asin. 1. 1. v. 32. Epid. 1. 1. v. 4. Poen. 5. 2. v. 95. Stich. 3. 2. v. 15. Rud. 1. 1. v. 19. Vide Lexic. Plaut.
units.tr: They used to bless and wish well with these formulas: May the gods give you whatever you wish! Asin. 1. 1. v. 32. Epid. 1. 1. v. 4. Poen. 5. 2. v. 95. Stich. 3. 2. v. 15. Rud. 1. 1. v. 19. See the Lexicon Plautinum.

units.la: IN votis usurpabant hanc Formulam: DI bene vortant! Trin. 2. 4. v. 100. In contractu Nuptiarum.
units.tr: In vows they used this formula: May the gods turn things out well! Trin. 2. 4. v. 100. In a marriage contract.

units.la: SÆPE multa volumus, & optamus, quæ nequicquam nobis obtingunt. Trin. 2. 4. v. 164.
units.tr: We often want and wish for many things which come to us in vain. Trin. 2. 4. v. 164.

units.la: SOLEBANT amici amicis optima queque vovere hac formulâ. DI duint tibi, quæcunque optes! Trin. 2. 4. v. 35.
units.tr: Friends used to wish their friends every good thing with this formula: May the gods grant you whatever you wish! Trin. 2. 4. v. 35.

units.la: SUB actionum principia solebant sic vovere: Queres bene vortat! Asin. Prol v. 2.
units.tr: At the start of undertakings they used to vow in this way: May it turn out well! Asin. Prol. v. 2.

units.la: E militiâ domum reversi salvi, vota Deo solvebant. Amph. 3. 2. v. 66. & 3. 3. v. 11.
units.tr: Returning home safe from military service, they paid their vows to God. Amph. 3. 2. v. 66 and 3. 3. v. 11.

units.la: NON omnia eadem æquè omnibus suavia sunt. Asin. 3. 3. v. 51.
units.tr: Not all things are equally pleasant to everyone. Asin. 3. 3. v. 51.

units.la: VOLUPTATIS. LIBIDINIS. CUPIDITATIS. IUCUNDITATIS. SUAVITATIS. GAUDII. LÆTITIÆ. HILARITATIS.
units.tr: PLEASURE. LUST. DESIRE. DELIGHT. SWEETNESS. JOY. GLADNESS. CHEERFULNESS.

units.la: Vide etiam Tit. Fortuna & Hominis.
units.tr: See also the heading Fortune and Man.

units.la: VOLUPTAS est malorum esca, quòd eâ non minus homines, quàm hamo piscess capiuntur. Merc. 5.3. v. 2.
units.tr: PLEASURE is the bait for evils, since men are caught by it no less than fish are caught by a hook. Merc. 5.3. v. 2.

units.la: QUODCUMQUE accidit homini libere, posse retur. Æquum esse putat, non reputat laboris quid sit, Nec æquum aut iniquum imperet, cogitabit. Amph. 1.1. v.17.
units.tr: Whatever happens to a man, let him think he can bear it freely. He thinks it fair and does not reckon what toil is; nor will he consider whether a command is fair or unfair. Amph. 1.1. v. 17.

units.la: HOMINES libidinosi, ut fruantur suis voluptatibus, omnia illis postponunt, etiam ipsam vitam. Bacch. 5.2. v.77.
units.tr: Lustful men, so that they may enjoy their pleasures, put everything before them, even life itself. Bacch. 5.2. v. 77.

units.la: ITA DIs placitum est: Voluptatem ut mœror comes sequatur. Amph. 2.2. v.5.
units.tr: So the gods have decided: that sorrow should follow pleasure as its companion. Amph. 2.2. v. 5.

units.la: Quæ sententia de Menandro sumta est his versibus: Ἐυξοις δ' ἀνυδλὴρ τῶν ἀπάντων, Σιμύλε, ἀγαθὸν, ὅταν μὴ ᾠσθέσθαι κακόν.
units.tr: This sentiment is taken from Menander, from these verses: "Of all things, Simylus, a good is not felt to be good unless an evil is also felt." [Ἐυξοις δ' ἀνυδλὴρ τῶν ἀπάντων, Σιμύλε, ἀγαθὸν, ὅταν μὴ ᾠσθέσθαι κακόν.]

units.la: Eurip. apud Plutar. περὶ εὐθυμίας. ἐκ ἀν γένοιτο χωρὶς ἐσθλὰ ἢ καλὰ ἀλλ' ἐσί τις σύνηθεσις, ὡς ἔχειν καλῶς. Vide alias sententias apud Rittershuf. in Notis ad Guntherum pag. 38.
units.tr: Euripides, quoted in Plutarch, On Cheerfulness: good or fair things could not come about apart from [their opposites], but there is a certain habituation, so that one has things well. [ἐκ ἂν γένοιτο χωρὶς ἐσθλὰ ἢ καλὰ ἀλλ' ἐσί τις σύνηθεσις, ὡς ἔχειν καλῶς.] See other sayings in Rittershusius's notes to Gunther, p. 38.

units.la: SI incolæ benè sunt morati, pulcrè munitum est oppidum. Perfidia, & peculatus ex urbe, & avaritia si exulant, quarta Invidia, quinta Ambitio, sexta Obtrectatio, septimum perjurium: octava Indiligentia: nona Injuria, decimum quod pessimum aggressu scelus. Hæc nisi urbe aberunt, centuplex murus rebus servandis parum est. Perf 4.4. v.6. & seqq.
units.tr: If the inhabitants are well behaved, the town is well fortified. If treachery, embezzlement of public funds, and avarice are banished from the city, and fourth envy, fifth ambition, sixth slander, and seventh perjury, eighth negligence, ninth injury, and tenth the crime worst in its approach, and if these are not driven out of the city, a wall a hundred times thicker is of little use for keeping things safe. Perf 4.4. v.6. & seqq.

units.la: Augustinus lib. 2. de Civ. Dei cap. 2 de Româ à Gothis vastatâ: In ruinâ urbis lapides & ligna, in civium autem vitâ omnia non muromurorum, seu morum monumenta atq; ornamenta ceciderunt: cum fanestioribus eorum corda cupiditatibus, quam ignibus tecta illius urbis arderent.
units.tr: Augustine, City of God book 2, chapter 2, on Rome laid waste by the Goths: In the ruin of the city, stones and timber fell; but in the life of the citizens, all the monuments and ornaments of morals, not of walls, fell, and their hearts, more than the houses of that city, burned with desires more than with fires.

units.la: Quumq; ruinosis procumbant oppida muris
units.tr: And since the towns collapse with ruined walls,

units.la: Majorem Morum patimur querimurq; ruinam.
units.tr: We suffer and lament a greater ruin of morals.

units.la: Vide Rittersh. ad Salvianum lib. 6. de Gubern. Dei. Nonne eadem & rerum ruina, & morum? Demosth. ἀνδρες πόλεις, ἡ ὑ τεί-χη. Alcaeus: ἄνθρες πόλιος, πύεγοι ἀξίιον.
units.tr: See Rittershusius on Salvian, On the Governance of God book 6. Is not the ruin of things and of morals the same? Demosthenes: men are cities, not walls [ἄνδρες πόλεις, οὐ τείχη]. Alcaeus: men are the city, not towers [ἄνδρες πόλις, οὐ πύργοι].

units.la: Vide etiam Rittersh. ad Oppian. Hal. lib. 5.

units.la: Dum inter homines fumus, colamus Humanitatem: non timori cuiquam, non periculo fimus: detrimenta, injurias, convitia, vellicationes contemnamus, & magno animo brevia feramus incommoda.
units.tr: While we are among men, let us cultivate humanity: let us be a source of fear to no one, of danger to no one; let us despise losses, injuries, reproaches and taunts, and with a great spirit bear the brief troubles of life.

units.la: Vir Clarissime:
units.tr: Most distinguished sir:

units.la: Ocos tuos Communes Philosophicos Plautinos accepi; quos & non semel, sed saepiùs ac saepiùs percurri. Diligentiam tuam mirificè laudo. Accuratissimus enim & exactissimus fuisti: nec adeò tam multa ab illo Comicorum Principe exspectassem, quàm multa nobis exhibuisti. Placent etiam Emblemata, quae subinde sententiis Plautinis à te sunt adjecta. Utinam plures in idem animi tui propositum concurrerent: & exemplo tuo Platonem, Aristotelem, Tullium, Plutarchum, caeterosque hujusmodi notae priores Authores Locos in Communes dissererent! sanè Commentarijs quotquot sunt Veterum multis intervallis ac spatijs eosanteponerem. Sed his de rebus inter nos aliquando, Deo dante, pleniùs ac familiariùs agemus. *** Vale.
units.tr: I have received your Common Places from Plautus, the Philosophical ones; these I have gone through not once but again and again. I praise your diligence greatly. For you have been most careful and most exact, and I would not have expected from that prince of comic poets so much as you have shown us. The Emblems also please me, which you have from time to time added to the Plautine sayings. Would that more men had the same purpose of mind as you, and that, following your example, the earlier authors of note, Plato, Aristotle, Tully, Plutarch and others of that kind, were to set out their passages under common headings! Indeed, I would prefer such work to all the commentaries of the ancients, however many there are, by a long way. But we shall discuss these matters between ourselves more fully and more familiarly one day, God willing. *** Farewell.

units.la: IDEM AD EUMDEM.
units.tr: IDEM AD EUMDEM.

units.la: Quae à te magno studio ad Comicorum Latinorum Principem sunt notata, modis omnibus mihi probantur, adeò ut Livoris Invidiaeq; morsus metuere nullâ cogitatione debeas. Resipsa te non superstitibus modo, sed & posteris prodesse voluisse: immò jam multis profuisse, ac quotidiè prodesse, satis superq; declarat. Carpant invidi, dummodò meliore successu, meliora scripsint, audeant vel praestent. Labor tuus, crede, nec tempore veterascet, nec ab alio superabitur. Adeò namq; fundum illum Plautinum necessarijs omnibus luculenter instruere coepisti, ut qui te sequi posthac vel imitarivoluerint, àte passim mutuum sint sumturi, tuáq; reposituri. Faustis ac feli-cibus auspicijs tantum perge: & Platonica (quorum specimen mihi misisti) Aristotelica, & id genus Electa, bono publico, per succedaneas vices nobis ede. Hoc si feceris, (quod te velle ac destinare video) futura secu-la uni tibi, quantum multis interpretibus aliis, debitura prafagio. Vale Vir Clarissime, a. d. 31. Iulij. Haidelbergæ. Anno 1617.
units.tr: What you have noted with great diligence on the Prince of Latin comic poets pleases me in every way, so that you need have no thought of fearing the bites of envy and spite. Indeed, the work itself clearly shows that you wished to benefit not only those still living but also posterity: in fact it has already benefited many, and benefits them daily, as is abundantly clear. Let the envious carp, provided that they write better things with better success, or dare or achieve more. Your labour, believe me, will neither grow old with time nor be surpassed by another. For you have begun so thoroughly to furnish that Plautine field with all the necessary aids that those who wish to follow you or imitate you hereafter will take from you on every side and will return to you what they have taken. Go on only with fortunate and happy auspices, and give us in successive turns your Platonica (of which you sent me a sample), your Aristotelica, and that kind of Electa, for the public good. If you do this (as I see you wish and intend), future ages will owe you alone as much as they owe to many other interpreters. Farewell, most distinguished sir. Heidelberg, 31 July 1617.

units.la: LABORES in Plautum tuos dudum est, cum ego, vel ob hoca-mare coepi, quòd publici saporis non sunt. Nam quos hodiè videmus plerosque, vel vani immensarum allegationum hamaxa-rij, vel reduviarum medici sunt. Et post hæc omnia tamen, si DIs placet, Induperatores Optimi-Maximi. At quàm diversâ tu longè viâ insistendum putares, ostendisti denuò nunc nuper Eclogis illis tuis, electis verè. Nihil ad gratiam dici puta: Opus istud tuum, ut Thesaurus est, ita inscribi quoq; velim. Nisi quòd & hoc supra Thesaurum habet, quod omnibus in commune stu-dijs nimium quantum prodest. Thesaurus defossus, nulli: effossus paucis prodest. Jam ego denuncio, Ordinem nostrum eâ re debi-turum tibi juxtà cæteros plurimùm: Cui sparsæ per Authorem ve-rè tuum, veteris Juris prudentiæ ramenta, in obryzæ nunc demùm massam redintegrata offers. †††Vale.
units.tr: Your labours on Plautus have long been in my thoughts, and I began to admire them partly because I loved this kind of work, since such things have no appeal to the general public. For most of those we see today are either empty wranglers of endless allegations or physicians of worthless scraps; and yet, if the gods are willing, after all this they become Emperors, Best and Greatest. You have shown again, in those recent Eclogues of yours, that you take a very different path, and truly a choice one. Take it that nothing I say is meant as flattery: I would like this work of yours to be titled as a treasury, as it is. Yet it has one advantage over a treasury: it benefits all scholars together, to a great degree. A buried treasure helps no one; a dug-up one helps only a few. I now declare that our Order will be greatly indebted to you, as to the others, for this reason: you offer us, restored in a mass of pure gold, the fragments of old legal learning scattered through your true work. Farewell.

units.la: VOD solet fieri ijs, qui circà vias in publico super-bas collocant Ædificiorum moles, ut obviantium experiantur varias sententias aquas,iniquas : idem accidit publica ingenij monumentain ora Virûm e-mittentibus. Inveniunt laudatores, omnia ex suis virtutibus comprobantes : æquitate singula & humanitate æstimantes : nec desunt tamen, atro quæq, sale perfundentes: quibus animi geniale pabulum est, alios vellicare. Ego cùm nullus dubitem, ELECTA mea PLAUTINA in posterioris Nationis homines vel jam incidisse, vel adhuc incidere posse, in gratiam Philologiæ studiosorum APHORISMOS aliquos brevioribus Notis conâtus sum reddere illustriores, faciliores, nihil interim abnuens censu-ras aliorum aut reprehensiones, dummodo absit venenata dicacitas. Admoneri, inquit Seneca, omnis bonus gaudet: neque quicquam ex erroribus suis timet.
units.tr: What happens to those who set up large buildings beside public roads is what happens to those who put out public monuments of their intellect: they meet with many opinions from passers-by, some fair and some unfair. Some admirers approve everything as the product of its author's virtues, and judge each item with fairness and kindness. Yet there are also those who sprinkle everything with bitter wit, for whom it is a congenial diet to pick at others. Since I do not doubt that my Selected Passages of Plautus have already fallen, or may yet fall, into the hands of men of a later generation, I have tried, for the benefit of students of philology, to make some of the aphorisms clearer and easier by means of shorter notes. I do not refuse the judgements and criticisms of others, provided they are free of poisonous sarcasm. Seneca says: "Every good man is glad to be admonished, and fears nothing from his own errors."

units.la: METHODO in illis usus sum elementari, iuxtà στοιχεῖα & ordinem litterarum, prout TITULI vel Artium, vel Antiquitatis, sese mihi offerebant: observata ubivis Titulorum ac Rerum ἀναμίᾳ. Placuit aliis, qui in pari LOCORUM COMMUNIUM studio diligenter versati sunt, alia μέθοδον: mihi hæc nostra omnium visa est accommodatissima. Neq; enim ad pompam tales ἐκλογὰς instituendæ sunt, sed ad Vsum. Quæ de re alibi fusius meminimē disserere. Cur verò è Comicorum principe M. Accio Plauto talem Electorum Sylvam potius collegerim, quàm ex alio Latinitatis Romanæ Auctore, exposui in Præmonitione ad Lectorem, ipsis Electis præfixâ: ubi & instituti mei rationes, & Plauti, adeoq. universa Comoediæ dignitatem iterùm assertum ivi. Nunc si qui Aphorismi in Electis nostris nonnullis fortean visi sint obscuriores, aut cæteroquin suspecti, conabor illos σὺν τοῖς μύθοις breviorибus istis Notis nostris paulò succinctius explicare, illustrare, ac, sicubi res feret, confirmare, ac defendere. Tu Lector benevole, εὐφήμει! & his nostris laboribus utere, fruere.
units.tr: I have used an elementary method in these notes, following the Greek alphabet [στοιχεῖα] and the order of the letters, according to the TITLES or the arts or antiquities as they presented themselves to me, while observing everywhere a mixing [ἀναμίᾳ] of titles and subjects. Others who have worked diligently on the study of common places preferred another method [μέθοδον], but this one of ours seemed to me the most suitable of all. For such selections [ἐκλογὰς] are to be made not for display but for use. I have mentioned elsewhere that I would discuss this matter more fully. Why I chose to gather such a Selected Forest from the prince of comic poets, M. Accius Plautus, rather than from another author of Roman Latinity, I explained in the Preface to the Reader prefixed to the Selections themselves, where I also again defended the reasons for my plan, Plautus, and so the whole dignity of Comedy. Now, if some aphorisms in our Selections seem rather obscure, or otherwise open to suspicion, I shall try, with the help of the fables [σὺν τοῖς μύθοις], to explain, illustrate and, where the matter allows, confirm and defend them somewhat more concisely in these Notes of ours. Kind reader, keep a holy silence [εὐφήμει]! Make use of these labours of ours and enjoy them.

units.la: IT. IV. ACTIONVM Aphorismus octavus sic habet: Pag.4. In seriis actionibus, ubi intentè quid agendum, utebantur hac formulâ: HOC AGE. Asin. Prolog. v. 1. Cap. 2. 3. v. 84. Perf. 4. 4. v. 35.]
units.tr: Book IV, Title of ACTIONS, the eighth aphorism reads thus: page 4. In serious actions, when something is to be done with close attention, they used this formula: HOC AGE ("attend to this"). Asinaria, Prologue, v. 1; ch. 2, 3, v. 84; Persa 4.4, v. 35.

units.la: Ab hâc formulâ minimè excludi debent res ludicræ voluptariæ, aut nugales etiam. Neque enim omnia hæc loca, quæ adduxi, de rebus seriis duntaxat capienda. At verò in Sacris potissimùm adhibitam illam formulam fuisse, ad notavi in Electis Tit. SACRIFICIORUM pag. 517. Quin & in Carnificinâ usitatam eandem, ex Suetonio notum est: ubi Cassius Chærea Caligulæ cervicem gladio cæsim percutere volens, præmisit hanc vocem; HOC AGE: cùm aliàs dicerent; FACTUM EST QUOD IMPERASTI: uti patet ex Sueton. Tiberio & Claudio. Itemque lib.1. Annal. Taciti. Vide etiam Tertull.lib. 1 v. in Marcion. cap.7. Contrâtamen sensit (ut refert Anton. Muret. lib. xv. Var. Lect. cap. XVII.) GABRIEL FAERNUS, qui in Terent. notat HOC AGE, esse solùm silentij formulam; sic: HOC AGE.st! Sed ibidem à Mureto deridetur.
units.tr: These should by no means be excluded from this formula: playful, pleasure-giving, or even trifling matters. For not all of the passages I have cited should be taken as referring only to serious matters. But that formula was used especially in sacred rites, as I noted in the Electa, title SACRIFICES, p. 517. It is also well known that the same formula was customary in executions, from Suetonius: when Cassius Chaerea wanted to strike Caligula's neck with a sword, he prefaced the blow with this word, HOC AGE; whereas on other occasions they said, FACTUM EST QUOD IMPERASTI, as is clear from Suetonius's Tiberius and Claudius. Likewise in the first book of Tacitus's Annals. See also Tertullian, Against Marcion, book 1, chapter 7. Yet, as Anton. Muret. reports (book 15, Various Readings, chapter 17), Gabriel Faernus held a different view. In his note on Terence he says that HOC AGE is merely a formula of silence; thus: HOC AGE. st! But Muretus mocks him for this in the same place.

units.tr: † Under the same title, the eleventh axiom reads: To begin is much more than to obtain easily. Poenulus 5.2, v. 14. The Greeks say one thing and the Greeks say another, ὑμεῖς ταῦτα τὰ ταῦτος.

units.la: Nimirùm quemadmodum non idem est rem aliquam inchoare, & eandem consummare; ita Græci in alium sensum pronunciârunt diverbio suo: Dimidium facti qui habet, jam plus toto confecisse.
units.tr: Clearly, just as it is not the same thing to begin something and to finish it, so the Greeks, in their own saying, gave it another meaning: whoever has the half of a deed has already accomplished more than the whole.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xx. QUOD BONUM FELIX FAUSTUM QUE SIT initiò rei gerendæ usurpabant. Aul.2.1.v.26.] Norit Lector. Barnabam Brissonium, Magnum illum Galliæ suæ φωτόξεα, similes ferè formulas in FORMULARIO collegisse: plura tamen loca ... à me adducta, omissa ab illo esse.
units.tr: † Ibid., axiom 20: they used to begin a undertaking with the words: WHAT IS GOOD, LUCKY AND PROPITIOUS BE (so). Aulularia 2.1, v. 26. Let the reader know that Barnabas Brissonius, that great light of his France, collected similar formulas in his Formulary; but he omitted many passages cited by me.

units.la: Tit. v. ADMONITIONUM. Aphor. iv. Errantes in viam redu- cere conuenit, ne pereant.] Aul.4.1.v.6. ubi servus sic loquitur: Qui amanti hero servitutem servit, quasi ego seruio, Si herum videt superare amorem, hoc serui esse officium reor, Retinere ad salutem: non eum, quò incumbat,
units.tr: Title V, ADMONITIONS. Aphorism 4: It is fitting to lead the erring back onto the road, lest they perish. Aulularia 4.1, v. 6, where the slave speaks thus: He who serves a master in love serves as I serve. If he sees the master overcome by love, this, I think, is the duty of a slave: to hold him back for his good, not to push him where he is about to fall.

units.la: eò impellere.
units.tr: not to push him there.

units.la: E quibus verbis præter hunc Aphorismum, quem adnotavi, a-lius quoque exstrui potest talis: Serui est, etiamsi non habeat in herum imperium, licet tamen ei genibus heri advolvi, orare, & blanditer obsecrare; quin & utraque manu medium invadere, & oblectari, perseverantemque ipso morari corpore, ne peccet. Sic Sallust. ad Q. Cæsarem Epist. 1. Ea clementia erit, retinuisse ab stultitiâ, & falsis voluptatibus. Hoc verò Axioma de officio Servorum in heros, alibi à me quoque observatum in Electis infrà Tit. Servorum pag. 543. Hic loci errantem herum in viam reducit Servus: eòque Admonitio illa ad hunc etiam Titulum referenda fuit.
units.tr: From these words, besides the aphorism I have noted, another may be built: It is the duty of a slave, even if he has no authority over his master, to fall at his master's knees, to beg, and to entreat him coaxingly; indeed to take hold of him with both hands in the middle, to delight him, and to keep him from sinning by staying with him in person. So Sallust, in his first letter to Caesar: That will be mercy: to have held him back from folly and false pleasures. I have observed this axiom about the duty of slaves toward their masters elsewhere too, in the Selections below, under the title Slaves, p. 543. Here the slave leads the erring master back onto the road, and so that Admonition should also be referred to this title.

units.la: ¶ Tit. vi. Adolescentiæ Aphorismus v. Sapè ætate pueri, ingenio senes sunt. ] Sic &c. eruitur ex Mercat. 5.4. v.15. Novus amator vetus puer. Nempe οι ... Recte Veteres pueri dici merentur, qui ingenio tamen senes: quando scilicet ad stultitiam redeunt, hoc est, ad Amores. Ita ætate pueri, sapè senes sunt.
units.tr: ¶ Title VI, Youth. Aphorism 5: Often boys are old in age, and old men are boys in mind. This is drawn out in the same way from Mercator 5.4, v. 15: A new lover is an old boy. Rightly, those are fittingly called old boys who are nevertheless old in mind, namely when they return to folly, that is, to their loves. So often boys in age, often old men.

units.tr: The Greek scholiast teaches the same thing in these words: ... To be understood of the same penalty.

units.la: Catullus Carmine xv. v.17. Ah tum te miserum, malique fati! Quem, attractis pedibus, patente portâ, Percurrent raphanique, mugilesq.
units.tr: Catullus, poem 15, v. 17: Ah, then you will be wretched and ill-fated, whom, with your feet bound, the radishes and mullets will run through, the gate standing open.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma secundum: Adultera & feminæ non domo solum exactæ, & dote privatæ fuerunt, sed etiam necatæ. Amph. 2. 2. v. 222. ] De Dote aperte ille locus loquitur. quod in Notis meis marginalibus ibidem expositi, his verbis: quin hoc te multem matrimonio] hoc est: Numquid contradicis, quin hoc matrimonium solvatur, & dotem amittas?
units.tr: † Ibid., axiom 2: Adulteresses and women were not only driven from the house and deprived of their dowry, but were even put to death. Amphitryon 2.2, v. 222. That passage speaks plainly of the dowry, as I explained in my marginal notes there, in these words: "quin hoc te multem matrimonio" ], that is: Do you not object that this marriage should be dissolved, and that you lose your dowry?

units.la: Quid Lex Iulia Adulteriis deprehensis irroget, satis notum est. Sed & Lex Solonis incognita non est, quâ Mulierem, apud quam Adulter fuerit deprehensus, ornari non finit, nec in fana ingredi: sin fecerit; tunc ejus vestes lacerare, ornatum diripere cuivis permisit, etiam verberare, dum ne occidat, nec mutilet: vti plurimus exponit Aeschynes contrà Timarchum. Poenam verò capitis multis primâ saeculis inductam, docet Lipsius ad Ann. les Taciti lib.iv.
units.tr: What the Julian Law imposes for adulteries detected is well known. But the law of Solon is not unknown either, by which a woman in whose house an adulterer had been caught was not allowed to adorn herself or enter temples; and if she did, it permitted anyone to tear her clothes, rip off her finery, and even beat her, provided he did not kill or maim her, as Aeschines explains at length in his speech against Timarchus. But that the death penalty was introduced in very early times is taught by Lipsius on the Annals of Tacitus, book 4.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma x v. Meretrices sine auro & argento ne quicquam præstant.] Si quis quæratur; quid sibi velit NEQUICQUAM, cui respondeo; dictionem esse latinissimam, ac significare; non quicquam. Cicero lib.i. Tusculan. Quæst. cap. xxxi. Secernere autem à corpore animum, nec quicquam aliud est, quàm emori discere.
units.tr: † Ibid., axiom 15: Prostitutes can accomplish nothing without gold and silver. If anyone asks what NEQUICQUAM means, I answer that it is a most Latin word, meaning not at all. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book 1, ch. 31: To separate the mind from the body is nothing other than learning to die.

units.la: † Ibid. Axiom. xxxiii. Meretrices quotiescunque pensum nequam absoluissent, corollas totidem Lucro cuiam Deo donârunt. ] Eò allusisse Plautum Asin. 4. i. v. 58. fatentur Viri doctissimi Lipsius & Casaubonus: quibus calculum meum haud injuriâ accenseo. Lector considered locum Plauti: neque abnuet; scio.
units.tr: † Ibid., axiom 33: Whenever prostitutes had finished their wretched task, they gave as many garlands to the god of gain. That Plautus alluded to this in Asinaria 4.1, v. 58, is affirmed by the most learned men, Lipsius and Casaubon, whose opinion I count my own, and not without reason. Let the reader consider the passage of Plautus; he will not refuse, I know.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma i x. Meretricula suis Amatoribus carere nequeunt, non minus ac cibo.] Sic Philenium Meretrix volenti Lenæ extrudere foràs Amatorem Argyrippum infit Asin. 3. i. v. 33. Patiar, si cibo carere me jubes. Neque verò sic capienda hæc verba, quasi ego statuam, aliquam intra dies aliquot mortuam Veneris abstinentiâ. hoc enim ne quidem Amatores absentes non perpetuò spurcam appetunt. Quin mutuus ille Amantium affectus versatur potius in ardenti amoris appetentiâ. Et tamen summam esse Amoris impatientiam constat ex Plauto Pseud. i. i. v. 92. Profectò nullo pacto posse vivere, inquit ibi Adolescens, si illa à me abalienatur, atque abducitur. Etalius Mercat. 2. 4. v. 1. & s. qq. Pentheum diripuisse ajunt Bacchas, nugas maximas fuisse credo, prout quo pacto ego diversus distrahor. Cur ego vivo? cur non morior? quid mihi est in vitâ boni? Certum est, ibo ad Medicum, & me ibi toxico morti dabo. Quando mihi adimitur quâ causâ vitam cupio vivere. Vide etiam Mercat. 3. 4. v. 15. Historiæ memorant Callirhoën Lyci Regis filiam, Diomedis amore captam, cùm voti compos fieri nequiret, ac Diomedem abnavigan-tem.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 9. Courtesans cannot do without their lovers, no less than without food.] So Philenium the courtesan, when the procuress wants to thrust her lover Argyrippus out of doors, says: I shall endure it, if you order me to go without food (Asin. 3.1 v. 33). These words should not be taken as though I were asserting that some woman, within a few days, dies from abstinence from love. For even absent lovers do not always crave a foul thing. Rather, that mutual affection of lovers consists in an ardent appetite for love. And yet it is clear that impatience of love can be extreme, from Plautus (Pseud. 1.1 v. 92): Surely I cannot possibly live, says the young man there, if she is alienated and taken away from me. Another character (Mercat. 2.4 v. 1 ff.) says: "They say the Bacchae tore Pentheus apart; I think those were mere trifles compared with how I am torn asunder. Why do I live? Why do I not die? What good is there in my life? I am resolved: I shall go to the doctor and there give myself death by poison. Since the reason for which I wish to live is taken from me." See also Mercat. 3.4 v. 15. Histories relate that Callirhoe, daughter of King Lycus, seized by love for Diomedes, when she could not gain her wish and saw Diomedes sailing away

units.la: B tem videret, laqueo sibi gulam præstrinxisse. De Bysal.iâ Massy.iio-rum Regis filiâ testatur Plutarchus, Calphurnij Crassi amore captam, cùm satisfacere amori ardentissimo nequiret, Crassum abeuntem, atque unicè deslentem, ferro jugulum sibi peremisse. De Sappho Lyricâ refert Naso, quòd amore Phaonis capta, cùm ille eam fugeret, ipsâ animi patientiâ se præcipitasse in mare de Monte Leucade.
units.tr: and strangled her throat with a noose. Plutarch testifies that the daughter of the king of the Massagetae, Byssalia, seized by love for Calphurnius Crassus, when she could not satisfy her most ardent love, and Crassus was leaving and she alone lamented him, slew herself with a sword. Naso reports of the lyric poet Sappho that, seized by love for Phaon, when he fled from her, she threw herself from the Leucadian cliff into the sea out of sheer impatience of mind.

units.la: Ibid. Axioma LXI. Meretrices comparantur τῇ φάτνῃ, præsepi: ubi scil.pabulum Adolescentum: ut Parasiti Præsepe dicuntur Curcul. 2. 1. v. 13. ] Parscilicet ratio est Parasitorum & Meretricum. Etilli namque & hæ Præsepi comparari possunt. Ratio comparationis non est obscura, proinde vberius non explicanda.
units.tr: Ibid. Axiom 61. Courtesans are compared to the manger [τῇ φάτνῃ], that is, the place where the young men's fodder is, just as parasites are called a manger (Curcul. 2.1 v. 13).] Clearly there is a reason for this, since parasites and courtesans alike can be compared to a manger. The basis of the comparison is not obscure, so it need not be explained at length.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphorismus LXVIII. Meretricibus lex posita, ne nimis acciperent. Tiuc.4.2 v.47.]
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorism 68. A law was laid down for courtesans that they should not take too much. (Truc. 4.2 v. 47.)

units.la: Objiciat aliquis: Si illud erat, cur tot è juventute evertbantur fundis, familijs?
units.tr: Someone may object: If that were so, why were so many young men ruined, stripped of their estates and families?

units.la: Respondeo esse παραλόγισμόν ὡς τῷ συμβεβηκότι: eodem modo, atque si quis sic argumentetur: Furibus, Adulteris, &c. lex non est p sita, ut furentur, mœchentur: Quia si id verum, cur tot è societate humanâ privantur suis possessionibus? cur tot honestæ matronæ faciunt factuαm pudoris? Αλογισμὸς certè ingens hæc foret. Atqui Aphorismus noster disserte habetur in Plauto, eo loco, quem adduxi.
units.tr: I answer that this is the fallacy of accident [παραλόγισμὸν ὡς τῷ συμβεβηκότι], in the same way as if someone argued: "The law has not been laid down that thieves and adulterers should steal and commit adultery, because if that were true, why are so many deprived of their possessions by human society? Why do so many honourable matrons take care to preserve their chastity?" This would surely be a huge fallacy [ἀλογισμός]. Yet this aphorism of ours is plainly found in Plautus, in the passage I have cited.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma LXXIIXX. Meretrices infantem ex stupro natum exposuerunt ad necem: si auctorem certum nescirent. Cistell.1.3.v.18.]
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 77 (sic). Courtesans exposed to death an infant born from fornication, if they did not know the certain father. (Cistell. 1.3 v. 18.)

units.la: Dicat quis: Alia ratio est Virginum, alia Meretricum. hæc Virgo fuit, qu: filiam peperit, quam postmodum Servo dedit exponendam ad necem. Quis verò Virginem dicat eam, quæ peperit? Vnicam nouimus ἀεὶπαρθένον, quæ naturæ cursum prætergressa est. Præterillam, Virginis definitionem nullam retinet, quæ peperit. Cæterùm Meretrices posse indicare auctorem suæ prolis, certissimum est, nisi quis credat, Meretrices absentes subigi, & διαπαρθένευσαι. Illæ quidem ad Nicrum & Rhenum juxta cum fœtu suo & Patre virgidemiam experiuntur per pontes.
units.tr: Someone may say: "The case of virgins is different from that of courtesans. This was a virgin who bore a daughter, whom she afterwards gave to a slave to be exposed to death." But who would call her a virgin who bore a child? We know of one ever-virgin [ἀεὶπαρθένον], who went beyond the course of nature. Apart from her, nothing retains the definition of a virgin for one who has borne a child. Moreover, that courtesans can name the father of their offspring is most certain, unless someone believes that courtesans are dealt with in their absence and play the virgin [διαπαρθένευσαι]. Indeed, they undergo a thrashing with rods on the bridges by the Neckar and the Rhine, together with their offspring and their father.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma XC. Post REM sequitur CONCEPTIO.] Id quidem ἀληθεύεικῶς colligitur ex Pers. 4. 4. v.18. Ubi cùm Toxilus ser-vus Dorpalo Lenoni persuadere cuperet, ut Virginè emeret, eo argumengumento, quòd indè maximum quæstum effet facturus; tandem infit: cum optimis Viris REM habe'is: gratiam tuam CONCIPIENT. Quibus verbis allusum ad σενο Agit enim cum Lenone, earum formularum pergnaro. Habebis REM, & indè mox CONCIPIES. Αρχιπροσσ manifestissima.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 90. Conception follows the deed.] This is indeed gathered [ἀληθεύεικῶς] from Persa 4.4 v. 18. There, when the slave Toxilus wants to persuade the procurer Dorpalus to buy a girl, on the argument that he will make a great profit from her, he finally says: You will have the deed with the best men, and your favour will conceive. These words allude to σενο. For he deals with a procurer, who knows these formulae well: you will have the deed, and soon you will conceive. The allusion is Αρχιπροσσ, most manifest.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma CII. Meretrices Canes aluerunt, quibus noua nomina indebantur. Epid. 2 2. v. 50.]
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 102. Courtesans fed dogs, to which new names were given. (Epid. 2.2 v. 50.)

units.la: Objiciat aliquis: Non fuerunt Meretrices, sed feminæ dotatæ. Resp. Feminæ igitur dotatæ Canes aluerunt.
units.tr: Someone may object: "They were not courtesans but dowered women." Answer: then dowered women fed dogs.

units.la: Rursùm dicat aliquis: Atqui nec canes ab ipsis enutritæ, multò minùs, ut noua acciperent nomina.
units.tr: Again someone may say: "But the dogs were not fed by them, much less did they receive new names."

units.la: Resp. Sic manifestissimè contradicitur textui. Sic enim habet: Caniquoque adeptu'st nomen. Vocatus ille Laconicus. Certè quidem non est novum, Meretriculas, siue Feminas, canes alere.
units.tr: Answer: this manifestly contradicts the text. For it says: Every dog has received a name. That Laconian dog was so named. Certainly it is not new for courtesans, or women, to feed dogs.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphor. CXXVIII. Lenæ comparantur portitoribus. Asin. I. 3. v. 7.] In explicatione huius thematis secutus sum sententiam Dionysii Lambini, Viri Clarissimi: neque quicquam demuto, firmissimè statuens; Portitores mare medium frequentasse, indice hoc loco Plauti. Adstipulatores quoque puto me habituram omnes Portitores maritimos.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphor. 128. Procuresses are compared to toll-collectors. (Asin. 1.3 v. 7.)
