In explaining this theme I have followed the opinion of the most distinguished Dionysius Lambinus, and I change nothing, firmly holding that toll-collectors frequented the middle of the sea, as this passage of Plautus shows. I think I shall also have all sea toll-collectors as supporters.

units.la: ¶ Tit. VIII. Ædium. Axiomate III. dixi, Ianuas in Græciâ in publicum aperiri solitas, idque comprobavi multis argumentis & exemplis. Si quis in ijs nolit acquiescere, doceat nos meliora: aut refutet nostra, si potest.
units.tr: ¶ Title 8, Of Houses. In Axiom 3 I said that in Greece the doors were customarily opened to the public, and I confirmed this by many arguments and examples. If anyone is unwilling to accept these, let him teach us better things, or refute our arguments if he can.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphorismus VIII. Clavi Laconica adulterinâ intus adaperta Aedes, & foris infecùs clausæ. Mostell. 2. 1. v. 57. 77.] Probavi id e verbis istis Theonis In qua quidem Theonis sententiâ veritatem huius rei attripio & tueor, donec contrarium quis ostendat. Quam eandem sententiam sequutus Scaliger & Casaubonus. Si cui secus videtur, ob clavem laconicam cælum non ruet. Iteùm si quis neget, quod dixi, nostrum Dieterich repræsentare clavem Laconicam, visat mihi omnes tabernas Serariorum in Germania, ac discer, verè me id pronuntiasse. Verum intùs aperiat clauis, an foris, quis curat? Meas quidem feras, quoties ordinarias clauês amiserat familia, præsertim cùm januis essent ejusmodi ferae, quas nostri Serarij appellant
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorism 8. A house was opened from within by a Laconian or adulterine key, and was shut tight from outside. (Mostell. 2.1 vv. 57, 77.) I proved this from the words of Theon. I maintain and defend the truth of this matter on the strength of Theon's opinion, until someone shows the contrary. Scaliger and Casaubon followed the same opinion. If anyone thinks otherwise, the sky will not fall because of a Laconian key. Again, if anyone denies what I have said, that our Dieterich represents the Laconian key, let him look at all the locksmiths' shops in Germany and learn that I spoke truly. But who cares whether the key opens from within or from without? Indeed, whenever the household had lost its ordinary keys, my beasts, especially since the doors were of that kind of iron fitting which our locksmiths call the Hoelschloß, these fellows often locked me in from inside, and earned full payment for my torment.

units.la: Sic. pellant Hoelschloß / homines isti sæpe mihi intús referárunt, ac pretium tulerunt integrum cruciatum. † Ibid. Axiomax i. Ad ostium adium sedebant ostiarij, sive Ianitores, incatenâ cum cane ferreo, picto scilicet, & alio Oblatratore, quasi alterius vicarío. Trin. 2.4. verf. 28. tutela ostiaria. Trucul. 2. 4. verf. 1. Ianua mordax. ] Ianitores sedisse in catenâ cum cane ferreo, Auctorum quâ veterum, quâ recentiorum omnia plena. Aliud verò est Canis, aliud Catena: quæ duo Disparata sunt, uti loquuntur Logici. Ferreus canis, est; canis pictus, ferreâ catenâ alligatus. Quærat quis: Quid ostiario præstabat canis ferreus, si aderat vivus? Respondeo de sententiâ omnium doctorum Virorum: pictum ideo ad parietem propter vivum, & verum, ut alterius picti imagine admoniti, à vivo illo & vero caverent. Addam Petronij verba pag. 74. Edit. Goldast. Ad sinistram intrantibus, non longe ab hostiarij cella, canis ingens catenâ vinctus in pariete erat pictus, superque quadratâ litterâ scriptum: CAVE CAVE CANEM.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 1. At the door of the house sat the doorkeepers, or porters, with a chained dog, painted of course, and another barker, as if a substitute for the other. (Trin. 2.4 v. 28, guardianship of the door; Truc. 2.4 v. 1, a biting door.)] That porters sat chained with an iron dog is everywhere in the authors, ancient and recent. But a dog is one thing, a chain another; these two are distinct things, as the logicians say. An iron dog is a painted dog bound with an iron chain. Someone may ask: "What use was an iron dog to the doorkeeper, if a live one was present?" I answer, in the opinion of all learned men: the dog was painted on the wall for the sake of the live and real one, so that, reminded by the image of another painted dog, people might beware of that live and real one. I shall add the words of Petronius, p. 74, Goldast edition: To those entering on the left, not far from the doorkeeper's cell, a huge dog bound with a chain was painted on the wall, and above it was written in square letters: BEWARE OF THE DOG, BEWARE OF THE DOG.

units.la: Ianitorem ve ò compedibus vinctum, ex his Ovidianis perspicuè constat lib. 1. Amor. Eleg. 6. v. 1.
units.tr: That the doorkeeper was sometimes bound in fetters is plainly clear from these lines of Ovid, Amores 1.6 v. 1:

units.la: Ianitor indignè durâ religate catenâ.
units.tr: The doorkeeper unworthily bound with a hard chain.

units.la: ¶ Tit. xiii. ÆRIS Axioma vii. In contractibus jurejurando se obstringebant: ut nisi pecunia præsens detur die dictâ, jusjurandum omittatur. Perf. 32. v. 4. ] Verissima hæc sunt, si modò vera, quæ scripsit Plautus dicto loco. Iuravit, inquit Leno, vicinus meus se hodie argentum daturum. Quod si non dederit, atque hic dies præterierit: Ego Argentum, ille jusjurandum amiserit. Hoc vult Leno: si die dictâ argentum non dederit vicinus; ego argentum amittam, & ille omnem fidem, ita gemino damno multabimur: ego argento, ille fide: hoc est: erit perfidus in me. Et hoc est; Iurisjurandum amittere.
units.tr: ¶ Title 13, Of Money. Axiom 7. In contracts they bound themselves by oath, so that unless money was paid on the appointed day, the oath would lapse. (Pers. 3.2 v. 4.) These things are very true, if what Plautus wrote in the passage cited is true. My neighbour, says the procurer, has sworn that he will give the silver today. But if he does not give it, and this day passes, I shall lose the silver, and he will lose his oath. The procurer means this: if on the appointed day my neighbour does not give the silver, I shall lose the silver, and he will lose all good faith; thus we shall both be fined by a double loss, I by the silver, he by his good faith. That is: he will be faithless towards me. And this is what it means to lose one's oath.

units.la: ¶ Tit.xv. AGRICULTURÆ Axioma I. Agri tamquam nutrices colebantur, ob felices eorum proventus. Trin. 2. 4. v. iii. ] Itaenim excudi debuit; non; alebantur. Ager autem NUTRIX dicebatur; quòd educaret familiam.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. XV. AGRICULTURAE Axiom I. Fields were cultivated like nurses, because of their happy yields. Trin. 2. 4. v. iii. ] It should have been printed thus; not colebantur but alebantur. A field was called a NURSE because it brought up the household.

units.la: ¶ Tit. xvii. AMBITIONIS Axioma xiv. Milites magnifici & inermes Vrbes vel bis capiunt. Vnde URBICAPI dicti. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 42. 51. Mil. 4.2. v. 46. ] Hæcista capienda. Thrasones enim πολίτης sunt, verbis; non vi, & armatâ manu : sicut Demetrius πολίορκητης dicitur, qui revera, & armatâ manu Urbes cepit.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. XVII. AMBITIONIS Axiom XIV. Soldiers, boastful and unarmed, capture cities even twice. Whence they are called city-takers. Bacch. 4. 9. v. 42. 51. Mil. 4. 2. v. 46. ] These words should be read as "to be captured." For braggarts are city-takers [πολίτης] in words only, not by force and an armed hand, just as Demetrius is called the city-besieger [πολιορκητής], who in fact took cities by an armed hand.

units.la: ¶ Tit. XIX. AMICITIÆ Axioma XXX.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. XIX. AMICITIAE Axiom XXX.

units.la: Amicitia quoque inter meretricium ordinem esse solet, non minus atque intra honestas Matronas, Cist. I. I. v. 24.] Objeét: Ita amicitia intra Latrones non minus esse solet, atque inter honestas personas.
units.tr: Friendship too is usually found among the order of prostitutes, no less than among honest matrons. Cist. 1. 1. v. 24. ] Objection: Friendship is likewise usually found among robbers, no less than among honest persons.

units.la: Resp. Quidni verò? Certe non minùs quoque inter Latrones constare potest Amicitia. Atque ita vere me scripsisse de improborum amicitiâ, ij demùm intelligent, qui diversas species amicitiæ ex Aristotele cognoverunt lib. VIII. Ethic. cap. III. quarum una est Honesta: altera, Iucunda: tertia, Vtilis.
units.tr: Answer: Why not indeed? Certainly friendship can exist among robbers no less. That I have written truly about the friendship of the wicked, only those will understand who have learned from Aristotle, Ethics Book VIII, chapter III, the different kinds of friendship: one is honourable, another pleasant, and a third useful.

units.la: Primam quidem συναναύμως & proprie Amicitiam verè dici, utpote quæ est κατ' ἀρετὴν, asserit Aristoteles: reliquas ἀμαναύμως quoque Amicitiæ nomen mereri, ibidem disputat Philosophus. Et talis esse potest Meretricium, talis Leonum.
units.tr: Aristotle maintains that the first is properly and strictly called friendship, since it is according to virtue; the same philosopher argues in the same place that the others also deserve the name of friendship, though in an equivocal sense. And such a friendship can be that of prostitutes, and such that of pimps.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma XXXI. Amici interdum in discrimen nos vocant: quod minimè sperabamus. Poen. 5. 4. v. 62.] Nota marginalis, quam ad illum locum appinxi, explicat hanc sententiam. Sic enim in orâ illius loci scripsi in Edit. secundâ Plautinâ: Etiam ij, qui pro me facere debent, mihi adversantur.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom XXXI. Friends sometimes bring us into danger, which we least expected. Poen. 5. 4. v. 62. ] The marginal note I added to that passage explains this sentiment. For thus I wrote in the margin of that place in the second Plautine edition: Even those who ought to act for me are opposed to me.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma XLIX. Quibus cum ætatem exegimus, absurdum est, non amplius nosse. Trin. 4.2.v.110. Ubi Seni Charmidi, interroganti: Norisne hominem? sic respondet Sycophanta: Næ tu me edepol arbitrare beluam: qui quidem non novisse possim, quicum ætatem exegerim.] Manifesta omnia: Latinitas latinissima. Proinde uberiore explicatione nihil opus.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom XLIX. With whom we have spent our lives, it is absurd not to know any longer. Trin. 4. 2. v. 110. Where the old man Charmides, asking, "Do you know the man?", the sycophant answers thus: "Indeed, do you take me for a beast, who could not fail to know the man with whom I have spent my life?" ] Everything is plain; the Latin is most Latin. Therefore no fuller explanation is needed.

units.la: ¶ Tit. XX. AMORUM Axiomate III. Locus Truc. I. 2. v. 89. Næ ut in ástu motitamur irâ] Sic quidem in primâ Editione expressèram eum locum: at postea nactus pretiosissimos MSS. Bibliothecæ Palatinæ, in secundâ Editione demonstravi, legendum: næ! ut in ástu mutuamur irâ. Et veram hanc lectionem nemo unquam everter, si vel ipse Plautus suat.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. XX. AMORUM Axiom III. Passage Truc. 1. 2. v. 89. Verily, how we exchange anger in the city. ] I had indeed printed that passage thus in the first edition; but afterwards, having obtained the most precious manuscripts of the Palatine Library, in the second edition I showed that it should be read: verily, how we exchange anger in the city. And no one will ever overturn this true reading, even if Plautus himself should sweat over it.

units.la: † Ibid. Axiomate XII. In loco Caf. 2.4. v. 56. [Qui amat, tamen hæreslesi esurit, nullum esurit.] Lectio hæc profecto nihil succi, nihil sanguinis habet. Illam igitur, quam in Editione secunda ex MSS. Pal. reporepòsui, deinceps strenuè defendam: Qui amat tantùm hercle si esurit, nullus esurit. Videat Lector Notas nostras Criticas.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom XII. In the passage Cas. 2. 4. v. 56. [Whoever loves, yet by Hercules, if he is hungry, is no one hungry.] This reading certainly has no juice and no blood. That reading, therefore, which in the second edition I restored from the Palatine manuscripts, I will henceforth vigorously defend: Whoever loves, but by Hercules, if he hungers, is no one hungry. Let the reader see our critical notes.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma LXIV. Amor non aliter alios complectitur, quàm se, & Genium suum. Curc. 5.2. v.29.] Existimo optimè me hanc sententiam è loco Plauti eruisse. Nam & sic eadem Fabulâ 2.3. v.22. & alibi. Alij indè elicere satagunt rationem, quare alter Parasitum vocárit Genium suum, vel quasi. Quàm commodè id fieri possit, ipsi viderint.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom LXIV. Love embraces others no differently than himself and his Genius. Curc. 5. 2. v. 29. ] I think I have rightly drawn this sentiment from a passage of Plautus. For it is so also in the same play, 2. 3. v. 22, and elsewhere. Others strive to elicit from this a reason why one man called his parasite his Genius, or as it were. How conveniently that can be done, they themselves will see.

units.la: † Ibid. Amor facit, ut sæpè disparis formæ, & ætatis copulentur. Afin: 1.3. v.4.] Explicant ista τπ... dictum Horatij de Clavo Cupidinis. Sic enim inquit lib.1. Odâ XXXIII. Sic visum Veneri, cui placet impares Formas, atque animos sub juga aënea Sævo mittere cum joco.
units.tr: † Ibid. Love often causes persons of unequal form and age to be joined. Asin. 1. 3. v. 4. ] These words explain the saying of Horace about the nail of Cupid. For thus he says in Book 1, Ode XXXIII: Thus it pleased Venus, who delights to put unequal forms and spirits under the bronze yoke with a cruel jest.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma XCI. Amatores initiatos Deo Munditianti: hoc est, Veneri: patet ex Casinâ 2.3. v.9.] Deus munditians sic dictus, à mundi-tijs; & est ipse AMOR. Quod ab alijs quoque jam pridem est explicatum: eoque nihil me fatigo amplius.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom XCI. Lovers initiated to the god Munditians: that is, to Venus; it is clear from Casina 2. 3. v. 9. ] The god Munditians is so called from munditiae (elegance), and he is Love himself. This has already been explained long ago by others, and so I trouble myself no further about it.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma CXI. Amor fustidit omnia adversa. Merc. 2.3. v.21. ubi adolescens sævitiam heri expertus, inquit: Arare mavolim, quàm sic amare. Verum esse hanc sententiam, quis abnegare poterit: Proin cui ea displicet, refutet licet.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom CXI. Love despises all adversities. Merc. 2. 3. v. 21, where the young man, having experienced the cruelty of his mistress yesterday, says: I would rather plough than love in this way. Who could deny that this sentiment is true? Therefore let anyone who dislikes it refute it.

units.la: Ibid. Axioma CXXXII. Senem osculari Mulierem turpe est. Merc. 3.3. v.12.] Id senex seni exprobrat his verbis: Iam ætatis plenus; animáque fœtidâ; Senex hir quofus; tu osculúre Mulierem? Vtine advenias vomitum excutias Mulieri?
units.tr: Ibid. Axiom CXXXII. It is shameful for an old man to kiss a woman. Merc. 3. 3. v. 12. ] The old man reproaches this to another old man in these words: Already full of years, and with a fetid soul, you old dotard; do you kiss a woman? Do you come to shake out your vomit on a woman?

units.la: Et paulò ante v.6. Itáne Vervex introeas?
units.tr: And a little before, v. 6: So you go in, you wether?

units.la: Vervecem ideò appellat Senem, quòd ad Venerem non minùs sit ineptus, quàm Aries Castratus.
units.tr: He calls the old man a wether because he is no less unfit for Venus than a castrated ram.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma CXXXVI. Amatores in foro fleterunt. Capt.3.1. v.18.] Objecd. Fortasse ad unum omnes sederunt. Resp. Fortasse omnes ad unum humi strati jacuerunt, vel in aëre pependerunt, alligati vexillo novo, vt à puellis tantò rectiùs dignoscerentur. Sic jocus deluditur joco.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom CXXXVI. Lovers have sat in the forum. Capt. 3. 1. v. 18. ] Objection: Perhaps they all sat down together. Answer: Perhaps they all lay flat on the ground, or hung in the air, tied to a new banner, so that they might be more readily distinguished by the girls. Thus a joke is mocked by a joke.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma CLII. Amor velut imber adobruit & proflernit juven-tutem. ] Aphorismus hic sumtus est ex Moftel. 1. 2. v. 61. ubi post-quàm Adolescens eleganti comparatione hominem novis ædibus similem prolixè expofu sst, velut ὁ ὑπερθηκ subdit:
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom CLII. Love, like a shower, overwhelms and prostrates youth. ] This aphorism is taken from Mostell. 1. 2. v. 61, where, after the young man has at length set out, with an elegant comparison, a man like a new house, he adds by way of hyperbole:

units.la: Continuò pro imbre Amor advenit in cor meum. Objectio:Imber gran-dis oportet fit, qui adolescentiam & prosternat, & obruat.
units.tr: Immediately Love came into my heart like a shower. Objection: The shower must be a great one, which both prostrates and overwhelms youth.

units.la: Resp. Certè grandis: quo inundari solet incauta illa ætas. Exem-pla passim obvia.
units.tr: Answer: Certainly a great one, by which that heedless age is wont to be flooded. Examples are everywhere to hand.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma CLIII. Amante solent insistere pedum plantam. Cas. 4.4.v.20. ] Quid sit; Pedum planta: quid item; Pedum plantam insi-stere; ex alio loco Plauti constare potest. Asin. 4. 1. v. 30. Neque illac ullo suo pede pedem homini premat. Hunc verò gestum Amatoribus esse familiarem, quis nescit?
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom CLIII. Lovers are wont to press the sole of the foot. Cas. 4. 4. v. 20. ] What the "sole of the foot" is, and likewise what "to press the sole of the foot" means, can be established from another passage of Plautus: Asin. 4. 1. v. 30: Nor will he press the foot of any man with his own foot there. But who does not know that this gesture is familiar to lovers?

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma CLXXXXI. Amantibus caput dicitur prurire, cùm sen-tiunt, se amore perire. ] Expressè & ἀμφοτέρων id affirmat Senex Bacch.s. 2. v. 74.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom CLXXXXI. The head is said to itch for lovers when they feel they are dying of love. ] The old man expressly affirms this, and with both, in Bacch. 5. 2. v. 74.

units.la: Objectio. Si hoc verum est, tum Amor ratione utitur. Resp. Certè quidem Amantes non sunt bruta exsensata. Sic Tiberius Cæsar ad Patres Conscriptos summam malorum suorum professus est, his verbis: Dī me Deaque pejus perʼant! quàm quotidiè perire sentio, si scio. Numquid & Tiberio caput prurijsse dicemus? Et Amantes mala sua non sentiant?
units.tr: Objection: If this is true, then Love makes use of reason. Answer: Certainly lovers are not senseless beasts. Thus Tiberius Caesar, addressing the Conscript Fathers, confessed the sum of his troubles in these words: May the gods and goddesses destroy me worse! How I feel myself perishing daily, if I know it. Shall we say that Tiberius's head itched too? And should lovers not feel their own evils?

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma CLXXXV. Amantes plerumque in forum processerunt libidinis suæ prædam inibi indagaturi. Habetur hoc disertim Casin.3.5. v.2. Atque id nemo vitij aut mendacij arguet, nisi ignarus discipli-næ quà veterum Romanorum, quà Sæculi hujus, & gentium ad-eò omnium.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom CLXXXV. Lovers for the most part came into the forum to hunt there for prey for their lust. This is stated expressly in Casina 3. 5. v. 2. And no one will charge this with vice or falsehood, unless he is ignorant of the discipline of the ancient Romans, of this age, and of all nations.

units.la: ¶ Tit.XX. ANIMALIUM. Aphorism.x. Catelli majusculi com-modati amicis ad caninam sobolem producendam. ] Sic colligo ex Cas.3. 2.v.22. Eodem modo ex hoc loco colligit Ianus Gruterus apud Taubmannum ibi loci: quem vide.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. XX. ANIMALIUM. Aphorism X. Rather large puppies were lent to friends for breeding canine offspring. ] I gather this from Cas. 3. 2. v. 22. Janus Gruterus gathers the same from this passage, as cited by Taubmann in that place; see him.

units.la: Objectio. Nostro sæculo quaruntur Catelli minuti: Ergò non Catelli majusculi.
units.tr: Objection: In our age small puppies are sought; therefore not larger puppies.

units.la: Resp. Est ἀγγοια ἐπιλέγχει Minimè namque ἀληθῶς ista sunt. Neque per Catellos majusculos ego intelligi velim Molossos aliquos vægrandes, vel Britannicos Doggios, aut tales, quales vernaculo sersermone nonnemo dépinxit. Grosse Starcke Rechelt. Aliter vero exlvsu quotidiano ⁠ ilta accipi solent.
units.tr: Answer: This objection refutes itself, for those things are by no means true. Nor would I have "larger puppies" understood as some very large Molossians or English mastiffs, or such as someone has depicted in the vernacular as big, strong hounds. Otherwise, in everyday usage, those words are taken in that sense.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma 1 x. Porci sacres ab insanis immolabantur. ] Constat id ex loco Men. 2, 2, v. 16. Men. Respondeme mihi, Adolescens; quibus hic pretijs porci væneunt Sacres sinceri? cyl. Nummo uno. Men. En! àme accipe; jube tepiari de mea pecunia. Nam ego quidem insanum esse te certò scio. Ex his verbis veritas Aphorismi satis patet. Et constat idem ex Varrone lib. 1. de Re rustica cap. 1. & 1v. Mureto lib. 111. Var. Lect. cap. v11; Turnebo lib. xx1x. cap. xxxi1. Rævardo lib. 111. cap. v11 1. Conject.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom LX. Sacred pigs were sacrificed by madmen. ] This is clear from Men. 2. 2. v. 16. Men.: Answer me, young man: at what price are pure sacred pigs sold here? Cyl.: For one penny. Men.: There! Take it, and have it cooked with my money. For I know for certain that you are mad. From these words the truth of the aphorism is sufficiently clear. The same is established from Varro, Book 1 on Rustic Matters, chapters 1 and 4; Muretus, Book 3 of Var. Lect., chapter 7; Turnebus, Book 29, chapter 31; Raevardus, Book 3, chapter 7, Conject.

units.la: ¶ Tit. xxIII. Annulorum Axioma v 1. Annulos dabant in signum & certitudinem rei. ] Eruitur id è verbis Sen. & Servi Bacch. 2. 3. v. 93. Nic. Quid opus est annulo? chr. Quia id signum est cum Theotimo, qui eum illi adferet: (supple; ut signo hoc viso, aurum ei reddat. Apparet itaque, in cuius rei certitudinem dati fuerint Annuli. Neque interest, utrum ostenderit annulum, an dederit. Utrumque factum.
units.tr: ¶ Title 23, Of Rings, Axiom 6. They gave rings as a sign and as a guarantee of a matter. ] This is drawn from the words of Seneca and Servius, Bacchides 2.3, v. 93. Nic. What need is there of a ring? Chr. Because it is the sign with Theotimus, who will bring it to him: (supply: so that, when this sign is seen, he may hand over the gold to him). It is clear, then, in whose guarantee the rings were given. It makes no difference whether he showed the ring or handed it over. Both happened.

units.la: ¶ Tit. xxvIII. Aquæ Aphorismus v 1. Aquarij aquas in ædes portabant, quà utebantur Mulieres ad balneum, sese eluendas. Inde Aquarij male coperunt audire. Poen. 1. 2. v 14.]
units.tr: ¶ Title 28, Of Water, Axiom 6. Water-carriers carried water into houses, where the women used it to wash themselves in the bath. From this the water-carriers came to be ill spoken of. Poenulus 1.2, v. 14.]

units.la: Aquarios ob vile id seruitium male audisse, tam est certum, quàm quod certissimum. Innuit id non obscu è Plautus loco allegato. Sed & alij Authores id evincunt. Quis igitur reprehendat hanc meam illationem?
units.tr: That water-carriers were ill spoken of because of that lowly service is as certain as anything can be. Plautus hints at it clearly in the passage cited. Other authors also prove it. Who, then, would find fault with this inference of mine?

units.la: Alibi male audiunt Aquarij; Ergo & apud Plautum male possunt audire. Videantur loca illa, quæ in Electis adduxi.
units.tr: Elsewhere water-carriers are ill spoken of; therefore they can also be ill spoken of in Plautus. Let those passages be looked at which I have adduced in the Electa.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma x. Aqua inest magna voluptas Rud. 1. 5. v. 1. Pindarus ⁠ At dicat quis: Eodem modo se cori inest magna voluptas, cui se involutiscarabaeus. Resp. Quid ni verò, scarabæus magnâ voluptate se involvat stercori? Ninimum voluptas omnis æstimatur ab objecto suo amabili.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 10. Water holds great pleasure Rudens 1.5, v. 1. Pindarus ⁠ But someone might say: In the same way there is great pleasure in dung, in which the beetle wallows. Reply: Why not, indeed? The beetle wraps itself in dung with great pleasure. Doubtless every pleasure is valued by its lovable object.

units.la: ¶ Ibid. Aphorismus xvi. Puteos è terra fodere solebant] Sic non loco, sed serio collegi ex Mostell. 2. 1. v. 32. Nempe in defectu aquæ salientis id fieri necessum fuit. Quærat quis: è terrâ autem? Cur non potius ex aëre? cur non omninò è flumine? Resp. Poterat amplius quis quærere: Cur non ex octavâ sphærâ cali? vel; ut quartum addatur Elemen-tum, tum, cur non ex ardenti igne flamma? Sed Dialectica haec nulla est. Sic enim deluderetur ipse Spiritus sanctus, è cujus instinctu Moses scripsit Genes. cap. xxvi. v. 19. Foderunt itaque servi Isaac in valle, & invenerunt ibi puteum aquarum vivarum. Jam si quis ita spiritum Sanctum arguat? In valle autem? cur non potius in aëre? cur non omnino in flumine? quanta haec foret blasphemia? quanta ἀλογία? Quid sit, fodere puteum vel suburbani vernae explicare possint.
units.tr: ¶ Ibid. Aphorism 16. They used to dig wells out of the earth.] I have gathered this not as a joke but seriously from Mostellaria 2.1, v. 32. Certainly, where there was no flowing spring, this had to be done. Someone may ask: out of the earth, though? Why not rather from the air? Why not altogether from a river? Reply: one could ask further, why not from the eighth sphere of heaven? Or, to add a fourth element, why not from burning fire, a flame? But this kind of dialectic is worthless. For in this way the Holy Spirit himself would be mocked, by whose inspiration Moses wrote in Genesis 26:19: And Isaac's servants dug in the valley, and found there a well of living waters. Now if someone accuses the Holy Spirit in this way: But in the valley? Why not rather in the air? Why not altogether in a river? How great would this blasphemy be! How great the absurdity [ἀλογία]! What it is to dig a well, even a slave-boy from the suburbs could explain.

units.la: Caeterum dicat quis: ad Plauti versum potius adducenda fuisse omnia ea, quae probarent; Remedia potius nobis expedienda, quam eorum nobis veniat usus: fera quae veniunt, nullius esse momenti. Bene? Idem monui ego in Notis ad eum locum: quas Lector in secundâ nostrâ Editione deprehender. Igitur quae quis meminit, mora mera est monerier. At vero sententia illa hic non potest habere locum Titulo A QV Æ PUTEORUM: sed potius Tit. ACTIONUM: autalibi.
units.tr: But someone may say that all those things which prove the point ought rather to have been brought to the Plautine verse; that remedies should rather be set out for us than their use come to us; that things which come from far off are of no importance. Very well. I made the same remark myself in the Notes on that passage, which the reader will find in our second edition. So "what one already remembers, it is mere delay to be reminded." But that opinion cannot have a place here under the title Of Wells; it belongs rather under the title Of Actions, or elsewhere.

units.la: Tit. xxxi. Argentariorum. Axioma ix. Argentum pu-
units.tr: Title 31, Of Bankers. Axiom 9. Silver pu-

units.la: rum & excoctum magis tinnulum sonum edit, quàm uvidum, adhuc in venis suis delitescens. Eandem sententiam tot dem litteris, totidem syllabis, ex loco Perf. 3.4.v.21. eruit quoque Ianus Gruterus apud Taubmanum. Proinde nihil demuto: sed Lectorem remitto ad collectanea Taubmanni. Quin & veritas Aphorismi tam est luculenta, ut ulteriori assertione non indigeat: modò cum candidi salis micâ accipiatur, & absit calumniandi libido.
units.tr: rum & excoctum magis tinnulum sonum edit, quàm uvidum, adhuc in venis suis delitescens. The same sentiment, with as many letters and as many syllables, is also drawn out from Persius 3.4, v. 21 by Janus Gruterus, as cited by Taubmann. Therefore I change nothing, but refer the reader to Taubmann's collections. Indeed, the truth of the aphorism is so clear that it needs no further assertion, provided it is taken with a grain of candid salt and the itch of calumny is absent.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphorismus xiii. Pecuniam solebant occupare, ne otiosa lan-guesceret. Ita quasi per jocum Danistarum indolem expressi, ex Epid. 2. 2. v. 113. Sedulò quippe lucripetæ isti cavent, ne Argentum otiosè domi delitescat, sed enixè laborant, ut nummus nummum pariat. Senecalib. v 11. de Benef. cap. x iv. Illic stat acerbus super caput creditor, qui nullum diem gratis (sine usurâ) occidere patitur.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorism 13. They used to lay out money, lest it lie idle. I have expressed the character of the usurers in this way, as if in jest, from Epidicus 2.2, v. 113. Those money-grubbers take care, indeed, that silver does not lie idle hidden at home, but they labour zealously so that coin begets coin. Seneca, On Benefits 7, ch. 14: There the harsh creditor stands over one's head, who allows no day to pass without interest.

units.la: ¶ Tit. xxxvii. Arithmetices. Aphorismo I. Medius digitus
units.tr: ¶ Title 37, Of Arithmetic. Aphorism 1. The middle finger

units.la: ineptâ ratione dicitur Impudicus, quia Medici eo digito vulnerum putredines tangere solent. De Medio digito varie variant Authores. Videat Lector, quae de eo prolixè commentatus est Alex. ab Alexandr. Genial. Dier. lib. iv. cap. xxvi. Sunt, qui Medicum ideo dictum velint, quod podici immitti soleat totus, totus utpote longior. Ego in diversitate ista opinionum quid amplius pronuncìem, non habeo, contentus ea exposuisse, quae faciunt ad antiquam computandi rationem.
units.tr: It is called impudent for a foolish reason, because doctors customarily touch the putrefaction of wounds with that finger. Authors vary in various ways about the middle finger. Let the reader see what Alex. ab Alexandr., Geniales Dies 4.26 has commented on it at length. Some want it called Medicus because it is usually thrust whole into the anus, being the longest. In this diversity of opinions I have nothing more to pronounce, content to have set out those things which bear on the ancient method of counting.

units.la: C
units.tr: C

units.la: ¶ Tit.xxxiv. Axioma ii. Sutores plerumque sedentarij & claudi- Aul.1.1.v.35. Tunc autem interdius quasi claudus Sutor domi sedet dies totos. Et Aul.3. 5.v.39. Sutores sedentarij. ] Locaista non loquuntur de uno Sutore: neque de certo aliquo Individuo, sed deIdeâ Indefi- nitè de sutoribus. Quæ Propositiones, juxtà doctrinam Logico- rum, æquipollent Particularibus. Quidam Sutores ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ sunt claudi, sunt sedentarij. Proinde qui ex istis locis Plautinis Sutores a- liquos statuit claudos, & sedentarios, non statim is centum aliquot, aut trecenta millia formare dicendus est sutores claudos, aut sedenta- rios.
units.tr: ¶ Title 34. Axiom 2. Cobblers are mostly sedentary and lame. Aulularia 1.1, v. 35. Then, indeed, in the daytime the lame cobbler sits at home all day long. And Aulularia 3.5, v. 39. Cobblers are sedentary.] These passages do not speak of one cobbler, nor of some particular individual, but of the class, indefinitely, of cobblers. Such propositions, according to the teaching of the logicians, are equivalent to particulars: some cobblers, for the most part [ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ], are lame, are sedentary. Therefore whoever takes these Plautine passages to set up some cobblers as lame and sedentary is not at once to be said to have formed a hundred or several hundred thousand lame cobblers or sedentary ones.

units.la: Quamquam qui hoc mihi imputare velit, eâdem se excuset fortè ὑπερβολὴ, quâ mihi utendum fuit, quando in Præfatione Lexici mei Plautini quondam scripsi; supra trecenta mill a locorum legi in Editione ultimâ Saxonicâ Plauti expressu inibi ex meâ primâ. Senecæ dictum est lib.vii. de Benef. cap. xxiii. In hoc omnis hyperbole extenditur, ut ad verum mendacio veniat. Numquam tantum sperat hyperbole, quantum audet: sed incredibilia affirmat, ut ad credibilia perve- niat.
units.tr: Yet whoever wishes to impute this to me may perhaps excuse himself by the same hyperbole [ὑπερβολὴ] which I once had to use when I wrote in the Preface of my Plautine Lexicon: more than three hundred thousand passages were read in the latest Saxon edition of Plautus, expressed there from my first. Seneca said, On Benefits 7, ch. 23: In this every hyperbole is extended, so that by a lie it comes to the truth. Hyperbole never hopes as much as it dares: it affirms incredible things so that it may arrive at credible ones.

units.la: Tit.xxxvii. Auctionis. Axioma quartum. Emere quoque solebant in conditionem meliorem, Capt.1.2.v.26. ] Emere in conditionem meliorem, est, quando pretium majus offertur. Siçenim Paulus Ic.lib.v. ad Sabinum, cujus verba exstant ff.lib.xviii. Tit.de in diem addictione. Ille fundus centum esto tibi emtus nisi quis intrà Kalen- das Ianuarias proximas meliorem conditionem f. ceritseu attulerit, quò res à Domino abeat.
units.tr: Title 37, Of Auctions. Axiom 4. They also used to buy on better terms Captivi 1.2, v. 26. ] To buy on better terms means when a higher price is offered. For thus Paulus the jurist, in book 5 on Sabinus, whose words are in the Digest, book 18, title On Sale Subject to a Day: Let that farm be bought by you for a hundred, unless someone within the next Kalends of January makes or brings a better term or price, so that the thing passes from the owner.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma vi. Nihil non nisi pecuniâ emitur. Asin.1.3.v.49. Si as habent, dant mercem. ] Germani Mercatores solemne hoc verbum usurpant: Hastu Gelt / so hab ich Wahr. Paraphrasi igituralià minimè opus, quâ explicetur hic noster Aphorismus.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 6. Nothing is bought except for money. Asinaria 1.3, v. 49. If they have coin, they give the goods.] German merchants use this familiar saying: "Hastu Gelt, so hab ich Wahr" (Have you money? Then I have the goods). So no paraphrase is needed at all to explain this aphorism of ours.

units.la: ¶ Ibid. Axioma viii. Mercatores Mercurium invocârunt, ut fœtus lucris afficiat. ] Ita quidem nonnemo malit legere Amph. Prol.v.21. sed rectius retinetur vulgata lectio, quam expressim in secundâ Editione Plauti,de consensu omnium MSS. Codd.
units.tr: ¶ Ibid. Axiom 8. Merchants invoked Mercury, that he might bless their gains with increase.] Indeed some would rather read it thus, Amphitruo Prologue, v. 21, but the received reading is more rightly kept, as it is expressly confirmed in the second edition of Plautus by the agreement of all the manuscripts.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xxxvi. Decima pars in Auctione Herculi consecratâ. Stich.2.1.v.80. ] Non hoc volo, quasi in omni Auctione, Pauperum a- què ac Divitum idobservatum, Neque enim universalem facio regu- lam. am: sed potissimùm de opulentioribus capiendum id censeo: eòque Indefinitam servo Propositionem: quæ æquipollet Particulari.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 36. A tenth part in an auction consecrated to Hercules. Stichus 2.1, v. 80. ] I do not mean this as if in every auction it was observed alike for poor and rich. For I do not make a universal rule, but I think this should be understood chiefly of the more wealthy; and so I keep an indefinite proposition, which is equivalent to a particular one.

units.la: ¶ Tit.xxxix. Augurii. Aphor. 1. In omnibus fere actionibus Augures solebant consulere. Asin. 2. 1. v. 11. ] Augures Accusandi casu positum. A quibus vero consulebantur? inquiat aliquis. Non dixerim ego: ab omnibus fere mortalibus? sed si loquor: In omnibus fere actionibus solebant consulere. Non nomino utique, quot & qui consulere soliti sint. Neque hoc admittendum puto, quando quis sic argumentatur: Quod si Augurium sumebant à Parrhá, à Cornice, à Pico, ubique locorum illas Aves obvias esse oportuit. Nam ab his duntaxat Avibus Augurianon capta. Ubivis enim obvia sunt Auguria Vulturum, Accipitrum, Aquilarum, Milvorum, Picorum, Hirundinum, Columbarum, Gallinarum, Corvorum, Noctuarum, Apum & id genus Avium. Ettamen, si à Parrhá, à Cornice, & Pico Auguria capta, certè præsentes illas Aves & obvias esse oportuit.
units.tr: ¶ Title 39, Of Augury. Aphorism 1. In nearly all actions augurs were used to be consulted. Asinaria 2.1, v. 11. ] Augures is put in the accusative case. But by whom were they consulted? someone will ask. Shall I not say, by nearly all mortals? But if I speak thus: In nearly all actions they were used to consult, I do not name at all how many and which people were accustomed to consult. Nor do I think this should be admitted when someone argues thus: If they took augury from the Parrha, from the Crow, from the Woodpecker, then those birds ought to have been met everywhere. For augury was not taken from these birds alone. Omens of vultures, hawks, eagles, kites, woodpeckers, swallows, doves, hens, ravens, owls, bees and birds of that kind are met everywhere. And yet, if augury was taken from the Parrha, the Crow and the Woodpecker, surely those birds too should have been present and met with.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma v 1. Omne principium rei omen erat bonum. Stich. 2. 5. v. 23. ] Objiciat aliquis: Nullum igitur poterat esse malum? Respondeo: Regula est Logicorum: Verba sunt intelligenda secundùm subjectam materiam. Omne bonum principium (quale erat illud servi) omen erat bonum. Sic enim diserte Stichus: Bona sinistra strenaque obvia pro esset mihi.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axioma v 1. Every beginning of a matter was a good omen. Stich. 2. 5. v. 23. Someone may object: Then nothing could be evil? I answer: it is a rule of the logicians that words must be understood according to their subject matter. Every good beginning (such as that of the slave) was a good omen. For Stichus says this plainly: May a good left-hand sign and a lucky meeting befall me.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma v r. Omen nostrum non est Adversariorum. Caf. 2. 8. Ibid. v. 78. ] Objectio: Vbiumquam quis attendit omini Adversarij sui?
units.tr: † Ibid. Axioma v r. Our omen is not our adversaries'. Caf. 2. 8. Ibid. v. 78. Objection: Does anyone ever pay attention to the omen of his adversary?

units.la: Respondeo: Neque ego id affirmo. Num ideò tamen falsum, quod noster vult Aphorismus? Quid sit Omen nostrum, in Notis ad eum locum exposui. Idem nempe est, quod, Auspicate, felicitér q.
units.tr: I answer: I do not affirm that. Is our maxim therefore false? What our omen means I have explained in the notes on that passage. It is the same as the phrase auspiciously, happily, etc.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xv. Aves visco capi solitæ, & fundis: quibus Aucupes folia farfari virgulti substernebant, ne ad fundas viscus adhærescerent. Poen. 2. 1. v. 33. ] Allegoria huius loci hæc est. Plautus loco dicto de Militea-git, homine volatico, pugnas suas pent ethronicas jactitante. Mirătur hanc ferociam Leno, & quærit; quomodo id potuerit? Pergit Miles exponere: viscum legioni dedi, fundasque: eò præsternebam folia farfari, ne ad fundas viscus adhærescerent. Hic igitur, quod in Aucupijs fit, Miles sibi applicat: & suæ arti capiendi vno die tot homines. Quis hanc non capit? Nihil verò ista ad Dialogos Lucani: in quiquibus sub velo ἀναγραφὴ multa item vera occultari, nemo nescit.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axioma xv. Birds that are wont to be caught with birdlime and slings, for which the fowlers spread leaves of coltsfoot under the bush, so that the birdlime would not stick to the slings. Poen. 2. 1. v. 33. The allegory of this passage is as follows. In the passage cited, the soldier, a flighty fellow, boasts of his battles, his pentathlon-like exploits. The pimp wonders at this boldness and asks how he could have managed it. The soldier goes on to explain: I gave birdlime and slings to the legion, and for that purpose I spread leaves of coltsfoot, so that the birdlime would not stick to the slings. Here the soldier applies to himself what fowlers do, and to his own skill in catching so many men in one day. Who does not see this? But these things have nothing to do with the Dialogues of Lucian, in which, under the veil of anagraphē [ἀναγραφὴ], many true things are likewise hidden, as everyone knows.

units.la: ¶ Tit. XLII. Balnei Aphor. VIII. In balneis luxu lavandi rem o-minem profligabant. Trin.2.4.v.5 Rud.2.7.v.21. Asin.1.2.v.9.] Loca omnia, è quibus talis regula petita, manifestissima sunt. Ecce Trin. 2.4.v.5. Servum sic alloquitur Adolescens:
units.tr: ¶ Tit. XLII. Baths, Aphor. VIII. In the baths they squandered every substance through the luxury of bathing. Trin. 2. 4. v. 5. Rud. 2. 7. v. 21. Asin. 1. 2. v. 9. All the passages from which this rule is drawn are perfectly clear. See Trin. 2. 4. v. 5, where the young man addresses his slave thus:

units.la: Minus quindecim dies sunt, quòm pro hisce Aedibus Minas quadraginta accepisti à Callicle.
units.tr: It is less than fifteen days since you received forty minae from Callicles for this house.

units.la: Excipit Adolescens: quid factum est eo? Respondet Servus: Comesum, expotum, exsutum, Elotum in balneis.
units.tr: The young man replies: What happened then? The slave answers: Eaten, drunk, sweated out, and washed away in the baths.

units.la: Deinde Rud.2.7.v.21. Servus joculariter ita loquitur: Eho! an te poenitet?
units.tr: Then in Rud. 2. 7. v. 21, the slave speaks jokingly in this way: Eho! Are you sorry?

units.la: In mari quod elavi, nisi hic in terra iterum elUAM.
units.tr: What I washed away in the sea, unless I wash it out again here on land.

units.la: Sic Asin.1 2.v.3.
units.tr: Likewise Asin. 1. 2. v. 3:

units.la: In Mari reperi: hic elavi Bonis.
units.tr: I found it in the sea; here I washed away my goods.

units.la: Et dubitare quis possit, à tribus istis locis recte inferri; per Luxum Balnearum multos sua Bona perdidisse?
units.tr: And who could doubt that these three passages rightly imply that by the luxury of the baths many men lost their goods?

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma XII. Ampulla rubida, rubiginosa strigilis fuit Parasi-tis: quà Divites in Balneis defricabant. Stich.2.1.v.74.] Scilicet ea fuit nota Divitum ad unum omnium, ut ament munditiem, ostentent pompam, splendorem admittant, aversentur, exsecrenturque sordida, rancida, & mutila instrumenta Parasiti. Quid inde? Non propterea falsum, Parasitos ijs instrumentis usos ad defricandum Diuites in balneis, quod ex Plauto, & alijs Auctoribus notissimum.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axioma XII. A reddish flask and a rusty strigil were the parasites' tools, with which the rich rubbed themselves down in the baths. Stich. 2. 1. v. 74. Clearly this was the common mark of the rich, that they loved cleanliness, displayed pomp and splendour, and shunned and cursed the dirty, rancid and broken tools of the parasite. What follows from this? Not that it is false that parasites used such tools to rub down the rich in the baths, which is very well known from Plautus and other authors.

units.la: ¶ Tit.XLIII. Belli. Axiomate XLVI Moftelb.2.1.v.11. sic ex MSS.Pall.legendum:
units.tr: ¶ Tit. XLIII. War. Axiom XLVI. Most. 2. 1. v. 11. The passage should be read thus, according to the Palatine manuscripts:

units.la: Vbi aliqui quindenis haflis corpus transfigi solent.
units.tr: Where some men are wont to have their bodies pierced by fifteen spears.

units.la: Vide Notas meas Criticas ad eum locum. Sunt tamen, quibus placet:
units.tr: See my critical notes on that passage. Some, however, prefer:

units.la: Vbi alij quique haflis corpus transfigi solent.
units.tr: Where other men are wont to have their bodies pierced by spears.

units.la: Sed perperàm.
units.tr: But this is wrong.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma XXVI. In bello rem bene gerentibus Rex Persarum pa-teram aureram dono dedit. ] Eò allusum Amph.1.1.v.262. Amphitruoni à Telebois data est patera aurea, qui potitare solitus est Pterela Rex. Neque verò hinc sequi potest: In omni portu Persico ideò fuisseconspectum Re-gem Persarum. Mala illatio; nulla consequentia. Veritas rei patet è VOPISCI Aureliano cap. v. Data est ei, cum legatus ad Persas esset, patera, qualis solet Imperatoribus dari a Rege Persarum, in qua insculptus erat Sol, &c. Ad hunc morem allusisse Plautum, nemo negare poterit.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axioma XXVI. In war, the King of the Persians gave a golden bowl as a gift to those who performed well. The allusion is to Amph. 1. 1. v. 262: A golden bowl was given to Amphitryon by the Teleboans, who was wont to be called King Pterelas. Nor can it follow from this that the King of the Persians was therefore seen in every Persian port. That is a bad inference, with no consequence. The truth of the matter is plain from Vopiscus, Aurelian, ch. v: When he was an envoy to the Persians, he was given a bowl of the kind that the King of the Persians usually gives to generals, on which the Sun was engraved, etc. No one can deny that Plautus was alluding to this custom.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma LXXXXI. Peditatus additus equitatui. Mil. I. I. v. 54.] Malit non nemo contrarium : Peditatui additum equitem. Es ist aber vier Hosen/eines Tuchs. Nihil omninò discriminis.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axioma LXXXXI. Infantry added to cavalry. Mil. 1. 1. v. 54. Some would prefer the opposite: a horseman added to the infantry. But it is four trousers of one cloth. There is no difference at all.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma LXXXVII. Milites magnum numerum Meretricum Ibid. secum duxerunt. Epid. 2. 2. v. 29. 30.] Hoc loco Plautus ait, revertente e bello juventute ad Lares patrios, commovisse ordinem Meretricum, & unamquamque occurrisse ultrò Amatori suo, illumque captasse. Quæ res in memoriam mihi revocavit, id, quod nonnullis absurdum videtur, etiam in bello Meretrices Militibus præsto fuisse. Negant utique in Militum comitatu vel unicam fuisse Meretriculam. Affero ego contrarium ex verbis Liuij. Scipio Africanus, inquit Livius, Numantiam obsedit, & corruptum licentiâ, luxuriâque exercitum, ad severissimam Militiæ disciplinam revocavit. Omnia enim Deliciarum instrumenta recidit: Duo millia Scortorum è castris ejecit.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axioma LXXXVII. Soldiers brought a great number of prostitutes with them. Epid. 2. 2. v. 29, 30. Here Plautus says that when the youth returned from war to the household gods of his fathers, the order of prostitutes was stirred, and each one ran up to her lover of her own accord and seized him. This reminded me of something that seems absurd to some people, namely that even in war prostitutes were at hand for the soldiers. They deny that there was even a single little prostitute in the soldiers' train. I bring forward the opposite from the words of Livy. Scipio Africanus, says Livy, besieged Numantia, and recalled his army, corrupted by licence and luxury, to the strictest military discipline. For he cut off all the instruments of pleasure; he drove two thousand prostitutes out of the camp.

units.la: Florus lib. II. cap. XVIII. Scorta, Calones, sarcinæ, nisi ad usum necessariæ, amputantur.
units.tr: Florus, Book II, ch. XVIII: Prostitutes, camp-followers and baggage are cut away, except what is necessary for use.

units.la: Scio, qui obtendat, non de Mulieribus, sed de Mulierosis ista Scorta accipienda.
units.tr: I know that someone may object that these prostitutes are to be understood not as women but as male prostitutes.

units.la: Falsum id esse, patet ex eo, quòd Livius ista Scorta vocat Deliciarum Instrumenta. At viri-Scorta quomodo Deliciarum instrumenta dici queant? Adhæc si duo millia virorum ejecta è castris: quantum putabimus restare potuisse de reliquo exercitu? Nugæ. Neque enim duo millia Virorum tam citò crescunt, ut fungi: eòque tam temerè tot milites è castris abigi minimè potuerunt.
units.tr: That this is false is clear from the fact that Livy calls these prostitutes instruments of pleasure. But how could male prostitutes be called instruments of pleasure? Moreover, if two thousand men were driven out of the camp, how much do we think could have remained of the rest of the army? Nonsense. For two thousand men do not grow so quickly like mushrooms, and so many soldiers could hardly have been driven out of the camp so carelessly.

units.la: Apud Florum verò ista Scorta à Calonibus apertè seperantur.
units.tr: In Florus, however, these prostitutes are clearly distinguished from the camp-followers.

units.la: Infert nonnemo: quin ne legitimæ quidem Uxores comitabantur maritos. Id verum post Augusti tempora, quando strictior Disciplina militaris exercita. Nam ante Augustum id licuisse: immò ab ipso Augusto non usque adeò severè prohibitum, quis colligat ex his Suetonij verbis: In re militari & commutavit multa, & instituit: atque etiam ad antiquum morem nonnulla revocavit: Disciplinam severissimè rexit, ne Legatorum quidem cuipiam, nisi GRAVATE, hibernisq; mensibus demum permisi: UXOREM invisere. Non igitur absolute id ab Imperatore inhibitum. Quod postea tamen ab aliis Impp. severius & strictius observatum.
units.tr: Someone infers: Not even lawful wives accompanied their husbands. This is true after the time of Augustus, when stricter military discipline was practised. That it was permitted before Augustus, and indeed was not forbidden so strictly even by Augustus himself, one may gather from these words of Suetonius: In military affairs he changed and instituted many things, and even revived some ancient customs; he kept discipline most strictly, so that to none of the legates, except when sick, and only in the winter months, was it permitted to visit his WIFE. So it was not absolutely forbidden by the Emperor. What was later observed more severely and strictly by other emperors is another matter.

units.la: Tit. XLIV. BENEFICIORUM. Axioma ultimum sic habet: De bonis bene partis liberales esse convenit: ideo, quia à Deo sunt. Trin.2. 2.v. 24. ] Ex hoc loco alius id elicit: q.d. Divina gratia tantum se poss fidere, ut non tibi solum, sed & Amicis bene facere possit. Bene utrumque. Vere utrumque.
units.tr: Tit. XLIV. BENEFITS. The last axiom reads: It is fitting that goods which have been well acquired should be shared generously, because they come from God. Trin. 2. 2. v. 24. From this passage someone draws the conclusion: that is, the divine grace is so trustworthy that it can do good not only to you but also to your friends. Both are well said; both are true.

units.la: ¶ Tit. XLV. BONORUM. Axioma v i. Quod quis in publico accepit, & quasi casu invenit, id proprium est. Rud. 4.3.v.33.& 4.4.v.27. ] Quid sibi velit, In publico accipere: quid, casu invenire: quid item; quasi-casu, è materiâ subjectâ contextûs Plautini haud est obscurum. Ecce enim priore loco Rud.4.3.v.33. Gripus Piscator dicit:
units.tr: ¶ Tit. XLV. GOODS. Axiom VI. What someone has received in public, and has found as if by chance, is his own property. Rud. 4. 3. v. 33 and 4. 4. v. 27. What is meant by to receive in public, what by to find by chance, and likewise what by as if by chance, is not obscure from the subject matter of the Plautine context. For see the first passage, Rud. 4. 3. v. 33, where the fisherman Gripus says:

units.la: Ecquem in Maridices esse Piscem MEUM?
units.tr: Is there anyone who can claim the fish in the sea as MINE?

units.la: Quos, quem capio siquidem cepi, MEI sunt: habeo pro MEIS: Nec manu adferuntur: neque illinc partem quisquam postulat.
units.tr: Whatever I catch, if indeed I have caught it, is MINE: I hold it as MINE. Nor is it brought by hand, nor does anyone demand a share of it from that quarter.

units.la: In Foro palam omnes vendo pro MEIS venalibus.
units.tr: In the Forum I sell openly, all things for sale as MINE.

units.la: Posteriori loco Rud.4.4.v.27. idem Gripus sic infert:
units.tr: In the second passage, Rud. 4. 4. v. 27, the same Gripus infers thus:

units.la: Si in Mari reti adprehendi, qui Tuum potius est, quam MEUM?
units.tr: If I caught in the net in the sea, which is rather YOURS than MINE?

units.la: En; Mare erat commune, & publicum: in quo Piscator piscces cæpit. Accepit igitur in publico. Ibidem casu: h.e. ... cæpit piscces. Et sic quasi-casu, est; ...
units.tr: See: the sea was common and public, and in it the fisherman caught fish. He therefore received them in public. And by chance, that is, ... he caught fish. And so as if by chance, is ...

units.la: ¶ Tit. XLVI. CALUMNIÆ Aphor. viii. Calumnias devitare non possumus, modo præter nostrum meritum ea nobis obtingant. Stich.1. 2.v. 58.] Nimirum in potestate nostra non est, ne Calumniatores reprehendant nostra benefacta. Id vero solatur Conscientias recte factorum, ne merito suo maledicta aliorum audiie cogantur. Et hoc est; præter nostrum meritum. Eandem mentem instillat Bonis Viris Seneca lib.iii. de Ira cap.xli. Conscientia satisfiat, nil in famam laboremus: sequatur vel mala, dum bene Merearis. Ubi Lipsius malit; dum bene merentes. Idem sub finem Epist. cxiii. Mala opinio bene parta del&et. Et Pythagoras scite admodum apud Stobæum serm.xliv. ...
units.tr: ¶ Tit. XLVI. SLANDER. Aphor. VIII. We cannot avoid slanders, provided that they fall upon us apart from our own deserving. Stich. 1. 2. v. 58. Certainly it is not in our power to keep slanderers from finding fault with our good deeds. But a clear conscience of right action consoles us, so that we are not compelled to hear the abuse of others on account of our own merit. And this is what is meant by apart from our own deserving. Seneca instils the same mind into good men in Book III of On Anger, ch. xli: Let your conscience be satisfied; let us not labour for reputation at all; let evils follow, provided you deserve well. Where Lipsius prefers: provided you are deserving well. The same author, near the end of Letter cxiii: A reputation won by good means delights. And Pythagoras, very wisely, in Stobaeus, serm. xliv. ...

units.la: ¶ Ibid. Aphor. xxix. Calumniatores furiosi, ut Sacerdotes Isidis Deae, qui in furore tympano usi: Poen. 5. 5. v. 38.] Plauti verba haec sunt: Ag. Num tili, Adulescens, mala, aut dentes pruriunt? Qui huic es molestus: an malam rem quaeritas? Anth. Quor non adhibuisti, dum isthaec loqueris, Tympanum? Nam te Cinaedum esse arbitror magis, quam Virum.
units.tr: ¶ Ibid. Aphor. xxix. Furious slanderers, like the priests of the goddess Isis, who in their frenzy used the drum: Poen. 5.5 v. 38.] These are the words of Plautus. Ag. Are your ears ringing, young man, or your teeth itching? Who is bothering you? Are you looking for trouble? Anth. Why didn't you bring a drum while you were saying those things? For I think you are more a Cinaedus than a man.

units.la: De Calumnijs & maledictis hic agi, manifeste locus arguit, inde à versu 30.
units.tr: That this passage deals with slanders and abuse is plain from the context, beginning at verse 30.

units.la: Tantum vero Sacerdotes Isidis usos Tympano, ego numquam dixerim. Hos vero Tympano usos, quis negare poterit? Notum quippe, Tympana & Cymbala ad furorem incutiendum in Orgijs adhibita. Notum item: eadem in Sacris Cybeles & Bacchi usurpari solita. Horat. lib. 1. Odâ xviii. v. 13. Saeva tene cum Berecynthio Cornu tympana.
units.tr: I would never say that the priests of Isis used the drum. But that those others used the drum, who can deny? It is well known that drums and cymbals were employed in the orgies to stir up frenzy. It is also well known that the same instruments were customarily used in the rites of Cybele and Bacchus. Horace, Odes 1.18, v. 13. Keep the savage drums with the Berecyntian horn.

units.la: En; cur saeva tympana dicit? non nisi ob furorem. Ibid. libr. 1. Odâ xvii. v. 5. Non Dindymene, non adytis quatit Mentem Sacerdotum incola Pythius, Non Liber aque: non acuta Sic geminant Corybantes aera.
units.tr: See, why does he call the drums savage? Only because of the frenzy. Horace, Odes 1.17, v. 5. Neither Dindymene nor the Pythian who dwells in the sanctuary shakes the minds of the priests so, nor does Liber, nor do the Corybantes so pound their sharp bronze.

units.la: Lucret. lib. iv. v. 623. Tympana tenta tonant palmis, & cymbala circum Concava, raucisono minitatur cornua cantu: Et Phrygio stimulat numero cava tibia mentis, Telaq; praeportant VIOLENTI signa FURORIS.
units.tr: Lucretius, Book 4, v. 623. The stretched drums thunder under the palms, and the hollow cymbals around, and the horns threaten with a hoarse song; the hollow pipe of Phrygian rhythm stirs the mind, and they carry weapons, the signs of raging madness.

units.la: ¶ Tit. xlvii. CANITIEI Axioma ii. Canities Parentum debet liberis stimulus esse ad Virtutem. Asin. 3. 1 v. 35. ] E Verbis Lenaeid petitur. Non vero refert, quaecumque fuerit. Nam Lena Philenio Puellae mater fuit, his verbis officium ei instillans: Meum caput contemples: siquidem ex re consultas tua.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. xlvii. GREY HAIR. Axiom ii. The grey hair of parents ought to be a spur to children towards virtue. Asin. 3.1 v. 35.] This is drawn from the words of the bawd. It does not matter which play it is. For the bawd Lena was the mother of the girl Philaenium, and in these words she instils a sense of duty in her: Look at my head, since you are consulting your own interest.

units.la: Unde Axioma pietatis, caeteroquin notissimum, non immerito elicitur. Nam certè Lena Canitiem proponit juniori puellae, quasi filiae suae.
units.tr: From this a maxim of piety, otherwise very well known, is not unreasonably drawn out. For surely the bawd holds up her grey hair to the younger girl, as if to her own daughter.

units.la: ¶ Tit. xlviii. CANTUS. Axioma iv. Cantu nocturno solebant se senes Senes recreare apud concubinas. Stich. 4. 1. v.66.] Natum hoc Axioma ex quorundam Criticorum lectione, qui eò loci ficeligunt.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. xlviii. SONG. Axiom iv. Old men used to refresh themselves with night-time song among their concubines. Stich. 4.1 v. 66.] This maxim arises from the reading of some critics, who there invent emendations.

units.la: Dabitur homini Amicanoctu,quæ in lecto occentet Senem.
units.tr: A girlfriend will be given to the man at night, who in bed will sing to the old man.

units.la: E quo loco quis rectè colligat, Senes cantu amasiæ sive Concubinæ oblectatos. Quis enim nescit, inter alia Veneris ἰλαγμὸς fuisse cantum? juxta illud Poetæ,
units.tr: From this passage one may rightly infer that old men were delighted by song from their mistresses or concubines. For who does not know that among the pleasures [ἰλαγμὸς] of Venus song was included, according to the saying of the poet:

units.la: Cantabant surdo, nudabant brachia cocco.
units.tr: They sang to the deaf man, and bared their arms in scarlet.

units.la: A verò in altera meâ Editione Plautinâ sequutus sum lectionem MSS.Pall. ubi retinetur optimo quoque sensu, accendet. Vide Notas nostras Criticas ad eum locum.
units.tr: But in my other Plautine edition I followed the reading of the Palatine manuscript, where he will kindle is retained, which makes good sense in every way. See our critical notes on that passage.

units.la: ¶ Tit. I. Carbonum. Carbones vivi etiam ex aquâ aridi exeunt. Rud. 2. 6. v. 50. ] Et hoc Axioma natum è lectione quorundam Criticorum, quibus sic placuit legi eò loci: Vtinam fortunâ nunc Anthracinâ uterer! idque ideò, quia paulò ante præcesserat: Vt fortunati sunt fabri ferrarij! qui apud Carbones aßident: semper calent. Hæc lectio sì adprobanda, de Carbonibus rectè id dicitur. At si pro, Anthracina, retinetur, Anatina, utique non de Carbonibus, sed Anatibus locus explicandus: aliudque tunc suborietur Axioma. In Editione nostrâ secundâ ex MSS. præstuli anatina.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. I. Of coals. Live coals come out dry even from water. Rud. 2.6 v. 50.] This maxim too arises from the reading of some critics, who preferred to read there: Would that I now used Anthracina fortune! This is because a little before had come: How fortunate are the smiths who sit beside the coals: they are always warm! If this reading is to be approved, it is rightly said of coals. But if Anthracina is kept, and Anatina is read, then the passage must be explained of ducks, not of coals, and another maxim then arises. In our second edition I preferred anatina from the manuscripts.

units.la: ¶ Tit. II. Carnis. Aphor. 11. Aprugna caro callum obducit. Perf. 2. 5. v. 4. Poen. 3. 2. v. 2. ] Quid sit callum obducere, explicat Cicero lib. II. Tusc. Et ipse labor quasi callum quoddam obducit dolori: Idem lib. III. Tusc. Quorum animus diuturnâ cogitatione callum vetustatis diduxerat. Sic Plautus dixit Aprugnam callum callere.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. II. Of flesh. Aphor. 11. Tough flesh grows a callus. Pers. 2.5 v. 4. Poen. 3.2 v. 2.] What it is to grow a callus Cicero explains in Tusculan Disputations, Book 2: Toil itself, as it were, draws a kind of callus over pain. The same in Tusculan Disputations, Book 3: Whose minds, by long reflection, had drawn out a callus of age. So Plautus said to have a callus of tough flesh.

units.la: Quærit nonnemo: Cui verò obducit? quomodo obducit? sibine, an alteri? Resp. Sibi certè aprugna caro callum obducit, utinduresçat magis. Ita ob duritiam, & condensationem durior fit, & callum obducit.
units.tr: Someone asks: On whom does it grow? How does it grow? On itself, or on another? Answer: Certainly tough flesh grows a callus on itself, so that it hardens more. Thus through hardness and condensation it becomes harder and grows a callus.

units.la: ¶ Tit. LVII. Colorum. Aphor. VIII. Color Puniceus ruber est. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 92. Rud. 4. 3. v. 59. ] Sic omninò legendum: non, uti Typographus mendosè excudit: niger est. Quis enim nescit puniceum colorem esse rubicundum?
units.tr: ¶ Tit. LVII. Of colours. Aphor. VIII. Purple colour is red. Pseud. 1.2 v. 92. Rud. 4.3 v. 59.] So it must be read in this way, not, as the printer carelessly printed it: is black. For who does not know that purple colour is reddish?

units.la: Virgil. lib. XII. Aeneid. v. 77.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid Book 12, v. 77.

units.la: Puniceis invecta rotis Aurora rubebit.
units.tr: Aurora, borne on purple wheels, will blush red.

units.la: ¶ Tit. LVIII. Comitatus. Mulieres, Matres-familiàs, Virgines, sine comite foràs prodire impudicum erat. Amph.3. 2. v.48.] Sic Pene-lope apud Homer.Odyss.6. v.181. Οἵη δ᾽ ἀκ κόσμει μετ᾽ ἀνέρας (Greek line)
units.tr: ¶ Tit. LVIII. Escort. Women, matrons, virgins, to go out without an escort was shameless. Amph. 3.2 v. 48.] So Penelope in Homer, Odyssey 6, v. 181: Such as she went among men in good order [Οἵη δ᾽ ἐκ κόσμου μετ᾽ ἀνέρας].

units.la: Morem hunc multæ matres-familiâs, virgines, non observant, quæ sine comitatu puellari domo egrediuntur in publicum. At suntaliæ plusculæ, quæ id sibi decorum ducunt, & honorificum.
units.tr: Many matrons and virgins do not observe this custom, who go out into public without a train of maidservants from home. But there are others, rather many, who count this as becoming and honourable for themselves.

units.la: ¶ Tit.LXI. Conjugii Aphor. III. Neque mei est instituti, omnia huc congerere, quæ in rem sunt. ] Nimirùm liberum mihi, uti meo arbitrio. Certè quidem ego aliis leges non fero. Fruantur quisque Authores suo arbitratu: multa pauca dicant, scribant. Idem mihi juris puto relictum.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. LXI. Of marriage. Aphor. III. It is not my plan to heap together here everything that bears on the matter.] Of course I am free to act as I judge. Certainly I do not impose laws on others. Let each author enjoy his own judgement; let them say and write much or little. I think the same right is left to me.

units.la: ¶ Ibid. Axioma LXIV. Votum maritorum apud Veteres fuit, Vxoribus supervivere, uti & contrà; Vxorum Maritis. Asin.I.I. v. 630. Cas.4. 4.v.1.Cist.I.I.v.86. Epid.2.I.v.8. Trin.I.2.v.19. Terent. Hecyrâ 2. I.v.10.] Etsi vulgò hæc nota sunt, tamen quia de sententia Juriscon-sultorum Superflua non nocent, nihil me peccasse arbitror, quod è verbis Plauti id observavi. Senecalib. VI. de Benef.cap.I. Etiam quod discere supervacuum est, prodesse cognoscere. Et sanè talia Vota Comici Poetæ in Fabulis suis prodiderunt ideò, quia familiaria & usitata esse solent. Testatur id Seneca lib.V.de Beneficijs cap.XVII. his verbis: Quotus quisque Vxoris optima mortem timet, ut non computet? Interim Universalem non facio sententiam. Nam cùm Propositio mea sit Indefinita, æquipollens Particulari, eò quòd contraria dari possint exempla, quivis facilè intelliget, de quibusdam saltim hujusmodi Votis meloqui.
units.tr: ¶ Ibid. Axiom LXIV. Among the ancients it was the husbands' wish to outlive their wives, and conversely; the wives' wish to outlive their husbands. Asin. 1.1 v. 630. Cas. 4.4 v. 1. Cist. 1.1 v. 86. Epid. 2.1 v. 8. Trin. 1.2 v. 19. Terence, Hecyra 2.1 v. 10.] Although these things are commonly known, yet since, according to the view of the jurists, superfluous things do no harm, I think I have done nothing wrong in noting this from the words of Plautus. Seneca, On Benefits, Book 6, ch. 1: Even what it is superfluous to learn, it is useful to know. And indeed comic poets have set down such vows in their plays because they are usually familiar and in common use. Seneca testifies to this in On Benefits, Book 5, ch. 17, in these words: How few of those who have an excellent wife fear her death, without reckoning it up? Meanwhile I am not making a universal statement. For since my proposition is indefinite, equivalent to a particular one, and contrary examples can be given, anyone will easily understand that I speak of certain such vows only.

units.la: Ibid. Axioma LXXV. Vxores irata suos maritos ne verbo quidem diguantur compellare, quicquid etiam muneris donent. Trucul.2.6.v.61.] Rursùm istum morem, non dico esse universalem: sed experientiam id edocere. Sunt enim mati, qui talem conjugio tam difficiles Uxores esse opor tebit.
units.tr: Ibid. Axiom LXXV. Angry wives do not deign even to address their husbands with a word, however many gifts they give. Truc. 2.6 v. 61.] Again, I do not say that this custom is universal, but experience teaches it. For there are husbands who will find such wives very difficult to have in marriage.

units.la: Expertos amare conqueri solent. Num propterea in OMNI conjugio tam difficiles Uxores esse oportebit.
units.tr: Those who have had experience of love are wont to complain. Will wives therefore have to be so difficult in every marriage?

units.la: Ibid. Axioma LXXVI. Mariti convivaturi clam Vxoribus vix abeunt. Ibid. Trucul.2.9.v.66.] Idem denuò inculco, minimè Universalem quidem hanc esse sententiam: sed de praxi tamen quotidianâ de-sumtam.
units.tr: Ibid. Axiom LXXVI. Husbands about to dine out scarcely leave without their wives' knowledge. Ibid. Truc. 2.9 v. 66.] Again I insist that this maxim is by no means universal, but is nonetheless drawn from everyday practice.

units.la: Ibid. Axioma LXXIX. Mors Vxoris grata maritis olim: & hodiè, Ibid.
units.tr: Ibid. Axiom LXXIX. The death of a wife was once welcome to husbands, and is so today too. Ibid.

units.la: D ὡς ἐπὶ πόλιν. Ciftell. 1.3. v.27. ] Iterum nolim hanc catholicam facere regulam. Satis id innuunt verba Graeca, quae adjeci: ὡς ἐπὶ πόλ.
units.tr: D as toward the city [ὡς ἐπὶ πόλ.]. Cist. 1.3 v. 27.] Again I would not wish to make this a universal rule. The Greek words I have added sufficiently indicate this: as toward the city [ὡς ἐπὶ πόλ.].

units.la: Ibid. Axioma lxxx. Magnum probrum erat, ante justas nuptias partum edere. Aul.2.3.v.9 ] Sic enim ibi Anus de filia Euclionis a Lyconide Adul. scente ante nuptias compresså: Nunc nobis prope est exitium mihi, atque herili filiae, Nunc probrum, atque partitudo prope est, ut fiat palam.
units.tr: Ibid. Axiom lxxx. It was a great disgrace to give birth before lawful marriage. Aul. 2.3 v. 9.] For so there the old woman speaks of Euclio's daughter, who was seduced before marriage by the young man Lyconides: Now ruin is near for me and for my master's daughter; now disgrace and childbirth are near, so that it will become public.

units.la: Objectio: Ergo biduum post nuptias edere partum, non erat probrosum. Resp. Sarcasmus hic est, non legitimus discursus. Nulla hic mentio bidui, aut mensium aliquot post nuptias: sed probi, quod in partitudine ante nuptias commisit filia Euclionis. Ante novem menses partum edere probrum fere haberi quis dubitavit umquam?
units.tr: Objection: So to give birth two days after marriage was not disgraceful. Answer: This is sarcasm, not a valid argument. There is no mention here of two days, or of some months after marriage, but of the disgrace which Euclio's daughter incurred by giving birth before marriage. Who has ever doubted that giving birth nine months before the wedding is generally regarded as disgraceful?

units.la: Ibid. Aphor. lxxxi. Parentes non parentes suos liberos in orbitatem, ut ipsi priventur iterum: eoque durum illis est si decedant. Capt.3.5.v.105.] Sic mendum Typographi corrigi debet, pro; Ciftell. In Ciftellaria namque ne quidem huiusmodi reperitur: sed in Captivis. Ubi benivolus Lector si inspiciat Notas nostras marginales, exinde cognoscet, quid sibi velint verba ista: Producere liberos in orbitatem. Taedet namque eadem hic rursum inculcare.
units.tr: Ibid. Aphor. lxxxi. Parents do not, by their children, bring their own children to bereavement, so that they themselves are deprived again; and so it is hard for them if the children die. Capt. 3.5 v. 105.] So the printer's error must be corrected, reading Captivi for Cistellaria. For in the Cistellaria nothing of this kind is found, but in the Captivi. If the kindly reader consults our marginal notes, he will learn from them what those words mean: to bring children to bereavement. For it is tiresome to repeat the same thing here again.

units.la: Ibid. Axioma lxxxiv. Multi parvi faciunt, quam ducant; ingenuamne, an libertinam: dummodo quaestuosa sit. &c. Mil.3.1.v.190.] Nullum hic fit convitium vel Aevo huius, vel Religioni Reformata. Nam cum dicitur, multos susque deque habere, quam ducant, nihil praeter, aut contra experientiam dicitur. Servi verba perspicua sunt apud Plautum: PA. Ecquam tu potes reperire formā lepidā mulierem? PE. Ingenuamne an liberam: PA. aeque istud facio, dummodo Eam des, quae sit quaestuosa, quae alat corpus corpore.
units.tr: Ibid. Axiom lxxxiv. Many men think little of whether they take a free-born wife or a freedwoman, so long as she is profitable. &c. Mil. 3.1.v.190.] No insult is offered here either to this age or to the Reformed religion. For when it is said that many men care nothing for whom they marry, nothing is said that is contrary to, or beyond, experience. The words of the servant are clear in Plautus: PA. Can you find a woman of attractive form for me? PE. Free-born or freed? PA. I don't care which, provided you give me one who is profitable, one who feeds her body with her body.

units.la: Eodem ingenio Servos alios reperiri, etiam hoc saeculo, quis inficias ibit? Ac si reperiantur, an propterea factum id nos adprobabimus? Multa, multa fiunt, sed MALE; secundum Accurfium.
units.tr: That such servants, of the same disposition, can be found even in this age, who will deny? And if they can be found, shall we therefore approve of the practice? Many things are done, many things, but BADLY, according to Accursius.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma lxxxv. Mariti magnam curam gerunt Uxorum: adeo ut plurimum eas metuant: si quid minus dextre agant.] Sic enim Servus alloquitur herum suum. Afin: 1.1. v.4. Itate obtestor tum per fenestram tuam Perque illam, quam tu metuis, uxorem tuam.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom lxxxv. Husbands take great care of their wives, so much so that they mostly fear them if they do anything less than skilfully.] For so a servant addresses his master. Asin. 1.1.v.4. I beg you by your window, and by that wife of yours whom you fear.

units.la: Quid sit; Curam gerere Vxorum: quid item; Minus dextrè aliquid agere: non nisi planè ἀὐνλαφώβνγ ignorat.
units.tr: Anyone who does not know what it is to take care of a wife, or what it is to do something less than skilfully, is simply ignorant.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xc. Dotis non habenda ratio: sive ea quidem certè non æstimanda ex divitijs. Aul. 2.1.v.45.] Sententia aperta. Optima Dos Virtus est. Quod ex alijs Aphorismis patet, quos è Plauto & alijs adnotavi.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom xc. The dowry is not to be taken into account; at any rate it is certainly not to be valued by riches. Aul. 2.1.v.45.] The meaning is plain. The best dowry is virtue. This is clear from the other aphorisms, which I have noted from Plautus and others.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xci Vxor receptitiam dotem servo suo dotali donavit. ] Eò allusum Asin. 1.1.v.71.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom xci. A wife gave her dowry-slave, the money she had received, to her own servant.] Alluded to in Asin. 1.1.v.71.

units.la: Dotalem servum Sauream Vxor tua
units.tr: Your wife brought in Saurea, the slave who came with her dowry,

units.la: Adduxit: cui plus in Manu fit, quàm tibi.
units.tr: To whom more is handed over in her hand than to you.

units.la: Non fictum, sed factum id fuisse, ostendunt hæc verba Catonis in suasione legis Voconiæ apud Agell. lib.xvii.cap.vi.
units.tr: That this was not invented but actually happened is shown by these words of Cato in his speech on the Voconian law, in Gellius, book 17, chapter 6.

units.la: Principio nobis mulier magnam dotem attulit. tum magnam pecuniam recipit, quam in Viri potestatem non committit, eam pecuniam Viro dat mutuam: postea ubi irata facta est, servum Receptitium sectari atque flagitare Virum jubet.
units.tr: At first the woman brought us a large dowry. Then she received a large sum of money, which she did not entrust to her husband's power, but lent it to him. Afterwards, when she became angry, she orders her husband to pursue and demand back the slave who had been received with the money.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphorismus xcviii. Damnosi mariti simulant se adire Amicos, cum ad vinum eunt. Asin. 5.2.v.14. ubi Mulier sic loquitur de marito.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorism xcviii. Spendthrift husbands pretend to visit friends when they go off to wine. Asin. 5.2.v.14., where the wife speaks thus of her husband.

units.la: Hoc ecastor est, quod ille it ad cœnam cottidiè.
units.tr: Surely that is what he does every day, going out to dinner.

units.la: Ait, se ire ad Archidemum, Chaream, Charestratum, Cliniam, Chremem, Cratinum, Diniam, Demosthenem: Is apud Scortum corruptela, & liberis nostris studet. ]
units.tr: He says he is going to Archidemus, Chaerea, Charestratus, Clinias, Chremes, Cratinus, Dinias, Demosthenes. He is busy with a whore, corrupting our children.

units.la: Quid hoc est? inquit nonnemo, Ire ad vinum: Ac pergit: eó ne portavi oportebat? an vinum potius ad ipsos veniret? Respondeo: Scomma hac Morionis, non docti viri est. Quid si lectica, aut quadrigis in cauponas vecti tales mauiu? quid si Equites eò pleno cursu accessissent! Atqui sic loquitur Plautus Asin.4.1.v.54.
units.tr: What is this? says someone: "to go to wine"? And he goes on: "Ought I to have carried him there? Or should the wine rather come to them?" I reply: this jest belongs to a buffoon, not to a learned man. What if such men were carried to the taverns in litters or chariots? What if knights had come there at full gallop! Yet Plautus speaks in just this way, Asin. 4.1.v.54.

units.la: Ne mater lena ad Vinum accedat interim.
units.tr: Lest in the meantime the procuress mother come to the wine.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma cix. Vxor dotata, honesta, indicta causa non poterat repudiari. Asin.5.1.v.49.] Ergò indotata, inquit nonnemo, inhonesta poterat repudiari. Respond. Eodem modo quis sic argumentari possit: Vxor dotata, honesta non potest abstinere à cibo & potu quotidiano: Ergò indotata, inhonesta id possunt. Item: Vxores dotatæ, honesta non incedunt quatuor pedibus: Ergo indotata, inhonesta incedunt quatuor pedibus. Item: Vxores dotatæ, honestæ, non oderunt suos maritos: Ergò indotatæ, inhonestæ oderunt suos maritos. Qui s hanc dialecticam ferat?
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom cix. A wife who was endowed and honest could not be repudiated without a cause. Asin. 5.1.v.49.] So, says someone, a wife who was not endowed and was dishonest could be repudiated. I reply: in the same way one could argue: a wife who is endowed and honest cannot abstain from daily food and drink; therefore a wife who is not endowed and is dishonest can. Likewise: endowed and honest wives do not walk on four feet; therefore unendowed and dishonest wives do walk on four feet. Likewise: endowed and honest wives do not hate their husbands; therefore unendowed and dishonest wives hate their husbands. Who could put up with this logic?

units.la: Cæterum formulam illam; Vitium dicere, non interpretor per, Exigere adibus, Quid sibi velit phrasis ea; expositi in Calligraphia Romana Titulo Calumniandi. Eadem usus est Terent. Hecyr. i. 2. v. 79. Non aliter locum Plautinum interpretatur Ianus Gruterus apud Taubmannum pag. 136. Quem vide.
units.tr: Moreover, I do not translate that phrase vitium dicere as to drive out of doors. What that expression means I have explained in my Roman Calligraphy under the title Calumniandi. Terence used it too, Hecyra 1.2.v.79. Janus Gruterus likewise interprets the Plautine passage in the same way, in Taubmann, page 136. See there.

units.la: ¶ Tit. LXIII. Conjugii. Axioma III. In Mulieribus etiam posteris temporibus apud Romanos non minus, quàm apud Græcos semper turpis habitus accubitus.] Testatur id Varro de Vitâ Pop. Rom. Ait enim, Viros discumbere solitos: Mulieres verò sedisse, quod turpis visu esset in Mulieribus accubitus. Testatur idem Valerius Maximus lib. II. cap. 1. Quod, inquit, genus severitatis et as nostra diligentius in Capitolio, quàm in domibus suis servat. Quibus verbis innuit, disciplinam illam jam aliquo modo antiquatam: Cùm impudicitiæ notabantur antea, si quæ forte accumberent. Quod in Cythèri reprehenditur apud Ciceronem in Convivio Eutrapeli. In eam quoque rem adduxi ex Bacch. 4. 4. v. 103. & 4. 8. v. 18. ubi Bacchides eodem cum Amatoribus cenitant lecto. Patet idem ex Cicer. in Verr. Accuf. 1. Postea quam, inquit, satis calere res Rubrio visa est! quæso, inquit, Philodame; cur ad nos intrà filiam tuam non vocari jubes? homo, qui & summâ gravitate, & jam id ætatis & parens esset, obstrepuit hominis improbo dicto. Inst.re Rubrius: tum ille, ut aliquid responderet, negavit, mores esse Græcorum, ut in convivio Virorum Mulieres accumberent. Atque huc allusisse dixi Terentium Eun. 4. 1. v. 11. ubi cùm Thraso introduci jussisset Pamphilam, indignata Thais: Minimè, inquit, gentium. In convivium tuillam? Idem ex loco Amphitruonis rectè colligi, res ipsa docet. Ibi enim cùm Alcumena cum Jove, quem suum maritum ipsa credidit (revera enim non fuit) idem se factitasse fateretur, his verbis:
units.tr: ¶ Title lxiii. Marriage. Aphorism iii. Among the Romans, even in later times, reclining at table was regarded as shameful for women, no less than among the Greeks.] Varro bears witness to this in his Life of the Roman People. For he says that men were accustomed to recline, but women sat, since reclining was unseemly to see in women. Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 1, bears witness to the same: This kind of strictness, he says, our people observe more carefully on the Capitol than in their own homes. By these words he hints that the custom was by then already in some measure out of date, since women who happened to recline were once branded as immodest. Ciceros Banquet of Eutrapelus reproves this in the case of Cytheris. I have also adduced for this point Bacchides 4.4.v.103 and 4.8.v.18, where the Bacchides recline on the same couch with their lovers.
