The same appears from Cicero against Verres, book 1: After the matter seemed to have grown warm enough, he says, "I beg you, Philodamus," said Rubrius, "why do you not order your daughter to be called in to us?" The man, who was of great dignity, and by now of an age to be a parent, cried out against the shameless remark. Then Rubrius, to make some reply, said that it was the custom among the Greeks for women to recline at a men's banquet. And I have said that Terence alluded to this in Eunuchus 4.1.v.11, where Thais, when Thraso had ordered Pamphila to be brought in, was indignant: Not at all, she said, not among any people! Should I bring her to the dinner? The matter itself shows that the same can be correctly gathered from the passage in Amphitryon. For there Alcmena, speaking with Jupiter whom she believed to be her husband (in fact he was not), admits that she had done the same thing, in these words:

units.la: Cœna appositæ est, canasti mecum: ego accubui simul.
units.tr: Dinner was served; you dined with me; I reclined at the same time.

units.la: Infit Amph: In eodem lecto? Alc. In eodem.
units.tr: Amphitryon begins: On the same couch? Alcmena: On the same.

units.la: Sos. Hei! non placet convivium.
units.tr: Sosia: Alas! I do not like this banquet.

units.la: Dicat quis: Alcumena ibi reprehenditur à Sofiâ, non quod accubuisset marito, sed quod eodem in lecto fuisset. Atqui accumbere: &, In eodem lecto esse, pro eodem hîc sumuntur. Nam sic repetendum: In eodem lecto: scil. accubuisti: ex præcedenti versu.
units.tr: Someone may say that Alcmena is here rebuked by Sosia not because she reclined with her husband, but because she was on the same couch. But to recline and to be on the same couch are here taken as the same thing. For it is to be read thus: On the same couch: that is, you reclined, from the preceding line.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xvii. in Legibus Bibendi. In commissationibus quisque suum vinum conferebat quasi in symbolam.] Eruitur id manifeste ex Stich. 5 4. v. 4.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom xvii, among the laws of drinking. At drinking parties each man brought his own wine, as a contribution to the cost.] This is clearly drawn from Stichus 5.4.v.4.

units.la: Sag quisquis praetereat commissatum volo vocari. St. Convenit: Dum quidem hercle quisque veniat cum vino suo.
units.tr: Agreed: whoever passes by, I want him invited to the drinking party. St. Agreed: provided, by heaven, that each man comes with his own wine.

units.la: Objectio: Glacialem commessationem, ubi nihil praeterea conferebatur!
units.tr: Objection: a frosty drinking party, where nothing else was contributed!

units.la: Respond. Nemo dicet, praeter vinum nihil collatum. Neminem vero ἀνυμβόλως venisse, patet ex loco Terentij Phorm. 2. 2. v. 25. Tén' ásymbolum venire? Neque vero semper vinum fuit collatum. Nam in isto convivio servili apud Plautum nulla fit mentio vini.
units.tr: Reply: no one will say that nothing was contributed besides wine. That no one came without contributing is clear from the passage of Terence, Phormio 2.2.v.25: Did you come without a contribution? [τὴν ἀσύμβολον]. Nor was wine always what was contributed. For in that servants' banquet in Plautus there is no mention of wine at all.

units.la: ¶ Tit. lxxx. Divitiarum. Aphorismus I. Divitiae saepe antepo-nuntur Pietati. Sic fecit Leno Pseud. 1. 3. v. 120.] Ex hoc loco Plautus est, qui malit inde colligere alias sententias, quod quidem mea pace illi facere licebit: dummodo ve itas mei Aphorismi mihi immota relinquatur, quem Illustravi dicto Senecae Epist. cxv. sine me vocari pessimum, ut dives vocer. Exempla e sacris litteris eundem Aphorismum confirmant: nec reluctatur quotidiana experientia.
units.tr: ¶ Title lxxx. Riches. Aphorism i. Riches are often preferred to piety. So the parasite does in Pseudolus 1.3.v.120.] Plautus is the source of this passage, and whoever prefers to draw other maxims from it may do so with my goodwill, provided the truth of my aphorism stays unshaken for me. I illustrated it with the saying of Seneca, Epistle 115: Let me be called wicked, so that I may be called rich. Examples from Holy Scripture confirm the same aphorism, and daily experience does not resist it.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma ii. Divites plerumque sunt impij: ex sententia Piscatoris. Rud. 4. 7. v. 8.] Ex hoc item loco aliam sententiam non nemo malit elicere. Atqui nostrum Axioma ex sacris quoque Litteris constat. Facilius est, inquit Salvator Jesus Christus, transfire per foramen acus, quam Divitem introire in regnum coelorum. Rationes a Theologis peti possunt.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom ii. The rich are for the most part impious, in the opinion of the fisherman, Rudens 4.7.v.8.] From this same passage someone may prefer to draw out another maxim. But our axiom is also grounded in Holy Scripture. It is easier, says our Saviour Jesus Christ, for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. The reasons can be sought from the theologians.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xxxiv. Divitiae raro cum virtute conjunctae. Afin. 2. 4. v. 91.] Veritatem hujus Axiomatis ipsa confirmat experientia. Si cui satuo aliter videatur, nihil repugnabo ego.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 34. Riches are seldom joined with virtue. Afin. 2.4 v.91. Experience itself confirms the truth of this axiom. If anyone thinks otherwise, I will not oppose him.

units.la: ¶ Tit. lxxxii. Eboris. Ebur suâ naturâ candidum, frustrà candefieret atramento. Mostel. 1. 3. v. 101. Unà ebur atramento candefacere postulat.] frustrà, valet, stultè & inepte. Totam sententiam explico in Notis marginalibus ad eum locum: his verbis: Quemadmodum si quis atramento velit Ebur candefacere; & stultè ageret: & nativum ejus colorem corrumperet: ita absurdum est, temalas cerussâ velle candefacere, cum malae ipsae cerussâ sint candidiores.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. 82. Ivory. Ivory, white by nature, would be whitened in vain with ink. Mostel. 1.3 v.101. You ask to whiten ivory with ink. In vain means foolishly and clumsily. I explain the whole sentiment in my marginal notes on that passage, in these words: Just as if someone wanted to whiten ivory with ink, he would act foolishly and would spoil its natural colour. So it is absurd to want to whiten the cheeks with white lead, when the cheeks themselves are whiter than white lead.

units.la: ¶ Tit. lxxxiii. Ebrietatis. Aphor. iv. Dolia cùm deplen-tur. tur, νψτ διοφωνπίων edunt sonum hac. Mil.3.2 v.44.] Sic legendum, non; replentur: sicuti meridosè excusum est. ⁊ Deplere, est; evacuare.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. 83. Drunkenness. Aphor. 4. When the casks are emptied ... Mil. 3.2 v.44. It should be read thus, not replentur (filled), as was carelessly printed. Deplere means to empty out.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xi. Ebrij crapulam amovere solent, secedendo nonnihil. Pseud.5.1.v.35.] Quid sit Crapula: quid item; eam amovere: quid denique; nonnihil secedendo: ex ipso contextu P'auti non satis est perspicuum: quando dicitur: Inde huc exij, crapulam dum amoverem. Neque opus est secare cuminum.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 11. Drunkards are accustomed to get rid of their hangover by withdrawing somewhat. Pseud. 5.1 v.35. What crapula is, what it means to get rid of it, and finally what withdrawing somewhat means, is not sufficiently clear from the context of Plautus itself, where it is said: I went out from here while I was getting rid of my hangover. And there is no need to split hairs over cumin.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xxx. Servis vilioribus posca præbebatur, seu levior potus mixtus aquâ. Mil.3.2.v.23. Alij ebrij sunt (ex optimo vino) alij poscam potitant] Objectio: Quid si mediocris tantum bonitatis fuerit? quid si infrà mediocritatem Resp. Neurrum sententiam meam impedit: dummodo ne posca sit. Veritatem lectionis confirmavi in Notis Criticis ad istum locum.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 30. Poor slaves were given posca, or a lighter drink mixed with water. Mil. 3.2 v.23. Others are drunk (on the finest wine), others drink posca. Objection: What if the wine were only of moderate quality? What if it were below moderate? Reply: Neither case hinders my view, provided it is not posca. I have confirmed the truth of this reading in my Critical Notes on that passage.

units.la: † Ibid. Axiomate xxxxi. Aul.3.6.v.36. Ego te hodie reddam madidum, si vivo probe.] Sic omninò esse legendum, evincit tota cohors MSS. Codd. sicut docui in Notis meis Criticis. Eodem modo loquitur Terent. Heaut. 5.1 v.45 At ne illud haud inultum, si vivo, feram. Ibid.v.77. Egone? si vivo, adeo exornatum dabo. Aliam lectionem sequutus erat Taubmannus ex Baptistâ Pio, sic:
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 41. Aul. 3.6 v.36. I will make you drunk today, if I live properly. That this must be read thus is proved by the whole company of manuscripts, as I showed in my Critical Notes. Terence speaks in the same way, Heaut. 5.1 v.45: But I will not bear that unavenged, if I live. Ibid. v.77: What, I? If I live, I will give her a very fine dressing. Taubmann followed a different reading from Baptista Pius, thus:

units.la: Ego te hodie reddam madidum, sed vino, probè.
units.tr: I will make you drunk today, but properly, with wine.

units.la: Contrà omnem rationem, contrà universum consensum Antiquitatis.
units.tr: Against all reason, against the universal agreement of antiquity.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphor. xxx. Murrhinam bibebant Veteres, svavem ac dulcem potum ad arcendam ebrietatem. Perf 1 3. v.8. Pseud.2.4.v.51.] ⁊ Arcere ebrietatem, est; eam defendere, prohibere, seu inhibere. Objectio: Sic erit necesse, ut vini potio præcesserit.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphor. 30. The ancients drank murrhine, a sweet and pleasant drink, to ward off drunkenness. Perf. 1.3 v.8. Pseud. 2.4 v.51. To ward off drunkenness is to defend against it, to prevent or inhibit it. Objection: So it would be necessary that the drinking of wine came first.

units.la: Resp. Per nullam Logicam id necesse est. Nam etiam ante inebriationem dulcibus potionibus usi; ut melle, murrhinâ, alijsque id genus dulciarijs haustibus. Quin & nonnulli post inebriationem potus adsumserunt. Utrumque patet ex istis verbis Plutarchi lib. iii. Sympos. Quæst.vii.
units.tr: Reply: No logic requires this. For they used sweet drinks even before intoxication, such as honey, murrhine, and other sweet refreshments of that kind. Indeed some also took drinks after becoming intoxicated. Both points are clear from these words of Plutarch, Symposiacs book 3, question 7.

units.la: Aristanetus Niceus in quibusdam libris se legisse ait, Dulcia vino admixta πάνεσι τὴν μέθην, reprimere & arcere ebrietatem: & Medicorum nonnullos præcipere ebrijs, ut dormituri panem melli intinctum edant. Si quod ergò dulcis sapor facit, ad retundendam meri vim, par est, multum nondum mutatâ dulcedine non inebriare.
units.tr: Aristaenetus of Nicaea says that in certain books he had read that sweet things mixed with wine restrain and check drunkenness [πανέσι τὴν μέθην]; and some physicians advise drunkards to eat bread dipped in honey before they go to sleep. If, then, the sweet taste helps to blunt the strength of undiluted wine, it is reasonable that, while the sweetness has not yet been changed by much drinking, one does not get drunk.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xxxv. Sorores illè (Stich.r.2.v.32.) Patri osculum præbent in sobrietatis argumentum.] Moris perpetui fuisse, excipere osculo cognatos, adgnatosque obvios, adeò verum est, ut Tiberius Imperator quotidiana illa osculà Edicto prohibuerit. Non verò propterea falsum, Sorores illas ad sobrietatem suam ostendendam Patri osculum præbuisse. Scio quem hujus meæ sententiæ habeam adstipulatorem, cujus auctoritatem tam facilè nemo elevare poterit. Conjectura petita est à consuetudine Romanâ, quam tangit Ag. Gell. lib. x. cap. xxiii. Qui de victu, atque cultu Pop. Rom. scripserunt, Mulieres Romæ, atque in Latio ætatem abstemias egisse, hoc est, vino semper, quod Temetum priscâ lingua appellabatur, abstinuisse dicunt: institutumque, ut cognatis osculà ferrent, reprehendendi causâ, ut odor indicium faceret, si bibissent: bibere autem solitas ferunt loream, passum, murrhinam, & quæ id genus sapiant, potu dulcia.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 35. Those sisters (Stich. 1.2 v.32) give their father a kiss as proof of sobriety. It was a constant custom to greet relatives and kinsfolk who met one with a kiss, so true is this that the Emperor Tiberius forbade those daily kisses by edict. It is not therefore false that those sisters gave their father a kiss to show their sobriety. I know whom I have as an ally in this view, and no one can easily diminish his authority. The conjecture is drawn from Roman custom, which Aulus Gellius touches on, book 10 chapter 23: Those who have written about the diet and dress of the Roman people say that the women at Rome and in Latium lived abstemious lives, that is, they always abstained from wine, which in the old language was called temetum; and it was the custom that they gave kisses to their relatives, for the purpose of reproof, so that the smell would reveal if they had drunk. They are said to have been accustomed to drink sweet drinks: lorea, passum, murrhine, and such things as taste of that kind.

units.la: Idem Cato memorat apud Plinium lib. xiv. Ideò propinquis feminis osculà dare, ut scirent, an temetum olerent.
units.tr: Cato also mentions the same, in Pliny book 14: For this reason women give kisses to their female relatives, so that they may know whether they smell of temetum.

units.la: ¶ Tit. LXXXIV. EDUCATIONIS. Axioma viii. Olim filios raro in Urbem dimiserunt ad spectacula: sed rus ablegabant. Mercat. Prol. v. 68.] Objectio: Non ablegabantur rure: sed ibidem degebant plures per annos. Resp. Nemo contradicit. Narratibidem Adulescens, Patrem exemplo propinquo se de hortari ab amoribus & desidiâ: eò quòd ipse arte cohibitus esset à Patre multò opere imminuto rustico se exercitum: Neque nisi quinto anno positum visere Urbem, atque extemplò indè ut spectaculum visset Peplum Rus rursum confestim exigi solitum à Patre. Numquid perspicua omnia? De Immundo rustico dixi in Lexico Plautino.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. 84. EDUCATION. Axiom 8. In former times they seldom sent their sons up to the City to the shows, but sent them away to the country. Mercat. Prol. v.68. Objection: They were not sent away to the country, but stayed there for several years. Reply: No one contradicts this. There a young man tells how his father, by a close example, urged him to keep away from love affairs and idleness, because the father himself had been restrained, having been kept busy at great length with rustic labour; and how he did not see the City until his fifth year, and as soon as he had seen the show, the Peplum, he was at once sent back to the country by his father, as was customary. Is everything clear? I have discussed the uncouth rustic in my Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xxxvi. Juventus Attica noctu solita graffationi-bus suis turbare publicam pacem. Eoque allusum Amph. i. i. v. 2. Stich. 4. 2. v. 33. Trin. 2. 2. v. 34.] Objectio: Ibi nulla juventus Attica: nulla Athenæ: cùm Thebis res acta. Resp. Ut ut Thebis res acta fingitur: acta tamen est hæc Fabula Romæ in Theatro. Juventutem itaque Romanam tangit Comicus, atque ad graffationem Atticam respicit.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 36. Attic youth were accustomed by night to disturb public peace with their raids. Alluded to there: Amph. 1.1 v.2; Stich. 4.2 v.33; Trin. 2.2 v.34. Objection: There is no Attic youth there, no Athens, since the action takes place at Thebes. Reply: Although the action is pretended to be at Thebes, this play was nonetheless performed at Rome, in the theatre. So the comic poet has in mind Roman youth, and refers to Attic raiding.

units.la: Vide quæ scripsi Tit. GRASSATIO NUM. Loco nimirum Amph. i. i. v. 2. allusum forte ad aliquam legem Pop. Rom. quâ cautum fuit, ne cui noctis conticinio per Urbem iter facere liceret, præserpræsertim temporibus belli Punici secundi, quibus Plautum vixis-se notum est.
units.tr: See what I wrote under the heading GRASSATIO. The allusion in Amph. 1.1 v.2 is perhaps to some law of the Roman people, by which it was provided that no one might travel through the City in the dead of night, especially in the times of the Second Punic War, in which Plautus is known to have lived.

units.la: Ibid. Aphorismus XXXIV. Honesta & libera Educatio etiam liberam formam conservat,præsertim puellis. Ciftell I.I.v.50. ] Axioma è verbis Lenæ desumtum, quæ fuit loco Matris. Non interest autem, quæ fuerit Lena, quales autem puellæ, Educationi enim id tribuit Lena, quando dicit: Siquidem ita eris, ut volo, numquam Hecate fies, h.e. numquam fies deformis Anus Proserpina: sed retinebis hunc ætatis florem, hanc formam virginalem: quemadmodum in Notis marginalibus exposui verba illa. Forma libera est ea, quam Terentius vocat egregiam. And.I.I.v.45. Et bonam. Ibid.v.92. Et honestam ac liberalem. Ibid.v.95.
units.tr: Ibid. Aphorism 34. An honest and free education preserves even a free appearance, especially in girls. Cist. 1.1 v.50. The axiom is taken from the words of the procuress, who stood in the place of a mother. It does not matter, however, what kind of procuress she was, or what sort of girls they were; for the procuress attributes this to education when she says: If you turn out as I wish, you will never become a Hecate, that is, you will never become a deformed old woman, a Proserpina; but you will keep this flower of youth, this virginal beauty. I explained those words in my marginal notes. A free form is that which Terence calls outstanding. And. 1.1 v.45. And good. Ibid. v.92. And honest and liberal. Ibid. v.95.

units.la: ¶ Tit.XCIV. FIDEI. Axioma 1. Ab ijs, qui nullius fidei, pignus fuit acceptum. Sic enim alloquitur Servus Parasitum Rud.2.7.v.23.] Alius quis sic circumscripsisset sententiam ejus loci: Peregrinus tantum fidei, quantum pignoris. Quantum verò hoc distat ab eo, quod posui?
units.tr: ¶ Tit. 94. FAITH. Axiom 1. From those who had no faith, a pledge was taken. For so the slave addresses the parasite, Rud. 2.7 v.23. Someone else might have paraphrased the sense of that passage thus: A stranger has as much faith as he has pledges. But how far does this differ from what I have put?

units.la: ¶ Tit.XCVIII. FORTITUDINIS. Romani eum demum ac formosum putárunt, qui esset fortis. Mil.4.3.v.13. ] Collectio hæc sumta ex ἀνδρεῖα τῶν fortis, quo dibi loci usurpat Plautus pro formoso & pulchro. Constat ex hoc dicto Virgilij lib.VII. Aen.v.656.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. 98. FORTITUDE. The Romans thought him alone a man and handsome who was brave. Mil. 4.3 v.13. The collection is taken from the Greek word for manly courage [ἀνδρεῖα], which Plautus in that place uses for handsome and beautiful. This is clear from this saying of Virgil, Aen. book 7 v.656.

units.la: Satus Herculepulchro Pulcher Aventinus.
units.tr: Born of Hercules, fair; Aventinus the handsome.

units.la: Neque impedit, quòd è verbis Militis eam sententiam exstruxi. Quam lectionem ejus loci sequar, exposui in Notis Criticis ad eum locum.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that I built that sentiment from the words of the Soldier. Which reading of that passage I follow, I have set out in my Critical Notes on that passage.

units.la: ¶ Tit.CV. FUNERIS. Axiomate 1. Seneca Epist XCIX. Quàm multis cùm maximè funus locatur?] Hunc locum Seneca omnes fere Antiquarij referunt ad morem veterem, quo Cadavera colloca-bant. Colvius ad lib.III. Florid.Apul. Et in primis Lipsius ad Senecam his verbis:
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CV. FUNERAL. Axiom 1. Seneca, Letter 99: How many people, when a funeral is being let out? Almost all the ancient writers refer this passage of Seneca to the old custom of laying out corpses. See Colvius on book III of Apuleius's Florida; and especially Lipsius on Seneca, in these words:

units.la: Funus locatur ] efferendum: nempe & urendum à Libitinariis.
units.tr: A funeral is let out: that is, to be carried out, namely, also burned, by the undertakers.

units.la: Ne quid dicam de Meurfio & Kirchmanno curiosis hujus Antiquitatis indagatoribus.
units.tr: Not to mention Meursius and Kirchmann, the curious investigators of this antiquity.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma IX. Bustirapi dicti per convivium, qui lucri causâ aliquid rapiebant è busto, seu convivio exsequiali: quod silentio solum licebat intueri. ] Sententiam hanc mille testibus affirmarem, nisi liquidò eam explicasset. plicasset Ianus Guilielmius lib.iii. Verisim.cap.xii.nec non Kirchmanus lib.iv. cap.xii. Fun. Rom.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom IX. Bustirapi were so called at a dinner: those who for gain snatched something from the pyre, or from the funeral feast, which they were allowed only to look at in silence. I would affirm this opinion with a thousand witnesses, if Janus Guilielmius had not explained it clearly in book III of his Verisimilia, chapter xii, and also Kirchmann in book IV, chapter xii, of De Funeribus Romanorum.

units.la: † Ibid. Pauperes, qui nec prædiolum, nec locum sepulturæ avitum haberent, extra portam Metiam sepultos, aut combustos. Ex iis meis verbis nemo sanæ mentis compos colligere poterit, eos quibus non erat ager hereditarius, extra portam Esquilinam Solummodo sepultos. Multo minus inde elici poterit, aliquos sepultos non combustos.
units.tr: † Ibid. The poor, who had neither a small farm nor an ancestral place of burial, were buried or burned outside the Metian gate. From these words of mine no one of sound mind will be able to conclude that those who had no hereditary field were buried only outside the Esquiline gate. Much less can it be inferred from them that some were buried and not burned.

units.la: ¶ Tit. cvi. Furum. Aphorismo iii. quæ de Quadruplatoribus dixi tantum abest, ut reprehendi possint, ut nonnemo fateatur, à quovis itaque intelligi, de quâ professione mihi gratulor.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CVI. Thieves. Aphorism iii. What I said about the Quadruplatores is so far from being open to blame that some admit it, so that it can be understood by anyone; and I congratulate myself on this profession.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma v. Nemo furti accusari potest, nisi manifeste deprehensus. Aul. 4. 10. v. 39. ] Hoc ita verum est, ut qui contrarium sentiat, fateatur oportet, eos ad Prætorem rapiendos, qui manus habent continentes. Certè Adolescens dives, apud Plautum, bonæque famæ de furto accusari à mendico, pro absurdissimo habet.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom v. No one can be accused of theft unless caught in the act. Aul. 4.10 v.39. This is so true that whoever thinks otherwise must admit that those who have their hands held should be dragged before the praetor. Certainly the rich young man in Plautus regards it as most absurd that a beggar should accuse a man of good reputation of theft.

units.la: † Ibid. Axiomate xiv. in loco Mil. 4. 2. v. 5. Vesperi suo vivere: admisi potius interpretationem Durantij, quàm Lambini: quòd ea visa esset probabilior, verior, concinnior, locoque Plauti accommodatior. Lambinianam tamen numquam planè improbavi.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom xiv, at the passage Mil. 4.2 v.5. To live by his evening meal: I preferred the interpretation of Durantius to that of Lambinus, because it seemed more probable, truer, more elegant, and better suited to the passage of Plautus. Yet I never entirely rejected the Lambinian one.

units.la: ¶ Tit. cxiii. Gynæceì. Axioma vi. Virgines, aut Matronæ honestiores numquam sine assectatione prodierunt in publicum. Atque eis comitatus ferè è spadonibus constabat. ] Notari velim particulam ferè. Nam id posterioribus sæculis demùm factitatum. Spadones enim post devictam Asiam Italiam invasisse; neque ante Plauti fuisse, satis est notum. Ego id ὠ; ἐπεισοκυμένως adjeceram: quia aliquando (tempus certum non indigetavi.) in Italiâ Matronæ tali spadonum pedisequio usæ sunt.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CXIII. Women's quarters. Axiom vi. Virgins or more honourable matrons never went out in public without an escort. And their retinue usually consisted of eunuchs. I would have the particle ferè (almost, usually) noted. For this was practised only in later centuries; it is well enough known that eunuchs invaded Italy after Asia was conquered, and were not there before Plautus. I had added it as an incidental qualification, because at some time (I have not determined which) matrons in Italy did use such an attendance of eunuchs.

units.la: ¶ Tit. cxiv. Axioma viii. Milites fuerunt cæsariati. Mil. 3. 1. v. 172.] Non de omnibus Militibus hoc accipiendum: Sed de nonnullis. Fecit enim Propositionem non Universalem, sed de-Ideâ Indefinitam, æquipollentem particulari.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CXIV. Axiom viii. The soldiers were beaten. Mil. 3.1 v.172. This is not to be taken of all soldiers, but of some. For he made a proposition not universal but indefinite in its sense, equivalent to a particular one.

units.la: ¶ Tit cxv. Hæreditatis. Axiomate primore scripsi, ex isto loco Plauti Mil. 3. 1. v. 115 Eos, qui hereditatem ambiunt, munera suis legatarijs solere mittere, hereditatis herciscundæ causâ. ] Contrà nonnemo sic objicit. Quid absurdius, quàm hercisciundæ hereditatis quid fieri vivo hærede? Numquam eius mentio, nisi à mortuo. Respond. Nihil hîcab-surdi surdi esse, clamat quotidiana experientiâ. Immò etiam vivo legata- rio mentio sæpè fit hæreditatis, cui creperi amici inhiant.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CXV. Inheritance. In the first axiom I wrote, from this passage of Plautus, Mil. 3.1 v.115: Those who court an inheritance are wont to send gifts to their legatees, for the sake of dividing the inheritance. On the contrary, someone objects thus: What is more absurd than that an inheritance should be divided while the heir is alive? Its mention never occurs except of a dead man. I reply: nothing here is absurd, as daily experience cries out. Indeed, even while a legatee is alive, mention is often made of the inheritance, for which eager friends gape.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphor.11. Hæredem faciebant eum, qui laudes decantaret vivi. Sic dicis causâ è verbis Servi erui hanc sententiam: qui cùm diffusim malè de Hero suo fuisset locutus, ita ab altero Servo joco excipitur Pseud.4.2.v.17. Omnia edepol mira sunt, nisi herus hunc hæredem facit. Nam is quidem illi ut meditatur, verba facit emortuo. Vides, Lector, jocum.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphor. 11. They made him heir who would praise the living man. For the sake of the jest, this sentiment is drawn from the words of a slave: when he had spoken ill of his master at length, he is answered with a joke by another slave, Pseud. 4.2 v.17. All things are wonderful, by Pollux, unless the master makes this man his heir. For he speaks to the dead man as he plots. You see, reader, the joke.

units.la: ¶ Tit.cxvi.Hominis. Aphor. xiii. Crepitum Philosophorum Stoicorum polentarium vocat Plautus è polentâ comestâ. Curc. 2.3.v.16. ] In hoc sequor Lambini, & aliorum Interpretum sententiam: secu- rus, quid alij contrà ogganniant.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CXVI. Of man. Aphor. xiii. Plautus calls the farting of the Stoic philosophers "polentarium", from the polenta they had eaten. Curc. 2.3 v.16. In this I follow the opinion of Lambinus and other interpreters, unconcerned about what others grumble to the contrary.

units.la: † Ibid. Axiomate ultimo dixi; ἰδιον hoc πνεῦμος corporis Physici: Venum corpus non posse esse in pluribus locis, redarguere posse vanitatem illius Dogmatis de πανταχοῦ corporis Christi. Innuitur id aliquot locis Plautinis. Amph.2.1.v.11.16.41.46. Mostell.3.3.v.106. Aulul.2.2.v.4. Neque verò mirum alicui videri debet, Dogma Christianum ex scriptore Ethnico posse revelli. Nam cùm Axioma hoc sit Physicum, nihil mirari possumà Plauto Naturæ omnis callentissimo, ut ut ille aliquot ante saeculis ante Christum natum vixerit, fuisse repetitum. Sic veritatem nihil impeditqui proferat.
units.tr: † Ibid. In the last axiom I said that this is a property of a physical body: A true body cannot be in several places at once, which can refute the vanity of that dogma about the omnipresence of Christ's body. This is hinted at in several places in Plautus: Amph. 2.1 v.11, 16, 41, 46; Mostell. 3.3 v.106; Aul. 2.2 v.4. Nor indeed should it seem strange to anyone that a Christian dogma can be drawn from a heathen writer. For since this axiom is physical, I can wonder at nothing: that it was repeated by Plautus, most skilled in nature, though he lived some centuries before the birth of Christ. Thus nothing prevents truth from being brought forward by anyone.

units.la: Etiam Aristoteles, Plato, alij, ante Christum natum vixerunt: & tamen ex ijsdem Authoribus Ethnicis multa dogmata Theologica, quæscilicet sunt mixti generis, confirmantur.
units.tr: Aristotle, Plato, and others also lived before the birth of Christ; and yet from these same heathen authors many theological dogmas, which are of a mixed kind, are confirmed.

units.la: ¶ Tit. cxxxvi. Lapidum. Aphor.1 Lapide veteriori. ] h. e. durior. Petitum hoc fuit è lectione Coleriana, quam loco Plauti intulerat ille Bacch. 5.2.v.31. Sed eam in secundâ Editione meâ Plauti- nâ ex MSS. Pa l. repuli. Vide Notas meas Criticas ad eum locum.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CXXXVI. Of stones. Aphor. 1. Lapide veteriori: that is, harder. This was taken from the reading of Colerus, which he had introduced into the passage of Plautus, Bacch. 5.2 v.31. But I rejected it in my second Plautine edition, on the authority of the Palatine manuscripts. See my Critical Notes on that passage.

units.la: ¶ Tit.cl. Litterarum, sive Epistolarum. Axioma viii. In Epistolis, si lata esset scribenda, ubi interdum Veteres genere litterarum contratiore, & accuratione. Bacch. 4.9.v.68. ] Nota quod dixi, Interdum. Nam non semper idfactum. Res enim læta magnis sæpè litteris transmissæ, minoribus tristes. Symmachus lib. i. Epist. xiii. Solet facunda esse læ titia: & angustiâ clausi pectoris adspernata gestire. Idem lib.iii. Epist. &c. Verba luxuriantia animi alacritatem testantur. testantur. Quin & tristia solent quandoque onus sui doloris depo- nere in sinum Amici diffusiore stilo.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CL. Of letters, or epistles. Axiom viii. In epistles, if the news is to be written joyfully, the Ancients sometimes used a more restricted kind of letter and care. Bacch. 4.9 v.68. Note what I said: sometimes. For this is not always done. Joyful matters are often sent in large letters, sad ones in smaller. Symmachus, book i, letter xiii: Joy is wont to be eloquent, and, scorning the narrowness of a closed heart, to exult. The same, book iii, letter etc.: Exuberant words bear witness to the cheerfulness of the mind. Indeed, sad matters too sometimes put down the burden of their grief in a friend's bosom in a more copious style.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CLIV. LUDORUM. Axioma VIII. In Amphitheatro ulti- mus locus, in quo Populus sedebat, CAVEA nominabatur. Amph. Prol. v.66. ] Id verum esse evincunt omnes passim Auctores. Vide Lip- sium & Fabrum de Amphitheatris. Nemo ver ò negavit umquam: alio nomine venisse locum medium, locum inferiorem, quamvis uterque et- jam excavatus. Et nota item est, Ima, Media, Prima, Ultima, Summa Ca- vea. Ultimum tamen locum, in quo Populus sedebat, CAVEAM nominatam, non nisi ignarus Antiquitatis dissitebitur.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CLIV. Of games. Axiom VIII. In the amphitheatre the highest place, where the people sat, was called the CAVEA. Amph. Prol. v.66. All the authors prove this to be true everywhere. See Lipsius and Faber on amphitheatres. No one has ever denied that another name was given to the middle place and the lower place, though each was also hollowed out. It is also known that there were the lowest, middle, first, last and highest cavea. Yet that the highest place, where the people sat, was called CAVEA, none but one ignorant of antiquity would deny.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma XXII. Gymnasia etiam ante Neronem fuerunt: quia Plautus eorum mentionem facit. Epid.2.2. v.14. ] Negavit id Petrus Fa- ber in Agonisticis: quem ut refellam, non est mei instituti. Utrum verò ante Julium Cæsarem itemque ante Scipionem Africanum Romæ fuerint Gymnasia, itidem non disputo.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom XXII. Gymnasia existed even before Nero, because Plautus makes mention of them. Epid. 2.2 v.14. Peter Faber denied this in his Agonistica; but to refute him is not part of my plan. Whether gymnasia existed at Rome before Julius Caesar, and likewise before Scipio Africanus, I likewise do not discuss.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CLV. Lusus. Aphorismus V. Noctu dormientibus ridiculi causa ora solebant pingere. Poen.5.5. v.11. ] Factum id non tantùm pu- gnis, sed & fuligine. Poen.4.4.v.23. Stulta soror es quàm volo; an verò pulchra videre, obsecro, si tibi illic non os oblitum est fuligine. Petronius: totam faciem ejus fuligine longâ perfricuit.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CLV. Play. Aphorism V. At night, for the sake of fun, they were wont to paint the faces of sleepers. Poen. 5.5 v.11. This was done not only with fists but also with soot. Poen. 4.4 v.23: You are a foolish sister, as I want. Or, pray, are you pretty to look at, if your face is not smeared with soot there? Petronius: he rubbed his whole face with a long coating of soot.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CLVI. LUXVS. dicitur Axiomate III. Inter alia instrumen- ta perditi luxûs & MATULAS in Triclinia inferri solitas: quas sæpè, vbi incaluissent, in capita sibi invicem illiserunt. ] Ad hunc morem allusum tribus locis apud Plautum.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. CLVI. LUXURY. Said in Axiom III. Among the other instruments of dissolute luxury, pots (matulae) were wont to be brought into the dining rooms, and these, when they had grown hot, they often struck against each other's heads. This custom is alluded to in three places in Plautus.

units.la: Curcul.3.1.v.26. Nam quid id refert meâ? An Aulâ quasiâ cum cinere effusus fiet.
units.tr: Curcul. 3.1 v.26. For what does that matter to me? Or will he be poured out with ashes, as if from a pot?

units.la: Capt.1.1.v.21. Qui colaphos perpeti potes? Parasitus, frangi Aulas in caput.
units.tr: Capt. 1.1 v.21. Can you endure blows? A parasite, with pots broken over his head.

units.la: Pers.1.2.v.8. Namque his (Parasitis cognomentum erat) duris ca- pitonibus. &c.
units.tr: Pers. 1.2 v.8: For these (the parasites had the nickname) hard-headed fellows, etc.

units.la: Objicit nonnemo: Plautina nihil loquuntur de Matulis, sed de Aulis. Respond. Res eodem redit. Nam & Aulæ, sive Ollæ pro Matulis s- surpatæ. Præterea notum est & Matulas in Convivijs Græcorum illatas. Quâ de re copiosè videatur CASAUBONUS ad libr.1. Athenæi. Cæterùm quod quis hoc loco infert, & quærit: Vbi aliquis de grege illo Parasitico ausus est referire Regem & Genium suum? frustrà sanè sanè est. Neque enim ignoramus verba Aristidis de Parasitis: ὠσὸ̈ ὰ̈ πὲρ ὃλ.ῶ· ... Itemq; illa Quintiliani Senioris : contumelias in quæstu habere, & injuria pasci.
units.tr: Someone objects: "The Plautine passages say nothing about the matulae, but about the aulae." Reply: the point comes to the same thing, since aulae, or ollae, were also used for matulae. Moreover, it is known that matulae were brought into the banquets of the Greeks. On this subject see Casaubon's commentary on the first book of Athenaeus, which is fuller. As for what someone infers and asks here, namely, "Where did anyone from that parasitical crowd dare to report the king and his genius?", that is certainly beside the point. For we are not unaware of Aristides' words about parasites: [Greek]. Likewise there is the saying of the elder Quintilian: to make insults a source of profit and to live on injury.

units.la: † Ibid. Canon 1 v. Luxus vestiarius tantus sæpè est, ut publica officia impediat. Aul.3.5.per totam Scenam. Epid.2.2.v.39. ] Per publica Officia intelligenda sunt debita Tributa. Quæab Officijs publicis excludi minimè possunt. Duo namque sunt Officij genera; ... teste Cicerone. Seneca de Constant. Sap. cap. xiv. quisquis erit, qui hoc salutationem publicum exercet. Plautus Truc.1.2.v.40. Illa,haud ego,habuit publicum. Glossæ: Publicum : ... Seneca Ep.ist.cxi, Qui ad Publica quoque accesserat. Et Epist. cxx. Quod agitarem Publicum. E quibus omnibus liquidò apparet: Tributa & Vectigalia inter Publica Officia recte referri.
units.tr: † Ibid. Canon 1 v.: Luxury in clothing is often so great that it hinders public offices. Aul. 3.5, throughout the scene. Epid. 2.2 v.39. By public offices we must understand the customary tributes, which cannot by any means be excluded from public duties. For there are two kinds of office, according to Cicero. Seneca, De constantia sapientis, ch. 14: whoever it is who carries on this public greeting. Plautus, Truc. 1.2 v.40: She, not I, had public... Glosses: Publicum: ... Seneca, Ep. 111: who had approached even public business. And Ep. 120: what I was pursuing as public business. From all of these it plainly appears that tributes and taxes are rightly counted among public offices.

units.la: ¶ Tit. clviii. Macies seu macritudo proprie est circa ossa.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. clviii. Emaciation, or leanness, properly concerns the bones.

units.la: Capt.1.2.v.32. ] Quæritaliquis: At improprie circa quæ est. Resp. Non circa ossa: sed circa carnes: non circa ungues, sed circa pellem: non circa crines & pilos, sed circa cutem. Sic apparet, improprie circa quæ fit macies.
units.tr: Capt. 1.2 v.32. Someone asks: "But improperly, about what things is it?" Answer: not about the bones but about the flesh; not about the nails but about the skin; not about the hair and bristles but about the skin. Thus it appears that emaciation occurs improperly about these things.

units.la: ¶ Tit. clxiii. Medicorum. Medici Plerumque sunt arrogantes, nimis sæpe morantur, ut magis ægros inveniant.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. clxiii. Of physicians. Physicians are for the most part arrogant, and they very often delay, so that they may find their patients worse.

units.la: ] Quod colligitur è querela Senis Menæch.5.3,v.6. Lumbi sedendo, oculi spectando dolent: Manendo Medicus, dum se ex operere excipiat. Odiosus tandem vix ab ægrotis venit: Ait se obligasse crus fractum Æsculapio: Apollini autem brachium.
units.tr: This is gathered from the complaint of an old man, Menaechmi 5.3 v.6: "My loins ache from sitting, my eyes from watching, while I wait for the doctor, who keeps taking himself off from work. At last the hateful fellow barely comes away from his patients. He says he has bound a broken leg to Aesculapius, but an arm to Apollo."

units.la: Absit verò, ut Aphorismus ille, quem ex istis verbis construxi, ad infamiam Æsculapij generis pertineat: aut per illum Integer Ordo infametur. Non ; non. Aliquorum ... non imputatur protinus toti Ordini. Numquid enim disertè dicitur, Plærumque? Thesis mea Universalis non est, sed Indefinita, ut loquuntur Logici, æquipollens Particulari.
units.tr: Far be it from me that the aphorism which I have constructed from these words should bring infamy on the family of Aesculapius, or that through it the whole profession should be defamed. No, no... the fault of some is not straightway imputed to the whole order. For is it not expressly said for the most part? My thesis is not universal but indefinite, as the logicians say, equivalent to a particular.

units.la: De Medicis verba sunt Senecæ lib.v1. de Benefic. cap.xxxvi. Gravissima est Medici infamia, opus quærere: videlicet; an ægri, aut magis ægri sint, addidit ibi Lipsius. De ijsdem extant hi versus Philemonis:
units.tr: The words about physicians are from Seneca, De beneficiis, book 6, ch. 36: The greatest infamy of a physician is to seek work, namely, whether the sick are sick, or sicker. Lipsius added this there. On the same subject these verses of Philemon also survive:

units.la: τλς
units.tr: [Greek verse, illegible in the scan]

units.la: [Greek line]
units.tr: [Greek verse, illegible in the scan]

units.la: [Greek line] Quis iste porro? Medicus. ô quàm se habet Medicus male omnis, nemo si male sese habet.
units.tr: [Greek verse, illegible in the scan] Who is that, then? A physician. Oh, how badly off is every physician, when no one is badly off.

units.la: § Tit. CLIV. MEMORIÆ. Memoria magis viget ante sumtum cibum. Amph. 2.1.v.97.] Nimirum, quò spirituum in cerebro tranquil- lior est agitatio, eò firmior fit impressio imaginum. at ventriculo cibis gravato exoritur ebullitio vaporum, è quibus quasi quædam spirituum nascitur constipatio: unde somnum ferè necesse est sub- oriri. Sic itaque interior ille sensus partes suas tam firmiter non ex- sequitur: atque si ventriculus sit inanis. Et hoc est, quod ait Seneca Epist.xv. Copiâ ciborum subtilitas animi elidi tur. Sic Galenus de saginâ & stupore Athletarum. [Greek] Verè quoque pronunciauit, qui, Vinum Mortem Memoriæ, appellavit.
units.tr: § Tit. CLIV. MEMORY. Memory flourishes more before food is taken. Amph. 2.1 v.97. Surely, the calmer the agitation of the spirits in the brain, the firmer the impression of images becomes. But when the stomach is weighed down with food, a boiling of vapours arises, from which a kind of constriction of the spirits is born; hence sleep almost necessarily follows. Thus that inner sense does not carry out its functions so firmly, as it would if the stomach were empty. This is what Seneca means in Ep. 15: By abundance of food the subtlety of the mind is crushed. So Galen, on the fatness and stupor of athletes: [Greek]. Rightly, too, did the one who called wine the death of memory speak the truth.

units.la: § Tit. CLXIV. Axioma x1. Aurichalcum Plautus pluris facit, quàm Talentum auri. Curcul.1.3.v.46. Pseud.2.3.v.22.] Ex his locis aperte id patet, quod posui. Vult alius, sibi ostendi è Plauto, permutatum fuisse Aurichalcum auro. Atqui nihil id necesse est: satis est, si constet ex prædictis locis, Plautum pluris fecisse Aurichalcum, quàm Talentum auri. Inspiciantur loca. Idem sensit Virgil.lib.xii. Aeneid.v.87. Ipse dehinc auro squalentem alboque Orichalco Circumdat loricam humeris.
units.tr: § Tit. CLXIV. Axiom 11. Plautus values orichalcum more than a talent of gold. Curc. 1.3 v.46; Pseud. 2.3 v.22. From these passages it is clear what I have set out. Someone else wishes it to be shown to him from Plautus that orichalcum was exchanged for gold. But that is not at all necessary: it is enough if it is established from the passages cited that Plautus valued orichalcum more than a talent of gold. Let the passages be examined. Virgil thought the same, Aeneid book 12 v.87: Then he himself girds his shoulders with a breastplate gleaming with gold and white orichalcum.

units.la: Idem fecit Homerus Hymno II. in Venerem. Meminit quoque Martianus tempore Alexandri Imperat. Anno ccxxv.l.Labeo.ff.de contrah. emtione. Videatur & Plinius lib.xxxiv.cap.11.
units.tr: Homer did the same in his Second Hymn, to Venus. Martianus also mentions it, in the time of Emperor Alexander, in the year 225. Labeo, Digest, de contrahenda emptione. See also Pliny, book 34, ch. 11.

units.la: § Tit. CLXIX. Mortis. In enumeratione causarum [Greek] [Greek] Casu vi. recitavi exemplum Severiani, qui priusquam jugularetur, ignem popposcit, atque ita incenso thure enecatus fuit. Hunc casum illustravi gemino alio simili. Uno petito ex Inscriptione Veteri: altero Juliani Imper. Quæ quidem duo paria exemplaest qui dicat Ridicule eò à me trahi. Neque enim quis se ipsum occidit, qui sanus casu necatur in somnis ex nidore prunarum. Ut huic objectioni satisfiat, notet mihi Lector, Veteré Inscriptionem, ut & exemplum Juliani me non tam habere ad certam quandam {Greek} inde eliciendam, quàm ad illustrandum illud Mortis genus, quo periit Severianus. Ita igitur Inscriptio Vetus:
units.tr: § Tit. CLXIX. Of death. In the enumeration of causes [Greek] [Greek]. In case 6 I cited the example of Severianus, who, before he was throttled, asked for fire, and so was killed by the burning of incense. I illustrated this case with two other similar ones: one taken from an ancient inscription, the other from Emperor Julian. These two pairs of examples... There is someone who says: "I am being ridiculously dragged there by me. For no one kills himself who, while sane, is accidentally killed in his sleep by the fumes of coals." To meet this objection, let the reader note that I do not so much use the ancient inscription, or the example of Julian, to draw some definite [Greek] from them, as to illustrate that kind of death by which Severianus perished. So the ancient inscription reads:

units.la: L. ÆMILIUS. PRUNA IN PENSILI POSITA URGUENTE FATO SANUM IPSE NECAVIT SE.
units.tr: L. Aemilius. A live coal placed in a hanging brazier; the fate pressing, he himself killed himself while sound.

units.la: Ubi & hoc negligendum, quòd ipse sanus seipsum occiderit. Eodem mortis genere perijt Julianus Imperator.
units.tr: Here this too should not be overlooked: he himself, being sound, killed himself. Julian the Emperor also perished by this same kind of death.

units.la: † Ibid. Casu postremo dixi: Mirum omninò videri posse, Fortunam prosperam Morte quosdam terminare voluisse, ne forsan adversa recurreret. Profectò omnino mirum id videri potest; tantum Gentilium fuisse vesaniam. Ut ut verò in Veterum lectione versatis illo ipso nihil magis est obvium, admiratione tamen illud non caret.
units.tr: † Ibid. I said at the end, by chance: It may seem altogether strange that some wished to end a prosperous fortune by death, lest adversity perhaps return. Indeed it may seem altogether strange; so great was the madness of the Gentiles. Yet however much this is most obvious to those versed in reading the ancients, it still does not lack the power to astonish.

units.la: ¶ Tit.CLXX. MORUM. Axioma VII. Mores rusticorum merum rus sapiunt. Sic Servus ille rusticus cùm salutaretur ab urbanâ Ancillâ Trucul.2.2.v.4. quàm inficetè respondet! Nihil moror non salveo, aegrotare malim, quàm tuâ salute esse sanior.
units.tr: ¶ Title CLXX. Of manners. Maxim VII. The manners of country folk taste wholly of the countryside. So that rustic slave, when greeted by the city maidservant of a harlot (Truc. 2.2.v.4), how wittily he replies! I care nothing for your greeting; I would rather be ill than healthier by your health.

units.la: Etsi verò ab Scorti ancilla salutatus fuit Servus, tamen ea Servi responsio nulli virtuti adscribi potest. Quid enim magis ab homine alienum, quàm non vicissim salute impertire aut redhostire hominem? Utique humanius Urbanam Ancillam excipere potuisset Servus, ruti natus, & educatus: cujus {Greek} non sine ratione Comicus sic introduxit: ut nimirùm liqueret, aliam educandi rationem, alios introducere mores.
units.tr: Although the slave was greeted by a harlot's maidservant, yet that slave's reply cannot be ascribed to any virtue. For what is more foreign to a man than not to return a greeting or wish health in return? Surely the slave, born and bred in the country, could have received the city maidservant more courteously; and the comic poet introduced him this way, not without reason: clearly to show that a different upbringing produces different manners.

units.la: ¶ Tit.CLXXI. MULIERUM. Axioma XXIII. Mulieres impudicae comparantur Navi, quòd domi stabant instar Navis instructae, & paratae, exspectantes, donec vocarentur. Caf.3.2.v.27. ] Objicit {Greek}: Atqui Mulier ista fuit pudica. Resp. Fortasis; inquam ego. Certè quidem jocus Senis non vsqueadeo fuit pudicus.
units.tr: ¶ Title CLXXI. Of women. Maxim XXIII. Unchaste women are compared to a ship, because they stood at home like a fitted and ready ship, waiting until they were called (Cas. 3.2.v.27). An objector says: "But that woman was chaste." I reply: "Perhaps so," I say. Certainly the old man's joke was not so very chaste.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma XLIV. Mulieres tonstrices dictae ab arte Mariti, Trucul.2.4.v.51. ] Et Feminas quoque Artem tonsoriam exercuisse, est {Greek}: nec feminas-conjuges tantùm, sed & Ancillas, patet ex Trucul.4.2.v.59. & 4.4.v.3. Immò & Virgines alias. Cicero Tuscul. fcul.lib.i. Regiæ Virgines ut tonstriculæ tondebant barbam, & capillos Patris. Videatur Inscriptio Antiqua pag. DLXXIX. S. Flora Mater Tonstrix. Tonstrices verò Mulieres ab arte Mariti dictas quoque quis negabit: cùm & hodiè eo nihil sit familiarius?
units.tr: † Ibid. Maxim XLIV. Women barbers are so called from the trade of their husband (Truc. 2.4.v.51). That women too practised the barber's art is evident, and not only wives but also maidservants, from Truc. 4.2.v.59 and 4.4.v.3. Indeed, other virgins too did so. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book I: Royal virgins, like little barbers, used to shave the beard and hair of their father. Let the ancient inscription on p. DLXXIX be consulted: S. Flora, mother, barber. Who, however, will deny that women barbers were so called from their husband's trade, since nothing is more familiar even today?

units.la: ¶ Tit. CLXXVIII. Nativitatis. Infantes expositi traditi Gladiatoribus] Expositionis hujus ratio non vsque adeò frequens fuit, Lanistæ tamen cùm tyrones, totamque familiam aluerint, è projectitijs & monstrosis fœtibus Gladiatores quoque formasse, quis abnuet? De Eunuchis quod ibidem dixi, Persis perquàm fuit solemne, uti testatur Dio Chrysostomus. Orat. de Pulchritudine. Et inprimis Herodotus lib. v i. his verbis: Posteaquàm Persæ potiti sunt Vrbibus Ioniæ, sub Dario Rege, formosissimos quosque puerorum seligentes castraverunt, exsectis testibus facientes Eunuchos.
units.tr: ¶ Title CLXXVIII. Of birth. Infants exposed were handed over to gladiators (Trucul.). The practice of exposure was not so very frequent, yet who will deny that the trainers, who reared recruits and their whole household, also formed gladiators from foundlings and monstrous births? As for eunuchs, which I also mentioned there, it was quite customary among the Persians, as Dio Chrysostom attests in his oration On Beauty. And above all Herodotus, book VI, in these words: After the Persians had taken the cities of Ionia under King Darius, they selected the most handsome of the boys, castrated them, cutting out the testicles, and made them eunuchs.

units.la: † Ibid. Diversa est lectio hujus loci Mil. 3.1. v.101. Tum piatricem cl. menter non potest, quin munerem.
units.tr: † Ibid. The reading of this passage in Miles 3.1.v.101 is different: "Then the patrician woman cannot but (clemently) ... the gift."

units.la: Probo lectionem vetustissimorum MSS. Codd. Pall. patricam: quasi, patriciam. Vide ibi Notas nostras Criticas.
units.tr: I approve the reading of the most ancient manuscripts, the Codices Palatini: patricam, as if it were patriciam. See our critical notes there.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xiv. Singularis Deorum benivolentia habebatur, & pietatis pudicitiæque puerperæ si gemmos peperisset. Amph. 5.1.v.38.] Hoc loco Bromia Ancilla laudat Dominam, quòd ita extraordinem Iuppiter ei faverit. Idem Tiberius apud Tacitum jactat, cùm Livia Druso nupta duos virilis sexûs simul enixa esset: quod Rarum, letumque, etiam modicis penatibus, tanto gaudio Principem affecit, ut non temperaverit, quin jactaret apud Patres: Nulli ante Romanorum ejusdem fastigii Viro geminam stirpem editam.
units.tr: † Ibid. Maxim XIV. The special goodwill of the gods was thought to be shown to a woman who, being pious and chaste, bore twins (Amph. 5.1.v.38). Here the maidservant Bromia praises her mistress, because Jupiter had favoured her so extraordinarily. The same Tiberius, in Tacitus, boasted when Livia Drusilla, married to him, had given birth to two male children at once: a rare and joyful event, even in modest households, which so moved the Emperor with joy that he could not refrain from declaring before the Fathers: "No man of the Romans of the same rank had ever before had a double offspring born to him."

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xiii. Mulieres à partione filiorum Plærumque animis fiunt elatiores. Trucul. 2.8.v.10. Ubi de Phronesio inquit Miles:
units.tr: † Ibid. Maxim XIII. Women are for the most part made more proud after bearing sons (Truc. 2.8.v.10). Where the soldier says of Phronesium:

units.la: Postquam filiolum peperit, animos sustulit.]
units.tr: After she bore a little son, she lifted up her spirits.

units.la: Thema hoc nolim esse generale: cùm in Ideâ id pono, Mulieres: &, Plærumque. Dictum quidem id de Meretrice: at non propterea fallum. Phronesium enim Mulier. Phronesium peperit. Phronesium animos sustulit post partionem. Aliquot igitur Mulieres à partione filiorum animis fiunt elatiores.
units.tr: I would not wish this maxim to be general, since I take it in the idea: "women" and "for the most part." It was said of a courtesan, yet it is not therefore false. For Phronesium is a woman; Phronesium bore a child; Phronesium lifted up her spirits after childbirth. Therefore some women are made more proud after bearing children.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CLXXIX. Navis. Axioma xxi. Cùm Ventus navem deserit, periculum est naufragij. Mostell. 3.2.v.49.] Quid fit, Deserere navim: vim: exposui in Editionis nostræ fecundæ Notâ marginali ad illum locum: quò Lectorem remitto.
units.tr: ¶ Title CLXXIX. Of ships. Maxim XXI. When the wind deserts the ship, there is danger of shipwreck (Mostell. 3.2.v.49). What it is to desert a ship I have explained in the marginal note on that passage in our second edition; I refer the reader there.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CLXXXII. Nominum. Axioma VI. Arrogantiæ est, sibi longa nomina adsciscere, quòd hodiè nimis quàm solemne est. Curc. 3. I. V. 40.] Si quæras, Ad quos? Respondeo: Apud Therapontigonos Platagi-doros, qui, dum nomina sua scribunt, explere solent totas ceras quattuor. Odiosum est, ad Individua descendere. Secus talia nomina plura subjungerem, in quibus
units.tr: ¶ Title CLXXXII. Of names. Maxim VI. It is a sign of arrogance to assume long names for oneself, which today is all too customary (Curc. 3.1.v.40). If you ask, "To whom?" I answer: "Among the Therapontigonians, the Plataghidoroi, who, when they write their names, are accustomed to fill four whole wax tablets." It is tiresome to go down to individuals. Otherwise I would add more such names, among which

units.la: Si ante lucem ire occipiam à primo nomine,
units.tr: If I begin from the first name before dawn,

units.la: Concubium sit noctis prius, quàm ad postremum perveniam.
units.tr: there will be a night's gloom before I reach the last.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CLXXXVII. Nuptiarum. Axioma I. Nuptiæ quandoque fiebant per sortitiones. In quâ sortitione sæpè devotationes. Cas. 2. 6. v. 36.] Infit hic quidam: Devotatio imminebat tantùm honestioribus: in quos quadrat rivalitas. Benè. Atqui Rivalitas etiam esse solet in natione servili: immò quàcumque aliâ: ut fert hominum malignitas, qui tales fibulas nectunt.
units.tr: ¶ Title CLXXXVII. Of weddings. Maxim I. Marriages were sometimes made by lot. In such a lot there were often curses (Cas. 2.6.v.36). Here someone begins: "Curses threatened only the more honourable people, against whom rivalry is directed." Well said. Yet rivalry also tends to exist among the servile class, indeed among any other class, as the malice of men brings it, who weave such snares.

units.la: † Ibid. Axiomate XL VII. Locus Casinæ 4. 3. v. 8.
units.tr: † Ibid. Maxim XLVII. Passage of Casina 4.3.v.8.

units.la: Quid si etiam offendam Hymaneum?
units.tr: What if I also offend Hymen?

units.la: omninò sic est legendus, & non aliter: uti nuper in Notis meis Criticis adseruì ex omnibus, ijsque optimis MSS. Pall. nec non plusculis Editionibus veteribus. Proinde in Morboniam abire jussi illud occentem: quod est à Baptistâ Pio.
units.tr: It must be read in exactly this way and in no other, as I lately asserted in my critical notes, from all, and the best, manuscripts of the Palatine and also several old editions. Accordingly, I bade the word occentem go off to Morbonia; this is from Baptista Pius.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CXCIII. Oleï. Ex oleo pulmenta quoque fiebant. Pseud. 1. 2. v. 84.] Regerit nonnemo: Illud omne, cui additur oleum, idne ex mero constat oleo? Respond. Constabit ex oleo, &c, cui additur oleum, ut fiat indè pulmentum.
units.tr: ¶ Title CXCIII. Of oil. Relishes were also made from oil (Pseud. 1.2.v.84). Someone objects: "Does every dish to which oil is added consist of pure oil?" Answer: It will consist of oil, etc., to which oil is added so that a relish may be made from it.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CXCV. Orationum. Magnates nonnisi rogati supplicitèr exorantur. Rud. 2. 4. v. 8.] Ita prorsùs legi debet Canon iste: neque aliter quoque distingui. Quod vitio Typographi neglectum. Omissa enim didiuncula nisi, quæ sic addita verum & germanum parit sensum.
units.tr: ¶ Title CXCV. Of speeches. The great ones are never persuaded by entreaty unless they are asked (Rud. 2.4.v.8). This rule ought to be read exactly thus, and cannot be punctuated otherwise. This was overlooked through a printer's error; for the omitted little word nisi, when added as here, produces the true and genuine sense.

units.la: ¶ CC. Palloris. Pallidi mortuis similiores, quàm vivis. Bacch. 5. 2. v. 22.] Si quæras; Quibus mortuis? triduanis? an qui mensem unum alterumve terræ infossi? Respondeo; Quoscumq; mortuos sumas licet, pallidos omnes invenies. Horat.
units.tr: ¶ CC. Of pallor. The pale are more like the dead than the living (Bacch. 5.2.v.22). If you ask: "Which dead? Those of three days, or those buried in the earth a month or so?" I answer: whichever dead you take, you will find them all pale. Horace:

units.la: Pallida mors æquo pulsat pede. &c. Dein; etsi alia quoque sunt, quæ Senes mortis similes faciunt, quàm pallor, frigus, paralysis, muccus, macies. &c. tamen & pallor Mortis similes reddit.
units.tr: Pale death knocks with impartial foot, etc. Further, although there are other things which make the old like the dead, such as pallor, cold, paralysis, mucus, leanness, etc., yet pallor too makes them like the dead.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CCI. PARASITORUM. Axioma XXXII. Parasiti avidum genus hominum, nescium saturari, ut etiam furfures subtus excutiat. Capt. 4.2.v.32. ] Parasitos famelicam esse nationem, patet quoque ex Sticho 2.1.v.1. ubi ait:
units.tr: ¶ Title CCI. Of parasites. Maxim XXXII. Parasites are a greedy race of men, unable to be satisfied, who would even shake out the bran from the bottom (Capt. 4.2.v.32). That parasites are a famished race is evident also from Stich. 2.1.v.1, where he says:

units.la: Ex ipsâ Fame natos Parasitos. Vide totum locum,
units.tr: Parasites born of Hunger herself. See the whole passage.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CCII. PARENTUM. Parentum imprecationis omnis aliquid habent. Asin. 3.3. v.155. ] Si quæras, bonine, an mali? Respondeo: Utrumque illis inest. Est enim Omen vocabulum μίσουs. Vide hujus Ominis exempla supra Tit. ABOMINATIONIS.
units.tr: ¶ Title CCII. Of parents. All curses of parents have something in them (Asin. 3.3.v.155). If you ask whether they are good or bad: I answer, both are in them. For omen is an ambiguous word. See examples of this omen above, under the title ABOMINATION.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CCVII. PAUPERTATIS. Aphorismus XVI. Egestas saepè cogit extrema pati, quod secus nemo faceret, si in re esset. Trin. 4.2.v.5. ] Regerit nonnemo: Num MENTIRI est extremum quid? Resp. Certè quidem. Egestas cogit saepè MENTIRI: cogit & FURARI: cogit & SUSPENDI. Annon haec extrema sunt? Quid sit, esse in re, non est obscurum. Res sunt Divitiae, mille mille locis Auctorum. Dehinc Plautus noster Trin.3.2.v.56. dixit: In divitiis esse. Ecce; hoc est, Esse in re.
units.tr: ¶ Title CCVII. Of poverty. Aphorism XVI. Want often forces people to suffer extremes, which no one would do if he were well off (Trin. 4.2.v.5). Someone objects: "Is LYING something extreme?" Answer: Certainly. Want often forces men to LIE; it forces them also to STEAL; it forces them even to HANG themselves. Are not these extremes? What it means to be in re, "well off," is not obscure: res means wealth, as in a thousand places of the authors. Then our Plautus says (Trin. 3.2.v.56): to be in riches. Behold: this is esse in re.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CCVIII. PECCATI. Aphorismus I. Eos, qui per imprudentiam peccârunt, veniam deprecari decet culpæ. Aul.4.10.v.8.22.62. ] Sic restitue mendam Typographicam. Excusum namque erat, impudentiam erroneè.
units.tr: Title CCVIII. OF SIN. Aphorism I. Those who have sinned through imprudence ought to beg pardon for their fault. Aul. 4.10.v.8.22.62. ] Restore the correct reading here. The printed text had "impudentiam" (shamelessness) by mistake; it should be "imprudentiam" (imprudence).

units.la: † Ibid. Aphorismus III. Laus maxima ducitur, sed si ad frugem redeant Adolescentes corrupti. Trin.2.1.v.35. ] Reclamat nonnemo, sic: Triplo major laus ducitur, si non opus fit eis ad bonam frugem redire, si perpetuò instituere Regiam Virtutis ac Doctrinae viam. Socratica sententia. Ac si jam corrupti sint Adolescentes, & tum animum rursùm applicent ad frugem, an non laus magna eos manebit? Immò maxima. Taliter ingeniatus fuit Adolescens ille apud Plautum.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorism III. Great praise is won, but only if the corrupted young men return to virtue. Trin. 2.1.v.35. ] Someone objects and proposes this instead: Three times greater praise is won if they need not return to good conduct, but keep forever to the royal road of virtue and learning. This is a Socratic saying. But if young men have already been corrupted and then turn their minds back to virtue, will not great praise still belong to them? Indeed, the greatest praise. The young man in Plautus was described in just this way.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CCIX. PEREGRINATIONIS. Canon II. Occurrentes de via, de semitâ decedere solent aliis: idque honoris causâ. Trin. 2.4. v.80. ] Quæritur: Quos vocas Occurrentes? qui ab Oriente veniunt? an qui ab Occasu? an qui ab Septentrione? an qui ab Meridie? Respondeo: A quocumque Mundi climate quis mihi occurrat: num honorem hunc F illi denegabo, ut decedam nonnihil de via, de semita? an incuisabo illum cornibus? Sint illi, quibus decedam, tenuiores, an ditiores: privati, an Magistratus: juniores, an seniores, Honoris profectò ratio talem deviationem requiret.
units.tr: ¶ Title CCIX. OF TRAVEL. Canon II. Those we meet on the road usually step aside from the path for others, and they do so out of respect. Trin. 2.4.v.80. ] The question is asked: Whom do you call "those we meet"? Those coming from the East? From the West? From the North? From the South? I answer: whatever part of the world anyone comes from to meet me, shall I deny him this mark of respect, so that I do not step a little off the road or path? Or shall I gore him with my horns? Whether those I step aside for are poorer or richer, private citizens or magistrates, younger or older, the reason of honour certainly calls for such a deviation.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma v. Peregrinationibus variis exerciti, solent esse arrogantes. Quod Charmides tribuit Sycophantæ. Trin. 4. 2. v. 104.] Versum hunc, è quo sententia deprompta, non tribuo Charmidi, sed rem tribuo Sycophantæ. Id verò inde quâ Methodo sic eruam, si quæris, Respondeo: Methodo Logicâ, manifestâ, particulari, syllogisticâ: quia confirmatur Thema conjunctum, medio termino, sumto ab effectu & adjuncto communi. Ea; meam Methodum. Et certè Thema ipsum cum ipsâ quotidianâ experientiâ consentit.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom v. Those who have wandered through many lands tend to be arrogant. Charmides attributes this to the Sycophant. Trin. 4.2.v.104. ] I do not assign this line, from which the saying is taken, to Charmides; I assign the matter to the Sycophant. If you ask how I reach this conclusion by method, I answer: by a logical method, clear, particular and syllogistic, because the connected thesis is confirmed by a middle term taken from the effect and a common attribute. That is my method. And indeed the thesis itself agrees with everyday experience.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xv i. Peregrinantes rerum visarum historiam domum reversi, conscribere solebant. Men. 2.1. v. 23.] Sic habet contextus Plautinus: Quin nos hinc domum redimus, nisi si historiam scripturi sumus. Jocum explicavi ad oram ipsius contextûs: nisi idcò tam diu peregrinamur, ut Historiam aliquam describamus rerum visarum. Quid potè dici magis perspicuum? Objicit: Quotusquisque Idiotaid (Historiam scribere) vel facit, vel facere potest? Resp. Neq; id necessum: neque ego dixi, aut volui, ut omnes Idiotæ Historias peregrinationum suarum describant: dummodo certum sit; Aliquos Peregrinantes id facere.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom xvi. Travellers who returned home used to write down the history of what they had seen. Men. 2.1.v.23. ] The Plautine context reads: "Why do we return home from here, unless we are going to write a history?" I have explained the joke in the margin beside the passage itself: unless we are travelling so long in order to describe some history of what we have seen. What could be said more plainly? Someone objects: how many laymen (idiotae) write a history, or can write one? I reply: this is not necessary, nor did I say or mean that all laymen write histories of their travels; it is enough that it is certain that some travellers do so.

units.la: † Ibid. Axiomate xx iv. Peregrè abituri Vicinis credebant Thesaurum suum. Trin. 1. 2. v. 17.] Quærit Titius: Cur non Parentibus? cur non fratribus? cur non Uxoril us? aut Adgnatis, aut Affinibus. Respondeo: Et Parentibus, & Fratribus, & Uxoribus & Adgnatis, & Affinibus integrum fuit illud facere. Aliqui verò maluerunt Vicinis suis credere. Neque verò ego dixerim, quòd Omnes id facere cogantur. Thesis namque mea hunc διαφέρει ἐξ ἡμῶν διφέρει excludit; quando in Idea aliquos duntaxat id solitos facere, pronunciavi. Logica Parei huiusmodi contradicentium διαφέρει γεφ καὶ captio sas δικαίως bellè docet refellere.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom xxiv. Those about to go abroad used to entrust their treasure to neighbours. Trin. 1.2.v.17. ] Titius asks: why not to parents? Why not to brothers, wives, kinsmen, or relatives by marriage? I answer: it was open to them to do this with parents, brothers, wives, kinsmen and relatives by marriage alike. But some preferred to entrust it to their neighbours. Nor would I say that all are compelled to do so. My thesis excludes this ambiguity (diaphora) [διαφέρει], since I declared that only some were in the habit of doing it. Parrhasius's logic teaches well how to refute this sort of contradiction by the fallacy of ambiguity [διαφέρει] and the captious argument [δικαίως].

units.la: ¶ Tit. ccxii. Pictura. Aphor. 11. Tabellas conficiebant Amantes ex cerà: in quibus picturam & imaginem depingebant eorum, quos amabant. Quò allusum Asin. 4. 1. v. 23.] Confirmavi in Electis hanc sententiam disertis Auctorum testimonijs.
units.tr: ¶ Title CCXII. PICTURE. Aphorism II. Lovers used to make tablets of wax, on which they painted the picture and image of those they loved. This is alluded to in Asinaria 4.1.v.23. ] I confirmed this saying in my Electa with the clear testimonies of authors.

units.la: Ovidius lib.II.de Remed. Am.v.327.
units.tr: Ovid, Remedia Amoris, Book II, v. 327.

units.la: Si potes, & ceras remove, quid imagine mutâ Carperis. hoc periit Laodamía modo.
units.tr: If you can, remove the wax as well: why do you lament a dumb image? In this way Laodamia perished.

units.la: Propertius lib.II. Eleg VIII.v.16.
units.tr: Propertius, Book II, Elegy VIII, v. 16.

units.la: Seu miseram in tabulâ pièta tabella movet.
units.tr: Or a little painted tablet moves the wretched girl.

units.la: Sensum loci Plautini expressi in Notis marginalibus ad cum locum: quem Lectorem vísere velim.
units.tr: I have set out the sense of the Plautine passage in the marginal notes on that place; I would like the reader to consult them.

units.la: ¶ Tit.CCXIII. PIGNORIS. Arrhabonem auferebant, si quid alij dabant mutuò. Poen.5.6.v.22. Quis non intelligit verba tam perspicua? Miles e loco é domo Leonis abstulerat Arrhabonem seu pignus, quod pro Minâ retineret, quam ei dederat.
units.tr: ¶ Title CCXIII. OF PLEDGE. They took back the earnest-money if they had lent anything to others. Poen. 5.6.v.22. Who does not understand words so clear? A soldier had taken from the house of Leo the earnest-money, or pledge, which he was to keep against the mina he had given him.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CCXIV. PISCIUM. Aphorismus VI. Passer marinus, sive Struthiocamelus ita volat, ut terrâ se non tollat, sed alarum passus velis unâ currens remiget. Rud. 4.2.v.17.] Sic totus Aphorismus re(aĉibendus. Vitio namque Typographi irrepserant duæ dictiunculæ in mari quas expungendas esse, indicabunt Notæ meæ marginales ad eum locum. Cæterum nescio quo errore relatum hoc thema fuerit ad Titulum PISCIUM, cùm pertineat ad Tit. AVIUM, quo deinceps oportebit referri. Est, qui dicat, Passerem marinum arenas amare. Ego in Gesnero pag.742. hæc verba lego: Struthiocamelus à terrâ non discedit unquam: ut Avem dicere non possis. Ibid. pag.743. Non bene volat propter corporis molem. Ibid. propter gravitatem neque altius extolli, neque volare potest: sed velociter terrâ graditur. Ibid. non volat, sed alis erectis currit ut equus: adeo celeriter, &c. De arenis nullus sermo.
units.tr: ¶ Title CCXIV. OF FISH. Aphorism VI. The sea sparrow, or ostrich-camel, flies in such a way that it does not lift itself from the ground, but runs with its wings spread like oars. Rud. 4.2.v.17. ] The whole aphorism must be read in this way. Through a printer's error two words, in mari (in the sea), had crept in; my marginal notes on that place show that they must be struck out. Otherwise I do not know by what error this thesis was referred to the title FISH, when it belongs under the title BIRDS, to which it should be referred next. Someone says that the sea sparrow loves sands. In Gesner, page 742, I read these words: The ostrich-camel never leaves the ground, so that you could not call it a bird. Ibid., page 743: It does not fly well because of the bulk of its body. Ibid.: Because of its weight it can neither rise higher nor fly, but it moves swiftly over the ground. Ibid.: It does not fly, but runs with its wings raised like a horse, so swiftly, etc. There is no talk of sands.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphor. VII. Pisces elixi suaviores quàm assi. Mostel. 5.2.v.108.] Quærit jocularitèr Arellius quidem: Leno tibi est inter pisces? Resp. Neque inter pisces, neque inter Aves, aut Apes mihi est Leno. Dum enim à Lenone proferuntur hæc verba: Elixus esse, quàm assus soleo suavior. ἀλλ ἀλλ ἀλλ alluditur ad geminam rationem coquendi Pisces: quod ad oram ejus loci in Notis meis adnotavi.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorism VII. Boiled fish are sweeter than roasted. Mostellaria 5.2.v.108. ] Arellius indeed asks jokingly: "Do you have a pimp among the fish?" I answer: I have a pimp neither among fish, nor among birds, nor among bees. For when the pimp utters these words, "I am usually sweeter boiled than roasted," there is an allusion to the twofold way of cooking fish; I noted this in my marginal notes beside that passage. [ἀλλ ἀλλ ἀλλ] (the repeated word) is the play on it.

units.la: ¶ Tit.CCXXI. PRÆSENTIÆ-PERSONÆ. Aphorismus practicus proponitur talis: Præsentia in omnibus locis prævalet, inprimis in militiâ. Amph.I.I.v.9.] De quâ præsentiâ, corporis, an animi loquar, Titulus ipse indicat: modò quis norit, quid sit PERSONA. Utraque sane præsentia, & corporis & animi, requiritur in rebus prosperè gerendis. dis. Regerit Sempronius quidam: Si occidi in prælio volumus, adsimus oporter. Resp. Quid ni vero! Alios quoque si occidere volumus, itidem absentes minimè nos esse oportebit.
units.tr: ¶ Title CCXXI. PRESENCE OF PERSON. The practical aphorism is put forward thus: Presence prevails in all places, especially in war. Amphitryon 1.1.v.9. ] Whether I speak of bodily or of mental presence, the title itself shows, provided one knows what PERSON means. Both kinds of presence, of body and of mind, are certainly needed for success in affairs. Someone named Sempronius objects: "If we want to be killed in battle, we must be present." I answer: why not indeed! But if we want others to be killed, likewise we must not be absent.

units.la: Eundem Aphorismum retuli quoque ad Tit. Belli in Electis pag. 130. quà scil. accipiendum id, de virtute Ducis & Imperatoris. Huc verò <bl>πρωτ</bl> pertinet, quà notat quamvis præsentiam etiam extrà bellum.
units.tr: I have also referred this same aphorism to the title WAR in the Electa, page 130, where it is to be understood of the courage of a commander and general. Here, however, it applies as well, since it notes presence even outside war.

units.la: § Tit. CCXXIII. Principis. Aphor. I. Cùm suspicamur Principem bona fide nobis se amicum præbere: Vultu, inquam, & voce, sed corde aliud volutare, hoc versu uti possumus: Quoi homini dii propitii sunt, ei non iratos esse puto. Curcul. 4.4.v.1.
units.tr: § Title CCXXIII. OF THE PRINCE. Aphorism I. When we suspect that the prince shows himself a friend to us in good faith, in face and voice, but in his heart turns over something else, we may use this line: "I think the gods are favourable to the man to whom they are favourable, and that they are not angry with him." Curculio 4.4.v.1.

units.la: Suppeditavit mihi hoc Thema Janus Gruterus, qui totidem dictionibus, totidem syllabis, totidem litteris illud refert in Florilegio Ethico-Politico o' parte primâ, paginâ 689.
units.tr: Janus Gruterus supplied me with this thesis, and he gives it in the same number of words, syllables and letters in his Florilegium Ethico-Politicum, part one, page 689.

units.la: Est tamen, qui Porro Quirites! heic exclamat. Notetis, inquit, vos Aulici summi, infimi, Medioxumi, illud Suspicamur: utique si ad triste m partem strenua est suspicio.
units.tr: Yet there is someone who here cries out, "O citizens!" He says: Notice, he says, you courtiers, high, low and middling, that "we suspect": especially if suspicion is active in the bad part.

units.la: Quid Gruterus ad suam hanc notam respondere fit, nescio. Seneca sapiens dictum est: Non criminationibus tantùm, sed suspicionibus impellimur, & ex vultu visuque alieno pejora interpretari solemus.
units.tr: I do not know what Gruterus answers to this note of his. A saying of the wise Seneca: We are moved not only by accusations but by suspicions, and we are used to interpreting worse things from another's face and look.

units.la: Ab hac quidem Suspicione non tantùm Tyranni immunes esse non possunt, sed quandoque etiam ne boni quidem Principes. Cn. Pompeius cùm ulceris causâ crus fascijs circumcinxisset, in affectati Regni Suspicionem incidit. Erant enim, qui affirmarent, nullam aliam ob causam eius ligasse diademate, quàm ut diadema sibi adscriberet, nihilque referret, quà in parte corporis gestaretur. Sic Titus, quòd Hierosolymis eversis non illico Romam venisset, creditus est, de Regno meditari. Credidit id Pater Vespasianus: crediderunt nonnulli alij. Unde liquet, Principes facile in Suspicionem factorum suorum venire posse: cùm præsertim multa per ambages agere solent: quod de Claudio refert Suetonius cap. XXVI. Et Tacitus lib. XI. Annal.
units.tr: Not only are tyrants unable to be free from this suspicion, but sometimes even good princes are not. When Gnaeus Pompey had bound his leg with bandages because of an ulcer, he fell under suspicion of aiming at kingship. For some asserted that he had bound it with a diadem for no other reason than to claim the diadem for himself, and that it made no difference on what part of the body it was worn. So Titus, because he did not come to Rome at once after Jerusalem was destroyed, was believed to be plotting for the kingdom. His father Vespasian believed it, and several others did too. From this it is clear that princes can easily fall under suspicion of their own deeds, especially since they often act by roundabout ways, as Suetonius reports of Claudius in chapter XXVI, and Tacitus in Annals, book XI.

units.la: De Tyrannis res est manifesta, his enim tutò numquam siditur: qui plærumque omnia sua Simulate agere solent. Cujus quidem dem Simulationis & Dissimulationis verum viuumque specimen esse potest Tiberius: adeò quidem,ut diceret ipse,si ex suis virtutibus nullam magis amplecti, & amare, quàm Dissimulationem: teste Suetonio cap. xxiv. & xxviii. Itemque Dione initio lib. lvii. Eodem ingenio præditus Caligula. Is aliquando lautiore Convivio effusus in cacchinnos, Coss. qui juxtà cubabant, quidnam videret blandè quærentibus: Quid, inquit, nisi uno meo nutu jugulari vtrumque vestrum statim posse. Alia Exempla nunc prætereo.
units.tr: The matter concerning tyrants is plain: one never trusts them safely, since they for the most part do all their business by pretence. Tiberius can be a true and living example of this pretence and dissimulation, so much so that he himself used to say that if he embraced and loved none of his virtues more than dissimulation. Suetonius attests this in chapters 24 and 28, and Dio likewise at the beginning of book 57. Caligula was endowed with the same disposition. Once, when he was poured out in loud laughter at a rather lavish banquet, the consuls who reclined beside him asked eagerly what he found so funny. "What," he said, "except that with one nod of mine each of you could be throttled at once." I now pass over other examples.

units.la: Subdit: Δεῖναι: Quem innuat voce illâ absolutâ Principis, nisi eum, sub quo vivit, sub quo docet? Proh hominum fidem! Quàm rursus Janum Gruterum pro se respondentem, hîc audire velim, de Principe, suóne, aut alio, Axioma suum scripserit. Et ego Principem meum innuam? Quæ verò hæc Dialectica? Ex particulari Indefinitâ procudere aliud particulare Singulare. Apage tam insidiosam Logicam! Aliter, aliter, & ego, & Gruterus (qui sub uno vivimus Principe & Rege) sentimus, loquimur, & scribimus de pientissimo nostro Magistratu: cujus Regiæ Majestatis gressus Æternus Deus dirigat ad Ecclesiæ Christianæ, & Reipublicæ salutem! Amen, Amen!
units.tr: He adds: [Δεῖνα]. "What else does that bare word 'Prince' point to, except the one under whom he lives and under whom he teaches?" Good heavens! I would like to hear here Janus Gruterus answering for himself again, and to learn whether he wrote his axiom about a Prince, his own or another's. And am I to name my own Prince? What kind of logic is this? To produce from a particular indefinite another particular singular! Away with such a treacherous logic! Gruterus and I, who live under one Prince and King, think, speak and write differently, and we do so about our most pious magistrate. May the eternal God direct the steps of his royal majesty to the salvation of the Christian Church and commonwealth! Amen, amen!

units.la: ¶ Tit. ccxxv. Pudoris. Axioma xiv. Virgines ægerrimè fe-runt, si Propudij insimulantur. Mil.2.4.v.11.43.] Sententia hæc è dicto Philocomasij èruta. Atqui sive ea Virgo, sive Mulier, sive Meretrix fuerit, perindè est. Nam propudij se insimulari feminineus inprimis sexus ægerrimè ferre solet.
units.tr: ¶ Title 225, Of Modesty. Axiom 14: Virgins take it very badly if they are accused of shameful conduct. Mil. 2.4 v.11.43. This saying is snatched from the words of Philocomasium. But whether that person was a virgin, a woman or a prostitute makes no difference. For women of all people are wont to take it very badly to be accused of harlotry.

units.la: ¶ Tit. ccxxxi. Romæ. Aphor. vii. Ad portam Oftiensem egentes stipem rogabant in sacculum. Capt.i.i.v.22.] Quid sit, Rogare in sacculum; patet ex textu Plautino: ire extrà portam ad sacculum: h.e. ad stipem colligendam. Nùspiam tamen alibi ego hàc formulà meminì.
units.tr: ¶ Title 231, At Rome. Aphorism 7: Beggars at the Ostian gate asked for alms into a purse. Capt. 1.1 v.22. What "to ask into a purse" means is plain from the Plautine text, "to go outside the gate to the purse", that is, to collect alms. Yet I do not recall this phrase anywhere else.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma ultimum. Extrà Portam erant Taberna: in quas fæx Populi diverti solebat.
