Pseud.2.2.v.63.] Qui sic inferunt: An nemo ho-nestior illum locum frequentavit? nulla utuntur Dialecticâ. Quid enim? An propterea fæci Populi eò diverti minimè licuit? Adiit certè eò Cacula Servus Militis.
units.tr: † Ibid. Last axiom: Outside the gate there were taverns, into which the dregs of the people used to turn aside. Pseud. 2.2 v.63. Those who infer, "Did no more honest man frequent that place?", use no logic at all. For what follows? Was it therefore by no means permitted for the dregs of the people to turn in there? Certainly Cacula, a soldier's slave, went there.

units.la: ¶ Tit. ccxxxii. Sacerdotum. Aphor.i. Arioli furiosi seipsos verbeverberare solent. Trucul. 2. 7. v. 41. ] Etsi Arioli etiam extrà furorem se-ipsos verberarint, tamen nemo negabit, quòd seipsos verberarint.
units.tr: ¶ Title 232, Of Priests. Aphorism 1: Frenzied Arioli are accustomed to beat themselves. Trucul. 2.7 v.41. Even though the Arioli also beat themselves outside of frenzy, no one will deny that they beat themselves.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma iii. Sacerdotibus ampletebantur sacrificaturi. Rud. 1. 5. v. 22. ] Si Mulieres eo loci Sacerdotes amplexantur. Et Religio-nis causâ id ab eis factum, indicio sunt illa Sacerdotis verba: Aequius erat candidatas venire, hostiatasque ad hoc Fanum.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 3: Those about to sacrifice embraced priests. Rud. 1.5 v.22. That is, if women embrace priests in that place. And that they did this for religious reasons is shown by those words of the priest: "It was more fitting that the candidates and the women bringing victims should come to this temple."

units.la: ¶ Tit. ccxxxiii. Sacrificiorum. Axioma xvii. In Sa-crificiis libis utebantur: quæ Fratres dicebantur. Mil. 1 1 v. 8. ] Id probatur ex Arnobio, cujus hæc sunt verba lib. vii. Cupientibus addi-scere, quid cum pultibus Deo fit, quid cum libis, quid diversi cum Fra-tribus, confectionis jure mul-tiplici, atque impensarum varietate condi-tis. Hoc si alius non intelligit, propriam ne nobis ignorantiam ob-trudat.
units.tr: ¶ Title 233, Of Sacrifices. Axiom 17: In sacrifices they used cakes, which were called "brothers". Mil. 1.1 v.8. This is proved from Arnobius, whose words in book 7 are these: "To those wishing to learn what is done with porridges for God, what with cakes, and what with the 'brothers', prepared in various ways, seasoned by a manifold art of cooking and a variety of expense." If anyone does not understand this, let him not thrust his own ignorance upon us.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xx. In sacrificiis vasa erant litterata: & ut plurimum Dei vel Dea in scripta. Rud. 2. 5. v. 21 ] Non dico Omnia Vasa fuisse litterata: eoque non necesse est, ut doceam, omnia vasa sa-crificiis destinata, fuisse litteris insignita.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 20: In sacrifices the vessels were inscribed, and for the most part the name of the god or goddess was written on them. Rud. 2.5 v.21. I do not say that all vessels were inscribed; so it is not necessary for me to show that all vessels destined for sacrifices were marked with letters.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xxi. Plerumque Samijs, seu fictilibus vasis usi tenacio-res: opulentiores verò Aureis. Capt. 2. 2. v. 41. ] Certè Patet Philola-ches homo dives ijs usus. At non Omnes ijs usos, patet ex par-ticulari istâ mea particulâ Plerumque.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 21: Mostly the more frugal used Samian or earthen vessels, but the wealthier used golden ones. Capt. 2.2 v.41. Certainly it is plain that Philolaches, a rich man, used these. But that not all used them is clear from this particular word of mine, "mostly".

units.la: Plauti verò ævo Vasa Aurea in usu quoque fuisse, satis arguit hic lo-cus. Docet enim me quis quæ Samijs vasis præstantiora fuerint, de quibus Plauti loco agitur. Cæterùm etsi non nego, fuisse quondam nefas, Templis Aurum inferre: quod ex Plutarcho alicubi constat: eò què usos potissimùm Vasis fictilibus: tamen ex eodem Plutar-cho in Tractatu: Quod non liceat funerari. Pag. 8. 8. Edit. Wechel. col-ligimus, Crateres aureos in usu fuisse. Dicit enim, Romanas mulieres mundum suum Apollini Pythio dedisse primitiarum loco: ex quo Aureus Crater confectus Delphos venit. Ex Auro item Lucerna fuit A-thenis in Templo Minervæ: ut videre est apud Pausaniam lib. 1. pag. 24. Edit. Wechel. Præterea quid illud est, quod legimus apud Vir-gilium lib. 11. Georg. v. 190.
units.tr: That golden vessels were also in use in Plautus's day this passage sufficiently shows. For someone teaches me which vessels were more excellent than Samian ones, which is the subject of the Plautine passage. Moreover, although I do not deny that it was once forbidden to bring gold into temples, which is established from Plutarch somewhere, and that they used earthen vessels chiefly, yet from the same Plutarch, in the tractate "That it is not lawful to be buried", p. 8, Wechel edition, we gather that golden mixing bowls were in use. For he says that Roman women gave their ornaments to Apollo Pythius in place of first-fruits, and from this a golden mixing bowl was made and sent to Delphi. Likewise there was a golden lamp at Athens in the temple of Minerva, as can be seen in Pausanias book 1, p. 24, Wechel edition. Besides, what is that which we read in Virgil, Georgics book 2, v. 190?

units.la: Hic tibi prævalidas olim, multòque fluentesSufficiet Bacchö vites: hic fertilis uva,Hic laticis qualem pateris libamus, & Auro. Sic Persius Sat.ii.v.69.
units.tr: "Here for you, long ago, very strong vines and abundant ones will suffice for Bacchus; here is the fruitful grape, here we pour libations from bowls and from gold."

units.la: Dicite Pontifices, in Sacris quid facit Aurum?
units.tr: Persius, Satire 2, v. 69: "Tell me, priests, what does gold do in sacred rites?"

units.la: Quo versuutitur quoque Alexander Severus Imper.apud Lampridium cap.xliv.
units.tr: To which passage the Emperor Alexander Severus also refers, in Lampridius, chapter 44.

units.la: Sicapud Livium lib.x.cap.xxiii. mentio fit Argenteorum Vasorum. Vasa Argentea trium mensarum in cellâ Jovis Capitolini fuerunt. De Paterâ Argenteâ, & Argenteo Salino vide Plinium lib.xiii. cap.xii. & Val.Max.lib.iv.cap.iv. Existis quidem omnibus liquidò apparet Aphorismum nostrum supra positum,esse verissimum.
units.tr: Thus in Livy, book 10, chapter 23, mention is made of silver vessels: there were silver vessels of three tables in the cell of Jupiter Capitolinus. On the silver patera and the silver salt-cellar see Pliny, book 13, chapter 12, and Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 4. Indeed, from all these it is clear that our aphorism set out above is most true.

units.la: ¶ Tit. ccxxxiv. Salis.
units.tr: ¶ Title ccxxxiv. Salt.

units.la: Sal modijs vendebatur vili pretio. Ejus igitur Annonæ ratio quoque habita olim fuit. Cafin.3.2. v.8.] Non dico, quòd Tantum modijs divenditum fit Sal. Et modijs, & aliâ quâcumq; mensurâ usitatâ admenfurari potuit.Ego quidem numquam ingressus sum Oppidum aliquod,ubi nulla Annonæ Salis ratio habita: coque in Rep. Romanâ tot legibus firmatâ id observatum, minimè minimum.Cui tamen Politico umquam obesse potest talis nota?
units.tr: Salt was sold by the peck at a cheap price. Therefore a regard for its price was also taken in former times. Casina 3.2 v.8. I do not say that salt was sold only by the peck. It could be measured out by the peck or by any other customary measure. For my part, I have never entered any town where no regard was taken of the price of salt. That this was observed in the Roman state, which was secured by so many laws, is not a very small point. Yet can such a remark ever harm a politician?

units.la: ¶ Tit.ccxxxvii. Salutationum.
units.tr: ¶ Title ccxxxvii. Greetings.

units.la: Aphorismus ultimus. Etiam Inimici salutandi: eisque dicendum Vale, atque Salve. Capt. 3.5.v.86.] Sententia hæc congruit cum Christianismi regulis & præceptis.
units.tr: Last aphorism. Even enemies are to be greeted, and to them one must say, Farewell and Hail. Captivi 3.5 v.86. This saying agrees with the rules and precepts of Christianity.

units.la: ¶ Tit. cclxxviii. Sanguinis.
units.tr: ¶ Title ccxxviii. Blood.

units.la: Præ metu sanguis dicitur emigrare è corpore. Moftel. 2.2. v. 75.] Si quæratur quis; quâ vià emigrarit? quibus fenestris? Respondeo: Emigravit pleno crepitu eximo guttu-re ventris. Hac viâ,inquam,his fenestris emigravit.
units.tr: Through fear, the blood is said to flee from the body. Mostellaria 2.2 v.75. If someone asks, by what way did it flee? through what windows? I answer: it fled with a loud crack, out of the narrow throat of the belly. By this way, I say, by these windows, it fled.

units.la: ¶ Tit.ccxxxix. Sapientiæ.
units.tr: ¶ Title ccxxxix. Wisdom.

units.la: Sapientia non semper annis acquiritur, sed ingenio. Trin. 2. 2. v. 68.] Ita erratum Typographicum emendandum. Editum enim perperàm fuit:sed atate. mendosè. Eandem sententiam confirmavi dictis in Electis Tit. Ætatis. pag.8.
units.tr: Wisdom is not always acquired with years, but with talent. Trinummus 2.2 v.68. The printer's error must be corrected in this way. It was wrongly printed as sed atate [but in age]. I confirmed the same saying by what I said in the Electa under the title Age, p. 8.

units.la: ¶ Tit. ccxliv. Senectutis.
units.tr: ¶ Title ccxliv. Old Age.

units.la: Aphor.ii. Senes Plærumque molles. Caf.2. 3. v.23.] Vitio vertitur Seni Stalioni, quòd unguentatus per vias inceffierit. Molles, non significat Nihili & Nauci: sicut quidam interpretatur. Nos mitiùs de Senibus sentimus. Ncq; Integri Ordines per hoc nostrum Axioma tangun-tur. tur: sed ex integro Ordine Plærumque unius & alterius commune enumeratur.
units.tr: Aphorism ii. Old men are for the most part soft. Casina 2.3 v.23. Stalino is blamed for old age because he walked about the streets scented with perfume. "Soft" does not mean worthless and good for nothing, as some interpret it. We judge old men more gently than that. Nor are whole orders touched by this our saying, but from the whole order a common feature of one or another is listed.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xiii. Senum vitium est Plærumque male o-lere sub axilli. Merc.3.3.v.14. Observavit hoc summus Juris Myst a Cujacrus, in Observat. Notavit idem Ramirez doctissimus Hispanorum ad Martialem. Itemque Savaro in Sidonium. Sed audi, Lector. Est nonnemo qui contradicit his verbis: Sub axillis ego os, vel podicem exspectabam. Resp. Is ipsus homo in ore an podice sit hirquosus, quis curat? Sed & Vniversalem mihi facit sententiam meam. Hic Senex talis fuit: Ergo O m n e s Senes male olent. Nulla profecto Logica haec est: de qua jam ad naufcam supra incul-cavi plura. Intolerabilis.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom xiii. It is a fault of old men that for the most part they smell bad under the armpits. Mercator 3.3 v.14. The great jurist Cujas observed this in his Observations. The most learned Spaniard Ramírez noted the same on Martial, and likewise Savaron on Sidonius. But listen, reader. There is someone who objects to these words: I was expecting the mouth, or rather the backside, under the armpits. I reply: who cares whether that man is goatish in the mouth or in the backside? He also makes my saying universal: This old man was such; therefore ALL old men smell bad. This is surely no logic at all, about which I have already said more than enough, to the point of nausea. Intolerable.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphor. xix. Senes Vxores suas perire volunt. Trin. 1.2. v.13.] Non loquor de Omnibus Senibus in Individuo: sed de aliquibus in specie. Vide quid scripserim supra ad Tit. lxi. Axioma lxiv.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorism xix. Old men want their wives to die. Trinummus 1.2 v.13. I am not speaking of all old men as individuals, but of some as a class. See what I wrote above at Title lxi, Axiom lxiv.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xxiv. Senes Plærumque sunt libidinosi. Pseud. 4.7.v.93. Stich.4.1.v.65.] Observavit idem summus Jurisconsultus Albericus Gentilis lib. 5. cap.iii. de Nuptiis, pag. 485. Est, qui hoc loco gravem mihi adversariam constituit, dum inter se committit has sententias Ἐπιφωνεῖς:
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom xxiv. Old men are for the most part lustful. Pseudolus 4.7 v.93; Stichus 4.1 v.65. The same great jurist Alberico Gentili observed this in book 5, chapter 3, On Marriage, p. 485. There is someone who sets up a serious opponent to me here, by putting these sayings together as epiphonemata [Ἐπιφωνεῖς]:

units.la: Senes plærumque sunt libidinosi.
units.tr: Old men are for the most part lustful.

units.la: Senes plærumque sunt sputatores, screatores, & muccidi.
units.tr: Old men are for the most part spitters, snorers and sniffers.

units.la: Senes ad Venerem inepti.
units.tr: Old men are unfit for love.

units.la: Senectus onus Aetnâ gravius.
units.tr: Old age is a burden heavier than Etna.

units.la: At vero optime, optime omnia consistunt: nec sunt αὐτοφυῆ Subjecta namque & praedicata non sunt ἀπὸ ταυτῆς: coque facile conciliari possunt in diversis subjectis: vel, ἀλλ' ἄλλο ἐξ ἄλλο.
units.tr: But indeed all these things fit together very well, and they are not self-evident [αὐτοφυῆ]. Subjects and predicates are not from the same [ἀπὸ ταυτῆς]; so they can easily be reconciled, in different subjects, or one thing from another [ἀλλ' ἄλλο ἐξ ἄλλο].

units.la: ¶ Tit. ccxlvii. Sermonis. Axioma penultimum: Omnes sapientes decet conferre, & fabulari. Rud.2.3.v.8. ] Quid sit, quod debeant conferre, & fabulari, expressi in Notis marginalibus ad illum locum: Debent de rebus veris inter se colloqui.
units.tr: ¶ Title ccxlvii. Speech. Penultimate aphorism: All wise men ought to converse and talk together. Rudens 2.3 v.8. What it is that they ought to converse and talk about, I have set out in the marginal notes on that passage: They ought to speak together about true things.

units.la: ¶ Tit. ccxlix. Servorum. Aphorismus xxi. Servis bonos nullus habebatur, multominus supplicatio honestior. Afin. 3.3.v.80.88. Trucul.2.7.v.30.] Excipit nonnemo: Falsissimum hoc est. Sic enim Servus Paedagogum herilium liberorum nemo agere potuisset. Resp. Quid audio? num Libanus, Leonida, Geta, Paedagogi fuerunt? Dein, quae hæc Logica? Lydus in Bacchidibus Servus-pædagogus fuit: Igitur Servi omnes sunt pædagogi. Repeto: Servis, quâ Servi, & heri sunt mancipia, hominos nullus habitus, nisi honos is fuit, quando ad pedes pendentium alligatum pondus, ne recalcitrarent, & verbera excuterent.
units.tr: ¶ Title ccxlix. Slaves. Aphorism xxi. No slave was held to be good, much less one who had been honourably flogged. Aulularia 3.3 v.80, 88; Truculentus 2.7 v.30. Someone objects: This is very false. For no slave could have acted as a tutor to his master's children. I reply: What am I hearing? Were Libanus, Leonida and Geta tutors? Further, what kind of logic is this? Lydus in the Bacchides was a slave-tutor; therefore all slaves are tutors. I repeat: slaves, as slaves, and especially as the property of masters, were held to be no men at all, unless this was an honour, when a weight was tied to their feet, hanging down, so that they would not kick out and shake off the blows.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma XLI. Servorum cibus sal fuit. Perf. 3.3.v.24.] Contradicit aliquis: Quid si etiam liberorum? Replico: Quid si etiam Servorum? Duplicat alius: At Leno vs fuit, qui sale usus, Respond. Inter Lenonem & servum quid interest? Quis negare poterit: salem opsonium fuisse tenuiorum?
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom xli. Salt was the food of slaves. Persius 3.3 v.24. Someone objects: What if it was also the food of free men? I reply: What if it was also the food of slaves? Another doubles the objection: But Leno used salt, a slave. I answer: What difference is there between a pimp and a slave? Who can deny that salt was the relish of the poorer sort?

units.la: † Ibid. Aphorismo XLVI. & LVI. Plaga pabulum & cibus servorum. Perf. 2.4.v.7. Pseud. 1.2.v.5. Asin. 3.3.v.38. ] Homo quidam ἀνὴρ ἐμπορος sic se isti sententiæ opponit: Num servi ab heris ita nutriti, ut venire à cibo inani, tergo lateribus, scapulisque saburrarentur. Item: an Domini vere nutrierunt Servos verberibus? Istos Sarcasmos pari quis venustate sic vicissim excipere posset:
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorisms xlvi and lvi. Blows are the fodder and food of slaves. Persius 2.4 v.7; Pseudolus 1.2 v.5; Asinaria 3.3 v.38. A certain man, a merchant, opposes this saying as follows: Were slaves nourished by their masters in such a way that they came to their food empty, with backs, sides and shoulders well stuffed? Again: did masters really feed their slaves with beatings? One could answer these sarcasms in turn with equal elegance:

units.la: Calumniatoris alius usus cibus & pabulum est, viris bonis maledicere: Igitur vere nutritur & saburratur calumniis & maledictis.
units.tr: The food and fodder of a slanderer is to speak ill of good men; therefore he is truly nourished and stuffed with slanders and insults.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphorismus XLVII. Magistratus Virgis in noxios utebatur: Dominis loris in servos. Pœn. Prol. v.26. ] Qui magistratus illi sint, & quibus in locis: & quos in noxios? patet ex ipso contextu Plautino. Inspiciatur locus. Publicam autem Magistratus pœnam inibi distingui à pœnâ domesticâ herorum in Servos, observavit quoque ex hoc loco Vir doctissimus Petrus Nannius lib.11. Miscell. cap.1x.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorism xlvii. Magistrates used rods against the guilty; masters used thongs against slaves. Poenulus Prologue v.26. What magistrates these are, and in what places, and against whom the guilty are punished, is clear from the Plautine context itself. Let the passage be looked at. The very learned Petrus Nannius also observed from this passage, in book 11 of the Miscellanies, chapter 9, that the public punishment by magistrates is distinguished here from the domestic punishment that masters inflicted on slaves.

units.la: † Ibid. Aphorismus LVIII. Servitia verberibus malacissati, ut statua verbere a nomen meruerint. Capt. 5.1.v.31.] Quærit nonnemo: Quid est MALACISSATUS? Hochteutsch Lathin. Respondeo: Malacissare est Hochgreckisch Lathin. Quo usus est Plautus nostér: si tamen ille Latine amplius loquitur. Bacch. 11.v.31. Nimirum ferus es. Pr. Mihi sum. Ba. Malacissandus es. Eodem usus est Seneca Epist. LXV. An potius optem, ut malacissandos articulo sexoleis meis porrigam? Ubi quidam libri: Malaxandos. Utrumvis recte, & Græciense: inquit Lipsius.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorism lviii. Slaves were softened by blows, so that they earned the name of statues from the beating. Captivi 5.1 v.31. Someone asks: What is MALACISSATUS? High German Latin. I answer: malacissare is High Greek Latin. Our Plautus used it, though he speaks Latin more often. Bacchides 1.1 v.31: "Surely you are wild." "I am tame." "You must be softened." Seneca used it too, Epistle 65: "Or would I rather wish that I might hand my soft limbs over to be softened by the sexual act?" Where some books have malaxandos. Either form is correct, and Greek-like, says Lipsius.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma LXXVII. Servi, ut liberos mentirentur cretam addiderunt in vestem: ut fallerent alios permixti. Aul. 4.9.v.7. ] Hic nostér Aphorismus jam olim à Magno Lipsio est propositus lib.1. Elect. cap. XIII. pag. 392.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom lxxvii. Slaves, so that they might pass for free men, added chalk to their clothing, so that they might deceive others by being mixed in. Aulularia 4.9 v.7. This aphorism of ours was already proposed long ago by the great Lipsius, book 1 of the Electa, chapter 13, p. 392.

units.la: G
units.tr: G

units.la: † Ibid. Aphor. lxxx. Servi vaso capite pileum accipiebant in Templo Feroniæ. Amph. i. v. 304. ] Objicit Titius: Igitur Templa Feroniæ omnibus patent: nam quod liber non fuit, quicunque extrà illud Templum manumissus. Respondet: Nulla hæc est Logica. Quasi vero qui Romæ manumissi, non etiam in Templo Feroniæ pileum acceperint.
units.tr: † Ibid. Aphorism lxxx. Slaves received a cap on a shaved head in the temple of Feronia. Amphitryon 1.1 v.304. Titius objects: Then the temple of Feronia is open to everyone, since anyone manumitted outside that temple was not free. He replies: This is no logic. As if those manumitted at Rome did not also receive the cap in the temple of Feronia.

units.la: ¶ Tit. cclxiii. Somni. Somnus meridianus homini de prandio non est bonus. Differte hoc dicit Plautus Mostell. 3. 2. v. 8: Et loca quæ in Electis adduxi, manifesta sunt.
units.tr: ¶ Title cclxiii. Sleep. A midday sleep is not good for a man after lunch. You will find this said by Plautus in the Mostellaria 3.2 v.8. The passages I cited in the Electa are clear.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xiii. Somnus in capitur commodè in curis. Trin. 3. 1. v. 20. ] Ita Typographicum corrigi debet: Perperam enim excusum fuit, sine curis.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom xiii. Sleep is taken conveniently in cares. Trinummus 3.1 v.20. The printer's error must be corrected in this way. It was wrongly printed as sine curis [without cares].

units.la: ¶ Tit. cclxv. Sortes. Ligno populno vel abiegno, immò querno durissimo, ne in aquâ subsiderent, conficiebantur fortilegia. ] Tangit id Plautus Casin. 2. 6. v. 26. 32. 61. 63.
units.tr: ¶ Title cclxv. Lots. Divination by lots was performed with wood of the poplar or fir, or rather very hard oak, so that they would not sink in water. Plautus touches on this in Casina 2.6 v.26, 32, 61, 63.

units.la: † Tit. cclxxi. Statura. Statura commoda, seu justa censebatur olim septem pedum: vel, ut alij, sex. Asin. 2. 3 v. 21. ] Non placet hoc Titio: at placuit tamen summis Viris: Isaaco Casaubono, Stevrechio, & Brodæo. Oggerit Titius: Ergo hodie aut aliâ sunt statura homines, aut alij pedes.
units.tr: † Title cclxxi. Stature. A convenient or proper stature was formerly judged to be seven feet, or, as others say, six. Asinaria 2.3 v.21. Titius does not like this, but it pleased very great men: Isaac Casaubon, Stevechius and Brodaeus. Titius objects: Then men are either of a different stature today, or the feet are different.

units.la: Respond. Nulla hæc est consequentia Logica. Hoc fatebor: Hodie ratio mensurandi justam staturam, alia esse potest. Quid hoc verò ad meum Thema? Quin necnecesse est, quod olim fuit, hodiè non esse.
units.tr: Reply. This is no valid logical consequence. I will grant this much: today the method of measuring a proper stature may be different. But what has this to do with my thesis? Indeed, it is not necessary that what was once so should be so now.

units.la: ¶ Tit. cclxix. Supplicirorum. Aphor. xx. Carnifices carceris custodes fuerunt. Rud. 2. 3. v. 19. ] Opponit Titius: Si perpetuò hoc verum, falsum igitur, quod extrà Vrbem habitarunt.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. 269. Of punishments. Aphor. 20. The executioners were the guards of the prison. Rud. 2.3 v.19. Titius objects: if this is always true, then it is false that they lived outside the City.

units.la: Respond. Ubi vero ego scripsi? Perpetuo? Probari mihi velim: Carnifices Numquam fuisse custodes carceris.
units.tr: Reply. Where did I write "always"? I would like it proved that executioners were never guards of the prison.

units.la: † Ibid. Axioma xxxv ii. Maleficis oculos eruebant. Men. 5. 2. v. 89. ] Universalem non facio sententiam: quasi Omnibus oculi eruti. nam & alia pænâ affecti.
units.tr: † Ibid. Axiom 37. They gouged out the eyes of wrongdoers. Men. 5.2 v.89. I do not make a universal statement, as if everyone had his eyes gouged out, for others were also punished in other ways.

units.la: Quærit Titius: Num Menæchmi socer maleficus? Respond. Si non fuit maleficus, pro eo tamen habitus est, quando de Oraculo Apollinis Menæchmus hoc ei malum minatur.
units.tr: Titius asks: was Menaechmus's father-in-law a wrongdoer? Reply: if he was not a wrongdoer, he was nevertheless regarded as one, since Menaechmus threatens him with this harm on the authority of Apollo's oracle.

units.la: ¶ Tit. cclxx. Sylvarum. Sylvanus præses Lucorum. Aul. 4. 6. v. 8.]
units.tr: ¶ Tit. 270. Of woods. Sylvanus, president of the groves. Aul. 4.6 v.8.]

units.la: v.8.] Male hoc loco ab aliis legi, lacus, cuici rationum argumentis in Notis meis Criticis ad eum locum.
units.tr: v.8.] This passage has been wrongly read by others as lacus. I have answered this with rationum argumentis (arguments of reason) in my Critical Notes on that passage.

units.la: ¶ Tit. ç CLXXXIX. Vicinitatis. Vicinis nihil denegandum. Quod fecit nequiter Euclio. Aul. 1.2. v.18.] Aphorismum hunc ita arjetat Titius. Ergo nihil Omnino denegandum. Respond. Ubi vero ego dixi; Nihil omnino? Verba sunt capienda secundum subjectam materiam. Nihil, inquam, eorum, quae vicinis denegare ipsa quasi Natura, vel honestas vetat. ꝑ NEQUITER, est, male perperam. Vide Lexicon Plautinum.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. 189. Neighbourhood. Nothing is to be denied to neighbours. What Euclio wickedly did. Aul. 1.2 v.18.] Titius twists this maxim thus: Therefore nothing at all is to be denied. Reply: where did I say "nothing at all"? Words must be taken according to the subject matter: nothing, I say, of those things which nature itself or honesty forbids us to deny to neighbours. NEQUITER means badly, wrongly. See the Plautine Lexicon.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CCCIIII. Voluptatis. Quodcunq; accidit homini libere, poseretur.] Sunt verba ipsius Plauti Amph. 1.1. v.17. Sed ad sensum supplete textus vocem omissam, Dominus. Sicui libeat haec verba ad alium Titulum referre, mea pace id facere poterit. Tanti enim non sunt.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. 304. Pleasure. Whatever happens to a man freely, is possessed.] These are the words of Plautus himself, Amph. 1.1 v.17. But in sense, supply the word omitted from the text, Master. If anyone likes to refer these words to another title, he may do so with my blessing, for they are not worth so much.

units.la: ¶ Tit. CCCV. Vvarum. V. nearum pestis est in volvulus. Ciftell. 4.2. v.63.] Ita Typographica menda fuit emendanda, non suggillanda à Titio. Excusum fuit pafis. male.
units.tr: ¶ Tit. 305. Vineyards. Of vines. The pest of vines is in the volvulus. Ciftell. 4.2 v.63.] Here a printer's error was to be corrected, not made a matter of reproach by Titius. It was printed pafis, wrongly.

units.la: Caeterum Involvulum esse pestem Vvarum, praeterquam quod Vinitores magno suo damno experiri solent, ipsa confirmat Sacra Scriptura. Deuter. cap. xxviii. v.39. Vineas plantabis, & coles, sed vinum non bibes, nec colliges; eo quod Vermis illud sit abscumturus. Cato de Re Rustica cap. xcv. remedium praescribit pro repellendo isto Vermiculo. Convolvulus in vinea nefit. &c. Vide totum caput.
units.tr: Moreover, that the Involvulum is a pest of vines, apart from what vinedressers commonly learn to their great loss, Holy Scripture itself confirms. Deut. ch. 28 v.39: You shall plant vineyards and dress them, but you shall not drink the wine nor gather it, because the worm will consume it. Cato, On Agriculture, ch. 95, prescribes a remedy for driving off this little worm: Let there be no bindweed in the vineyard, etc. See the whole chapter.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.
